These lipophilic ligands penetrate the cell membrane and bind to intracellular receptors. The drug-receptor complex then acts as a transcription factor, producing very slow responses (usually hours) via gene regulation.

In an unconscious, vomiting patient with status epilepticus, the intravenous (IV) route is most appropriate because it provides immediate drug effect, bypasses first-pass metabolism, and is reliable regardless of gastrointestinal function. The oral and sublingual routes require a cooperative patient, and rectal and subcutaneous routes have slower and more variable absorption.
questions.question: A patient with severe status epilepticus is unconscious and actively vomiting. Which route of drug administration is MOST appropriate?
The CYP2E1 enzyme, which metabolizes chlorzoxazone, is induced by ethanol and inhibited by disulfiram. This is clinically important because disulfiram is used to treat:
questions.explanation: Disulfiram (Antabuse) inhibits CYP2E1 and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, used for treating alcohol use disorder by creating aversive acetaldehyde accumulation when alcohol is consumed. CYP2E1 is induced by chronic alcohol consumption, explaining increased tolerance to alcohol. Disulfiram's CYP2E1 inhibition also has implications for drugs metabolized by CYP2E1, such as chlorzoxazone.

options: It tastes better under the tongue
It is insoluble in gastric contents
Oral route causes excessive renal excretion
Sublingual route produces lower peak plasma levels
It undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism when taken orally, leaving very little active drug to reach systemic circulation. The sublingual route bypasses the liver's portal circulation, allowing the drug to enter the systemic circulation directly, achieving adequate plasma levels and rapid relief of angina within 1-3 minutes.
questions.question: Nitroglycerine is specifically given sublingually rather than orally primarily because:

questions.explanation: Bioequivalence is achieved when the rate and extent of absorption of a drug from a test product are not statistically significantly different from those of the reference standard when administered at the same molar dose. Bioequivalence requirements are imposed by regulatory agencies as a condition of marketing approval for generic drug products.
questions.question: Bioequivalence between two drug products is achieved when:
options: They contain identical active ingredients and same dose
They have the same chemical structure and formulation
They are manufactured by the same pharmaceutical company
Their rate and extent of absorption are not statistically different
Their pharmacodynamic profiles are clinically comparable

questions.explanation: The nasal mucosa can readily absorb many drugs, and the digestive juices and liver are bypassed because the venous drainage from the nasal mucosa goes directly to the systemic circulation rather than through the portal vein. This makes the nasal route useful for drugs with high first-pass metabolism when formulated as sprays or nebulized solutions.
options: Drugs given nasally must cross the blood-brain barrier
Nasal administration always causes rhinitis symptoms
Only systemic routes can bypass digestive enzymes
The nasal mucosa allows absorption bypassing liver
All drugs are absorbed faster nasally than orally
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the nasal route is CORRECT?
Enzyme induction by a drug like rifampicin increases its own and other drugs' metabolism through:
options: Covalent binding to active sites of enzymes
Enhanced renal tubular secretion of substrates
Increased synthesis of microsomal CYP enzymes
questions.explanation: Enzyme inducers like rifampicin increase the synthesis (transcription and translation) of microsomal CYP enzymes, increasing enzyme quantity and overall metabolic capacity. This results in faster metabolism of the inducer itself and other co-administered drugs metabolized by the same enzymes. Induction typically develops over days to weeks after starting the inducing drug.

questions.question: Salt of heavy metals and base compounds are excreted from which site respectively?
questions.explanation: Heavy metal salts are excreted from the intestine, and base compounds are excreted from the stomach. Volatile compounds are excreted from the lungs. The liver removes some drugs from plasma and secretes them into bile for fecal excretion. However, the kidney (renal excretion) remains the major organ for elimination of most drugs and their metabolites.

questions.question: CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole would be expected to increase plasma levels of:
questions.explanation: Midazolam, felodipine, lovastatin, buspirone, and sildenafil are major CYP3A4 substrates. CYP3A4 inhibitors like ketoconazole (and atazanavir, cimetidine, clarithromycin) reduce their metabolism, leading to elevated plasma levels. The clinically serious consequence is increased risk of muscle toxicity from statins and prolonged sedation from midazolam.

Efficacy is the capacity to produce a desired effect — it is the maximum response achievable from a given drug regardless of dose. It represents the intrinsic capability of the drug to activate the receptor and produce a biological effect. Two drugs may have the same efficacy (same Emax) but different potency (different EC50 values).
questions.question: Efficacy of a drug is defined as:
options: The amount of drug needed for 50% maximum response
The maximum response achievable regardless of dose
The drug concentration at half-maximum effect
The ratio of EC50 to TD50
The selectivity of the drug for its receptor subtype
Enhance patient care and safety regarding medicines
Increase drug sales in developing countries
questions.explanation: Pharmacovigilance aims to enhance patient care and patient safety in relation to the use of medicines, and to support public health programmes by providing reliable, balanced information for effective assessment of the risk-benefit profile of medicines. It involves detection, assessment, understanding, and prevention of adverse reactions and drug-related problems.
questions.question: Pharmacovigilance aims primarily to:

options: Direct physical chemical tissue damage from UV light
Cell-mediated immune response producing papular rash
Drug accumulation in skin absorbing light energy
Dose-related toxicity from UV radiation exposure
questions.question: Photoallergic reactions differ from phototoxic reactions in that photoallergic reactions involve:
questions.explanation: Photoallergic reactions involve a cell-mediated (Type IV delayed hypersensitivity) immune response. The drug or its metabolite acts as a hapten, induces sensitization, and on subsequent UV exposure produces a papular or eczematous rash. Unlike phototoxic reactions (which cause sunburn-like damage and are dose-related), photoallergic reactions require prior sensitization and are not dose-dependent.

options: Cause cancer and genetic mutations in adult tissue
Cause fetal abnormalities when given to a pregnant mother
Cause liver damage via toxic metabolite formation
Cause bone marrow suppression in adults
questions.question: Teratogenicity refers to the capacity of a drug to:
questions.explanation: Teratogenicity is the capacity of a drug to cause fetal abnormalities when administered to the pregnant mother. The embryo has very dynamic biological systems, and drug effects are often irreversible. The type of malformation depends on both the drug and the stage of pregnancy when the teratogen is used. Key examples include thalidomide (limb defects) and valproate (neural tube defects).

questions.question: Which route of administration is primarily used for contraceptive implants providing drug release over months or years?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous implants (like the levonorgestrel implant - Jadelle or Implanon) are deposited in the loose subcutaneous tissue and provide sustained drug release over months to years. The subcutaneous tissue is less vascular than muscle, providing slow, constant absorption that is ideal for long-acting contraceptive delivery with excellent patient compliance.

Pharmacosurgery is not a recognized division of pharmacology. The established divisions include pharmacokinetics (fate of drug in the body), pharmacodynamics (effects of drugs), pharmacogenetics (genetic basis of drug responses), therapeutics (treatment of disease), toxicology (toxic effects), pharmacovigilance, and pharmacoeconomics.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered a division of pharmacology?
Radioactive radiation affects hepatic drug metabolism primarily by acting to:
options: Decrease microsomal enzyme activity except reductase enzymes
Decrease all microsomal enzyme activity equally
Enhance drug conjugation reactions in phase 2
Increase hepatic blood flow and drug clearance
questions.explanation: Radioactive radiation decreases the activity of microsomal enzymes but specifically spares (or may even enhance) reductase enzymes. This selective effect on oxidative but not reductive enzymes is a recognized factor affecting drug metabolism in patients undergoing radiation therapy, potentially requiring dose adjustments for hepatically metabolized drugs.

options: High water solubility and large molecular weight
questions.question: Drugs excreted through the lungs are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Drugs excreted through the lungs are volatile substances with lipophilic properties, excreted by simple diffusion. Examples include general anesthetic agents (halothane, isoflurane), alcohol, ethereal oil, guaiacol, and creosote. The rate of excretion depends on blood flow (cardiac output) and ventilation. Expectorants are also excreted through this route.

options: Increased sensitivity to the agonist drug
Increased affinity but unchanged receptor number
Reduced total receptor number and diminished response
questions.question: Downregulation of receptors is associated with prolonged receptor activation and leads to:
questions.explanation: Downregulation is a reduction in the total number of receptors due to prolonged receptor activation (e.g., chronic agonist use or prolonged inhibition of neurotransmitter metabolism). Downregulation reduces the cell's sensitivity to further stimulation and produces tolerance, requiring higher agonist doses to achieve the same effect. It is a cellular homeostatic mechanism.

Physiological antagonism occurs when two drugs with opposing pharmacological effects act at different receptors or physiological systems. Example: histamine (causing bronchoconstriction via H1 receptors) vs. adrenaline (causing bronchodilation via beta-2 receptors) — they produce opposing effects through different receptor systems without competing for the same receptor.
options: Two drugs compete for the same receptor binding site
A drug prevents another from being absorbed from the GI tract
A drug chemically inactivates another drug in the body
Two drugs with opposing effects act at different receptors or systems
An antagonist blocks all available receptors completely
questions.question: Physiological antagonism occurs when:

options: The ability of the drug to activate the receptor after binding
The ability of the drug to combine with (bind to) the receptor
The maximum effect produced by the drug
The drug concentration producing 50% maximal response
The intrinsic biological activity of the drug
questions.question: Affinity of a drug for its receptor is defined as:
questions.explanation: Affinity is the ability of a drug to combine with (bind to) its receptor. It reflects how strongly and readily the drug binds to the receptor. A drug with high affinity binds at very low concentrations, while a drug with low affinity requires higher concentrations for receptor binding. Affinity is quantified as the dissociation constant (Kd) — lower Kd means higher affinity.

options: Probenecid competes with penicillin for glomerular filtration
Probenecid inhibits renal blood flow to the tubule
Probenecid increases protein binding reducing penicillin filtration
Probenecid and penicillin compete for the same acidic tubular secretion carrier
Probenecid blocks active tubular reabsorption of penicillin
questions.explanation: Probenecid and penicillin are both acidic drugs that compete for the same acidic drug carrier system in the proximal renal tubule. Probenecid, having higher affinity for this carrier, competitively inhibits tubular secretion of penicillin and cephalosporins. This interaction was historically used intentionally to maintain higher penicillin levels during wartime penicillin shortages.
questions.question: Probenecid reduces gout by blocking uric acid reabsorption. However, it also inhibits excretion of penicillin because:

questions.explanation: Tetracycline chelates (binds) calcium, leading to its accumulation in bones and teeth during calcification. This depot storage property explains tetracycline's contraindication in children under 8 years and pregnancy, as it causes permanent discoloration of developing teeth and may impair bone development. The calcium-chelating property is also why calcium-containing products reduce tetracycline absorption.
options: It chelates calcium in calcifying tissues
It is highly lipophilic and crosses bone cell membranes
It is actively secreted by osteoblasts
It binds specifically to periosteal receptors
It undergoes specific renal tubular reabsorption
questions.question: Tetracycline accumulates in bones and teeth because:

questions.explanation: Supersensitivity or hypersensitivity refers to an enhanced response to an agonist that may occur as a result of unmasking of receptors (removal of masking protein increases receptor activity) or accentuation of signal amplification (increase in receptor activity or enzymatic activity). This can occur after denervation or prolonged antagonist use leading to upregulation.
options: Protein binding increasing free drug concentration
Reduced receptor affinity for its natural ligand
Unmasking of receptors or accentuation of signal amplification
questions.question: Hypersensitivity (supersensitivity) of receptors results from:

options: Fixed at 0.75 for most oral medications
Less than 1 due to incomplete absorption
questions.explanation: The peroral route always has bioavailability less than 100% (f < 1) due to multiple factors including binding to food substances, first-pass hepatic metabolism, enzymatic degradation in the GI tract, and incomplete absorption. This contrasts with IV administration where f = 1 (100% bioavailability) because drug enters circulation directly.
questions.question: The peroral route has a bioavailability (f) value that is always:
A partial agonist when administered alone will produce:
options: No effect at any dose level
Sub-maximal response even at full receptor occupancy
An effect equal to competitive antagonist
Inverse effect opposite to full agonist
questions.explanation: A partial agonist has affinity but sub-maximal intrinsic activity (0 < AI < 1), meaning it produces less than the maximum possible tissue response even when all receptors are occupied. When co-administered with a full agonist, a partial agonist acts as a competitive antagonist by displacing the full agonist and reducing the overall response to the partial agonist's maximum.

questions.question: First-order kinetics of drug elimination means that:
options: A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time
Elimination rate is determined by enzyme saturation
Elimination rate is independent of concentration
Half-life increases as drug concentration increases
A constant fraction (percentage) of drug is eliminated per unit time
questions.explanation: First-order (linear) kinetics means a constant fraction (percentage) of the drug is eliminated per unit time, so elimination rate is proportional to the drug concentration. As concentration decreases, elimination rate decreases proportionally. The half-life is constant and independent of drug concentration. Most drugs follow first-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.

questions.question: In the concentration-response curve, drug X plus competitive antagonist compared to drug X alone shows:
options: Reduced Emax with the same EC50
Rightward shift with the same Emax
questions.explanation: Adding a competitive antagonist shifts the concentration-response curve of the agonist to the right (higher concentrations needed) while preserving the same Emax (maximum effect is unchanged). This parallel rightward shift without reduction in Emax is the defining characteristic of competitive (surmountable) antagonism, distinguishable from non-competitive antagonism which reduces Emax.

Drug-induced disease (iatrogenic disease) is a functional disturbance caused by a drug that persists even after the offending drug has been discontinued. Examples include NSAID-induced peptic ulcer (which may persist despite stopping NSAIDs), isoniazid-induced hepatitis, and antibiotic-induced vaginal discharge. The persistence after drug withdrawal distinguishes it from regular side effects.
questions.question: Drug-induced disease (iatrogenic disease) is defined by which feature?
options: Functional disturbance that resolves immediately upon drug discontinuation
Acute allergic reaction occurring only while the drug is taken
Functional disturbance that persists even after the drug is stopped
Dose-dependent toxic effects from drug overdose
Genetic syndrome triggered by first exposure to a drug

questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble drugs (e.g., tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, isoniazid) diffuse readily into breast milk and can reach significant concentrations that may affect the nursing infant. The rate of drug penetration to breast milk should be considered before prescribing to nursing mothers to avoid toxic effects on babies, including potential bone/dental toxicity, aplastic anemia, or hepatotoxicity.
questions.question: An important clinical concern when prescribing lipid-soluble drugs to nursing mothers is:
options: Reduced drug efficacy due to dilution in breast milk
Drug binding to milk proteins limiting systemic effect
Drug precipitation in milk reducing bioavailability
Increased maternal drug metabolism during lactation
Drug accumulation causing toxicity in nursing infant

questions.explanation: A clearance factor of 0.5 (60/120 ml/min compared to inulin) means that half of the drug filtered by the glomeruli is reabsorbed in the convoluted tubules. If clearance factor = 1, neither reabsorption nor secretion occurs. If clearance factor > 1, the drug is actively secreted by the tubules in addition to being filtered.
questions.question: A drug has a renal clearance of 60 ml/minute. Its clearance factor compared to inulin is 0.5. This means:
options: The drug is actively secreted by renal tubules
The drug is not filtered by glomeruli
The drug is not reabsorbed or secreted in tubules
Half of the filtered drug is reabsorbed in tubules
The drug has no renal excretion mechanism

questions.explanation: The LADMER system represents Liberation of active ingredient from the dosage form, Absorption into systemic circulation, Distribution and metabolism in the body, Excretion from the body, and achievement of Response. It describes the complex dynamic processes that determine drug behavior and effect following administration.
questions.question: The LADMER system in pharmacokinetics represents:
options: Lipophilicity, Absorption, Dose, Metabolism, Elimination, Rate
Loading, Administration, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination, Residual
Liberation, Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, Response
Latency, Affinity, Distribution, Mechanism, Efficacy, Response
Liberation, Agonism, Distribution, Modulation, Excretion, Reversal

questions.explanation: Active transport is identical to facilitated diffusion in using specific carrier proteins, but differs crucially in that ATP (energy) powers drug transport against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This saturable process can be competitively inhibited by drugs with higher affinity for the carrier, as exemplified by probenecid blocking penicillin secretion.
options: Uses specific carrier proteins for drug transport
Is inhibited by chemically similar drug compounds
Can move drugs against their concentration gradient using ATP
Does not require energy for membrane transport
Is limited to lipophilic and nonpolar drug molecules
questions.question: Active transport of drugs across membranes differs from facilitated diffusion in that active transport:

options: Deep fascia of skeletal muscle tissue
The dermis just below the epidermis
The outermost superficial layer of the skin
questions.question: A drug administered intradermally for BCG vaccination enters which specific anatomical layer?
questions.explanation: Intradermal (ID) injection delivers the drug into the superficial layer of the skin (dermis just beneath the epidermis), creating a characteristic bleb or wheal. BCG and tuberculin (Mantoux test) are classic intradermal injections. This route is used for skin testing and some vaccines, where local immune responses are desired.

options: Slowing renal elimination through tubular secretion
Increasing drug binding to plasma proteins
Reducing hepatic first-pass metabolism of the drug
Using insoluble salts or suspensions in non-aqueous vehicles
Enhancing enterohepatic recirculation of the drug
questions.explanation: Depot or reservoir intramuscular preparations achieve prolonged drug effects by using insoluble salts (e.g., benzathine penicillin) or suspensions in non-aqueous (oily) vehicles. These formulations release drug slowly at the injection site, providing sustained plasma levels over days to weeks, improving compliance and ensuring consistent drug exposure.
questions.question: The depot or sustained-release intramuscular preparation achieves prolonged drug effect primarily by:

options: The entire filtered drug is reabsorbed in tubules
Two-thirds of the filtered drug is reabsorbed
One-third of the drug cleared is by active tubular secretion
The drug has 100% glomerular filtration and no secretion
The drug only undergoes passive tubular reabsorption
questions.question: A drug with renal clearance of 180 ml/minute (clearance factor = 1.5) indicates that:
questions.explanation: A clearance factor of 1.5 (180/120) means the filtered drug is not reabsorbed and that one-third (0.5 of 1.5) of the total drug cleared is actively secreted by the renal tubules in addition to glomerular filtration. Active tubular secretion adds to glomerular filtration to increase overall drug elimination beyond the GFR.

options: Antibiotics increase intestinal motility and absorption
Gut flora is involved in enterohepatic drug recycling
Gut flora reduces blood flow to intestinal mucosa
questions.question: Oral contraceptive bioavailability increases when an antibiotic that alters gut flora is co-administered. This suggests that:
questions.explanation: Some drugs (including certain oral contraceptive steroids) undergo enterohepatic circulation where conjugated drug excreted in bile is hydrolyzed by intestinal bacteria back to the active form and reabsorbed. Antibiotics that reduce gut flora can disrupt this cycle, potentially reducing drug levels — however, increased bioavailability may also result if bacterial inactivation of drug is reduced.

The loading dose (LD) is calculated as the product of the target plasma concentration (Cp) and the volume of distribution (Vd): LD = Cp — Vd. This ensures that the drug rapidly attains the desired therapeutic concentration, particularly important for drugs with long half-lives where waiting for steady-state would be clinically unacceptable.
questions.question: The loading dose of a drug is primarily calculated using which pharmacokinetic parameter?
options: Area under curve and peak drug level
Renal clearance and protein binding rate
Target plasma concentration and volume of distribution

questions.question: CYP2D6 genetic polymorphism is clinically significant for codeine because poor metabolizers:
options: Cannot convert codeine to morphine causing lack of efficacy
Have excessive analgesia from codeine overdose
Experience severe respiratory depression from codeine
Develop rapid tolerance to codeine's effects
Have increased bioavailability of oral codeine
questions.explanation: CYP2D6 poor metabolizers cannot convert codeine (a prodrug) to its active metabolite morphine through O-demethylation. This results in lack of analgesic efficacy from codeine in poor metabolizers. Conversely, ultra-rapid metabolizers convert codeine to morphine excessively quickly, potentially causing opioid toxicity even at standard doses.

Codeine undergoes N-dealkylation to form norcodeine and O-dealkylation (demethylation by CYP2D6) to form morphine. The conversion of codeine to morphine is responsible for the majority of codeine's analgesic effect. Poor metabolizers of CYP2D6 cannot convert codeine to morphine and therefore experience inadequate analgesia from codeine.
questions.question: Codeine is metabolized by N-dealkylation and O-dealkylation to produce respectively:

questions.explanation: Most drugs interact with specific biomolecules, but notable exceptions include: antacids (neutralize gastric acid chemically), EDTA (chelates heavy metals), cholestyramine (binds bile acids in gut lumen), and activated charcoal (adsorbs toxins non-specifically). These drugs act through physicochemical mechanisms rather than receptor-mediated signal transduction.
options: Antacids, EDTA, cholestyramine, and activated charcoal
questions.question: Which notable exceptions act WITHOUT binding to specific bio-molecular receptors?
Oral drug absorption via the peroral route is susceptible to first-pass effect because:
options: Drugs are absorbed from the stomach into lymphatics
Absorbed drugs pass through the portal vein to the liver
The liver directly secretes absorbed drugs into bile
Intestinal enzymes completely inactivate absorbed drugs
Plasma proteins rapidly bind drugs in intestinal vessels
questions.explanation: The first-pass effect occurs because drugs absorbed perorally are transported from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver via the portal vein before reaching systemic circulation. In the liver, significant drug metabolism can occur, reducing the amount of active drug reaching the systemic circulation and lowering oral bioavailability.

questions.question: The principle of stimulation as a mechanism of drug action is exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Stimulation as a mechanism of drug action involves enhancement of existing bodily activities. Adrenaline (epinephrine) stimulates beta-1 adrenoceptors in the heart, causing tachycardia — a classic example of pharmacological stimulation. Barbiturates causing CNS depression is an example of depressant action, while L-dopa is an example of replacement therapy.

options: Drug accumulating in skin, absorbing light, causing tissue damage
Cell-mediated immune response on UV exposure
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the skin
Type III immune complex deposition in the skin
questions.question: Phototoxic reactions to drugs are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Phototoxic reactions occur when a drug or its metabolite accumulates in the skin, absorbs UV light, and undergoes a photochemical reaction followed by a photobiological reaction resulting in local tissue damage resembling severe sunburn — blistering and erythema. Examples include tetracyclines and NSAIDs. Photoallergic reactions, in contrast, involve cell-mediated (Type IV) immune response.

options: Drug concentration continues to rise indefinitely
Drug is completely eliminated between doses
Rate of drug input equals rate of drug output
Drug plasma level equals the initial loading dose level
Drug distribution is limited to the central compartment
questions.question: Accumulation of drug in blood and tissue occurs with multiple dosing until a steady state is reached. At steady state:
questions.explanation: At steady state, the rate of drug input (from each dose) equals the rate of drug output (elimination), resulting in stable average plasma drug concentrations. Steady state is typically reached after 4-5 half-lives of repeated dosing at regular intervals. A loading dose can be used to rapidly achieve therapeutic concentrations while waiting for steady state to develop with maintenance dosing.

questions.question: Relative bioavailability compares drug absorption of two products given via:
options: The same route at the same molar dose
Different routes with different dose sizes
The same route and different doses
questions.explanation: Relative bioavailability compares the extent of drug absorbed from a test product to that from a reference standard, both administered via the same route. Relative bioavailability = AUC of Drug A / AUC of standard — 100%. This is used in bioequivalence studies to compare generic and innovator products given orally at the same molar dose.

options: Basic drugs like quinidine and amitriptyline
Acidic drugs like warfarin and NSAIDs
Neutral lipophilic drugs of any class
questions.question: Albumin in plasma predominantly binds which chemical class of drugs?
questions.explanation: Acidic drugs are strongly bound to albumin (the most abundant plasma protein), while basic drugs are weakly bound to albumin and therefore the clinical importance of albumin binding for basic drugs is often limited. Examples of highly albumin-bound acidic drugs include warfarin, NSAIDs, and penicillins. Basic drugs bind more to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein.

questions.question: The kidney is the major organ of drug excretion. Drugs are excreted renally through:
options: Passive diffusion through the collecting duct
questions.explanation: Drugs are excreted by the kidney through two main mechanisms: glomerular filtration (passive filtration of free, unbound drug) and tubular secretion (active transport by carrier systems in proximal tubule epithelium). In addition, some drugs undergo tubular reabsorption, which reduces net excretion. The net renal clearance represents the balance of these three processes.

questions.question: Bioavailability requirement imposed by regulatory agencies specifies that for bioequivalence, the rate and extent of absorption must be:
questions.explanation: Bioequivalence requires that the rate and extent of absorption of a test drug are not statistically significantly different from those of the reference standard when administered at the same molar dose. Regulatory agencies (FDA, EMA) impose bioequivalence requirements as a condition of marketing generic drugs, ensuring generic products provide equivalent therapeutic outcomes to innovator products.
options: Greater than 80% of the reference standard
Not statistically significantly different from the reference standard
Equal to or greater than the reference standard

questions.explanation: Intrinsic activity (efficacy) is the ability of the drug to activate the receptor after receptor occupation. A full agonist has maximal intrinsic activity (AI = 1), a partial agonist has sub-maximal intrinsic activity (0 < AI < 1), a competitive antagonist has no intrinsic activity (AI = 0), and an inverse agonist has negative intrinsic activity (AI between 0 and -1).
options: The ability of the drug to bind to its receptor
The selectivity of drug for a particular receptor type
The rate of drug-receptor complex formation
The ability of the drug to activate the receptor after binding
The duration of drug-receptor complex occupancy
questions.question: Intrinsic activity (efficacy) of a drug is defined as:

options: NSAIDs inhibiting prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin
NSAIDs blocking renin secretion in kidneys
NSAIDs competing with antihypertensives for plasma binding
NSAIDs activating aldosterone secretion from adrenals
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase, reducing synthesis of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) and prostacyclin (PGI2) — prostaglandins that promote natriuresis and vasodilation. This inhibition causes sodium and water retention and increases vascular resistance, thereby antagonizing the antihypertensive effects of beta-blockers, diuretics, and ACE inhibitors. This interaction can cause blood pressure to become uncontrolled.
questions.question: The NSAIDs antagonizing beta-blockers, diuretics, and ACE inhibitors antihypertensive effect is due to:

questions.explanation: Amphetamine undergoes oxidative deamination (to phenylacetone) and aromatic hydroxylation (to 4-hydroxyamphetamine) as first-phase metabolic transformations. These reactions are mediated by monoamine oxidase (MAO) and CYP enzymes respectively. The metabolites are then available for phase 2 conjugation before renal excretion.
questions.question: Amphetamine undergoes which specific first-phase metabolic transformation?

options: High molecular weight and ionic character
Water solubility and polar molecular structure
High plasma protein binding and hydrophilicity
Small molecular size, lipophilicity, and nonionic state
Large molecular size and charged ionic state
questions.explanation: Small, nonionic, lipid-soluble drugs permeate plasma membranes most readily by passive diffusion. Lipophilicity allows the drug to partition into the lipid bilayer, nonionic state prevents repulsion from charged membrane components, and small molecular size facilitates membrane traversal. This combination is the pharmacokinetic ideal for passive absorption.
questions.question: Which of the following drug properties MOST favors rapid and efficient passive membrane diffusion?

options: Decrease the rate of absorption of most oral drugs
Decrease the extent of absorption of all oral drugs
Increase the rate of absorption of most oral drugs
Block enterohepatic circulation of oral drugs
Reduce first-pass metabolism of oral drugs
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide increases gastric motility and accelerates gastric emptying, thereby speeding the transit of drug from the stomach to the small intestine (the primary site of drug absorption). This increases the rate of absorption for most oral drugs. However, it may slightly reduce the extent of absorption for drugs best absorbed slowly in the stomach.
questions.question: The GI motility affects oral drug absorption. Metoclopramide, which increases gastric motility, would be expected to:

questions.explanation: Drug accumulation occurs when a drug is given repeatedly at intervals shorter than those required to completely eliminate the drug from the previously given dose. It results in progressive increase of drug concentration in blood and tissues until a steady state is reached where input and output are at equilibrium.
questions.question: Drug accumulation during multiple dosing occurs when:
options: The drug has a very short half-life
Doses are given less frequently than needed
Doses are given more frequently than elimination allows
The volume of distribution is very small

questions.question: Pharmacoeconomics evaluates pharmaceutical drugs primarily by comparing their:
questions.explanation: Pharmacoeconomics compares the value of one pharmaceutical drug or drug therapy to another by evaluating cost (expressed in monetary terms) and effects (expressed in terms of monetary value, efficacy, or enhanced quality of life). It serves to guide optimal healthcare resource allocation in a standardized and scientifically grounded manner.
options: Mechanism of action and receptor affinity
Cost expressed in monetary terms and therapeutic effects
Drug passes from hepatic artery into bile then to intestine
Drug undergoes first-pass metabolism in the liver
Lipid-soluble drugs excreted in bile are reabsorbed from intestine
Bile acids stimulate intestinal drug absorption
Intestinal flora metabolize drugs before hepatic excretion
questions.question: Enterohepatic circulation refers to the process where:
questions.explanation: Enterohepatic circulation is the process where lipid-soluble drugs passing into the intestine from bile are reabsorbed into the bloodstream. This cycle continues until the drug undergoes biotransformation and loses its lipophilic properties. Enterohepatic circulation prolongs drug effects by repeatedly recycling the drug and contributes to the half-life of drugs like morphine, contraceptive steroids, and digoxin.

An inverse agonist has affinity for the receptor but a negative intrinsic activity (AI between 0 and -1), producing an effect opposite to that of the agonist. Example: beta-carbolines binding to benzodiazepine receptors produce anxiety, hypertonia, and convulsions — opposite to the anxiolytic and anticonvulsant effects of benzodiazepines. A competitive antagonist has zero intrinsic activity with no effect alone.
options: Has zero affinity for the receptor
Cannot be displaced by agonists at the receptor
Acts at allosteric sites different from the agonist site
Requires higher doses than a competitive antagonist
Has affinity and a negative intrinsic activity producing opposite effect
questions.question: An inverse agonist differs from a competitive antagonist in that an inverse agonist:
Biliary excretion of drugs by active transport occurs for drugs secreted regardless of:
questions.explanation: Active transport by the liver into bile occurs irrespective of the concentration or chemical gradients. The liver actively secretes endogenous substances like bile acids, bilirubin, and certain drugs (erythromycin, rifampicin, tetracycline, penicillin, chloramphenicol) into bile against concentration gradients. This is an energy-dependent process independent of concentration differences.
options: Their molecular weight or structural formula
Their concentration or chemical gradient in bile

questions.question: The intravenous route cannot be used for which type of drug formulation?
options: Isotonic drug solutions for large-volume infusion
questions.explanation: Oil-based or oily drug preparations (such as depot IM preparations using non-aqueous vehicles) cannot be given intravenously because oil droplets could cause pulmonary embolism and vascular damage. IV formulations must be aqueous, sterile, pyrogen-free, and compatible with blood. Depot preparations are specifically used for IM or SC routes.

questions.question: The intramuscular injection sites include all of the following EXCEPT the:
options: Deltoid muscle of the upper arm
Triceps muscle of the upper arm
Biceps femoris of the posterior thigh
questions.explanation: Standard intramuscular injection sites include the deltoid, triceps, and gluteus maximus as mentioned in pharmacology texts, as well as the vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh). The biceps femoris (posterior thigh) is not a standard IM injection site due to risk of injury to the sciatic nerve and poor accessibility.

options: Individual differences in drug receptor expression
Integrated drug level and effect relationships
Indirect drug-drug interactions via enzyme induction
Insertions or deletions of nucleotide sequences in genes
Inhibitory deletion of metabolizing enzyme genes
questions.explanation: Indels (Insertions/Deletions) are insertions or deletions of one or more nucleotides within a gene sequence. They represent a major type of genetic variation along with SNPs. Indels can cause frameshifts, premature stop codons, or altered splicing, often causing complete loss of enzyme function. They contribute to genetic polymorphism in drug metabolism and response genes.
questions.question: Indels in pharmacogenetic context refer to:

questions.explanation: Depot storage of lipophilic drugs in fat tissue is clinically significant because these drugs accumulate gradually and are released slowly from fat stores. In obese patients, lipophilic drugs like thiopental may have prolonged duration of action compared to lean patients, because the large fat depot slowly releases drug back into plasma long after discontinuation.
options: Fat enhances drug metabolism through lipases
Lipophilic drugs accumulate and are slowly released prolonging effects
Drug release from fat is rapid upon discontinuation
Fat storage activates prodrugs to their active form
Drug binding to fat increases plasma protein binding
questions.question: Depot storage of drugs in fat tissue is clinically significant because:
The ABCDE classification of adverse drug events was developed by:
questions.explanation: The ABCDE classification system for adverse drug events was developed by Rawlins and Thompson of Newcastle. They initially classified adverse events into Type A and Type B based on mechanism. The classification was subsequently expanded to include Types C (Chronic effects), D (Delayed effects), and E (End-of-treatment effects) to better categorize the temporal and mechanistic patterns of adverse drug reactions.

questions.question: The glomerular filtration clearance factor of 1.0 (unity) means:
options: All filtered drug is reabsorbed in tubules
The drug undergoes active tubular secretion
The drug is not filtered at all by the glomeruli
The drug is completely protein-bound in plasma
The drug is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted
questions.explanation: A clearance factor of 1.0 (unity) means the drug's renal clearance equals the GFR (approximately 120 ml/min = inulin clearance). This indicates the drug is freely filtered at the glomerulus and neither reabsorbed nor secreted in the convoluted tubules. Clearance < 1 indicates net reabsorption, while clearance > 1 indicates net tubular secretion.

options: Reduce the cost of drug manufacturing
Predict the chemical structure of new drugs
Maintain drug concentration below toxic and above efficacy level
Determine the route of drug excretion
Identify drug-drug interactions at receptor level
questions.question: The primary goal of pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) integration is to:
questions.explanation: The primary goal of PK-PD integration is to maintain drug concentrations at lower than toxic levels and higher than (or not below) the efficacy level. This ensures drugs remain within the therapeutic window, maximizing therapeutic benefit while minimizing the risk of toxicity or therapeutic failure.

options: Half-life is unaffected by dose in all cases
Half-life decreases due to enhanced renal excretion
Half-life increases as kinetics shift toward zero-order
Half-life doubles for each doubling of dose
questions.question: Dose size is listed as a factor influencing half-life because at higher doses with saturable elimination:
questions.explanation: At high drug doses that saturate elimination pathways (enzyme saturation, protein binding saturation), drug kinetics shift from first-order (constant half-life) toward zero-order kinetics (constant elimination rate). As a result, half-life effectively increases with dose in this range. This is clinically important for drugs like phenytoin and aspirin at high doses, where small dose increases cause disproportionately large plasma level increases.

questions.question: A physician chooses the intravenous route for drug administration in an emergency. A critical disadvantage of this choice is:
options: Slower absorption compared to other routes
High concentration achieved too rapidly causing adverse effects
Drug is rapidly metabolized before effect
Poor volume capacity limiting dose range
questions.explanation: A critical disadvantage of IV administration is that a high drug concentration is attained very rapidly, which increases the risk of adverse effects and toxicity. There is also a risk of embolism, the requirement for expertise, difficulty in recovery if an adverse event occurs, the need to administer the drug slowly, and the cost of equipment.

options: How the body handles the administered drug
What the drug does to the body
The study of drug receptor interactions only
The mechanism of drug adverse reactions
The classification of drugs by their chemical structure
questions.question: Which of the following best describes pharmacokinetics?
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to the drug — it encompasses Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion (ADME). In contrast, pharmacodynamics describes what the drug does to the body, including its mechanisms of action and effects.

The sublingual route has an onset of action of approximately 3-5 minutes, owing to rapid absorption through the richly vascularized mucosa under the tongue. This is faster than intramuscular (10-20 min) and oral (30-90 min) routes but slower than intravenous (30-60 seconds) and inhalation (2-3 min) routes.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly characterizes the time to onset of the sublingual route?
The blood-testis barrier and blood-placenta barrier serve what pharmacological purpose?
options: Enhancing drug metabolism in specialized tissues
Preventing drug accumulation in highly perfused organs
Protecting reproductive tissues from potentially harmful drug exposure
Facilitating drug excretion through specialized secretory pathways
questions.explanation: The blood-testis and blood-placenta barriers serve to protect reproductive cells and the developing fetus from potentially harmful xenobiotics, including drugs. These barriers limit passage of many drugs, though lipophilic molecules can still cross. This is why drug safety in pregnancy and male fertility must be carefully considered, especially for drugs with teratogenic potential.

questions.question: The SerT (serotonin transporter) long vs short repeat variants affect pharmacotherapy with:
questions.explanation: The serotonin transporter (SerT) gene has short and long promoter repeat variants that affect serotonin transporter expression and function. These polymorphisms affect the clinical response to SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), including both efficacy and side effect profiles. Patients with certain SerT variants may have different antidepressant responses and risk of adverse effects.

Erythromycin, chloramphenicol, rifampicin, tetracycline, penicillin, contrast media, and hydantoin are secreted by active transport into bile regardless of their concentration in bile. This active biliary secretion is important for drugs excreted predominantly via the biliary route, and can be exploited for treating biliary tract infections with appropriate antibiotics.
questions.question: Which drugs are excreted by active transport into bile, irrespective of their concentration in bile?

options: Imatinib and tyrosine kinase in CML; trastuzumab and HER2 in breast cancer
Metformin and biguanide target in diabetes
questions.question: The development of novel medicines based on pharmacogenetic principles is exemplified by which pairing?
questions.explanation: The development of imatinib targeting the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase in CML and trastuzumab targeting HER2 in breast cancer exemplify pharmacogenetically-guided novel drug development. Both drugs were specifically designed to target molecular aberrations identified through genetic analysis of cancer cells, representing the paradigm of molecular targeted therapy in oncology.

options: The quantity of drug absorbed and present in the body
The time to maximum drug concentration
The peak plasma concentration of the drug
The volume of plasma cleared of drug per minute
The rate of drug elimination from the body
questions.question: The total area under the curve (AUC) in pharmacokinetics measures:
questions.explanation: The Area Under the Curve (AUC) is the integral of drug blood level over time from zero to infinity. It measures the total quantity of drug absorbed and available in the body over time. AUC is used to calculate absolute and relative bioavailability, and is a key parameter in bioequivalence studies and exposure-response analysis.

options: Disease state altering receptor number via gain of function
Loss of receptor function due to autoimmune destruction
Tachyphylaxis due to repeated agonist stimulation
questions.question: Alpha-2A adrenergic receptor overexpression in beta-cells represents which mechanism of altered drug receptor response?
questions.explanation: Increased expression of the alpha-2A adrenergic receptor in Type 2 DM beta cells represents a gain-of-function mutation causing disease state alteration of receptor expression. The increased receptor number leads to constitutive suppression of insulin secretion. This is an example of how disease states can alter the number of available receptors, affecting drug response and requiring different therapeutic approaches.

options: Clearance to half-life of the drug
Minimum dose to maximum therapeutic dose
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index (TI) is the ratio of TD50 (toxic dose in 50% of subjects) divided by ED50 (effective dose in 50% of subjects). In animal studies, it uses LD50/ED50. A higher ratio indicates better safety. Drugs like digoxin, cocaine, and vancomycin have narrow therapeutic indices, requiring careful dose monitoring.
questions.question: A drug's therapeutic index (TI) is calculated as the ratio of:

questions.explanation: The primary advantage of intravenous over intramuscular administration is that the drug directly reaches the bloodstream, producing an immediate, accurate, and measurable effect. The response to the drug can be precisely monitored and the infusion stopped or adjusted as needed. However, IV is also the most risky route due to the risk of rapid adverse reactions.
questions.question: What is the primary advantage of intravenous drug administration over intramuscular administration?
The first phase of drug metabolism (non-synthetic phase) involves which reactions?
options: Conjugation with glucuronic acid and glycine
questions.explanation: The first phase (non-synthetic phase) of drug metabolism involves oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, and dehalogenation. These reactions prepare the drug for the second phase by introducing or exposing functional groups (-OH, -NH2, -COOH, -SH) that serve as handles for conjugation reactions in phase 2 metabolism.

questions.question: Volume of distribution depends on which of the following factors?
questions.explanation: Volume of distribution (Vd) depends on blood flow rate in diffused tissues, plasma protein binding, tissue binding, and the drug's lipophilicity and ionization. High tissue binding (lipophilic drugs) and low plasma protein binding give large Vd values. The Vd determines the loading dose required and predicts how well a drug will be removed by hemodialysis.
options: Urine flow rate and renal blood flow
Drug molecular weight and ionization state only
Blood flow rate in diffused tissues and tissue binding
Drug taste and palatability for oral preparations

questions.question: A second messenger is generated in the signal transduction process of which receptor type?
questions.explanation: G protein-coupled receptors (Type 2/metabotropic receptors) generate second messengers as part of their signal transduction process. Activation of GPCRs leads to G protein-mediated activation of effector enzymes (adenylyl cyclase, phospholipase C) that produce second messengers: cyclic AMP (cAMP), inositol trisphosphate (IP3), diacylglycerol (DAG), and calcium ions.

questions.question: Type C adverse drug events are characterized by:
options: Rapid acute reactions within minutes of administration
Chronic effects after prolonged drug administration
Delayed effects making them difficult to diagnose
Effects occurring only in genetically susceptible patients
questions.explanation: Type C adverse drug events are chronic effects that develop after prolonged (chronic) drug administration. Examples include analgesic nephropathy following prolonged use of some analgesics, and tardive dyskinesia developing after long-term antipsychotic drug use. These chronic toxicities may not be apparent from short-term clinical trials, which is a limitation of pre-approval drug safety assessment.

options: Protein binding saturation at high drug concentrations
Glomerular filtration rate reduction with age
Urine pH affecting tubular reabsorption of ionizable drugs
questions.question: Urinary excretion variation as a factor influencing half-life is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Urine pH is a key factor influencing drug half-life through its effect on tubular reabsorption. Acidic urine promotes ionization and trapping of basic drugs (reduced reabsorption, shorter half-life), while alkaline urine promotes ionization and trapping of acidic drugs. Changes in urine pH from diet, disease, or drugs can significantly alter the half-life of ionizable drugs.

The maintenance dose (MD) = Clearance (CL) — Target average steady-state plasma concentration (CpSSav). This formula ensures the rate of drug administration equals the rate of elimination at the desired therapeutic plasma level. Knowing the drug's clearance and target concentration allows calculation of appropriate maintenance doses for individual patients.
options: Target plasma concentration multiplied by volume of distribution
AUC multiplied by elimination rate constant
Loading dose divided by number of doses per day
Clearance multiplied by target average steady-state concentration
Half-life divided by volume of distribution
questions.question: The maintenance dose of a drug is calculated as:

questions.explanation: Acidic, hydrophilic, ionized drug metabolites excreted in bile and entering the intestinal lumen will not undergo enterohepatic circulation because they cannot passively diffuse back through intestinal membranes (which require lipophilicity). They remain in the intestinal lumen and are eventually excreted in feces. Enterohepatic recycling is limited to lipid-soluble, non-ionized molecules.
options: Be reabsorbed passively into the systemic circulation
Stimulate bile salt production in the liver
Be excreted in feces without further absorption
questions.question: Acidic drugs that undergo biliary excretion and enter the intestine as ionized, non-lipophilic metabolites will:

options: Faster absorption than the sublingual route
Higher bioavailability than the sublingual route
No first-pass effect unlike the sublingual route
Better patient tolerance and longer drug contact time
Suitable for a wider range of drug types
questions.explanation: Both sublingual and buccal routes bypass first-pass metabolism and provide rapid absorption. The buccal route (drug placed between cheek and gum) offers the advantage of longer contact time with the mucosa and better patient tolerance for drugs that may cause discomfort under the tongue, though absorption characteristics are otherwise similar.
questions.question: A drug is given as a buccal tablet for its advantage over sublingual administration. The main extra advantage of the buccal route is:

questions.explanation: An aqueous drug solution provides the fastest oral absorption because the drug is already dissolved and does not require time for tablet disintegration or drug dissolution. Tablets and capsules must first disintegrate and dissolve before absorption can begin. Enteric-coated tablets and sustained-release preparations intentionally delay or slow drug release.
questions.question: Drug formulation affects absorption. Which formulation generally provides the fastest oral absorption?

questions.explanation: A very large volume of distribution indicates that the drug is extensively distributed into peripheral tissues relative to plasma. This means the drug concentration in plasma is low compared to the total drug in the body. Drugs with large Vd tend to be lipophilic, poorly protein-bound to plasma proteins, or highly bound to tissue proteins.
questions.question: A drug with a very large volume of distribution (Vd) implies:
options: The drug is extensively distributed into peripheral tissues
The drug is highly protein-bound in plasma
The drug is confined mainly to plasma
The drug has rapid renal clearance
The drug has poor membrane permeability
Dose-related pharmacological effects at therapeutic doses
Toxic effects proportional to drug plasma levels
Stereotype symptoms unrelated to drug's pharmacodynamic profile
Delayed-onset effects related to drug accumulation
questions.question: Drug allergy is characterized as immunologically mediated reaction producing:
questions.explanation: Drug allergy (hypersensitivity) is an immunologically mediated reaction producing stereotype symptoms that are unrelated to the drug's pharmacodynamic profile and largely independent of dosage. It occurs only in a small percentage of the population who have been previously sensitized. IgE-mediated type I reactions (anaphylaxis), type II, III, and IV reactions are all forms of drug allergy.

options: Addition of oxygen to the drug molecule
Removal of a chlorine group from the drug
Transfer of electrons from the drug molecule
Addition of a water molecule causing drug disintegration
Reduction of drug by addition of hydrogen
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis is a first-phase metabolic reaction in which a water molecule is added to a substance, resulting in disintegration of the substance into smaller molecules. Esters and amide drugs commonly undergo hydrolysis. Classic examples include acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) hydrolyzed to salicylic acid and acetic acid, and acetylcholine hydrolyzed to choline and acetic acid.
questions.question: Hydrolysis as a first-phase metabolic reaction involves:
The passage of a drug through aqueous channels (pores) across membranes is characterized by:
options: Requirement for energy and specific carriers
Saturable kinetics with maximum transport rate
No energy, no carrier, limited to small hydrophilic drugs
questions.explanation: Passage through aqueous channels requires no energy and no carrier proteins. It is limited to small hydrophilic drugs (less than 200 daltons molecular weight) that can pass through the pores along their concentration gradient. This is distinct from facilitated diffusion (uses carriers) and active transport (uses energy), and from passive diffusion (requires lipophilicity).

questions.question: The intraosseous route of drug administration is primarily used in:
questions.explanation: The intraosseous (IO) route is used primarily in pediatric emergencies when intravenous access cannot be established quickly, particularly during cardiac arrest or circulatory collapse. Drug injected into the bone marrow enters the venous sinusoids and reaches systemic circulation within 30-60 seconds, comparable to intravenous delivery.
options: Elective surgical procedures under general anesthesia
Pediatric emergencies when IV access fails

questions.explanation: Half-life (t½) = 0.693 / elimination rate constant (k). Therefore, t½ = 0.693 / 0.693 per hour = 1 hour. The value 0.693 represents the natural logarithm of 2 (ln 2), which arises from the mathematical relationship between half-life and first-order elimination: the time for drug concentration to halve is constant for first-order processes.
questions.question: The half-life of a drug with elimination rate constant (k) of 0.693 per hour is:

questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion requires carrier proteins (non-covalent binding of drug to carrier) but does not require energy (ATP). It allows drugs to cross membranes more rapidly than simple passive diffusion, moving along the concentration gradient. Chemically similar drugs compete for the same carrier. Active transport, in contrast, uses ATP to move drugs against their gradient.
questions.question: Facilitated diffusion of drugs differs from active transport in that facilitated diffusion:
options: Uses carriers but does not require energy
Can move drugs against the concentration gradient
Does not involve specific carrier proteins
Is faster than passive diffusion at all times

questions.explanation: The maintenance dose is the dose size required to maintain clinical effectiveness or the therapeutic concentration in blood according to the dosage regimen. It replaces drug that has been eliminated, keeping plasma concentrations within the therapeutic window throughout the course of treatment.
options: Reduce the toxicity of the initial loading dose
Replace lost drug to maintain the therapeutic level
Override the first-pass effect in oral dosing
Prevent renal accumulation of active metabolites
questions.question: A maintenance dose is designed to:
Which of the following drugs is classified as having a low therapeutic index?
questions.explanation: Digoxin, cocaine, and vancomycin are classic examples of drugs with a low (narrow) therapeutic index, meaning the toxic dose is close to the therapeutic dose. These drugs require careful monitoring of plasma levels to avoid toxicity. Digoxin toxicity can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, and vancomycin requires trough level monitoring.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a generic drug product?
options: A product marketed under its nonproprietary name
A product marketed under its brand name only
A product with a unique patented chemical formula
A product reserved for hospital pharmacy usage
A product bioequivalent only to the innovator drug
questions.explanation: A generic product is a drug product marketed under the nonproprietary or common name of the drug. Unlike brand-name drugs (drug specialties), generic products are not sold under a registered trademark of a single company. They must meet bioequivalence requirements set by regulatory agencies.

Physical dependence is an altered physiological state produced by repeated drug use that necessitates the continued presence of drug to maintain physiological equilibrium. Discontinuation of the drug results in a withdrawal syndrome (abstinence syndrome) — a constellation of physiological symptoms. Examples include alcohol, opioids, antidepressants, and stimulants like cocaine causing physical dependence.
options: The belief that well-being requires the drug's action
Compulsive drug-seeking behavior without physiological need
Altered physiological state requiring continued drug presence
Mild discomfort on drug withdrawal without physical symptoms
questions.question: Physical drug dependence is characterized by:
Drug idiosyncrasy is best described as:
options: Appearance of toxic effects at therapeutic doses
Genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a chemical
Exaggerated pharmacological response to a drug
A secondary consequence of primary drug action
questions.explanation: Drug idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a chemical. Such adverse effects are restricted to individuals with a particular genotype. A classic example is hemolytic anemia in G6PD-deficient patients exposed to oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone). The reaction is predictable once the genetic susceptibility is known, but not from the drug's normal pharmacology.

options: Compulsive drug use despite harmful consequences
Mild discomfort on withdrawal without compulsive use
Drug use taking precedence over other activities
Tendency to relapse after promising to stop
questions.question: Drug addiction is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Drug addiction is characterized by overwhelming compulsive involvement with drug use, with taking the drug taking precedence over other activities, and strong tendency to relapse. Drug habituation (not addiction) is characterized by mild discomfort on withdrawal without significant physical dependence. Addictive drugs include cocaine, cannabis, amphetamines, and opioids.

questions.question: After 4 half-lives, what approximate percentage of a drug dose remains in the body?
questions.explanation: After each half-life, 50% of the remaining drug is eliminated. After 1 t½: 50% remains. After 2 t½: 25% remains. After 3 t½: 12.5% remains. After 4 t½: 6.25% remains. After 5 t½: 3.125% remains (≈97% eliminated). Clinically, 4-5 half-lives is considered sufficient for near-complete drug elimination.

options: Therapeutic drug monitoring of plasma levels
Dose reduction based on renal function testing
HLA pharmacogenetic screening before drug administration
Allergy testing with skin prick tests
questions.explanation: Abacavir hypersensitivity (associated with HLA-B5701) and carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (associated with HLA-B1502 in Asian populations) are HLA-mediated adverse drug reactions preventable through HLA pharmacogenetic screening. Current guidelines mandate HLA testing before initiating abacavir and carbamazepine in relevant populations.
questions.question: Abacavir hypersensitivity and carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome are examples of adverse drug reactions prevented through:
The combination of salbutamol (beta-2 agonist) and propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker) represents which type of drug interaction?
questions.explanation: Salbutamol and propranolol represent pharmacodynamic (receptor-level) antagonism. Propranolol blocks the beta-2 receptors that salbutamol acts on, thereby opposing bronchodilation. This interaction is clinically dangerous in asthma patients, as propranolol can cause severe bronchospasm. Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in asthmatic patients for this reason.

questions.question: Phenobarbital and diazoxide are metabolized faster in children than adults. This is clinically relevant because:
options: Children require lower doses of these drugs
These drugs accumulate more in children
Children may require higher mg/kg doses than adults
These drugs have narrower therapeutic indices in children
questions.explanation: Children (not newborns) have more active microsomal enzymes than adults for certain drugs like phenobarbital and diazoxide, metabolizing them faster. This means children may require relatively higher mg/kg doses to achieve therapeutic levels compared to adults. This contrasts with neonates who have immature metabolism and need lower doses.

options: Variable between pH 5 and 9 based on diet
questions.explanation: Urine under normal physiological conditions is a weak acid with pH between 6 and 7 (approximately 6.0-6.5). This mildly acidic pH has significant implications for the tubular reabsorption and excretion of weak acid and weak base drugs. Urine pH can be manipulated therapeutically (acidification or alkalinization) to manage drug overdose or optimize drug elimination.
questions.question: The urine pH under physiological conditions is:

questions.explanation: Autocoids are biological substances produced in the body, such as histamine and prostaglandins (PG). They are local hormones or mediators that act near their site of synthesis and are classified under 'Natural (biological)' drug types in pharmacology. They play important roles in inflammation, allergy, and normal physiological regulation.
questions.question: The term autocoid refers to:
options: A synthetic drug acting on adrenergic receptors
A drug produced from plant alkaloid extraction
A biological agent such as histamine or prostaglandin
A receptor with natural ligand affinity

questions.explanation: Drug intolerance is the appearance of characteristic toxic effects of a drug in an individual at therapeutic doses. The individual shows an unusually low threshold for drug toxicity at doses that are well-tolerated by most patients. Example: a single dose of chloroquine causing vomiting and abdominal pain. It differs from idiosyncrasy (which is genetically determined) and allergy (which is immunological).
options: Appearance of characteristic toxic effects at therapeutic doses
A genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a chemical
An immunological mechanism with specific antibodies
A dose-related exaggeration of the desired drug effect
Development only with prolonged drug administration
questions.question: Intolerance as an adverse drug effect is characterized by:

questions.explanation: CYP2C9 metabolizes warfarin and NSAIDs (including diclofenac, meloxicam, naproxen). CYP2C9 poor metabolizers have reduced warfarin clearance, predisposing them to bleeding tendency with standard doses. They also have reduced metabolism of NSAIDs and oral hypoglycemic agents like glipizide, with potential for hypoglycemia and GI bleeding.
questions.question: CYP2C9 deficiency would be MOST clinically significant for patients taking:
options: Codeine and tramadol for pain management
Efavirenz and ritonavir for HIV infection

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic advantage of the transdermal route over oral administration?
questions.explanation: The transdermal route provides stable plasma drug concentrations without the fluctuations seen with oral dosing, while also avoiding first-pass hepatic metabolism. Transdermal delivery requires highly lipid-soluble and potent drugs (since the patch cannot be too large), and is unsuitable for large hydrophilic molecules or large drug volumes.
options: Suitable for drugs with high molecular weight
Provides stable plasma levels with no first-pass effect
Allows administration of water-soluble hydrophilic drugs
Permits administration of large drug volumes
Achieves faster onset of action than oral route

questions.explanation: Synergism occurs when two drugs produce a combined effect that is greater than the sum of their individual effects (supra-additive effect). An example is sequential blockade of folate synthesis by sulphamethoxazole (blocking dihydropteroate synthase) and trimethoprim (blocking dihydrofolate reductase) — combined, they produce far greater antimicrobial effect than either alone.
questions.question: Synergism between two drugs means that their combined effect is:
options: Equal to the sum of their individual effects
Equal to the effect of the more potent drug only
Greater than the sum of their individual effects

questions.explanation: Salbutamol administered as a nebulized solution or fine powder (aerosol) is the classic example of a drug applied topically to the bronchi and lungs. It acts locally on bronchial smooth muscle beta-2 receptors for rapid bronchodilation. Aerosols and nebulized solutions allow high local concentrations with minimal systemic side effects.
questions.question: Topical drugs applied to the bronchi and lungs work as aerosols. An example is:
options: Tetracycline applied as a topical ointment
Salbutamol administered as a nebulized solution
Lidocaine gel applied to the urethra
Metronidazole given as a rectal suppository

questions.explanation: When the tubular secretion carrier system is saturated with drugs, the rate of drug elimination will not increase even if blood drug concentration increases. This represents zero-order kinetics (saturable kinetics), where elimination rate is constant at maximum tubular transport capacity. This explains why some drugs have dose-dependent elimination rates at high plasma concentrations.
options: Drug elimination rate increases proportionally with concentration
Drug transitions to glomerular filtration exclusively
Drug elimination rate remains constant regardless of blood level
Drug undergoes biliary excretion as alternative
questions.question: The renal tubular secretion carrier system for acidic drugs can be saturated. When saturated:

questions.explanation: Abacavir hypersensitivity reaction is strongly associated with the HLA-B5701 allele. This serious, potentially life-threatening immune-mediated reaction occurs in patients with this allele. Current guidelines mandate HLA-B5701 screening before initiating abacavir. Patients who test positive should not receive abacavir as the risk of hypersensitivity is very high.
questions.question: The HLA-B5701 allele is associated with hypersensitivity to which antiretroviral drug?

questions.answerText:
A(i) MG is an autoimmune disorder characterised by weakness or fatiguability of muscles after exercise. Antibodies are produced against acetylcholine receptors in the muscles. Though mainly autoimmune, a rare familial form is autosomal recessive. Types: Juvenile MG (most common in this age group); neonatal transient MG; congenital MG.

A(ii) Clinical features:
- Occurs >10 years in 75% of cases.
- Affects more girls.
- Commonly affects cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X, XI.
- Respiratory muscle may also be affected.
- Signs and symptoms: ptosis (usually bilateral, may be unilateral); diplopia (due to weakness of ≥1 extra-ocular muscle); poor chewing and inability to close mouth properly (if masseter affected); symptoms worsen with activity and improve with rest.

A(iii) Investigations:
1. Clinical test: ask patient to do repetitive movements (e.g., sustained upward gaze); eyelids drop — demonstrates fatigability.
2. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies — if facility is available.
3. Edrophonium (Tensilon) Test: Tensilon is a strong short-acting anticholinesterase that increases ACh concentration at the neuromuscular junction; given IV (0.2 mg/kg); within minutes the ptosis/weakness improves — confirms diagnosis.
4. Neostigmine (0.04 mg/kg) — long-acting; less likely to be used for diagnosis.
5. Chest X-ray — to rule out thymic hyperplasia or thymoma (seen as thymic shadow on X-ray).

B. In MG, autoimmune antibodies destroy ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction. During repeated muscle activity, ACh is repeatedly released and depleted faster than it can be replenished, resulting in progressive failure of neuromuscular transmission and worsening weakness. At rest, ACh accumulates at the junction and enough receptors remain functional for transmission to recover, explaining symptomatic improvement with rest.

C(i) MG — first line: anticholinesterases (Neostigmine, Pyridostigmine, Ambemonium). In non-responsive cases, steroids are added. DMD — Steroids (prednisolone) in low dose to increase the period of ambulation.
C(ii) MG — Thymectomy (removal of thymoma). DMD — Orthopaedic surgery to manage contractures and deformities; no equivalent surgical cure.
C(iii) MG — with optimal treatment most patients can live normal lives; remission in about 25% after about 2 years of treatment; some patients die from respiratory embarrassment. DMD — ambulation impossible by age 12 years; death before 20 years from cardiomyopathy; prognosis poor.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Amniocentesis:
• Definition: withdrawal of amniotic fluid.
• Timing: usually at 16–18 weeks of gestation, when the ratio of viable to non-viable cells is maximal.
• Tests on amniotic fluid cells:
  - Fetal sexing: visualisation of Barr body, often as a preliminary step
  - Fetal karyotyping: classical karyotyping; interphase cytogenetics (in situ hybridisation with non-radioactively labelled probes)
  - Fetal enzyme assay: primarily for inborn errors of metabolism
  - Fetal DNA diagnosis: linkage to restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLP); direct detection
• Tests on amniotic fluid supernatant:
  - Amniotic fluid biochemistry: alpha-fetoprotein (for open neural tube defects); 17α-hydroxyprogesterone (for 21-hydroxylase-deficient adrenogenital syndrome)
• Conditions it can diagnose: open neural tube defects, chromosomal abnormalities (Down syndrome, sex chromosome aneuploidies), inborn errors of metabolism, CAH, haemoglobinopathies (via DNA), and many single-gene disorders.

A(ii) Amniocentesis vs CVS:
• Amniocentesis: done at 16–18 weeks; amniotic fluid obtained; tests include karyotyping, enzyme assay, AFP, DNA analysis.
• Chorionic villus sampling (CVS): sampling of chorionic villus from the fetus, usually at 8–10 weeks. Each biopsy yields 5–30 mg of tissue, used for fetal sexing, fetal karyotyping, biochemical studies, and DNA analysis.
• Key advantage of CVS: can be done much earlier than amniocentesis (8–10 weeks vs 16–18 weeks), so selective termination of pregnancy can be done earlier and with fewer complications.

B(i) Additional prenatal diagnostic techniques:
Non-invasive:
• Ultrasonography: visualisation of the fetus using ultrasound. Optimal time 16–18 weeks, although anencephaly is detectable as early as 10–12 weeks. Advantage: no proven hazard to mother or fetus; can be repeated as many times as needed.
• Radiography: useful in skeletal dysplasias; optimal time 20 weeks. Limited use.

Invasive (mostly obsolete):
• Cordocentesis: taking a fetal blood sample; possible from 18 weeks onwards. Useful in blood disorders (e.g. haemophilia, haemoglobinopathies).
• Fetoscopy: endoscopic visualisation of the fetus at 18–20 weeks.
• Fetal skin biopsy: useful in some serious skin conditions.
• Fetal liver biopsy: useful in some metabolic disorders.

A(i) Describe the prenatal diagnosis technique of amniocentesis under the following headings: definition, timing, tests performed on cells, tests performed on supernatant, and specific conditions it can diagnose.
A(ii) Compare amniocentesis with chorionic villus sampling (CVS) in terms of timing, tissue obtained, tests available, and the key advantage of CVS.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Vital capacity: the largest volume a subject can expire after a single maximal inspiration. Forced vital capacity (FVC): the vital capacity when expiration is performed as rapidly as possible. FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second): volume expired during the first second of FVC. FEV1/FVC ratio: normal value ≥75% (though this depends on age, sex, and height). This ratio is reduced in obstructive airway diseases like asthma, emphysema, and bronchitis.

A(ii) PEFR (peak expiratory flow rate): the maximum expiratory flow rate achieved during a forced expiration; measured in ml/min. Advantage: more convenient to measure than FEV1; FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC require a spirometer, while PEFR only requires a Wright Peak Flow Meter.

A(iii) Demonstration of reversible airway obstruction: pulmonary function test (FEV1 or PEFR) measured before and after β2-agonist administration. An improvement of greater than 12% after 10 minutes confirms reversibility consistent with asthma.

B(i) Bronchial provocation test: determines airways responsiveness to provoking stimuli; expressed as the provoking dose/concentration causing a 20% fall in FEV1, or the slope of a dose-response curve.

B(ii) Laboratory evaluation: full blood count and absolute eosinophil count; specific IgE antibody measurements — in vivo (skin prick tests) and in vitro (radioallergosorbent test, RAST).

B(iii) Chest radiography: warranted in an acutely symptomatic patient if complications are suspected — pneumonia, pneumothorax, or pneumomediastinum; otherwise not really necessary.

C. Follow-up after discharge: observed for at least 24 hours before discharge; discharged with sufficient medication for at least 3 days; instructed on use of MDI, spacer, or nebuliser; PEFR measurements should be made at least 3 times a day until reassessed within 3 days of discharge to assess PEFR deterioration; identify trigger factors (inciting agents) of the acute attack; a written plan of action should be given to the patient.

A. Describe the pulmonary function tests used in the assessment of bronchial asthma:
(i) Define vital capacity, forced vital capacity (FVC), FEV1, and FEV1/FVC ratio with normal values.
(ii) Define peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) and state its advantage over FEV1.

B. Describe the investigations used in the long-term assessment of a child with asthma:
(i) Bronchial provocation test
(ii) Laboratory evaluation — name all tests
