C. Explain the follow-up plan after hospital discharge for an acute asthma exacerbation.

A 12-month-old infant presents with a 2-day history of fever, irritability, ear-pulling, and refusal of feeds. The mother reports the child has had frequent colds. On examination the child is febrile (T 38.8°C), has an immobile red tympanic membrane, and there is serous fluid in the middle ear visible on otoscopy. The child attends a daycare centre and lives with five siblings.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List all the risk factors for this condition.
(iii) What are all the possible complications?
(iv) Outline the treatment, distinguishing neonatal management from management in older children.
(v) How does this condition differ from chronic otitis media?
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute otitis media (AOM).

(ii) Risk factors: age (six to eighteen months most likely); attending daycare centre; recent illness (cold or sinus infection); history of allergies (allergic rhinitis or sinusitis); exposure to secondhand smoke; family members prone to ear infections; using a pacifier; blockage of the Eustachian tube by acute coryza/common cold, allergies, exposure to cigarette smoke, infected or hypertrophied adenoids, or being fed lying down (bottle while lying on back). The infant's Eustachian tube is shorter, wider, and straight, predisposing to infection.

(iii) Complications: hearing loss; mastoiditis; petrositis; labyrinthitis; meningitis; brain abscess.

(iv) Treatment — Neonates: parenteral ampicillin/sulbactam plus amikacin (cefuroxime plus amikacin in some descriptions); also parenteral cefuroxime plus amikacin is listed. Sepsis screen in toxic neonates. Older children: oral amoxicillin (first line); co-amoxiclav (second line); oral co-trimoxazole and IM procaine penicillin may be useful in areas of low resistance. Supportive: ear (aural) toiletting for otorrhoea; antipyretic/analgesic (paracetamol/ibuprofen).

(v) Chronic otitis media is defined as a perforated, painless, discharging ear, almost always with an immobile tympanic membrane. Complications unique to chronic otitis media include: cholesteatoma; mastoiditis; CNS involvement (otogenic tetanus, meningitis, facial nerve palsy, lateral sinus thrombosis, abscesses — brain, subdural, eustachian). Treatment: ear (aural) toiletting; flavine-in-spirit dressing; systemic antibiotics (controversial).

A(i) Definition: inflamed tonsils and pharynx. Types: exudative tonsillopharyngitis; diphtheritic tonsillopharyngitis; vesicular or ulcerative tonsillopharyngitis.

A(ii) Causative organism: Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus. Older children: fever, sore throat, dysphagia, headache, malaise. Young children: fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

A(iii) Physical signs: pyrexia T>38°C; exudative tonsillar enlargement; oedema; erythema; lymphoid hyperplasia of the pharynx; anterior cervical lymphadenitis.

A(iv) Investigations: culture of throat swab; FBC — polymorphonuclear leucocytosis (useful but not diagnostic); blood culture in very ill patients; rapid latex agglutination test on throat swabs (10–60 minutes) — specific but low sensitivity.

B. Suppurative complications: acute otitis media (spread via Eustachian tube); acute sinusitis (spread to paranasal sinuses); peritonsillar cellulitis and abscess (spread to peritonsillar space); retropharyngeal abscess (spread to retropharyngeal lymph nodes); suppurative cervical lymphadenitis (spread to cervical lymph nodes). Delayed non-suppurative complications: acute rheumatic fever (immune-mediated response to streptococcal antigen affecting the heart) and acute glomerulonephritis (immune complex deposition in the glomeruli following streptococcal infection).

C. Antibiotics are indicated if symptomatic pharyngitis and: a positive rapid streptococcal antigen test; clinical diagnosis of scarlet fever; a household contact with documented streptococcal pharyngitis; a past history of acute rheumatic fever; or a recent history of acute rheumatic fever in a family member. Antibiotic choices: oral penicillin V 250 mg qds × 10 days; single IM injection of benzathine penicillin G (600,000–900,000 units for children ≥12 years); oral erythromycin (30–50 mg/kg/day) in 3–4 divided doses for penicillin-allergic patients; oral amoxicillin; oral azithromycin. Supportive: analgesic/antipyretic (paracetamol/ibuprofen); adequate fluid and caloric intake.
questions.question:
A. Describe exudative (streptococcal) tonsillopharyngitis under the following headings:
(i) Definition and types of acute tonsillopharyngitis
(ii) Causative organism and clinical features in older children versus young children
(iii) Physical signs
(iv) Investigations and diagnosis

B. Explain the clinical basis for the suppurative and delayed non-suppurative complications of Group A β-haemolytic streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis.

A 7-year-old child presents with dyspnoea on exertion and is found on examination to have a soft and delayed P2, a possible single S2, a left parasternal heave, an ejection click at the pulmonary area, and an ejection systolic murmur. The chest X-ray shows a pulmonary knuckle (post-stenotic dilatation), reduced pulmonary vascular markings, and a normal heart size.

(i) State the diagnosis and classify all the types of this condition, including any syndromes associated with specific subtypes.
(ii) Explain the embryological/pathological basis and the haemodynamic changes that produce the clinical features.
(iii) Describe the full investigation findings — CXR, ECG, echo, and cardiac catheterisation.
(iv) Outline the management for both mild and severe forms, naming the specific procedures used and indications for each.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pulmonary Stenosis (PS). Classification by anatomical level:
- Valvar: the commonest type; if unicuspid, presents in the neonatal period as critical stenosis
- Infundibular: fibromuscular band obstruction
- Supravalvar: rare; associated with hypercalcaemia; commonly found in infants <9 months; if co-exists with similar lesion on the left (aortic stenosis) it is called Williams Syndrome (features: mental retardation, elfin facies, hypercalcaemia, aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis — "Double Arterial Stenosis")
- Peripheral: unilateral or bilateral stenosis of branches of pulmonary trunk; caused by drugs (e.g. thalidomide) or rubella infection

(ii) Obstruction at the RVOT impedes blood flow out of the right ventricle, increasing RV workload → RVH. If severe (critical stenosis, e.g. unicuspid valve), foramen ovale remains open due to high right-sided pressure, leading to right-to-left atrial shunting and cyanosis. The ejection click is produced by forced or pressurised flow of blood against the wall of the pulmonary artery; it indicates less severe obstruction.

(iii) CXR: post-stenotic dilatation of the pulmonary artery (pulmonary knuckle — unlike TOF which shows a pulmonary bay); reduced pulmonary vascular markings; heart size usually normal unless obstruction is severe.
ECG: right ventricular hypertrophy (overwhelming evidence); in very severe forms, T-wave inversion in V1–V6 (RV-apex forming).
Echo (now replaces catheterisation for diagnosis): Doppler sample volume; transthoracic echo demonstrates the obstruction.
Cardiac catheterisation: increased right ventricular pressure (gradient); normal or reduced pulmonary artery pressure; right ventriculography shows post-stenotic dilatation on lateral view; demonstrates high pressure gradient between pre- and post-stenotic areas.

(iv) Management:
Mild (RV pressure <60 mmHg): conservative management.
Severe (RV pressure >60 mmHg): urgent relief of obstruction to avoid hypertrophied muscle outgrowing its blood supply (causing angina).
Procedures:
- Ventriculotomy
- Pulmonary valvotomy/infundibular resection
- Balloon valvuloplasty (inflated with normal saline in case balloon ruptures) — now the accepted standard procedure; can be done as a day case

questions.question:
A 13-year-old girl is brought in with a 2-week history of palpitations, weight loss despite increased appetite, irritability, deterioration in school performance, and a visible swelling in the front of her neck. On examination there is a diffuse goitre, tachycardia, warm moist skin, fine tremor, and mild exophthalmos.

(i) State the diagnosis and identify all predisposing factors.
(ii) Describe the pathophysiology, including the role of autoimmunity.
(iii) List all management options and state which is preferred in children.
(iv) What are the surgical risks, and what are the disadvantages of radioactive iodine?
questions.answerText:
(i) Graves' disease (diffuse toxic goitre / autoimmune hyperthyroidism). Predisposing factors: autoimmune pathogenesis; five times more common in girls than boys; can occur at any age but peak incidence is in adolescents; the condition may be autonomous or arise from a diffuse goitre; thyroid stimulating antibodies bind to TSH receptor.

(ii) Pathophysiology: Graves' disease is an autoimmune thyroid disease in which thyroid stimulating antibodies bind to the TSH receptor, causing autonomous, unregulated production of T4 and T3. Serum T4, FT4, T3, and FT3 are elevated while TSH is very low (negative feedback). Lymphocytic infiltration and swelling of retro-orbital tissue cause exophthalmos. Local thickening of subcutaneous tissue over the shin causes pretibial myxoedema. The hypermetabolic state produces tachycardia, weight loss, sweating, tremor, diarrhoea, and heat intolerance. Onset is usually gradual.

(iii) Management options:
• Medical (preferred in children): anti-thyroid drugs — propylthiouracil, methimazole/carbimazole, ipodate sodium. Treatment usually needed for 2–3 years. Symptomatic relief: sedation, bed rest, beta-adrenergic blockers (propranolol 2.5–10.5 mg/kg/day, max 120 mg/day every 6–8 hours) to control tremor and agitation — contraindicated in asthma and heart block
• Surgical: subtotal thyroidectomy. Indicated when there is toxicity to drugs, failure to cure after an adequate course of medical treatment, non-compliance, or failure of drugs to shrink a large conspicuous goitre
• Radioactive iodine

(iv) Surgical disadvantages (risks): mortality; injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve; hypoparathyroidism; hypothyroidism.
Radioactive iodine disadvantages: hypothyroidism; unknown genetic effects; complete control requires weeks/months of treatment.

(i) Primary lung abscess (localised area of suppuration due to destruction of lung parenchyma with formation of a cavity containing purulent material). Primary — because this occurs in a previously healthy patient with no underlying medical disorders, caused by aspiration or pneumonia in the healthy host.

(ii) Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus. In previously normal (healthy) hosts: S. aureus, H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, and viridians streptococci. In immunocompromised hosts: anaerobes, Gram-negative organisms, Candida, Aspergillus. Anaerobes occur exclusively in secondary abscesses.

(iii) Pathophysiology: patients predisposed to aspiration commonly have periodontal disease. A bacterial inoculum (mouth anaerobes) from the gingival crevice reaches the most dependent portions of the lung (posterior segments of upper lobes and superior segment of lower lobes). Infection initiated because bacteria are not cleared by host defence mechanisms → aspiration pneumonitis → tissue necrosis 7–14 days later → lung abscess. Pathological sequence: pulmonary parenchyma obstructed, infected, suppurative, necrotic; inflammatory changes → suppuration and thrombosis of local blood vessels → necrosis and liquefaction; granulation tissue forms around periphery; abscess commonly ruptures into a bronchus → contents coughed up or aspirated into other lung areas → additional abscess formation. Other mechanisms: bacteraemia or tricuspid valve endocarditis causing septic emboli.

(iv) Complications: overexpansion of the abscess; tension pneumothorax; empyema; spontaneous rupture with seeding to other parts of the lungs.

(v) Management — Medical: antibiotics must include antistaphylococcal agent; metronidazole for anaerobes; physiotherapy — postural drainage and chest percussion to reduce secretion. Surgical: if no response to medical therapy — pneumonotomy or lobectomy. Surgery is indicated when there is failure of medical treatment.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child presents with a 10-day history of productive cough with foul-smelling sputum, high fever (40°C), chest pain, dyspnoea, and haemoptysis. Examination reveals tachycardia, tachypnoea, decreased chest movement, dullness on percussion, decreased breath sounds with fine crackles and bronchial breath sounds. Chest radiograph shows a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the right lower lobe. The child is not immunocompromised and has no prior lung disease.

(i) What is the diagnosis and how is it classified in this patient?
(ii) State the most common causative organisms, distinguishing those that affect previously healthy hosts from those that affect immunocompromised patients.
(iii) Describe the full pathophysiology, from aspiration through to abscess formation.
(iv) List all the complications.
(v) Outline the full management, including indications for surgery.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology and epidemiology:
- Acute spastic paralytic illness due to tetanus toxin; Clostridium tetani – Gram +ve, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacilli
- Worldwide occurrence but endemic in some developing countries
- Neonatal tetanus kills 500,000 babies/year
- Non-neonatal forms due to penetrating injuries by dirty objects like nails, glass fragments, unsterile injections, animal bites, deep seated abscesses (CSOM), ear-piercing, unsterile circumcision, compound fractures, scarifications, intestinal surgery or contaminated sutures
- Neonatal tetanus: affects infants of unimmunized mothers; unhygienic cord care practices, circumcision, ear-piercing, scarification
A(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Wounds with low oxidation-reduction potential (dead/devitalized tissue, foreign body, active infection) facilitate germination of spores
- Tetanospasmin released in wound binds to peripheral motor neuron terminal, enters axon, via retrograde intraneuronal transport reaches nerve cell body in brainstem and spinal cord
- Toxin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA
- Reduced inhibition → muscle rigidity (sustained muscle contraction) and spasms; sympathetic hyperactivity and increased catecholamines; weakness and paralysis
- Localized tetanus: toxin effect on nerves supplying only the affected muscle
- Generalized tetanus: spread of toxin through lymphatics and blood to multiple nerve terminals
B(i) Clinical presentation:
- Generalized: incubation period 2-14 days to months; trismus (locked jaw), headache, restlessness, irritability, rigidity, opisthotonos, intermittent spasms; patient is conscious, anxious and fearful; ±fever; dysuria, urinary retention; autonomic involvement: tachycardia, arrhythmias, labile hypertension, diaphoresis
- Localized: rigidity and spasms limited to muscles adjacent to site of entry
- Cephalic: limited to bulbar musculature; poor prognosis
B(ii) Neonatal tetanus:
- Always generalized
- Symptoms: excessive crying, refusal to suck, trismus, rigidity, spasms
- Worse prognosis than post-neonatal tetanus
C(i) Diagnosis, differential diagnosis, prognosis:
- Mainly clinical; no abnormal EEG, CSF, or EMG findings
- Differential diagnosis: para/retropharyngeal or dental abscess with trismus; brainstem encephalitis; rabies; hypocalcaemia
- Prognosis: guarded
- Poor prognostic indicators: short incubation period <7 days; period of onset <48 hours; cephalic; neonatal > post-neonatal; generalized > localized; temperature >40°C; tachycardia >120/min (>150/min in neonates)
C(ii) Management and prevention:
- Nurse in quiet dark environment (ideally ICU)
- Neutralize unbound toxin: Human TIG single dose of 3,000-6,000 U for children/adults, 500 U for neonates; alternatively ATS single dose of 50,000-100,000 U after testing for sensitivity
- Eradicate organisms: metronidazole (preferred); penicillin G as alternative; 10-14 days
- Muscle relaxants: oral diazepam 5 mg/kg/day x 2-6 weeks; others: MgSO4, midazolam, chlorpromazine, phenobarbitone
- Wound debridement and care
- Supportive care: fluid/electrolyte balance, nutritional support
- Prevention – active immunization (Td schedule): Td1 at first contact (no protection); Td2 4 weeks later (80% for 3 years); Td3 6 months later (95% for 5 years); Td4 1 year later (99% for 10 years); Td5 1 year later (99% for life)
questions.question:
Describe the pathogenesis and management of tetanus under the following headings, distinguish neonatal from post-neonatal tetanus, and explain the basis of prevention.
A(i) Aetiology and epidemiology including causes of neonatal tetanus
A(ii) Pathogenesis: how the toxin causes muscle rigidity, spasms, and autonomic instability
B(i) Clinical presentation: generalized, localized, and cephalic forms
B(ii) Neonatal tetanus: distinctive features and clinical manifestations
C(i) Diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and prognosis
C(ii) Management and prevention including active and passive immunization schedules

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: IE is a septicaemic illness that causes damage to the endocardium and heart valves (unlike ARF which is due to antibody formation).
Pathogenesis steps:
1. Damage to endothelium (or presence of foreign material within the heart)
2. Formation of sterile vegetation on the damaged surface (non-bacterial endocarditis)
3. Transient bacteraemia and adherence of organisms to the sterile vegetation
4. Infective endocarditis: progressive enlargement of vegetation
5. Proliferation of valve leaflet; embolisation of infected emboli

A(ii) Causative organisms:
Most common: Streptococcus viridans (found in mouth — commonest, causing subacute IE in those with pre-existing heart abnormality)
Others: Streptococcus faecalis; other streptococci (beta-haemolytic, pneumococci); Staphylococcus aureus (and coagulase-negative staph); Gram-negative organisms (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, HACEK group — Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella); Fungi (Candida — in immunosuppression/very rare)

A(iii) Predisposing cardiac lesions (five):
1. Congenital heart disease (complex CHD, uncorrected PDA, uncorrected small VSD)
2. Rheumatic heart disease
3. Bicuspid aortic valve
4. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
5. Prosthetic valves / surgically constructed shunts / following palliative surgery
Non-cardiac predisposing factors (five):
1. Dental caries/dental manipulation
2. Cardiac catheterisation
3. Prolonged IV cannulation/indwelling central catheters
4. IV drug abuse
5. Urethral catheterisation/bladder instrumentation; endoscopic procedure; immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy, steroids)

B(i) Antibiotic regimens:
- Strep. viridans: Penicillin (crystalline/IV) — very good; or Ampicillin; or Amoxycillin; ± Gentamicin; ± Probenecid (to delay excretion of penicillin). OR: Ceftriaxone
- Staphylococcus aureus: Cloxacillin (Oxacillin/Nafcillin) + Gentamicin; Vancomycin if indicated
- Unknown organism: Penicillin + Cloxacillin + Gentamicin
Duration: For six weeks (all cases)

B(ii) Surgical indications (four):
1. Valve replacement (for destroyed valve)
2. Correction of underlying heart defect
3. Embolectomy
4. Removal of mycotic aneurysm
(Also: heart failure not responding to medical treatment; persistent bacteraemia)

B(iii) Prophylaxis strategy:
Aim: To ensure adequate blood levels of antibiotic in circulation BEFORE the intended procedure, in order to kill bacteria in the bloodstream before they can lodge in the heart.
Patients: Those with predisposing cardiac lesions (prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired CHD, cardiac transplant, congenital heart disease). Identify patients at risk.
Timing: Given 1–2 hours before surgery (and after); single dose 30–60 minutes before procedure.
Oral options: Penicillin; amoxycillin (50 mg/kg for children); erythromycin (for penicillin-allergic patients)
Parenteral options: Penicillin; amoxicillin; vancomycin; gentamicin (for GUT surgery)
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross pathology, pathogenesis, and clinical presentation of Infective Endocarditis (IE) under the following headings:
A(i) Define IE and state how vegetations form, from damaged endothelium to infective endocarditis (describing the steps in the pathogenesis)
A(ii) List the causative organisms, starting with the most common subacute organism through to fungi
A(iii) List the predisposing cardiac lesions (at least five) and five non-cardiac predisposing factors

B. Describe the treatment of IE under the following headings:
B(i) State the antibiotic regimen for Streptococcus viridans, Staphylococcus aureus, and unknown organism, and state how long treatment should be given
B(ii) List four surgical indications in IE
B(iii) Describe the antibiotic prophylaxis strategy, including the aim, which patients receive it, when the drug is given, and the oral and parenteral drug options

Describe the management of sickle cell disease in the steady state and during crises under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the full steady-state management of SCD including prophylactic measures, immunisation, and supplementation.
A(ii) Describe the management of vaso-occlusive crisis: distinguish mild-to-moderate from severe VOC and state all interventions including drug doses and routes.
B(i) Describe the management of infections in SCD: common organisms, antibiotic choices, and the mechanism of increased susceptibility.
B(ii) Describe the management of leg ulcers and haematuria in SCD.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Steady-state management:
- Determine and record physical/haematological parameters.
- Avoid factors that encourage sickling (hypoxia, dehydration, fever, acidosis, cold, infections, bacteria, presence of WBC).
- Folic acid supplementation.
- Malaria prophylaxis.
- Immunisation: Pneumococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B.
- Iron-chelation therapy: may be indicated for patients with stroke or cardiomyopathy requiring long-term transfusion programme; aim is to prevent haemosiderosis. Subcutaneous desferrioxamine 35–45 mg/kg/night; continuous ambulatory IV desferrioxamine; oral chelating agent Deferiprone (L1) — 1,2-dimethyl-hydroxypyrid-4-one.
- Hydroxyurea 15 mg/kg/24 hrs (to increase HbF); monitor FBC, LFT and HbF.
- Laser photocoagulation for proliferative retinopathy.
- Total hip replacement with prostheses for avascular necrosis.

A(ii) VOC management:
Mild to moderate VOC: Bed rest at home; Liberal oral fluids; Analgesics; Identify and treat cause.
Severe VOC: Admit; Administer analgesics commensurate with degree of pain; IV fluids 2000–2500 ml/m²/24 hrs in form of ½ strength Darrows in 5% dextrose (No. 18 solution can also be used); Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA), Nurse-Controlled Analgesia (NCA); Epidural infusions; Psychological intervention — cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) can reduce distress; Identify and treat cause.

B(i) Management of infections:
Common organisms: H. influenzae, Pneumococcus, Salmonella spp., S. aureus.
Antibiotic choices:
- Chloramphenicol + Erythromycin.
- Crystalline penicillin + Chloramphenicol.
- Chloramphenicol + Cloxacillin.
- Cephalosporins.
Mechanism of increased susceptibility:
- Microvascular thrombosis/infarction in the lungs → impaired local ventilation/resultant hypoxia.
- Metabolic abnormalities in leucocytes.
- Progressive splenic infarction/fibrosis → functional asplenia (by age 5, 95% of children with SCA have functional asplenia).
- High serum iron levels (promotes bacterial growth, multiplication, virulence, and inhibits the RES).
- Defective alternate pathway of complement.

B(ii) Leg ulcers management:
- Bed rest.
- Elevation of affected limb.
- Daily Eusol/Zinc sulphate dressings.
- Maintenance transfusion.
- Oral zinc sulphate.
- Epanutin.
- Skin grafting.

Haematuria management:
- Usually stops spontaneously.
- Conservative treatment: liberal fluids (to reduce clot formation); correct anaemia.
- Epsilon amino caproic acid (antifibrinolytic agent) is useful in management.

questions.question:
A. Describe coeliac disease under the following headings:
A(i) The causative dietary proteins, the cereals in which they are found, and the specific immune effector mechanism
A(ii) The histological appearance on jejunal biopsy that confirms the diagnosis (gold standard) and the serological marker most specific for the condition
A(iii) The extra-intestinal and autoimmune conditions associated with coeliac disease
A(iv) The specific skin manifestation and its biopsy finding

B. Explain the clinical basis for the following:
B(i) Why coeliac disease is described as rare in Black Africans
B(ii) Why the age of peak adult incidence falls in the 3rd–4th decade

C. Distinguish coeliac disease from tropical sprue on the basis of:
C(i) Epidemiological feature and response to treatment
C(ii) Serological differentiation
questions.answerText:
A(i) Coeliac disease is caused by intolerance to gluten, a protein complex found specifically in wheat, barley, and rye. The immune mechanism involves a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response in the small intestinal mucosa triggered by gliadin, the immunotoxic fraction of gluten, in genetically predisposed individuals with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes.
A(ii) The gold standard investigation is jejunal biopsy showing flat mucosa with subtotal villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia. The reversal of these changes on a gluten-free diet confirms the diagnosis. The serological marker most specific for coeliac disease (greater than 99% specificity) is IgA endomysial antibody (EMA), alongside IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG).
A(iii) Coeliac disease is associated with other autoimmune conditions, particularly insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM/Type 1 diabetes) and autoimmune thyroid disease. Shared HLA-DQ2/DQ8 haplotypes predispose individuals to multiple autoimmune conditions.
A(iv) The skin manifestation is dermatitis herpetiformis, presenting with blistering subepidermal eruptions (vesicles) that are intensely pruritic, distributed on extensor surfaces. Skin biopsy shows IgA deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction.
B(i) Coeliac disease is rare in Black Africans, likely due to low prevalence of predisposing HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 haplotypes in this population. It is most common in Caucasian populations of European descent.
B(ii) The mode of inheritance of coeliac disease is unknown despite familial clustering, as multiple genetic and environmental factors contribute to disease expression. The adult peak in the 3rd–4th decade likely reflects the cumulative effect of ongoing gluten exposure combined with a delayed or triggered immune response, often diagnosed during workup for unexplained anaemia or infertility.
C(i) Tropical sprue occurs in individuals residing in or returning from tropical regions and is believed to be of infectious aetiology (possibly bacterial overgrowth). Unlike coeliac disease, it responds to tetracycline and folate supplementation, not a gluten-free diet.
C(ii) Coeliac disease is associated with positive IgA endomysial antibodies and anti-tTG, which are negative in tropical sprue. Both may show villous atrophy on biopsy, but the specific serological markers distinguish them.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy and clinical features of Neurofibromatosis (NF) under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, inheritance pattern, and pathognomonic features
A(ii) Café au lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules — their appearance, number, and clinical significance
A(iii) Other associations (neurological, skeletal, endocrine, neoplastic, visceral, and vascular)

B. State the classification of neurofibromatosis (NF1 through NF8), and explain how the zones of the disease relate to the type of NF.

C. Explain why genetic counselling is a key component of management, and outline all the elements of the management plan.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Neurofibromatosis (Von Recklinghausen's disease) is an autosomal disorder with complete penetrance and variable expressivity, characterised by multiple café au lait macules, axillary freckling (Crowe's sign), multiple neurofibromas, and pigmented iris hamartoma (Lisch nodules).

A(ii)
- Café au lait macules: at least 5 lesions, 0.5 cm in diameter; present at birth or soon after; pathognomonic of NF when found with axillary freckling (Crowe's sign).
- Neurofibroma: tumours of Schwann cell origin; can be molluscioid or plexiform; appear in late childhood or early adolescence; found anywhere except palms and soles.
- Lisch nodules: iris hamartomas found in 94% of patients with NF.

A(iii) Other associations: neurological, skeletal, endocrine, neoplastic, visceral, and vascular abnormalities.

B. Classification:
- NF1: family history, café au lait spots, Crowe's sign, Lisch nodules, and neurofibromas
- NF2: central (bilateral acoustic neuroma)
- NF3: mixed pattern
- NF4: neurofibromas and café au lait spots ± family history
- NF5: segmental, no family history, no Lisch nodules
- NF6: multiple café au lait spots, no neuroma
- NF7: late onset after 30 years
- NF8: does not fit into the above
The type depends on which features predominate and their distribution.

C. Genetic counselling is essential because NF is an autosomal disorder with complete penetrance and variable expressivity, meaning offspring are at risk of inheriting the condition.
Management plan: thorough evaluation; close follow-up; look out for associated complications; surgical removal (of neurofibromas as needed); genetic counselling.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents with a whitish pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in the left eye noticed by his mother. His father had the same condition in one eye as a child. On examination there is strabismus.
(i) What is the spot diagnosis and what is the significance of the family history in determining the likely type — unilateral or bilateral?
(ii) State ALL the predisposing/genetic factors and describe the pathology including sites of metastasis.
(iii) Describe the full pathophysiology from the genetic mutation to tumour development.
(iv) Outline the complete management, specifying how treatment choice differs between early and advanced stage disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Retinoblastoma.
- Leukocoria (cat-eye reflex or leucocoria) is an early feature of retinoblastoma.
- 2/3 of cases are unilateral; 10–20% of these unilateral cases are inherited in autosomal dominant fashion.
- 1/3 of cases are bilateral and almost all are inherited in autosomal dominant fashion.
- Family history of the condition in the father strongly suggests an inherited (autosomal dominant) form; bilateral disease is likely if inherited.
(ii) Predisposing/genetic factors and pathology:
- Arises from mutation or deletion of chromosome 13.
- Autosomal dominant inheritance for the bilateral/inherited form.
- Incidence: age 1–3 years.
Pathology and metastasis:
- Malignant tumour arising from the retina.
- Metastasizes to: Brain, Orbits, Liver, Bones, Face, Lung, Lymph nodes, Bone marrow.
(iii) Pathophysiology:
- Mutation or deletion of chromosome 13 underlies tumour development.
- This leads to a malignant tumour arising from the retina.
- The tumour may grow to protrude from the eye and cause strabismus, proptosis (in late cases), and mass effect.
- Metastatic spread occurs haematogenously to the sites listed above.
(iv) Management:
Earlier stage:
- Laser therapy (photocoagulation).
- Cryotherapy: the use of cold to freeze.
Advanced stage:
- Chemotherapy.
- Radiotherapy: external beam is done here; it causes secondary orbit tumour.
Note: In Ibadan, surgery (Enucleation) is done for most cases (with radiotherapy).

questions.question:
A. Describe the classification of severity of pneumonia in children, using respiratory rate thresholds and clinical signs:
(i) Non-severe pneumonia — criteria by age group
(ii) Severe pneumonia — additional signs required
(iii) Very severe pneumonia — features

B. Explain the clinical and physiological basis of each of the following physical signs encountered in pneumonia:
(i) Grunting
(ii) Flaring alae nasi
(iii) Intercostal indrawing
(iv) Lower chest wall indrawing

C. Using the physical signs table, describe all the physical signs of lobar consolidation on examination of the chest (chest deformity, chest movement, mediastinal shift, vocal fremitus, percussion, breath sounds, added sounds, and vocal resonance).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Non-severe pneumonia: cough or difficult breathing and fast breathing — age <2 months: >60 breaths/min; age 2 up to 12 months: >50 breaths/min; age 1 up to 5 years: >40 breaths/min.

A(ii) Severe pneumonia: cough or difficult breathing plus at least one of — lower chest wall indrawing; nasal flaring; grunting (in young infants).

A(iii) Very severe pneumonia: cough or difficult breathing plus at least one of — central cyanosis; inability to breastfeed or drink, or vomiting everything; convulsions, lethargy, or unconsciousness; severe respiratory distress.

B(i) Grunting: an expiratory sound, usually low-pitched with musical qualities. In older children it is frequently a sign of chest pain in pneumonia with pleuritis, or of pneumonia when many alveoli are affected. Also seen in neonatal RDS and pulmonary oedema.

B(ii) Flaring alae nasi: widening of nostrils; occurs in pneumonia complicated by pleuritis.

B(iii) Intercostal indrawing: retraction of soft tissue between the ribs during inspiration; it is a sign of hyperinflation and a flattened diaphragm due to small airway obstruction.

B(iv) Lower chest wall indrawing: inward movement of the lower chest wall during inspiration; occurs when intrathoracic pressure is lowered in bronchial asthma, bronchiolitis, and laryngotracheobronchitis — these cause airway obstruction and reduce intrathoracic pressure.

C. Lobar consolidation — Chest deformity: none. Chest movement: diminished or absent. Mediastinal shift: none. Vocal fremitus: increased. Percussion note: dull. Breath sounds: bronchial. Added sounds: crepitations (crackles). Vocal resonance: increased — often with whispering pectoriloquy and aegophony.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross pathophysiology of distributive shock and obstructive shock:
A(i) Distributive shock — haemodynamics, maldistribution mechanism, causes (sepsis, spinal cord injury, anaphylaxis, drug intoxication), and why it is the opposite of hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock in terms of CO and SVR
A(ii) Obstructive shock — mechanism, causes (pericardial tamponade, tension pneumothorax, critical coarctation, aortic stenosis, hypoplastic left heart), and management approach including the role of prostaglandin E in neonates with ductal-dependent lesions

B. Explain why distributive and obstructive shock can initially present identically to hypovolemic shock, and how to distinguish them after the initial fluid challenge.

C. State how metabolic acidosis develops in any type of shock, and explain how sodium bicarbonate, glucose management, and calcium relate to cardiovascular function in the shocked child.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Distributive shock: high CO and low SVR — the opposite of hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock. Mechanism: maldistribution of blood flow causing inadequate tissue perfusion; due to release of endotoxin, vasoactive substances, complement cascade activation, and microcirculation thrombosis. Early septic shock is the most common form.
Causes: anaphylaxis, anaphylactoid reactions, spinal cord injury/spinal shock, head injury, early sepsis, drug intoxication (barbiturates, phenothiazines, antihypertensives).
Management: goal is to maintain intravascular volume and minimise interstitial fluid (primary problem is decrease in SVR); use crystalloid initially; can give up to 40 ml/kg without monitoring CVP; vasoactive/cardiotonic agents often necessary; treat the cause (e.g., antimicrobial therapy).

A(ii) Obstructive shock: low CO secondary to physical obstruction to flow; compensatory increased SVR. Causes: pericardial tamponade, tension pneumothorax, critical coarctation of the aorta, aortic stenosis, hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
Management: initial fluid challenge; treat the cause (pericardial drain, chest tube, surgical intervention); if the patient is a neonate with a ductal-dependent lesion, give prostaglandin E (PGE); further evaluation, invasive monitoring, pharmacologic therapy, appropriate consultations.

B. Initial presentation of both distributive and obstructive shock can be identical to hypovolemic shock (all three show signs of low cardiac output). After initial fluid challenge: hypovolemic shock responds well to fluid. Obstructive shock: no improvement or worsening after volume → treat the obstructive cause. Distributive shock: may improve initially but requires vasoactive agents if SVR remains low. Cardiogenic shock: if no improvement or worsens after giving volume → suspect cardiogenic shock.

C. Metabolic acidosis in shock: develops secondary to tissue hypoperfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid accumulation. Profound acidosis depresses myocardial contractility and impairs effectiveness of catecholamines. Treatment: fluid administration and controlled ventilation.
Sodium bicarbonate: dose 1–2 mEq/kg or ½ correction = 0.3 × weight × base deficit; risks include hyperosmolarity, hypocalcaemia, hypernatraemia, left-ward shift of oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.
Glucose: hypoglycaemia can lead to CNS damage and is needed for proper cardiovascular function; in neonates replace with 10% dextrose; in children with 25% glucose.
Calcium: important for cardiac function and for the pressor effect of catecholamines.

questions.question:
A. Describe the complete history of a child presenting with suspected heart disease, under the following headings:
A(i) Onset and duration — how age at presentation guides the differentiation between congenital and acquired heart disease, with examples of exceptions in each direction
A(ii) Key symptoms to elicit — list all symptoms, explain the mechanism for each, and state what each symptom indicates

B. Describe the specific history components:
B(i) Pregnancy and birth history — what to ask about and the specific congenital heart disease each risk factor is associated with
B(ii) Family and social history — what factors increase the risk of specific heart diseases
B(iii) Past medical and neonatal history — what specific questions to ask and their significance in the context of different heart conditions
questions.answerText:
A(i) Onset and duration:
- For younger children (<5 years): think of congenital causes
- For older children (>5 years): think of acquired heart disease first
Exceptions to this rule:
Congenital heart diseases that are asymptomatic in early life and present in the 2nd or 3rd decade:
- Small VSD (often closes spontaneously)
- Coarctation of the aorta — commonly presents at 12 years with features of heart failure due to effects on left ventricle
- Atrial Septal Defect — many are asymptomatic in the first decade of life
Acquired heart diseases that can present in infancy (though commoner in older children):
- Rheumatic heart disease (most common acquired HD in developing countries)
- Infective heart disease
- Pericardial effusion

A(ii) Key symptoms and mechanisms:
- Cough — common; from pulmonary congestion
- Breathlessness — common; from pulmonary oedema/congestion
- Cyanosis — bluish discolouration; occurs especially in cyanotic heart disease (right-to-left shunts)
- Failure to thrive/small for gestational age — compromised supply of nutrients in the circulation from reduced cardiac output
- Delayed developmental milestone — occurs in severe heart disease; may be part of a syndrome (e.g. Down syndrome: mental retardation + ASD)
- Convulsions/fainting — seen in obstructive heart disease (e.g. aortic stenosis) and TOF (hypercyanotic spells)
- Stroke — occurs in polycythaemia (hyperviscosity, e.g. in TOF) and infective endocarditis (emboli)
- Pedal/abdominal/facial swelling — indicates right-sided heart failure; in paediatrics, usually both sides are in failure
- Palpitations — mother notices when carrying child to her chest
- Feeding difficulties/sucking difficulty — baby cannot hold breath long enough to suck; points to heart failure
- Excessive sweating — from increased adrenergic activity
- Recurrent chest infections — pointer to chronic heart disease

B(i) Pregnancy/birth history:
- Intrauterine infection (fever/rashes during pregnancy): rubella → PDA, VSD, PS
- Duration of pregnancy (preterm) → PDA
- Teratogenic drugs: thalidomide, cytotoxic, steroids → various CHD
- X-radiation → CHD
- Maternal diabetes mellitus → TGA
- Birth asphyxia (reduced oxygen tension) → PDA (hypoxia is needed to keep ductus open)
- Maternal diabetes mellitus → TGA is commonest

B(ii) Family and social history:
- Low socioeconomic status → risk factor for acute rheumatic fever and endomyocardial fibrosis
- High socioeconomic status (obesity) → hypertension
- Family history of hereditary problems
- CHD is commoner among siblings
- PDA associated with high altitude and birth asphyxia

B(iii) Past medical history:
- Previous history of fever: very important in rheumatic heart disease (ARF precedes RHD)
Neonatal/infancy history — ask about: cough; breathlessness; cyanosis; feeding difficulties; frequent chest infections (pointer to chronic heart disease); birth asphyxia (predisposes to PDA since reduced oxygen tension is needed to close the duct).
Developmental milestones: rubella and other congenital abnormalities are associated with delayed milestones.

questions.question:
A. Describe the clinical features, investigations, diagnosis, and management of cerebral palsy:
A(i) Clinical features: early pointers in the first year of life and features found on physical examination in older children.
A(ii) The role of investigations: state which investigations are recommended, what each detects, and what condition must always be excluded to confirm a diagnosis of CP.
A(iii) Prevention: describe primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.

B. Explain the following statements:
B(i) "The earlier the rehabilitation starts, the better for the child."
B(ii) "A positive family history rules out cerebral palsy, except in rare cases."

C. Describe the pharmacotherapy options for cerebral palsy — the aim of drug treatment, the drugs used, and their limitations.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Clinical features:
Early pointers in the 1st year of life: feeding difficulties; hypotonia (floppy infant); head lag; neonatal seizures; persistence of primitive reflexes (grasp, Moro, sucking); abnormal posturing (spastic grasp, scissoring, tongue thrusting, persistent thumb adduction); hand preference in the 1st year of life (normally develops by 3 years — early preference is abnormal); hypertonia.
Later/physical examination: commonest presentation is delayed developmental milestones (especially motor); disorders of movement (hemiplegic gait — flexion of elbow and wrist, extension of lower limb, circumduction movement); scissoring of lower limbs (most noticeable in diplegia); spasticity; prolonged fisting; tongue thrusting (common in athetoid type); microcephaly (always check head circumference); abnormal hand preference; persistent Moro reflex beyond 4 months; obligate ATNR (very abnormal even in the neonatal period).

A(ii) Investigations:
- Diagnosis is clinical; no specific chemical test required.
- Exclude progressive disorders (degenerative CNS disorders; metabolic disorders) — positive family history rules out CP in most cases; a hereditary progressive condition should be considered.
- G6PD screening: because G6PD deficiency in the mother can cause kernicterus in successive children, producing CP — this is the exception to the family history rule.
- Blood group.
- EEG.
- Skull X-ray: intracranial calcification, skull defects.
- CT scan of cranium: cerebral atrophy, cystic lesions, dysgenesis.
- MRI.
- Chromosomal studies: to rule out Down syndrome and others.
What must always be excluded: progressive CNS disorders (e.g., muscular dystrophy, spinal cord tumour, Werdnig–Hoffman Disease, brain tumours, Down syndrome, peripheral neuropathies, myelomeningocoele).

A(iii) Prevention:
Primary: proper supervision of pregnancy and delivery to prevent severe birth asphyxia — recognition of high-risk pregnancy; referral; improvement in obstetric care; improvement in care of the newborn; proper management of neonatal jaundice.
Secondary: management of the condition (as described above) to minimise disability.
Tertiary: rehabilitation — maximising residual function and quality of life.

B(i) "The earlier the rehabilitation starts, the better for the child": during the period of brain immaturity and active neurodevelopment, early physiotherapy and multidisciplinary intervention can exploit neuroplasticity — the brain's capacity to form new connections and compensate for damaged areas. Early intervention prevents contractures, deformities, and learned disuse, and promotes the acquisition of developmental milestones at a time when the brain retains greatest capacity for reorganisation.

B(ii) "A positive family history rules out cerebral palsy, except in rare cases": CP is caused by a fixed, nonprogressive lesion; it is not an inherited degenerative disease. If a sibling has the same motor disorder, it suggests a hereditary progressive CNS disease rather than CP. The exception: if the mother is G6PD deficient, she may have successive children with neonatal jaundice (hyperbilirubinaemia) → kernicterus → CP; in this rare case, the family history reflects a metabolic (G6PD) cause rather than a genetic progressive neurological condition.

C. Pharmacotherapy in CP:
- Drug treatment is limited.
- Aim: to reduce spasticity when it is very high.
- Drugs: muscle relaxants — disadvantage: they are sedative.
  • Nitrazepam.
  • Dantrolene.
  • Botulinum toxin — injected directly into the spastic muscles; effect is short-acting (recently introduced).
  • IT Baclofen.
  • Benzodiazepines (general).
  • Anticonvulsants: to control seizures where present.
- Limitation: drugs have significant sedative side effects and do not treat the underlying brain lesion; effect of botulinum toxin is short-acting.

(i) Surgical intervention — specifically lobectomy — is indicated because this patient has failed medical treatment and the disease is localised to the left lower lobe. Justification: medical treatment can halt the potentially reversible cylindrical form, but saccular bronchiectasis represents irreversible destruction of structural components of the airway wall and in a localised, well-defined case after failure of medical therapy, surgical resection is appropriate.

(ii) Three types: (a) Cylindrical bronchiectasis (Group I) — dilation is regular, with the airway continuing to have a regular outline. (b) Varicose bronchiectasis (Group II) — dilation is irregular, with areas of dilation and constriction. (c) Saccular bronchiectasis (Group III) — dilation is marked, with destruction of structural components of the airway wall.

(iii) Evaluation investigations: Infection: sputum or BALF for M/C/S; mycobacterial/fungal cultures; viral culture; skin tests (PPD, fungal); serological studies; HIV tests. Immunodeficiency: FBC; quantitative immunoglobulins; IgG subclasses; WBC function (nitroblue tetrazolium dye test, chemotactic assays); total haemolytic complement. Aspiration: barium swallow; extended oesophageal pH monitoring. Ciliary dysfunction: nasal/tracheal epithelium — light and electron microscopy. Cystic fibrosis: sweat test.

(iv) Kartagener syndrome: a triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. The underlying mechanism is a congenital abnormal ciliary function (primary ciliary dyskinesia). Acquired ciliary dysfunction can also occur as a result of infection.

(v) The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ content of sweat are increased throughout the patient's life in cystic fibrosis. A positive sweat test (elevated sweat chloride) confirms the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis as a cause of bronchiectasis in that patient.
questions.question:
A 5-year-old child presents with persistent cough, foul-smelling purulent sputum, fever, and dyspnoea that have been present for 3 months. He is malnourished. On examination there is finger clubbing, dullness to percussion, and bronchial breath sounds localised to the left lower zone. CT scan confirms extensive saccular left lower lobe bronchiectasis. He failed a 12-week course of oral antibiotics.

(i) What is the most appropriate next management step for this patient and the justification?
(ii) Using the classification, name the three types of bronchiectasis and describe the distinguishing pathological feature of each type.
(iii) State the evaluation investigations needed to identify the cause and predisposing factors of bronchiectasis.
(iv) What is Kartagener syndrome, and what is the underlying pathological mechanism?
(v) How does the sweat test help diagnose cystic fibrosis, which is a cause of bronchiectasis?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and age-specific cut-offs:
- Definition: Hb or Haematocrit level lower than age-adjusted reference range; reduced RBC mass that leads to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity that fails to meet the metabolic demands of the body.
- Post-neonatal Hb <11 g/dL.
Age-specific cut-offs:
- 0.5–4 years: <11 g/dL.
- 5–7 years: <11.5 g/dL.
- 8–11 years: <12.0 g/dL.
- 12–14 years: Male <12.5 g/dL; Female <12.0 g/dL.
- Term infant physiologic anaemia: Hb falls to 9–11 g/dl at 2–3 months; preterm: falls to 7–9 g/dl by 3–6 weeks.

A(ii) Three pathogenic mechanisms:
1. Reduced red cell production:
- Bone marrow failure: aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 infection), Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.
- Anaemia of chronic disorders and renal disease (e.g. osteomyelitis, SLE, Rheumatoid arthritis).
- Impaired erythropoietin production: chronic renal failure, hypothyroidism, severe PEM.
- Defect in red cell maturation: nutritional (folate, vit B12, Iron), sideroblastic anaemias, maturational arrest, congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias.
- Other microcytic anaemias: Pb poisoning (basophilic stippling and ↑blood lead).
2. Increased red cell destruction (Extracellular):
- Mechanical injuries: HUS, cardiac valvular defects.
- Antibodies: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
- Infections: malaria.
- Drugs, toxins; Thermal injuries — severe burns.
Intracellular causes:
- Membrane defects: hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis.
- Enzyme defects: G-6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency.
- Haemoglobinopathies: SCD, Thalassaemias.
- Porphyrias; Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
3. Blood loss: Gastrointestinal, pulmonary, intracranial; Bleeding disorders e.g. haemophilia.

B(i) Compensatory mechanisms:
- Increased cardiac output (HR and stroke volume).
- Shunting of blood to vital organs.
- Increased RBC 2,3-DPG to enhance oxygen delivery.
- Few clinical disturbances until Hb <7–8 g/dl because of these compensatory mechanisms; chronic anaemia allows body to adjust and ameliorate effects; acute anaemia — symptoms are pronounced.
Physical signs: Tachycardia, Tachypnoea, Congestive cardiac failure (cardiomegaly, tender hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm), Splenomegaly (haemolytic anaemias), Stigmata of SCD (bossing of skull, habitus), Dysmorphic features.

B(ii) Investigation pathway:
Red cell indices: MCV, MCH, RDW (increased in anisocytosis).
Microcytic hypochromic: iron deficiency, chronic inflammation, thalassaemias, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anaemia.
Macrocytic: Vit B12 deficiency, folic acid deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism, accelerated erythropoiesis, hypoplastic/aplastic anaemia.
Red cell morphology: Schistocytes or fragmented RBC (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia); Spherocytes; Ghost or bite cells (G6PD deficiency); Sickle-shaped cells (SCD); Target cells (HbS, C); Stippled RBC (Pb poisoning); Increased polychromasia (reticulocytosis).
Reticulocyte count: normal 0.5–1.5%; indicates active erythropoiesis.
Specific tests:
- Blood film for malaria parasite.
- Haemoglobin electrophoresis (haemoglobinopathies).
- Enzyme assays: G6PD, pyruvate kinase.
- Serum bilirubin, LDH (haemolytic anaemia).
- Coombs' test (autoimmune haemolytic anaemia).
- Osmotic fragility test (spherocytosis).
- Stool exam: occult blood, parasites e.g. hookworm.
- Bone marrow exam; Serum Iron, TIBC, Ferritin; Folate, Vitamin B12; Ham's test (PNH); Thyroxine (T4), TSH.
questions.question:
Describe childhood anaemia comprehensively under the following headings:
A(i) Define anaemia in childhood with age-specific cut-off values for Haemoglobin.
A(ii) Describe the three pathogenic mechanisms of anaemia with all the specific causes under each mechanism.
B(i) Describe the compensatory physiological mechanisms that occur in anaemia and explain why clinical features may be absent until Hb falls below a critical level.
B(ii) Describe the investigation pathway for anaemia, covering red cell indices, morphology, and specific tests for haemolytic versus nutritional anaemia.

A 7-year-old child presents with a 6-week history of a scaly, itchy patch on the scalp with a boggy, tender swelling at the centre. He has siblings with similar scalp patches.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis? State the genera of dermatophytes and their biological sources.
(ii) Describe the full range of clinical presentations of dermatophyte infections (tinea types).
(iii) Describe the management — systemic and topical — and state what topical therapy alone can and cannot achieve.
(iv) State the additional management required for a Kerion, and explain why the other siblings must also be examined.
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Tinea Capitis with Kerion formation. Dermatophytes are fungi capable of infecting or colonising keratinised tissue such as nails, hair, and stratum corneum; they have low mortality but high morbidity and are very common in the tropics.
Genera: Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton.
Biological sources: anthropophilic (humans), zoophilic (animals), and geophilic (soil).

(ii) Clinical presentations (tinea types): Tinea capitis (scalp); Tinea corporis (body); Tinea manum (hand); Tinea incognito; ID reaction.

(iii) Management:
Systemic antifungals for Tinea capitis: Griseofulvin (fulcin), itraconazole.
Topical therapy: limits spread but does not cure the infection. Topical therapy alone is insufficient for Tinea capitis and must be combined with systemic antifungals.

(iv) Kerion requires a short course of steroids in addition to systemic antifungals.
Siblings must also be examined because dermatophytes are transmitted between humans (anthropophilic sources) and spread through close contact; examining siblings allows early detection and treatment to prevent further spread within the household.

A(i) Inspection — General:
- Features of acute or chronic illness; nutritional status
- Dysmorphic features (e.g. Down facies: slanting epicanthic fold, flat nasal bridge, flat occiput); Congenital rubella syndrome (cleft lip/palate, polydactyly/syndactyly, talipes)
- Skin colour: pink or blue (central cyanosis)
- Digital clubbing; pedal oedema; dyspnoea
Specific cardiovascular inspection:
- Praecordial bulge — due to cardiomegaly, indicates chronicity (likely congenital)
- Chest symmetry; abnormal pulsations in the neck
- JVP: not sensitive in children <2 years because of short neck; important in older children; indicates right-sided heart failure

A(ii) Palpation:
Pulse rate: neonates — upper limit 160 bpm; <100 = bradycardia.
Rhythm: regularly irregular (e.g. sinus arrhythmia, often normal in children); irregularly irregular (common cause: atrial fibrillation).
Always palpate peripheral pulses (radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis) to detect coarctation of the aorta.
Apex beat: normal location — 4th or 5th left intercostal space medial to mid-clavicular line. Displaced downward and outward suggests enlargement (usually dilatation). Character: heaving (LVH); tapping (suggests mitral stenosis).
Left parasternal heave: heaving there suggests RVH.
Thrills (palpable murmur): Systolic at apex — mitral regurgitation; at aortic area — aortic stenosis. Diastolic at apex — mitral stenosis. At lower left parasternal — VSD.

B(i) Bounding/collapsing pulse (hyperdynamic circulation):
Cardiac causes: PDA, aortic incompetence
Non-cardiac causes: fever, chronic anaemia
Small volume pulse:
Cardiac causes: aortic stenosis, mitral stenosis, pericardial effusion
Non-cardiac: shock from any cause

B(ii) Blood pressure: normal difference between upper and lower limbs should be ≤20 mmHg. If >20 mmHg, coarctation of the aorta is suggested. In infants with coarctation: a 20 mmHg systolic pressure difference between upper and lower limbs is the normal cut-off (even a small difference can be significant in neonates). Blood pressure is usually assessed last in children because of the discomfort it causes.

B(iii) Percussion has little value in children. Auscultation is organised by four areas:
- Area 1 (Right upper sternal edge): Aortic valve area
- Area 2 (Left upper sternal edge): Pulmonary valve area
- Area 3 (Left lower sternal edge): Tricuspid valve area
- Area 4 (Apex): Mitral valve area
Also auscultate intervening spaces between the valve areas.
questions.question:
A. Describe the physical examination of the cardiovascular system in a child, covering:
A(i) Inspection — all the general and specific cardiovascular findings to look for on inspection, including jugular venous pressure (JVP) and praecordial findings
A(ii) Palpation — pulse characteristics (rate, rhythm, volume with causes for each abnormality), apex beat location and character, left parasternal heave, and thrills

B. Describe:
B(i) The types of pulse volume abnormality — bounding and small volume — with all cardiac and non-cardiac causes of each
B(ii) Blood pressure assessment in children with heart disease — what a disparity between upper and lower limb pressures signifies and the normal versus abnormal threshold
B(iii) Explain why percussion has little value in children, and how auscultation is organised — naming the four auscultatory areas and what each corresponds to

A. Describe the gross anatomy and pathology of the valves in Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) under the following headings:
A(i) State the types of valvular lesion that occur in RHD, naming the commonest lesion in paediatrics and the lesion most likely to be congenital rather than rheumatic in children
A(ii) List the five symptoms and seven physical signs described for chronic RHD
A(iii) Describe the ECG findings and CXR findings in chronic RHD

B. Explain the mechanism by which chronic mitral valve disease in RHD leads to:
B(i) A loud P2 on auscultation
B(ii) Left ventricular failure followed by right ventricular failure
B(iii) State how RHD is prevented at the primary and secondary levels, including drugs and doses
questions.answerText:
A(i) Types of valvular lesion in RHD:
1. Mitral incompetence — commonest lesion in paediatrics
2. Mitral stenosis — patient is usually older (takes time to develop)
3. Aortic incompetence
4. Aortic stenosis — not common in children; more likely to be congenital in children and rheumatic in adults
The faulty valves heal by fibrosis.

A(ii) Symptoms (five):
1. Breathlessness
2. Cough
3. Palpitations
4. Easy fatiguability
5. Pedal swelling (features iv and v indicate decompensation)

Physical signs (seven):
1. Active praecordium (at apex)
2. Increased JVP
3. ± Loud P2 (due to backflow of blood from left atrium into lungs)
4. Apical pansystolic murmur loudest at apex, radiating to the axilla (mitral incompetence)
5. ± Diastolic murmur at the apex (mitral stenosis)
6. ± Diastolic murmur in aortic area with collapsing pulse (aortic incompetence)
7. Signs of heart failure (tender hepatomegaly)

A(iii) ECG findings:
- Evidence of left atrial hypertrophy/enlargement: broad, flat (P mitrale/notched) or biphasic P wave
- Increased PR interval
- Left ventricular hypertrophy
- ± Right ventricular hypertrophy (if long-standing hypertension)
CXR findings:
- Cardiomegaly
- Hump on left border/mitralised left heart border
- Splaying of the carina
- Double density at the right heart border
- Pulmonary congestion

B(i) Loud P2 mechanism: Backflow of blood from the incompetent mitral valve causes left atrial hypertension, which raises pulmonary venous and pulmonary arterial pressures. Pulmonary hypertension causes a loud pulmonary component of S2 (P2).

B(ii) Left then right failure: Mitral incompetence causes volume overload of the left atrium and left ventricle first, leading to left ventricular failure (breathlessness, pulmonary congestion). The resulting pulmonary hypertension then increases right ventricular afterload, eventually causing right ventricular failure (elevated JVP, tender hepatomegaly, pedal swelling).

B(iii) Prevention:
Primary (prevention of ARF):
- Recognise sore throat and treat with procaine penicillin (most sore throats are viral)
- Health education
Secondary (prevention of recurrence):
- Benzathine penicillin/erythromycin (monthly benzathine penicillin dose: 1.2 mega units/month; erythromycin: 125–250 mg twice daily as alternative)
- Health education

(i) Diagnosis: Neonatal Tetanus. Causative organism: Clostridium tetani, a Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium. The disease is caused by the exotoxin Tetanospasmin, a potent neurotoxin.

(ii) Risk factors:
- Home delivery
- Unhygienic cutting of the cord
- Contamination of umbilical stump
- No maternal immunisation

(iii) Resuscitation and supportive therapy:
- Ensure adequate hydration and calories
- Skilled nursing care: regular turning, airway suctioning, maintain spasm chart
- Nurse in a quiet, dark environment
- Oxygen supplementation when necessary
- Pyridoxine 100 mg three times daily
- Physiotherapy during recovery

(iv) Definitive management:
Eradication of organism: Wound debridement (cord care); IM Procaine Penicillin 25,000–30,000 IU/kg daily for 10 days OR IV Metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg/dose 8-hourly; treat concurrent sepsis with IV Amikacin or IV Cefuroxime.
Neutralisation of toxin: IM Human Tetanus Immunoglobulin — neonates 500 U; OR IM Equine ATS 10,000–20,000 IU.
Control of spasms (oral by NGT): Diazepam 1–2 mg/kg/dose 6-hourly; Phenobarbitone 4–6 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses; Chlorpromazine 5–10 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses; IM Paraldehyde 0.3 mg/kg or 1 ml/year (max 5 ml) for breakthrough spasms; IV Diazepam infusion; therapeutic paralysis with non-depolarising NM blocker plus mechanical ventilation for unresponsive spasms.
Active immunisation: 0.5 ml tetanus toxoid stat; complete course after discharge.
questions.question:
A 7-day-old neonate is brought to the emergency ward with a 2-day history of inability to open the mouth, spasms, and apnoea. He was delivered at home and the umbilical cord was cut with a non-sterile blade. His mother received no antenatal care.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the causative organism and its toxin?
(ii) State the embryologic/pathologic basis of why this neonate is at risk, listing all the risk factors given in the lecture.
(iii) Outline the initial resuscitation priorities and supportive care measures.
(iv) Detail the definitive management under each principle: eradication of organism, neutralisation of toxin, control of spasms, and active immunisation of the patient.

questions.answerText:
(i) Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS).

(ii) Predisposing factors: post-term pregnancy (meconium is rarely found in amniotic fluid prior to 34 weeks GA; MAS occurs in term and post-term infants); fetal distress (hypoxic stress in utero promotes passage of meconium); placental insufficiency; maternal hypertension/pre-eclampsia; oligohydramnios; maternal drug abuse (tobacco, cocaine); prolonged rupture of membranes; poor progress in labour.

(iii) Three mechanisms: (a) Airway obstruction — partial obstruction causes air trapping and hyperdistension of alveoli, which may rupture → pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, pneumopericardium (air block syndrome); complete obstruction → atelectasis → ventilation-perfusion mismatch. (b) Surfactant dysfunction — free fatty acids (palmitic, stearic, oleic acids) in meconium have higher surface tension than surfactant and strip it from the alveolar surface → diffuse atelectasis. (c) Chemical pneumonitis — enzymes, bile salts, and fats in meconium irritate the airway and parenchyma → diffuse pneumonia; many infants have pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) from chronic in utero stress and thickening of pulmonary vessels.

(iv) Investigations: Arterial blood gases — expected: respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, ↑pCO2, ↓pO2). Pulse oximetry — continuous oxygen saturation monitoring. Serum E&U — SIADH and acute renal failure are frequent complications of perinatal stress. FBC — neutropenia/neutrophilia may indicate bacterial infection; ↓platelets ↑risk of haemorrhage. CXR — expected: patchy infiltration, coarse streaking of both lung fields, increased AP diameter, flattened diaphragm, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax. Blood culture. Blood glucose. ECHO — assess cardiac structure, severity of pulmonary hypertension, right-to-left shunting.

(v) Medical care: Prevention (paramount). If meconium detected: amnioinfusion with warm saline to dilute meconium. At delivery: careful suctioning of posterior pharynx; if meconium present and infant not vigorous — intubate and suction. Optimal thermal environment; minimal handling; oxygen (headbox, intranasal catheter); IPPV; mechanical ventilation; surfactant (thought to reduce air leaks); NPO; IVF 10% dextrose/water on day 1, electrolytes added thereafter; antibiotics; correct acidosis. Surgical care: pneumothorax → pleural chest tube connected to underwater drain.
questions.question:
A 10-day-old neonate born to a 30-year-old unbooked mother at 44 weeks gestation via emergency Caesarean section for post-term pregnancy, fetal distress, and poor progress in labour presents with cyanosis, grunting, alar flaring, subcostal recession, tachypnoea (RR 98 cpm), and barrel chest. Liquor at delivery was stale meconium-stained and foul-smelling. Apgar scores were 4 at 1 minute, 7 at 5 minutes, and 9 at 10 minutes.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the factors in the maternal history and delivery that predisposed to this condition.
(iii) Describe the three mechanisms by which aspirated meconium produces respiratory compromise.
(iv) List the investigations indicated and interpret what findings are expected.
(v) Outline medical management including surgical care for complications.

Describe the phases, laboratory confirmation, and treatment of malaria in pregnancy and in children under five, using content, and explain the specific complications seen in each group.
A(i) Why pregnant women (especially primigravidae) are at increased risk of severe malaria
A(ii) How malaria in pregnancy causes maternal anaemia, low birth weight, and infant mortality
B(i) How malaria can affect the fetus: congenital/perinatal malaria features and timing of first signs
B(ii) Children under 5 in Nigeria: burden of malaria mortality, factors that influence susceptibility, and host protective factors
C(i) Treatment of uncomplicated malaria in children: ACTs available, weight-based dosing for Artemether-Lumefantrine
C(ii) Aims of treatment for uncomplicated versus severe malaria and what treatments are NOT recommended in severe malaria
questions.answerText:
A(i) Why pregnant women are at increased risk:
- Pregnancy, especially primigravidae and in 2nd half of pregnancy, is a predisposing factor for complications of P. falciparum malaria
- Pregnancy is listed among predisposing factors alongside children <5 years, immunosuppressed and immunocompromised patients, and post-splenectomy patients
- Human factors that affect transmission include pregnancy status
A(ii) Malaria in pregnancy:
- Up to 15% maternal anaemia
- 35% of preventable low birth weight
- Leads to infant mortality
- Congenital malaria causes spontaneous abortion, miscarriage, stillbirth and neonatal death
B(i) Congenital/perinatal malaria:
- Malaria may rarely be prenatally or perinatally acquired
- Congenital malaria causes spontaneous abortion, miscarriage, stillbirth and neonatal death
- First sign or symptom usually about 2 weeks (10-30 days) but may occur as early as 14 hours
- Signs and symptoms are non-specific: may include fever, restlessness, jaundice, poor feeding, cyanosis, hepatosplenomegaly, apnoea
B(ii) Children under 5 in Nigeria:
- 86% of malaria victims worldwide are children less than 5 years
- 90% of all malaria mortality is in children under 5 years
- Nigeria, DRC, Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Côte d'Ivoire and Mali account for 60% of deaths due to malaria
- Factors influencing susceptibility: age (children more susceptible); endemicity (adults and older children in endemic areas are less susceptible); Duffy blood group antigen alleles
- Protective host factors: sickle cell trait (heterozygous state); haemoglobin F also has protective effects against severe malaria
C(i) Treatment of uncomplicated malaria in children (Artemether-Lumefantrine dosing):
- Each tablet contains 20 mg artemether and 120 mg lumefantrine
- 5-<15 kg: 1 tab twice daily x 3 days
- 15-<25 kg: 2 tabs twice daily x 3 days
- 25-<35 kg: 3 tabs twice daily x 3 days
- >35 kg: 4 tabs twice daily x 3 days
- Important: the 6 doses must be taken by the patient
- If patient vomits within 30 minutes, repeat dose; persistent vomiting → consider severe malaria
C(ii) Aims of treatment and what NOT to use in severe malaria:
- Uncomplicated malaria treatment aims: to cure the infection; to prevent the emergence of resistance to antimalarials; to prevent the spread of resistance to antimalarials
- Severe malaria treatment aims: to prevent death; to prevent recrudescence; avoidance of minor adverse effects; to prevent neurological deficit (cerebral malaria); to save mother's life in severe malaria in pregnancy
- Treatments NOT recommended in severe malaria: corticosteroids and other anti-inflammatory agents; agents used for cerebral oedema (e.g. urea); adrenaline; heparin

questions.question:
A 15-month-old child is admitted with sudden-onset haematemesis and melaena. On examination he is pale, tachycardic (HR 148 bpm), and hypotensive (BP 70/40 mmHg). The abdomen reveals splenomegaly and prominent dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus. History notes he had omphalitis treated at birth. His INR is 2.02 and platelet count is 62,000/mm³. Serum ALP is 505 U/L and ALT is 65 U/L.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the anatomical vascular structure most likely involved.
(ii) What specific sign do the dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus represent, and what does the biochemical pattern of markedly elevated ALP with only mildly elevated ALT indicate?
(iii) Name the endoscopic therapeutic procedure that is first-line for the active bleeding, and identify the primary structure at risk from this intervention if performed in the oesophagus.
(iv) Identify the neonatal event that most likely caused the underlying vascular pathology, and describe the Doppler ultrasound finding that would confirm the chronic nature of this vascular change.
(v) State the haemodynamic parameters most critical to monitor in this acute phase, and identify two immediate pharmacological measures to reduce portal pressure.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is variceal haemorrhage from portal hypertension. The most likely anatomical vascular structure involved is the oesophageal or gastric varices, which are portosystemic collaterals formed under elevated portal pressure (defined as portal pressure above 10–12 mmHg).
(ii) The dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus represent caput medusa — portosystemic collaterals via umbilical vein shunts — and is a pathognomonic sign of portal hypertension. The biochemical pattern of markedly elevated ALP (505 U/L) with only mildly elevated ALT (65 U/L) indicates a predominantly cholestatic pattern, suggesting biliary obstruction or cholestatic liver disease rather than hepatocellular injury.
(iii) Endoscopic variceal band ligation or endoscopic sclerotherapy is first-line. In the oesophagus, the primary structure at risk from inadvertent deep injection or perforation during sclerotherapy is the oesophageal wall and the surrounding mediastinal structures, with risk of oesophageal perforation and mediastinitis.
(iv) Omphalitis (umbilical infection) at birth most likely caused portal vein thrombosis, a recognised cause of extrahepatic portal hypertension. On Doppler ultrasound, cavernous transformation of the portal vein — a network of collateral venous channels (multiple small tortuous vessels replacing the normal portal vein structure) developing around a chronically thrombosed portal vein — would confirm the chronic nature of this vascular pathology.
(v) Heart rate, blood pressure, and haematocrit are the most critical parameters to monitor in active variceal haemorrhage, as tachycardia and hypotension signal haemodynamic compromise requiring urgent transfusion. Pharmacological measures to reduce portal pressure include octreotide infusion (which reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure) and vasopressin analogues; surgical portosystemic shunt is not first-line.

questions.question:
Describe the pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and management of pertussis under the following headings, explain why infants under 3 months present differently, and distinguish pertussis from other causes of chronic cough in children.
A(i) Causative organism, epidemiology, and mode of transmission
A(ii) Pathogenesis of pertussis toxin effects on the respiratory epithelium and immune system
B(i) Three clinical phases: features, timing, and complications
B(ii) Why infants <3 months do not produce the characteristic whoop, and what they present with instead
C(i) Diagnosis: clinical case definition, laboratory methods and media used
C(ii) Management goals, antibiotic treatment, contact prophylaxis, and prevention
questions.answerText:
A(i) Organism, epidemiology, transmission:
- Bordetella pertussis, B. parapertussis: small gram negative pleomorphic coccobacillus
- Mode of spread: droplets
- Peak incidence between July and October
- Peak age: 1-5 years, but also affects infants and older people
- Source: adults with subclinical infection
- Attack rate almost 100%
- Risk factors: overcrowding, poor ventilation, poor vaccine coverage
- Vaccination/infection does not confer lifelong immunity; no chronic carrier state
- Incubation period: 3-12 days
A(ii) Pathogenesis of pertussis toxin:
- Pertussis toxin causes: epithelial damage; histamine sensitivity; insulin secretion; leucocyte dysfunction
B(i) Three clinical phases:
1. Catarrhal phase (2 weeks): low grade fever, congestion, rhinorrhoea, sneezing, lacrimation, conjunctival suffusion
2. Paroxysmal phase (2-6 weeks): initial dry cough, irritative and intermittent; evolves into bouts of intense non-staccato cough followed by a whoop; associated symptoms: subconjunctival haemorrhage, petechiae, seizures from intracranial bleeds/hypoxia
3. Convalescent phase (2-4 weeks): recovery begins; immunization shortens all stages
Complications: pneumonia; otitis media; subconjunctival, intracranial, subdural, pulmonary haemorrhage; epistaxis; apnoea; encephalopathy; hernias; dehydration; malnutrition; urinary incontinence
B(ii) Infants <3 months:
- No whoop in infants <3 months (gasp, cyanosis, apnoea, bulging red eyes) instead of the characteristic whoop
- Because their small airways and insufficient muscular force do not generate the inspiratory force needed to produce a whoop; they present with gasp, cyanosis, and apnoea which are potentially life-threatening
C(i) Diagnosis:
- Mostly clinical
- Case definition: cough >14 days + 1 of (paroxysms, whoop, post-tussive vomiting)
- Lymphocyte leucocytosis (15,000-100,000/cc) in late catarrhal or early paroxysmal phase
- CXR is not pathognomonic
- Deep nasopharyngeal aspirate for MCS: Regan-Lowe transport medium; culture on Regan-Lowe Charcoal agar + 10% horse blood; Stainer-Scholte media + cyclodextrin
- PCR; serology – ELISA; direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing
C(ii) Management:
- Goals: limit spread, prevent/treat complications, maximize nutrition and rest to aid recovery without sequelae
- Erythromycin 40-50 mg/kg/day for patient and close contacts
- Close contacts <7 years: give booster dose of vaccine
- Prevention: immunization

(i) Acute bronchiolitis.

(ii) Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) – mainly; Parainfluenza virus types 1, 2, and 3; Adenovirus; Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

(iii) Oedema of the bronchiolar mucosa plus accumulation of mucus and cellular debris plus constriction of the muscles of the bronchiolar wall leads to reduction in the size of the lumen of the bronchioles. Resistance to airflow increases, more marked at expiration. If obstruction is complete → atelectasis. If incomplete → air trapping and hyperinflation → impairment of normal gaseous exchange at alveolar level → hypoxaemia early and hypercapnia later. Downward displacement of the diaphragm from hyperinflation makes the liver and spleen palpable.

(iv) Hospitalisation: sustained SpO2 below 92% in room air; age less than six months; cannot maintain oral hydration; markedly elevated respiratory rate; history of chronic cardiorespiratory disease. ICU referral: desaturation in 40% O2 (3–4 l/min O2); central cyanosis; extra-pulmonary symptoms; apnoea or acidosis. Mechanical ventilation if: PaO2 <60 mmHg, PaCO2 >45 mmHg, pH less than 7.25.

(v) Mainstays: fluid replacement (infants mildly dehydrated from decreased intake and increased losses); oxygen supplementation (hypoxaemia is the most common laboratory abnormality). Bronchodilators: controversial; a trial of albuterol/salbutamol (0.15 mg/kg/dose) is reasonable and clinical response assessed every 5–10 minutes. Nebulisation with racemic epinephrine is superior to salbutamol. Antibiotics, ribavirin (now found not useful; palivizumab preferred for prevention), and ipratropium bromide have not been shown to influence the course of bronchiolitis.
questions.question:
A 4-month-old male infant presents in the rainy season with a 3-day history of coryza and low-grade fever, followed by cough, fast breathing, and refusal of feeds. On examination he has nasal flaring, subcostal retractions, prolonged expiration, fine crepitations, diffuse wheezing, and a hyper-resonant percussion note. The liver and spleen are palpable.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the causative agents responsible for this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology that produces the clinical picture, including the mechanism of air trapping and impairment of gaseous exchange.
(iv) State the indications for hospitalisation and the indications for paediatric intensive care referral.
(v) Outline the mainstays of therapy and the role of bronchodilators.

On the paediatric ward, a house officer auscultates a 6-year-old child and notes a murmur. The mother says the child was diagnosed with a heart problem at birth but has been relatively well. Examination reveals the child is acyanotic, has a mildly active praecordium, and there is a to-and-fro (continuous) murmur heard maximally in the left infraclavicular area (under the left clavicle), with bounding pulses in all four limbs. Chest X-ray shows increased pulmonary vascular markings. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
