(i) What is the spot diagnosis, and state the anatomical structure involved.
(ii) Explain why this lesion produces a continuous murmur — describe the pressure relationship between the two vessels throughout the cardiac cycle.
(iii) State three factors that predispose to persistent patency of this structure after birth.
(iv) Describe the complete pathophysiological consequence of a large defect of this type on both the pulmonary and systemic circulation (using the same framework as for VSD).
(v) State the pharmacological treatment for closure and the surgical option if medical closure fails. Explain why normal saline — and not glucose — is used during balloon valvuloplasty in pulmonary stenosis, making the general principle about replacement fluids explicit.
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).
Anatomical structure involved: The ductus arteriosus — a normal fetal structure that connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta (persisting patent after birth instead of closing within 48 hours).

(ii) Continuous murmur — pressure relationship:
PDA produces a continuous (to-and-fro/machinery) murmur because the pressure in the aorta exceeds the pressure in the pulmonary artery throughout both systole AND diastole. Blood therefore flows continuously from the aorta into the pulmonary artery in both phases. The murmur has a higher pitch in systole and lower pitch in diastole. It is heard loudest under the left clavicle (left infraclavicular area).

(iii) Three predisposing factors for persistent patency:
- Preterm delivery (immature closure mechanism)
- Birth asphyxia (reduced oxygen tension)
- High altitude (reduced ambient oxygen — PDA is commoner at high altitude)
- Maternal rubella infection
(Any three accepted)

(iv) Pathophysiological consequences (same framework as VSD):
Pulmonary circuit: Aorta → PDA → pulmonary artery → lungs receive large amount of blood → reflex vasospasm → increased pulmonary venous return → increased preload to left atrium and left ventricle → vicious cycle of volume overload → pulmonary vascular disease.
Systemic circuit: Reduced systemic perfusion (diastolic runoff through PDA) → hypoperfusion of peripheral tissues → vasomotor centre compensates with tachycardia → wet lungs → less compliant lungs → hypoxia → accessory muscle recruitment → intercostal/subcostal recession. Kidney retains fluid → worsens preload → congestive heart failure (left failure first, then right failure from pulmonary vascular resistance and fluid retention).

(v) Pharmacological treatment: Indomethacin (prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor) — inhibits prostaglandin, causing ductal smooth muscle constriction and closure.
Surgical option if medical closure fails: Surgical ligation of the ductus arteriosus.

Note on fluids (balloon valvuloplasty in PS): Normal saline is used because it stays in the intravascular space. Glucose is NOT used because it redistributes rapidly out of the intravascular compartment (into cells), providing no lasting volume benefit. In general: plasma and normal saline are used for intravascular replacement because they remain in the intravascular space (same principle as in TOF plasma exchange, where glucose is explicitly contraindicated for the same reason).

(i) Diagnosis: neonatal tetanus. Source: unhygienic cord care (cord cut with dirty blade). Other possible neonatal entry points: circumcision, ear-piercing, scarification; in the mother's history, unimmunized status (no transplacental protection).
(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Clostridium tetani spores contaminate the wound (umbilical cord stump)
- Wounds with low oxidation-reduction potential (dead/devitalized tissue, foreign body, active infection) facilitate germination of spores and release of toxin
- Tetanospasmin released in the wound binds to peripheral motor neuron terminal, enters axon, and via retrograde intraneuronal transport reaches nerve cell body in brainstem and spinal cord
- The toxin blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA
- Reduced inhibition → muscle rigidity (sustained muscle contraction) and spasms; sympathetic hyperactivity and increased catecholamines
- In neonatal tetanus: always generalized; symptoms include excessive crying, refusal to suck, trismus, rigidity, and spasms
(iii) Full management:
- Nurse in quiet dark environment (ideally ICU)
- Neutralize unbound toxin: Human TIG single dose of 500 U for neonates; alternatively Tetanus antitoxin (ATS) single dose of 50,000-100,000 U after appropriate testing for sensitivity and desensitization
- Eradicate organisms: metronidazole (preferred) or penicillin G 10-14 days
- Muscle relaxants: oral diazepam 5 mg/kg/day x 2-6 weeks; others: MgSO4, midazolam, chlorpromazine, phenobarbitone; neuromuscular blockers with respiratory support in ICU if needed
- Supportive care: fluid and electrolyte balance, nutritional support
- Wound care: debridement and cleaning of umbilical cord stump
(iv) Td immunization schedule for mothers (prevention of neonatal tetanus):
- Td1 at first contact: no protection
- Td2 4 weeks later: 80% protection for 3 years
- Td3 6 months later: 95% protection for 5 years
- Td4 1 year later or in subsequent pregnancy: 99% protection for 10 years
- Td5 1 year later or in subsequent pregnancy: 99% protection for life
questions.question:
A 3-week-old neonate presents with irritability, excessive crying, refusal to suck, and muscle stiffness. His mother is unimmunized and the umbilical cord was cut with a dirty blade. He developed trismus 2 days ago.
(i) State the diagnosis, the source of infection in this case, and other possible entry points for the same condition in neonates.
(ii) Describe the pathogenesis of this condition from wound contamination to clinical manifestation.
(iii) Outline the full management including neutralization of toxin, antimicrobial therapy, muscle relaxants, supportive care, and nursing environment.

A. Describe the clinical features of pulmonary stenosis under the following headings:
A(i) Explain why most children with pulmonary stenosis are asymptomatic, identifying the anatomical mechanism responsible
A(ii) List the symptoms and signs when the obstruction is severe, including auscultatory findings
A(iii) State the CXR and ECG findings in valvar pulmonary stenosis

B. Describe the management of pulmonary stenosis under the following headings:
B(i) The criterion (in terms of right ventricular pressure) that distinguishes conservative from interventional management, and explain why urgent relief is needed when this threshold is exceeded
B(ii) List the three procedures available for relief of the obstruction and state what substance is used for balloon inflation in valvuloplasty and why

C. Distinguish between valvar, infundibular, supravalvar, and peripheral types of pulmonary stenosis: state the anatomical location of each, and for supravalvar and peripheral types, name the specific syndrome and aetiological agent respectively.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Most children with pulmonary stenosis are asymptomatic because the high pressure on the right side keeps the foramen ovale open, acting as a decompression mechanism. Mild to moderate lesions are common in older children and adults.

A(ii) Symptoms/signs in severe pulmonary stenosis:
- Cyanosis (through ASD or patent foramen ovale)
- Dyspnoea on exertion — severe
- Left parasternal heave (due to right ventricular hypertrophy)
- P2 is soft and delayed
- S2 may be single (indicates high severity)
- Ejection click (indicates the obstruction is less severe — due to forced/pressurised flow of blood against wall of pulmonary artery)

A(iii) CXR findings (valvar PS):
- Post-stenotic dilatation of pulmonary artery (pulmonary knuckle) — unlike TOF where it is a pulmonary bay
- Reduced pulmonary vascular markings
- Heart size usually normal unless obstruction is severe
ECG findings:
- Right ventricular hypertrophy (overwhelming evidence)
- In very severe form: T-wave inversion from V1 to V6 (RV-apex forming)

B(i) Criterion: Right ventricular pressure < 60 mmHg → conservative management.
Right ventricular pressure > 60 mmHg → urgent relief needed.
Reason: When RV pressure exceeds 60 mmHg, the hypertrophied muscle can outgrow its blood supply, causing angina. Urgent relief prevents irreversible myocardial damage.

B(ii) Three procedures:
1. Ventriculotomy
2. Pulmonary valvotomy/infundibular resection
3. Balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon inflation substance: Normal saline (not air, not gas).
Reason: Just in case the balloon ruptures — normal saline is safe; air or gas would cause fatal embolism.

C. Types of pulmonary stenosis:
- Valvar: Obstruction at the level of the pulmonary valve leaflets (associated with ejection click and post-stenotic dilatation)
- Infundibular: Fibromuscular band below the valve (no post-stenotic dilatation, no ejection click from the valve itself)
- Supravalvar: Rare; associated with hypercalcaemia; co-exists with aortic stenosis (double arterial stenosis); part of Williams syndrome (elfin facies, mental retardation, hypercalcaemia); commonly found in infants <9 months
- Peripheral: Stenosis of branches of the pulmonary trunk; may be unilateral or bilateral; caused by (i) drugs e.g. thalidomide; (ii) rubella infection

questions.question:
A 4-month-old infant presents with a 3-week history of poor weight gain, refusal to feed, excessive perspiration, and breathlessness. On examination there is tachycardia with gallop rhythm, tachypnoea, cardiomegaly, and a soft tender hepatomegaly.

(i) What is the diagnosis? Define the condition and state the pathophysiological mechanism from oxygen supply deficit to end-organ changes.
(ii) List all the common causes of this condition in the local environment as described.
(iii) Outline the initial resuscitation steps and monitoring parameters.
(iv) State the definitive drug treatment under each category: inotropic agents, ACE inhibitors and vasodilators, PDE inhibitors, and diuretics, listing specific drugs in each group.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Cardiac failure (heart failure) in infancy. Definition: cardiac output insufficient to meet the metabolic needs of the body. Pathophysiology: systemic oxygen supply is less than demand → compensatory mechanisms activated → salt and water retention; increased adrenergic activity; increased red cell mass; hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes; hyperplasia of cardiac fibroblasts; alteration of pattern of expression of cardiomyocyte-specific and non-muscle myocyte-specific genes → increased preload, increased afterload, and myocardial dysfunction.

(ii) Common causes in this environment: Pneumonia; Severe anaemia; Acyanotic congenital heart diseases; Acquired heart diseases e.g., Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD).

(iii) Initial resuscitation:
- Cardiac position
- Ensure clear airway
- Give oxygen
- Total fluid at ¾ maintenance, preferably oral if no contraindication
- Monitor oxygen saturation and other vital signs closely
- Treat the underlying cause

(iv) Drug treatment:
Inotropic agents: digoxin, dopamine, dobutamine, isoprenaline.
ACE inhibitors and vasodilators: captopril, enalapril, hydralazine, nitroglycerine, sodium nitroprusside, PGE-1 infusion, tolazoline.
PDE inhibitors: amrinone, milrinone.
Diuretics: furosemide, ethacrynic acid, spironolactone.

questions.question:
A. Describe immunity and immunisation under the following headings:
A(i) Definition of immunity
A(ii) Types of immunisation (active and passive), including the two situations in which passive immunisation commonly occurs
A(iii) Constituents of immunising agents beyond the vaccine itself

B. Distinguish between live attenuated vaccines and inactivated vaccines, covering their mechanism, dosing characteristics, and examples of each type currently available.

C. Explain the clinical basis of herd immunity and the level of vaccination coverage at which spread of disease is effectively stopped.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Immunity: the ability to fight disease, or the ability of the body to tolerate material that is indigenous to it and eliminate material that is foreign. The immune system identifies harmful substances called antigens and destroys them using antibodies and other specialised cells.

A(ii) Active immunisation: administration of a vaccine that stimulates the body to produce antibody or cell-mediated immunity or both. Passive immunisation: temporary protection through administration of exogenously produced antibody. Two situations: (1) transplacental transfer of antibodies to the fetus, which may protect for the first 3–6 months of life; (2) injection of immunoglobulin (e.g., hepatitis B immune-globulin, tetanus immune globulin).

A(iii) Constituents beyond the vaccine:
- Suspending fluid (sterile water or saline, or complex fluid with small amounts of protein)
- Preservatives, stabilisers, and antibiotics (inhibit bacterial growth, stabilise the antigen; allergic reactions may occur if the recipient is sensitive)
- Adjuvant (e.g., an aluminium salt) to enhance immunogenicity; vaccines with adjuvant should be injected deeply into muscle to prevent local irritation, inflammation, or necrosis.

B. Live attenuated: derived from weakened disease-causing viruses or bacteria; grow in the vaccinated individual but do not cause clinical disease; usually one dose provides lifelong immunity (except oral vaccines such as OPV, which require multiple doses). Examples: BCG, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, yellow fever, OPV, oral typhoid vaccine, rotavirus vaccine.
Inactivated: grown in culture media and inactivated with heat or chemicals; do not grow in the vaccinated individual; require multiple doses; first dose primes, protective immunity develops after second or third dose; antibody titres diminish with time requiring booster doses. Examples (whole-cell): viral — polio, rabies, hepatitis A; fractional — subunits (hepatitis B, acellular pertussis) and toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus).

C. Herd immunity is the level of resistance of a community to a particular disease. When a critical percentage of the population is vaccinated (>80%), spread of disease is effectively stopped. Susceptible persons are reduced to a small proportion, and the occurrence of an epidemic is unlikely; eventually the disease may be eliminated.

A(i) Definition and laboratory criteria:
- TLS is a constellation of metabolic disturbances which occurs when large numbers of neoplastic cells are killed rapidly, leading to release of intracellular ions and metabolic by-products into systemic circulation.
- Laboratory TLS (Cairo and Bishop): ≥2 of the following metabolic abnormalities during the same 24-hour period within 3 days before or up to 7 days after initiation of therapy:
  - Hyperkalemia: K >6 mEq/L (or 25% increase).
  - Hyperuricemia: uric acid >8 mg/dl (or 25% increase).
  - Hyperphosphatemia: PO₄ >6.5 mg/dl (or 25% increase).
  - Hypocalcemia: ionized calcium <1.5 mEq/L (3 mg/dl) (or 25% decrease).
- Uric acid nephropathy and acute kidney injury are clinical TLS features.

A(ii) Risk factors:
- Bulky tumours (>10 cm in diameter) and/or white blood cell count >50,000/uL.
- Rapidly proliferating tumours.
- Chemosensitive tumours.
- Pre-treatment Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) >2× Upper Limit of Normal.
- Organ infiltration or bone marrow involvement.
- High LDH (2× ULN) plus pre-existing renal insufficiency: strong prognostic indicators.
- Poor urine output.
- Increased pre-treatment serum uric acid.
- Commonly in Burkitt lymphoma, T-cell ALL, also hepatoblastoma and neuroblastoma.

B(i) Mechanisms of renal failure:
- Precipitation of urate in acidic urine.
- Precipitation of xanthine when urine pH >7.5.
- Precipitation of Ca₃(PO₄)₂ in renal vessels and tubules.
- Increased xanthine level after starting allopurinol.
- Treatment: Dialysis.

B(ii) Management of specific abnormalities:
Hyperuricaemia: Aim to (1) decrease uric acid production, (2) increase uric acid solubility in urine, (3) decrease uric acid concentration in urine. Use: Allopurinol, Hydration with IVF at 3–6 L/m²/day, alkalinisation of urine with 50–100 mEq of NaHCO₃/L, Uricase.
Hyperkalaemia (K+ >6 mEq/L): Stop K+ intake; drive K+ into cells with IV NaHCO₃ 1–2 mEq/kg, 0.1 U/kg insulin + IV 50% glucose 1 ml/kg, aerosolised salbutamol; IV Calcium gluconate 100–200 mg/kg/dose slowly; ion exchange resin (kayexalate) 1 g/kg p.o. + 50% sorbitol; Dialysis.
Hyperphosphatemia (PO₄ >6.5 mEq/L): Causes reciprocal depression of serum Ca; Ca × PO₄ >60 → metastatic calcification; symptoms include pruritus, conjunctivitis, arthritis, renal failure.
Hypocalcemia: Ionized calcium calculation: Serum Calcium (mg/dl) + 0.8(4 − serum albumin [g/dl]).

Describe the classification, pathophysiology, clinical features, and management of Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS).
A(i) Define TLS and state the laboratory criteria used for its diagnosis (Cairo and Bishop classification).
A(ii) List all the risk factors for TLS.
B(i) Explain the mechanisms by which renal failure develops in TLS.
B(ii) Describe the management of each specific metabolic abnormality in TLS (hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia).

questions.answerText:
(i) The radiological sign is the 'double bubble' sign. It consists of two gas-filled structures: the first (larger) bubble represents the stomach in the left upper quadrant, and the second represents the proximal duodenum (duodenal cap) in the right upper quadrant, separated by the pylorus. The absence of gas distal to these two structures is the defining feature.
(ii) The most likely diagnosis is duodenal atresia or annular pancreas in a neonate presenting with bilious vomiting and the 'double bubble' sign on plain abdominal X-ray. Both conditions cause complete or near-complete obstruction at or just distal to the ampulla of Vater, explaining the bilious nature of the vomiting.
(iii) Polyhydramnios was present antenatally because complete duodenal obstruction prevents the fetus from swallowing and absorbing amniotic fluid in the normal volume. The obstructed duodenum leads to accumulation of amniotic fluid above the level of obstruction and subsequently polyhydramnios.
(iv) Differential pathological diagnoses producing the double bubble or similar high intestinal obstruction signs include: duodenal atresia, duodenal stenosis, annular pancreas, malrotation with Ladd's bands causing duodenal compression, and duodenal web. The absence of all distal gas distinguishes complete obstruction (atresia) from partial obstruction.
(v) Urgent surgical intervention is necessary because: complete duodenal obstruction causes progressive gastric and duodenal distension; bilious vomiting leads to rapid fluid and electrolyte loss with dehydration; ongoing inability to absorb feeds causes nutritional failure; and delay risks aspiration of vomitus. The anatomy of the obstruction requires surgical bypass (duodenoduodenostomy or duodenojejunostomy) to restore intestinal continuity, which cannot resolve spontaneously.
questions.question:
A term neonate is born at 39 weeks gestation to a mother whose antenatal ultrasound showed polyhydramnios. At birth, bilious vomiting begins within 6 hours. On examination the upper abdomen appears distended while the lower abdomen is scaphoid. A plain abdominal X-ray shows two large gas-filled structures — one in the left upper quadrant and one in the right upper quadrant — separated by a soft tissue band, with no gas visible in the rest of the abdomen.

(i) Describe the radiological sign and the two anatomical structures it represents.
(ii) What is the most likely diagnosis or group of diagnoses causing this radiological appearance?
(iii) Explain why polyhydramnios was present antenatally in this condition.
(iv) What are the differential pathological diagnoses to be considered for this appearance?
(v) Outline the clinico-anatomical reasoning that makes urgent surgical intervention necessary in this presentation.

A 4-year-old unimmunized girl presents with low-grade fever, malaise, mild sore throat, and a greyish-brown adherent membrane on the right tonsil that bleeds when an attempt is made to remove it. Her neck shows soft tissue swelling.
(i) State the diagnosis, the causative organism, and the specific characteristic of the membrane.
(ii) Describe how the exotoxin of this organism causes systemic complications outside the throat.
(iii) State the differential diagnosis of the pharyngeal and laryngeal forms of this condition.
(iv) Outline the full treatment with rationale for each step, and the antibiotic choices with duration.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: tonsillar/pharyngeal diphtheria (classical diphtheria). Causative organism: Corynebacterium diphtheriae – Gram +ve, non-sporulating, aerobic/anaerobic bacilli.
Characteristics of the membrane:
- Pseudomembrane formation is the hallmark
- Formed from necrosed epithelial cells + fibrin + leucocytes + RBCs + organisms matted together
- Grey/brown in colour
- Firmly adherent to the tissue where destruction occurs (bleeds when attempts are made to remove it)
The swelling of the neck (soft tissue oedema + cervical lymphadenitis) – described as "Bull neck" – seen in cases >6 years
(ii) Systemic complications of the exotoxin:
- Exotoxin occasionally absorbed into blood causing:
  - Renal: necrosis of renal tubules → renal failure or hypotension
  - Bone marrow: thrombocytopaenia
  - Heart: cardiomyopathy (myocarditis); cardiac toxicity appears 1-2 weeks after initial symptoms; arrhythmias, heart block, circulatory collapse; immune-mediated; takes 2-10 weeks to manifest fully; fatal
  - Nerves: peripheral neuropathy (demyelination); neuropathies appear 2-6 weeks after; may involve any nerves (cranial and peripheral); peripheral polyneuropathy is symmetric and progresses distally; does not leave permanent damage if patient survives
- Another mechanism: antigen-antibody complex deposition in heart and nerves (takes 2-3 weeks to manifest)
(iii) Differential diagnosis:
- Pharyngeal: streptococcal or EBV pharyngitis (throat is angry red, more constitutional symptoms, patient more toxic); peritonsillar abscess; pharyngeal candidiasis (grayish-whitish plaques/patches, not a single membrane); Vincent's angina; Ludwig's angina
- Laryngeal: viral croup (acute LTB, less toxic, responds to steroids/adrenaline); acute epiglottitis (H. influenzae, very toxic, cherry red epiglottis, drooling, prefers sitting, life-threatening); laryngeal tumours
- Nasal diphtheria: foreign body in nostrils
- Peripheral neuropathy: poliomyelitis; Guillain-Barré syndrome (progresses proximally, unlike diphtheria neuropathy which progresses distally)
(iv) Full treatment with rationale:
1. Neutralizing antitoxins: specific diphtheria antitoxins administered to neutralize the circulating unbound exotoxin and prevent further cardiac and neural complications; must be given as early as possible
2. Antibiotics: IV crystalline penicillin 100-140 IU/kg for 2 weeks in divided doses OR erythromycin 40-50 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks; rationale: to kill the bacteria, thereby stopping production of more toxins
3. Supportive care: clear secretions; maintain good hygiene; maintain fluid balance
4. Toxoid after recovery: to actively immunize patient since clinical disease may not confer reliable immunity
5. Contacts: treat all household or school contacts with erythromycin for 7 days to prevent spread; also notify appropriate authorities

(i) Infective Endocarditis — subacute type. Duke criteria analysis:
Major criteria satisfied:
1. Two or more positive blood cultures for organisms typical of IE (Streptococcus viridans — most common IE organism)
2. Echocardiographic evidence — oscillating intracardiac mass (vegetation) on the aortic valve
= 2 MAJOR criteria → DEFINITE IE (diagnosis is made with 2 major criteria alone).

(ii) Predisposing factors: bicuspid aortic valve (a predisposing cardiac lesion); dental manipulation (dental extraction → transient bacteraemia).
Pathogenic sequence: dental extraction → bacteraemia with Streptococcus viridans (normally resident in the mouth) → damaged endothelium of bicuspid aortic valve (already abnormal) → formation of sterile non-bacterial thrombus on damaged surface → bacteria adhere from transient bacteraemia → infective endocarditis → progressive enlargement of vegetation → proliferation of valve leaflet → infected emboli and valve destruction.

(iii) Management:
Antibiotics for Streptococcus viridans (bactericidal, given parenterally):
- Ceftriaxone, OR
- Ampicillin + Gentamicin, OR
- Crystalline penicillin IV ± Probenecid ± Gentamicin
Duration: 6 weeks (all IE antibiotics given for 6 weeks)
Treatment of heart failure (from aortic regurgitation): digoxin and diuretics
Surgical: valve replacement (aortic valve); embolectomy if embolic complications; removal of mycotic aneurysms if present; correction of underlying aortic valve lesion.

(iv) Embolic complications (systemic — from aortic/mitral valve):
- CNS: cardiovascular accident (stroke), cerebral abscess from mycotic aneurysm → subarachnoid haemorrhage
- Renal: acute renal failure
- Splenic: splenic infarction
- Mesenteric arteries: acute abdomen
- Coronary arteries: angina, myocardial infarction
Mycotic aneurysms: from microabscesses in vessel walls causing false aneurysm formation.
Immunological (late manifestations, commoner in subacute form):
- Petechiae; splinter haemorrhages
- Osler's nodes (painless swelling in pulps of fingers)
- Roth spots (exudates in the eye)
- Microscopic haematuria; nephritis (glomerulonephritis)
- Arthritis; digital clubbing; Janeway lesions; rheumatoid factor positivity
questions.question:
A 9-year-old boy with a known bicuspid aortic valve is scheduled for a dental extraction. His cardiologist prescribes antibiotic prophylaxis. The following week, he develops persistent fever, a new diastolic murmur at the aortic area, and Osler's nodes. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus viridans. Echocardiography reveals an oscillating vegetation on the aortic valve.

(i) State the diagnosis and classify this case using the Duke major and minor criteria — how many major and how many minor criteria are satisfied here, and what does that mean for the diagnosis?
(ii) Explain the predisposing factors for this child and trace the pathogenic sequence from dental manipulation to vegetation formation on the aortic valve.
(iii) Describe the management — antibiotic regimen, duration, surgical options — for this specific child.
(iv) State the full range of embolic and immunological complications that could develop, and the site-specific consequences of systemic embolisation from the aortic valve.

A 3-year-old boy presents with 5 days of high fever, rigors, and pallor. He lives in Lagos and has had no recent prophylaxis. His blood glucose is 1.8 mmol/l, haemoglobin is 4.2 g/dl, and his blood smear shows P. falciparum with 8% parasitized erythrocytes. He is arousable but confused.
(i) What is the diagnosis and how does it meet the criteria for severity?
(ii) State all the predisposing factors that increase the risk of this complication.
(iii) Outline the urgent resuscitative steps that should be taken immediately on arrival.
(iv) State the specific antimalarial drug of choice for this condition, its dosing regimen, and what to give once oral feeding is tolerated.
questions.answerText:
(i) Severe/complicated P. falciparum malaria. Criteria met include: hyperparasitaemia (>5% parasitized erythrocytes or >250,000 parasites/μl); severe anaemia (Hb <5 g/dl in the presence of parasite count >10,000/μl); hypoglycaemia (blood glucose <2.2 mmol/l); and impaired consciousness (rousable mental condition).
(ii) Predisposing factors for complications of P. falciparum malaria: children less than 5 years; pregnancy, especially in primigravidae and in the 2nd half of pregnancy; immunosuppressed patients on steroids, anti-cancer drugs, immunosuppressant drugs; immunocompromised patients with advanced tuberculosis and cancers; post splenectomy; lack of previous exposure to malaria (non-immune) or lapsed immunity; pre-existing organ failure; internally displaced persons.
(iii) Urgent treatment steps:
- Ensure airway is patent; gentle suction of nostrils and the oro-pharynx
- Nurse the patient lying on the side or with the head sideways
- Insert a naso-gastric tube (NGT)
- Establish an intravenous line for giving drugs and fluids
- Correct hypoglycaemia: give 0.5 ml/kg of 50% dextrose diluted to 10-15% in children
- Give 20-30 ml/kg of normal saline for dehydration/shock and reassess within 30 minutes
- Give urgent blood transfusion for severe anaemia: use packed cells (10 ml/kg in children); blood must be screened for HIV, Hepatitis B and C
(iv) The recommended treatment is Artesunate Injection: give 2.4 mg/kg IV bolus, repeat 2.4 mg/kg after 12 hours and then 2.4 mg/kg daily until patient can tolerate oral medication (or for a minimum of 48 hours). Once parenteral treatment has been commenced it should be given for a minimum of 24 hours before changing to oral even if the patient is ready for oral administration earlier. Thereafter give follow-on treatment using a full 3-day course of ACT.

questions.question:
Describe the physiological basis and normal haematological indices in the newborn.
A(i) State the normal haemoglobin range for term and preterm babies and explain what happens to Hb, erythropoietin, and reticulocytes after birth.
A(ii) State the normal WBC count on Day 1, Week 1, and at 1 month, and give the normal neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages at Day 1 and Day 14.
B(i) State the normal platelet count and the reticulocyte count at Day 1, Day 7, and 1 month.
B(ii) Describe the foetal blood volume distribution (baby vs. placenta) and explain why 2,3-DPG increases after birth and what its physiological effect is.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Haemoglobin ranges:
- Term babies: 14–20 g/dl (cord blood 16.8 g/dl).
- Preterm babies: 14 g/dl at 28 weeks (1–2 g/dl less than term babies).
- Haematocrit: 45–65% (lower in preterm).
After birth: O2 saturation increases to 95%; erythropoietin production is reduced; erythropoiesis and reticulocytes are reduced; Hb reduces to minimum values by 8–12 weeks of life, after which erythropoiesis resumes. HbA/HbF starts to increase after birth.

A(ii) WBC counts:
- Day 1: 6–35,000/µl; Week 1: 8–16,000/µl; 1 Month: 6–14,000/µl. Values are a little lower in preterms.
Neutrophils: Day 1: 50–80%; Day 4: 35–60%; Day 7: 35–45%; 3 months: 25–45%.
Lymphocytes: Day 1: 31%; Day 7: 41%; Day 14: 48%.

B(i) Normal platelet count: 150,000–400,000/µl (up to 600,000/µl by 2–4 months).
Reticulocyte count: 2–8% Day 1; 0.5–5% Day 7; 0–0.5% at 1 month.

B(ii) Foetal blood volume is approximately 115 ml/kg: 75 ml in the baby, 40 ml in the placenta.
In utero: aortic O2 saturation is approximately 45%; increased erythropoietin production, erythropoiesis, and reticulocytes (3–7%).
After birth: 2,3-DPG increases; this increases O2 delivery to tissues, supporting the newborn's switch from placental to pulmonary gas exchange.

questions.question:
Describe the fluid and electrolyte physiology of the newborn, covering homeostasis, body fluid compartments, and the regulation of extracellular fluid volume.
A(i) State the total body water as a percentage of body weight in a term baby, a 4–6-month-old, and an adult, and subdivide into ECF and ICF values for each.
A(ii) Define plasma osmolality, state its normal value, name the principal solutes in the ECF and ICF, and explain how ADH and aldosterone regulate ECF tonicity and volume.
B(i) Describe maintenance fluid requirements: state how to calculate them, the daily electrolyte requirements, and the components of obligatory water loss.
B(ii) List four conditions that increase maintenance fluid requirements and three conditions that require a reduction in maintenance fluid.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Total body water and compartments:
- Term baby: TBW 75%; ECF 35–44%; ICF 33%.
- 4–6 months: TBW 60%; ECF 23%; ICF 37%.
- 12 months: TBW 60%; ECF 26–30%; ICF 37%.
- Puberty: TBW 60%; ECF 20%; ICF 40%.
- Adult: TBW 50–60%; ECF 20%; ICF 40%.
ECF subdivisions: plasma (5%); interstitial (15%); transcellular (2%) — GI secretions, urine, CSF, pleural, peritoneal, synovial.

A(ii) Plasma osmolality: concentration of solute particles in plasma; normal value 285–295 mosm/kg/H2O.
ECF principal solutes: Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO3⁻, glucose, urea. ICF principal solute: mainly K⁺.
ADH: regulated by tonicity (not volume) of body fluid; increases water reabsorption in collecting ducts of kidney → concentrated urine.
Aldosterone: released in response to (i) decreased effective circulating volume; (ii) stimulation of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis; (iii) rising plasma K⁺. It enhances distal renal tubular reabsorption of Na⁺ in exchange for K⁺ (and H⁺).
ANF: polypeptide hormone secreted by cardiac atria in response to atrial dilatation; inhibits renin secretion and aldosterone synthesis; inhibits ADH release; increases GFR and renal Na excretion.

B(i) Maintenance fluid: quantity of fluid needed daily to maintain fluid balance, taking into account insensible H2O losses and water lost in sweat, urine, and stool (assuming patient is afebrile and relatively inactive). Greater for LBW and preterm infants. Approximately 1 ml water is needed for each kcal expended.
Components of obligatory water loss: insensible loss — evaporative from lungs (2/3) and skin (1/3) = 40%; urine (water to excrete solute load) = 50–55%; faecal loss = 5–10%.
Daily electrolyte requirements: Na, K, Cl = 2–3 mmol of each electrolyte/kg/day.

B(ii) Conditions increasing fluid requirements: increased insensible H2O loss in preterm; phototherapy (allow 20–40 ml/kg/day extra); persistent pyrexia (increase by 12% for each °C above 37.5°C); radiant warmer; increased urine volume (glycosuria, acute tubular necrosis); abnormal fluid losses — third space losses (diarrhoea, vomiting, tube drainage); hypermetabolic states — severe thermal injuries, salicylate intoxication, hyperthyroidism (increase up by 25–50%).
Conditions requiring reduction: oedematous and antidiuretic states; infants nursed in high environmental humidity; sedated or paralysed patients (> 40% reduction needed because of decreased energy need); presence of compromised renal function.

questions.question:
A 3-day-old male neonate delivered at term in a peripheral clinic is brought to the hospital by his mother after she notices yellow colouration of the eyes and skin. He was delivered normally and cried immediately at birth. The family is from a sub-Saharan African ethnic background. On examination the neonate is jaundiced up to the abdomen (Kramer zone III), is mildly lethargic but rousable, and has no pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, or skin petechiae. Serum bilirubin is 18.5 mg/dL (total), with conjugated fraction at 0.8 mg/dL. The rate of rise over the past 12 hours has been 6 mg/dL.

(i) Classify this jaundice as physiologic or pathologic, citing the specific criteria met, and state the single most likely aetiological diagnosis given the epidemiological context.
(ii) State at least three risk factors in this history that predispose this neonate to the condition.
(iii) Explain the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which the identified aetiological agent causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
(iv) Outline the management approach, including the treatment indicated by the bilirubin level, and state the most serious neurological complication if treatment is delayed.
questions.answerText:
(i) This jaundice is pathologic. Pathologic criteria met include: a rate of rise exceeding 5 mg/dL/day (or 0.5 mg/dL/hour) — this infant's rate is 6 mg/dL in 12 hours; total serum bilirubin of 18.5 mg/dL exceeding the threshold of 12 mg/dL in a term infant; and lethargy suggesting impending toxicity. The most likely aetiological diagnosis given the sub-Saharan African ethnic background is G6PD deficiency, which in the Ibadan series (Effiong and Laditan, 1976) accounted for 59% of aetiological factors in neonates with significant hyperbilirubinaemia, making it the dominant cause in this Nigerian cohort.
(ii) Risk factors include: male sex (G6PD deficiency is X-linked and more commonly expressed in males); sub-Saharan African ethnicity (high G6PD deficiency prevalence in this population); delivery in a peripheral clinic with likely lack of newborn screening and monitoring; and age below 12 months (children under 12 months have higher body water content and greater susceptibility to rapid bilirubin accumulation).
(iii) G6PD deficiency impairs the pentose phosphate pathway, reducing NADPH production and glutathione regeneration. Without adequate glutathione, red blood cells are vulnerable to oxidative haemolysis, especially with certain drugs, foods (fava beans), or infections. Increased red cell destruction generates an elevated bilirubin load from haem catabolism, overwhelming the hepatic conjugation capacity of the immature neonatal liver and producing unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
(iv) Management: the elevated total bilirubin with a rapid rate of rise in a lethargic neonate indicates phototherapy at minimum, and the rate of rise suggests exchange transfusion may be needed. Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin in skin to water-soluble photoisomers excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. If bilirubin continues to rise despite phototherapy or reaches exchange transfusion thresholds, exchange transfusion removes bilirubin and haemolysed red cells. The most serious neurological complication of untreated severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is kernicterus — bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia and brainstem — causing permanent neurological damage.

questions.question:
A 4-day-old female neonate, born at 33 weeks via elective caesarean section, presents with tachypnoea and mild grunting. Her chest X-ray shows a 'sunburst pattern' that cleared within 48 hours. However, she is now noted to have profuse bloody stools at 18 days, abdominal distension, and apnoea, with an abdominal X-ray revealing pneumatosis intestinalis.
(i) Name the two diagnoses in sequence (early and late), and for each state the key diagnostic criterion.
(ii) For the first diagnosis, state three risk factors.
(iii) For the second diagnosis, state which factor is described as the single greatest risk factor.
(iv) State the prevention strategies for the second condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Two diagnoses in sequence:
Early (Day 4): Transient Tachypnoea of the Newborn (TTN) — key diagnostic criterion: CXR shows 'sunburst pattern' that clears in 24 hours; benign and self-limiting; child recovers in 24–72 hours.
Late (Day 18): Necrotising Enterocolitis (NEC) — key diagnostic criterion: radiological signs including pneumatosis intestinalis (plus intestinal dilatation, ileus, portal vein gas, ascites, pneumoperitoneum).

(ii) Risk factors for TTN: Preterm birth; maternal diabetes; maternal sedation; caesarean delivery.
(Three from: preterm birth; maternal diabetes; maternal sedation; caesarean delivery.)

(iii) Single greatest risk factor for NEC: Prematurity is the single greatest risk factor (mean GA 30–32 weeks).

(iv) Prevention strategies for NEC:
The ultimate goal is prevention; unfortunately this can best be accomplished only by preventing premature birth.
Other preventive strategies:
1. Induction of GI maturation (prenatal steroid therapy).
2. Breastfeeding (IgA).
3. Very slow introduction of feeding may be useful.

(i) Most likely differentials in order: (1) Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS/hyaline membrane disease) — most likely given prematurity (30 weeks), very low birth weight (1.0 kg), and granular opacities; (2) Congenital pneumonia — given pre-eclampsia, maternal illness, and homogenous opacity in left hemithorax.

(ii) RDS specific CXR: bilateral diffuse reticular granular or ground-glass appearance; air bronchograms; poor lung expansion; cardiac silhouette normal or enlarged. Congenital pneumonia CXR: may show homogenous opacities, patchy infiltrates, similar to RDS and pneumonia, but distinguishing features include clinical context (evidence of infection, maternal chorioamnionitis). In RDS, the granular (ground-glass) appearance with air bronchograms is characteristic; in congenital pneumonia, opacities may be more heterogeneous.

(iii) Antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone 12 mg IM given twice 48 hours before delivery) reduce the risk of RDS. Mechanism: corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by stimulating surfactant production and release. The risk of RDS is reduced by antenatal corticosteroid use (as well as by prolonged rupture of membranes, chronic or pregnancy-associated hypertension, and maternal opiate addiction).

(iv) Blood gas abnormalities in severe RDS: respiratory acidosis (raised pCO2, low pH); metabolic acidosis; hypoxia (low pO2). Normal values for comparison: pO2 in term infants ~90 mmHg by 24 hrs; pCO2 35–40 mmHg; pH 7.35–7.40.

(v) Supportive treatment of RDS: surfactant replacement therapy; oxygen (to maintain SaO2 90–95%); continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP); assisted mechanical ventilation; temperature regulation; fluids, electrolytes, and nutrition; circulation and anaemia management; antibiotic administration; support of parents and family. Acute complications: alveolar rupture; infections; intracranial haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia; PDA; pulmonary haemorrhage; necrotising enterocolitis/GI perforation; apnoea of prematurity. Chronic complications: chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia); retinopathy of prematurity (ROP); neurologic impairment; familial psychopathology.
questions.question:
A 30-week preterm male neonate presents to the Special Care Baby Unit with signs of respiratory distress at 3 days of life. Chest radiograph shows homogeneous opacities in the left hemithorax and granular opacities in the right hemithorax. He was born to a mother with severe pre-eclampsia who received 2 doses of dexamethasone 48 hours before delivery. Birth weight was 1.0 kg.

(i) Based on the radiograph description and clinical context, what are the two most likely diagnoses in differential order?
(ii) What chest radiograph finding specifically characterises RDS, and how does it differ from that seen in congenital pneumonia?
(iii) Which maternal factor in this case is protective against RDS, and by what mechanism?
(iv) What blood gas abnormalities are expected in severe RDS?
(v) Describe the full supportive treatment of RDS and state the acute and chronic complications.

A 4-year-old girl is brought with a 3-day history of generalised tonic–clonic convulsions that have not stopped for the past 40 minutes. She has a known history of epilepsy on phenobarbitone but her mother ran out of medication 2 weeks ago. She has not regained consciousness between attacks.

(i) State the diagnosis and its definition.
(ii) List the aetiological causes of this condition.
(iii) Outline the stepwise emergency management of this child, listing the drugs in the correct sequence, doses, and routes of administration.
(iv) State the monitoring parameters required during management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Status Epilepticus. Definition: a life-threatening seizure that is prolonged for >30 minutes with no recovery in between the attacks. Generalised tonic–clonic status is most alarming because of the risk of hypoxia.

(ii) Aetiological causes:
a. Febrile seizure.
b. Non-compliance with drugs (sudden withdrawal of AED — as in this child).
c. Stress including intercurrent infections.
d. Brain pathology: tumour, trauma, infection, infarction, drugs.

(iii) Stepwise emergency management:
Step 1 — ABC of resuscitation; give oxygen; check blood sugar.
Step 2 — Rectal diazepam; secure IV access.
Step 3 (if seizures continue after 10 minutes) — IM Paraldehyde 1 ml/year of life.
Step 4 (if no response) — IV Phenytoin 18–20 mg/kg slowly over 20 minutes.
Step 5 (if no response) — IV Phenobarbitone 15–20 mg/kg over 10 minutes (given slowly).
Step 6 (if no response) — Induction of anaesthesia with sodium thiopentone; intubate after general anaesthesia.
Additional: IM Paraldehyde 0.1 ml/kg may be used as an alternative.

(iv) Monitoring parameters:
- Blood sugar estimation (to detect hypoglycaemia and monitor glucose correction).
- Respiratory status (risk of respiratory arrest from diazepam; bulbar compromise from prolonged seizures).
- Oxygen saturation/airway patency.
- IV access — to ensure availability of IV route for drugs.
- Seizure cessation and return of consciousness between attacks.

questions.question:
A 6-month-old infant presents with breathlessness, poor feeding, excessive sweating, recurrent chest infections, and failure to thrive. Examination reveals a hyperactive praecordium, tachycardia, subcostal and intercostal recession, tender hepatomegaly, and a pansystolic murmur best heard at the mid-left sternal edge radiating to the back.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? State the factors that predispose to this condition.
(ii) Describe the full pathophysiological sequence by which a large defect leads to congestive heart failure, including the vicious cycles set up in both the pulmonary and systemic circulations.
(iii) List the complications that arise at the late stage when pulmonary vascular disease becomes irreversible, and state why surgery is then contraindicated.
(iv) State the investigations and their expected findings, and describe the management options.
questions.answerText:
(i) Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) — the most common congenital heart disease (35% of congenital heart diseases in Ibadan). Predisposing factors (exert effect during morphogenesis — 12th day to 6–8th week of intrauterine life):
- Irradiation
- Drugs taken by the mother (e.g. thalidomide, cytotoxic, steroids)
- Specific chromosomal anomalies (e.g. Trisomy 21, Trisomy 18, Trisomy 13)
- Specific gene defects; intrauterine infection (e.g. rubella)

(ii) Pulmonary vicious cycle: high left-sided pressure (130–140 mmHg) drives blood through the VSD into the right ventricle → right ventricle pumps excess blood to lungs → lungs develop reflex vasospasm → increased pulmonary vascular resistance → thickening of pulmonary vessels → increased afterload on right ventricle → right ventricular failure. Left-sided cycle: reduced stroke volume from left ventricle → hypoperfusion of peripheral tissues → vasomotor centre increases heart rate → shortened systolic interval → reduced left ventricular filling → more blood damped into lungs (wet lungs) → reduced lung compliance → hypoxia → accessory muscles summoned → intercostal and subcostal indrawing. Fluid retention (kidney perceives hypovolaemia) worsens preload → left ventricular failure first, then biventricular congestive heart failure.

(iii) When pulmonary vascular disease becomes irreversible, the right-sided pressure rises above left-sided pressure, causing Eisenmenger Complex/Syndrome — desaturation occurs on the left side. Surgery is contraindicated because suprasystemic pressure on the right side causes post-cardiotomy syndrome; the myocardium requires a lot of oxygen after surgery, and the irreversible vascular changes cannot be reversed.

(iv) Investigations:
- CXR: pulmonary plethora (increased vascular markings); cardiomegaly if heart failure has set in
- ECG: initially shows LVH, then biventricular changes
- ECHO: shows the defect; Doppler colour flow demonstrates left-to-right shunt
- Cardiac catheterisation: pulmonary wedge vascular pressure (in Woods units) when pulmonary vascular disease is suspected pre-surgery
Management: Treatment of congestive heart failure (digoxin and diuretics). Definitive: patch repair under profound hypothermia.

questions.question:
A 3-month-old infant presents with cyanosis and heart failure. Examination shows features of a univentricular heart. ECG demonstrates right atrial hypertrophy, superior axis deviation, and left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography confirms absence of the right atrioventricular connection with a rudimentary right ventricle.

(i) State the diagnosis and explain how the ventriculo-arterial connection determines whether the child presents primarily with cyanosis alone or with cyanosis plus heart failure.
(ii) State the risk factors and predisposing conditions for this disease group and describe the full range of complications that arise.
(iii) Describe the investigations and their expected findings, distinguishing the ECG pattern that is suggestive of this diagnosis in a cyanosed child.
(iv) State the surgical management, name the operation, describe the procedure, and justify its use.
questions.answerText:
(i) Tricuspid Atresia (TA) — also called univentricular heart (commonest example of univentricular heart disease); right ventricle is rudimentary; the right atrioventricular connection is absent.
Clinical presentation depends on ventriculo-arterial (V-A) connection:
- If V-A concordance (RV→PA): features are due to reduced pulmonary blood flow; presents haemodynamically similar to TOF — predominantly cyanosis
- If V-A discordance (RV→Aorta, LV→PA): the morphological right ventricle (which is rudimentary) connects to the aorta; presents with cyanosis AND heart failure
Summary: presentation consists of cyanosis ± heart failure.

(ii) Predisposing factors/causes of congenital heart disease that apply to this group (exert effect during morphogenesis — 12th day to 6–8th week of intrauterine life): irradiation; drugs (thalidomide, cytotoxic, steroids); intrauterine infection (rubella — PDA, VSD, PS); chromosomal anomalies (Trisomy 21 — AV septal defect/VSD/ASD; Trisomy 18 — VSD/ASD; Trisomy 13 — VSD; Turner's syndrome — coarctation); familial/environmental factors; preterm delivery; birth asphyxia; maternal diabetes mellitus (TGA).
Complications: most patients die in first year of life without intervention; heart failure; progressive cyanosis and hypoxia; growth retardation.

(iii) CXR: features are variable depending on V-A connection; odd-looking shaped heart because the right ventricle is absent; increased pulmonary vascular markings (if V-A discordance like TGA) OR reduced markings (if V-A concordance like TOF).
ECG: suggestive but not diagnostic; shows right atrial hypertrophy (large if ASD is small, and vice-versa), superior axis deviation (ERAD/ELAD/LAD), and left ventricular hypertrophy. These three features together in a cyanosed child are suggestive of tricuspid atresia.
Echocardiography: absent right atrioventricular connection; ASD; LV is main chamber; rudimentary RV chamber; V-A connection defined.
Cardiac catheterisation: shows no entrance into right ventricle.

(iv) Medical: treat heart failure. Most patients give up in first year without intervention.
Surgical — definitive: Fontan's Operation — a classical operation for those with reduced pulmonary blood flow. Procedure: connecting the right atrium directly to the pulmonary artery. A valve conduit is used to allow blood to flow in one direction — to the pulmonary artery. This bypasses the absent right ventricle and allows deoxygenated blood from the right atrium to reach the lungs.

A(i) Classification of malaria endemicity:
- Hypoendemicity: spleen rate ≤10% and parasite rate ≤10% in children aged 2-9 years; areas where there is a little transmission and effects during the average year on the general population are unimportant
- Mesoendemicity: spleen rate 11-50% and parasite rate 11-50% in children aged 2-9 years; typically found among rural communities in subtropical zones where wide geographical variations in transmission risk exist
- Hyperendemicity: spleen rate constantly >50% in children aged 2-9 years, also high in adults (>25%); parasite rate constantly >50% in children aged 2-9 years; areas where transmission is intense but seasonal; immunity insufficient in all age groups
- Holoendemicity: spleen rate constantly >75% in children aged 2-9 years but low in adults; parasite rate constantly >75% among infants aged 0-11 months; intense transmission resulting in a considerable degree of immunity outside early childhood
A(ii) Burden of malaria:
- 300-500 million clinical cases per year worldwide; over 1 million deaths per year with >90% in Africa
- 81% of cases occur in Africa; 86% of victims were children less than 5 years
- Nigeria, DRC, Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Côte d'Ivoire and Mali account for 60% of deaths due to malaria
- 90% of all malaria mortality is in children under 5 years
- Major cause of poor child development: impairment of physical growth; impairment of cognitive function; disability from severe form of disease; 40 million DALYs lost annually
- In pregnancy: up to 15% maternal anaemia; 35% of preventable low birth weight
B(i) Fever paroxysms and periodicity:
- Fever paroxysms coincide with rupture of schizonts and are due to synchronous release of merozoites, antigens, and other pyrogenic substances such as tumour necrosis factor-α and interleukins
- P. malariae: quartan fever, 72-hour periodicity (malaria quartan)
- P. vivax and P. ovale: tertian fever, 48-hour cycles (malaria tertian)
- P. falciparum: often exhibits continuous fever rather than periodic paroxysm (malaria tropical: irregular high fever); periodicity less apparent, especially in children; fatality can be as high as 30% if not urgently addressed
- A typical malaria illness is characterized by acute febrile attacks (malaria paroxysms): fever, fatigue, high fever, rigors, sweats, headache, myalgia, abdominal and back pains, nausea, vomiting, pallor and diarrhoea
B(ii) Host factors modifying susceptibility:
- Age: children and pregnant women are more susceptible; adults and older children in endemic areas are less susceptible due to acquired immunity
- Duffy blood group antigen alleles: affect P. vivax susceptibility; new findings show Duffy negative subjects also infected with P. vivax
- Sickle cell trait (heterozygous state): confers protection against severe malaria
- Haemoglobin F also has protective effects against severe malaria
- P. vivax and P. ovale primarily infect immature RBCs while P. malariae infects only mature RBCs; these infections are usually mild
- P. falciparum can infect both mature and immature RBCs (up to 60%); causes the most severe disease
C(i) Health education for malaria prevention:
- Health education should focus on: importance of early diagnosis and prompt treatment; seeking early treatment and taking appropriate antimalarials promptly in adequate doses when having fever; counselling about illness and treatment
- Prevention and personal protection: mosquito screening devices in the design of houses and protective dressing; use of insecticide-treated nets (ITN)/materials should be encouraged; use of insecticides and mosquito repellants
- Environmental management: especially reducing mosquito breeding sites
C(ii) Community mobilization strategies:
- Use community health workers to follow up patients
- Work with existing community development committees and other community organizations and leaders
- Work with people from other sectors (like partners and stakeholders) that are concerned with social and economic development of the community
questions.question:
Describe the phases, spectrum, and prevention of malaria under the following headings, explain the classification of malaria endemicity, and relate the burden of malaria in Nigeria to global figures.
A(i) Classification of malaria endemicity: hypo, meso, hyper, holoendemic – definitions, spleen rates, parasite rates, and characteristics of each zone
A(ii) Burden of malaria: global morbidity and mortality, disability-adjusted life years lost, and specific impact on child development
B(i) Malaria fever paroxysms: mechanism of release of pyrogenic substances, periodicity of each Plasmodium species, and why P. falciparum fever is different in children
B(ii) Host factors (blood group, haemoglobin type, age) that modify susceptibility to malaria
C(i) Health education for malaria prevention: personal protection, ITNs, insecticides, environmental management
C(ii) Community mobilization strategies for malaria control

A 9-year-old girl with a known heart murmur since birth presents with a 3-week history of fever, malaise, and progressive breathlessness. Her mother reports she had a tooth extraction 4 weeks ago without antibiotic cover. On examination, she is febrile, has splinter haemorrhages under the fingernails, a new pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, tender hepatomegaly, and microscopic haematuria on urinalysis. Two-dimensional echocardiography shows an oscillating mass on the mitral valve.

(i) State the diagnosis and identify the most likely predisposing factor in this patient.
(ii) List five other recognised predisposing factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe four late autonomic/immunological manifestations (beyond fever and murmur) that can develop in this condition and explain their mechanism.
(iv) State two systemic complications that can result from embolisation of vegetations from the mitral or aortic valve.
(v) List four surgical indications for this condition and justify which one applies most to this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (subacute).
Most likely predisposing factor: Dental manipulation (tooth extraction 4 weeks ago) without antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient with pre-existing congenital heart disease (VSD murmur since birth).

(ii) Other predisposing factors:
- Cardiac catheterisation
- Prolonged IV cannulation
- Septicaemic illness (especially Staph. aureus, Gram-negative organisms)
- IV drug abuse
- Urethral catheterisation/bladder instrumentation
- Endoscopic procedure
- Immunosuppression (malignancy, steroid therapy, chemotherapy, HIV)

(iii) Late autonomic/immunological manifestations:
- Petechiae: immune complex/vasculitis
- Splinter haemorrhages: microemboli or vasculitis affecting nail-bed vessels
- Osler's nodes: painless swelling found in the pulps of the fingers — immunological
- Roth's spots: exudates/haemorrhages in the eye — immune complex
- Janeway lesions: immunological/embolic
- Microscopic haematuria/nephritis: immune complex glomerulonephritis
(Any four accepted)

(iv) Systemic embolic complications from mitral/aortic valve vegetations:
- CNS: cardiovascular accident (stroke)
- Renal: acute renal failure
- Mesenteric arteries: acute abdomen
- Coronary arteries: angina/myocardial infarction
- Mycotic aneurysm (e.g. subarachnoid haemorrhage in the brain)
(Any two accepted)

(v) Surgical indications:
- Valve replacement (for destroyed valve leaflets)
- Correction of underlying heart lesion (e.g. VSD)
- Embolectomy
- Removal of mycotic aneurysm
The indication most applicable to this patient is correction of the underlying congenital heart lesion (VSD), because the pre-existing structural defect created the damaged endothelium that allowed vegetation formation; eliminating this substrate reduces the risk of recurrence.

A(i) Neonatal cholestasis is defined as conjugated bilirubin exceeding 15% of total bilirubin, or above 2.0 mg/dL. Its incidence is approximately 1 in 2500 live births. Prolonged neonatal jaundice lasting more than 14–21 days should prompt evaluation for cholestasis by fractionating serum bilirubin.
A(ii) Extrahepatic causes include biliary atresia (the most important, with progressive fibro-obliterative destruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts, requiring urgent surgical intervention) and choledochal cysts (presenting with the classic triad of jaundice, abdominal pain, and a palpable right upper quadrant mass). Biliary atresia must be diagnosed urgently before 8 weeks of age.
A(iii) Metabolic: galactosaemia (accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate from galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (accumulation of abnormal misfolded protein in hepatocytes), and cystic fibrosis (viscid secretions causing mucus plugging of bile ducts). Viral: hepatitis B virus (detectable by HBsAg), herpes simplex virus, CMV, and enteroviruses. Bacterial: syphilis, E. coli (beta-haemolytic), Listeria monocytogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Parasitic: Toxoplasma gondii (a TORCH infection). Chromosomal: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18).
B(i) Hepatobiliary scintigraphy uses Tc-99m-labelled iminodiacetic acid (IDA) derivatives taken up by hepatocytes and excreted into bile. Absent excretion into the bowel at 24 hours despite hepatic uptake strongly suggests biliary atresia, while present excretion argues against it.
B(ii) Urine-reducing substances (Clinitest) detect non-glucose sugars in urine. A positive result in a cholestatic neonate indicates galactosaemia (galactosuria), as galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency causes galactose to spill into urine. This is critical because continuing lactose-containing feeds in galactosaemia worsens liver damage.
B(iii) Liver biopsy is the most definitive investigation when non-invasive tests are inconclusive. It distinguishes biliary atresia (bile duct proliferation, portal fibrosis) from neonatal hepatitis (giant cell transformation), storage diseases, and metabolic hepatopathies.
C. The pathological progression follows: initiation of insult → liver cell inflammation (hepatitis) → inflammation of biliary tracts (cholangitis) → progressive necrosis → narrowing and obliteration of biliary ducts constituting biliary atresia. This progressive fibroinflammatory process means that early Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy — ideally before 8 weeks — can restore bile drainage before irreversible biliary cirrhosis develops. Delayed surgery beyond this window allows progressive hepatic fibrosis leading to cirrhosis and liver failure.
questions.question:
A. Describe the classification of neonatal cholestasis under the following headings:
A(i) Definition (conjugated bilirubin threshold and when to evaluate)
A(ii) Extrahepatic causes — name at least two, and identify the one most important to diagnose urgently
A(iii) Intrahepatic causes — list the metabolic, infective (viral, bacterial, parasitic), and chromosomal categories with at least one example each

B. Describe the investigation pathway for neonatal cholestasis, explaining the specific information provided by:
B(i) Hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA scan) and the radiopharmaceutical used
B(ii) Urine-reducing substances test and what a positive result indicates
B(iii) The investigation that is most definitive when all non-invasive tests are inconclusive

C. Explain why the pathological progression from cholestasis to biliary atresia makes early diagnosis and surgery critically time-sensitive, describing the sequential pathological steps.

A 15-year-old female presents with fluctuating bilateral ptosis and diplopia that worsen in the evenings and improve with rest. She also reports difficulty chewing, especially towards the end of meals. No sensory deficits are found. Reflexes are intact. A bedside test is performed and her ptosis reverses within 2 minutes.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what test was performed? Name the drug used, its pharmacological mechanism, dose, and route.
(ii) Which cranial nerves are most commonly affected in this condition?
(iii) What investigation is used to rule out an underlying structural cause in the chest, and what does it look for?
(iv) Describe the complete treatment, including first-line drugs, second-line options, and surgical treatment with its indication.
(v) State the differential diagnoses of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Myasthenia Gravis. The bedside test performed is the Edrophonium (Tensilon) Test. Drug used: Edrophonium (Tensilon). Mechanism: it is a strong short-acting anticholinesterase that increases the concentration of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by preventing its breakdown; this improves neuromuscular transmission and reverses the ptosis/weakness. Dose: 0.2 mg/kg IV. Route: intravenous. Within few minutes, the weakness/ptosis improves.

(ii) Cranial nerves most commonly affected: III (oculomotor — ptosis, diplopia from extra-ocular muscle weakness), VII (facial — facial weakness), IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory). Respiratory muscles may also be affected.

(iii) Chest X-ray: to rule out thymic hyperplasia or thymoma (seen as a thymic shadow on the chest X-ray in the anterior mediastinum).

(iv) Complete treatment:
First-line: anticholinesterase drugs — Neostigmine, Pyridostigmine, Ambemonium (these increase ACh at the NMJ to improve neuromuscular transmission).
Second-line: in non-responsive cases, give steroids.
Surgical treatment: Thymectomy (removal of the thymoma) — indicated when a thymoma is identified on chest X-ray.

(v) Differential diagnoses:
1. Hyperthyroid myopathy.
2. Hypothyroid myopathy.
3. Aminoglycoside myopathy (e.g., Gentamicin).
4. Botulism.

(i) Diagnosis: Neonatal polycythaemia / hyperviscosity state, with necrotising enterocolitis as a complication.
Definition: Venous PCV > 65%. As venous PCV rises above 65%, viscosity of blood increases and O2 transport reduces — high viscosity impairs flow through small vessels, reducing oxygen delivery to tissues.

(ii) Aetiological factors:
- Placental insufficiency; materno-foetal transfusion from delayed cord clamping; twin-twin transfusion; IDM (infant of diabetic mother); congenital adrenal hyperplasia; Trisomy 13, 18, 21; neonatal thyrotoxicosis; Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; maternal drugs (e.g. propranolol).

(iii) Clinical features:
- General: Plethora; jaundice; cyanosis; prolonged capillary refill.
- Respiratory: Tachypnoea; dyspnoea.
- GIT: Feeding problems; NEC.
- CNS: Irritability; jitteriness; lethargy; seizures.
- Laboratory: Hyperbilirubinaemia; hypoglycaemia; hypocalcaemia; prominent vascular markings on CXR.
- May be asymptomatic.

(iv) Management:
- PCV < 70% and asymptomatic: Observe.
- Symptomatic: Erythrophoresis (partial exchange transfusion with normal saline or albumin).
Volume (ml) = Blood volume × (observed PCV - desired PCV) / actual PCV.
questions.question:
A 26-week preterm infant with birth weight 800 g develops metabolic acidosis, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and thrombocytopenia at age 4 weeks. On examination there is polycythaemia with venous PCV 72%.
(i) State the full diagnosis including the complication, define polycythaemia as used, and explain why O2 transport is impaired.
(ii) List all the aetiological factors for polycythaemia in the newborn.
(iii) Describe the clinical features of polycythaemia under general, respiratory, GIT, CNS, and laboratory categories.
(iv) Outline the management of polycythaemia according to PCV level and presence of symptoms.

questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA).

(ii) Classification as right-to-left shunt: In TGA, there is ventriculo-arterial discordance — the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle. The SVC and IVC return deoxygenated systemic blood, which ends directly into the aorta. The systemic and pulmonary circuits are in parallel — deoxygenated blood continues to circulate systemically and oxygenated blood continues to recirculate through the lungs — making the condition incompatible with life unless there is a point of mixing. (Note: it is not called right-to-left shunt because of a simple defect — it is because of the SVC and IVC ending as aorta.)

(iii) Two communications that allow survival: ASD (atrial level); VSD (ventricular level); arterial fistula/PDA (arterial level) — any two.
Emergency bedside procedure: Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy — a balloon catheter is passed through the right-sided route into the right atrium, crosses the foramen ovale into the left atrium, the balloon is inflated, and pulled back to create a patent atrial septal defect, allowing mixing of blood.

(iv) Medical management on admission:
- Treatment of heart failure: diuretics and digoxin
- Supportive: manage respiratory distress, correct acidosis
(Heart failure is common in TGA; management involves the above.)

(v) Two definitive surgical operations:
1. Mustard operation (open heart surgery): The atrial septum is removed and an atrial baffle is created to divert blood from the right atrium into the left ventricle and thence to the pulmonary artery. The patient becomes pink dramatically. Prognosis is good.
2. Arterial switch operation (open heart surgery): Surgical correction at the level of the great arteries.
questions.question:
A 10-day-old neonate presents to the emergency room in severe respiratory distress and cardiovascular collapse. The mother reports that the baby appeared slightly blue at birth but seemed to improve over the first few days. He began feeding poorly and became progressively breathless and grey on day 8. On examination, he is cyanosed, tachycardic, hypotensive, and has markedly reduced femoral pulses with bounding brachial pulses. Auscultation reveals a loud single S2 and an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette on chest X-ray with markedly increased pulmonary vascular markings.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis?
(ii) Explain why this condition is classified as right-to-left shunt in terms of the anatomical arrangement of the great vessels, and why it is incompatible with life without additional communications.
(iii) Identify two communications that allow the baby to survive, and state what emergency bedside procedure was performed by the cardiologist using a balloon catheter.
(iv) Describe the medical management on admission.
(v) Name the two definitive surgical operations for this condition and briefly state what each involves.

A 2-hour-old term male neonate develops grunting and respiratory distress. He passed meconium in utero. The amniotic fluid was thick and meconium-stained. At birth he was depressed and required bag-and-mask ventilation.
(i) State the diagnosis, explain the aetiopathogenesis, and state why this is a problem of term and late-preterm infants specifically.
(ii) List the common causes of respiratory distress in the newborn under the categories of pulmonary (common) and pulmonary (less common).
(iii) List all four upper airway structural causes of respiratory distress given.
(iv) Define tachypnoea and bradypnoea as thresholds given and list all signs of respiratory distress as enumerated.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS).
Aetiopathogenesis: Intrauterine asphyxia causes foetal distress → the foetus passes meconium into the amniotic fluid → meconium is inhaled (aspirated) before, during, or after delivery → airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, and surfactant inactivation → respiratory distress.
It is a problem of term and late-preterm infants specifically because preterm infants rarely pass meconium in utero (immature GI motility); meconium in liquor is predominantly a feature of term and post-term infants subject to intrauterine stress.

(ii) Causes of respiratory distress:
Common pulmonary causes: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn; meconium aspiration syndrome; congenital/neonatal pneumonia; respiratory distress syndrome (HMD); pneumothorax.
Less common pulmonary causes: Upper airway obstruction; space-occupying lesions (diaphragmatic hernia; congenital lobar emphysema; congenital cystic malformations); pulmonary hypoplasia; pulmonary haemorrhage; chronic lung diseases (BPD).

(iii) Upper airway structural causes: Vasomotor rhinitis; choanal atresia; laryngeal web; and (from less common column) diaphragmatic hernia (space-occupying lesion compressing airway).
The four specifically named upper airway causes: vasomotor rhinitis; choanal atresia; laryngeal web; and upper airway obstruction (as a category).

(iv) Tachypnoea: RR > 60/min. Bradypnoea: below normal respiratory rate (bradypnoea is a sign; tachypnoea is defined as RR > 60/min; bradypnoea = slow respiratory rate below normal range of 30–40/min).
Signs of respiratory distress:
Tachypnoea (RR > 60/min); bradypnoea; intercostal indrawing; lower chest wall indrawing; subcostal indrawing; flaring of ala nasi; grunting; cyanosis.
Note: Not all respiratory distress has a respiratory cause.

questions.question:
A preterm infant born at 30 weeks gestation presents at 3 days of life with tachypnoea, bounding pulses, a to-and-fro continuous murmur loudest in the infraclavicular area, and features of congestive heart failure. The chest X-ray shows increased pulmonary vascular markings and cardiomegaly.

(i) Identify the structure responsible for these findings and explain why it persists in this clinical setting.
(ii) Describe the haemodynamic changes set up by this structure — explaining why it behaves haemodynamically like a VSD rather than an ASD.
(iii) List the full clinical features — symptoms and signs — of this condition, and distinguish the murmur character from that of other continuous murmurs.
(iv) Outline the investigations and expected findings, and state all management options.
questions.answerText:
(i) Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) — persistent patency of a normal fetal structure between the pulmonary artery and descending aorta. It normally closes 48 hours after delivery. In preterm infants, reduced oxygen tension (from prematurity and risk of birth asphyxia) is needed to close the duct; failure of this mechanism keeps it patent. The ductus arteriosus closure is mediated by prostaglandin effects (indomethacin has a dilatatory effect on the ductus).

(ii) PDA is classified as a left-to-right shunt because blood flows from the aorta (higher pressure) into the pulmonary artery. It involves the high pressure system — aorta to pulmonary artery — unlike ASD which is associated with the low-pressure atrial system (gradient only 3–4 mmHg). Haemodynamic changes are essentially similar to VSD: excessive blood recirculates through the lungs, causing pulmonary congestion and eventual congestive heart failure through the same vicious cycles of increased preload, pulmonary hypertension, and fluid retention.

(iii) Clinical features (depend on size of defect):
Small defect: insignificant
Large defect symptoms: small for gestational age; tachypnoea; features of congestive heart failure.
Signs: bounding/collapsing pulses; to-and-fro/continuous machinery murmur — very characteristic in the infraclavicular area; continuous because it spans both systole and diastole, with higher pitch in systole and lower pitch in diastole. Unlike venous hum (benign, at base of neck, less loud), the PDA murmur is loudest under the left clavicle and is pathological.

(iv) Investigations:
- CXR: increased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary plethora); cardiomegaly if heart failure has set in
- ECG: initially LVH, then biventricular changes
- ECHO with Doppler: demonstrates the duct and left-to-right shunt
- Cardiac catheterisation: confirms the defect; measures pressures
Management: treat congestive heart failure (digoxin and diuretics). Medical closure: indomethacin (prostaglandin inhibitor) — especially in preterm neonates. Surgical ligation: definitive treatment for persistent PDA.

(i) Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) — the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease worldwide. The four components are:
- Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO) — usually infundibular
- Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)
- Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
- Over-riding (dextropositioned) aorta

(ii) Embryologically, the heart develops from a single heart tube. In TOF, the arterial septum divides unequally — the left half is much bigger than the right — resulting in pulmonary stenosis and an over-riding aorta. This unequal septation also causes the VSD. Haemodynamically, RVOTO raises right ventricular pressure, leading to RVH; when RV pressure exceeds LV pressure, desaturated blood shunts right-to-left through the VSD into the aorta, causing cyanosis.

(iii) Management of hypercyanotic spell (emergency):
- Place child in knee-chest position — most important step
- Give oxygen by face mask or nasal catheter
- Give intravenous propranolol 0.1 mg/kg/dose (alternative: IM/IV morphia 0.1 mg/kg/dose)
- Give sodium bicarbonate IV, dose 1 mEq/kg

(iv) Palliative surgery: Blalock-Taussig shunt — shunts blood from systemic to pulmonary circulation.
Classical: subclavian artery cut and anastomosed to pulmonary artery (no post-op radial pulse).
Modified: Gore-tex graft interposed; subclavian artery preserved; used for smaller patients.
Criteria for successful shunt: disappearance of cyanosis; shunt murmur heard; improved symptomatology; PCV falls and stabilises at 45–55%; CXR shows no more pulmonary oligaemia.
Definitive treatment: open heart surgery to close the VSD, requiring cardiopulmonary bypass (heart-lung machine).
questions.question:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a history of cyanosis since infancy, easy fatiguability, effort intolerance, and episodes of assuming a squatting or knee-chest position after exertion. The mother reports episodes when the child becomes deeply blue, cries uncontrollably, and occasionally loses consciousness.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and state the four structural components that define it?
(ii) Explain the embryological basis of this condition and the haemodynamic changes that produce cyanosis.
(iii) Describe the immediate steps for managing a hypercyanotic/hypoxic spell in this child.
(iv) State the palliative surgical procedure available and the criteria for a successful outcome. What is the definitive treatment?

A 4-year-old presents with a 5-week history of intensely itchy papules and burrows on the web spaces of the fingers and toes, and the extensor surfaces. Multiple classmates have similar lesions.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis? State the causative organism, mode of transmission, and incubation period.
(ii) Describe all the sites of predilection.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology — why pruritus occurs and what lesions are formed.
(iv) Outline the complete management of the child and explain why treatment of household members and classmates is mandatory.
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Scabies. Causative organism: Sarcoptes scabiei. Mode of transmission: fomites. Incubation period: 4–6 weeks.

(ii) Sites of predilection: extensor surfaces; webs of toes and fingers; rarely scalp; soles of foot in infants.

(iii) Pathophysiology: the mite Sarcoptes scabiei burrows into the skin, causing an inflammatory reaction; the primary lesions are papules, burrows, and vesicles; intense pruritus results from the host's hypersensitivity reaction to mite proteins, eggs, and faeces within the burrow.

(iv) Management of the child:
- 12.5–25% benzyl benzoate
- Ivermectin
- Permethrin
- Antihistamines (for pruritus)
- Antibiotics (for secondary bacterial infection)
Treatment of household members and classmates (all contacts) is mandatory because scabies is transmitted via fomites and close contact; untreated household members and classmates serve as reservoirs for re-infestation, making individual treatment alone insufficient to eradicate the outbreak.

(i) Diagnosis and confirmation:
- Diagnosis: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL).
- Definitive diagnosis is confirmed with Bone Marrow Aspiration showing leukaemia cells (lymphoblasts).
- Note: Presence of blasts in peripheral film alone is NOT diagnostic.
- ALL is the commonest childhood malignancy in Caucasians; accounts for 7.1% in Ibadan; peak age 2–5 years; occurs more often in Down's syndrome.
(ii) ALL versus AML:
ALL:
- Commoner in children; peak age 2–5 years.
- Peripheral blood: blast cells (lymphoblasts); WBC usually high but may be low or normal; platelet count usually low; anaemia present.
- Clinically significant hyperleucocytosis at WBC >300,000/mm³ in ALL.
