- Prognosis: In good centres 80% cure can be achieved. Better in non-B, non-T cell type; worse with B cell, T cell, and pre-B types. Better for ages 2–10 years; worse in males and in blacks.
AML:
- Less common in children.
- Clinically significant hyperleucocytosis at WBC >200,000/mm³ in AML (lower threshold than ALL).
- Prognosis: Worse than ALL; prognosis is worse with AML overall.
(iii) Hyperleucocytosis and associated oncologic emergency:
- Clinically significant hyperleucocytosis in ALL: WBC >300,000/mm³. (Defined as WBC count >100,000/mm³; incidence 9–13% of ALL with 5% mortality.)
- At WBC 90,000/mm³ the patient is approaching this threshold; Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS) may develop spontaneously or with treatment.
Metabolic abnormalities constituting TLS (≥2 of the following within 3 days before or up to 7 days after therapy):
- Hyperkalemia: K >6 mEq/L (or 25% increase).
- Hyperuricemia: uric acid >8 mg/dl (or 25% increase).
- Hyperphosphatemia: PO₄ >6.5 mg/dl (or 25% increase).
- Hypocalcemia: ionized calcium <1.5 mEq/L (3 mg/dl) (or 25% decrease).
- Uric acid nephropathy and acute kidney injury are clinical TLS features.
(iv) Treatment, relapse sites, and poor prognostic factors:
Treatment regimen — COAP:
- Cyclophosphamide.
- Oncovin (Vincristine).
- Adriamycin.
- Prednisolone.
- Radiotherapy can also be used; Bone marrow transplantation.
Sites of relapse:
- Bone marrow (commonest site).
- CNS.
- Testes.
Factors that determine poor prognosis in ALL:
- Age: <2 years or >10 years.
- Race: worse in blacks.
- Sex: worse in males (testes are sanctuary sites).
- WBC: worse if initial value >50,000/mm³.
- Type: worse with B cell, T cell, and pre-B types; better in non-B, non-T cell.
- AML has a worse prognosis than ALL overall.
questions.question:
A 9-year-old presents with fever, generalised lymphadenopathy predominantly in the neck, hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, and bleeding gums. The WBC is 90,000/mm³ with numerous blast cells on peripheral film. Bone marrow aspiration confirms >80% lymphoblasts.
(i) What is the diagnosis and how is it confirmed (state the definitive diagnostic criterion)?
(ii) Using the WHO/clinical classification, distinguish ALL from AML in terms of patient age predilection, peripheral blood findings, and prognostic differences.
(iii) This patient's WBC is 90,000/mm³. At what WBC threshold does Hyperleucocytosis become clinically significant in ALL, and what additional oncologic emergency may develop? State all the metabolic abnormalities that constitute this emergency.
(iv) State the treatment regimen for ALL and describe ALL the sites of relapse and the factors that determine a poor prognosis.

Describe the anatomy and pathological significance of haemoglobinopathies under the following headings:
A(i) Define haemoglobinopathy and distinguish between qualitative and quantitative types, giving the principal examples.
A(ii) Describe the normal haemoglobin variants and the structural changes in HbS and HbC.
B(i) Describe the epidemiology and genetics of sickle cell disease including haplotypes, mode of inheritance, and frequency in Nigeria.
B(ii) Explain the diagnostic approach to haemoglobinopathies, distinguishing the laboratory methods used in neonates versus older children.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and types:
- Haemoglobinopathy refers to abnormalities of the globin component of the haemoglobin molecule. Abnormalities of the haem component are referred to as the porphyrias.
- May be qualitative or quantitative.
- Sickle cell disease = qualitative haemoglobinopathy.
- Thalassaemia = quantitative haemoglobinopathy.

A(ii) Normal Hb variants and structural changes:
- Normal Hb: Hb F (α₂γ₂): predominant from 9/12 to 1 year, then <2%; Hb A₂ (α₂δ₂): 2.5–3.5%; Hb A (α₂β₂): >95%.
- Most variants substitute a single amino acid in the α or β chain.
- HbS: Glu→Val at position 6 of the β chain (thymine for adenine at sixth codon of beta gene); encodes valine instead of glutamine.
- HbC: substitution of glutamic acid by lysine at position 6 of the beta chain. HbC trait frequency varies from 3–4% in Nigeria to 15–20% in parts of Ghana and Burkina Faso.
- Altered solubility or abnormal properties of aggregation: HbS, HbC.
- Thalassaemias: abnormal and unbalanced rates of production of normal polypeptide chains.

B(i) Epidemiology, genetics and haplotypes:
- HbS gene is due to spontaneous mutation which occurred at least thrice in different parts of Africa: Atlantic, Central, and Bantu-speaking Africa. First observed in 1910 by J.B. Herrick.
- Mode of inheritance: Autosomal recessive.
- HbS prevalent in malaria-endemic regions (balanced polymorphism); distribution worldwide, with greatest incidence in tropical Africa.
- In Nigeria: 2–3% of newborns are homozygous; frequency of S gene in Nigeria = 25%; incidence in general population 1:300. In Ibadan: HbSS 3.1%, HbS+C 1.1%, HbA+S 23.7%.
- Haplotypes (named after places of first description):
  1. Senegal: Atlantic coast of West Africa — least severe clinical course on average.
  2. Benin: Central West Africa (Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire) — intermediate severity.
  3. Bantu/Central African Republic: Zaire, CAR, Angola, Kenya — most severe.
  4. Asian: Eastern Saudi Arabia, Central India — more benign course.

B(ii) Diagnostic approach:
Neonates: HPLC (High Performance Liquid Chromatography), Isoelectric focussing.
Post-neonatal (older children): Cellulose acetate electrophoresis; citrate agar electrophoresis.
Solubility test: 4 drops blood + 2 ml freshly prepared Na dithionite + K₂PO₄; HbA/CC/DD = clear solution; HbSS = precipitate above, clear solution beneath; HbAS = precipitate above, pink solution beneath. NB: HbD has the same electrophoretic mobility as HbS, so a sickling test and solubility studies must also be done.
Other: PCV, Blood film appearance; Lab findings in HbSS: Hb 5–9 g/dl, retic 5–15%, WBC 12–20,000, normal MCV, target cells, poikilocytosis, sickled RBC, Howell-Jolly bodies.

A(i) Bell's Palsy is a disorder of cranial nerve VII. It is associated with herpes zoster or otitis media infection.

A(ii) Clinical features:
- Onset: tends to be sudden in onset.
- Weakness of one side of the face (unilateral facial weakness).
- Bell's sign or phenomenon: the angle of the mouth is deviated to the normal (unaffected) side.
- Eye finding: on the weak side, the eye cannot close; when the patient attempts to close the eye, the eyeball rolls upward (Bell's phenomenon).
- Hyperacusis: because the stapedius muscle (dampening effect on the stapes) is paralysed, the dampening effect is removed, causing increased sensitivity to sound (hyperacusis) and ringing in the ear.

A(iii) Treatment:
- There is no definite treatment for Bell's Palsy.
- It disappears within a few weeks.
- The single most important management step: protect the eye during the illness — instil artificial tears or normal saline; use a plaster to cover the eye at night (prevents corneal exposure and injury from inability to close the eye).

B(i) Anatomical basis of hyperacusis: the facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the stapedius muscle in the middle ear. The stapedius normally dampens excessive vibration of the stapes (ossicle), protecting the cochlea from loud sounds. When CN VII is damaged, the stapedius is paralysed, removing this dampening effect, and resulting in hypersensitivity to sound (hyperacusis) and ringing in the ear (tinnitus).

B(ii) Inability to close the eye: CN VII supplies the orbicularis oculi muscle, which closes the eyelids. When CN VII is paralysed, the orbicularis oculi cannot contract to close the eye. On attempted closure, the intact superior rectus muscle (CN III) causes the eyeball to roll upward — this is Bell's phenomenon.

B(iii) Deviation of mouth to normal side: CN VII supplies all muscles of facial expression on the ipsilateral side, including the orbicularis oris, buccinator, and other perioral muscles. When these are paralysed on the affected side, the intact muscles on the normal side pull the angle of the mouth toward the normal side.

C. Peripheral vs. central (UMN) facial palsy:
- Peripheral (Bell's Palsy): affects all muscles of facial expression on the ipsilateral side, including the upper face (brow and forehead); patient cannot wrinkle the forehead on the affected side; no brow-sparing; may have hyperacusis and taste disturbance.
- Central (UMN) palsy: the upper face (forehead/brow) is relatively spared because the cortical motor area for the upper face has bilateral representation; patient can still wrinkle the forehead; brow-sparing is present; weakness is limited to the lower face (nasolabial fold flattening, mouth weakness); associated neurological findings may include hemiplegia or other ipsilateral cortical signs.
questions.question:
A. Describe Bell's Palsy under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, aetiology, and associated conditions.
A(ii) Clinical features: onset, nature of facial weakness, Bell's sign, the eye finding on attempted closure, and hearing-related symptoms with their anatomical basis.
A(iii) Treatment and the single most important management step.

B. Explain the anatomical basis for each of the following features of Bell's Palsy:
B(i) Hyperacusis.
B(ii) Inability of the eye to close (with the eyeball rolling up on attempted closure).
B(iii) Deviation of the angle of the mouth to the normal side.

C. Distinguish Bell's Palsy (peripheral cranial nerve VII palsy) from a central (UMN) facial nerve palsy, based on: muscles affected, brow-sparing, and associated neurological findings.

questions.answerText:
(i) Epiglottitis. The lateral radiograph identifies the swollen epiglottis (wide and thumb-like with shallow pre-epiglottic space); normally the epiglottis appears thin or triangular.

(ii) Primary cause: Haemophilus influenzae type b (direct invasion of the involved tissues is probably the initiating pathophysiological event). In immunosuppressed patients: Candida, herpes simplex, varicella, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococci.

(iii) Cellulitis of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and arytenoid cartilage causes swelling that compresses the supraglottic airway; this results in high fever, stridor, drooling, and the characteristic posture. Because of the risk of sudden, unpredictable airway obstruction, it is a medical emergency.

(iv) Supraglottic causes: epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, diphtheria. Glottic and subglottic causes: croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, vocal cord paralysis. Intrathoracic causes: foreign bodies, congenital webs, vascular slings.

(v) If the airway is patent, do not disturb the child. Immediate endotracheal intubation must be performed once diagnosis is made — most anaesthesiologists prefer general anaesthesia (not muscle relaxants). After the airway is secured, blood culture and epiglottis culture are obtained. Start intravenous antibiotics covering H. influenzae: ceftriaxone or equivalent cephalosporin. IV antibiotics for 2–3 days, then oral antibiotics to complete a 10-day course. Extubation when direct inspection shows significant reduction in epiglottis size (usually 24–48 hours). Humidified oxygen and IV fluids are also given.
questions.question:
A 4-year-old child presents with a 2-day history of high fever, drooling, aphonia, and acute-onset stridor. The child appears toxic, prefers to sit leaning forward with the mouth open and tongue protruding. A lateral neck radiograph shows a wide, thumb-like epiglottis with a shallow pre-epiglottic space.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and which structure is identified on the radiograph?
(ii) Which aetiological agent is primarily responsible and which other organisms are implicated in immunosuppressed patients?
(iii) What compressed or affected structures produce the clinical features?
(iv) List the differential diagnoses of acute stridor in children, categorising them by anatomical level.
(v) State the immediate management including airway intervention and antibiotic therapy.

A(i) Describe the process of genetic counselling under the following headings: definition of consultand and proband, principles of accurate diagnosis, depth of explanation, and calculation of recurrence risk.
A(ii) State all available reproductive options that should be discussed with a couple who have had a child with an autosomal recessive disorder.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis of why the frequency of congenital malformations increases from 2–3% at birth to 6% in 2-year-olds and 8% in 5-year-olds, and distinguish between major and minor malformations and their clinical significance.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Genetic counselling:
• Definition: genetic counselling is the communication of information and advice about inherited conditions. A person seeking advice is called a CONSULTAND; the affected individual who caused the consultand(s) to seek advice is called the PROBAND. Often the proband is a child, but may also be the consultand or a more distant relative.
• Accurate diagnosis: accurate diagnosis is essential for meaningful genetic counselling. Without a firm diagnosis, recurrence risks and management cannot be accurately conveyed.
• Principles: adequate time should be allowed in an appropriate setting; if the proband is a child, both parents should be counselled; counselling should include all aspects of the condition; the depth of explanation should be matched to the educational level of the consultand; time should be taken to deal with guilt and perceived social stigma; misconceptions about the condition and of heredity in general may need to be dealt with.
• Recurrence risk: a recurrence risk should always be calculated for the consultand; the recurrence risk should be explained against the background of the general population risk for the condition; reproductive options should be discussed.

A(ii) Reproductive options to discuss:
• Proceed to a further pregnancy (with or without prenatal diagnosis)
• Artificial insemination by donor (AID)
• In vitro fertilisation (with or without pre-implantation diagnosis)
• Adoption
• Contraception (reversible or non-reversible)

B(i) Increasing frequency of congenital malformations with age:
• At birth, 2–3% of newborns have major congenital malformations. Additional malformations are detected after birth: thus the frequency is 6% in 2-year-olds and 8% in 5-year-olds. An additional 2% will be detected later in life (during imaging procedures, at surgery, at autopsy).
• The increase reflects that many malformations are internal (cardiac, renal, neurological) and only become clinically apparent when the child fails to achieve developmental milestones, when symptoms arise, or when investigated for other reasons.
• Major vs minor malformations: Major malformations have major medical, surgical, or cosmetic consequences. Minor malformations do not have major medical, surgical, or cosmetic consequences. Single minor malformations are present in about 14% of newborns; minor malformations are clinically significant because they may point to the presence of associated major anomalies (e.g. single umbilical artery). The aetiology of congenital malformations: idiopathic 60%, multifactorial 20%, monogenic 7.5%, chromosomal 6%, maternal illness 3%, congenital infection 2%, drugs/X-ray/alcohol 1.5%.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old girl is brought with progressive right-sided proptosis and a whitish reflex from her right eye (leukocoria). Ophthalmoscopy confirms an intraocular mass. Her mother mentions that a sibling had the same condition affecting both eyes.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and describe its genetic basis and pattern of inheritance.
(ii) List ALL the clinical features and sites of metastasis.
(iii) What treatment modalities are available, and how does the stage influence the choice?
(iv) Describe Rhabdomyosarcoma: its origin, peak age groups, sites of presentation, the unique variant called Sarcoma Botryoides, and its treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Retinoblastoma.
Genetic basis and inheritance:
- Is a malignant tumour arising from the retina.
- 2/3 of cases are unilateral; 10–20% of these unilateral cases are inherited in autosomal dominant fashion.
- 1/3 of cases are bilateral and almost all are inherited in autosomal dominant fashion.
- It arises from mutation or deletion of chromosome 13.
- Incidence: age 1–3 years.
(ii) Clinical features:
- Cat-eye reflex or leucocoria (leukocoria): an early feature.
- Mass protruding from the eye.
- Strabismus.
- Proptosis: in late cases.
Sites of metastasis: Brain, Orbits, Liver, Bones, Face, Lung, Lymph nodes, Bone marrow.
(iii) Treatment modalities and stage influence:
Earlier stage: Laser therapy (photocoagulation); Cryotherapy (use of cold to freeze).
Advanced stage: Chemotherapy; Radiotherapy (external beam — causes secondary orbit tumour).
Note: In Ibadan, surgery (Enucleation) is done for most cases (with radiotherapy).
(iv) Rhabdomyosarcoma:
- Arises from the same embryonic mesenchyme as striated muscle; is the commonest soft tissue sarcoma.
- Three peak age groups: 2–6 years and 15–19 years. Sex: Male > Female.
Sites (in order of frequency): Head and neck region — 40% (commonest site; may present as jaw tumour, making it a strong differential diagnosis of Burkitt's Lymphoma); Extremities — 20%; Urinary tract — 20%; Others: Trunk, Retroperitoneal, GIT.
Sarcoma Botryoides: a form of rhabdomyosarcoma occurring in girls; presents as a grape-like tumour projecting into body cavity e.g. vagina, uterus, bladder, nasopharynx.
Treatment: depends on site and extent; modalities: Surgery (subtotal excision or debulking); Radiotherapy; Chemotherapy — Vincristine, Adriamycin, Cyclophosphamide.

(i) Using the classification table — Appearance: Abnormal (irritable); Work of Breathing: Normal; Circulation: Abnormal → This corresponds to Decompensated shock. The circulatory/cardiovascular system is the primary system affected.

(ii) Blood pressure 60 mmHg is below the lower limit. Formula: hypotension = systolic BP <70 + 2n mmHg (where n = age in years). For a 2-year-old: lower limit = 70 + (2 × 2) = 74 mmHg; 60 mmHg is below this threshold, confirming hypotension. Hypotension is a very late sign; 25% of blood volume must be lost before a drop in blood pressure occurs; minimal changes in blood pressure in children may indicate shock.

(iii) Circulation assessment parameters: heart rate and rhythm; pulse rate and synchronicity (peripheral and central); capillary refill time; skin colour and temperature; blood pressure.
Disability — glucose management ('Don't Ever Forget Glucose' — DEFG): close monitoring of random blood sugar (RBS); correct hypoglycaemia when present: 2–4 ml/kg of D10 (10% dextrose water). Also assess: level of consciousness (AVPU scale or GCS); pupillary response (PERRL — pinpoint, dilated, or unequal). Consider adrenal insufficiency in refractory shock.

(iv) Compensated shock: clinical signs of inadequate perfusion but normal blood pressure; vital organ functions are maintained. Signs: tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, fussy/irritable child (early signs of shock).
Decompensated shock: severely impaired perfusion; organ and cellular function deteriorates. Signs: absent pulses, cool extremities, mottled skin, altered sensorium, hypotension develops.
Reason early recognition is critical: shock progression is unpredictable; the sequence is: compensated shock (possibly hours) → hypotensive shock (potentially minutes) → cardiac arrest. Early recognition and prompt intervention are critical to halting the progression. Only 10% of children who progress to cardiopulmonary arrest are successfully resuscitated; whereas 92% of children with respiratory arrest only have no subsequent neurologic impairment.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old is rushed to the emergency unit. She is irritable, with cool and mottled extremities, a capillary refill time of 4 seconds, and weak peripheral pulses. Her respiratory rate is 60/min. Her blood pressure is 60 mmHg systolic (age-based lower limit is 74 mmHg).

(i) Using the primary assessment framework described, identify the physiological state (from the appearance/work-of-breathing/circulation classification table) and name the organ/system affected.
(ii) What is the significance of her blood pressure reading, and what formula is used to calculate hypotension in children?
(iii) List all the structures and parameters assessed under Circulation in the primary assessment, and state the glucose management approach under Disability.
(iv) Distinguish between the findings expected in compensated and decompensated shock using all the clinical signs stated, and explain why early recognition and prompt intervention are described as critical.

A public health officer is reviewing child mortality data for a sub-Saharan African country. The under-five mortality rate is 110 per 1000 live births, and the country is listed among those with the highest child mortality burden.

(i) State the global burden of under-five mortality (total deaths in 2013, daily toll, and the comparison between WHO African and European regions).
(ii) List all the countries named as having the highest child mortality burden.
(iii) Describe the global trend in under-five mortality from 1990 to 2013, including percentage reduction and the annual rate of acceleration noted, and the target that was not met.
(iv) Identify the three factors responsible for high rates in low-income countries, and explain the projected impact on under-five deaths if no progress is made in sub-Saharan Africa by 2050.
questions.answerText:
(i) Global burden (2013 figures): 6.3 million children under age five died in 2013, nearly 17,000 every day (according to WHO). The risk of a child dying before completing five years is highest in the WHO African region (90 per 1000 live births), about 7 times higher than in the WHO European region (12 per 1000). In 2013, the under-five mortality rate in low-income countries was 76 deaths per 1000 live births — almost 13 times the average rate in high-income countries (6 per 1000).

(ii) Countries with the highest child mortality burden: Afghanistan, Mali, Somalia, Central African Republic, Guinea-Bissau, Chad, Niger, Angola, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, South Sudan, Zambia, Gambia, Comoros, Burundi.

(iii) Global trend: globally, under-five mortality decreased by 49%, from an estimated rate of 90 deaths per 1000 live births in 1990 to 46 per 1000 in 2013. The average annual rate of reduction has accelerated — from 1.2% per year (1990–1995) to 4.0% for 2005–2013. About 17,000 fewer children died every day in 2013 than in 1990. However, this remains insufficient to reach MDG 4 (which required a two-thirds reduction). Three WHO regions achieved >60% decline (Americas, European, Western Pacific); the WHO African Region's share of under-five deaths is increasing despite decreasing rates.

(iv) Three factors responsible for high rates in low-income countries: place of delivery; antenatal visits during pregnancy; source of drinking water.
Projected impact (Sub-Saharan Africa by 2050): by 2050, 37% of the world's children under age five will live in Sub-Saharan Africa, while close to 40% of all live births will take place in that region. Therefore, the number of under-five deaths may stagnate or even increase without much progress in that region.

(i) Diagnosis: Valvar aortic stenosis.
Justification of clinical clues:
- Ejection click at the apex: Indicates valvar obstruction (an ejection click is generated by forced/pressurised flow against the wall of the aorta/pulmonary artery — specifically a valvar click; it is heard at the apex and is due to the tensing of the abnormal valve leaflets at the start of ejection). Present in valvar AS; absent in subvalvar and supravalvar.
- ESM at right upper sternal edge: The aortic area — this is where aortic stenosis murmur is loudest (valvar AS).
- Post-stenotic dilatation of ascending aorta on CXR: Confirms valvar obstruction — the jet from the valve strikes the aortic wall downstream, causing post-stenotic dilatation. In subvalvar AS, the jet dissipates before the valve, so post-stenotic dilatation is less marked.

(ii) Mechanism of reversed (paradoxical) splitting of S2:
In severe aortic stenosis, the left ventricle takes longer to empty due to obstruction. This delays aortic valve closure (A2) beyond pulmonary valve closure (P2). Therefore, P2 occurs BEFORE A2 (opposite of normal). On inspiration, increased right heart filling moves P2 earlier, bringing P2 and A2 closer together (splitting narrows on inspiration). On expiration, P2 moves away from A2 (splitting widens on expiration) — this is the paradoxical/reversed splitting pattern.

(iii) Mechanism of anacrotic (slow-rising, small-volume) pulse:
The obstruction at the aortic valve reduces and delays peak aortic flow during systole. The pulse therefore rises slowly (prolonged upstroke) and achieves a lower peak (small volume). The resulting pulse is of small volume and slow-rising — termed anacrotic or pulsus parvus et tardus.

(iv) Differences in subvalvar AS:
- Murmur location: Loudest at 3rd or 4th right intercostal space (slightly lower than in valvar AS, which is 2nd right intercostal space — aortic area)
- Ejection click: Absent in subvalvar AS (the click is a valvar event; in subvalvar, the valve itself is normal, so no click)
- Pulse in each arm: Equal bilaterally in subvalvar AS. In supravalvar AS, right arm pulse is greater than left arm pulse (due to blood jet directed into the right brachiocephalic artery — Coanda effect)
- Post-stenotic aortic dilatation: Less prominent or absent in subvalvar AS

(v) Differential diagnosis of ESM at right upper sternal edge: Aortic regurgitation (diastolic component); hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; systemic hypertension.
Confirming findings:
CXR: Normal initially; post-stenotic dilatation of ascending aorta (cardiomegaly with prominence of ascending aorta); ± calcification of aortic valve in older patients
ECG: May be normal; or left ventricular hypertrophy; inverted T-wave
ECHO: Thickened valve; LVH; Doppler demonstrates turbulence across the obstruction; shows the anatomical change (valve morphology)
questions.question:
A 3-year-old child is evaluated for a murmur discovered at a health check. He is acyanotic, well-nourished, and has no dysmorphic features. On auscultation there is an ejection click at the apex, an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge, and a reversed (paradoxical) splitting of S2. Blood pressure shows a small pulse volume with a slow-rising (anacrotic) pulse. CXR shows post-stenotic dilatation of the ascending aorta. ECHO shows a thickened valve with left ventricular hypertrophy.

(i) Identify the diagnosis and the specific type (valvar, subvalvar, or supravalvar) based on the clinical clues given, justifying each clue.
(ii) Explain the mechanism of the reversed (paradoxical) splitting of S2 in this condition.
(iii) Explain the mechanism of the anacrotic pulse.
(iv) Describe how the clinical findings would differ if the lesion were subvalvar rather than valvar (murmur location, ejection click presence, pulse finding in each arm).
(v) State the differential diagnosis that must be considered and list the CXR, ECG, and ECHO findings that confirm this diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) causing virilisation of a female infant. Embryological basis: absent cortisol leads to excessive ACTH production as a result of failure of the negative feedback mechanism. ACTH drives adrenal hyperplasia, which stimulates other pathways in cholesterol metabolism above the enzyme block, leading to excess androgen production. Virilisation of the female infant occurs in utero; she presents at birth with ambiguous genitalia — clitoral enlargement and labial fusion (the clitoris may be mistaken for a penis, leading to a mistaken diagnosis of hypospadias). Internal genitals are normal female. The enzyme defect is 21-hydroxylase deficiency (accounts for 90–95% of all CAH).

(ii) Investigations confirming diagnosis and severity:
• Plasma 17-OHprogesterone: elevated (in 21-hydroxylase and 11-hydroxylase deficiency)
• Urinary 17-ketosteroids: elevated (elevated in 21-OHlase; pregnenatriol also elevated)
• Plasma cortisol: reduced
• Serum Na+, Cl-, HCO3-: reduced; K+: elevated; acidosis; hypoglycaemia — confirm salt-losing form
• Urinary pregnenatriol: elevated in 21-hydroxylase deficiency
• Buccal smear and karyotyping to confirm 46,XX
• Skeletal survey: bone age may be advanced if diagnosis is delayed

(iii) Salt-losing crisis resuscitation: IV Normal saline and 5% dextrose (or plasma if in shock); IV Hydrocortisone 50 mg immediately. Correct electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypoglycaemia). Monitor TPR, BP, blood glucose.

(iv) Long-term management:
• Medical: hydrocortisone IM for 7–10 days initially (under 2 years: 25 mg/24 hrs; under 5 years: 50–75 mg/24 hrs, in 2–3 divided doses). Then oral hydrocortisone 20–25 mg/m²/day every 8 hours to suppress ACTH. Fludrocortisone 100 mcg/day orally to replace aldosterone. Deoxycorticosterone acetate in addition to hydrocortisone. Salt supplementation 2–3 g/day for salt losers.
• Surgical: female genital abnormalities are surgically corrected (clitoroplasty, vaginoplasty).
• Monitoring: serial urinary ketosteroids; watch for under-treatment (raised 17-OHprogesterone, androstenedione, renin, advanced bone age, virilisation) and over-treatment (suppressed growth, hypercortisolism).
questions.question:
A newborn girl is noted to have ambiguous external genitalia. The clitoris is enlarged and there is labial fusion. The karyotype is 46,XX. Investigations show markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, low plasma cortisol, elevated ACTH, and elevated urinary ketosteroids.

(i) State the diagnosis, embryological basis, and the specific enzyme defect.
(ii) What investigations confirm the diagnosis and indicate severity?
(iii) What is the resuscitation approach if the infant presents in a salt-losing crisis?
(iv) What are the surgical and long-term medical management options?

Describe neonatal jaundice (hyperbilirubinaemia) comprehensively.
A(i) Describe the metabolism of bilirubin from haem to excretion, naming the enzymes and proteins involved.
A(ii) State the physiological reasons why newborns produce bilirubin at a 2–3 fold greater rate than adults.
B(i) Distinguish between physiological and non-physiological jaundice using the criteria given (onset, peak level, duration).
B(ii) List the causes of non-physiological (pathological) jaundice under the categories of haemolysis, obstruction, and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Bilirubin metabolism:
- Haem (mainly from haemoglobin) is converted to biliverdin by microsomal haem oxygenase; biliverdin is converted to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase. Biliverdin is colourless and non-toxic; bilirubin is yellow and potentially toxic at high levels. Byproducts: iron (Fe, almost 100% re-circulated) and carbon monoxide (CO, excreted via lungs).
- About 80% of bilirubin from catabolism of RBCs in RES. About 20% from myoglobin, haem-containing enzymes (cytochromes, catalase/peroxidases, tryptophan pyrrolase), and ineffective erythropoiesis.
- Bilirubin transported on albumin to the liver; uptake from blood into liver cell cytoplasm is against concentration gradient (active process), facilitated by ligandins in the cytoplasm.
- In the liver: conjugation occurs upon reaction with UDP-glucuronic acid, catalysed by UDP-glucuronyl transferase, to form bilirubin mono- and di-glucuronides (mainly).
- Bilirubin-diglucuronide excreted into bile and bile canaliculi → duodenum → stercobilin (gives stool its normal yellowish-brown colour).
- In newborns (relatively sterile gut): bilirubin hydrolysed back to unconjugated → reabsorbed via enterohepatic circulation → unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

A(ii) Reasons for increased bilirubin production in newborns:
- 1 g of haemoglobin in a child yields more bilirubin than in adults.
- Shortened red cell life span (70 days vs. adult).
- Concentration of ligandin and glucuronyl transferase are lower (immature) in newborns, especially preterm.
- Enhanced enterohepatic circulation (babies on exclusive breastfeeding, on broad-spectrum antibiotics).
- Delayed passage of meconium, which also contains bilirubin.

B(i) Physiological jaundice:
- Appears after first 48 hours of life; peak level < 170 µmol/L (< 12 mg/dl in term; < 15 mg/dl in preterm); resolves by Day 7 in term (Day 14 in preterm).
Non-physiological (pathological) jaundice criteria:
- Jaundice manifesting within 24 hours of age.
- Peak SBR > 12 mg/dl unconjugated in term or > 15 mg/dl in exclusively breastfed babies, or direct bilirubin > 1.5–2 mg/dl.
- Jaundice in a sick neonate (e.g. septicaemia, NEC).
- Rate of rise of SBR > 5 mg/dl/24 hrs.
- Prolonged jaundice: > 7 days in term or > 14 days in preterm.
- Hepatosplenomegaly or anaemia.

B(ii) Causes of non-physiological jaundice:
Haemolysis: G6PD deficiency (leading cause in Nigeria); ABO incompatibility (worse in group B individuals); Rhesus incompatibility; hereditary spherocytosis.
Obstruction / conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia:
- Extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
- Intrahepatic biliary obstruction.
- Neonatal hepatitis syndrome.
- Inspissated bile syndrome (bile viscosity/stasis; seen in sickle cell anaemia).
- Hirschsprung's disease; upper GI obstruction.
- Total parenteral nutrition (hyperalimentation).
Other: Dubin-Johnson syndrome (disorder of transport); Crigler-Najjar syndrome (not common in Nigeria).

A(i) HAV is transmitted via the faecal-oral route. Its incubation period is 2–7 weeks, during which HAV RNA is present in high concentrations in faeces toward the end — the peak infectious period before clinical symptoms appear.
A(ii) Phase 1 (viral replication): subclinical, no symptoms. Phase 2 (prodromal): non-specific symptoms including anorexia, nausea, vomiting, changed taste, malaise, fatigue, arthralgia, pruritus, and low-grade fever; bilirubinuria appears at this phase before clinical jaundice. Phase 3 (icteric): jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, tender hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly develop. Phase 4 (convalescent): resolution of symptoms and gradual biochemical recovery; urobilinogenuria appears, reflecting recovering bile excretion.
A(iii) In acute HAV infection, serum aminotransferases (AST and ALT) are elevated, reflecting hepatocellular necrosis. Alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are elevated. The leucocyte count characteristically shows leucopaenia. Bilirubinuria is present.
A(iv) HAV vaccine is administered as two doses. After the first dose, 97–100% of recipients develop protective antibody levels within 1 month. Essentially 100% achieve protective levels after the second (booster) dose given 6–18 months later. Vaccine efficacy against clinical hepatitis A is 94–100%.
B(i) HAV infection confers lifelong immunity because natural infection produces persistent anti-HAV IgG antibodies. Unlike HCV, where anti-HCV antibodies are non-protective (approximately 75–85% of acutely infected adults develop chronic HCV), anti-HAV IgG provides durable protection and HAV does not cause chronic hepatitis.
B(ii) HAV spreads efficiently via the faecal-oral route in close living environments. HAV RNA is present in faeces before symptoms appear, making index cases infectious without being identifiable, and household contacts share toilet facilities and prepare food together, facilitating transmission.
C(i) HEV infection is particularly dangerous in pregnant women, especially during the third trimester, carrying mortality rates up to 20–25% compared to less than 1% in the general population. HAV mortality in the general population is less than 0.01%.
C(ii) HAV has a licensed vaccine (two-dose schedule) and standard immune serum globulin (ISG) for post-exposure passive prophylaxis. HEV has no routinely available licensed vaccine in most countries and no passive prophylaxis.

A. Describe Hepatitis A virus (HAV) under the following headings:
A(i) Route of transmission and incubation period
A(ii) The four clinical phases of acute hepatitis, specifying the key features of each
A(iii) Serological and haematological findings in acute HAV infection
A(iv) Vaccine schedule and the seroconversion rate after the first dose

A 10-year-old child with a 2-year history of jaundice and abdominal distension is admitted for investigation. Examination reveals scleral icterus, palmar erythema, spider angiomas on the upper chest and arms, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren's contracture, and asterixis. Laboratory results: serum bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL (conjugated 3.1 mg/dL), AST 94 U/L, ALT 78 U/L, ALP 385 U/L, GGT 210 U/L, albumin 2.2 g/dL, INR 2.7, platelet count 58,000/mm³.

(i) Identify the biochemical pattern indicated by the elevated ALP and GGT, and distinguish this from the significance of elevated AST and ALT.
(ii) Explain the mechanism responsible for each of the following examination findings: gynaecomastia, spider angiomas, and Dupuytren's contracture.
(iii) Interpret the albumin of 2.2 g/dL and the INR of 2.7, stating what each reflects about hepatic function.
(iv) State the primary investigation that would provide histological diagnosis of aetiology and degree of fibrosis, and name the five parameters of the Child-Pugh classification for assessing severity of chronic liver disease.
(v) Using the Child-Pugh parameters, classify this child's hepatic status based on the available laboratory values.
questions.answerText:
(i) Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and GGT indicate a cholestatic pattern — cholestasis or biliary obstruction. Elevated aminotransferases AST and ALT are markers of ongoing hepatocellular necrosis or injury — they are intracellular hepatic enzymes released into the bloodstream upon hepatocyte damage. ALT is more liver-specific; AST is also elevated in muscle disease.
(ii) Gynaecomastia results from impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogens, leading to relative hyperoestrogenism — the liver normally inactivates circulating oestrogens through conjugation and excretion, and this fails in chronic liver disease. Spider angiomas result from oestrogen excess causing arteriolar dilatation; they are distributed in the area drained by the superior vena cava — upper trunk, face, arms, and hands. Dupuytren's contracture involves progressive fibrosis of the palmar fascia, causing flexion deformity of the fingers; it is listed among the signs of chronic liver disease with a multifactorial pathogenesis related to altered fibroblast activity.
(iii) Albumin of 2.2 g/dL (below the normal 3.5–5 g/dL) reflects impaired hepatic synthetic function — the liver synthesises albumin, and hypoalbuminaemia indicates significant hepatocellular dysfunction. It also contributes to ascites formation through reduced oncotic pressure. INR of 2.7 reflects impaired hepatic synthetic function for coagulation factors II, V, VII, IX, and X. Both vitamin K malabsorption from cholestasis and intrinsic synthetic failure contribute to the elevated INR.
(iv) Liver biopsy is the primary investigation that provides histological diagnosis including degree of fibrosis (staging), inflammatory activity (grading), and specific aetiological features. The five parameters of the Child-Pugh classification are: serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time (PT/INR), degree of ascites, and grade of hepatic encephalopathy.
(v) Using Child-Pugh: serum bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL = score 3; albumin 2.2 g/dL = score 3; INR 2.7 = score 3; asterixis indicates hepatic encephalopathy = score 2–3; ascites is present = score 2–3. Total score is in the range 13–15, placing this child in Child-Pugh Class C (score 10–15), indicating decompensated cirrhosis — the most severe category.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old girl presents with a 3-month history of recurrent brief episodes (5–15 seconds) of starring, eye blinking, and apparent day-dreaming, occurring up to 30 times daily. She is unaware of the episodes. Her teacher reports she "switches off" during class. She never falls during attacks and returns immediately to normal afterwards. A doctor in the outpatient clinic hyperventilates her for 30 seconds and precipitates a typical episode.

(i) State the diagnosis and the specific EEG finding that confirms it.
(ii) List the predisposing or risk factors for this condition developing into a persistent problem.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of why hyperventilation precipitates an attack.
(iv) State the drug treatment of choice and the expected long-term prognosis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Childhood Absence Epilepsy (Petit Mal). The specific EEG finding is a 3 cycles/second (3 Hz) spike-wave discharge pattern, which is characteristic.

(ii) Predisposing or risk factors / factors relevant to the natural history:
- Age of onset 4–8 years is typical.
- The attack is usually precipitated by hyperventilation (as demonstrated here).
- Female sex (more common in girls).
- Family history (genetic predisposition — the condition tends to aggregate in families).
- Risk of not outgrowing: while most children outgrow the disease by teenage years, some continue into adolescence.
- Complex febrile seizures, family history of afebrile seizure, and abnormal neurological examination increase risk of epilepsy persistence (from febrile seizure context, applicable here as risk factors for epilepsy generally).

(iii) Pathophysiology of hyperventilation-induced attack: hyperventilation causes hypocapnia (reduced CO₂ levels in the blood), which leads to cerebral vasoconstriction and a reduction in cerebral blood flow. This change in cerebral neuronal excitability (or perfusion) can precipitate the synchronised abnormal discharge characteristic of absence seizures. The attack is usually precipitated by hyperventilation, and this can be induced in hospital to help confirm the diagnosis.

(iv) Drug treatment of choice:
- Ethosuximide (first choice for absence seizures).
- Sodium Valproate 20–40 mg/kg/day (alternative).
Expected long-term prognosis: most children outgrow childhood absence epilepsy by teenage years. Prognosis is generally good.

questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the upper respiratory tract, including:
(i) the boundaries of the upper respiratory tract
(ii) the structures it contains
(iii) how the Eustachian tube is related to this tract

B. Explain the anatomical reason why acute otitis media (AOM) is more common in infants than in older children.

C. Distinguish between acute otitis media and otitis media with effusion (OME) them.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Boundaries: The upper respiratory tract is the airway above the vocal cords (glottis). One definition places it outside the thorax / above the sternal angle; another as the airway above the glottis or vocal cords; yet another as the airway above the cricoid cartilage. A useful working definition is the airway above the vocal cords.

A(ii) Structures: The nose (with two internal nares), sinuses, pharynx (naso-, oro-, and hypopharynx), and larynx.

A(iii) The Eustachian tubes open at the nasopharynx near the adenoids.

B. AOM is common in infants because of the high frequency of common colds and the anatomy of the infant's Eustachian tube, which is shorter, wider, and straight compared with that of older children. These anatomical features allow pathogens to pass more easily from the nasopharynx into the middle ear.

C. Acute otitis media is acute inflammation of the middle ear resulting in an effusion and associated with rapid onset of symptoms such as otalgia, fever, irritability, anorexia, or vomiting. Otitis media with effusion (OME) is defined as an asymptomatic middle ear effusion that often follows AOM, but may have no such antecedent history — fluid remains trapped in the ear even after the infection is gone, without the acute symptoms of AOM.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the classification of Diabetes Mellitus in children, under the following headings: immune-mediated Type 1, Type 2, genetic defects of beta-cell function (with examples), and other specific types.
A(ii) Explain the pathophysiology of Type 1 DM in children: the sequence from insulin deficiency to hyperglycaemia, osmotic diuresis, ketosis, acidosis, and electrolyte imbalance.
B(i) Distinguish between the partial remission (honeymoon) phase and the preclinical phase of Type 1 DM, including what each implies about beta-cell function, antibody markers, and clinical management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification of Diabetes Mellitus in children:
• Type 1 diabetes: a) Immune mediated b) Idiopathic — β-cell destruction leading to absolute insulin deficiency
• Type 2 diabetes: a) Typical b) Atypical — insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency secondary to secretory defects
• Genetic defects of β-cell function:
  a) MODY syndromes
  b) Mitochondrial DNA mutations
  c) Wolfram syndrome (DI, DM, optic atrophy, deafness [DIDMOAD])
  d) Thiamine responsive
• Other specific types: drug or chemical induced; diseases of the exocrine pancreas; infections; variants of Type 2 diabetes; genetic syndromes with diabetes and insulin resistance/insulin deficiency; gestational diabetes; neonatal diabetes (insulin-requiring hyperglycaemia in the first 3 months of life, rare, 1:400,000, associated with IUGR)

A(ii) Pathophysiology of Type 1 DM:
• Insulin is essential to process CHO, fat, and protein. It lowers blood glucose levels by glucose uptake into muscle cells and fat cells, stimulates glycogenesis, inhibits glycogenolysis, and inhibits the breakdown of fat to triglycerides, free fatty acids, and ketones (lipolysis).
• Lack of insulin → reduced glucose oxidation in muscle and fat cells; proteolysis and amino acid release; glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis → all result in hyperglycaemia; glucose intake still continues.
• The kidneys cannot reabsorb the excess glucose load → glycosuria → osmotic diuresis → thirst and dehydration. Untreated patients excrete a high glucose load, causing polyphagia.
• Increased fat and protein breakdown → ketone production → weight loss; acidosis results from ketosis.
• Acidosis leads to increased renal excretion of K+ and PO4. Na+ loss is due to osmotic diuresis and vomiting. Hypokalaemia is due to vomiting, osmotic diuresis, and hyperaldosteronism. Coma is likely due to ketosis, acidosis, dehydration, and hyperosmolality.

B(i) Preclinical phase vs partial remission (honeymoon) phase:
• Preclinical DM: occurs months to years preceding the clinical presentation of T1DM. Beta-cell autoimmunity is detectable as antibody markers before symptoms: GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies in 60–90% of new cases), ICA (islet cell antibody, present in 90% of newly diagnosed, detectable up to 20 years earlier in at-risk groups), IA (insulin antibodies in younger patients), IA-2 (high risk of developing disease in cohorts). IVGTT may show impaired first-phase insulin response. There are no symptoms; the patient is not on insulin. Clinical relevance: identifies individuals at high risk before irreversible beta-cell loss.
• Partial remission (honeymoon) phase: defined as when the patient requires <0.5 units of insulin/kg/day and has an HbA1c <7%. It is due to partial recovery of the damaged beta cells. Commences within days or weeks of start of insulin therapy and may last for weeks to months. Ketoacidosis at presentation and young age reduce the likelihood of a remission phase. Management: insulin must still be continued even at very low doses; the phase is transient and is followed by chronic lifelong dependency on administered insulin.

A(i) EPI history in Nigeria:
- 1974: WHO created EPI, originally aimed to protect against 6 killer diseases: TB, Polio, Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis, and Measles; adopted globally
- 1978: Nigeria launched EPI; low immunization coverage recorded in all parts of the country; low public mobilization and awareness, poor cold chain maintenance
- By 1990: high level of 80% coverage achieved in some areas but not maintained due to poor implementation, economic recession, political instability, and withdrawal of foreign donors; inadequate and irregular supply of vaccines
- By 1996: national data showed <30% coverage; EPI reviewed and re-launched as National Programme on Immunization (NPI) to reflect national commitment and ownership
- NPI merged with NPHCDA in May 2007; mandate: protect children from vaccine-preventable diseases
- Newer vaccines introduced: Pentavalent (2012), PCV (2014), IPV (2015), Rotavirus (2015), Meningitis A Conjugate (2019)
A(ii) Definitions:
- Immunization: the process of inducing immunity artificially
- Vaccination: the administration of a vaccine for the prevention of disease
- Vaccine: any preparation which when administered is able to stimulate the immune system to produce specific responses that inactivate, destroy or suppress a given pathogen
- Active immunization: induces immunity similar to that achieved from natural infection; involves stimulating immune system to produce antibodies or cell mediated immunity; able to prevent clinical disease
- Passive immunization: administration of exogenously preformed antibodies; immunity is temporary
B(i) Herd immunity:
- The level of resistance of a community or group of people to a particular disease
- Occurs through clinical or subclinical infection in the community, and/or high and continuous immunization rate
- When a critical percentage of the population is vaccinated, spread of disease is effectively stopped (>80%)
- Herd immunity provides an immunological barrier to spread of disease in the community
- With sufficiently high herd immunity, occurrence of an epidemic is unlikely
- Susceptible persons are reduced to a small proportion; eventually the disease may be eliminated
B(ii) Guiding principles for community immunization planning:
- Epidemiology of the disease: incidence and prevalence; immunization given in terms of priority to children and others at risk
- Age-specific morbidity and mortality: routine vaccines recommended at youngest age at which significant risk and protective immunologic response can be expected
- Special circumstances: some vaccines recommended only in special circumstances (e.g. pneumococcal vaccine and haemoglobinopathies); vaccines used to control outbreaks
- Routes of immunization: oral (OPV), IM (IPV, pentavalent, PCV), SC (measles, DPT), intradermal (BCG)
C(i) Barriers and missed opportunities:
- Consumer factors: ignorance, wrong information, lack of motivation
- Sociocultural: education, place of delivery, religion, maternal age
- Community factors: traditional rulers, religious leaders
- Systems: practice policies, vaccine costs, lack of tracking, long waiting, poor funding, donor activities, lack of political will, political interference, low staff morale, poor monitoring
- Missed opportunities: non-availability of vaccine; not checking immune status; failure to give simultaneous injections; failure to provide information to parents; failure to immunize every day; failure to open multiple-dose vials for few clients; asking parents to pay for vaccine or vaccination services
C(ii) Vaccine hesitancy:
- Delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services
- It is complex, context specific, and varies across time, place and vaccines
- Affected by 3 major factors: complacency, convenience, and confidence
- Considered one of top 10 global health threats by WHO
- COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy driven by myths and misconceptions cutting across: its existence, vaccines, origin/cause, clinical features, risk perception, and treatment
- Mechanisms driving myths and misconceptions: social media, politicians, religious leaders

Describe the immunization programme in Nigeria under the following headings, explain the principles of herd immunity, and analyse why immunization coverage has declined and what the barriers are.
A(i) History and evolution of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) in Nigeria
A(ii) Definitions: immunization, vaccination, active immunization, passive immunization, and vaccine
B(i) Principles of herd immunity and its critical threshold
B(ii) Guiding principles for planning immunization in a community
C(i) Barriers to immunization and missed opportunities
C(ii) Vaccine hesitancy: definition, key drivers, and factors that contribute to it

A. Describe the classification of seizure disorders under the following headings:
A(i) Aetiological classification with specific examples under each category.
A(ii) Classification by seizure type: partial seizures (simple and complex) and generalised seizures (list all sub-types with their defining features).
A(iii) Syndromic classification: describe the defining features, age of onset, EEG pattern, treatment, and prognosis of: Rolandic epilepsy, Childhood Absence Epilepsy (Petit Mal), West Syndrome/Infantile Spasms, and Lennox–Gastaut Syndrome.

B. Explain the basis for the statement that "classification of seizure type is important for choice of appropriate treatment and prognosis."

C. State the principles of long-term drug treatment of epilepsy, including when to start, how to use drugs, and when and how to stop.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiological classification:
- Congenital: CNS malformation (neurocutaneous syndromes — neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge–Weber; cerebral dysgenesis; porencephaly); genetic syndromes; intrauterine infections.
- Acquired: trauma (birth trauma causing seizure and cerebral palsy; asphyxia); infections (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria); febrile seizure; metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia); toxic (lead poisoning; drugs); CNS neoplasm; vascular (AVM, CVA).

A(ii) Partial seizures:
- Simple partial: motor, sensory, autonomic, or psychic features; NO loss of consciousness; no impairment of consciousness.
- Complex partial: some impairment/alteration of consciousness; automatism (psychomotor epilepsy); may progress to generalised seizure.
Generalised seizures:
- Absence (Petit Mal): brief lapses of consciousness; no aura; no post-ictal symptoms; occurs many times a day; typical (<12 seconds) or atypical (has motor component).
- Myoclonic: brief contraction of muscles; seen in several syndromes.
- Clonic: rhythmic contraction of limbs.
- Tonic: sustained contraction.
- Tonic–clonic (Grand Mal): most common; aura; patient may cry and fall; tonic then clonic; salivation/urination during attack; post-ictal: drowsiness, headache, Todd's paralysis (<24 hours).
- Atonic: patient loses muscle tone and collapses.

A(iii) Epileptic syndromes:
- Rolandic Epilepsy: commonest (15–25% of childhood epilepsy); onset 3–12 years; attacks at night; tingling on lips/tongue; tonic/clonic seizures; EEG — spikes in Rolandic (centrotemporal) area; treatment — Carbamazepine/Sodium Valproate; prognosis — good, outgrow by puberty (14–18 years).
- Childhood Absence Epilepsy: onset 4–8 years; brief starring/loss of responsiveness; attacks precipitated by hyperventilation; EEG — 3 cycles/sec spike-wave discharge; treatment — Ethosuximide, Sodium Valproate; most outgrow by teenage.
- West Syndrome/Infantile Spasms: onset first year of life (peak 4–6 months); occurs in children with underlying brain injury (severe perinatal asphyxia, cerebral dysgenesis, tuberous sclerosis); sudden flexion/extension jerk; attacks in clusters; EEG — hypsarrhythmia; treatment — ACTH, steroids, Clonazepam, Vigabatrin; prognosis — poor (associated brain damage, death, or mental retardation).
- Lennox–Gastaut: onset 2–3 years (range 1–14 years); most severe form; mixed seizures (tonic, atonic, atypical absence); mental retardation/regression; behavioural abnormalities; causes include perinatal brain injury, congenital malformations, genetic disorders, severe CNS infections; treatment — Sodium Valproate, Lamotrigine, Clonazepam; prognosis — poor, seizures difficult to control.

B. Different seizure types respond to different drugs (e.g., ACTH is first choice for infantile spasm; Ethosuximide for absence; Phenobarbitone for simple partial; Carbamazepine for complex partial). Prognosis also differs widely — Rolandic epilepsy has a benign prognosis with remission at puberty, while Lennox–Gastaut has a poor prognosis with persistent intellectual and behavioural deficits.

C. Principles of long-term treatment:
- Counselling at first visit about long-term treatment.
- Drug treatment usually started after ≥2 episodes.
- Start with small dose and increase gradually until seizure is controlled.
- Use single drug if possible (controls seizure in about 70% of cases and minimises side effects).
- Continue the drug for 2–4 seizure-free years.
- On stopping: tail off gradually over 3–6 months.

A(i) Acute pneumonia is the acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by micro-organisms (community-acquired pneumonia is that acquired within the community or developing within 48 hours of hospital admission).

A(ii) The lungs are composed of thousands of tubes (bronchi) that subdivide into smaller airways (bronchioles), which end in small sacs (alveoli). The alveoli contain capillaries where oxygen is added to the blood and carbon dioxide is removed. When a person has pneumonia, pus and fluid fill the alveoli, which interferes with oxygen absorption, making breathing difficult.

A(iii) Patchy infiltrate on chest radiograph points to bronchopneumonia (multiple segments involved). Lobar or segmental consolidation suggests lobar pneumonia (a single lobe). Pneumatocoele (overdistended alveoli) indicates necrotising pneumonia, common with S. aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas. Presence of abscesses and pneumatocoele in an infant suggests S. aureus until proven otherwise.

B. Spread beyond parenchyma produces acute complications: heart failure; empyema; atelectasis; respiratory failure; pneumatocoele; pneumothorax; pyopneumothorax; pleural effusion; septicaemia; subcutaneous emphysema (rare, especially in measles pneumonia). Chronic complications: lung abscess; bronchiectasis.

C. Older children/adolescents: brief mild URTI followed by sudden onset of chills and rigors, high fever, cough, and chest pain; immunocompetent older children may not be extremely ill. Infants: mild URTI with stuffy nose, fretfulness, and diminished appetite, leading to abrupt onset of fever, restlessness, apprehension, and respiratory distress; some have few or non-specific findings; others may have fever only or signs of generalised toxicity. Clinical features depend on age of patient, immune and nutritional status, peculiarities of the infecting organisms, and severity of infection.

C. Explain why the clinical presentation of pneumonia differs between older children and infants.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Transient Tachypnoea of the Newborn (TTN) — also called wet lung disease or delayed clearance of lung water. It is benign and self-limiting; child recovers in 24–72 hours.
Distinction from RDS:
- TTN: CXR shows 'sunburst pattern'; clears in 24 hours; benign and self-limiting; common in near-term and term infants.
- RDS: CXR shows fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) appearance with air bronchogram sign developing during first 6 hours of life; associated with surfactant deficiency; progressive deterioration over 3–5 days (if child does not die, begins to recover); most common in < 34 weeks' gestation.

(ii) Risk factors for TTN: Preterm birth; maternal diabetes; maternal sedation; caesarean delivery.
Patients at risk of having increased lung fluids at birth: preterms; babies born without prior labour or following precipitate labour; born via caesarean section; born following intrauterine asphyxia.

(iii) Signs of respiratory distress in the newborn:
- Tachypnoea (RR > 60/min); bradypnoea; intercostal indrawing; lower chest wall indrawing; subcostal indrawing; flaring of ala nasi; grunting; cyanosis.
Note: Not all respiratory distress has a respiratory cause.

(iv) Extra-pulmonary causes:
Vascular: Hypovolaemia; anaemia; polycythaemia; congenital heart disease; persistent foetal circulation.
Metabolic: Acidosis; hypoglycaemia; hypothermia.
Neuromuscular: Cerebral oedema; cerebral haemorrhage; drugs; muscular disorders; spinal cord problems; phrenic nerve damage.
questions.question:
A 35-week premature male neonate develops mild respiratory distress, mild depression at birth, and tachypnoea (RR 80/min) with a chest X-ray showing a 'sunburst pattern' that clears within 24 hours.
(i) State the diagnosis, and distinguish it from Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in terms of onset, CXR findings, and natural course.
(ii) List all the risk factors for this condition.
(iii) Enumerate all the signs of respiratory distress in the newborn.
(iv) List all the non-respiratory (extra-pulmonary) causes of respiratory distress under vascular, metabolic, and neuromuscular categories.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Left ventricular failure before right:
In a large left-to-right shunt, the increased pulmonary blood flow returns via pulmonary veins to the left atrium and left ventricle. This causes progressive volume overload and dilatation of the left ventricle first. Left ventricular failure therefore occurs before right-sided failure. The right side fails secondarily — from increasing afterload (pulmonary vascular resistance rises) and increasing preload (fluid retention).

A(ii) Fluid retention mechanism and vicious cycle:
Reduced systemic cardiac output → peripheral tissue hypoperfusion → kidney perceives this as hypovolaemia → initiates fluid retention (increased preload to already overloaded heart) → worsens heart failure → further reduces cardiac output → more fluid retention. This vicious cycle eventually causes congestive cardiac failure (decompensation). Dilatation occurs first, then hypertrophy.

A(iii) Pulmonary vascular resistance:
Initially, increased pulmonary blood flow causes reflex vasospasm. With time, this causes thickening of pulmonary vessel walls — initially reversible, eventually irreversible obliterative pulmonary vascular disease. When pulmonary vascular resistance rises to suprasystemic levels (Eisenmenger syndrome), surgery is contraindicated because closing the defect would leave the right ventricle with no outlet for its suprasystemic pressure → post-cardiotomy syndrome (the myocardium requires a lot of oxygen after surgery and cannot sustain suprasystemic pressures).

B(i) Pressure gradient:
- VSD: Peak systolic pressure — left ventricle 130–140 mmHg vs. right ventricle 30 mmHg → very high gradient → large shunt
- ASD: Left atrium 8–9 mmHg vs. right atrium 5 mmHg → gradient only 3–4 mmHg → small shunt → usually asymptomatic
- PDA: Aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary artery pressure throughout systole AND diastole → continuous high-pressure shunt; essentially similar haemodynamics to VSD (both are high-pressure systems)

B(ii) Initial ECG changes:
- VSD: Initially shows left ventricular hypertrophy (volume overload of LV); then biventricular hypertrophy as pulmonary hypertension develops
- ASD: Right ventricular hypertrophy (right heart volume overload); right axis deviation
- PDA: Left ventricular hypertrophy initially (similar to VSD — high-pressure left-to-right shunt)

B(iii) Murmur characteristics:
- VSD: Pansystolic/holosystolic murmur; variable pitch; loudest at mid-left sternal edge; radiates to the back (not the axilla)
- ASD: Ejection systolic murmur (pulmonic flow murmur) at left upper sternal edge; wide, fixed splitting of S2
- PDA: Continuous (to-and-fro/machinery) murmur; starts in systole, continues through S2 into diastole; higher pitch in systole, lower in diastole; loudest in the left infraclavicular area

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Pyogenic/bacterial meningitis (inflammation of the meninges caused by bacteria).
Contraindications to LP:
1. Raised ICP.
2. Thrombocytopenia.
3. Coagulopathy.
4. Infection of overlying skin at LP site.
5. Very ill patients with imminent cardiorespiratory collapse.

(ii) Pathogenesis: Bacteraemia (from URTI, contiguous spread from otitis media, mastoiditis, penetrating head injury, myelomeningocele) → bacteraemia → penetration of blood-brain barrier → invasion of the meninges → release of acute phase reactants (IL-1, TNF, cytokines) → meningitis → sequelae.

(iii) Organisms:
1–2 months: Organisms seen in neonates (G-ve bacilli, Group B Streptococcus, Staph aureus, Listeria monocytogenes) plus those in the 3 months–12 years group.
3 months–12 years: Haemophilus influenzae; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Neisseria meningitidis.

(iv) Other investigations: PCV; FBC; random blood sugar; blood culture; transfontanelle USS.
CSF in pyogenic meningitis:
- Appearance: Purulent/turbid.
- WBC: Increased ++ (neutrophils predominate, N > L).
- Protein: Elevated.
- Sugar: Reduced CSF:blood sugar ratio (hypoglycorrhachia); organisms on Gram stain and/or culture positive.
questions.question:
A 5-day-old term male neonate is admitted with fever (39.2°C), bulging anterior fontanelle, high-pitched cry, and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture is performed.
(i) State the diagnosis, and list five specific contraindications to lumbar puncture.
(ii) Describe the pathogenesis of this condition from the portal of entry to the development of sequelae, including the inflammatory mediators.

A premature male infant born at 28 weeks is admitted to the neonatal unit. By 6 hours of life he has worsening grunting, intercostal indrawing, cyanosis, and fine inspiratory crepitations. His chest radiograph shows a fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) appearance with air bronchogram signs.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and list four predisposing factors for this condition.
(ii) Describe the pathophysiology (mechanism) of this condition step by step.
(iii) State how the condition could have been prevented antenatally and at birth.
(iv) Outline the management, including respiratory support modalities and pharmacological treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) / Hyaline Membrane Disease (HMD) — described as 'Progressive atelectasis of prematurity.'
Predisposing factors: Prematurity (< 34 weeks); infant of diabetic mother (IDM); second twin (Twin 2); perinatal asphyxia; male sex (male > female).
Risk is reduced in: PROM, IUGR, maternal stress (e.g. pre-eclampsia).

(ii) Pathophysiology (step by step):
1. Inadequate surfactant synthesis.
2. High alveolar surface tension.
3. Reduced lung compliance.
4. Progressive expiratory atelectasis.
5. Hypoxia → respiratory distress.
6. Increased capillary permeability → exudation of fluid → oedema.

(iii) Prevention:
- Prenatal glucocorticoid administered for > 24 hours before delivery.
- Surfactant replacement given before 1–2 hours of life.
- Early CPAP instituted from the delivery room.

(iv) Management:
Investigations: CXR; chest ultrasound; electrolytes/urea/creatinine; arterial blood gas; sepsis screen as indicated.
Treatment:
- Respiratory support: oxygen; CPAP; mechanical ventilation.
- Surfactant rescue therapy.
- Fluid and nutritional support.
- Antibiotics.

questions.question:
A day-old male infant born at 30 weeks' gestation, weighing 1.2 kg, is noted to have increasing pallor, apnoeic episodes, tachycardia, and poor weight gain from week 6 of life. Blood investigations show Hb 7.5 g/dl. No blood loss or haemolysis is identified.
(i) State the diagnosis, explain why it occurs in preterm infants at an earlier time point than in term infants, and name the exaggerated physiological process involved.
(ii) List all the reasons for the exaggeration of physiological anaemia in preterm infants.
(iii) State the clinical manifestations.
(iv) Outline the complete management including transfusion criteria, nutritional supplements, and pharmacological agents with their specific doses.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Anaemia of Prematurity — an exaggeration of physiological anaemia.
It occurs earlier in preterm infants because minimum Hb values are reached at 6 weeks (1–3 months) compared to 8–12 weeks in term infants. Preterm infants start to produce erythropoietin again only when Hb falls to 7–9 g/dl, in contrast to 10–11 g/dl in term infants, because their tissues have lower O2 requirements.

(ii) Reasons for exaggeration in preterm infants:
- Minimum values reached earlier than in term babies (6 weeks).
- Reduced RBC survival.
- Iatrogenic — repeated phlebotomy for investigations.
- Relatively more rapid somatic growth rate.
- Vitamin E deficiency.

(iii) Clinical manifestations: Pallor; apnoea; poor weight gain; tachypnoea; tachycardia.

(iv) Management:
- Blood transfusion if symptomatic: 10 ml/kg of packed cells over 1–3 hours.
- Folic acid 5 mg weekly to babies < 2 kg from 2 weeks of age.
- 10 mg a-tocopherol acetate (Vitamin E) daily to babies < 1.5 kg from 2 weeks.
- FeSO4 50 mg daily or 6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron from 2 kg or 10–14 weeks of age.
- rHuEpO 100–200 iu/kg 5×/week or 400 iu/kg/day 3×/week + iron + Vitamin E.

A(i) Abdominal ultrasound is highly sensitive for detecting gallstones (cholelithiasis), biliary dilatation indicating obstructive jaundice, choledocholithiasis, bilomas (bile collections), and cholecystitis. As a first-line modality it requires no ionising radiation, is widely available, economical, and can be performed at the bedside.
A(ii) MRCP provides high-resolution images of the biliary tree (intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts), pancreatic duct, and hepatic parenchyma without ionising radiation, intravenous contrast, or endoscopic intervention. It has largely replaced diagnostic ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) for evaluation of biliary and pancreatic pathology, reserving ERCP for therapeutic interventions such as stone extraction or stenting.
A(iii) Doppler ultrasonography in portal hypertension demonstrates portal blood flow direction (hepatopetal vs hepatofugal), velocity, and can diagnose cavernous transformation, portal vein thrombosis, or splenic vein thrombosis — haemodynamic information not obtainable by standard ultrasound or CT. Its specific advantage is that it is safe (no radiation), economical, and assesses portal flow direction and velocity. Its limitation is operator dependency and circadian variation in portal flow.
B(i) HIDA scan uses Tc-99m-labelled iminodiacetic acid (IDA) derivatives taken up by hepatocytes and excreted into bile. In neonatal cholestasis, absent excretion into the bowel at 24 hours despite hepatic uptake strongly suggests biliary atresia; present excretion argues against it.
B(ii) Tc-99m RBC scintigraphy (tagged red blood cell scan) uses radiolabelled red blood cells that accumulate at the active bleeding site within the GI tract. It is sensitive for detecting active GI bleeding at rates as low as 0.1–0.5 mL/min, indicated when intermittent or slow GI bleeding is suspected and endoscopy is inconclusive.
B(iii) Meckel's scan uses Tc-99m pertechnetate, which is taken up by gastric mucosa (including ectopic gastric mucosa). It is indicated for suspected Meckel's diverticulum — which contains ectopic gastric mucosa that secretes acid causing peptic ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa, producing painless lower GI bleeding typically in children under 2 years.
C. CT is not affected by patient body habitus or overlying bowel gas (which limits ultrasound), and provides comprehensive cross-sectional images of all abdominal organs simultaneously. CT is preferred over ultrasound: (1) in obese patients or when bowel gas obscures the ultrasound field, impairing organ visualisation; and (2) for detailed evaluation of complex abdominal masses, mesenteric pathology, or trauma — where spiral CT with 3D angiographic reconstruction provides more accurate visualisation of portal vasculature, collateral vessels, and venous anatomy than ultrasound.
