A. Describe the murmurs heard in congenital heart disease under the following headings:
A(i) Timing — define the three types and give two causes for each
A(ii) Intensity — state the grading system and distinguish the grades that produce a thrill from those that do not
A(iii) Location — state the valve area where each of the following murmurs is heard loudest: pansystolic murmur of VSD, pansystolic murmur of mitral incompetence, ejection systolic murmur of aortic stenosis, ejection systolic murmur of pulmonary stenosis

B. Distinguish between a venous hum and the murmur of patent ductus arteriosus under the following headings:
B(i) Nature and location of each murmur
B(ii) How to clinically differentiate them at the bedside
questions.answerText:
A(i) Timing:
- Systolic (between S1 and S2): e.g. pansystolic in VSD, mitral incompetence, tricuspid incompetence; ejection systolic in pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, ASD
- Diastolic (between S2 and S1): e.g. aortic incompetence (high-pitched); mitral stenosis (low-pitched/rumbling, mid-diastolic)
- Continuous (starts in systole, continues through S2 into diastole): e.g. PDA; arterio-venous malformations (e.g. coronary artery AV fistula)

A(ii) Grading system:
- Grade I/6: extremely soft
- Grade II/6: soft but louder than Grade I
- Grade III/6: loud enough to be heard but does not produce a thrill
- Grade IV/6: very loud; thrill present
- Grade V/6: very loud; thrill present; heard with stethoscope held at an angle to the chest wall
- Grade VI/6: very loud; thrill present; heard with stethoscope held away from the chest
Grades III and IV are most commonly found. Grades I–III do not produce a thrill; Grades IV–VI produce a thrill.

A(iii) Location:
- Pansystolic murmur of VSD: loudest at the left lower sternal edge (VSD is 99 times more common than tricuspid incompetence at this site)
- Pansystolic murmur of mitral incompetence: loudest at the apex
- Ejection systolic murmur of aortic stenosis: loudest at the right upper sternal edge
- Ejection systolic murmur of pulmonary stenosis: loudest at the left upper sternal edge

B(i) Nature and location:
- Venous hum: benign; heard at the base of the neck from the large venous system; not as loud as the murmur in PDA
- PDA murmur: continuous (to-and-fro/machinery murmur); heard loudest in the infraclavicular area under the left clavicle; continuous because it spans both systole and diastole

B(ii) Bedside differentiation:
- Venous hum is benign/not pathological and is not heard as far down as the infraclavicular area, whereas the PDA murmur is pathological and is loudest under the left clavicle
- The venous hum arises from the large venous system at the base of the neck; the PDA murmur arises from aortopulmonary flow throughout the cardiac cycle

questions.question:
A. Describe bronchial asthma under the following headings:
(i) Definition
(ii) The three key characteristics of asthma
(iii) The three clinical patterns of asthma in childhood

B. Describe the pathogenesis of allergic asthma, including:
(i) the three stages: sensitisation, early (immediate) response, and late-phase response
(ii) the cells and mediators involved at each stage
(iii) the three mechanisms that produce airway obstruction

C. Distinguish between Inducers and Inciters (trigger factors) of asthma, giving at least three examples of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airway in which many cellular elements play a role; the chronic inflammation causes associated increase in airways hyperresponsiveness that leads to recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing particularly at night or early in the morning; these episodes are usually associated with widespread or variable airflow obstruction that is often reversible either spontaneously or with treatment.

A(ii) Three characteristics: (a) variable airway obstruction (severe or minor), often (not always) reversible; (b) chronic airway inflammation; (c) airway hyperresponsiveness.

A(iii) Clinical patterns: (1) Atopic/Extrinsic asthma — commonest in childhood; (2) Non-atopic/Intrinsic asthma; (3) Mixed.

B(i–ii) Sensitisation: CD4+ TH2 lymphocytes and B cells interact; B cells produce allergen-specific IgE which binds to high-affinity receptors on mast cell surfaces — this is sensitisation. Early (immediate) response: re-exposure to allergen causes molecular bridging of receptor-bound IgE → mast cell activation → release of preformed and newly generated mediators: histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4), and cytokines → mucosal oedema and bronchospasm. Late-phase response: if no intervention, influx of inflammatory cells (mainly eosinophils and neutrophils) → further airway narrowing and airflow obstruction.

B(iii) Airway obstruction due to: (a) swelling of the airway mucosa due to inflammation; (b) mucus clogs in the airways; (c) bronchospasm of the muscles around the airways.

C. Inducers: all environmental factors that initiate asthma in a genetically predisposed individual — e.g. allergens (dust mites, pollens, moulds), air pollution, viral respiratory infections, formula feeds (non-breastfeeding in first 6 months). Inciters (trigger factors): factors involved in re-occurrence after the first attack — e.g. viral URTI (most important in childhood), aero-allergens, exercise, irritant fumes, emotion, cold air. Many inducers are also inciters.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the pathogenetic mechanisms used to classify congenital malformations (malformation, deformation, disruption, and dysplasia), giving one example of each.
A(ii) Describe how patterns of multiple malformations are classified (association, sequence, complex, and syndrome) with one example of each.
B(i) Explain the physician's responsibilities when a child with a congenital malformation is born, and describe how parental reactions typically progress. State what factors influence parental responses.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pathogenetic mechanisms:
• Malformation (true malformation): an error of morphogenesis. Example: myelomeningocoele, exomphalos. The abnormality arises from an intrinsically abnormal developmental process from the start.
• Deformation: mechanical effects on a normally formed part. Example: talipes equinovarus. An extrinsic mechanical force distorts a normally formed structure.
• Disruption: tissue loss or necrosis of a normally formed part. Example: amniotic band disruption. An external event (amniotic band) destroys previously normal tissue.
• Dysplasia: abnormal organisation of cells into tissues. Example: achondroplasia. The basic defect is at the level of cellular organisation within a tissue type.

A(ii) Patterns of multiple malformations:
• Associations: non-random occurrence of malformations that cannot be explained as a sequence or syndrome. Example: the VATER association (Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Tracheo-Esophageal fistula, Renal anomalies).
• Sequences: a pattern of anomalies derived from a single structural defect or mechanical factor. Example: the Potter-oligohydramnios sequence (oligohydramnios from renal agenesis causes compression deformities of the fetus).
• Complexes: malformations resulting from disturbance of a developmental field. Example: hemifacial microsomia.
• Syndromes: a recognised pattern of malformations with a single specific cause. Example: Down syndrome.

B(i) Physician's responsibilities and parental reactions:
Physician's responsibilities:
• Accurate diagnosis
• Initial communication with parents, the patient, the family
• Non-abandonment of the family
• Facilitation of the coping process
Principles of initial communication:
• Avoid information overload
• Use appropriate language
• Use an individualised approach
• Remain realistic and honest
• Be gentle and sensitive
Parental reactions (typical progression):
1. Shock → disappointment → guilt (sense of retribution)
2. Grief → fear → anger → shame (stigma)
3. Denial (intellectualisation) → blame
4. Diminished self-esteem → depression
5. Reorganisation → equilibrium
Factors influencing parental responses:
• The existence of other children
• Prior stability of family relationships
• Economic considerations
• Ethnic/cultural/religious factors

A(i) Components of the standard ECG:
- P wave: represents atrial depolarisation (atrial hypertrophy)
- PR interval: represents conduction from atria to ventricles (conduction defects); normal values — children: 0.16s, adolescents: 0.18s, adults: 0.2s
- QRS complex: represents ventricular depolarisation (ventricular hypertrophy)
- T wave: represents ventricular repolarisation
- QT interval: total ventricular electrical activity
- Isoelectric line: baseline between complexes

A(ii) Systematic ECG analysis:
- Rhythm: sinus rhythm or other (arrhythmia)
- Rate: normal, increased (tachycardia), decreased (bradycardia); neonate upper limit 160 bpm; age-dependent
- P wave: atrial hypertrophy (broad/flat P — left atrial; peaked P — right atrial; notched P — P mitrale; biphasic P)
- PR interval: conduction defects (prolonged PR in ARF)
- Axis: 0–90° normal; right axis deviation (RAD); left axis deviation (LAD); superior axis (ERAD/ELAD — in Paediatrics, superior/inferior axis preferred over RAD/LAD)
- QRS complexes: ventricular hypertrophy (LVH or RVH)
- T wave: inversion (in severe conditions)

B(i) Tetralogy of Fallot ECG:
- Right axis deviation (RAD)
- Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)
- ± Right atrial hypertrophy (RAH)
Basis: RVOTO causes progressive RVH; right-to-left shunting further increases RV work.

B(ii) TGA ECG:
- Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)
- ± Right atrial hypertrophy (RAH)
- Right axis deviation (RAD)
Basis: the aorta arises from the right ventricle, which pumps at systemic pressure; the RV is therefore the systemic ventricle and hypertrophies.

B(iii) Tricuspid Atresia ECG (suggestive but not diagnostic):
- Right atrial hypertrophy (RAH) — large if ASD is small and vice-versa
- Superior axis deviation (ERAD/ELAD)
- Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)
These three features together in a cyanosed child are suggestive of tricuspid atresia. Basis: the LV is the main functional ventricle (hence LVH); the rudimentary RV and absent AV connection make the right atrium hypertrophy to overcome obstruction; superior axis from the unusual depolarisation pattern.

B(iv) Acute Rheumatic Fever ECG: prolonged PR interval (>0.16s in children, >0.18s in adolescents, >0.2s in adults) — due to myocarditis delaying AV conduction.
Chronic RHD ECG:
- P mitrale (broad, notched, biphasic P wave) — left atrial hypertrophy/enlargement from long-standing mitral valve disease
- Increased PR interval
- LVH
- ± RVH (if long-standing pulmonary hypertension)

B(v) Pulmonary Stenosis:
Mild to moderate: right ventricular hypertrophy (overwhelming evidence).
Very severe: T-wave inversion in V1 to V6 (RV-apex forming) — indicates the right ventricle is so hypertrophied it has rotated to form the cardiac apex.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross anatomy of the thyroid gland:
• Position: situated in the neck in front of the larynx and trachea at the level of the 5th, 6th, 7th cervical and 1st thoracic vertebrae.
• Structure: weight 25 g; surrounded by a fibrous capsule; consists of two lobes joined by an isthmus. Parathyroid glands are located on the posterior aspects.
• Products: produces T4, T3, and calcitonin (from parafollicular/C cells).
• Origin: the thyroid is the earliest endocrine gland in mammals; it originates from embryonic endoderm; formed from the pharyngeal floor and the ultimo branchial body. Its median part originates from the median endoderm of the foregut at the level of the 1st and 2nd pharyngeal pouches; the growth is ventral and caudal; closely associated with the developing heart. The lateral primordium (from the ultimo branchial body, primordium of the parafollicular cells) fuses with the medial enlargement at the 8th–9th week of gestation.

A(ii) Zone/component to pathology relationships:
• Follicular cells (produce T3/T4): deficiency → congenital hypothyroidism (from thyroid dysgenesis, ectopy, or dyshormonogenesis), acquired hypothyroidism (from Hashimoto's thyroiditis, post-thyroidectomy, iodine deficiency); excess → hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodular goitre). Graves' disease arises from a diffuse goitre when thyroid stimulating antibodies bind to the TSH receptor.
• Parafollicular/C cells (from ultimo branchial body, produce calcitonin): involved in calcium homeostasis; not a common site of paediatric thyroid disease.
• Thyroid gland size (goitre): diffuse enlargement or nodular goitre. During adolescence the thyroid may become diffusely enlarged (colloid/simple goitre); this usually resolves spontaneously. Subacute thyroiditis follows viral URTI with fever, a tender gland, transient hyperthyroidism, then transient hypothyroidism, then recovery.
• Hashimoto's/lymphocytic thyroiditis: autoimmune; autoantibodies present in 95% of cases; most common cause of juvenile thyroid disease; may present with hypo- or hyperthyroidism or be asymptomatic; F>M, age 3–6 years; TPO antibodies present.

B(i) Iodine deficiency and endemic cretinism:
• Low iodine intake (<50 mcg/day) leads to compensatory changes so that T3 is secreted in preference to T4, because thyroglobulin will contain relatively more MIT than DIT. Consequently thyroid hormones are reduced and TSH secretion rises. The increased TSH induces thyroid enlargement (goitre) and the rate of iodine uptake rises dramatically — the adaptive response that produces goitre.
• Endemic cretinism is a syndrome of intellectual impairment, deafness, and diplegia resulting from severe iodine deficiency during fetal and early neonatal life. Iodine deficiency in early fetal life is thought to cause the neurological form: mental retardation, spasticity, ataxia, and defects in speech and hearing to the point of deaf-mutism.
• Neurological damage is irreversible even with later iodine supplementation because thyroid hormone is necessary for normal brain growth and myelination during the critical early developmental window. Neurological damage that has already occurred cannot be repaired by subsequent iodine or thyroxine supplementation. Neurologic damage, once it occurs, is untreatable. Prevention through iodine supplementation (iodized salt, iodinated poppy seed oil) before and during pregnancy is therefore the only effective strategy.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the thyroid gland, including its structure, position, blood supply axis (as described), and its relationship to the parathyroid glands.
A(ii) State how each zone or functional component of the thyroid relates to specific common pathologies (goitre, hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, thyroiditis).
B(i) Explain why iodine deficiency leads to goitre and endemic cretinism, and why neurological damage in cretinism may spread to cause permanent functional deficit even if iodine is later supplemented.

A. Describe the serological markers of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection under the following headings:
A(i) HBsAg: when it appears in acute infection, when it disappears in recovery, and what its persistence beyond 6 months signifies
A(ii) HBeAg: its clinical significance and the perinatal transmission risk it predicts
A(iii) Anti-HBc IgM: its role in distinguishing acute from chronic infection and the window period
A(iv) Anti-HBs: what clinical states it indicates and the protective titre threshold

B. State the chronic HBV phase characterised by HBeAg positivity, high viral DNA, normal or minimally elevated aminotransferases, and minimal hepatic inflammation, and explain why this phase is relevant to perinatal transmission.

C. Explain why chronic HBV infection predisposes to hepatocellular carcinoma at approximately 100-fold the risk of uninfected individuals, and through what sequential process HCC typically develops.
questions.answerText:
A(i) HBsAg is the first serological marker to appear in acute HBV infection, detectable at approximately 6 weeks after exposure. In acute infection with recovery, HBsAg disappears by approximately 3 months. Its persistence beyond 6 months is the defining serological criterion for chronic HBV infection.
A(ii) HBeAg positivity indicates active HBV replication and high infectivity, correlating with high serum HBV DNA levels. The greatest risk of perinatal HBV transmission — 70–90% risk of persistent HBV infection in the infant by 6 months — occurs in infants born to HBeAg-positive mothers without prophylaxis.
A(iii) IgM Anti-HBc appears shortly after HBsAg and confirms acute infection, particularly during the 'window period' when HBsAg may have already cleared but Anti-HBs has not yet appeared. IgG Anti-HBc persists for life and indicates prior natural infection.
A(iv) Anti-HBs indicates protective immunity, whether from natural infection resolution or HBV vaccination. A titre greater than 10 mIU/mL is considered protective. It is the sole marker present in vaccinated individuals, as Anti-HBc is absent in vaccination.
B. The immunotolerant phase of chronic HBV is characterised by HBeAg positivity, high serum HBV DNA, normal or minimally elevated transaminases, and little hepatic inflammation. The immune system does not mount an effective response, allowing ongoing viral replication without significant liver damage. This phase is critical to perinatal transmission because infants infected perinatally enter this immunotolerant phase and have a 90% risk of developing chronic HBV infection.
C. The relative risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in chronic HBV infection is approximately 100-fold compared to uninfected individuals. HCC typically develops 25–30 years after initial HBV infection through the sequential process of chronic hepatitis → cirrhosis (defined histologically by bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodule formation distorting hepatic architecture) → hepatocellular carcinoma, with a 10-year HCC risk up to 15%.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old boy born at 29 weeks gestation presents with delayed walking, bilateral lower limb spasticity greater than upper limb spasticity, and a scissor gait. His parents report a normal MRI showing periventricular leukomalacia. IQ assessment is within normal limits. Seizures have not been reported.

(i) Identify the specific type of cerebral palsy, and explain why periventricular leukomalacia particularly produces this pattern.
(ii) State the functional classification of this child's cerebral palsy, given he can walk with assistance.
(iii) List the investigations recommended in the management of this child.
(iv) Describe the differential diagnoses that should be excluded before confirming a diagnosis of CP.
(v) Explain the statement "a positive family history rules out cerebral palsy in most cases," and give the exception stated.
questions.answerText:
(i) Specific type: Spastic Diplegia. This sub-type is especially common in preterm infants because of the high incidence of intraventricular haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia in this age group. The periventricular white matter contains the descending motor fibres for the lower limbs, which lie closest to the ventricles; damage here preferentially affects lower limb function while sparing upper limb function and intelligence (IQ usually normal; seizures are rare in this sub-type).

(ii) Functional classification: Class II — slight to moderate limitation of activity (child can walk with assistance but has limitation).
The four functional classes are: Class I — no limitation; Class II — slight to moderate limitation; Class III — moderate to great limitation; Class IV — no useful physical activity.

(iii) Investigations in management of CP:
- G6PD screening (positive family history rules out CP, except in rare cases if the mother is G6PD deficient — so G6PD screening is done).
- Blood group.
- EEG (for seizure assessment).
- Skull X-ray (intracranial calcification, skull defects).
- CT scan of the cranium (shows cerebral atrophy, cystic lesions, dysgenesis).
- MRI.
- Chromosomal studies to rule out Down syndrome and others.
- Biochemical tests to exclude progressive disorders: degenerative CNS disorders; metabolic disorders.

(iv) Differential diagnoses:
1. Muscular dystrophy.
2. Spinal cord tumour.
3. Werdnig–Hoffman Disease.
4. Brain tumours.
5. Down syndrome.
6. Spinal cord injury.
7. Peripheral neuropathies.
8. Myelomeningocoele.

(v) CP is a nonprogressive disorder; a positive family history of the same condition suggests a genetic/hereditary progressive disorder, which rules out CP (since CP is due to a fixed, nonprogressive brain insult). The exception: in rare cases where the mother is G6PD deficient (G6PD deficiency can cause hyperbilirubinaemia/kernicterus in successive children, potentially causing CP in more than one child in the same family), a positive family history does not exclude CP.

(i) Diagnosis: Early-onset neonatal sepsis (EONS) — neonatal sepsis refers to acute inflammatory response to infections caused by bacterial, fungal, parasitic, or viral pathogens. Early onset = bacteraemia within 72 hours (< 5 days old).
Likely organisms (maternal genitourinary tract organisms): Group B Streptococci, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae.

(ii) Maternal risk factors: Prolonged rupture of membranes (> 24 hrs); chorioamnionitis; maternal peripartal fever, leucocytosis, foetal heart rate > 160/min; foul-smelling amniotic fluid; premature labour and delivery; manipulative/operative delivery.
Neonatal risk factors: Birth asphyxia; instrumentation/catheterisation/IVF; hospitalisation; low birthweight; prematurity; presence of open congenital anomalies.

(iii) Clinical signs by system:
- Respiratory: retractions, tachypnoea, cyanosis, apnoea, grunting (lung is most common site of infection in neonate).
- Cardiovascular: poor perfusion, tachycardia, hypotension, shock, acidaemia.
- Temperature: thermal instability — hyperthermia more common in term; hypothermia more common in preterms.
- Gastrointestinal: poor feeding, abdominal distension, regurgitation, ileus, NEC.
- Neurological: seizures, lethargy, hypotonia, decreased activity.
- Skin: petechiae, purpura, pallor.
- Metabolic: glucose instability, metabolic acidosis.

(iv) Investigations:
- Cultures: blood, CSF, urine, tracheal aspirates (gram stain and culture via endotracheal tube).
- CXR and abdominal X-ray.
- Leukocyte profiles: total WBC < 5,000/mm³; absolute neutrophil count < 1,000/mm³; bands: PMN ratio > 0.2 (highest predictive accuracy and sensitivity for bacteraemia).
- Thrombocytopenia.
Treatment: Based on clinical pattern; antibiotics covering the likely organisms. Cultures guide definitive therapy.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Clinical presentation comparison:
Burkitt's Lymphoma: Peak age 7 years (range 3–13 years); short history (83% within 3 months); multiple abdominal organs involved, usually with retroperitoneal tumour mass; hard craggy mass (single or multiple); hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, palpable ovarian masses in girls; kidney most frequently affected; no abdominal organ is spared; associated jaw swelling or CNS abnormalities; lymphadenopathy minimal in endemic BL.
Wilm's Tumour: 78% diagnosed at 1–5 years; peak age 3–4 years; flank mass initially painless that does NOT cross the midline; hypertension in 25% of cases; haematuria in 15% of cases; polycythaemia; bleeding abnormalities due to acquired von Willebrand disease.
Neuroblastoma: 50% of patients <2 years, 75% <4 years; abdominal mass usually CROSSES the midline; 65% evolve within the abdomen; most commonly presents as asymptomatic abdominal mass with metastasis at onset in 75% of cases; pelvic involvement: constipation and urinary retention.

A(ii) Presenting syndromes unique to Neuroblastoma:
- Pepper syndrome: massive involvement of liver with metastatic disease + respiratory distress.
- Horner's syndrome: unilateral ptosis, myosis, enophthalmos, anhidrosis.
- Hutchinson's syndrome: limping and irritability in young child associated with bone and BM metastasis.
- Opsomyoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet): myoclonic jerking and random eye movement + cerebellar ataxia.
- Kerner-Morrison syndrome: intractable secretory diarrhoea associated with VIP secretion.
- Raccoon eyes: periorbital haemorrhage secondary to metastatic tumour.

B(i) Imaging and biochemistry differentiation:
- USS/IVU in BL: distortion of calyces or non-excretion of contrast material; single or multiple masses; downward and lateral displacement of kidney; usually preserved calyceal architecture (on USS).
- IVU in Wilm's Tumour: distorted calyces or non-excretion of dye; CT is preferable; intrarenal tumour usually >10 cm on USS.
- IVU in Neuroblastoma: downward and lateral displacement of the kidney but preserved calyceal architecture.
- Urine/serum biochemistry: Neuroblastoma — urine/serum VMA and HVA increased by at least 3 SD above the mean for age per/mg creatinine in the sample (elevated in >90% of cases); elevated carcinoembryonic antigen. Wilm's Tumour: elevated serum CEA; serum Ca elevated in mesoblastic nephroma.
- Diagnosis confirmation: BL by FNAC/ascitic cytology; Neuroblastoma by biopsy; Wilm's Tumour by biopsy/CT.

B(ii) Hypertension mechanisms:
- Wilm's Tumour: hypertension in 25% of cases — renin induced by tumour cells or compression of vasculature.
- Neuroblastoma: hypertension due to catecholamine release from adrenal medulla (though rare because of the type of catecholamines secreted by most neuroblastomas) or renal vascular compression.
questions.question:
Describe the common differential diagnoses of abdominal tumours in children under the following headings:
A(i) Compare the clinical presentation of Burkitt's Lymphoma versus Wilm's Tumour versus Neuroblastoma with respect to age, mass characteristics, and organ involvement.
A(ii) Describe the presenting syndromes unique to Neuroblastoma.
B(i) Describe how ultrasound, IVU, and urine/serum biochemistry are used to differentiate these three tumours.

Describe the gross epidemiology, aetiology, and clinical classification of malaria, explain the mechanism of fever periodicity for each Plasmodium species, and relate the diagnostic methods to their specific utility in clinical management.
A(i) Causative species of human malaria: distribution, characteristics of each species, and which RBCs each species infects
A(ii) Transmission: vector, factors affecting transmission, incubation periods by species
B(i) Classification of malaria for clinical management and the WHO definition of each class
B(ii) Mechanism of fever paroxysms and the characteristic periodicity of each species
C(i) Microscopic diagnosis: thick film versus thin film, parasite density determination, and limitations
C(ii) Non-microscopic tests: RDTs, PCR, serology; advantages and issues with RDTs
questions.answerText:
A(i) Causative species:
- P. falciparum: most fatal type; commonest in tropics and subtropics; infects both mature and immature RBCs (up to 60% of RBCs); causes the most severe form
- P. vivax: most common worldwide; has widest geographical range (temperate to tropical); infects only immature RBCs; usually mild
- P. ovale: uncommon in Africa; found mainly in tropical Africa and West Pacific; infects only immature RBCs; usually mild
- P. malariae: patchily present; produces long-lasting infections; infects only mature RBCs; usually mild
- P. knowlesi: zoonotic infection seen mostly in forested regions of South East Asia
A(ii) Transmission:
- Transmitted primarily by bite of infected female Anopheles mosquito
- Transmission factors: mosquitoes, humans, parasite, environment, control measures
- Human factors: age, history of exposure, genotype, pregnancy status
- Incubation periods: P. falciparum 9-14 days; P. vivax 12-17 days; P. ovale 16-18 days; P. malariae 18-40 days
- Areas of transmission are divided into stable and unstable; transmission may be year-round or seasonal
B(i) Classification:
- Uncomplicated malaria: symptomatic infection with malaria parasitaemia without evidence of vital organ dysfunction or life-threatening clinical symptoms and signs
- Severe or complicated malaria: malaria with evidence of vital organ dysfunction; a patient has severe malaria when there is P. falciparum asexual parasitaemia and no other confirmed cause of symptoms, in the presence of one or more life-threatening features
B(ii) Fever paroxysms:
- Fever paroxysms are due to synchronous release of merozoites, antigens, and other pyrogenic substances such as tumour necrosis factor-α and interleukins
- P. malariae: quartan fever, 72-hour periodicity
- P. vivax and P. ovale: tertian fever, 48-hour cycles
- P. falciparum: often exhibits continuous fever rather than periodic paroxysm, especially in children; periodicity less apparent; fatality can be as high as 30% if not urgently addressed
C(i) Microscopic diagnosis:
- Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smears; both thick and thin smears examined
- Thick film: identifies degree of parasitisation; quantification; monitoring response to treatment; sensitivity 86-98% by skilled microscopist
- Thin film: identifies the Plasmodium species
- P. falciparum smears best obtained after a febrile paroxysm; a single negative blood smear does not exclude malaria
- Parasite density: infected RBCs counted in relation to pre-determined number of WBCs; average 8,000/μl taken as standard; 200 leucocytes counted in 100 fields
- Plus system: + (1-10/100 thick fields); ++ (11-100/100 thick fields); +++ (1-10/thick field); ++++ (>10/thick field)
C(ii) Non-microscopic tests:
- RDTs: detects specific antigens (proteins) produced by malaria parasites via colour change on nitrocellulose strip; Quality-assured HRP-2 based RDT is recommended for all age groups; sensitivity of 95% at parasite densities of 200/μl; detects antigen, not parasites; parasite load is not quantified
- Issues with RDTs: HRP-2 RDTs could remain positive >2 weeks after treatment; occasionally negative in presence of parasites; degraded by excessive heat; limited shelf life (18-24 months)
- PCR: used for parasite diagnosis in tertiary institutions and research (e.g. resistance testing)
- Detection of antibodies by Radio immuno assay, immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay; serology useful for epidemiological surveys not clinical diagnosis

questions.question:
A 3-year-old child develops fever, lethargy, and a purpuric rash. He is rushed to the emergency room in shock. He is given IV fluids and antibiotics for meningococcal septicaemia. On day 2 his serum sodium is 122 mmol/L, urine sodium is 68 mmol/L, urine specific gravity is 1.024, urine output is 0.4 ml/kg/hr, and his CVP is 10. He is euvolemic.

(i) What is the electrolyte diagnosis, and which specific laboratory pattern confirms the subtype?
(ii) List four causes of this condition.
(iii) Outline the treatment for the symptomatic acute form.
(iv) How does this condition differ from Diabetes Insipidus on laboratory parameters?
questions.answerText:
(i) Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH) causing hypo-osmolar, euvolemic hyponatraemia. Laboratory pattern: serum Na ≤130 mmol/L, urine Na ≥60 mmol/L (alternative references cite ≥20 mmol/L), serum osmolality ≤275 mosmol/kg, urine SG ≥1.020, urine output <1 ml/kg/hr, CVP ≥8 — all consistent with SIADH. Defined as inappropriate high secretion of ADH in the presence of concentrated urine and euvolemic hyponatraemia.

(ii) Causes of SIADH:
• CNS disorders (as in meningococcal septicaemia with CNS involvement)
• Respiratory diseases
• Tumours
• Drugs
• Pain
• Cortisol deficiency
• Hypothyroidism
• Pregnancy
• Cerebrovascular accident (CVA)

(iii) Treatment of symptomatic acute hyponatraemia:
• Calculate mEq Na required: (desired Na − patient's Na) × 0.6 × weight in kg
• Use 3% saline = 513 mEq Na/L (approximately 0.5 mEq/cc)
• Give at rate of 1 ml/kg/hr; not faster than 1 mEq/L/hr
• Monitor serum Na 2–4-hourly until stable
• Fluid restriction (primary treatment for euvolemic SIADH)
• For chronic SIADH: very slow correction ≤0.5 mEq/L/hr; correct half the Na deficit on day 1 and the rest over the next 24–48 hours; may try lithium or demeclocycline in chronic SIADH
• Treat the underlying cause (meningococcal disease in this case)

(iv) SIADH versus Diabetes Insipidus:
• Serum Na: SIADH ≤130 mmol/L vs DI ≥150 mmol/L
• Urine Na: SIADH ≥60 mmol/L vs DI ≤40 mmol/L
• Serum osmolality: SIADH ≤275 mosmol/kg vs DI ≥305 mosmol/kg
• Urine SG: SIADH ≥1.020 vs DI ≤1.005
• Urine output: SIADH <1 ml/kg/hr vs DI >3 ml/kg/hr
• CVP: SIADH ≥8 vs DI ≤4

questions.question:
A. Describe the systematic approach to interpreting a chest X-ray in a child with suspected heart disease, under the following headings:
A(i) Heart size — how it is assessed in different age groups and the causes of an enlarged heart
A(ii) Heart shape — the four abnormal silhouettes, the condition each suggests, and the structural explanation for each shape

B. Describe the assessment of:
B(i) The aortic arch — normal and abnormal positions, causes of a right-sided arch, and what it signifies
B(ii) The pulmonary artery and lung fields — findings when enlarged versus absent/small, and the disease states each pattern points to
B(iii) Explain why these chest X-ray findings, taken together with clinical features, guide further investigation and management
questions.answerText:
A(i) Heart size: in children >5 years, the heart should not exceed 50% of the chest width (cardiothoracic ratio). In infants, 50–60% is allowed; 50% is the upper limit for children <2 years.
Causes of enlarged heart:
- Heart failure — from chamber dilatation/hypertrophy
- Pericardial effusion

A(ii) Abnormal heart shapes:
- Boot-shaped (coeur en sabot): apex is lifted, pulmonary artery is small — suggests Tetralogy of Fallot
- Egg-on-side: suggests Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA)
- Cottage loaf/Snowman/Figure-8 shape: suggests Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage (TAPVD) — all pulmonary veins drain abnormally, usually into the superior vena cava
- Globular heart shape: causes — pericardial effusion, endomyocardial fibrosis, dilatation of all chambers

B(i) Aortic arch: normally arches over the left side. Right-sided aortic arch (arches right but apex points left, i.e. still laevocardia): causes — Tetralogy of Fallot (commonest, seen in about 25%), pulmonary atresia, truncus arteriosus. In dextrocardia, a right-sided arch is normal.

B(ii) Pulmonary artery and lung fields:
Large pulmonary artery: causes — left-to-right shunt, pulmonary hypertension from any cause
Small/absent pulmonary artery: causes — pulmonary atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot
Increased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary plethora): left-to-right shunt, heart failure
Decreased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligaemia): severe obstruction — Tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary atresia

B(iii) The CXR findings together with the clinical picture narrow the differential and direct further investigation: ECG confirms the rate, rhythm, axis, and ventricular hypertrophy pattern; echocardiography (M-mode for measurements and cardiac function; 2D for structural defects; Doppler for pressures; colour flow for direction of blood flow) is now the primary modality. Cardiac catheterisation is reserved for complex anatomy, pressure measurement, and therapeutic procedures such as Rashkind's atrial septostomy.

questions.question:
A. Describe poliomyelitis under the following headings:
A(i) Aetiology: the virus, its serotypes, and the most common cause of paralytic disease.
A(ii) Pathogenesis: route of transmission, stages of infection, and predilection sites in the nervous system.
A(iii) The four clinical modes of presentation, with their relative frequencies and distinguishing features.

B. State the specific management of:
B(i) Acute phase (paralytic) poliomyelitis, including the most important single measure, positioning, and one critical contraindication.
B(ii) Long-term management.

C. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) and Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV), and state which is used in Nigeria and why.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: Polio virus is an RNA enterovirus with 3 serotypes — 1, 2, 3. Type I is the most frequent cause of poliomyelitis. Humans are the only known reservoir.

A(ii) Pathogenesis: Transmission is mainly by faeco-oral route; occasionally by oro-oral (saliva) route. The virus enters the lymph nodes in the GIT, multiplies in the reticuloendothelial system, then passes through the blood (viraemia) to migrate to the nervous system. It has a predilection for: anterior horn cells in the spinal cord (cervical and lumbar expansion — paralysis of limbs); cranial nerve nuclei in the medulla; and other sections (cerebral cortex, cerebellum, thalamus, hypothalamus). End result: flaccid paralysis.

A(iii) Four clinical modes:
1. Asymptomatic/Inapparent infection — 90–95% of infections; detected by serology showing high titre antibody; person sheds virus and infects others.
2. Abortive polio — 4–8% of patients; minor illness; fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation; lasts 1–3 days; diagnosis made during epidemics.
3. Non-paralytic polio — 1–5% (Lagunju: 1–2%); major illness; symptoms as in abortive but more intense; stiffness and pain of neck, back, and calf muscles; increased/decreased reflexes; NO sensory deficit; no paralysis; recovery in 2–10 days.
4. Paralytic polio — <1% of infections; flaccid paralysis of >1 muscle group; asymmetrical/spotty/haphazard; subtypes: spinal, bulbar (most severe/life-threatening — high mortality), bulbospinal.

B(i) Acute phase management:
- Bed rest — most important; muscle stress or strain precipitates and worsens paralysis.
- Analgesics and hot packs for pain relief.
- Appropriate posture (supine: knee slightly flexed, ankle perpendicular, trunk straight with sand bags).
- Monitor for worsening paralysis and bulbar involvement.
- ICU care and mechanical ventilation for bulbar polio.
- Critical contraindication: DO NOT GIVE INTRAMUSCULAR INJECTIONS to any patient with polio (precipitates paralysis).

B(ii) Long-term: physiotherapy to strengthen non-paralysed muscles; use of special ambulatory devices; surgery to correct contractures and deformities; social rehabilitation.

C. OPV advantages: cheap; easily administered; effective; increases herd immunity (especially important in low-hygiene environments like Nigeria). OPV disadvantage: causes Vaccine-Associated Polio Paralysis (VAPP) in immunosuppressed individuals (very rare).
IPV advantages: very effective; does not cause paralysis (used for immunosuppressed cases and household family). IPV disadvantages: more expensive; requires more gadgets (needles); requires higher technical skills.
Nigeria uses OPV because it is cheap, easily administered, and increases herd immunity — important in the Nigerian environment.

questions.question:
A 10-day-old preterm male infant (born at 27 weeks) develops seizures. He was delivered after a complicated labour with fetal distress. His blood sugar on arrival is 1.8 mmol/L. Cranial ultrasound reveals intraventricular haemorrhage.
(i) List at least five possible aetiological causes of neonatal seizures, categorised under perinatal, metabolic, and infectious causes.
(ii) Describe the four main seizure patterns seen in neonates, with the clinical features of each.
(iii) Distinguish clinically between jitteriness and seizures using the parameters given (stimulus sensitivity, cessation, rhythmicity, frequency, EEG, and autonomic disturbance).
(iv) State the time-based aetiological diagnosis guide: which conditions present on Day 1, which on Days 1–3.
questions.answerText:
(i) Aetiological causes of neonatal seizures:
Perinatal causes:
- Neonatal encephalopathy (20–40% of seizures).
- Intracranial haemorrhages — CNS trauma, subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), periventricular haemorrhage (PVH).
- Focal infarcts.
Metabolic causes:
- Hypoglycaemia.
- Hypocalcaemia (most common metabolic cause for neonatal seizures).
- Hypomagnesaemia; hypo/hypernatraemia; pyridoxine dependency.
- Inborn errors of metabolism (disorders of amino acid metabolism).
Infectious causes:
- Intracranial: meningitis; encephalitis (herpes, coxsackie, echo, CMV); toxoplasmosis.
- Extracranial: septicaemia; tetanus; severe respiratory distress.
Other: developmental defects (cerebral dysgenesis, hydrocephalus, microcephaly, neuronal migration defects); polycythaemia; unknown/idiopathic (3–25%); benign familial epilepsy (does not continue after neonatal period).

(ii) Seizure patterns:
1. Subtle seizure (50% of seizures): tonic horizontal deviation of eyes; staring look; repetitive blinking/fluttering of eyelids; oro-buccal movements (chewing, lip smacking, sucking, yawning); tonic posturing of a limb; apnoea; swimming/bicycling movements.
2. Clonic — Focal/Multifocal: twitching migrates haphazardly from one limb to another; occurs due to HIE and birth trauma.
3. Tonic seizure: stiffening similar to decerebrate posture but with eye signs and heavy breathing; often associated with apnoea; seen in IVH, preterm, and kernicterus.
4. Myoclonic seizures: rare in newborns; single/multiple flexion movements, slow and jerky; seen in developmental defects and anencephaly.
(Focal clonic: localised, often associated with loss of consciousness; signs of bilateral cerebral disorder; common in metabolic disorder, birth trauma, and cerebral infarction.)

(iii) Jitteriness vs. Seizures:
- Stimulus sensitivity: Jitteriness = ++; Seizure = absent.
- Cessation: Jitteriness = passive flexion / gentle grasp; Seizure = not stopped by these manoeuvres.
- Rhythmicity: Jitteriness = rhythmic oscillation; Seizure = fast and slow components.
- Frequency of jerks: Jitteriness = 5–6/sec; Seizure = 2–3/sec.
- Abnormal gaze/eye movement: Jitteriness = nil; Seizure = present.
- Autonomic disturbance: Jitteriness = nil; Seizure = increase in HR and BP.
- EEG: Jitteriness = normal; Seizure = abnormal.

(iv) Time-based aetiological diagnosis:
- Day 1: Birth asphyxia (HIE); cerebral trauma; pyridoxine dependency; narcotic withdrawal; inborn errors of metabolism.
- Days 1–3: Intracranial haemorrhage; hypocalcaemia; hypoglycaemia.

questions.question:
A. Describe Infective Endocarditis (IE) under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, classification, and the organisms responsible — listing in order of frequency
A(ii) Pathogenesis — the prerequisites for IE and the sequence from damaged endothelium to infective endocarditis

B. Describe:
B(i) The predisposing factors (cardiac and non-cardiac) and the epidemiology of IE in children
B(ii) The clinical features of IE, classifying them according to the mechanisms that produce them
B(iii) The Duke diagnostic criteria — major and minor
questions.answerText:
A(i) IE is a microbial infection of the endocardial (endothelial) surface of the heart; a cause of significant morbidity and mortality and a dreaded complication of structural heart disease.
Classification:
- Clinical course: acute vs subacute
- Aetiologic agent: bacterial vs fungal (very rare others)
- Valve affected: native vs prosthetic
Organisms (in order of frequency): Streptococci (alpha-haemolytic — most common; beta-haemolytic — uncommon; pneumococci — rare); Staphylococci (S. aureus — second most common; coagulase-negative staph — uncommon but increasing); HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella); Neisseria species; Fungi (e.g. Candida — in immunosuppression).

A(ii) Prerequisites for IE: damage to the endothelium → formation of non-bacterial (sterile) thrombus on damaged surface → transient bacteraemia with adherence of organisms → infective endocarditis → progressive enlargement of vegetation → infected emboli and proliferation of valve leaflet.

B(i) Predisposing factors:
Cardiac: complex congenital heart disease, uncorrected PDA, uncorrected small VSD, bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic mitral valve, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, prosthetic valves, surgically constructed shunts.
Non-cardiac: indwelling central catheters, injection drug use, immunosuppression, septicaemic illness (affects normal hearts), dental manipulation, urethral catheterisation, endoscopic procedures.
Epidemiology: commoner among older children and adults; less common in infancy; no sex predilection (one source states commoner in males).

B(ii) Clinical features classified by mechanism:
Bacteraemia: fever (99%), arthralgia, myalgia, headache.
Valvulitis: cardiac murmur (changing murmur 21%), heart failure (9%).
Immunological response: Osler's nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid factor, microscopic haematuria.
Emboli (systemic — from mitral/aortic valve or right-to-left shunt): CNS — CVA; renal — acute renal failure; mesenteric — acute abdomen; coronary — angina/MI; mycotic aneurysms (e.g. subarachnoid haemorrhage).
Emboli (pulmonary — in left-to-right shunts e.g. VSD): acute chest syndrome.
Other: petechiae (21%), splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, digital clubbing, hepatosplenomegaly (14%), dental caries (14%), splenomegaly (7%).

B(iii) Major criteria: two positive blood cultures for organisms typical of IE; three positive blood cultures for organisms consistent with IE; serologic evidence of Coxiella burnetii; echocardiographic evidence — oscillating intracardiac mass on a valve/supporting structures/path of regurgitant jets, cardiac abscess, new dehiscence of prosthetic valve, new valvular regurgitation.
Minor criteria: predisposing heart disorder or IV drug abuse; fever ≥38°C; vascular phenomena (arterial embolism, septic pulmonary embolism, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival petechiae, Janeway lesions); immunological phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor); microbiologic evidence not meeting major criteria.

questions.question:
A 2-day-old preterm male neonate (28 weeks' gestation) develops increasing abdominal distension, bloody stools, temperature instability, and apnoeic episodes. Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis and portal vein gas.
(i) State the diagnosis, and classify the stage according to Bell's staging criteria.
(ii) List the specific risk factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathogenesis of this condition in the sequence given.
(iv) Outline the medical and surgical management, and state the prognosis when NEC totalis is found.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Necrotising Enterocolitis (NEC).
Bell's staging: Pneumatosis intestinalis + portal vein gas + systemic signs = Stage IIB (Definite NEC: moderately ill + X-ray signs + systemic toxicity) or Stage IIIA (Advanced NEC: severely ill + IIB findings + ascites, bowel intact).
Full staging criteria:
- IA: Suspected NEC (clinical signs + non-diagnostic X-rays).
- IB: Suspected NEC (IA + bloody stool).
- IIA: Definite NEC (mildly ill + X-ray signs).
- IIB: Definite NEC (moderately ill + X-ray signs + systemic toxicity).
- IIIA: Advanced NEC (severely ill + IIB + ascites, bowel intact).
- IIIB: Advanced NEC (severely ill, perforated bowel).

(ii) Risk factors: Prematurity (single greatest risk factor; mean GA 30–32 weeks); hypoxia; feeding; bacteria. Others: cyanotic heart diseases; polycythaemia; twin gestation.

(iii) Pathogenesis (sequence):
Hypoxaemia / acidosis / low cardiac output / hypothermia → decreased splanchnic blood flow → mucosal oedema (from hypertonic feed) and intestinal colonisation (E. coli & Klebsiella) + absent normal colostrum / immature gut immunity + invasive infection → transmural bowel necrosis → perforation → endotoxin release → DIC → septic shock.

(iv) Medical management: NPO; IVF; NaHCO3; FFP; inotropic agents; antibiotics.
Surgical: If patient fails to improve or there is perforation → resection of the necrotic bowel; viable bowel exteriorised as stomas.
NEC totalis (necrosis from duodenum to rectum) is found in 14% of infants; prognosis is very poor.
Prevention: Prevent premature birth (ultimate goal); induction of GI maturation (prenatal steroid therapy); breastfeeding (IgA); very slow introduction of feeding.

(i) Transient Tachypnoea of the Newborn (TTN), also known as Respiratory Distress Syndrome type II or 'wet lung' disease.

(ii) Pathophysiology — Normal: In fetal life, lungs are expanded with an ultrafiltrate of fetal serum fluid. During and after birth, this fluid must be removed. Passage through the birth canal squeezes the thorax, eliminating liquid in the lungs. Pulmonary capillaries and lymphatics remove remaining fluid. In TTN: liquid in the lung is removed slowly or incompletely due to decreased thoracic birth squeeze (e.g. caesarean section without labour) or decreased respiratory efforts → retained fluid → tachypnoea and respiratory distress. Recovery is usually complete within 3 days.

(iii) Risk factors: caesarean delivery; prolonged labour; maternal asthma and smoking; precipitate labour; macrosomia of the fetus; excessive maternal sedation → poor respiratory drive.

(iv) CXR findings: prominent vascular markings (perihilar); fluid in lung tissue; over-aeration (symmetric); small pleural fluid; occasionally the right side may appear more opacified than the left; sometimes cardiomegaly. Radiological resolution usually by 2nd or 3rd day.

(v) Treatment: supportive — NGT feeding or IVF; supplemental O2 (cyanosis resolves with minimal O2); good thermal environment; antibiotics when sepsis is clinically suspected (aminoglycoside + cephalosporin); no benefits with diuretics. Prognosis: excellent — generally self-limited without significant morbidity or mortality; however there is increased risk of hospitalisation from asthma during preschool years. If radiological resolution is not complete by day 3 or respiratory symptoms persist longer than 5 days, consider another diagnosis.
questions.question:
A neonate is born at 36 weeks gestation via emergency Caesarean section for antepartum haemorrhage. At birth the infant is noted to be dyspnoeic and tachypnoeic (RR 68 cpm) with subcostal recession and grunting. By day 2 of life the respiratory rate falls to 40 cpm and the child is no longer dyspnoeic.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the pathophysiology of this condition, contrasting it with the normal mechanism of lung fluid clearance after birth.
(iii) List the risk factors for this condition.
(iv) Describe the expected chest radiograph findings.
(v) Outline the treatment and prognosis.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Social paediatrics deals with non-biomedical aspects of diseases in children. It is a global, holistic, and multidisciplinary approach to child health that considers the health of the child within the context of their family, society, environment, and school; it integrates the physical, mental, and social dimensions of child health, development, and care; covers prevention and promotion of health and quality of life.
Three areas: (1) child health problems with social causes; (2) child health problems with social consequences; (3) child health care in society.

A(ii) Four areas of child health care: curative paediatrics; health promotion; disease prevention; rehabilitation.
Three determinants: socio-economic, political, and cultural determinants of health and disease.

A(iii) Components:
Behavioural: child and caregiver (parents/guardian).
Environmental physical: immediate or community physical environment.
Environmental non-physical: non-physical community environment.
Behaviour is a function of knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, actual life experiences, societal norms, and enabling factors (e.g., poverty). These affect presentation, course, and final outcome of disease.

B. Social determinants:
- Social structure: family units (family size, spacing), extended family, clan, larger community
- Social status: education, employment
- Resources: availability, distribution/allocation, planning (involvement of appropriate interest groups)
- Population dynamics: developing countries are mostly rural dwellers
- Governance: political commitment/will of government; corruption
- Religious issues: taboos
- Peculiar problems: natural disasters (floods, famine, hurricanes, tsunamis, earthquakes); communal conflicts/civil wars/terrorism; child abuse/neglect; street children/child labour/child marriage; drug abuse; orphans

C. Role of the paediatrician: understand the relationship between all components of health (physical, mental, social, and spiritual); adopt a holistic approach to child healthcare.
Home visits/seminars purpose: facilitates understanding of the peculiar social circumstances of each child visited with respect to — the epidemiology of the disease; effects of the disease on child, family, and community; effect of the family or community on the child's condition; fashioning preventive strategies for the child and community at large; rehabilitation; the role of the family, community, and government in health promotion.
Requirements: good knowledge base of the biomedical aspect of the disease; vigilance; open mind (it goes beyond poverty and poor hygiene); there is something to learn from every case.
questions.question:
A. Describe social paediatrics under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and the three areas it acts in
A(ii) The four areas of child health care it encompasses and the three determinants of health and disease
A(iii) The three components (behavioural, environmental physical, environmental non-physical) and how each affects presentation, course, and outcome of disease

B. State the specific social determinants of health and disease, covering social structure, resources, population dynamics, governance, religious issues, and peculiar problems.

C. Explain the role of the paediatrician in social paediatrics, and describe the purpose and requirements for home visits/social paediatrics seminars.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Werdnig–Hoffman Disease is an autosomal recessive disorder. It results from destruction and degeneration of motor neurones in the spinal cord and the brain stem in utero, following prolongation of the normal process of programmed cell death (apoptosis). It is the most severe form of Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA).

A(ii) Clinical features:
- Reduced foetal movements in utero.
- Infant is severely hypotonic at birth with a frog-like posture.
- Weak cry.
- Tongue fasciculations — diagnostic sign.
- Reflexes absent.
- Difficulty with swallowing and accumulation of secretions in the mouth.
- No associated sphincteric or sensory impairment (posterior columns intact).
- Normal IQ — intellect is preserved.
- May manifest in utero as reduction in fetal movement (kicking).
- Death usually occurs in the 2nd year of life.

A(iii) Investigations:
1. Electromyography (EMG): shows fibrillation.
2. Muscle biopsy: shows degeneration of muscles.
3. Biopsy of anterior horn cells (on post-mortem): shows atrophy of anterior horn cells and cranial motor nuclei.
Cause of death: respiratory failure, as muscles (including respiratory muscles) become paralysed; in children, death is from recurrent aspirations and respiratory infections.

B. In Werdnig–Hoffman Disease, the lesion is confined to the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and cranial motor nuclei; the cerebral cortex, which mediates intellect and higher function, is entirely spared — hence intellect is normal. In cerebral palsy, the damage is to the developing brain itself (cerebral cortex and/or subcortical structures); depending on the extent and location of brain damage, cognitive function and intellect may be significantly impaired, especially in quadriplegia (poor mentation, cognitive dysfunction, and mental retardation are common).

C. Comparison:
- Werdnig–Hoffman: site — anterior horn cell (lower motor neurone); inheritance — autosomal recessive; onset — in utero/birth; key clinical sign — tongue fasciculations, frog-like posture; investigation — EMG fibrillation, muscle biopsy degeneration.
- DMD: site — muscle (myopathy); inheritance — X-linked; onset — after 3 years; key clinical sign — Gower's sign, calf pseudohypertrophy; investigation — CK >10× normal, myopathic EMG.
- Myasthenia Gravis: site — neuromuscular junction; inheritance — autoimmune (juvenile), rare autosomal recessive; onset — usually >10 years; key clinical sign — ptosis, diplopia worsening with activity; investigation — Tensilon test positive, anti-AChR antibodies.
questions.question:
A. Describe Werdnig–Hoffman Disease (Infantile Spinal Muscular Atrophy) under the following headings:
A(i) Genetic basis, mode of inheritance, and pathological process.
A(ii) Clinical features: posture at birth, tone, reflexes, motor and sensory profile, intellectual status, and the pathognomonic sign.
A(iii) Investigations and cause of death.

B. Explain why the intellect is preserved in Werdnig–Hoffman disease, whereas it may be impaired in cerebral palsy, using the anatomical location of the pathological lesion in each condition.

C. Compare Werdnig–Hoffman Disease with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and Myasthenia Gravis under the headings of: site of lesion in the motor unit, mode of inheritance, onset, key clinical sign, and investigation finding.

A. Describe bilirubin metabolism under the following headings:
A(i) Production and initial steps of haem catabolism
A(ii) Plasma transport and hepatic uptake
A(iii) Hepatic conjugation and the specific enzyme involved
A(iv) Enterohepatic circulation and urinary/faecal excretion

B. Explain the clinical basis for each of the following:
B(i) Why jaundice is not clinically detectable until bilirubin exceeds a defined threshold
B(ii) Why bilirubinuria precedes visible jaundice in hepatitis

C. Distinguish between unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin with respect to:
C(i) Water solubility and albumin binding
C(ii) Ability to appear in urine
questions.answerText:
A(i) Haem from red cell breakdown is converted to biliverdin by haem oxygenase, then biliverdin reductase catalyses the reduction of biliverdin to bilirubin. This unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble and non-water-soluble at this stage.
A(ii) Unconjugated bilirubin is transported in plasma tightly bound to albumin. After hepatic uptake, it binds intracellularly to ligandin (Y protein) and Z protein, which facilitate transport within the hepatocyte to the endoplasmic reticulum for conjugation.
A(iii) Within the endoplasmic reticulum, bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronyltransferase. Bilirubin monoglucuronide reacts with a second glucuronic acid via transesterase to form bilirubin diglucuronide — the major form of conjugated bilirubin secreted into bile.
A(iv) In the intestine, bacterial action converts conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen, some of which is reabsorbed and excreted in urine (enterohepatic circulation). The remainder is oxidised to stercobilin and excreted in stool, giving it its brown colour.
B(i) Jaundice becomes clinically apparent as yellowish discolouration of skin, sclera, and mucous membranes only when serum bilirubin exceeds 5 mg/dL. Below this threshold, bilirubin elevation is subclinical.
B(ii) Only conjugated (water-soluble, direct) bilirubin appears in urine because unconjugated bilirubin is tightly bound to albumin and cannot pass the glomerular filter. Hepatocellular damage in hepatitis causes early regurgitation of conjugated bilirubin into the bloodstream during the prodromal phase, before visible scleral icterus, producing bilirubinuria.
C(i) Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble and tightly bound to albumin; conjugated bilirubin diglucuronide is water-soluble and has lower albumin affinity.
C(ii) Only conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin can pass the glomerular filter and appear in urine; unconjugated bilirubin bound to albumin cannot be filtered renally.

questions.question:
A neonate born at 28 weeks gestation is now day 5 of life in the neonatal unit. He is on respiratory support. The nurse notices he is tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and has bounding pulses. On auscultation, a continuous murmur is heard under the left clavicle. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings.

(i) State the diagnosis and explain why this lesion is classified as a left-to-right shunt.
(ii) State three predisposing factors that keep this fetal structure patent after birth.
(iii) Describe the mechanism of normal closure of this structure after birth and state which pharmacological agent exploits this mechanism to achieve closure.
(iv) Describe four complications that can result if this lesion is left untreated (using the same pathophysiological framework as for VSD).
(v) State the drug used to close this lesion pharmacologically, and describe the surgical treatment if pharmacological closure fails.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).
Classification as left-to-right shunt: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta. After birth, because the aorta has higher pressure than the pulmonary artery, blood flows from the aorta (left) into the pulmonary artery (right) — hence left-to-right shunt. The haemodynamic changes are essentially similar to VSD; both involve a high-pressure system unlike ASD which is a low-pressure system.

(ii) Predisposing factors that keep the ductus patent:
- Preterm delivery (immature closure mechanism; PDA is commoner at high altitude and after birth asphyxia — both conditions maintain low oxygen tension)
- Birth asphyxia (reduced oxygen tension needed to close the duct)
- High altitude (reduced ambient oxygen)
- Maternal rubella (congenital rubella syndrome includes PDA)
(Any three accepted)

(iii) Mechanism of normal closure: Closure is caused by prostaglandin effect — indomethacin (prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor) has a constrictive/closing effect; prostaglandin has a dilatory effect (keeps duct open). After birth, rising oxygen tension inhibits prostaglandin, causing ductal smooth muscle to constrict and close within 48 hours.
Pharmacological agent exploiting this mechanism: Indomethacin (prostaglandin inhibitor) — closes the PDA.
(Note: Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open in duct-dependent lesions — the reverse.)

(iv) Complications if untreated:
- Congestive heart failure (from left ventricular volume overload, identical mechanism to large VSD)
- Pulmonary hypertension (from increased pulmonary blood flow and reflex vasospasm, causing thickening of pulmonary vessels)
- Eisenmenger syndrome (if pulmonary vascular resistance becomes irreversible and exceeds systemic — right-to-left shunt occurs)
- Infective endocarditis (turbulent flow damages endothelium)
- Failure to thrive/small for gestational age (from hypoperfusion of peripheral tissues)
(Any four accepted)

(v) Pharmacological closure: Indomethacin (prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor).
Surgical treatment if pharmacological closure fails: Surgical ligation of the ductus arteriosus (closed-heart surgery).

questions.question:
A newborn infant is delivered at 35 weeks gestation. At birth, the infant is noted to have a frog-like posture, is severely hypotonic, has a weak cry, and tongue fasciculations are visible. The mother reports reduced fetal movements throughout the third trimester. Deep tendon reflexes are absent. IQ testing is not yet applicable. No sensory deficits are detected.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and its mode of inheritance?
(ii) Describe the pathological process at the cellular level that causes this condition.
(iii) State the expected findings on investigations (EMG, muscle biopsy, and post-mortem anterior horn cell biopsy).
(iv) State the prognosis and the cause of death in this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Werdnig–Hoffman Disease (Infantile Spinal Muscular Atrophy / SMA Type I). Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive.

(ii) Pathological process: there is atrophy and degeneration of the anterior horn cells due to disturbance of controlled cell growth, development, and cell death (prolongation of the normal process of programmed cell death — apoptosis). This results in destruction and degeneration of motor neurones in the spinal cord and the brain stem in utero. It is the most severe form of Spinal Muscular Atrophy.

(iii) Investigations:
- Electromyography (EMG): shows fibrillation — evidence of denervation of muscle.
- Muscle biopsy: shows degeneration of muscles.
- Biopsy of anterior horn cells (on post-mortem): shows atrophy of anterior horn cells and cranial motor nuclei.

(iv) Prognosis: very poor. Death usually occurs in the 2nd year of life from recurrent aspirations and respiratory infections. The cause of death is respiratory failure, as the respiratory muscles become progressively paralysed.

(i) Diagnosis: measles.
Pathognomonic sign: Koplik spots
- Precise characteristics: greyish white dots as small as grains of sand with a reddish area surrounding them
- Location: on the palate and buccal mucosa, usually opposite the lower molars
- Very transient: last 12-18 hours
- They represent the pathognomonic enanthem consisting of serous exudate and proliferation of endothelial cells
- The red mottling on the hard and soft palate is called exanthem (distinct from Koplik spots)
(ii) WHO clinical case definition and laboratory confirmation:
- WHO clinical case definition: maculopapular rash (non-vesicular) and fever (>38°C) with at least one of the three symptoms: cough, coryza and conjunctivitis
- FBC: leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis
- Laboratory confirmation:
  - Isolation of the measles virus from a clinical specimen (e.g. nasopharynx, urine)
  - Significant rise in measles IgG by any standard serologic assay (e.g. EIA, HA)
  - Positive serologic test for measles IgM antibody
(iii) Complications by system:
- Respiratory: bronchopneumonia (viral giant cell and bacterial); laryngotracheobronchitis (croup); activation of TB lesion
- Neurological: febrile seizure; encephalomyelitis (1-2/1000, appears 2-5 days after onset of rash); SSPE (mean incubation ~10.8 years, chronic degenerative disease with behavioural and intellectual deterioration and seizures); ADEM; haemorrhagic measles
- Cardiovascular: myocarditis (infrequent; child can develop heart failure)
- GIT: gastroenteritis; malnutrition; cancrum oris; hepatitis (rare)
- Ophthalmic: blindness due to Vitamin A deficiency; conjunctivitis
- Other: subcutaneous emphysema from mediastinal emphysema; purpura fulminans; DIC
(iv) Management and prevention:
- Supportive and symptomatic: antipyretic, eye drops, clean the eyes, calamine lotion, adequate fluid intake
- Specific agent: high dose Vitamin A significantly reduces risks of morbidity and mortality
- Other management: antibiotics for bacterial complications; management of heart failure; nutritional rehabilitation; rehydration; management of croup
- Prevention: live attenuated vaccine; national programme uses monovalent measles vaccine in freeze-dried form reconstituted with diluent; also available as MMR (combination with rubella and mumps)
- Efficacy: 85%; side effects: 10% develop low grade fever, 5% develop mild generalized non-infectious rash
- Duration of immunity: lifelong; no contraindications even where child is sick or malnourished
- Dose: 0.5 ml SC, upper left arm; schedule at 9 months (MCV1) and 15 months (MCV2)
questions.question:
A 2-year-old presents with 3 days of high fever, barking cough, red eyes with photophobia, and profuse rhinorrhoea. On day 4, a maculopapular rash appears starting on the face and spreads downward. Examination reveals white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars.
(i) State the diagnosis. Identify and name the pathognomonic sign and describe its precise characteristics.
(ii) Describe the WHO clinical case definition and the laboratory tests that confirm this diagnosis.
(iii) List all complications under each system (respiratory, neurological, GIT, ophthalmic, cardiovascular).
(iv) Describe management including specific agent proven to reduce morbidity and mortality, and the vaccine used for prevention.

A 5-year-old child presents with sudden onset of choking, followed by a brief asymptomatic interval. Two weeks later she returns with haemoptysis, recurrent right-sided pneumonia, and a persistent wheeze. Chest radiograph shows unilateral hyperinflation with mediastinal shift to the left on expiration, and a radio-opaque object in the right main bronchus.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the most common airway foreign bodies and the pattern of their natural history?
(iii) What investigations are recommended?
(iv) Which procedure is used to manage this condition, and what are the possible complications if the condition is left untreated?
(v) Name the congenital laryngeal abnormality most commonly associated with additional anatomical findings in children with stridor.
questions.answerText:
(i) Foreign body aspiration causing right bronchial obstruction with obstructive emphysema and unilateral pneumonia.

(ii) Most common airway foreign bodies: nuts, carrot pieces, beans, sunflower/watermelon seeds; conforming objects (bolus of amala), and balloons — spherical objects are common. Natural history: choking/coughing/gagging → asymptomatic interval (up to half of cases diagnosed beyond one week) → complications (haemoptysis, pneumonia, lung abscess).

(iii) Investigations: inspiratory and expiratory chest radiograph (not reliable alone); lateral decubitus views; examination and films usually normal in the first 24 hours; if radio-opaque, the object may be visible on neck or chest radiograph. Flexible fibreoptic bronchoscopy may locate the foreign body.

(iv) Flexible fibreoptic bronchoscopy is used to remove the foreign body. If left untreated, complications include haemoptysis, pneumonia, and lung abscess, and chronic retention can lead to bronchiectasis.

(v) Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital laryngeal abnormality. In about 35% of infants with laryngomalacia, an additional anatomical finding (e.g. tracheomalacia, subglottic stenosis, vocal cord paralysis) is also present. Tracheomalacia is occasionally accompanied by bronchomalacia.

(i) Spot diagnosis: Inguinal hernia. In infants with an inguinal hernia, immediate referral to surgery is required.
Full list of diagnoses not to miss in children and infants:
- Meningitis and cerebral malaria (in any sick or febrile child, this is the diagnosis to exclude)
- Intussusception (in the screaming child)
- Epiglottitis (distinguish from croup)
- Hernia (inguinal hernia in infants needs immediate referral to surgery)
- Dehydration after diarrhoea and/or vomiting (do not underestimate)
- Appendicitis (uncommon in children but may rapidly progress to perforation)
- Diabetes mellitus
- Asthma (under-diagnosed; consider in child with recurrent cough)
- Torsion of the testes (more often in the older child/adolescent; refer at once, minutes matter)
- Perthes disease (beware the child with a limp)
- Urinary tract infection (pyrexia with no obvious cause merits a urine culture)
- Non-accidental injury
- Failure to thrive (all practitioners should have a percentile chart of height and weight)
- Developmental problems: CDH (Ortolani's manoeuvre), squint, undescended testes, hearing defects, scoliosis

(ii) UTI: important not to miss; pyrexia with no obvious cause merits a urine culture. One proven UTI means a referral for IVU/USS. Renal damage can occur at an early age and may be preventable.

(iii) CDH: vital that it is detected early. Manoeuvre: Ortolani's manoeuvre.

(iv) Squint: refer constant squints as early as possible in the first weeks of life. Inconstant squints need referral if persisting after 6 months. Early treatment of squint is essential. Serious diagnosis squint can mask: Retinoblastoma (can present as squint).
questions.question:
A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the general paediatric clinic with a swelling in the right groin that becomes more prominent when he cries. He was noted to have been irritable since yesterday.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis? State the complete list of diagnoses not to miss in children and infants (all that apply to infants and older children).
(ii) State all the risk factors and complications for urinary tract infection in children as described, and explain the diagnostic workup required following one proven UTI.
(iii) Describe the approach to congenital dislocation of the hip (CDH) — why early detection is vital and what manoeuvre is used.
(iv) State the approach to squint (strabismus) in infants and children, including the timing of referral for constant versus inconstant squints, and what serious diagnosis squint can mask.

questions.answerText:
(i) The child has severe dehydration (approximately 10% weight loss: from 11 kg to 10 kg = 1 kg = 10% of body weight). Clinical signs of severe dehydration include lethargy, sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle, very dry mucous membranes, and skin pinch going back very slowly. Given that the diarrhoea fluid is watery and the clinical picture shows signs of collapse, this is most consistent with isonatraemic (isotonic) dehydration (the most common type, 80%), where lost fluid is similar in Na+ concentration to blood and Na+ and H2O losses are proportionate.

(ii) Affected systems and consequences: Total body water (TBW) depletion in both intracellular and extracellular compartments. ECF depletion leads to poor skin turgor, sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle, hypotension, tachycardia. ICF depletion leads to lethargy and altered sensorium. Renal consequence: very decreased urine output (kidneys conserving water). GI consequence: ongoing losses from diarrhoea. Risk of shock if untreated.

(iii) Three types of dehydration based on serum Na:
• Isonatraemic (80%): Na 130–150 mEq/L; lost fluid similar in Na to blood; no osmotic gradient; ICF volume unchanged.
• Hyponatraemic (5–10%): Na <130 mEq/L; more Na than H2O lost; ECF hypotonic relative to ICF; H2O shifts from ECF to ICF, worsening intravascular volume depletion for a given amount of TBW loss; caused by electrolyte-rich fluid losses replaced by plain water, or diuretic use.
• Hypernatraemic (5–10%): Na >150 mEq/L; less Na than water lost; ECF relatively preserved because water moves from ICF space; patient appears less dehydrated for a given amount of TBW loss compared to isotonic dehydration; degree of dehydration is usually underestimated; cardiovascular instability does not develop until large amounts of fluid are lost.

(iv) Management sequence for this child with severe dehydration:
• Prevention/treatment goal: correct dehydration, prevent dehydration, maintain or improve nutrition, treat aetiological agents.
• Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) is inappropriate for initial treatment of severe dehydration with signs of shock, patients with paralytic ileus, or marked abdominal distension.
• Intravenous Therapy (IVT): Give 20–30 ml/kg IV boluses of Ringer's lactate or normal saline until organ perfusion is restored, then continue rehydration.
• If child cannot drink, continue with IVT: 0.45% saline in 5% dextrose (or 0.18% saline in 4.3% dextrose based on serum sodium values). Calculate deficit and maintenance. Give ½ deficit and ⅓ maintenance in 7 hours and the remaining deficit and maintenance in 16 hours. Add KCl (10–20 mmol/500 ml bag) as soon as urine is passed.
• For isonatraemic dehydration: treat as per standard protocol. Reassess frequently.
• High-risk factors present in this child: age below 12 months (18 months — borderline), frequent stools >8/day, vomiting >2/day.
• Correct metabolic acidosis: if pH <7.2 or base deficit >−10, use 0.6 × wt(kg) × base deficit; give half over 1 hour and remaining half over 8–12 hours.
questions.question:
An 18-month-old child is brought with a 3-day history of watery diarrhoea (10 stools/day) and vomiting (5 times/day). He is lethargic, with sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor with slow return (>2 seconds), and very decreased urine output. Weight 10 kg; recent weight was 11 kg.

(i) Identify the organs and structures affected and the type of dehydration present.
(ii) List the compressed or affected physiological systems and their consequences.
(iii) Name the differential fluid types that may account for different dehydration patterns, and give the clinico-anatomical reasoning distinguishing them.
(iv) Outline the complete management sequence for this child's condition.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute Leukaemia; most likely Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL) — commoner in children; also Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML).
Classification: ALL (commoner in children) and AML. It is the commonest childhood malignancy in Caucasians; accounts for 7.1% in Ibadan. Peak age 2–5 years. Occurs more often in Down's syndrome.
(ii) Clinical features:
General: Fever, Lassitude, Pallor.
Bone Marrow: Anaemia, Infections, Bleeding (especially skin and buccal mucosa).
Extramedullary invasion: Lymphadenopathy, Hepatosplenomegaly.
Other sites: CNS, Testes, Bones and Joints, Skin.
(iii) Investigations:
- Full blood count: shows anaemia.
- WBC: usually high, but may be low or normal.
- Platelet count: usually low due to associated DIC.
- Peripheral blood film: blast cells are seen.
- Bone marrow aspiration: shows leukaemia cells; this is the diagnostic investigation.
Note: Presence of blasts in peripheral film alone is NOT diagnostic.
Differential diagnosis: Infectious leukaemoid reaction, Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura, Aplastic anaemia, Rheumatic fever, Rheumatoid arthritis.
(iv) Treatment: Chemotherapy — COAP regimen: Cyclophosphamide, Oncovin, Adriamycin, Prednisolone; Radiotherapy can also be used; Bone marrow transplantation.
Sites of relapse: Bone marrow (commonest), CNS, Testes.
Prognostic factors:
- Age: Better for those between 2–10 years; worse <2 years and >10 years.
- Race: Worse in blacks.
- Sex: Worse in males.
- WBC: Worse if initial value >50,000/mm³.
- Type: Worse with AML; in good centres 80% cure in ALL; better in non-B, non-T cell, and worse with B cell, T cell, and pre-B.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old presents with a 3-week history of pallor, fever, and easy bruising. Examination shows generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse bone tenderness. WBC is elevated. Bone marrow aspiration confirms blast cells.
(i) What is the diagnosis and how is it classified in children?
(ii) List ALL clinical features as grouped under general, bone marrow, extramedullary invasion, and other sites of involvement.
(iii) What investigations are performed and how is the diagnosis confirmed?
(iv) State the treatment regimen used and the sites of relapse. Describe the factors determining prognosis.

A 6-week-old male infant born at term after an uncomplicated delivery presents with breathlessness, excessive sweating on the forehead during feeds, and inability to complete feeds. His mother noticed palpitations when she held him to her chest. On examination, he is small for gestational age, tachypnoeic, and tachycardic. There is a praecordial bulge and a hyperactive praecordium. On auscultation, a pansystolic murmur is heard loudest at the mid-left sternal edge radiating to the back, with a loud P2. Chest X-ray shows increased pulmonary vascular markings and cardiomegaly.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis?
(ii) Identify four predisposing or causative factors for this condition.
(iii) Using the two-flow-chart model, describe the pathophysiological sequence by which this condition leads to congestive heart failure, covering both the pulmonary and systemic circulation.
(iv) State the hallmark physical sign of heart failure in children found on abdominal examination and explain why it occurs.
