(v) Describe the treatment of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Ventricular septal defect (VSD) with congestive heart failure.

(ii) Predisposing/causative factors:
- Intrauterine infections (e.g. rubella: associated with PDA, VSD, PS)
- Chromosomal abnormalities (e.g. Trisomy 21/Down syndrome: AV septal defect/VSD/ASD; Trisomy 18: VSD/ASD; Trisomy 13: VSD)
- Drugs (e.g. thalidomide, cytotoxic drugs, steroids)
- X-radiation
- Preterm delivery
- Birth asphyxia
- Familial/environmental factors (commoner among siblings)
(Any four accepted)

(iii) Pathophysiological sequence:
Pulmonary circuit: The large pressure gradient (left ventricular systolic pressure 130–140 mmHg vs. right ventricular 30 mmHg) drives blood through the VSD into the right ventricle → right ventricle pumps increased volume to the pulmonary artery → lungs receive excessive blood, causing reflex vasospasm → increased pulmonary venous return → increased preload to the left atrium and ventricle → increased left ventricular wall tension → more blood shunted via the VSD → vicious cycle. The damped blood into the lung and reflex vasospasm thicken pulmonary vessels, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (right ventricular afterload).
Systemic circuit: Reduced stroke volume reaches the aorta → hypoperfusion of peripheral tissues → vasomotor centre discharges, increasing heart rate → shortens systolic time interval → reduces left ventricular filling → more blood dampened into lungs (wet lungs) → lungs less compliant → hypoxia → apneustic centre summons accessory muscles of respiration → intercostal and subcostal recession. Kidney perceives hypoperfusion as hypovolaemia → fluid retention → worsens preload → congestive heart failure (left failure first, then right failure from increased preload and pulmonary vascular resistance).

(iv) Hallmark of heart failure on abdominal examination: Tender hepatomegaly.
Mechanism: Acute liver congestion stretches the hepatic capsule, making the liver tender. It is the hallmark of congestive heart failure in children.

(v) Treatment: Batch repair under profound hypothermia. Very rarely on bypass. (Medical: digoxin and diuretics for heart failure; cardiac catheterisation to determine pulmonary wedge vascular pressure if pulmonary vascular disease is suspected before surgery.)

A(i) Management of Type 1 DM in children:
• Insulin types: three basic formulations — short-acting (e.g. regular, soluble, lispro); medium- or intermediate-acting (e.g. isophane, lente); long-acting (e.g. ultralente). Lispro insulin is an analogue of human insulin with rapid onset and shorter duration than modified regular insulin; ideally suited for meal times.
• Dosing rule of thumb: prepubertal children — 0.5–1 U/kg/day with 60–70% given in the morning and 30–40% in the evening. Adolescents may require up to 2 U/kg/day. About one-third is short-acting formulation and two-thirds is medium- to long-acting formulation.
• Basal-bolus concept: Basal insulin (suppresses glucose production between meals and overnight) = 40–50% of daily needs. Bolus insulin (meal time, limits post-meal hyperglycaemia, immediate rise and sharp peak at 1 hour) = 50–60% of total daily insulin requirement. Regimens: MDI (Multiple Dose Insulin) or CSII (Continuous Subcutaneous Insulin Infusion — insulin pump).
• Dietary macronutrient distribution: carbohydrates 50–60% of daily energy intake (no more than 10% from sucrose or refined carbohydrates); fat <30%; protein 10–20%.

A(ii) Monitoring:
• HbA1c: best method for medium- to long-term diabetic control monitoring. HbA1c levels should be checked every 3 months. Most clinicians aim for HbA1c values of 7–9%.
• Target blood glucose range: aim to keep blood glucose concentrations as close as possible to reference ranges, 80–180 mg/dl.
• Monitoring of growth and development using percentile charts is a crucial element. Poor gain of height and weight, hepatomegaly, and late puberty may indicate persistently poorly controlled DM.
• Microalbuminuria screening: from age 12 years, annual urinalysis is needed to test for microalbuminuria (slightly increased albumin excretion rate, AER) as an indicator of risk for diabetic nephropathy.

B(i) Acute vs long-term complications:
Acute complications (reflect difficulties maintaining balance between insulin therapy, dietary intake, and exercise):
• Hypoglycaemia: sweatiness, confusion, behavioural changes, and coma when blood glucose falls below 30–40 mg/dL
• Hyperglycaemia: blood sugar rises if insulin is insufficient for a given glucose load
• Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): most important cause of mortality and severe morbidity in children with DM; life-threatening medical emergency

Long-term complications (from prolonged hyperglycaemia and metabolic consequences of insulin deficiency):
• Retinopathy
• Cataracts
• Hypertension
• Progressive renal failure
• Early coronary artery disease
• Peripheral vascular disease
• Neuropathy (both peripheral and autonomic)
• Increased risk of infection
• Injection-site hypertrophy
• Growth failure; delayed puberty

Associated autoimmune diseases: common with IDDM, particularly in children who have HLA-DR3; up to 20% of children with diabetes have thyroid autoantibodies.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the management of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus in children under the following headings: insulin types available, the traditional dosing rule of thumb by pubertal status, the basal-bolus concept (percentage allocation), and dietary distribution of macronutrients.
A(ii) Explain the monitoring approach in children with Type 1 DM, including: the role of HbA1c, the target blood glucose range, the frequency of HbA1c testing, and at what age microalbuminuria screening begins.
B(i) Distinguish between the acute and long-term complications of Type 1 DM in children, providing a complete list under each category.

questions.answerText:
A(i) SAM is defined by any one of: (1) MUAC less than 11.5 cm in children aged 6–59 months; (2) weight-for-height Z-score (WHZ) below –3 SD (or below –3 Z-score); or (3) presence of bilateral pitting oedema (nutritional).
A(ii) Kwashiorkor is primarily caused by protein deficiency and is characterised by bilateral pitting oedema, miserable affect, skin changes (flaky paint dermatosis, depigmentation), hair changes, hepatomegaly from fatty infiltration, and low serum albumin (hypoalbuminaemia). Marasmus results from combined severe caloric and protein deficiency, producing profound wasting (loss of muscle and fat) without oedema, and tends to preserve serum albumin through adaptive protein catabolism — this is the primary biochemical difference.
A(iii) Protein-energy malnutrition causes predominantly T-cell immune impairment with thymic atrophy and reduction in T-lymphocyte numbers and function, particularly CD4+ cells. The thymus is the organ affected, undergoing severe atrophy. This leads to increased susceptibility to viral, fungal, and intracellular bacterial infections.
B(i) Iron is withheld during the acute stabilisation phase because the antioxidant systems are severely depleted in SAM. Free iron is a potent generator of reactive oxygen species via the Fenton reaction, causing oxidative damage to cells and tissues already compromised by malnutrition. Iron supplementation begins in the rehabilitation phase once antioxidant capacity has been partially restored.
B(ii) Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate refeeding triggers insulin release, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium from the extracellular compartment into cells for anabolic processes. The most dangerous shift is severe hypophosphataemia, which can cause cardiac failure, respiratory failure, and neurological dysfunction. This is prevented by gradual refeeding as per the WHO SAM protocol.
C(i) Stunting is measured using height-for-age Z-score (HAZ below –2 SD). Wasting (acute malnutrition) is measured using weight-for-height Z-score (WHZ below –2 SD) or MUAC below 12.5 cm.
C(ii) Stunting reflects chronic malnutrition — prolonged inadequate nutrition and/or recurrent infections impairing linear growth over time. The critical window of vulnerability for stunting is the first 1000 days of life (from conception to 2 years of age), after which stunting becomes largely irreversible. Wasting reflects acute malnutrition — recent or current inadequate dietary intake or illness-driven weight loss.
questions.question:
A. Describe severe acute malnutrition (SAM) under the following headings:
A(i) The three anthropometric/clinical criteria that individually define SAM
A(ii) The distinction between marasmus and kwashiorkor in terms of primary deficiency, oedema, and serum albumin
A(iii) The primary immune defect of protein-energy malnutrition, including the organ affected and the lymphocyte subset predominantly impaired

B. Explain the clinical basis for each of the following:
B(i) Why iron is withheld during the acute stabilisation phase of SAM treatment
B(ii) Why refeeding syndrome occurs on transition to the rehabilitation phase, and which electrolyte shift is most dangerous

C. Distinguish stunting from wasting on the basis of:
C(i) The anthropometric measure used for each
C(ii) The type of nutritional insult (acute vs chronic) each reflects and the critical window of vulnerability for stunting

A. Describe the classification and pathophysiology of obstructive heart lesions in congenital heart disease:
A(i) Define obstruction as a category and give examples of right ventricular outlet tract obstruction, left ventricular outlet tract obstruction, and peripheral obstruction
A(ii) Compare the incidence of the three main obstructive lesions (pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, coarctation of the aorta) from the Ibadan data, and explain why coarctation is the most clinically urgent in the neonatal period

B. For each of the three obstructive lesions, state:
B(i) The types/classification of each
B(ii) The key distinguishing clinical signs — including the specific pulse character, murmur type, and location — that differentiate one from the other at the bedside
B(iii) Explain why disease of these lesions may lead to a distant functional deficit — specifically, why untreated coarctation leads to left ventricular failure and why untreated severe AS in infancy leads to heart failure
questions.answerText:
A(i) Obstruction impedes blood flow out of the heart, increasing cardiac workload — either intra-cardiac or extra-cardiac.
- Right Ventricular Outlet Tract (RVOT) obstruction: pulmonary stenosis
- Left Ventricular Outlet Tract (LVOT) obstruction: coarctation of the aorta; also aortic stenosis
- Peripheral obstruction: e.g. branches of the pulmonary trunk

A(ii) Incidence from Ibadan (635 cases, 1965–1975):
- Pulmonary stenosis (isolated): 9%
- Aortic stenosis: 7.5%
- Coarctation of the aorta: 12% (but more clinically urgent)
Coarctation is the most clinically urgent: it is the commonest primary cardiovascular lesion causing heart failure in the acyanotic neonate in the first week of life. Severe coarctation presents at birth with acute cardiovascular collapse when the ductus arteriosus closes (especially in pre-ductal coarctation where ductal flow was supplying the lower body).

B(i) Types:
Pulmonary stenosis: valvar (commonest), infundibular (fibromuscular band), supravalvar (rare — Williams Syndrome), peripheral (branches — from drugs or rubella).
Aortic stenosis: valvar (bicuspid/unicuspid), subvalvar (fibromuscular diaphragm, elongated stenotic tunnel), supravalvar (Williams Syndrome component).
Coarctation of the aorta: concentric or cylindrical; sites — thoracic, abdominal, or complete tubular hypoplasia of arch; pre-ductal, juxta-ductal, or post-ductal.

B(ii) Key distinguishing bedside features:
Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at left upper sternal edge (pulmonary area); soft and delayed P2; ejection click (shows less severity); left parasternal heave (RVH); post-stenotic dilatation (pulmonary knuckle) on CXR. Pulse normal unless critical.
Aortic stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at right second intercostal space; aortic ejection click at apex; small-volume, slow-rising (anacrotic) pulse; heaving apical impulse (LVH); systolic thrill at right second ICS; reversed S2 splitting or single S2; in supravalvar type, right arm pulse > left arm pulse.
Coarctation of the aorta: reduced femoral pulses; upper limb hypertension; disparity between upper and lower limb BP >20 mmHg; continuous murmur over scapular (collateral flow); ejection systolic murmur + ejection click; increased apical impulse (LVH); rib notching on CXR.

B(iii) Distant functional deficit mechanisms:
Coarctation → LV failure: the aortic obstruction increases afterload on the left ventricle massively; the LV must generate high pressure to push blood past the obstruction; sustained pressure overload leads to LVH, which eventually decompensates → left ventricular failure (and right ventricular failure from secondary pulmonary hypertension).
Severe AS in infancy → heart failure: severe aortic stenosis ± coarctation of the aorta is the commonest cause of heart failure in the first year of life. Critical obstruction reduces cardiac output → the presentation is hypoplastic left heart syndrome with heart failure. Severe obstruction in the fetus means the left ventricle does not develop adequately (hypoplasia).

(i) Von Gierke disease (Type I Glycogen Storage Disease). Enzyme defect: deficiency of Glucose-6-phosphatase. The condition is autosomal recessive. It presents during the first 2 years of life, with hepatomegaly present at birth (though not initially noticed).

(ii) Risk factors and complications:
• Autosomal recessive inheritance (recurrence risk one in four per sibling)
• Clinical features: failure to thrive, abdominal pain, progressive enlargement of the abdomen, episodes of hypoglycaemia during stress (vomiting, convulsions, loss of consciousness)
• Hyperglycaemia after meals; obesity in some cases (glucose converted to fat and stored)
• Excessive mobilisation of fat and protein: increased ketone bodies, metabolic acidosis
• Prothrombin deficiency leading to bleeding tendencies
• No response to adrenaline or glucagon injection (confirms enzyme block)
• Impaired glucose tolerance test

(iii) Medical management (first-line):
• Frequent meals high in protein (to maintain blood glucose and prevent hypoglycaemic episodes), ± steroids.
• Dietary management is first-line because the underlying defect (inability to release glucose from glycogen stores) is addressed by maintaining continuous glucose supply through frequent feeding, particularly overnight and during illness.
• There is no specific enzyme replacement therapy for this condition; management is dietary and supportive.
• Liver biopsy confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating glycogen accumulation.
questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents with progressive abdominal distension, severe hepatomegaly noted since infancy, recurrent episodes of loss of consciousness during febrile illness, and failure to thrive. On investigation, fasting blood sugar is 2.1 mmol/L, there is no response to adrenaline or glucagon injection, and liver biopsy shows massive glycogen accumulation.

(i) Name the diagnosis and specify the enzyme defect.
(ii) What are the risk factors and the full range of complications?
(iii) What surgical or medical management options are available, and which is first-line?

A 6-year-old boy is brought to clinic with a 2-year history of weakness of the face, expressionless face, inability to close the eyes fully, and difficulty drinking from a cup. On examination there is bilateral facial weakness, weakness of orbicularis oculi and orbicularis oris, but calf muscles appear normal. Serum CK is marginally elevated.

(i) What is the diagnosis and what is its mode of inheritance?
(ii) How does this condition differ from Bell's Palsy with respect to aetiology, nature of facial weakness, laterality, and associated features?
(iii) State the prognosis and life expectancy for this condition.
(iv) List all four types of muscular dystrophy, with their key distinguishing features.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy. Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant.

(ii) Differences from Bell's Palsy:
- Aetiology: Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy is a genetic myopathy (autosomal dominant); Bell's Palsy is a disorder of cranial nerve VII, associated with herpes zoster or otitis media infection.
- Nature of weakness: Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy causes progressive muscle degeneration (myopathy — intrinsic muscle disease); Bell's Palsy is a neuropathy (cranial nerve VII dysfunction) that tends to be sudden in onset.
- Laterality: Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy is bilateral; Bell's Palsy involves weakness of one side of the face.
- Associated features: Bell's Palsy has Bell's sign/phenomenon (eyeball rolls up when patient attempts to close the eye), hyper-acusis (damage to stapedius muscle removes dampening effect), ringing in the ear, and deviation of angle of mouth to the normal side. Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy has expressionless face and orbicularis involvement without these features. Bell's Palsy disappears within a few weeks with conservative treatment; Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy is chronic and progressive.

(iii) Prognosis: Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy is compatible with life (normal life expectancy). It is a milder, less common form of muscular dystrophy. Progression is slower than DMD.

(iv) Four types of muscular dystrophy:
1. Pseudohypertrophic (Duchenne) Muscular Dystrophy: X-linked; most severe; onset after 3 years; waddling gait, Gower's sign, calf pseudohypertrophy; CK >10× normal; death before 20 years from cardiomyopathy.
2. Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy: autosomal dominant; less common, milder; onset first decade; facial weakness, expressionless face; CK normal or slightly elevated; compatible with life.
3. Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophy: autosomal recessive; onset late childhood; slowly progressive; affects pelvic girdle mainly, may affect shoulder girdle; compatible with life.
4. Becker Pseudohypertrophy: X-linked; mild form of DMD; presents later; progresses slowly; increased CK; better prognosis.

(i) Diagnosis: cerebral malaria. For diagnosis, all three criteria must be met:
- P. falciparum malaria parasitaemia
- Unrousable coma: Glasgow Coma Scale <11, Blantyre Coma Scale <3; unrearousable coma not attributable to any other cause; coma must persist for at least 30 minutes after a generalized convulsion
- Absence of other causes of coma
Note: convulsions associated with loss of consciousness persisting for >30 min after a seizure with P. falciparum malaria parasitaemia is also considered cerebral malaria.
(ii) Differential diagnoses:
- Meningitis: patient may have a stiff neck
- Encephalopathy: repeated convulsions or deep coma from other causes
- Diabetes mellitus: patient may be dehydrated, acidotic or in coma
- Septicaemia: usually very ill and toxic with warm extremities
- Epilepsy: usually no temperature; history of convulsions before
- Acute renal failure from other causes: usually associated with reduced or no urine output
- Viral haemorrhagic fevers: usually associated with jaundice and bleeding tendency
(iii) Investigations and clinical monitoring:
Investigations:
- Blood smear for malaria parasites
- Haematocrit (PCV)/Haemoglobin
- Blood sugar level
- Lumbar puncture in unconscious patients
- Urinalysis for sugar and blood
Clinical monitoring:
- Monitor vital signs (pulse, temperature, respiratory rate, blood pressure) at least 6 hourly, more frequently initially
- Monitor input and output: strict 24-hour input/output chart
- Monitor level of consciousness at least 6 hourly
- Frequently turn patient in bed to avoid bedsores
- Keep a clear drug chart recording dose, time given, and number of times per day
- Monitor parasitaemia by daily blood smear; if high after 2-3 days, review adequacy of drug dose
(iv) Management of convulsions:
- Ensure patent airway and that the patient is breathing
- Correct hypoglycaemia or control temperature
- In children: give rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg OR IM paraldehyde 0.1 ml/kg
- If convulsions continue: give IM phenobarbitone 10-15 mg/kg
- If a patient has a seizure and does not recover within 30 minutes from that seizure, it should be considered as severe malaria and managed accordingly
questions.question:
A 9-year-old boy presents with 2 days of fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Three weeks earlier he had a confirmed P. falciparum infection treated at a peripheral clinic. He is now deeply unresponsive, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8, and blood smear is positive for P. falciparum.
(i) State the diagnosis and the criteria that must all be met for this diagnosis to be made.
(ii) List the differential diagnoses of deep coma with fever in a child in a malaria-endemic area.
(iii) State the investigations required at this point and the clinical monitoring parameters to be used during admission.
(iv) Outline the management of convulsions that occur in this child.

A. Describe Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) under the following headings:
A(i) Aetiology, pathogenesis, and the pattern of cardiac damage it produces
A(ii) The modified Jones' criteria for diagnosis — all major and minor criteria, and the evidence of recent streptococcal infection required

B. Describe the management of ARF:
B(i) Specific drug treatment — agents, doses, and the rationale for long-term prophylaxis
B(ii) Distinguish ARF from five important differential diagnoses and explain why each can be confused with it
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus of Lancefield causing pharyngitis (not skin sepsis, which causes acute glomerulonephritis). Pathogenesis: the organism in the throat generates antibody or antigen-antibody complexes deposited in the heart and joints; not everyone with streptococcus in the throat develops pharyngitis, and not everyone with pharyngitis develops ARF. It causes pancarditis:
- Pericarditis: thin fibrinous sticky exudate ("bread-and-butter") or small frank pericardial effusion
- Myocarditis: direct myocardial damage
- Endocarditis: mitral valve (most commonly), aortic valve, tricuspid valve (occasionally), pulmonary valve (rarely)
Histopathological hallmark: Aschoff Nodules — aggregates of inflammatory cells, pathognomonic of ARF.

A(ii) Major criteria ("CASES"): Carditis, Arthritis (pain and swelling, fleeting/migratory, large joints), Subcutaneous nodules (over bony surfaces, indicate ongoing carditis), Erythema marginatum (transient skin rash, spares face, not common in Negroids), Sydenham's chorea (CNS manifestation, basal ganglia, commoner in adolescent girls).
Minor criteria (3 clinical, 2 laboratory): Fever, Arthralgia, Previous history of ARF; elevated acute phase reactants (WCC, ESR, C-reactive protein), prolonged PR interval on ECG (normal: children 0.16s, adolescents 0.18s, adults 0.2s).
Evidence of recent streptococcal infection: ASOT >333 Todd units (IU); positive throat swab culture.
Diagnosis: 2 major criteria OR 1 major + 2 minor criteria + evidence of recent streptococcal infection.

B(i) Bed rest. Aspirin (salicylate) as anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and analgesic: maximum dose 100 mg/kg/day in divided doses (side effects: gastric erosion — take with meals; metabolic acidosis — monitor electrolytes). Prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for life-threatening carditis (side effects: salt and water retention; glycosuria — monitor urinalysis). Treatment of heart failure with digoxin and diuretics. Procaine penicillin for 7–10 days to eliminate the organism and stop antibody production.
Long-term prophylaxis (to prevent second attack, which is more severe): Benzathine penicillin (Penadur) 1.2 mega/month for at least 3 years; alternatives (less effective) — oral penicillin V 125–250 mg twice daily, or oral erythromycin 125–250 mg twice daily.

B(ii) Differential diagnoses:
- Malaria: fever and joint pains may overlap; no carditis or chorea
- Sickle cell disease: characterised by bone pains rather than joint pains; can have septic arthritis
- Acute leukaemia (leukaemoid reaction): bone pain, fever, but distinct haematological findings
- Rheumatoid arthritis: joint pains tend to be symmetrical, affect small joints of hands and feet, non-flitting
- Infective endocarditis: fever + murmur + heart failure, but embolic phenomena, positive blood cultures, and predisposing heart lesion distinguish it

questions.question:
A. Describe unconjugated bilirubin transport and the factors affecting kernicterus risk under the following headings:
A(i) The protein carrier in plasma, the normal molar ratio of bilirubin:albumin, and what happens when this ratio is exceeded
A(ii) Two conditions that increase the risk of dissociation of bilirubin from albumin and increase the free bilirubin fraction
A(iii) The intracellular binding proteins within the hepatocyte that facilitate bilirubin transport to the endoplasmic reticulum

B. Explain the clinical basis for each of the following observations in neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia:
B(i) Why the prevalence of significant hyperbilirubinaemia in Nigerian hospital practice is estimated at 23–60%, substantially higher than in Western countries
B(ii) Why the Ibadan series (Effiong and Laditan, 1976) identified G6PD deficiency as accounting for 59% of aetiological factors in outborn neonates with significant hyperbilirubinaemia

C. Describe the pathophysiology of kernicterus:
C(i) The form of bilirubin responsible, and the specific brain structures where it deposits
C(ii) The preventive treatment modalities available, how phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin, and when exchange transfusion is indicated instead
questions.answerText:
A(i) Unconjugated bilirubin is transported in plasma tightly bound to albumin at a normal molar ratio of 0.5–1:1. When the molar ratio exceeds 1:1 — meaning albumin binding sites are saturated — free unconjugated bilirubin dissociates from albumin and can cross the blood-brain barrier, causing kernicterus.
A(ii) Two conditions that increase dissociation: (1) acidosis — at pH below 7.4, the albumin-bilirubin binding affinity decreases, releasing free bilirubin; (2) displacement by competing ligands — certain drugs (e.g., sulphonamides) and free fatty acids from intravenous lipid infusions compete with bilirubin for albumin binding sites, releasing free unconjugated bilirubin into the circulation.
A(iii) After hepatic uptake, unconjugated bilirubin binds intracellularly to ligandin (Y protein) and Z protein, which facilitate its transport within the hepatocyte to the endoplasmic reticulum where conjugation with glucuronic acid occurs via UDP-glucuronyltransferase.
B(i) The prevalence of significant hyperbilirubinaemia in Nigerian hospital practice is estimated at 23–60%, substantially higher than in Western countries, reflecting the high incidence of G6PD deficiency (the dominant aetiological factor in sub-Saharan African populations), ABO incompatibility, neonatal sepsis, and low birth weight — multiple compounding aetiological factors operating simultaneously in this population and setting.
B(ii) G6PD deficiency has a very high prevalence in sub-Saharan African populations, including Nigeria, because the enzyme deficiency confers partial protection against falciparum malaria in heterozygous females, maintaining the G6PD-deficient allele at high population frequency. In outborn neonates — delivered without hospital monitoring, often exposed to oxidative triggers such as traditional herbal medicines, naphthalene (mothballs), or infections — oxidative haemolysis from G6PD deficiency is triggered before the infant reaches hospital, explaining the 59% proportion.
C(i) Kernicterus is caused by free (unbound) unconjugated bilirubin, which is lipid-soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier. It deposits in the basal ganglia (particularly the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei) and brainstem nuclei, causing permanent neurological damage with choreoathetosis, auditory neuropathy, and intellectual impairment.
C(ii) Prevention: phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin to water-soluble photoisomers (lumirubin and configurational isomers) through photoisomerisation, which are excreted in bile and urine without requiring hepatic conjugation. Exchange transfusion is indicated when the rate of rise of bilirubin exceeds 5 mg/dL/day despite phototherapy, when bilirubin reaches exchange transfusion thresholds on standard charts, or when signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy appear; it physically removes bilirubin, haemolysed red cells, and maternal antibodies from the circulation.

questions.question:
A 5-week-old infant is referred for evaluation of jaundice that has persisted since the first week of life. The parents are of Nigerian origin. The infant is breastfed. On examination there is hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Stool colour has been pale over the last 2 weeks. Total serum bilirubin is 11.2 mg/dL, direct (conjugated) bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL. The urine-reducing substance test is positive.

(i) State the diagnosis category indicated by the laboratory results and the specific diagnosis suggested by the positive urine-reducing substance test.
(ii) Identify the enzyme deficiency responsible for the specific metabolic diagnosis, and explain the mechanism by which the accumulation causes hepatocellular damage.
(iii) Identify at least two other metabolic and one viral cause of neonatal cholestasis that must be excluded in this investigation workup.
(iv) Outline the specific treatment for the metabolic diagnosis identified, the dietary measure required, and two fat-soluble vitamins that must be supplemented in all neonatal cholestasis cases and the basis for their deficiency.
questions.answerText:
(i) The laboratory results — conjugated bilirubin of 4.3 mg/dL (exceeding 15% of total bilirubin and above 2.0 mg/dL) — indicate neonatal cholestasis. The positive urine-reducing substance test indicates the specific diagnosis of galactosaemia: the Clinitest detects galactose (a non-glucose sugar) spilling into the urine, which is characteristic of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency in galactosaemia.
(ii) Galactosaemia results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). This enzyme normally converts galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate. Without it, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates within hepatocytes (as well as renal tubules and brain cells). The intracellular accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate is hepatotoxic, causing hepatocyte injury, inflammation, fibrosis, and ultimately cirrhosis if lactose-containing feeds are not eliminated.
(iii) Other metabolic causes to exclude: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (accumulation of abnormal misfolded protein in hepatocytes leading to hepatocyte damage); cystic fibrosis (viscid secretions causing mucus plugging of bile ducts — confirmed with sweat chloride testing); hypothyroidism and hypopituitarism (combined hormone deficiency impairing bilirubin conjugation); and TPN-associated cholestasis (particularly in premature infants requiring prolonged parenteral nutrition). Viral cause to exclude: hepatitis B virus (detectable by HBsAg), and TORCH infections including herpes simplex virus, CMV, and enteroviruses (blood, urine, and CSF cultures for these).
(iv) Specific treatment for galactosaemia: immediate elimination of all lactose-containing feeds (breast milk and standard infant formula both contain lactose). The infant must be switched to a lactose-free formula. This is both diagnostic (improvement confirms galactosaemia) and life-saving. Fat-soluble vitamins requiring supplementation: bile acids are essential for micellar solubilisation and intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. Cholestasis with impaired bile secretion leads to their malabsorption. Vitamin K deficiency causes coagulopathy (prolonged PT/INR) and vitamin D deficiency causes rickets; both require supplementation. Cholestyramine may be used to bind bile acids in the intestinal lumen, reducing enterohepatic recirculation and pruritus.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents with headaches and is found to have hypertension during a school medical check. On examination, the radial pulses are bounding, but the femoral pulses are markedly reduced. Blood pressure in the right arm is 160/90 mmHg and in the right leg is 120/60 mmHg (difference of 40 mmHg systolic). There is a continuous murmur heard over the scapular area. Chest X-ray shows rib notching of ribs 3–8 posteriorly.

(i) Identify the diagnosis and state the most common anatomical site of this lesion.
(ii) Identify three clinical types of this lesion based on position relative to the ductus arteriosus.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of (a) the reduced femoral pulses, (b) the continuous murmur over the scapular area, and (c) the rib notching on chest X-ray.
(iv) State the threshold blood pressure difference between upper and lower limbs that suggests this diagnosis, and identify which investigation is used to delineate the anatomy.
(v) List the four surgical/interventional procedures available for this condition, and state the primary indication for urgent surgical intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Coarctation of the aorta.
Most common anatomical site: Thoracic aorta — most commonly the juxtaductal position (near the ductus arteriosus). Sites include thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta, or the entire arch (complete tubular hypoplasia).

(ii) Three types based on position relative to ductus arteriosus:
1. Pre-ductal coarctation
2. Juxta-ductal coarctation
3. Post-ductal coarctation

(iii) Anatomical basis:
(a) Reduced femoral pulses: The narrowing of the aorta reduces blood flow distal to the obstruction, diminishing pulse volume in the lower limb vessels including the femoral arteries.
(b) Continuous murmur over the scapular area: Collateral circulation develops through intercostal arteries to bypass the coarctation; these enlarged, tortuous collateral vessels carry continuous turbulent flow, generating the murmur heard over the scapular region.
(c) Rib notching: The enlarged intercostal collateral arteries run in the costal grooves and erode the inferior surfaces of ribs 3–8 posteriorly, producing the notching seen on CXR. (This indicates established collateral circulation.)

(iv) Blood pressure threshold: A difference of more than 20 mmHg (normal difference ≤ 20 mmHg) between upper and lower limb systolic pressure suggests coarctation of the aorta.
Investigation to delineate anatomy: Cardiac catheterisation.

(v) Surgical/interventional procedures:
1. Classical resection and end-to-end anastomosis
2. Subclavian flap repair
3. Modified subclavian flap repair with stent (complication: re-coarctation)
4. Percutaneous transluminal balloon aortoplasty
Primary indication for urgent surgical intervention: Symptomatic patients and those with associated heart failure (including neonates). Asymptomatic patients with hypertension receive medical treatment for hypertension and heart failure; surgical relief is after 6 months of life.

(i) Laryngomalacia (congenital laryngeal stridor). The dominant feature in more than half of cases is floppy arytenoid cartilages. Congenital deformities or flabbiness of the epiglottis and supraglottic aperture and weakness of the airway walls lead to collapse and some airway obstruction with inspiration.

(ii) Congenital causes of upper airway obstruction: laryngomalacia; laryngeal web; subglottic stenosis; laryngocoele; tracheo-oesophageal fistula; craniofacial anomalies.

(iii) Treatment: it is a self-limiting condition; specific treatment is usually not necessary. Symptoms subside by the age of 12–18 months. Reassure the parents; advise to feed slowly; advise to place the child in the prone position. In rare cases where the condition does not improve, tracheotomy is done.

(iv) In about 35% of infants with laryngomalacia, an additional anatomical finding is also present: tracheomalacia, subglottic stenosis, or vocal cord paralysis. Tracheomalacia is occasionally accompanied by bronchomalacia.

(v) Diagnosis is confirmed by direct laryngoscopy under general anaesthesia. Differential diagnosis includes malformations of the laryngeal cartilages or vocal cords, intraluminal webs, generalised severe chondromalacia of the larynx and trachea, tumours of the larynx, mucus retention cysts, branchial cleft cysts, thyroglossal duct remnants, hypoplasia of the mandible, macroglossia, haemangioma, lymphangioma, Pierre Robin syndrome, congenital goitres.
questions.question:
A 4-week-old male neonate presents with inspiratory and expiratory noisy breathing since birth that worsens when he lies supine, during feeding, and when he cries. He has a weak cry and mild chest retractions with suprasternal and supraclavicular indrawing during inspiration. There is no fever. His weight gain has been slow.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what anatomical feature is predominantly responsible?
(ii) List the congenital causes of upper airway obstruction described.
(iii) Describe the treatment of this specific condition.
(iv) Name the additional anatomical findings associated with this condition in about 35% of cases.
(v) How is the diagnosis confirmed?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: Erb's Palsy is due to damage to C5 and C6 nerve roots (upper roots of the brachial plexus). It usually occurs during the birth of a baby, especially large babies (macrosomia), due to pulling of the head at the second stage of labour. It also occurs in breech delivery (bottom-first delivery).

A(ii) Clinical presentation:
- Weakness of muscles supplied by C5 and C6, resulting in:
  • Loss of abduction of the shoulder.
  • Inability to externally rotate the shoulder.
  • Inability to supinate the forearm.
- Characteristic posture: the arm is held adducted, internally rotated, and pronated ("waiter's tip" position, though this term is used in some sources for Klumpke's).
- Loss of biceps reflex (C5, C6).

A(iii) Management:
- Wearing a long-sleeve shirt for the baby and pinning it down to the pillow (to immobilise and support the limb).
- Early physiotherapy.
- Gentle massage and other physical exercises.
- Surgery if required: should be done before 4 years of age.
Prognosis: most recover fully, but a few do not recover completely.

B. Anatomical basis for the posture: C5 supplies abductors (deltoid, supraspinatus) and external rotators of the shoulder; C6 supplies the biceps (flexion and supination of forearm) and other supinators. When C5 and C6 are damaged, the muscles producing abduction, external rotation, and supination are paralysed. The unopposed action of the adductors, internal rotators, and pronators then produces the characteristic posture of adduction, internal rotation, and pronation. Loss of biceps reflex reflects C5/C6 arc disruption.

C. Comparison:
C(i) Erb's Palsy: C5 and C6 (upper roots). Klumpke's Paralysis: C7, C8, T1 (lower roots of brachial plexus).
C(ii) Erb's Palsy: weakness of shoulder abductors, external rotators, elbow flexors, and forearm supinators; arm held adducted, internally rotated, pronated (waiter's tip variant of Klumpke's refers to the hand deformity — Klumpke's gives rise to Waiter's tip hand). Klumpke's Paralysis: damage to lower roots — weakness of intrinsic hand muscles (supplied by C8/T1 via ulnar nerve); results in claw hand / Waiter's tip hand deformity.
C(iii) Erb's Palsy: pulling of the head at second stage of labour (big babies, vertex delivery) or breech delivery. Klumpke's Paralysis: excessive traction on the lower brachial plexus — may occur in breech delivery with arm above head, or shoulder dystocia.
questions.question:
A. Describe Erb's Palsy under the following headings:
A(i) Aetiology: which nerve roots are damaged, the obstetric mechanism of injury, and the circumstances in which it occurs.
A(ii) Clinical presentation: which movements are lost and the characteristic posture of the arm.
A(iii) Management and prognosis.

B. Explain the anatomical basis for the specific posture of the arm in Erb's palsy (adduction, internal rotation, pronation, loss of biceps reflex).

C. Compare Erb's Palsy with Klumpke's Paralysis:
C(i) Nerve roots involved.
C(ii) Muscles affected and resulting deformity.
C(iii) Clinical setting in which each occurs.

A 2-year-old male child with known Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is brought in unconscious by his mother. She reports he has been vomiting for 2 days, has a fruity smell to his breath, and his abdomen is distended. On examination he is severely dehydrated, breathing deeply and rapidly (Kussmaul breathing), blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg, and his blood glucose is 28 mmol/L.

(i) State the diagnosis and its three cardinal diagnostic features.
(ii) Describe the complete resuscitation and management sequence.
(iii) What specific electrolyte danger must be anticipated, and how is it managed?
(iv) What complication must be monitored for during treatment, and how is it treated?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). Three cardinal features:
• Hyperglycaemia: blood glucose >300 mg/dl (>11.1 mmol/L or >200 mg/dl in some criteria)
• Ketonuria: >5 mmol/L (and ketonaemia)
• Metabolic acidosis: bicarbonate <15 mmol/L and/or venous pH <7.3

(ii) Resuscitation and management sequence:
• Laboratory baseline: blood glucose, electrolytes (E&U), calcium, phosphorus, venous pH, acid-base status (arterial if shock present), FBC, urea and creatinine, triglycerides, urinalysis for ketones, infection workup if indicated. Hourly blood glucose; 2–4-hourly electrolytes and venous pH depending on severity.
• Expansion of intravascular volume: 0.9% normal saline at 20 ml/kg over 30 minutes; repeat if necessary, then continue at one-half maintenance.
• Potassium replacement: commence as soon as resuscitation is completed and prior to commencing insulin infusion (withhold if renal failure suspected until electrolytes are available and a catheter is inserted).
• Insulin therapy: IV infusion pump at 0.1 U/kg/hr; reduce when glucose falls below 250 mg/dl, then start IV 5% dextrose.
• Bicarbonate: generally not required. May be considered after consultation in the severely shocked patient with severe acidosis (arterial pH <7.0 and/or HCO3 <5 mmol/L). Cardiac monitoring required.
• Ongoing monitoring: blood glucose hourly, electrolytes 2-hourly, TPR.
• Recovery: wean off IV insulin, commence subcutaneous insulin, commence feeds.

(iii) Hypokalaemia. Although potassium may appear normal, increased, or reduced initially due to acidosis-driven shifts, total body potassium is depleted by vomiting, osmotic diuresis, and hyperaldosteronism. As insulin drives glucose into cells it carries potassium intracellularly, causing dangerous hypokalaemia. Management: commence potassium replacement (10–20 mmol/500 ml bag) as soon as resuscitation is completed and urine is passed; withhold if renal failure is suspected. ECG monitoring is required.

(iv) Cerebral oedema: the major life-threatening complication during DKA treatment, presenting with bradycardia, hypertension, and anisocoria (signs of raised intracranial pressure). Treatment: IV Mannitol; ICU care.

questions.question:
Describe Necrotising Enterocolitis (NEC).
A(i) Describe the pathogenesis of NEC step by step, naming the initiating physiological derangements, the intermediate processes at the intestinal wall, and the terminal systemic events.
A(ii) State how the gross pathological stages of NEC (Bell's staging criteria IA through IIIB) relate to the clinical and radiological findings at each stage.
B(i) Explain how NEC progresses from localised mucosal injury to systemic collapse — identifying the structure whose necrosis leads to perforation, the substance released into the circulation, and the two systemic syndromes that follow.
B(ii) State the three preventive strategies, explain the physiological rationale for each, and state the prognosis when NEC totalis is found at surgery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pathogenesis of NEC step by step:
1. Initiating physiological derangements: Hypoxaemia; acidosis; low cardiac output; hypothermia.
2. Intermediate intestinal process: Decreased splanchnic blood flow → mucosal oedema (from hypertonic feed) and intestinal colonisation with E. coli and Klebsiella + absent normal colostrum + immature gut immunity → invasive infection.
3. Terminal systemic events: Transmural bowel necrosis → perforation → endotoxin release → DIC → septic shock.

A(ii) Bell's staging criteria — clinical and radiological correlates:
- IA: Suspected NEC — clinical signs only + non-diagnostic X-rays.
- IB: Suspected NEC — IA features + bloody stool.
- IIA: Definite NEC — mildly ill + X-ray signs (pneumatosis intestinalis, intestinal dilatation, ileus).
- IIB: Definite NEC — moderately ill + X-ray signs + systemic toxicity.
- IIIA: Advanced NEC — severely ill + IIB findings + ascites; bowel intact.
- IIIB: Advanced NEC — severely ill, perforated bowel (pneumoperitoneum on X-ray).

B(i) Progression from localised to systemic:
- The structure whose necrosis leads to perforation: the bowel wall (transmural bowel necrosis → perforation of the intestinal wall).
- Substance released: endotoxin (from gram-negative bacteria released into the bloodstream on perforation).
- Two systemic syndromes: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) and septic shock.
Additional radiological progression: intestinal dilatation → ileus → portal vein gas → ascites → pneumoperitoneum (perforation).

B(ii) Three preventive strategies and rationales:
1. Preventing premature birth (ultimate goal) — prematurity is the single greatest risk factor (mean GA 30–32 weeks); prevention of prematurity removes the primary predisposing factor.
2. Induction of GI maturation with prenatal steroid therapy — glucocorticoids accelerate maturation of the gut mucosa and immune defences, reducing susceptibility to mucosal injury and invasion.
3. Breastfeeding (IgA) — breast milk provides secretory IgA and colostrum that support gut immunity, which is otherwise absent in premature infants; very slow introduction of feeding may also be useful.
Prognosis when NEC totalis is found: In 14% of infants, NEC totalis (necrosis from duodenum to rectum) is found at surgery; prognosis is very poor.

(i) Jones Criteria fulfilled:
Major criteria:
1. Carditis (diastolic murmur at the apex)
2. Arthritis (fleeting joint pain affecting the knees — migratory arthritis of large joints)
Minor criteria:
1. Fever
2. ECG: prolonged PR interval (0.22 seconds — above the normal upper limit of 0.16 s for children)
Evidence of recent streptococcal infection: ASO titre 400 Todd units > 333 Todd units = suggestive of ARF.
Diagnosis confirmed: 2 major criteria (carditis + arthritis) + evidence of recent streptococcal infection = meets Jones criteria for ARF.

(ii) Murmur at the apex in ARF vs. chronic RHD:
Acute ARF: Care-Coombs murmur (heard in the acute phase of ARF) — different from the murmur of mitral incompetence; it is a diastolic murmur at the apex during acute inflammation. Patient may present with this murmur due to valve involvement.
Chronic RHD (mitral incompetence): Apical pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex, radiating to the axilla — this is the murmur of established mitral valve incompetence from fibrotic valve changes.

(iii) Pathological process in carditis (pancarditis):
- Pericarditis: thin fibrinous sticky exudate (bread-and-butter pericarditis); or small frank pericardial effusion. If small, a pericardial friction rub is heard.
- Myocarditis: usually direct inflammatory involvement; manifests as tachycardia (partly from fever, partly direct myocardial involvement).
- Endocarditis: affects the mitral valve most commonly; then aortic; occasionally tricuspid; rarely pulmonary. Leads to valve regurgitation (murmurs).

(iv) Drug treatment:
Anti-inflammatory drugs:
1. Aspirin (salicylate): maximum dose 100 mg/kg/day in divided doses; 3–4 times daily with meals (to prevent gastric erosion); monitor electrolytes (risk of metabolic acidosis)
2. Corticosteroid (e.g. prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day): for patients with life-threatening carditis; monitor urinalysis for glycosuria
Organism eradication: Procaine penicillin — given for 7–10 days (streptococci are very sensitive)
Heart failure treatment (if present): Digoxin and diuretics

(v) Histopathological findings:
1. Pathognomonic lesion: Aschoff nodule — aggregates of inflammatory cells; pathognomonic of ARF
2. What it consists of: Aggregates of inflammatory cells (a perivascular granulomatous lesion with fibrinoid necrosis, also described as aggregates of inflammatory cells; pathognomonic of ARF)
questions.question:
A 5-year-old child with progressive breathlessness and exercise intolerance is found to have the following on examination: fleeting joint pain affecting the knees (now resolved), fever for 3 weeks, and a diastolic murmur at the apex. ASO titre is 400 Todd units. The ECG shows a PR interval of 0.22 seconds. The cardiologist diagnoses the child with ARF complicated by carditis and decides to commence treatment.

(i) Using the Jones criteria, state precisely which criteria are fulfilled in this patient and confirm the diagnosis.
(ii) Describe the murmur heard at the apex during acute ARF and distinguish it from the murmur of established mitral incompetence in chronic RHD.
(iii) Describe the pathological process occurring in the pericardium, myocardium, and endocardium during acute ARF carditis.
(iv) State the complete drug treatment: name the anti-inflammatory drugs (with doses), the organism-eradicating drug (with duration), and the drug for heart failure if present.
(v) State two histopathological findings in the heart in acute ARF: the pathognomonic lesion and what it consists of.

questions.answerText:
(i) Differential diagnoses:
- TB meningitis (given lymphocytic CSF picture and subacute onset)
- Meningitis from other organisms (bacterial meningitis would show low glucose and high neutrophils)
- Viral encephalitis
- Encephalopathy (repeated convulsions or deep coma)
- Diabetic coma (dehydrated, acidotic)
Key distinguishing investigation: lumbar puncture for CSF chemistry and GeneXpert (for TB meningitis); blood smear (already negative); blood sugar; CT/MRI of brain for TB meningitis/tuberculoma
(ii) CSF interpretation:
- TB meningitis: elevated protein, elevated WBCs with lymphocytes, normal glucose – consistent with TB meningitis
- Measles encephalitis CSF: elevated protein, elevated WBC and lymphocytes, glucose is normal (similar picture; therefore distinguishing TB meningitis from viral encephalitis requires GeneXpert or culture)
- Most likely diagnosis here: TB meningitis
(iii) Treatment for TB meningitis:
- Regimen 2: 2RHZE/10RH (total 12 months)
- Drugs and doses: Rifampicin 10-20 mg/kg/day; Isoniazid 10-15 mg/kg/day; Pyrazinamide 25-30 mg/kg/day; Ethambutol 20-25 mg/kg/day
- Intensive phase: 2 months RHZE; Continuation phase: 10 months RH
- Steroids indicated for TB meningitis: steroids have been shown to improve survival and reduce complications in TB meningitis; also indicated for TB pericarditis, TB pleural effusion, hypo-adrenalism, TB laryngitis, endobronchial TB, severe hypersensitivity reaction, renal tract TB, massive lymph node enlargement with pressure effect
(iv) Extrapulmonary TB sites and presentations:
- TB adenitis: asymmetric, painless lymph node enlargement >1 month; ±discharging sinus; most commonly in neck area; investigations: FNA for cytology and culture; lymph node biopsy for histology
- Pleural TB: signs of respiratory distress, reduced breath sounds, dull percussion note, ±chest pain; investigations: CXR, pleural tap
- TB meningitis: headache, irritability, vomiting, lethargy, convulsion, neck stiffness; investigations: CSF chemistry and GeneXpert
- Miliary TB: non-specific symptoms, lethargy, fever, wasted; investigations: CXR, CSF tap, FNAC lymph node
- Abdominal TB: abdominal swelling with ascites, abdominal masses; investigations: USS, ascitic tap, FNAC
- Spinal TB (Pott's disease): deformity of spine (gibbus), lower limb weakness/paralysis; investigation: X-ray of the spine
- Pericardial TB: signs and symptoms of heart failure, distant heart sound, apex beat difficult to palpate; investigations: CXR, echocardiography, pericardial tap
questions.question:
A 10-year-old child develops fever, headache, and vomiting 4 days after a positive malaria smear was treated with artemether-lumefantrine. He now has neck stiffness and is lethargic. Repeat blood smear is negative for malaria.
(i) What conditions must now be considered in the differential diagnosis and what investigation distinguishes them?
(ii) A lumbar puncture is performed: CSF shows elevated protein, elevated WBCs with lymphocytes, and normal glucose. What is the most likely diagnosis now, and how does CSF in malaria encephalitis compare?
(iii) State the treatment for the most likely diagnosis, including drug, dosage, duration, and indications for steroids.
(iv) Identify all the sites of extrapulmonary TB and their typical presentations.

Describe Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and the coagulation factors most affected.
A(ii) Causes of DIC in the newborn and in older children.
B(i) Pathophysiology: how the coagulation cascade is disrupted leading to both haemorrhage and thrombosis.
B(ii) Laboratory findings used to confirm the diagnosis.
B(iii) Distinguish between the treatment principles for DIC versus the treatment of its underlying cause.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and coagulation factors:
- DIC is a clinical syndrome characterised by excessive activation of the clotting system leading to consumption of coagulation factors with consequent intravascular fibrin deposition, generalised haemorrhage and haemolytic anaemia.
- It is an acquired haemorrhagic disorder associated with an underlying disease; the most common form of consumption coagulopathy in children.
- Clotting factors affected: Factors II, V, VIII, and Fibrinogen.
- Also: Protein C, Protein S, and Antithrombin III are consumed.

A(ii) Causes:
Neonatal causes: Infections, Severe Birth Asphyxia, Severe Hyaline Membrane Disease, NEC, Meconium Aspiration, Hypothermia, Renal Vein Thrombosis, Use of Vascular Catheters, Giant Haemangioma, Haemolytic Transfusion Reactions, Homozygous Protein C and S deficiency, Massive Trauma.
Older children: Infections (Meningococcus, Rickettsia), Incompatible blood transfusion, Malignancies, Snake envenomation, Head injury, Shock, Acidosis, Hypoxia, Tissue necrosis, Endothelial injury.

B(i) Pathophysiology:
- A trigger leads to Thrombin formation → consumption of clotting factors and platelets → Haemorrhage.
- Fibrinaemia → microvascular thrombosis.
- Fibrinolysis → Fibrin Degradation Products (FDP) → further Haemorrhage.
- Tissue necrosis results in infarction of large areas of skin, subcutaneous tissue or kidneys.
- Anaemia from microangiopathic haemolysis.

B(ii) Laboratory findings:
- Low haematocrit.
- Blood smear shows fragmented, burr and helmet red cells; thrombocytopaenia.
- Prolonged PT, PTTK, TT.
- Elevated FDP.

B(iii) Treatment principles:
- Treat the underlying cause.
- Blood component replacement.
- Heparin (noted as a treatment option).

A(i) HCV is transmitted primarily by parenteral routes including blood transfusion and intravenous drug use, with perinatal and sexual transmission also possible. Faecal-oral transmission does not occur because HCV is an enveloped virus that does not survive intestinal passage and replication, unlike HAV and HEV which are non-enveloped and spread efficiently via contaminated food and water.
A(ii) Unlike HAV, HCV infection typically progresses to chronicity in most infected individuals because anti-HCV antibodies are non-protective — the virus mutates rapidly (high genetic variability), evading immune clearance. No vaccine is currently available for HCV.
A(iii) Approximately 75–85% of acutely infected adults develop chronic HCV infection.
B(i) HDV is a defective RNA virus because it lacks genes encoding the envelope protein needed for its own assembly. It requires the HBsAg envelope of HBV for its assembly and propagation. HDV can only infect HBV-positive individuals — either as simultaneous co-infection or as superinfection of a chronic HBV carrier.
B(ii) Two patterns: (1) Co-infection — simultaneous acute HBV and HDV, which may cause more severe acute hepatitis but usually resolves with HBV clearance; (2) Superinfection — HDV infecting a chronic HBV carrier, which causes more severe progressive liver disease and accelerated cirrhosis compared to HBV alone.
B(iii) HBV vaccination produces protective anti-HBs antibodies that prevent HBV infection. Since HDV requires HBsAg for replication, preventing HBV infection also prevents HDV infection in previously uninfected individuals, thus HBV vaccination indirectly prevents HDV.
C(i) AFP greater than 400 ng/mL with a hepatic mass on imaging is virtually diagnostic of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which develops as a complication of chronic HBV or HCV infection. AFP is a serum tumour marker produced by malignant hepatocytes.
C(ii) Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), particularly the M2 subtype, is highly specific for primary biliary cirrhosis (cholangitis) — a chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease causing destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts. This is distinct from antinuclear antibody (ANA) which is associated with autoimmune hepatitis.
C(iii) Low ceruloplasmin with elevated 24-hour urinary copper indicates Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), a hereditary disorder of copper metabolism causing hepatic and neurological disease. Slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings and liver biopsy copper quantification complete the diagnosis.

C. Explain the basis for the following laboratory findings in chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, stating what each finding reflects:

A. Describe non-traumatic paraplegia in childhood under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and the epidemiology in Nigeria (including the leading causes and overall mortality).
A(ii) Aetiological classification: congenital causes and acquired causes (infectious, vascular, neoplastic, autoimmune, drug-induced).
A(iii) Classification of non-traumatic paraplegia: compressive vs. non-compressive; spastic vs. flaccid — with disease examples for each.

B. Explain the clinico-anatomical basis of the following features in a child with Pott's disease (TB spine):
B(i) Gibbus deformity and paravertebral shadow on X-ray.
B(ii) Bladder and bowel incontinence.

C. Describe the investigations required for the assessment of a child with non-traumatic paraplegia, and explain what each investigation detects.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: non-traumatic paraplegia refers to impairment or paralysis of motor or sensory function of the lower extremities, due to a compromise in the integrity of the spinal cord either by compression or destruction. In Nigeria, a study at UCH showed 92.7% of cases were caused by infectious processes (polio and TB spine). Overall mortality was 7.2%; 50% of deaths were caused by malignancies. Prognosis was best in TB causes.

A(ii) Aetiological classification:
Congenital: spina bifida (cystica or occulta); syringomyelia; diastematomy-elia; tethered cord.
Acquired:
- Infectious: TB spine (Pott's disease) — commonest cause of non-traumatic paraplegia; poliomyelitis; epidural abscess; osteomyelitis of the spine; paravertebral abscess; HIV myelopathy.
- Vascular: infarction; dural fistula; intravertebral disc embolus; sickle cell disease; aneurysm.
- Neoplasm: Burkitt's lymphoma; leukaemia; rhabdomyosarcoma; meningioma; neurofibroma.
- Autoimmune: Guillain–Barré Syndrome; multiple sclerosis; chronic polyneuropathy; sarcoidosis; transverse myelitis.
- Drugs: isoniazid; vincristine.

A(iii) Classification:
- Compressive (UMN features — spastic): extradural — Pott's disease, epidural abscess, metastasis; intradural extramedullary — neurofibroma; intradural intramedullary — astrocytoma, ependymoma.
- Non-compressive (LMN features — flaccid): paralytic poliomyelitis, multiple sclerosis, sickle cell disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, Guillain–Barré Syndrome, diphtheria.
- Flaccid paraplegia examples: polio, Burkitt's lymphoma, sickle cell disease.
- Spastic paraplegia examples: Pott's disease, epidural abscess.

B(i) Gibbus deformity: destruction of vertebral bodies by Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes collapse of the vertebral column, producing an angular kyphosis (gibbus). The paravertebral shadow on X-ray represents a cold abscess (paravertebral abscess or psoas abscess) forming from caseous material tracking along tissue planes around the destroyed vertebral body.

B(ii) Bladder and bowel incontinence: spinal cord compression disrupts the descending supraspinal pathways that control the autonomic and somatic supply to the bladder and bowel (including the sacral micturition and defaecation centres), resulting in loss of voluntary bladder and bowel control, causing incontinence or retention.

C. Investigations and what each detects:
- Spinal X-ray: vertebral body destruction, paravertebral shadow (Pott's disease), kyphosis.
- MRI: best for cord compression, soft tissue involvement, abscess, disc herniation, tumour extent.
- CT myelogram: cord compression, thecal involvement.
- ESR: elevated in TB and epidural abscess (inflammatory/infectious aetiology).
- CXR: pulmonary TB (primary focus).
- Blood: FBC (anaemia, leucocytosis), E&U, Creatinine (renal function).
- Stool culture: to isolate poliovirus.
- Lumbar puncture: CSF analysis for infection, protein, cells, cytology (neoplasm).
- Mantoux test: for pulmonary TB (positive in TB exposure).

(i) Most likely diagnosis: TB spine (Pott's disease) with spinal cord compression. Classification: compressive paraplegia (extradural lesion compressing the cord) with upper motor neuron features; spastic paraplegia.

(ii) Organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis. TB spine (Pott's disease) is the commonest cause of non-traumatic paraplegia in Nigeria. According to a study in UCH, 92.7% of non-traumatic paraplegia was caused by infectious processes (polio and TB spine).

(iii) Investigations:
- Spinal X-ray (shows vertebral body destruction and paravertebral shadow).
- MRI (best for cord involvement and soft tissue).
- CT myelogram.
- ESR — increased in TB and epidural abscess.
- CXR — for pulmonary TB.
- Blood: FBC, E&U, Creatinine.
- Mantoux test (Tuberculin skin test) — for pulmonary TB.
- Lumbar puncture.

(iv) Specific management: Anti-tuberculous drugs for at least 12 months; analgesia; steroids; antibiotics if superimposed infection; incision and drainage if abscess present; radiotherapy/chemotherapy if neoplasm is a co-existing cause.
Supportive management: physiotherapy; bladder care/training; bowel care; frequent turning to prevent decubitus ulcers; assisted mobility.

(v) Complications: decubitus (pressure) ulcers; deep venous thrombosis; urinary tract infection; orthostatic pneumonia; hydronephrosis.
questions.question:
A 3-year-old child is brought in with a 3-week history of fever, weight loss, cough, and midline back swelling. Examination reveals a gibbus deformity of the thoracic spine. There is progressive weakness and sensory loss of the lower limbs, with loss of bladder and bowel control. Plain spinal X-ray shows vertebral body destruction with paravertebral shadow.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and how would you classify this type of paraplegia (compressive vs. non-compressive; spastic vs. flaccid)?
(ii) Name the specific infective organism and state the commonest cause of non-traumatic paraplegia in Nigeria.
(iii) List the investigations required to confirm the diagnosis, staging, and extent of cord involvement.
(iv) Outline the specific and supportive management of this child.
(v) Enumerate the complications that may arise if this condition is not managed appropriately.

A 32-week preterm male infant, born to a diabetic mother, is admitted to the neonatal unit and develops progressive respiratory distress within hours of birth. His CXR shows a fine reticulogranular appearance with air bronchogram sign.
(i) State the diagnosis and classify this infant's level of risk based on the predisposing factors listed.
(ii) Explain the full pathophysiology of this condition step by step.
(iii) Describe the natural clinical course and the full clinical signs including CXR findings.
(iv) State all three antenatal and immediate post-delivery preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) / Hyaline Membrane Disease (HMD) — 'Progressive atelectasis of prematurity.'
This infant has multiple risk factors: prematurity (< 34 weeks); infant of diabetic mother (IDM) — both high-risk categories.
Risk-reducing factors (not applicable here): PROM, IUGR, maternal stress (e.g. pre-eclampsia) reduce risk.

(ii) Pathophysiology (step by step):
1. Inadequate surfactant synthesis.
2. High alveolar surface tension.
3. Reduced lung compliance.
4. Progressive expiratory atelectasis.
5. Hypoxia.
6. Respiratory distress.
7. Increased capillary permeability.
8. Exudation of fluid → oedema.

(iii) Clinical course and signs:
Natural course: Progressive deterioration over 3–5 days; if child does not die, begins to recover.
Clinical signs:
- Onset near time of birth.
- Tachypnoea; chest wall indrawing; expiratory grunt; cyanosis; fine inspiratory crepitations; hypothermia; peripheral oedema.
CXR: Characteristic fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) appearance with air bronchogram sign, which develops during first 6 hours of life.

(iv) Prevention:
1. Prenatal glucocorticoid for > 24 hours before delivery.
2. Surfactant replacement before 1–2 hours of life.
3. Early CPAP from the delivery room.

(i) Diagnosis: Iron Deficiency Anaemia.
Causes: Inadequate intake, prematurity, hookworm, occult blood loss.
(ii) Complete clinical features:
- Pallor.
- Blue sclera.
- Irritability.
- Pagophagia (desire to eat ice).
- Rigid nails.
- Koilonychia.
- Pica (eating non-food stuff).
- Geophagia (eating of soil).
- Anorexia.
- Features of cardiac failure.
- Haemic murmur.
- Features of adverse neurologic function (short attention span).
Laboratory findings:
- Microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
- ↓MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume).
- ↓MCHC (Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration).
- RDW increased (anisocytosis).
(iii) Transfusion criteria and protocol:
Yes — this child meets criteria for blood transfusion: Hb 4.5 g/dl is below the severe threshold of Hb <5 g/dl; she also has haemic murmur and features of cardiac decompensation.
Transfusion protocol:
- Severe anaemia (Hb <5 g/dl): Blood transfusion is indicated.
- Check if there is acute blood loss (>10% of volume) or ongoing bleeding → Transfuse with whole blood (≤5 days) at 20 ml/kg.
- If stable (no ongoing loss), transfuse with packed cells at 15 ml/kg.
- Give IV Frusemide 1–2 mg/kg stat (except in hypovolaemia).
- All cases of anaemia must be fully investigated — FBC, blood culture etc. — find the cause and treat appropriately.
- For treatable cause (iron deficiency): specific replacement therapy (Iron for several months) should be used; mild to moderate cases are treated with haematinics: Iron, Folic acid, Vitamin B₁₂.
(iv) Compensatory physiological mechanisms:
1. Increased cardiac output (increased Heart Rate and Stroke Volume).
2. Shunting of blood to vital organs.
3. Increased RBC 2,3-DPG to enhance oxygen delivery.
Clinical signs typically appear when Hb <7–8 g/dl: few clinical disturbances occur above this level because compensatory mechanisms are effective. In chronic anaemia the body adjusts and ameliorates effects; in acute anaemia symptoms are more pronounced.
questions.question:
A 3-year-old girl is brought with a 2-month history of progressive pallor and poor appetite. She has been exclusively eating maize porridge. On examination she is pale, has blue sclerae, koilonychia, and a haemic murmur. Her Hb is 4.5 g/dl. There are no blast cells on peripheral film.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what are its causes?
(ii) Describe the complete clinical features of this condition and the laboratory findings that confirm it.
(iii) This child has Hb 4.5 g/dl. Does she meet criteria for blood transfusion? If yes, state the transfusion protocol (volume, rate, diuretic use). If no, state what should be used instead and why.
(iv) Describe the three compensatory physiological mechanisms that occur in anaemia and explain at what haemoglobin level clinical signs typically appear.

Describe the approach to blood transfusion in children under the following headings:
A(i) What are the major indication and the goals of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion?
A(ii) List the specific concerns regarding blood transfusion in neonates and older children, including both acute and long-term risks.
B(i) Describe the transfusion protocol for older children with Sickle Cell Disease including the specific indications for direct transfusion versus EBT.
B(ii) State the steps for selection, preparation, and safe administration of blood.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Major indication and goals:
- Major indication: to prevent or treat symptoms of tissue hypoxia by augmenting the oxygen-carrying capacity in blood.
- For treatable causes of anaemia, specific replacement therapy (e.g. vitamin B₁₂, iron, folate) should always be used before transfusion is considered.
- A dose of 15 ml/kg of packed red cells with a haematocrit of approximately 60% will increase haemoglobin by approximately 3 g/dL. Transfused red cells have a half-life of approximately 30 days in the absence of other processes causing red cell loss.

A(ii) Concerns in paediatric blood transfusion:
Acute concerns (Neonates/Preterms): Vulnerable to potential infective (e.g. CMV) and toxic effects (additives) of transfusion; Immature immune system (risk of graft vs. host disease) and metabolic processes (additives effects e.g. adenine); Still undergoing rapid neurodevelopment (effect of lead); A single unit may represent a much greater proportion of blood volume than in an adult; Iso/alloantibodies concerns; Plasma or platelets from group O donors transfused into non-group-O children may cause significant haemolysis from anti-A,B.
Long-term concerns: Infections with long incubation period e.g. HTLV — may cause chronic neurological disorders or adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma decades later; Iron overload in chronic transfusion programmes (β-thalassaemia, myelodysplasia) — liver cirrhosis, cardiac problems, endocrine impairment; Alloimmunisation — in females and sickle cell disease (all children with SCD should receive fully Rh-matched and Kell-negative blood).

B(i) Transfusion protocol for older children with Sickle Cell Disease:
Indications for transfusion: Symptomatic anaemia/signs of heart failure, Complicated crisis unresponsive to drugs, Evidence of infection/septicaemia, Ongoing haemolysis, Splenic sequestration, Oxygen dependency (not ventilated), Priapism, Acute chest syndrome, CVA/TIA, Mechanical ventilation PCV <20%.
- Transfuse with packed cells 15 ml/kg.
- Direct transfusion or EBT for CVA/TIA.
If PCV <15%: Transfuse with packed cells at 15 ml/kg.
If acute blood loss (>10% volume, signs of shock, PCV ≤20%, ongoing bleeding): Transfuse with whole blood (≤5 days) at 20 ml/kg.

B(ii) Selection, preparation, and safe administration:
- Decide if there is sufficient indication for transfusion.
- RBC must be compatible with ABO antibodies in recipient's serum and crossmatched to confirm compatibility.
- Decide how much rise in haematocrit is required.
- Informed consent must be obtained.
- Review patient and document findings before, during, and after transfusion.
- Cross-check blood label and detail descriptions with patient's data before transfusion.
- Transfusion period should never exceed 4 hours.
- May need to give diuretic except in hypovolaemia.
- Give IV Frusemide 1–2 mg/kg stat.
- Monitor vital signs every 15–30 minutes.

A(i) Right-sided study: catheter passed via femoral vein → inferior vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery. Assesses right heart anatomy and pressures.
Left-sided study: catheter passed via femoral artery → descending aorta → left ventricle. Assesses left heart anatomy; bleeding is the major complication.

A(ii) Uses of cardiac catheterisation:
- Confirm structural defects e.g. ASD, VSD, PDA
- Measure pressures (including pressure gradient across obstructions — pre- and post-stenotic areas)
- Oximetry — oxygen saturation measurement
- Angiography — to delineate anatomy, demonstrate direction of shunts, assess pulmonary artery size and level of obstruction
- Pulmonary wedge vascular pressure (in Woods units) when pulmonary vascular disease is suspected pre-surgery
- Therapeutic: Rashkind's atrial septostomy in TGA; balloon valvuloplasty in pulmonary stenosis

A(ii) [continued — cardiac catheterisation vs echocardiography]: cardiac catheterisation is no longer used routinely for VSD; is still useful for complex anatomy and when pulmonary vascular disease is suspected.

B(i) M-mode (Motion) echocardiography: older; used for measurements and to assess cardiac function; NOT good for structural defects.
2-Dimensional echocardiography: shows cross-sections of the heart; extremely useful for structural defects e.g. detecting holes, VSD, PDA. Doppler: assesses pressures and turbulence across obstructions. Colour flow Doppler: demonstrates direction of blood flow (left-to-right or right-to-left shunts). Advantage over catheterisation: non-invasive; can be repeated many times.

B(ii) Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy: a balloon catheter is advanced via cardiac catheterisation into the right atrium, crossed through the foramen ovale into the left atrium, the balloon is inflated, then pulled back forcefully to create an ASD. This allows mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and is life-saving in TGA.

C. Arterial blood gases: arterial sample taken from the right radial artery after administering 100% oxygen for 10 minutes (hyperoxia/nitrogen washout test). In cyanotic congenital heart disease: reduced PO2, reduced pH, increased PCO2. If the cause of cyanosis is a respiratory disorder, cyanosis improves with 100% oxygen. If it is cardiac in origin, the cyanosis does not improve with 100% oxygen.
questions.question:
A. Describe cardiac catheterisation as an investigation in paediatric cardiology:
A(i) The two types — the route followed by the catheter in each, and what each type assesses
A(ii) The uses/indications of cardiac catheterisation in congenital and acquired heart disease

B. Describe echocardiography as a diagnostic tool:
B(i) The two forms of echocardiography and what each can assess — including its advantage over cardiac catheterisation
B(ii) Describe the specific therapeutic application of cardiac catheterisation in Transposition of Great Arteries, naming the procedure, its technique, and why it is used

C. State how arterial blood gases help distinguish cardiac from respiratory cyanosis, describing the test used and its interpretation

questions.answerText:
A(i) Age-based guidance:
- Age < 5 years: think of congenital heart disease first
- Age > 5 years: think of acquired heart disease first
Exceptions:
- Congenital heart diseases that may be asymptomatic early and present in the 2nd or 3rd decade: small VSD; coarctation of aorta (commonly presents at 12 years with heart failure due to left ventricular effects); atrial septal defect (many are asymptomatic in the first decade)
- Acquired heart disease (e.g. rheumatic heart disease, infective heart disease, pericardial effusion) does occur in infants, though commoner in older children

A(ii) Symptoms in infancy raising suspicion of CHD:
- Cough
- Breathlessness
- Cyanosis
- Feeding difficulties
- Frequent chest infections (pointer to chronic heart disease)

A(iii) Pregnancy/birth history predisposing factors:
- PDA: preterm delivery (duration of pregnancy); birth asphyxia (reduced oxygen tension); rubella infection during pregnancy
- TGA: maternal diabetes mellitus
- Pulmonary stenosis/VSD/PDA (as a group): congenital rubella syndrome; drugs (thalidomide, cytotoxic drugs, steroids); X-radiation

B(i) Socioeconomic risk factors:
- Low socioeconomic status: predisposes to acute rheumatic heart fever and endomyocardial fibrosis
- High socioeconomic status/obesity: predisposes to hypertension

B(ii) Three chromosomal abnormalities:
1. Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome): AV septal defect and VSD/ASD; dysmorphic feature: slanting epicanthic fold (Down facies), flat nasal bridge, flat occiput; associated with mental retardation (commoner among the Mongols)
2. Turner syndrome (XO): Coarctation of the aorta (specifically listed)
3. Congenital rubella syndrome: PDA; dysmorphic features include mental retardation, deafness, bilateral cataracts, microcephaly, cleft lip or palate, polydactyly or syndactyly, talipes deformity
(Trisomy 18 or 13 may be substituted for Turner: Trisomy 18 = VSD/ASD; Trisomy 13 = VSD)
questions.question:
A. Describe the clinical history-taking for a child suspected of having congenital heart disease under the following headings:
A(i) State how age at presentation (below or above 5 years) guides the distinction between congenital and acquired heart disease, and give two exceptions for each direction
A(ii) List the symptoms in infancy that should raise suspicion of congenital heart disease
A(iii) State the pregnancy and birth history features that specifically predispose to the following: PDA, TGA, and pulmonary stenosis/VSD/PDA (as a group)

B. Describe the role of family and social history in paediatric cardiac evaluation:
B(i) State two socioeconomic risk factors and the specific heart diseases they predispose to
B(ii) State three chromosomal abnormalities mentioned, the cardiac lesion(s) associated with each, and one dysmorphic feature of each

A 6-year-old boy presents with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal swelling and pain. On examination there is a hard, craggy abdominal mass with hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. There is also a swelling of the left maxilla with loosening of adjacent teeth.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What are the three aetiological factors associated with this condition?
(iii) What investigations would you perform to confirm the diagnosis and assess tumour burden?
(iv) Describe the chemotherapy regimen used as the mainstay of treatment, including all drugs and schedule.
questions.answerText:
(i) Burkitt's Lymphoma (BL).
(ii) Three aetiological factors:
- Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): its viral genome is found in 95% of cases in the endemic area; chronic EBV infection is thought to cause proliferation of lymphocytes.
- Chronic malarial infection: impairs immune surveillance (P. falciparum).
- Chromosomal translocation: 8:14 (constitutes about 80%), 8:22 (15%), and 2:8; chromosome 8 is common to all and possesses the c-myc gene, which is critical in the regulation of cell proliferation.
(iii) Investigations:
- Tumour aspirate for cytology / percutaneous aspiration under ultrasound guidance (FNAC).
- X-ray of jaw: shows loss of dental lamina, dural thin rim of cortical bone outlining teeth, osteolytic lesion, dental anarchy.
- Full blood count (baseline for chemotherapy).
- Electrolyte, Urea and Creatinine (to monitor metabolic complications e.g. Tumour Lysis Syndrome).
- Calcium and Phosphorus.
- Abdominal ultrasound and IVU for kidney masses.
- Chest X-ray.
- Spinal CSF for cytology: mandatory for all cases.
