- Serum LDH: useful marker for tumour burden; used to monitor treatment regression and relapse.
(iv) Chemotherapy regimen "COMP or COAP":
- Oral Prednisolone
- IV Cyclophosphamide
- IV Vincristine
- IV Cytosine arabinoside or methotrexate
- Intrathecal cytosine arabinoside or methotrexate
Six cycles are given; each cycle of treatment is 2 weeks and is given for the first 5 days of each cycle except when bone marrow complication occurs.

questions.question:
Describe the immune and metabolic complications of Hyperleucocytosis as an oncologic emergency.
A(i) Define Hyperleucocytosis and state the WBC thresholds that make it clinically significant for each leukaemia type.
A(ii) Describe the pathophysiology of Hyperleucocytosis.
B(i) Describe ALL clinical features of Hyperleucocytosis by organ system.
B(ii) Outline the complete management protocol for Hyperleucocytosis including drug doses, monitoring parameters, and the use of leukapheresis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and clinically significant WBC thresholds:
- Hyperleucocytosis is defined as WBC count >100,000/mm³.
- Incidence: 9–13% of ALL with 5% mortality; 5–22% of AML with 23% mortality; nearly 100% in CML.
- Clinically significant hyperleucocytosis occurs with WBC:
  - >200,000/mm³ in AML.
  - >300,000/mm³ in ALL.
  - >600,000/mm³ in CML.

A(ii) Pathophysiology:
- Myeloblasts and monoblasts are rigid and sticky.
- Increase viscosity of blood.
- Tumour emboli form in the microvasculature.
- Vascular obstruction and haemorrhage result.

B(i) Clinical features by organ system:
CNS: Blurred vision, Confusion, Delirium, Papilloedema, Intracerebral haemorrhage/stroke (especially in CML).
Respiratory: Tachypnea, Dyspnea, Hypoxia, CXR — diffuse interstitial infiltrates.
Genitourinary: Renal failure, Priapism.
Musculoskeletal System: Dactylitis.

B(ii) Complete management protocol:
- Hydration and alkalinisation: IVF 5% D in 1/5 saline + 50–100 mEq/L NaHCO₃ at 2–4× maintenance.
- Mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg.
- Allopurinol 100 mg/m²/dose 8-hourly.
- Leukapheresis/Exchange Transfusion.
- Platelet transfusion.
- Avoid blood transfusion and diuretics (keep PCV ≤30%).
- Chemotherapy.
- Dialysis.
Monitoring parameters:
- E&U, Cr, Ca, P, Uric acid 6-hourly.
- FBC 6-hourly.
- Urine output, specific gravity and pH.
- Cardiac monitoring.
- Respiratory and cerebral monitoring.

(i) Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA): atrioventricular concordance but ventriculo-arterial discordance — the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. The systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel rather than in series; SVC and IVC blood flows to the aorta (systemic circuit) without being oxygenated, while oxygenated pulmonary venous return goes back to the lungs. This is incompatible with life unless there is a communication to allow mixing — at atrial level (ASD), ventricular level (VSD), or arterial level (PDA).

(ii) Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy: performed via cardiac catheterisation (right-sided study). A balloon catheter is passed via the femoral vein → IVC → right atrium → across the foramen ovale into the left atrium. The balloon is inflated, then pulled back forcefully to tear open the atrial septum, creating an ASD. This allows mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood at the atrial level, sustaining life.

(iii) Surgical options:
- Blalock-Hanlon Atrial Septectomy: not open heart; surgically creates an opening for mixing of blood
- Mustard's Operation: open heart; atrial septum is removed and an atrial baffle diverts right atrial blood into the left atrium and left ventricle; patient becomes pink dramatically; good prognosis
- Arterial Switch Operation: open heart surgery; anatomically corrects the positions of the great arteries

(iv) Classical TGA: atrioventricular concordance + ventriculo-arterial discordance.
Congenitally Corrected TGA: atrioventricular discordance + ventriculo-arterial discordance. Right atrium connects to the left ventricle; left atrium connects to the right ventricle; left ventricle connects to the pulmonary artery; right ventricle connects to the aorta. Blood thus follows the correct physiological path — deoxygenated blood from right atrium → left ventricle → pulmonary artery; oxygenated blood from left atrium → right ventricle → aorta. Therefore, there should be no symptoms from the transposition itself; symptoms arise only from associated lesions such as VSD, pulmonary stenosis, bleeding disorders, or valve incompetence.
questions.question:
A neonate presents at birth with severe cyanosis, breathlessness, cough, and features of heart failure. The chest X-ray shows an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette, cardiomegaly, right ventricular and right atrial enlargement, and increased pulmonary vascular markings. ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy, right atrial hypertrophy, and right axis deviation.

(i) State the diagnosis and explain why this condition is incompatible with life without a communication between the two sides of the heart.
(ii) Name the therapeutic cardiac catheterisation procedure that can be performed urgently, describe how it is carried out, and explain why it is life-saving.
(iii) Describe the surgical options available, distinguishing between the operation that creates atrial mixing and the one that corrects the great vessel positions.
(iv) Distinguish this condition from Congenitally Corrected TGA — state the atrioventricular and ventriculo-arterial connections in each, and why Congenitally Corrected TGA may be asymptomatic.

A 4-year-old child presents with 4 days of fever and severe pallor. Examination reveals a temperature of 39.8°C, splenomegaly, and a blood glucose of 2.0 mmol/l. A thick blood film confirms P. falciparum infection. He is responsive but unable to sit without support.
(i) Classify this illness and name the life-threatening features present.
(ii) What factors determine the severity of P. falciparum illness in any given patient?
(iii) Describe the laboratory monitoring required throughout admission.
(iv) State the supportive treatment for each of the following: high temperature, pulmonary oedema, and renal failure.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is severe/complicated malaria. Life-threatening features present:
- Prostration or extreme weakness: inability to sit upright in a child that could previously do so
- Hypoglycaemia: whole blood glucose concentration <2.2 mmol/l (<40 mg/dl)
- Hyperpyrexia: core body temperature >40°C (the stated temperature of 39.8°C approaches this threshold; the clinical picture supports severity)
Other applicable criteria include hyperparasitaemia, severe anaemia, circulatory collapse, impaired consciousness, and acidaemia.
(ii) Factors that influence severity:
- Species of Plasmodium: severe malaria is only caused by P. falciparum
- Endemicity: adults and older children in endemic areas are less susceptible
- Host factors:
  - Age: children and pregnant women are more susceptible
  - Duffy blood group antigen alleles
  - The sickle cell trait (heterozygous state)
  - Haemoglobin F also has protective effects against severe malaria
- Parasite drug resistance
(iii) Laboratory monitoring:
- Monitor parasitaemia by daily blood smear; if high after 2-3 days, review adequacy of drug dose
- Monitor blood glucose: do blood glucose or maintain dextrose-containing infusion
- Monitor haemoglobin/haematocrit
(iv) Supportive treatments:
- High temperature: give paracetamol (oral/rectal) if temperature is >38.5°C; wipe the body with wet towel and fan the patient to lower the temperature
- Pulmonary oedema: prop up the patient, give oxygen and furosemide 2-4 mg/kg IV; exclude anaemia as the cause of heart failure
- Renal failure: if patient is dehydrated, give 20 ml/kg of normal saline and challenge with furosemide 1-2 mg/kg; pass a urinary catheter to monitor urinary output; if patient does not pass urine within 24 hours, refer for peritoneal or haemodialysis

questions.question:
A 6-year-old child known to have sickle cell disease presents with fever, cough, and right-sided chest pain. Chest radiograph shows right-sided homogenous opacity with blunting of the costophrenic angle. Chest examination reveals decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and absent vocal resonance on the right. Blood culture is positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae.

(i) What complication of pneumonia has developed?
(ii) Classify the fluid in terms of the biochemical criteria given.
(iii) What does the colour of the pleural fluid obtained at pleuracentesis indicate about the likely organism?
(iv) Outline the full treatment of this condition, specifying definitive antibiotic therapy for each likely causative organism.
(v) What are all the complications of pleural effusion/empyema?
questions.answerText:
(i) Empyema (purulent pleural effusion) — an acute complication of pneumonia.

(ii) Biochemical classification — Exudate: total protein >3 g/dL; pleural protein/serum protein ratio >0.5; predominant polymorphonuclear cells (except in malignant or tuberculous effusions with higher percentage of mononuclear cells); specific gravity >1020.

(iii) Pleural fluid colour and organism: thickly purulent → S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, Hib; thinly purulent → S. pyogenes; straw-coloured → TB; bloody → malignancy, TB, trauma; serous → nephrotic syndrome, CHF, cirrhosis; milky → lymphatic obstruction, TB. In this case (S. pneumoniae): thickly purulent.

(iv) Treatment — Large empyema: chest tube thoracic drainage (CTTD). Thinly purulent: aspiration using a syringe and 3-way tap. Tuberculous and malignant effusions: aspiration only if patient is dyspnoeic; careful CTTD. Definitive antibiotic therapy: S. aureus → cloxacillin or flucloxacillin or cefuroxime plus amikacin. Other pyogenic organisms (including S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Strep. pyogenes) → chloramphenicol + erythromycin, or cefuroxime plus amikacin. Tuberculosis → see PTB regimen. Malignancy → cytotoxic drugs.

(v) Complications: Pulmonary — empyema necessitans; pockets of loculated pus; bronchopleural fistula. Cardiac — purulent pericarditis. Skeletal — rib osteomyelitis. CNS — meningitis. Haematological — anaemia, septicaemia.

(i) Two likely diagnoses in a well, breastfed, jaundiced neonate:
1. Breast Feeding Jaundice (early type):
- Onset: 2–4 days; peaks at 3–6 days (> 12.0 mg/dl); returns to < 3.0 at > 3 weeks.
- Prevalence: approximately 12% in breastfed infants.
- Believed to be due to decreased oral intake (decreased PO).
2. Breast Milk Jaundice (late type):
- Onset: 4–7 days; peaks 5–15 days (> 10.0 mg/dl); returns to < 3.0 at > 9 weeks.
- Prevalence: 2–4% of breastfed infants.
In contrast, physiological jaundice: does not occur early (onset usually after 36 hours); peak < 170 µmol/L in term infants; resolves by Day 7 in term.

(ii) Aetiological factors in breastfeeding jaundice:
- Fluids: breastfed infants have decreased oral intake → increased weight loss and dehydration.
- Inhibition of hepatic excretion: suspected factors in breast milk include pregnanediol, free fatty acids, lipase.
- Intestinal re-absorption of bilirubin: delayed passage of meconium allows ß-glucuronidase to deconjugate bilirubin, increasing enterohepatic circulation. ß-glucuronidase present in guts of some babies and mothers and in breast milk.
- Sterile GI: no conversion of bilirubin to urobilinogen.
- Breast milk contains glucuronidase.

(iii) Management of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia:
- Be aggressive. Note that preterm infants develop kernicterus earlier because of lower serum protein levels and immature blood-brain barrier.
- Phototherapy: used when SBR > 12.5 mg/dl.
- Exchange blood transfusion (EBT): when SBR approaching > 20 mg/dl.
- EBT: fresh whole blood compatible with both mother and child.
- Give extra fluid allowance during phototherapy (20–30 ml/kg/day) for insensible water loss.
- Protect the eyes with goggles.

(iv) Investigations for jaundice:
- Serum bilirubin (total, direct, indirect).
- PCV/Hb; blood film (high reticulocyte count suggests haemolysis).
- Blood group of mother and child.
- Coombs test.
- Peroxidase haemolysis test.
- Exclude carotinaemia.
- For anaemia, infection.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: examine for masses in the abdomen; Dubin-Johnson syndrome (disorder of transport); Crigler-Najjar syndrome.
questions.question:
A 28-day-old term male infant presents with a one-week history of persistent jaundice. He is exclusively breastfed, appears well, and has no fever or hepatosplenomegaly. Total bilirubin is 14 mg/dl (predominantly unconjugated). His birth was uneventful with no history of blood incompatibility.
(i) State the two most likely diagnoses in this age group in an otherwise well breastfed infant and distinguish between them based on onset, peak, and duration.
(ii) List the aetiological factors in breastfeeding jaundice.
(iii) State the management of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a preterm infant, including why preterm infants need earlier intervention.
(iv) State the investigations required to work up a neonate with suspected jaundice.

A 6-week-old female infant is referred because of prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, constipation, and a hoarse cry since birth. On examination she is hypotonic, has coarse facial features, macroglossia, a large posterior fontanelle (>1 cm), and an umbilical hernia.

(i) State the spot diagnosis and the pathophysiological basis of the condition.
(ii) List four predisposing factors or causes.
(iii) Describe the approach to confirming the diagnosis and the biochemical tests required.
(iv) Outline the treatment and monitoring plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital Hypothyroidism (CH). Pathophysiological basis: Thyroid hormones T4 and T3 are essential for normal growth, development and metabolism. The pituitary and thyroid glands develop from the buccopharyngeal cavity between 4 and 10 weeks' gestation. The thyroid arises from the fourth brachial pouches. Errors in formation or migration of thyroid tissue result in thyroid aplasia, dysplasia, or ectopy. By 10–11 weeks the fetal thyroid can produce thyroid hormone. Inadequate thyroid hormone production causes the clinical picture of cretinism: hypothermia, hypotonia, poor feeding, prolonged jaundice (from impaired hepatic enzyme activity), and coarse features from myxoedematous infiltration.

(ii) Causes/predisposing factors:
• Thyroid dysgenesis: agenesis (complete absence), ectopy (lingual or sublingual thyroid)
• Dyshormonogenesis (mostly familial autosomal recessive): peroxidase defect, organification defect (Pendred syndrome), thyroglobulin defect, deiodinase defect
• TSH or TRH deficiency (secondary/tertiary hypothyroidism)
• Maternal autoimmune disease; iatrogenic (maternal use of thioamides, iodine excess, radioactive iodine therapy)
• Iodine deficiency (endemic cretinism)

(iii) Diagnosis: Measurement of T4 or TSH, or both, in blood collected on filter paper spots (neonatal screening). Done within the 2nd and 6th day of life. Biochemical tests Group A (to establish dysfunction): plasma free T4 (normal 9–23 nmol/L), plasma total T4 (normal 70–150 nmol/L), plasma TSH (normal 0.15–3.5 mU/L), plasma free T3. Biochemical tests Group B (to determine cause): thyroid auto-antibodies, serum thyroglobulin, thyroid enzyme activities, ultrasound, radioiodide uptake. Radiological: bone age is retarded and epiphyseal dysgenesis may be present.

(iv) Treatment: Oral L-T4 10 mcg/kg/day once daily. Monitoring: Recheck T4 and TSH 2–4 weeks after initial treatment, then every 1–2 months in the first 6 months, every 3–4 months between 6 months and 3 years, then every 6–12 months to end of growth. Goal: normalise TSH and maintain T4 and FT4 in the upper half of the reference range. The best index of adequate treatment is suppression of TSH to normal levels. Mental attainment depends on degree of hypothyroidism, age at diagnosis, and adequacy of treatment.

questions.question:
During a surgical ward round, a 9-year-old girl recovering from an appendicectomy develops sudden-onset severe dehydration, hypotension, tachycardia, and altered consciousness on day 2 post-operatively. Her mother reports she has been on oral prednisolone for asthma for the past 8 months. Investigations show hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia.

(i) Name the diagnosis. What is the embryological and anatomical basis of the underlying gland's function?
(ii) List four risk factors or causes that predispose to this acute presentation.
(iii) Describe the resuscitation and immediate management steps.
(iv) State the definitive long-term management and how adequacy of replacement is monitored.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute Adrenal Insufficiency (Adrenal Crisis). The adrenal glands are located at the cranial pole of the kidneys. The cortex is subdivided into three zones: outer zona glomerulosa (produces mineralocorticoids, principally aldosterone, responsive to angiotensin and potassium), middle zona fasciculata and inner zona reticularis (responsive to ACTH, synthesise glucocorticoids and adrenal androgens respectively). Secondary adrenal insufficiency occurs when lack of CRH or ACTH causes hypofunction. Prolonged exogenous corticosteroid use suppresses the HPA axis; the stress of surgery unmasks relative insufficiency because the gland cannot mount the expected cortisol response.

(ii) Risk factors/causes:
• Prolonged exogenous corticosteroid use (iatrogenic): withdrawal after prolonged use (>2 weeks), or failure to administer stress-dose steroids during illness/surgery
• Primary acquired: autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex; adrenal haemorrhage or infarction (e.g. meningococcal septicaemia); infections (TB, AIDS, fungal, histoplasmosis); malignancy; leukodystrophy
• Primary congenital: adrenal hypoplasia congenita, aplasia, adrenal hyperplasia
• Drugs: megestrol acetate; congenital or acquired hypopituitarism

(iii) Resuscitation: IV access and infusion of isotonic NaCl (20–30 ml/kg bolus if in shock). May require glucose supplementation for hypoglycaemia. Administer IV Hydrocortisone (stress-dose steroid). Correct electrolyte abnormalities. Monitor: TPR, BP, blood glucose, electrolytes. Identify and manage precipitating factors (in this case, surgical stress).

(iv) Long-term management: patients need glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for life. Carry means of identification (e.g. steroid card/bracelet). Parental steroid coverage must be used in major stress, trauma or surgery and during any major procedure. Periodic monitoring: general wellbeing, BP (postural hypotension), electrolytes, presence or absence of pedal oedema, Cushingoid features, and growth (over-replacement leads to poor growth).

questions.question:
A 3-year-old child with known Tetralogy of Fallot is listed for palliative surgery before definitive repair. The surgeon plans a Blalock-Taussig shunt.

(i) What is the haemodynamic problem this shunt is designed to correct, and what is the target of the shunting?
(ii) Distinguish between the classical and the modified Blalock-Taussig shunt in terms of surgical technique, the vessel used, and the postoperative difference in radial pulse.
(iii) What graft material is used in the modified shunt, and state two disadvantages of this modification?
(iv) State three clinical and two objective (investigative) indices of a successful shunt.
(v) State the embryological variant of arterial anatomy that is present in 25–30% of TOF patients and is also seen in pulmonary atresia and truncus arteriosus.
questions.answerText:
(i) Haemodynamic problem: Reduced pulmonary blood flow due to right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (pulmonary stenosis — usually infundibular) and right-to-left shunting through the VSD causing cyanosis.
Target: Blood is shunted from the systemic circulation into the pulmonary circulation to increase pulmonary blood flow and improve oxygenation.

(ii) Classical vs. Modified Blalock-Taussig shunt:
- Classical: The subclavian artery is cut (divided) and anastomosed directly with the pulmonary artery. Postoperatively, no radial pulse is felt on the ipsilateral side (collateral arteries open up to supply the limb).
- Modified: The subclavian artery is NOT divided; a graft is interposed between the subclavian artery and the pulmonary artery. The radial artery (pulse) is intact at the end of surgery. Used for smaller patients.

(iii) Graft material in modified shunt: Gore-tex graft.
Two disadvantages:
- The patient will outgrow the graft
- Clot formation in the graft

(iv) Indices of successful shunt:
Clinical:
1. A shunt murmur (continuous, like in PDA) may be heard immediately
2. Cyanosis should start disappearing
3. Symptomatology improves (patient becomes more fit; reduced risk of hypercyanotic spells)
Objective:
1. PCV should start falling and stabilise at 45–55%
2. Chest X-ray: no more pulmonary oligaemia

(v) Embryological variant: Right-sided aortic arch (present in 25–30% of TOF patients). It is also seen in pulmonary atresia and truncus arteriosus. (In dextrocardia, a right-sided arch can be considered normal; in laevocardia, it is always abnormal.)

questions.question:
Describe the structural and biological basis of the management of Sickle Cell Disease under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the role of ion channels in sickle cell pathophysiology, including the Gardos pathway, K-Cl cotransport, and the effect of cell dehydration.
A(ii) Describe the pharmacological and biological agents used to induce HbF synthesis or reduce sickling, with mechanism of action for each.
B(i) Describe the principles and selection criteria for Bone Marrow Transplantation in SCD.
B(ii) Distinguish between the management of haemolytic crisis, aplastic crisis, and priapism in SCD.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Ion channels in SCD pathophysiology:
- One distinguishing characteristic of sickle erythrocytes is cell dehydration, due to loss of cell potassium via 4 major mechanisms:
  1. Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channel (Gardos pathway): when intracellular free Ca²⁺ increases, large K⁺ loss with accompanying Cl⁻ and water movement occurs. Gardos channel belongs to a family of Ca²⁺-activated channels.
  2. K-Cl cotransport: active almost exclusively in normal reticulocytes, not normal mature red cells; activation in SCD is most likely due to oxidative damage to the RBC.
  3. Deoxygenation-induced Na and K fluxes and Na-K pump.
  4. Oxidative damage to the cell membrane and K loss.
- Cell dehydration raises intracellular HbS concentration, markedly affecting polymerisation (delay time is inversely proportional to the 15th–35th power of HbS concentration).

A(ii) Agents to induce HbF or reduce sickling:
- Hydroxyurea: 15 mg/kg/24 hrs, gradually increased to maximum 30 mg/kg/24 hrs; monitor FBC, LFT and HbF; increases HbF by usually 10–15%; does not cause myelosuppression in the manner of other agents. (Note: NICOSAN does not cause myelosuppression unlike hydroxyurea.)
- Recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO): induces HbF synthesis.
- Resveratrol (natural dietary polyphenol); Butyric acid.
- Clotrimazole: potent inhibitor of Gardos channel; at 20 mg/kg/day shows channel inhibition, reduced erythrocyte dehydration, increased cell K⁺ content, and increased Hb levels.
- Oral Mg supplementation: increases RBC Mg, inhibits K-Cl cotransporter, reduces dense erythrocytes and sickling.
- NICOSAN (NIPRISAN): ethanol/water extract from 4 local herbs; developed by NIPRD Abuja; increases solubility of deoxy-HbS; slightly shifts O₂ dissociation curve to the left.
- Sodium cromoglycate (inhalation): reduces concentration of sickled cells.
- Fagara zanthoxyloides (Zanthoxylum zanthoxyloides): contains 2-hydroxymethyl benzoic acid. Also Ceteidil and Ciklavit (aqueous extract of Cajanus cajan — contains amino acids, zinc, antioxidants).

B(i) Bone marrow transplantation:
- Has curative potential for patients with SCD.
- Problems: short-term and long-term toxicity; lack of suitable stem cell donors; limited access.
- Selection criteria: Stroke/CNS haemorrhage, Recurrent acute chest syndrome, Sickle nephropathy, Bilateral proliferative retinopathy and visual impairment, Recurrent debilitating pain.
- Stem cells originally procured by direct puncture and aspiration of bone marrow and re-infused intravenously (bone marrow transplantation).

B(ii) Management of specific crises:
Haemolytic crisis: Admit; give O₂; Transfuse in presence of anaemic heart failure, PCV below 15%, significant fall in PCV below steady state, overwhelming infection; Diuretics.
Aplastic crisis: Intermittent oxygen; Whole blood transfusions; Steroid therapy; ?Bone marrow transplantation. Precipitated by parvovirus; Dx: ↓PCV, ↓Retic, normal WBC and platelet.
Priapism: Sedatives/anxiolytics; Analgesics; Intracavernous injection of adrenergic agonists e.g. Etilefrine; EBT; Surgery if ICI fails: caverno-spongiosum anastomosis.

questions.question:
Describe the pathogenesis and clinical features of meningitis in childhood.
A(i) State the causative organisms for each of the three age groups: neonates, 1–2 months, and 3 months–12 years.
A(ii) Describe the pathogenesis from bacteraemia/URTI to the development of meningitis and its sequelae, including the inflammatory mediators involved.
B(i) List the non-specific and specific clinical features, and the features of raised intracranial pressure.
B(ii) State the typical CSF findings in pyogenic meningitis compared to viral meningitis, TB meningitis, and normal CSF across all four parameters (appearance, WBC, protein, sugar).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Causative organisms by age group:
- Neonates: Gram-negative bacilli, Group B Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Listeria monocytogenes.
- 1–2 months: Organisms seen in neonates plus those in the 3 months–12 years group.
- 3 months–12 years: Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis.

A(ii) Pathogenesis: Bacteraemia / URTI or contiguous spread (otitis media, mastoiditis, penetrating head injury, myelomeningocele) → bacteraemia → penetration of blood-brain barrier → invasion of the meninges → release of acute phase reactants (IL-1, TNF, cytokines) → meningitis → sequelae.

B(i) Non-specific features: Fever, lethargy, vomiting, irritability, refusal of feeds, cough, catarrh.
Features of raised ICP: Bulging anterior fontanelle, abnormal pupils (unequal, dilated), vomiting, papilloedema, hypertension, bradycardia (Cushing's triad), abnormal respiration (apnoea, hyperventilation).
Specific features: Convulsions (20–30%); bulging anterior fontanelle; neck pain; photophobia; headache; coma; features of raised ICP.
Signs of meningeal irritation: Neck stiffness; positive Kernig's sign (extension of leg on thigh impossible when thigh is flexed at right angles with trunk in supine position); positive Brudzinski's sign (involuntary flexion of knee/hip following flexion of neck in supine position, or passive flexion of one leg producing similar movement on the other side). Note: these signs are unusual in infants and young children.

B(ii) CSF findings:
- Normal CSF: Clear/colourless; WBC < 5/mm³; nil protein; nil.
- Pyogenic meningitis: Purulent/turbid; WBC increased++ (N > L); elevated protein; reduced CSF:blood sugar ratio (hypoglycorrhachia); organisms on gram stain and/or culture.
- Viral meningitis: Turbid/hazy; WBC increased+ (L > N); protein increased; sugar relatively normal.
- TB meningitis: Clear/xanthochromic; WBC increased (L > N); protein increased; reduced sugar.

A(i) Gross anatomy of the pituitary gland and hypothalamus:
• Hypothalamus: the part of the brain made up of the floor and part of the lateral walls of the 3rd ventricle. Plays a central role in the endocrine system. Produces releasing factors directly into the adenohypophyseal portal vasculature. Also produces 2 hormones — vasopressin (VP) and oxytocin (OXT) — that are secreted into the capillary beds supplying the posterior pituitary, where they are ultimately released into circulation.
• Pituitary gland — two parts:
  - Adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary): develops from roof of mouth (oral ectoderm — Rathke's pouch). Receives releasing hormones from the hypothalamus via the portal vasculature.
  - Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary): develops from neural tissue of the area of ventricle III of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm). Does not produce its own hormones; stores and releases vasopressin and oxytocin produced by the hypothalamus.
• Communication: the hypothalamus produces releasing hormones (e.g. TRH, GnRH, GHRH, CRH) delivered via the hypophyseal portal system to the anterior pituitary. The delivery of these releasing hormones, which have short half-lives, is dependent upon an intact pituitary stalk.
• Hormone types: steroids (e.g. testosterone, oestrogen); proteins (e.g. TSH, ACTH, LH, hCG); polypeptides <84 amino acids (e.g. insulin, glucagon); miscellaneous (e.g. thyroxine and T3).

A(ii) Zones and pathologies:
• Adenohypophysis: excess ACTH → Cushing's disease (ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma, usually a microadenoma, accounts for 80–90% of ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome, most common cause after 7 years). Deficient TSH → secondary hypothyroidism. Deficient ACTH → secondary adrenal insufficiency. Deficient GnRH/gonadotrophins → hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (delayed puberty).
• Neurohypophysis/hypothalamus: deficient ADH secretion → central Diabetes Insipidus (primary: familial, non-familial; secondary: from CNS pathology). Excess or inappropriate ADH → SIADH.
• Feedback loops: long loop (target organ → pituitary → hypothalamus); short loop (pituitary → hypothalamus). Disruption of feedback leads to either excess or deficiency of end-organ hormones.

B(i) Disease at the hypothalamic level and spread of functional deficit:
• The pituitary stalk is critical: the delivery of short half-life releasing hormones (TRH → TSH; CRH → ACTH; GnRH → LH/FSH) is entirely dependent on an intact pituitary stalk. If a mass (e.g. craniopharyngioma, hypothalamic tumour) or infiltrative disease compresses or destroys the stalk, all releasing hormones fail to reach the anterior pituitary, causing pan-hypopituitarism.
• Thyroid axis: TRH is produced by hypothalamic nuclei and secreted into the portal system → TSH → T4/T3 synthesis. Stalk interruption → no TRH → low TSH → secondary hypothyroidism.
• Adrenal axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol/androgens. Stalk disruption → no ACTH → secondary adrenal insufficiency (relative insufficiency in stress). TSH, ACTH, and gonadotrophin deficiency may coexist in pan-hypopituitarism from hypothalamic/stalk disease.
• A feedback loop exists between the pituitary and hypothalamus (short loop) and between the target organ to the pituitary and thence the hypothalamus (long loop); this acts to control synthesis such that once enough hormone is produced, it feeds back to the hypothalamus and secretion of releasing factors stops. Loss of any level disrupts the entire downstream cascade.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pituitary gland and hypothalamus, including: embryological origin of each part, anatomical position, communication between the hypothalamus and the pituitary, and the hormones produced.
A(ii) Explain how each zone or part of the pituitary–hypothalamic axis relates to common pathologies in paediatric endocrinology (deficient, excess, and regulatory disorders).
B(i) Explain why disease at the level of the hypothalamus may spread to cause functional deficit in the thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal axes, and why the pituitary stalk is critical to this process.

questions.answerText:
(i) Galactosaemia. Specific enzyme deficiency: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency. This enzyme catalyses the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate. The condition is autosomal recessive.

(ii) Risk factors and complications:
• Risk factor: ingestion of lactose (milk); autosomal recessive inheritance (recurrence risk one in four per sibling)
• Pathophysiology/complications: accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate, which cannot enter the glycolytic pathway, causing hypoglycaemia. Toxic effects on the liver (progressive hepatomegaly, jaundice in 1st or 2nd week of life), kidney, brain, and lens (inhibition of cell metabolism). Complications: death in untreated cases; infantile cataract in survivors; mental retardation due to growth retardation; proteinuria and generalised amino aciduria from renal tubular damage; galactosuria

(iii) Diagnosis: enzyme defect detectable in cord blood. Treatment: exclusion of all foods containing lactose and galactose from the diet.

(iv) First-line treatment is dietary elimination of lactose and galactose. Because galactose-1-phosphate accumulation is directly caused by galactose ingestion (lactose in milk is split by lactase to glucose and galactose), removing the substrate prevents further toxic accumulation in the liver, kidney, brain, and lens. This is the only effective intervention since there is no enzyme replacement therapy available. Breast milk and standard formula must be replaced with lactose-free or galactose-free alternatives immediately.
questions.question:
A 5-day-old term neonate presents with feeding refusal, vomiting, and jaundice beginning on day 2 of life. On examination there is progressive hepatomegaly. By day 7 the infant develops cataracts. There is galactosuria on urinalysis.

(i) State the diagnosis and the specific enzyme deficiency responsible.
(ii) List the risk factors and complications of this condition.
(iii) What are the management and treatment options?
(iv) Justify the chosen first-line treatment.

A. Describe pyogenic meningitis under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and causative organisms, classified by age group.
A(ii) Routes of infection (pathogenesis).
A(iii) CSF findings: compare the typical CSF picture in pyogenic, tuberculous, and viral meningitis across appearance, pressure, cell count and type, gram stain, culture, protein, and sugar.

B. Explain the clinical and epidemiological basis for the following:
B(i) Why Streptococcus pneumoniae is particularly common in certain groups of patients.
B(ii) Why Neisseria meningitidis is responsible for epidemic pyogenic meningitis in Northern Nigeria.

C. Distinguish between pyogenic meningitis and each of the following:
C(i) Brain abscess.
C(ii) Viral encephalitis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges. Pyogenic meningitis is caused by bacteria. Organisms by age:
- Neonate/<2 months: Klebsiella sp., Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, H. influenzae type B.
- 2 months–1 year: H. influenzae type B, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis.
- >12 years (uncommon): S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis.

A(ii) Routes of infection:
- Haematogenous — most common; usually secondary to chest or lung infections.
- Contiguous sites: otitis media, sinusitis, mastoiditis, cerebral abscess.
- Trauma: compound skull fracture causing direct implantation of bacteria.
- Direct invasion: dermoid sinus, meningomyelocoele (any organism may be seen).

A(iii) CSF comparison:
- Pyogenic: cloudy/turbid/purulent; pressure increased; WBC increased (1000s, mainly polymorphs); gram stain positive; culture positive; protein increased; sugar decreased.
- Tuberculous: clear/slightly turbid/xanthochromic; pressure increased; WBC increased (100s, mainly lymphocytes); gram stain negative; culture positive on Lowenstein–Jensen medium; protein markedly increased (may form clot/spider web); sugar decreased.
- Viral: clear; pressure increased; WBC increased (mainly lymphocytes); gram stain negative; culture negative; protein increased; sugar normal.

B(i) S. pneumoniae is particularly common in: sickle cell disease (HbSS), patients who have had splenectomy, immunocompromised patients, and those on steroids.

B(ii) N. meningitidis is responsible for epidemic pyogenic meningitis in the Northern part of Nigeria; it occurs during the dry season and a meningococcal vaccine is used where the epidemic is common.

C(i) Brain abscess differs from pyogenic meningitis by: presence of abscess at other sites/focus of spread (e.g., osteomyelitis, congenital heart disease); presence of localising signs; and prominent raised intracranial pressure.
C(ii) Viral encephalitis presents with fever, seizure, and coma but is differentiated by CSF analysis: viral meningitis shows clear CSF, lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal sugar, and negative gram stain/culture.

questions.question:
A 3-month-old infant born to a mother who had a febrile illness with a rash during the first trimester of pregnancy presents with cyanosis, feeding difficulties, and failure to thrive. On examination, the infant has bilateral cataracts, microcephaly, deafness, and a continuous murmur in the infraclavicular region. The chest X-ray shows increased pulmonary vascular markings.

(i) State the unifying diagnosis, name the cardiac lesion, and explain the embryological basis of how the maternal infection produced this cardiac defect.
(ii) State all the predisposing factors for congenital heart disease generally, indicating the exact developmental window during which they exert their effect.
(iii) Describe the management of the identified cardiac lesion — medical and surgical — and the mechanism by which a specific pharmacological agent acts on the ductus.
(iv) State what investigations would confirm the cardiac diagnosis and what the expected findings would be.
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital Rubella Syndrome with Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA). The full syndrome consists of: mental retardation, deafness, bilateral cataracts, microcephaly, and PDA (the characteristic cardiac lesion).
Embryological basis: rubella virus, acquired during the first trimester (during morphogenesis — 12th day to 6–8th week of intrauterine life), acts as a teratogen affecting the developing cardiovascular structures. The ductus arteriosus normally closes 48 hours after delivery due to rising oxygen tension after birth. Intrauterine rubella infection disrupts normal prostaglandin-mediated closure mechanisms, leaving the ductus patent; additionally, reduced oxygen tension associated with the infection and its effects on neonatal circulation maintains ductal patency.

(ii) Predisposing factors for congenital heart disease (exert effect during morphogenesis — 12th day to 6–8th week of intrauterine life):
- Irradiation
- Drugs taken by the mother: thalidomide, cytotoxic agents, steroids
- Intrauterine infections: rubella (→ PDA, VSD, PS)
- Specific chromosomal anomalies: Trisomy 21/Down syndrome (AV septal defect, VSD/ASD); Trisomy 18/Edward's syndrome (VSD/ASD); Trisomy 13/Patau's syndrome (VSD); Turner's syndrome XO (coarctation)
- Specific gene defects
- Familial/environmental factors (CHD commoner among siblings); PDA associated with high altitude and birth asphyxia
- Preterm delivery (→ PDA)
- Maternal diabetes mellitus (→ TGA)

(iii) Medical: treat congestive heart failure with digoxin and diuretics. Indomethacin: a prostaglandin inhibitor (the ductus arteriosus closure is caused by prostaglandin effect; indomethacin has a dilatatory effect, so its inhibition promotes closure) — used especially in preterm neonates for medical closure of PDA.
Surgical: ligation of the PDA — definitive surgical treatment for persistent PDA that fails medical closure.

(iv) Investigations:
- CXR: increased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary plethora); cardiomegaly if heart failure has set in
- ECG: initially LVH, then biventricular changes
- ECHO with Doppler colour flow: demonstrates the duct and confirms left-to-right shunt; defines cardiac anatomy
- Cardiac catheterisation: confirms the PDA; measures pressures; demonstrates left-to-right shunt via angiography

A(i) Shock is a physiologic state characterised by inadequate tissue perfusion to meet metabolic demands and tissue oxygenation. It is an acute, life-threatening syndrome characterised by circulatory dysfunction resulting in inadequate delivery of oxygen and other nutrients to meet tissue metabolic demands. It progresses into anaerobic metabolism and accumulation of lactic acid, culminating in loss of normal cellular function, cell death, organ dysfunction, and eventually death if not recognised and treated.

A(ii) Cardiac output (CO) = Stroke Volume × Heart Rate. DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10. CaO2 = Hb × 1.34 × SaO2 + (PaO2 × 0.003); haemoglobin carries more than 99% of oxygen under standard conditions.
Stroke volume determinants: Preload (LVEDV — reflects patient's volume status, measured by CVP or PCWP, follows Starling curve); Afterload (resistance to ventricular ejection, determined by vascular tone and transmural pressure); Myocardial Contractility (influenced by coronary perfusion, baseline myocardial function, cardiotonic medications).

A(iii) Neural sympathetic: baroreceptors (carotid body, aortic arch), volume receptors (right atrium, pulmonary vascular), chemoreceptors (aortic and carotid, medullary), cerebral ischaemic response. Humoral: adrenal medulla catecholamines, hypothalamo-pituitary response (ACTH, vasopressin), renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

B. Hypovolemic: inadequate blood volume (diarrhoea, burns, haemorrhage, vomiting); low preload → decreased SV → decreased CO; compensatory increase in HR and SVR. Cardiovascular: decreased preload, increased afterload, no change in contractility.
Distributive (septic): high CO and low SVR; maldistribution of blood flow; due to endotoxin, vasoactive substances, complement cascade. Early: increased preload, decreased afterload; late: decreased preload, decreased afterload, decreased contractility.
Cardiogenic: low CO and high SVR; primary cardiac dysfunction; increased LV afterload → pulmonary oedema and RV failure. Causes: congenital heart disease, arrhythmias, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy. Cardiovascular: increased afterload, decreased contractility.
Obstructive: low CO secondary to physical obstruction; increased SVR. Causes: pericardial tamponade, tension pneumothorax, critical coarctation, aortic stenosis, hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

C. Compensated shock: clinical signs of inadequate perfusion but normal BP — vital organ functions maintained (tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, fussy/irritable child). Decompensated shock: severely impaired perfusion; absent pulses, cool extremities, mottled skin, altered sensorium, hypotension develops. Hypotension is a very late sign because 25% of blood volume must be lost before a drop in blood pressure occurs; minimal changes in blood pressure may already indicate shock.
questions.question:
A. Describe the physiologic basis of shock under the following headings:
A(i) Definition of shock
A(ii) Determinants of cardiac output, oxygen delivery (DO2 formula), and stroke volume (preload, afterload, contractility)
A(iii) Compensatory mechanisms that defend blood pressure in shock, covering both neural (sympathetic) and humoral pathways

B. Describe the four types of shock (hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive) — their pathophysiology, causes, and cardiovascular changes in preload, afterload, and contractility.

C. Distinguish between compensated and decompensated shock in terms of clinical signs and explain why hypotension is a very late sign in children.

questions.answerText:
(i) Pertussis (whooping cough). Causative organism: Bordetella pertussis (B. Parapertussis) – small gram negative pleomorphic coccobacillus. Note: infants less than 3 months do not produce the classic whoop; instead they present with gasp, cyanosis, and apnoea.
(ii) Risk factors and epidemiological features:
- Overcrowding, poor ventilation, poor vaccine coverage are risk factors; poverty
- Peak incidence between July and October
- Mode of spread: droplets
- Peak age is 1-5 years, but also affects infants and older people
- Source: adults with subclinical infection
- Attack rate is almost 100%
- Vaccination/infection does not confer lifelong immunity
- No chronic carrier state
- Incubation period: 3-12 days
(iii) Three clinical phases:
1. Catarrhal phase (2 weeks): low grade fever, congestion, rhinorrhoea, sneezing, lacrimation, conjunctival suffusion
2. Paroxysmal phase (2-6 weeks): initial dry cough, irritative and intermittent, evolves into bouts of intense non-staccato cough followed by a whoop; in infants <3 months: gasp, cyanosis, apnoea, bulging red eyes; associated symptoms include subconjunctival haemorrhage, petechiae, seizures from intracranial bleeds/hypoxia
3. Convalescent phase (2-4 weeks): recovery begins; immunization shortens all stages
(iv) Laboratory findings and treatment:
- Mostly clinical; case definition: cough >14 days + 1 of (paroxysms, whoop, post-tussive vomiting)
- Lymphocyte leucocytosis (15,000-100,000/cc) in late catarrhal or early paroxysmal phase
- Deep nasopharyngeal aspirate for MCS using Regan-Lowe transport medium; PCR; serology (ELISA); direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing
- Treatment goals: limit spread, prevent/treat complications, maximize nutrition and rest to aid recovery without sequelae
- Erythromycin 40-50 mg/kg/d for patient and close contacts
- Close contacts under 7 years: give booster dose of vaccine
questions.question:
A 6-month-old unimmunized infant presents with 10 days of low-grade fever, congestion, and rhinorrhoea. In the last 3 days she has developed severe bouts of cough followed by a gasp and cyanosis, with post-tussive vomiting.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the causative organism.
(ii) List the risk factors and epidemiological features of this condition.
(iii) Describe the three clinical phases in order and their characteristic features.
(iv) State the laboratory findings that support the diagnosis and the treatment goals with specific management.

A 30-minute-old male neonate born at term via emergency caesarean section for fetal distress is brought to the resuscitation bay. He is limp, pale, not breathing, and his heart rate is 40 beats per minute. He scores 2 on his 1-minute Apgar.
(i) State his diagnosis and classify the severity of birth asphyxia based on the Apgar score given.
(ii) List four maternal and four foetal predisposing factors for birth asphyxia.
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitation steps (ABC) for this neonate in the delivery room.
(iv) Name five organ systems affected by severe birth asphyxia and one complication in each.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Birth asphyxia — defined as reduced oxygen saturation (hypoxaemia) and increased acid in blood (acidaemia) from CO2 retention and lactic acid accumulation. Apgar score of 1–3 = Severe birth asphyxia.

(ii) Maternal/Prenatal factors: Pneumonia / asthmatic attack; cardiac arrhythmias / heart failure; anaemia due to haemoglobinopathy; hypertension (due to arteriosclerosis); uterine rupture; narcotics (via respiratory depression in mother or direct effect on baby); prolonged obstructed labour; placental insufficiency.
Foetal factors: Prematurity (affects respiratory centre); postmaturity (due to placental insufficiency); developmental anomalies (diaphragmatic hernia, choanal atresia, hypoplasia); cord problems (knotting, compression or prolapse); congenital infection (e.g. congenital pneumonia).

(iii) ABC of resuscitation in the delivery room:
A — Clear the airway.
B — Ensure ventilation with 100% oxygen.
C — Ensure circulation; give volume expander if in shock.
Additional agents: Naloxone 0.1 mg/kg to reverse effects of narcotics; sodium bicarbonate 2 mEq/L diluted (only when baby has ventilation); 50% dextrose 0.5–1 mg/kg diluted.

(iv)
- CNS: Hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE); also seizures, intracranial haemorrhage, SIADH (inadequate urine output, hyponatraemia, oedema, weight gain).
- CVS: Left ventricular dysfunction due to myocardial ischaemia; tricuspid incompetence; patent ductus arteriosus; patent foetal circulation.
- Renal: Acute tubular necrosis; acute cortical necrosis; urinary retention; different kidney failure requiring fluid challenge.
- GIT: Necrotising enterocolitis (due to ischaemia causing bacterial proliferation).
- Haematologic: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); increased risk of infection; hypo- or hyperglycaemia.

(i) Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

(ii) The four anatomical components are:
- Pulmonary stenosis (usually infundibular)
- Right ventricular hypertrophy
- Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
- Over-riding (dextropositioned) aorta
Embryological basis: The arterial septum divides unequally — the left half is much bigger than the right — causing pulmonary stenosis and over-riding aorta. This unequal septation is also responsible for the formation of the VSD. Right ventricular hypertrophy is secondary to the obstruction.

(iii) Squatting folds the femoral and popliteal vessels, increasing resistance and consequently pressure in the systemic circulation, which raises left ventricular afterload and reduces right-to-left shunting through the VSD. More blood is then pumped to the lungs for oxygenation. A secondary mechanism is compression of the femoral and popliteal veins, reducing venous return and thus reducing pressure on the right side.

(iv) Steps in immediate management of a hypercyanotic spell:
1. Place the patient in the knee-chest position — most important
2. Give oxygen by face mask or nasal catheter
3. Give intravenous propranolol (dose: 0.1 mg/kg)
   Alternative: subcutaneous or intramuscular morphia (relaxes the infundibulum)
4. Give sodium bicarbonate (dose: 1 mEq/kg)

(v) Definitive treatment: Open heart surgery to close the VSD, requiring cardiopulmonary bypass (heart-lung machine).
questions.question:
A 4-year-old child is brought to clinic with a history of cyanosis noticed since infancy, easy fatiguability, and squatting after exertion. On examination, he is small for age, cyanosed, with digital clubbing. Palpation reveals a left parasternal heave and a systolic thrill along the left upper sternal edge. Auscultation reveals a single soft second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area. Chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart with reduced pulmonary vascular markings and a right-sided aortic arch.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the four anatomical components of this condition and explain the embryological basis for all four arising from a single developmental defect.
(iii) Describe the physiological mechanism by which squatting relieves the child's symptoms.
(iv) The child suddenly develops a hypercyanotic spell in the waiting room. List, in order of priority, the steps in immediate management of this emergency.
(v) What is the definitive surgical treatment?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aims of investigations: to aid diagnosis; to define the extent of disease; to follow up response to treatment.

A(ii) Chest radiograph: PA view is sufficient for lobar or bronchopneumonia except to demonstrate additional features like pleural effusion. Patchy consolidation (bronchopneumonia), lobar or segmental consolidation (lobar pneumonia), or mixed picture may be shown. Lobar consolidation in older children is common with S. aureus. Pneumatocoele also common with Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, and Proteus. No pneumatocoele but pneumonia with acute otitis media → S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae. Associated pleural effusion → assume S. aureus (though S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae can also cause it). Air bronchograms, hilar opacity, cavitation with amphoric breath sounds and whispering pectoriloquy.

A(iii) FBC and differential: PCV may be low or normal. Blood film may show toxic granulations. Usually there is leucocytosis; leucopenia is an ominous sign. Differential WBC: neutrophilia if bacterial; lymphocytosis if viral.

B. Blood culture: low yield — 10–30% positive; usually done in severe pneumonia. Sputum examination (MCS): very low yield because young children rarely expectorate; when they do, sputum acquires contaminants from the upper airway. Lung aspirate: high yield but invasive; MCS of aspirate for bacteria detection, isolation, and sensitivity; immunofluorescence and cell culture for viruses; aspirate analysed for other organisms; serological tests for antigens not routinely done; indications — severely ill patient, immunocompromised patient likely to have unusual organisms, research purposes; requires expertise and good microbiology laboratory.

C. Oxygen therapy — Absolute indications: central cyanosis; severe lower chest wall indrawing; oxygen saturation <90%. Other indications: tachypnoea 20 breaths/min above age-specific cut-off point; restlessness (not due to meningitis); titubation; tachycardia. Methods: face mask or nasal prongs at 3–4 litres/min; nasopharyngeal catheter at 1–2 litres/min (supplies about 40% oxygen); headbox; oxygen concentrator when medical oxygen is not affordable; pulse oximetry to ensure adequate oxygenation.
questions.question:
A. Describe the investigations used in the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia in children:
(i) State the aims of investigations in pneumonia.
(ii) Describe what chest radiograph may show and what specific radiological patterns suggest which aetiological agents.
(iii) Describe the FBC findings and what the differential white cell count indicates.

B. Explain the indications and limitations of blood culture, sputum examination, and lung aspirate in the diagnosis of childhood pneumonia.

C. Describe the oxygen therapy for pneumonia, giving the absolute and other indications for oxygen therapy, and the methods of delivery.

A 5-year-old girl has had cough for 6 weeks with progressive weight loss, low-grade fever, and night sweats. Her mother has been on TB treatment for 3 months. Examination reveals cervical lymphadenopathy and phlycternular conjunctivitis. Chest X-ray shows hilar enlargement.
(i) State the diagnosis and outline the investigations needed to confirm it, including specimen types and diagnostic tests.
(ii) Identify the clinical signs of hypersensitivity to tubercle bacilli and explain their significance.
(iii) State the treatment regimen appropriate for this child, including drugs, doses, and duration.
(iv) What conditions increase the risk of TB infection, and how should newborns of mothers with TB be managed?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: pulmonary tuberculosis (primary complex with hilar adenopathy). Investigations:
- Bacteriological confirmation: Xpert MTB/RIF (now 1st line, detects M. tb Complex and Rifampicin resistant strains; results in 2 hours; requires only one sample); AFB for microscopy (2 sputum samples – on spot and early morning, after overnight fast); culture (gold standard) on Lowenstein Jensen solid medium or MGIT liquid agar
- Specimens: sputum obtained by coughing up or sputum induction; gastric washing/aspirate in children
- HIV test for all cases of TB
- Chest X-ray: perihilar adenopathy ("doughnut" or "hamburger" sign on lateral view); consolidation; cavitation
- Mantoux test: ≥10 mm is positive irrespective of BCG vaccination; ≥5 mm is positive in HIV-infected and severely malnourished children
- Other: histological examination useful for TB adenitis; CSF analysis for TB meningitis (CSF chemistry and GeneXpert)
(ii) Signs of hypersensitivity to tubercle bacilli:
- Erythema nodosum and phlycternular conjunctivitis
- Phlycternular conjunctivitis: red eye associated with white speck(s) at the border of the cornea
- These are muco-cutaneous manifestations of the hypersensitivity reaction and indicate that the host has mounted a cellular immune response to M. tuberculosis
(iii) Treatment regimen:
- This child has PTB (not TB meningitis, miliary TB, or osteoarticular TB): use Regimen 1 (2RHZE/4RH)
- Intensive phase: 2 months RHZE daily
- Continuation phase: 4 months RH daily; total duration 6 months
- Drug doses: Rifampicin 10-20 mg/kg/day; Isoniazid 10-15 mg/kg/day; Pyrazinamide 25-30 mg/kg/day; Ethambutol 20-25 mg/kg/day
- DOTS desirable at least during the intensive phase to improve compliance
(iv) Conditions increasing risk of TB infection:
- HIV infection; malnutrition; other infections (measles, pertussis)
- Prolonged corticosteroid or other immunosuppressive therapy
- Haematologic and reticuloendothelial diseases (e.g. leukaemia and Hodgkin's disease)
- Diabetes mellitus; chronic malabsorption syndromes
Management of newborn of a mother with TB:
- Mother's treatment should be commenced or continued if already started
- Baby should start INH soon after delivery
- CXR if symptomatic
- If CXR is normal, continue INH for 6 months
- If CXR is abnormal, treat as TB with combination chemotherapy

questions.question:
A young woman in her second trimester of pregnancy presents with breathlessness on exertion. She recalls that as a child she was told she had a "hole in the heart" but was otherwise well. Examination reveals a wide fixed split of S2, a pulsatile flow murmur at the pulmonary area, and a markedly dilated right atrium on echocardiography. A male colleague of hers, a professional footballer, was found to have the same condition incidentally.

(i) State the diagnosis and explain the pathogenesis and why the pressure gradient across this defect is small compared with VSD and PDA.
(ii) Explain why this condition often presents symptomatically in pregnancy and why it may be asymptomatic for decades in males.
(iii) Describe the full clinical features — the specific auscultatory findings and the cardiac chamber most likely to dilate — and the investigation findings.
(iv) Outline the management of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) — specifically secundum ASD. Pathogenesis: failure of complete septation during morphogenesis affects the atrial septum; blood shunts left-to-right due to a higher left atrial pressure (8–9 mmHg) than right atrial pressure (5 mmHg).
The shunting is minimal because the pressure gradient is small — only 3–4 mmHg (left atrium 8–9 mmHg vs right atrium 5 mmHg). This contrasts with VSD and PDA which involve the high-pressure systems (systemic ventricle → right ventricle pressure gradient of ~100 mmHg; aorta → pulmonary artery), explaining their much larger shunts and earlier symptomatic presentation.

(ii) In pregnancy, the hyperdynamic circulation markedly increases cardiac output, exposing a previously compensated shunt and precipitating symptoms. In males, ASD is often an accidental discovery because the heart adapts to the volume overload for many years — as in Kanu Nwankwo (Nigerian footballer) .

(iii) Auscultatory findings:
- Wide fixed splitting of S2 — the hallmark; fixed means it does not vary with respiration (in contrast to normal S2 which widens on inspiration)
- Pulmonic flow murmur — ejection systolic murmur at left upper sternal edge due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve
The heart adapts to volume overload with huge dilatation of the right atrium (left atrium usually normal).
Investigations:
- ECHO: detects the ASD, demonstrates dilated right atrium, quantifies shunt
- ECG: may show right atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy
- CXR: increased pulmonary vascular markings if shunt is significant; right heart enlargement

(iv) Management:
- Small asymptomatic ASD with no haemodynamic compromise: conservative/observation
- Significant ASD causing haemodynamic compromise: closure
Surgical closure: patch repair (open heart surgery)
Catheter-based closure: device closure (for suitable secundum ASDs)
Treatment of complications (e.g. heart failure in pregnancy): digoxin and diuretics
Prevention of recurrence: long-term prophylaxis not required for ASD (unlike ARF); antibiotic prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures if not yet closed

(i) Diagnosis: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA).
Hyperoxia test: When 100% oxygen is given, cyanosis improves if the cause is respiratory (PO2 rises significantly). Failure to improve (or only marginal improvement in PO2) indicates cardiac cyanosis — specifically a right-to-left shunt bypassing the lungs. This confirms TGA (or another cyanotic CHD). It is done routinely: arterial sample from right radial artery after 100% oxygen for 10 minutes.

(ii) Anatomical arrangement:
Normal: Atrioventricular concordance (right atrium → right ventricle; left atrium → left ventricle) AND ventriculo-arterial concordance (right ventricle → pulmonary artery; left ventricle → aorta).
TGA: Atrioventricular concordance (normal AV connections) BUT ventriculo-arterial discordance — the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle.

(iii) Loud (single) S2: The aorta is anterior to the pulmonary artery in TGA. The anterior position of the aorta makes A2 louder (transmitted through the chest wall more easily). Additionally, because of increased blood flow in the pulmonary artery, P2 may also be loud (though the PA lies behind the aorta). The result is a loud, often single-sounding S2.

(iv) Emergency catheter-based procedure: Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy — a balloon catheter is passed via the femoral vein → right atrium → across the foramen ovale → left atrium; the balloon is inflated and pulled back forcefully to create an atrial septal defect, allowing mixing of blood.
Surgical alternative if catheter procedure is insufficient: Blalock-Hanlon Atrial Septectomy — not an open heart surgery; surgically creates an opening for mixing of blood.

(v) Two open-heart surgical operations:
1. Mustard operation: The atrial septum is removed and an atrial baffle is created to divert all blood from the right atrium into the left atrium and left ventricle (and thence to the pulmonary artery). The patient becomes pink dramatically. Good prognosis.
2. Arterial switch operation: Corrects the transposition at the level of the great arteries.
questions.question:
A newborn female is delivered at term to a mother with known diabetes mellitus. At birth she is noted to be mildly cyanosed with a respiratory rate of 70/min. She has difficulty feeding. On examination, there is tachycardia, a loud single S2, and an egg-on-side appearance on chest X-ray with markedly increased pulmonary vascular markings. The 100% oxygen test (hyperoxia test) fails to improve cyanosis significantly.

(i) State the diagnosis and explain the significance of the hyperoxia test result in distinguishing cardiac from respiratory cyanosis.
(ii) Describe the anatomical arrangement of the great vessels in this condition as compared with the normal arrangement, using the terms concordant and discordant.
(iii) Explain why a loud (single) S2 is heard in this condition.
(iv) State the emergency palliative catheter-based procedure that must be performed at this stage, and one surgical alternative if this catheter procedure is insufficient.
(v) Name the two open-heart surgical operations available and briefly describe what each achieves.

A 2-year-old child presents with a 1-year history of delayed walking. She has never walked independently. On examination she has scissoring of the lower limbs, increased tone in all four limbs with the lower limbs more affected, and a history of prolonged birth asphyxia. Head circumference is below the 3rd centile. A persistent Moro reflex is elicited at 14 months.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what specific type/sub-type best fits this child's presentation?
(ii) List the predisposing (aetiological) factors for this condition, classified as prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology linking birth asphyxia to this child's motor disorder.
(iv) Outline the management of this child, listing every member of the multidisciplinary team and the role of each.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Cerebral Palsy — Spastic Diplegia. Lower limbs are more severely affected than upper limbs (scissoring gait, lower limb spasticity predominant); this sub-type is especially common in preterm infants with anoxic brain damage and in those with intraventricular haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia.

(ii) Aetiological factors:
Prenatal: radiation; anoxia; intrauterine infections (TORCHES — manifested as skin rash and fever during pregnancy); developmental anomaly (e.g., encephalocoele, cerebral cysts); drugs (alcohol, narcotics); metabolic (phenylketonuria, hypoglycaemia); toxins; genetic (some syndromes associated with brain dysgenesis); vascular accident resulting in infarction.
Perinatal: low birth weight; anoxia (e.g., birth asphyxia → hypoxic encephalopathy → cerebral palsy); trauma; prematurity (gestational age).
Postnatal: trauma (falls, child abuse, RTA); infections (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria); toxins (bilirubin/kernicterus); drugs; metabolic (hypoglycaemia); cerebral hypoxia (FB aspiration, near-drowning).

(iii) Pathophysiology: birth asphyxia causes hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy. Lack of oxygen leads to failure of oxidative phosphorylation, cellular energy depletion, excitotoxic neuronal injury, and ultimately permanent, nonprogressive damage to the developing brain. The periventricular white matter is particularly vulnerable in the perinatal period; damage here produces spasticity predominantly in the lower limbs (spastic diplegia).

(iv) Multidisciplinary team management:
- Paediatric Neurologist: overall coordination of neurological care, anticonvulsants for seizures.
- Physiotherapist: main treatment modality; passive then active exercises; reduce spasticity; prevent contractures. The earlier rehabilitation starts, the better for the child.
- Ophthalmologist: assessment and management of visual defects (strabismus, optic atrophy, nystagmus).
- Audiologist/ENT Surgeon: hearing assessment; all children with CP must have hearing and visual assessment.
- Speech Therapist: management of speech defects, feeding difficulties, language.
- Clinical Psychologist: behavioural and cognitive assessment.
- Occupational Therapist: functional independence and adaptive aids.
- Educator: learning disability and special educational needs.
- Social Worker: family support, social rehabilitation.
- Orthopaedic Surgeon: to release contractures, correct hip dislocation, rhizotomy.
- Drug treatment: muscle relaxants to reduce high spasticity (Nitrazepam, Dantrolene, Botulinum toxin injected directly into spastic muscles — short-acting effect); Baclofen.

questions.question:
A. Describe intracranial infections in childhood under the following headings:
A(i) The reasons why the brain is normally protected from infection, and the factors that make it vulnerable when those protections fail.
A(ii) Tuberculous meningitis: stages of clinical presentation, distinguishing CSF findings, and the prognosis according to stage at commencement of therapy.
A(iii) Viral encephalitis: definition, aetiology, clinical features, and complications (early and late).

B. Explain why bacterial infections of the CNS often lead to death or significant neurological sequelae, using the pathophysiological mechanisms described.

C. Distinguish pyogenic meningitis from viral encephalitis and from tuberculous meningitis, using: CSF appearance, WBC count and type, protein, glucose ratio, gram stain, and overall prognosis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Normal protection: the brain is normally a sterile site protected by the bony skull and the blood–brain barrier (BBB). When these fail, the brain becomes vulnerable because of: deficient local host defences that do not suppress multiplication of pathogens; detrimental effects of cerebral blood flow (CBF) alterations; harmful effects of raised ICP caused by brain swelling and mass lesions; destruction of brain tissue by the inflammatory process; and limited repair mechanism of neuronal tissue.

A(ii) Tuberculous meningitis stages:
Stage I: non-specific symptoms — fever, headache, weight loss, irritability, drowsiness.
Stage II: lethargy, nuchal rigidity, seizures, positive Kernig's sign, vomiting, signs of brainstem involvement, cranial nerve palsies, focal neurological signs.
Stage III: hemiplegia or paraplegia, coma, decerebrate rigidity, opisthotonus; fundoscopy may show papilloedema and choroidal tubercles.
CSF: straw-coloured or clear; WBC 10–500 cells/cmm predominantly lymphocytes; protein >1 g/dl; glucose <40 mg/dl; ZN stain may yield AFB; culture may be positive.
Prognosis: Stage I — good. Stage III — mortality is high; survivors have complications (blindness, deafness, paraplegia, mental retardation, speech disturbance, cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus).

A(iii) Viral encephalitis: a widespread or focal inflammation of the brain parenchyma resulting in a marked disturbance of cerebral function, usually in the absence of a metabolic or toxic cause.
Aetiology: idiopathic in at least 50%; RNA viruses (mumps, measles, rabies, eastern equine viruses); DNA viruses (herpes, EBV, poxviruses); bacteria, rickettsiae, spirochetes, fungi (Candida, Histoplasma, Aspergillus); protozoa (Plasmodium, Toxoplasma gondii, Entamoeba sp.); post-infectious/allergic (cell-mediated antigen–antibody complexes).
Clinical: prodromal symptoms (cough, coryza, vomiting); mild neck stiffness, mental dullness, ataxia, speech alteration, focal neurological deficit, decerebrate or decorticate rigidity; may range from mild to irreversible coma.
Early complications: SIADH, cortical blindness, aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, heart failure, DIC. Late complications: epilepsy, mental retardation, cerebral palsy, motor deficit, psychosis/behavioural problems.

B. Brain damage in bacterial meningitis is often a consequence of the overwhelming inflammatory response rather than invasion of pathogens. Release of acute-phase reactants (IL-1, TNF, cytokines) causes brain oedema, raised ICP, vasculitis, cerebral infarction, and destruction of neuronal tissue; because neuronal tissue has limited repair mechanisms, the resulting damage is often permanent and leads to death or significant sequelae.

C. CSF comparison:
- Pyogenic: purulent/turbid; WBC increased markedly (neutrophils); protein markedly increased; glucose ratio <1/2; gram stain positive.
- Viral encephalitis: clear or slightly turbid; WBC increased (lymphocytes); protein increased; glucose ratio normal; gram stain negative.
- Tuberculous: xanthochromic/clear; WBC 10–500 (lymphocytes); protein very high (>1 g/dl, may form clot); glucose <40 mg/dl (<1/2); ZN stain may be positive; prognosis depends on stage — Stage III is poor.

A(i) Obstructive airway diseases are diseases that cause obstruction at various parts of the respiratory tract. Two main divisions: (1) Extra-thoracic or upper airway obstruction (from anterior nares to the pharynx); (2) Intrathoracic or lower airway obstruction (larynx to alveoli).

A(ii) Extra-thoracic/upper airway obstruction: affects mainly the inspiratory phase of respiration; important feature is STRIDOR. Intrathoracic/lower airway obstruction: affects mainly the expiratory phase of respiration.

A(iii) Congenital causes of upper airway obstruction: laryngomalacia; laryngeal web; subglottic stenosis; laryngocoele; tracheo-oesophageal fistula; craniofacial anomalies. Acquired causes: infections — laryngotracheobronchitis; epiglottitis; retropharyngeal abscess; peritonsillar abscess; bacterial tracheitis; diphtheria. Burns — thermal; chemical. Foreign body aspiration. Trauma. Allergy — spasmodic laryngitis. Neoplasm.

B. Pathophysiology: oedema of bronchiolar mucosa + accumulation of mucus and cellular debris + constriction of muscles of bronchiolar wall → reduction in size of lumen → resistance to airflow at inspiration and expiration, more marked at expiration. If obstruction is complete → atelectasis. If incomplete → air trapping and hyperinflation → impairment of gaseous exchange at alveolar level → hypoxaemia early and hypercapnia later. Indication for mechanical ventilation: PaO2 <60 mmHg; PaCO2 >45 mmHg; pH less than 7.25.

C. Clinical features: usually begins with upper respiratory infection → cough, fast breathing, fever, refusal of feeds, vomiting, fretfulness, wheezing, chest retraction, cyanosis; hyperresonant percussion note; prolonged expiration; diminished breath sounds; fine crepitations; palpable liver and spleen due to downward displacement of diaphragm from hyperinflation.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is kwashiorkor with severe acute malnutrition (SAM): bilateral pitting oedema qualifies as SAM by oedema criteria, confirmed by MUAC of 10.2 cm (below 11.5 cm) and WHZ of –4.1 (below –3 SD). The blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/L represents hypoglycaemia, defined in SAM as blood glucose below 3 mmol/L. Bradycardia and hypothermia indicate life-threatening metabolic decompensation.
(ii) In SAM, depleted glycogen stores and impaired gluconeogenesis — from deficiency of gluconeogenic substrates (amino acids, glycerol) due to severe protein-energy depletion — prevent adequate glucose production during fasting. Impaired Na-K ATPase activity from energy deficit and micronutrient deficiency further compromises cellular metabolism. Children with SAM are unable to maintain normoglycaemia during illness or prolonged fasting.
(iii) Immediate resuscitation: hypoglycaemia is treated with 10% dextrose IV bolus (5 mL/kg) or oral glucose if the child can swallow, followed by frequent feeding every 2–3 hours to prevent recurrence. Hypothermia is managed by warming and frequent feeds. Bradycardia raises concern for hypokalaemia-induced cardiac arrhythmia — hypokalaemia prolongs the QT interval and increases risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias including ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation; potassium supplementation is mandated. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (amoxicillin) are given to all SAM children as per WHO protocol because SAM is associated with bacterial translocation and subclinical sepsis.
(iv) Phase 1 — Stabilisation: F-75 therapeutic milk (75 kcal/100 mL, 0.9 g protein/100 mL, low fat, restricted sodium). This provides maintenance energy without overloading the damaged gut and corrects metabolic derangements. Phase 2 — Rehabilitation: F-100 or Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF — peanut butter, dry skimmed milk powder, vegetable oil, sugar, and a micronutrient supplement) to achieve catch-up growth. The specific electrolyte risk at transition is refeeding syndrome: carbohydrate refeeding triggers insulin release, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, causing severe hypophosphataemia with risk of cardiac failure and respiratory failure. This is prevented by gradual refeeding per WHO SAM protocol.
questions.question:
A 22-month-old child is admitted to the paediatric ward from a rural community. The child is lethargic and does not respond to voice. The mother reports he has had diarrhoea for 3 weeks and has stopped eating over the past 5 days. On examination: bilateral pitting oedema to mid-thigh, MUAC 10.2 cm, weight-for-height Z-score –4.1, heart rate 54 bpm (bradycardic), temperature 35.8°C (hypothermic), and bedside glucose is 2.1 mmol/L. The skin has flaky paint dermatosis on the lower extremities.

(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis for impaired gluconeogenesis leading to this metabolic complication in this condition.

questions.answerText:
(i) Infant A: Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA) — presents in infancy at or near birth with cyanosis, breathlessness, and heart failure from increased pulmonary blood flow. Embryological/pathological basis: atrioventricular concordance but ventriculo-arterial discordance — the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. CXR egg-on-side with increased PVM reflects cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary blood flow.
Infant B: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) — presents later (often >1 year, sometimes 5–7 years) without heart failure, with squatting, cyanosis, and boot-shaped heart with reduced PVM. Embryological basis: atrioventricular concordance AND ventriculo-arterial concordance but with unequal division of the arterial septum — left half bigger → pulmonary stenosis, over-riding aorta, and (from unequal septation) VSD; VSD causes RVH.

(ii) Infant A — emergency management in first 48 hours:
Medical: treatment of heart failure — diuretics and digoxin.
Maintain/create mixing point to sustain oxygenation: PGE-1 infusion to keep ductus arteriosus patent if not yet closed (maintaining PDA mixing).
Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy (therapeutic cardiac catheterisation, emergency): balloon catheter via femoral vein → IVC → right atrium → foramen ovale → left atrium → inflate balloon → pull back forcefully to create ASD → allows mixing at atrial level → patient becomes less cyanosed and more stable.

(iii) Infant B — TOF expected findings:
Clinical features: cyanosis (degree varies with severity of obstruction); small for gestational age; polycythaemia (conjunctival suffusion, reddened buccal mucosa); digital clubbing; ± breathlessness (from polycythaemia or metabolic acidosis, NOT from heart failure or pulmonary congestion); left parasternal heave (RVH); systolic thrill along left upper sternal edge; single and soft S2; ejection systolic murmur at pulmonary area (LUSE) OR pansystolic murmur of VSD at LLSE (not both heard simultaneously).
ECG: right axis deviation; right ventricular hypertrophy; ± right atrial hypertrophy.
Echo (2D): RVH, VSD, over-riding aorta, pulmonary outflow tract stenosis.
Blood gases: reduced PO2 (hypoxia from right-to-left shunting — desaturated blood in systemic circulation); reduced pH (metabolic acidosis from hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism); increased PCO2 (compensatory hyperventilation is overwhelmed in severe cases). In TOF, breathlessness when present is due to polycythaemia or metabolic acidosis (compensatory hyperventilation), NOT pulmonary congestion.

(iv) Surgical options:
Infant A (TGA):
- Palliative: Blalock-Hanlon Atrial Septectomy (non-open heart, creates atrial communication); Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy (catheter-based)
- Definitive: Mustard's Operation (open heart — atrial baffle diverts blood; patient becomes pink dramatically); Arterial Switch Operation (open heart — anatomically corrects great vessel positions)
Infant B (TOF):
- Palliative: Blalock-Taussig Shunt (shunts blood from systemic to pulmonary circulation to improve oxygenation); classical (subclavian artery cut and anastomosed to PA) or modified (Gore-tex graft interposed; used for smaller patients)
- Definitive: open heart VSD patch repair with relief of pulmonary obstruction, requiring cardiopulmonary bypass (heart-lung machine)
questions.question:
