questions.answerText:
A(i) Epidemiology:
- Measles is endemic in most of the world; highly infectious
- Median age of measles infection in Nigeria = 17 months
- Transplacentally acquired immunity present in first 6 months of life
- By 1 year, 1/3 of children would have had measles; before 3rd year, 3/4 of children would have had measles
- Period of communicability: 4 days before and 5 days after appearance of rash
- Seasonal variation: in temperate countries, transmission peaks in late winter and early spring; in tropics, dry season (February/March); however in large, crowded cities with low measles vaccine coverage, transmission can be continuous throughout year
- No vector, no animal reservoir, one serotype
- Risk factors: overcrowding, malnourished or immunocompromised children
- Case fatality rate: 2-15% in developing countries; <0.2/10,000 in developed countries
A(ii) Pathogenesis of immunosuppression:
- Measles virus infection causes immunosuppression marked by decreases in delayed-type hypersensitivity, interleukin-12 production, and antigen-specific lymphoproliferative responses that persist for weeks to months after acute infection
- Immunosuppression may predispose individuals to severe bacterial infection, particularly bronchopneumonia (a major cause of measles deaths)
- In cellular immune deficiency, measles virus causes progressive and often fatal giant cell pneumonia (Warthin-Finkeldey)
B(i) Measles vaccine:
- Type: live attenuated
- Preparation: national programme uses monovalent measles vaccine in freeze-dried form reconstituted with a diluent; also available in combination with rubella and mumps as MMR
- Schedule: 9 months (MCV1); 15 months (MCV2); routine immunization is the foundation of effective measles control
- Efficacy: 85% (up to 15% of children do not seroconvert and are thus not protected)
- Side effects: 10% of children develop low grade fever; 5% develop mild generalized non-infectious rash
- Duration of immunity: lifelong
- Contraindications: none, even where the child is sick or malnourished
- Administration: 0.5 ml dose SC, upper left arm
B(ii) MMR and autism:
- There is no scientific evidence that the risk of autism is higher among children who receive measles or MMR vaccine than among unvaccinated children
C(i) Immunization strategies:
- Routine immunization: foundation of effective measles control; schedule 9 months ±6 months
- Supplemental immunization – "catch-up" campaign: a one-time effort to vaccinate all children under age 15 to reduce susceptible individuals (never vaccinated and primary vaccination failures); builds herd immunity
- "Follow-up" campaign: periodic mass immunization campaigns every 2-4 years following catch-up campaigns; purpose is to reduce any build-up of susceptible individuals born after previous SIA or <9 months at time of catch-up campaign
C(ii) Passive immunization and malnutrition:
- Passive immunity: immune serum globulin within 5 days after exposure
- Malnourished/immunocompromised children are listed as risk factors for measles infection and severity
- Complications occurring in malnourished children: malnutrition is listed as a GIT complication; blindness due to Vitamin A deficiency; high dose Vitamin A significantly reduces risks of morbidity and mortality (Vitamin A deficiency worsens measles prognosis)
- In cellular immune deficiency (which includes severe malnutrition), measles causes progressive and often fatal giant cell pneumonia

A(ii) Pathogenesis of measles-induced immunosuppression and why this leads to secondary infections

A(i) Describe the structure of Calcium and Vitamin D metabolism under the following headings: calcium distribution in the body, role of calcium, role of PTH, role of calcitonin, and the synthesis pathway of Vitamin D.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of Rickets: why Vitamin D deficiency leads to this specific skeletal disease and what biochemical pattern results.
B(i) Distinguish between the role of PTH and calcitonin in calcium homeostasis, and explain which is more clinically important in the acute management of hypocalcaemia and hypercalcaemia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Calcium and Vitamin D metabolism:
• Calcium distribution: calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body; the average adult body contains approximately 1 kg total. 99% of the body's Ca2+ is in bones. 50% of ingested calcium is absorbed in the jejunum. Protein-bound calcium is approximately 50%. Normal total calcium: 9–10.5 mg/dL (2.2–2.6 mmol/L). Calcium is filtered in the glomerulus; reabsorption occurs throughout the nephrons.
• Role of calcium: cellular functions (muscle contraction, hormonal secretion, cell division); enzymatic activities; nerve conduction; fertilisation; vision; maintains intercellular adhesions; promotes plasma membrane integrity; ensures blood clotting; Ca salts (99%) provide rigid framework for body movements; provides reservoir of Ca and PO4 for times of need. Daily requirement: 800 mg.
• Role of PTH: functions to raise plasma calcium via bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption; stimulates the metabolism of Vitamin D to its active hormonal form 1,25(OH)2D3.
• Role of calcitonin: functions to reduce blood calcium levels; physiological antagonist of PTH; enhances excretion of calcium into urine; inhibits bone resorption.
• Vitamin D3 synthesis: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is generated in the skin when UV-B light energy is absorbed by the precursor molecule 7-dehydrocholesterol. Converted in the liver by 25-hydroxylase to 25OHD3. Then converted in the kidney by 1-hydroxylase (or 24-hydroxylase) to the active form 1,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol). Foods containing Vitamin D: livers of fatty fish, cod liver oil, egg yolk, cheese, butter. Functions of Vitamin D: promotes calcium absorption from the gut; promotes calcium reabsorption from the kidney; promotes calcium mobilisation from bone via resorption; enhances phosphate absorption by the intestine.

A(ii) Rickets: deficiency of Vitamin D leads to inadequate mineralisation of the organic bone matrix (osteoid). New bone formation is initiated by osteoblasts responsible for matrix deposition and subsequent mineralisation. Without Vitamin D, calcium absorption from the gut is reduced; PTH rises in compensation (secondary hyperparathyroidism) to maintain serum calcium by increasing bone resorption. Phosphate is lost via the kidneys. The result is soft, deformed bones. Serum chemistry: low Ca2+, high PTH, high alkaline phosphatase, high or low 25(OH)D3, low 1,25(OH)2D3. Clinical features: slow growth, skull bossing, delayed closure of fontanelles, chest deformities, kyphosis/lordosis/scoliosis, muscular weakness, delay in walking, increased susceptibility to infections especially chest infections, delayed tooth eruption, enlarged ankles and wrists epiphyses, lower limb deformities (genu valgum/varum, windswept deformity). Treatment: oral Vitamin D, calcium, monitoring, surgical intervention.

B(i) PTH vs calcitonin in calcium homeostasis:
• Low plasma calcium stimulates PTH release; PTH acts to resorb Ca2+ from the pool in bone and to enhance renal reabsorption of Ca2+, and stimulates conversion of Vitamin D to its active form.
• High plasma calcium stimulates calcitonin secretion; calcitonin lowers plasma calcium by inhibiting bone resorption and enhancing renal excretion of calcium.
• Clinically: PTH is more important in acute hypocalcaemia management — its absence (hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome) causes acute hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures, and cardiac effects (prolonged QT). Treatment is directed at giving calcium. In hypercalcaemia, calcitonin (4 units/kg, inhibits bone resorption) is one of several agents used alongside saline hydration, furosemide, steroids (when due to tumour, Vitamin D toxicity, or granulomatous disease), and bisphosphonates (mithramycin in hyperparathyroidism or malignancy with bone involvement).

A(i) Calcium homeostasis — bone cells and regulatory responses:
• Bone composition: organic matrix (mainly collagen) + inorganic mineral phase of Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 (hydroxyapatite).
• Osteoblasts: promote bone synthesis; initiate new bone formation; responsible for matrix deposition and its subsequent mineralisation.
• Osteoclasts: promote bone resorption; secrete enzymes on the bone surface, dissolving and removing matrix.
• Factors affecting bone growth: Ca, P, fluoride, and Growth Hormone.
• Bone turnover: mediated by osteoclast activating factors (OAFs).
• Response to low plasma calcium: stimulates PTH release → PTH acts to resorb Ca2+ from the pool in bone and to enhance renal reabsorption of Ca2+; PTH also stimulates conversion of Vitamin D to its active form 1,25(OH)2D3, which promotes calcium absorption from the gut, reabsorption from the kidney, and mobilisation from bone.
• Response to high plasma calcium: stimulates calcitonin secretion → calcitonin lowers plasma calcium by inhibiting bone resorption and enhancing excretion of calcium into urine.

A(ii) Treatment of hypocalcaemia and hypercalcaemia:
• Hypocalcaemia: identify and treat the underlying cause. Give calcium supplementation. Clinical features: muscle twitch, paraesthesia, spasm, seizure, bradycardia, T-wave inversion, prolonged QT interval, Chvostek's and Trousseau's sign. Causes: blood transfusion, sepsis, respiratory alkalosis, hypoparathyroidism, Vitamin D deficiency, DiGeorge syndrome, drugs (phenytoin, aminoglycosides, frusemide, glucocorticoid, HCO3, phenobarbitone).
• Hypercalcaemia treatment (total Ca >15 mg/dl or symptomatic is considered an emergency):
  - Identify and treat cause
  - Saline hydration: 200–250 mg/kg/day (adult 70–80 mEq/hr)
  - Frusemide 1–2 mg/kg/day 4-hourly
  - Calcitonin 4 units/kg: inhibits bone resorption
  - Steroids: especially if high Ca due to tumour, Vitamin D toxicity, or granulomatous disease (decreases gut Ca absorption)
  - Mithramycin: in hyperparathyroidism or malignancy with bone metastases; 15–25 mcg/kg IV over 3–8 hours (decreases bone resorption)
  - Dialysis with calcium-free dialysate
  - Binding Ca with chelators and PO4 (associated with soft tissue deposition of Ca complexes; used as last resort; PO4 0.15–0.3 mmol/kg IV over 6 hours)

B(i) Cardiac dysfunction in calcium disorders:
• Hypocalcaemia: cardiac effects include bradycardia and T-wave inversion. Prolonged QT interval is a feature of hypocalcaemia. Prolonged QT arises because a low ionised calcium concentration prolongs the plateau phase (phase 2) of the cardiac action potential, delaying repolarisation, which predisposes to arrhythmias and potentially torsades de pointes.
• Hypercalcaemia: cardiac effects include hypertension, shortened QT interval, and U waves. Shortened QT interval and U waves are features of hypercalcaemia. Elevated ionised calcium shortens the plateau phase of the cardiac action potential, accelerating repolarisation. Very high calcium levels can cause bradycardia, heart block, and cardiac arrest.
• Note: alkalosis decreases ionised calcium and acidosis increases ionised calcium, influencing the degree of cardiac effect independent of total serum calcium.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy and metabolic role of calcium homeostasis under the following headings: role of bone cells (osteoblasts and osteoclasts), factors affecting bone growth, and how low versus high plasma calcium triggers corrective hormonal responses.
A(ii) State the treatment of hypocalcaemia and hypercalcaemia, including all specific agents, doses, and their mechanisms.

A 2-year-old child presents with profuse diarrhoea and vomiting. She is in shock with absent peripheral pulses, hypotension, and altered consciousness. Initial boluses of 60 ml/kg of normal saline have been given with partial improvement but she remains haemodynamically unstable. Her PCV is 12%.

(i) Identify the diagnosis and classify the type of shock, including the pathophysiological chain from inadequate blood volume to cellular dysfunction.
(ii) State the formula for lower limit of systolic blood pressure in children and the early versus late signs of shock as described.
(iii) Outline the specific fluid therapy for haemorrhagic shock and the criteria for blood transfusion, including the role of group O blood in emergencies.
(iv) Explain the management of metabolic acidosis and electrolyte imbalances in shock, listing all the risks associated with sodium bicarbonate administration.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hypovolemic shock. Type: Hypovolemic (inadequate blood volume). Pathophysiology: inadequate blood volume → inadequate O2-carrying capacity → low preload → decreased stroke volume → decreased cardiac output → compensatory increased heart rate and SVR → if uncompensated → inadequate tissue perfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid accumulation → loss of normal cellular function → cell death → organ dysfunction → death.

(ii) Lower limit of systolic BP formula: 70 + (2 × age in years) mmHg.
Early signs of shock: sinus tachycardia; delayed capillary refill; fussy, irritable child.
Late signs of shock: bradycardia; altered mental status (lethargy, coma); hypotonia, decreased deep tendon reflexes; Cheyne-Stokes breathing; hypotension (a very late sign).

(iii) Haemorrhagic shock treatment: PRBCs or whole blood; treat the cause (stop the bleeding). Transfuse if significant blood loss is known or if patient is unstable after 60 ml/kg crystalloid. In non-hypotensive children with severe anaemia, blood transfusion is superior to crystalloid boluses. In emergency: can give group O PRBCs before cross-matching is complete, or type-specific non-cross-matched blood products.

(iv) Metabolic acidosis: develops secondary to tissue hypoperfusion; profound acidosis depresses myocardial contractility and impairs effectiveness of catecholamines. Treatment: fluid administration and controlled ventilation. Sodium bicarbonate: 1–2 mEq/kg; or ½ correction = 0.3 × weight (kg) × base deficit. Risks of sodium bicarbonate: hyperosmolarity, hypocalcaemia, hypernatraemia, left-ward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.
Electrolytes: calcium is important for cardiac function and pressor effect of catecholamines; hypoglycaemia can lead to CNS damage and impairs cardiovascular function; check BUN and creatinine to evaluate renal function; hyperkalemia can occur from renal dysfunction and/or acidosis.

(i) The diagnosis is dysentery — defined as diarrhoea with visible blood in the stool, indicating mucosal invasion. The single most common causative bacterial genus is Shigella (bacillary dysentery). Stool microscopy showing red blood cells and polymorphonuclear leucocytes is consistent with invasive bacterial colitis.
(ii) Risk factors include: low-resource community setting with likely poor water sanitation and inadequate faecal disposal; household contact exposure (sibling with similar illness, sharing toilet facilities and food preparation areas); age 5 years (children under 5 have immature immune defences and greater exposure risk in endemic settings); and the faecal-oral route enabled by inadequate handwashing with soap.
(iii) The most severe serotype is Shigella dysenteriae type 1, which produces Shiga toxin (the most potent bacterial toxin) and is associated with: (1) haemolytic uraemic syndrome (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, and acute renal failure); (2) severe and epidemic forms of bacillary dysentery with high mortality; and (3) Reiter's syndrome (reactive arthritis) — a post-infectious syndrome involving uveitis, urethritis, and reactive arthritis.
(iv) Management: mild dehydration is managed with oral rehydration therapy (ORT) exploiting the functional SGLT1 transporter. Management objectives include correcting dehydration and maintaining nutrition. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for all cases of diarrhoea because empirical universal antibiotic use promotes resistance and is not needed for self-limiting illness. Antibiotics ARE indicated here because: dysentery from Shigella requires treatment; azithromycin is the preferred antibiotic for Shigellosis in children, and ciprofloxacin is an alternative. The most important community-level preventive measure is handwashing with soap and improved sanitation.
questions.question:
A 5-year-old child from a low-resource community setting presents with a 3-day history of bloody diarrhoea, frequent small-volume stools (approximately 10 per day) with mucus and blood, abdominal cramps, and fever of 39.2°C. He is alert and active, with mild dehydration by assessment (sunken eyes, slightly dry mucous membranes, drinks eagerly). His older sibling recently had a similar illness. Stool microscopy reveals red blood cells and polymorphonuclear leucocytes.

(i) State the diagnosis, the clinical definition that applies, and the single most common causative bacterial genus.
(ii) Identify at least three risk factors in this history that predispose to this condition or to its transmission.
(iii) State three specific complications associated with the most severe serotype of this organism, and name that serotype.
(iv) Outline the management, including the approach to the identified degree of dehydration and the specific antibiotic recommended, and explain why empirical antibiotics are NOT recommended for all cases of diarrhoea but ARE indicated here.

questions.answerText:
A(i) GBS (also known as acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy / Landry's ascending paralysis) results from demyelination of peripheral nerves following a preceding microbial infection. Axonal degeneration may also occur. It is believed to result from autoimmune demyelination of peripheral nerves by antibodies and WBC. Associated organisms: mumps virus, ECHO, influenza, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Mycoplasma, Campylobacter. Onset of symptoms: 2–4 weeks after the preceding infection.

A(ii) Clinical features:
- Rapid onset of weakness starting in the lower limbs.
- Weakness progresses (ascends) to involve muscles of the upper limbs, respiration, and facial muscles.
- Paralysis is flaccid; deep tendon reflexes are absent.
- Limb involvement is bilateral and symmetrical.
- Associated paraesthesia (pins and needles, numbness) in many cases; sensory loss is rare but sensory impairment occurs.
- Autonomic dysfunction: tachycardia.
- Involvement of respiratory and bulbar muscles may rapidly lead to death.
- Recovery occurs in reverse order (upper limbs recover first, lower limbs last); median recovery 7 months; >90% recover completely.

A(iii) CSF findings: protein — increased; cells — few or absent. Characteristic finding: cytoalbuminologic dissociation — pleocytosis may occur initially which later drops, and protein level becomes high.

B. The ascending pattern reflects the anatomy of demyelination starting in the peripheral, distal nerves of the lower limbs and progressing proximally to involve the intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles and cranial nerves. When intercostal muscles are paralysed (as in poliomyelitis), respiratory failure results — this is the cause of death.

C. Comparison with paralytic poliomyelitis:
- Pattern: GBS — ascending, symmetrical; Polio — spotty, haphazard, asymmetrical.
- Symmetry: GBS — bilateral and symmetrical; Polio — asymmetrical.
- Sensory: GBS — paraesthesia common, sensory loss rare; Polio — no sensory deficit (does not affect posterior column tract).
- CSF: GBS — high protein, few or no cells (cytoalbuminologic dissociation); Polio — viral/aseptic picture.
- Prognosis: GBS — >90% recover completely in few weeks; Polio — weakness present 12 months after onset is usually permanent.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Barium swallow evaluates the oesophagus, pharynx, and upper GI tract. It is indicated for structural abnormalities including strictures, webs, rings, hernias, and motility disorders. It provides real-time fluoroscopic assessment of swallowing mechanics.
A(ii) Small bowel follow-through evaluates the mucosal fold pattern, motility, transit, and structural abnormalities of the entire small intestine. It is indicated in suspected coeliac disease and Crohn's disease of the small intestine. Specific signs: the 'string sign of Kantor' describes severe narrowing of the terminal ileum to a thin thread due to Crohn's disease stricture; 'cobblestone' mucosa with skip lesions and 'rose thorn' (spiculated) ulcers indicates Crohn's disease.
A(iii) Double-contrast barium enema uses a thin coating of high-density barium on the colonic mucosa combined with air insufflation to distend the bowel, providing superior mucosal detail. This enhances detection of polyps, early cancers, and inflammatory mucosal changes compared to single-contrast technique.
A(iv) In suspected intestinal perforation, water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) is used instead of barium because barium sulphate in the peritoneal cavity causes a severe granulomatous reaction (barium peritonitis) that is more dangerous than the underlying perforation. Water-soluble contrast is safely absorbed if it leaks into the peritoneum.
B. Ultrasound is the first-line GI imaging modality in paediatric patients because it uses no ionising radiation, is widely available, and can assess bowel wall thickness, intussusception, appendicitis, and abdominal masses. CT is not affected by body habitus or overlying bowel gas and provides comprehensive views, but involves radiation exposure. USS criteria for acute appendicitis: a non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure exceeding 6 mm in outer diameter, with periappendiceal fat stranding and tenderness.
C. Three neonatal plain X-ray signs: (1) 'Double bubble' sign — two gas-filled structures representing stomach and proximal duodenum separated by the pylorus, with no distal gas; caused by complete duodenal obstruction (duodenal atresia or annular pancreas) preventing air from passing distally. (2) 'Ground-glass' or 'soap bubble' appearance — air mixed with inspissated meconium in the terminal ileum in meconium ileus; caused by cystic fibrosis producing viscid mucus secretions that trap air within thickened meconium. (3) Free gas under the right hemidiaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) on erect CXR — a translucent crescent of gas; caused by bowel perforation allowing air to escape into the peritoneal cavity and rise to the highest point beneath the diaphragm.

A 9-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, irritability, and refusal to feed. On examination he is febrile, lethargic, with a bulging anterior fontanelle. Neck stiffness is noted. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are positive.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and which organism is most probable at this age?
(ii) Describe the pathological basis of the signs of meningeal irritation seen in this infant.
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitation and initial antibiotic management, including drugs, doses, and the rationale for route of administration.
(iv) State the definitive antibiotic regimen after CSF culture results are available, the duration of treatment, and the adjunctive agent proven to reduce complications such as deafness.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: Pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis. At the age of 2 months–1 year, the most probable organisms are Haemophilus influenzae (type B), Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Neisseria meningitidis.

(ii) Pathological basis: Inflammation of the meninges causes exudate formation around the brain, which may lead to cerebral oedema. Arteritis causes reduced blood supply and infarction. This brain damage results in various neurological deficits including cranial nerve palsy and seizures. In infants, signs of meningeal irritation (neck stiffness, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs) may be minimal or absent; bulging and tense anterior fontanelle and irritability may be the only signs.

(iii) Immediate management:
- Admit the patient.
- There is no room for oral or intramuscular drugs; all antibiotics must be given intravenously so they can cross the blood–brain barrier.
- First choice while awaiting CSF results: IV Crystalline Penicillin 300,000 iu/kg/day (covers S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis) + IV Chloramphenicol 100 mg/kg/day (covers H. influenzae type B).
- Second choice (more expensive): 3rd-generation cephalosporin, e.g., Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, or Ceftazidime.
- Administer IV dexamethasone 20–30 minutes before the first dose of antibiotics and continue for 4 days; this reduces the inflammatory response and decreases complications such as deafness.
- Give IV fluids at 2/3 of maintenance because of the risk of SIADH.
- Give anticonvulsants for seizures; monitor head circumference for hydrocephalus.

(iv) After culture results: change to the recommended drug based on sensitivity unless the patient is already responding to initial therapy. Duration: at least 10–14 days, or continue for 5 days after fever has disappeared. IV dexamethasone should be given before the first dose of antibiotics and continued for 4 days after antibiotics are stopped.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of polyuria producing large volumes of dilute urine, excessive thirst, and nocturia. His random blood sugar is normal. Urinalysis shows very low specific gravity (1.002). Serum sodium is 153 mmol/L. He is of normal weight and has no recent head trauma.

(i) Identify the organ/system involved and the two subtypes of this disorder.
(ii) What are the compressed or affected downstream structures and physiological consequences?
(iii) What differential conditions could produce a similar picture, and how would you distinguish them?
(iv) Describe the clinico-anatomical and physiological reasoning that leads to the diagnosis, including the key investigation.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is Diabetes Insipidus (DI), a disorder of the posterior pituitary–kidney axis. The two subtypes are:
• Central (neurogenic) DI: excessive flow of dilute urine secondary to lack of ADH secretion (primary: familial, non-familial; secondary: from CNS pathology)
• Nephrogenic DI: failure of the kidney to respond to adequate amounts of ADH (primary: X-linked or autosomal recessive; secondary: renal disease, hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia, systemic diseases; drugs that inhibit ADH secretion: naloxone, ethanol; drugs that inhibit peripheral action: lithium, demeclocycline, mannitol, cytotoxic drugs, angiographic drugs)

(ii) Consequences: ADH normally increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts of the kidney, producing concentrated urine. In DI, this reabsorption fails. The resulting massive water loss leads to hypernatraemia (serum Na ≥150 mmol/L), high serum osmolality (≥305 mosmol/kg), very low urine osmolality, and low urine specific gravity (≤1.005). Urine output exceeds 3 ml/kg/hr. Severe dehydration and cardiovascular instability may follow.

(iii) Differential diagnosis includes: SIADH (which presents with the opposite picture: serum Na ≤130, urine Na ≥60, urine SG ≥1.020, urine output <1 ml/kg/hr, CVP ≥8); primary polydipsia (water intoxication — euvolemic hyponatraemia, serum Na <130, high urine output but driven by excessive intake); causes of osmotic diuresis such as Diabetes Mellitus (which is excluded here by normal blood sugar). Laboratory comparison: in DI, serum Na ≥150, urine Na ≤40, serum osmol ≥305, urine SG ≤1.005, urine output >3 ml/kg/hr, CVP ≤4.

(iv) Clinical reasoning: The combination of very dilute urine, hypernatraemia, and normal blood glucose points to a defect in water conservation rather than glucose-driven osmotic diuresis. The key investigation is the water deprivation test, which differentiates DI subtypes and primary polydipsia. If urine remains dilute despite water deprivation but concentrates after exogenous ADH (desmopressin), the diagnosis is central DI; if urine remains dilute even after ADH administration, nephrogenic DI is confirmed.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the management of hypernatraemic dehydration under the following headings: why severity is underestimated, the first resuscitation step, the rate of sodium correction, preferred fluid route, and the preferred intravenous fluid if IV fluids are required.
A(ii) Describe the management of hyperkalaemia in a child, listing each treatment step in order, the mechanism of action of each step, and when dialysis is indicated.
B(i) Distinguish between isonatraemic and hyponatraemic dehydration: definition, pathophysiology of fluid shifts, and clinical implications for resuscitation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Management of hypernatraemic dehydration:
• Why severity is underestimated: the degree of dehydration in hypernatraemic patients is usually underestimated because the hypertonic serum tends to keep the extracellular fluid space intact. Thus cardiovascular instability does not develop until the patient has lost large amounts of fluid.
• First resuscitation step: if the patient is in shock, resuscitate first with 20 ml/kg normal saline (or Ringer's lactate).
• Rate of sodium correction: aim to correct the deficit plus maintenance slowly over 48–72 hours. Rate of lowering serum Na should be <10 mmol Na/L/day (or 0.5 mmol/L/hr).
• Preferred fluid route: ORT (oral rehydration therapy) is safer than IV fluids in lowering serum Na. If the child can drink, use "Slow ORT" over 12 hours.
• Preferred IV fluid: if IV fluid is used, 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose is preferred if serum Na >160 mmol/L.
• If the child develops convulsions during rehydration: give anticonvulsants; 20% mannitol may also be used.

A(ii) Management of hyperkalaemia (step by step):
• Step 1: Treat cause; remove K+ from IVF or diet.
• If K+ >6.5 mmol/kg: needs immediate treatment:
  a) CaCl (10%) 0.1–0.25 ml/kg IV over 10–30 minutes: antagonises the neuromuscular effects of hyperkalaemia (membrane stabilisation); does not lower K+.
  b) Insulin (0.1–0.2 units/kg) and Glucose (0.5–1 g/kg) IV push then as infusion; max 10 units insulin; monitor glucose during infusion: drives K+ from ECF to ICF.
  c) NaHCO3 (onset 3–4 hours): 1–2 mmol/kg IV over 10–30 minutes; redistributes K+ from ECF to ICF.
  d) Salbutamol nebulisation: drives K+ intracellularly via β2 receptor stimulation.
  e) Kayexalate 1 g/kg (max 30 g) PO, NG, PR; onset 1 hour; exchanges Na+ for K+ in the GI tract, removing K+ from the body.
  f) Dialysis: if all else fails — removes K+ from the body; used when other measures are insufficient or the patient is in renal failure.

B(i) Isonatraemic vs hyponatraemic dehydration:
• Isonatraemic dehydration (most common: 80%): Na 130–150 mEq/L. Occurs when lost fluid is similar in Na+ concentration to blood. Na+ and H2O losses are proportionate in both intra- and extravascular compartments. No osmotic gradient across the cell wall exists; ICF volume remains unchanged. Resuscitation: treat as per standard protocol.
• Hyponatraemic dehydration (5–10%): Na <130 mEq/L. Occurs when lost fluid contains more Na+ than the blood (relatively more Na than H2O is lost). Because serum Na is low, intravascular H2O shifts to extravascular space, worsening intravascular volume depletion for a given amount of TBW loss. ECF is hypotonic relative to ICF, thus H2O shifts from ECF to ICF. Caused by renal (diuretic use, renal salt wasting) or extra-renal losses (GI, skin) of electrolyte-rich fluid, replaced by plain water.
• Clinical implication for resuscitation: if serum Na <120 mEq/L, treat — calculate deficit: (135 − serum Na) × 0.6 × wt in kg; correct deficit over 24–48 hours. Initial N/S to correct ECF volume deficit. The shift of water into cells means cardiovascular collapse occurs earlier than in isonatraemic dehydration.

questions.question:
Describe the comprehensive epidemiology, pathogenesis, and clinical features of childhood tuberculosis under the following headings, and explain why children are particularly vulnerable.
A(i) Global and Nigerian burden of tuberculosis and causes of resurgence in incidence
A(ii) Epidemiology of M. tuberculosis transmission and characteristics of mycobacteria that make it difficult to treat
B(i) Pathogenesis of primary TB: cellular immune response, granuloma formation, and conditions increasing risk of infection
B(ii) Conditions that increase risk of TB infection and the timetable from primary infection to various forms of EPTB
C(i) Symptoms and anthropometric signs of presumptive TB in children
C(ii) Diagnosis: how to approach a child with presumptive TB, specimens, tests, and when to treat without bacteriological confirmation
questions.answerText:
A(i) Global and Nigerian burden:
- TB is the world's deadliest infectious disease, killing more than HIV and malaria combined
- Every year, 10 million people develop active TB; 1.6 million people lose their lives – 3 every minute
- >4 million cases of TB go undetected
- Global new TB cases: 10.4 million (WHO 2016); <15 years of age: 6.9%; 250,000 children die annually
- 56,000 cases of TB in children estimated in 2016; case notification for childhood TB: 5%
- Nigeria: TB incidence 338/100,000 (2012 national prevalence survey)
- PLWHIV: 1.2 million (11%) of all new cases; MDR TB new cases: 480,000
- Causes of resurgence: worsening economic situations; HIV pandemic; multidrug resistance; decline of national TB control programmes; conflicts and wars → large numbers of displaced persons living in poor conditions
A(ii) Transmission and mycobacterial characteristics:
- Sources: most important is sputum of persons with open tuberculosis
- Airborne: droplet nuclei remain suspended in air for several hours; one cough produces 3,000 droplet nuclei
- Ingestion: M. bovis via milk from infected cattle
- Primary infection in children most often follows prolonged close contact with untreated adult with cavitary disease
- Characteristics of mycobacteria: multiples slowly; resistant to many antimicrobial drugs; remains viable in macrophages by subverting macrophage-killing; its waxy coat together with its many component substances depress immune responses against it
B(i) Pathogenesis and conditions increasing risk:
- Immune response involves interactions between tubercle bacilli, specific lymphocyte subpopulations, and tissue macrophages; antibodies play no role in inhibiting bacterial growth or creating immunity
- Cellular immune response begins after viable bacilli are inhaled
- TB → granulomatous inflammation (specific type of chronic inflammation)
- Tubercle: characterized by central area of caseous necrosis
- Primary complex: local infection at portal of entry + regional lymph node
- Infection → disease when tubercle bacilli overcome immune defenses
- 70-90% of exposed individuals develop no symptoms (inhalation of insufficient organisms or adequate immunity)
- Risk of primary infection developing into active disease: ~15% in first 10 years
- Conditions increasing risk: HIV infection; malnutrition; other infections (measles, pertussis); prolonged corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy; haematologic and reticuloendothelial diseases (leukaemia, Hodgkin's); diabetes mellitus; chronic malabsorption syndromes
B(ii) Timetable of TB:
- Pulmonary TB: within a few months
- Miliary and meningeal TB: 2-6 months
- TB adenitis: 3-9 months
- Bones and joints: several years
- Renal and genital TB: >10 years
- PTB from reactivation of dormant focus: many years after primary infection
C(i) Symptoms and anthropometric signs:
- Symptoms: cough ≥2 weeks; weight loss/FTT; fever ±night sweats; history of contact with adult with TB symptoms in last 2 years; history of death in family attributable to TB/HIV/AIDS
- General examination: chronically ill, wasted, febrile, pallor, lymphadenopathy especially cervical, phlycternular conjunctivitis
- Anthropometric: underweight (60-80% of normal body weight); marasmic (<60% of normal body weight); stunted (height <90% of expected); MUAC in children 1-5 years: normal range 13.5-16 cm
- Systemic: abdominal distension with/without ascites and/or hepatosplenomegaly; gibbus (angulation of spine) ±decreased power and increased lower limb reflexes (UMN signs)
C(ii) Approach to diagnosis:
- TB case: one who is bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed by a clinician to have TB
- Bacteriological confirmation: Xpert MTB/RIF (now 1st line); AFB microscopy; culture
- Specimens: sputum (by coughing or induced); gastric washing/aspirate in children
- HIV test for all cases of TB
- When bacteriological confirmation not feasible: in areas of high transmission such as Nigeria, children under five years can still be treated on clinical basis
- Chest X-ray and Mantoux test support the diagnosis; CSF chemistry and GeneXpert for TB meningitis

A(i) Worldwide incidence: 4–9 per 1000 live births.
Top five in Ibadan series (1965–1975, 635 cases):
1. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD): 35%
2. Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA): 22%
3. Coarctation of the aorta (CoA): 12%
4. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF): 10%
5. Pulmonary Stenosis (isolated): 9%
(Also: Aortic Stenosis 7.5%; ASD 7.0%; TGA 4.5%)
Most common congenital heart disease worldwide: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) — isolated VSD accounts for 25% worldwide; in Ibadan it is 35%; in some countries it is 40%.

A(ii) Four classifications:
1. Left-to-right shunt: Oxygenated blood recirculates in lungs — cyanosis is not a problem unless heart failure ensues. Example: VSD
2. Right-to-left shunt: Desaturated blood bypasses the lungs — associated with cyanosis (arterial desaturation). Example: Tetralogy of Fallot
3. Transposition: Circulations are in parallel — incompatible with life unless there are points of mixing. Example: TGA
4. Obstruction: Impedes blood flow out of the heart — may be intracardiac or extracardiac; increases workload on the heart. Example: Pulmonary stenosis (RVOT), Coarctation of aorta (LVOT)

B(i) Failure to thrive in left-to-right shunts (two mechanisms):
1. Hypoperfusion of peripheral tissues: Reduced stroke volume from the left ventricle (blood diverted through the shunt) → reduced systemic delivery of nutrients → failure to thrive and small for gestational age
2. Feeding difficulties: Child cannot hold breath to suck (breathless) → inadequate caloric intake → failure to thrive; excessive sweating (from increased adrenergic activity) worsens caloric losses

B(ii) TOF — stroke and cerebral abscess (two separate mechanisms):
Stroke: Polycythaemia (PCV may reach 88%) from chronic hypoxia → hyperviscosity syndrome → slowing of blood flow → formation of clot → thrombotic or embolic phenomenon → cardiovascular accident/stroke
Cerebral abscess: In right-to-left shunt, bacteria entering the bloodstream can bypass the pulmonary filter (which would normally trap them) → paradoxical embolism → bacterial seeding of the brain → cerebral abscess. (The pulmonary filter is bypassed via the VSD.)

B(iii) Risk of infective endocarditis in CHD: Turbulent blood flow through abnormal cardiac structures (congenital defects — VSD, PDA, bicuspid aortic valve, etc.) damages the endothelium, creating a substrate for bacterial adherence and vegetation formation. 
Specific portal of entry: Dental caries/dental manipulation — the most commonly identified portal allowing Streptococcus viridans (normally found in the mouth) to enter the bloodstream.

C. Teratogenic factors and window of vulnerability:
Teratogenic factors:
- Intrauterine infections (e.g. rubella)
- Drugs (thalidomide, cytotoxic drugs, steroids)
- X-radiation
- Chromosomal abnormalities (Trisomy 21, 18, 13; Turner syndrome XO)
- Specific gene defects
- Familial/environmental factors
- Preterm delivery / birth asphyxia
Window of vulnerability: Factors exert their effect during the first half of the first trimester — during morphogenesis — from the 12th day to the 6th or 8th week of intrauterine life.

Describe the physiology of foetal and neonatal circulation and the changes that occur at birth.
A(i) Describe the path of oxygenated blood in the foetal circulation from the placenta to the left ventricle, naming the structures used.
A(ii) Name the factors that keep the ductus arteriosus open in the foetus and state the treatment for a clinically significant patent ductus arteriosus in a neonate less than 2 weeks old.
B(i) State the normal cardiovascular and respiratory parameters of the newborn (heart rate, thresholds for tachycardia, respiratory rate, threshold for tachypnoea, urine output, SG, and GFR range).
B(ii) Explain why PDA is more common in preterm infants, and state two physiological events that occur in the pulmonary and systemic circulations immediately at birth.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Foetal circulation path: Oxygenated blood from placenta → umbilical vein → IVC → right atrium → left atrium (through the foramen ovale) → left ventricle. Deoxygenated blood from upper and lower parts of the body enters SVC and IVC. Oxygen saturation in the left ventricle is approximately 45%.

A(ii) Factors that keep the ductus arteriosus open:
- Hypoxia; prostaglandin E2; anaemia; metabolic acidosis; fluid overload.
Treatment of PDA (< 2 weeks old): Oxygen; fluid restriction + anti-failure treatment; indomethacin (in infants < 2 weeks old).

B(i) Normal parameters of the newborn:
- CVS: Heart rate 120–140/min; tachycardia > 160/min.
- Respiratory: RR 30–40/min; tachypnoea > 60/min.
- Urine output: 1 ml/kg/hr on Day 1, then 2–4 ml/kg/hr after 24 hours (alternative references cite 2–3 ml/kg/hr).
- Specific gravity: 1006–1012.
- GFR: varies with gestational age (0.35 ml/min–2.2); averages 40 ml/min per 1.73 m² (40–65 in first few days); end of first year: 90–150 ml/min/1.73 m².

B(ii) PDA is more common in preterms because of their immature control mechanisms and the factors listed (hypoxia, prostaglandin E2, anaemia, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload) being more prevalent.
At birth, the newborn switches from dependence on placenta to pulmonary gas exchange: (1) Pulmonary vascular resistance falls as the lungs expand, increasing pulmonary blood flow. (2) Adequacy of pulmonary function is required for successful transition. Foetal lung is fluid-filled (20–30 ml/kg) and does not partake in gas exchange; lung fluids are cleared near term, during labour, and while passing through the birth canal.

A(i) Pulse:
Rate: Age-dependent cut-off. Neonate upper limit: 160/min (vs. adult 100/min). Below 100/min = bradycardia.
Rhythm:
- Regularly irregular: not necessarily abnormal — many children have sinus arrhythmia (heart rate changes with respiration); often better seen on ECG
- Irregularly irregular: a common cause is atrial fibrillation
Volume:
- Bounding/collapsing (hyperdynamic): Cardiac causes — PDA; aortic incompetence. Non-cardiac — fever; chronic anaemia
- Small volume: Cardiac causes — aortic stenosis; mitral stenosis; pericardial effusion. Non-cardiac — shock from any cause
Note: Always palpate peripheral pulses to pick coarctation of the aorta.

A(ii) Apex beat:
Normal location: 4th or 5th left intercostal space, medial to mid-clavicular line.
Displacement downward and outward: suggests enlargement — usually dilatation; also caused by massive pleural effusion on the right side (check trachea) or dextrocardia.
Character: heaving/hyperactive = LVH; tapping = mitral stenosis.

A(iii) JVP:
- In children <2 years: not sensitive/reliable because of the short neck
- In older children: important sign of elevated right atrial pressure
- Increase signifies: right-sided heart failure / systemic venous congestion

B(i) Heaving apex: suggests left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) — note it is possible to have hypertrophy without dilatation, in which case the apex is not displaced.
Tapping apex: suggests mitral stenosis (palpable S1 from thickened, stiff mitral valve).

B(ii) Left parasternal heave: indicates right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH). Palpated at the left sternal border (left parasternal region).

C. Abnormal pulse volume:
Bounding/collapsing pulse — cardiac causes:
1. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
2. Aortic incompetence
Small volume pulse — cardiac causes:
1. Aortic stenosis
2. Mitral stenosis (also: pericardial effusion)

A(i) Five components of the motor unit in anatomical order:
1. Anterior horn cell (in the spinal cord).
2. Motor nerve fibre.
3. Motor end plate (neuromuscular junction).
4. Muscle.
5. (Sensory receptor in muscle and sensory nerve fibre — completing the reflex arc.)

A(ii) Classification with examples:
- Anterior horn cell disorders: Poliomyelitis; Werdnig–Hoffman Disease.
- Nerve fibre disorders (neuropathies): Polyneuropathies — Guillain–Barré Syndrome, Diphtheritic Polyneuropathy; Mononeuropathies — Erb's Palsy, Bell's Palsy, Klumpke's Paralysis.
- Neuromuscular junction disorders: Myasthenia Gravis.
- Muscle disorders (myopathies): Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy; Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy; Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophy; Becker Pseudohypertrophy.

A(iii) UMN lesion features (compressive paraplegia — e.g., Pott's disease): increased tone/spasticity; hyperreflexia; positive Babinski sign; no muscle wasting; paralysis affects whole limbs.
LMN lesion features (non-compressive — e.g., paralytic poliomyelitis, GBS): decreased tone (flaccidity); absent or reduced reflexes; muscle wasting (atrophy); fasciculations may be present; sensory deficit may occur.

B. Poliomyelitis (anterior horn cell): virus destroys anterior horn cells → LMN lesion → flaccid asymmetrical paralysis, absent reflexes, wasting, no sensory deficit (posterior columns spared).
GBS (peripheral nerve): autoimmune demyelination of peripheral nerves → LMN lesion → ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, paraesthesia, cytoalbuminologic dissociation in CSF.
MG (neuromuscular junction): autoantibodies destroy ACh receptors → failure of neuromuscular transmission → fatiguable weakness (ptosis, diplopia), worsening with activity, improving with rest, normal reflexes and tone.
DMD (muscle): absence of dystrophin → progressive degeneration of muscle fibres → proximal weakness, pseudohypertrophy, elevated CK, myopathic EMG, normal reflexes (initially).

C. Classification of non-traumatic paraplegia:
- Compressive — UMN features (spasticity): Pott's disease (TB spine), epidural abscess, neoplasm. Important because compression may be surgically reversible.
- Non-compressive — LMN features (flaccidity): paralytic poliomyelitis, GBS, multiple sclerosis, sickle cell disease. Management is medical/supportive.
Clinical importance: compressive lesions may require urgent surgical decompression; failure to distinguish means a potentially reversible cause may be missed. MRI is the investigation of choice to demonstrate cord compression.

questions.answerText:
A(i) NTCP (Na-Taurocholate Cotransporting Polypeptide) is located on the basolateral membrane of hepatocytes. Its primary substrates are conjugated bile acids (bile salts). It is sodium-dependent and accounts for approximately 80% of conjugated bile acid uptake into hepatocytes.
A(ii) OATP (Organic Anion Transporting Protein) is also located on the basolateral membrane. It handles unconjugated bile acids, organic anions, steroids, and drugs.
A(iii) BSEP (Bile Salt Export Pump) is located on the canalicular (apical) membrane of hepatocytes. Its primary substrates are bile acids, which it exports into the bile canaliculus.
A(iv) MDR2/MRP2 (Multi-Drug Resistant Protein 2) is located on the canalicular membrane. It transports conjugated bilirubin (bilirubin diglucuronide) across the canalicular membrane into bile. MDR3 transports phospholipids at the canalicular membrane.
A(v) NTCP accounts for approximately 80% of conjugated bile acid uptake into hepatocytes across the basolateral membrane. Both NTCP and OATP are reduced or downregulated in liver injury, which serves to protect hepatocytes from further accumulation of toxic bile acids and organic anions during cholestasis.
B. PFIC type 2 results from BSEP (Bile Salt Export Pump) deficiency, encoded by the ABCB11 gene. BSEP is the primary canalicular transporter for bile acids; its deficiency causes intrahepatic bile acid accumulation and progressive cholestatic liver disease, often requiring liver transplantation.
C. Canalicular transporter defects (BSEP, MDR2) impair the secretion of bile constituents from hepatocytes into the bile canaliculus at the cellular level. This causes bile constituents to accumulate within the hepatocyte and regurgitate into the bloodstream, producing intrahepatic cholestasis without any anatomical obstruction of the macroscopic extrahepatic bile ducts. The bile duct lumen itself remains patent; the failure is at the subcellular transport level.

Describe the types of vaccines used in childhood immunization under the following headings, explain the immunological basis of each type, and relate each type to the diseases for which it is used in the Nigerian immunization schedule.
A(i) Live attenuated vaccines: how they are produced, mechanism of action, advantages, disadvantages, and examples
A(ii) Inactivated vaccines: types (whole cell, fractional, polysaccharide, conjugate, recombinant), mechanism, and examples
B(i) Other vaccine components (suspending fluid, preservatives, adjuvants) and their roles
B(ii) Active versus passive immunization: mechanisms, duration of protection, and examples
C(i) Nigerian NPI schedule: vaccines given at each age from birth to 15 months
C(ii) Contraindications and conditions that are NOT contraindications to immunization
questions.answerText:
A(i) Live attenuated vaccines:
- Produced by modifying a naturally occurring organism (wild type) usually by repeated culturing; retain the ability to replicate and produce immune response similar to natural infection
- Circulating antibody may interfere with response
- Examples of live attenuated viruses: poliomyelitis, measles, rubella, mumps, rabies, varicella, yellow fever, rotavirus, influenza
- Examples of live attenuated bacteria: Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG), typhoid
- Usually only one dose provides lifelong immunity, except those administered orally (e.g. OPV) which require multiple doses
A(ii) Inactivated vaccines:
- The organism is inactivated with heat and/or chemicals (formalin); non-replicating so cannot cause disease
- Less interference from circulating antibodies; requires more doses (3-5); mostly humoral immune response; antibody titres diminish with time
- Whole organism: viral (poliomyelitis Salk, hepatitis A, rabies, influenza); bacterial (pertussis, typhoid, cholera, plague, anthrax)
- Fractional – subunit: hepatitis B, acellular pertussis, human papilloma virus; toxoids: diphtheria, tetanus
- Polysaccharide: pneumococcal, meningococcal, salmonella typhi; not very immunogenic
- Conjugate polysaccharide: Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcal
- Recombinant: hepatitis B, HPV, influenza; mRNA vaccines
B(i) Other vaccine components:
- Suspending fluids: sterile water, saline or complex fluid containing small amounts of proteins
- Preservatives, stabilizers, antimicrobial agents: gelatin, 2-phenoxyethanol, specific antimicrobial agents; THIMEROSAL contains ethyl mercury
- Adjuvants: enhance immune response; aluminium salts, ASO4; vaccines with adjuvant should be injected deeply into muscle to prevent local irritation, inflammation or necrosis
B(ii) Active versus passive immunization:
- Active immunization: induces immunity similar to natural infection; involves stimulating immune system to produce antibodies or cell mediated immunity; immunity is durable/long-lasting
- Passive immunization: administration of exogenously preformed antibodies; immunity is temporary; two situations: transplacental transfer of antibodies to fetus (provides protection for first 3-6 months of life); injection of immunoglobulin for prevention of specific infections (e.g. hepatitis B immunoglobulin, tetanus immunoglobulin)
C(i) Nigerian NPI schedule:
- Birth: OPV 0, BCG, HBV1
- 6 weeks: OPV1, PENTA1 (HBV, DPT, HIB), PCV1, ROTA1
- 10 weeks: OPV2, PENTA2, PCV2, ROTA2
- 14 weeks: OPV3, PENTA3, PCV3, IPV
- 9 months: MCV1, YF, MEN A
- 15 months: MCV2
- 9-13 years: HPV – 2 doses 6 months apart
C(ii) Contraindications and non-contraindications:
- True contraindications: anaphylaxis; known allergy to constituents of vaccine; encephalopathy; progressive neurologic disorders; immunodeficiency disorder or immunosuppressive therapy; pregnancy; any illness requiring hospital admission (defer immunization)
- NOT contraindications: URTI; mild fever; diarrhoea; cerebral palsy; breast feeding; antimicrobial therapy

questions.question:
A. Describe adolescence under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, etymology, age range, and the three stages with their respective age boundaries
A(ii) Global and Nigerian population figures for adolescents
A(iii) Why adolescence is considered a critical and important period in the life cycle, including the rights and transitions involved

B. Describe the key challenges facing adolescents in the areas of sexual health and contraception, including the failure rates and limitations of barrier methods, IUCDs, and hormonal methods, and the prevalence of sexual activity by age 18.

C. Explain the approach to managing STDs in adolescents and the principles of abstinence-based education.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The term adolescent comes from the Latin word 'adolescere' meaning 'to grow up'. An adolescent is an individual aged between 10 and 19 years. Three stages: Early: 10–13 years; Middle: 14–15 years; Late: 16–19 years.

A(ii) Global: 1.2 billion, constituting 20% of the global population. Nigeria: 22% of the Nigerian population.

A(iii) Adolescence is a critical period for developing habits and skills that create a strong foundation for healthy lifestyles and behaviour over the full lifespan. It is a time of major transitions, when young people develop many of the habits, patterns of behaviour, and relationships they will carry into adult lives. Like everyone else, adolescents have a right to life, development, health, and access to health services. They experience significant physical, psychological, and social transitions which carry both risks and opportunities for impact as they grow to adults.

B. Sexual activity: 60% of females and 70% of males have their first sexual intercourse by age 18; 20–30% of 15-year-olds are sexually active; approximately one fifth of these girls will become pregnant, the majority within the first 6 months of sexual activity. Contraception is used only by a minority.
Barrier methods: high failure because used inconsistently; provide a measure of protection against STI; diaphragm has the highest failure rate (few teenage girls remember to insert it before intercourse); condom requires the male to take responsibility.
IUCD: unacceptable level of STI with consequent sequelae of PID, ectopic pregnancy, and later infertility — completely contraindicated for adolescents.
Hormonals (OCP and Depo Injectables): provide contraception but do not protect against STIs; many adolescents do not make this distinction; depo injections have large amounts of hormones found to disturb development; compliance to taking OCPs daily is poor.

C. STDs in adolescents: occur frequently but adolescents may be ignorant or ashamed to seek care; often cannot afford treatment and do not want parents to know. Treatment is the same as for adults. If money is available, informing parents can be done after a firm relationship has been established with the consent of the adolescent. In those aged 18 and above, this remains a matter between the doctor and patient.
Abstinence-based education: highlights the dignity of the human body and the importance of womanhood; teaches that abstinence is possible by guarding the senses and avoiding occasions of difficulty; has been found not only possible but welcome to adolescents; a 'cult' of being proud to be a virgin has started as the best way to combat HIV/AIDS and teenage pregnancy.

A(i) Historical development:
- 1796: Edward Jenner discovered that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox were protected against smallpox; he inoculated fluid from cowpox lesions into susceptible individuals, thus immunization was born
- Artificial induction of immunity antedated understanding of the germ theory of disease
- Effective immunisation led to: eradication of smallpox globally; near-eradication of polio worldwide; significant reduction in incidence of most vaccine-preventable diseases
- 1974: WHO created EPI; original 6 killer diseases: TB, Polio, Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis, and Measles
- Immunization is one of the two most cost-effective means of preventing infectious diseases (the second is sanitation)
- New vaccines added: yellow fever (1986 for Africa), hepatitis B (1992), Hib (1997)
- Nigeria: 1978 EPI launched; by 1990 coverage of 80% achieved in some areas; by 1996 <30% coverage; re-launched as NPI in 1997; merged with NPHCDA in 2007
A(ii) Determinants of immunogenicity:
- Vaccine-related: chemical and physical state of antigen; dose of antigen; timing; presence of adjuvant; route of administration
- Child-related: genetic characteristics; age; nutrition; infection; immune status
B(i) Live attenuated vs inactivated vaccines:
- Live attenuated: derived from disease-causing viruses/bacteria weakened under laboratory conditions; will grow in vaccinated individual but will not cause clinical disease; usually one dose provides lifelong immunity (except oral vaccines like OPV requiring multiple doses); circulating antibody may interfere; examples: BCG, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, yellow fever, OPV, oral typhoid, rotavirus
- Inactivated: organism inactivated with heat and/or chemicals (formalin); non-replicating, cannot cause disease; less interference from circulating antibodies; requires more doses (3-5); mostly humoral immune response; antibody titres diminish with time; first dose does not produce protective immunity but "primes"; examples: polio (Salk), rabies, hepatitis A; fractional: hepatitis B, acellular pertussis, toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus)
B(ii) Polysaccharide vs conjugate vaccines:
- Polysaccharide vaccines: composed of long chains of sugar molecules making up surface capsule of certain bacteria; not very immunogenic
- Pure polysaccharide vaccines available for: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Salmonella typhi
- Conjugate polysaccharide vaccines: polysaccharide linked to a protein carrier; improve immunogenicity especially in young children
- Examples: Hib, pneumococcal (PCV), meningococcal conjugate
C(i) Special circumstances:
- HIV: all vaccines if asymptomatic; BCG and yellow fever contraindicated if symptomatic; IPV preferred to OPV; live vaccines generally not given to immunocompromised children
- Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine special indications: sickle cell anaemia (SCA), anatomic asplenia, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure, HIV, organ transplant
- For cerebrospinal meningitis and rabies: specific vaccines indicated
C(ii) Adverse reactions and contraindications:
- Adverse reactions: pain, swelling, redness, soreness; fever; anaphylaxis; encephalopathy (convulsions, coma); rash/urticaria
- True contraindications: anaphylaxis; known allergy to constituents; encephalopathy; progressive neurologic disorders; immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive therapy; pregnancy; any illness requiring hospital admission
- NOT contraindications: URTI; mild fever; diarrhoea; cerebral palsy; breast feeding; antimicrobial therapy
- Measles vaccine: no contraindications even where child is sick or malnourished

questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). The sign demonstrated when he rises from the floor by climbing up his own legs is Gower's sign, which is due to weakness of pelvic girdle muscles.

(ii) Predisposing/genetic factors:
- DMD is an X-linked inherited disease with spontaneous mutation.
- It is due to deletion of the short arm of the X-chromosome at the point carrying the dystrophin gene. Dystrophin is needed for muscular contraction.

(iii) Pathophysiology of calf enlargement:
- The enlargement is pseudohypertrophy resulting from fatty infiltration of the degenerating muscle fibres. This gives the calf muscles a hypertrophied appearance despite the underlying weakness and fibre degeneration. Occasionally, pseudohypertrophy of brachioradialis and other muscles also occurs.

(iv) Management:
- Pharmacological: Steroids (prednisolone) in low dose increase the period of ambulation by about 2 years.
- Physiotherapy: general and respiratory physiotherapy to maintain muscle function and remove secretions.
- Orthopaedic: to manage contractures and deformities.
- Genetic counselling: for the family.
- Prognosis: by 12 years, ambulation becomes impossible; death occurs before 20 years from cardiomyopathy.

questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) presenting as a salt-losing syndrome. The most common enzyme defect is 21-hydroxylase deficiency (accounts for 90–95% of all CAH cases). In males, the genitalia may not be ambiguous in the 21-hydroxylase type, making diagnosis difficult unless there is a known family history.

(ii) In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, cortisol synthesis is blocked. Absent cortisol causes excessive ACTH production due to failure of the negative feedback mechanism. ACTH drives adrenal hyperplasia and excess androgen production. 50–75% of severe cases have a defect of aldosterone synthesis, leading to salt loss. Without aldosterone, sodium is not retained; the infant develops hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, and hypoglycaemia, culminating in dehydration and shock within 2–4 weeks of life.

(iii) Resuscitation: IV Normal saline and 5% dextrose (or plasma if in shock); IV Hydrocortisone 50 mg. Correct electrolyte abnormalities. Monitor TPR, blood pressure, blood glucose, and electrolytes.

(iv) Definitive long-term treatment: Oral hydrocortisone 20–25 mg/m²/day every 8 hours to suppress ACTH and over-production of androgen. Fludrocortisone 100 mcg/day orally to suppress plasma renin. Salt losers also need additional dietary salt 2–3 g/day. Female genital abnormalities are surgically corrected. Follow-up includes monitoring growth velocity, sexual development, and serial urinary ketosteroid estimation.

questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: laryngeal diphtheria (given the progression from catarrhal prodrome to hoarseness, stridor, and croupy cough with dyspnoea).
Alternative diagnoses and distinguishing features:
- Viral croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis): preceded by URTI, no pseudomembrane, no toxic appearance, less systemic toxicity, responds to steroids and adrenaline; the normal pharynx and prior URTI in this child overlap with viral croup
- Acute epiglottitis (H. influenzae): more abrupt onset, very toxic child, "cherry red" epiglottis on laryngoscopy, child prefers sitting upright (tripod position), no barking cough, drooling
In diphtheria specifically: pseudomembrane firmly adherent to tonsils/pharynx/larynx; more toxic appearance; cervical lymphadenitis and bull neck; preceding upper respiratory features
(ii) Complications of laryngeal diphtheria:
- Respiratory obstruction: often the cause of death; pseudomembrane in the larynx causes hoarseness, stridor, croupy cough, dyspnoea, and risk of suffocation
- Cardiac toxicity (1-2 weeks after initial symptoms): arrhythmias, heart block, circulatory collapse; cardiomyopathy is immune-mediated and fatal
- Neuropathies (2-6 weeks after): cranial and peripheral neuropathies; may resemble GBS; symmetric, affects proximal muscles more than distal, progresses distally
- Renal failure or hypotension
- Bronchopneumonia
(iii) Pathological lesions in diphtheria (pseudomembrane formation):
- Pseudomembrane formation is the hallmark
- Necrosed epithelial cells + fibrin + leucocytes + RBCs + organisms matted together = grey/brown pseudomembrane
- Exotoxin causes tissue necrosis by inhibition of protein synthesis
- Lesions at sites of secretion causing local tissue destruction
- Pseudomembrane is firmly adherent to the tissue where destruction occurs
(iv) Definitive treatment for diphtheria:
- Neutralizing antitoxins: given to neutralize unbound circulating exotoxin and prevent further systemic complications (cardiac, neural)
- Antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin) x 14 days: to kill the bacteria, thereby stopping the production of more toxins
- Supportive care: clear secretions, maintain good hygiene, maintain fluid balance
- Toxoid given after recovery: to immunize the patient since clinical disease does not reliably confer immunity
- Treat carriers and unimmunized close contacts with penicillin or erythromycin x 7 days to prevent spread

questions.answerText:
A(i) Epidemiology: distribution worldwide; incidence 10–20%; in this environment's paediatric age group, 60% of cases are seen before 3 years and 80% before 5 years. Male-to-female ratio = 1.3:1; at puberty the sex ratio changes and returns at adulthood. Commoner among Caucasians, in industrialised countries, among the affluent, and in urban areas. Nigerian data: Falade et al using ISAAC questionnaire — Phase One: 6–7 year-olds 4.8%, 13–14 year-olds 10.7%; Phase Three: 6–7 year-olds 5.6%, 13–14 year-olds 13%.

A(ii) Host risk factors: hereditary — genes play an important role; twins study shows genetic factor contribution of 35–70%; multiple genes and chromosomal regions likely involved. Environmental risk factors: allergens; air pollution; viral respiratory infections.

A(iii) Three environmental variables: (1) allergens; (2) air pollution; (3) viral respiratory infection.

B(i) TH2 lymphocytes are central cells in orchestrating local eosinophilia, mast cell replenishment, and IgE production; they recognise and respond directly to allergens. B cells produce allergen-specific IgE. IgE binds to high-affinity receptors on mast cell surfaces (sensitisation). Re-exposure causes receptor bridging → mast cell release of leukotrienes, histamine, prostaglandins → airway obstruction. Eosinophils are the inflammatory cells most closely associated with asthma; they appear to play a role in virtually all severities.

B(ii) Three main components of the immune system: antibodies; inflammatory cells; inflammatory mediators.

B(iii) IgE is fundamental to the allergic immune response. Th2 cells stimulate B cells to produce IgE via IL-4. Natural state of the foetus is skewed towards Th2 production; in most, this is displaced by Th1 predominance required to fight infections (viral, parasitic) — which may explain the hygiene hypothesis.

C. Airway remodelling: refers to development of structural changes in the airway accompanying long-standing and severe airway inflammation — thickening of airway walls with increases in submucosal tissue, the adventitia, and smooth muscle; also includes fibrosis, goblet-cell hyperplasia, and neovascularisation. This development and fibrosis account for 'fixed' airflow obstruction in asthma unresponsive to steroids, bronchodilators, or both. Clinical significance: preventing the progressive loss of lung function in childhood may require recognition and treatment of disease during the first five years of life.
