A(i) Describe Phenylketonuria (PKU) under the following headings: definition/pathogenesis, mode of inheritance, biochemical basis, and clinical consequences.
A(ii) Compare Galactosaemia and Fructosaemia: enzyme defect in each, mode of inheritance, key clinical difference in timing of presentation, and treatment.
B(i) Distinguish between Hurler's syndrome (Type 1 mucopolysaccharidosis) and Hunter's syndrome (Type 2) under the headings: mode of inheritance, sex affected, key distinguishing clinical feature, and urine biochemistry.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Phenylketonuria (PKU):
• Definition/pathogenesis: an inborn disorder of amino acid metabolism — a genetic disorder in which a specific enzyme defect results in accumulation of substrate and alternate metabolic products.
• Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive (inborn error of amino acid metabolism).
• Biochemical basis: deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to accumulation of phenylalanine and its alternate metabolic products (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate).
• Clinical consequences: if untreated — intellectual disability (mental retardation), neurological damage. Neonatal screening allows early diagnosis and dietary phenylalanine restriction to prevent intellectual deficit.

A(ii) Galactosaemia vs Fructosaemia:
• Galactosaemia: enzyme defect — Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency (catalyses conversion of Ga-1-p to G-1-p); autosomal recessive. Presentation: baby normal at birth; vomits on milk diet; jaundice in 1st–2nd week; progressive hepatomegaly; diarrhoea; progressive wasting; cataracts in survivors; renal tubular damage. Treatment: exclusion of all foods free from lactose and galactose. Diagnosis: enzyme defect detectable in cord blood.
• Fructosaemia: enzyme defect — Fructose-1-phosphate aldolase deficiency (converts F-1-p to G-1-p); autosomal recessive. Key clinical difference: baby is okay when fed with breast milk only but hypoglycaemia develops when fed on fructose or sucrose (not from birth as in galactosaemia, since breast milk contains no fructose). Vomiting, anorexia, failure to thrive; MR if hypoglycaemia is prolonged; proximal tubular defect with proteinuria and aminoaciduria. Diagnosis: oral fructose tolerance test (results in fall in blood glucose). Treatment: exclusion of fructose and sucrose from the diet.

B(i) Hurler's syndrome vs Hunter's syndrome:
• Hurler's syndrome (Type 1 MPS):
  - Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive
  - Sex affected: both sexes
  - Key distinguishing features: overproduction of acid mucopolysaccharide; grotesque facial appearance (gargoylism); mental defect; dwarfism; corneal opacity (cloudy cornea); hepatosplenomegaly; umbilical hernia common; features manifest about 6 months of age
  - Urine biochemistry: large quantities of dermatan sulphate in urine
• Hunter's syndrome (Type 2 MPS):
  - Mode of inheritance: sex-linked recessive (X-linked)
  - Sex affected: only boys affected
  - Key distinguishing features: similar to Hurler's but NO cloudy cornea; about half are deaf
  - Urine biochemistry: elevated heparan sulphate and dermatan sulphate in urine

questions.question:
A(i) Describe Cushing's syndrome in children under the following headings: definition, distinction between Cushing's syndrome and Cushing's disease, frequency of ACTH-dependent versus ACTH-independent causes by age, and clinical features.
A(ii) State the investigations used to confirm the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome and the treatment options.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and physiological basis for why glucocorticoid excess causes growth arrest and reduced final height in children, distinguishing this from the mechanism of weight gain.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cushing's syndrome in children:
• Definition: Cushing's syndrome is glucocorticoid excess (hypercortisolism). Cushing's disease specifically refers to hypercortisolism caused by pituitary overproduction of ACTH (adrenal hyperplasia due to oversecretion of pituitary ACTH). Ectopic ACTH syndrome and iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome are distinct entities. Iatrogenic causes (exogenous hydrocortisone or other glucocorticoids) are the most common cause in childhood when excluded.
• Frequency by age:
  - ACTH-dependent: age <5 years — 50% of CS; age >5 years — 80–90% of CS. ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma (corticotropinoma) accounts for 80–90% of ACTH-dependent CS at all ages; usually a microadenoma; may invade the cavernous sinus.
  - ACTH-independent: age <5 years — 50% of CS; age >5 years — 10–20% of CS. Includes adrenocortical neoplasms (risk of malignancy significant in young children), macronodular disease (very rare in children), micronodular disease (PPNAD), McCune-Albright syndrome.
  - After 7 years of age, most cases are due to Cushing's disease. Before 7 years, adrenal tumours are the most common cause.
• Clinical features: increase in body fat, plethora, increased body hair, hypogonadism, hypertension, polycythaemia, hyperglycaemia, glycosuria, thinning of bones, purple/dark lines on thighs, hips and breasts, lassitude, moon-shaped face, muscle weakness. In children: central obesity, moon facies, hirsutism, facial flushing (80%); striae, hypertension, muscular weakness, back pain, buffalo hump, psychological disturbance, acne, easy bruising (35–80%). Earliest most reliable signs in children: weight gain and growth arrest.

A(ii) Investigations and treatment:
• Investigations: increased urinary free cortisol level; dexamethasone suppression test; ACTH level (low in primary adrenal disease; high in ectopic disease; plasma cortisol levels).
• Treatment: surgical excision of adrenal tumours; trans-sphenoidal microsurgery for Cushing's disease; withdrawal of exogenous steroid if possible. Medical drugs (inhibitors of adrenal steroidogenesis: ketoconazole, mitotane, etomidate; hypothalamic modulators: bromocriptine, cyproheptadine, octreotide, valproic acid). Post-treatment monitoring: treatment of eventual secondary adrenal insufficiency; treatment of eventual GH deficiency and hypopituitarism; prevention/treatment of osteoporosis; psychological counselling.

B(i) Growth arrest from glucocorticoid excess:
• Glucocorticoids suppress growth by two mechanisms: (1) increasing hypothalamic somatostatin (which inhibits growth hormone release), and (2) acting directly on the epiphysis.
• Long-term hypercortisolism reduces the final height by 1.5–2 SD.
• Weight gain mechanism is distinct: glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis and decrease cellular glucose use; they mobilise amino acids and fatty acids; they inhibit the effects of insulin; they give rise to ketones in metabolism. The resulting metabolic milieu promotes fat deposition, particularly central obesity, moon facies, and buffalo hump — which proceeds independently of the growth-suppressive mechanism. Thus a child may gain weight (fat) while experiencing growth arrest (reduced linear growth from epiphyseal suppression).

questions.question:
A 14-year-old boy presents with dyspnoea on exertion, syncope on exercise, and chest pain on effort. Examination reveals a small-volume, slow-rising pulse, a heaving apical impulse, a systolic thrill at the right second intercostal space, a possible single or reversed S2, an ejection systolic murmur at the right intercostal space with an aortic ejection click at the apex, and a 4th heart sound. The right arm pulse is stronger than the left arm pulse.

(i) State the diagnosis, classify all types, and identify which specific subtype is indicated by the stronger right arm pulse.
(ii) Describe the predisposing and pathological basis of this condition — distinguishing the presentation in infancy from presentation in older patients.
(iii) Describe the full investigation findings — CXR, ECG, echo, and cardiac catheterisation.
(iv) Outline the management of mild and symptomatic disease, including specific procedures.
questions.answerText:
(i) Aortic Stenosis (AS). Classification:
- Valvar AS: bicuspid or unicuspid valve alone — the commonest; bicuspid aortic valve is common in middle age (often asymptomatic ± calcification visible on lateral CXR)
- Subvalvar AS: involves fibromuscular diaphragm with elongated stenotic tunnel; murmur is maximum at 3rd or 4th right intercostal space
- Supravalvar AS: component of Williams Syndrome — mental retardation, elfin facies, hypercalcaemia, aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis
The stronger right arm pulse (right arm > left arm) indicates supravalvar AS: the jet of blood produces flow preferentially into the right brachiocephalic artery, then to the right radial artery.

(ii) Pathological basis: obstruction to left ventricular outflow increases LV afterload → LV hypertrophy → heaving apical impulse. Severe obstruction causes reduced cardiac output → small-volume slow-rising (anacrotic) pulse. Reversed splitting of S2 occurs because the aortic valve closes after the pulmonary valve (normally it closes first) when LV systole is prolonged by severe obstruction. In infancy: severe aortic stenosis ± coarctation of the aorta is the commonest cause of heart failure in the first year of life; usually associated with heart failure (hypoplastic left heart syndrome). In older patients: mild/moderate AS is asymptomatic (incidental ejection systolic murmur); severe AS presents with the triad of dyspnoea on exertion, syncope on exercise, and angina of effort.

(iii) CXR: normal initially; with time, post-stenotic dilatation of the ascending aorta develops (from jet flow); cardiomegaly with prominence of ascending aorta; ± calcification of aortic valve in older patients.
ECG: may be normal; or shows left ventricular hypertrophy with inverted T waves.
ECHO: shows anatomical change; thickened valve and LVH; Doppler demonstrates turbulence across the obstruction.
Cardiac catheterisation: measures the pressure gradient and for left ventriculography.

(iv) Mild AS: conservative; antibiotic prophylaxis before any dental or surgical procedure lasting over 72 hours (starting from 24 hours before, then during and after).
Symptomatic AS:
- Aortic valvotomy
- Valve replacement — if there is calcific stenosis

A(i) LBW definition: An infant weighing < 2.5 kg at birth irrespective of gestational age. (8% in Ibadan; 21% in India.)
Methods of gestational age assessment:
1. Physical signs — e.g. Farr scoring system: consists of skin, lanugo hair, immature external genitalia, palmar and plantar crease.
2. Neurological signs — e.g. Amiel-Tison.
3. Combined physical and neurological signs — e.g. Dubowitz and Ballard Scoring System.

A(ii) Symmetrical (uniformly retarded) IUGR:
- Occurs earlier in pregnancy (e.g. congenital rubella syndrome).
- Head, length, and weight are all proportionally small.
Asymmetrical (disproportionate) IUGR:
- Occurs late in pregnancy.
- Head size is normal (brain growth least affected by IUGR) → head-body disproportion so marked it may suggest hydrocephalus.
- Length of child is normal; weight is small.
- Physical appearance (wizened): loss of buccal fat; hungry-looking; scaphoid abdomen (from shrunken liver).

B(i) Comparison of SGA vs. Immature/AGA infants (selected categories):
- Early weight change: SGA = 0–3% loss, then gains rapidly; Immature = 10% loss, then gains slowly.
- Pulmonary problems: SGA = less; Immature = hyaline membrane disease (L/S ratio < 2:1).
- Infection (congenital): SGA = yes; Immature = no.
- Hyperbilirubinaemia: SGA = yes; Immature = yes.
- Haematology: SGA = normal or polycythaemia; Immature = anaemia.
- Congenital malformation: SGA = more common; Immature = less common.
- Intracranial haemorrhage: SGA = less common; Immature = yes (due to immaturity of germinal matrix underlying the ventricle).
- Persistent foetal circulation: SGA = yes; Immature = less.
- Hypoglycaemia in SGA: due to reduced hepatic glycogen stores; reduced gluconeogenesis; increased basal metabolic rate.

B(ii) Important causes of LBW in Nigeria: Toxaemia of pregnancy; placental insufficiency; antepartum haemorrhage; infections (cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis — both cause SGA; bacterial infections not associated with growth retardation); inherited factors/familial; trisomies (13, 18, 21); alcohol (foetal alcohol syndrome); smoking (low oxygen causing SGA and polycythaemia).
Management:
- Improve survival by 3-fold through warmth, nutrition, and skilled care.
- Child may be nursed in incubator until approximately 1.5 kg (corresponding to 32 weeks of gestation).
- Feeding: orogastric tube feeding; confirm tube position by testing aspirate with litmus paper (acidic) or placing open end of tube in water (bubbles if in trachea).
- Treat complications: PDA; NEC; RDS/apnoea; respiratory problems.
- Prevention of iron and folic acid deficiencies: start at postnatal age of 4–6 weeks (when anaemia of prematurity occurs).
- Improved maternal nutrition; careful monitoring of high-risk pregnancy (multiple pregnancy, APH, pregnant women with sickle cell disease).
questions.question:
Describe the low birth weight (LBW) infant, covering gestational age assessment, intrauterine growth restriction, and management.
A(i) Define LBW and state three methods of gestational age assessment with examples of the tools used for each,.
A(ii) Distinguish between symmetrical and asymmetrical IUGR in terms of timing, head and body measurements, and the physical appearance described.
B(i) Compare the problems of SGA and immature/AGA infants in the table format given, covering at least eight categories (weight change, pulmonary problems, infection, hypoglycaemia, etc.).
B(ii) State the important causes of LBW in Nigeria as listed, and outline the management of the LBW neonate, including criteria for incubator care, feeding method, and when to start iron and folic acid.

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the heart as evaluated in a paediatric cardiac patient under the following headings:
A(i) The four auscultatory areas of the heart: their names and surface anatomical positions
A(ii) The normal location of the apex beat and the significance of its displacement

B. The following abnormal heart shapes are seen on chest X-ray. For each shape, state the condition it suggests and describe the underlying anatomical/pathological basis:
B(i) Boot-shaped heart
B(ii) Egg-on-side
B(iii) Cottage loaf/Snowman/Figure-of-8
B(iv) Globular heart

C. Explain how left atrial enlargement in rheumatic heart disease produces the CXR findings of (i) splaying of the carina, (ii) double density at the right heart border, and (iii) mitralised left heart border (hump on left border), and state the underlying valvular pathology that causes each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Four auscultatory areas:
1. Aortic area: Right upper sternal edge (RUSE)
2. Pulmonary area: Left upper sternal edge (LUSE)
3. Tricuspid area: Left lower sternal edge (LLSE)
4. Mitral/Apex area: Apex (4th/5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line)
(Also auscultate intervening spaces between valve areas)

A(ii) Normal apex beat location: 4th or 5th left intercostal space, medial to mid-clavicular line.
Displacement downward and outward suggests enlargement — either hypertrophy or dilatation (usually more dilatation).
Other causes of displacement: massive pleural effusion on the right side (check for tracheal displacement); dextrocardia.
Character of apex beat: heaving/hyperactive suggests LVH; tapping suggests mitral stenosis.
Left parasternal heave suggests RVH.

B(i) Boot-shaped heart: Tetralogy of Fallot — the apex is lifted; the pulmonary artery is small (pulmonary bay). RVH lifts the apex; the small pulmonary artery creates the concave pulmonary bay.

B(ii) Egg-on-side: Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA) — the arrangement of the great vessels creates an egg-shaped silhouette with increased pulmonary vascular markings.

B(iii) Cottage loaf/Snowman/Figure-of-8: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage (TAPVD) — all pulmonary veins drain abnormally (anywhere besides the normal right atrium), usually into the superior vena cava, creating the upper lobe of the snowman figure.

B(iv) Globular heart: Pericardial effusion; endomyocardial fibrosis; dilatation of all chambers.

C. Left atrial enlargement in RHD:
(i) Splaying of the carina: The enlarged left atrium pushes upward against the carina (tracheal bifurcation), widening the angle between the two main bronchi.
(ii) Double density at the right heart border: The enlarged left atrium projects posteriorly and to the right, creating a second shadow behind the right atrial border on CXR — seen as double density.
(iii) Hump on left border/mitralised left heart border: Enlargement of the left atrial appendage creates a bulge on the left heart border between the pulmonary artery knuckle and the left ventricle.
Underlying valvular pathology: mitral incompetence (commonest lesion in paediatrics) and mitral stenosis (patient usually older), from rheumatic valve fibrosis. Aortic incompetence is also seen (diastolic murmur in aortic area with collapsing pulse).

A(i) Definition: acute inflammation of the nasal and pharyngeal epithelia, which affects primarily the nose. Synonyms: common cold, nasopharyngitis, rhinopharyngitis, acute viral rhinitis.

A(ii) Aetiology: Rhinoviruses (commonest); coronavirus; influenza; parainfluenza; RSV; adenovirus; enterovirus; human metapneumovirus. Occasionally Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus.

A(iii) Transmission: (a) Airborne droplets (aerosols) — least important; (b) direct contact with infected nasal secretions; (c) fomites (contaminated objects).

A(iv) Incubation: 1–6 days. Frequency: 6–12 episodes per year. Duration: usually 7 days. Classical triad: sneezing, rhinorrhoea, and blocked nostrils; also cough, headache, low-grade fever. Rhinorrhoea progresses: thin → mucoid → mucopurulent.

A(v) Signs: swollen nasopharyngeal mucosa; cervical lymphadenitis. Other symptoms: sore throat, malaise, loss of appetite.

B. Complications and basis: Acute otitis media — infection spreads via the Eustachian tube from the nasopharynx. Sinusitis — spread to adjacent paranasal sinuses. Tonsillitis — extension to tonsillar tissue. Laryngotracheobronchitis (viral croup) — spread downward to larynx, trachea, and bronchi. Bronchiolitis — further spread to bronchioles. Pneumonia — extension to lung parenchyma.

C. Streptococcal pharyngitis: rapid onset; fever; cough unusual; headache; GIT symptoms common; red pharynx; enlarged tonsils classically covered with yellow, blood-tinged exudates. Viral pharyngitis: insidious onset; rhinorrhoea; cough; diarrhoea; conjunctivitis; coryza; hoarseness; vesicles on the pharynx.
questions.question:
A. Describe acute coryza (common cold) under the following headings:
(i) Definition and synonyms
(ii) Aetiology — name all causative agents mentioned
(iii) Mode of transmission
(iv) Clinical features: incubation period, frequency per year, duration, classical triad of symptoms, and progression of nasal discharge
(v) Signs on examination

B. Explain the clinical basis for each complication that may follow acute coryza.

C. Distinguish streptococcal pharyngitis from viral pharyngitis using the features given.

A 5-year-old girl presents to the paediatric endocrinology clinic with precocious development of breast buds and pubic hair. Her mother noticed these changes over the past 6 months. On examination, growth velocity is accelerated, bone age is advanced by 2 years, and a brain MRI shows a hypothalamic mass.

(i) Identify the type of precocious puberty and the underlying mechanism in this case.
(ii) What anatomical landmarks and structures are involved in normal puberty regulation?
(iii) What nerve or structure is at risk from the mass found?
(iv) What management options exist for this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) This is True (Central) Precocious Puberty. In girls, secondary sex characteristics normally appear after 7.5 years; their appearance before this age constitutes precocious puberty. True precocious puberty is defined as pubertal changes that proceed in an orderly fashion (breast bud → pubic hair → growth spurt → menstruation), indicating that the pituitary and hypothalamic centres are intact. In this case, a hypothalamic mass is activating the GnRH–gonadotrophin axis prematurely. CNS pathology is found more frequently in boys than in girls with precocious puberty, but any CNS lesion can activate the axis.

(ii) Normal puberty regulation: puberty involves acquisition of secondary sexual characteristics and attainment of reproductive capacity through secretion of gonadal hormones as a result of the influence of GnRH (Gonadotrophin Releasing Hormone). The hypothalamus is the part of the brain made up of the floor and part of the lateral walls of the third ventricle. It produces releasing factors directly into the adenohypophyseal portal vasculature. Intact pituitary stalk is required for delivery of these short half-life releasing hormones. The feedback loop exists between the pituitary and hypothalamus (short loop) and between the target organ to the pituitary and thence the hypothalamus (long loop). Any disturbance of this chain of events leads to abnormal pubertal development.

(iii) A hypothalamic mass may compress or disrupt: the pituitary stalk (disrupting delivery of releasing hormones); the optic chiasm (causing visual field defects); the third ventricle (causing hydrocephalus). The delivery of releasing hormones is dependent on an intact pituitary stalk, and the hypothalamus produces vasopressin (VP) and oxytocin (OXT) released into the posterior pituitary — a mass may impair these functions.

(iv) Management: Treat the underlying cause (surgical or radiotherapy for the hypothalamic mass, as appropriate). Counselling and emotional support. Sexual education at the level of the child's development.

questions.question:
A medical student is reviewing the following four serological profiles in patients referred for hepatology assessment. For each profile, reason through the interpretation:

Profile A: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, Anti-HBc IgM positive, Anti-HBs negative.
Profile B: HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc positive.
Profile C: HBsAg positive, Anti-HBe positive, HBeAg negative, HBV DNA low.
Profile D: HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc negative.

(i) For Profile A, state the diagnosis, the degree of infectivity, and the most likely phase of infection.
(ii) For Profile B, identify the clinical state and explain how it differs from the result produced by HBV vaccination alone.
(iii) For Profile C, identify the phase of chronic HBV infection and its clinical significance with respect to infectivity and hepatic inflammation.
(iv) For Profile D, identify what this pattern represents and which of the five markers is the key differentiator from Profile B.
(v) State the approximate worldwide carrier number of chronic HBV, and describe the sequential pathway through which chronic HBV infection leads to hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.answerText:
(i) Profile A: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, IgM Anti-HBc positive. This is acute HBV infection with active viral replication. HBeAg positivity indicates active replication and high infectivity, correlating with high serum HBV DNA. IgM Anti-HBc confirms acute or recent infection. HBsAg appears first at approximately 6 weeks after exposure.
(ii) Profile B: HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc positive. This represents resolved past HBV infection with current protective immunity. The presence of Anti-HBc confirms prior natural infection. Vaccination produces Anti-HBs without Anti-HBc; the presence of Anti-HBc is the distinguishing feature, as it is absent in vaccinated individuals who never had natural infection. Anti-HBs titre above 10 mIU/mL is considered protective.
(iii) Profile C: HBsAg positive, Anti-HBe positive, HBeAg negative, low HBV DNA. This represents the inactive phase (third phase) of chronic HBV infection, characterised by HBeAg negativity, anti-HBe positivity, low serum HBV DNA concentrations, and minimal hepatic inflammation. It reflects seroconversion — resolution of active replication — and low-grade infectivity during convalescence or transition to the inactive carrier state. However, reactivation remains possible.
(iv) Profile D: HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc negative. This pattern represents vaccination-induced immunity. The key differentiator from Profile B (past natural infection with recovery) is the absence of Anti-HBc: natural infection always produces Anti-HBc, while vaccination produces only Anti-HBs.
(v) Approximately 400–500 million people worldwide are chronic HBV carriers. The sequential pathway from chronic HBV to hepatocellular carcinoma is: chronic hepatitis (ongoing immune-mediated hepatocyte destruction) → cirrhosis (bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodule formation distorting hepatic architecture) → hepatocellular carcinoma. This typically develops 25–30 years after initial infection, with up to a 15% 10-year HCC risk, and a 100-fold relative risk compared to uninfected individuals.

(i) Hypercyanotic/hypoxic/cyanotic blue spell — an emergency in TOF requiring immediate intervention to avoid brain damage. The mechanism: the infundibular region (which is muscular) goes into spasm rapidly, causing worsened cyanosis.
Precipitating factors:
- Emotion/excessive crying
- Excessive cold
- Dehydration
- Infections
- Hypoglycaemia
- Metabolic acidosis

(ii) Mechanism of squatting/knee-chest position:
(a) Pressure effect on shunting (major mechanism): compression of femoral and popliteal vessels increases resistance in the systemic circulation → increased systemic pressure → increased left ventricular afterload → reduces right-to-left shunting through the VSD → more blood is pumped to the lungs for oxygenation.
(b) Reduction of venous return: compression of femoral and popliteal veins reduces venous return to the right atrium → less blood to the right → reduced pressure on the right side → less right-to-left shunting.

(iii) Complications classified by mechanism:
Due to chronic hypoxia:
- Growth retardation
- Metabolic acidosis (reduced HCO3)
Due to polycythaemia (physiological response to chronic hypoxia, e.g. PCV 82%–88%):
- Cardiovascular accident/stroke — from hyperviscosity syndrome (slowed blood flow → thrombotic or embolic phenomenon)
- Cerebral abscess
- Iron deficiency — paradoxical; iron-deficiency picture on blood film because of the large number of red cells and inadequate iron (NOT iron-deficiency anaemia); must give iron supplement
- Bleeding diathesis — also from polycythaemia; thrombocytopaenia contributes
Hypercyanotic spells — as above
Infective endocarditis — patients are prone

(iv) Plasma exchange formula:
Exchange Volume = [(Actual PCV – Desired PCV) / Actual PCV] × Blood Volume
Blood Volume = 80 ml × Body weight (kg)
Example (10 kg patient, PCV 80%, target 55%): Exchange Volume = [(80–55)/80] × (80×10) = (25/80) × 800 = 250 mL
Target PCV range: 45–55% (not to normal, because of the ongoing cyanosis)
Maximum volume on any one occasion: not more than 20–25% of patient's blood volume (to prevent acute metabolic acidosis)
Replacement fluid: plasma (preferred) or normal saline — stay in intravascular space. Do NOT use glucose.
Complications of plasma exchange:
- Transfusion complications (e.g. infections)
- Air or fat embolism
- Anxiety — procedure is invasive; premedicate with morphia before and after
- Metabolic acidosis — premedicate with sodium bicarbonate before and after
questions.question:
A 5-year-old known TOF patient on oral propranolol is brought to the emergency department deeply cyanosed, unresponsive, and having a convulsion after a bout of crying. His PCV is 82%. His ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy and right axis deviation.

(i) What is the immediate emergency and state all the precipitating factors for this type of event?
(ii) Describe the mechanism by which squatting/knee-chest position provides physiological adaptation to hypoxia in this child — all mechanisms involved.
(iii) Describe the complications of the underlying condition, classifying them by pathophysiological mechanism.
(iv) A decision is made to perform plasma exchange before surgery. State the formula for calculating the volume to exchange, the acceptable target PCV range, the maximum volume to be exchanged at one time, and the complications of the procedure.

A. Describe the well child visit programme:
A(i) The AAP-recommended minimum number of visits and their age distribution from birth to 18 years, and the situations in which the frequency of visits should be increased
A(ii) The specific developmental and immunisation milestones at each visit from birth to 9 months

B. Explain how the well-child visit relates to common pathologies by stating the goals of the well-child visit — covering relationship-building, risk detection, disease prevention, and anticipatory guidance.

C. Explain why the growth chart (percentile graph) is important in detecting obesity early, what about childhood obesity and type II diabetes in children, and what environmental exposure is stated to cause cognitive deficit, behaviour disorders, and slowed growth.
questions.answerText:
A(i) AAP-recommended minimum frequency:
- 5 health supervision visits from birth to 2 years of age
- 3 visits from 2–6 years of age
- 4 visits from 6–18 years of age
Situations where frequency should be increased: first-born, adopted, and foster children; parents with a particular need for education and guidance; disadvantaged social or economic environment; presence or possibility of perinatal disorders, congenital defects, or familial disease; acquired illness or previously identified disease or problems. Each child and family must be treated individually and the number of visits adjusted accordingly.

A(ii) Birth (newborn visit): feeding discussed; BCG, 1st OPV, and 1st Hepatitis B vaccine given by the 2nd day of life.
2–4 week visit: discuss parents' exhaustion; reactions of siblings to the new baby; baby's sleep and feeding patterns; physician may prescribe Vitamins A, D, and C with iron for the exclusively breastfed infant.
2-month visit: assess social smile, eye contact, and cooing; immunisation: 1st DPT + OPV + 2nd Hepatitis B vaccine.
3-month visit: immunisation: 2nd DPT + OPV.
4-month visit: questions about addition of solids (exclusive breastfeeding encouraged to 6 months); immunisation: 3rd DPT + OPV.
6-month visit: assess laughing/squealing, alertness, babbling (vowel sounds), rolling over, sitting with or without support, picking up and transferring toys; iron-fortified food discussion; immunisation: 3rd Hepatitis B vaccine.
9-month visit: child enters dangerous developmental stage — parents counselled on accident-proofing; immunisation: measles vaccine + yellow fever vaccine; haemoglobin genotype often done at this visit.

B. Goals of the well-child visit:
- Establish a relationship of trust and open communication with the patient and family
- Gain understanding of the child's cultural, ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic background
- Observe and inquire about the child's relationship to parents and family members
- Detect stresses affecting the family and anxieties the child experiences
- Inquire about the child's environment
- Determine the risk for genetically transmitted diseases
- Detect early developmental and behavioural problems and monitor remediation
- Detect early disease processes through interview, physical examination, and screening
- Provide health maintenance (immunisations)
- Provide appropriate counselling and anticipatory guidance
- Communicate that the physician is available to help and provide support

C. Growth chart: the percentile graph shows the range of normal weight or heights from the 1st to 100th percentile for age. Obesity can be prevented by using the chart properly; when a child leaves his percentile curve to a higher one, dietary quality and eating habits should be explored; at this stage it is easy to guide parents to healthier eating. An increase in type II diabetes has been reported in children and adolescents due to obesity. After age 2, weight and height should be checked once a year. Environmental exposure causing cognitive deficit, behaviour disorders, and slowed growth: children exposed to lead (from batteries and peeling paint) — lead levels of 10 µg/dl have been associated with cognitive deficit, behaviour disorders, and slowed growth.

questions.question:
A preterm male neonate born at 30 weeks gestation to a diabetic mother via emergency Caesarean section presents within minutes of birth with tachypnoea, grunting, intercostal and subcostal retractions, nasal flaring, and increasing cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse reticular granular (ground-glass) appearance with air bronchograms and poor lung expansion.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the risk factors that predispose to this condition, distinguishing those that affect the state of lung development at birth from those that impair surfactant production, release, or function.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology, tracing events from surfactant deficiency through to hyaline membrane formation.
(iv) Outline the management, including both prenatal and postnatal interventions and the acute and chronic complications.
questions.answerText:
(i) Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) / Hyaline Membrane Disease.

(ii) Risk factors affecting lung development: infants of diabetic mothers; delivery before 37 weeks gestation; multifetal pregnancies; history of prior affected infants; preterm male or white infants; thoracic malformations (lung hypoplasia, diaphragmatic hernia). Factors impairing surfactant: caesarean section delivery without labour; precipitous delivery; asphyxia; cold stress. Secondary surfactant deficiency: intrapartum asphyxia; pulmonary infections; pulmonary haemorrhage; meconium aspiration pneumonia; oxygen toxicity with barotrauma or volutrauma.

(iii) Pathophysiology: Surfactant deficiency + small respiratory units + compliant chest wall → atelectasis → ventilation-perfusion mismatch → hypoxia. Decreased lung compliance + small tidal volumes + increased physiological dead space + increased work of breathing → hypercarbia. Hypercarbia + hypoxia + acidosis → pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction → increased right-to-left shunting through foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus → reduced pulmonary blood flow → ischaemic injury to surfactant-producing cells and vascular bed → effusion of proteinaceous material into alveolar spaces → hyaline membrane formation.

(iv) Management: prenatal — antenatal corticosteroids reduce risk; monitoring of lung maturity. Delivery and resuscitation. Postnatal: surfactant replacement therapy; oxygen; continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP); assisted mechanical ventilation; temperature regulation; fluids, electrolytes, and nutrition; circulatory support and anaemia management; antibiotic administration. Acute complications: alveolar rupture; infections; intracranial haemorrhage; PDA; pulmonary haemorrhage; necrotising enterocolitis; apnoea of prematurity. Chronic complications: chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia); retinopathy of prematurity; neurologic impairment; familial psychopathology.

(i) Myelomeningocoele is classified as a Malformation (true malformation), defined as an error of morphogenesis. Myelomeningocoele and exomphalos are examples of malformations. A malformation is a primary structural defect arising from an intrinsically abnormal developmental process.

(ii) Indications for prenatal diagnosis in this pregnancy (both pre-pregnancy and during-pregnancy indications apply):
Prior to/predating pregnancy indications present:
• Increased maternal age (mother is 38 years — advanced maternal age increases chromosomal risk)
• Previous obstetric history (prior child with a neural tube defect — family history)
During-pregnancy indications:
• Elevated or low maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is specifically associated with open neural tube defects
• Abnormal ultrasound appearance
• Consanguinity (if applicable) and ethnic origin

(iii) Prenatal investigation techniques for neural tube defects:
• Amniocentesis (at 16–18 weeks of gestation, when the ratio of viable to non-viable cells is maximal): amniotic fluid biochemistry including alpha-fetoprotein (elevated in open neural tube defects) and acetylcholinesterase. Also allows fetal karyotyping and fetal DNA diagnosis.
• Ultrasonography (optimal time 16–18 weeks, though anencephaly detectable as early as 10–12 weeks): visualises the neural tube defect directly, cranial shape (lemon sign, banana sign for Arnold-Chiari), and associated anomalies. Advantage: no proven hazard to mother or fetus; can be repeated.
• Chorionic villus sampling (at 8–10 weeks): can be done earlier than amniocentesis; useful for fetal sexing, karyotyping, biochemical studies, and DNA analysis. Advantage: selective termination if needed can be done earlier and with fewer complications.

(iv) Genetic counselling principles: accurate diagnosis is essential for meaningful counselling. Adequate time should be allowed in an appropriate setting. Both parents should be counselled. Counselling must cover all aspects of the condition; depth matched to educational level. Time must be taken to deal with guilt and perceived social stigma. A recurrence risk should always be calculated and explained against the background of the general population risk. Neural tube defects have multifactorial aetiology (20% of congenital malformations are multifactorial). Reproductive options include: proceeding to a further pregnancy with prenatal diagnosis; adoption; artificial insemination by donor; in vitro fertilisation with or without pre-implantation diagnosis; contraception (reversible or non-reversible).
questions.question:
A couple attends a genetics clinic. Their first child was born with a lumbosacral myelomeningocoele and has hydrocephalus. The mother is now 8 weeks pregnant. She is 38 years old.

(i) Name the pattern of congenital malformation present in their previous child, and classify it by pathogenetic mechanism.
(ii) State all relevant indications for prenatal diagnosis in this pregnancy.
(iii) Name the specific prenatal investigations appropriate for neural tube defects, state the timing for each technique, and describe what each detects.
(iv) What information should be provided during genetic counselling, and what are the reproductive options?

questions.answerText:
(i) Bronchiectasis.

(ii) Aetiology/predisposing factors — Infections (most common): tuberculosis; pertussis, measles (complicated by pneumonia); adenovirus; Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Congenital and genetic disorders: cystic fibrosis; Marfan syndrome; alpha-1-antiproteinase (antitrypsin) deficiency; congenital bronchiectasis. Ciliary abnormalities: Kartagener syndrome (triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis with underlying congenital abnormal ciliary function); acquired ciliary dysfunction from infection. Immunodeficiency. Foreign body aspiration. Asthma. Others: bronchogenic cyst, chronic sinusitis, recurrent aspiration (e.g. tracheo-oesophageal fistula, cerebral palsy), inhalation of noxious gases, racial predilections.

(iii) Complications: brain and lung abscess; empyema and pyopneumothorax; bronchopleural fistula; severe atypical pneumonia; haemoptysis; amyloidosis; cor pulmonale in advanced disease.

(iv) Medical management: chest physiotherapy; antibiotics; bronchodilator; good nutrition; bronchoscopy to remove foreign body or thick secretions. Surgical management: indicated when medical treatment fails and disease is localised. Justification: medical treatment can halt progression of the potentially reversible cylindrical form (Group I) to the irreversibly destructive saccular bronchiectasis (Group III), making early aggressive medical therapy the priority intervention.
questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents with a 6-week history of daily productive cough worse in the morning, foul-smelling sputum, haemoptysis, intermittent fever, and weight loss. He had severe measles with pneumonia two years ago and has never been fully vaccinated. Examination reveals finger clubbing, Harrison's sulci, cyanosis, and localised dullness with bronchial breath sounds at the left lower zone.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) List the aetiological and predisposing factors them.
(iii) State all the complications that may arise.
(iv) Outline both the medical and surgical management options, and justify which medical intervention can prevent progression to the most destructive form of the disease.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Four major acquired heart diseases in children in developing countries:
- Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF)
- Chronic Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD)
- Infective Endocarditis (IE)
- Others: Endomyocardial Fibrosis, Pericardial Effusion
Anatomy of cardiac damage in ARF — pancarditis (affects all three layers):
- Pericarditis: forms thin fibrinous sticky exudate — "bread-and-butter" appearance — or small frank pericardial effusion
- Myocarditis: direct damage; can be fatal in the first attack
- Endocarditis: Mitral valve (most commonly — endocarditis +++), Aortic valve (+), Tricuspid valve (occasionally), Pulmonary valve (rarely)
Histopathological hallmark: Aschoff Nodules — aggregates of inflammatory cells; pathognomonic of ARF.

A(ii) Pathogenesis comparison:
ARF — immune-mediated: the organism (Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus) in the throat generates antibody or antigen-antibody complexes; these complexes are deposited in the heart and joints. The organism itself does NOT directly infect the heart — cardiac damage is from the immune (antibody) response. This is why not everyone with streptococcus in the throat develops pharyngitis, and not everyone with pharyngitis develops ARF.
IE — direct microbial infection: the organism directly infects the endocardial surface after adhering to a damaged endothelium or non-bacterial thrombus; it is a septicaemic illness. Unlike ARF, the organism itself is present in the heart tissue (vegetation); treatment requires bactericidal antibiotics for 6 weeks to eradicate the organism from the vegetation.

B(i) Sydenham's Chorea in ARF (also called St Vitus' Dance): arises from involvement of the basal ganglia — a CNS manifestation. Presents starting with dropping objects, progressing to involuntary movements. Most commoner among adolescent girls. The cardiac damage is said to be worse than joint damage because: "ARF licks the joint but bites the heart" — arthritis is self-limiting, fleeting, and fully reversible; carditis causes pancarditis which can be fatal in the first attack and leads to permanent fibrotic valvular damage (chronic RHD) with subsequent decompensation; subcutaneous nodules indicate ongoing carditis.

B(ii) IE — pathways of distant organ dysfunction from left-sided valve vegetation:
Embolic (systemic, from mitral/aortic valve):
- CNS: cerebral embolism → stroke/CVA; mycotic aneurysm from microabscesses → subarachnoid haemorrhage
- Renal arteries: emboli → renal infarction → acute renal failure; immune complex deposition → nephritis/glomerulonephritis → haematuria
- Splenic arteries: splenic infarction
- Mesenteric arteries: bowel infarction → acute abdomen
- Coronary arteries: myocardial infarction → angina
Immunological (late, subacute form):
- Petechiae, splinter haemorrhages (small emboli or vasculitis)
- Osler's nodes (painful swellings in finger pulps from microemboli/immune complexes)
- Roth spots (retinal exudates — immune complex vasculitis)
- Janeway lesions; arthritis; digital clubbing; rheumatoid factor positivity

B(iii) Chronic RHD with mitral incompetence → right ventricular failure (anatomical sequence):
Mitral incompetence → regurgitation of blood from left ventricle back into left atrium during systole → left atrial volume and pressure overload → left atrial dilatation → increased pulmonary venous pressure → pulmonary congestion → pulmonary oedema → reactive pulmonary arterial hypertension (vasoconstriction and vessel wall hypertrophy) → increased right ventricular afterload → right ventricular hypertrophy → eventually right ventricular failure → raised JVP, hepatomegaly, peripheral oedema.
CXR evidence of this sequence: hump on left border (left atrial enlargement); splaying of the carina (left atrium pushes up bronchi); double density right heart border (left atrium behind right heart); pulmonary congestion (increased PVM); loud P2 on auscultation (pulmonary hypertension) → cardiomegaly involving all chambers.

questions.answerText:
(i) Neuroblastoma.
(ii) Presenting syndromes:
- Pepper syndrome: massive involvement of the liver with metastatic disease plus respiratory distress.
- Horner's syndrome: unilateral ptosis, myosis, enophthalmos, anhidrosis.
- Hutchinson's syndrome: limping and irritability in the young child associated with bone and bone marrow metastasis.
- Opsomyoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet syndrome): myoclonic jerking and random eye movement plus cerebellar ataxia.
- Kerner-Morrison syndrome: intractable secretory diarrhoea associated with VIP secretion.
- Raccoon eyes: periorbital haemorrhage secondary to metastatic tumour.
- Hypertension, tachycardia, headaches, palpitation, sweating and flushing (rare, due to type of catecholamines secreted).
- Pelvic involvement: constipation and urinary retention.
- Exophthalmos and non-tender bluish subcutaneous nodules.
(iii) IVU difference:
- In Neuroblastoma: IVU shows downward and lateral displacement of the kidney, but calyceal architecture is usually preserved.
- In Wilm's Tumour: IVU shows distorted calyces or non-excretion of contrast dye (non-functional kidney), as it is an intrarenal tumour.
(iv) Chemotherapy regimen:
- VCAC: Vincristine, Cyclophosphamide, Adriamycin, Cisplatin/Cisplatinum.
- Surgery is also used.
Prognosis determinants:
- Age: better if <1 year.
- Site: worse in abdominal tumour.
- Stage: worsens with advancing stage.
- Pathology: the less the differentiation, the worse the prognosis; there may be spontaneous regression/differentiation into benign ganglioneuroma.
- Amplification of the proto-oncogene myc-n, deletions on chromosome 1 and DNA ploidy all carry a poor prognosis.
questions.question:
A 3-year-old presents with a large abdominal mass crossing the midline with systemic features including bone pain, irritability, and periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes"). Urine Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is elevated.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Describe the full spectrum of presenting clinical syndromes associated with this tumour.
(iii) How does the IVU finding in this tumour differ from that in Wilm's tumour?
(iv) What chemotherapy regimen is used, and what determines the prognosis?

A 7-year-old girl presents with a 4-week history of progressive abdominal distension and an abdominal mass. On examination the mass is firm, crosses the midline, and involves multiple abdominal organs. There is minimal peripheral lymphadenopathy. Ascitic fluid cytology reveals characteristic large cells with basophilic cytoplasm, fat vacuoles, and nuclei with multiple nucleoli.
(i) What is the diagnosis? Describe the cytological and histological appearances that confirm it.
(ii) Using staging criteria, stage this patient and describe how the stage determines prognosis.
(iii) A 10-year-old boy in the same ward has cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with pleural effusion, but NO jaw involvement and NO abdominal mass. What tumour is this more likely to be, and how does its clinical picture differ from the first patient?
(iv) Describe the pre-chemotherapy management that must be initiated before starting cytotoxic drugs in either patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Burkitt's Lymphoma (BL).
Cytological appearance (on FNAC): Burkitt's cells — basophilic moderate cytoplasm containing fat vacuoles; nucleus has about 2–5 nucleoli.
Histological appearance (on excisional biopsy): typical starry-sky appearance — stars are histiocytes interspersed among lymphoid cells; blue sky is basophilic lymphoid cells.
It is a malignant lymphoma of B-lymphocyte origin; the fastest growing tumour in man with a 24-hour doubling time; hence the short interval of onset of symptoms to presentation (83% within 3 months).
(ii) Staging and prognosis:
- Stage A: Solitary extra-abdominal site (e.g. jaw) — better prognosis.
- Stage B: Multiple extra-abdominal sites — better prognosis.
- Stage C: Intra-abdominal tumour ± facial tumour — worse prognosis.
- Stage AR: Abdominal tumour which has been completely (≥90%) resected — better prognosis.
This patient has Stage C (intra-abdominal tumour involving multiple organs, crossing midline with ascites).
Factors associated with worse prognosis: Stage C, D; CNS involvement; Bone marrow involvement; Peripheral blood manifestation; Male gender; Age >13 years.
(iii) More likely diagnosis for second patient: Other Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (e.g. Precursor T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma or large cell lymphoma).
Clinical differences from BL:
- Lymphadenopathy is common (50–80%) — cervical and supraclavicular — unlike endemic BL where lymphadenopathy is minimal.
- Usually associated with thoracic presentation: mediastinal masses causing pain, dysphagia, dyspnoea, SVC syndrome, pleural effusion.
- Right iliac fossa masses (rare in BL) may mimic appendicitis in other small noncleaved cell lymphomas.
- Diagnosis: Lymph node biopsy, FNAC of abdominal masses.
- Serum LDH is a useful marker for tumour burden and monitoring treatment response.
(iv) Pre-chemotherapy management:
- Allopurinol 100 mg/m² (to prevent tumour lysis syndrome/hyperuricaemia).
- Electrolyte, Urea and Creatinine monitoring (to monitor for metabolic complications).
- Blood complications management.
- Management of metabolic disturbance (10% die due to Tumour Lysis Syndrome).
- Antiemetics.
- Nutritional support.
- Psychological support.
- Full blood count as baseline for chemotherapy.
- Calcium and Phosphorus monitoring.

A(i) Normal portal pressure is 5–10 mmHg. Portal hypertension is defined as elevation of portal pressure above 10–12 mmHg.
A(ii) Presinusoidal: portal vein thrombosis (from umbilical infection, neonatal dehydration, intra-abdominal infection, or hypercoagulable states) — blood flow is obstructed before reaching the hepatic sinusoids. Sinusoidal (intrahepatic): cirrhosis — bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodule formation distorts the hepatic architecture and increases sinusoidal resistance. Postsinusoidal: Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis/obstruction) and veno-occlusive disease — outflow from hepatic veins is obstructed.
A(iii) Portosystemic collaterals include: (1) Oesophageal and gastric varices — formed through anastomoses between the left gastric (portal) vein and oesophageal veins (systemic); (2) Caput medusa — via the umbilical vein connecting the portal system to the anterior abdominal wall veins (systemic); (3) Rectal haemorrhoids — through anastomoses between the superior rectal vein (portal territory) and the middle/inferior rectal veins (systemic territory).
A(iv) Caput medusa — tortuous, dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus — is the clinical sign produced by portosystemic collaterals via the umbilical vein shunts and is a pathognomonic sign of portal hypertension.
B. HVPG is measured via transjugular catheterisation as the difference between wedged hepatic venous pressure and free hepatic venous pressure. The hepatic vein serves as a safe indirect measure because it reflects sinusoidal pressure without requiring direct portal puncture. HVPG greater than 5 mmHg defines portal hypertension; HVPG greater than 12 mmHg predicts variceal bleeding risk.
C. Hepatocellular dysfunction and portosystemic shunting generate vasodilatory humoral factors — primarily nitric oxide and glucagon — that cause splanchnic vasodilatation. This reduces effective arterial blood volume, triggering compensatory sodium and water retention and producing the hyperdynamic circulation characterised by high cardiac output with low peripheral vascular resistance, bounding pulses, and warm extremities.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Preterm Labour (PTL) = regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks' gestation (ACOG definition).
Incidence: 10–12% of all pregnancies; related to 80% of perinatal mortality; single greatest cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality in developed countries; most common cause of hospitalisation during pregnancy.
Maternal risk factors: Age (< 18 and > 40); race (nonwhite); poverty; tobacco use; drugs; prior preterm birth; prior 2nd trimester loss or bleeding; psychological stress; poor nutrition; low pre-pregnancy weight and poor weight gain; anatomic anomaly (fibroids, placenta praevia); increased uterine volume (multiple gestation, polyhydramnios); trauma/abruption; cervical incompetence/short cervix; oligohydramnios; infections (chorioamnionitis; Chlamydia and gonorrhoea; Group B Streptococcus; asymptomatic bacteriuria, UTI, pyelonephritis).

A(ii) PPROM definition: Rupture of membranes prior to 37 weeks and at least 1 hour before onset of labour. Average 8% of all pregnancies; 20–40% before 37 weeks; same risk factors as PTL — infection is often the culprit.
Bacterial vaginosis (BV): Known association between PTL and BV; found in 10–25% of pregnant women; 50% asymptomatic. Treatment of BV in high-risk women has been shown to reduce PPROM, not necessarily PTL. Trials for screening and treatment have varying results.

B(i) Foetal fibronectin (FFN): A glue-like substance that helps maintain placental attachment to the decidua. Not detectable in vaginal secretions after 20 weeks to term. If present after 20 weeks in cervical/vaginal fluids = disruption of maternal-foetal boundaries. Negative if < 50 µg/ml.
Clinical use: High specificity — after a negative test, 124 of 125 women will not deliver in the next 14 days. Positive result: 1 in 6 women will deliver in next 14 days. May aid in early discharge vs. increased vigilance. FDA approved.

B(ii) Progesterone mechanism: Inhibits oxytocic effect of prostaglandin F2a and stimulation of alpha adrenergics, acting as a tocolytic. No known teratogenic effects. May cause pain, swelling, bruising from injection, but no known maternal/foetal metabolic or haemodynamic effects.
Dosing regimen: Weekly IM injection of 250–1,000 mg alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate from 16–37 weeks in women at risk for PTL.
Possible neonatal outcomes reduced: NEC; IVH; perinatal morbidity. (Other studies do not demonstrate benefit.)
