A 6-year-old girl presents with her first generalised convulsion lasting 10 minutes in the setting of a high fever. She has no CNS infection, no prior history of afebrile seizures, and no neurological abnormality. She is in your emergency unit.
(i) State the diagnosis, define it precisely, and classify this episode.
(ii) List at least six risk factors for this condition.
(iii) Outline the acute management, including the drugs, doses, and routes of administration for each drug.
(iv) State the criteria for hospital admission and describe the prognosis including the risk of epilepsy and factors that increase this risk.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Simple febrile seizure.
Definition: A seizure occurring in association with a febrile illness in the absence of a CNS infection or acute electrolyte imbalance in children > 1 month of age without prior afebrile seizures; also defined as seizures occurring during a fever in the absence of intracranial infections, metabolic disturbance, or history of afebrile seizures.
Classification: Simple febrile seizures occur for less than 15 minutes, are generalised in nature, occur as a single episode within 24 hours, and occur in a neurologically normal child. 70% of cases are simple. This episode qualifies as simple.

(ii) Risk factors: Developmental delay; discharge from a neonatal unit after 28 days; day care attendance; viral infections (HHV6, influenza, adenovirus, parainfluenza); a family history of febrile seizures; certain vaccinations (flu, DPT, MMR); possible iron and zinc deficiencies; possible genetics (25% of cases have a positive family history).

(iii) Acute management:
- ABC of resuscitation; check blood sugar; abort seizure.
- Rectal diazepam: 5 mg in children = 3 years; 10 mg in children > 3 years.
- IM paraldehyde: 1 ml per year of age up to 5 years (e.g. 1-year-old: 1 ml; 2-year-old: 2 ml; 5 years and beyond: 5 ml).
- Buccal midazolam: 3 months–< 1 year: 2.5 mg; 1 year–< 5 years: 5 mg; 5 years–< 10 years: 7.5 mg; 10 years–< 18 years: 10 mg.

(iv) Criteria for hospital admission (SIGN 2005, ILAE 2009):
Age < 1 year; first episode < 18 months; febrile seizure in children without a reliable familiar context; GCS < 15 one hour after seizure; meningeal signs; raised ICP; acutely ill child; signs of aspiration; high parental/carer anxiety; complex febrile seizures.
Prognosis: Can recur frequently (up to 32%, with 75% recurring in the first year). Risk factors for recurrence: age < 18 months; duration of fever < 1 hour before seizure onset; first-degree relative with febrile seizures; temperature < 40°C. Children without underlying developmental problems do not have long-lasting neurological effects. Mortality is extremely rare. Increased risk of epilepsy: 2% in simple febrile; 6–49% in complex febrile seizures. Risk increases with: family history of epilepsy; cerebral palsy; hydrocephalus; Apgar score < 7 at 5 minutes; complex febrile seizures.

questions.question:
A. Describe the normal and abnormal heart sounds heard on auscultation of the cardiovascular system, under the following headings:
A(i) Normal S1 and S2 — components and timing
A(ii) Wide splitting of S2 — types and causes
A(iii) Single S2, triple rhythm, and ejection click — causes of each

B. Distinguish between systolic and diastolic murmurs, stating:
B(i) The types of each with their causes
B(ii) The grading system for murmur intensity
B(iii) The clinical basis for a continuous/machinery murmur and the condition it characterises
questions.answerText:
A(i) S1 is due to closure of atrioventricular valves; mitral valve closes a split second before and is louder than the tricuspid. S2 is due to closure of semilunar valves; aortic valve closes slightly earlier than pulmonary. S2 has a normal physiological split into its aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) components.

A(ii) Wide splitting (non-fixed): wider during inspiration than expiration because the right side fills more during inspiration. Causes: aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block.
Wide and fixed split S2: the split does not vary with respiration. Cause: secundum ASD.

A(iii) Single S2 (A2 and P2 fused): causes — severe aortic stenosis/atresia, severe pulmonary stenosis/atresia.
Triple rhythm (S3): heard in myocardial heart disease and heart failure; when associated with tachycardia it is called gallop rhythm.
Ejection click: occurs just before S1; louder on expiration, may disappear on inspiration; generated from aortic or pulmonary valve. Causes: valvar aortic stenosis, valvar pulmonary stenosis, dilated pulmonary artery, dilated aorta.

B(i) Systolic murmurs:
- Pansystolic/holosystolic (spans S1 to S2): VSD, mitral incompetence, tricuspid incompetence
- Ejection systolic murmur (crescendo-decrescendo, diamond-shaped): pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, ASD
Diastolic murmurs (generally less loud):
- Aortic incompetence — high-pitched
- Mitral stenosis — low-pitched/rumbling, mid-diastolic

B(ii) Grading: Grade I — extremely soft; Grade II — louder but still soft; Grade III — loud, audible to medical students, no thrill; Grade IV — produces a palpable thrill; Grade V — heard with stethoscope at an angle to the chest; Grade VI — heard with stethoscope away from the chest.

B(iii) Continuous (machinery/to-and-fro) murmur starts anywhere in systole, continues through S2 into diastole. Causes: patent ductus arteriosus (loudest under the left clavicle); arteriovenous malformations e.g. coronary artery AV fistula; combination of aortic incompetence with VSD/ASD/PDA; collateral circulations in coarctation of the aorta.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old girl presents with gradual onset of weight loss, anorexia, abdominal distension with ascites, and back pain with progressive weakness of the lower limbs for 3 months. Her TST is 14 mm. She has no cough.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the two extrapulmonary TB sites responsible for the clinical picture.
(ii) Describe the clinical features, investigations, and X-ray findings for spinal TB, including the feared neurological complication.
(iii) State the treatment regimen and its total duration for this form of TB, and the indications for steroid use.
(iv) Describe the timetable showing when each form of extrapulmonary TB typically appears after primary infection.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) with two sites:
- Abdominal TB (causing abdominal distension with ascites and abdominal masses)
- Spinal TB – Pott's disease (causing back deformity, lower limb weakness/paralysis)
(ii) Spinal TB:
- Clinical features: deformity of the spine (gibbus – angulation of the spine); lower limb weakness or paralysis; increased lower limb reflexes (upper motor neuron signs); decreased power in lower limbs
- Investigations: X-ray of the spine
- X-ray findings: gibbus (angular deformity/"hunchback"); vertebral collapse; disc space narrowing
- Feared neurological complication: lower limb weakness/paralysis from cord compression by the caseous abscess or gibbus deformity, manifesting as increased lower limb reflexes and decreased power (upper motor neuron pattern)
Abdominal TB investigations: abdominal ultrasound scan; ascitic tap; FNAC; abdominal X-ray
(iii) Treatment regimen and steroid indications:
- Spinal TB (osteoarticular TB) falls under Regimen 2: 2RHZE/10RH
- Total duration: 12 months (2 months intensive phase RHZE + 10 months continuation phase RH)
- Drugs: H = Isoniazid 10-15 mg/kg/day; R = Rifampicin 10-20 mg/kg/day; Z = Pyrazinamide 25-30 mg/kg/day; E = Ethambutol 20-25 mg/kg/day
- Indications for steroids in TB treatment: TB meningitis; TB pericarditis; TB pleural effusion; hypo-adrenalism; TB laryngitis; endobronchial TB; severe hypersensitivity reaction associated with TB and anti-TB drugs; renal tract TB; massive lymph node enlargement with pressure effect
(iv) Timetable of extrapulmonary TB after primary infection:
- Pulmonary TB: within a few months
- Miliary and meningeal TB: 2-6 months
- TB adenitis: 3-9 months
- Bones and joints: several years
- Renal and genital TB: >10 years
- PTB from reactivation of a dormant TB focus takes a number of years after primary infection

questions.question:
A. Describe Aortic Stenosis (AS) in children under the following headings:
A(i) State the three anatomical types, and for each type: its specific anatomical location of obstruction, its auscultatory characteristics (where the murmur is loudest and any specific pulse finding), and its associations (syndrome, if any)
A(ii) Describe the incidence of AS in the Ibadan series and state the commonest cause of heart failure in the first year of life from left ventricular outflow obstruction

B. Describe the clinical presentation of severe aortic stenosis:
B(i) Three symptoms in older patients and their physiological basis
B(ii) Three physical signs and how each arises
B(iii) State the investigation findings on CXR, ECG, and ECHO

C. State the treatment of aortic stenosis: conservative management and the procedures for symptomatic patients, including what antibiotic prophylaxis is given and for how long.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Three anatomical types of AS:
1. Valvar AS (bicuspid or unicuspid):
- Location: at the level of the aortic valve leaflets
- Auscultation: ejection systolic murmur at right upper sternal edge (2nd right intercostal space); aortic ejection click at the apex; reversed splitting of S2; ± diastolic murmur; ± 4th heart sound
- Association: Bicuspid aortic valve — common in middle age, usually asymptomatic with/without calcification (seen on lateral CXR); in infancy, severe AS ± coarctation = commonest cause of heart failure in first year of life (hypoplastic LHS)

2. Subvalvar (fibromuscular diaphragm/elongated stenotic tunnel):
- Location: below the valve (fibromuscular band)
- Auscultation: murmur maximum at 3rd or 4th right intercostal space (slightly lower than aortic area)
- No specific syndrome

3. Supravalvar:
- Location: above the valve (aortic root/ascending aorta)
- Specific finding: Right arm pulse is greater than left arm pulse (blood jet directed into right brachiocephalic artery — Coanda effect)
- Association: Williams syndrome (mental retardation, elfin facies, hypercalcaemia, aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis — double arterial stenosis)

A(ii) Incidence in Ibadan: 0.6% (7.5%) of 635 cases of CHD over 10 years (rare in Ibadan).
Commonest cause of heart failure in first year of life from LVOT obstruction: Severe aortic stenosis ± coarctation of the aorta (hypoplastic left heart syndrome).

B(i) Three symptoms in severe AS (older patients):
1. Dyspnoea on exertion — LV cannot increase output on demand; pulmonary congestion
2. Syncope on exercise — inadequate cerebral perfusion from fixed cardiac output
3. Angina of effort — subendocardial ischaemia from hypertrophied LV with increased oxygen demand and reduced coronary reserve

B(ii) Three physical signs:
1. Pulse of small volume and slow-rising (anacrotic): obstruction reduces and delays peak aortic flow
2. Systolic thrill at 2nd right intercostal space (aortic area): turbulent flow across stenotic valve
3. S2 may be single OR reversed splitting: A2 is delayed (LV empties slowly), so A2 follows P2; on expiration the gap between P2 and A2 widens (paradoxical/reversed splitting)

B(iii) Investigations:
CXR: Normal initially; post-stenotic dilatation of ascending aorta develops with time; cardiomegaly with prominence of ascending aorta; ± calcification of aortic valve in older patients
ECG: May be normal; or shows LVH; inverted T-wave
ECHO: Shows thickened valve; left ventricular hypertrophy; Doppler demonstrates turbulence across the obstruction; shows anatomic change

C. Treatment:
Conservative (mild): Antibiotic prophylaxis when going for dental or surgical procedures — given for over 72 hours (starting 24 hours before, during, and after the procedure)
Symptomatic patient:
1. Aortic valvotomy
2. Valve replacement — if there is calcific stenosis

A. A critically ill child is any child with a severe problem with the airway, breathing, or circulation, or acute deterioration of conscious state; including apnoea, upper airway obstruction, hypoxaemia, central cyanosis, severe respiratory distress; total inability to feed; shock, severe dehydration, active bleeding requiring transfusion; unconsciousness or seizures.

A(i) Airway:
Positioning: responsive child — position of comfort; unresponsive — turn child to the side.
Check if airway is patent and maintainable: head tilt-chin lift; suctioning; relieve foreign body if present; insertion of oropharyngeal airway.
If patency cannot be maintained by simple manoeuvre, advanced airway: endotracheal tube; CPAP/non-invasive ventilation; cricothyrotomy.

A(ii) Breathing assessment: respiratory rate and pattern; respiratory effort; chest expansion and air movement; lung and airway sounds; O2 saturation by pulse oximetry. Signs of probable respiratory failure: very rapid or inadequate respiratory rate (apnoea).

A(iii) Circulation assessment: heart rate and rhythm; pulse rate and synchronicity (peripheral and central); capillary refill time; skin colour and temperature; blood pressure.
Normal BP (1–10 years): 90 + 2n mmHg (n = age in years).
Hypotension: <70 + 2n mmHg.

B. Disability:
Level of consciousness: AVPU scale or GCS.
Pupillary response (PERRL): pinpoint, dilated, or unequal pupils.
Glucose level: must always be checked.

C. Classification table (Appearance / Work of Breathing / Circulation):
- Stable: Normal / Normal / Normal
- Respiratory distress: Normal / Abnormal / Normal
- Respiratory failure: Abnormal / Abnormal / ±Normal
- Compensated shock: Normal / Normal / Abnormal
- Decompensated shock: Abnormal / Normal / Abnormal
- CNS/metabolic dysfunction: Abnormal / Normal / Normal
- Cardiopulmonary failure: Abnormal / Abnormal / Abnormal
Early recognition and prompt intervention are critical to halting progression to cardiopulmonary arrest.
questions.question:
A. Define who is a critically ill child and describe the full primary assessment (ABCDE) of a critically ill child under each heading:
A(i) Airway — positioning and interventions from simple to advanced
A(ii) Breathing — parameters assessed and signs of probable respiratory failure
A(iii) Circulation — parameters assessed, formula for normal and hypotensive blood pressure

B. Describe the Disability assessment, including the tools used for consciousness, pupillary responses, and the metabolic parameter that must be checked.

C. Explain the clinical basis of the classification table (Appearance, Work of Breathing, Circulation) as it relates to six physiological states: stable, respiratory distress, respiratory failure, compensated shock, decompensated shock, and cardiopulmonary failure.

questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Impetigo (bullous form). Clinical types: Bullous impetigo (Staph. aureus); Impetigo contagiosa (mixed Staph. aureus + Streptococcus pyogenes). Infection due to Strep. pyogenes and Staph. aureus, especially in hot humid climates; small, thin-walled vesicles or pustules rupture to form characteristic yellow-brown crust. Bullous form due to strains of Staph. aureus that produce a toxin causing a sub-corneal split; may lead to Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).

(ii) Predisposing factors: poor personal hygiene, warm moist climate; nasal colonisation also occurs.
Impetigo contagiosa: thin-walled vesicles/pustules rupturing to form characteristic yellow-brown crust (superficial).
Ecthyma: due to Staph. or/and Streptococcus but deeper than impetigo; involves the whole of the epidermis; usually a firm crust on a superficial ulcer surrounded by erythema.

(iii) Known complication: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (APSG) may complicate streptococcal infection. Both Staph. aureus and Strep. pyogenes are NOT part of normal skin flora.

(iv) Management:
Topical antibiotics: mupirocin in limited lesions; application of topical antibiotics in minor trauma in children in areas of high risk may be helpful. Note: topical antibiotics will not eradicate nasal carriage.
Systemic antibiotics: penicillin, cloxacillin, or clindamycin.
Secondary infection of primary skin disease also requires treatment with systemic agents.
questions.question:
A 5-year-old child presents with multiple yellow-brown crusted lesions on the face and arms. Some lesions are bullous. He lives in a hot, humid environment with poor personal hygiene.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis? State the causative organisms for each clinical type and the pathogenic mechanism of the bullous form.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and distinguish clinically between impetigo contagiosa and ecthyma.
(iii) State the known complication of streptococcal skin infection and the relationship of both Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes to normal skin flora.
(iv) Outline the full management — topical and systemic antibiotics — and state what topical antibiotics cannot achieve even when applied in minor trauma.

A 10-year-old boy presents with a 2-year history of progressive symmetric weakness starting in the legs and spreading upward to the arms. Two weeks before admission he had a febrile diarrhoeal illness. On examination he is afebrile, has reduced power in all four limbs (lower > upper), absent deep tendon reflexes, bilateral symmetrical involvement, and mild sensory impairment. CSF examination shows high protein with few cells.

(i) What is the diagnosis? Distinguish this from paralytic poliomyelitis based on the clinical and CSF findings.
(ii) List all the organisms/conditions associated with this diagnosis.
(iii) State the life-threatening complication and the monitoring required.
(iv) Outline the complete management, justifying the use of plasmapheresis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS).
Distinction from paralytic poliomyelitis:
- GBS: paralysis is bilateral and symmetrical, ascending pattern, sensory impairment common, DTR absent; CSF shows cytoalbuminologic dissociation (high protein, few or no cells); associated preceding infection with the listed organisms; recovery is generally complete in >90%.
- Poliomyelitis: paralysis is spotty, haphazard, asymmetrical; NO sensory deficit; CSF shows aseptic/viral meningitis picture; virus isolated on stool culture; weakness present at 12 months is usually permanent.

(ii) Associated organisms/conditions:
- Mumps virus, ECHO virus, Influenza virus, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Mycoplasma.
- Also: vaccinations against rabies and influenza (as stated in the chapter text).
- Infectious mononucleosis; and other post-infectious causes.

(iii) Life-threatening complication: paralysis of intercostal muscles leading to respiratory failure and death. Monitoring required: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, signs of respiratory compromise (breathlessness, use of accessory muscles, apnoea), and bulbar muscle involvement. Cranial nerve involvement should be monitored.

(iv) Management:
i. Bed rest.
ii. Mechanical ventilation if there is respiratory compromise.
iii. Steroids — may or may not be used.
iv. Plasmapheresis: the patient's blood is filtered; red cells are removed, reconstituted with donor plasma, and re-infused; the patient's own plasma (containing the pathogenic antibodies against peripheral nerves) is discarded. This is life-saving because it removes the autoimmune antibodies responsible for the demyelination.
Prognosis: recovery is complete in a few weeks in >90% of cases; a few die from respiratory embarrassment.

(i) Hyperhaemolytic crisis (rapid RBC destruction, increased baseline jaundice, cola-coloured urine, drop in PCV, increased reticulocyte count).
Four main types: vaso-occlusive crisis (painful episodes in body sites, occurs with or without intercurrent illness); aplastic crisis (temporary destruction of RBC precursors by parvovirus B19, recovery in 10 days, severe pallor, rapid fall in PCV, reticulocyte count <1%); sequestration crisis (sites: spleen, liver, lungs; varying pallor, organomegaly, low PCV, increased retic count); hyperhaemolytic crisis (rapid RBC destruction, increased baseline jaundice, cola-coloured urine, drop in PCV, increased retic count).
Other complications: acute chest syndrome, priapism, stroke.

(ii) Hyperhaemolytic crisis involves increased jaundice and cola-coloured urine. Distinguished from aplastic crisis: aplastic crisis — severe pallor, weakness, rapid fall in PCV, reticulocyte count <1% (bone marrow suppression by parvovirus B19); hyperhaemolytic crisis — increased jaundice, drop in PCV, increased reticulocyte count (active haemolysis). Risk factors for crises: intercurrent illness (as trigger).

(iii) Vaso-occlusive crisis: bed rest; liberal fluids; analgesics; reassurance; treatment of precipitating cause; rule out osteomyelitis if bone VOC; continue routine drugs and vitamin C; avoid precipitating factors.
Hyperhaemolytic crisis: monitoring vital signs, PCV, jaundice, urine rack; may need blood transfusion; treat precipitating cause; continue routine drugs.

(iv) Acute chest syndrome: treat potential underlying infections; adequate pain management; maintain hydration with caution; maintain oxygenation; exchange transfusion; incentive spirometry. Justification for exchange transfusion: reduces the proportion of HbS-containing cells, improving oxygen delivery to the lungs.
Stroke: immediate exchange blood transfusion; hydration; monitor for seizures and treat. Prevention of recurrence: hypertransfusion regimen 3–4 times per year to bring HbS to 30% (caution: iron overload); bone marrow transplantation; surgery. Justification for exchange transfusion: lowers HbS proportion rapidly, halting the vascular occlusion causing CNS damage.
questions.question:
An 8-year-old known sickle cell disease patient is brought in with bilateral leg pain and mild jaundice. His PCV is 16% (baseline 22%), reticulocyte count is elevated, and urine is cola-coloured.

(i) What type of sickle cell crisis is this? List all four main types of crises and the other complications mentioned.
(ii) State the risk factors for this type of crisis and distinguish it from aplastic crisis using the key haematological differences stated.
(iii) Describe the management of vaso-occlusive crisis and hyperhaemolytic crisis.
(iv) Describe the management of stroke and acute chest syndrome as given, justifying one intervention used in each.

A 3-year-old boy with a 10-day history of productive cough, fever, and weight loss has enlarged, painless cervical lymph nodes with skin erythema and early fluctuation. His Mantoux is 13 mm. He has no history of BCG vaccination.
(i) State the diagnosis and outline all the investigations required to confirm it.
(ii) Describe the pathogenesis from inhalation of M. tuberculosis to the development of TB adenitis.
(iii) State the treatment regimen for TB adenitis, including drugs, doses, and total duration.
(iv) List the side effects of each first-line anti-TB drug.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: TB adenitis (scrofula). Investigations:
- Bacteriological: Xpert MTB/RIF (now 1st line); AFB for microscopy; culture on Lowenstein Jensen or MGIT media
- Specimens: fine needle aspirate (FNA) for cytology and culture; lymph node biopsy for histology
- Mantoux test: ≥10 mm positive (irrespective of BCG); already 13 mm – positive
- HIV test for all cases of TB
- Chest X-ray (to assess pulmonary involvement)
(ii) Pathogenesis to TB adenitis:
- M. tuberculosis inhaled as airborne droplet nuclei; one cough produces 3,000 droplet nuclei
- Organisms inhaled, replicate locally in tracheal and bronchial epithelium
- A cellular immune response begins after viable bacilli are inhaled
- Primary complex forms: primary focus (sub-pleural lesion) + regional lymph node that drains the area (e.g. hilar or paratracheal nodes for lung)
- TB granuloma develops: focal area of granulomatous inflammation characterized by central caseous necrosis
- Fibrosis/encapsulation of nodes with viable TB bacilli persisting within the node for years – source of reactivation TB
- For cervical adenitis: primary focus may be in the oropharynx or tonsil draining to cervical nodes; or haematogenous spread from primary pulmonary focus; appearing 3-9 months after primary infection
(iii) Treatment regimen for TB adenitis:
- TB adenitis is a form of EPTB that is NOT TB meningitis, miliary TB, or osteoarticular TB
- Use Regimen 1: 2RHZE/4RH; total duration 6 months
- Intensive phase: 2 months RHZE daily
- Continuation phase: 4 months RH daily
- Drug doses: Rifampicin 10-20 mg/kg/day; Isoniazid 10-15 mg/kg/day; Pyrazinamide 25-30 mg/kg/day; Ethambutol 20-25 mg/kg/day
(iv) Side effects of first-line anti-TB drugs:
- Rifampicin: orange discoloration of urine and tears; gastrointestinal disturbance; hepatotoxicity; thrombocytopaenia
- Isoniazid: peripheral neuritis; hepatotoxicity; psychosis
- Pyrazinamide: hyperuricaemia; skin rash; hepatotoxicity
- Ethambutol: optic neuritis; hepatotoxicity

questions.question:
A. Describe the CXR evaluation of heart size and shape in congenital heart disease under the following headings:
A(i) State the normal cardiothoracic ratio for children under 1 year, for those under 2 years, and for those above 5 years, and list four causes of cardiomegaly on CXR
A(ii) For a right-sided aortic arch on CXR: list three conditions in which it is seen; state in which percentage of Tetralogy of Fallot cases it is found; and explain when a right-sided arch can be considered normal

B. Describe the situs and cardiac position as evaluated on CXR:
B(i) Define situs solitus, situs inversus, and ambiguus, and state which structure's position on CXR is used to determine atrial situs
B(ii) Define laevocardia, dextrocardia, and mesocardia
B(iii) Give a clinical example of situs inversus with dextrocardia — state what the liver shadow and stomach gas bubble positions would be on CXR

C. Explain the CXR finding of the following conditions:
C(i) What the pulmonary artery appearance is in post-stenotic dilatation vs. TOF (pulmonary bay) and how each arises
C(ii) What is shown by pulmonary plethora vs. oligaemia and give two causes of each
questions.answerText:
A(i) Normal cardiothoracic ratio:
- Children under 1 year: up to 60% (50–60% allowed)
- Under 2 years: 50% should be the upper limit
- Above 5 years: should not be enlarged beyond 50%
Four causes of cardiomegaly:
1. Heart failure (chamber dilatation/hypertrophy)
2. Pericardial effusion
3. Endomyocardial fibrosis
4. Individual chamber enlargement

A(ii) Right-sided aortic arch:
Three conditions in which it is seen:
1. Tetralogy of Fallot (commonest — NOT seen in all cases, only about 25–30%)
2. Pulmonary atresia
3. Truncus arteriosus
Percentage in TOF: 25–30% of patients.
When normal: In dextrocardia, where the apex points to the right, a right-sided aortic arch can be considered normal.

B(i) Situs:
- Situs solitus: Normal — liver shadow on the right, stomach gas bubble on the left
- Situs inversus: Mirror image — liver shadow on the left, stomach gas bubble on the right
- Situs ambiguus: Liver shadow in the middle
The structure used to determine atrial situs: Left bronchus (normally longer than right). If the left bronchus is seen on the right on CXR, it is 99% certain that the right atrium is on the left (situs inversus).

B(ii) Cardiac position:
- Laevocardia: Apex pointing to the left (normal)
- Dextrocardia: Apex pointing to the right
- Mesocardia: Apex direction indeterminate

B(iii) Situs inversus with dextrocardia:
Liver shadow: On the left (mirrored)
Stomach gas bubble: On the right (mirrored)
Apex: Pointing to the right

C(i) Pulmonary artery appearance:
- Post-stenotic dilatation (valvar PS): The jet flow through the stenotic valve is directed at the wall of the main pulmonary artery, causing it to dilate — seen as a pulmonary knuckle (prominent main pulmonary artery segment on CXR).
- TOF (pulmonary bay): The small/absent pulmonary artery (due to infundibular/subvalvar stenosis reducing PA flow) creates a concavity (bay) in the area where the pulmonary artery knuckle normally is — seen as a pulmonary bay.

C(ii) Pulmonary plethora vs. oligaemia:
Plethora (increased PVM): Caused by (1) large left-to-right shunts; (2) heart failure; (3) pulmonary venous obstruction
Oligaemia (decreased PVM): Caused by (1) Tetralogy of Fallot; (2) Pulmonary atresia; (both are severe obstructions to pulmonary blood flow)

(i) This child has severe dehydration. Signs justifying this classification include: lethargic/drowsy and unresponsive (inability to drink), very sunken eyes with absent tears, parched mucous membranes, no urine output (oliguria/anuria), absent detectable blood pressure (shock), and profound weakness. Inability to drink, lethargic or drowsy/unconscious state, very sunken eyes with absent tears, and parched mucous membranes characterise severe dehydration, indicating loss exceeding 10% of body weight.
(ii) Vibrio cholerae O1 produces cholera toxin (CT), which activates adenylyl cyclase in intestinal enterocytes. This causes massive cyclic AMP (cAMP) accumulation, leading to opening of CFTR chloride channels with consequent massive chloride secretion and water efflux into the intestinal lumen — a pure secretory mechanism. There is little or no structural mucosal damage in cholera, distinguishing it from invasive/inflammatory diarrhoea.
(iii) Immediate resuscitation: severe dehydration with shock requires urgent intravenous fluid resuscitation — oral rehydration is contraindicated in a child who is unable to drink, lethargic, or in shock. IV Ringer's lactate or normal saline is administered rapidly. ORT is not appropriate at this stage because the child cannot drink safely and absorption depends on an intact enough gut for the sodium-glucose cotransporter to function. Recovery of consciousness and ability to drink signals readiness to transition to ORT.
(iv) ORT exploits the fact that the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) in the enterocyte brush border remains functional even during secretory diarrhoea caused by cholera toxin. Glucose enhances sodium absorption via SGLT1, which brings water with it by osmosis, effectively correcting dehydration despite ongoing diarrhoea. The antibiotic indicated for confirmed cholera is azithromycin (or doxycycline in older children), which reduces the duration and volume of diarrhoea and bacterial shedding, though ORS remains the cornerstone of treatment.
questions.question:
A 4-year-old child living in a flood-affected Nigerian community is brought to the health post unable to drink, lying limp and unresponsive, with no tears, very sunken eyes, a parched mouth, and no urine output in 8 hours. The community health worker reports 'rice-water' stools since the previous day. Temperature is 36.1°C. Glucose stick test: 3.2 mmol/L. Blood pressure is undetectable. Stool culture later confirms Vibrio cholerae O1.

(i) Classify the degree of dehydration and identify the signs that justify this classification.
(ii) Describe the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which Vibrio cholerae O1 produces this degree of fluid loss, naming the enterotoxin and the intracellular pathway activated.
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitation protocol, specifying the intravenous fluid strategy, and explain why oral rehydration is not appropriate at this stage.
(iv) State the principles underlying oral rehydration therapy (ORT) for subsequent management, identifying the transporter exploited, and name the antibiotic indicated for confirmed cholera.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Polysaccharide vaccines: a unique type of inactivated subunit vaccine composed of long chains of sugar molecules making up the surface capsule of certain bacteria. They are not very immunogenic. Three diseases for which pure polysaccharide vaccines are available: pneumococcal disease (Pneumococcal Polysaccharide Vaccine); meningococcal disease; Salmonella Typhi.

A(ii) Recombinant vaccines: produced by genetic engineering technology; produced by inserting genetic material from a disease-causing organism into a harmless cell, which replicates the proteins of the disease-causing organisms; the proteins are then purified and used as vaccine. Example: Hepatitis B vaccine — produced by insertion of a segment of the hepatitis B virus gene into the gene of a yeast cell; the modified yeast cell produces pure hepatitis B surface antigen when it grows.

A(iii) Guiding principles in planning for immunisation in a community:
- Epidemiology of the disease: incidence and prevalence; immunisation given in order of priority (children and others at risk, e.g., elderly, health workers)
- Age-specific morbidity and mortality: routine vaccines recommended at the youngest age at which significant risk exists and a protective immunologic response can be expected
- Some vaccines recommended only in special circumstances (e.g., pneumococcal vaccine in haemoglobinopathies)
- Vaccines also used to control outbreaks (e.g., meningococcal disease)
- Routes of immunisation: oral (OPV), IM (IPV), SC (measles), intradermal (BCG)

B. Adverse effects: mild — fever, pain at injection site (clear up quickly). Controversial/reported serious: diphtheria/tetanus toxoid and encephalopathy, brachial neuritis, Guillain-Barré; Hib vaccine and early onset of Hib disease; rubella and chronic arthritis; MMR and thrombocytopenia and autism — most of these reports not supported by scientific evidence (the MMR-autism paper was retracted).
True contraindications: anaphylactic hypersensitivity to a prior dose; moderate to severe acute illness.

C. Herd immunity: the level of resistance of a community or group of people to a particular disease. It occurs through: clinical or subclinical infection in the community; high and continuous immunisation rates. When a critical percentage of the population is vaccinated (>80%), spread of disease is effectively stopped because the susceptible persons are reduced to a small proportion. When there is herd immunity, it provides an immunological barrier to the spread of disease in the community; with sufficiently high herd immunity, the occurrence of an epidemic is unlikely; eventually the disease may be eliminated.
questions.question:

A(i) Polysaccharide vaccines — including why they are not very immunogenic and the three diseases for which pure polysaccharide vaccines are available
A(ii) Recombinant vaccines — the process of production and an example
A(iii) The guiding principles in planning for immunisation in a community

B. State the known or controversial adverse effects and true contraindications to immunisation.

C. Explain the concept of herd immunity in full, including the threshold of coverage required, the mechanism by which it protects susceptible individuals, and the possible outcome when herd immunity is sufficiently high.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Origin, synthesis, transport, and mode of action of thyroid hormones:
• Origin: produced by the follicular cells of the thyroid gland. The thyroid originates from embryonic endoderm; its median part originates by proliferation and invagination of the median endoderm of the foregut at the level of the first and second pharyngeal pouches, commencing between the 2nd and 3rd weeks of gestation. The parafollicular cells (C cells) originate from the ultimo branchial body. Located at the level of the 5th–7th cervical and 1st thoracic vertebrae; weight 25 g.
• Synthesis steps:
  1. Trapping of iodide from plasma by the thyroid gland under the influence of TSH (blocked by thiocyanate and perchlorate).
  2. Oxidation of iodide to iodine by thyroid peroxidase.
  3. Incorporation of iodine into tyrosine on thyroglobulin in the colloid to form MIT and DIT (inhibited by carbimazole and propylthiouracil).
  4. Coupling of iodotyrosyl residues to form T3 and T4.
  5. Splitting off of T3 and T4 from thyroglobulin by proteolytic enzymes stimulated by TSH (inhibited by iodide); released into circulation.
  6. T4 is produced exclusively by the thyroid gland. Biologically active T3 is formed by peripheral deiodination of the outer β ring of T4 in the liver, kidney, and muscle. Inner α ring deiodination produces inactive rT3.
• Transport: almost entirely bound to plasma proteins. TBG binds about 70% of plasma T4 and 80% of plasma T3. Approximately 0.05% of plasma T4 and 0.2% of plasma T3 are free (biologically active fraction).
• Mode of action: free fraction is biologically active; actively transported into cells by an ATP-dependent adenylate cyclase. T3 acts mainly at the nucleus where it binds to specific receptors which activate T3-responsive genes, stimulating basal metabolic rate and metabolism of lipids, carbohydrate, and proteins. Thyroid hormone is necessary for normal brain growth and myelination, normal neuronal connections, and epiphyseal maturation.

A(ii) Monitoring thyroid replacement in congenital hypothyroidism:
• Medication: L-T4 10 mcg/kg/day by mouth once daily.
• Monitoring schedule: Recheck T4 and TSH 2–4 weeks after initial treatment; every 1–2 months in the first 6 months; every 3–4 months between 6 months and 3 years of age; every 6–12 months from 3 years to end of growth.
• Goal: normalise TSH and maintain T4 and FT4 in the upper half of the reference range. Best index of adequate treatment is suppression of TSH to normal levels. Somatic growth may be corrected. Assess permanence: thyroid scan shows ectopic/absent gland = permanent CH; if TSH <50 mU/L and no increase in TSH after newborn period, trial off therapy at 3 years.

B(i) Brain damage is irreversible because thyroid hormone is necessary for normal brain growth, myelination, and formation of normal neuronal connections. The most critical period for brain development affected by hypothyroidism is the first few weeks or months of life. Thyroxine must be available during this critical window; if absent, neuronal migration, synaptogenesis, and myelination are permanently disrupted. Once this developmental window closes, neural circuits cannot be re-established even with subsequent T4 replacement. Somatic growth deficits (short stature, delayed bone age, epiphyseal dysgenesis) may be corrected because bone growth plates remain responsive to thyroid hormone and growth hormone at later ages, allowing catch-up growth with adequate T4 replacement.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, synthesis steps, transport, and mode of action of thyroid hormones T3 and T4.
A(ii) State the safe approach to monitoring thyroid replacement therapy in congenital hypothyroidism, including which investigations should be used and at what intervals.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity (neurological or growth deficit) seen in untreated congenital hypothyroidism, specifically why brain damage is irreversible but somatic growth deficits may be corrected.

An 8-year-old boy presents with a 6-week history of early-morning headache relieved by standing, projectile vomiting on waking from sleep, and bilateral papilloedema. His mother reports recent-onset head tilting to the right and diplopia.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what does the clinical presentation indicate about the site and mechanism of disease?
(ii) List ALL the investigations that would be performed, including their expected findings.
(iii) What treatment modalities are available and which is preferred for each histological tumour type?
(iv) What features of CNS malignancy carry localising versus non-localising significance, and how does the site (infratentorial versus supratentorial) differ in Nigerian versus worldwide populations?
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: CNS Malignancy (Brain Tumour).
- Early-morning headache relieved by standing, projectile vomiting on waking, bilateral papilloedema, and head tilting indicate features of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) from an intracranial mass.
- Diplopia and 6th cranial nerve palsy are present; note that 6th cranial nerve palsy does NOT have any localising value.
- Head tilting to one side is a feature of CNS tumour.
- Clinical features depend on histological characteristics and rate of growth of tumour.
(ii) Investigations and expected findings:
- Skull X-ray: showing copper-beating or silver-beating appearance (raised ICP).
- Plain radiography: raised ICP.
- Angiography.
- Myelography.
- Cranial CT.
- MRI and Nuclear MRI.
- CSF Cytology.
- EEG: for localisation of tumour.
- Endocrine tests depending on the tumour: ACTH, TSH, GH, LH and FSH.
(iii) Treatment modalities by tumour type:
- Surgery: for craniopharyngioma.
- Radiotherapy: for brain stem glioma (may be the main modality).
- Combination chemotherapy.
- Treatment depends on localisation.
Side effects of radiotherapy (relevant here): Early — alopecia, skin erythema and desquamation, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, bone marrow suppression. Late — impaired growth and development of epiphyseal growth plates, development of secondary tumours.
(iv) Localising versus non-localising features and site differences:
- 6th cranial nerve palsy: does NOT have any localising value.
- Focal neurological deficits: have localising value (depend on side of brain affected).
- Rapid head enlargement, papilloedema, early morning headache, projectile vomiting, and diplopia: features of raised ICP, not specific to tumour location.
Site differences: Worldwide, >50% of CNS malignancies arise in the posterior fossa (infratentorial). In Ibadan (Nigeria), most CNS tumours are hemispheric (supratentorial). Peak age is common in the second half of the first decade. Primary tumours are commoner; secondary tumours are rare. Majority arise from glial cells e.g. Astrocytoma, Ependymomas.

questions.question:
A. Describe the right-sided cardiac catheterisation route in children under the following headings:
A(i) The route of the catheter from peripheral access to the pulmonary artery
A(ii) Three specific pieces of information obtained during a right-sided study
A(iii) State the major complication of cardiac catheterisation

B. Describe the left-sided cardiac catheterisation route and state what additional therapeutic procedure can be performed via cardiac catheterisation in transposition of the great arteries (TGA), including the technique.

C. Explain why echocardiography is now preferred over cardiac catheterisation as the primary diagnostic tool for congenital heart disease in children, distinguishing between M-mode, 2D, Doppler, and colour flow mapping.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Right-sided catheterisation route:
Femoral vein → Inferior vena cava → Right atrium → Right ventricle → Pulmonary artery

A(ii) Information obtained during right-sided study:
- Anatomy: to confirm structural defects (e.g. ASD, VSD, PDA)
- Pressures: to measure pressures within each chamber (which can now also be calculated with M-mode echo)
- Oximetry: oxygen saturation measurement at each level

A(iii) Major complication of cardiac catheterisation: Bleeding

B. Left-sided catheterisation route:
Femoral artery → Descending aorta → Left ventricle
Therapeutic procedure in TGA: Rashkind's Atrial Septostomy — a balloon catheter is passed via the right-sided route into the right atrium, crosses the foramen ovale into the left atrium, then the balloon is inflated and pulled back forcefully to make the foramen ovale patent and create an atrial septal defect; this allows mixing of blood between the two parallel circuits.

C. Echocardiography is preferred because:
- It can be repeated many times safely (unlike catheterisation, which is highly invasive)
- M-mode (Motion mode): used for measurements and to assess cardiac function; NOT good for structural defects
- 2D (two-dimensional) mode: shows cross-sections of the heart; extremely useful for structural defects (e.g. detecting holes, VSD, ASD)
- Doppler: demonstrates pressures and turbulence across obstructions
- Colour flow mapping: demonstrates the direction of blood flow (e.g. left-to-right shunt in VSD)
Cardiac catheterisation is now used selectively — mainly when pulmonary vascular disease is suspected (to measure pulmonary wedge pressure in Wood units) or when combined with therapeutic intervention.

questions.question:
Describe the timetable, investigation, and treatment of the different forms of tuberculosis in children under the following headings, and explain the basis of the Mantoux test interpretation.
A(i) Pulmonary TB in children: pathological findings and radiological features
A(ii) Presumptive TB case: important symptoms and signs to look for in a child
B(i) Mantoux test: how it is done, how to interpret results in immunocompetent and immunocompromised children
B(ii) Bacterial investigations for TB: Xpert MTB/RIF versus AFB smear microscopy versus culture; strengths and limitations of each
C(i) Side effects of all four first-line anti-TB drugs and which drug requires special monitoring
C(ii) Prevention of TB in the community and management of contacts including the newborn of a mother with TB
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pulmonary TB in children:
- Commonest form of TB; occurs alone or in combination with other forms (70% of cases)
- PTB in children consists mainly of primary complex and direct progression of its components
- Pathological findings: hilar enlargement → bronchial compression with resulting hyperinflation or atelectasis; consolidation (patchy or lobar ±pneumothorax and pleural effusion); cavitation
- Radiological features: perihilar adenopathy (perihilar and sub-carinal enlarged lymph nodes encircling the carina with some airway obstruction – "doughnut" or "hamburger" sign as seen on lateral view); cavity formation
- Differential diagnosis: pneumonia (bacterial, viral, mycoplasma); lung abscess; bronchiectasis; pulmonary fungal infections; pulmonary neoplasm
A(ii) Presumptive TB – symptoms and signs:
- Important symptoms: cough ≥2 weeks; weight loss/FTT; fever ±night sweats; history of contact with adult with TB symptoms in last 2 years; history of death in family attributable to TB/HIV/AIDS
- Signs – general physical examination: chronically ill, wasted, febrile, pallor, lymphadenopathy especially cervical, phlycternular conjunctivitis (red eye with white speck(s) at border of cornea)
- Anthropometric: underweight (60-80% of normal body weight); marasmic (<60% of normal); stunted (height <90% expected); MUAC in 1-5 years: normal 13.5-16 cm
- Other systemic: abdominal distension with/without ascites and/or hepatosplenomegaly; gibbus (angulation of spine) ±decreased power and increased LL reflexes (UMN)
B(i) Mantoux test:
- Interpretation: 0-4 mm = negative; 5-9 mm = borderline; ≥10 mm = positive irrespective of BCG vaccination
- ≥5 mm = positive in HIV-infected children and severely malnourished children (marasmus, kwashiorkor)
- A positive test occurs when a person is infected with M. tb but does not necessarily indicate disease
B(ii) Bacterial investigations:
- Xpert MTB/RIF: new automated NAAT endorsed by WHO; now 1st line for diagnosis of both DS-TB and DR-TB; detects M. tb Complex and Rifampicin resistant strains; requires only one sputum sample; results ready in 2 hours; non-respiratory samples (gastric aspirate, extra-pulmonary TB) can also be tested; not useful for monitoring
- AFB microscopy: useful for PTB diagnosis where Xpert MTB/RIF is not available; also for monitoring; 2 sputum samples: on spot and early morning after overnight fast; sensitivity 86-98% by skilled microscopist; lower sensitivity at low parasitaemias
- Culture: gold standard; expensive; solid media (Lowenstein Jensen – traditional, slow, up to 6 weeks); MGIT liquid agar (shorter turnaround)
C(i) Side effects of anti-TB drugs:
- Rifampicin: orange discoloration of urine and tears; gastrointestinal disturbance; hepatotoxicity; thrombocytopaenia
- Isoniazid: peripheral neuritis; hepatotoxicity; psychosis
- Pyrazinamide: hyperuricaemia; skin rash; hepatotoxicity
- Ethambutol: optic neuritis; hepatotoxicity (requires monitoring of vision)
C(ii) Prevention and contact management:
- Community prevention: case-finding and effective treatment; contact tracing and INH chemoprophylaxis; BCG vaccination; improvement in the general standard of living
- Contacts: children who are contacts of smear-positive TB cases should have clinical investigations; screen with symptoms, CXR and TST
- Newborn of a mother with TB: mother's treatment commenced or continued; baby starts INH soon after delivery; CXR if symptomatic; if CXR normal, continue INH for 6 months; if CXR abnormal, treat as TB with combination chemotherapy

A(i) Definition: seizures occurring in young children as a result of elevated body temperature in the absence of a pathology in the brain. Affects 2–3% of young children between the ages of 3 months and 5 years. 25% of cases have a positive family history. Common causes of fever: malaria, URTI, pharyngo-tonsillitis, otitis media, bronchopneumonia, UTI, measles. Seizures are usually brief, generalised tonic–clonic, and occur in conjunction with a rapid rise in body temperature.

A(ii) Classification:
Simple febrile seizure: single attack in a 24-hour period; seizures are generalised; last <15 minutes; commoner form.
Complex febrile seizure: multiple attacks in a 24-hour period; seizures are focal; duration >15 minutes.

A(iii) Management:
1. ABC of resuscitation (airway, breathing, circulation).
2. Establish IV line; check blood sugar — if <40 mg/dl correct hypoglycaemia (give 2–4 ml/kg of 10% D/W or 50% glucose 1–2 ml/kg diluted 1:2).
3. Abort the seizure with an anticonvulsant: rectal diazepam (age <3 years: 5 mg; age >3 years: 10 mg); IV diazepam 0.1–0.3 mg/kg/dose given slowly; IM paraldehyde 1 ml/year of life.
4. Detailed history and thorough physical examination to determine underlying cause.
5. Investigations: LP for CSF analysis (to rule out meningitis); blood film for malaria parasites; chest X-ray; urine m/c/s; random blood sugar.
6. Treat the underlying cause of fever (tepid sponging, antipyretics for temperature).
7. Reassure parents: the disease is not fatal; child will not necessarily become epileptic; no brain damage.

B(i) In children <18 months, the classic signs of meningeal irritation (neck stiffness, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs) may be absent or minimal. Therefore, meningitis cannot be excluded on clinical grounds alone, and a lumbar puncture for CSF analysis is mandatory to rule out meningitis in this age group.

B(ii) Drug is not the first line of treatment for febrile seizures. There is no longer a need for phenobarbitone for prophylaxis. Parental counselling, teaching recurrent management, and selective use of diazepam (for young age, multiple past attacks, or parental anxiety) are preferred, because the risk of epilepsy development is very small (about 1%) and recurrence does not increase that risk.

C. Distinction between febrile seizures and epilepsy:
- Febrile seizures: occur with fever; no brain pathology; age 3 months to 5 years; recurrence in 33%; risk of epilepsy very small (~1%); long-term management is counselling and selective diazepam.
- Epilepsy: afebrile seizures; defined as recurrent afebrile seizures (more than 1 episode); affects ~1% of population; various aetiologies (idiopathic, perinatal injury, CNS infections, congenital malformations, trauma, neurocutaneous syndromes, genetic, tumours); long-term management requires AEDs continued for 2–4 seizure-free years, then tapered over 3–6 months.
questions.question:
A. Describe febrile seizures under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, epidemiology, and the common causes of fever that precipitate them.
A(ii) Classification: distinguish simple from complex febrile seizures across all defining features.
A(iii) Management: outline all steps from seizure cessation to discharge, including investigations.

B. Explain the following:
B(i) The basis for performing a lumbar puncture in children under 18 months with febrile seizures, even when no neck stiffness is present.
B(ii) Why drug prophylaxis (phenobarbitone) is no longer the first-line long-term management for febrile seizures.

Describe the general principles of cancer treatment in children under the following headings:
A(i) Genetic and environmental aetiological factors.
A(ii) The role of surgery and radiotherapy, including side effects of radiotherapy.
B(i) Describe the mechanism of action and side effects of each major group of cytotoxic drugs used in paediatric oncology.
B(ii) Describe immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies, using Rituximab as an example.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiological factors:
Genetic Factors:
- Mutations in tumour suppressor genes (anti-oncogenes) e.g. retinoblastoma.
- Activation of proto-oncogenes e.g. by chromosomal translocation thereby deregulating gene expression.
- Cancer predisposition syndromes e.g. Xeroderma pigmentosum: defects in repair of DNA damaged by UV light → cancer.
Environmental Factors:
- Ionizing radiation e.g. leukaemia/atomic bomb.
- UV radiation e.g. Xeroderma pigmentosum.
- Drugs e.g. intrauterine DES – adenocarcinoma of vagina; treatment of aplastic anaemia with anabolic steroids – hepatocellular carcinoma; immunosuppressive agents – NHL.
- Viruses e.g. EBV: Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

A(ii) Surgery and Radiotherapy:
Surgery: Complete excision e.g. early nephroblastoma; Debulking e.g. rhabdomyosarcoma; May follow neo-adjuvant chemotherapy. Determinants of modality: histology, size/stage, experience, location.
Radiotherapy: May be the main modality e.g. brain stem glioma; may follow/precede surgery. Early side effects: alopecia, skin erythema and desquamation, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, bone marrow suppression. Late side effects: impaired growth and development of epiphyseal growth plates, development of secondary tumours.

B(i) Major cytotoxic drug groups:
- Alkylating agents (CC non-specific) e.g. cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide: inhibit DNA replication, RNA transcription; chromosomal breakages. S/E: haemorrhagic cystitis and fibrosis (prevent with mesna), myelosuppression, pulmonary fibrosis, infertility, darkening of nail bed.
- Antibiotics (CCNS) e.g. daunorubicin, doxorubicin: intercalate DNA helix, prevent DNA replication and RNA transcription. S/E: local vesicant; daunorubicin and doxorubicin are cardiotoxic causing cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias.
- Antimetabolites e.g. methotrexate, 5-FU, cytosine arabinoside: specific for S phase; inhibit enzymatic steps for synthesis of nucleic acids; methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. S/E: myelosuppression, stomatitis, mucositis.
- Vinca alkaloids e.g. vincristine, vinblastine: specific at M phase; inhibit microtubule formation causing mitotic arrest at metaphase. S/E: local vesicant, neuropathy.
- Enzymes e.g. L-asparaginase: specific for G1 phase. Major S/E: hypersensitivity — urticaria → anaphylaxis.

B(ii) Immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies (MABs):
- MABs bind to target antigens on cancer cells and mark them for destruction; each MAB is specific for a particular antigen.
- Rituximab: for follicular or refractory low-grade NHL; 90% of B-cell lymphomas have the CD20 antigen; Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody targeting B lymphocytes for destruction. Fifty percent of cases respond with full or partial remission.
- MABs can also be bound to a chemotherapy agent (two mechanisms attack the cell) or combined with radioactive substances (e.g. radioactive iodine) so the tumour receives a large dose while normal tissue is spared.

A(i) Airway: always provide supplemental oxygen. Endotracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is suggested if respiratory failure or airway compromise is likely (elective is safer). Benefits: decreases negative intrathoracic pressure; improves oxygenation and O2 delivery; decreases O2 consumption; allows hyperventilation if necessary.

A(ii) Vascular access: if unstable, have 60–90 seconds for peripheral IV; IO if less than 4–6 years old; central venous catheter as alternative. Fluid: isotonic — NS, Ringer's Lactate, or 5% albumin. Volume: 20–50 ml/kg rapidly if cardiac function is normal. PRBCs: to replace blood loss or if still unstable after 60 ml/kg of crystalloid (anaemia is poorly tolerated in the stressed, hypoxic, haemodynamically unstable patient). In non-hypotensive children with severe anaemia, blood transfusion is superior to crystalloid boluses. In haemorrhage: give group O PRBCs before cross-matching is complete, or type-specific non-cross-matched blood in an emergency.

A(iii) Dopamine: 1–5 mcg/kg/min (dopaminergic); 5–15 mcg/kg/min (more beta-1); 10–20 mcg/kg/min (more alpha-1); useful in distributive shock. Dobutamine: 2.5–15 mcg/kg/min (mostly beta-1, some beta-2); useful in cardiogenic shock. Epinephrine: 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min (mostly beta-1, some beta-2); >0.1–0.2 mcg/kg/min (alpha-1). Norepinephrine: 0.05–0.2 mcg/kg/min (only alpha and beta-1); use up to 1 mcg/kg/min. Milrinone: 50 mcg/kg load then 0.375–0.75 mcg/kg/min; phosphodiesterase inhibitor; increased inotropy and peripheral vasodilation (greater effect on pulmonary vasculature). Phenylephrine: 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min (pure alpha).

B. Metabolic acidosis: develops secondary to tissue hypoperfusion; profound acidosis depresses myocardial contractility and impairs catecholamines. Treatment: fluid administration and controlled ventilation. Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg, or ½ correction = 0.3 × weight (kg) × base deficit; risks: hyperosmolarity, hypocalcaemia, hypernatraemia, left-ward shift of oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.
Electrolytes: calcium is important for cardiac function and pressor effect of catecholamines; hypoglycaemia causes CNS damage and impairs cardiovascular function; check BUN and creatinine (renal function); hyperkalemia can occur from renal dysfunction and/or acidosis.
Hyperammonaemia: mild elevations common with shock; levels >1000 consistent with inborn errors of metabolism; consider Reye syndrome, toxins, hepatic failure.

C. Hypovolemic shock: initial presentation — low preload, decreased SV, decreased CO, compensatory increased HR and SVR. Response to fluids: responds well to isotonic crystalloid 20–50 ml/kg. Subsequent management: reassess perfusion, urine output, vital signs; treat the cause.
Cardiogenic shock: initial clinical presentation can be identical to hypovolemic shock. However, if no improvement or if patient worsens after giving volume — suspect cardiogenic shock. Subsequently needs invasive monitoring, further evaluation, pharmacologic therapy, and consultation with intensivist/cardiologist; balancing fluid therapy and inotropic support is very difficult.
questions.question:
A. Describe the management of shock in a child under the following headings:
A(i) Airway and breathing management, including indications for intubation and the benefits of controlled ventilation in shock
A(ii) Circulatory resuscitation — IV/IO access, fluid of choice, volume, and rate; the role of PRBCs in haemorrhagic and severe anaemic shock

C. Distinguish between hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock in terms of initial clinical presentation, response to initial fluid therapy, and how subsequent management differs.

questions.answerText:
A(i) A localized area of suppuration due to destruction of lung parenchyma with formation of a cavity containing purulent material.

A(ii) Primary: occurs in a previously healthy patient with no underlying medical disorders; caused by aspiration or pneumonia in the healthy host. Secondary: occurs in a patient with underlying or predisposing conditions; caused by a pre-existing condition (obstruction, spread from an extrapulmonary site, bronchiectasis, and/or immunocompromised state). Lung abscesses most likely occur in immunocompromised patients; in those with severe infections elsewhere (embolic spread); or in those with recurrent aspiration, malnutrition, or blunt chest trauma.

A(iii) Pathophysiology: patients predisposed to aspiration commonly have periodontal disease; a bacterial inoculum (mouth anaerobes) from the gingival crevice reaches the most dependent lung portions. Infection is initiated because bacteria are not cleared by host defence mechanisms → aspiration pneumonitis → tissue necrosis 7–14 days later → lung abscess formation. Other mechanisms: bacteraemia or tricuspid valve endocarditis causing septic emboli. Pathology: parenchyma becomes obstructed, infected, then suppurative and necrotic; inflammatory changes → suppuration and thrombosis of local blood vessels → necrosis and liquefaction; granulation tissue forms around periphery; abscess commonly ruptures into a bronchus.

A(iv) Posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segment of the lower lobes are involved most frequently because these are the most dependent portions when aspiration occurs.

B. Complications: overexpansion of the abscess (CXR shows enlarging thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level); tension pneumothorax; empyema; spontaneous rupture with seeding to other parts of the lungs. CXR of abscess: thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level.

C. Medical: antibiotics — must include antistaphylococcal agent; metronidazole for anaerobes; physiotherapy — postural drainage and chest percussion to reduce secretion. Surgical: if no response to medical therapy — pneumonotomy or lobectomy.

questions.answerText:
(i) This clinical picture — secondary amenorrhoea, defeminisation followed by virilisation (hirsutism, clitoral enlargement, voice deepening), and a solid ovarian mass in a young woman — is most consistent with a sex-cord stromal tumour specifically an arrhenoblastoma (Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour / androblastoma).

(ii) Pathophysiology: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours secrete androgens. Androgen excess causes: initial defeminisation (loss of female secondary sexual characteristics, secondary amenorrhoea), followed by progressive virilisation (hirsutism, clitoral enlargement, deepening of the voice). The solid ovarian mass on ultrasound is consistent with this tumour type.

(iii) Complications if untreated:
• Progressive virilisation: irreversible voice changes, clitoral hypertrophy, male-pattern baldness
• Infertility from androgen-induced anovulation
• Psychological and psychosocial consequences
• Risk of malignant change (not infrequently malignant but usually low grade with an indolent course)
• Spread if malignant: transperitoneal seeding, lymphatic spread

(iv) Management options:
• Surgical: for a young woman wishing to preserve fertility, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of the affected ovary alone) is appropriate if the tumour is confined to one ovary and intraoperative features are benign. A biopsy of the contralateral ovary should be performed to exclude occult tumour.
• If malignant or bilateral: staging laparotomy with TAH-BSO, omentectomy, peritoneal cytology, and pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy followed by platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy.
Justification: Unilateral oophorectomy is justified in young patients with apparently localised disease because sex cord stromal tumours are not infrequently malignant but usually low grade; preserving the contralateral ovary and uterus maintains reproductive potential while removing the androgen source.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS).
Differential diagnosis:
- Poliomyelitis (paralytic).
- Transverse myelitis.
- Diphtheritic polyneuritis.
- Hysterical paralysis.
- Sciatic nerve injury.

(ii) Expected CSF findings:
- Protein: increased.
- Cells: few or absent (pleocytosis may occur initially but later drops).
- The characteristic pattern is called cytoalbuminologic dissociation: high protein with few or no cells.

(iii) Immediate life-threatening complication: paralysis of intercostal muscles and respiratory muscles, leading to respiratory failure and death. Specific treatment: Mechanical ventilation to support respiration until the disease resolves. Plasmapheresis (filtering the patient's blood, removing red cells, reconstituting with donor plasma, re-infusing the cells, and discarding the patient's plasma that contains pathogenic antibodies against peripheral nerve myelin) — life-saving.

(iv) Drug treatments:
- Bed rest.
- Mechanical ventilation (for respiratory compromise).
- Steroids — may or may not be used (controversial).
- Plasmapheresis — life-saving.

(v) Prognosis: Not bad. Recovery is complete in a few weeks in >90% of cases. A few die from respiratory embarrassment.
Pattern of recovery: recovery begins in the reverse order to the paralysis — upper limbs recover first and lower limbs last; median recovery 7 months.
questions.question:
An 8-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset progressive ascending weakness of all four limbs over 3 days, absent reflexes, and mild fever. He had a diarrhoeal illness 3 weeks ago. A lumbar puncture is planned.

(ii) What CSF findings will you expect, and what is the name given to the characteristic CSF pattern in this condition?
