(iv) List all drug treatments for this condition, including those whose role is described as controversial.
(v) State the prognosis and the pattern of recovery.

questions.answerText:
(i) Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). Each finding corresponds to a structural component or pathological consequence:
- Boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) / upturned apex: right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) — the apex is lifted because the enlarged RV rotates it upward and to the left; this is suggestive but not diagnostic of TOF
- Pulmonary artery bay (concavity in the left heart border where the MPA shadow should be): pulmonary stenosis with small pulmonary artery — the infundibular obstruction and small pulmonary artery produce an absent or small pulmonary artery knuckle
- Reduced pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligaemia): right-to-left shunting through the VSD + severe pulmonary obstruction → less blood reaching the lungs
- Right-sided aortic arch: over-riding/dextropositioned aorta — present in 25–30% of TOF cases; the aorta arches to the right; also seen in pulmonary atresia and truncus arteriosus
- ECG: RVH + RAH + RAD — all reflect the chronic pressure overload and hypertrophy of the right ventricle and right atrium from RVOTO

(ii) Structures affected:
Right ventricle: markedly hypertrophied (pressure overload from infundibular obstruction); forms the apex.
Pulmonary artery: small and obstructed; pulmonary bay on CXR.
Aorta: over-rides the ventricular septum (dextropositioned); receives desaturated blood from the right ventricle.
VSD: allows right-to-left shunting of desaturated blood into the aorta (systemic circulation) → cyanosis; the pressure on both sides of the VSD is equalised (right = left) due to the non-restrictive large VSD.
Right atrium: enlarges secondarily (RAH on ECG) as RV pressure rises.

(iii) Differential diagnosis of cyanotic congenital heart disease by age and presence of heart failure:
6-month-old with HEART FAILURE + cyanosis: differentials — TGA (commonest), Tricuspid atresia.
6-month-old with NO heart failure: differentials — TOF (first), Tricuspid atresia. Note: TGA usually associates with heart failure (increased pulmonary blood flow and large shunts).
Other differentials: pulmonary atresia ± VSD (extreme TOF, presents earlier); univentricular heart disease.
CXR shape differentiates:
- Boot-shaped + reduced PVM + no heart failure → TOF
- Egg-on-side + increased PVM + cardiomegaly + heart failure → TGA
- Variable odd-looking heart + variable PVM + cyanosis ± HF → Tricuspid atresia
- When cyanosis + heart failure occurs in OLDER children → think Eisenmenger syndrome

(iv) Blood film paradox: the blood film paradoxically shows iron deficiency (not iron deficiency anaemia) despite markedly elevated PCV (e.g. 82–88%). The reason: the chronic hypoxia of TOF drives erythropoiesis (increased red blood cell production) as a physiological compensatory mechanism. This rapid and massive production of red cells consumes iron stores faster than they can be replaced → iron deficiency develops despite the large number of red cells (polycythaemia). There are inadequate iron stores relative to the high demand from ongoing erythropoiesis. Therefore, iron supplementation must be given to these patients, while keeping the PCV at 45–55% through plasma exchange when the PCV exceeds 60%.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child presents with cyanosis, failure to thrive, and easy fatiguability. Chest X-ray shows a normal-sized heart with a boot-shaped (coeur en sabot) silhouette, a pulmonary artery bay, reduced pulmonary vascular markings, and a right-sided aortic arch. ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy, right atrial hypertrophy, and right axis deviation.

(i) Identify the cardiac condition from these imaging and clinical clues, and state which of the four structural components each radiological/ECG finding corresponds to.
(ii) Describe all the structures and chambers affected or compressed/altered in this condition, explaining the resulting physiology.
(iii) List the differential diagnoses for a cyanotic child at this age — distinguishing the child with heart failure from the one without, and explaining how the chest X-ray shape and presence or absence of heart failure helps differentiate between them.
(iv) Explain the anatomical and clinico-pathological reasoning for why blood film in this condition paradoxically shows iron deficiency despite a markedly elevated PCV.

Describe the haematologic problems in the newborn under the following headings:
A(i) Normal haematological indices for term and preterm neonates (Hb, Haematocrit, Platelets, Reticulocytes, WBC).
A(ii) Physiological basis of the changes in oxygen delivery that occur after birth.
B(i) Describe anaemia of prematurity: definition, reasons for its exaggeration compared to term physiologic anaemia, its clinical manifestations, and its management.
B(ii) Distinguish between early-onset and late-onset neonatal anaemia: causes and treatment approach for the shocked neonate.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Normal haematological indices:
- Hb: Term Babies 14–20 g/dl (cord blood 16.8 g/dl); Preterm Babies 14 g/dl at 28 weeks (1–2 g/dl below term babies).
- Haematocrit: 45–65% (lower in preterm).
- WBC: Day 1: 6–35,000/µl; Week 1: 8–16,000/µl; 1 Month: 6–14,000/µl (a little lower in preterms).
- Platelets: 150,000–400,000/µl (up to 600,000/µl by 2–4 months).
- Reticulocytes: 2–8% Day 1; 0.5–5% Day 7; 0–0.5% at 1 Month.
- Neutrophils: Day 1: 50–80%; Day 7: 35–45%; Lymphocytes: Day 1: 31%; Day 14: 48%.

A(ii) Physiological basis of O₂ delivery changes after birth:
- In utero: Aortic O₂ sat. ~45%; increased erythropoietin production, erythropoiesis, and reticulocytes (3–7%); foetal Hb increases with gestational age; foetal blood volume ~115 ml/kg (75 ml in baby, 40 ml in placenta).
- After birth: O₂ sat. increases to 95%; reduced erythropoietin production, erythropoiesis and reticulocytes; Hb reduces to minimum values by 8–12 weeks (after which erythropoiesis resumes); HbA/HbF starts to increase; 2,3-DPG increases; O₂ delivery to tissue increases.

B(i) Anaemia of Prematurity:
Definition: Exaggeration of physiologic anaemia in preterm infants.
Reasons for exaggeration: Minimum values reached earlier (6 weeks vs 1–3 months in term); Reduced RBC survival; Iatrogenic — repeated phlebotomy for investigations; Relatively more rapid somatic growth rate; Vitamin E deficiency; Preterm infants start to produce erythropoietin again when Hb falls to 7–9 g/dl (vs 10–11 g/dl in term) because their tissues have lower O₂ requirements.
Manifestations: Pallor, Apnoea, Poor weight gain, Tachypnoea, Tachycardia.
Management: Blood transfusion if symptomatic (10 ml/kg packed cells over 1–3 hrs); Folic acid 5 mg weekly to babies <2 kg from 2 weeks of age; 10 mg α-tocopherol acetate (vit E) daily to babies <1.5 kg from 2 weeks; FeSO₄ 50 mg daily or 6 mg/kg/d elemental iron from 2 kg or 10–14 weeks; rHuEPO 100–200 iu/kg 5×/wk or 400 iu/kg/d 3×/wk + iron + vit E.

B(ii) Early-onset vs late-onset neonatal anaemia:
Early onset (first few days): Causes — Rh haemolytic disease, ABO haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis, α-thal, Fetal haemorrhage (abruptio placentae, placenta previa, vasa previa), Feto-maternal transfusion, Twin-twin transfusion, Neonatal haemorrhage (birth trauma, cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haematoma, rupture of liver/spleen).
Late-onset anaemia: Appears later in neonatal period; causes include mild HDN, chronic blood loss e.g. GI bleeding, Infections with DIC, G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis, α-thalassaemia, Congenital marrow aplasia/hypoplasia, Repeated venepuncture.
Treatment for shocked neonate (BP <25 mmHg, PCV <30%, pH <7.1): Transfuse 15–20 ml/kg whole blood over 5–10 minutes. If not in shock but severe anaemia: Give 20 ml/kg of whole blood over 2–3 hrs with IV frusemide 2 mg/kg OR packed cells 10–15 ml/kg (2–3 ml/kg/hr). Very severe anaemia (Hb <8 g/dl) with CCF: EBT with packed cells.

A(i) Spinal cord compression:
- About 4% of children with cancers develop symptoms of spinal compression.
- Associated with: Lymphomas, Leukaemia, Sarcomas, Neuroblastomas.
Mechanisms:
- Direct extension of the tumour.
- Metastatic spread to the vertebrae with secondary cord compression.
- Spread to the epidural space via infiltration of the vertebral foramina.
- Subarachnoid spread down the spinal cord from primary CNS tumour (such as Medulloblastoma).

A(ii) Clinical features:
- Back pain.
- A dermatome of increased sensation.
- Paralysis of the limbs below the level of compression.
- Decreased sensation below the level of compression.
- Urinary and faecal incontinence.
- Hyperreflexia.
Investigation: Main stay is MRI (X-ray is only abnormal in 30–35% of cases).
Treatment: Dexamethasone; Immobilize; Surgery; Emergency radiotherapy; Chemotherapy.

B(i) Pancytopenia in oncology:
- Pancytopenia refers to a reduction in all three elements of the blood: erythrocytes, leucocytes, and platelets.
- May result from: Displacement of normal haematopoietic precursor cells by infiltration of bone marrow by leukaemia or solid tumour; Chemotherapy; Radiotherapy.
- Consequences: Haemorrhage, Anaemia, and Increased susceptibility to infection.
- Treatment: Replacing the cell line that is reduced and treating the cause.

B(ii) Febrile neutropenia treatment:
- Initiate broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour of patient's arrival.
High Risk: Initial therapy with a broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g. cefepime, ceftazidime) or a carbapenem, Piperacillin-Tazobactam. Vancomycin is used in cases of radiographically documented pneumonia, clinically suspected central venous line site infection, skin or soft tissue infection at any site, MRSA, substantial mucositis.
Low Risk: Initial oral therapy with oral ciprofloxacin + amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for 72 hours. Duration of therapy should be individualised. Antifungal may be needed if fever persists >3 days (amphotericin B, fluconazole, itraconazole). Frequent or close monitoring is required.
questions.question:
Describe spinal cord compression and pancytopenia as oncologic emergencies under the following headings:
A(i) What percentage of children with cancer develop symptomatic spinal compression? List all the mechanisms by which spinal cord compression occurs.
A(ii) Describe ALL the clinical features of spinal cord compression.
B(i) Define pancytopenia in the context of oncology and explain how it arises from cancer and its treatment.
B(ii) Describe febrile neutropenia treatment protocols distinguishing high-risk from low-risk patients and the specific antibiotics used.

Describe the clinical approach to, and management of, neonatal anaemia from early-onset causes.
A(i) Define anaemia in the newborn, list the causes of early-onset anaemia (first few days after birth), and categorise them as haemolytic or haemorrhagic.
A(ii) Describe the clinical assessment of a neonate with suspected anaemia — what to look for in the history and examination.
B(i) State the investigations required.
B(ii) Outline the treatment based on severity: (1) shock, (2) severe anaemia without shock, (3) very severe anaemia with CCF, with specific volumes, blood products, and infusion rates.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Anaemia = Hb < normal for gestational and postnatal age.
Early-onset anaemia (first few days): most frequently due to haemolytic disease or haemorrhage.
Haemolytic causes:
- Rh haemolytic disease.
- ABO haemolytic disease.
- Infections.
- Other causes of haemolysis: G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis, a-thalassaemia.
Haemorrhagic causes:
- Foetal haemorrhage — abruptio placentae, placenta praevia, vasa praevia (APH).
- Feto-maternal transfusion; twin-twin transfusion.
- Neonatal haemorrhage — birth trauma; cephalhaematoma; subgaleal haematoma; rupture of liver/spleen.
- Congenital hypoplastic anaemia.

A(ii) Clinical assessment:
History: APH; multiple delivery; difficult delivery; instrumental delivery; poor feeding; breathlessness.
Examination: Colour; bruises; cephalhaematoma; rigid abdomen; pulse volume; heart rate; BP; respiratory rate.

B(i) Investigations: PCV; Hb; WBC; peripheral blood film appearance.

B(ii) Treatment based on severity:
1. Shock (BP < 25 mmHg, PCV < 30%, pH < 7.1): Transfuse 15–20 ml/kg whole blood over 5–10 minutes.
2. Severe anaemia without shock: Give 20 ml/kg of whole blood over 2–3 hours with IV frusemide 2 mg/kg; OR packed cells 10–15 ml/kg at 2–3 ml/kg/hr. Note: 2 ml/kg of packed cells will raise Hb by 0.5–1 g/dl.
3. Very severe anaemia (Hb < 8 g/dl) with CCF: Exchange blood transfusion (EBT) with packed cells.

questions.question:
Describe the pathophysiology of homeostasis and negative feedback control mechanisms in the body, with specific examples.
A(i) Define homeostasis and explain how negative feedback control systems work in maintaining the internal environment, using two specific examples (CO2 regulation and arterial BP regulation).
A(ii) Explain positive feedback mechanisms, state why they generally lead to instability and death, and give one example where positive feedback is useful.
B(i) Define the three types of dehydration based on serum sodium level, state which is most common and why, and explain the significance of isotonic dehydration.
B(ii) Describe isonatraemic dehydration: what it is, why it is the most common type, and state the serum Na range that defines it.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Homeostasis: Maintenance of static or constant conditions in the internal environment. All organs and tissues are involved and serve as control systems to maintain homeostasis. The actual environment of cells is the interstitial component of the ECF, and cell function depends upon the constancy of this fluid.
Negative feedback: If some factor becomes excessive or deficient, a control system initiates a feedback consisting of a series of changes that returns the factor to the normal value.
Example 1 — CO2 regulation: ↑CO2 in ECF → excites respiratory centre → ↑pulmonary ventilation → ↓CO2 in ECF (returns to normal).
Example 2 — Arterial BP regulation: ↑arterial BP → baroreceptors in carotid and aortic arch send impulses to brain to inhibit the vasomotor centre → ↓impulses sent through sympathetic nerves to heart and blood vessels → ↓BP.

A(ii) Positive feedback leads to instability and often death; in rare instances it can be useful.
Example of useful positive feedback: Blood clotting — blood vessel ruptures and a blood clot starts forming; clotting factors are activated within the clot, which also activate yet-unactivated clotting factors → more clot formation. This cycle amplifies until haemostasis is achieved.

B(i) Types of dehydration based on serum Na:
- Isonatraemic (isotonic): Na 130–150 mEq/L.
- Hyponatraemic (hypotonic): Na < 130 mEq/L.
- Hypernatraemic (hypertonic): Na > 150 mEq/L.
Most common: Isonatraemic (80%). It is most common because it occurs when the lost fluid has a similar Na concentration to blood, which is the typical scenario in most diarrhoeal illnesses.

B(ii) Isonatraemic dehydration: Most common (80%); occurs when lost fluid is similar in Na⁺ concentration to blood. Serum Na range: 130–150 mEq/L.

A(i) Pleural effusion is excessive fluid in the pleural cavity. Transudate: total protein <3 g/dL; pleural protein/serum protein ratio <0.5; total leucocyte count <2,000/mm3 with mononuclear predominance; specific gravity <1012. Exudate: total protein >3 g/dL; pleural protein/serum protein ratio >0.5; predominant polymorphonuclear cells (except in malignant or tuberculous effusions which have higher mononuclear cells); specific gravity >1020.

A(ii) Four clinical types: purulent (empyema); bloody (haemothorax); thin fluid (serous); chyle (chylothorax).

A(iii) Bacterial: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pyogenes, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Others: viral, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, heart failure, liver cirrhosis.

B. Pleural effusion vs pneumothorax — Chest deformity: none in both. Chest movement: diminished/absent in both. Mediastinal shift: displaced to opposite side if large (effusion); displaced to opposite side if tension (pneumothorax). Vocal fremitus: absent (effusion); decreased (pneumothorax). Percussion: stony dull (effusion); hyperresonant/tympanitic (pneumothorax). Breath sounds: diminished vesicular, sometimes bronchial at upper level (effusion); diminished vesicular or absent (pneumothorax). Added sounds: pleural rub may initially be present (effusion); none (pneumothorax). Vocal resonance: diminished/absent, sometimes aegophony at upper level of fluid (effusion); diminished (pneumothorax).

C. Pleural fluid colour at pleuracentesis: straw-coloured → TB; bloody → malignancy, TB, trauma; thickly purulent → S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, Hib; thinly purulent → S. pyogenes; serous → nephrotic syndrome, CHF, cirrhosis; milky → lymphatic obstruction, TB.

A 12-year-old unimmunized boy presents with trismus, opisthotonos, and intense intermittent muscle spasms. He had a puncture wound from a rusty nail 10 days earlier. He is conscious and anxious.
(i) State the diagnosis and causative organism, including its characteristics.
(ii) Describe the pathogenesis of the muscle rigidity and autonomic features.
(iii) Outline immediate management including neutralization of toxin, control of spasms, and eradication of the organism.
(iv) State the poor prognostic indicators for this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: generalized tetanus. Causative organism: Clostridium tetani – Gram +ve, spore-forming obligate anaerobic bacilli.
(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Tetanus caused by direct contamination of wounds with clostridial spores
- Wounds with low oxidation-reduction potential (dead or devitalized tissue, foreign body, active infection) facilitate germination of spores and release of toxin
- Tetanospasmin released in the wound binds to the peripheral motor neuron terminal, enters the axon, and via retrograde intraneuronal transport reaches the nerve cell body in the brainstem and spinal cord
- The toxin blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
- Reduced inhibition → muscle rigidity (sustained muscle contraction) and spasms; sympathetic hyperactivity and increased catecholamines; weakness and paralysis
- Generalized tetanus: spread of toxin through lymphatics and blood to multiple nerve terminals → trismus, rigidity, opisthotonos, intermittent spasms
- Autonomic involvement: tachycardia, arrhythmias, labile hypertension, diaphoresis
(iii) Immediate management:
- Nurse in quiet dark environment (ideally ICU)
- Neutralize unbound toxin: Human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) single total dose of 3,000-6,000 U for children and adults; alternatively Tetanus antitoxin (ATS) single dose of 50,000-100,000 U after appropriate testing for sensitivity and desensitization
- Eradicate organisms: penicillin G 10-14 days; alternatives: metronidazole or erythromycin
- Muscle relaxants: oral diazepam 5 mg/kg/day x 2-6 weeks; others: MgSO4, Midazolam, Chlorpromazine, Phenobarbitone
- Neuromuscular blockers with respiratory support in ICU if needed
- Supportive care: fluid and electrolyte balance, nutritional support, wound debridement and care
(iv) Poor prognostic indicators:
- Short incubation period (<7 days)
- Period of onset <48 hours
- Cephalic tetanus
- Neonatal tetanus (worse prognosis than post-neonatal)
- Generalized (worse than localized)
- Temperature >40°C
- Tachycardia >120/min (>150/min in neonates)

questions.question:
A. Describe the aetiology and epidemiology of community-acquired pneumonia in children under five years, including:
(i) all bacterial, viral, atypical bacterial, protozoal, and fungal causative organisms listed
(ii) all risk factors for pneumonia in under-five children

B. Explain how the aetiological agent influences the chest radiograph findings and blood picture in pneumonia, using the specific correlations given.

C. State the treatment algorithm for pneumonia based on nutritional status and severity, specifying which antibiotics are used for different patient groups.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae; Staphylococcus aureus; haemolytic streptococcus; Escherichia coli; Klebsiella sp.; Proteus mirabilis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; non-typhoidal Salmonella. Viruses: measles; RSV; adenovirus; parainfluenzae; influenzae A&B; herpes simplex type 1. Atypical bacteria: Mycoplasma pneumoniae; Ureaplasma urealyticum; Chlamydia. Protozoa: Pneumocystis carinii (jiroveci). Fungi: Candida; Aspergillus; Histoplasma.

A(ii) Risk factors: low birth weight; infancy; outdoor air pollution; indoor air pollution; cigarette smoke; crowding (poor housing, large family size >6); malnutrition (non-breastfeeding, vitamin A deficiency, protein-energy malnutrition); HIV/AIDS (in symptomatic HIV-infected children: increased incidence and severity of bacterial pneumonia).

B. Lobar consolidation on CXR is common in older children with S. aureus. Pneumatocoele is common with Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, and Proteus (indicates necrotising pneumonia). Patchy consolidation suggests bronchopneumonia. No pneumatocoele/abscess but pneumonia with acute otitis media: S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae. Associated pleural effusion: assume S. aureus (though S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae can also cause it). FBC: polymorphonuclear leucocytosis points to bacterial; lymphocytosis if viral; leucopenia is an ominous sign.

C. Well-nourished patients — Non-severe: cotrimoxazole (TMP/SMX) → if no response, procaine penicillin or ampicillin → if no response, crystalline penicillin 48 hours → discharge on amoxicillin for 5 days. Severe (well-nourished): chloramphenicol + erythromycin for 7 days; add gentamicin if needed. Severe malnutrition: cefuroxime + gentamicin for 3–5 weeks; ceftriaxone/cefotaxime for Gram-negative organisms (Klebsiella, Proteus). Neonate to 3 months: treat as sepsis — 1st line cephalosporins (cefuroxime) plus aminoglycosides (gentamicin); ceftazidime if Pseudomonas suspected. Ribavarin if RSV is life-threatening/with BPD/CHD; rimantadine for influenza A&B pneumonia.

A(i) Venous segment components:
Right: Superior vena cava (SVC), Inferior vena cava (IVC), Coronary sinus.
Left: Pulmonary veins.
Connection: if transposition occurs in the atria, each atrium takes along the veins attached to it. For example, if transposition occurs on the right side, the pulmonary veins are taken along, thereby crossing the midline and can become obstructed (causing pulmonary venous obstruction and increased pulmonary venous pressure).

A(ii) Persistent Truncus Arteriosus — four types:
Type I: Common trunk; pulmonary artery is an offshoot of the trunk
Type II: Right and left pulmonary arteries have a common trunk but in the posterior aspect
Type III: Right and left pulmonary arteries are side branches of the trunk
Type IV: No pulmonary artery; the lungs are perfused by bronchial arteries — this type has the worst prognosis because no dedicated pulmonary vasculature exists for oxygenation.

B(i) Left-to-right shunt: the essential pathology is that oxygenated blood recirculates in the lungs, therefore cyanosis is not a problem unless heart failure ensues. Examples: VSD, ASD, PDA. These involve pressure gradients from the left (higher pressure) to the right (lower pressure).

B(ii) Right-to-left shunt: desaturated blood bypasses the lungs, therefore associated with cyanosis — arterial desaturation from birth. Examples: TOF, TGA (when classified by direction of systemic venous flow to aorta), Tricuspid Atresia. Cyanosis occurs because haemoglobin in the systemic arterial blood is not fully oxygenated.

B(iii) Transposition: the systemic and pulmonary circulations are in parallel rather than in series. SVC and IVC blood flows to the aorta (bypasses the lungs), while oxygenated pulmonary venous blood returns to the lungs again — no net oxygenation. This is totally incompatible with life unless there are points of mixing to allow some oxygenated blood to enter the systemic circulation. Mixing points:
- Atrial level: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
- Ventricular level: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
- Arterial level: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA/fistula)

B(iv) Obstruction: impedes blood flow out of the heart; increases cardiac workload as a result of impedance — can be intra-cardiac or extra-cardiac.
RVOT obstruction: pulmonary stenosis
LVOT obstruction: coarctation of the aorta; also aortic stenosis
Peripheral obstruction: e.g. stenosis of branches of the pulmonary trunk

C. Incidence data from Ibadan (635 cases, 1965–1975):
VSD: 35% (most common); PDA: 22%; Coarctation of aorta: 12%; TOF: 10%; Pulmonary stenosis: 9%; Aortic stenosis: 7.5%; ASD: 7.0%; TGA: 4.5%.
Overall incidence of congenital heart disease: 4–9 per 1000 live births worldwide. VSD is the most common congenital heart disease both globally (25–40% of all CHD) and in the Ibadan series (35%).

B(ii) Right-to-left shunt — essential pathology and why cyanosis occurs
B(iii) Transposition — why it is incompatible with life without mixing points, and what the mixing points are
B(iv) Obstruction — the pathological effect and examples of RVOT, LVOT, and peripheral obstruction

A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency ward unconscious, with a history of fever for 3 days and two generalised convulsions. On examination he is unresponsive to pain, has extreme opisthotonus, disconjugate eye movement, and cool, clammy skin. Temperature is 39.5 °C.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis? State the three criteria required to define this condition.
(ii) List the predisposing (risk) factors and describe the histopathological hallmark.
(iii) Describe the full range of neurological and general clinical features.
(iv) Outline the complete stepwise urgent treatment and specific antimalarial treatment, including first-line and second-line regimens.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Cerebral Malaria. A diffuse symmetrical encephalopathy resulting from severe Plasmodium falciparum infection. Mortality ratio: 25–50%. Fatal in 24–72 hours in the absence of treatment.
Three criteria: (1) Unarousable coma persisting for at least 30 minutes after a convulsion; (2) asexual forms of P. falciparum parasitaemia; (3) exclusion of other causes of encephalopathy.

(ii) Risk factors: being a child <10 years of age and living in a malaria-endemic region.
Histopathological hallmark: sequestration of cerebral capillaries and venules with parasitised and non-parasitised RBCs (NPRBCs).

(iii) General features: fever (37.5–41°C), anorexia, vomiting and cough, deep breathing with a clear chest (metabolic acidosis), cold clammy skin with a core-to-skin temperature difference of 10°C; some patients are in shock with systolic BP <50 mmHg.
Neurological features: convulsions usually generalised and often repeated (before or after onset of coma); subtle seizure activity — repetitive tonic-clonic eye movement, intermittent nystagmus, salivation, minor twitching of a single digit or corner of the mouth; coma (unarousable); passive resistance to head flexion but no meningeal signs; extreme opisthotonus; disconjugate eye movement; decerebrate and decorticate postures; absent corneal and Doll's eye reflex in profound coma; increased or decreased muscle tone; absent abdominal and cremasteric reflexes; retinal haemorrhages, exudates and papilloedema.

(iv) Urgent treatment:
1. Treat convulsions: IM paraldehyde 1 ml/year of life (max 5 ml); IV phenobarbitone or phenytoin 15 mg/kg stat (loading dose) then 5 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses.
2. Treat hypoglycaemia (RPG <40 mg/dl): IV 10% dextrose water 2–4 ml/kg stat, then repeat RPG; maintain on 10% dextrose water.
3. Treat hypovolaemic shock: IV normal saline 20 ml/kg bolus; re-assess and repeat if necessary.
4. Treat anaemia: monitor PCV; transfuse with packed cells (10–12 ml/kg) if PCV <15% or PCV >15% with signs of cardiac decompensation.
5. Nursing care: care of the unconscious patient; strict input/output monitoring; monitor GCS 4-hourly; feed via NG tube at maintenance; correct electrolyte and acid-base imbalances.
Specific antimalarial — 1st line: IV quinine 10 mg/kg in 10 ml/kg of 10% dextrose water over 2 hours, repeat 8-hourly until child can tolerate oral; then oral quinine 10 mg/kg three times daily to complete 7 days OR oral Coartem (appropriate dose for weight).
2nd line: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg stat, then 1.2 mg/kg 12 hours later, then 1.2 mg/kg daily for 6 days; OR IM artemether 3.2 mg/kg stat, then 1.6 mg/kg daily for 6 days.

questions.question:
Describe the pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and management of diphtheria under the following headings, explain why respiratory diphtheria is the most life-threatening form, and distinguish diphtheria from other causes of upper airway obstruction in children.
A(i) Aetiology, epidemiology, and mode of spread
A(ii) Pathogenesis of tissue injury and pseudomembrane formation
B(i) Clinical manifestations at each anatomical site (nasal, tonsillar/pharyngeal, laryngeal, cutaneous)
B(ii) Systemic complications (cardiac, neurological, renal) and their mechanisms
C(i) Diagnosis, differential diagnosis at each site, and treatment
C(ii) Why laryngeal diphtheria is more dangerous than tonsillar disease, and how to distinguish from viral croup and epiglottitis
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology, epidemiology, mode of spread:
- Corynebacterium diphtheriae: Gram +ve, non-sporulating, aerobic/anaerobic bacilli; 3 biotypes: gravis, intermedius, mitis (mitis is less toxigenic, less severe disease)
- Humans are the only known reservoirs; rare in advanced countries; still reported in the tropics
- Peak age 2-14 years (especially unimmunized); peak incidence in winter
- Spread via respiratory droplets, skin exudates (cases/carriers); also from skin infection by direct contact
- Incubation period 2-4 days; risk factors: poverty, overcrowding, poor hygiene and homelessness
A(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Bacteriophage encodes for gene producing exotoxin (tox+); fragments A and B
- Exotoxin causes tissue necrosis by inhibition of protein synthesis
- Pseudomembrane formation is the hallmark: necrosed epithelial cells + fibrin + leucocytes + RBCs + organisms = grey/brown pseudomembrane
- Exotoxin occasionally absorbed into blood causing: renal (necrosis of renal tubules), bone marrow (thrombocytopaenia), heart (cardiomyopathy/myocarditis), nerves (peripheral neuropathy/demyelination)
- Another mechanism is antigen-antibody complex deposition in heart and nerves (takes 2-3 weeks to manifest)
B(i) Clinical manifestations:
- Nasal (mostly infants): common cold, mucopurulent, serosanguinous discharge and shallow ulcers
- Tonsillar/pharyngeal (classical): malaise, low grade fever, mild sore throat, pseudomembrane in 1-2 days; some develop high grade fever, toxicity, cervical lymphadenitis, tonsillar and uvular enlargement, oedema of neck ("Bull neck" in >6 years)
- Laryngeal: hoarseness, stridor, croupy cough, dyspnoea; high risk of suffocation
- Cutaneous (commoner in warm climates): extremities more likely than head/trunk; chronic non-healing shallow ulcers with pain, tenderness, erythema, exudative lesions
- Unusual sites: aural diphtheria, conjunctivitis, vulvovaginitis
B(ii) Systemic complications:
- Cardiac toxicity 1-2 weeks after initial symptoms: arrhythmias, heart block, circulatory collapse; cardiomyopathy is immune-mediated, takes 2-10 weeks to set; is fatal
- Neuropathies 2-6 weeks after: may resemble GBS; local or cranial neuropathies; peripheral polyneuropathy is symmetric, affects proximal more than distal muscles; unlike GBS (which progresses proximally) it progresses distally; does not leave permanent damage if patient survives
- Renal: renal failure or hypotension
- Respiratory obstruction: often the cause of death
C(i) Diagnosis, differential diagnosis, treatment:
- Diagnosis is mostly clinical: pseudomembrane, fever
- Culture of organism on Tindale's media (Tellurite) - black colonies with halos; Loffler's media - metachromatic granules; PCR detects toxin-producing gene; serology (Elek test, EIA)
- Differential: nasal (FB in nostrils); pharyngeal (Strept or EBV pharyngitis, peritonsillar abscess, pharyngeal candidiasis, Vincent's or Ludwig's angina); laryngeal (viral croup, epiglottitis, laryngeal tumors); cutaneous (impetigo)
- Treatment: neutralizing antitoxins; antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin) x 14 days; supportive care; toxoid after recovery; treat carriers/unimmunized close contacts with penicillin or erythromycin x 7 days
C(ii) Why laryngeal diphtheria is more dangerous:
- Laryngeal diphtheria causes hoarseness, stridor, croupy cough, dyspnoea, and has a high risk of suffocation
- Respiratory obstruction is often the cause of death in diphtheria
- Viral croup (acute LTB): caused by viral organisms, no pseudomembrane, child less toxic
- Acute epiglottitis: caused by H. influenzae, is life threatening; distinguished by more acute presentation and 'cherry red' epiglottis; the child is more toxic and prefers sitting upright
- Peripheral neuropathy in diphtheria must be distinguished from Guillain-Barré Syndrome: diphtheria neuropathy is symmetric and progresses distally, GBS is also symmetric but progresses proximally

A(i) Types of pulmonary vascular marking abnormality:
Increased (pulmonary plethora): Caused by (1) large left-to-right shunts; (2) heart failure; (3) pulmonary venous obstruction. Normal pulmonary vascular markings extend two-thirds laterally from the hilum — any markings beyond this boundary indicate plethora.
Decreased (pulmonary oligaemia): Caused by severe obstruction — (1) Tetralogy of Fallot; (2) pulmonary atresia; (3) severe pulmonary stenosis.

A(ii) CXR appearance of pulmonary artery:
- Valvar pulmonary stenosis: Post-stenotic dilatation of the pulmonary artery — seen as a pulmonary knuckle (prominent main pulmonary artery); reduced pulmonary vascular markings beyond; heart size usually normal unless obstruction is severe.
- Tetralogy of Fallot: Pulmonary bay (small/absent pulmonary artery segment); reduced pulmonary vascular markings; boot-shaped heart; right-sided aortic arch in 25–30% of cases.
- Large left-to-right shunt: Enlarged/prominent main pulmonary artery; increased pulmonary vascular markings throughout; cardiomegaly if heart failure present.

B(i) Axis designations:
- 0° to 90°: Normal
- Right Axis Deviation (RAD)
- Left Axis Deviation (LAD)
- Extremely Right or Left Axis Deviation (Superior axis = ERAD or ELAD or LAD)
Superior axis significance:
- With acyanosis: alerts to Atrioventricular Septal Defect (AVSD)
- With cyanosis: points to univentricular disorder, most commonly Tricuspid Atresia

B(ii) Prolonged PR interval in a child with recent sore throat: This is a minor criterion in the Jones criteria for Acute Rheumatic Fever, indicating first-degree AV block from cardiac inflammation following Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis.
Normal PR interval range:
- Children: 0.16 s
- Adolescents: 0.18 s
- Adults: 0.2 s

Describe the approach to a neonate with early-onset anaemia due to haemolytic disease of the newborn, focusing on ABO and Rhesus incompatibility.
A(i) Explain the mechanism by which ABO incompatibility causes haemolysis in the newborn, including which blood group combinations are at highest risk and why G6PD deficiency worsens the outcome.
A(ii) Describe Rhesus haemolytic disease: define the condition, state the conditions that must be met for RhHDN to occur, and state why it is rarer in Blacks.
B(i) List the investigations for a neonate suspected to have HDN, and state the treatment threshold for phototherapy and exchange blood transfusion (EBT).
B(ii) State the complications of phototherapy and the care measures required during phototherapy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) ABO incompatibility: Worst in Group B individuals — e.g. if the mother is O and the child is A or B. The mother's anti-A or anti-B IgG antibodies cross the placenta and haemolyse the baby's RBCs. G6PD deficiency worsens the outcome because G6PD-deficient RBCs are more susceptible to oxidative haemolysis, increasing the rate of haemolysis and the severity of jaundice.

A(ii) Rhesus haemolytic disease of the newborn (RhHDN): Mother is Rh-negative and infant is Rh-positive. Rhesus antigens: C, c, D, d, E, e; D antigen is most important. Rhesus negative: occurs in 15% Whites, 5% Blacks.
For RhHDN to occur: Mother must have been sensitised to the D antigen by: (i) abortion of Rh-positive foetus; (ii) delivery of Rh-positive infant; (iii) transfusion with Rh-positive blood. Subsequent pregnancy with Rh-positive foetus results in more severe disease. Both direct and indirect Coombs tests will be positive.
It is rarer in Blacks because: fewer Blacks are Rh-negative (fewer chances of an Rh-positive man marrying an Rh-negative woman); concurrence of ABO incompatibility and Rh incompatibility protects against RhHDN.

B(i) Investigations for HDN: Blood group of mother and child; Coombs test; PCV/Hb; blood film (high reticulocyte count suggests haemolysis); peroxidase haemolysis test; serum bilirubin.
Treatment thresholds:
- Phototherapy: used when SBR > 12.5 mg/dl.
- Exchange blood transfusion (EBT): when SBR approaching > 20 mg/dl.
Note: Be aggressive in preterm — they develop kernicterus earlier because of lower serum protein levels and immature blood-brain barrier.
Fresh whole blood compatible with both mother and child is used for EBT.

B(ii) Complications of phototherapy: Increase in insensible water loss and dehydration; nasal obstruction by eye pads; bronze baby syndrome (due to effect of phototherapy on direct/conjugated bilirubin).
Care during phototherapy: Give extra fluid allowance (20–30 ml/kg/day) for insensible water loss; protect eyes with goggles; wavelength of the ultraviolet light is 420 nm; distance is 45 cm (if further, it is less effective).

questions.question:
A 4-year-old child presents with a painless right-sided abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. The blood pressure is elevated. There is no haematuria on urinalysis.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) List ALL the congenital abnormalities known to be associated with this condition.
(iii) State the most common metastatic site and the investigations that would be performed, including their expected findings.
(iv) Outline the staging system and the treatment options available, justifying the approach for early versus advanced disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) Wilm's Tumour (Nephroblastoma).
(ii) Associated congenital abnormalities:
- Aniridia (absence of iris).
- Hemihypertrophy.
- Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, visceromegaly, many embryonal tumours; associated with lesion of chromosome 11).
- Genitourinary tract abnormalities: horse-shoe kidney, dysplasia of kidney, cystic disease of kidney, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, duplication of collecting system, pelvic kidneys.
- WAGR syndrome: Wilm's tumour, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformation, Mental Retardation.
- Denys-Drash syndrome: Wilm's tumour, Nephropathy, and genital abnormalities.
(iii) Most common metastatic site is the Lungs (85%), followed by the liver (8%).
Investigations and expected findings:
- USS: intrarenal tumour, usually >10 cm at diagnosis.
- CT scan (preferable).
- IVU: distorted calyces or non-excretion of the dye (non-functional kidney).
- Serum Calcium: elevated in mesoblastic nephroma (seen in neonates and infants).
- Elevated serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).
- Urinalysis for haematuria (present in 15% of cases, more often microscopic).
(iv) Staging and treatment:
- Stage I (limited to one kidney) and Stage II (extends beyond capsule, can be completely resected): Nephrectomy ± Radiotherapy.
- Advanced cases (Stage III–V): Chemotherapy with VAC regimen — Vincristine, Actinomycin D/Adriamycin, Cyclophosphamide.
- 5-year survival: Stage I = 97%, Stage II = 94%; prognosis worsens with advancing stage, unfavourable histology (anaplasia), and age >2 years.

(i) The diagnosis is kwashiorkor. The anthropometric classification is severe acute malnutrition (SAM), as the weight-for-height Z-score is –3.8 (below –3 SD), and bilateral pitting oedema is itself a defining criterion of SAM with oedema.
(ii) Predisposing factors include: abrupt cessation of breastfeeding when displaced by a new sibling (the word 'kwashiorkor' derives from the Ga language of Ghana, meaning 'the disease the older child gets when the next baby is born'); protein-energy deficiency during a critical growth period; likely dietary shift to carbohydrate-predominant weaning foods deficient in protein; and vitamin A and antioxidant deficiency, which has been implicated in free radical damage and inflammatory mediator release contributing to oedema.
(iii) Oedema in kwashiorkor results primarily from hypoalbuminaemia reducing plasma oncotic pressure, allowing fluid to shift into the interstitium. Free radical damage and inflammatory mediator release from dietary antioxidant deficiency are additional proposed mechanisms.
(iv) SAM inpatient management follows two phases: the stabilisation phase uses F-75 therapeutic milk (75 kcal/100 mL, 0.9 g protein/100 mL, low fat, restricted sodium) to provide maintenance energy without overloading the damaged gut and to correct metabolic derangements safely. The rehabilitation phase uses F-100 or Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF — composed of peanut butter, dry skimmed milk powder, vegetable oil, sugar, and a balanced micronutrient supplement) to achieve catch-up growth at 5–10 times the normal rate for age. Iron is withheld during the acute stabilisation phase to avoid oxidative damage, as the antioxidant systems are severely depleted in SAM and free iron generates harmful reactive oxygen species.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought to the nutrition rehabilitation unit. The mother reports that the child, who was previously well, developed swelling of the feet and legs over the past month after a new sibling was born and breastfeeding was abruptly stopped. On examination the child has bilateral pitting oedema up to the knees, a miserable affect, hair that is sparse and easily plucked, areas of flaky paint skin changes with depigmentation on the trunk, and a protuberant abdomen. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL. Weight-for-height Z-score is –3.8.

(ii) Identify at least three predisposing factors evident in this presentation.
(iii) Explain the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for the oedema.
(iv) Outline the feeding management, specifying the two phases and the formula used in each, and state why iron is withheld in the first phase.

A 6-year-old child with a history of sickle cell disease is admitted with fever, progressive breathlessness, a new loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, and splenomegaly. There is a history of dental extraction 6 weeks ago without prophylaxis. Blood cultures (three samples) grow Streptococcus viridans. Echocardiography shows a small oscillating vegetation on the tricuspid valve.

(i) State the diagnosis and identify the likely portal of entry of the organism.
(ii) Why is sickle cell disease listed as a predisposing factor for infective endocarditis?
(iii) Describe four peripheral/embolic/autonomic signs you would specifically look for on examination to complete the clinical picture of this condition, distinguishing those caused by embolisation from those caused by immune complexes.
(iv) State the antibiotic treatment for this specific organism including the drugs, doses, and duration.
(v) Name two surgical options available for this patient and justify which is most appropriate.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (subacute), tricuspid valve, caused by Streptococcus viridans.
Portal of entry: Dental manipulation (tooth extraction 6 weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis) — Streptococcus viridans is found in the mouth and enters the bloodstream during dental procedures.

(ii) Why sickle cell disease predisposes to IE: Sickle cell disease is listed as a differential diagnosis because patients are more prone to infections and septicaemic illness; septicaemia is itself a predisposing factor for IE, particularly from Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative organisms. Additionally, sickle cell patients may develop functional asplenia, further reducing immunity.

(iii) Four peripheral/embolic/autonomic signs:
Embolic (direct organism seeding/clot):
1. Splinter haemorrhages — linear haemorrhages under the fingernails from microemboli or vasculitis
2. Janeway lesions — embolic/immunological palmar/plantar lesions
Immune complex (late/autonomic manifestations):
3. Osler's nodes — painless swelling found in the pulps of the fingers (immune complex)
4. Roth's spots — exudates in the eye (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres — immune complex)
Also: Petechiae; microscopic haematuria; arthritis; digital clubbing; nephritis

(iv) Antibiotic treatment for Streptococcus viridans:
Drugs: Penicillin (crystalline/IV) — very good; OR Ampicillin; OR Amoxycillin; ± Gentamicin (for Gram-negative cover); ± Probenecid (to delay excretion of penicillin in advanced countries). Newer alternative: Ceftriaxone.
Drugs should be bactericidal and given parenterally.
Duration: Six weeks.

(v) Two surgical options:
1. Valve replacement (of the destroyed tricuspid valve)
2. Correction of the underlying heart defect (if a congenital defect is present contributing to the endothelial damage)
Most appropriate: Valve replacement if the tricuspid valve is destroyed and heart failure does not respond to medical treatment — surgical options include valve replacement and correction of underlying heart lesions, with heart failure refractory to medical treatment as the indication for surgery.

A(i) Sequential Segmental Analysis: a system for describing congenital heart diseases, adopted in 1971 by consensus. The heart is seen to develop from partitioning of a single tube; failure of septation (incomplete or complete) leads to abnormalities.
Four segments:
- Venous segment: SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus
- Atrial segment: right and left atria
- Ventricular segment: right and left ventricles
- Arterial segment: aorta and pulmonary artery

A(ii) Atrial Situs: determined by the location of the morphological right atrium.
Situs Solitus: morphological right atrium in the right (normal) position; left bronchus is normally longer than the right bronchus.
Situs Inversus: morphological right atrium is on the left side; when the left bronchus appears on the right in a chest X-ray (shorter, equal to the right), it is 99% certain that the right atrium is now on the left side.
Atrial Isomerism: occurs when both bronchi are of the same length. Right atrial isomerism: both bronchi have the length of a right bronchus — two sino-atrial nodes are present. Left atrial isomerism: both bronchi have the length of a left bronchus. Because there are no two distinct atria, the atrioventricular connection is described as ambiguous.

B(i) Structural features to distinguish right from left ventricle:
- Trabecular pattern: right ventricle — coarse; left ventricle — fine
- Valve: right ventricle — tricuspid; left ventricle — mitral (bicuspid)
In a univentricular heart, the valve present is used to identify which side is present.

B(ii) Atrioventricular Concordance: right atrium connected to right ventricle (via tricuspid valve); left atrium connected to left ventricle (via mitral valve); requires situs solitus.
Atrioventricular Discordance: right atrium connected to left ventricle; left atrium connected to right ventricle; mitral valve now on the right side, tricuspid on the left; requires two distinct atria, two distinct ventricles, two atrioventricular ostia; occurs with situs solitus or inversus.
Ambiguous connection: occurs in right or left atrial isomerism where the minimum requirements (two distinct atria) are not met.

B(iii) Over-riding valve: the valve overlaps the ventricular septum but the tension apparatus (chordae tendineae and papillary muscles) remains in the ipsilateral ventricle.
Straddling valve: the valve overlaps and part of the tension apparatus is in the contralateral ventricle.
Clinical significance: both can occur in VSD; surgeons must take care of them during repair to avoid damaging the tension apparatus.
In Classical TGA (ventriculo-arterial discordance): atrial situs solitus + concordant AV connection + discordant VA connection — the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle.
questions.question:
A. Describe the Sequential Segmental Analysis system as used to classify congenital heart diseases:
A(i) Define the system, state when it was adopted, and list the four segments of the heart it describes
A(ii) Describe Atrial Situs — define situs solitus, situs inversus, and atrial isomerism (right and left), explaining how the chest X-ray (specifically the bronchi) is used to determine atrial situs

B. Describe the connection between the atria and ventricles:
B(i) Structural features used to distinguish morphological right from morphological left ventricle
B(ii) Define atrioventricular concordance and discordance — the requirements for each and the anatomical features that define each
B(iii) Explain the terms over-riding and straddling valves and their clinical significance, and state what ventriculo-arterial discordance means in Classical TGA

questions.answerText:
(i) This is a very severe / life-threatening acute exacerbation of bronchial asthma. Life-threatening features: cyanosis; a silent chest; poor respiratory effort; fatigue or exhaustion; agitation or reduced level of consciousness.

(ii) Immediate management: Give 100% oxygen immediately. Adrenaline 0.3 ml subcutaneously (0.01 ml/kg of 1:1000, maximum 0.3 ml); may be repeated maximum 2 times after 20 minutes (3 doses in 1 hour). Short-acting β2 agonist via oxygen-driven nebuliser (3 times in 1 hour). Oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg. If no response after 15–30 minutes: continue oxygen; nebulised salbutamol every 30 minutes or continuously; add ipratropium bromide. If still no response: IV aminophylline 5 mg/kg stat then aminophylline drip 1 mg/kg/hr; IV hydrocortisone sodium succinate; ipratropium bromide 0.25 mg added to nebulised beta2 agonist. If no response: intubation and mechanical ventilation. Admit to ICU.

(iii) Oral corticosteroids are more effective than inhaled or nebulised corticosteroids. They should be given early during an acute asthma exacerbation — within 45 minutes of onset of symptoms. Dose: oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg. Extra care should be taken in children on oral steroids during episodes of increased stress (e.g. surgery).

(iv) Preventers (anti-inflammatory): inhaled corticosteroids — beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone, flunisolide, triamcinolone; oral corticosteroids — prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone. Controllers (sustained bronchodilator, weak/unproven anti-inflammatory): long-acting β2 agonists — salmeterol, formoterol; sustained-release theophylline tablets; leukotriene antagonists — montelukast, zarfirlukast. Relievers (quick relief): short-acting β2 agonists — salbutamol, terbutaline, fenoterol; anticholinergics; short-acting theophyllines.

(v) Unnecessary therapy: antibiotics, cough syrups, mucolytics, antihistamines, mist tents, lung lavage, ionisers, and physiotherapy (breathing exercises) are unnecessary.
questions.question:
A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency room with acute onset of severe breathlessness. He is too breathless to talk or feed, with marked tachypnoea, tachycardia, and a silent chest on auscultation. He has a known history of bronchial asthma. SaO2 is 84% in room air.

(i) What is the severity classification of this acute exacerbation and what are the life-threatening features?
(ii) Describe the immediate emergency management step-by-step, including drugs, doses, and routes of administration.
(iii) What is the role of oral corticosteroids in acute asthma management, and when should they be given?
(iv) List the agents classified as Preventers, Controllers, and Relievers in the long-term management of asthma.
(v) State which drugs are considered unnecessary in the management of asthma.

A 3-year-old child presents with a 2-day history of barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, fever, and progressive respiratory distress. He had coryzal symptoms 3 days prior. On examination he has moderate chest retraction, anxious appearance, and decreased breath sounds. Lateral neck radiograph shows subglottic narrowing. Croup score is 7.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the most common causative organism?
(ii) What anatomical structure is narrowed, and which conditions must be excluded on the basis of the differential diagnosis?
(iii) Describe the clinical scoring system for assessing children with stridor (Wesley, 1975), including all parameters and their score values.
(iv) List the complications of this condition.
(v) Outline the full treatment of laryngotracheobronchitis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Laryngotracheobronchitis (viral croup) — the commonest form of croup; commonest occurs in children aged 6 months to 3 years. Most common causative viruses: parainfluenza virus types 1–3 (55%) and RSV (12%); measles and adenovirus are also listed as causes.

(ii) The anatomical structure narrowed is the subglottic region of the larynx and trachea. Differential diagnoses to exclude: laryngeal diphtheria (membrane in the pharynx); epiglottitis (sudden onset; lateral radiograph shows supraglottic opacity); foreign body in the larynx (history; lateral radiograph shows radio-opaque body); retropharyngeal abscess (lateral radiograph shows widening of the retropharyngeal space).

(iii) Wesley croup scoring system (1975): Stridor — 0: none; 1: with agitation; 2: mild at rest; 3: severe at rest. Retractions — 0: none; 1: mild; 2: moderate; 3: severe. Air entry — 0: normal; 1: mild; 2: moderate; 3: severe. Colour — 0: normal; 4: cyanotic in room air; 5: cyanotic in 40% oxygen. Level of consciousness — 0: normal; 1: restless if disturbed; 2: restless undisturbed; 3: lethargic.

(iv) Complications: pneumonia; congestive heart failure; pulmonary oedema.

(v) Treatment: humidified oxygen; adequate fluid and calorie intake; mild sedative if patient is very restless (chloral hydrate); antibiotics (not routinely indicated but should be used if there is evidence of superimposed bacterial infection); racemic epinephrine by inhalation — provides rapid but transient relief; steroid (dexamethasone or hydrocortisone); tracheostomy if respiratory obstruction progresses.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross features of atopic dermatitis (AD) under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and epidemiology (prevalence, sex ratio, socioeconomic association, age of onset)
A(ii) Aetio-pathogenesis — food allergens, microorganisms, and immunological mechanism (IgE, T-cell dysregulation, cytokines)
A(iii) Signs and symptoms across age groups and complications

B. Explain how the zones of the condition relate to common pathologies (infantile, childhood, adolescent/adult presentations).

C. State the therapeutic objectives and outline the full management — including topical drugs (with the two-step steroid approach), systemic drugs, immune modulators, and adjuncts.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Atopic eczema (AD) is a characteristic type of chronic dermatitis frequently associated with atopy and an elevated IgE level; the diagnosis is made on a combination of history and morphological findings. Worldwide occurrence reported in all races; about 3% of children under age 5 years had AD with a male-to-female ratio of 1.2:1; higher incidence in higher socioeconomic groups (hygiene hypothesis); majority of patients present within the first 5 years; increasing incidence in the developing world. Genetics: AD runs in families; about 75% of patients have a personal or family history of other atopic diseases (allergic rhinitis, asthma, hay fever); inheritance is polygenic.

A(ii) Food allergy: common in children, decreases as the child grows; triggers include nuts, wheat products, colouring agents, egg and egg products, cow's milk. Microorganisms: Pityrosporum, Staphylococcus. Immunology: increased IgE production; T-cell dysregulation — cells differentiate into TH2 cells producing cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13) which promote B-cell proliferation and IgE synthesis, which suppresses TH1 cell-mediated immunity, leading to increased susceptibility to viral and bacterial infection.

A(iii) Signs and symptoms: pruritus, xerosis, hyperlinearity of the palms, eczematous lesions, prurigo, lichenification, Dennie-Morgan fold, hand and foot involvement. Complications: infection, exfoliative dermatitis, xerosis, growth retardation, eye changes (keratoconus, posterior and anterior subcapsular cataract), Dennie-Morgan fold. Associations: nail pitting, posterior and anterior subcapsular cataracts, atopy, thyroid antibodies, Down syndrome.

B. Infantile AD affects the face and trunk; childhood AD involves the flexural surfaces; adolescent/adult AD shows lichenification and flexural involvement. Each zone relates to a recognisable pattern of morphological findings alongside the pruritus.

C. Therapeutic objectives: reduce signs and symptoms; prevent or reduce recurrences; prevent disease or treatment complications.
Management: initial assessment for allergens/precipitating factors, extent, severity, psychological distress and family impact; education; hydration of skin to relieve symptoms and increase absorption of topical drugs; reduce number of baths or use of soaps; acute control of pruritus and inflammation; avoidance of trigger factors (diet, clothing).
Topical drugs: topical steroids (mild, moderate, potent, very potent) — two-step approach: start with a strong steroid, prescribe for 7 days and review, then step down to a weaker steroid if considerable improvement; topical antibiotics; topical calcineurin inhibitors.
Systemic drugs: antihistamines, systemic steroids, antibiotics.
Immune modulators: mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporin A, ascomycin compounds, interferon gamma, systemic corticosteroids, leukotriene inhibitors, azathioprine/oral pimecrolimus.
Adjuncts: evening primrose oil, Chinese herbs, Acalypha, multivitamins/pyridoxine/vitamin E.

questions.question:
A 9-month-old infant is brought to the emergency room with a 2-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea (more than 8 stools per day) and vomiting. The mother stopped breastfeeding 3 weeks ago and switched to infant formula prepared with tap water. On examination the child is restless and irritable, has very sunken eyes with no tears, a depressed anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and drinks eagerly when offered fluids. Temperature is 38.2°C. Stool electron microscopy later reveals non-enveloped, double-stranded RNA viral particles.

(i) Identify the degree of dehydration and the most likely causative organism, including its group classification most responsible for human infections.
(ii) State at least three risk factors present in this scenario that predisposed this child to the illness and/or to rapid dehydration.
(iii) Describe the complications that may arise if this child is not promptly treated.
(iv) Outline the management approach, justifying the fluid treatment selected, and state the single specific preventive measure available for the identified causative organism.
questions.answerText:
(i) The child has moderate dehydration, characterised by restlessness/irritability, very sunken eyes, absent tears, a depressed fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and thirst with eager drinking. A child who drinks poorly or is unable to drink signals severe dehydration. The causative organism is Rotavirus; Group A rotavirus causes the vast majority of human infections, particularly in infants and young children worldwide.
(ii) Risk factors present in this scenario include: age below 12 months (children under 12 months have higher body water content per unit body weight, a larger body surface area to body weight ratio, and higher metabolic rates predisposing to rapid dehydration); early introduction of infant formula before 6 months or cessation of breastfeeding (formula lacks protective antibodies, growth factors, secretory IgA, and lactoferrin present in breast milk, and is often prepared with contaminated water); stool frequency exceeding 8 per day; and vomiting, which impairs oral rehydration and increases fluid losses.
(iii) Complications if untreated include: progression to severe dehydration with oliguria; acute renal failure from pre-renal aetiology; electrolyte imbalance including hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia; metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss; and in severe cases, shock, circulatory collapse, and death. Secondary lactose intolerance may also complicate recovery.
(iv) Management: moderate dehydration is managed with oral rehydration therapy (ORT), exploiting the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) which remains functional during secretory diarrhoea. Management objectives include preventing further dehydration, correcting existing dehydration, maintaining nutrition, and treating aetiological agents if indicated. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for all cases. The specific preventive measure for rotavirus is the Rotavirus vaccine, which is recommended for prevention of rotavirus diarrhoea.

A(i) Bronchiolitis is an acute, infectious, inflammatory disease of the lower respiratory tract resulting in obstruction of the small airways.

A(ii) Epidemiology: bronchiolitis is the most frequent lower respiratory tract infection during infancy requiring hospitalisation. 25% of children under one and 13% of children aged one to two years will have respiratory infections; of these, half will have a wheezing associated respiratory disease. RSV can be cultured from one third of outpatients and from 80% of those less than 6 months old who are hospitalised. Two RSV subtypes: A and B; type A causes the majority of severe infections; one subtype usually predominates during a given season, creating 'good' and 'bad' years.

A(iii) Risk factors for early onset disease and hospitalisation: low birth weight; prematurity; lower socioeconomic group; crowded living conditions; parental smoking; absence of breastfeeding; day care attendance.

B. The relationship between acute bronchiolitis in infancy and subsequent development of asthma remains confusing. Some studies show that asymptomatic children examined 10 years after an acute episode of bronchiolitis may have abnormal small airway resistance and decreased transcutaneous oxygen saturation (SpO2), and up to 50% will have recurrent wheezing later in life. However, these are retrospective studies with no controls; the majority of these children had either a family history of allergy, prematurity, small for gestational age, or were born into families with exposure to passive cigarette smoke. Sequelae: a significant proportion have hyperreactive airways, with wheezy episodes and possibly bronchial asthma later.

C. Distinguishing asthma from bronchiolitis: Asthma — uncommon under the age of 1 year; positive family history; recurrent attacks; blood and sputum eosinophilia. Bronchiolitis — most common under 2 years of age; commoner in males (M:F 2:1); incidence highest during rainy season and cold harmattan months; no family history of atopy necessarily; single or first episode typically. Bacterial pneumonia and congestive heart failure are also in the differential of bronchiolitis.
questions.question:
A. Describe the definition, epidemiology, and risk factors of acute bronchiolitis:
(i) Define bronchiolitis.
(ii) State the epidemiological facts, including the proportion of infants affected, the role of RSV, and the two RSV subtypes.
(iii) List all the risk factors for early onset disease and subsequent hospitalisation.

B. Explain the long-term morbidity and association of bronchiolitis with asthma, including what studies have shown and the confounding factors mentioned.

C. Distinguish bronchial asthma from acute bronchiolitis using the features listed as differential diagnoses.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis and mode of inheritance:
- Most likely diagnosis: G6PD (Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase) deficiency.
- Mode of inheritance: X-linked recessive; X-linked disorders more likely in males.
(ii) Substances/drugs that precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deficiency:
- Naphthalene (moth balls), Sulphones, Sulphonamides, Quinine, Nitrofurantoin, Nalidixic acid, Chloramphenicol, Fava beans.
(iii) Clinical and laboratory presentation:
Iron Deficiency Anaemia:
- Causes: Inadequate intake, prematurity, hookworm, occult blood loss.
- Clinical features: Pallor, blue sclera, irritability, pagophagia (desire to eat ice), rigid nails, koilonychia, pica (eating non-food stuff), geophagia (eating of soil), anorexia, features of cardiac failure, haemic murmur, features of adverse neurologic function (short attention span).
- Lab: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia; ↓MCV, ↓MCHC.
- Treatment: Iron for several months.
G6PD Deficiency:
- X-linked recessive; haemolysis precipitated by specific drugs/substances (listed above).
- Blood film: Ghost cells or bite cells.
- Enzyme assay for G6PD is diagnostic.
- Jaundice and dark urine (haemolysis).
(iv) Management of childhood anaemia:
- Depends on severity and cause; treat the underlying cause.
- Mild to moderate: haematinics — Iron, Folic acid, Vitamin B₁₂.
- Corticosteroids: for autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and PNH.
- Recombinant Erythropoietin: useful in anaemia of chronic diseases (e.g. CRF), anaemia from chemotherapy, AIDS, prematurity. Not indicated for immediate correction (correction occurs after 2–8 weeks of EPO).
- Blood transfusion: for severe anaemia Hb <5 g/dl; use packed cells or whole blood depending on cause and haemodynamic state; give IV Frusemide 1–2 mg/kg stat.
questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy with a family history of jaundice presents with pallor, jaundice, and mild fever. He recently took an antimalarial (quinine) prescribed for malaria. His blood film shows ghost cells and bite cells.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and its mode of inheritance?
(ii) List all the substances and drugs that precipitate haemolysis in this condition.
(iii) Describe the full clinical and laboratory presentation of iron deficiency anaemia, distinguishing it from G6PD deficiency anaemia.
(iv) Describe the management of childhood anaemia including the role of specific haematinics, corticosteroids, erythropoietin, and blood transfusion.

A 7-year-old girl presents with a 3-week history of fever, joint pains affecting the knee and then the shoulder sequentially, and breathlessness. She had a sore throat 4 weeks ago, inadequately treated. On examination, she is febrile (38.8°C), has a tachycardia of 130/min, tender swollen right knee (now improving), and a diastolic murmur at the apex. ESR is markedly elevated, ASO titre is 480 Todd units.

(i) What is the diagnosis? State the criteria used and which combination of criteria is met in this patient.
(ii) Describe the pathogenesis of cardiac damage in this condition, naming the specific histopathological lesion that is pathognomonic of the disease.
(iii) Which heart valves are affected in order of frequency?
(iv) Describe the treatment of this patient, covering bed rest, anti-inflammatory therapy with dosing, organism eradication, and management of cardiac complications.
(v) Describe the long-term prophylaxis: drug, dose, and duration.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF).
Criteria used: Modified Jones Criteria (Bence-Jones Criteria).
Criteria met in this patient:
- Major criteria: Carditis (diastolic murmur at apex from mitral valve involvement) + Arthritis (fleeting/migratory arthritis affecting large joints)
- Minor criteria: Fever; elevated ESR (acute phase reactant)
- Evidence of recent streptococcal infection: ASO titre >333 Todd units (here: 480) = suggestive of ARF
Combination: Two major criteria (carditis + arthritis) + evidence of recent streptococcal infection = fulfils diagnostic criteria.

(ii) Pathogenesis: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus in the throat generates antibodies or antigen-antibody complexes which are deposited in the heart and joints. It causes pancarditis (affecting pericardium, myocardium, and endocardium). The cardiac damage is more severe than joint damage.
- Pericarditis: thin fibrinous sticky exudate (bread-and-butter pericarditis) or small frank pericardial effusion
- Myocarditis: usually direct
- Endocarditis: affects mitral, aortic, occasionally tricuspid, and rarely pulmonary valves
Pathognomonic histological lesion: Aschoff nodules — aggregates of inflammatory cells (pathognomonic of ARF).

(iii) Heart valves in order of frequency:
1. Mitral valve (most commonly)
2. Aortic valve
3. Tricuspid valve (occasionally)
4. Pulmonary valve (rarely)

(iv) Treatment:
- Bed rest
- Aspirin (salicylate) as anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and analgesic: maximum dose 100 mg/kg/day in divided doses; given 3–4 times a day with meals (to prevent gastric erosion)
- Corticosteroid (e.g. prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day) for patients with life-threatening carditis; monitor urinalysis for glycosuria and electrolytes for salt/water retention
- Organism eradication: Procaine penicillin for 7–10 days (streptococci are very sensitive to it)
- Heart failure treatment: digoxin and diuretics

(v) Long-term prophylaxis:
Drug: Benzathine penicillin (Penadur) — long-acting
Dose: 1.2 mega units/month (adult dose: 2–4 mega units)
Duration: Usually given for 3 years after the first attack; prolonged in those with worse cardiac involvement
Alternatives (not as effective): Oral penicillin V (125–250 mg twice daily); oral erythromycin (125–250 mg twice daily)

(i) Infective Endocarditis (IE) — subacute form (commoner in children with underlying/pre-existing heart disease). Most likely organism given dental history: Streptococcus viridans (found in the mouth) — the commonest cause of subacute IE. The pathological lesion is a vegetation: formed by progressive enlargement of infected thrombus on the damaged endocardium → proliferation of valve leaflet. The lesion may generate infected emboli (explaining the right hemiplegia — CVA from systemic embolisation to the CNS).

(ii) Surgical procedures:
- Valve replacement — for the damaged mitral valve
- Embolectomy — to remove the embolic material causing hemiplegia (coronary, mesenteric, cerebral)
- Removal of mycotic aneurysm — from microabscesses weakening vessel walls (e.g. subarachnoid haemorrhage from cerebral mycotic aneurysm)
- Correction of underlying heart lesion (the rheumatic mitral valve disease)

(iii) Blood cultures: take at least three samples; if not possible to wait, take samples at least one hour apart to maximise yield. Antibiotic regimen for Streptococcus viridans:
- Ceftriaxone, OR
- Ampicillin + Gentamicin (for Gram-negative cover), OR
- Penicillin (crystalline/IV) — very effective; ± Probenecid (used in advanced countries to delay penicillin excretion); ± Gentamicin
All antibiotics given parenterally (bactericidal drugs are preferred); duration: 6 weeks.

(iv) Prophylaxis:
Identify patients at risk: prosthetic cardiac valves; previous IE; unrepaired congenital heart disease; cardiac transplant recipients; surgically constructed shunts.
Additional patient-based measures: good oral and dental hygiene; health education.
Aim: to ensure adequate blood levels of antibiotic in circulation before the intended procedure, to kill bacteria in the bloodstream before they can lodge in the heart.
Oral prophylaxis: amoxycillin 50 mg/kg PO, OR ampicillin PO (given as a single dose 30–60 minutes before the procedure); alternatives — erythromycin, penicillin.
Parenteral prophylaxis: penicillin, amoxicillin, vancomycin, gentamicin (for GUT surgery).
Given 1–2 hours before the procedure and after.
questions.question:
A 10-year-old with a known history of rheumatic heart disease presents with 3 weeks of persistent fever, malaise, changing cardiac murmur, and recent dental extraction. Examination reveals petechiae, splinter haemorrhages, a new pansystolic murmur at the apex, right hemiplegia, and microscopic haematuria. Three sets of blood cultures are taken.

(i) State the diagnosis, the most likely organism given the history, and name the pathological lesion found on the valve.
(ii) Name the surgical procedure on the valve and additional surgical procedures that may be needed to manage the complications present in this child.
(iii) Describe the anatomical landmarks for safe blood culture collection and the antibiotic regimen — drugs, doses, duration — for the most likely organism.
(iv) Describe the prophylaxis for IE — who should receive it, what drugs are used and when, and the aim of prophylaxis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulopathy (DIC).
Predisposing factors: Severe birth asphyxia; septicaemia; hypothermia; hypotension; acidosis; hypoxia.

(ii) Laboratory picture of DIC:
- Prolonged PT; prolonged PTT; prolonged thrombin time.
- Increased FDP (fibrin degradation products).
- Reduced platelets < 100,000/mm³.
- Fragmented RBCs on peripheral blood film.
Distinction from HDN:
- In HDN: PT and PTT are prolonged, but thrombin time and fibrinogen levels are normal; no fragmented RBCs; child is generally well.
- In DIC: thrombin time is prolonged; fibrinogen is reduced; FDP elevated; platelets reduced; fragmented RBCs present; child is sick (from underlying cause such as sepsis or asphyxia).

(iii) Treatment:
- Treat underlying cause.
- Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) 10–15 ml/kg.
- Platelet transfusion.
- Exchange blood transfusion (EBT) with fresh whole blood.
- Vitamin K (? as adjunct).

(iv) Other causes of neonatal thrombocytopenia: Septicaemia; DIC; transient ITP (immune thrombocytopenic purpura); Kasabach-Merritt syndrome.
Clinical presentation: Purpura; ecchymoses; large haematomas.
questions.question:
A 2-week-old male neonate presents with purpura, ecchymoses, prolonged bleeding from venepuncture sites, and spontaneous bleeding. He was delivered by a septic mother, and blood tests show prolonged PT, prolonged PTT, prolonged thrombin time, increased FDP, reduced platelets (< 100,000/mm³), and fragmented RBCs on peripheral blood film.
(i) State the diagnosis and list its predisposing factors.
(ii) Describe the laboratory picture fully and distinguish it from haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
(iii) State the treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The MDGs are 8 goals drawn from the Millennium Declaration adopted by 191 nations (signed by 147 heads of state) during the UN Millennium Summit in September 2000; they were to be achieved by 2015. The 8 MDGs break down into 18 quantifiable targets measured by 48 indicators. They were a universal framework for development and a means for developing countries and their development partners to work together in pursuit of a shared future for all.

A(ii) Goal 4 — Reduce child mortality. Target 5: reduce by two-thirds the mortality rate among children under five years. Indicators: Under-Five Mortality Rate (UNICEF); Infant Mortality Rate (UNICEF); Proportion of 1-year-old children immunised against measles (UNICEF).
Goal 5 — Improve maternal health. Target 6: reduce by three-quarters the maternal mortality ratio. Indicators: Maternal Mortality Ratio (WHO); Proportion of births attended by skilled health personnel (UNICEF).
Goal 6 — Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseases. Target 7: halt and begin to reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS. Target 8: halt and begin to reverse the incidence of malaria and other major diseases. Indicators include: HIV prevalence among 15–24-year-old pregnant women; condom use rate; prevalence and death rates associated with malaria; proportion of population in malaria risk areas using effective malaria prevention and treatment; prevalence and death rates associated with TB; proportion of TB cases detected and cured under DOTS.

B(i) SDGs arose from the MDGs through the Rio +20 conference of 2012, as a follow-up initiative of the United Nations; based on a resolution to create "the future we want." They cover 2015–2030 (Transforming Our World: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development) and consist of 17 goals, 169 targets, and 304 indicators.

B(ii) Three dimensions of sustainable development: Environment, Economics, and Society. Broadly aimed at: ending poverty and hunger; improving health and education; making cities more sustainable; combating climate change; promoting living in a way that does not harm generations to come.

C. The MDG Monitor shows how countries are progressing. It is designed as a tool for policymakers, development practitioners, journalists, students, and others to: track progress through interactive maps and country-specific profiles; learn about countries' challenges and achievements; support organisations working on the MDGs. Success assessment: strong government leadership; good policies and practical strategies for scaling up public investments; adequate financial and technical support from the international community.
Obstacles to progress: insecurity and instability in conflict and post-conflict countries (makes long-term development extremely difficult; failure to achieve MDGs can increase risk of instability); global economic recession; natural and man-made disasters.
