questions.answerText:
A(i) Five parameters of the Apgar score and their scoring:
1. Appearance/Colour: 0 = pale or central cyanosis; 1 = peripheral cyanosis; 2 = completely pink.
2. Pulse/Heart rate: 0 = absent; 1 = < 100 b/min; 2 = > 100 b/min.
3. Grimace/Irritability: 0 = none; 1 = grimace; 2 = cry/sneezing / active avoidance.
4. Activity/Muscle tone: 0 = flaccid; 1 = some flexion / fairly active; 2 = well flexed and active.
5. Respiration: 0 = absent; 1 = weak irregular; 2 = regular.
Maximum score = 10.

A(ii) Score ranges and management:
= 7: Normal — requires no active resuscitation; suctioning.
6: Mild birth asphyxia — more suctioning, but avoid vigorous suctioning to avoid vagal reflex.
4–5: Moderate birth asphyxia — oxygen by face mask; occasionally bag and mask.
1–3: Severe birth asphyxia — clearing of airways; endotracheal intubation and ventilation by bag and mask.

B(i) The 1-minute score is used to determine the amount of resuscitation required. The 5-minute score is used to prognosticate, especially on brain outcome; if it remains low after 5 minutes, the child is likely to have long-term sequelae.

B(ii) Primary apnoea occurs after initial hypoxia with gasping, followed by a period of apnoea; resuscitation at this stage has a good prognosis. Secondary (terminal) apnoea follows if intervention is not offered after the first gasping phase — circulatory collapse occurs, and the patient becomes pale (asphyxia pallida). Note: human beings can only sustain hypoxia for about 5 minutes before brain damage ensues.
questions.question:
Describe the Apgar scoring system used to assess the neonate at birth.
A(i) Name the five parameters scored, state the scoring range for each, and give the maximum possible score.
A(ii) State what each score range means clinically and what immediate management each level requires.
B(i) Explain the clinical significance of the 1-minute and 5-minute scores respectively.
B(ii) Distinguish between primary and secondary apnoea and state the prognostic implication of each.

A 2-year-old boy presents with a first episode of generalised convulsion lasting 8 minutes, occurring on the first day of fever. His temperature is 39.2°C. He is fully conscious between attacks. His neurological examination is normal. His elder sister had similar episodes.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and which sub-type does this episode represent? Justify your answer.
(ii) List the risk factors for recurrence of this condition after the first episode.
(iii) Enumerate the risk factors that increase the chance of development of epilepsy in this child.
(iv) Describe the management of this episode, including: steps to abort the seizure, investigations required, and long-term counselling of the parents.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Febrile seizure. Sub-type: Simple febrile seizure, because it is a single attack in a 24-hour period, the seizure is generalised, and it lasted less than 15 minutes.

(ii) Risk factors for recurrence (occurs in 33% of patients; 75% within 12 months of first attack):
- Young age (<18 months) at the time of the first attack.
- Family history of febrile seizures.
- Short duration of fever before the seizure onset.
- Seizure occurring at a relatively lower fever temperature.

(iii) Risk factors for development of epilepsy (note: this risk is small; recurrence does not increase the risk):
- Abnormal development before the first seizure.
- Family history of afebrile seizure.
- Complex febrile seizure.

(iv) Management:
Step 1 — Abort the seizure: IV (parenteral) diazepam 0.1–0.3 mg/kg given slowly to avoid respiratory arrest; or IM paraldehyde 0.1 ml/kg.
- Rectal diazepam: age <3 years give 5 mg; age >3 years give 10 mg.
Step 2 — Control the temperature: tepid sponging and antipyretics.
Step 3 — Investigate: full blood count; blood film for malaria parasite; lumbar puncture for CSF analysis to rule out meningitis (especially in children <18 months who may not show the usual signs of meningitis).
Step 4 — Treat the underlying cause of fever.
Step 5 — Reassure the parents that the disease is not fatal, the child will not necessarily become epileptic, and there is no brain damage.
Long-term: counsel parents about recurrent management; drug is not the first line of treatment; diazepam is used for prevention/treatment of future episodes in young age, multiple past attacks, or high parental anxiety.

A(i) Rational use and prescribing phases:
- WHO 1988 definition: rational use requires that patients receive medicines appropriate to their clinical needs, in doses to meet individual requirements, for an adequate period of time, at the lowest cost to them. CORRECT DRUG; CORRECT DOSE; CORRECT DURATION
- Four phases: (i) perception of need – is an antibiotic necessary? (ii) choice of antibiotic – what is the most appropriate antibiotic? (iii) choice of regimen – what dose, route, frequency and duration are needed? (iv) monitoring efficacy – is the treatment effective?
A(ii) Factors guiding antibiotic choice:
- Etiological agent: clinical assessment may allow a likely source of infection; empirical treatment aimed at these organisms; laboratory investigations to establish definitive microbiological diagnosis
- Patient – age: tetracycline contraindicated in children (may discolour teeth); neonates have immature liver and renal function affecting metabolism/excretion; antibiotics may adversely affect growing tissues
- Renal and hepatic function: aminoglycosides and glycopeptides need careful use in renal failure; beta-lactams precipitate seizures in renal impairment; doses of macrolides, chloramphenicol, metronidazole, rifampin, and isoniazid reduced in hepatic failure
- Pregnancy: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines avoided; trimethoprim, metronidazole, and macrolides enter breast milk; penicillins, cephalosporins and macrolides appear safe
- Site of infection: antibiotics must achieve sufficient local concentration; abscesses require drainage; necrotic material requires debridement
- Immune status: AIDS, haematological malignancies influence both likelihood and likely etiology
- Allergy: determination of previous allergic drug reactions is important
B(i) Routes, dosage, and duration:
- Parenteral: seriously ill patients; drugs not orally absorbed (e.g. aminoglycosides, glycopeptides); oral route contraindicated
- Oral: most appropriate when feasible
- Topical: superficial skin infections, mucosal candidiasis, middle ear and superficial ocular infections
- Dosage: dose influenced by severity of infection, age, and weight; standard treatment guidelines should be followed; less frequency improves compliance
- Duration: depends on site and severity of infections, causative organisms, and patient's response to treatment
B(ii) Consequences and the four Es:
- Consequences of irrational use: antimicrobial resistance; adverse drug reactions; increased cost burden
- Four Es of irrational antibiotic use:
  1. Lack of Education: suboptimal approach to diagnosis, lack of knowledge of natural course of viral diseases
  2. Experience: diagnostic and prescribing habits of doctors
  3. Expectations: belief that patient expects antibiotics
  4. Economics: time pressures, need to return to work
C(i) Mechanisms of resistance:
- Intrinsic resistance: may be part of genetic makeup; antibiotic target may be absent from bacterial genome
- Acquired resistance: mutation in bacterial chromosome or acquisition of extrachromosomal DNA; spread via vertical transmission of mutations during growth and by horizontal genetic exchange
- Plasmid-mediated: resistance genes on plasmids can be exchanged between different bacterial strains or species; plasmids carrying several resistance genes can confer resistance to multiple antibacterials
- Cross-resistance: resistance mechanism encoded by single gene conveys resistance to more than one antibacterial
C(ii) Strategies and CARAT:
- CARAT (Council of Appropriate and Rational Antibiotic Therapy): independent multidisciplinary panel
- Five CARAT criteria: evidence-based results; therapeutic benefits; safety; cost effectiveness; optimal drug use and duration (shorter course, more aggressive therapy)
- Educating practitioners: seminars, panel discussions, updates
- Educating consumers: no self-medication, no own antibiotic kit, emphasis on dose and duration
- Reading fine print of advertisements
- Multifactorial interventions aimed at both physicians and patients can reduce inappropriate antibiotic prescription
questions.question:

A(i) Definition of rational use of drugs (WHO 1988), and the four phases of prescribing an antibiotic
A(ii) Factors related to the etiological agent, the patient (age, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy, immune status), and the antibiotic that guide choice
B(i) Routes of administration and when each is indicated; dosage regimen principles; duration of treatment
B(ii) Consequences of irrational antibiotic use and the four Es of irrational use
C(i) Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance: intrinsic, acquired (mutation, plasmid-mediated), and cross-resistance
C(ii) Strategies to promote rational antibiotic use and the CARAT criteria

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: CP is a disorder of posture and movement resulting from a permanent, nonprogressive lesion to the immature or developing brain. Also known as Little's disease or static encephalopathy. Epidemiology: incidence 2–4/1000; no appreciable difference between developed and developing countries; commonest neurological disease in the Paediatric Neurologic Clinic (at least 1/3 of cases at UCH).

A(ii) Physiologic classification:
- Spastic: increased muscle tone; intellect usually spared; most common type.
- Athetoid (Dyskinetic): slow writhing movement of limbs and trunk from damage to basal ganglia; common in kernicterus (bilirubin level >20 mg%); features include tongue thrusting, athetosis, chorea, dental enamel dysplasia, impaired upward gaze, deafness.
- Rigid: damage to basal ganglia; types — lead pipe (more common) or cog-wheel.
- Ataxic: involvement of cerebellum; associated with nystagmus; problems with balance and depth perception.
- Tremor, Atonic, Mixed/Unclassified.

A(iii) Topographic classification:
- Monoplegia: one limb (very uncommon).
- Hemiplegia: one side of body; associated seizures; usually spastic.
- Triplegia: three limbs.
- Quadriplegia/Tetraplegia: all four limbs; poor mentation, cognitive dysfunction, mental retardation.
- Diplegia: lower limbs more affected than upper limbs; especially common in preterm infants with anoxic brain damage.
- Double hemiplegia: upper limbs more affected (spastic) than lower limbs.
- Paraplegia: involvement of lower limbs.

B. Athetoid/Dyskinetic CP — caused by bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus); bilirubin is toxic to the basal ganglia, producing involuntary writhing movements. Spastic diplegia — caused by intraventricular haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia, particularly in preterm infants; damage to periventricular white matter tracts produces spasticity predominantly in the lower limbs. Spastic quadriparesis — caused by diffuse brain injury; widespread cortical and subcortical damage produces weakness in all four limbs with seizures and severe mental retardation.

C. Associated deficits include: mental retardation; seizure disorder; hearing impairment; visual defects (strabismus, optic atrophy, nystagmus, refractive errors); speech defects (delayed, poor articulation, loss of voice modulation); learning disability; ADHD; failure to thrive; gait abnormalities; hip subluxation. These may sometimes be more severe than the motor impairment because they directly interfere with the child's education, social functioning, and overall development. All children with CP must have hearing and visual assessment.
questions.question:

A 9-month-old infant presents with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea (more than 10 stools per day) and vomiting. She is under 12 months old and was recently weaned. On examination she has sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, and reduced urine output. She is unable to drink.

(i) Identify the clinical condition and the degree of dehydration suggested by the findings; list all the high-risk factors for dehydration in a child with diarrhoea.
(ii) State what determines whether oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is inappropriate or unsuccessful, and identify the structures/systems that are compromised.
(iii) Describe the intravenous therapy (IVT) required: initial bolus for shock, then calculation and schedule of deficit and maintenance replacement.
(iv) Reason through the appropriate fluid composition for IV replacement, and explain why the management objectives must also include maintenance of nutrition and treatment of the aetiological agent.
questions.answerText:
(i) Clinical condition: Acute diarrhoea with severe dehydration. High-risk factors for dehydration in a child with diarrhoea: age below 12 months; discontinuation of breast feeding; frequent stools (>8/day); vomiting (>2/day); severe malnutrition.

(ii) ORT is inappropriate in: initial treatment of severe dehydration with signs of shock; patients with paralytic ileus or marked abdominal distension; patients unable to drink (though ORS can be given via NG tube if IV is not possible).
ORT is unsuccessful in: patients with very rapid stool loss (>15 ml/kg/hr); patients with severe, repeated vomiting; patients with glucose malabsorption (rare).

(iii) IVT:
In severe dehydration with shock: give 20–30 ml/kg IV boluses of Ringer's lactate or normal saline until organ perfusion is restored; then continue rehydration with ORT.
If child cannot drink, continue IVT using 0.45% saline in 5% dextrose (or 0.18% saline in 4.3% dextrose based on serum sodium values).
Schedule: give ½ deficit and ⅓ maintenance in 7 hours; give remaining deficit and maintenance in 16 hours. Add KCl (10–20 mmol/500 ml bag) as soon as urine is passed. Reassess frequently.

(iv) Fluid composition: isotonic crystalloid (Normal Saline: Na⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154; Ringer's Lactate: Na⁺ 130, Cl⁻ 109, K⁺ 4, Ca²⁺ 3, buffer: lactate). NS can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis. Inotropic and vasoactive drugs are not a substitute for fluid.
Management objectives: prevent dehydration; correct dehydration; maintain or improve nutrition; treat aetiological agents if any.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child is brought to the cardiology clinic. On inspection, the examining nurse notes praecordial bulge and a hyperactive praecordium. On palpation, the apex beat is displaced downward and outward. Auscultation reveals a wide, fixed splitting of the second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge. The ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy. Chest X-ray shows an enlarged right atrium.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? Explain why the S2 has wide fixed splitting in this condition.
(ii) Explain the pressure gradient responsible for shunting in this condition and compare it with the pressure gradient in VSD and PDA.
(iii) What does the praecordial bulge signify in terms of chronicity?
(iv) State three conditions that produce an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, and state how this condition is distinguished from the others on auscultation.
(v) Describe the natural history: why may this condition be asymptomatic for years, and what complication may arise in adulthood from the long-standing right atrial dilatation?
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) — secundum type.
Wide fixed splitting of S2: The shunting through the ASD equalises the volume loads of both atria throughout the respiratory cycle. Normally, inspiration increases right heart filling and widens S2 splitting. In ASD, the equalization of atrial volumes means the right ventricular ejection time remains prolonged throughout both inspiration and expiration — so splitting is always wide and does not vary with respiration (fixed).

(ii) Pressure gradient:
- ASD: The pressure gradient is small — left atrium has 8–9 mmHg vs. right atrium 5 mmHg = gradient of only 3–4 mmHg. This is why shunting is minimal and haemodynamic changes are gradual.
- VSD: Peak systolic pressure on left is 130–140 mmHg vs. right ventricle at 30 mmHg = high pressure gradient → large haemodynamically significant shunt.
- PDA: Similar to VSD — high-pressure system; aortic pressure far exceeds pulmonary artery pressure → significant shunting. ASD is associated with a low-pressure system unlike VSD and PDA.

(iii) Significance of praecordial bulge: It is due to cardiomegaly (long-standing cardiac enlargement). It shows the chronicity of the illness — a long-standing illness that is likely congenital.

(iv) Three conditions producing ejection systolic murmur at LUSE:
1. Pulmonary stenosis
2. ASD (pulmonic flow murmur — from increased flow through the pulmonary valve due to volume overload)
3. (Pulmonary hypertension may also be considered)
Distinguishing ASD: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 (not seen in PS or other causes of ESM at LUSE). PS also has an ejection click (absent in ASD).

(v) Natural history:
- ASD is usually asymptomatic in early life because the pressure gradient is very small (3–4 mmHg), so the haemodynamic load builds gradually over years. The heart adapts with right atrial and right ventricular dilatation. In males, it is often an accidental discovery (e.g. Kanu Nwankwo, Nigerian footballer).
- Adult complication: The long-standing right atrial dilatation leads to atrial arrhythmias (specifically atrial fibrillation — listed as a complication of ASD dilatation; irregular rhythm with irregularly irregular pulse).

questions.question:
A. Describe paediatric heart failure (CHF) under the following headings:
A(i) List the causes of heart failure by age group: fetus, premature neonate, full-term neonate, infant, and child/adolescent
A(ii) Classify the pathophysiological groups and the haemodynamic groups of paediatric heart failure, giving examples for each group

B. Describe the pathophysiology of CHF:
B(i) The compensatory mechanisms activated when systemic O2 supply is less than demand
B(ii) The mechanism of salt and water retention in CHF — tracing the sequence from limited O2 delivery through to increased intravascular fluid volume

C. State the clinical features of CHF and list all drug classes used in its management, giving examples of agents in each class
questions.answerText:
A(i) Causes of paediatric heart failure by age:
Fetus: cardiac arrhythmias (SVT, AF, complete heart block, VT); severe anaemia (Rh incompatibility, ABO incompatibility, fetal-maternal transfusion, intrauterine infection); myocardial ischaemia; Ebstein anomaly; AV valve insufficiency; critical AS; AV malformation.
Premature neonate: PDA, cor pulmonale, VSD, PPH of newborn; HLHS, CoA ± VSD, interrupted aortic arch ± VSD, critical AS, truncus arteriosus, UVH + increased PBF, TGA + VSD.
Full-term neonate: TAPVR + venous obstruction, cardiac arrhythmias (SVT, VT, CHB), AV malformation, asphyxial cardiomyopathy, viral myocarditis.
Infant: VSD, PDA, complete AVC, UVH, TAPVR, AV malformation, anomalous left coronary artery, metabolic cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrhythmias, Kawasaki, TGA with VSD.
Child/adolescent: cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive, metabolic/genetic, drug-induced, toxins, infections, collagen vascular disease); Eisenmenger syndrome; primary pulmonary hypertension; RHD; ARF; endocarditis; cor pulmonale; tachyarrhythmias; chronic anaemia; post-open heart surgery with residual lesion.

A(ii) Pathophysiological groups: preload (severe anaemia, AV malformation, AVVR, PDA, VSD, truncus arteriosus, TGA+VSD); afterload (critical AS, CoA ± VSD, interrupted aortic arch ± VSD, HLHS); myocardial dysfunction (congenital, infections, cardiomyopathy, carnitine deficiency, iatrogenic, secondary to valvular or ischaemic disease).
Haemodynamic groups: (1) Diminished systemic output due to excessive pulmonary blood flow — atrial level shunts (TAPVR, common atrium); ventricular level shunts (VSD, AVCD, UVH); great vessel shunts (PDA, truncus arteriosus, AP window, AV fistula). (2) Obstruction — AV valve obstructions (MS, TS); ventricular obstruction (AS); great vessel obstruction (CoA). (3) Myocardial dysfunction. (4) Arrhythmias (SVT, VT, CHB). (5) Diastolic dysfunction (cardiomyopathy, hypertension).

B(i) Compensatory mechanisms: salt and water retention; increased adrenergic activity; increased red cell mass; hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes; hyperplasia of cardiac fibroblasts; alteration of pattern of expression of cardiomyocyte-specific and non-muscle myocyte-specific genes.

B(ii) Salt and water retention sequence: limited O2 delivery → redistribution of cardiac output away from kidney → circulating and local renin, angiotensin II, and catecholamines → renal vasoconstriction, reduced GFR, reduced filtration fraction → increased peritubular protein concentration → proximal tubular Na+ and fluid reabsorption → increased aldosterone activity → Na+ reabsorption and K+ excretion at distal tubule → reduced fluid volume in distal tubule → release of ADH → distal tubule water reabsorption → increased intravascular fluid volume → cardiac dilatation → stroke volume → LV and LA volume → cardiac compliance exhausted → LV, LA, and pulmonary venous pressures → atrial distension → release of ANF.

C. Clinical features: sympathetic overdrive (tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, cold extremities, cold sweat, hypotension, pallor, pulsus alternans); increased pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary vascular congestion and oedema, frequent respiratory infections, diastolic flow rumble across AV valves); fluid retention (hepatomegaly, peripheral oedema, JVD); general — failure to thrive, effort intolerance, syncope, chest discomfort.
Drug management:
- Inotropic agents: digoxin, dopamine, dobutamine, isoprenaline
- PDE inhibitors: amrinone, milrinone
- Diuretics: furosemide, ethacrynic acid, spironolactone, hydrochlorothiazide, bumetanide, metolazone
- ACE inhibitors and vasodilators: captopril, enalapril, hydralazine, nitroglycerine, sodium nitroprusside, PGE-1 infusion, tolazoline
- Antiarrhythmic drugs
- Others: prednisolone, L-carnitine, IV immunoglobulins, beta blockers
- Newer interventions: IABP, ventricular assist devices

questions.question:
A 10-year-old child on chemotherapy for Burkitt's lymphoma develops a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, decreased urine output, and muscle weakness. ECG shows widened QRS complexes and peaked T-waves. Serum K⁺ is 6.8 mEq/L, uric acid is 9.5 mg/dl, and PO₄ is 7.0 mEq/L.
(i) What syndrome is this? Which tumours are most commonly associated with it?
(ii) Describe in detail the clinical consequences of hyperphosphataemia in TLS.
(iii) Describe the classification of TLS using the Cairo and Bishop system.
(iv) Outline the specific treatment for hyperkalaemia in TLS.
questions.answerText:
(i) Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS).
Most commonly associated tumours: Burkitt lymphoma and T-cell ALL; also hepatoblastoma and neuroblastoma.
Risk factors making these tumours prone: Bulky tumours, rapidly proliferating, chemosensitive, high LDH, high pre-treatment uric acid, organ infiltration, bone marrow involvement. Sevinir et al retrospective study on 327 children: 5.8% TLS overall; 15.9% in NHL and 0.47% in ALL.
(ii) Clinical consequences of hyperphosphataemia:
- Serum PO₄ >6.5 mEq/L.
- From tumour lysis and renal failure.
- Causes reciprocal depression of serum Ca (hypocalcaemia).
- Ca × PO₄ >60 → metastatic calcification.
- Symptoms: pruritus, conjunctivitis, arthritis, renal failure.
(iii) Cairo and Bishop classification:
Laboratory TLS: ≥2 of the following metabolic abnormalities during the same 24-hour period, within 3 days before or up to 7 days after initiation of therapy:
- Hyperkalemia: K >6 mEq/L or 25% increase.
- Hyperuricemia: UA >8 mg/dl or 25% increase.
- Hyperphosphatemia: PO₄ >6.5 mg/dl or 25% increase.
- Hypocalcemia: ionized calcium <1.5 mEq/L (3 mg/dl) or 25% decrease.
Clinical TLS: Laboratory TLS PLUS one or more of: increase in creatinine ≥1.5× ULN, cardiac arrhythmia or sudden death, or seizure. (Note: Uric acid nephropathy and acute kidney injury are clinical TLS features.)
(iv) Specific treatment for hyperkalaemia:
- Stop K⁺ intake.
- Drive K⁺ into the cells:
  (a) IV NaHCO₃ 1–2 mEq/kg.
  (b) 0.1 U/kg of insulin + IV 50% glucose 1 ml/kg.
  (c) Aerosolised salbutamol.
- IV Calcium gluconate 100–200 mg/kg/dose slowly.
- Ion exchange resin (kayexalate): 1 g/kg p.o. + 50% sorbitol.
- Dialysis.

A(i) Pathophysiology of HDN: After birth, there is a slight reduction in levels of Vitamin K, which leads to a reduction of Vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors, usually between the 2nd and 7th days of life — a normal phenomenon. Exaggeration of this process leads to haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN).
Vitamin K-dependent factors: Factors II, VII, IX, X (PT measures vitamin K deficiency; PTT measures factors XII, XI, VIII, X, V, II, I and is prolonged in DIC, heparin therapy, haemophilia, and severe vitamin K deficiency).
Timing: Early < 24 hours; Classic 2nd–7th day; Late > 1 week.

A(ii) Predisposing factors: Birth asphyxia; maternal drugs (phenobarbitone, aspirin, coumarin); exclusive breastfeeding; broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy; parenteral nutrition.

B(i) Clinical features:
- Bleeding sites: GI, nasal, subgaleal, intracranial, post-circumcision.
- General condition: Well child (in classic HDN).
- Laboratory: PT and PTT prolonged; thrombin time and fibrinogen levels are normal (distinguishes from DIC where thrombin time and fibrinogen are also abnormal).

B(ii) Treatment: IV Vitamin K1 1–5 mg stat; exchange blood transfusion (EBT) with fresh whole blood in severe cases.
Prevention: IM Vitamin K 1 mg at birth; 0.5 mg weekly to babies on parenteral nutrition.
questions.question:
Describe the haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN) comprehensively.
A(i) Explain the pathophysiological basis of classic HDN, name the vitamin K-dependent factors involved, and state the timing of the condition (early, classic, late).
A(ii) List the predisposing/risk factors for HDN.
B(i) Describe the clinical features of HDN, including the bleeding sites, the child's general condition, and the laboratory findings expected.
B(ii) State the treatment and prevention of HDN, including drugs, doses, and route.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is ileocolic intussusception. The specific ultrasound sign is the 'target sign' (also called the 'donut sign') — a concentric ring pattern in cross-section — which is pathognomonic of intussusception representing the telescoping of one bowel segment into another. The condition most commonly occurs at the ileocaecal region.
(ii) The classic clinical triad is: (1) intermittent colicky abdominal pain with episodes of drawing up the legs; (2) palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass; and (3) passage of 'currant jelly' stools (blood mixed with mucus from mucosal ischaemia). Vomiting may also be present.
(iii) Hydrostatic or pneumatic (air) enema under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance is both diagnostic and therapeutic, reducing the intussusception non-surgically. Contraindications include signs of bowel perforation (pneumoperitoneum on X-ray), peritonitis, haemodynamic instability or shock, and clinical suspicion of gangrenous bowel.
(iv) A barium enema is absolutely contraindicated in suspected bowel perforation. If barium sulphate enters the peritoneal cavity through the perforation, it causes a severe granulomatous reaction — barium peritonitis — which is more dangerous than the underlying perforation and carries a very high mortality.
(v) If non-surgical reduction fails, surgical reduction (open or laparoscopic) is performed. The surgical finding that distinguishes viable from non-viable bowel is colour, turgor, and peristalsis of the reduced bowel: viable bowel returns to normal pink colour, normal consistency, and shows active peristalsis after reduction; non-viable (gangrenous) bowel remains dark purple-black, does not recover its turgor or colour, and lacks peristalsis, requiring segmental bowel resection.
questions.question:
A 10-month-old infant is brought by his mother after 8 hours of intermittent, severe colicky abdominal pain with episodes of drawing up the legs. Between episodes the child is pale and lethargic. The mother reports one episode of vomiting and the passage of reddish jelly-like stool. On abdominal examination a sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. The abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a concentric ring pattern in cross-section.

(i) State the diagnosis, the specific ultrasound sign described, and the anatomical region where this condition most commonly occurs.
(ii) Identify three clinical features in this presentation that collectively constitute the classic triad of this condition.
(iii) What non-surgical procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic for this condition, and under what circumstances is it contraindicated?
(iv) Identify the radiological investigation that is absolutely contraindicated in suspected bowel perforation in this setting, and state the specific complication of using this agent in the peritoneal cavity.
(v) If non-surgical reduction fails, what operation is required, and what is the surgical finding that distinguishes viable from non-viable bowel at this stage?

A 7-year-old boy with known congenital hepatic fibrosis presents to the emergency department with his parents, who report he has been increasingly drowsy and confused over 24 hours, and started to 'wave his hands strangely.' He had a large upper GI bleed 2 days ago requiring blood transfusion. On examination he has a distended abdomen with shifting dullness, splenomegaly, and asterixis on outstretched hands. His serum ammonia is elevated.

(i) Identify the specific neurological complication, name the clinical sign elicited, and state the primary neurotoxic substance responsible.
(ii) Identify at least three predisposing factors in this presentation that precipitated the current neurological complication.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism linking the variceal haemorrhage to the rise in the identified neurotoxic substance.
(iv) Describe the physical examination signs of ascites demonstrated, and explain the humoral mechanism responsible for ascites formation in portal hypertension.
(v) Name the primary diuretic agents used to manage cirrhotic ascites, stating the rationale for choosing each.
questions.answerText:
(i) The specific neurological complication is portosystemic (hepatic) encephalopathy. The clinical sign demonstrated is asterixis (hepatic flap or flapping tremor), elicited by outstretched hands. The primary neurotoxic substance responsible is ammonia (NH₃).
(ii) Predisposing factors in this presentation include: the large upper GI bleed (haematemesis) — blood in the intestinal lumen provides a large nitrogenous substrate load for bacterial ammonia production; portosystemic shunting from the underlying congenital hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension, allowing ammonia to bypass hepatic detoxification; impaired urea cycle function in the damaged liver; and reduced effective hepatic mass for ammonia detoxification.
(iii) The variceal haemorrhage delivered a large quantity of blood into the intestinal lumen. Intestinal bacteria catabolise this blood (a protein substrate) producing large quantities of ammonia. Ammonia is normally detoxified in the liver via the urea cycle. With portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatocellular function, ammonia accumulates in the systemic circulation, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and impairs neuromuscular coordination, causing encephalopathy. This explains the 24-hour lag between the bleed and encephalopathy onset.
(iv) Shifting dullness and fluid wave (fluid thrill) are the physical examination signs of ascites demonstrated. Ascites develops from a combination of: (1) vasodilatory humoral factors — primarily nitric oxide and glucagon — generating splanchnic vasodilatation that reduces effective arterial blood volume; (2) compensatory sodium and water retention; and (3) hypoalbuminaemia (impaired hepatic albumin synthesis) reducing plasma oncotic pressure, allowing fluid to shift into the peritoneal cavity.
(v) Spironolactone (an aldosterone antagonist) is the primary diuretic because secondary hyperaldosteronism drives sodium retention in portal hypertension, and spironolactone blocks this mechanism directly. Furosemide (a loop diuretic) may be added for a synergistic effect. The combination is more effective than either alone while preserving potassium balance.

questions.answerText:
(i) Coarctation of the aorta (CoA) — the commonest primary cardiovascular lesion causing heart failure in the acyanotic neonate in the first week of life. In Ibadan, it accounts for 2% of 635 cases of congenital heart disease over 10 years at UCH.
Associated conditions: commonly associated with aortic stenosis; in infancy often associated with heart failure. Types: concentric or cylindrical; sites — thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta, or complete tubular hypoplasia of the entire arch; pre-ductal, juxta-ductal, or post-ductal coarctation.

(ii) Upper limb hypertension results from obstruction to aortic flow, increasing afterload on the left ventricle and raising pressure proximal to the coarctation (i.e. in vessels supplying the upper limbs). Reduced femoral pulses occur because blood pressure distal to the obstruction is reduced. The normal difference should be ≤20 mmHg; a difference >20 mmHg suggests coarctation. The continuous scapular murmur is due to collateral circulation that develops to bypass the obstruction.

(iii) Investigations:
- CXR: cardiomegaly (if in heart failure); rib notching (if collateral circulation established); ± incidental aortic knuckle
- ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy; occasionally right ventricular hypertrophy (if interrupted aortic arch + VSD + pulmonary hypertension)
- Cardiac catheterisation: to delineate the anatomy and demonstrate the pressure gradient across the obstruction

(iv) Management:
Medical: treat hypertension and heart failure while awaiting surgery (for asymptomatic patients with hypertension — defer surgery until after 6 months of life).
Surgical: urgent surgical relief for symptomatic patients and those with heart failure.
Procedures:
- Classical resection and end-to-end anastomosis
- Subclavian flap repair
- Modified subclavian flap repair with stent (complication: re-coarctation)
- Percutaneous transluminal balloon aortoplasty

A(ii) Atrial situs:

- Situs inversus: Mirror image — when the left bronchus is seen on the right on chest X-ray, it is 99% certain that the right atrium is now on the left side
- Atrial isomerism: Both bronchi are of the same length (either both have the length of a right bronchus = right isomerism = two sino-atrial nodes, or both have the length of a left bronchus = left isomerism). Identified on CXR by equal bronchial lengths.

A(iii) Concordant AV connection — requirements:

(b) Left atrium must be connected to the left ventricle
(c) Situs solitus
Discordant AV connection — requirements:
(a) Right atrium connected to left ventricle; left atrium connected to right ventricle
(b) 2 distinct atria, 2 distinct ventricles, 2 AV ostia

Congenitally Corrected TGA:

A(i) Aetiological agents (Mycobacterium complex):
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. bovis, M. africanus, M. microti
- Characteristics of mycobacteria: multiples slowly; resistant to many antimicrobial drugs; remains viable in macrophages by subverting macrophage-killing; its waxy coat together with its many component substances depress immune responses against it
A(ii) Sources of infection and modes of spread:
- Most important source is sputum of persons with open tuberculosis
- Inhalation (airborne): when a person with pulmonary or laryngeal TB coughs or sneezes, droplet nuclei containing M. tb can remain suspended in the air for several hours; one cough can produce 3,000 droplet nuclei
- Ingestion: M. bovis can be transmitted by ingestion of milk from infected cattle
- Primary infection in children most often follows prolonged close contact with an untreated adult with cavitary disease
- Uncommon: contact with infectious discharges e.g. drainage from discharging sinuses; aerosol-producing procedures such as autopsies and tissue irrigation
B(i) Pathogenesis to primary complex:
- 70-90% of individuals exposed will not develop symptoms (inhalation of insufficient organisms or adequate immunity)
- Primary complex = primary focus + regional lymph nodes
- Primary focus: a few mm to 2 cm, usually sub-pleural; may be symptomless or cause minor symptoms
- TB granuloma: focal area of granulomatous inflammation characterized by central caseous necrosis
- Risk of primary infection developing into active disease is ~15% in the first 10 years after infection
- Primary complex can heal or progress; spread of primary focus to contiguous lung → TB pneumonia; inflamed nodes compress neighbouring bronchi → atelectasis/emphysema; erosion through bronchial wall → endobronchial TB
B(ii) Haematogenous dissemination and systemic disease:
- Erosion of nodes into blood vessels → haematogenous spread to other organs
- Diffuse infection of the lungs: "miliary" TB
- Brain: TB brain abscess; Meninges: TB meningitis
- Bones: TB osteomyelitis, commonly affects the spine ("Potts' disease")
- Pericardium: TB pericarditis and pericardial effusion
- Disseminated disease most likely in the immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, malnutrition) and at extremes of age
C(i) Drug resistance:
- Pathogenesis: spontaneous mutation, cross resistance (resistance to other medications from the same class)
- DR-TB transmitted same way as DS-TB
- Types: drug resistance among new cases (primary) and among previously treated cases (acquired)
- MDR: resistance to Rifampicin and Isoniazid
- XDR: resistance to Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Quinolone, and Aminoglycoside
C(ii) Treatment regimens:
- Regimen 1 (2RHZE/4RH): for PTB and all forms of EPTB except TB meningitis, miliary TB, osteoarticular TB; total 6 months (2 months intensive RHZE + 4 months continuation RH)
- Regimen 2 (2RHZE/10RH): for TB meningitis, miliary TB, osteoarticular TB (spine, joints); total 12 months (2 months intensive RHZE + 10 months continuation RH)
- Treatment divided into intensive phase (first 2 months) and continuation phase; DOTS desirable at least during intensive phase

A. Describe the causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in the neonate under the following categories, naming at least two specific diseases per category:
A(i) Increased bilirubin load from haemolysis
A(ii) Defective hepatic uptake or conjugation
A(iii) Inhibition of conjugation — including one drug and one maternal factor

B. Explain the clinical basis for each of the following:
B(i) Why preterm neonates develop pathologic jaundice at a lower serum bilirubin threshold than term neonates
B(ii) Why polycythaemia causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia

C. Distinguish physiologic neonatal jaundice from pathologic neonatal jaundice on the basis of:
C(i) Timing of onset, peak serum bilirubin level, and rate of rise
C(ii) Conjugated bilirubin fraction
questions.answerText:
A(i) Increased bilirubin load from haemolysis: ABO incompatibility (Group O mother with high titres of IgG anti-A or anti-B antibodies carrying a Group A or B infant) and Rh isoimmunisation (maternal IgG anti-D antibodies crossing the placenta coating Rh-positive fetal red cells causing extravascular haemolysis). Also G6PD deficiency (oxidative haemolysis from impaired glutathione regeneration), pyruvate kinase deficiency (reduced ATP causing red cell fragility), congenital spherocytosis (defects in membrane proteins spectrin/ankyrin causing spherical fragile erythrocytes), and extravascular blood breakdown from cephalohaematoma.
A(ii) Defective hepatic uptake or conjugation: Crigler-Najjar syndrome (complete or partial hereditary deficiency of UDP-glucuronyltransferase); Gilbert's disease (liver cell membrane defect impairing hepatic uptake with mild reduction in glucuronyltransferase activity); and hypothyroidism (reduces UDP-glucuronyltransferase activity and maturation).
A(iii) Inhibition of conjugation: Novobiocin (a drug that inhibits bilirubin conjugation); breast milk jaundice (inhibitory substances in breast milk — believed to include beta-glucuronidase and unsaturated fatty acids — inhibit UDP-glucuronyltransferase activity, peaking at 2 weeks and resolving by 3–12 weeks); and Lucey-Driscoll syndrome (Transient Familial Neonatal Hyperbilirubinaemia — a serum inhibitor of UDP-glucuronyltransferase transmitted from mother via serum, distinct from breast milk jaundice).
B(i) Preterm neonates have greater blood-brain barrier permeability and lower serum albumin levels, meaning free unconjugated bilirubin dissociates more readily and penetrates the brain at lower total bilirubin concentrations. The threshold for pathologic jaundice in preterm neonates is therefore serum bilirubin exceeding 15 mg/dL (versus 12 mg/dL in term infants) to define pathologic jaundice, reflecting lower brain protection at lower levels.
B(ii) Polycythaemia increases the total haem substrate available for catabolism. The breakdown of excess red blood cells produces proportionally more unconjugated bilirubin, overwhelming the conjugation capacity of the immature neonatal liver and resulting in hyperbilirubinaemia.
C(i) Physiologic jaundice appears on day 2–3 of life and resolves by day 10, with serum bilirubin below 12 mg/dL in term infants and a rate of rise below 5 mg/dL/day. Pathologic jaundice appears within the first 24 hours, or total bilirubin exceeds 12 mg/dL in a term infant (15 mg/dL in preterm), or the rate of rise exceeds 5 mg/dL/day.
C(ii) In physiologic jaundice, conjugated bilirubin fraction is less than 2 mg/dL (or below 15% of total bilirubin). The presence of conjugated bilirubin above 2 mg/dL defines pathologic cholestatic jaundice, distinguishing it from unconjugated physiologic jaundice.

questions.question:
A. Describe the pathophysiology of intestinal malabsorption under the following categories, naming at least one specific disease for each:
A(i) Small intestinal mucosal disease causing villous atrophy
A(ii) Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causing fat malabsorption
A(iii) Physical brush border coating interfering with absorption
A(iv) Protein-losing enteropathy via lymphatic dysfunction

B. Describe the following diagnostic investigations for malabsorption, explaining the physiological principle underlying each:
B(i) D-xylose absorption test — what it measures and what abnormal result indicates
B(ii) Hydrogen breath test — the substrate used and the principle of detection
B(iii) Jejunal biopsy — the specific histological pattern in coeliac disease

C. Explain why cystic fibrosis causes fat malabsorption, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and steatorrhoea, linking the underlying genetic defect to the intestinal consequence, and state which vitamins are specifically deficient.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Small intestinal mucosal disease: coeliac disease causes flat mucosa with subtotal villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia from immune-mediated T-cell destruction of villi triggered by gliadin. Tropical sprue also causes villous atrophy but in individuals from tropical regions responding to tetracycline.
A(ii) Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency: cystic fibrosis causes malabsorption through exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — viscid secretions block pancreatic ducts leading to destruction of acini and deficiency of lipase, protease, and amylase — resulting in steatorrhoea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
A(iii) Physical brush border coating: Giardia intestinalis (lamblia) causes malabsorption by physically coating the intestinal brush border, mechanically interfering with nutrient and enzyme contact. It also disrupts tight junctions and causes villous blunting without invading the mucosa.
A(iv) Protein-losing enteropathy via lymphatic dysfunction: intestinal lymphangiectasia involves dilated lacteals that leak protein-rich lymph (chylomicrons, lymphocytes) into the intestinal lumen, causing hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and fat malabsorption.
B(i) The D-xylose absorption test assesses small intestinal mucosal function; D-xylose is a pentose sugar absorbed passively in the proximal small intestine and excreted unchanged in urine. Reduced urinary excretion indicates mucosal disease (such as coeliac), while normal levels point to pancreatic or luminal causes of malabsorption.
B(ii) The hydrogen breath test uses a carbohydrate substrate (such as lactose or lactulose). Unabsorbed carbohydrate reaches the colon where bacterial fermentation produces hydrogen gas, which is absorbed and exhaled. A rise in exhaled hydrogen above baseline indicates malabsorption or bacterial overgrowth.
B(iii) Jejunal biopsy in coeliac disease shows flat mucosa with subtotal villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia — loss of the normal finger-like villi with compensatory elongation of crypts. This reverses on a gluten-free diet, confirming the diagnosis.
C. Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, producing dysfunctional chloride channels generating viscid secretions. Viscid secretions block pancreatic ducts, leading to acinar destruction and deficiency of lipase, protease, and amylase. Without lipase, dietary fats cannot be digested and absorbed, producing steatorrhoea. Bile acids are essential for micellar solubilisation and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; impaired fat absorption also impairs absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K specifically, leading to night blindness (A), rickets (D), neuropathy (E), and coagulopathy (K).

questions.question:
Describe febrile neutropenia and Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS)/Superior Mediastinal Syndrome (SMS) as oncologic emergencies under the following headings:
A(i) Define neutropenia (with classifications) and febrile neutropenia; distinguish high-risk from low-risk patients.
A(ii) Describe the indications and mechanism of action of G-CSF/GM-CSF, including potential risks.
B(i) Define SVCS and SMS, state the major aetiological tumours, and describe the clinical presentation of each.
B(ii) Outline the complete treatment of SVCS/SMS.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and classification of neutropenia and febrile neutropenia:
- Neutropenia: absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, or <1000/uL with anticipated decline to <500/uL in the next 48 hours.
- Classifications: Mild neutropenia: 500–1000/uL; Moderate neutropenia: 200–499/uL; Severe neutropenia: <200/uL.
- Febrile Neutropenia: Fever ≥38.3°C or temperature >38.0°C sustained for more than 1 hour in a person with neutropenia.
High-risk patients: ANC <500 cells/microL anticipated to last >7 days; Hepatic or renal insufficiency; Co-morbidities.
Low-risk patients: Neutropenia expected to resolve within 7 days; Stable and adequate hepatic and renal function; No active co-morbidities.

A(ii) G-CSF/GM-CSF:
- Increases proliferation of granulocytes and macrophages.
- Ameliorates and prevents profound neutropenia and its potentially life-threatening infections in patients with non-myeloid malignancies.
- Reduces antibiotic usage and shortens hospital stay.
- Prevents delay in delivery of chemotherapy.
- Risk: Can stimulate leukaemic clone causing relapse.
Indications: Pre-existing neutropenia due to disease; Previous irradiation of the pelvis; To accelerate granulocyte recovery following BM transplant; Mobilise haematopoietic progenitor cells into peripheral blood for collection by leukopheresis.
Dose: SC 5 mcg/kg/d until ANC is 5000–10,000/uL.

B(i) SVCS and SMS:
- SVCS: signs and symptoms that occur following obstruction to blood flow through the SVC. Extrinsic: compression of SVC. Intrinsic: thrombosis formation.
- SMS: signs and symptoms that occur as a result of obstruction of the airways (trachea, main bronchi) or great thoracic vessel compression, usually from a mediastinal mass.
Major aetiological tumours: Lymphomas, Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (particularly T-cell), Sarcomas, Neuroblastoma, Germ cell tumours.
SVCS presentation: Oedema; Plethora of face, neck, upper chest and arms; Oedema of conjunctiva; Distended neck veins and chest veins; Cerebral symptoms: headaches, dizziness, confusion, loss of consciousness, visual distortion.
SMS presentation (caused by local mass effect, systemic effect, infection): Trachea/bronchi: Stridor, dyspnoea, cough, features of lung collapse; Oesophagus: Dysphagia; Left recurrent laryngeal nerve: Hoarseness; Phrenic nerve: Hemidiaphragm paralysis; Sympathetic trunk: Horner's syndrome.

B(ii) Treatment of SVCS/SMS:
- Elevation of the head/keep patient propped up.
- Supplemental oxygen administration via face mask.
- Maintenance of a calm and quiet environment with minimal handling.
- Avoid sedatives.
- Moderate diuresis with loop diuretics.
- Steroids: dexamethasone given 6-hourly.
- Endovascular stents to relieve obstruction.
- Tissue diagnosis.
- Radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours: effect is seen within 72 hours.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old child is brought unconscious to the emergency unit. The child had been previously well. On triage, the child has snoring respirations, poor colour, and a capillary refill time of 5 seconds.

(i) Name the immediate life-threatening problem and outline the stepwise airway management from least to most invasive.
(ii) State the indications for IPPV by bag-valve-mask, the consequence if BVM ventilation is unsuccessful, and the landmarks used for intraosseous (IO) access including when IO is preferred.
(iii) What is the physiological definition of the circulatory problem demonstrated, and what is the initial fluid bolus prescribed?
(iv) State the post-resuscitation steps, and list the constraints to emergency paediatric care in Nigeria.
questions.answerText:
(i) Immediate problem: Airway obstruction with circulatory compromise (shock). Stepwise airway management:
1. Head tilt-chin lift manoeuvre
2. Suction airway
3. Oro-pharyngeal airway
4. Endotracheal intubation
5. Cricothyrotomy

(ii) Indications for IPPV by BVM: poor colour; bradycardia unresponsive to supplemental O2; gasping; apnoea.
If BVM ventilation is unsuccessful or prolonged PPV is required → endotracheal intubation.
IO access: recommended in children six years or younger after 90 seconds or 3 attempts at peripheral intravenous access. Crystalloid solution (normal saline or Ringer's lactate), 20 ml/kg bolus over 20 minutes.

(iii) Shock is a physiologic state where delivery of oxygen and substrates are inadequate to meet tissue metabolic needs. Circulatory management: IV normal saline 20 ml/kg rapidly; re-assess and give more boluses if still in shock; urethral catheterisation to monitor urinary output.

(iv) Post-resuscitation:
- Re-assessment of status is ongoing
- Laboratory and radiological information is obtained
- Aetiology of respiratory failure or shock is determined
- Transfer to facility where child can get maximum care

Constraints to emergency paediatric care in Nigeria:
- Lack of a functional Emergency Medical Services (EMS) system
- Shortage of manpower
- Financial constraints
- Inadequate infrastructures
- Late presentation in hospitals

A(i) Definitions and classification:
- Uncomplicated malaria: symptomatic malaria with no vital organ dysfunction or life-threatening manifestations; no life-threatening features
- Severe malaria: P. falciparum asexual parasitaemia and no other confirmed cause of symptoms with the presence of one or more life-threatening clinical or laboratory features; a life-threatening condition where the goal of treatment is to prevent death
- Classification: assess for symptoms (fever, chills, headache, joint weakness, fatigue, abdominal and back pains, nausea, vomiting, pallor) and signs (raised temperature ≥37.5°C, enlarged spleen/liver, pallor); exclude signs of severe disease
A(ii) Life-threatening features with thresholds:
- Cerebral malaria: deep unarousable coma; GCS <11 or Blantyre <3; coma persisting ≥30 min after convulsion
- Severe anaemia: haematocrit <15% or haemoglobin <5 g/dl in presence of parasite count >10,000/μl
- Renal failure: urine output <400 ml/24 hours in adults (<12 ml/kg/24 hours in children) and serum creatinine >265 μmol/l
- Hypoglycaemia: whole blood glucose <2.2 mmol/l (<40 mg/dl)
- Circulatory collapse (algid malaria): systolic BP <70 mmHg (>5 years) or <50 mmHg (1-5 years) with cold clammy skin or core-skin temperature difference >10°C
- Pulmonary oedema/ARDS; abnormal bleeding/DIC (≥3 convulsions/24 hours); acidemia (pH <7.25); macroscopic haemoglobinuria; prostration; hyperparasitaemia (>5% parasitized erythrocytes or >250,000/μl); hyperpyrexia (>40°C); hyperbilirubinaemia (>43 μmol/l)
B(i) Treatment of uncomplicated malaria:
- Treatment of choice: Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapy (ACT)
- Artemether-Lumefantrine: 5-<15 kg: 1 tab twice daily x 3 days; 15-<25 kg: 2 tabs twice daily x 3 days; 25-<35 kg: 3 tabs twice daily x 3 days; >35 kg: 4 tabs twice daily x 3 days; 6 doses must be taken
- Artesunate-Amodiaquine: 4.5-<9 kg (2-11 months): 25/67.5 mg, 1 tab once daily x 3 days; >9-<18 kg (1-5 years): 50/135 mg, 1 tab once daily x 3 days; >18-<36 kg (6-13 years): 100/270 mg, 1 tab once daily x 3 days; 36 kg+ (14+ years): 100/270 mg, 2 tabs once daily x 3 days
- If patient vomits within 30 minutes, repeat dose; if vomiting persists, consider severe malaria
- Febrile seizure: if no recovery within 30 minutes, treat as severe malaria
- Inadequate response: evaluate, exclude sub-optimal dosing; if unresponsive consider another ACT
B(ii) Treatment of severe malaria:
- First line: Artesunate Injection 2.4 mg/kg IV bolus; repeat 2.4 mg/kg after 12 hours; then 2.4 mg/kg daily until oral tolerated (minimum 48 hours); parenteral for minimum 24 hours before switching oral even if patient ready
- Follow-on: full 3-day course of ACT
- Alternative (Artemether IM): 3.2 mg/kg IM on first day; 1.6 mg/kg daily for maximum 3 days; then full 3-day course of ACT
- Alternative (IV Quinine): 20 mg/kg loading dose in 10 ml/kg 4.3% dextrose/0.18% saline over 4 hours; then 10 mg salt/kg every 12 hours; switch to oral ACT once patient can tolerate
C(i) Risk groups and differential diagnoses:
- At risk for severe malaria: children <5 years; pregnant women; people returning from malaria-free areas; people who have had splenectomy
- Differential diagnoses of coma with fever: meningitis (stiff neck); encephalopathy; diabetes mellitus (dehydrated, acidotic); septicaemia (very ill, toxic, warm extremities); epilepsy (no temperature, prior history); acute renal failure; viral haemorrhagic fevers (jaundice, bleeding tendency)
C(ii) Health education and community control:
- Health education: importance of early diagnosis and prompt treatment; seeking early treatment and taking appropriate antimalarials promptly in adequate doses; counsel about illness and treatment
- Personal protection: mosquito screening devices in the design of houses; protective dressing; use of insecticide-treated nets (ITN)/materials; use of insecticides and mosquito repellants
- Environmental management: reducing mosquito breeding sites
- Community mobilization: use community health workers to follow up patients; work with existing community development committees and other community organizations and leaders; work with partners from other sectors

questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is biliary atresia. Criteria supporting this include pale (acholic) stools, dark urine, jaundice persisting beyond 14–21 days, hepatomegaly, and absent bowel excretion on HIDA scan despite hepatic uptake. Conjugated bilirubin exceeding 15% of total bilirubin or above 2.0 mg/dL confirms neonatal cholestasis, of which biliary atresia is the most important extrahepatic cause.
(ii) The underlying process is progressive fibro-obliterative destruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts. The pathological progression follows: initiation of the insult → liver cell inflammation (hepatitis) → inflammation of biliary tracts (cholangitis) → progressive necrosis → narrowing and obliteration of the biliary ducts constituting biliary atresia.
(iii) Resuscitation and supportive measures include: correction of the prolonged prothrombin time with intravenous vitamin K, which addresses fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption from cholestasis. Fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K) is essential. Cholestyramine may be used to bind bile acids in the intestinal lumen, reducing enterohepatic circulation and relieving pruritus. Nutritional support with medium-chain triglyceride-enriched feeds is important.
(iv) The definitive surgical treatment is the Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy. Timing is critical because early surgery — ideally before 8 weeks of age — significantly improves prognosis by restoring bile drainage before irreversible biliary cirrhosis develops. Delayed surgery beyond this window leads to progressive hepatic fibrosis and eventual liver failure, making liver transplantation the only remaining option.

A 14-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of painless, progressive swelling of the right side of his face. On examination there is a hard, craggy jaw mass and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. He has fever, drenching night sweats, and significant weight loss.
(i) What two diagnoses must be distinguished and what clinical and histological features differentiate them?
(ii) What investigation is essential to diagnose each tumour?
(iii) What is the staging system for Burkitt's Lymphoma?
(iv) Describe the specific chemotherapy regimen for each tumour.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnoses to distinguish and differentiating features:
- Burkitt's Lymphoma (BL): hard craggy jaw/abdominal mass; short history (83% within 3 months); lymphadenopathy is minimal in endemic BL unlike other Non-Hodgkin's lymphomas; no significant constitutional symptoms typical of HL; multiple abdominal organ involvement frequent.
- Hodgkin's Disease (HD): presents with progressive painless enlargement of lymph nodes; constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, drenching night sweats — "B symptoms") are prominent; cervical lymphadenopathy most common; differential diagnosis of tuberculosis. Characteristic cell is the Reed-Sternberg cell with "owl-eye" appearance; associated with EBV. Histologic types: lymphocyte-predominant (best prognosis), nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-depleted (worst prognosis).
(ii) Essential investigation for diagnosis:
- Burkitt's Lymphoma: ultrasound-guided FNAC; ascitic fluid cytology; FNAC shows Burkitt's cells (basophilic moderate cytoplasm with fat vacuoles, nucleus with 2–5 nucleoli); excisional biopsy if FNAC fails — shows starry-sky appearance.
- Hodgkin's Disease: Lymph node biopsy.
(iii) Staging of Burkitt's Lymphoma:
- Stage A: Solitary extra-abdominal site (e.g. jaw).
- Stage B: Multiple extra-abdominal sites.
- Stage C: Intra-abdominal tumour ± facial tumour.
- Stage AR: Abdominal tumour which has been completely (≥90%) resected.
(iv) Chemotherapy regimens:
- Burkitt's Lymphoma: COMP or COAP — Oral Prednisolone, IV Cyclophosphamide, IV Vincristine, IV Cytosine arabinoside or Methotrexate, Intrathecal Cytosine arabinoside or Methotrexate. Six cycles, 2 weeks each, given for first 5 days per cycle.
- Hodgkin's Disease: MOPP — Nitrogen mustard, Oncovin, Procarbazine, Prednisolone. (Note: Radiotherapy responds well but is avoided in children because of affectation of growth plates.)

(i) The diagnosis is coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). The cereals to be eliminated are wheat, barley, and rye, which contain the immunotoxic gliadin fraction of gluten. Rice, maize, and other grains do not contain gliadin and are safe. Type 1 diabetes (IDDM) is relevant because coeliac disease is associated with other autoimmune conditions, particularly insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and autoimmune thyroid disease, due to shared HLA-DQ2/DQ8 haplotypes that predispose individuals to multiple autoimmune conditions. The co-existence of both increases the index of suspicion for coeliac disease.
(ii) The gold standard investigation is jejunal biopsy. Histological findings expected: flat mucosa with subtotal villous atrophy (loss of normal finger-like villi), crypt hyperplasia (elongation of the crypts), and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. These changes reverse on a gluten-free diet, confirming the diagnosis. The biopsy should be taken from the proximal small intestine — the jejunum (obtained at upper GI endoscopy, typically at the duodenojejunal junction or second part of the duodenum).
(iii) The skin manifestation is dermatitis herpetiformis, presenting with blistering subepidermal eruptions (vesicles) that are intensely pruritic and symmetric, distributed on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). Skin biopsy shows IgA deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction, which is the specific and characteristic microscopic finding.
(iv) IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA) and IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) would be falsely negative in patients with IgA deficiency. The clinical implication is that IgA deficiency must be excluded before relying on negative EMA/tTG serology to rule out coeliac disease; in IgA-deficient patients, IgG-based anti-tTG or IgG EMA should be measured instead.
(v) Two absorption tests available: D-xylose absorption test and hydrogen breath test. D-xylose absorption test principle: D-xylose is a pentose sugar absorbed passively in the proximal small intestine without requiring pancreatic enzymes or bile acids. It is not metabolised and is excreted unchanged in urine. After oral ingestion, a 5-hour urine collection measures the excreted amount. Reduced urinary excretion indicates proximal mucosal disease (such as coeliac), while a normal result suggests that malabsorption is of pancreatic or luminal origin rather than mucosal.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis and mechanism:
- Most likely: Neonatal anaemia due to acute haemorrhage — likely birth trauma (subgaleal haematoma, cephalhaematoma, or rupture of liver/spleen from difficult instrumental delivery), or feto-maternal/twin-twin transfusion.
- Mechanism: Neonatal haemorrhage from birth trauma (cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haematoma, rupture of liver, spleen, etc.) leads to acute blood loss, causing shock and anaemia with PCV <30% and BP <25 mmHg.
(ii) Immediate resuscitation based on severity:
- Shock (BP <25 mmHg, PCV <30%, pH <7.1): Transfuse 15–20 ml/kg whole blood over 5–10 minutes.
- Not in shock but severe anaemia: Give 20 ml/kg of whole blood over 2–3 hrs with IV frusemide 2 mg/kg OR packed cells 10–15 ml/kg (2–3 ml/kg/hr); 2 ml/kg of packed cells will raise Hb by 0.5–1 g/dl.
- Very severe anaemia (Hb <8 g/dl) with CCF: Exchange Blood Transfusion (EBT) with packed cells.
- Neonatal transfusion protocol (symptomatic): Lethargy, Tachycardia >180/min, Respiratory signs including tachypnoea, Haemic murmurs, Heart failure → Transfuse.
(iii) Indications for EBT in neonatal anaemia:
- Anaemia in the first 72 hours, PCV <30%.
- Mechanical ventilation, PCV <30%.
- Oxygen dependency (not ventilated), PCV <25–30%.
- Very severe anaemia with CCF.
(iv) Hyperviscosity/Polycythaemia in the newborn:
- Definition: Venous PCV >65%. As venous PCV rises above 65%, viscosity of blood increases and O₂ transport reduces.
- Aetiology: Placental insufficiency; Materno-foetal transfusion from delayed cord clamping; Twin-twin transfusion; Infant of diabetic mother (IDM).

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Erb's Palsy (Brachial plexus injury — upper roots). The nerve roots involved are C5 and C6.

(ii) Mechanism of injury: Erb's Palsy usually occurs during birth, especially in large babies (macrosomia), due to excessive lateral traction on the head at the second stage of labour — this stretches and tears the upper roots (C5, C6) of the brachial plexus. It also occurs in breech delivery (bottom-first).

(iii) Structures at risk: muscles supplied by C5 and C6 — specifically the shoulder abductors (deltoid, supraspinatus), external rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor), elbow flexors (biceps brachii), and forearm supinators (biceps, supinator). Loss of these produces the posture of adduction, internal rotation, and pronation, and absent biceps reflex (C5, C6 arc).
The hand intrinsic muscles are spared because they are supplied by C8 and T1 (via the ulnar nerve), which are the lower roots of the brachial plexus — these roots are not damaged in Erb's Palsy (only the upper roots C5, C6 are damaged). This distinguishes Erb's Palsy from Klumpke's Paralysis (C7, C8, T1), which affects the intrinsic hand muscles and gives rise to a "waiter's tip hand" deformity.

(iv) Management:
- Wearing a long-sleeve shirt for the baby and pinning it down to the pillow (to immobilise the limb in a position that prevents further stretch injury and contracture).
- Early physiotherapy.
- Gentle massage and other physical exercises to maintain joint range and muscle function.
- Surgery if required: should be done before 4 years of age (to release contractures or explore nerve repair).
Prognosis: most recover fully, but a few do not recover completely.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Three cardinal symptoms: cough; attacks of wheeze; breathlessness.

A(ii) Features giving clue to diagnosis: repeated wheeze (>2 episodes); recurrent or persistent cough; night-time disturbance by wheeze or cough.

A(iii) Precipitating factors: viral URTI; exercise or excitement; family emotional disturbances; potential allergens (pets, pollens, dust, feathers); cigarette smoke.

A(iv) Supporting features: presence of collateral allergy (allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis); past medical history of infantile eczema (atopic dermatitis); family history of atopy; therapeutic response to a bronchodilator makes the diagnosis more likely.

B. Classification of acute exacerbations: Mild; Moderate; Severe/life-threatening. Recognition of acute severe asthma: too breathless to talk; too breathless to feed; tachypnoea; tachycardia. Life-threatening features: cyanosis; a silent chest; poor respiratory effort; fatigue or exhaustion; agitation or reduced level of consciousness. Classification for long-term management: Intermittent; Mild persistent; Moderate persistent; Severe persistent.

C. Goals of acute therapy: to reduce wheeze and cough; relieve airflow obstruction and hypoxaemia as rapidly as possible; reduce the risk and number of acute exacerbations; plan prevention of future relapses; minimise adverse effects of treatments, sleep disturbances, and absences from school; close monitoring of patient's condition and response to treatment is crucial. Treatment is tailored to the severity of asthma. Long-term management: focuses on controlling asthma by treating the underlying airway inflammation; inhaled corticosteroids are the agent of choice in preventive care; leukotriene modifiers are very useful; long-acting beta2 agonists are useful; oral theophylline cannot be recommended in children because of potential serious side effects (cardiac arrhythmias or convulsions if therapeutic blood levels are exceeded).

(i) The complication described is Acute Chest Syndrome (also called Pulmonary Infarction/Respiratory complication of SCD).
Respiratory complications in SCD include: Pneumonia, Pulmonary infarction, Fat embolism, Hypoxaemia (due to intrapulmonary R-L shunts, membrane diffusion defects, and a shift of the dissociation curve to the RIGHT), Restrictive impairment of ventilatory function.
(ii) Complications by organ system:
- MSS: Osteomyelitis, Bone infarction/osteonecrosis, Pathological fractures, Avascular necrosis, Chronic leg ulcers, Digital clubbing.
- Hepato-biliary: Hepatomegaly/hepatic necrosis (ischaemic damage), Sickle-cell hepatopathy, Cirrhosis/haemosiderosis, Cholelithiasis, Choledocholithiasis, Hepatic coma (rare).
- Genito-urinary: Enuresis/polyuria due to hyposthenuria, Pyelonephritis, Haematuria, Progressive azotaemia/renal failure, Priapism, Nephrotic syndrome, Renal medullary carcinoma.
- Cardiovascular: Cardiomegaly, Ischaemic damage to the myocardium, Congestive cardiac failure, Cor pulmonale.
- Neurological: Convulsions, CVA (aphasia, spastic hemiplegia — thrombotic/haemorrhagic); risk factors for infarction: prior TIA, low steady state Hb, elevated BP, recent acute chest syndrome. Risk factors for intracranial haemorrhage: low steady state Hb and high leucocyte count.
- Ocular: Dilatation/tortuosity of retinal vessels, Retinal haemorrhage, Proliferative retinopathy, Retinal detachment, Visual impairment.
- Endocrine: Reduced growth hormone from anterior pituitary, Reduced cortisol levels, Pancreatic insufficiency.
- Psychosocial: Persistent jaundice, Frequent ill health, Delayed puberty, Poor growth, Non-acceptance by society, Uncertainty about future, Economic burden.
(iii) Investigations and peripheral blood film findings:
- Haemoglobin electrophoresis (cellulose acetate, citrate agar); HPLC and isoelectric focussing for neonates.
- Solubility test: 4 drops blood + 2 ml freshly prepared Na dithionite + K₂PO₄; HbSS shows precipitate above, clear solution beneath.
- Lab: Hb 5–9 g/dl, increased retic count 5–15%, WBC 12–20,000, normal MCV, normal or slightly increased platelets.
- Peripheral blood film: target cells, poikilocytosis, anisocytosis, hypochromic cells, sickled RBC, Howell-Jolly bodies, nucleated RBC (severe anaemia), markedly hyperplastic bone marrow with erythroid predominance.
(iv) Acute management: Give O₂; IV fluids; O₂ therapy; Antibiotics; Transfuse in presence of: anaemic heart failure, PCV below 15%, significant fall in PCV below steady state, overwhelming infection; EBT (or straight PRBC Tx).
Long-term management for CNS infarction: Long-term programme of partial EBT or hypertransfusion is commenced especially if there is evidence of permanent endothelial damage on angio or CT/MRI scan; aim is to permanently reduce sludging by decreasing viscosity. Transcranial Doppler (TCD) is used to monitor cerebral flow and predict those liable to stroke; blood flow velocity in cerebral arteries >200 cm/sec on TCD is an indication for initiating transfusions to maintain HbS below 30%.

questions.answerText:
(i) Eisenmenger syndrome (Eisenmenger Complex).
Haemodynamic mechanism: In a large VSD, the high pulmonary blood flow causes progressive thickening of pulmonary vessel walls, initially causing reversible pulmonary vascular disease, then irreversible obliterative changes. As pulmonary vascular resistance rises, it eventually exceeds systemic vascular resistance. At this point, the pressure gradient that previously drove blood from left to right reverses — blood now flows from right to left through the VSD, causing cyanosis (arterial desaturation).

(ii) Contraindication to surgery: When the pulmonary vascular disease is irreversible and pulmonary pressure is suprasystemic, closing the VSD would result in post-cardiotomy syndrome — after surgery, the right ventricle would face suprasystemic afterload with no outlet through the VSD, leading to acute right heart failure. The myocardium requires a lot of oxygen after surgery and cannot sustain suprasystemic pressures.

(iii) Investigation to determine pulmonary vascular disease: Cardiac catheterisation — no longer used routinely; it is needed only to determine pulmonary wedge vascular pressure.
Unit of measurement: Wood units.

(iv) Natural history of pulmonary vascular changes:
1. Initially: reflex vasospasm in response to high pulmonary blood pressure
2. Thickening of pulmonary vessel walls (smooth muscle hypertrophy and intimal proliferation) — initially reversible
3. Progressive irreversible obliterative pulmonary vascular disease
4. Eisenmenger syndrome: suprasystemic pulmonary vascular resistance → reversal of shunt → cyanosis

(v) Definitive repair: Batch repair (patch repair of VSD) under profound hypothermia. Very rarely on bypass. This is performed before Eisenmenger syndrome develops.

(i) Vaccines due at 9 months (Nigerian NPI schedule):
- MCV1 (Measles-Containing Vaccine 1): route: subcutaneous (SC), 0.5 ml, upper left arm
- Yellow Fever (YF): route: subcutaneous (SC), 0.5 ml, upper right arm
- MEN A (Meningitis A Conjugate Vaccine): route: intramuscular (IM)
(ii) Whether diarrhoea, mild fever, and antimicrobial therapy are contraindications:
- These are NOT contraindications to immunization:
  - URTI: not a contraindication
  - Mild fever: not a contraindication
  - Diarrhoea: not a contraindication
  - Antimicrobial therapy: not a contraindication
  - Cerebral palsy: not a contraindication
  - Breast feeding: not a contraindication
- Justification: delaying immunization for these common conditions results in missed opportunities and lowers coverage; the vaccines are safe to administer; not immunizing every day and failure to check immune status are listed as missed opportunities that reduce coverage
(iii) Cold chain and preparation for live attenuated vaccine:
- The national programme uses monovalent measles vaccine in freeze-dried form and it has to be reconstituted with a diluent before administration
- The vaccine must be reconstituted correctly; once reconstituted it has a limited viability
- Failure to open multiple-dose vials for few clients is listed as a missed opportunity, implying multi-dose vials should be opened when needed regardless of the number of clients
- Vaccine costs and lack of vaccine availability are barriers to immunization; vaccines must be properly stored
- Yellow fever vaccine is also live attenuated and requires similar cold chain storage and reconstitution
(iv) Modifications for symptomatic HIV-positive child:

- Live vaccines generally not given to immunocompromised children
- IPV is preferred to OPV in HIV-positive children
- All vaccines may be given if the child is asymptomatic HIV-positive
