A(i) Describe the structure of the adrenal gland under the following headings: location, gross structure, zones of the cortex, and hormones produced by each zone.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of the salt-losing crisis in 21-hydroxylase deficiency: why it occurs, and why it is more difficult to diagnose in males than in females.
B(i) Distinguish between 21-hydroxylase deficiency and 11-hydroxylase deficiency in terms of biochemistry, clinical presentation, and the presence or absence of hypertension.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Structure of the adrenal gland:
• Location: located at the cranial pole of the kidneys. Accessory adrenal tissue may occur adjacent to the main glands, near the gonads or within the gonads.
• Gross structure: made up of the adrenal cortex and medulla.
• Zones of the cortex (three zones):
  - Outer zona glomerulosa: produces mineralocorticoids, principally aldosterone; primarily responsive to angiotensin and potassium.
  - Middle zona fasciculata: responsive to ACTH; primarily synthesises glucocorticoids.
  - Inner zona reticularis: responsive to ACTH; primarily secretes C19 steroids (adrenal androgens).
• Medulla: produces adrenaline and noradrenaline.

A(ii) Clinical basis of salt-losing crisis in 21-hydroxylase deficiency:
• Absent cortisol leads to excessive ACTH production due to failure of the negative feedback mechanism. ACTH drives adrenal hyperplasia. Resulting hyperplasia leads to excess androgen production from pathways above the enzyme block.
• 50–75% of severe 21-hydroxylase deficiency cases have a defect of aldosterone synthesis, leading to salt loss. Without aldosterone, sodium is not retained: serum Na+, Cl−, HCO3− fall; K+ rises; acidosis, hypoglycaemia, dehydration, and shock develop within 2–4 weeks of life.
• More difficult in males: in females, the genitalia are ambiguous at birth (clitoral enlargement, labial fusion), alerting the clinician immediately. In males, the genitalia may not be ambiguous in the 21-hydroxylase type, and diagnosis may be missed unless there is a known family history. The salt-losing male may be mistaken for a case of pyloric stenosis or gastroenteritis.

B(i) 21-hydroxylase versus 11-hydroxylase deficiency:
• Biochemistry: 21-hydroxylase produces 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androgenic precursors above the block → elevated 17-OHprogesterone, elevated urinary pregnenatriol. 11-hydroxylase produces its immediate precursor deoxycortisol and increased deoxycorticosterone (DOC) → elevated urine deoxycortisol, elevated DOC.
• Clinical: both cause virilisation in females and increased masculinisation/precocious puberty in males. 11-hydroxylase is the second commonest type and their urine contains large amounts of deoxycortisol.
• Hypertension: 11-hydroxylase deficiency produces excess deoxycorticosterone, which has mineralocorticoid activity and causes hypertension, and prevents salt-losing syndrome even when enough aldosterone is not produced. 21-hydroxylase deficiency, by contrast, causes salt-losing syndrome (in 50–75% of severe cases) and does NOT cause hypertension from this mechanism.

A(i) Aetiology, infectivity, epidemiology:
- Measles virus is an RNA virus; family: Paramyxoviridae; genus: Morbillivirus; only 1 antigenic type
- Virus found in nasopharyngeal secretions, blood and urine during prodromal period and few days after rash appears
- Spread by droplet spray during the prodromal period; infected person is contagious from 9th-10th day after exposure to 3rd day after onset of rash
- Recommended period of isolation: 7th day after exposure until 5 days after rash has appeared
- Measles is endemic in most of the world; highly infectious; median age in Nigeria = 17 months
- Transplacentally acquired immunity present in first 6 months; by 1 year, 1/3 of children would have had measles
- Incubation period: 10-14 days; period of communicability: 4 days before and 5 days after appearance of rash
- Case fatality rate: 2-15% in developing countries; no vector, no animal reservoir, one serotype
A(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Initial infection and viral replication occur locally in tracheal and bronchial epithelial cells
- After 2-4 days, measles virus infects local lymphatic tissues, perhaps carried by pulmonary macrophages
- Following amplification in regional lymph nodes, a predominantly cell-associated viraemia disseminates the virus to various organs prior to appearance of rash
- Lesions in skin, mucous membranes of nasopharynx, bronchi, intestinal tract and conjunctiva
- Pathognomonic enanthem: Koplik spots consist of serous exudate and proliferation of endothelial cells
- In cellular immune deficiency: measles causes progressive and often fatal giant cell pneumonia (Warthin Finkeldey)
- Immunosuppression marked by decreases in delayed-type hypersensitivity, interleukin-12 production, and antigen-specific lymphoproliferative responses, persisting for weeks to months
B(i) Three stages:
1. Incubation period: 10-14 days with few signs or symptoms
2. Prodromal period (3-5 days): mild to moderate fever, slight backing cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; Koplik spots – pathognomonic, on palate and buccal mucosa usually opposite lower molars, greyish white dots with reddish area, transient, lasting 12-18 hours
3. Final stage: abrupt rise in temperature with appearance of rash; rash starts as macules behind ears, along hairline, entire face, upper arm; within 24 hours becomes maculopapular; spreads to back, abdomen, entire arms and thigh; reaches legs on 3rd day; severity related to extent and confluence of rash; desquamation follows fading
B(ii) Complications:
- Reported in 1 out of 15 cases
- Respiratory: bronchopneumonia (viral giant cell and bacterial); laryngotracheobronchitis (croup); activation of TB lesion
- Neurological: febrile seizure; encephalomyelitis (1-2/1000, appears 2-5 days after onset of rash); SSPE (mean incubation ~10.8 years, chronic degenerative disease with behavioural/intellectual deterioration and seizures)
- GIT: gastroenteritis, malnutrition, cancrum oris
- Myocarditis; blindness due to Vit A deficiency; subcutaneous emphysema; ADEM; haemorrhagic measles; DIC
B(i cont'd)/C(i) Differential diagnosis:
- Roseola: rash appears as temperature decreases
- Rubella: associated tender lymphadenopathy, less striking rash
- Drug reaction: no cough, history of drug ingestion
- Enteroviral infections: rash less striking, less fever
- Rickettsial infection: rash spares the face
- Scarlet fever: rash is diffuse, finely papular with goose flesh texture on an erythematous base
C(ii) Management and prevention:
- Supportive and symptomatic: antipyretic, eye drops, clean the eyes, calamine lotion, adequate fluid intake
- Management of complications: antibiotics, management of heart failure, nutritional rehabilitation, high dose Vit A (significantly reduces risks of morbidity/mortality), rehydration, management of croup
- Prevention: live attenuated vaccine; national programme uses monovalent measles vaccine in freeze-dried form reconstituted with diluent; also available as MMR
- Efficacy: 85% (up to 15% of children do not seroconvert); side effects: 10% develop low grade fever, 5% develop mild generalized non-infectious rash; duration of immunity: lifelong
- No contraindications, even where child is sick or malnourished; dose 0.5 ml SC, upper left arm
- Routine schedule at 9 months (±6 months); passive immunity with immune serum globulin within 5 days after exposure

questions.answerText:
A(i) Molecular basis:
- HbS is the result of a single base-pair change, thymine for adenine, at the sixth codon of the beta gene. This change encodes Valine instead of glutamine (glutamic acid) in the sixth position on the beta-globin molecule.
- Alternatively stated: Glu → Val at position 6 of the beta chain.

A(ii) Mechanism of polymerisation and sickling:
- Deoxy HbS polymerises to form tactoids (spindle-shaped liquid crystalline bodies), deforming the RBC with increased mechanical fragility and haemolysis, predominantly at extra-vascular sites.
- Sickling occurs at the venous end of capillaries; unsickling occurs at the arterial end.
- Initially there are series of sickle-unsickle cycles; finally cells become irreversibly sickled.
- The delay time (latent phase before explosive polymer growth) is inversely proportional to the 15th–35th power of HbS concentration; small changes in HbS concentration markedly affect polymerisation.
- Factors enhancing sickling: hypoxia, presence of WBC, bacteria, fever, dehydration, metabolic acidosis.

B(i) Vascular consequences:
- Blocks microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → infarction → pain and organ failure.
- Shortened RBC lifespan (17 days) → chronic anaemia (PCV ~24%) → increased BM activity (6–8×) → widening diploe of skull.
- Increased adhesiveness of sickle reticulocytes, coupled with increased leucocyte count, leads to thrombotic coagulopathy.
- Pathologic changes occur in all organs from the combined effects of chronic hypoxia, recurrent infections, and infarction.

B(ii) Infections in SCD:
- Progressive splenic infarction/fibrosis leads to functional asplenia; by age 5 years, 95% of children with SCA have functional asplenia.
- High serum iron levels (from chronic haemolysis, frequent transfusions, and compensatory increased gut absorption) promote growth, multiplication, and virulence of several bacterial organisms.
- Defective alternate pathway of complement (excessive properdin consumption or depressed macrophage synthesis of properdin related to splenic dysfunction).
- Metabolic abnormalities in leucocytes.
- Common organisms: H. influenzae, Pneumococcus, Salmonella spp., S. aureus.

B(iii) Distinction:
- Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis: blocks microcirculation in bone, abdomen, and other organs; management includes identifying and treating precipitating cause, bed rest, liberal fluids (P.O./IV at least 1.5 maintenance), analgesics; usually lasts less than 1 week.
- Acute splenic sequestration crisis: pooling of blood in the spleen causes shock and rapid splenic enlargement; commonest in younger children; severe pallor, may lead to death; management includes urgent blood transfusion, treating precipitating cause, parenteral steroids, packed cell transfusion 5–10 ml/kg, partial EBT, and splenectomy.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions:
- Neonatal period: 0–28 days.
- Perinatal period: 1st week of life (from 28/40 weeks gestational age).
- Term: > 37–42 weeks.
- Preterm: < 37 completed weeks.
- Very preterm: < 32 weeks.
- Late preterm: > 34 weeks – 36 weeks + 6 days.
- Post-term: > 42 weeks.
- LBW (Low birthweight): weighing < 2,500 g.
- Macrosomic: > 4,000 g.
- Chronological age: age from date of birth.
- Real age (corrected age) = chronological age minus the number of weeks preterm.

A(ii) Objectives of perinatology:
1. Early identification of high-risk pregnancies.
2. Proper perinatal and neonatal care of high-risk babies to: present to families a healthy infant with maximum potential for growth and development; decrease neonatal mortality and morbidity.
Categories of high-risk infants:
- Delivered before 37 weeks or after 42 weeks.
- Weighing < 2,500 g (LBW) or > 4,000 g (macrosomic).
- Deviate from expected size and development (SGA < 10th centile or LGA > 90th centile for GA).
- Born to mothers with history of serious neonatal illness or death of a sibling, or > 2 previous foetal deaths.
- With birth asphyxia or requiring active resuscitation (bag and mask ventilation).
- Delivered to mothers with infections or illness during pregnancy (hypertension, pre-eclampsia, DM, drug addicts, APH, elderly primip > 35 years, teenage mothers).
- Maternal history of drug usage (narcotics, thiazides, steroids, tetracycline, anticonvulsants, cytotoxic drugs, nicotine, alcohol).
- IDMs; preterm/postdate/LBW/macrosomic infants.
- Mothers with eclampsia/hypertensive disorders, APH, oligo/polyhydramnios or PROM, sickle cell anaemia.
- Meconium stained liquor; severely asphyxiated infants; multiple pregnancies; congenital malformations; maternal age = 16 or = 40 years; previous perinatal deaths or preterm births.

B(i) Essential care of the normal newborn:
- Resuscitation: materials, personnel, procedure (NRP), Apgar scoring.
- Physical examination: general, vital signs, and anthropometry.
- Keep warm (thermal control).
- Cord care.
- Feeding; hygiene; watch for jaundice; immunisation. No routine drugs.

B(ii) Normal birthweight range: 2.5 kg–3.99 kg.
Corrected (real) age = chronological age less the number of weeks preterm. Example: a baby born at 28 weeks who is now 16 weeks old has a corrected age of 16 - (40 - 28) = 4 weeks.
questions.question:

A(i) Define the following terms: neonatal period, perinatal period, term, preterm, very preterm, late preterm, post-term, LBW, and macrosomic.
A(ii) State the objectives of perinatology and list ten categories of high-risk infants.
B(i) Describe the essential care of the normal newborn immediately after birth, covering the five key areas.
B(ii) State the normal birthweight range and explain what corrected (real) age means, giving the formula.

Describe the neonatal immune system and why neonates are at increased risk of infection.
A(i) State the four components of the neonatal immune system that are immature and ineffective, and explain how WBC function is impaired compared to adults using the specific parameters given.
A(ii) Explain how maternal antibody transfer protects the neonate and what limits this protection.
B(i) Distinguish between Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis (EONS) and Late-Onset Neonatal Sepsis (LONS) using the five criteria (timing, clinical pattern, acquisition, obstetrical associations, mortality).
B(ii) State the laboratory investigations for neonatal sepsis in full, including all culture sources, all leukocyte profile criteria for bacteraemia, and the role of thrombocytopenia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Immature/ineffective components: Antibodies; complement; neutrophils; skin/mucosal barriers.
WBC function impaired:
- Immature: decreased chemotaxis; decreased deformability; decreased phagocytosis; reduced storage pool.
- Adults have a circulating pool 14-fold greater than their storage pool; neonates have only a 2-fold difference.
- Defective phagocyte migration and less effective neutrophil killing of ingested bacteria.
- Neutrophils from sick neonates have greater deficits in killing capacity.
- Antibody-dependent and independent cell-mediated immunity is also deficient → prone to viral infections.
- Males have higher predisposition than females.
- Low birthweight babies have defective IgG response to infections.
- Deficiency of alternate pathway of complement activation and classic pathway to some extent.

A(ii) Maternal antibody transfer: Antibody transfer increases with gestational age; most transfer occurs during the 3rd trimester. Protection is limited because: (i) preterm infants receive less; (ii) there is no guarantee that maternal antibodies to the specific infecting organism are present.
Immature skin and mucosal surfaces: reduced layers; reduced junctions between cells; reduced secretory IgA. Umbilical cord and catheter breaches provide portals of entry.

B(i) EONS vs. LONS:
- EONS: < 5 days old; fulminant, multi-system illness; obstetrical complications; prematurity; perinatal acquisition; high mortality (5–50%).
- LONS: 5 days to 3 months old; sepsis or meningitis; perinatal or postnatal acquisition; lower mortality (2–6%).

B(ii) Laboratory investigations:
Cultures:
- Blood.
- CSF.
- Urine.
- Tracheal aspirates (gram stains and cultures via endotracheal tube).
- Amniotic fluid, gastric aspirate, ear canal, skin cultures/gram stains identify flora of foetal environment but do not confirm neonatal sepsis.
- CXR and abdominal X-ray.
Leukocyte profiles (highest predictive accuracy and sensitivity for bacteraemia):
- Total WBC < 5,000/mm³.
- Absolute neutrophil count < 1,000/mm³.
- Bands: PMN ratio > 0.2.
- Note: Leukocytosis may be a stress reaction and not indicative of sepsis.
Thrombocytopenia: a marker of sepsis.
Bacterial antigen identification: Latex agglutination or counter immune electrophoresis (CIE) — may not be reliable.

A(i) EPI was created in 1974, following the success of the smallpox eradication programme. Original 6 killer diseases: Tuberculosis, Polio, Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis, and Measles. Additional vaccines since recommended by WHO: yellow fever in 1986 (for Africa only); hepatitis B in 1992; Hib in 1997 (according to national capacities and priorities).

A(ii) Nigeria launched EPI in 1978; low immunisation coverage recorded nationwide due to low public mobilisation and awareness, and poor cold chain maintenance. By 1990, high coverage of 80% was achieved in some areas but not maintained — due to continuing economic recession, political instability, withdrawal of foreign donors, inadequate and irregular supply of vaccines, and poor utilisation of immunisation services. In 1996, the Federal Government organised a review and re-launched the EPI as the National Programme on Immunisation (NPI) to reflect national commitment and ownership.

A(iii) Routine immunisation strategies: fixed facility; outreach; mobile.
Supplemental immunisation strategies: National Immunisation Days (NIDs) — nationwide mass campaigns to boost and sustain coverage; Mop-up campaigns.

B. Drop-out: a comparison of the number of children who start receiving immunisations and the number who do not complete it; measures immunisation programme continuity. A drop-out rate of 10% or less is acceptable, though full immunisation is always the goal.
Missed opportunity: a health facility visit by a child who is eligible to receive a vaccine but does not receive it. Reasons at provider level: invalid contraindications, fear of adverse events (usually not supported by scientific data). Reasons at systemic level: clinic with a policy of not vaccinating on particular days, or irregular immunisation service.

C. Vaccine-related determinants: chemical and physical state of the antigen, dose of the antigen, timing, presence of adjuvant, route of administration. Child-related determinants: genetic characteristics, age, nutrition, infection, immune status. No vaccine has 100% efficacy; efficacy ranges from 71% to about 95% with an average of about 80% in most. Hence, children who have received a full course of a vaccine may still acquire the disease on exposure.

questions.answerText:
(i) Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) in childhood. Risk factors present in this patient:
• Obesity (>85% of children with T2DM are obese; obesity contributes to insulin resistance and is associated with a 40% decrease in insulin-mediated glucose disposal)
• Female sex (girls are nearly twice as likely to develop T2DM as boys)
• Family history of DM in first- and second-degree relatives (74–100% of T2DM have a family history)
• Puberty (associated with increased insulin resistance; insulin-mediated glucose disposal is reduced by approximately 30% between Tanner stages 2 and 5)
• Clinical signs of insulin resistance: acanthosis nigricans and hypertension

(ii) Screening for complications is essential because onset of DM usually precedes diagnosis by several years, so end-organ effects may already be present. Screen for:
• Microalbuminuria (urine albumin ≥30 mg/24 h or 30 mg albumin/g creatinine, confirmed in 2–3 samples) — indicates nephropathy risk
• Dyslipidaemia: hypertriglyceridaemia and reduced HDL cholesterol are hallmarks of T2DM lipidaemia
• Hypertension: accounts for 35–75% of DM complications both micro- and macrovascular
• Retinopathy: ophthalmology referral
• Hepatic steatosis (NAFLD): present in 25–45% of T2DM cases; advanced cases lead to cirrhosis

(iii) Management options: lifestyle modification (dietary caloric restriction and increased physical activity); oral hypoglycaemic agents; ± insulin therapy; control of comorbidities with regular screening. First-line approach is lifestyle modification (dietary restriction and increased physical activity) because it directly addresses the underlying insulin resistance and obesity without pharmacological risk, and approximately one-third to one-half of patients who present with metabolic decompensation will require aggressive fluid and insulin therapy to reverse DKA before lifestyle measures can be instituted.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Three groups of paediatric tumours:
1. Embryonal neoplasms: due to faulty development of embryonal cells, leading to persistence and proliferation of cells resembling fetal tissue. Examples: Germ cell tumours, Nephroblastoma, Medulloblastoma, Neuroblastoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, Retinoblastoma, Primitive neuroectodermal tumour.
2. Juvenile neoplasms: due to malignant transformation in mature tissue cells, but prevalent in the younger age group. Examples: Cerebral astrocytoma and ependymoma, Ewing's sarcoma, Osteosarcoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.
3. Adult-type tumours: rarely seen in children and histologically identical to adult counterparts. Examples: Hepatocellular carcinoma, Renal cell carcinoma, Synovial cell carcinoma, Schwannoma, Carcinoma e.g. nasopharyngeal.

A(ii) Types of radiation and techniques:
Types of radiation: X-rays (delivered by linear accelerator); Gamma rays (emitted from radioactive isotope e.g. cobalt 60); Beta particles (emitted from radioactive isotopes e.g. iridium 192, iodine-131, gold 198, caesium 137); Electron beam (produced by linear accelerator).
Techniques: Teletherapy (source at a distance); Brachytherapy (source within or in close proximity to tumour, delivers continuous dose — Interstitial brachytherapy; Contact brachytherapy e.g. intracavitary, intraluminal, endovascular, surface); Systemically delivered radio-isotope.
Fractionated RTH/External beam irradiation: total dose delivered in small daily fractions over a period of time. Types: Standard/conventional fractionation, Hyperfractionation, Accelerated fractionation.

B(i) The 4Rs of radiotherapy:
- Repair of cellular damage.
- Repopulation by tumour cells.
- Reoxygenation.
- Redistribution of cells in the cell cycle.
These form the biological basis for delivering radiation in fractions: fractionation allows normal tissue to repair between doses while tumour cells are progressively killed.

B(ii) Side effects:
Acute side effects (depend on area irradiated):
General: fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea and vomiting (related to metabolic effects of tumour breakdown, bone marrow depression, and reaction to anxiety and stress).
Specific: Skin desquamation; Alopecia; Mucositis, dysphagia, xerostomia; Diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; Dysuria; Bone marrow depression — decrease in red cells, platelets, and leucocytes.
Late effects: Fibrosis, atrophy (non-stochastic effect); Carcinogenesis (damage to somatic cells); Genetic mutation (damage to germ cells); Impaired growth and development of epiphyseal growth plates; Development of secondary tumours.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the types of radiation used and the techniques of radiotherapy delivery available for childhood cancers.

A. Describe the gross anatomy and clinical features of Tuberous Sclerosis under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, inheritance pattern, and characteristic skin findings (ash-leaf hypopigmentation, Shagreen's patch, periungual fibromas, and facial lesions)
A(ii) Neurological features — the nature of tubers, subependymal nodules, and their clinical consequences
A(iii) Other system involvement (renal, cardiac, skeletal, dental)

B. Explain how the skin and neurological zones of tuberous sclerosis relate to common pathologies — specifically why infantile spasms, seizures, and mental retardation occur.

C. Outline the full management of tuberous sclerosis and neurofibromatosis side by side, highlighting the components that are common to both neurocutaneous syndromes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Tuberous Sclerosis: autosomal dominant, characterised by the presence of cerebral tubers, retinal phakomas, and a variety of skin findings. Skin findings: ash-leaf-shaped area of hypopigmentation; Shagreen's patch; periungual fibromas; facial lesions — adenoma sebaceum (hamartomas of fibrous and vascular tissue), which may be present by age 3 in 40% of patients.

A(ii) Neurological: gliotic tissue (tubers) in the brain; subependymal nodules may project into the 3rd and 4th ventricles and are calcified; consequences: infantile spasms, seizures, and mental retardation.

A(iii) Other system involvement:
- Renal: hamartomas, cystic renal lesions
- Cardiac: multiple rhabdomyoma, pheochromocytoma
- Skeletal: bony cysts, periosteal thickening of bone, hyperostosis of the cranium
- Dental: pits in teeth

B. Skin lesions are hamartomas; the cerebral tubers are also hamartomas (gliotic tissue), causing structural disruption to brain architecture. Subependymal nodules that calcify and project into the ventricles cause obstructive hydrocephalus and pressure on surrounding tissue. The tubers disrupt normal cortical organisation and neuronal signalling, leading to infantile spasms and seizures; cumulative seizure burden and direct hamartomatous involvement of cognitive areas lead to mental retardation.

C. Tuberous Sclerosis management: genetic counselling; use of anticonvulsants; cosmetic surgery; follow-up for complications.
Neurofibromatosis management: thorough evaluation; close follow-up; look out for associated complications; surgical removal; genetic counselling.
Common to both: genetic counselling; close follow-up for complications; surgical intervention where appropriate. Both are autosomal conditions requiring a multidisciplinary approach.

A(i) Gross anatomy of the immune system:
• Innate immunity: made up of the skin, white blood cells called phagocytes, the complement system, and chemicals called interferons. When phagocytes encounter an invading organism, they surround and engulf it to destroy it. The complement system also attacks bacteria. This is the immunity people are born with.
• Adaptive immunity: develops throughout life; adapts to fight specific invading organisms. Divided into humoral and cellular components.
  - Humoral immunity (B lymphocytes): B lymphocytes manufacture proteins called antibodies. The humoral response is particularly useful for attacking bacteria.
  - Cellular immunity (T lymphocytes): useful for attacking viruses, some parasites, and possibly cancer cells. T lymphocyte subtypes: helper T-cells — play a role in recognising invading organisms and help killer T-cells to multiply; killer T-cells — destroy the target organism.
• Complement: part of the non-specific innate response; attacks bacteria directly.
• Natural killer cells: part of the non-specific innate response.

A(ii) Broad division of congenital immunodeficiency disorders:
• T-lymphocyte deficiency: example — DiGeorge syndrome (X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome also listed); inheritance — chromosomal (DiGeorge is a developmental defect of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches).
• B-lymphocyte deficiency: example — X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (XLA); Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID); Selective IgA deficiency (most common: 1:300); inheritance — X-linked recessive (XLA) or variable.
• Combined T- and B-cell defects: example — Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID); inheritance — X-linked or autosomal recessive.
• Neutrophil defects: example — chronic granulomatous disease; inheritance — X-linked or autosomal recessive.
• Deficiency of complement components: inheritance — autosomal.

B(i) T-lymphocyte vs B-lymphocyte deficiency — susceptibility difference:
• T-lymphocyte deficiency (DiGeorge syndrome): T-cells are essential for cellular immunity — attacking viruses, some parasites, and possibly cancer cells; helper T-cells recognise invading organisms and amplify the killer T-cell response. Without T-cells: particularly vulnerable to viral infections, intracellular pathogens, fungal infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii), mycobacteria, and protozoal parasites. Combined defects (SCID — both T and B) present the most severe vulnerability to all classes of organisms.
• B-lymphocyte deficiency (X-linked agammaglobulinaemia): B-lymphocytes manufacture antibodies used to attack bacteria, particularly encapsulated extracellular bacteria. Without antibodies: particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus), as well as some enteroviruses. These children tolerate viral infections better than T-cell-deficient children because cellular immunity (T-cells) is preserved.
• Clinical basis: the difference reflects which arm of the adaptive immune response is absent. Antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity primarily defends against extracellular bacteria; cellular immunity primarily defends against intracellular organisms, viruses, fungi, and parasites. A person with an immunodeficiency disorder may get more frequent infections, heal more slowly, and have a higher incidence of some cancers — the type of organism reflects which defect is present.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the immune system relevant to congenital immunodeficiency, including: innate versus adaptive components, B-lymphocyte function, T-lymphocyte subtypes and their roles, and the complement system.
A(ii) State the broad division of congenital immunodeficiency disorders, giving one example of each division and its mode of inheritance.
B(i) Explain why T-lymphocyte deficiency (as in DiGeorge syndrome) renders the child particularly vulnerable to certain classes of pathogens compared with B-lymphocyte deficiency (as in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia), and explain the clinical basis of this difference.

A. Describe Tricuspid Atresia (TA) under the following headings:
A(i) Define the condition, state why it is also called univentricular heart disease, and describe the anatomical abnormality
A(ii) Explain how the clinical presentation varies depending on the ventriculo-arterial connection — distinguish between concordant and discordant presentations
A(iii) State the ECG features that, when seen together in a cyanosed child, are suggestive of tricuspid atresia

B. Describe the management of tricuspid atresia:
B(i) What happens if no intervention is taken?
B(ii) State the definitive surgical operation, what it involves anatomically, and what haemodynamic problem it addresses
B(iii) State the most diagnostic investigation and what it shows
B(iv) Using the differential diagnosis framework, state when you would suspect TGA versus TOF versus TA, based on age of presentation and presence or absence of heart failure
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and anatomy:
Tricuspid atresia is also called univentricular heart disease — it is the commonest example of univentricular heart disease. The right atrioventricular connection is absent (the tricuspid valve is absent/atretic). The right ventricle is rudimentary (non-functional). All circulation must pass through the left ventricle, which is the sole functional ventricle.

A(ii) Clinical presentation by ventriculo-arterial connection:
a. Ventriculo-arterial concordance (RV → PA): Features are due to reduced pulmonary blood flow — presents haemodynamically similar to TOF (cyanosis without heart failure; reduced pulmonary vascular markings).
b. Ventriculo-arterial discordance (RV → Aorta; LV → PA): Patient presents with cyanosis AND heart failure (increased pulmonary blood flow causes heart failure; parallel circuits cause cyanosis).
In summary: Presentation consists of cyanosis ± heart failure.

A(iii) ECG features suggestive of TA in a cyanosed child:
1. Right atrial hypertrophy (large if ASD is small, and vice versa)
2. Superior axis deviation
3. Left ventricular hypertrophy
These three features together in a cyanosed child are suggestive of tricuspid atresia.

B(i) Without intervention: Most patients usually give up (die) in the first year of life if no intervention is taken.

B(ii) Definitive surgical operation: Fontan's operation.
What it involves: Connecting the right atrium to the pulmonary artery; a valve conduit is used to allow blood to flow in one direction (to the pulmonary artery).
Haemodynamic problem addressed: The operation is classical for those who have reduced pulmonary blood flow (ventriculo-arterial concordant type) — it allows deoxygenated blood from the right atrium to reach the lungs without passing through the rudimentary right ventricle.

B(iii) Most diagnostic investigation: Echocardiography (2D mode) — very diagnostic; shows the absent right AV connection, rudimentary right ventricle, and the ventriculo-arterial connection pattern.
Cardiac catheterisation shows no entrance into the right ventricle.

B(iv) Differential diagnosis framework:
- 6-month-old with cyanosis AND heart failure: TGA (most commonly associated with heart failure) OR Tricuspid atresia with ventriculo-arterial discordance. (Also: pulmonary atresia ± VSD.)
- 6-month-old with cyanosis and NO heart failure: Think of TOF first (then tricuspid atresia with ventriculo-arterial concordance — presents like TOF).
- Older child with cyanosis (>1 year, e.g. 7 years): TOF — patients are usually older before presentation (some reach 5–7 years). In TOF, TGA, and TA, in TOF patients are usually older while TGA and TA patients die earlier without intervention.
- Older child with cyanosis appearing for the first time after years of acyanotic CHD: Eisenmenger syndrome.

A(i) Chronic RHD implies permanent valvular damage with chronic cardiac decompensation. The flabby valves healed by ARF heal by fibrosis, causing permanent structural change. Valve lesions in order of frequency in paediatrics:
- Mitral incompetence — commonest lesion
- Mitral stenosis — patient is usually older as it takes time to develop
- Aortic incompetence
- Aortic stenosis — not common in children; more likely to be congenital in children and rheumatic in adults

A(ii) Symptoms (± previous history suggestive of ARF): breathlessness, cough, palpitations, easy fatiguability (decompensation), pedal swelling (decompensation).
Signs:
- Active praecordium at apex; increased JVP
- Loud P2 — due to backflow of blood from left atrium into lungs
- Apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla — murmur of mitral incompetence
- ± Diastolic murmur at the apex — mitral stenosis
- ± Diastolic murmur in aortic area along with collapsing pulse — aortic incompetence
- Signs of heart failure: tender hepatomegaly

B(i) CXR findings:
- Cardiomegaly (LA, LV, RA, RV)
- Hump on left border/mitralised left heart border — due to left atrial enlargement
- Splaying of the carina — due to left atrial enlargement pushing up the carina
- Double density right heart border — left atrium enlarged behind right heart border
- Pulmonary congestion — increased pulmonary vascular markings

B(ii) ECG findings:
- P mitrale/notched P wave — broad, biphasic P wave; seen in mitral disease — indicates left atrial hypertrophy/enlargement
- Increased PR interval
- Left ventricular hypertrophy
- ± Right ventricular hypertrophy — if long-standing pulmonary hypertension
P mitrale basis: left atrial enlargement delays atrial depolarisation, producing a broad bifid P wave.

B(iii) Management:
Medical: treatment of heart failure — digoxin and diuretics (ACE inhibitors e.g. captopril/enalapril now being used).
Surgical: valve repair or valve replacement.
Primary prevention: prevent the first attack of ARF — prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis with IM procaine penicillin; health education.
Secondary prevention: prevent recurrence of ARF — IM benzathine penicillin 1.2 mega units monthly, OR oral penicillin V 125–250 mg twice daily, OR oral erythromycin 125–250 mg twice daily for penicillin-sensitive patients; health education.

A(ii) Describe all the clinical features — symptoms and signs — distinguishing the murmur of each valve lesion and its radiation

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Neonatal Jaundice (NNJ). Jaundice refers to yellowish discolouration of the sclera and/or skin due to accumulation of bilirubin in the blood; it becomes clinically visible from serum bilirubin level ≥5 mg/dl.
Common causes: ABO incompatibility, Rhesus isoimmunisation, Prematurity, G6PD deficiency, Infection, Extravascular blood, Physiologic jaundice.

(ii) Risk factors / key assessments:
History: time of onset, progression, use of naphthalene balls, family history, level of activity/feeding, pregnancy, labour and delivery history.
Examination: clinical estimation of jaundice, pallor, level of hydration, area of trauma (bruises, cephalhaematoma, ICH), neurologic findings (lethargy, poor suck).

(iii) Investigations: serum bilirubin (conjugated and unconjugated), blood grouping of baby and mother, Coombs test, G6PD screen, FBC differential, PBF, blood culture, E&U + creatinine.
Phototherapy indications: serum bilirubin >12 mg/dl in a term neonate; half of exchange blood transfusion level in a preterm neonate; can also be used prophylactically.

(iv) EBT:
Indications: SB ≥18 mg/dl in a term neonate; SB ≥10 × weight in a preterm; values below these if there is anaemia, sepsis, rate of rise ≥5 mg/dl in 24 hours, or cord blood SB >5 mg/dl.
Volume: double volume — 160 ml/kg.
Blood requirements: compatible blood, fully cross-matched blood, fresh whole blood (<72 hours).
Aliquot sizes: 5 ml for ≤2 kg; 10 ml for 2–3 kg; 20 ml for >3 kg.
Other procedure steps: IV calcium gluconate 1 ml per 100 ml of blood; withhold oral feeds 1 hour before procedure; monitor vital signs every 15 minutes; ensure asepsis; take consent.
Complications: catheter-related (infection, haemorrhage, NEC, air embolism), arrhythmias, intestinal perforation, portal and splenic vein thrombosis, fluid overload, hypovolaemic shock, hypothermia, anaemia, electrolyte imbalance.
questions.question:
A 3-day-old term neonate presents with progressive yellowing of the skin and sclerae noted since day 1 of life. The mother is blood group O and the baby is blood group A. The baby appears lethargic and is feeding poorly.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and list all the common causes of this condition?
(ii) State the risk factors for severe disease and the key assessments (history and examination) that must be performed.
(iii) List the investigations required and state the indications for phototherapy in a term neonate.

questions.answerText:
A(i) DMD is an X-linked inherited disease with spontaneous mutation. It is due to deletion of the short arm of the X-chromosome at the point where it carries the dystrophin gene. Dystrophin is needed for muscular contraction; its absence leads to progressive degeneration of muscle fibres.

A(ii) Clinical features:
- Age of diagnosis: usually after 3 years.
- Delayed developmental milestones; walking/standing on toes.
- Characteristic waddling gait (like a duck) — evidence of weakness of pelvic girdle muscles.
- Difficulty in climbing a staircase.
- On examination: hypertrophy of calf muscles (pseudohypertrophy from fatty infiltration); occasional pseudohypertrophy of brachioradialis.
- Gower's sign: typical of DMD, due to weakness of pelvic girdle muscles.
- Intelligence is below normal in 30% of cases.

A(iii) Investigations:
- Serum creatine kinase (CK): >10 times the upper limit of normal (160 iu/L), as CK is the muscle enzyme released after muscle death.
- Muscle biopsy: shows degeneration of muscle fibres.
- Electromyography (EMG): shows myopathic changes different from neuropathic changes.

B. Progressive degeneration of muscle fibres causes increasing weakness. By age 12, ambulation becomes impossible. Death occurs before 20 years, resulting from cardiomyopathy.

C. Comparison:
- Becker Pseudohypertrophy: X-linked; mild form of DMD; presents later than DMD; progresses slowly; increased CK; prognosis is better.
- Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy: autosomal dominant; less common, milder; onset in the first decade; features are weakness of facial muscles, expressionless face, orbicularis oculi or oris involvement; CK is normal or slightly increased; compatible with life.
- DMD: X-linked recessive; most severe; onset after 3 years; rapidly progressive; CK markedly elevated; fatal before age 20.
questions.question:
A. Describe Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) under the following headings:
A(i) Genetic basis and mode of inheritance; the pathogenesis at the molecular level.
A(ii) Clinical features: age of diagnosis, motor presentation, characteristic gait, physical examination findings, and intellectual involvement.
A(iii) Relevant investigations and findings.

B. Explain why a child with DMD becomes wheelchair-dependent by age 12 years.

C. Distinguish DMD from Becker Pseudohypertrophy and Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy under the headings of: inheritance, severity, age of presentation, progression, and prognosis.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) neutrophil count exceeding 250 cells/mm³, regardless of Gram stain or culture results. Common causative organisms are Gram-negative bacteria translocating from the intestinal lumen. Empirical first-line treatment is a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime) initiated immediately on diagnosis.
A(ii) Hepatorenal syndrome is initiated by extreme splanchnic vasodilatation (mediated primarily by nitric oxide and glucagon), which reduces effective arterial blood volume. Compensatory renal vasoconstriction reduces GFR. The kidneys are structurally normal — the syndrome is purely functional and potentially reversible with liver transplantation, which corrects the underlying hepatic dysfunction driving the haemodynamic abnormality.
A(iii) The primary neurotoxic substance is ammonia (NH₃). Ammonia is produced in the intestine from nitrogenous substrates (dietary protein and blood in the gut lumen) by bacterial catabolism. Normally, ammonia is detoxified in the liver via the urea cycle converting ammonia to urea. In portal hypertension, portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatocellular function allow ammonia to bypass hepatic detoxification, accumulate in the systemic circulation, and cross the blood-brain barrier causing encephalopathy.
B(i) Thrombocytopaenia and leucopaenia result from hypersplenism — sequestration and destruction of platelets and leucocytes in the congested, enlarged spleen (splenomegaly from elevated portal pressure). The enlarged spleen is the responsible organ. Reduced thrombopoietin synthesis by the diseased liver is a secondary contributing factor.
B(ii) Coagulopathy arises from two mechanisms: (1) impaired hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, fibrinogen) — reflecting hepatocellular dysfunction; and (2) fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption from cholestasis — as bile acids are essential for micellar absorption of vitamin K. IV vitamin K is the appropriate first intervention because if the coagulopathy responds, it indicates that hepatic synthetic function is partially preserved and the coagulopathy is primarily from vitamin K malabsorption; non-response suggests intrinsic synthetic failure.
C(i) Idiopathic portal hypertension is characterised by portal hypertension with near-normal hepatocellular synthetic function (normal albumin, normal prothrombin time), distinguishing it from cirrhosis where synthetic function is significantly impaired.
C(ii) Cirrhosis is defined histologically by bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodule formation that distorts the normal hepatic architecture. In idiopathic portal hypertension, liver biopsy may show periportal fibrosis without the nodule formation and architectural distortion that defines cirrhosis.
questions.question:
A. Describe the following complications of portal hypertension under the stated headings:
A(i) Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): defining diagnostic criterion, the most common causative organisms, and first-line empirical treatment
A(ii) Hepatorenal syndrome: the initiating haemodynamic mechanism, whether the kidneys are structurally damaged, and the potential for reversibility
A(iii) Hepatic encephalopathy: the primary neurotoxic substance, how it is produced in the gut, and the normal hepatic detoxification pathway that fails

B. Explain the haematological consequences of portal hypertension and why each arises:
B(i) Thrombocytopaenia and leucopaenia — the mechanism and the organ responsible
B(ii) Coagulopathy — the two contributing mechanisms, and why intravenous vitamin K is the appropriate first intervention

C. Distinguish the following features of idiopathic portal hypertension from cirrhotic portal hypertension:
C(i) Hepatic synthetic function
C(ii) Histological finding on liver biopsy

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Convulsing child (acute seizures). Causes in a child >2 months: meningitis, cerebral malaria, febrile convulsions, hypoglycaemia, head injury.
Causes in a child <2 months (for completeness as stated): perinatal asphyxia, metabolic problems (hypoglycaemia), electrolyte imbalance (hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia), birth injury (intracranial haemorrhage), meningitis, severe unconjugated NNJ.

(ii) Initial intervention to abort seizure: IM paraldehyde 0.15 ml/kg or 1 ml/year of life. May need phenobarbitone or phenytoin subsequently.

(iii) Investigations:
- PCV (packed cell volume)
- Random plasma glucose (RPG)
- CSF analysis (lumbar puncture)
- Blood film for malaria parasite
- E&U + creatinine ± calcium, phosphate
- Others as necessary

(iv) Management of underlying causes:
1. Cerebral malaria: Quinine is the drug of choice.
2. Meningitis: appropriate drugs (antibiotics as clinically indicated).
3. Electrolyte imbalance: correct the specific electrolyte abnormality.
4. Hypoglycaemia: IV 10% dextrose water 2–4 ml/kg OR IV 50% dextrose water 1 ml/kg (1:4 dilution); follow up with dextrose water infusion; monitor RPG. If temperature ≥38.5°C, give paracetamol. For kerosene poisoning: treatment is symptomatic; avoid emesis.

Airway management (immediate): maintain a clear airway — airway suctioning, oropharyngeal airway, turn neck to one side to avoid aspiration. Also assess: quick history (duration, previous history, drug ingestion, fever, type and number of convulsions); quick examination (pallor, jaundice, signs of increased ICP — unequal pupils, abnormal posture).
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought in with active generalised tonic-clonic convulsions lasting 20 minutes. She has had fever for 2 days and was noted to be pale at triage. She has not received any anticonvulsant prior to arrival.

(i) What is the clinical diagnosis, and list all the causes of convulsions in a child older than 2 months?
(ii) What is the initial intervention to abort the seizure (drug, dose, and route)?
(iii) List all the bedside and laboratory investigations that must be done.
(iv) Detail the management of each identifiable underlying cause — cerebral malaria, meningitis, electrolyte imbalance, and hypoglycaemia —, including drugs and doses.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Left-to-right shunts: the essential pathology is that oxygenated blood recirculates in the lungs; cyanosis is not a problem unless heart failure ensues (unlike right-to-left shunts where desaturated blood bypasses the lungs — arterial desaturation from birth).
Conditions and Ibadan incidence (635 cases over 10 years):
- VSD: 35% (worldwide: isolated VSD accounts for 25% of all CHD; worldwide CHD incidence 4–9 per 1000 live births)
- PDA: 22%
- Coarctation of aorta: 12% (listed in the Ibadan table as left-sided/obstructive but haemodynamically creates a left-to-right circulation effect)
- ASD: 7.0%

A(ii) VSD: failure of complete septation of a portion of the interventricular septum; variable size depending on the stage at which partitioning was arrested.
Small defect: haemodynamic change not significant.
Large defect: higher left-sided pressure (systolic 130–140 mmHg) vs right (30 mmHg) drives a large portion of stroke volume right → increased pulmonary blood flow → reflex pulmonary vasospasm → thickening of pulmonary vessels → increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Initially reversible; later becomes irreversible → pulmonary vascular disease.
Eisenmenger Complex/Syndrome: when pulmonary vascular resistance rises to suprasystemic levels, right-sided pressure exceeds left-sided pressure → shunt reverses (now right-to-left) → desaturation on the left side → cyanosis. Surgery is contraindicated at this stage (suprasystemic right-sided pressure; post-cardiotomy syndrome risk).

B(i) Symptoms of VSD:
- Breathlessness and panting — pulmonary congestion
- Recurrent chest infections/pneumonia — wet lungs provide medium for infection
- Fever — from infections; persistent fever if complicated by infective endocarditis
- Failure to thrive; small for gestational age — hypoperfusion of tissues
- Unconsolable cry
- Excessive sweating — increased adrenergic activity
- Cold clammy extremities — peripheral vasoconstriction
- Palpitations — mother notices when carrying child
- Difficulty feeding/sucking — cannot hold breath to suck

B(ii) Signs of VSD:
Inspection: increased praecordial activity at onset (medial and anterior rotation); praecordial bulge; if in heart failure: sweating (forehead and face), breathlessness, subcostal and intercostal recession, moist palms, reduced urinary output.
Palpation: cold clammy extremities; poor pulse volume (if heart failure); evidence of systemic congestion; tender hepatomegaly — hallmark of congestive heart failure (acute liver congestion stretches the capsule); BP may be normal or hypotensive in heart failure.
Auscultation: pansystolic/holosystolic murmur radiating to the back (not the axilla); variable pitch depending on VSD size; best heard at mid-left sternum; ± diastolic rumble (gallop rhythm); loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension).

B(iii) ASD vs VSD:
ASD: the shunting is minimal because the atrial pressure gradient is small — only 3–4 mmHg (LA 8–9 mmHg vs RA 5 mmHg). VSD: involves the high-pressure system — systolic gradient ~100 mmHg (LV 130–140 mmHg vs RV 30 mmHg). Therefore VSD produces much greater haemodynamic effects.
ASD murmur: wide FIXED splitting of S2 (hallmark — does not vary with respiration); pulmonic flow murmur (ejection systolic at pulmonary area). ASD is usually asymptomatic in early life.
VSD murmur: pansystolic/holosystolic murmur, best at mid-left sternum, radiating to the back.
Chamber dilatation: ASD → right atrium dilates hugely (left atrium usually normal). VSD → left ventricle dilates first (from increased preload); then right heart involvement.
questions.question:
A. Describe the group of congenital heart diseases classified as left-to-right shunts:
A(i) Define the essential haemodynamic pathology of left-to-right shunts and list the three conditions in this group, with their incidence from Ibadan data
A(ii) Describe the pathogenesis and location of the defect in VSD — including the size-dependent haemodynamic effects and the pathophysiological basis of Eisenmenger Complex/Syndrome

B. Describe the full clinical presentation of VSD:
B(i) All the symptoms — and the physiological mechanism for each
B(ii) All the signs — covering inspection, palpation, and auscultation findings
B(iii) Distinguish the clinical features of ASD from VSD — including the specific murmur of each, the pressure gradient that drives each shunt, and the typical chamber that dilates in each

questions.explanation: Serial ophthalmological screening in infants with retinopathy of prematurity aims to detect early progression to more severe stages that require timely treatment to prevent retinal detachment and vision loss, making ongoing monitoring essential rather than a one-time assessment. It does not replace the need for broader developmental follow-up, which addresses other aspects of preterm outcome. Delaying treatment when indicated would be inappropriate and could worsen visual outcomes.
options: Early detection of progression to a stage requiring treatment
Confirming that no further eye examinations are ever needed
Providing a one-time assessment with no further monitoring required
Delaying any potential treatment as long as possible regardless of stage
Replacing the need for any general growth and development follow-up
questions.question: An infant born preterm at 28 weeks is noted on ophthalmological screening to have early retinal changes consistent with retinopathy of prematurity. What is the primary goal of continued serial screening in this infant?

A 5-year-old with type 1 diabetes develops sudden severe headache, vomiting, and reduced consciousness during treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis. What is the most likely life-threatening complication?
questions.explanation: Cerebral oedema is a rare but life-threatening complication of diabetic ketoacidosis treatment in children, typically occurring within the first 24 hours and presenting with headache, altered consciousness, and other neurological signs, requiring immediate recognition and treatment with hyperosmolar therapy. This differs from a hypoglycaemic seizure, which would be associated with a low blood glucose reading rather than ongoing DKA management. Careful fluid management protocols aim to reduce this risk.

A dysmorphic feature is a medical term for a physical difference in body structure that is suggestive of a congenital disorder, genetic syndrome, or birth defect. It may be an isolated minor variant or one of a combination of features signalling a serious multisystem syndrome. Systematic dysmorphological assessment (head-to-toe) is essential in paediatric practice to identify syndromic diagnoses.
options: A structural sign of a genetic disorder
Any difference in body size compared to the average
A biochemical abnormality detected on newborn screening
A functional deficit without structural anomaly
questions.question: A dysmorphic feature is best described as:

questions.explanation: RSV colonises the nasopharynx and causes upper respiratory symptoms but is far more important as the predominant cause of acute bronchiolitis in infants under 2 years. RSV bronchiolitis is the most frequent lower respiratory tract infection requiring hospitalisation during infancy. Understanding this dual role guides both upper and lower respiratory tract infection management.
questions.question: Which organism can colonise the nasopharynx and occasionally cause coryza, but is more importantly associated with severe lower respiratory tract disease in young infants?
A neonate's ECG shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with an independent, slow ventricular escape rhythm. Which diagnosis does this represent?
questions.explanation: Complete heart block is defined by total dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity, with the ventricles maintaining an independent, usually slow, escape rhythm. This is distinct from first-degree and Mobitz type I block, which both retain some relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. In neonates, this finding may be congenital, often associated with maternal autoimmune disease.

questions.question: A newborn is noted to have a continuous murmur and differential cyanosis, with respiratory distress attributed partly to cardiac shunting rather than primary lung disease. What is the most important initial step in distinguishing cardiac from pulmonary causes of neonatal cyanosis?
options: Hyperoxia test comparing pre- and post-ductal oxygen saturation or arterial blood gas response to 100% oxygen
Immediate cardiac surgery without further assessment
Chest X-ray alone is always sufficient to distinguish the two
Assuming the cause is always pulmonary in origin
Waiting 48 hours before any further evaluation
questions.explanation: The hyperoxia test, assessing the change in oxygenation with administration of 100% oxygen, helps distinguish cyanotic congenital heart disease (where oxygenation improves minimally due to fixed shunting) from primary pulmonary causes of cyanosis (where oxygenation typically improves more substantially), guiding urgency of further cardiac evaluation. Assuming a purely pulmonary cause without this assessment risks delaying diagnosis of a duct-dependent cardiac lesion. Prompt differentiation is critical since some cardiac lesions require urgent prostaglandin therapy to maintain ductal patency.

Hypoglycaemia in a neonate causes CNS depression, seizures, and apnoea due to glucose being the primary CNS fuel. Reduced respiratory drive from CNS hypoglycaemia presents as apnoea or irregular breathing. This is why blood glucose monitoring (RPG) is essential in all neonates with respiratory distress, as hypoglycaemia both masquerades as and complicates primary respiratory disease.
questions.question: Hypoglycaemia in a neonate can cause respiratory distress because:
options: Glucose is the only substrate for surfactant synthesis
Hypoglycaemia causing CNS depression and reduced respiratory drive
Low glucose increases pulmonary vascular resistance

questions.question: A pleural fluid total protein of 3.5 g/dL and specific gravity of 1025 indicates:
questions.explanation: An exudate is characterised by total protein greater than 3 g/dL, specific gravity greater than 1020, pleural protein to serum protein ratio greater than 0.5, and predominance of polymorphonuclear cells (except in TB and malignancy). A total protein of 3.5 g/dL and specific gravity of 1025 meet exudate criteria. Exudates typically result from inflammatory or malignant processes rather than hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance.

Small gastric capacity and high metabolic needs mean that well term neonates, including smaller infants around 2 kg, generally require frequent feeding approximately every 2 to 3 hours to meet caloric and fluid needs and to establish good milk supply. Widely spaced feeds every 8 to 12 hours would be inadequate for these needs. Feeding only on persistent crying risks missing earlier hunger cues and inadequate intake.
questions.question: A neonate is fed at a frequency appropriate for a well term infant weighing 2 kg. Which feeding schedule would generally be recommended for this infant?
options: Feeding strictly only when the infant cries persistently
A fixed single large feed once every 12 hours
Feeding every 8 hours regardless of infant cues
Frequent feeds approximately every 2 to 3 hours
Feeding only once daily to avoid overfeeding

questions.question: In the pathophysiology group 'diminished systemic output due to primary diastolic dysfunction', which condition represents the most extreme form in children?
options: Dilated cardiomyopathy with severely reduced ejection fraction
Constrictive pericarditis with fibrotic pericardial constriction
Restrictive cardiomyopathy with severely impaired filling
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy with systolic obstruction
Tricuspid atresia with absent right AV connection
questions.explanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy represents the most severe form of primary diastolic dysfunction, where marked ventricular stiffness severely impairs ventricular filling, causing very high filling pressures despite preserved or relatively normal systolic function. Cardiac output is profoundly reduced from the restriction in stroke volume. In children, restrictive cardiomyopathy carries the worst prognosis of all cardiomyopathies, and many require cardiac transplantation. It must be distinguished from constrictive pericarditis, which is surgically correctable.

questions.question: In bacterial tracheitis, which differentiates it from viral croup, the key feature is:
options: It responds fully to nebulised adrenaline
Toxic; high fever and purulent tracheal secretions
It is associated with barking cough alone
questions.explanation: Bacterial tracheitis (membranous laryngotracheobronchitis) is characterised by toxic appearance with high fever, severe stridor, and purulent/membranous tracheal secretions. Unlike viral croup which is typically non-toxic, bacterial tracheitis resembles epiglottitis in severity. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism, and treatment requires airway management and antistaphylococcal antibiotics.

Bronchiolitis is specifically defined as acute, infectious, inflammatory disease of the lower respiratory tract resulting in obstruction of the small airways (bronchioles). It is predominantly caused by RSV and is the most frequent lower respiratory tract infection during infancy requiring hospitalisation. The small airway calibre in infants makes even minor mucosal inflammation highly obstructive.
questions.question: Bronchiolitis is defined as an acute, infectious, inflammatory disease of the lower respiratory tract resulting in obstruction of:

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates (principally lactose) in breast milk supply energy for growth and body functions, allow protein to be used efficiently for tissue building rather than energy, allow normal fat metabolism, and provide building blocks for essential body compounds. Lactose also promotes bifidobacterial colonisation.
questions.question: Carbohydrates in breast milk primarily serve to:

questions.explanation: Severe RSV bronchiolitis in early infancy is strongly associated with subsequent recurrent wheezing and an increased risk of developing asthma in later childhood, a relationship known as the RSV-asthma link. Whether RSV causes airway damage predisposing to asthma or whether a genetic predisposition to atopy explains both the severe bronchiolitis and later asthma is still debated. Rhinovirus-associated wheezing carries similar long-term risk.
questions.question: A potential long-term consequence of severe RSV bronchiolitis in early infancy is:
Pyrazinamide's most specific adverse effect is which metabolic complication?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide specifically causes hyperuricaemia by reducing renal uric acid excretion, which can precipitate gout in predisposed individuals. Other side effects include skin rash and hepatotoxicity. Monitoring serum uric acid and liver enzymes is recommended during pyrazinamide-containing regimens.

questions.question: Which statement about the sequence of developmental milestones is most accurate?
options: It varies widely between different children
It is the same as growth milestones
It is consistent across children but the rate varies
It differs depending on the child's culture
It can be skipped in some children without significance
questions.explanation: The sequence of developmental milestones is constant across children—children always achieve head control before sitting, and sitting before walking—though the rate (timing) varies between individuals. Cultural and environmental factors may modify the rate but not the sequence. Understanding this principle helps distinguish true delay from developmental variation.

Inborn errors of metabolism characteristically present after an initial period of apparent wellness, followed by progressive deterioration with feeding intolerance, vomiting, and lethargy as toxic metabolites accumulate, which helps distinguish this cause from hypoxic-ischaemic or purely birth-related causes presenting immediately at or very soon after delivery. An examination that remains entirely normal throughout would be atypical for a significant metabolic derangement causing seizures. Metabolic causes often require more than a single anticonvulsant dose and ongoing metabolic correction for control.
options: Seizures that resolve permanently after a single dose of any anticonvulsant
Seizures occurring immediately at birth with no preceding well period
Seizures accompanied exclusively by a normal, unremarkable examination throughout
Onset after a period of apparent wellness, with progressive deterioration and feeding intolerance
Seizures occurring only in the context of a documented difficult delivery
questions.question: A neonate is diagnosed with an inborn error of metabolism after presenting with seizures alongside vomiting, poor feeding, and lethargy. Which additional feature would most strongly support this metabolic diagnosis over other common causes of neonatal seizures?

questions.explanation: Meningism (meningismus) is meningeal irritation without true inflammation of the meninges. It produces neck stiffness and may mimic meningitis clinically. CSF examination, however, is normal in meningism. It is found in young children with high fever, severe systemic infections, or toxic states. LP is needed to distinguish true meningitis (abnormal CSF) from meningism (normal CSF).
questions.question: Meningism (meningismus) is defined as:
options: Confirmed bacterial meningitis in young children

questions.explanation: The WHO clinical case definition of pertussis requires cough lasting more than 14 days combined with at least one of: paroxysms of coughing, whoop (inspiratory whooping sound), or post-tussive vomiting. This clinical definition is useful in settings where laboratory confirmation is not available.
questions.question: What is the WHO clinical case definition of pertussis?
options: Cough of any duration with lymphocytosis >15,000
Cough with stridor lasting more than 7 days in children
Cough >14 days plus paroxysms, whoop, or post-tussive vomiting
Cough with confirmed B. pertussis culture only
Cough with chest X-ray changes and fever

questions.explanation: Two immunological parameters are used to monitor HIV severity in children: CD4+ T cell count/percentage and HIV RNA viral load (copies per ml). CD4 count reflects immune status while viral load reflects viral replication activity. Both guide treatment initiation decisions, monitor treatment response, and predict risk of disease progression.
questions.question: Which parameter, along with CD4, is used for monitoring severity of HIV/AIDS in children?

options: Pericarditis exclusively affects only the inferior leads
Pericarditis never causes any ST segment change
Ischaemia always produces diffuse changes across all leads
Ischaemia is characterised by ST depression only, never elevation
Pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation; ischaemia causes localised, reciprocal changes
questions.explanation: Pericarditis characteristically produces diffuse, concave ST elevation across multiple, non-contiguous leads without the reciprocal ST depression typically seen in territorial myocardial ischaemia. Ischaemic ST elevation instead follows a specific coronary artery distribution with corresponding reciprocal changes. This distinction remains a useful diagnostic principle when pericarditis is suspected in children.
questions.question: A child with acute pericarditis has an ECG showing diffuse, concave ST segment elevation across multiple leads without reciprocal changes. How does this differ from an ST elevation pattern of localised myocardial ischaemia?
In lead V1, a dominant R wave in a child of 5 years old suggests which abnormality given the expected normal RS progression for that age?
questions.explanation: In a 5-year-old, the ECG should show an 'adult' RS progression with a dominant S in right ventricular leads (V1). The 'infant' RS pattern (dominant R in RV leads + dominant R in LV leads) should have transitioned to the adult pattern by 18 months. Persistence of a dominant R in V1 at 5 years is therefore abnormal and suggests right ventricular hypertrophy. An 'adult' RS pattern seen in a neonate would, conversely, suggest LVH.
options: Left ventricular hypertrophy since V1 normally shows LV electrical activity
Normal neonatal pattern that persists until school age
Biventricular hypertrophy as V1 receives electrical input from both ventricular chambers
Right ventricular hypertrophy since the infant RS pattern has persisted abnormally
Right bundle branch block as the only cause of a dominant R in V1

questions.explanation: CSF in measles encephalitis typically shows increased protein, increased lymphocytes, and normal glucose. This pattern is consistent with viral/aseptic meningitis. The CSF findings reflect the inflammatory nature of post-measles encephalomyelitis, which is immune-mediated (not direct viral infection of the CNS).
questions.question: A child is diagnosed with measles encephalitis. CSF analysis is most likely to show which finding?
options: Clear fluid with xanthochromia and RBCs
Increased protein, increased lymphocytes, normal glucose

questions.explanation: After meconium and transitional stools, the normal breastfed neonate passes yellow-green, seedy, slimy stools. Formula-fed infants tend to have paler, more formed stools. Blood in stool, sudden change in consistency, or markedly increased frequency requires evaluation.
questions.question: Normal stool colour and consistency in a breastfed neonate after transitional stools is:

options: Tracheomalacia or vascular ring causing extrinsic airway compression
Gastro-oesophageal reflux alone without structural cause
questions.explanation: Positional variation in respiratory noise, worsening when supine, raises suspicion for a structural airway abnormality such as tracheomalacia or an external vascular ring compressing the trachea, which can cause both inspiratory and expiratory sounds distinct from typical wheeze. Simple viral wheeze does not typically show this pronounced positional dependence. Further investigation with bronchoscopy or MRI/CT angiography may be needed to define the anatomy.
questions.question: A 2-year-old with recurrent wheeze is noted to have symptoms that worsen specifically when lying flat and improve when upright, with a harsh inspiratory and expiratory noise. What underlying cause should be considered?

questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis is a chronic structural complication of recurrent lower respiratory infections and is NOT a direct complication of acute coryza. Acute coryza spreads via anatomical spaces to cause acute otitis media, sinusitis, tonsillitis, epiglottitis, laryngitis, tracheitis, laryngotracheobronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia. Bronchiectasis develops over a more prolonged pathological course.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a complication of acute coryza?

questions.explanation: The Fontan procedure connects systemic venous return directly to the pulmonary arteries without an intervening functional right ventricular pump, relying on passive flow, which is appropriate when only a single functional ventricle exists. This achieves separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood despite the absence of two functioning ventricles. It does not attempt to reconstruct the missing tricuspid valve or right ventricle.
questions.question: A child with tricuspid atresia has undergone staged surgical palliation culminating in a Fontan procedure. What is the fundamental principle behind this operation?
options: Pulmonary venous blood is redirected to the right atrium
Systemic venous return passes directly to the pulmonary arteries
The left ventricle is disconnected from the systemic circulation
A new tricuspid valve is created from pericardial tissue
The right ventricle is reconstructed to function normally

questions.explanation: Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (particularly S. epidermidis) is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in neonates with central venous catheters and in early post-cardiac surgery patients, due to its ability to form biofilms on prosthetic materials and catheter surfaces. It is a component of normal skin flora that becomes pathogenic with vascular access. Management requires prolonged vancomycin therapy and removal of the infected catheter or prosthetic material when feasible.
questions.question: Which organism is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in neonates with central venous catheters or after cardiac surgery?
options: Streptococcus viridans from oral flora colonisation
Candida albicans from fungal superinfection of gut flora
Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus from pharynx
Enterococcus faecalis from urinary tract instrumentation

questions.question: Surfactant replacement therapy is MOST appropriately given in a neonate with:
questions.explanation: Exogenous surfactant therapy is the specific treatment for RDS (hyaline membrane disease) caused by surfactant deficiency in preterm lungs. It is administered intratracheally and reduces surface tension, prevents alveolar collapse, and significantly reduces RDS mortality.

questions.question: Prolonged jaundice (beyond 14 days in term neonates) with pale stools and dark urine MOST suggests:
questions.explanation: The combination of prolonged jaundice beyond 14 days with pale acholic stools and dark urine (direct hyperbilirubinaemia) is the classic presentation of biliary atresia, a surgical emergency. Early Kasai portoenterostomy within the first 60 days maximises biliary drainage.

Bell's staging: Stage IA = suspected NEC (clinical signs + non-diagnostic X-ray); IB = suspected NEC + bloody stool; IIA = definite NEC—mildly ill with radiological signs (pneumatosis); IIB = definite NEC with systemic toxicity; IIIA = advanced NEC with ascites but intact bowel; IIIB = perforation.
questions.question: In Bell's staging of NEC, Stage IIA indicates:
options: Definite NEC: mildly ill with radiological signs
Advanced NEC with intact bowel and ascites

questions.question: A vaccine cold chain is interrupted for several hours during a heatwave, and vaccine vials are exposed to elevated temperature. What is the appropriate action before use?
options: Assume all vaccines remain fully potent after any brief exposure
Assess vaccine viability using appropriate indicators before administering
Discard all vaccines automatically regardless of exposure duration
Administer the vaccines immediately without any assessment
Refreeze the vaccines rapidly and use them as normal
questions.explanation: Following a cold chain break, vaccine viability should be assessed, for example using vaccine vial monitors or manufacturer guidance, before deciding whether the vaccines remain usable, rather than assuming automatic fitness or automatic discard. Simply refreezing does not restore lost potency in heat-sensitive vaccines. This structured assessment protects both vaccine efficacy and resource use.

options: Increased pulmonary blood flow from left-to-right shunting
Reduced pulmonary blood flow from right ventricular outflow obstruction
Pulmonary venous congestion from mitral stenosis
questions.question: A 3-month-old with a large VSD is found on chest X-ray to have cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings. What does this radiographic pattern indicate?
questions.explanation: In a large left-to-right shunt such as VSD, excess blood flows into the pulmonary circulation, producing plethoric lung fields and cardiomegaly on chest X-ray. This contrasts with the oligaemic lung fields seen in lesions with reduced pulmonary flow like Tetralogy of Fallot. The pattern directly reflects the volume of shunted blood reaching the lungs.

By around day 5 to 6 of exclusive breastfeeding, stools normally become soft, yellow, and seedy, passed several times a day, reflecting normal transitional and mature breastfed stool patterns. Hard, infrequent stools would suggest inadequate intake or another problem. Pale, clay-coloured stools with dark urine would raise concern for a biliary or hepatic problem rather than being a normal finding.
questions.question: A neonate's stool pattern is being assessed on day 6 of exclusive breastfeeding. Which stool characteristic would be considered a normal finding at this stage?
options: Hard, pale, infrequent stools passed once every few days
Persistently black, tarry stools continuing beyond the first week
Soft, yellow, seedy stools passed several times daily
Completely white, clay-coloured stools with dark urine
Watery, green, foul-smelling stools with mucus and blood
Using a spacer device correctly with each dose
Rinsing the mouth after inhaled corticosteroid use
Poor coordination between actuation and inhalation leading to reduced drug delivery
Shaking a metered-dose inhaler before use
Waiting the recommended interval between puffs
questions.question: A 5-year-old with known asthma is being counselled about inhaler technique at a routine review. Which finding on inhaler technique assessment would most likely explain poor symptom control despite correct medication prescription?
questions.explanation: Poor coordination between pressing the inhaler and inhaling, particularly with a metered-dose inhaler without a spacer, significantly reduces the amount of drug reaching the lower airways and is a common, correctable cause of apparently poor asthma control. The other listed actions (correct spacer use, mouth rinsing, shaking the inhaler, waiting between puffs) all represent correct technique rather than problems. Technique review and correction should be routine at every asthma follow-up visit.

Cyanotic congenital heart disease (e.g., transposition of the great arteries) produces central cyanosis that fails to improve significantly with supplemental oxygen—the hyperoxia (nitrogen washout) test. This distinguishes cardiac from respiratory causes of cyanosis.
questions.question: The most common cause of neonatal cyanosis in the first day of life that does NOT respond to 100% oxygen is:
Tachypnoea in a neonate is defined as a respiratory rate above:
questions.explanation: In neonates, tachypnoea is defined as a respiratory rate greater than 60 breaths per minute. This is the most sensitive and earliest sign of respiratory distress and requires prompt assessment to determine the underlying cause.

questions.question: An adolescent is scheduled to receive a booster dose of a vaccine given earlier in childhood. What is the primary immunological rationale for this booster?
questions.explanation: Booster doses are given because protective antibody levels from earlier vaccination can decline over time, and a booster restimulates the immune system to restore higher protective levels through immunological memory. It is not the child's first exposure to the antigen, since the primary series was completed earlier. Boosters do not treat active infection and are a form of active, not passive, immunity.
options: To restore antibody levels that have declined over time
To replace the need for the original primary vaccine series
To introduce the child to the antigen for the very first time
To provide passive immunity transferred from another individual
To treat an active infection already present in the child

questions.question: The Blalock-Hanlon atrial septectomy was historically used for TGA. What has replaced it as the standard initial palliation?
questions.explanation: The Blalock-Hanlon surgical atrial septectomy has been replaced by the Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy, a catheter-based procedure performed in the cardiac catheterisation laboratory or at the bedside under echocardiographic guidance. Rashkind septostomy is less invasive, can be performed in critically ill neonates, and effectively enlarges the interatrial communication to improve bidirectional mixing of blood in TGA, serving as a bridge to definitive arterial switch surgery.
options: Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy as a catheter-based procedure
Pulmonary artery banding to protect the left ventricle
Mustard's intra-atrial redirection procedure used as primary palliation
Systemic-to-pulmonary shunting for augmenting the mixing
Complete arterial switch in the first 24 hours of life

questions.explanation: Herpes simplex type I pneumonia primarily affects malnourished children in whom cellular immunity is significantly impaired, allowing reactivation of latent herpetic infection to spread to the lower respiratory tract.
