questions.question: A 6-year-old boy has chronic nasal congestion, mouth breathing, and snoring, with enlarged adenoids noted on examination, but no evidence of sleep apnoea on assessment. What is the most appropriate initial management?

questions.explanation: The Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respiration) is a late and ominous sign of critically raised intracranial pressure and impending brainstem herniation, reflecting the body's attempt to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure. Recognising this triad requires immediate action to reduce intracranial pressure and prevent herniation. Waiting for further deterioration risks irreversible brainstem injury.
questions.question: A child with a known intracranial tumour and signs of rapidly rising intracranial pressure develops bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular breathing. What is this triad best termed?

options: It should be disregarded unless anaemia is also present
It is significant solely for epidemiological reporting purposes
It only matters when combined with a positive rapid diagnostic test
It classifies the illness as severe malaria regardless of other symptoms
It has no bearing on management if the child appears clinically well
questions.explanation: Hyperparasitaemia above the defined threshold is itself a WHO criterion for severe malaria because of the associated risk of rapid deterioration, even before other complications become apparent. This means high-density parasitaemia mandates severe malaria management regardless of how well the child currently appears. It carries direct clinical, not merely epidemiological, importance.
questions.question: A child in a malaria-endemic country presents with fever and is found to have a very high parasite density on blood film, exceeding the threshold used to define hyperparasitaemia. What is the clinical significance of this finding?

questions.explanation: Lack of expected improvement with appropriate asthma therapy should prompt reassessment of the diagnosis itself, alongside checking adherence and inhaler technique, since an alternative or additional diagnosis (such as an anatomical abnormality or another chronic respiratory condition) may be responsible for the ongoing symptoms. Escalating treatment blindly without this reassessment risks continued ineffective management. A systematic 'diagnosis, technique, adherence' review is a recommended step in refractory paediatric respiratory symptoms.
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has a chronic cough and is diagnosed with asthma, but re-evaluation after 3 months of appropriate inhaled corticosteroid therapy shows no improvement in symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step before escalating asthma therapy further?
options: Reassess the diagnosis and consider alternative causes, alongside checking adherence and inhaler technique
Immediately triple the inhaled corticosteroid dose without further assessment
Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist without reassessing the diagnosis
Assume the child is simply non-compliant with no further evaluation
Refer directly for lung transplantation assessment

questions.explanation: Acute pericarditis classically produces diffuse, concave upward (saddle-shaped) ST elevation across multiple leads without the reciprocal ST depression pattern seen in myocardial infarction. PR segment depression is an additional characteristic feature of pericarditis, reflecting atrial involvement. In children, viral pericarditis is the most common cause. This diffuse pattern helps distinguish pericarditis from the regional, convex ST elevation of myocardial infarction.
questions.question: ST segment elevation in a paediatric ECG with concave upward morphology and diffuse distribution is most characteristic of which condition?
options: Acute myocardial infarction with convex upward ST elevation
Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain in V5–V6 only
Acute pericarditis with diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation
Right ventricular hypertrophy with strain in V1–V2 only
Hyperkalaemia with tall T waves and QRS widening

questions.question: Chorioamnionitis in the mother is a major risk factor for EONS. Which clinical sign in the mother is MOST specific for chorioamnionitis?
questions.explanation: Foul-smelling amniotic fluid is the most specific clinical sign of chorioamnionitis, indicating advanced infection with anaerobic organisms. Other features include maternal fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and foetal tachycardia >160/min, but these are less specific individually.

questions.question: Which of the following respiratory signs is caused by increased intrathoracic pressure secondary to gas trapping in a child with lower airway obstruction?
questions.explanation: Harrison's sulcus is a permanent deformity of the ribs (a horizontal groove along the lower costal margin) that results from chronic increased use of the accessory muscles of respiration combined with soft rib cage in childhood, typically from chronic obstructive lower airway disease such as asthma or bronchiectasis. Intercostal indrawing reflects acute gas trapping, while Harrison's sulcus reflects chronic remodelling from sustained increased work of breathing.

questions.question: Which WHO Clinical Stage 3 condition is diagnosed presumptively on clinical signs in HIV-infected children?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis in HIV-infected children is a Stage 3 condition that can be diagnosed presumptively on clinical signs and simple investigations (CXR, tuberculin test) without microbiological confirmation. LIP, unexplained anaemia, and bronchiectasis also require confirmatory tests to classify as Stage 3, unlike pulmonary TB which can be clinically diagnosed.

options: Connecting the right atrium or caval veins directly to the pulmonary artery
Creating a BT shunt from the subclavian to pulmonary artery
Redirecting aortic blood through an intra-atrial baffle
Inserting a valved conduit from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery
Performing a definitive repair of the tricuspid valve using a bioprosthesis
questions.question: The definitive surgical correction for tricuspid atresia is the Fontan operation. This procedure achieves palliation by:
questions.explanation: The Fontan operation connects the right atrium (or superior/inferior vena cava in total cavopulmonary connections) directly to the pulmonary artery, bypassing the absent right ventricle. Pulmonary blood flow is therefore driven by systemic venous pressure rather than ventricular pumping. Success requires low pulmonary vascular resistance, good left ventricular function, and adequate pulmonary artery size. It is the definitive palliation for single ventricle physiology including tricuspid atresia.

questions.question: Which pathological structure is formed at the site of primary TB infection, combining the local focus and regional lymph node?
questions.explanation: The primary complex (Ghon's complex) consists of the primary focus (Ghon's focus) at the site of initial infection plus the regional lymph node that drains that area. In the lungs, this typically involves the hilar or paratracheal lymph nodes. This combination characterizes primary TB infection in children.

options: Clearing mucus obstructing the upper airway
Cooling the airway to reduce inflammation
Generating positive end-expiratory pressure to keep alveoli open
Indicating a primary cardiac rather than respiratory problem
Signalling pain from the birth process itself
questions.explanation: Grunting occurs when the infant partially closes the glottis during expiration, generating positive end-expiratory pressure that helps keep alveoli open and improve gas exchange in the setting of reduced lung compliance. It is not primarily a pain response or a mechanism for airway clearance. While cardiac disease can cause respiratory distress, grunting itself reflects a compensatory respiratory mechanism, not a specific cardiac signal.
questions.question: A neonate develops signs of respiratory distress including nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and audible expiratory grunting shortly after birth. What is the primary physiological purpose of the grunting sound?

questions.explanation: Postnatal antiretroviral prophylaxis aims to reduce the risk that any virus the infant was exposed to during pregnancy, labour, or early breastfeeding establishes a persistent infection, functioning as a preventive rather than curative measure. It does not eliminate the need for subsequent virological testing to determine actual infection status. It is time-limited, not a source of lifelong protection.
options: To cure any HIV infection already established in the infant
To reduce the risk of transmission from residual maternal virus exposure
To provide complete lifelong protection against future exposure
To replace the need for any later virological testing
To treat an infection that has already definitely occurred
questions.question: An infant exposed to HIV is given antiretroviral prophylaxis after birth. What is the primary purpose of this postnatal prophylaxis?
Roseola infantum is differentiated from measles because the rash in roseola appears when?
questions.explanation: In roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, caused by HHV-6), the rash appears as the temperature decreases and the fever resolves. This is the reverse of measles, where the temperature rises sharply with rash onset. This clinical distinction helps differentiate the two conditions without laboratory testing.
options: At the peak of the fever before it breaks
Only on the trunk, never on the face

questions.explanation: Congenital CMV infection classically causes periventricular calcifications (deposited around the ventricles) on CT or MRI. This pattern distinguishes it from toxoplasmosis (scattered 'pepper-salt' calcifications throughout the brain) and tuberous sclerosis (subependymal calcifications). Congenital CMV is the most common congenital viral infection and may cause a spectrum from asymptomatic infection to severe sensorineural deafness, intellectual disability, and microcephaly.
questions.question: Which condition causes periventricular calcifications seen on CT scan of the neonatal brain?

questions.explanation: High-flow nasal cannula therapy delivers warm, humidified oxygen at high flow rates (1-2 L/kg/min), generating a degree of positive airway pressure that helps stent open collapsed or obstructed small airways in bronchiolitis, improving ventilation-perfusion matching and reducing the work of breathing. It has become the standard step-up therapy before CPAP or intubation in moderate-severe bronchiolitis in high-income centres.
questions.question: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy in severe bronchiolitis works by:
options: Positive pressure stenting open obstructed airways
Delivering antivirals directly to the bronchioles
Preventing aspiration by elevating the head

questions.explanation: In symptomatic HIV-infected children, the incidence and severity of bacterial pneumonia are increased compared to HIV-negative children, though the pneumonia may appear similar in terms of causative organisms. This reflects the acquired immunodeficiency that impairs humoral and cellular immune responses to common respiratory pathogens. Management must include both antiretroviral therapy and prompt antibiotic treatment.
questions.question: In symptomatic HIV-infected children with pneumonia, the pattern of infection compared to HIV-negative children is:

options: Systemic (right) ventricular dysfunction and atrial arrhythmias
questions.explanation: After atrial switch procedures such as Mustard or Senning, the anatomical right ventricle continues to support the systemic circulation long-term, predisposing to progressive systemic ventricular dysfunction and atrial arrhythmias from the extensive atrial baffle surgery. These are recognised late complications specific to atrial switch repairs. The arterial switch operation, now preferred, avoids this problem by restoring the left ventricle as the systemic pump.
questions.question: A child who had a Mustard procedure for TGA in infancy is now being followed up in adolescence. Which long-term complication is this individual particularly at risk of?

questions.explanation: Multifocal clonic seizures, where rhythmic jerking migrates unpredictably from one limb to another, are most commonly associated with HIE and birth trauma. They represent widespread cortical hyperactivity and are seen in severe perinatal insults affecting multiple cortical regions.
questions.question: Multifocal clonic seizures in a neonate, where twitching migrates haphazardly from limb to limb, are MOST associated with:

questions.explanation: Pott's disease (TB of the spine) causes compressive extradural pathology, producing upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive) in the lower limbs due to compression of the spinal cord. It is classified as compressive paraplegia. The classical presentation includes a 'gibbus' (angular kyphosis from vertebral collapse), back pain, and TB systemic symptoms (cough, fever, weight loss). Treatment includes anti-TB drugs and possibly surgical decompression.
questions.question: Pott's disease (TB spine) is the COMMONEST cause of non-traumatic paraplegia in Nigeria. It is an example of which category of spinal cord pathology?

questions.explanation: Nasal diphtheria presents with unilateral, serosanguineous, or mucoid nasal discharge, and its differential diagnosis includes other causes of nasal discharge in children. While the Mantoux test is specific to Mycobacterium tuberculosis exposure, among the listed options nasal diphtheria must be considered when a grey membrane or serosanguineous discharge is present. Wegener granulomatosis and congenital syphilis also enter the differential.
questions.question: A child presents with nasal discharge and the Mantoux test is positive. Which differential diagnosis must be considered?

A term infant develops severe hypoxia disproportionate to the degree of lung disease seen on chest X-ray, with echocardiography showing elevated pulmonary artery pressure and right-to-left shunting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn occurs when the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance after birth fails to occur, causing right-to-left shunting through fetal channels and severe hypoxia that appears disproportionate to the degree of parenchymal lung disease on imaging. This differs from conditions like transient tachypnoea, where hypoxia is generally proportionate to the mild imaging findings. Management includes oxygen, ventilatory support, and pulmonary vasodilators such as inhaled nitric oxide in severe cases.
options: Simple transient tachypnoea of the newborn
Isolated atrial septal defect without pulmonary hypertension
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia without pulmonary hypertension

questions.explanation: Rolandic epilepsy is a benign, age-related idiopathic focal epilepsy with a genetic predisposition (autosomal dominant with age-related penetrance), characterised by centrotemporal (Rolandic) spikes on EEG. 'Benign' refers to its excellent prognosis—nearly all children outgrow it by puberty (14–18 years) without cognitive sequelae. It is the most common form of childhood epilepsy, constituting 15–25% of all cases.
options: Structural lesion in the temporal lobe
questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes the aetiology of Rolandic epilepsy?

questions.explanation: Pneumocystis carinii (now P. jirovecii) is a protozoal opportunistic pathogen that causes severe interstitial pneumonia in immunocompromised children, particularly those with HIV infection. It is listed among the aetiological agents of childhood pneumonia and requires specific treatment with high-dose cotrimoxazole. Children with HIV and pneumonia should therefore be screened for PCP.
questions.question: Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) pneumonia should be considered in a child with pneumonia who also has:

options: Progressive PR interval prolongation with occasional dropped beats
Fixed PR interval with consistently dropped QRS complexes
Short PR interval with delta waves from pre-excitation
Absent P waves with regular ventricular ectopic rhythm
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.explanation: Complete (third-degree) AV heart block is defined by complete dissociation between atrial (P wave) and ventricular (QRS complex) activity, where no P waves conduct to the ventricles. The atria and ventricles beat independently at their own intrinsic rates (atrial faster, ventricular escape slower). This is also termed AV dissociation in the context of complete block. The PR interval varies unpredictably, and the escape QRS may be narrow (junctional) or wide (ventricular).
questions.question: Third-degree (complete) AV heart block is defined on ECG as which finding?
The FIRST-LINE treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is:
questions.explanation: Phototherapy is the first-line treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. Light at 460–490 nm converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers (lumirubin) that can be excreted without conjugation. Exchange transfusion is reserved for phototherapy failure or impending kernicterus.

questions.question: Which vaccine can only be given as a live attenuated organism and cannot be inactivated without losing efficacy?
questions.explanation: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) is a live attenuated vaccine derived from M. bovis that must remain viable to provide protection. It cannot be effectively produced as an inactivated vaccine without losing immunogenicity, since its protective mechanism relies on the organism replicating within macrophages and stimulating cell-mediated immunity.

questions.question: A mother asks how secretory IgA in breast milk helps protect her infant against infection. Through which primary mechanism does this immunoglobulin exert its protective effect?
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA in breast milk acts locally within the infant's gastrointestinal tract, coating the mucosal surface to prevent adherence and invasion by both bacterial and viral pathogens, rather than being absorbed systemically to act within the bloodstream. It does have a dietary protein component, but its described protective role here is immunological, not purely nutritional. It supports, rather than replaces, the infant's own developing immune system, and its protective effect is not limited only to viral pathogens.
options: Working only against viral pathogens, with no effect on bacteria
Replacing the need for any of the infant's own immune development
Acting exclusively as a source of dietary protein with no immune function
Directly entering the infant's bloodstream to attack circulating pathogens
Coating the infant's gut mucosa to prevent pathogen adherence and invasion

questions.question: Digitalis effect on the ECG is most characteristically recognised by which finding?
questions.explanation: Digitalis effect on the ECG produces the characteristic 'reverse tick' or sagging ST depression — a downward-sloping ST segment with T wave inversion, most prominent in the lateral leads. This reflects digitalis's effect on myocardial repolarisation and shortened action potential. Digitalis toxicity may cause AV block, junctional tachycardia, or ventricular arrhythmias. Distinguishing digitalis effect (therapeutic) from toxicity (pathological arrhythmia) is clinically important.
options: Downward-sloping ST depression with T wave inversion (sagging baseline)
Tall tented T waves with a markedly and abnormally shortened QT interval
Peaked P waves with right axis deviation
Prolonged QTc interval with torsades de pointes episodes
Widened QRS with delta wave formation

questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome results from prenatal alcohol exposure and causes a recognisable pattern of growth restriction, CNS dysfunction (intellectual disability, behavioural problems), and characteristic facial features (thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures). Alcohol is the most common preventable teratogen in developed countries. There is no safe level of alcohol consumption during pregnancy.
options: Macrocephaly, tall stature, and intellectual precocity
Limb defects only from alcohol use in third trimester
questions.question: Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is characterised by which combination of features?

questions.explanation: Global developmental delay evaluation should prioritise identifying treatable causes such as congenital hypothyroidism or inborn errors of metabolism, since early treatment can significantly alter outcomes. Chromosomal abnormalities and fixed structural malformations, while important to identify for prognosis and counselling, do not offer the same opportunity for reversal. Screening for reversible causes is therefore an early priority in the diagnostic pathway.
questions.question: A 2-year-old has global developmental delay. Initial evaluation should prioritise identifying which category of potentially treatable cause?
options: Metabolic or endocrine disorders such as hypothyroidism

questions.explanation: Two elevated sweat chloride results combined with identification of two disease-causing CFTR mutations provide definitive confirmation of a cystic fibrosis diagnosis, supporting comprehensive multidisciplinary management going forward. Carrier status would involve only one mutated allele without clinical disease, which does not fit this scenario of confirmed biochemical and genetic abnormality. Early definitive diagnosis allows prompt initiation of appropriate long-term management to optimise outcomes.
questions.question: A 3-year-old with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections is found to have an elevated sweat chloride on two occasions. Genetic testing confirms two CFTR mutations. What does this combination of results confirm?
options: A diagnosis that requires no further monitoring
A definitive diagnosis of cystic fibrosis
Carrier status only, not affected disease
An incidental finding of no clinical significance
A diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia instead
Isolated ostium secundum atrial septal defect
questions.explanation: A common AV valve with an inlet VSD and primum-type ASD defines a complete atrioventricular septal defect, the commonest cardiac lesion in Down syndrome. The mixed systolic and diastolic murmurs arise from valve regurgitation and increased flow across the common valve. Isolated VSD or ASD would not show a common AV valve on echocardiography.
questions.question: A child with Down syndrome presents with a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, and echocardiography showing a common atrioventricular valve with an inlet ventricular septal defect. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options: Limb reduction defects and renal agenesis
questions.explanation: Phenytoin (fetal hydantoin syndrome) causes hypoplasia of the distal phalanges (fingertip and nail hypoplasia), mental deficiency, and craniofacial dysmorphism. This is distinct from the fetal valproate syndrome (NTDs, facial dysmorphism) or fetal alcohol syndrome. Recognition of drug-specific teratogenic patterns guides antenatal counselling for women with epilepsy who require anticonvulsant therapy.
questions.question: Phenytoin use during pregnancy is associated with which pattern of congenital anomalies?

questions.explanation: A tall, peaked P wave in lead II, often termed P pulmonale, reflects right atrial hypertrophy or enlargement, commonly seen in conditions producing right atrial pressure or volume overload such as tricuspid valve disease or pulmonary hypertension. This differs from the broad, notched P wave morphology of left atrial hypertrophy. Its presence should prompt evaluation for right-sided cardiac pathology.
questions.question: A child's ECG shows a tall, peaked P wave in lead II exceeding 2.5 mm in amplitude. Which chamber abnormality does this most likely represent?

questions.explanation: The upper respiratory tract is defined as the region above the laryngeal opening or epiglottis. Structures above this boundary include the nostrils, nasal cavity, pharynx, and epiglottis. This anatomical landmark distinguishes upper from lower respiratory infections.
questions.question: The upper respiratory tract is defined as the region ABOVE an imaginary line drawn through the:

questions.explanation: Tongue fasciculations (visible twitching of the tongue at rest) are pathognomonic of Werdnig-Hoffman disease (Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type I), resulting from anterior horn cell degeneration. Unlike other causes of floppy infant syndrome, SMA type I presents with a frog-like posture, absent reflexes, and tongue fasciculations but preserved intelligence. Respiratory failure typically causes death before age 2.
questions.question: Tongue fasciculations are pathognomonic of which condition causing hypotonia in infancy?

options: Mild immunosuppression requiring monitoring alone without treatment
Severe immunosuppression requiring urgent antiretroviral therapy
No significant immunosuppression requiring only routine monitoring
Advanced immunosuppression that has already resolved spontaneously
A normal finding for this specific age group
questions.explanation: A CD4 percentage below the age-specific severe threshold, such as around 12% in a child of this age, indicates severe immunosuppression according to WHO criteria, warranting urgent initiation of antiretroviral therapy. This is not a normal or mild finding. Immunosuppression at this level does not resolve without treatment.
questions.question: An HIV-infected 3-year-old has a CD4 percentage of 12%. According to WHO immunological classification, what level of immunosuppression does this represent?
Stranger anxiety normally begins to appear at approximately what age?
questions.explanation: Stranger anxiety (wariness or distress on encountering unfamiliar people) typically emerges around 8–9 months as the infant develops object permanence and attachment to primary caregivers. This is a normal social-emotional milestone that reflects cognitive and emotional maturity. Its absence or its persistence beyond the expected developmental period can signal social-emotional or attachment difficulties.

questions.question: In children with foreign body aspiration, the peak age of occurrence is:
questions.explanation: Foreign body aspiration peaks at 2 to 3 years of age when children are mobile, curious, and tend to place objects in their mouths, yet lack the protective mechanisms of older children. The history of sudden onset of choking or coughing is the most important diagnostic clue. Organic materials such as groundnuts are particularly dangerous because they swell and cause inflammatory bronchitis.

questions.question: A child is treated empirically for a presumed bacterial infection, but blood culture results return showing no bacterial growth after 48 hours, and the child has improved clinically. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
options: Assume the culture was performed incorrectly and repeat it immediately
Add a second broad-spectrum antibiotic despite clinical improvement
Continue the same antibiotic regimen for an extended, indefinite duration
Conclude that bacterial infection is definitely still present regardless of the result
Consider that the infection may not have been bacterial and reassess continued antibiotic need
questions.explanation: A negative culture combined with clinical improvement should prompt reassessment of whether a bacterial cause was actually present, since some presumed bacterial infections resolve as self-limiting viral illnesses or without significant bacterial involvement, and unnecessary continuation of antibiotics should be reconsidered. Automatically repeating the culture or adding further antibiotics without clinical justification does not reflect rational practice. Concluding bacterial infection is definitely present despite negative evidence and clinical improvement is not well supported.

options: Herpes simplex virus type 1 and cytomegalovirus
Respiratory syncytial virus and influenza A
questions.explanation: Coxsackie B virus (an enterovirus) is the most common cause of viral myocarditis in neonates and infants, causing inflammatory destruction of cardiomyocytes, oedema, and myocardial dysfunction presenting as acute heart failure. Neonatal Coxsackie B myocarditis carries a high mortality. The virus may be acquired perinatally from the mother. Echocardiography shows global ventricular dysfunction, and management is supportive with inotropic support and IVIG in some protocols.
questions.question: Viral myocarditis as a cause of heart failure in full-term neonates most commonly results from infection with which group of viruses?

questions.explanation: Erythema marginatum is a major Jones criterion characterised by an evanescent (rapidly changing), non-pruritic, pink or red ring-shaped (annular or serpiginous) rash with central clearing and erythematous advancing borders, located predominantly on the trunk and proximal limbs but sparing the face. It appears and disappears within hours, worsens with fever, and is present in only 5–10% of ARF cases. Its evanescent nature and central clearing distinguish it from fixed rashes of other diagnoses.
options: Fixed, pruritic, butterfly-shaped rash on the face
Petechial haemorrhagic rash on the lower limbs from vasculitis process
Evanescent, non-pruritic, pink ring-shaped rash on the trunk and limbs
Vesicular rash following a dermatomal distribution from viral infection
Desquamating rash on the hands and feet following fever
questions.question: The erythema marginatum rash of ARF has which specific morphological characteristics distinguishing it from other rashes?

questions.explanation: Sudden-onset choking and unilateral wheeze during eating, without a preceding coryzal illness, strongly suggests foreign body aspiration, particularly with high-risk foods such as nuts in toddlers. Bronchiolitis and viral-induced wheeze typically follow a preceding respiratory illness and cause bilateral, not unilateral, findings. Recognising this acute choking history is essential to prompt urgent bronchoscopy for removal.
questions.question: A previously well 2-year-old presents with sudden-onset coughing, choking, and unilateral wheeze while eating peanuts, with no preceding illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Congenital subglottic stenosis is different from acquired subglottic stenosis because acquired subglottic stenosis is typically caused by:
questions.explanation: Acquired subglottic stenosis is most commonly caused by prolonged or traumatic endotracheal intubation, which leads to subglottic mucosal injury, ulceration, granulation tissue formation, and eventual fibrotic stenosis. This is an important iatrogenic complication in neonatal intensive care. Congenital subglottic stenosis results from failure of the subglottis to fully canalise during foetal development.

questions.question: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) used as insulating fluids and plasticisers are teratogenic, with exposed offspring showing which characteristic feature?
questions.explanation: Polychlorinated and polybrominated biphenyls (PCBs) cause a characteristic clinical picture in exposed offspring termed 'cola baby,' featuring cola-coloured skin hyperpigmentation, exophthalmos, natal (neonatal) teeth, and developmental delay. This was documented in Yusho (Japan) and Yu-cheng (Taiwan) poisoning incidents from PCB-contaminated cooking oil. Recognition of this pattern aids environmental cause identification.

Mycobacterium bovis is transmitted to humans primarily through ingestion of unpasteurized milk from infected cattle, causing primary intestinal or cervical lymph node tuberculosis. M. tuberculosis is primarily airborne. Pasteurization of milk effectively eliminates M. bovis transmission, explaining its rarity in developed countries.
questions.question: Which Mycobacterium species is transmitted through ingestion of contaminated unpasteurized milk?

options: Sensory aura with no motor component
Complex automatisms without loss of consciousness
questions.explanation: Atonic (akinetic) seizures involve a sudden loss of postural muscle tone, causing the child to abruptly collapse to the ground or slump—hence 'drop attacks.' They carry a high risk of head and facial injury, requiring protective helmets. They may manifest as head nodding or knee buckling. Sodium valproate is the main pharmacological treatment, with protective helmets and face guards as physical measures.
questions.question: Atonic seizures (drop attacks) are characterised by:
Goals of asthma therapy in acute exacerbations include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Relieve airflow obstruction as rapidly as possible
Cure the underlying atopic tendency permanently
Close monitoring of patient condition and treatment response
questions.explanation: Goals of acute asthma therapy include relieving airflow obstruction and hypoxaemia rapidly, reducing wheeze and cough, minimising adverse effects, reducing sleep disturbances and school absences, and closely monitoring response to treatment. Curing the underlying atopic tendency permanently is not a goal of acute therapy; asthma management aims for control rather than cure. Long-term management addresses underlying inflammation.

questions.question: A child points at desired objects and follows pointing by another person. These behaviours are best described as part of which developmental domain?
questions.explanation: Pointing to share interest (proto-declarative pointing) and responding to another's pointing are manifestations of joint attention, a critical social-communicative milestone emerging around 12 months. Joint attention is considered a precursor to language development and a key diagnostic marker in autism screening. Its absence by 12–14 months is a red flag for autism spectrum disorder.

options: Mild asphyxia requiring only routine observation
Severe asphyxia requiring the most aggressive classification
An invalid score requiring immediate recalculation only
Normal, reassuring condition requiring no intervention
questions.question: A neonate has an APGAR score of 4 at 1 minute of life. According to standard grading, how is this score generally classified?
questions.explanation: An APGAR score in the range typically associated with moderate depression, such as a score of 4 to 5 at 1 minute, is generally classified as moderate birth asphyxia, prompting continued resuscitative efforts and close monitoring. This is neither a normal nor merely mildly concerning score. The lowest scores, rather than this moderate range, would correspond to the most severe classification.

Percussion of the precordium is explicitly described as being of little value in the cardiovascular examination of children, due to the difficulty in accurately delineating cardiac borders in the small paediatric chest. In contrast, auscultation is of immense diagnostic value. The four cornerstones of paediatric CVS examination in decreasing clinical yield are: auscultation, palpation, inspection, and percussion.
questions.question: Which investigation is considered 'of little value' in the physical examination of the paediatric cardiovascular system?

options: Congenital viral infection affecting the bone marrow
A normal, uncomplicated term delivery with no other risk factors
Intrauterine growth restriction with placental insufficiency
Neonatal sepsis with associated consumptive coagulopathy
Maternal alloimmune antibodies against fetal platelets
questions.question: A neonate develops thrombocytopenia, and the clinician considers a list of possible causes. Which of the following would NOT typically be considered a cause of neonatal thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: An uncomplicated, healthy term delivery without other risk factors is not itself a recognised cause of neonatal thrombocytopenia, whereas sepsis, maternal alloimmune antibodies, growth restriction, and congenital infection are all established causes through different mechanisms such as consumption, immune destruction, or impaired marrow production. Recognising which factors are genuine risk factors helps focus the diagnostic evaluation of a thrombocytopenic neonate. A normal delivery in isolation does not explain a low platelet count.

options: A normal anatomical variant with no pathological significance
A dilated bronchus with an adjacent smaller pulmonary artery, characteristic of bronchiectasis
A discrete pulmonary nodule suggestive of malignancy
A pneumothorax with a visible air-fluid level
Diffuse ground-glass opacification throughout the lung fields
questions.explanation: The 'signet ring sign' on high-resolution CT refers to a dilated, thick-walled bronchus appearing larger than its adjacent pulmonary artery branch, resembling a signet ring, and is a classic radiological indicator of bronchiectasis. This differs from normal bronchovascular anatomy, where the bronchus and artery are typically similar in size. Recognising this sign supports the diagnosis and helps quantify the extent of bronchiectatic change.
questions.question: A 6-year-old with recurrent chest infections and bronchiectasis undergoes high-resolution CT of the chest, which shows the 'signet ring sign'. What does this finding represent?

options: Absence of both sinoatrial nodes in the heart
Presence of two sinoatrial nodes in the heart
Fusion of atria into a single common atrial chamber
Complete atrioventricular block from absent AV node
questions.explanation: Right atrial isomerism implies duplication of right atrial morphology, which carries the structural consequence of having two sinoatrial (SA) nodes, since each morphological right atrium normally contains one SA node. This has significant electrophysiological implications, including potential conduction abnormalities. Left atrial isomerism conversely is associated with absence or abnormality of the SA node, predisposing to bradyarrhythmias.
questions.question: Right atrial isomerism in sequential segmental analysis implies which specific structural and electrical consequence?

questions.explanation: Headaches specifically associated with near work such as reading, relieved by rest, and without red-flag features raise suspicion for an uncorrected refractive error or accommodative strain, making a visual assessment the appropriate initial step. Neuroimaging and lumbar puncture are unnecessary without additional concerning features. Correcting a refractive error may fully resolve this type of headache.
options: Refer for formal visual acuity and refraction assessment
questions.question: A 7-year-old with recurrent headaches is noted to have symptoms only when reading, relieved by resting the eyes, with no other red-flag features. What is the most appropriate initial step?

questions.explanation: Brief staring episodes with eyelid fluttering, abrupt onset and offset, no post-ictal confusion, and multiple daily occurrences are characteristic of childhood absence epilepsy, often provoked by hyperventilation. Complex focal seizures typically last longer and are followed by post-ictal confusion. The abrupt resumption of normal activity without confusion is the key discriminating feature.
questions.question: A 5-year-old has episodes of staring, eyelid fluttering, and unresponsiveness lasting 10 seconds, occurring multiple times daily, with immediate resumption of activity and no post-ictal confusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Central cyanosis and lethargy are danger signs that classify a child into the very severe pneumonia category in the WHO classification. These signs indicate life-threatening hypoxaemia and impaired consciousness requiring immediate hospitalisation, parenteral antibiotics, and oxygen therapy. Prompt recognition of these danger signs is critical to preventing death.
questions.question: A 3-year-old with cough develops central cyanosis and lethargy. According to WHO classification, this child most likely has:

options: Vesicular lesions in a dermatomal distribution
Pink rings with pale centres that spread and fade
Coalescing purpuric lesions with a non-blanching character
Target lesions with three distinct concentric zones
Fine, sandpaper-like erythema that blanches uniformly across the trunk
questions.explanation: Erythema marginatum, a major Jones criterion, presents as pink, non-pruritic rings with pale centres, mainly on the trunk and proximal limbs, characteristically evanescent and spreading with a serpiginous, map-like border. This distinguishes it from the sandpaper texture of scarlet fever rash, the dermatomal distribution of herpes zoster, or the target lesions of erythema multiforme. Recognising this specific morphology supports the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.
questions.question: A child with acute rheumatic fever develops erythema marginatum. Which morphological feature helps distinguish this rash from other paediatric exanthems?
Which condition is associated with jaundice, anaemia, and hepatosplenomegaly in a newborn?
questions.explanation: HDN presents with the triad of anaemia (from haemolysis), jaundice (from unconjugated bilirubinaemia), and hepatosplenomegaly (from extramedullary haematopoiesis). This triad distinguishes HDN from physiological jaundice, which occurs without anaemia or organomegaly.

options: Breakdown of previously normal tissue from interrupted blood supply
Response of tissues to unusual mechanical forces
Abnormal structure due to abnormal constituent tissues
Primary abnormal formation of tissues from the outset
Normal formation followed by environmental disruption
questions.explanation: A malformation is a primary structural defect in which tissues form abnormally from the outset of organogenesis—examples include congenital heart disease, neural tube defects, and cleft lip/palate. This is distinct from a deformation (abnormal mechanical forces on normal tissue), a disruption (breakdown of previously normal tissue), or a dysplasia (abnormal constituent tissue). Accurate classification guides aetiological investigation and recurrence risk counselling.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a 'malformation' in the context of errors of morphogenesis?

options: Administering digoxin to improve contractility alongside the tachyarrhythmia
Performing emergency cardiac transplantation before function deteriorates
Controlling or terminating the tachyarrhythmia to restore normal rate
Initiating ACE inhibitors as the primary and sole treatment
Prescribing corticosteroids to reduce arrhythmia-related myocarditis
questions.explanation: Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is a reversible form of dilated cardiomyopathy where control or termination of the responsible arrhythmia (SVT, permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia, incessant atrial tachycardia) allows gradual recovery of ventricular function over weeks to months. This makes accurate arrhythmia diagnosis critical — what appears to be idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy may in fact be arrhythmia-induced and fully reversible if the tachycardia is controlled pharmacologically or by ablation.
questions.question: Tachyarrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy in a child is potentially reversible. Which key management principle allows recovery of ventricular function?

questions.explanation: The PR interval represents the time from the onset of atrial depolarisation (beginning of the P wave) to the onset of ventricular depolarisation (beginning of the QRS complex), encompassing AV nodal, bundle of His, and bundle branch conduction time. Normal PR interval in children under 1 year is 0.07–0.12 sec, 0.08–0.16 sec in children over 1 year, and 0.10–0.20 sec in adults. Prolongation indicates first-degree heart block.
questions.question: Which ECG component represents the duration of atrioventricular conduction from atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation?
A child with diphtheria is treated with erythromycin. What is the primary purpose of giving this antibiotic in addition to antitoxin?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics such as erythromycin eradicate Corynebacterium diphtheriae, stopping further toxin production and reducing transmissibility, but they do not neutralise toxin already released into the circulation. Antitoxin is specifically required to neutralise that circulating toxin. Antibiotics cannot substitute for antitoxin in active disease.
options: To treat the myocarditis that may develop later
To eliminate the organism and halt further toxin production
To replace the need for antitoxin administration entirely
To directly neutralise toxin already circulating in the blood
To prevent an allergic reaction to the antitoxin

questions.question: Iron supplementation in a preterm neonate less than 2 kg is started at:
questions.explanation: Iron supplementation (FeSO4) at 6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron is initiated at 2 weeks of age in preterm neonates below 2 kg. Preterm infants have lower iron stores and faster growth rates, making early supplementation essential to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia.

FFP is given at 10–15 ml/kg in neonatal DIC to replace consumed clotting factors including fibrinogen, and Factors V, VIII, and XIII. It is a key supportive treatment alongside platelet transfusion and treatment of the underlying trigger.
questions.question: In DIC, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is given at which dose in neonates?

options: A traumatic lumbar puncture artefact only
Tuberculous meningitis with its typical chronic pattern
Normal age-appropriate CSF findings requiring no treatment
Viral meningitis with a typical lymphocytic pattern
questions.explanation: A CSF profile showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein is characteristic of bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis, reflecting an acute bacterial inflammatory process within the central nervous system. Viral meningitis typically shows a lymphocyte-predominant pattern with normal or only mildly reduced glucose. Tuberculous meningitis usually has a more gradual, lymphocytic pattern rather than this acute neutrophilic picture, and this profile is not consistent with a normal or purely traumatic result.
questions.question: A neonate develops fever, irritability, and a bulging fontanelle on day 7 of life. Lumbar puncture reveals a high white cell count with predominant neutrophils, low glucose, and elevated protein. What does this CSF pattern most strongly suggest?

options: Newborns in the first week of life
questions.explanation: Bronchiolitis requiring hospitalisation predominantly affects infants under 2 years of age, with peak incidence in the first 6 months of life when the bronchiolar diameter is smallest. RSV is responsible for the majority of hospitalisations. The younger and smaller the infant, the higher the risk of apnoea and respiratory failure requiring ICU care.
questions.question: Bronchiolitis is the MOST frequent lower respiratory tract infection requiring hospitalisation in which age group?

questions.explanation: The measles virus is a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus belonging to the family Paramyxoviridae and genus Morbillivirus. It has only one antigenic type (serotype). It is found in nasopharyngeal secretions, blood, and urine during the prodromal period and a few days after the rash appears.
questions.question: The measles virus belongs to which family and genus?

questions.explanation: Generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and recurrent parotid enlargement, in the absence of AIDS-defining illnesses, are typical WHO Clinical Stage 2 features reflecting mild-to-moderately symptomatic paediatric HIV disease. This is a less advanced picture than Stage 3 or Stage 4 disease, which include more severe opportunistic infections and wasting. The WHO paediatric staging system applies specifically to children, not only adults.
questions.question: A 5-year-old with HIV who has never received antiretroviral therapy presents with generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and recurrent parotid swelling but no AIDS-defining illness. According to WHO staging, this combination best fits which stage?
options: WHO Clinical Stage 1, reflecting asymptomatic infection
WHO Clinical Stage 3, reflecting advanced symptomatic disease
A staging category reserved only for adults, not children
WHO Clinical Stage 4, reflecting severe immunosuppression
WHO Clinical Stage 2, reflecting mild-to-moderate symptomatic disease

questions.question: The prognosis of Werdnig-Hoffman disease is:
questions.explanation: The prognosis of Werdnig-Hoffman disease (SMA Type I) is very poor. Death typically occurs before 2 years of age from recurrent aspiration pneumonias and progressive respiratory failure, as the bulbar and respiratory muscles are progressively affected. There is no curative treatment traditionally, though newer SMN-targeting therapies (e.g., nusinersen, risdiplam) have changed this in centres where they are available, improving survival significantly.

questions.question: Predisposing factors for haemorrhagic disease of the newborn include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Early introduction of formula reduces HDN risk because formula is supplemented with Vitamin K. Risk factors for HDN include maternal use of anticonvulsants (phenobarbitone, phenytoin), warfarin, exclusive breastfeeding (low Vitamin K in breastmilk), and broad-spectrum antibiotics (reduce gut flora producing Vitamin K2).

options: Prominent right atrium on PA chest X-ray
Normal cardiac silhouette with increased vascular markings only
Right ventricular enlargement with upturned apex
Left atrial and left ventricular enlargement
questions.explanation: In a large PDA, the extra blood flowing from the aorta to the pulmonary circulation returns to the left heart via the pulmonary veins, causing volume overload of the left atrium and left ventricle. Chest X-ray therefore shows left atrial (LA) and left ventricular (LV) enlargement alongside pulmonary plethora. This left-sided volume overload pattern is characteristic of large PDA, contrasting with the right-sided overload seen in ASD.
questions.question: In a large PDA producing a significant left-to-right shunt, which radiological finding specifically reflects increased left-sided cardiac volume overload?

options: Aortic valve alone without mitral involvement
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is the most commonly and severely affected valve in acute rheumatic carditis, typically producing mitral regurgitation acutely, with the aortic valve being the second most frequently involved. Right-sided valves are rarely primarily affected. This pattern of predominant left-sided valve involvement is characteristic of rheumatic heart disease throughout its acute and chronic phases.
questions.question: A child with acute rheumatic fever develops carditis. Which cardiac valve is most commonly and severely affected first?

questions.explanation: Because tachyarrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy results from a reversible functional insult rather than permanent structural myocardial damage, ventricular function typically improves gradually, often substantially, over weeks to months once sinus rhythm is restored and maintained. This favourable prognosis distinguishes it from many other paediatric cardiomyopathies. Continued surveillance is still required to confirm recovery and detect any recurrence of arrhythmia.
questions.question: A child previously diagnosed with tachyarrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy has now achieved sustained sinus rhythm with anti-arrhythmic therapy. What is the expected outcome for ventricular function?
options: Ventricular function remains permanently and irreversibly impaired
Immediate and complete normalisation within hours
Gradual, often substantial recovery of ventricular function over weeks to months
No relationship between rhythm control and ventricular recovery

questions.explanation: Positive stool culture for poliovirus is the DIAGNOSTIC investigation for poliomyelitis. Virus excretion in stool begins before symptom onset and continues for 3–8 weeks. The virus can also be isolated from the throat, urine, and CSF in the first week. Clinical diagnosis is based on typical history and flaccid paralysis, but stool culture provides definitive confirmation. This is critical for national eradication programme certification.
questions.question: The DIAGNOSTIC investigation for paralytic poliomyelitis is:
A febrile child with a heart rate of 220 beats per minute has narrow, regular QRS complexes on ECG with no clearly discernible P waves. Which arrhythmia is most likely?
questions.explanation: Supraventricular tachycardia in children typically presents with a very rapid, regular, narrow-complex rhythm with absent or difficult-to-identify P waves, often exceeding rates achievable by sinus tachycardia alone. Sinus tachycardia usually shows a clearly identifiable P wave before each QRS and rarely exceeds 220 bpm in this manner. Ventricular tachycardia would instead show broad QRS complexes.

A single unprovoked afebrile seizure with a normal examination and full recovery does not routinely require immediate antiepileptic therapy, as the recurrence risk after one seizure is around 40 to 50 percent and treatment is usually deferred until a second event or high-risk features are present. Investigations can be arranged electively rather than emergently. Overtreatment exposes the child to unnecessary medication risk.
questions.question: A 4-year-old has a first afebrile generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes with full recovery within 30 minutes. Examination and development are normal. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

questions.explanation: Rhinovirus is the most common cause of acute coryza (nasopharyngitis), accounting for the majority of upper respiratory tract infections. The classical triad of sneezing, rhinorrhoea, and blocked nostrils is characteristic. Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus is only an occasional bacterial cause.
questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with sneezing, rhinorrhoea, and blocked nostrils for 3 days. The MOST likely causative organism is:
A child with longstanding, uncorrected congenital heart disease is noted to have an asymmetrical anterior chest wall bulge overlying the heart. What does this most likely indicate?
questions.explanation: A praecordial bulge develops when a chronically enlarged heart exerts sustained pressure on the still-pliable paediatric chest wall during growth. It signifies long-standing, rather than acute, cardiac enlargement. Pericardial effusion and costochondral problems do not typically produce this gradual bony remodelling.
options: Congenital sternal deformity unrelated to the heart
Chronic cardiac enlargement during skeletal growth

questions.question: The average length of a term neonate at birth and the expected length at 1 year is:
options: 45 cm at birth, 65 cm at 1 year
50 cm at birth, 75–80 cm at 1 year
55 cm at birth, 80 cm at 1 year
48 cm at birth, 70 cm at 1 year
52 cm at birth, 85 cm at 1 year
questions.explanation: Term neonates are approximately 50 cm at birth and grow to 75–80 cm by 12 months of age. This represents an increase of approximately 25–30 cm in the first year. Adequate nutrition is essential to achieve this growth velocity, as infants who are malnourished show linear growth faltering.

Apnoea of prematurity is defined as cessation of breathing for more than 20 seconds, or for a shorter duration if accompanied by bradycardia (HR <100/min) or cyanosis. It results from immaturity of the respiratory control centres and is treated with methylxanthines (caffeine).
questions.question: Apnoea of prematurity is defined as cessation of breathing for more than:

questions.explanation: Oral prednisolone for moderate acute asthma exacerbation at the emergency room is given at 1-2 mg/kg as part of the acute management protocol. This dose provides rapid systemic anti-inflammatory effect sufficient to reverse the acute exacerbation. A short course (3-5 days) is typically given without the need for tapering when the duration is brief.

questions.explanation: After the loading dose of 15–20 mg/kg IV, phenobarbitone maintenance is 3.5–5 mg/kg/day (divided into two doses in older infants, usually once daily in neonates). Maintenance is continued for 2 weeks to 2 months depending on aetiology and EEG findings before considering weaning.
questions.question: The maintenance dose of phenobarbitone in neonatal seizures is:

options: An abnormally low count requiring urgent haematology referral
Definite evidence of an active bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
A laboratory error requiring the sample to be repeated immediately
The wide normal physiological variation in white cell counts at this early age
An abnormally high count diagnostic of leukaemia at this age
questions.explanation: White cell counts in neonates show wide physiological variation, particularly on day 1 of life, and a value within this broad normal range does not by itself indicate infection, laboratory error, or a haematological malignancy. Isolated interpretation of the white cell count without considering the full clinical picture and other laboratory parameters can be misleading in either direction. This wide normal range is an important consideration when using white cell count as part of a sepsis evaluation in a neonate.
questions.question: A neonate's white blood cell count is checked on day 1 of life as part of a sepsis evaluation, and the result falls within the range considered normal for this specific age. What does a white cell count within the range of roughly 6,000 to 35,000 per microlitre on day 1 primarily reflect?

questions.explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically occurs in tall, thin adolescent males, presenting with sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, with reduced breath sounds and hyperresonant percussion on the affected side due to rupture of a subpleural bleb. Pneumonia would typically show dullness and crackles rather than hyperresonance. Recognising this classic body habitus and presentation supports prompt chest imaging and appropriate management.
questions.question: A 15-year-old tall, thin boy presents with sudden-onset unilateral chest pain and breathlessness while playing basketball, with reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Delayed developmental milestones in children with congenital heart disease are primarily attributed to chronic tissue hypoxia, which reduces oxygen delivery to the developing brain and impairs neurological maturation. This is most pronounced in cyanotic heart disease with right-to-left shunting. Additionally, chromosomal syndromes such as Down syndrome may cause both the cardiac defect and the developmental delay independently.
questions.question: Delayed developmental milestones in a child with congenital heart disease occur primarily as a consequence of which mechanism?
options: Recurrent bacterial meningitis from cerebral emboli
Chronic tissue hypoxia reducing cerebral metabolism
Neurotoxic side effects of cardiac medications on the CNS
Poor nutrition from cardiac cachexia alone
Chromosomal anomaly independent of cardiac disease

questions.question: In paediatric heart failure, tachyarrhythmias cause diminished systemic output through which primary mechanism?
questions.explanation: Tachyarrhythmias reduce diastolic filling time, which decreases ventricular preload and stroke volume, ultimately reducing cardiac output despite the higher rate. At very high rates, the reduction in stroke volume outweighs the rate increase, causing net reduction in cardiac output. Additionally, tachycardia increases myocardial oxygen demand. Sustained tachycardia (tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy) can cause reversible dilated cardiomyopathy if left untreated for weeks to months.
options: Direct myocardial toxicity from rapid pacing reducing contractility
Reduced diastolic filling time reducing stroke volume and cardiac output
Excessive ventricular filling from prolonged diastole reducing stroke volume
Coronary artery spasm from sympathetic activation during tachycardia
AV valve regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction at high rates

questions.question: On examining a toddler with congenital heart disease, the clinician palpates a sustained, forceful and laterally displaced apex beat. This finding is most consistent with which chamber abnormality?
questions.explanation: A heaving, displaced apex beat reflects left ventricular dilatation and hypertrophy from chronic volume overload, as occurs with large left-to-right shunts such as VSD or PDA. Right ventricular overload instead produces a left parasternal heave rather than apex displacement. Atrial enlargement does not typically alter the character of the apex beat.

questions.question: A right QRS axis deviation on the paediatric ECG, when seen in the context of cyanotic heart disease with pulmonary oligaemia, most strongly suggests which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Right axis deviation combined with right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG in the context of cyanotic heart disease with pulmonary oligaemia is most characteristic of Tetralogy of Fallot. The RVOTO causes pressure-overload RVH, and the right axis reflects the dominant right ventricular vector. Tricuspid atresia produces superior axis + LVH, while AV canal produces superior axis + BVH. These ECG-axis signatures aid in differential diagnosis of cyanotic CHD.

options: Hepatitis B vaccine produced using recombinant DNA technology
Tetanus toxoid produced by chemical inactivation of toxin
Pertussis whole-cell vaccine produced from killed bacteria
BCG vaccine produced by serial laboratory attenuation
Oral polio vaccine produced from a live attenuated virus strain
questions.explanation: The hepatitis B vaccine is a well-known example of a recombinant vaccine, in which the gene encoding a viral surface antigen is inserted into a yeast or other expression system to produce the antigen without using the whole virus. BCG and oral polio vaccines are produced through laboratory attenuation of live organisms, not recombinant technology. Tetanus toxoid and whole-cell pertussis vaccines use inactivation methods rather than genetic engineering.
questions.question: A vaccine manufacturer produces a recombinant vaccine using genetic engineering techniques. Which example best illustrates this vaccine production method?

questions.explanation: In vitamin K deficiency, prothrombin time is typically prolonged but corrects after vitamin K administration, whereas a prolonged prothrombin time that fails to correct suggests underlying hepatic synthetic dysfunction rather than simple vitamin K lack. A completely normal coagulation screen would be inconsistent with significant hepatic impairment. An isolated platelet abnormality does not reflect the synthetic clotting factor problem being assessed here.
options: A completely normal coagulation screen despite severe liver disease
An isolated abnormality confined only to the platelet count
A prolonged prothrombin time that fails to correct with vitamin K administration
A prothrombin time that fully corrects after vitamin K is given
A shortened prothrombin time with no other abnormality
questions.question: A neonate's coagulation screen is requested as part of evaluating prolonged jaundice with suspected liver dysfunction. Which result pattern would be most consistent with significant hepatic synthetic impairment rather than simple vitamin K deficiency?

Definite non-accidental suffocation without further investigation needed
Sudden infant death syndrome or an unsafe sleep environment as contributing factors
questions.question: A term infant is found unresponsive and not breathing, with a preceding history of being placed prone to sleep on a soft mattress. After resuscitation attempts, what is this scenario most consistent with?
questions.explanation: Unsafe sleep practices, including prone positioning and soft bedding, are well-established modifiable risk factors for sudden infant death syndrome, and such presentations require careful multidisciplinary review, though this does not automatically imply non-accidental injury without further specific evidence. Recognising and addressing modifiable risk factors, such as promoting supine sleeping and firm mattresses, is central to public health prevention strategies. A thorough, non-accusatory but thorough case review is standard practice following unexpected infant death.

options: Caused by bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
Always preceded by acute otitis media
questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion (OME) is defined as an asymptomatic middle ear effusion, sometimes called glue ear, that often follows AOM but may occur without prior AOM. Unlike AOM, it lacks the acute inflammatory signs of fever and otalgia. OME can cause conductive hearing loss and is a common cause of childhood hearing impairment.
questions.question: Otitis media with effusion (OME) differs from acute otitis media in that OME is:

questions.explanation: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is currently recommended only for high-risk cardiac patients: those with unrepaired cyanotic CHD, prosthetic cardiac valves or repair material, previous infective endocarditis, or surgically repaired CHD with residual defects near prosthetic material. The regimen is amoxicillin 50 mg/kg (max 2g) orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure. Clindamycin is used for penicillin-allergic patients. Low and moderate-risk lesions no longer warrant routine prophylaxis per current guidelines.
options: All children with any congenital heart defect regardless of its complexity
Only children with no structural heart disease who have dental caries
High-risk patients including unrepaired cyanotic CHD and prosthetic valves
All children with a previous episode of streptococcal pharyngitis infection
Children with a family history of infective endocarditis only
questions.question: Dental prophylaxis for prevention of infective endocarditis is currently recommended for which specific group of paediatric patients?

questions.explanation: Approximately one-third (33%) of children who have a first febrile seizure will have a recurrence. Of those who recur, about 75% do so within 12 months of the first episode. The risk is higher with young age at first episode (<18 months), family history of febrile seizures, lower temperature at onset, and shorter duration of fever before seizure. Parental counselling about this recurrence risk is essential.
questions.question: The recurrence rate after a first febrile seizure is approximately:

questions.explanation: Fresh frozen plasma contains a broad range of clotting factors and is used in DIC to replace multiple consumed factors simultaneously, addressing the coagulopathy component of the condition. Packed red cells and platelet concentrate address anaemia and thrombocytopenia respectively but do not replace the range of clotting factors needed. Cryoprecipitate targets specific factors such as fibrinogen and is not the primary broad-spectrum replacement product used first-line.
options: Whole blood used exclusively instead of any component product
Cryoprecipitate used as the sole product in every case
questions.question: A neonate with suspected DIC requires correction of both clotting factor deficiency and ongoing bleeding. Which blood product is most appropriate to replace multiple clotting factors simultaneously?

options: Osler nodes, caused by immune complex deposition in the fingers
Roth spots, caused by retinal microembolism or vasculitis
Janeway lesions, caused by septic microemboli to the skin
Splinter haemorrhages, caused by microemboli under the nailbed
Erythema marginatum, caused by streptococcal cross-reactivity
questions.explanation: Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with pale, white centres seen on fundoscopy in infective endocarditis, thought to result from retinal microembolism or immune-mediated vasculitis. They are a recognised, though non-specific, peripheral stigma of endocarditis distinct from the skin and nail findings such as Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages. Their presence supports the clinical suspicion of endocarditis in an appropriate context.
questions.question: A child with infective endocarditis undergoes fundoscopic examination, revealing retinal haemorrhages with pale centres. What are these findings called, and what is their underlying cause?
The MOST common METABOLIC cause of neonatal seizures is:
questions.explanation: Hypocalcaemia is the most common metabolic cause of neonatal seizures, typically presenting between days 1–3 (early hypocalcaemia in IDM, asphyxiated, or preterm neonates) or days 4–7 (late neonatal hypocalcaemia associated with high-phosphate feeds or hypomagnesaemia).

Serial ultrasound biometry (measuring head circumference, abdominal circumference, and femur length) is the standard method for diagnosing IUGR by tracking deviation from expected growth trajectories. A single measurement is insufficient; serial measurements define the growth pattern.
