For children under 2 months, the threshold is more than 60 breaths per minute, and for children aged 1 to 5 years, more than 40 breaths per minute. These age-specific thresholds are essential for community case management.

Pulmonary sequestration is defined by non-functioning lung tissue that lacks a normal connection to the tracheobronchial tree and receives its blood supply from a systemic (rather than pulmonary) artery, distinguishing it anatomically from other congenital lung malformations such as congenital pulmonary airway malformations, which typically retain pulmonary arterial supply. Recognising this anomalous systemic supply is critical for surgical planning, as inadvertent injury to this vessel during resection can cause significant haemorrhage. This anatomical distinction is a key differentiator tested in the assessment of congenital lung malformations.
options: Systemic (rather than pulmonary) arterial blood supply to non-functioning lung tissue
Complete absence of any blood supply to the affected tissue
Normal connection to the tracheobronchial tree with normal function
Presence exclusively within the pleural space rather than lung parenchyma
Direct communication with the gastrointestinal tract
questions.question: A 6-year-old with a chronic cough undergoes chest CT, which reveals a pulmonary sequestration with an anomalous systemic arterial supply. What key anatomical feature distinguishes a pulmonary sequestration from other congenital lung malformations?

questions.explanation: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV), discovered in 2001, has been increasingly recognised as a second major cause of bronchiolitis and croup in infants, causing a clinical syndrome essentially indistinguishable from RSV bronchiolitis. Rhinovirus, adenovirus, and parainfluenza are also important bronchiolitis pathogens. Co-infection with RSV and hMPV is associated with more severe disease.
questions.question: Which of the following viruses, besides RSV, has been increasingly recognised as a cause of bronchiolitis?

A 6-year-old boy with poorly controlled asthma despite maximal inhaled therapy is found to have significant environmental tobacco smoke exposure at home. What is the most important intervention to address alongside pharmacological optimisation?
questions.explanation: Environmental tobacco smoke exposure is a well-recognised trigger that worsens asthma control and increases exacerbation frequency, so addressing this modifiable environmental factor through smoking cessation support for household members is an essential complementary intervention alongside optimising pharmacological therapy. Escalating to advanced therapies without addressing an ongoing modifiable trigger is unlikely to achieve optimal control. A holistic approach addressing environment, adherence, and technique should precede escalation to more intensive therapies.
options: Immediate escalation to biologic therapy regardless of exposure
Smoking cessation support for household members and reduction of environmental exposure
Ignoring the exposure as it has no bearing on asthma control
Recommending long-term hospital admission instead of home management
Doubling all current medication doses without addressing exposure

questions.explanation: Unlike other forms of tracheoesophageal fistula associated with oesophageal atresia, which present immediately with feeding difficulty at birth, the H-type fistula occurs with a patent oesophagus, allowing relatively normal feeding, so the diagnosis may be delayed until recurrent aspiration pneumonia or choking with feeds prompts further investigation. This later presentation contrasts with the immediate, dramatic presentation of atresia-associated fistulas. A high index of suspicion is needed in children with recurrent unexplained respiratory infections and feeding-related symptoms.
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections since infancy is diagnosed with an H-type tracheoesophageal fistula, a subtype without associated oesophageal atresia. Why might this specific subtype present later than other forms of tracheoesophageal fistula?
options: Because it never causes any respiratory symptoms
Because it is always diagnosed prenatally without exception
Because the oesophagus remains patent, allowing near-normal feeding, so symptoms may be subtler and diagnosis delayed
Because it is more common in older children than infants
Because it causes immediate complete inability to feed from birth

questions.explanation: A positive tuberculin skin test with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms indicates latent tuberculosis infection rather than active disease, and treatment with a preventive antibiotic regimen, such as isoniazid, reduces the risk of future progression to active disease, which is particularly important in young children. Active disease would require multi-drug therapy and further investigation for extent of disease. Distinguishing latent from active infection is essential for appropriate treatment intensity.
questions.question: A 3-year-old close contact of a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis has a positive tuberculin skin test but a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Latent tuberculosis infection, treated with a course of preventive therapy
Active pulmonary tuberculosis requiring four-drug therapy
No infection present, requiring no further action
Tuberculosis meningitis requiring urgent lumbar puncture

questions.question: A 4-year-old has developmental regression, hepatosplenomegaly, and coarse facial features. Which category of disorder is most strongly suggested by this combination?
questions.explanation: Developmental regression with coarse facial features and hepatosplenomegaly is a classic pattern for lysosomal storage disorders, such as mucopolysaccharidoses, in which progressive accumulation of undegraded substrates affects multiple organ systems. Mitochondrial disorders more typically present with multisystem energy-dependent organ failure without this specific coarse facies and organomegaly combination. Recognising this triad guides targeted enzyme and metabolic testing.

questions.question: A 9-year-old girl has recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches lasting 4 hours, associated with photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea, relieved by sleep. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Unilateral throbbing pain with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, and relief with sleep, in a child with a normal examination, fits the paediatric criteria for migraine without aura. Tension headaches are typically bilateral and band-like without these associated features. A normal examination supports a primary rather than secondary headache disorder.

options: Vitamin D, which addresses bone metabolism rather than seizures
Vitamin A, which addresses vision rather than seizures
Vitamin E, which addresses oxidative stress rather than seizures
Vitamin K, which addresses bleeding rather than seizures
questions.question: A neonate develops recurrent seizures that fail to respond to standard anticonvulsant therapy, and a specific vitamin-responsive metabolic condition is suspected. Administration of which vitamin is characteristically diagnostic and therapeutic in this specific condition?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxine-dependent seizures are a rare but important cause of anticonvulsant-resistant neonatal seizures, and administration of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) can be both diagnostic, through prompt seizure cessation, and therapeutic in this specific condition. Vitamins K, A, D, and E address entirely different physiological processes and do not have this specific diagnostic and therapeutic role in seizure management. Recognising this rare but treatable cause is important when standard anticonvulsants fail.

options: Recommend switching immediately to an entirely different vaccine brand
Suggest the child should never receive any injectable vaccine again
Advise permanent discontinuation of all further vaccination
Advise that this always indicates a dangerous allergic reaction
Reassure that these are common, expected, self-limiting reactions
questions.question: A caregiver reports that her child develops a mild fever and local swelling after each dose of a vaccine. What is the most appropriate guidance regarding future doses?
questions.explanation: Mild fever and local swelling are common, expected, and generally self-limiting reactions to many vaccines, reflecting normal immune stimulation rather than a dangerous reaction, and do not usually warrant discontinuing future scheduled doses. Only true severe allergic or anaphylactic reactions would typically prompt reconsideration of further doses of that specific vaccine. Reassurance and simple symptomatic care are usually all that is needed.

options: Immediately at birth, with no further decline afterwards
Only after 12 months of age in preterm infants
At exactly the same postnatal age as term infants
Earlier than in term infants, often around 4 to 8 weeks
Only in the first 24 hours of life
questions.explanation: Anaemia of prematurity reaches its nadir earlier than the physiological anaemia nadir of term infants, often around 4 to 8 weeks of postnatal age, reflecting a more pronounced and earlier decline in haemoglobin related to reduced erythropoietin response and shorter red cell lifespan in preterm infants. It does not occur at the same timing as in term infants, nor is it confined to the first 24 hours or delayed until after 12 months. Recognising this earlier nadir helps guide monitoring and potential intervention.
questions.question: A neonate develops anaemia of prematurity, an exaggeration of the normal physiological anaemia seen in all infants. At approximately what postnatal age does this anaemia typically reach its lowest point (nadir) in a preterm infant?

questions.explanation: Cardiac toxicity (myocarditis/cardiomyopathy) from diphtheria exotoxin occurs 1–2 weeks after initial symptoms. Peripheral neuropathy (via antigen-antibody complex deposition) develops 2–6 weeks after onset and may resemble Guillain-Barré syndrome. These delayed complications are caused by systemic toxin absorption, not direct infection.
questions.question: Diphtheria exotoxin absorbed into the bloodstream causes cardiac toxicity presenting approximately how long after initial symptoms?
options: 6–8 weeks after the acute illness resolves

questions.question: A child with hypercalcaemia would be expected to show which change in the QTc interval on ECG?
options: Prolonged QTc from delayed ventricular repolarisation
ST elevation from calcium-mediated coronary vasospasm
No change in QTc as calcium does not affect repolarisation
Widened QRS from calcium's effect on myocardial conductance
Shortened QTc from accelerated ventricular repolarisation
questions.explanation: Hypercalcaemia shortens the QTc interval by accelerating ventricular repolarisation, as elevated extracellular calcium shortens the plateau phase (phase 2) of the cardiac action potential. Conversely, hypocalcaemia prolongs the QTc interval. Hyperkalaemia produces tall T waves; hypokalaemia causes T wave flattening and U waves. These electrolyte-ECG relationships are an important component of systematic paediatric ECG interpretation in metabolic or critical care settings.

options: H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis
coli, Listeria) and adults (predominantly S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis).
questions.question: The meningitis pathogen spectrum in children 3 months to 12 years is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: The classic pathogen triad of bacterial meningitis in children aged 3 months to 12 years is Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Neisseria meningitidis. This differs from neonates (GBS, E. coli, Listeria) and adults (predominantly S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis).

questions.question: An HIV-exposed infant is being managed under a PMTCT programme. At what timing relative to delivery does most mother-to-child transmission occur when no interventions are given?
questions.explanation: In the absence of any intervention, the largest proportion of mother-to-child HIV transmission occurs during labour and delivery, when the infant is exposed to maternal blood and genital secretions, rather than during the earlier antenatal trimesters. This is why intrapartum interventions such as antiretroviral prophylaxis are a cornerstone of PMTCT programmes. Transmission does not occur after infancy from this maternal exposure route.
options: Equally distributed across each trimester of pregnancy
Only after the infant reaches two years of age
Exclusively during the first trimester of pregnancy
During labour and delivery (the intrapartum period)
Exclusively during the second trimester of pregnancy

questions.question: Secretory IgA in breast milk protects the neonate by:
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA (sIgA) in breast milk coats the mucosal surfaces of the gut, oral cavity, airways, and inner ears, preventing pathogens from adhering to the epithelium—a process called immune exclusion. Unlike serum IgA, sIgA is not destroyed by digestive enzymes, allowing it to act throughout the GI tract.

questions.question: Mitochondrial DNA is ALWAYS inherited from:
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is always inherited exclusively from the mother because only egg cells, not sperm, retain their mitochondria during fertilisation. This maternal inheritance pattern means that mitochondrial diseases are passed from mothers to all their children, but only daughters can transmit them further. Examples of mitochondrial disorders include MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes).

questions.question: A critically ill child with suspected severe sepsis requires immediate antibiotic therapy. Which route of administration is most appropriate for ensuring reliable and rapid drug levels?
options: Oral administration to avoid the discomfort of injections
Delayed administration until oral intake is tolerated
Intravenous administration for rapid, reliable systemic levels
Rectal administration as the preferred first choice
Topical application directly onto the skin surface
questions.explanation: In a seriously ill child, especially with sepsis, the intravenous route ensures rapid and reliable achievement of therapeutic drug levels, bypassing concerns about unreliable gut absorption. Oral administration may be inadequate or unreliable in a very sick child with poor perfusion or vomiting. Topical or rectal routes are not appropriate for treating systemic sepsis.

questions.question: In neonatal resuscitation, bag-and-mask ventilation is indicated when a neonate's heart rate falls below:
questions.explanation: Positive pressure ventilation via bag-and-mask is initiated when a neonate's heart rate falls below 100 beats/min despite initial steps, or when breathing is absent or gasping. Chest compressions are added if the heart rate remains below 60 beats/min despite effective ventilation.

questions.question: A child in the paroxysmal phase of pertussis develops recurrent severe coughing fits leading to facial petechiae and subconjunctival haemorrhage. What mechanism best explains these findings?
options: An allergic reaction to antibiotic treatment given earlier
An underlying bleeding disorder unrelated to the cough
Vitamin K deficiency triggered by the infection
Markedly raised intrathoracic pressure during coughing paroxysms
Secondary bacterial sepsis causing disseminated bleeding
questions.explanation: The severe, repetitive coughing paroxysms of pertussis markedly raise intrathoracic and venous pressure, which can rupture small capillaries in the face and conjunctivae, producing petechiae and subconjunctival haemorrhage. This is a mechanical consequence of coughing rather than a coagulation disorder. It is not related to vitamin K status or antibiotic allergy.

Ataxia telangiectasia combines progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections due to combined immunodeficiency, with elevated alpha-fetoprotein supporting the diagnosis. Friedreich ataxia instead presents with areflexia, pes cavus, and cardiomyopathy without telangiectasia or immunodeficiency. The combination of neurological, cutaneous, and immune features is distinctive.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy has progressive gait unsteadiness, dysarthria, and oculocutaneous telangiectasia, with recurrent sinopulmonary infections. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Immediate initiation of daily prophylactic medication
Routine neuroimaging before any other management
Strict elimination diet without evidence of a specific trigger
Lifestyle modification addressing identified triggers before considering prophylactic medication
questions.question: A 7-year-old boy has recurrent headaches associated with a strong family history of migraine, triggered specifically by skipping meals and poor sleep. What is the most appropriate first-line management approach?
questions.explanation: For paediatric migraine, addressing identifiable lifestyle triggers such as irregular meals, poor sleep hygiene, and dehydration is recommended as first-line management before considering daily prophylactic medication, which is generally reserved for frequent or disabling attacks unresponsive to these measures. Neuroimaging is not routinely required when the history and examination are typical of migraine without red-flag features. A stepwise approach avoids unnecessary medication exposure in children.

options: Mitral regurgitation causing increased diastolic flow across the mitral valve
Mitral stenosis from commissural fusion during acute inflammation
Pericardial rub from fibrinous pericarditis mimicking a true diastolic murmur
Pulmonary regurgitation (Graham-Steell murmur) from severe pulmonary hypertension
Tricuspid stenosis causing diastolic rumble at the LLSE
questions.explanation: The Carey-Coombs murmur is an apical mid-diastolic murmur heard in acute rheumatic carditis, caused by the increased mitral valve diastolic flow resulting from significant mitral regurgitation flooding the left atrium and increasing the flow back across the mitral valve in diastole. It is a functional diastolic flow murmur — not organic mitral stenosis — and typically resolves when the acute carditis subsides. It is an important physical sign of active rheumatic carditis requiring anti-inflammatory treatment.
questions.question: The apical diastolic murmur (Carey-Coombs murmur) heard in acute rheumatic carditis is caused by which mechanism?
A neonate's birthweight triples by approximately:
questions.explanation: Birthweight doubles by 4–6 months and triples by 12 months in a normally growing infant. This rapid growth rate reflects the high caloric and protein demands of infancy and is a key parameter in assessing nutritional adequacy.

questions.question: Circumduction of the lower limb during walking is a characteristic gait pattern of which CP subtype?
questions.explanation: Circumduction—a semicircular swinging of the lower limb during gait caused by spasticity of the knee extensors—is the characteristic gait of spastic hemiplegia. The ipsilateral upper limb is held in elbow flexion and wrist pronation. This distinctive gait pattern results from the combination of spasticity and weakness on one side of the body and is used in clinical grading of severity.

options: Oesophageal atresia with or without tracheoesophageal fistula
questions.explanation: Oesophageal atresia presents with excessive frothy secretions, choking and cyanosis with feeding attempts, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach, with the tube visibly coiling in the blind-ending upper oesophageal pouch on X-ray. Pyloric stenosis instead presents later, typically around 3 to 6 weeks, with projectile vomiting rather than immediate feeding difficulty from birth. Prompt recognition prevents aspiration and allows timely surgical correction, often combined with a fistula repair.
questions.question: A newborn develops choking, cyanosis, and excessive frothy secretions during the first feed, with a nasogastric tube unable to be passed into the stomach on X-ray, coiling in the upper oesophagus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the commonest intracranial tumour in children, arising in the infratentorial compartment (cerebellum—specifically the vermis). It is a malignant tumour with poor prognosis that typically causes hydrocephalus by obstructing CSF flow. On CT it appears hypodense (sometimes hyperdense in the vermis) with brilliant enhancement post-contrast. Calcification is uncommon. It can spread via CSF seeding.
questions.question: The COMMONEST intracranial tumour in children overall (including infratentorial) is:

options: Any detectable antibody at any titre
Positive ELISA alone without confirmatory testing
Positive p24 antigen with negative ELISA
questions.explanation: In children above 18 months of age, a positive HIV antibody test (ELISA) followed by a positive confirmatory test (Western blot or immunofluorescence assay) definitively indicates HIV infection, because maternal antibodies have cleared by this age. Below 18 months, maternal antibodies make antibody testing unreliable.
questions.question: What defines a positive HIV antibody test for children ABOVE 18 months of age?

questions.explanation: The haemodynamic group 'diminished systemic output due to myocardial dysfunction' encompasses conditions that directly impair myocardial contractility: congenital cardiac muscle abnormalities (structural defects of the myocardium), infections (viral myocarditis, septic cardiomyopathy), cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, metabolic), iatrogenic injury (anthracyclines), and ischaemic heart disease (anomalous coronary artery, Kawasaki coronary aneurysms). Management targets the specific myocardial pathology alongside standard heart failure therapy.
questions.question: The haemodynamic consequence of myocardial dysfunction in heart failure — 'diminished systemic output due to myocardial dysfunction' — includes which group of conditions?
options: ASD, VSD, and PDA causing volume overload of the ventricle
Aortic stenosis and coarctation causing pressure overload obstruction states overall
Congenital cardiac muscle abnormalities, infections, cardiomyopathy, and ischaemia
Arrhythmias causing rate-mediated reduction in cardiac output
Pericardial effusion causing tamponade and reduced diastolic filling further

questions.explanation: In a systematic step-by-step ECG interpretation, individual components such as rate, rhythm, axis, and waveform morphology are assessed first, with final clinical correlation and comparison to prior tracings performed last to integrate all findings into an overall diagnostic impression. This ensures no individual component is overlooked before drawing conclusions. It is a standard, structured approach recommended for accurate paediatric ECG interpretation.
options: Overall clinical correlation and comparison with previous tracings
questions.question: A child undergoing systematic ECG interpretation has already assessed rate, rhythm, axis, and each waveform in sequence. Which component is conventionally assessed last in this systematic approach?

questions.explanation: Universal Precautions, as defined by the CDC, are a set of precautions designed to prevent transmission of HIV, Hepatitis B virus (HBV), and other blood-borne pathogens when providing first aid or healthcare. They assume all blood and body fluids are potentially infectious, regardless of patient HIV status.
options: WHO; designed to prevent only airborne pathogens
ECDC; designed for hospital-acquired infections only
CDC; prevents HIV, HBV, blood-borne pathogens
UNICEF; designed for mother-to-child transmission prevention
Infectious Diseases Society; for multidrug-resistant organisms
questions.question: Universal precautions are defined by which organization and are designed to prevent transmission of which pathogens?

options: The Glasgow coma scale for consciousness
The APGAR score assessed at birth
The Bell staging system for bowel disease
questions.question: A preterm infant is assessed using a scoring tool that evaluates physical and neuromuscular maturity signs to estimate gestational age when the actual dates are uncertain. Which tool is being used?
questions.explanation: The Ballard score, closely related to the Dubowitz method, evaluates physical and neuromuscular maturity signs to estimate gestational age, which is particularly useful when maternal dates are uncertain or unavailable. The APGAR score assesses immediate postnatal condition, not gestational age. Bell staging assesses necrotising enterocolitis severity, and the Glasgow coma scale assesses consciousness, both unrelated to gestational age estimation.

A neonate in haemorrhagic shock (BP <25 mmHg, PCV <30%, pH <7.1) requires urgent transfusion of 15–20 ml/kg whole blood over 5–10 minutes to restore circulating volume. Packed cells are used when anaemia is less acute and haemodynamic stability is preserved.
questions.question: A neonate in hypovolaemic shock from blood loss should receive which initial transfusion?
What is the hallmark histological finding at the site of Koplik spots?
questions.explanation: Koplik spots consist of serous exudate and proliferation of endothelial cells. The general measles histological finding at skin and mucosal lesions is serous exudate and proliferation of mononuclear cells with few polymorphonuclear cells around capillaries, with hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue particularly in the appendix.
options: Dense plasma cell infiltration with amyloid

questions.question: The sweat test in the evaluation of bronchiectasis is used to diagnose:
questions.explanation: The sweat test (measuring sodium and chloride content of sweat) is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis, where sweat electrolytes are elevated throughout the patient's life due to defective CFTR chloride channel function. Cystic fibrosis is one of the congenital and genetic causes of bronchiectasis. A sweat chloride above 60 mmol/L on two occasions is diagnostic.

questions.question: Polycythaemia in a child with cyanotic congenital heart disease is a compensatory response to which stimulus?
questions.explanation: Polycythaemia in cyanotic congenital heart disease is a physiological compensatory response to chronic arterial hypoxaemia. Hypoxia stimulates the kidneys to produce erythropoietin, which drives red cell production in the bone marrow, increasing the haematocrit and oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. While initially compensatory, extreme polycythaemia (PCV > 60%) leads to hyperviscosity syndrome with thrombotic and haemorrhagic complications.
options: Iron deficiency stimulating erythropoiesis through direct marrow effect
Chronic carbon dioxide retention stimulating respiratory drive
Elevated right ventricular pressure increasing right heart output
Chronic arterial hypoxaemia stimulating renal erythropoietin secretion
Aldosterone excess from cardiac failure retaining erythrocytes

questions.explanation: Overnight polysomnography is the gold-standard investigation for confirming and quantifying obstructive sleep apnoea in children, measuring respiratory events, oxygen desaturation, and sleep architecture during sleep. Daytime tests such as spirometry or peak flow do not capture the nocturnal respiratory events characteristic of this condition. Confirming the diagnosis guides decisions about adenotonsillectomy, the most common effective treatment in children with tonsillar hypertrophy.
options: Arterial blood gas during the day
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy has loud snoring, witnessed apnoeic pauses during sleep, and daytime sleepiness, with tonsillar hypertrophy noted on examination. What is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm obstructive sleep apnoea?

questions.explanation: Chronic constitutional symptoms including night sweats and weight loss combined with a cavitating lung lesion should prompt urgent investigation for tuberculosis, including appropriate sample collection for microscopy, culture, and molecular testing, particularly relevant depending on local disease prevalence and exposure history. Assuming a purely viral or purely malignant cause without appropriate infectious disease workup risks delayed diagnosis and ongoing transmission risk. Prompt recognition and isolation precautions are important both for the child's treatment and public health control.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy has a several-week history of low-grade fever, cough, and drenching night sweats, with significant weight loss, and a chest X-ray showing a cavitating upper lobe lesion. Given his age and the pattern described, what is the most important next step?
options: Reassure that this is a typical viral illness requiring no further action
Investigate urgently for tuberculosis, including sputum or gastric aspirate for microscopy and culture
Start empirical treatment for asthma without further investigation
Assume malignancy is most likely and proceed directly to biopsy without infectious workup

questions.explanation: Tetracycline has immunomodulatory properties beyond its antibacterial activity. It inhibits matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), reduces host-mediated collagen breakdown, and modulates inflammatory cytokines. This makes it effective in periodontal inflammation (used as an adjunct to scaling and root planing). Dapsone similarly has immunomodulatory activity in autoimmune diseases.
questions.question: Which antibiotic has immunomodulatory activity specifically effective in periodontal inflammation?
options: Metronidazole for its anti-anaerobic properties only

questions.question: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes diastolic dysfunction and may also cause dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction. These are categorised under which haemodynamic pathophysiological group?
options: Increased preload from volume overload progressively causing ventricular dilation
Myocardial dysfunction from infections or ischaemic injury
Primary diastolic dysfunction and afterload obstruction from hypertrophy
Pericardial constraint limiting ventricular filling from outside
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) causes primary diastolic dysfunction from abnormal ventricular relaxation and compliance due to myocardial hypertrophy, and in the obstructive subtype (HOCM), dynamic systolic outflow obstruction from the hypertrophied septum and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Both mechanisms reduce cardiac output. HCM is also the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes and requires specific management including avoidance of strenuous exercise.

questions.question: In the management of infective endocarditis caused by viridans streptococcal infection, the preferred antibiotic regimen is based on which principle?
options: Short course oral amoxicillin for 5 days to eradicate biofilm
Combination oral therapy with amoxicillin and metronidazole for 2 full weeks
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone as definitive treatment for sensitive organisms only given
Prolonged intravenous bactericidal therapy (4–6 weeks) with penicillin ± gentamicin
Topical antiseptics applied directly to affected valves during surgery
questions.explanation: Infective endocarditis requires prolonged intravenous bactericidal therapy (4–6 weeks) because vegetations are avascular fibrin matrices that prevent antibiotic penetration and phagocyte access. High-concentration bactericidal antibiotics are needed to sterilise the vegetation. Penicillin G (or ampicillin) combined with gentamicin is standard for sensitive viridans streptococcal IE. Bacteriostatic agents alone are insufficient. Blood culture clearance, echocardiographic response, and inflammatory marker trends guide treatment adequacy.

Nebulised 3% hypertonic saline is used in some centres for bronchiolitis based on the hypothesis that it draws fluid from the oedematous airway mucosa via osmosis, reducing mucosal oedema, and also hydrates and thins mucus secretions, facilitating mucociliary clearance. Systematic reviews show modest benefit in reducing length of hospital stay. It is generally given with a bronchodilator to prevent bronchoconstriction.
questions.question: Nebulised 3% hypertonic saline in bronchiolitis is thought to work by:
options: Drawing water into airway, reducing oedema
Killing RSV directly within the airways
Stimulating surfactant release from type II cells
Reducing body temperature in febrile infants

questions.question: A child is found to have a congenital anomaly detected only in the lower urinary tract. The rest of the examination is normal. This is MOST accurately described as:
questions.explanation: A single isolated anomaly, particularly when minor (not requiring medical management), is best described as an isolated minor birth defect. The distinction between isolated defects, syndromes (multiple features from common aetiology), sequences (cascading defects), and associations (non-random co-occurrence) is fundamental to dysmorphological assessment and guides the extent of investigation.

questions.question: Poiseuille's law applied to airway physiology states that resistance is inversely proportional to:
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law states that resistance to flow is inversely proportional to the radius raised to the fourth power (R ??1/r??. This means that halving the airway radius increases resistance 16-fold, explaining why even minor degrees of subglottic oedema in a child cause dramatic increases in airway resistance and respiratory distress. This law underlies the clinical significance of small amounts of mucosal swelling in paediatric airways.

questions.question: A newborn is placed skin-to-skin with the mother immediately after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery in a facility with limited resources. What is the primary purpose of this practice for thermal management?
questions.explanation: Skin-to-skin contact is a simple, low-resource method of preventing neonatal heat loss by using maternal body warmth, which is particularly valuable immediately after delivery when infants are vulnerable to rapid temperature drop. It does not replace routine clinical assessment or specific interventions such as vitamin K administration. Its primary purpose here is thermal, not nutritional or antiseptic.
options: Eliminating the need for any vitamin K administration
Replacing the need for any subsequent clinical assessment
Sterilising the infant's skin surface after delivery
Preventing heat loss through direct maternal warmth and contact
Providing the infant's entire nutritional requirement immediately

questions.question: In neonatal meningitis, which CSF finding is MOST characteristic of bacterial (pyogenic) aetiology?
questions.explanation: Pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis CSF shows turbid/cloudy fluid, predominantly neutrophilic pleocytosis, very low glucose (<40 mg/dl or <50% of blood glucose), and elevated protein. This pattern distinguishes it from viral (clear, lymphocytic, normal glucose) and tuberculous (clear/turbid, lymphocytic, low glucose) meningitis.
options: Turbid fluid, neutrophilia, very low glucose
Xanthochromic fluid, red cells, normal protein
Clear fluid, mixed pleocytosis, normal glucose

questions.question: Proximal tubular sodium reabsorption in heart failure is enhanced by which specific mechanism involving peritubular protein concentration?
questions.explanation: In heart failure, reduced cardiac output decreases renal blood flow and increases filtration fraction (relatively more plasma filtered than blood flow reduced). This increases peritubular protein (oncotic) concentration, which drives enhanced proximal tubular sodium and fluid reabsorption by Starling forces. This is a key mechanism of early Na+ retention in heart failure preceding aldosterone-mediated distal tubular effects. It contributes significantly to the oedema and hypervolaemia of congestive heart failure.
options: Decreased peritubular protein concentration reduces oncotic tubular reabsorption
Aldosterone acts on the proximal tubule as its primary reabsorption site
Reduced GFR increases tubular transit time facilitating passive Na+ reabsorption further
Angiotensin II directly acts on the proximal tubule to stimulate Na+ secretion
Increased peritubular protein concentration enhances proximal tubular Na+ reabsorption

questions.question: A neonate with TGA undergoes balloon atrial septostomy shortly after birth. What is the physiological goal of this procedure?
questions.explanation: In TGA, the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel, so survival depends on mixing between the two circuits. Balloon atrial septostomy enlarges the atrial communication, improving intercirculatory mixing and systemic oxygenation as a bridge to definitive surgery. It does not act on the ductus, outflow tract or septum directly.
options: Improving mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood at the atrial level

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has progressive gait difficulty, frequent falls, and is noted on examination to have brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses, and increased tone in both legs but normal arm function and normal cognition. Which category of diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Hereditary spastic paraplegia presents with progressive lower limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses reflecting corticospinal tract dysfunction, typically sparing the arms and cognition in the pure form. Duchenne dystrophy instead causes a primary myopathic pattern with reduced, not increased, reflexes as disease progresses. Recognising the upper motor neuron pattern with leg predominance helps direct genetic testing toward this diagnosis.

questions.question: An adolescent presents with tremor, dysarthria, behavioural change, and a golden-brown ring around the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism causing hepatic and neurological manifestations including tremor, dysarthria, and behavioural change, with the Kayser-Fleischer ring representing copper deposition in the cornea. Sydenham chorea does not cause corneal ring findings or hepatic involvement. Early diagnosis is critical since copper-chelation therapy can prevent irreversible neurological damage.

questions.question: A national immunization schedule specifies that MCV2 (second dose of measles vaccine) is given at an older age than MCV1. What is the main purpose of scheduling a second dose later in childhood?
questions.explanation: The second measles vaccine dose provides an additional opportunity for children who did not seroconvert after the first dose to develop protective immunity, thereby increasing overall population and individual protection. It does not replace the importance of the first dose, and it is not intended to treat an existing infection. It increases, rather than reduces, the level of protection achieved.
options: To replace the need for the first dose entirely
To reduce protection compared with giving a single dose
To treat any measles infection acquired between the two doses
Giving non-responders to the first dose a further chance to seroconvert
To provide passive immunity transferred from another person

questions.question: What does the interagency coordination committee (ICC) for immunization in Nigeria do?
questions.explanation: The ICC (Interagency Coordination Committee) for Immunization, constituted in July 2004, serves as a forum for regular information sharing and networking among major immunization stakeholders (NPHCDA, development partners, UNICEF, WHO, USAID) to ensure synergy and complementarity. The Honourable Minister of Health chairs the ICC, with NPHCDA as its secretariat.
options: Determines the price of vaccines in Nigeria
Forum for stakeholder information-sharing and synergy
Provides direct funding to primary health centres
Audits immunization records at state level
Further evaluation, including protracted bacterial bronchitis
Assume the cough is habitual and provide reassurance only
Repeat the same antibiotic course again without reassessment
questions.question: A 5-year-old has a chronic wet cough for 6 weeks that has not responded to a course of antibiotics, with normal chest X-ray. What is the most appropriate next step in the diagnostic pathway?
questions.explanation: A persistent wet cough not responding to an initial antibiotic course should prompt further specific evaluation, including consideration of protracted bacterial bronchitis (which may need a longer antibiotic course) and specialist referral if the cough remains unexplained or is not resolving as expected. Repeating the same treatment without reassessment or assuming a purely habitual cause risks missing an underlying diagnosis. A wet, productive cough in particular warrants more focused evaluation than a dry cough.

The seven airway As for systematic assessment of stridor are: Age, Acuity of onset, Appearance, Alteration in mental status, Acoustic quality of sound, Air-shadow interface (X-rays), and Airway examination. Antibiotic response is not part of this systematic framework. The seven As provide a structured clinical assessment that helps identify the likely site and cause of upper airway obstruction.
questions.question: The 'seven airway As' used for systematic assessment of stridor include all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Neovascularisation from chronic retinal hypoxia damage
Papilloedema from cerebral venous sinus thrombosis process occurring
Cotton-wool spots from retinal artery occlusion
Oval haemorrhages with pale centres from microemboli and vasculitis
questions.explanation: Roth spots are oval retinal haemorrhages with pale (white or pale) centres, most commonly seen on fundoscopy in subacute bacterial endocarditis. They result from microemboli causing retinal vasculitis with central fibrin/platelet aggregation. While pathognomonic of SBE historically, they may also occur in leukaemia, severe anaemia, and diabetic retinopathy. Their presence in a febrile child with a cardiac murmur should prompt urgent investigation for infective endocarditis.
questions.question: Roth spots, seen on fundoscopy in a child with infective endocarditis, consist of which pathological finding in the retina?
Aspergillus fumigatus is relevant to asthma management because it can cause:
options: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in atopic asthmatics
Lobar pneumonia in all asthmatic children
questions.explanation: Aspergillus fumigatus is an outdoor mould that can cause allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) in atopic asthmatic patients, characterised by eosinophilia, elevated IgE, central bronchiectasis, and poorly controlled asthma. It is both an allergen triggering asthma exacerbations and a cause of ABPA. Treatment includes oral corticosteroids and itraconazole.

questions.question: Neonatal tetanus typically presents between:
questions.explanation: Neonatal tetanus (caused by Clostridium tetani infecting the umbilical stump) presents classically between days 3–14 of life with trismus (lockjaw), inability to suck, opisthotonus, and generalised muscle spasms. Prevention is through maternal tetanus immunisation and clean cord care.

Haemophilia A is a factor VIII deficiency causing prolonged bleeding time and PTT but does not cause thrombocytopenia. Neonatal thrombocytopenia is caused by platelet destruction (sepsis, DIC, transient ITP, Kasabach-Merritt) or reduced production (congenital marrow failure).
questions.question: Causes of neonatal thrombocytopenia include all EXCEPT:

options: Close monitoring with serial abdominal examinations and radiographs
Bowel rest with cessation of enteral feeds
Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy directed at likely pathogens
Continuing full enteral feeds unchanged throughout the acute illness
questions.question: A preterm neonate with NEC is managed medically in the initial stages before any decision about surgery is made. Which of the following would NOT typically be part of this initial medical management?
questions.explanation: Continuing full enteral feeds unchanged during acute NEC is inappropriate and would worsen bowel injury, since standard initial medical management specifically requires bowel rest with cessation of feeds, alongside nasogastric decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and close serial monitoring. All the other listed measures are appropriate, evidence-based components of initial medical management. Recognising which intervention does not belong is important to avoid a harmful management error.

questions.question: Finger clubbing in a child with chronic cough and foul-smelling sputum is MOST likely due to:
questions.explanation: Finger clubbing (Hippocratic clubbing) in a child with chronic cough, purulent sputum, and haemoptysis is most likely a manifestation of chronic hypoxia from suppurative lung disease, particularly bronchiectasis. Chronic hypoxia stimulates periosteal vascular proliferation and soft tissue changes at the fingertips. It is a clinical sign of significant chronic pulmonary pathology and warrants thorough investigation.

A large, unrepaired ventricular septal defect is the most common underlying defect leading to Eisenmenger syndrome, because large VSDs expose the pulmonary vasculature to systemic pressure and flow from early infancy, causing irreversible pulmonary vascular disease if not repaired. ASD can also cause Eisenmenger syndrome but does so later in life. Early surgical closure of large VSDs prevents this devastating complication.
options: Atrial septal defect in an adult
Patent ductus arteriosus with ductal closure
Ventricular septal defect in an unrepaired child
Pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left atrial shunting
Coarctation of the aorta with left ventricular hypertrophy
questions.question: The 'differential diagnosis of cyanotic congenital heart disease' includes Eisenmenger syndrome. Which underlying congenital defect most commonly leads to Eisenmenger syndrome?

options: Normal variation with no cause for concern
Pneumothorax as a complication of severe asthma
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is a recognised, though uncommon, complication of severe asthma exacerbations, resulting from high intrathoracic pressures and alveolar rupture, and should be suspected when there is sudden asymmetry in breath sounds or a disproportionate change in clinical status. This is distinct from simple worsening bronchospasm, which would typically cause bilateral rather than unilateral findings. Prompt recognition allows appropriate imaging and management alongside ongoing asthma treatment.
questions.question: A 7-year-old with known asthma presents with sudden worsening of breathlessness and unilateral reduced breath sounds during a severe exacerbation. What complication should be considered?

questions.explanation: Minimising additional lung injury in bronchopulmonary dysplasia involves using the lowest effective oxygen concentration to avoid oxygen toxicity, alongside gentle ventilation strategies that avoid excessive tidal volumes (volutrauma) and pressure (barotrauma). Targeting very high saturation levels can worsen oxidative injury rather than help. Adequate nutrition, rather than withholding it, supports lung growth and repair.
questions.question: A preterm infant with bronchopulmonary dysplasia is being managed on the neonatal unit. Which strategy is most important in minimising further lung injury during ongoing respiratory support?
options: Using the lowest effective oxygen concentration and gentle ventilation strategies
Maximising oxygen saturation targets above 98% at all times
Using high tidal volume ventilation to fully expand the lungs
Avoiding all nutritional support to reduce metabolic demand
Prolonged paralysis to prevent spontaneous breathing

questions.explanation: Scissoring gait—where the thighs adduct and cross during walking due to spasticity of the hip adductors—is the classic gait pattern of spastic diplegia. It is typically seen in preterm infants who survive with periventricular leukomalacia. The upper limbs are minimally involved, distinguishing diplegia from quadriplegia. Gait analysis is an important tool in rehabilitation planning for these children.
questions.question: A scissoring gait in a child with CP most characteristically indicates which subtype?

options: Reassurance and observation without further intervention
Prompt airway assessment with readiness for emergency intubation
Immediate administration of oral antibiotics alone
Nebulised bronchodilator therapy as the sole treatment
Delaying any intervention until antitoxin takes full effect
questions.explanation: Progressive stridor with retraction in laryngeal diphtheria signals impending airway obstruction from the pseudomembrane, so securing the airway takes priority over other measures. Bronchodilators do not address a mechanical membrane obstruction. Antitoxin works to neutralise circulating toxin but does not immediately relieve mechanical obstruction.
questions.question: A 5-year-old with laryngeal diphtheria develops increasing stridor, suprasternal retraction, and restlessness. What is the most urgent management priority?

options: A single gene causing multiple phenotypic effects
A syndrome with a single Mendelian cause
A chromosomal translocation affecting two chromosomes
A sequence of anomalies from a single primary defect
questions.question: An 'association' in clinical genetics refers to:
questions.explanation: An association in genetics refers to a non-random co-occurrence of two or more anomalies that happen together more (or less) often than expected by chance, without the implied single aetiology of a syndrome. The VACTERL association is the classic example. Unlike syndromes, associations do not have an identified underlying unifying cause and represent statistical co-occurrence patterns.

questions.question: In a child with a large left-to-right shunt from any cause, the chest X-ray will most characteristically demonstrate which pattern?
questions.explanation: A large left-to-right shunt results in cardiomegaly from volume overload of the affected cardiac chambers and increased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary plethora) from the excessive pulmonary blood flow. These two radiological features together are characteristic of significant left-to-right shunts. In contrast, right-to-left shunts produce oligaemia and a characteristic boot-shaped or egg-shaped cardiac silhouette.
options: Oligaemic lung fields with a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette
Cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings
Normal-sized heart with prominent aortic knuckle
Normal cardiac silhouette with bilateral pleural effusions
Right-sided cardiomegaly with leftward tracheal shift
Bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy
Unilateral upper motor neuron facial weakness sparing the forehead
Brainstem lesion causing facial nerve palsy
questions.question: Bell's palsy is characterised as a:
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic unilateral lower motor neuron (LMN) palsy of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). It affects all branches of the nerve, including those to the forehead (distinguishing it from UMN lesions, which spare the forehead due to bilateral cortical representation). Features include inability to close the eye, drooping of the mouth, loss of nasolabial fold, and sometimes impaired taste. Most cases resolve spontaneously.

questions.question: The incubation period of poliovirus infection is:
questions.explanation: The incubation period of poliovirus infection is approximately 10–14 days, with a range of 5–30 days. This relatively long incubation period has implications for outbreak investigation, contact tracing, and post-exposure prophylaxis with OPV. Paralysis typically develops 1–10 days after the prodromal symptoms, progresses over 3–5 days, and then plateaus. Understanding the incubation period aids outbreak timeline reconstruction.

Because HRP2 antigen can persist for weeks after successful treatment, a positive RDT during this period does not necessarily indicate active infection or treatment failure. Clinical assessment and, where possible, microscopy should guide retreatment decisions. Relying on RDT alone risks unnecessary re-treatment.
questions.question: A community health worker uses an RDT to diagnose malaria in a febrile 3-year-old but the test remains faintly positive for weeks after full treatment despite clinical recovery. What is the practical implication for management?
options: RDT alone should not be used to diagnose recurrent illness in this window
The persistent positivity indicates development of drug resistance
The RDT result confirms ongoing active parasitaemia requiring therapy
A repeat RDT after one week will reliably become fully negative
The child must always be re-treated whenever the RDT is positive

questions.explanation: Breastmilk jaundice typically begins after the first week and peaks at around 2 weeks of age, gradually declining over subsequent weeks, distinguishing its timeline from early pathological jaundice presenting in the first 24 hours. It does not appear only in the first hour of life or persist unrecognised until as late as 6 months. This distinct, benign pattern differs from other more urgent causes of neonatal jaundice.
questions.question: A neonate develops jaundice attributed to breastmilk jaundice, a benign and self-limiting condition distinct from breastfeeding failure jaundice. At what typical timing does breastmilk jaundice usually peak?
options: Not until after 6 months of age
Only during the first hour after birth
Exclusively during intrauterine life before birth
Within the first 24 hours of life
Around 2 weeks of age, following an earlier onset

questions.question: A 4-month-old with bronchiolitis has mild respiratory distress, is feeding adequately, and has oxygen saturation of 95% on air. What is the most appropriate management approach?
questions.explanation: Most infants with bronchiolitis have a self-limiting illness and can be managed supportively at home with safety-netting advice, since bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics have not been shown to improve outcomes in typical viral bronchiolitis. Routine chest physiotherapy is also not recommended and can be distressing without proven benefit. Adequate feeding and oxygenation, as in this case, support a plan for outpatient management with clear reattendance advice.
options: Supportive care with safety-netting for outpatient management
Chest physiotherapy as a primary treatment

questions.question: Tuberculous lymphadenitis of superficial nodes typically occurs within which timeframe after primary TB infection?
questions.explanation: Tuberculous lymphadenitis of superficial lymph nodes (most commonly cervical) occurs 3–9 months after primary TB infection. Initially, nodes are discrete, mobile, firm, and non-tender. Later, they become matted with periadenitis and may form discharging sinuses. Systemic constitutional symptoms may or may not be present.
options: Immediately at time of primary infection
Only in patients with HIV co-infection

questions.explanation: Congenital syphilis characteristically presents with a combination of findings including hepatosplenomegaly, a characteristic skin rash, and skeletal abnormalities such as periostitis or osteochondritis, reflecting multisystem involvement by Treponema pallidum. The isolated single findings listed as alternatives are each more typical of other specific congenital infections, such as rubella (cataracts, deafness) or toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis), rather than of congenital syphilis's characteristic multisystem pattern.
options: Isolated chorioretinitis with no other organ involvement
Isolated limb hypoplasia with no other organ involvement
Isolated sensorineural deafness with no other organ involvement
Isolated cataracts with no other organ involvement
Hepatosplenomegaly, skin rash, and skeletal abnormalities such as periostitis
questions.question: A neonate with congenital syphilis is being evaluated for characteristic clinical findings. Which combination of features would be most consistent with this diagnosis?
An echocardiogram of an infant with a VSD shows bidirectional shunting across the defect. What does this finding suggest about pulmonary vascular resistance?
questions.explanation: Bidirectional shunting occurs when pulmonary and systemic pressures become nearly equal, allowing flow to move in either direction depending on the phase of the cardiac cycle. This reflects early pulmonary vascular disease progressing toward Eisenmenger physiology. It is an important echocardiographic clue that the shunt lesion is becoming less safely operable.
options: The defect is too small to generate any shunt
Pulmonary vascular resistance is approaching systemic levels
Pulmonary vascular resistance is normal for age
Systemic vascular resistance has fallen below pulmonary resistance
Pulmonary vascular resistance is markedly reduced
Pulmonary atresia with associated ventricular septal defect
questions.explanation: Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) produces the characteristic 'egg-on-side' appearance on chest X-ray due to the narrow mediastinum created by the anteroposterior relationship of the aorta and pulmonary artery, combined with an enlarged heart. The parallel great vessel orientation eliminates the normal shadow of the main pulmonary artery, creating the narrow pedicle. Increased pulmonary vascular markings are also present due to high pulmonary blood flow.
questions.question: Which cardiac defect is associated with the 'egg-on-side' appearance on chest X-ray?
Maternal prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM >24 hours) increases neonatal sepsis risk PRIMARILY because:
options: Allows ascending colonisation of amniotic cavity
It directly causes umbilical cord compression
questions.explanation: PROM lasting more than 24 hours removes the physical barrier of intact membranes, allowing ascending migration of vaginal flora (GBS, E. coli, Klebsiella) into the amniotic cavity. This causes chorioamnionitis and perinatal acquisition of organisms leading to EONS.

questions.question: In the standard 12-lead ECG analysis, which component is assessed LAST in the systematic 9-step paediatric ECG analysis described?
questions.explanation: The systematic paediatric ECG analysis follows the sequence: Rhythm ? Rate ? P waves ? PR interval ? QRS axis ? QRS morphology ? T wave ? ST segment ? QT interval. The QT interval is assessed last (step 9), requiring correction for heart rate using Bazett's formula. This systematic 9-step approach ensures that no component is missed and reduces diagnostic errors in paediatric ECG interpretation.

questions.question: The heart failure associated with acute rheumatic carditis is treated with which combination of specific interventions?
options: Salicylates alone at 50 mg/kg/day without any cardiac medications
Cardiac catheterisation and valvuloplasty during the acute carditis phase of illness
IM procaine penicillin alone without anti-inflammatory agents
Bed rest only without pharmacological management
Prednisolone for carditis plus standard heart failure therapy (diuretics, digoxin)
questions.explanation: Heart failure from acute rheumatic carditis is managed with prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) to suppress the active cardiac inflammation alongside standard heart failure therapy including diuretics (furosemide) to reduce pulmonary congestion and digoxin for inotropic support if needed. IM procaine penicillin eradicates the precipitating streptococcal infection. Bed rest limits cardiac workload during the acute phase. These combined measures constitute comprehensive management of heart failure in acute rheumatic carditis.

questions.question: Which opportunistic infection characteristically causes PCP (Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia) in paediatric HIV?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis carinii) causes PCP, a severe life-threatening pneumonia in immunocompromised children with HIV. It is a WHO Stage 4 condition. PCP typically presents with progressive dyspnoea, hypoxia, and a CXR showing bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is recommended for all HIV-exposed infants.

options: Pulmonary vascular resistance exceeds systemic resistance
Venous return from the lungs exceeds systemic venous return
Aortic valve incompetence significantly augmenting left ventricular stroke output
Right atrial pressure being lower than pulmonary artery pressure
Left ventricular pressure normally exceeds right ventricular pressure
questions.question: A ventricular septal defect (VSD) produces a left-to-right shunt because of which fundamental haemodynamic principle?
questions.explanation: A VSD produces a left-to-right shunt because systemic vascular resistance and left ventricular pressure normally exceed pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular pressure. Blood therefore flows from the high-pressure left ventricle through the defect to the lower-pressure right ventricle and pulmonary circulation. The magnitude of the shunt depends on defect size and the ratio of pulmonary to systemic vascular resistance.

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder requires symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity present in multiple settings before age 12, causing functional impairment. Oppositional defiant disorder centres on defiant and hostile behaviour rather than inattention. The cross-setting nature of the symptoms is a key diagnostic requirement distinguishing ADHD from situational behavioural problems.
questions.question: A 7-year-old boy has difficulty sustaining attention, is easily distracted, and is impulsive across school and home settings, present since before age 12. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Kernicterus causing CP is the result of bilirubin toxicity to which specific structure?
questions.explanation: Bilirubin preferentially accumulates in the basal ganglia (particularly the globus pallidus) and causes kernicterus, manifesting as dyskinetic CP. The resulting movement disorder (athetosis, dystonia) reflects basal ganglia dysfunction. Early recognition and treatment of hyperbilirubinaemia (phototherapy, exchange transfusion) prevents kernicterus and the resultant CP.

questions.question: A 2-year-old presents at night with a barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor at rest, following a day of coryzal symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Croup classically presents with a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor, often worse at night, following a preceding viral coryzal illness, most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus. Epiglottitis instead has a more rapid, toxic-appearing presentation with drooling and minimal cough. The characteristic barking cough and preceding coryza are key features distinguishing croup from other causes of stridor.

questions.question: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate anticonvulsant for febrile seizure prophylaxis according to current guidelines?
questions.explanation: Phenobarbitone prophylaxis for febrile seizures is no longer recommended because its cognitive side effects outweigh the modest reduction in seizure recurrence. Current guidelines do not favour continuous AED prophylaxis for simple febrile seizures. Intermittent diazepam (rectal or oral) at fever onset may be used for high-risk children (young age, multiple prior episodes, parental anxiety). Parental reassurance and education remain the cornerstone of management.
options: Intermittent rectal diazepam at onset of fever
Oral diazepam 1 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses from onset of fever
No drug prophylaxis for most simple febrile seizures

questions.question: Varicella-zoster virus is NOT listed as a cause of childhood pneumonia, but measles virus is. The key difference is that measles pneumonia mainly affects:
questions.explanation: Measles-associated pneumonia predominantly affects unvaccinated children, making it a vaccine-preventable cause of respiratory mortality. In regions with low vaccine coverage, measles virus remains a significant cause of pneumonia-related child deaths. Universal measles vaccination is therefore one of the most cost-effective interventions to reduce childhood pneumonia and overall mortality.
options: Unvaccinated children especially where vaccination is not done
Only neonates in the first week of life

questions.explanation: Non-invasive respiratory support such as high-flow nasal cannula oxygen or continuous positive airway pressure is typically used as an escalation step for infants with bronchiolitis showing signs of impending respiratory failure, including recurrent apnoea, before resorting to invasive mechanical ventilation. Chest tube insertion is unrelated to bronchiolitis management. Early use of non-invasive support can prevent the need for intubation in many cases.
questions.question: A 6-month-old infant with severe bronchiolitis and recurrent apnoeic episodes is being assessed for respiratory support. Which respiratory support option is most appropriate as an early escalation before invasive ventilation?
options: Nebulised adrenaline as the definitive treatment
High-flow nasal cannula or continuous positive airway pressure

questions.explanation: Measles is communicable from 4 days before rash appearance to 5 days after rash onset. Virus is found in nasopharyngeal secretions, blood, and urine during the prodromal period and first few days of rash. The recommended isolation period is from 7th day of exposure until 5 days after the rash appears.
options: 7 days before rash to 7 days after rash onset
From day 1 of fever until complete rash resolution
4 days before to 5 days after rash onset
questions.question: What is the period of communicability for measles?

questions.explanation: Spinal polio is the most common form of paralytic poliomyelitis, involving the skeletal muscles innervated by spinal nerves. Clinical features include loss of neck control, inability to sit up, weakness of the limbs, paralysis of abdominal muscles, severe constipation, bladder paralysis, and urinary retention. Bulbar polio (cranial nerve involvement) and bulbospinal polio (combined) are less common but carry higher mortality.
questions.question: In paralytic poliomyelitis, which type is most common?

options: Need assessment; antibiotic choice; regimen; monitoring
Clinical assessment, dosing, monitoring, and stopping
questions.explanation: Rational antibiotic prescribing involves four phases: (i) Perception of need – is an antibiotic necessary? (ii) Choice of antibiotic – which is most appropriate? (iii) Choice of regimen – dose, route, frequency, and duration? (iv) Monitoring efficacy – is the treatment working? This framework ensures appropriate antibiotic use and prevents resistance.
questions.question: What is the FOUR-PHASE process of rational antibiotic prescribing?

options: Elevated glucose with few white cells
Elevated protein with low glucose and neutrophil pleocytosis
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis classically produces a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, raised protein from blood-brain barrier disruption, and low glucose due to bacterial and leukocyte consumption. Viral meningitis instead usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose. This CSF pattern helps distinguish bacterial from viral aetiology while awaiting culture results.
questions.question: In a 10-month-old with suspected bacterial meningitis, which finding on cerebrospinal fluid analysis would be most typical?

A high-risk premature infant with chronic lung disease is being considered for RSV prophylaxis during the winter season. What is the mechanism of action of palivizumab, the agent used for this purpose?
options: A monoclonal antibody providing passive immunity against RSV
A live attenuated vaccine stimulating active immunity
An antiviral agent that directly inhibits viral replication
An inhaled corticosteroid reducing airway inflammation
questions.explanation: Palivizumab is a monoclonal antibody administered by monthly injection during RSV season to provide passive immunity against respiratory syncytial virus, reducing the risk of severe bronchiolitis in high-risk infants such as those with chronic lung disease or significant prematurity. It is not a vaccine stimulating the infant's own immune response, and it does not treat established infection. Its high cost limits use to carefully selected high-risk populations.

options: A normal expected finding in asthma
Evolving type 2 respiratory failure and exhaustion, requiring urgent escalation of care
An artefact requiring repeat sampling only
questions.explanation: A rising PaCO2 with falling pH in a child with severe asthma indicates progression to type 2 respiratory failure due to fatigue and inadequate alveolar ventilation, an ominous sign requiring urgent escalation of care, potentially including intensive care involvement and consideration of ventilatory support. This is not a normal or reassuring finding and does not represent improvement. Early recognition of this deterioration is critical to prevent respiratory arrest.
questions.question: A 6-year-old with a severe asthma exacerbation becomes increasingly drowsy, and arterial blood gas now shows a rising PaCO2 with a falling pH. What does this combination most importantly indicate?

questions.explanation: Intellectual disability (formerly mental retardation) requires deficits in both intellectual functions (IQ typically below 70) and adaptive behaviour (conceptual, social, and practical skills), with onset during the developmental period (before age 18). This dual criterion prevents misclassification based on IQ alone and recognises that real-world functioning is as important as test scores.
questions.question: Mental retardation is now classified as intellectual disability. It is defined by deficits in intellectual functions AND:

questions.explanation: Simultaneous voltage criteria for hypertrophy in both right and left precordial leads suggest biventricular hypertrophy, which can occur in dilated cardiomyopathy where both ventricles are affected by the disease process. This differs from isolated chamber hypertrophy patterns seen in lesions affecting only one ventricle. Recognising biventricular involvement supports the diagnosis of a global myocardial process rather than an isolated pressure or volume overload lesion.
questions.question: An ECG in a child with dilated cardiomyopathy shows large-amplitude QRS complexes in both right and left precordial leads with deep Q waves and tall R waves. What does this pattern suggest?
A neonate with seizures is being evaluated for prognosis. Which factor listed would generally be associated with the WORST prognosis following neonatal seizures?
options: Severe, refractory hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy as the underlying cause
A completely normal neurological examination between seizure episodes
Seizures that resolve promptly with a single anticonvulsant dose
A normal neuroimaging study with no structural abnormality
A single brief seizure due to transient, easily corrected hypoglycaemia
questions.explanation: Severe, refractory hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is associated with a poor neurodevelopmental prognosis following neonatal seizures, reflecting the severity of the underlying brain injury rather than the seizures themselves being the primary determinant. In contrast, seizures from a transient, correctable cause such as brief hypoglycaemia, a normal interictal examination, prompt response to treatment, and normal imaging are generally associated with a more favourable outcome. The underlying cause and its severity, more than the seizure activity itself, largely determine long-term prognosis.

questions.question: Minimal enteral nutrition (trophic feeds) in very preterm infants is intended primarily to:
questions.explanation: Trophic or minimal enteral nutrition in infants below 32 weeks is given in small volumes not for caloric goals but to stimulate gut maturation, promote intestinal colonisation, enhance mucosal immunity, and reduce the risk of NEC and cholestatic jaundice.

Approximately 25% of children under 1 year will have respiratory infections, and 13% of children aged 1-2 years. Of those children with respiratory infections, approximately half will have a wheezing-associated respiratory disease (WARD). RSV can be cultured from one-third of these cases, underlining its role as the dominant bronchiolitis pathogen.
questions.question: Approximately what percentage of children under 1 year will have a respiratory infection, and of these, approximately half will have wheezing-associated respiratory disease?

questions.explanation: Congenital heart disease is a non-respiratory (cardiovascular) cause of respiratory distress in neonates. Cyanotic heart disease produces cyanosis and tachypnoea that do not improve with oxygen supplementation, distinguishing it from primary respiratory causes.
questions.question: Which is a NON-respiratory cause of respiratory distress in the newborn?

questions.explanation: Children typically experience 6 to 8 episodes of acute coryza per year, though some sources cite 6 to 12 episodes. The high frequency reflects the multiple serotypes of rhinovirus and other respiratory pathogens, combined with the immature immune systems of young children. This distinguishes it from conditions requiring further investigation.
questions.question: The average frequency of acute coryza episodes in a child per year is:

questions.explanation: Children under 5 years bear the greatest burden of severe malaria in endemic Africa, accounting for 90% of all malaria mortality. They lack naturally acquired immunity, have immature immune systems, and their fetal haemoglobin has been replaced by adult haemoglobin, making them maximally vulnerable between 6 months and 5 years.
questions.question: Which group is at GREATEST risk for severe and complicated malaria in endemic African settings?

questions.explanation: Choanal atresia results from failure of the nasal passages to canalise, causing cyclical cyanosis that worsens during feeding (when the infant must breathe through the nose) and improves with crying (mouth breathing), confirmed by inability to pass a catheter through the nares. Laryngomalacia instead causes positional stridor rather than this specific feeding-related cyanosis pattern. Bilateral choanal atresia is a neonatal emergency requiring urgent airway management.
questions.question: A newborn has episodes of cyanosis that worsen with feeding and improve with crying, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed through one or both nostrils. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Crying selectively increases coronary blood flow only
Crying has no physiological effect on shunt lesions
Crying causes immediate closure of the foramen ovale
Increased pulmonary vascular resistance and reduced pulmonary blood flow during crying-induced Valsalva-like effects
Crying always improves oxygenation by increasing respiratory rate
questions.explanation: Crying can transiently raise intrathoracic pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance, reducing pulmonary blood flow in lesions where flow depends on a pressure gradient across a shunt, thereby worsening desaturation. Calming the infant helps restore more favourable haemodynamics. This is why minimising distress is an important supportive measure in cyanotic neonates awaiting definitive treatment.
questions.question: A neonate with a cyanotic congenital heart lesion is noted to desaturate further with crying and improve somewhat with calming measures. What is the underlying reason for desaturation during crying in duct-dependent or shunt-dependent lesions?

questions.explanation: Atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunting is an acyanotic defect — blood flows from left to right, increasing pulmonary blood flow without causing systemic desaturation. It belongs to the left-to-right shunt group of acyanotic congenital heart disease. Cyanotic CHD includes Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, tricuspid atresia, Eisenmenger syndrome, univentricular hearts, and pulmonary atresia — all conditions with right-to-left shunting causing systemic arterial desaturation.
options: Transposition of the great arteries physiology variant
Atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunting
questions.question: The differential diagnosis of cyanotic congenital heart disease includes all the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Risk factors for febrile seizures include: developmental delay, day care attendance (increased viral exposure), family history (25% have positive family history suggesting genetic predisposition), viral infections (HHV-6, influenza), certain vaccines (DPT, flu, MMR), and iron/zinc deficiencies. Sex is not a major risk factor.
questions.question: Risk factors for febrile seizures include all the following EXCEPT:

options: Absent tricuspid valve with only an ASD and a markedly dominant right ventricle present overall
Imperforate pulmonary valve with intact ventricular septum
Absent right AV connection, ASD, dominant left ventricle, and rudimentary right ventricle
Common AV valve with superior bridging leaflet
Absent left AV connection with a right-dominant ventricle finding
questions.question: In Tricuspid Atresia, echocardiography most characteristically demonstrates which set of anatomical findings?
questions.explanation: In tricuspid atresia, echocardiography confirms the absent right atrioventricular connection, an obligatory ASD (for right atrial decompression), a dominant left ventricle as the main pumping chamber, and a rudimentary right ventricle. The ventriculo-arterial connection determines whether there is pulmonary stenosis/atresia or increased pulmonary blood flow. These findings form the diagnostic echocardiographic signature of tricuspid atresia.

options: Tetanus, transmitted readily between household members
Measles, among susceptible unimmunized close contacts
Tuberculosis, with guaranteed transmission on any exposure
Diphtheria, with universally complete secondary attack rates
Hepatitis B, spread easily through casual contact
questions.explanation: Measles is classically described as having an attack rate approaching 100% among susceptible, unimmunized close contacts because of its high infectivity and efficient respiratory transmission. Tetanus is not transmitted person to person at all. Diphtheria and tuberculosis, while transmissible, do not have secondary attack rates approaching this level in typical exposures.
questions.question: A country plans a mass immunization campaign against a disease with historically very high attack rates in unimmunized populations. Which vaccine-preventable disease is classically associated with an attack rate approaching 100% among susceptible contacts?

options: Risk of direct spread to the bloodstream via umbilical vessels
It exclusively affects the skin with no risk of deeper spread
It cannot occur in neonates delivered by caesarean section
It is only a cosmetic concern with no infective significance
It is always a benign, self-limiting finding requiring no concern
