Start oral antibiotics after blood culture
Perform CT brain before any treatment

questions.question: A preterm neonate weighing 1.6 kg is being planned for iron supplementation. At what timing is iron supplementation typically initiated in such an infant?
options: Delayed until the infant reaches one year of age
From around 2 months of age, once enteral feeds are established
Only after the infant reaches full term equivalent age
Never required for preterm infants of this weight
Immediately at birth before any feeding begins
questions.explanation: Preterm infants have reduced iron stores and rapid postnatal growth, so iron supplementation is generally started around 2 months of age, once feeding is established, to prevent iron deficiency anaemia. Starting immediately at birth is not standard practice, and delaying until full term equivalent age or one year would risk significant deficiency in this high-risk group. This is a recognised and necessary supplement, not one that can be omitted.

Laryngomalacia typically follows a benign course, with most infants experiencing spontaneous improvement in stridor by 12 to 18 months of age as laryngeal cartilage matures and stiffens, and only a minority with severe disease require surgical intervention such as supraglottoplasty. It does not always indicate an underlying syndrome, though severe or atypical cases warrant further evaluation. Reassurance with appropriate safety-netting is usually appropriate for typical, uncomplicated cases.
questions.question: A 2-year-old with recurrent stridor since birth, worse when supine, is diagnosed with laryngomalacia. Parents ask about the expected clinical course. What is the most accurate response?
options: The condition will definitely worsen and always requires surgery
Symptoms will persist unchanged throughout childhood
This condition typically resolves within the first week of life
Most cases improve spontaneously by 12 to 18 months of age as the airway matures
Laryngomalacia always indicates an underlying serious congenital syndrome

questions.question: A newborn has a skin-covered midline lumbar defect noted only on examination, with a tuft of hair overlying the area, but no palpable mass and normal neurological examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spina bifida occulta is a failure of vertebral arch fusion without herniation of neural tissue, often marked only by a cutaneous sign such as a hairy patch, dimple, or lipoma, with a normal neurological examination in most cases. Meningocele and myelomeningocele instead present with a visible or palpable sac. This distinction is important since occulta usually requires no urgent intervention but may need imaging to exclude tethered cord.

questions.question: The Ziehl-Neelsen stain demonstrates acid-fast bacilli. Why is M. tuberculosis classified as 'acid-fast'?
questions.explanation: M. tuberculosis is classified as acid-fast because once stained with carbol fuchsin (Ziehl-Neelsen stain), the organism retains the red dye even after treatment with acidified organic compounds (acid-alcohol decolourant). This property is due to the unique mycolic acid-rich cell wall. Bright red rods on blue background confirms acid-fast bacilli.
options: It grows optimally in acidic media at pH <5
It produces acid when metabolizing glucose
It requires acidic pH for spore germination
It is identified by acid phosphatase production
Retains carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol decolourisation

questions.question: Folic acid deficiency during the periconceptional period primarily predisposes to:
questions.explanation: Periconceptional folic acid deficiency is the most important preventable cause of neural tube defects (NTDs), including spina bifida, anencephaly, and encephalocele. Folic acid supplementation (400–800 µg/day) starting before conception and continuing through the first trimester reduces NTD risk by up to 70%. This is the basis for national fortification programmes in many countries.

Head circumference (OFC) in term neonates increases at approximately 0.5 cm/week, while preterm infants grow at 0.8–1 cm/week to achieve catch-up growth. Suboptimal head circumference growth (head-sparing fails) indicates severe malnutrition or brain injury affecting brain growth.
questions.question: Postnatal head circumference growth rate for term infants is approximately:

options: Presence of coarse trabeculation and tricuspid valve
Relative size of the ventricular chamber on echocardiography imaging
Site of origin of the pulmonary artery from that specific ventricle
Thickness of the ventricular free wall
questions.explanation: The right ventricle is morphologically identified by its coarse trabecular pattern and the presence of the tricuspid valve, which has three leaflets and chordae tendinae inserting directly into the ventricular wall. The left ventricle has fine trabeculation and is associated with the mitral (bicuspid) valve. These morphological markers are critical in sequential segmental analysis when the spatial positions of chambers are abnormal.
questions.question: Which morphological feature most reliably distinguishes the right ventricle from the left ventricle in sequential segmental analysis?

options: Intussusception associated with mesenteric lymphoid hyperplasia
Vitamin A toxicity affecting the bowel wall
Simple lactose intolerance triggered by the fever
Uncomplicated measles enteritis without further concern
Normal post-measles desquamation of the gut lining
questions.explanation: Measles can cause mesenteric lymphoid hyperplasia, which predisposes to intussusception, presenting with severe abdominal pain and bloody mucoid stool. This is a surgical emergency rather than simple enteritis. Vitamin A toxicity and lactose intolerance do not produce this presentation.
questions.question: A child with confirmed measles develops sudden severe abdominal pain, and stool testing reveals blood mixed with mucus. Which complication should be suspected?

questions.explanation: SGA infants should be fed at the minimum expected weight for their actual age rather than actual body weight, which is lower due to IUGR. Using actual weight underfeeds the infant and prevents catch-up growth. This approach ensures adequate caloric density to support the metabolic demands of catch-up growth.
questions.question: An SGA infant's caloric needs should be calculated based on:
Croup is a GENERIC term for a group of conditions characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Croup is a generic term for a heterogeneous group of largely infectious conditions characterised by barking or brassy cough, stridor, and possibly hoarseness and respiratory distress. Croup, particularly viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), is typically non-toxic in appearance with low-grade or no fever, distinguishing it from epiglottitis which presents with high fever and a toxic, septic appearance. Toxicity suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis.

MAS chest X-ray shows hyperinflation (from partial airway obstruction creating ball-valve air trapping) with coarse, irregular infiltrates and patchy areas of consolidation and atelectasis. RDS chest X-ray characteristically shows homogeneous bilateral granular (ground glass) opacities with air bronchograms from diffuse atelectasis without air trapping. These contrasting X-ray patterns reflect the different underlying pathophysiology of the two conditions.
questions.question: Which finding on chest X-ray in MAS differs from that seen in RDS?
options: Bilateral granular opacities (ground glass) vs. coarse irregular infiltrates
Both show identical ground glass opacities
MAS shows pleural effusions; RDS does not
Both conditions are diagnosed without chest X-ray
Hyperinflation with coarse infiltrates vs. granular opacities

questions.explanation: Kangaroo mother care (skin-to-skin contact) is the gold standard for thermal regulation in stable preterm and LBW neonates in resource-limited settings. It reduces hypothermia-related mortality and promotes breastfeeding and bonding, with outcomes comparable to incubator care.
questions.question: For a newborn's thermal management, the ideal method used in low-resource settings for a stable preterm neonate is:

options: High-pitched inspiratory sound from the larynx
Biphasic musical sound from the trachea
questions.question: Stertor, which differs from stridor, is described as:
questions.explanation: Stertor is a low-pitched inspiratory snoring sound originating from the nose or nasopharynx, produced by partial obstruction at these sites. It differs from stridor which is a higher-pitched sound from laryngeal or subglottic obstruction. Stertor is commonly associated with adenoid hypertrophy, nasal polyps, or choanal stenosis rather than laryngeal disease.

questions.question: Following neonatal seizures, maintenance anticonvulsants are typically continued for:
options: Until 6 months of age in all cases
Until a normal EEG is obtained at 1 year
questions.explanation: Maintenance phenobarbitone is generally continued for 2 weeks to 2 months depending on the underlying aetiology. Transient metabolic causes have low recurrence risk and short treatment. HIE has 30–50% recurrence risk, requiring longer coverage. Cortical malformations have high risk, requiring prolonged or lifelong therapy.

An epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu, and oroalimentary automatisms such as lip-smacking are classic semiological features localising seizure onset to the temporal lobe, often involving mesial structures such as the hippocampus. Frontal lobe seizures instead more typically present with prominent motor activity and briefer post-ictal confusion. Recognising this semiology helps direct further presurgical evaluation in drug-resistant cases.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of déjà vu, a rising epigastric sensation, and lip-smacking automatisms, followed by post-ictal confusion. Which lobe of the brain is most likely the seizure focus?
Which is the MOST common site of diphtheria infection in infants?
questions.explanation: The nose is the most common site of diphtheria infection in infants, presenting as nasal diphtheria with serosanguinous or purulent discharge and shallow ulcers. In older children, the tonsils and pharynx are the most common sites (classical diphtheria). Nasal diphtheria is often milder but can seed other sites.

Fetal blood volume is approximately 115 ml/kg, of which about 75 ml/kg is in the baby and 40 ml/kg is in the placenta. This placental blood can be transfused to the neonate if cord clamping is delayed, contributing to physiological polycythaemia.
questions.question: The total fetal blood volume in a term neonate is approximately:

questions.explanation: Bronchiolitis typically affects infants under 12 months, presenting with a preceding coryzal illness followed by cough, tachypnoea, and widespread fine inspiratory crackles with or without wheeze, most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus. Bacterial pneumonia would more typically show focal, rather than widespread, crackles and higher fever. The age and clinical pattern are key to distinguishing bronchiolitis from other causes of respiratory distress in infancy.
questions.question: A 5-month-old infant presents with a 2-day history of coryza, followed by cough, tachypnoea, and widespread fine crackles with wheeze on auscultation, feeding poorly. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A preterm infant born at 29 weeks gestation is being monitored for growth using length and weight measurements. Postnatal head circumference growth in term infants is used as a comparison reference; approximately what weekly rate would be considered normal in a term infant for comparison?
options: A fixed 10 cm total increase only in the first week
No increase at all expected in the first year
About 5 cm per week from birth
About 0.5 cm per day throughout infancy
About 0.5 cm per week in the early months
questions.explanation: Normal postnatal head circumference growth in term infants is approximately 0.5 cm per week during the early months, a reference point that is useful for comparison when assessing preterm infants for appropriate catch-up or concerning patterns of head growth. A rate as high as 5 cm per week or 0.5 cm per day would be markedly abnormal and concerning for pathological causes such as hydrocephalus. No head growth at all in the first year would indicate a serious growth problem.

The National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) has the mandate to protect Nigerian children from vaccine-preventable diseases through provision of vaccines. Following NPI restructuring, NPHCDA serves as the secretariat for the Interagency Coordination Committee (ICC) for Immunization. NPHCDA merged with NPI in May 2007.
options: It provides only financial support without operational role
Protects children via vaccines; serves as NPHCDA secretariat
Manages only adult HIV treatment centres
It has no formal role in PMTCT
questions.question: What is the role of NPHCDA in Nigeria's PMTCT programme?

questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis/acidaemia in severe malaria is defined as arterial pH <7.25 or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L. It results from anaerobic glycolysis, impaired hepatic lactate clearance, and renal failure. Acidosis is manifested clinically as respiratory distress (deep Kussmaul breathing) and predicts high mortality.
questions.question: Acidaemia/acidosis in severe malaria is defined by which blood gas parameter?
options: pCO2 >60 mmHg on arterial blood gas

questions.question: A child presents with cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue oedema of the neck ('bull neck'). This finding in diphtheria is more common in which age group?
questions.explanation: 'Bull neck' describes massive cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue oedema from extensive diphtheria toxicity in the tonsillar/pharyngeal region. It occurs predominantly in children above 6 years who have severe classical diphtheria. It indicates severe toxin absorption and carries a poor prognosis.

Haemoglobin breakdown: Hb ? haem (haem oxygenase) ? biliverdin (biliverdin reductase) ? unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin ? transported bound to albumin ? conjugated in liver to diglucuronide (direct bilirubin) ? excreted in bile. This sequence is central to understanding neonatal jaundice pathophysiology.
options: Haem to biliverdin to bilirubin to conjugated
questions.question: Which is the CORRECT sequence in neonatal bilirubin metabolism?

questions.explanation: The ECG in Tetralogy of Fallot characteristically shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH), reflecting the pressure-overloaded right ventricle from RVOTO. Right atrial hypertrophy (RAH) may also be present. Superior axis deviation is more characteristic of AV septal defect and tricuspid atresia, not Fallot's. These ECG changes are consistent with and supportive of the clinical and radiological diagnosis.
options: Left axis deviation with isolated left ventricular hypertrophy
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy
Normal axis with isolated left atrial hypertrophy only
Left bundle branch block from surgical injury
questions.question: Which ECG finding is characteristic of Tetralogy of Fallot and reflects the predominant haemodynamic abnormality?

questions.explanation: Multiple-trigger wheeze describes children whose wheeze is provoked by a range of stimuli beyond viral infections, including exercise and allergen exposure, with symptoms also occurring between acute episodes, and this phenotype is more likely to respond to regular preventer therapy such as inhaled corticosteroids. Episodic viral wheeze, by contrast, occurs only with viral triggers and resolves completely between episodes. Correctly distinguishing the phenotypes helps individualise long-term management.
questions.question: A 4-year-old has wheeze triggered by viral infections, exercise, and exposure to pets, with symptoms also present between acute episodes. What wheeze phenotype does this best represent?

questions.explanation: Small VSDs, particularly perimembranous and muscular types, can close spontaneously in childhood through the adherence of fibromuscular tissue or redundant tricuspid valve tissue (aneurysm of the membranous septum) to the defect margin. This gradual sealing reduces the murmur and abolishes the shunt. Spontaneous closure occurs in up to 50% of small VSDs, particularly in the first two years of life.
questions.question: Which statement best describes the physiological mechanism of spontaneous closure of small ventricular septal defects in childhood?
options: Progressive pulmonary hypertension gradually reducing left-to-right flow
Fibromuscular tissue or tricuspid valve tissue seals the defect
Calcification of the defect edges obliterates the opening
Progressive right ventricular hypertrophy occludes the opening
Antibiotic therapy promoting fibrosis and eventual closure

questions.explanation: Because maternal antibodies persist in infants for many months, antibody-based tests cannot reliably distinguish true infection from passive maternal antibody in a child under 18 months, so virological testing such as PCR is required for diagnosis at this age. CD4 count assists staging but does not diagnose infection. Clinical staging alone is inadequate for definitive diagnosis in an exposed infant.
questions.question: An HIV-exposed infant is 10 weeks old. Which test is most appropriate to confirm or exclude HIV infection at this age?
options: CD4 count as the sole diagnostic test
Clinical staging without any laboratory testing
Standard HIV antibody rapid test alone
HIV DNA or RNA virological testing (PCR)

questions.question: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) occurs predominantly in neonates born before:
questions.explanation: ROP is a proliferative retinal vascular disorder predominantly affecting neonates born before 32 weeks or weighing less than 1500 g, especially those requiring supplemental oxygen. Regular ophthalmologic screening is mandatory for these infants.

options: Political priority of the ruling government
Availability of vaccine in sufficient quantities
Proximity of the community to urban health facilities
Epidemiology of the disease including incidence and prevalence
questions.question: Which guiding principle determines vaccine priority in community immunization planning?
questions.explanation: The epidemiology of the disease (incidence, prevalence, severity, age distribution, and community impact) is the fundamental guiding principle for determining vaccine priority in community immunization planning. Higher burden diseases receive higher priority. Economic considerations, cold chain capacity, and community acceptance also influence planning but are secondary to epidemiological need.

Koplik's spots, small white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars, are pathognomonic of the prodromal stage of measles. They appear 1-2 days before the measles rash during the catarrhal phase which mimics acute coryza. Recognising Koplik's spots allows early diagnosis and public health isolation measures.
questions.question: Koplik's spots on the buccal mucosa during a coryza-like illness should alert the clinician to:

questions.explanation: Laryngeal web is caused by persistence of a web (incomplete luminal formation) in the anterior portion of the larynx and presents at birth with stridor, weak hoarse cry, and respiratory distress. Unlike laryngomalacia which produces a weak but normal-pitched cry, laryngeal web causes a distinctively hoarse cry. Treatment involves incision or excision followed by repeated dilatation, or CO2 laser lysis.
questions.question: A neonate with stridor, weak hoarse cry, and respiratory distress present from birth, where direct laryngoscopy shows a web in the anterior larynx, is diagnosed with:

questions.explanation: Impaired social communication combined with restricted, repetitive behaviours and interests, typically emerging before age 3, defines autism spectrum disorder according to standard diagnostic criteria. Specific language impairment affects language without the accompanying social and behavioural features. The combination of both domains, not language delay alone, is required for this diagnosis.
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has impaired social communication, restricted repetitive behaviours, and delayed language, first noticed by his parents around 18 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The safety of any infant feeding choice for an HIV-exposed infant depends heavily on maternal and infant access to effective antiretroviral therapy (which reduces transmission risk during breastfeeding) and, if replacement feeding is chosen, reliable access to clean water and adequate resources to prepare it safely. Preference alone, without regard to these factors, could result in an unsafe choice. Birth weight and household composition are not the primary determinants.
options: The mother's personal preference alone without other considerations
The season of the year in which the infant was born
The number of older siblings already in the household
Access to antiretroviral therapy and safe water for replacement feeding
The infant's birth weight alone as the deciding factor
questions.question: An HIV-positive mother is counselled about infant feeding options. Which factor is MOST important in determining the safest feeding choice in her specific setting?

options: Not classified in children's WHO staging
questions.question: Herpes zoster in an HIV-infected child is classified in which WHO clinical stage?
questions.explanation: Herpes zoster (shingles) in HIV-infected children is a WHO Clinical Stage 2 condition, representing reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus. Stage 2 also includes papular pruritic eruptions, seborrhoeic dermatitis, molluscum contagiosum, recurrent oral ulcerations, parotid enlargement, and recurrent URTIs. Chronic herpes simplex >1 month is Stage 4.

Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of muscle tone leading to head drops or falls, often with brief duration, and carry a risk of injury requiring protective headgear in some children. Myoclonic seizures instead cause brief, shock-like muscle jerks rather than loss of tone. Correctly classifying seizure type is important for guiding antiepileptic drug selection.
questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with sudden loss of muscle tone causing head drops and falls, without loss of consciousness duration beyond a second, occurring multiple times daily. What seizure type does this best represent?

questions.explanation: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a severe childhood epileptic encephalopathy characterised by multiple seizure types, a slow (less than 2.5 Hz) spike-and-wave EEG pattern, and significant cognitive impairment, and is typically resistant to standard antiepileptic therapy. Childhood absence epilepsy instead shows a single seizure type with a faster 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern and a much better prognosis. Recognising this syndrome guides use of specific therapies such as the ketogenic diet.
questions.question: A 6-year-old with a known seizure disorder has frequent multiple seizure types including tonic, atonic, and atypical absence seizures, with a slow spike-and-wave pattern on EEG and significant developmental impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are triggered by crying or frustration, with breath-holding leading to transient cyanosis and brief loss of consciousness followed by rapid spontaneous recovery, and are considered benign. Pallid breath-holding spells instead follow pain or fright and cause pallor through a vagal mechanism rather than cyanosis. Reassurance and exclusion of cardiac causes are usually sufficient.
questions.question: A 4-year-old holds his breath and turns blue during a tantrum, followed by brief loss of consciousness with rapid full recovery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Ethambutol causing additive optic toxicity with ARVs
Rifampicin inducing CYP450 enzymes reducing ARV concentrations
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP450 enzymes, which dramatically reduces the plasma concentrations of many antiretroviral drugs (particularly non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and protease inhibitors). This interaction necessitates careful selection of ARV regimens in TB/HIV co-infected patients.
questions.question: Which anti-TB drug is specifically avoided in children with HIV on ART due to significant drug interactions?
The PR interval in a 6-month-old infant falls within which normal range?
questions.explanation: The normal PR interval in infants under 1 year of age is 0.07–0.12 seconds, reflecting faster AV conduction in young children with higher heart rates. In children over 1 year, it is 0.08–0.16 sec; in adolescents, 0.10–0.18 sec; and in adults, 0.10–0.20 sec. PR intervals vary with both age and heart rate. A PR interval exceeding the age-specific upper limit indicates first-degree AV block, while shortening may indicate pre-excitation or junctional rhythms.

Diphtheria toxoid immunity wanes over time without booster doses, so children and adults who have not received scheduled boosters can still become susceptible despite prior completion of the primary series. This does not indicate vaccine failure across the board. Vaccination cannot cause the disease it protects against.
options: An entirely new organism unrelated to Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Complete and permanent failure of all diphtheria vaccines
A laboratory error in the diagnosis of diphtheria
Vaccination itself directly causing the current infection
Waning vaccine-induced immunity requiring periodic booster doses
questions.question: A previously healthy child develops diphtheria despite reportedly completing routine childhood immunisation. What is the most likely explanation for this breakthrough infection?

questions.explanation: Undernutrition is implicated in 53% of all deaths among children under five globally, often as an underlying or contributing factor rather than the direct cause of death. Malnourished children with pneumonia have significantly higher case fatality rates. Nutritional interventions are therefore integral to reducing not just malnutrition-specific deaths but also pneumonia mortality.
questions.question: Undernutrition is implicated in what proportion of all deaths among children under five globally?

questions.explanation: The lung is the most common site of infection in neonatal sepsis. Pneumonia—congenital or postnatal—is frequently the entry point or primary focus of septicaemia. This is partly because neonates aspirate amniotic fluid containing maternal organisms during delivery.
questions.question: The MOST common site of infection in neonatal sepsis is:
In alpha-thalassaemia of sufficient severity (Hb Bart's hydrops), the predominant haemoglobin is:
questions.explanation: In alpha-thalassaemia major (loss of all 4 alpha globin genes), Hb Bart's (gamma-4 tetramers) predominates in the fetus. Hb Bart's has extremely high oxygen affinity and delivers no oxygen to tissues, causing severe fetal hypoxia, hydrops fetalis, and usually intrauterine death.

questions.question: A jaundiced neonate has a positive direct Coombs test along with anaemia and a rapidly rising bilirubin. What does the positive direct Coombs test specifically indicate?
options: Antibody coating of the infant's own red blood cells
A laboratory artefact requiring repeat testing before any conclusion
A finding unrelated to bilirubin metabolism
Complete absence of haemolysis in this infant
Presence of free antibody in the maternal serum alone
questions.explanation: The direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test detects antibody already bound to the surface of the infant's own red blood cells, indicating an immune-mediated haemolytic process such as Rh or ABO incompatibility, consistent with the anaemia and rising bilirubin described. It does not simply reflect free antibody in maternal serum, which would instead be assessed by the indirect Coombs test. This finding is directly relevant to, not unrelated to, the bilirubin elevation seen.

options: Only after the child reaches school age
By around 4 to 6 months of age
questions.question: A neonate is noted to have a strong grasp reflex when an object is placed in the palm, and a Moro reflex on sudden movement. At approximately what age would these primitive reflexes be expected to have disappeared if development is normal?
questions.explanation: Primitive reflexes such as the grasp and Moro reflex are normally present in early infancy and are expected to diminish and disappear by around 4 to 6 months as cortical control matures; their persistence beyond this age can suggest an underlying neurological concern. They are not expected to vanish within the first day of life. Persistence throughout childhood would be abnormal, not a normal developmental pattern.

questions.question: The chest radiograph in transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN) classically shows:
questions.explanation: TTN (wet lung disease) shows a 'sunburst' or perihilar streaky pattern on chest X-ray representing retained lung fluid, which clears within 24–48 hours. This is different from RDS, which shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is an important differential diagnosis for acute rheumatic fever because both can present with fever and joint involvement, though the arthritis pattern and other associated features help distinguish them. Iron deficiency, febrile convulsions and vitamin D deficiency do not typically mimic this clinical picture. Careful clinical and serological assessment helps differentiate these overlapping presentations.
questions.question: A child is being evaluated for possible acute rheumatic fever, but the clinical picture also raises suspicion for an alternative diagnosis with overlapping features such as fever and joint pain. Which condition would appropriately be considered in this differential?

options: Cause direct mechanical injury to the developing brain
Cause autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue
questions.explanation: Endocrine disruptors are exogenous chemicals that mimic, block, or interfere with hormones in the endocrine system, disrupting normal hormonal signalling. Examples include bisphenols (estrogen-like), nitrofen (thyroid-disrupting), and DDT. They pose the greatest risk during prenatal and early postnatal development when organ and neural systems are forming. They are found in everyday products including plastics, cosmetics, and pesticides.
questions.question: Endocrine disruptors are hazardous environmental chemicals PRIMARILY because they:

options: Hyperkalaemia causing tall tented T waves
questions.explanation: Hyperkalaemia causes tall, tented (peaked) T waves rather than flat or inverted T waves, so it is the exception. Flattened or inverted T waves in left ventricular leads are associated with myocardial disease, pericardial disease, LVH with strain, hypokalaemia, and digitalis toxicity. Hypothyroidism and LVH are also recognised causes. Distinguishing T wave morphology in the correct clinical context is essential for accurate paediatric ECG interpretation.
questions.question: Flattened or inverted T waves on ECG in LV leads of a child are associated with all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Low maternal CD4 count without seroconversion
questions.explanation: Mixed feeding (combining breast milk with other fluids or foods) significantly increases HIV transmission risk during breastfeeding compared to exclusive breastfeeding. Breaks in gut epithelial integrity caused by early introduction of other foods allow HIV in breast milk to enter the infant's circulation. Exclusive breastfeeding with ARV prophylaxis minimizes risk.
questions.question: Which factor most increases MTCT risk during breastfeeding when seroconversion occurs?

questions.explanation: Immunization and sanitation are the two most cost-effective means of preventing infectious diseases. Effective sanitation prevents faeco-oral transmission of diseases (polio, cholera, typhoid), while immunization provides direct protection. Together, they address the two major routes of infectious disease transmission in developing countries.
questions.question: Immunization is considered one of the two most cost-effective means of preventing infectious diseases. What is the second?

questions.explanation: In children aged 1–5 years, Category III (severe immunosuppression) is defined as CD4 <500 cells or CD4 percentage <15%. Category I (no suppression) is >1,000 cells/>25%, and Category II (moderate suppression) is 500–999 cells/15–24%. For children 6–12 years, Category III is CD4 <200 cells/<15%.
questions.question: What CD4 percentage threshold defines Category III (severe immunosuppression) in a 3-year-old HIV-infected child?
Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS) causes heart failure in which neonatal period and through which haemodynamic mechanism?
questions.explanation: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS) causes life-threatening heart failure in the full-term neonate as the ductus arteriosus begins to close. The hypoplastic left ventricle cannot support systemic circulation, making the infant entirely dependent on right-to-left ductal flow for systemic perfusion. As the ductus closes, systemic cardiac output collapses, producing circulatory shock. Prostaglandin E1 to maintain ductal patency is the critical emergency intervention.
options: In premature neonates from increased pulmonary blood flow states
In infants from mitral regurgitation increasing left atrial pressure even further
In children from progressive right ventricular hypertrophy
In full-term neonates from inadequate systemic perfusion after ductal closure

questions.explanation: Progressive neurological decline in a child with an underlying spinal dysraphism such as spina bifida occulta suggests a tethered spinal cord, in which the cord is abnormally fixed and becomes stretched with growth, causing ischaemic injury. This differs from a static congenital deficit and requires neurosurgical evaluation for possible detethering. Recognising this progressive pattern distinguishes it from a fixed, non-progressive lesion.
questions.question: An 8-year-old with spina bifida occulta develops progressive lower limb weakness, worsening bladder dysfunction, and back pain as they grow. What is the most likely underlying explanation?
Which antibiotics need dose reduction in patients with HEPATIC failure?
questions.explanation: Drugs primarily metabolized by the liver require dose reduction in hepatic failure to prevent toxic accumulation. These include macrolides, chloramphenicol, metronidazole, rifampicin, and isoniazid. Aminoglycosides and glycopeptides require careful monitoring in renal (not hepatic) failure. Beta-lactams can precipitate seizures in renal impairment.

questions.question: A newborn has a lumbosacral skin-covered swelling containing neural tissue, with associated lower limb weakness and a neurogenic bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A lumbosacral swelling containing neural tissue with associated motor and bladder dysfunction indicates a myelomeningocele, the most severe form of open neural tube defect. A simple meningocele contains only meninges and cerebrospinal fluid without neural elements, and typically causes no neurological deficit. The presence of neurological deficit is the key distinguishing clinical clue.

A simple febrile seizure is generalised, lasts less than 15 minutes, and does not recur within 24 hours, with full return to baseline. Complex febrile seizures are focal, prolonged beyond 15 minutes, or recurrent within the same illness. This distinction determines the intensity of subsequent investigation and counselling.
questions.question: A 2-year-old has a seizure during a fever of 39.2°C. The seizure is generalised, lasts 3 minutes, and the child returns to baseline within an hour. This is best classified as:

questions.explanation: Isolated thrombocytopenia without other clinical features of sepsis or meningitis is not a stand-alone indication for lumbar puncture. LP is indicated in positive blood cultures, suspected meningitis (neurological signs, bulging fontanelle), failed antibiotic response, and any neonate with seizures in the context of suspected infection.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an indication for lumbar puncture in neonatal sepsis evaluation?

A neonate with TGA is noted to have both atrioventricular concordance and ventriculo-arterial discordance, but is asymptomatic with normal oxygen saturations at birth due to an associated large VSD and mild pulmonary stenosis. What is the most likely explanation for this relatively stable presentation?
options: The child does not actually have TGA despite the echocardiographic findings
The pulmonary stenosis has completely obstructed all pulmonary flow
The VSD has functionally converted this into biventricular circulation without transposition
VSD shunting with mild pulmonary stenosis balances mixing and flow
questions.explanation: In some cases of TGA with VSD, associated pulmonary stenosis limits excessive pulmonary blood flow while the VSD still allows adequate intercirculatory mixing, resulting in a more balanced and initially stable physiology compared with TGA alone. This combination still requires surgical correction, but the presentation may be less acutely life-threatening than TGA with intact septum. It does not represent spontaneous correction of the underlying transposition.

Hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema reflect systemic venous congestion, a hallmark of right-sided heart failure, whereas pulmonary crackles and tachypnoea are more indicative of left-sided congestion. In infants, however, biventricular failure often coexists, but hepatomegaly is a particularly sensitive early sign of right-sided involvement. This distinction helps localise the predominant haemodynamic burden clinically.
questions.question: An infant with heart failure is noted to have hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema. Which side of cardiac failure do these findings predominantly reflect?
options: Primary hepatic disease unrelated to the heart
Left-sided heart failure with pulmonary congestion
Right-sided heart failure with systemic venous congestion
Isolated diastolic dysfunction of the left ventricle
Isolated arrhythmic cause without structural disease
Cardiac catheterisation with oxygen saturation oximetry
ECG voltage criteria for biventricular hypertrophy
Chest X-ray assessment of pulmonary vascular marking prominence
Echocardiography with pulsed Doppler velocity measurement
questions.question: Which investigation most accurately quantifies the ratio of pulmonary to systemic blood flow (Qp:Qs) in a child with a suspected large intracardiac shunt?
questions.explanation: Cardiac catheterisation with oximetry remains the gold standard for quantification of the Qp:Qs ratio in intracardiac shunts. By measuring oxygen saturations at multiple sites in the heart and great vessels, the Fick principle allows calculation of pulmonary and systemic blood flows. A Qp:Qs >2:1 typically indicates a haemodynamically significant shunt warranting intervention, and this method also assesses pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.question: Acute pneumonia is defined as acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by microorganisms, distinguishing it from aspiration pneumonitis, which becomes true pneumonia only when:
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical inflammation of the lung parenchyma from inhalation of sterile gastric contents, not a true infection. It becomes acute pneumonia only when secondary bacterial infection supervenes. This distinction is clinically important because aspiration pneumonitis alone does not require antibiotics, whereas aspiration pneumonia does.

questions.question: What is the incubation period of measles?
questions.explanation: The incubation period of measles is 10–14 days (some sources state 10–12 days). During this period, there are very few or no symptoms. The prodromal stage begins at the end of the incubation period and lasts 3–5 days, characterized by fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots before the rash appears.

Mastitis and other breast conditions increase local inflammation and viral shedding into breast milk, thereby increasing the risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission during breastfeeding. This risk applies specifically to breastfed infants exposed to the affected milk. The condition does not reduce transmission risk by any mechanism.
questions.question: A breastfeeding HIV-positive mother develops acute mastitis during the breastfeeding period. How does this condition affect the risk of mother-to-child transmission?
options: It only affects transmission risk if the infant already has fever
It affects only formula-fed infants, not breastfed ones
It increases transmission risk due to higher viral shedding in breast milk
It decreases transmission risk by reducing milk volume
It has no effect on transmission risk during breastfeeding

questions.explanation: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome in a young child is a paraneoplastic phenomenon strongly associated with underlying neuroblastoma, and its recognition should prompt urgent screening for an occult tumour, typically with abdominal imaging and urinary catecholamine metabolites. A simple post-viral cerebellitis would not typically produce the characteristic chaotic eye movements (opsoclonus) seen in this syndrome. Early tumour detection and treatment can also improve the neurological outcome.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of unsteady gait, and examination reveals opsoclonus and myoclonus of the limbs. What underlying diagnosis is most important to exclude?

options: Sudden complete closure of the VSD reducing pulmonary flow
Acute pulmonary haemorrhage from rupture of dilated pulmonary vessels entirely
Ventricular fibrillation from severe right ventricular hypertrophy alone
Acute infundibular spasm causing dynamic RVOTO and increased R-L shunting
questions.explanation: Hypercyanotic (Tet) spells result from acute dynamic infundibular spasm, which dramatically increases RVOTO, reducing pulmonary blood flow and massively increasing right-to-left shunting through the VSD. This causes severe arterial desaturation, metabolic acidosis, and hypoxia, which further relaxes systemic vessels — creating a vicious cycle. Prompt management includes knee-chest position, oxygen, morphine, and intravenous propranolol or sodium bicarbonate.
questions.question: Hypercyanotic spells (Tet spells) in Tetralogy of Fallot are pathophysiologically attributed to which acute event?
Airway hyperresponsiveness in asthma is defined as the propensity of the airway to:
questions.explanation: Airway hyperresponsiveness (hyperreactivity) is defined as the propensity of the airway to constrict too easily and too much in response to various stimuli including allergens, exercise, cold air, and irritants. It is quantified as the provoking dose (or concentration) of methacholine or histamine causing a 20% fall in FEV1 (PC20 or PD20). Airway hyperresponsiveness is a central feature of asthma and correlates with disease severity.

options: Prevents gestational diabetes in subsequent pregnancies
Reduces risk of breast and ovarian cancer
questions.explanation: Documented maternal benefits of breastfeeding include uterine involution, reduced postpartum bleeding, lactational amenorrhoea (contraceptive effect), reduced breast and ovarian cancer risk, personal fulfilment, and cost savings. Prevention of gestational diabetes in future pregnancies is not a recognised direct breastfeeding benefit.
questions.question: Breastfeeding benefits the mother by all the following EXCEPT:
A neonate with TGA and inadequate mixing despite a patent ductus arteriosus is being considered for balloon atrial septostomy. Under which imaging guidance is this procedure most commonly performed?
questions.explanation: Balloon atrial septostomy is typically performed at the bedside under echocardiographic guidance, allowing real-time visualisation of the atrial septum and catheter position without the delays of transporting a critically ill neonate. MRI is not practical for this urgent bedside procedure. This approach allows rapid improvement in mixing when clinically indicated.

options: Inactivated vaccines have smaller antigen particles
Inactivated vaccines need repeated doses to build immunity
Live vaccines cause disease that requires multiple vaccine exposures to cure
Inactivated vaccines are given orally and have poor bioavailability
Multiple doses ensure herd immunity regardless of individual response
questions.explanation: Inactivated vaccines cannot replicate in the host, so they do not produce the sustained antigen presentation that live vaccines achieve. The first dose typically primes (rather than fully protects) the immune system, and 2–5 doses are needed to achieve protective immunity. Antibody titres also decline over time, often requiring booster doses.
questions.question: Why do inactivated vaccines generally require more doses than live attenuated vaccines?
Complete heart block in the fetus causing heart failure occurs primarily through which mechanism?
options: Tachycardia from accessory pathway activation causing high-output cardiac failure
AV nodal destruction from maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies causing bradycardia and low output
Severe bradycardia from hypothyroidism reducing metabolic rate
Ventricular premature beats causing ineffective cardiac contraction
Right heart obstruction from hydrops causing bradycardia from atrial distension changes noted
questions.explanation: Congenital complete heart block (CHB) in the fetus is most commonly caused by transplacental passage of maternal anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies in mothers with connective tissue diseases (SLE, Sjögren syndrome), which destroy the fetal AV node. The resulting severe bradycardia (30–50 bpm) reduces cardiac output, causing fetal hydrops and congestive heart failure. Fetal surveillance and maternal corticosteroids or hydroxychloroquine may limit progression.

questions.question: A neonate with TGA has an associated large VSD. How does this typically affect the clinical presentation compared with TGA with an intact septum?
options: Cyanosis is often less severe because of greater intercirculatory mixing
The neonate is asymptomatic and requires no intervention
Heart failure never develops in this combination
The VSD eliminates the need for any surgical intervention
Cyanosis is markedly more severe due to reduced mixing
questions.explanation: A VSD in the setting of TGA provides an additional site for mixing between the systemic and pulmonary circulations, often resulting in less profound cyanosis than TGA with an intact septum, though heart failure from pulmonary overcirculation may develop instead. Some intervention is still required, typically the arterial switch operation with VSD closure. Complete absence of symptoms would be atypical given the significant intracardiac shunting.

questions.question: A child with acute coryza develops yellowish nasal discharge. The MOST appropriate next step is:
questions.explanation: Mucopurulent (yellowish) rhinorrhoea in acute coryza is NOT an indication for antibiotic therapy, as the aetiology is predominantly viral. Antibiotics are only warranted when there is clear evidence of bacterial superinfection. Treatment of acute coryza remains largely symptomatic.

questions.question: In a neonate presenting with meningitis, which organism is the LEAST likely causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) is a pathogen predominantly affecting children aged 3 months to 12 years and is not a typical neonatal organism. Neonatal meningitis is caused by organisms responsible for neonatal sepsis: Group B Streptococcus, Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella), Staphylococcus aureus, and Listeria monocytogenes. This age-specific microbiological pattern guides empirical antibiotic selection.

options: Total lung capacity measured by body plethysmography alone
Diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide as the sole marker
questions.question: A 5-year-old with cystic fibrosis is due for routine spirometry. Which pulmonary function parameter is most useful for monitoring disease progression over time?
questions.explanation: FEV1 is the most widely used and clinically meaningful spirometric parameter for monitoring progression of obstructive lung disease such as cystic fibrosis, with a declining trend indicating worsening lung function over time. While other measures provide additional information, FEV1 remains the primary marker tracked in routine clinical follow-up. Serial measurement allows early identification of decline and timely intervention.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent respiratory symptoms, and detailed history reveals that symptoms are worse specifically in a particular room of the house with visible mould growth. What is the most appropriate initial recommendation regarding this environmental factor?
options: No action is needed as mould has no respiratory relevance
Immediate permanent relocation of the family is always required
Address the mould source and improve ventilation in the affected area
Ignore the history since environmental triggers are never relevant to respiratory symptoms
Recommend daily oral antibiotics to counteract mould exposure
questions.explanation: Mould exposure is a recognised environmental trigger that can worsen respiratory symptoms, particularly in children with underlying atopic or asthmatic tendencies, and addressing the source directly through remediation and improved ventilation is a reasonable and proportionate first-line environmental intervention. Assuming no relevance or jumping to drastic measures such as relocation without first attempting remediation are both disproportionate responses. Identifying and addressing specific environmental triggers is an important complementary part of managing chronic respiratory symptoms.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl presents with new-onset squint, and examination reveals leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in the affected eye. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude urgently?
questions.explanation: Leukocoria in a young child is a red-flag sign requiring urgent ophthalmological assessment to exclude retinoblastoma, a potentially life-threatening intraocular malignancy that is highly treatable when detected early. While congenital cataract can also cause leukocoria, malignancy must be excluded first given the stakes involved. Prompt referral avoids delay in diagnosis and treatment of this vision- and life-threatening condition.

The brain is protected from infection primarily by two barriers: the bony skull, which provides mechanical protection from external invasion, and the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which restricts passage of pathogens and inflammatory mediators from the bloodstream. Deficiencies in either barrier (skull fracture, immature or inflamed BBB) significantly increase susceptibility to CNS infection. Understanding these barriers guides pathogenesis and treatment strategies.
questions.question: The brain is normally sterile and protected from infection by which primary structural barriers?

questions.explanation: Biphasic stridor of intermediate pitch indicates obstruction at the extrathoracic trachea level, specifically the glottis and subglottis. Supraglottic obstruction causes high-pitched inspiratory stridor, while intrathoracic tracheal obstruction causes expiratory stridor (wheeze). Biphasic stridor occurs because the obstruction at the glottis/subglottis affects both phases of breathing.
questions.question: In the classification of stridor by anatomical location, biphasic stridor of intermediate pitch indicates obstruction at:

options: Use of a standard blood agar plate exclusively
Delayed transport allowing bacterial multiplication first
Storage of the sample at room temperature before plating
Refrigeration of the swab for one week before use
questions.explanation: Bordetella pertussis is fastidious and requires prompt inoculation onto specialised Bordet-Gengou medium for optimal recovery, since delays or use of standard media reduce culture yield. Prolonged storage or delayed transport allows organism viability to fall. This is why culture sensitivity for pertussis is often disappointing in practice.
questions.question: A child with suspected pertussis has a nasopharyngeal aspirate sent for culture. Which specific transport and culture medium consideration is most important for organism recovery?

questions.explanation: Nasal toiletting, as recommended for primary health care management of coryza, involves the gentle removal of nasal secretions using rolled tissue or gauze. This technique is safe, effective, and appropriate for infants who are obligatory nasal breathers. Mechanical suctors and nasal decongestants carry risks of mucosal injury and rebound congestion respectively.
questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes nasal toiletting in the management of coryza in infants?
options: Irrigation with normal saline under pressure
Secretion removal with tissue or gauze

questions.question: ADHD is characterised by inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity. According to developmental norms, ADHD behaviours must be present:
questions.explanation: For an ADHD diagnosis, symptoms must have been present before age 12 years and must occur in more than one setting (e.g., home and school). Symptoms must cause significant functional impairment and not be better explained by another disorder. The cross-setting requirement prevents over-diagnosis of situational behavioural problems as ADHD.
options: For a minimum period of 2 weeks

questions.question: A neonate develops meningitis in the first week of life. Which organism is the MOST common cause of neonatal meningitis at this early age?
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis in the first week of life, consistent with its role as a leading early-onset sepsis pathogen acquired from the maternal genital tract. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b are more typically associated with meningitis in older infants and children rather than in the very early neonatal period. Tuberculous meningitis usually has a more insidious, delayed presentation rather than this acute early-onset pattern.
options: Haemophilus influenzae type b, typically seen after early infancy
Streptococcus pneumoniae, typically seen in older infants
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically presenting more insidiously
Group B Streptococcus, consistent with early-onset disease patterns
Neisseria meningitidis, typically seen in older children
A biphasic sound at the level of the larynx
An inspiratory wheeze from small airways
A low-pitched expiratory sound with musical quality
questions.explanation: Grunting is described as a low-pitched expiratory sound, usually with musical qualities, produced when the child closes the glottis during exhalation to maintain positive end-expiratory pressure and prevent alveolar collapse. It is a sign of severe respiratory distress and is frequently seen in neonatal RDS and in children with pneumonia affecting many alveoli. Grunting in young infants is a danger sign of very severe disease.
questions.question: Grunting in a child with pneumonia is described as:

A term infant develops encephalopathy following a difficult delivery with evidence of fetal distress. Using the Sarnat staging system, lethargy, mild hypotonia, and weak suck without seizures would be classified as which stage?
questions.explanation: Sarnat stage I hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is characterised by mild hyperalertness or lethargy, mild hypotonia, and a weak suck, without seizures, and generally carries a good prognosis. Stage II includes lethargy, more marked hypotonia, and seizures, while stage III involves stupor or coma, flaccid tone, and absent primitive reflexes with a poor prognosis. Accurate staging helps predict outcome and guides consideration of therapeutic hypothermia.

questions.question: Haemoptysis in bronchiectasis is caused by:
questions.explanation: Haemoptysis in bronchiectasis occurs when the chronic inflammatory process erodes the bronchial vasculature within the dilated, infected bronchial walls. It ranges from blood-streaked sputum to massive, life-threatening haemoptysis requiring bronchial artery embolisation. Haemoptysis is particularly common in saccular bronchiectasis due to the extensive vascular proliferation in the abnormal airway walls.

CSF rhinorrhoea is listed among the differential diagnoses of nasal discharge and should be suspected following head trauma or basal skull fracture. Unlike mucoid or mucopurulent discharge of infectious origin, CSF rhinorrhoea appears clear and watery and tests positive for beta-2 transferrin. Missing this diagnosis can lead to meningitis if the CSF leak is untreated.
questions.question: CSF rhinorrhoea, which may mimic nasal discharge, should be suspected in a child with:
Meconium aspiration into the lungs MOST commonly causes respiratory distress through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Meconium causes a ball-valve obstruction leading to air-trapping and hyperinflation, combined with chemical pneumonitis from meconium's irritant properties. Meconium also inactivates surfactant, worsening atelectasis. These three mechanisms collectively cause severe respiratory distress in MAS.

questions.question: The term 'univentricular heart with increased pulmonary blood flow' is most correctly applied in which clinical scenario?
options: Single ventricle physiology with an unobstructed pulmonary artery
Tricuspid atresia with a restrictive VSD and pulmonary stenosis
Tetralogy of Fallot with a large VSD and severe right ventricular outflow obstruction
Hypoplastic left heart with aortic atresia
Complete heart block with junctional rhythm
questions.explanation: A univentricular heart with increased pulmonary blood flow (UVH + increased PBF) occurs when a functionally single ventricle has an unobstructed pulmonary artery, allowing excessive pulmonary blood flow and leading to early congestive heart failure. Pulmonary artery banding may be required as a palliative procedure to limit pulmonary blood flow and protect pulmonary vasculature until definitive Fontan repair. This is a key pathophysiological category in paediatric heart failure.

options: Aluminium salts: enhance the immune response as an adjuvant
Gelatin: stabilizes the antigen during freeze-drying
Thimerosal: inhibits microbial growth in multidose vials
2-phenoxyethanol: serves as a carrier protein for conjugate vaccines
Formaldehyde: suspending fluid maintaining vaccine pH
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a preservative used in vaccines and its function?
questions.explanation: Thimerosal is a preservative containing ethylmercury that inhibits bacterial and fungal growth in multidose vaccine vials. Aluminium salts function as adjuvants (enhancing immune response). Gelatin is a stabilizer (maintaining antigen structure during storage). Formaldehyde is used to inactivate organisms or toxins. 2-phenoxyethanol is another preservative.

options: Ensuring resuscitation equipment and a trained team are ready
Preparing only suction equipment and nothing else
Assuming resuscitation will not be needed since risk factors are only theoretical
Delaying preparation until the infant is actually born and assessed
Notifying only the family without preparing any equipment
questions.question: A resuscitation team anticipates the delivery of an infant with known risk factors for asphyxia, such as a non-reassuring fetal heart pattern in labour. What is the most important action to prepare in advance?
questions.explanation: When risk factors for possible birth asphyxia are identified antenatally or during labour, anticipation and advance preparation of a trained team and full resuscitation equipment is critical, since asphyxia can evolve rapidly and delay in readiness worsens outcomes. Waiting until after birth to prepare equipment would waste crucial time. Preparation should be comprehensive, not limited to a single piece of equipment.

Placental malaria has been shown to increase the risk of MTCT of HIV in studies conducted in Uganda and Kenya. Malaria causes placental inflammation and parasitaemia, disrupting the placental barrier and increasing viral load in the placenta, thereby facilitating HIV transmission from mother to fetus during pregnancy.
questions.question: Placental malaria increases the risk of MTCT in which countries as demonstrated in research?

options: Hind milk has a notably lower fat content than foremilk
Hind milk contains significantly less protein than foremilk
Hind milk and foremilk are identical in fat content
Hind milk has a notably higher fat content than foremilk
Hind milk contains no lactose at all, unlike foremilk
questions.explanation: Hind milk, released later in a feed as the let-down reflex progresses, has a notably higher fat content compared with the thinner, more lactose-predominant foremilk released at the start of a feed, contributing importantly to the infant's total caloric intake during that feeding session. It is not identical to foremilk in fat content, nor does it lack lactose entirely. This distinction is relevant when counselling mothers about ensuring infants feed long enough at each breast to obtain adequate hind milk.
questions.question: A mother is advised that hind milk, obtained later in a breastfeeding session, differs in composition from foremilk obtained at the start of the same feed. What is the primary compositional difference between hind milk and foremilk?

questions.explanation: Certain treatable metabolic causes of infantile seizures, such as pyridoxine dependency and biotinidase deficiency, should be considered in infants with early-onset seizures or spasms, as supplementation can dramatically improve seizure control and outcome if identified early. Vitamin D, iron, zinc, and vitamin C deficiencies are not established causes of infantile spasms. A trial of pyridoxine may be both diagnostic and therapeutic in resistant neonatal or infantile seizures.
questions.question: A 9-month-old boy presents with hypsarrhythmia on EEG and infantile spasms. Family history reveals a maternal uncle with intellectual disability and seizures. Which underlying metabolic condition should be specifically screened for as a treatable cause?
The MOST common organism causing early-onset neonatal sepsis in maternal genitourinary infections is:
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the most common cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis in developed settings, colonising the maternal vagina and being transmitted to the neonate during delivery. E. coli is the second most common. GBS prophylaxis in culture-positive mothers prevents many cases.
options: coli is the second most common. GBS prophylaxis in culture-positive mothers prevents many cases.

questions.question: A community reports an outbreak of measles predominantly among children older than the routine vaccination age. What does this pattern most likely indicate about the local immunisation programme?
options: Complete vaccine failure across the entire population
A new, more virulent strain that evades all immunity
Suboptimal vaccine coverage leaving a cohort of susceptible children
Normal expected disease pattern regardless of coverage
questions.explanation: An outbreak concentrated in older, under-vaccinated children usually reflects accumulated susceptibility from gaps in coverage over preceding years rather than a failure of the vaccine itself. This pattern is a coverage and programmatic issue. It does not indicate a new immune-evading strain or vaccine-caused disease.

Vegetation on the mitral valve detected by echocardiography in a febrile child with a new murmur is the diagnostic hallmark of infective endocarditis. Echocardiographic evidence of vegetation (an oscillating intracardiac mass on a valve) is a major Duke criterion. Transesophageal echocardiography (TOE) is more sensitive than transthoracic echo (TTE) for detecting small vegetations and perivalvular abscesses. The combination of vegetation, fever, and positive blood cultures constitutes definitive infective endocarditis by Duke criteria.
questions.question: The echocardiographic finding of vegetation on the mitral valve in a febrile child with a new murmur is MOST consistent with which diagnosis?
options: Acute rheumatic fever with new mitral regurgitation
Congenital mitral regurgitation from myxomatous disease
Dilated cardiomyopathy with secondary mitral regurgitation
Mitral valve prolapse with ruptured chordae tendinae
Infective endocarditis with vegetation on the mitral valve

questions.explanation: Term neonates have a normal haemoglobin of 14–20 g/dl, with cord blood Hb averaging 16.8 g/dl. This high Hb reflects compensatory erythropoiesis in the relatively hypoxic intrauterine environment. It falls to its nadir at 8–12 weeks as erythropoiesis decreases postnatally.
questions.question: Normal haemoglobin range for a term neonate is:

questions.explanation: Between 70–90% of individuals exposed to M. tuberculosis will not develop infection. Possible reasons include inhalation of an insufficient number of organisms and adequate immune responses preventing infection from becoming established. Factors such as malnutrition, HIV, and extremes of age increase susceptibility to infection.
questions.question: What percentage of individuals exposed to TB will NOT develop any symptoms or infection?

questions.explanation: Tall, tented (peaked) T waves are the earliest and most characteristic ECG change in hyperkalaemia. They reflect the effects of elevated extracellular potassium on myocardial repolarisation, shortening the action potential duration. As hyperkalaemia progresses, the PR interval lengthens, QRS widens, and ultimately a sine wave pattern or ventricular fibrillation may occur. Tall T waves may also be seen in LVH with strain and early myocardial infarction.
questions.question: Tall, tented T waves on the paediatric ECG are most characteristically associated with which metabolic disturbance?

A neonate develops respiratory distress that does not correspond to a primary lung pathology; instead, examination reveals pallor and a low haematocrit. Which category of cause does this best represent?
questions.explanation: Severe anaemia is a recognised non-respiratory cause of respiratory distress in the newborn, since reduced oxygen-carrying capacity can produce tachypnoea and distress despite normal lung parenchyma, distinguishing it from primary pulmonary or structural causes. Structural, surfactant, aspiration, and fluid-related causes are pulmonary in origin, unlike this haematological explanation. Recognising non-respiratory causes broadens the differential diagnosis in a distressed neonate.
options: Surfactant deficiency as the primary underlying process
Transient tachypnoea as the primary underlying process
A structural airway malformation causing the distress
Meconium aspiration as the primary underlying process
A non-respiratory (haematological) cause of respiratory distress

questions.question: A child with tetanus has spasms triggered by minimal handling during nursing care. Which nursing practice modification is most appropriate to reduce this triggering?
options: Encouraging frequent visitors to provide stimulation
Performing all care with bright lighting for better visibility
Grouping necessary care activities to minimise total handling episodes
Increasing the frequency of routine handling and repositioning
Playing loud music to distract the child during care
questions.explanation: Because minimal stimuli can provoke spasms in tetanus, nursing care should be organised to group necessary interventions together and minimise the number and frequency of handling episodes, reducing spasm triggers. Increasing handling frequency or adding noise and light would worsen, not reduce, spasm frequency. This principle underlies the overall quiet, minimal-stimulation approach to tetanus nursing.

In large left-to-right shunt lesions such as VSD, excessive pulmonary blood flow steals from the systemic circulation, reducing effective systemic output despite normal myocardial contractility, placing this in the specific haemodynamic category of excessive pulmonary flow rather than primary pump or diastolic failure. Recognising this distinct mechanism guides management toward reducing shunt volume rather than purely inotropic support. This differs from failure due to intrinsic myocardial disease.
options: Diminished systemic output due to a tachyarrhythmia
Diminished systemic output due to obstruction to ventricular outflow
Diminished systemic output due to primary myocardial dysfunction
Diminished systemic output due to excessive pulmonary blood flow
Diminished systemic output due to primary diastolic dysfunction
questions.question: An infant with heart failure secondary to a large VSD is assessed for possible causes of diminished systemic output. Which pathophysiological grouping does an uncorrected large left-to-right shunt lesion belong to?
Which specific laboratory investigation should be performed in the initial assessment of a child with newly diagnosed heart failure to identify a metabolic cause?
options: Serum troponin I and CK-MB for myocardial necrosis
Serum electrolytes, glucose, lactate, and urine organic acids/acylcarnitine profile
Thyroid function tests alone to exclude hypothyroidism
Blood culture and inflammatory markers for an infective aetiology source
Full blood count for anaemia as the sole initial metabolic screening test to be performed
questions.explanation: Initial metabolic investigations in a child with unexplained heart failure should include serum electrolytes, glucose, lactate (for mitochondrial disorders), and urine organic acids and acylcarnitine profile (for fatty acid oxidation defects and organic acidaemias). These are essential to identify treatable metabolic cardiomyopathies. A specific metabolic diagnosis changes management profoundly — for instance, carnitine supplementation reverses carnitine deficiency cardiomyopathy. Genetic and enzymatic studies follow if metabolic screening is positive.

Noonan syndrome shares phenotypic overlap with Turner syndrome, including short stature, webbed neck, and pulmonary stenosis, but occurs in both sexes and has a normal karyotype, distinguishing it genetically from Turner syndrome, which requires a 45,X or mosaic karyotype abnormality. This distinction is important because the two conditions have different inheritance patterns and associated risks. Molecular testing for RAS-MAPK pathway genes confirms Noonan syndrome.
questions.question: A 3-year-old girl has short stature, a webbed neck, low-set ears, and pulmonary stenosis, with normal chromosomes on karyotype. What is the most likely diagnosis given normal karyotyping?

options: Promoting premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and worsening hypoxaemia
Permanent cure of the underlying structural lesion
Immediate and complete resolution of cyanosis
questions.explanation: High-concentration oxygen can promote constriction and premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, which is catastrophic in duct-dependent pulmonary circulation, as it removes the sole source of pulmonary blood flow and worsens hypoxaemia. Oxygen therapy in these infants must therefore be used cautiously, alongside prostaglandin E1 to maintain ductal patency. It does not correct the underlying structural cardiac lesion.
questions.question: A neonate with severe cyanotic congenital heart disease and known duct-dependent pulmonary blood flow is inadvertently given supplemental oxygen at very high concentration. What adverse effect might this have?

options: Any antibiotic preparation preventing bacterial infections
A passive immunization agent containing preformed antibodies
A chemical agent that kills pathogens on contact
An immunosuppressive agent used to prevent organ rejection
Stimulates immunity to inactivate or suppress a pathogen
questions.question: What is a VACCINE as defined in immunology?
questions.explanation: A vaccine is any preparation which, when administered, is able to stimulate the immune system to produce specific responses (antibodies and/or cell-mediated immunity) that inactivate, destroy, or suppress a given pathogen. This definition encompasses live, inactivated, subunit, conjugate, toxoid, and recombinant vaccine technologies.

A previous history of a life-threatening or near-fatal asthma episode is a well-recognised risk factor for future severe exacerbations and should prompt a lower threshold for early, aggressive treatment and closer observation during any subsequent presentation, even if the current episode initially appears less severe. This history remains clinically relevant and should always be factored into risk stratification. Documenting and flagging this history in the child's records supports safer, more responsive care in future encounters.
questions.question: A 7-year-old presents with acute wheeze and is noted to have a history of a similar episode requiring paediatric intensive care admission previously. How does this history influence the current assessment approach?
options: It has no bearing on current management since each episode is unrelated
It means the child cannot have simple mild asthma this time
It should lower the threshold for early, aggressive treatment and closer monitoring given the history of a life-threatening episode
Previous intensive care admission means no further escalation is ever possible
It is only relevant to future employment, not current clinical care

questions.explanation: Rifampicin is dosed at 10–20 mg/kg/day in children. In addition to the harmless orange discoloration of body fluids, rifampicin can cause gastrointestinal disturbances, hepatotoxicity (requiring LFT monitoring), and thrombocytopenia. It is a potent enzyme inducer affecting many co-administered drugs including oral contraceptives and antiretrovirals.
questions.question: What is the rifampicin dose range in children and which dose-related adverse effect requires monitoring?
Preterm delivery and birth asphyxia share a common cardiovascular complication. Which condition is associated with BOTH of these perinatal events?
questions.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is associated with both preterm delivery and birth asphyxia as perinatal precipitating factors. Prematurity results in incomplete ductal smooth muscle development, while hypoxia in birth asphyxia reduces the oxygen tension needed to trigger ductal closure. High altitude is another environmental factor associated with PDA through a similar hypoxic mechanism.

Algid malaria (circulatory collapse) is defined as systolic blood pressure <70 mmHg in patients >5 years of age (<50 mmHg in children aged 1–5 years) with cold clammy skin or a core-skin temperature difference >10°C. It represents peripheral circulatory failure and carries a poor prognosis.
questions.question: Which describes Algid malaria as a feature of severe falciparum malaria?
options: It represents peripheral circulatory failure and carries a poor prognosis.

questions.question: An ECG in a child shows a sawtooth baseline pattern of atrial activity at a rate of around 300 per minute with variable ventricular conduction. Which arrhythmia does this describe?
questions.explanation: Atrial flutter produces a characteristic regular sawtooth pattern of atrial deflections, typically at a rate around 300 per minute, with variable degrees of AV conduction determining the ventricular rate. Atrial fibrillation instead shows an irregularly irregular baseline without discrete flutter waves. This distinction is important because management strategies differ between the two atrial arrhythmias.

Erb's palsy (upper brachial plexus palsy) results from injury to the C5 and C6 nerve roots, typically from excessive lateral neck traction during difficult delivery. The classic posture is the 'waiter's tip' position—shoulder adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended and pronated, wrist flexed. Klumpke's paralysis affects C8 and T1 (lower brachial plexus), producing intrinsic hand muscle weakness with possible Horner's syndrome.
questions.question: Erb's palsy results from injury to which nerve roots?

questions.explanation: A minor anomaly is a structural difference of no significant medical consequence in isolation (e.g., single palmar crease, ear pit, clinodactyly). However, multiple minor anomalies co-occurring in the same individual significantly increase the probability of an underlying major anomaly or genetic syndrome. The threshold commonly used is three or more minor anomalies, which warrants systematic evaluation for an associated major defect.
options: Minor alone; significant if multiple coexist
A defect involving a vital organ
A chromosomal deletion detectable on FISH only
An anomaly requiring genetic counselling exclusively
questions.question: In dysmorphology assessment, the term 'minor anomaly' implies:

questions.explanation: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia presents with a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen (bowel in thorax), breath sounds heard in the chest, mediastinal shift away from the lesion, and severe respiratory distress. It is a surgical emergency.
questions.question: A diaphragmatic hernia in a neonate typically presents with which combination of findings?
options: Abdominal distension, absent breath sounds, bradycardia
Scaphoid abdomen, chest breath sounds, distress

questions.explanation: Maternal pre-eclampsia, placental insufficiency, and oligohydramnios are associated with increased risk of foetal distress and meconium passage in utero, which can lead to MAS. Foetal distress causes intestinal hyperperistalsis and relaxation of the anal sphincter leading to meconium passage. Maternal drug abuse (especially tobacco and cocaine) also promotes in utero meconium passage.
questions.question: Which maternal factor is associated with increased risk of meconium passage in utero?

questions.explanation: The APGAR score assesses five components: Appearance (colour), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration (respiratory effort). Blood glucose is not part of the APGAR score but is separately monitored in neonates at risk of hypoglycaemia. Each component is scored 0-2 giving a maximum total of 10.
questions.question: The APGAR score is assessed at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Which of the following is NOT one of the five components?

courses.title: Pharmacology II

questions.question:
Classification of target organ toxicity.
(a) Classify organ-specific toxic effects and describe the main forms for each.
(b) Explain the pharmacological basis of the susceptibility of the liver, kidney and nervous system.
(c) Distinguish between hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity (and neurotoxicity).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Types: blood/vascular, dermal, ocular, genetic, hepatic, immune, renal, nervous, reproductive and respiratory toxicity.
