• Blood and cardiovascular: carbon monoxide hypoxia (affinity for haemoglobin 200 times that of oxygen), chloramphenicol leucopenia, benzene leukaemia, cardiac cell death from anticancer drugs.
• Hepatotoxicity forms: steatosis, chemical hepatitis, necrosis, cholestasis, hepatic cancer, cirrhosis, hypersensitivity. Nervous: neuronopathies, axonopathies, demyelination, interference with neurotransmission.
• Respiratory: irritation, asthma/bronchitis, emphysema, allergic alveolitis, fibrosis, pneumoconiosis, lung cancer; reproductive: infertility, abortion, birth defects; immune: hypersensitivity, immunodeficiency.
(b)
• The liver has a large blood supply, high metabolic capacity and clears xenobiotics, so it faces high doses of toxicants and toxic metabolites.
• The kidney receives a high volume of blood flow and filters and concentrates toxins; its excretory function makes it vulnerable to metals.
• Nervous system vulnerability: cell-specific injury (triethyltin demyelination, methylmercury hippocampal damage), bupivacaine reducing neural perfusion; elevated intracellular calcium and free radicals.
• Eye: methanol damages optic nerves, corticosteroids cause cataracts, acids and alkalis corrode the cornea.
(c)
• Hepatotoxicity involves liver, bile duct and gall bladder, diagnosed by clinical pathology and histopathology.
• Nephrotoxicity reduces waste excretion, fluid and electrolyte balance, erythropoietin synthesis and pH balance.
• Neurotoxicity damages CNS and peripheral nerves; the CNS is the target organ most frequently involved in systemic effects.
• Peripheral neuropathy occurs with isoniazid, ototoxicity with aminoglycosides, furosemide and salicylates.

(a)
• Direct-acting agonists bind cholinergic receptors: acetylcholine, carbachol, pilocarpine, bethanechol.
• Indirect-acting agents inhibit cholinesterase (physostigmine, pyridostigmine, neostigmine, donepezil); reversible ones bind for minutes to hours, irreversible ones form a permanent covalent bond.
(b)
They mimic ACh, acting directly on receptors or indirectly by inhibiting the enzyme that degrades ACh; at low doses mainly muscarinic, at high doses nicotinic receptors are stimulated.
(c)
Effects: increased gastric secretion, GI motility and urinary frequency; miosis; reduced intraocular pressure; increased salivation and sweating; decreased heart rate; vasodilation.
(d)
• Carbachol and pilocarpine treat glaucoma and lower pressure in eye surgery; pilocarpine treats dry mouth; bethanechol raises bladder and GI tone.
• Pyridostigmine and physostigmine treat myasthenia gravis; physostigmine reverses anticholinergic poisoning; donepezil treats mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; ACh agents reverse muscle relaxants.
(e)
• Adverse effects reflect widespread muscarinic stimulation: bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, abdominal cramps, increased secretions, nausea, vomiting, lacrimation, sweating, salivation, bronchial secretions.
• Central and other effects: headache, dizziness, convulsions, loss of binocular accommodation; ocular ACh effects include corneal swelling and clouding.
• Limitations: antihistamines antagonize cholinergic agents; pilocarpine and cevimeline are limited by lack of selectivity.
(f)
• Pilocarpine: tertiary alkaloid, uncharged, stable to AChE, muscarinic, penetrates the CNS; used for glaucoma and xerostomia.
• Carbachol: carbamic acid ester, quaternary, poor AChE substrate, muscarinic and nicotinic (releases epinephrine), rarely used, little systemic penetration in the eye.
• Bethanechol: unsubstituted carbamoyl ester, muscarinic only because of its beta-methyl, selective for bladder and GI tract, about 1 hour duration.
questions.question:
For cholinergic agonists (parasympathomimetics):
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanism of action.
(c) State their pharmacological effects.
(d) State their therapeutic uses.
(e) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(f) Distinguish between pilocarpine, carbachol and bethanechol.

A patient has fatigue, pallor and shortness of breath, with large immature red cells in the bone marrow, a lack of intrinsic factor and neurological defects (pernicious anaemia).
(a) State the first-line drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on mechanism and pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the adverse effects.
(d) State the alternative agent and when it is not suitable.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin, equivalent effects) by parenteral replacement; monthly injections usually produce a response.
(b)
• Vitamin B12, a cobalt-containing molecule, is with folic acid a cofactor in DNA synthesis; deficiency shows first as anaemia because red cells are produced continuously.
• Deficiency anaemia is almost always caused by inadequate absorption (lack of intrinsic factor, gastric resection), so parenteral replacement is used.
• Deficiency can cause neurologic defects that become irreversible if untreated; about 3-4 micrograms daily is adequate.
(c)
Neither form has significant toxicity.
(d)
• Folic acid, also needed for DNA synthesis, treats anaemia from dietary insufficiency or malabsorption and is given orally.
• Folic acid corrects the anaemia but not the neurologic deficits of B12 deficiency, so B12 deficiency must be ruled out before folic acid is used alone.
• Folic acid is absorbed in the ileum, has no recognised toxicity, and supplementation before and during pregnancy lowers neural tube defect risk.

(a)
• Succinylcholine is a rapid-acting, rapid-recovery muscle relaxant; usual paralysis lasts 2 to 6 min but an occasional patient is paralysed for hours.
• The cause was identified as an 'atypical' plasma (serum) cholinesterase; normally succinylcholine is hydrolysed by pseudocholinesterase to succinylmonocholine and choline.
(b)
• Genetic variants of human serum cholinesterase (a single gene locus) alter its metabolism of succinylcholine; this is an idiosyncratic, genetically determined reaction.
• Atypical cholinesterase occurs in homozygous form in about 1 in 3500 Caucasians.
• It carries a single substitution at nucleotide 209 that changes aspartic acid 70 to glycine.
• Reduced affinity for succinylcholine means none is hydrolysed in blood, so a large overdose reaches the nerve-muscle junction and causes prolonged paralysis with apnoea.
(c)
Prevention: pharmacogenetics aims at dose optimisation and avoidance of adverse reactions by using the patient's genetic make-up.
questions.question:
A patient given the muscle relaxant succinylcholine stays paralysed and apnoeic for hours instead of the usual few minutes.
(a) Identify the cause and the drug-metabolising defect responsible.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) State how the problem can be prevented.

For haematopoietic growth factors:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at receptor level (target cells and receptors).
(b) State how the members relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Erythropoietin, produced by the kidney, activates receptors on erythroid progenitors in bone marrow, stimulating red cell production and release; reduced synthesis underlies the anaemia of renal failure.
• Filgrastim (G-CSF) and sargramostim (GM-CSF) stimulate production and function of neutrophils; GM-CSF also stimulates other myeloid and megakaryocyte progenitors.
• Oprelvekin (IL-11) stimulates primitive megakaryocytic progenitors; romiplostim and eltrombopag are thrombopoietin receptor agonists.
• Haematopoiesis occurs mainly in bone marrow and needs vitamin B12, iron and erythropoietin (erythrocyte factors), oprelvekin (platelet factor), and G-CSF and GM-CSF (granulocyte factors).
(b)
• ESAs (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin, methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta) treat anaemia of renal failure and anaemias with cancer chemotherapy, HIV, bone marrow transplantation or bone marrow disorders.
• G-CSF and GM-CSF speed neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy, treat neutropenias, reduce time to engraftment after autologous transplant and mobilize stem cells (with plerixafor, a CXCR4 inhibitor).
• Oprelvekin reduces platelet transfusions after chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia; romiplostim (subcutaneous) and eltrombopag (oral) treat chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenia.
• Pegfilgrastim and darbepoetin have much longer half-lives.
(c)
• ESA complications are hypertension and thrombosis; keep haemoglobin at or below 12 g/dL because higher levels raise mortality and cardiovascular events.
• G-CSF toxicity is minimal (bone pain); GM-CSF causes fever, arthralgias, capillary damage with oedema; allergic reactions are rare.
• Oprelvekin: fatigue, headache, dizziness, fluid retention.
• Eltrombopag use is restricted by hepatotoxicity and haemorrhage risk.

(a)
• Nicotine (from Nicotiana tabacum) is a tertiary amine; lobeline (from Lobelia inflata) has similar actions but is less potent.
• Nicotine is readily absorbed from the respiratory tract, buccal membranes and skin, and efficiently from the intestine.
• Chewing tobacco is absorbed more slowly than inhaled nicotine and so has a longer duration of effect.
• Elimination is mainly by the kidney and is diminished if urine is alkaline; it is excreted in milk.
• Half-life after inhalation or parenteral administration is about 2 hours.
(b)
• Nicotine is available as gum, nasal spray and transdermal patch to help achieve abstinence from tobacco.
• Efficacy results mainly from preventing a withdrawal or abstinence syndrome; varenicline, a synthetic agonist selective for CNS receptors, is also used.
• Nicotine is the only ganglion stimulant with a therapeutic use (smoking addiction).
(c)
• Nicotine stimulates then depresses all autonomic ganglia, with net effects on heart rate and other systems depending on summation of stimulatory and inhibitory actions; it also causes neuromuscular block by desensitization.
• In the CNS low doses give analgesia, large doses stimulation then depression; death results from respiratory failure from central paralysis and peripheral muscle blockade.
• Vomiting results from central (chemoreceptor trigger zone) and peripheral actions.
• Pleasure-reward and dependence relate to release of excitatory amino acids, dopamine and other biogenic amines.
questions.question:
For nicotine:
(a) Describe its pharmacokinetics.
(b) State its dosing considerations and clinical use.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of its toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic; ototoxicity occurs with aminoglycosides, furosemide and salicylates.
(b)
• Gentamicin accumulates in the internal ear and kidney, damaging them when used at high concentration over a long period.
• It is highly ionised and hydrophilic, restricted largely to extracellular fluid (Vd about 15 L).
• The kidney is vulnerable because of high blood flow and because it filters and concentrates toxicants.
• Renal failure lowers clearance, so drugs are retained for longer and toxic effects result.
(c)
Prevention: use appropriate dose, route and frequency, check history of reaction and interactions; dose adjustment is required for narrow therapeutic index drugs in liver or kidney disease.
questions.question:
A patient on prolonged high-dose gentamicin develops damage to the inner ear and kidney.
(a) Identify the causative drug and class.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State how the toxicity can be prevented.

A patient chronically taking rifampin takes paracetamol and is at risk of liver injury.
(a) State the risk factors for toxicity.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, St John's wort and chronic alcohol intake are enzyme inducers.
• The liver is highly susceptible to xenobiotics because of its large blood supply and metabolic role.
(b)
• Enzyme induction speeds metabolism of the substrate drug; where a drug yields reactive metabolites it may worsen metabolite-mediated tissue toxicity.
• Paracetamol is an example of a drug with a highly toxic metabolite.
• Acetaminophen is also conjugated with glucuronic acid, sulfate and glutathione.
• Forms of hepatotoxicity include steatosis, hepatitis, necrosis, cholestasis and cirrhosis.

questions.question:
Pharmacokinetics of drug absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
(a) Describe the mechanisms of transport across membranes and the factors affecting absorption.
(b) Explain the pH-partition hypothesis, its limits, bioavailability and first-pass effect.
(c) State the dosing considerations and interactions.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Four mechanisms: passive diffusion (most drugs, down gradient; lipid-soluble drugs by lipid:water partition coefficient), facilitated diffusion (carrier, no energy, saturable), active transport (against gradient, energy, saturable, selective), pinocytosis (large substances).
• Physiological factors: gastric pH 1-3 versus intestinal 5-8, blood flow, surface area (villi and microvilli), gastric emptying, motility, food, disease state and age.
• Physicochemical factors: solubility, particle size (smaller dissolves faster), dosage form (solutions and suspensions faster than capsules or tablets) and ionisation state.
(b)
• Weak acids (aspirin, acetaminophen, levodopa) and weak bases (pyrimethamine, atropine, diazepam) follow Henderson-Hasselbalch: at pH = pKa half is ionised.
• pH-partition: only the unionised lipid-soluble form crosses; in the acidic stomach weak acids (aspirin) are absorbed while weak bases (pyrimethamine) are ionised and poorly absorbed.
• Limit: the small intestine's very large surface area overrides ionisation, so acids are still well absorbed there and quaternary ammonium compounds are absorbed despite being ionised.
• Bioavailability is the fraction reaching the circulation unchanged (IV = 100%); oral drugs lose dose to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism in gut wall and liver.
(c)
• Where first pass is extensive a much larger oral dose is needed than a parenteral dose, or another route (IV, IM, SC, sublingual) is used, e.g. insulin, morphine, pentazocine, glyceryl trinitrate.
• Food slows gastric emptying and lowers absorption of many drugs; milk retards tetracycline while fatty meals enhance artemether-lumefantrine; diarrhoea cuts absorption.
• Monitoring: drug concentrations are determined during therapy to adjust the regimen; AUC reflects extent and tmax reflects rate of absorption.
(d)
• Very poor bioavailability from extensive pre-systemic metabolism causes therapeutic failure; slow gastric emptying exposes drugs to degradation, and gastric acid destroys penicillin.
• Digestive enzymes destroy polypeptides such as insulin; emesis and low solubility also limit absorption.

(a)
Triple therapy for 14 days: a proton pump inhibitor plus clarithromycin 500 mg plus metronidazole 500 mg, amoxicillin 1 g or tetracycline, twice daily; first-line in areas of low clarithromycin resistance.
(b)
• Eradication of H. pylori is standard care in gastric or duodenal ulcers.
• PPIs (omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole) are prodrugs activated in acid that bind cysteine sulfhydryl groups of the H+/K+-ATPase irreversibly; acid secretion resumes only after new pumps are made (24-48 hours).
• Give about 30 minutes before meals; rapidly absorbed, highly protein bound, metabolized by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4; 2-5 days of once-daily dosing reach about 70% inhibition.
(c)
• Adverse effects: nausea, abdominal pain, constipation, flatulence, diarrhoea, subacute myopathy, arthralgias, headache, rash.
• Interactions: warfarin, diazepam, cyclosporin; omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and induces CYP1A2; lost acidity reduces absorption of ketoconazole, ampicillin esters, iron salts and calcium (hip fractures).
• In severe hepatic disease esomeprazole and lansoprazole clearance falls and dose reduction is recommended.
(d)
Non-bismuth quadruple, bismuth-based and levofloxacin-containing regimens; H2 blockers, misoprostol, sucralfate and bismuth are other agents.
questions.question:
A patient has dull gnawing abdominal pain relieved by eating and antacids, and has a duodenal ulcer with Helicobacter pylori infection.
(a) State the first-line drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on mechanism and pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects and interactions.
(d) State the alternative or second-line regimens and when they are preferred.

A child living in a home with deteriorating lead paint is found to have a blood lead concentration of 20 microgram/dL or greater.
(a) State the risk factors for lead toxicity and the circumstances of exposure.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity.
(c) Outline management, including the antidote.
(d) Justify the preferred management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Today the largest source of lead poisoning in children is dust and chips from deteriorating lead paint; playing on bare contaminated soil also raises blood lead.
• Absorption in children may exceed 50% (adults absorb 35-50% through drinking water); lead crosses the placenta to the fetus.
• Other sources: leaded gasoline, plumbing/food cans, crystals and ceramics, traditional medicines and cosmetics, workplace and hobbies.
(b)
• Lead inhibits or mimics calcium, replaces calcium in bone, binds sulfhydryl and amide groups of enzymes and competes with essential cations.
• It generates reactive oxygen species and disrupts calcium-dependent neuronal signalling; haemoglobin biosynthesis is disrupted giving anaemia.
• The nervous system is the most vulnerable target (lower IQ, impaired neurobehavioural development, poor attention).
(c)
• EDTA is given as a chelating drug for lead poisoning; it acts chemically without a receptor.
• Exposure control: lead removed from gasoline, paint and cans, children screened, housing abated.
(d)
Lead is redistributed from liver to its storage site in bone within a month, and dust re-contaminates cleaned houses, so chelation plus source removal is needed.

questions.question:
A patient with a stomach ulcer is treated with omeprazole plus amoxicillin.
(a) Name the drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the genetic test that can guide therapy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, lansoprazole) are used to treat acid reflux and stomach ulcers.
• H. pylori is associated with gastric ulcer in 70% and duodenal ulcer in 90%.
(b)
• Omeprazole is metabolised by CYP2C19; omeprazole is also a CYP2C19 inhibitor and rifampicin as an inducer.
• Ulcer cure rates with omeprazole plus amoxicillin by CYP2C19 phenotype: rapid metabolisers 28.6%, intermediate 60%, poor 100%.
(c)
CYP2C19 genotype can be identified by the AmpliChip P450 test to aid therapeutic strategy and dose.

(a)
• Succinylcholine (suxamethonium), a depolarizing blocker, in a patient with a genetic variant of serum (plasma) cholinesterase.
• Carriers of such variants respond abnormally, with substantial prolongation of paralysis and apnoea.
(b)
• Atypical cholinesterase: single substitution at nucleotide 209, changing aspartic acid 70 to glycine.
• Silent cholinesterase: frame-shift mutation at glycine 117 gives no active enzyme; K variant: threonine in place of alanine 539, about 33% lower activity; all arise from a single locus.
• Succinylcholine is normally hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase (action under 5 minutes); when it is not hydrolysed in blood, a large dose reaches the neuromuscular junction and causes prolonged paralysis.
• Its action is also prolonged by various factors that reduce plasma cholinesterase activity.
• Phase I block is augmented, not reversed, by cholinesterase inhibitors; later phase II resembles non-depolarizing block and is reversed by them.
(c)
Pharmacogenetic disorders may not be recognised until the drug is given.
questions.question:
After intravenous succinylcholine for surgical relaxation, a patient remains paralysed with apnoea far longer than the usual 2-6 minutes.
(a) Identify the causative drug and the likely cause of the reaction.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) State why the problem may go unrecognised until the drug is given.

Pharmacokinetics of drug distribution.
(a) Describe the determinants of distribution, plasma and tissue binding, barriers and the volume of distribution.
(b) State the dosing considerations, interactions and monitoring.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity and therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Distribution is movement from blood to tissues and site of action; highly perfused organs (heart, brain, liver, kidney) receive drug first, then muscle, skin and fat.
• Albumin binds acidic drugs and alpha-1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs; binding is reversible and only free drug produces effect.
• Tissue reservoirs: fat (thiopental), bone and teeth (tetracycline and heavy metals); fat is a stable depot because of low blood flow.
• Barriers: the blood-brain barrier is crossed by lipophilic diazepam; penicillin crosses only when meningeal inflammation disrupts it; the placenta is also a barrier.
• Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration; Vd of 3 L means plasma only (heparin), 15 L ECF (gentamicin), 42 L total body water (phenytoin), above 42 L tissue accumulation (digoxin).
(b)
• Vd is used to calculate a loading dose, while clearance is used for maintenance dose.
• Displacement from protein binding by compounds with higher affinity is a source of important drug interactions.
• Vd is lower than expected in obesity and larger in oedema; hypoalbuminaemia, heart failure and cirrhosis alter distribution.
• Monitoring: plasma drug concentrations are recorded during therapy to adjust the regimen.
(c)
• Excessive protein binding slows reaching the site and elimination, prolonging action; hypoalbuminaemia in severe liver disease raises unbound drug and side effects.
• Gentamicin accumulating in inner ear and kidney damages them; thiopental stored in fat sedates an obese person longer than a lean one.
• Tissue binding is a reservoir that prolongs action at the site or a distant site.

(a)
• Bleeding is the chief complication of heparin and LMWH; in blood heparin binds many proteins, causing unpredictable pharmacokinetics.
• Contraindications: hypersensitivity, bleeding disorders, alcoholism, recent surgery of the brain, eye or spinal cord.
• Renal insufficiency prolongs LMWH half-life, so dose reduction is needed.
(b)
• Heparin binds antithrombin III, a conformational change catalyzing thrombin inhibition about 1000-fold and inactivating factor Xa, so fibrin formation is prevented.
• The effect is monitored with aPTT or anti-Xa level; LMWHs usually need no coagulation monitoring.
(c)
Discontinue the drug, or treat with protamine sulfate.
(d)
• Protamine combines ionically with heparin when infused slowly, forming a stable 1:1 inactive complex.
• Titrate carefully (1 mg per 100 units of heparin) because protamine is a weak anticoagulant and excess may trigger or worsen bleeding.
questions.question:
A patient on heparin for acute venous thromboembolism develops excessive bleeding.
(a) Identify the risk factors for the toxicity.
(b) Explain the mechanism of heparin action and of the bleeding.
(c) State the management, including the antidote.
(d) Justify the preferred option and its precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
L-dopa is an example of replacement as a principle of drug action (replacement in Parkinsonism).
(b)
Levodopa is converted to active dopamine in basal ganglia nerve terminals; it is an inactive precursor (prodrug).
(c)
• It is absorbed from the GIT and crosses the blood-brain barrier via a transport mechanism.
• Levodopa is a weak acid.
questions.question:
A patient with Parkinsonism is prescribed levodopa.
(a) State the principle of drug action indicated.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Nystagmus is a nervous-system adverse effect of phenytoin; ataxia occurs with streptomycin, phenytoin and lithium.
(b)
• Phenytoin is a weak acid, relatively lipid-soluble (Vd about 42 L, well distributed) and an enzyme inducer; it is a CYP2C9 substrate (aromatic hydroxylation).
• The organ system affected is the nervous system.
(c)
• Differential causes of ataxia: streptomycin and lithium; other nervous-system effects include convulsions (isoniazid, lignocaine) and extrapyramidal symptoms (chlorpromazine, metoclopramide).
• Dicumarol and disulfiram inhibit phenytoin metabolism; sodium valproate, isoniazid, cimetidine and chloramphenicol are listed CYP inhibitors.
(d)
• Inhibition of metabolism raises concentration and adverse effects, while inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, barbiturates) lower it.
• Liver disease, age and enzyme changes alter metabolism, and narrow therapeutic index drugs need dose adjustment.
questions.question:
A patient taking phenytoin develops ataxia and nystagmus.
(a) Identify the clues and the drug adverse-effect category.
(b) State the enzymes and organ system involved.
(c) List differential drug-related causes.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for a change in therapy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pharmacogenetics studies how a single gene's variation influences drug response; pharmacogenomics studies multiple genes across the genome.
• Determinants include drug targets, drug-metabolising enzymes and drug transporters affecting pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.
• Phase 1 enzymes are the CYPs; phase 2 enzymes include TPMT, NAT and UGTs; transporters include MDR1 (P-glycoprotein) and SerT; receptors include the beta-adrenergic receptor.
(b)
• Imatinib acts on the tyrosine kinase receptor in chronic myeloid leukaemia; trastuzumab acts on HER2 in breast cancer.
• Albuterol (bronchodilator) response depends on the beta-adrenergic receptor genotype.
• Abacavir hypersensitivity is strongly associated with HLA-B*5701; carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN with HLA-B*1502.
• Pharmacogenetics gives dose optimisation, personalised medicine, lower healthcare cost, novel drug development.
(c)
• Abacavir is among drugs known for severe cutaneous reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome; carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN is the HLA-B*1502 example.
• Poor TPMT activity causes bone marrow suppression; G6PD deficiency causes haemolysis; atypical cholinesterase causes prolonged apnoea.
• Slow acetylators on procainamide may develop SLE, while fast acetylators may not benefit from isoniazid or hydralazine.
• 20-40% of patients benefit from an approved drug and 70-80% of drug candidates fail in clinical trials.
questions.question:
Pharmacogenetics of drug targets and hypersensitivity genes (HLA, enzymes and receptors).
(a) Describe how genetic variation affects drug targets, enzymes and transporters.
(b) State how gene-drug pairs relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

For sulfasalazine and mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid compounds):
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics and delivery.
(b) State their dosing considerations and uses.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of their toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• 5-ASA differs from salicylic acid only by an amino group at the 5 (meta) position and acts topically on diseased mucosa; 5-ASA alone is absorbed from the proximal small intestine.
• Azo compounds link 5-ASA by an azo bond to sulfapyridine (sulfasalazine), another 5-ASA (olsalazine) or an inert carrier (balsalazide); the azo structure reduces small intestinal absorption.
• Bacterial azoreductase in the terminal ileum and colon cleaves the bond, releasing 5-ASA there.
• Sulfasalazine is a prodrug given orally with about 10% absorbed; 5-ASA stays in the gut (active); sulfapyridine is absorbed.
• Asacol is 5-ASA coated in pH-sensitive resin dissolving at pH 7; Pentasa uses time-release microgranules releasing 5-ASA through the small intestine.
(b)
• Rectal forms: Canasa (suppositories), Rowasa (enema) for distal ulcerative colitis, proctitis and proctosigmoiditis.
• Uses: first-line induction and maintenance of remission in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease; sulfasalazine also in rheumatoid arthritis.
• Mesalamine formulations are sulfa-free, well tolerated and suit sulfa-sensitive patients; folic acid should be provided with sulfasalazine.
(c)
• Sulfapyridine, the absorbed moiety, accounts for the side effects of sulfasalazine.
• Toxicity: crystalluria, bone marrow depression, megaloblastic anaemia from folic acid deficiency, male oligospermia.
• 5-ASA itself causes interstitial nephritis.
• Anti-inflammatory action: inhibition of prostaglandins and leukotrienes, reduced neutrophil chemotaxis, antioxidant.

(a)
Codeine is used for cough and for analgesia.
(b)
It requires activation by CYP2D6 to exert its analgesic effect.
(c)
• CYP2D6 metabolises codeine (O-dealkylation is a phase I oxidative reaction); over 100 CYP2D6 polymorphisms give ultrarapid, extensive and poor metabolisers.
• Because of genetic polymorphism, 2-10% of the population cannot metabolise codeine and are resistant to its analgesic effect.
• In poor metabolisers failure to convert to the active metabolite (morphine) may cause lack of efficacy, unlike other CYP2D6 substrates where poor metabolisers have more adverse effects.
• CYP2D6 inhibitors: paroxetine, quinidine; inducers: rifampicin, dexamethasone.
(d)
• Constipation is a side effect of codeine (therapeutic in diarrhoea).
• CYP2D6 genotyping (e.g. AmpliChip test) may aid therapeutic strategy and dose.
questions.question:
A patient is given codeine and the adequacy of pain relief is found to differ between individuals on the same uniform dose.
(a) Identify the drug and its indication.
(b) State how it is activated to exert its analgesic effect.
(c) Describe the pharmacokinetic basis of the variable response.
(d) State the adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index with numerous interactions; INR is the standard for monitoring.
• CYP2C9 inhibitors that raise bleeding risk include amiodarone, azole antifungals, cimetidine, clopidogrel, cotrimoxazole, disulfiram, fluoxetine, isoniazid, metronidazole, sulfinpyrazone, tolcapone and zafirlukast.
• Other risks: displacement from albumin by sulfonamides; antibiotics that remove gut flora (they synthesize vitamin K) raise INR; hepatic impairment, heart failure and hyperthyroidism enhance the effect.
(b)
• Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X, leaving factors with 10-40% of normal activity.
• Inhibition of its CYP2C9 metabolism raises warfarin effect; peak effect is delayed 72-96 hours until circulating factors are depleted.
(c)
• Minor bleeding: withdraw the drug or give oral vitamin K.
• Severe bleeding: larger intravenous vitamin K doses; whole blood, frozen plasma or plasma concentrates of blood factors for rapid reversal.
(d)
Vitamin K reversal takes about 24 hours, the time needed to degrade already synthesized clotting factors, so plasma or factor concentrates are used when rapid reversal is needed.
questions.question:
A patient stabilized on warfarin is given a new drug, such as metronidazole or an azole antifungal, and presents with bleeding and a raised INR.
(a) Identify the interaction and the risk factors.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the interaction.
(c) State the management, including the antidote.
(d) Justify the preferred management option.

For ganglion-acting drugs:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at the ganglionic nicotinic receptor level (blockers and stimulants).
(b) State how members relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The primary receptors at autonomic ganglia are nicotinic cholinergic receptors; ganglion blockers reduce transmission in all ganglia, sympathetic and parasympathetic, and uncover the predominant system at each tissue.
• They act by interfering with ACh release, prolonged depolarization or interfering with the post-synaptic action of ACh.
• Depolarizing ganglion blockers (nicotine, large dose) give initial stimulation then block; competitive blockers include the quaternary amines hexamethonium and chlorisondamine, the secondary amine mecamylamine, and trimetaphan.
• Examples: tetraethylammonium, mecamylamine, hexamethonium, trimetaphan, pentolinium, pempidine; ganglion stimulants include nicotine and lobeline (tertiary amines) and tetramethylammonium.
(b)
• Trimetaphan: short-acting, IV, histamine liberator, used in hypertensive emergency and for controlled hypotension in surgery; mecamylamine (a secondary amine) was introduced for hypertension and is the only one currently available in the US.
• Ganglion blockers have been supplanted by better agents for chronic hypertension and by nitroprusside for controlled hypotension; their clinical use is obsolete.
• Nicotine is used in gum, nasal spray and patch to prevent withdrawal in tobacco abstinence; varenicline is a CNS-selective agonist for nicotine addiction.
• Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release in autonomic ganglia.
(c)
• Blockade effects: arterioles and veins (vasodilation), heart (tachycardia), iris (mydriasis), ciliary muscle (cycloplegia), GIT (hypomotility), bladder (urinary retention), salivary glands (xerostomia), sweat glands (anhidrosis).
• Adverse reactions: visual disturbance, dry mouth, constipation, postural hypotension and syncope; severe: marked hypotension, paralytic ileus, urinary retention, cycloplegia.
• Nicotine first stimulates then depresses all ganglia, stimulates the CNS and induces vomiting via the chemoreceptor trigger zone.
• Large doses of nicotine cause death through respiratory failure.

questions.question:
Pharmacodynamics of receptors and other drug targets.
(a) Describe the receptor types and their speed and signalling mechanisms.
(b) State how enzymes, ion channels and receptors relate to specific drug examples.
(c) Explain why drugs may act without receptors and why effects may extend to other organ systems.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A receptor is a biomolecule, generally a protein, that responds to binding of a ligand (neurotransmitter, hormone) to produce a physiological change.
• Ligand-gated channels (nicotinic, GABA): protein subunits forming a central pore; fastest, milliseconds.
• G-protein coupled receptors: seven membrane-spanning helices linked to a second messenger; seconds, e.g. beta-adrenoceptor with cAMP.
• Enzyme-linked receptors (insulin, growth factors, cytokines): intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; slow; cell growth and inflammatory mediator release.
• Intracellular (nuclear) receptors for thyroid and steroid hormones: very slow, usually hours.
(b)
• Targets: enzymes (Na/K-ATPase; ACE inhibitors), ion channels (quinidine on Na+; nifedipine on L-type Ca2+), receptors (GPCRs, nuclear receptors).
• Cited target shares: cellular receptors 52%, enzymes 28%, hormones and factors 11%, DNA 2%, unknown 7%.
(c)
• Drugs acting without a receptor: antacids, EDTA, cholestyramine, activated charcoal, mannitol, Mg(OH)2.
• Receptors are also free-floating enzymes (trypsin, thrombin), DNA/RNA (cisplatin) and cell-surface carbohydrates.
• Adverse effects arise from untargeted receptors (lateral or parallel stimulation), e.g. constipation from morphine and GI irritation from NSAIDs.
• Receptors adapt: down-regulation with agonists causes tolerance; up-regulation with antagonists causes rebound.

questions.question:
Pharmacodynamic drug interactions at the receptor and effector level.
(a) Describe antagonism, additive effect, potentiation and synergism.
(b) State how drug pairs relate to specific outcomes.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antagonism: one drug opposes another's effect, whether at the receptor (competitive/non-competitive) or physiologically or chemically.
• Additive: effects sum, as with H1 antihistamine (mepyramine) and alcohol worsening drowsiness.
• Potentiation: chloroquine effect increased by chlorpheniramine.
• Synergism: sequential blockade by sulphamethoxazole and trimethoprim; gentamicin and ampicillin for Gram-negative bacilli.
(b)
• Antagonism examples: salbutamol versus propranolol; tricyclic antidepressants versus guanethidine; NSAIDs versus beta-blockers, diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
• Mechanism of NSAID antagonism: NSAIDs inhibit PGE2 and PGI2 secretion.
• Agonist plus partial agonist: the partial agonist competes with the full agonist.
(c)
• Drug effects extend because receptors in several organs are shared; sedative-hypnotics cause daytime somnolence, antihypertensives orthostatic hypotension.
• NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis by cyclooxygenase-1 inhibition, so GI mucosa loses protection and gastric secretion rises, causing ulcers.
• Rebound hypertension follows abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal; up-regulation contributes.
• Special precautions: check interactions and history of reactions; the multi-drug and elderly populations have more adverse effects.

questions.question:
A worker exposed to an insecticide develops profuse sweating, salivation, lacrimation, increased bronchial secretions, vomiting, miosis, abdominal cramps, bradycardia, hypotension, involuntary urination and defecation, muscle twitching and fasciculations, followed by confusion and convulsions.
(a) Identify the type of agent responsible and the properties that increase its toxicity.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the toxicity.
(c) Outline the management, including the antidotes.
(d) Justify the preferred antidote combination and state its limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• An organophosphate irreversible anticholinesterase; these form irreversible bonds with AChE and also block trypsin and thrombin.
• Organophosphates are highly lipid soluble (echothiophate is polar) and penetrate the CNS rapidly; they are used as pesticides and as nerve gases (tabun, sarin, soman).
(b)
• Covalent attachment to the esteratic site gives phosphorylated AChE, followed by aging; ACh accumulates at synapses and causes toxic effects.
• Muscarinic effects: sweating, salivation, lacrimation, secretions, bronchospasm, vomiting, miosis, cramps, hypotension, bradycardia, urination and defecation.
• Nicotinic effects: twitching, fasciculations, weakness, paralysis. Central effects: restlessness, confusion, convulsions, coma, death from respiratory failure.
(c)
• Remove the victim from exposure; decontaminate; gastric lavage; give atropine; give pralidoxime or obidoxime; resuscitate; artificial ventilation; anticonvulsants.
• Atropine antagonizes the muscarinic effects: given early, in larger dose and repeated.
• Oximes (pralidoxime, obidoxime, methoxime) reactivate phosphorylated AChE through the oxime group and rapidly reactivate the enzyme at neuromuscular junctions.
(d)
• Atropine blocks muscarinic effects while the oxime restores enzyme activity; oximes are used in moderate-severe cases, early, with a larger dose of atropine, and are more effective on tremor.
• Limitations: ineffective against aged phosphorylated AChE; central reactions if given IV above 500 mg/min; iodine toxicity; overdose inhibits AChE.

(a)
• Arginine vasopressin (ADH) stimulates water reabsorption in distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts, reducing urine volume.
• This is mediated by V2-type receptors on the tubular cell surface leading to intracellular cAMP.
• Release is influenced by plasma osmolarity and by blood volume and arterial pressure (baroreceptor stretch normally inhibits secretion).
• Release also rises with severe pain, fear, nausea, general anaesthesia and nicotine, morphine and other opiates, angiotensin II, prostaglandin E2 and noradrenaline.
(b)
• Hyposecretion (hypothalamic damage or tumour) causes diabetes insipidus; hypersecretion causes SIADH.
• Oxytocin stimulates rhythmic uterine smooth muscle contraction in childbirth (contributing to but not essential for labour) and milk ejection on suckling.
• Oxytocin release follows sensory stimulation of the nipple and uterus; its disorders are rarely encountered.
(c)
• In large quantities AVP acts directly as a vasoconstrictor on blood vessels.
• SIADH can arise from ectopic AVP-secreting tumours (malignant bronchial neoplasm), severe pneumonia or acute bronchitis, head injury and brain lesions.
• SIADH may also arise from antidepressant or antipsychotic therapy (fluoxetine, sertraline, imipramine, amitriptyline, haloperidol).
• In advanced HIV disease, hyponatraemia may be due to SIADH, usually with pulmonary or CNS disease.
questions.question:
Pharmacodynamics of the posterior pituitary hormones (vasopressin and oxytocin).
(a) Describe their actions at receptor level and control of release.
(b) State how each hormone relates to specific disorders.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

A patient takes a tricyclic antidepressant and needs pupillary dilation for funduscopic examination; narrow anterior chamber angles are found.
(a) Identify the drug classes that dilate the pupil and their mechanisms.
(b) State the receptors and tissues of the eye involved.
(c) State the drug-related causes of altered pupil size or pressure.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for the choice of drug in this and other patients.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mydriatics are sympathomimetic agents (epinephrine, phenylephrine; indirect cocaine, hydroxyamphetamine) and cholinergic antagonists (atropine, scopolamine, homatropine, tropicamide, cyclopentolate).
(b)
Iris dilator muscle: alpha-1 receptors (active mydriasis); iris sphincter and ciliary muscle: M3 receptors (blockade gives passive mydriasis and cycloplegia); ciliary epithelium: beta-2 receptors secrete aqueous humour.
(c)
• Topical sympathomimetics dilate the pupil; topical parasympathomimetics constrict it; oral or intravenous opioids give pin-point pupils.
• Mydriatics can raise intraocular pressure and precipitate closed-angle glaucoma in narrow angles.
(d)
• Contraindications: closed-angle glaucoma, Down's syndrome, pregnancy; phenylephrine should not be used with reserpine, tricyclic antidepressants or MAO inhibitors.
• Tropicamide: fastest onset, shortest duration, little cycloplegia, drug of choice for routine dilation; cyclopentolate: faster cycloplegia, used for cycloplegic refraction, often in children.
• Atropine: most potent, long acting, used when complete cycloplegia is required; homatropine: weak, prolonged, standard for anterior uveitis; scopolamine: reserved for patients allergic to other agents, more CNS effects.

(a)
• Beta-1, beta-2 and beta-3 receptors all stimulate Gs, activate adenylyl cyclase and raise cAMP.
• Beta-1 receptors are in heart and kidney: increased force (inotropy) and rate (chronotropy), and renin release.
• Beta-2 receptors in smooth muscle, liver and skeletal muscle: cAMP and PKA phosphorylate and inactivate myosin light chain kinase, giving relaxation; K+ efflux hyperpolarizes bronchial smooth muscle.
• Beta-2 receptors also raise plasma glucose in liver, stimulate muscle glycogenolysis and K+ uptake; beta-3 receptors in adipose tissue stimulate lipolysis.
(b)
• Beta-1 agonist dobutamine: increases output without much rate rise in cardiac failure; beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol) treat asthma and COPD; ritodrine treats premature labour.
• Beta-blockers treat angina, hypertension, arrhythmias, heart failure, pheochromocytoma, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, migraine prophylaxis, variceal bleeding.
• Beta-3 agonists include mirabegron and vibegron.
(c)
• Beta-blocker effects: bradycardia, reduced contractility and cardiac output, slowed AV conduction, bronchoconstriction (asthma, COPD), prolonged hypoglycaemia (diabetics), raised LDL and triglycerides, lower HDL, hypokalaemia.
• Other adverse effects: fatigue, insomnia, nightmares, sexual dysfunction in men.
• Beta-2 agonists cause headache, anxiety, nausea, tremor, nervousness and palpitations, reduced by inhalation.
• Caution with cardiovascular disease; avoid use in Prinzmetal angina.
• Effects depend on the degree of sympathoadrenal tone.
questions.question:
For beta-adrenoceptors:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at receptor level (subtypes and signalling).
(b) State how agonists and antagonists relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Routes are local (given at the site of action) or systemic; systemic routes are enteral (translingual, buccal, sublingual, oral/peroral, rectal) or parenteral (not via the GI tract).
• Parenteral examples: IV, IM, SC, intra-arterial, epidural, intrathecal, intradermal, intra-articular, intraosseous, intraperitoneal, intracardiac, intralymphatic, intracerebroventricular; inhalation and topical/transdermal routes are also described.
(b)
• Sublingual: quick onset and bypass of portal circulation and first pass (nitroglycerin, buprenorphine). Rectal: usable for GIT-irritant drugs and for patients vomiting or unable to swallow.
• Topical: high local concentration without systemic effect; transdermal patches of lipophilic drugs (fentanyl, nitroglycerin) give slow, long-lasting effect. Inhalation: rapid, large surface area, no hepatic first pass.
• IV: 100% bioavailability (F=1), immediate effect, suited to life-threatening emergencies and highly irritant drugs. IM: rapid, full absorption from rich blood supply, depot injections and suspensions possible.
(c)
• Oral: slow onset; not usable in unconscious patients; limited by low solubility, poor permeability, emesis, digestive enzymes, low gastric pH, food, and metabolism before reaching the general circulation.
• Sublingual: distasteful drugs unsuitable and high-molecular-weight drugs not absorbed. Rectal: unreliable absorption and possible inflammation. Topical: most drugs are large and poorly lipid-soluble; irritation, contact dermatitis, epidermal enzymes.
• Inhalation: irritation, difficulty regulating the dose, transport to site not guaranteed. IM: nerve injury, abscess, painful, small volumes only, aseptic conditions.
• IV: pain, close monitoring, cannot be retrieved once injected, vein patency needed, infection risk, no oily vehicles, no self-medication.
(d)
• Peroral: swallowed and absorbed from the GIT; bioavailability below 100% (food binding, first pass, enzymatic action); cheap, convenient, recovery by lavage possible; effect in 30-90 min.
• Sublingual (oral): absorbed from the mouth cavity, no first pass, rapid absorption, drug stability, but only small doses and unpleasant taste; effect in 3-5 min.
• Choice depends on convenience, state and age of patient, desired onset, the drug (insulin works by one route only), gastric pH, enzymes and first pass.
questions.question:
Routes of drug administration.
(a) Classify the routes into local and systemic, and enteral and parenteral, giving examples.
(b) State the advantages of the sublingual, rectal, topical/transdermal, inhalation, intravenous and intramuscular routes.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of the limitations of the oral, sublingual, rectal, topical, inhalation, intramuscular and intravenous routes.
(d) Distinguish between the peroral and sublingual routes.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Muscarinic receptors are seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors; five types (M1-M5) are found in human cells.
• M1, M3, M5 couple to Gq, stimulating phospholipase C (PIP2 to IP3 and diacylglycerol), raising Ca2+ and activating protein kinase C: excitation.
• M2 and M4 couple to Gi, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase (lower cAMP) and opening K+ channels (GIRKs), lowering Ca2+ conductance and hyperpolarizing the cell: inhibition.
• Activation by ACh gives brief decreases in heart rate; the subtypes are distinguished by antagonists.
(b)
• M1: cortical neurons, autonomic ganglia, gastric and salivary glands; pirenzepine is used for peptic ulcer.
• M2: cardiac muscle (cardiac inhibition); M3: glandular and smooth muscle, GI tract and eye (secretion, contraction, accommodation); M4 and M5: CNS.
• Uses of antimuscarinics: ipratropium/tiotropium in asthma and COPD; oxybutynin and tolterodine in overactive bladder; atropine for bradycardia; hyoscine for motion sickness; benztropine for Parkinsonism.
(c)
• Muscarinic receptors are present in eye, heart, GI tract, bronchi, glands, bladder and CNS, so blockade gives mydriasis and cycloplegia, tachycardia, decreased secretions and motility, urinary retention.
• Atropine in high doses causes excitement, hallucinations and coma; it decreases sweating (fever in infants) and sphincter contraction.
• Precautions: glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, urinary or GI obstruction, infectious diarrhoea, reflux esophagitis, tachyarrhythmias, angina, hyperthyroidism, pregnancy.
• Ocular effect: worsens glaucoma by blocking the iris circular muscle and relaxing the ciliary muscle.
• Because M1, M3, M5 excite and M2, M4 suppress excitability, effects differ across tissues.
questions.question:
For muscarinic receptors:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at receptor level (receptor type and signal transduction of each subtype group).
(b) State how the subtypes relate to specific locations and therapeutic uses of muscarinic antagonists.
(c) Explain why antimuscarinic effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

For antidiarrhoeal drugs:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanisms of action.
(c) State their therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between octreotide and the opioid antimotility agents.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Oral rehydration therapy is the cornerstone; drug classes are bulk-forming and hygroscopic agents (carboxymethylcellulose, calcium polycarbophil, kaolin-pectin).
• Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam); bismuth (bismuth subsalicylate); opioids (diphenoxylate, difenoxin, loperamide); octreotide.
(b)
• ORT works because Na+ and Cl- absorption linked to glucose uptake stays intact in the small bowel.
• Bulk agents absorb water (calcium polycarbophil absorbs 60 times its weight) and may bind toxins and bile salts; sequestrants bind bile acids and toxins; bismuth is antisecretory, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial; opioids reduce motility and secretion via mu-receptors.
(c)
• Cholestyramine for bile salt-induced diarrhoea (distal ileal resection) and pruritus of biliary obstruction; bismuth for travellers' diarrhoea; bulk agents for mild diarrhoea of irritable bowel; loperamide for travellers' and chronic diarrhoea.
• Pharmacotherapy is for significant or persistent symptoms; dehydration and electrolyte imbalance matter especially in infants, young children and the elderly.
(d)
• Most treatments give only symptomatic relief by reducing motility; this is dangerous in infective diarrhoea (systemic invasion, toxic megacolon).
• Cholestyramine may worsen steatorrhoea after extensive ileal resection; bismuth causes dark stools (bismuth sulfide); opioid overdose gives CNS depression and paralytic ileus.
• Octreotide causes gallstones, hypo- or hyperglycaemia, nausea, bloating and injection-site pain.
(e)
• Octreotide is an octapeptide somatostatin analogue given subcutaneously or IV (half-life 1-2 hours; long-acting forms exist) that inhibits hormone secretion (serotonin, gastrin, VIP, insulin, secretin).
• It treats severe secretory diarrhoea from hormone-secreting tumours, chemotherapy-induced, HIV and diabetic diarrhoea.
• Opioid antimotility agents act on mu-receptors of the enteric plexus to reduce motility, are orally active, and treat common and travellers' diarrhoea.

(a)
Warfarin is a widely prescribed anticoagulant used to prevent blood clots.
(b)
• It has a narrow range between efficacy and toxicity, and the dose needed to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation varies 10-fold between people.
• CYP2C9 is the enzyme responsible for its metabolism; SNPs in the CYP2C9 gene decrease enzyme activity.
• Mean daily dose (mg) by genotype: *1/*1 5.63; *1/*2 4.88; *1/*3 3.32; *2/*2 4.07; *2/*3 2.34; *3/*3 1.60.
• CYP2C9 genotype explains only about 10-20% of the variability in warfarin dose; other genetic and non-genetic factors contribute.
(c)
• Bleeding tendency is the clinical consequence of a defective CYP2C9 gene.
• Interactions: warfarin plus a barbiturate (inducer) gives decreased anticoagulation; warfarin plus metronidazole (inhibitor) gives haemorrhage.
questions.question:
A patient requiring prevention of blood clots is to be started on warfarin.
(a) Name the drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on pharmacokinetics and pharmacogenetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Isoniazid (INH) has an anti-tuberculosis effect.
(b)
• Isoniazid is first acetylated by NAT (phase II) and then hydrolysed to isonicotinic acid (phase I), a reversal of the usual order.
• Fast acetylators may not benefit from the anti-tuberculosis effect; slow acetylation alleles are common among Caucasians and Africans.
• Isoniazid is also a CYP inhibitor.
(c)
• Adverse effects: peripheral neuropathy, convulsions, and hepatitis (a drug-induced disease).
• N-acetylation of isoniazid may form reactive species responsible for its hepatotoxicity.
• Acetylator phenotype or genotype testing is one approach.
questions.question:
A patient with tuberculosis is treated with isoniazid.
(a) Name the drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects and the testing approach.

A young patient given metoclopramide for vomiting develops spasmodic torticollis, oculogyric crises and motor restlessness.
(a) Identify the causative drug and reaction.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) State the treatment.
(d) State how it can be prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Metoclopramide, a substituted benzamide D2 receptor antagonist closely related to the phenothiazines, producing extrapyramidal movement disorders.
(b)
• It acts centrally on the chemoreceptor trigger zone and also blocks dopamine receptors elsewhere in the CNS.
• Movement disorders are more common in children and young adults.
• Other unwanted effects: fatigue, stimulation of prolactin release causing galactorrhoea and menstrual disorders.
• It is given orally, with plasma half-life 4-5 hours.
(c)
H1 antihistamines have central anticholinergic action that blocks the extrapyramidal effects of metoclopramide while supplementing its antiemetic action.
(d)
• Domperidone does not readily penetrate the blood-brain barrier and is less prone to central side effects.
• Metoclopramide also acts peripherally to increase oesophageal, gastric and intestinal motility, explaining its use in reflux and hepatic and biliary disorders.

questions.question:
A patient receiving heparin develops an abnormally low platelet count with venous and arterial embolism.
(a) Identify the causative drug and the reaction.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) State the treatment.
(d) State the contraindications of heparin.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), a serious reaction to heparin with abnormally low circulating platelets.
(b)
• The reaction is immune-mediated and carries a risk of venous and arterial embolism.
• Heparin preparations come from porcine sources and may be antigenic: chills, fever, urticaria and anaphylactic shock can occur; other effects are bleeding and osteoporosis on long-term use.
(c)
• Stop heparin when HIT or severe thrombocytopenia develops.
• Replace it with another anticoagulant such as argatroban, a small-molecule thrombin inhibitor binding only the active site, excreted in bile and safer in renal insufficiency.
• Lepirudin is also approved for HIT; it binds thrombin irreversibly, is renally excreted and may provoke anti-hirudin antibodies.
• LMWHs can show cross-sensitivity and are not recommended in HIT.
(d)
Heparin is contraindicated in hypersensitivity, bleeding disorders, alcoholism or recent brain, eye or spinal surgery.

(a)
Chloroquine (retinal toxicity is also associated with chlorpromazine).
(b)
• Binding to the intracellular pigment melanin lets some chemicals accumulate in melanin-containing cells.
• The release of melanin-bound toxicant is thought to contribute to the retinal toxicity.
• Chloroquine is a weak base; lipophilic amine xenobiotics also accumulate in lysosomes and mitochondria.
• Chemicals in the circulation can distribute to the eye and cause corneal opacity, retinal and optic nerve damage.
• A single dose of chloroquine may cause vomiting and abdominal pain in some individuals (intolerance).
(c)
Prevention: avoid inappropriate use, use the appropriate dose, route and frequency, and check history of reaction and interactions.
questions.question:
A patient on prolonged chloroquine therapy develops retinal toxicity.
(a) Identify the causative drug.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State how it can be prevented.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Epinephrine is the drug of choice for type I hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis, and for acute asthma when bronchoconstriction has diminished respiratory function.
• It is also used to restore cardiac rhythm in cardiac arrest and in local anaesthetic solutions (such as 1:100,000) to prolong anaesthesia by vasoconstriction.
(b)
• It acts directly on alpha and beta receptors (alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, beta-2, beta-3); beta-2 action gives powerful bronchodilation and inhibits mediator release (histamine) from mast cells.
• At low doses beta effects (vasodilation) predominate; at high doses alpha vasoconstriction predominates; it strengthens cardiac contraction and rate and releases renin via beta-1.
(c)
• Catecholamines are ineffective orally because COMT and MAO in the gut wall and liver inactivate them; after subcutaneous injection respiration improves within minutes.
• Metabolism is by COMT (to metanephrine) and MAO, ending in vanillyl mandelic acid excreted by the kidney.
(d)
Adverse effects: increased myocardial oxygen demand, hyperglycaemia (liver glycogenolysis, glucagon release, reduced insulin) and lipolysis.
questions.question:
A patient with severe anaphylaxis (a type I hypersensitivity reaction) is treated with intramuscular or subcutaneous epinephrine.
(a) Name the drug indicated and its other emergency uses.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics.
(d) State its adverse effects and cautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Pilocarpine is the drug of choice for emergency lowering of intraocular pressure in open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma; in acute narrow-angle glaucoma it is combined with physostigmine.
(b)
• It contracts the iris sphincter and meridional ciliary fibres near the trabecular meshwork, opening the trabecular spaces so aqueous humour drains more easily and the angle opens.
• Onset is within minutes, lasting 4-8 hours, and it can be repeated.
(c)
• Ocular effects: corneal edema, ciliary spasm, blurred vision, retinal detachment, induced myopia, pain, cataracts, raised pressure, angle narrowing.
• Systemic effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating, bradycardia, hypotension, pulmonary edema, bronchospasm, urinary retention.
• Contraindications: retinal detachment, cataracts, uveitis, severe myopia. Parameter: intraocular pressure (normal 10-15 mmHg; in glaucoma 30 mmHg or more).
(d)
• Carbachol when glaucoma is resistant to pilocarpine or physostigmine; echothiophate in resistant cases.
• Miotics have largely been replaced for chronic open-angle glaucoma by topical beta blockers (timolol), prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost), alpha-2 agonists (apraclonidine, brimonidine) and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide).
• Surgery: a hole made through the iris by surgery or laser facilitates drainage in angle-closure.
questions.question:
A patient has raised intraocular pressure and glaucoma, which may be open-angle (slow, painless optic nerve damage) or angle-closure (a medical emergency).
(a) State the first-line drug for emergency lowering of pressure.
(b) Give the rationale based on mechanism and pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects, contraindications and the parameter monitored.
(d) State the alternative or second-line agents and when they are preferred.

A patient has subacute onset of proximal weakness of the legs and hips with dry mouth, constipation and postural hypotension; weakness temporarily improves after repeated muscle activity, and a lung tumour is suspected.
(a) Identify the condition and its mechanism.
(b) State the structures and organ systems affected.
(c) Give the differential diagnoses of neuromuscular transmission failure and how they differ.
(d) State the therapy used in the related conditions (myasthenia gravis and botulism).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), an autoimmune disease with antibodies against presynaptic membrane Ca2+ channels; it correlates with small cell lung cancer.
• Less Ca2+ enters the terminal, so less ACh is released.
(b)
• Skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction (weakness, fatigue) and autonomic function (dry mouth, constipation, impotence, postural hypotension).
• The triad is proximal weakness, areflexia and autonomic dysfunction.
• Improvement with activity occurs because a calcium gradient builds and endogenous calcium outcompetes the antibodies.
(c)
• Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic ACh receptors; eye muscles first (ptosis, diplopia); worse in the evening; decrement above 10% on repetitive stimulation, whereas LEMS gives an increment.
• Botulism: toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking ACh exocytosis, giving descending flaccid paralysis; aminoglycoside antibiotics and botulinum toxin block ACh release.
(d)
For myasthenia gravis: anticholinesterases, corticosteroids, plasmapheresis; for botulism: antitoxin and ventilation.

questions.question:
A patient with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease is to start cholinesterase inhibitor therapy.
(a) Name the drugs used and the one given once daily.
(b) Give the rationale based on mechanism and pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects and cautions.
(d) State the alternative agents and how they differ.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Donepezil, centrally acting and long acting, once-daily, used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease to improve memory, learning, cognition and behaviour.
• Tacrine, rivastigmine and galantamine are also used for symptomatic therapy.
(b)
• They inhibit cholinesterase, raising ACh; these agents act indirectly with central effects.
• Pharmacokinetic reasoning: they are lipophilic and enter the brain; tacrine is a lipophilic acridine that crosses the blood-brain barrier.
(c)
• Side effects of cholinergic agonists: bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, headache, dizziness, convulsions, abdominal cramps, increased secretions, nausea, vomiting, lacrimation, sweating, salivation.
• Antihistamines antagonize cholinergic agents.
(d)
• Tacrine: longer duration of action; rivastigmine: cerebro-selective ChE inhibitor; galantamine: alkaloid inhibitor of cerebral cholinesterase.
• Pyridostigmine and neostigmine are used in myasthenia gravis, not Alzheimer's.

(a)
• Sulfasalazine (5-ASA plus sulfapyridine); 5-ASA compounds are first-line for induction and maintenance of remission in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
• Sulfasalazine alone is also used in rheumatoid arthritis; rectal formulations treat active distal ulcerative colitis, proctitis and proctosigmoiditis.
(b)
5-ASA acts topically on diseased mucosa: it inhibits prostaglandins and leukotrienes, decreases neutrophil chemotaxis and scavenges free radicals.
(c)
• It is a prodrug given orally; only about 10% is absorbed.
• In the terminal ileum and colon bacterial azoreductase cleaves it into 5-ASA (not absorbed, active) and sulfapyridine (absorbed, causes side effects).
(d)
• Adverse effects: crystalluria, bone marrow depression, megaloblastic anaemia, folic acid deficiency (provide folic acid), male oligospermia, interstitial nephritis from 5-ASA.
• Mesalamine formulations are sulfa-free and useful in patients sensitive or allergic to sulfa drugs.
questions.question:
A patient has mild to moderate ulcerative colitis with diarrhoea, abdominal pain and bleeding, and an azo compound containing 5-aminosalicylic acid is started.
(a) Name the drug indicated and its uses.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics.
(d) State its adverse effects and contraindications.

A patient has double vision, drooping of the upper eyelids, difficulty speaking and swallowing and general muscle fatigue that is worse in the evening; myasthenia gravis is diagnosed.
(a) State the first-line symptomatic drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on the pathophysiology, mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects, contraindications and the parameter used to distinguish crises.
(d) State the alternative or second-line agents and when they are preferred.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Reversible anticholinesterases such as neostigmine and pyridostigmine give symptomatic treatment; physostigmine also relieves weakness.
(b)
• Autoimmune disease: antibodies against nicotinic ACh receptors (rarely anti-MuSK) block ACh action, causing weakness; anticholinesterases increase ACh in the cleft and enhance conduction.
• Neostigmine is synthetic with direct and indirect actions, has stronger effect on skeletal muscle, and is polar so it cannot enter the CNS.
• Edrophonium is short acting (5-10 minutes).
(c)
• Adverse effects: muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic effects, treated with atropine; overdose causes cholinergic crisis.
• Contraindications of neostigmine: mechanical ileus, urinary obstruction, bronchial asthma, poisoning with depolarizing relaxants.
• Edrophonium differentiates myasthenic crisis from cholinergic crisis; a decrement above 10% on repetitive nerve stimulation is a diagnostic criterion.
(d)
• Corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus, mycophenolate) suppress the immune response.
• Rituximab for refractory cases, especially anti-MuSK; plasmapheresis removes antibodies; IV immunoglobulin with plasmapheresis for crises; ventilatory support for respiratory crisis.

questions.question:
A patient has urinary retention from an atonic bladder after surgery, without obstruction, and a choline ester that is not hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase is selected.
(a) Name the drug indicated and state its uses.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action, including the structural basis of its selectivity.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics.
(d) State its adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bethanechol, a direct-acting cholinergic agonist, increases tone and motility of the bladder and GI tract and relaxes their sphincters so they empty.
• It treats the atonic bladder (postpartum, postoperative, spinal cord injury), non-obstructive retention, neurogenic atony and megacolon.
(b)
• It selectively activates muscarinic receptors in smooth muscle and glands; it stimulates the detrusor while the trigone and sphincter relax, and raises intestinal tone and motility.
• It is an unsubstituted carbamoyl ester, not hydrolysed by AChE (other esterases inactivate it); the added beta-methyl removes nicotinic action.
(c)
• Well absorbed orally (variable); widely distributed and can cross the blood-brain barrier; minimally metabolized, mostly parent drug.
• Half-life about 30-90 minutes; excreted mainly unchanged in urine; short action so frequent dosing is needed; oral dose 10-50 mg three to four times daily.
(d)
• Adverse effects: sweating, salivation, flushing, decreased BP with reflex tachycardia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, bronchospasm.
• Atropine sulfate may overcome severe cardiovascular or bronchoconstrictor responses.

questions.question:
A patient with schizophrenia shows hallucinations and delusions.
(a) Identify the drug class used for this condition.
(b) State the mechanism related to the disease.
(c) Describe pharmacokinetic points.
(d) State the adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Antipsychotic drug therapy (examples: haloperidol, chlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine, fluphenazine).
(b)
Active symptoms are associated with increased activity of dopamine D2 synapses in the limbic system; 5-HT overactivity, glutamatergic and GABA hypoactivity and alpha-1 adrenergic overactivity are also implicated.
(c)
Chlorpromazine is extensively metabolised in the intestine; haloperidol and clozapine are CYP2D6 substrates; nicotine induces CYP2A6 with interactions with antipsychotics.
(d)
• Extrapyramidal symptoms (chlorpromazine) and tardive dyskinesia (type C effect); SIADH (haloperidol); drug-induced diabetes (atypical antipsychotics).
• CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have more adverse effects; chlorpromazine contributes to retinal toxicity via melanin binding.

(a)
• Phase I: oxidation (N-, S-, O-dealkylation, N- and S-oxidation, aromatic hydroxylation), reduction (carbonyl, azo, nitro) and hydrolysis (esters and amides).
• Examples: salicylic acid to gentisic acid; prontosil to sulfonamide; pethidine to pethidinic acid; atropine and acetylcholine hydrolysed.
• Phase II: glucuronidation (UDP-glucuronyltransferase, microsomes), acetylation (N-acetyltransferase, cytosol), glutathione, glycine, sulphate and methyl conjugation, and water conjugation (epoxide hydrolase).
• Enzymes are microsomal (CYP450, NADPH-cytochrome c reductase, UDP-glucuronyltransferase in smooth ER) or non-microsomal (esterases, amidases, hydrolases in cytoplasm and mitochondria).
(b)
• Metabolism usually yields polar, inactive products but can produce a more active drug from a prodrug (enalapril to enalaprilat; cyclophosphamide; levodopa to dopamine).
• Toxication yields electrophiles or free radicals; paraquat, doxorubicin and nitrofurantoin accept electrons giving superoxide.
• Ethylene glycol forms oxalic acid causing acidosis; amygdalin forms cyanide; nitrate is reduced to methaemoglobin-forming nitrite.
• Conjugation is not always terminal: acyl glucuronidation of NSAIDs, O-sulfation of N-hydroxyacetylaminofluorene and N-acetylation of isoniazid form reactive species; sulfation activates minoxidil.
(c)
• Phase I is non-synthetic functionalisation (-OH, -NH2, -SH) usually reducing activity; phase II is synthetic conjugation with endogenous groups giving highly polar, inactive products.
• The order may reverse: isoniazid is first acetylated (phase II) then hydrolysed to isonicotinic acid (phase I).
• Phase II transferases are in microsomes or cytosol and use high-energy intermediates such as UDP-glucuronic acid.
• Metabolism is more important for lipid-soluble drugs because polar drugs are excreted in urine.
questions.question:
Classification of drug metabolic reactions into phase I and phase II.
(a) Classify the reactions with examples, enzymes and sites.
(b) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxic metabolite formation and of altered activity after metabolism.
(c) Distinguish between phase I and phase II reactions.

For the 5-HT3 and NK1 receptor antagonist antiemetics:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at receptor level.
(b) State how the members relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other systems and cause adverse effects, interactions or precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) selectively block 5-HT3 receptors in the periphery (visceral vagal afferents) and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, the primary site.
• Cytotoxic drugs, radiation and GI irritants release 5-HT from enterochromaffin cells onto 5-HT3 receptors on extrinsic primary afferent neurones.
• NK1 antagonists (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, netupitant, rolapitant) cross the blood-brain barrier and block central NK1 receptors in the area postrema; substance P causes vomiting.
• NK1 antagonists have no affinity for serotonin, dopamine or corticosteroid receptors; 5-HT3 antagonists do not inhibit dopamine or muscarinic receptors.
(b)
• 5-HT3 antagonists are primary agents for acute CINV and for postoperative and radiation nausea and vomiting; alone they have little efficacy for delayed emesis, and motion sickness is poorly controlled.
• Ondansetron and granisetron prevent emesis in 50-60% of cisplatin-treated patients; efficacy is enhanced with a corticosteroid, an NK1 antagonist and a D2 antagonist.
• NK1 antagonists with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone prevent acute and delayed emesis from highly emetogenic regimens (acute emesis 80-90% vs under 70%; delayed over 70% vs 30-50%).
• Fosaprepitant is an IV prodrug of aprepitant; netupitant is a combination product with palonosetron.
(c)
• 5-HT3 antagonists cause headache, dizziness, constipation (slowed colonic transit), small QT prolongation (most with dolasetron), and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or SNRIs; no effect on oesophageal or gastric motility.
• NK1 antagonists are well tolerated (fatigue, dizziness) but are metabolized by CYP3A4; aprepitant induces CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 and lowers INR on warfarin.
• Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise aprepitant levels; avoid inducers such as St. John's wort; rolapitant moderately inhibits CYP2D6.
• They may inhibit metabolism of chemotherapy drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 (docetaxel, paclitaxel, etoposide, irinotecan, imatinib, vinblastine, vincristine).

questions.question:
A patient presents after an overdose of diazepam.
(a) State the risk factors for toxicity.
(b) Explain the mechanism of accumulation and of enhanced elimination.
(c) Outline management of the overdose.
(d) Justify the preferred option.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Diazepam is a weak base and very lipophilic, so it crosses the blood-brain barrier and distributes into the brain rapidly.
• In liver cirrhosis the half-life of diazepam and chlordiazepoxide is greatly increased, prolonging their effects.
• Cimetidine, an inhibitor of cytochrome P450, reduces diazepam metabolism; metabolism may be reduced at extremes of age.
(b)
• Inhibited or impaired metabolism leads to drug accumulation with increased intensity and duration of action.
• A weakly basic drug ionises in acidic urine, so its tubular reabsorption falls and it is readily excreted.
(c)
Ammonium chloride acidifies the urine and enhances diazepam elimination; this ion-trap approach is used in acute intoxication.
(d)
Weak bases are polar and excreted faster in acidic urine; in alkaline urine a weak base stays unionised and is reabsorbed, so acidification (not alkalinisation) is preferred.

(a)
• An antiplatelet drug; antiplatelet drugs are used for platelet-rich "white" arterial thrombi and prevent platelets from clumping.
• Aspirin is a key component of antiplatelet treatment to reduce death from myocardial infarction or stroke.
(b)
• It irreversibly inhibits COX-1 (and COX-2 at higher doses); COX-1 inhibition is the main antithrombotic mechanism.
• Prostaglandin H2 formation is blocked, so thromboxane A2, which activates platelets and stimulates aggregation, cannot be synthesized.
• Inhibition lasts the lifespan of a platelet (7-10 days); very low doses block the platelet chemical needed for clumping.
(c)
Given orally; bioavailability 68%; peak plasma concentration within 30-40 minutes; plasma half-life 15-30 minutes.
(d)
• Adverse effects: GI bleeding, Reye's syndrome in children, ringing in the ears, worsened asthma, nausea.
• Bleeding risk is smaller with low doses (75-100 mg).
questions.question:
A patient has had a myocardial infarction, a platelet-rich arterial thrombotic disease, and low-dose aspirin is started.
(a) State the drug class indicated and the role of aspirin.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics.
(d) State its adverse effects and contraindications.

Pharmacodynamics of adrenergic receptor-acting drugs (beta-agonists and beta-blockers).
(a) Describe their action at the receptor level.
(b) State how the subclasses (agonists and antagonists) relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Beta-adrenoceptors are G-protein coupled receptors with seven membrane-spanning helices linked to a second messenger; the beta-adrenoceptor uses cAMP and the effect is seen within seconds.
• An agonist has affinity plus maximal efficacy; a partial agonist has sub-maximal efficacy and competes with a full agonist; an antagonist has affinity but lacks efficacy.
• Beta-agonists attach to adrenergic receptors of the sympathetic nervous system and mimic norepinephrine; beta-blockers attach and block norepinephrine action.
(b)
• Beta-agonist bronchodilators (albuterol) are used for asthma attacks, given by pressurised inhaler.
• Beta-blockers (atenolol) are adrenergic antagonists; the beta-adrenergic receptor is also a pharmacogenetic target (albuterol).
(c)
• Salbutamol is functionally antagonised by propranolol; NSAIDs antagonise beta-blockers, diuretics and ACE inhibitors by inhibiting PGE2 and PGI2.
• Continuous agonist exposure down-regulates receptors, reducing beta-agonist response in asthmatics; beta-2 agonist tachyphylaxis arises after 1 dose by uncoupling of receptor from effector.
• Continuous antagonist exposure up-regulates receptors; abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker causes rebound, e.g. rebound hypertension.
• The beta-blocker metoprolol is a CYP2D6 substrate, so CYP2D6 poor metabolisers are predisposed to adverse effects.
• Receptors act to propagate, amplify and integrate signals and to adapt to long-term change to maintain homeostasis.

(a)
• Some drugs are secreted into bile from the liver and leave in faeces, e.g. rifampicin, indomethacin, vecuronium; organic acids and bases, neutral substances and metals (As, Pb, Hg) use the biliary route under active transport.
• Conjugated metabolites such as glucuronides are hydrolysed by intestinal bacteria, releasing the active drug, which is reabsorbed into the portal vein, returns to the liver and is re-conjugated and re-excreted: enterohepatic circulation.
• Direct intestinal excretion is a slow route that is major for compounds with low biotransformation and low renal or biliary clearance.
• Lungs excrete gases and volatile agents by passive diffusion (ethanol, anaesthetic gases); elimination is roughly inversely proportional to absorption.
• Milk (more acidic than plasma, about pH 6.5) takes lipid-soluble xenobiotics to the nursing infant; sweat and saliva are minor routes and sweat toxicants may cause dermatitis.
(b)
• Enterohepatic circulation can retain up to 20% of total drug in the body and may continue for several weeks after the drug is stopped.
• Examples of drugs with prolonged action through enterohepatic circulation: digoxin, morphine, chloramphenicol.
• Clearance by organs is additive (total = renal + hepatic + other).
(c)
• Recirculation increases the volume of distribution and makes elimination slower than expected, prolonging pharmacological action.
• Repeated recirculation prolongs the half-life of a chemical and toxicity can be enhanced.
• Toxic substances may pass into cow's milk and then to people, and liver and kidney disease reduce excretion and prolong drug action.
questions.question:
