Pharmacokinetics of biliary, enterohepatic and other non-renal routes of drug excretion.
(a) Describe biliary excretion, enterohepatic circulation and the other routes (faecal, respiratory, milk, sweat, saliva).
(b) State the dosing considerations and interactions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity and prolonged action.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Folic acid is given orally and absorbed in the ileum; methyl-FH4 is the form carried in blood and entering cells.
• Methyl-FH4 is functionally inactive until demethylated in a vitamin B12-dependent reaction; folate is taken up into hepatocytes and bone marrow cells by active transport.
• In cells folic acid is reduced and formylated, then converted to the active polyglutamate form; folinic acid (synthetic FH4) is converted much faster.
• Reduction of folic acid by dihydrofolate reductase yields FH2 and FH4, one-carbon transfer cofactors needed for purine and pyrimidine synthesis and conversion of dUMP to dTMP.
• Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is cobalt-containing and a cofactor with folate in DNA synthesis; its absorption needs intrinsic factor from the stomach.
(b)
• Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia is almost always from inadequate absorption, so give parenteral hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin (monthly injections); about 3-4 micrograms is adequate daily.
• Folic acid deficiency is treated with oral supplementation; daily requirement is about 0.2 mg in non-pregnant adults and rises in pregnancy.
• Supplement folic acid before and during pregnancy to reduce neural tube defects.
(c)
• Folic acid corrects the anaemia but not the neurologic deficits of vitamin B12 deficiency, so deficiency of B12 must be ruled out first or neurological damage may become irreversible.
• Pernicious anaemia results from lack of intrinsic factor, so oral B12 relies on absorption that fails.
• Neither vitamin B12 form has significant toxicity; folic acid has no recognised toxicity.
• Folic acid unwanted effects are not expected even at large doses, except possibly with vitamin B12 deficiency.
questions.question:
For folic acid and vitamin B12:
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, activation).
(b) State their dosing considerations and routes.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of therapeutic failure and the precautions in using folic acid.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bioassay measures the biological activity or potency of a substance in a biological system, comparing potency or relative potency to a standard.
• Biological systems include living cells or tissues, whole organisms, animals (rat, guinea pig, rabbit, cat, dog, monkey) and humans.
• In vitro: in glass (test tubes, 96-well plates) with isolated cell lines, bacteria, viruses or fungi; e.g. antimalarial activity against P. falciparum NF54 and anticancer activity against MCF-7.
• In vivo: animal studies (pre-clinical) and clinical trials in whole living organisms.
• Ex vivo: living tissue taken from an organism (guinea pig colon, frog heart).
• In silico: experiments performed by computer simulation, used to predict drug interactions with the body and pathogens.
(b)
• In vivo systems are complex, and behaviour or brain function cannot be reproduced in a test tube; computer models are not yet as robust as a living organism.
• In vitro work isolates cells from their usual surroundings for detailed analysis; the complexity of a living animal cannot be easily replicated.
• Failure to develop the bioassay correctly causes problems with approval, invalid assays and out-of-specification results.
• Most problems are avoided by correct development, qualification, validation and control of the reference standard.
(c)
• In vitro uses isolated, purified, cultivated cells that can be reconstructed or modified and renamed; ex vivo uses living tissues taken directly with minimal alteration.
• Biological products (vaccines, hormones, antibodies, cell and gene therapies) need one or more bioassays.
questions.question:
Classification of bioassay types.
(a) Classify bioassays into in vitro, in vivo, ex vivo and in silico, with examples.
(b) Explain the pharmacological basis of the limitations of each type and of unreliable bioassays.
(c) Distinguish between in vitro and ex vivo bioassays.

A neonate receiving theophylline is found to have caffeine in the blood.
(a) Identify the metabolic mechanism and clue.
(b) State the enzymes or pathways and organ affected.
(c) List other drugs showing altered metabolite production in children.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for dosing in special populations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Caffeine production in a neonate receiving theophylline is an example of a metabolite seen in children that is not usually seen in adults.
• Such metabolites may explain some efficacy or toxicity of drugs in children.
(b)
• Phase I and phase II pathways may not be active at birth because of maturational changes.
• The liver is the major organ of metabolism; its size, blood perfusion and protein-synthetic capacity determine the rate of hepatic elimination.
(c)
Other agents with changed metabolite production in children: valproic acid, paracetamol, chloramphenicol, cimetidine, salicylamide.
(d)
• In the elderly, hepatic blood flow falls by 40% or more and liver size by about 17-36%, with diminished enzyme activity.
• The blood-brain barrier is not fully developed at birth, so some xenobiotics are more toxic to newborns than to adults.
• Immature GI function in children and declining function in the elderly delay or reduce absorption.

questions.question:
For laxatives:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State the mechanism of action of each class.
(c) State the therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between saline laxatives and the non-absorbable sugars (lactulose and sorbitol).
questions.answerText:
(a)
Four classes: bulk-forming (psyllium, methylcellulose, polycarbophil), stool surfactants/softeners (docusate, glycerin suppository, mineral oil), osmotic (saline, sugars, polyethylene glycol), stimulant (anthraquinones, castor oil).
(b)
• Bulk-forming agents are hydrophilic colloids that absorb water, forming a bulky emollient gel that distends the colon and promotes peristalsis.
• Surfactants soften stool by letting water and lipids penetrate; mineral oil lubricates and retards water absorption.
• Osmotic agents are soluble, non-absorbable compounds that increase stool liquidity through obligate fluid retention.
• Stimulant laxatives act by poorly understood mechanisms: direct stimulation of the enteric nervous system and colonic fluid and electrolyte secretion; castor oil is hydrolysed to ricinoleic acid, an irritant.
(c)
Used for constipation after fibre, fluid and habit measures fail; docusate in hospitalised patients; mineral oil for faecal impaction; PEG for colonic cleansing before procedures.
(d)
• Bacterial digestion of fibre causes bloating and flatus; mineral oil aspiration causes lipid pneumonitis and long-term use impairs absorption of vitamins A, D, E, K.
• Magnesium laxatives risk hypermagnesemia in renal insufficiency; anthraquinones with chronic use give melanosis coli; phenolphthalein was withdrawn for possible cardiac toxicity.
(e)
• Saline laxatives contain magnesium cations or phosphate anions (magnesium sulfate, hydroxide, citrate, sodium phosphate; milk of magnesia).
• Sorbitol and lactulose are non-absorbable sugars used to prevent or treat chronic constipation.
• The sugars are metabolized by colonic bacteria, producing severe flatus and cramps; the magnesium salts carry the risk in renal insufficiency.
• Polyethylene glycol (about 3350) is a balanced isotonic preparation.

questions.question:
A patient who ate seeds or berries of belladonna or datura has hyperthermia, delirium, dry mouth, tachycardia, ileus and urinary retention; seizures, coma and respiratory arrest may follow.
(a) Identify the toxicity and the plants responsible.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the toxicity.
(c) State the management, including the antidote.
(d) Justify the preferred antidote.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Anticholinergic overdose syndrome (belladonna poisoning); atropine is derived from Atropa belladonna (deadly nightshade) and Datura stramonium (thorn apple).
(b)
• Atropine is a competitive, reversible antagonist at muscarinic receptors (affinity, no efficacy, slow dissociation); blockade is overcome by more ACh or agonist.
• Effects: mydriasis and cycloplegia, decreased secretions and GI motility, tachycardia from vagal blockade, cutaneous vasodilation, decreased sweating (fever), urinary retention.
• CNS: stimulation, excitement, agitation, hallucinations, then coma at high doses.
(c)
• Gastric lavage with tannic acid; cold sponging or ice bags; physostigmine subcutaneously or intravenously; diazepam to control convulsions.
• Physostigmine is used to reverse anticholinergic poisoning (antidote).
(d)
• Physostigmine is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor, raising ACh to overcome the competitive blockade; it is a tertiary amine that crosses the blood-brain barrier, so it reverses central effects.
• Neostigmine is polar and cannot enter the CNS; physostigmine's short half-life (about 30-60 minutes) needs repeated dosing.

questions.question:
For antiemetic drugs:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanisms of action.
(c) State their therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between metoclopramide and domperidone.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anticholinergics (hyoscine, dicyclomine); H1 antihistamines (promethazine, diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, cinnarizine, cyclizine); 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron).
• Dopamine antagonists (phenothiazines, haloperidol, droperidol, olanzapine, metoclopramide, domperidone); NK1 antagonists (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, netupitant, rolapitant); cannabinoid nabilone; dexamethasone.
(b)
• Hyoscine blocks the cholinergic link from the vestibular apparatus to the vomiting centre; antihistamines act through anticholinergic, antihistamine, weak antidopaminergic and sedative properties.
• 5-HT3 antagonists block 5-HT3 receptors peripherally and in the CTZ; D2 antagonists block the CTZ; NK1 antagonists block substance P centrally in the area postrema.
(c)
Hyoscine for short journeys and motion sickness; antihistamines for motion and morning sickness; 5-HT3 antagonists for postoperative, radiation and cisplatin emesis; NK1 antagonists with 5-HT3 and dexamethasone for acute and delayed chemotherapy emesis.
(d)
• Hyoscine and antihistamines cause sedation and dry mouth; hyoscine has poor efficacy for other emetic causes and brief duration; antihistamines are not effective against drugs acting on the CTZ.
• Phenothiazines and haloperidol cause sedation, hypotension and extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonias, tardive dyskinesia); 5-HT3 antagonists cause headache, constipation and QT prolongation, and alone do not prevent delayed emesis.
• NK1 antagonists inhibit and induce CYP3A4 and have many drug interactions (aprepitant lowers INR on warfarin); nabilone causes drowsiness, mood change and hallucinations.
• H1 antihistamines protect against motion sickness for 4-6 hours; promethazine is used for severe morning sickness and has been used for space motion sickness.
(e)
• Metoclopramide (a D2 antagonist) acts centrally on the CTZ and peripherally to increase gut motility; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes movement disorders, restlessness, torticollis and prolactin release.
• Domperidone does not readily penetrate the blood-brain barrier, so produces fewer central effects; both are given orally with plasma half-lives of 4-5 hours.
• Both treat vomiting from cytotoxic therapy and GI symptoms.

questions.question:
A patient with HIV infection is started on antiretroviral therapy.
(a) State the drug classes indicated.
(b) Explain the mechanism of action at each stage of the viral life cycle.
(c) State the adverse effects and monitoring.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Classes: nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (zidovudine, lamivudine, emtricitabine, didanosine, tenofovir), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir) and fusion inhibitors; zidovudine was the first (1986).
• HIV-1 responds better to NNRTIs; HIV-2 does not respond to NNRTIs.
(b)
• HIV is a retrovirus: single-stranded RNA transcribed to DNA by reverse transcriptase, then integrated into the host genome.
• NRTIs and NNRTIs prevent formation of proviral DNA by inhibiting reverse transcriptase through two different mechanisms.
• Protease inhibitors block virion maturation (protein processing and virus assembly); fusion inhibitors prevent fusion with CD4 cells.
(c)
• Lactic acidosis (most with NRTIs, can be fatal); lipodystrophy in 33-75% on HAART; indinavir renal calculi in 10% (hydration is mainstay).
• Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) with NNRTIs, abacavir and amprenavir; zidovudine causes eyelash elongation and bluish nails.
• Investigations for HIV care include viral load and drug sensitivity testing, LFT, RFT, lipids, glucose, G6PD, CBC and CD4.

(a)
• Alpha-1 receptors couple via Gq/11 to phospholipase C, forming IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases stored Ca2+ and Ca2+ rises, triggering smooth muscle contraction.
• Alpha-2 receptors couple via Gi, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP and PKA, reducing phosphorylation of N-type Ca2+ channels and vesicular release of neurotransmitter.
• Alpha-2 effects also include opening K+ channels (hyperpolarization); located presynaptically, postsynaptically, on pancreatic beta cells (inhibit insulin) and platelets.
• Alpha-2 agonists act at CNS sites to decrease sympathetic outflow, NE release and vascular smooth muscle contraction.
(b)
• Alpha-1 agonists (phenylephrine, methoxamine, midodrine) act as pressor agents; oxymetazoline and xylometazoline as nasal decongestants.
• Alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, methyldopa, guanfacine) lower sympathetic outflow in hypertension; apraclonidine and brimonidine treat glaucoma; they also ease withdrawal from narcotics, alcohol and tobacco.
• Alpha-1 antagonists (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin) treat primary hypertension and benign prostatic hypertrophy (more urine flow); yohimbine is an alpha-2 antagonist.
(c)
• Alpha-1 blockade causes nasal stuffiness, miosis, postural hypotension and reflex tachycardia, failure of ejaculation and diarrhoea.
• Alpha-1 agonists cause hypertension, headache, reflex bradycardia, restlessness and rebound hypertension after abrupt withdrawal.
• Alpha-2 agonists cause sedation, dry mouth, bradycardia, orthostatic hypotension, impotence and constipation.
• Yohimbine increases heart rate, blood pressure and can cause severe tremors.
• Phenylephrine should not be used with reserpine, tricyclics or MAOIs.
questions.question:
For alpha-adrenoceptors:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at receptor level (alpha-1 and alpha-2 signalling).
(b) State how agonist and antagonist members relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Enzyme induction: tobacco is an inducer of CYP1A2, whose substrates include theophylline and caffeine.
• Nicotine also induces its own metabolising enzyme, CYP2A6, leading to multiple potential drug interactions.
(b)
• Cytochrome P450 enzymes sit in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells; induction raises their synthesis.
• The inducing agent and other substrates of the induced enzyme are metabolised more rapidly, lowering pharmacological action or causing therapeutic failure.
(c)
• Other inducers: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates, St John's wort, chronic alcohol; benzo[a]pyrene and phenytoin are enhancing theophylline metabolism.
• Fluvoxamine is a CYP1A2 inhibitor (it would raise levels instead).
(d)
Exposure to tobacco smoke is a recognised factor altering drug response; nicotine interactions also involve antiarrhythmics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, caffeine, oral oestrogens, pentazocine and insulin (delayed absorption from skin vasoconstriction).
questions.question:
A patient who smokes tobacco and takes theophylline shows a weaker effect of the drug than expected.
(a) Identify the drug-class mechanism involved.
(b) State the enzymes and organ system affected.
(c) List differential drug-related causes of reduced effect.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for the choice or change of therapy.

For heparin and low molecular weight heparins (LMWHs):
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion).
(b) State their dosing considerations and monitoring.
(c) State the relevant interactions or special populations.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Heparin does not readily cross membranes, so it is given intravenously or subcutaneously; LMWHs are usually subcutaneous (enoxaparin can be given IV in myocardial infarction).
• IV heparin acts within minutes (1-2 hours after subcutaneous injection); maximum anti-Xa activity of LMWHs occurs about 4 hours after subcutaneous injection.
• In blood heparin binds many proteins that neutralize it, making pharmacokinetics unpredictable; binding is variable in thromboembolic disease.
• It is taken up by the monocyte/macrophage system, depolymerized and desulfated to inactive products excreted in urine.
• LMWHs (about one-third the size of heparin) are eliminated mainly in urine; half-life of heparin about 1.5 hours; LMWH 3-12 hours.
(b)
• Heparin starts as an IV bolus, then lower doses or infusion titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa level.
• LMWHs usually need no coagulation monitoring because their kinetics are predictable.
(c)
• In renal impairment LMWH half-life is prolonged and dose is reduced; in renally impaired, pregnant and obese patients monitor factor Xa levels.
• Heparin and LMWHs are the anticoagulants of choice in pregnancy because they do not cross the placenta.
(d)
• Binding to antithrombin III accelerates inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa, so the chief toxicity is bleeding; protamine sulfate (1 mg per 100 units) reverses it.
• Porcine-derived heparin is antigenic: chills, fever, urticaria, anaphylaxis; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (stop and use argatroban; LMWH cross-reactive).
• Long-term use causes osteoporosis; contraindicated in hypersensitivity, bleeding disorders, alcoholism and recent brain, eye or spinal surgery.

(a)
• Miotics: muscarinic agonists (acetylcholine, carbachol, pilocarpine) and anticholinesterases (echothiophate, physostigmine).
• Mydriatics: sympathomimetics (epinephrine, phenylephrine; indirect cocaine, hydroxyamphetamine) and cholinergic antagonists (atropine, scopolamine, homatropine, tropicamide, cyclopentolate).
(b)
• Miotics stimulate M3 receptors of the iris sphincter (miosis) and ciliary muscle (accommodation, wider trabecular spaces, more aqueous drainage).
• Sympathomimetics stimulate alpha-1 receptors of the dilator muscle (active mydriasis, without cycloplegia); antimuscarinics block M3 receptors causing passive mydriasis and cycloplegia.
• Indirect-acting sympathomimetics inhibit NE re-uptake, making more available to stimulate alpha-1 receptors.
(c)
Miotics: eye surgery miosis and glaucoma; mydriatics: surgical dilation, cycloplegic refraction, funduscopy, preventing lens adhesion in uveitis, conjunctival hyperaemia, Horner's syndrome diagnosis.
(d)
• Miotic ocular effects: corneal edema, ciliary spasm, blurred vision, retinal detachment, myopia, cataracts, raised IOP and angle narrowing; systemic: nausea, bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, urinary retention; use has fallen because newer agents have fewer effects.
• Mydriatic effects: photophobia, blurred and lost near vision, dryness, raised IOP, closed-angle glaucoma; systemic hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmias; contraindicated in closed-angle glaucoma, Down's syndrome and pregnancy.
• Miotics are contraindicated in retinal detachment, cataracts, uveitis and severe myopia.
(e)
• Tropicamide has very little cycloplegia, the fastest onset and shortest duration, and is the drug of choice for routine dilation.
• Atropine is the most potent mydriatic and cycloplegic with a long duration, used when complete cycloplegia is required and not for routine dilation.
• Cycloplegic potency order: atropine, scopolamine, cyclopentolate, homatropine, tropicamide (little).
questions.question:
For drugs acting on the pupil and ciliary muscle (miotics and mydriatics):
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanisms of action.
(c) State their therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Thiopurines (azathioprine, mercaptopurine/6-MP, 6-thioguanine) are used to treat cancer such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
• They also have implications in transplant, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, dermatology and Crohn's disease.
(b)
• Thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT, a phase II enzyme) metabolises them; TPMT polymorphisms give high, normal or low/no activity.
• Decreased TPMT activity predisposes to severe, life-threatening toxicity from these drugs.
(c)
• Individuals with inherited TPMT deficiency are unusually sensitive to myelosuppression and prone to rapid bone marrow suppression after starting treatment.
• Substantial dose reductions may be required in these patients.
• Genetic testing for TPMT is routine at some cancer centres (a CLIA-approved test exists).
questions.question:
A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is to be treated with mercaptopurine.
(a) Name the drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on pharmacokinetics and pharmacogenetics.
(c) State the major adverse effect and the parameter to monitor.

Tolerance and tachyphylaxis.
(a) Classify the types of tolerance and give examples.
(b) Describe the features and examples of tachyphylaxis.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of their limitations.
(d) Distinguish between tolerance and tachyphylaxis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tolerance is reduced response after repeated administration, requiring higher doses; it is dose-dependent and chronic.
• Pharmacokinetic tolerance: persistent exposure induces clearance mechanisms, e.g. ethanol induction of CYP450.
• Pharmacodynamic tolerance: receptors down-regulated or second messengers dampened.
• Physiological tolerance: homeostatic mechanisms restore the balance while receptor responses remain the same.
• Learned (behavioural) tolerance: compensatory behaviour, e.g. an alcoholic remaining functional while intoxicated.
(b)
• Tachyphylaxis is a rapid decrease in response to repeated doses over a short period; features: same dose, not dose-dependent, rate-sensitive.
• Examples: ephedrine and metaraminol (depleted noradrenaline stores; three doses), methylphenidate (3-4 hours), nitroglycerin infusion (hours).
• Beta-2 agonists (after 1 dose, resolves in a week), nicotine (after one dose), and prazosin (counterproductive sympathetic response).
(c)
• Giving larger doses may not restore the maximal effect in tachyphylaxis; receptor down-regulation reduces beta-agonist response in asthmatics.
• Distinguish tolerance in host cells from resistance of micro-organisms or malignant cells in chemotherapy.
(d)
• Tolerance is slow, dose-dependent and chronic, tachyphylaxis rapid (few doses) and not dose-dependent.
• Mechanisms of tachyphylaxis resemble tolerance, but receptors cannot be withdrawn and resynthesised that fast.

questions.question:
Pharmacodynamics and pharmacology of nicotine and tobacco constituents.
(a) Describe nicotine's action at receptor level.
(b) State how the constituents of tobacco relate to specific effects.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nicotine stimulates brain nicotinic cholinergic receptors, releasing dopamine and other neurotransmitters and activating the reward system; it is the main addictive substance.
• Cravings may begin within days of first use.
• Tachyphylaxis to nicotine develops after a single dose by incompletely understood mechanisms.
(b)
• Most dangerous constituents: nicotine (a stimulant), carbon monoxide (about 800 times the level considered safe) and tar; phenols are irritants that may contribute to lung cancer.
• Tobacco smoke has over 7,000 harmful compounds; the cilia's cleansing function is impaired by nicotine.
(c)
• Nicotine stimulates the CNS and adrenals, raising adrenaline, heart rate, respiratory rate, vessel constriction and blood pressure.
• Nicotine induces CYP2A6 with interactions: antiarrhythmics (flecainide, lidocaine, mexiletine), antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, caffeine, oral oestrogens, pentazocine, theophylline.
• Insulin absorption is delayed by skin vasoconstriction.
• Nicotine increases AVP release; tobacco use is the single most preventable cause of death.
• Smoking raises blood and urine cadmium and chromium(VI) exposure, and tobacco induces CYP1A2.
• Secondhand exposure also puts non-smokers at risk.

(a)
• Dabigatran is a substrate of P-glycoprotein; verapamil, dronedarone, quinidine, ketoconazole and clarithromycin raise its concentration, while rifampicin lowers it.
• Higher risk: renal impairment and age over 75; elimination is renal.
(b)
• Dabigatran etexilate is a prodrug hydrolysed by plasma esterases to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor binding the active site and inhibiting free and clot-bound thrombin.
• P-gp inhibition raises plasma levels and so bleeding risk; GI effects (dyspepsia, abdominal pain, GI bleeding) are common.
(c)
• Idarucizumab may be used to reverse bleeding in severe cases.
• Avoid abrupt discontinuation, which raises thrombotic risk; it is contraindicated with mechanical prosthetic heart valves.
(d)
• Idarucizumab is the antidote for dabigatran, whereas direct factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban) currently have no antidote.
• Plasma levels of dabigatran need not be monitored, unlike warfarin.
questions.question:
A patient taking dabigatran etexilate for non-valvular atrial fibrillation is also given clarithromycin and develops severe bleeding.
(a) Identify the interaction and risk factors.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the interaction.
(c) State the management, including the antidote.
(d) Justify the preferred option.

A pregnant patient requires anticoagulation for an acute deep vein thrombosis.
(a) Identify the drug class indicated.
(b) State the enzymes or factors affected.
(c) Name the alternatives and why they are unsuitable.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for the choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Heparin or low molecular weight heparins (enoxaparin, dalteparin); they treat acute venous thromboembolism.
• They are the anticoagulants of choice in pregnant women.
(b)
• Heparin binds antithrombin III, inactivating thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa; its pentasaccharide sequence permits binding and catalyzes thrombin inhibition about 1000-fold.
• LMWHs complex with antithrombin III and inactivate factor Xa but bind thrombin less.
(c)
Warfarin crosses the placenta, is teratogenic and is contraindicated in pregnancy; relative resistance also arises from raised coagulation factors in pregnancy.
(d)
• Heparin and LMWHs do not cross the placenta because of their large size and negative charge.
• LMWHs have predictable pharmacokinetics and need less monitoring; factor Xa levels are monitored in pregnant, renally impaired and obese patients.
• Adverse effects: bleeding (protamine reverses), HIT, osteoporosis; LMWH dose is reduced in renal impairment.

(a)
• Type A (augmented): extension of pharmacology, predictable, common, dose-related, less severe; sub-classes exaggerated desired effect (orthostatic hypotension, hypoglycaemic shock after insulin) and undesired lateral effect (constipation from morphine).
• Type B (bizarre): not an extension of pharmacology, unpredictable, may occur at very low doses; immunologic (IgE, radiocontrast) or idiosyncratic (G6PD haemolysis).
• Type C chronic (analgesic nephropathy, tardive dyskinesia), type D delayed (thalidomide teratogenicity, stilbestrol carcinogenesis), type E end-of-treatment (opioid and antiepileptic withdrawal, hypnotic rebound).
(b)
• Side effects occur at therapeutic doses (codeine causing constipation); secondary effects are indirect (tetracycline superinfection, steroid opportunistic infections); toxic effects follow absolute or relative overdose.
• Photosensitivity is phototoxic (sunburn-like) or photoallergic (cell-mediated rash); teratogenicity depends on drug and stage (first 2 weeks failure of pregnancy; 3 weeks-3 months deformities; NSAIDs close the ductus arteriosus).
• Carcinogenicity and mutagenicity involve reactive oxygen species (tobacco, radioisotopes, estrogens, some anticancer drugs); iatrogenic disease persists after stopping (NSAID ulcer, isoniazid hepatitis).
(c)
• Type A is based on drug pharmacology and is mostly preventable; type B is based on patient peculiarity, less common, often non-dose-related, more serious and needs withdrawal.
• Severity grades: minor (no therapy), moderate (change of therapy, antidote or prolonged admission), severe (life-threatening, permanent damage), lethal.
• Prevention: avoid inappropriate use, correct dose/route/frequency, elicit history of reactions and allergy, check interactions and use correct technique.
(d)
• Idiosyncrasy: genetically determined abnormal reactivity restricted to a genotype. Intolerance: characteristic toxic effects at therapeutic doses (chloroquine single dose vomiting).
• Allergy: immune-mediated, stereotyped symptoms unrelated to pharmacodynamics, largely dose-independent, occurring in a small percentage.
• Adverse reactions are commoner in multiple drug therapy and the elderly, and may arise after stopping the drug.
questions.question:
Classification of adverse drug effects.
(a) Classify adverse effects into types A to E with examples.
(b) Describe side, secondary, toxic and other effects, intolerance, idiosyncrasy, allergy, photosensitivity, teratogenicity and carcinogenicity.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of type A and type B reactions and how adverse effects are graded and prevented.
(d) Distinguish between idiosyncrasy, intolerance and drug allergy.

For drugs used in peptic ulcer disease:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanisms of action.
(c) State their therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acid inhibitors: H2 antagonists, proton pump inhibitors, prostaglandin analogues (misoprostol); neutralizers: antacids (Mg and Al salts, sodium bicarbonate, alginates, simeticone).
• Cytoprotectives: sucralfate and colloidal bismuth; H. pylori therapy: amoxicillin, clarithromycin, tinidazole, metronidazole, tetracycline.
(b)
• Misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) inhibits acid secretion and raises blood flow, mucus and bicarbonate.
• Sucralfate (aluminium hydroxide with sulfated sucrose) forms gels with mucus and inhibits pepsin; bismuth is toxic to H. pylori and prevents its adherence.
(c)
• PPIs: gastric and duodenal ulcer, non-ulcer dyspepsia, GERD, stress-related bleeding prevention, gastrinoma; eradication of H. pylori is standard care in ulcers.
• Antacids neutralize acid and raise gastric pH; H2 antagonists suppress basal and nocturnal acid secretion, a measure of duodenal ulcer healing.
(d)
• Misoprostol causes diarrhoea and uterine contraction, so is contraindicated in pregnancy; magnesium salts cause diarrhoea and aluminium constipation, so are mixed.
• Sodium bicarbonate liberates CO2 (belching, acid rebound) and can cause alkalosis; antacids chelate other drugs, so take 2 hours apart.
• Sucralfate needs acid for activation (antacids reduce efficacy), reduces absorption of several drugs and causes constipation; bismuth may cause encephalopathy in renal impairment and blackens tongue and faeces.
(e)
• PPIs are prodrugs activated in acid, irreversibly inhibit the proton pump, are the most potent suppressors, last 24-48 hours; given before meals.
• H2 antagonists are reversible competitive blockers of H2 receptors, less potent but suppress 24-hour acid by about 70% including nocturnal secretion; tolerance may occur.
• Interactions and adverse effects differ: PPIs via CYP2C19/1A2 and acid loss; cimetidine causes endocrine effects.

(a)
• Metyrosine (alpha-methyl-L-tyrosine), a tyrosine analogue that inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase and decreases catecholamine stores.
• It is used occasionally in pheochromocytoma, particularly with extensive metastatic disease, or pre-operatively in patients with high catecholamine levels.
(b)
Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to DOPA and is the rate-limiting step; DOPA decarboxylase (needs vitamin B6) forms dopamine; dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (copper dependent) forms NE; PNMT forms epinephrine in the adrenal medulla.
(c)
• Reserpine blocks vesicular uptake (VMAT) and depletes catecholamines; guanethidine and bretylium block NE release.
• Cocaine and imipramine block NET (uptake 1) and potentiate NE; carbidopa and benserazide inhibit DOPA decarboxylase.
• Menkes disease: copper deficiency lowers DBH, raising the DOPA:DHPG ratio.
(d)
• Metyrosine acts at the rate-limiting step so it lowers production at the start of the pathway.
• Beta-blockers also list pheochromocytoma among their uses.
questions.question:
A patient with pheochromocytoma has high circulating catecholamines and is awaiting surgery.
(a) Identify the drug class or mechanism that can reduce catecholamine synthesis.
(b) State the enzymes and steps affected.
(c) State other drugs that alter catecholamine stores or action.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for the choice of therapy.

For the P2Y12 receptor antagonists (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor):
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics.
(b) State their dosing considerations and interactions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects or therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clopidogrel (thienopyridine) is a prodrug: 85% is hydrolysed to an inactive metabolite and the rest is activated by CYP3A4/3A5, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19; bioavailability 50%, peak in 1 hour, half-life 8 hours.
• Prasugrel is a third-generation thienopyridine prodrug activated by CYP450; bioavailability 80%, peak in 30 minutes, half-life 7 hours.
• Ticagrelor is a non-thienopyridine reversible blocker; bioavailability about 36%, peak 1.5 hours, half-life 7 hours; CYP3A4/3A5 metabolism with an active metabolite.
• Cangrelor is a reversible blocker with over 90% inhibition and half-life 2-5 minutes; platelet function recovers within 60 minutes of stopping.
(b)
• Clopidogrel needs an initial loading dose for rapid onset; its CYP dependence makes it prone to interactions (omeprazole and other PPIs reduce its effect).
• Active metabolites of clopidogrel and prasugrel bind irreversibly, inhibiting the platelet for its lifespan.
• CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 polymorphisms do not influence prasugrel metabolism.
• Twenty-four hours after the last dose ticagrelor effect has fallen by 50%; 20% remains after 3 days.
(c)
• Adverse effects: clopidogrel dyspepsia, rash, diarrhoea; prasugrel rash, rare hypersensitivity and angioedema; ticagrelor dyspnoea or GI symptoms.
• Prasugrel gives more reliable conversion, faster onset and more effective inhibition than clopidogrel.
• Cangrelor suits perioperative bridging of high-risk patients because of its short half-life.
• Blocking P2Y12 reduces ADP-mediated shape change, aggregation and coagulation promotion.

(a)
• Clearance = rate of elimination / plasma concentration; units L/hr; it is additive across organs and is the most important parameter for maintenance dosing.
• Half-life is time for concentration to fall by half; elimination rate constant k is fraction removed per unit time; after 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 half-lives 50, 75, 87.5, 93.8, 96.9, 98.4% is eliminated.
• Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration; used to calculate a loading dose.
• Bioavailability by AUC; absolute bioavailability compares oral with IV AUC; steady state is when input equals output; accumulation occurs on multiple dosing until steady state.
(b)
• Loading dose initiates therapeutic concentration; maintenance dose sustains it; dose size, dosing interval and dosage regimen are designed from pharmacokinetic variables.
• Half-life determines how often a drug is taken and how long it takes to wear off; older, younger or sick people clear drugs more slowly.
• Factors influencing half-life: dose size, urinary pH, age, protein binding, enzyme inducers and inhibitors, and liver and kidney disease.
• Monitoring is determination and recording of drug concentrations during therapy to adjust the regimen.
• Clearance depends on dose size, blood flow and intrinsic organ function; renal failure lowers clearance.
(c)
• The therapeutic goal is to keep concentration below toxic and not below effective; an overly long half-life or low clearance causes accumulation.
• Rapid elimination or sub-therapeutic accumulation risks therapeutic failure; for narrow therapeutic index drugs dose adjustment is needed in organ failure.
• Sustained-release forms reduce extreme peaks and troughs.
questions.question:
Pharmacokinetic parameters: clearance, half-life, volume of distribution and dosage regimen.
(a) Describe each parameter and how it is obtained.
(b) State dosing considerations, interactions and monitoring.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity or therapeutic failure.

A worker with long-term occupational exposure to an agricultural chemical has weakness, restlessness, anxiety, tremor and miosis, and plasma cholinesterase activity is reduced.
(a) Identify the drug class and mechanism involved.
(b) State the receptors and organ systems affected.
(c) Name other drug-related causes of a cholinergic picture and how they differ.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for the choice of therapy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chronic intoxication with irreversible anticholinesterases (organophosphates), which bind the esteratic site of AChE covalently so ACh accumulates.
(b)
• Muscarinic receptors: eye, exocrine glands, respiration, GI tract, urinary tract and CVS.
• Nicotinic receptors: ganglionic (raised BP and heart rate) and neuromuscular (skeletal muscle tremor); central effects: excitation and convulsion, then depression.
(c)
• Reversible anticholinesterases bind for minutes to hours; neostigmine overdose causes cholinergic crisis; neostigmine is polar and cannot enter the CNS.
• Direct agonists: pilocarpine poisoning (profuse sweating, salivation; uncharged, penetrates CNS) and bethanechol (sweating, salivation, flushing, reflex tachycardia, bronchospasm).
(d)
• Atropine antagonizes muscarinic effects; for pilocarpine toxicity parenteral atropine at doses crossing the blood-brain barrier is used; for bethanechol atropine sulfate overcomes severe cardiovascular or bronchoconstrictor responses.
• For organophosphates an oxime reactivates AChE: used early, in moderate-severe cases, ineffective once the enzyme has aged.

questions.question:
Pharmacokinetics and pharmacogenetics of polymorphic cytochrome P450 enzymes.
(a) Describe polymorphisms, phenotypes and key isoforms (CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6).
(b) State dosing considerations, interactions and monitoring (genotyping).
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity and therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A polymorphism occurs in over 1% of the population (a mutation in under 1%); SNPs and insertion-deletions may change protein function, quantity or mRNA stability.
• CYP2D6 has over 100 polymorphisms giving ultrarapid, extensive and poor metabolisers; CYP2D6 handles about 25% of drugs and CYP3A about 50%.
• CYP2C9 metabolises warfarin, NSAIDs (diclofenac, meloxicam, naproxen), glipizide, phenytoin and losartan; CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole and lansoprazole.
• CYP2D6 substrates include metoprolol, tricyclics, codeine, paroxetine, haloperidol and clozapine.
(b)
• Warfarin mean daily dose falls from 5.63 mg (*1/*1) to 1.60 mg (*3/*3); genotype explains about 10-20% of the variation.
• Atomoxetine: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have 10-fold higher plasma concentrations (about 7% of Caucasians are poor metabolisers).
• Ulcer cure with omeprazole and amoxicillin: 28.6% rapid, 60% intermediate, 100% poor CYP2C19 metabolisers.
• Genotyping uses molecular tests such as the Roche AmpliChip CYP450 test for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19; phenotyping uses drug administration and metabolic ratio.
(c)
• Poor metabolisers have higher plasma concentrations and more adverse effects (fluoxetine death in a child; antipsychotics), except where activation is needed.
• Codeine needs CYP2D6 activation, so 2-10% of people cannot metabolise it and are resistant to analgesia.
• Decreased CYP2C9 activity gives bleeding tendency with warfarin and hypoglycaemia with oral hypoglycaemics.
• Environmental and drug-interaction influences are not captured by genotyping.

questions.question:
For neuromuscular blocking drugs:
(a) Classify them (by pharmacokinetics, chemistry and mechanism) with examples.
(b) State their mechanism of action.
(c) State their pharmacological effects and therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between depolarizing and non-depolarizing blockers.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• By duration: long (d-tubocurarine, metocurine, pancuronium, doxacurium), intermediate (vecuronium, rocuronium, atracurium), short (mivacurium).
• By chemistry: natural alkaloids (tubocurarine, alcuronium), ammonio steroids (pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium), benzylisoquinolines (atracurium, mivacurium).
(b)
Non-depolarizing agents prevent ACh access to the nicotinic receptor (competitive); depolarizing agents (succinylcholine, decamethonium) depolarize the end plate and cause block.
(c)
They interfere with transmission at the end plate and lack CNS activity; uses: surgical relaxation (intracavitary surgery), tracheal intubation, control of ventilation, attenuating convulsions.
(d)
• Tubocurarine lowers arterial pressure through ganglion block and histamine release (bronchospasm); gallamine and pancuronium block mAChRs, causing tachycardia.
• Succinylcholine causes bradycardia (preventable with atropine), raised intraocular pressure, prolonged paralysis when plasma cholinesterase is reduced, and malignant hyperthermia.
• Limitation: long-acting agents give persistent block and difficult complete reversal; they are quaternary, poorly absorbed, given IV, and do not cross the placenta or blood-brain barrier.
(e)
• Non-depolarizing block is reversed by anticholinesterases and shows enhanced tetanic fade; no initial fasciculations.
• Depolarizing block is not reversed by anticholinesterases; it produces initial fasciculations and postoperative muscle pain; tetanic fade is less.
• Succinylcholine has two phases: phase I (depolarized, unresponsive membrane, flaccid paralysis, augmented by cholinesterase inhibitors); phase II (repolarized but desensitized, resembling non-depolarizing block).
• Succinylcholine is hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase (short action); non-depolarizers have more autonomic effects.
• Neither crosses the blood-brain barrier.

questions.question:
A patient taking procainamide develops systemic lupus erythematosus.
(a) Identify the causative drug and the genetic phenotype.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State how it can be prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Procainamide is a substrate of N-acetyltransferase (NAT), a phase II enzyme.
• The slow acetylator phenotype may predispose to SLE when procainamide is used.
(b)
• NAT acts in the cytosol using acetyl-CoA on amines; of 27 variants described, NAT2*5, *6, *7 and *14 slow-activity alleles are common among Caucasians and Africans.
• Phenotypes are slow and fast acetylators.
(c)
• Prevention: pharmacogenetic evaluation by phenotyping (give the drug, then measure the metabolic ratio) or genotyping (molecular test of the polymorphic site).
• Phenotyping is tedious and impractical before dosing; genotyping cannot detect environmental or drug-interaction influences or rare alleles.

questions.question:
For catecholamine synthesis and adrenergic transmission (enzyme and transporter level):
(a) Describe the biosynthetic steps and enzymes of norepinephrine and epinephrine.
(b) State how drugs acting at each step relate to their therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain how termination of action and metabolism extend effects to other tissues and drug interactions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tyrosine is hydroxylated to DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step.
• DOPA decarboxylase (vitamin B6 dependent) forms dopamine, which VMAT moves into vesicles; dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (copper dependent) forms NE in the vesicles.
• In the adrenal medulla PNMT methylates NE to epinephrine; adrenal medullary release is about 80% epinephrine and 20% NE; glucocorticoid controls epinephrine.
• NE release needs Ca2+ entry and exocytosis; presynaptic alpha-2 receptors give negative feedback.
(b)
• Metyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase (pheochromocytoma); carbidopa and benserazide inhibit decarboxylase, enhancing levodopa in Parkinson's disease.
• Reserpine blocks vesicular uptake and depletes catecholamines; guanethidine and bretylium block NE release.
• Cocaine and imipramine block NET (uptake 1); ephedrine, tyramine and amphetamine act indirectly by releasing NE.
(c)
• Uptake 1 (NET) removes about 87% of released NE, ENT (uptake 2) about 5% and diffusion about 8%; over 70% of recaptured NE returns to vesicles.
• MAO (neuronal) and COMT (extraneuronal, liver) metabolize catecholamines; the major urinary end product is vanillyl mandelic acid (VMA).
• Liver and kidney clear over 60% of circulating catecholamines; uptake inhibitors such as cocaine and imipramine potentiate NE.
• Menkes disease (copper deficiency) lowers dopamine-beta-hydroxylase activity.
• NET also occurs in adrenal medulla, liver and placenta.

(a)
• Acute iron toxicity, seen almost exclusively in young children who accidentally ingest iron tablets.
• Parenteral iron bypasses intestinal regulation and can deliver more iron than can be safely stored; free inorganic iron given parenterally is dose-dependently toxic.
(b)
• Signs of gastroenteritis (vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea) are followed by shock, lethargy and dyspnoea.
• The patient may improve or progress to metabolic acidosis, coma and death.
(c)
• Whole bowel irrigation to flush unabsorbed pills.
• Intravenous deferoxamine, a potent iron chelator, binds absorbed iron and promotes its excretion.
• Supportive therapy for GI bleeding, metabolic acidosis and shock.
(d)
• Activated charcoal does not bind iron and is ineffective, so irrigation and chelation are used.
• Chronic overload (hemochromatosis) without anaemia is best treated by phlebotomy, one unit weekly; chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox) is less efficient and hazardous but may be the only option in refractory anaemia such as thalassemia major.
questions.question:
A young child accidentally ingests many iron tablets and develops vomiting, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, followed by shock, lethargy and dyspnoea.
(a) Identify the toxicity and the risk factors.
(b) Explain the course of the toxicity.
(c) State the management, including the antidote.
(d) Justify the preferred options.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Drug transporters influence absorption, distribution and elimination and mostly belong to the ABC family (MDR1) or the SLC family (SerT).
• ABC transporters are active, energy-dependent (ATP) efflux pumps; P-glycoprotein (MDR1) exudes chemicals from cells and MRP effluxes conjugates of glucuronic acid and glutathione.
• SLC carriers work mainly by facilitated diffusion and move glucose, neurotransmitters, nucleotides, essential metals and peptides; OAT and OCT carry organic anions and cations into kidney and liver.
• P-glycoprotein in luminal membranes of brain capillary endothelial cells contributes to the blood-brain barrier.
• P-gp substrates: digoxin, quinidine, verapamil, colchicine, morphine, clarithromycin, etoposide, vinblastine, cefotetan, cefazolin, efavirenz, ritonavir, tamoxifen, cyclosporin, tacrolimus, dexamethasone.
(b)
• OATs and OCTs are a site for drug interactions because drugs compete for the transporter.
• Carriers are saturable and can be competitively inhibited by chemically similar drugs.
• MDR1 and SerT polymorphisms vary between people.
(c)
• In chemotherapy, efflux transporters contribute to resistance to anticancer drugs.
• Transporters facilitate delivery of toxicants: paraquat enters pneumocytes by carrier-mediated uptake and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels admit lead and barium ions.
• Export from cells (P-gp extrusion) opposes distribution of intracellular toxicants to their targets.
• Binding to metallothionein in acute cadmium intoxication reduces concentration at the target.
questions.question:
Pharmacokinetics of drug transporters (P-glycoprotein and other ABC and SLC transporters).
(a) Describe the transporters and their role in absorption, distribution and elimination.
(b) State dosing considerations and interactions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity and therapeutic failure.

A patient has dry mouth (xerostomia) following radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, and a muscarinic agonist is prescribed.
(a) Name the drug indicated and state its other uses.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics.
(d) State its adverse effects and contraindications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pilocarpine, a direct-acting muscarinic agonist, treats dry mouth after head and neck radiotherapy and dry mouth in Sjogren's syndrome.
• Ophthalmic pilocarpine is a miotic used for glaucoma; it is the drug of choice for emergency lowering of intraocular pressure (open-angle and angle-closure) and reverses atropine-induced mydriasis.
• It strongly stimulates sweat, tears and saliva, but this use is limited by lack of selectivity.
(b)
It activates muscarinic receptors, causing smooth muscle contraction, glandular secretion and ocular effects; it is a tertiary amine, uncharged and stable to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase.
(c)
• Rapidly absorbed orally; large volume of distribution; crosses the blood-brain barrier.
• Hepatic CYP metabolism; major metabolite is pilocarpic acid; half-life about 1-2 hours; excreted mainly in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites; duration varies with route.
• Oral dose 5-7 mg three times daily, starting at 5 mg; not more than 10 mg as a single dose; treatment takes up to 12 weeks.
(d)
• Adverse effects: blurred vision, night blindness, brow ache; poisoning gives exaggerated parasympathetic effects (profuse sweating, salivation); parenteral atropine counteracts toxicity.
• Contraindications to miotics: retinal detachment, cataracts, uveitis, severe myopia; antihistamines antagonize cholinergic agents.

(a)
• Schizophrenia: dopamine hypothesis, with increased D2 activity in the limbic system; also 5-HT overactivity, glutamatergic and GABA hypoactivity and alpha-1 adrenergic overactivity.
• Depression: monoamine hypothesis, with abnormality in serotonin (5-HT), noradrenaline and dopamine systems; altered receptors, turnover and the HPA axis; tryptophan, the 5-HT precursor, is reduced in untreated patients.
(b)
• Antipsychotics named: haloperidol, chlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine, fluphenazine, thiothixene; antidepressants named: fluoxetine, sertraline, imipramine, amitriptyline, paroxetine (SSRI), venlafaxine (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), clomipramine, fluvoxamine, trazodone.
• Lithium (a mineral source) is a mood stabiliser used for mania.
• Reduced cingulate cortex activity after 8 weeks of venlafaxine predicted treatment efficacy in generalised anxiety.
(c)
• Endocrine: antidepressants and antipsychotics (fluoxetine, sertraline, imipramine, amitriptyline, haloperidol) can cause SIADH; atypical antipsychotics cause drug-induced diabetes.
• Nervous system: extrapyramidal symptoms (chlorpromazine, metoclopramide), tardive dyskinesia (type C), ataxia (lithium).
• Eye: chlorpromazine and chloroquine retinal toxicity by melanin binding; loss of libido with antidepressants.
• Metabolism: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have more adverse effects (fluoxetine death in a child, antipsychotics), with more reactions, higher cost and longer stay; chlorpromazine is extensively metabolised in the intestine.
• Nicotine induces CYP2A6, interacting with clomipramine, fluvoxamine, imipramine, trazodone, chlorpromazine, clozapine, fluphenazine, haloperidol and olanzapine.
• Withdrawal: antidepressants cause physical dependence and withdrawal syndrome.
questions.question:
Pharmacodynamics of antipsychotic and antidepressant drug action at the neurotransmitter and receptor level.
(a) Describe the receptor and transmitter systems relevant to antipsychotic and antidepressant therapy.
(b) State how members relate to their uses.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• AChE (true cholinesterase) is at cholinergic sites and gray matter and hydrolyses ACh very rapidly (less than 1 millisecond); butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) is in plasma, liver and intestine, hydrolyses slowly, and handles esters such as procaine and succinylcholine.
• Anticholinesterases are similar to ACh and combine with AChE in place of ACh, preventing ACh hydrolysis, raising ACh at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.
• AChE is more sensitive to physostigmine; butyrylcholinesterase is more sensitive to organophosphates.
• Reversible agents are hydrolysed within a short time; irreversible organophosphates (dyflos, parathion, malathion, isoflurophate, echothiophate) form very stable covalent bonds, so the body must make new cholinesterase.
(b)
• Reversible: edrophonium (5-10 minutes; diagnosis of myasthenia, differentiates crises, curare poisoning), neostigmine (myasthenia, paralytic ileus, bladder, reversal of non-depolarizers, supraventricular tachycardia), pyridostigmine, physostigmine (glaucoma, atropine poisoning).
• Alzheimer's: tacrine, rivastigmine, donepezil, galantamine.
• Irreversible organophosphates have toxicological importance; echothiophate is the exception, used in resistant glaucoma.
(c)
• Muscarinic effects: miosis, bronchoconstriction and secretions, bradycardia, vasodilation, increased GI peristalsis and secretions, bladder contraction, salivation.
• Nicotinic effects include twitching, fasciculations, weakness and paralysis; central effects include convulsions, coma and respiratory failure.
• Neostigmine is polar and cannot enter the CNS; adverse cholinergic effects are treated with atropine.
• Neostigmine contraindications: mechanical ileus, urinary obstruction, bronchial asthma, depolarizing relaxant poisoning.
• Organophosphate toxicity: atropine plus oxime reactivators, limited by aging.
questions.question:
For cholinesterases and anticholinesterases:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics of the enzymes and drugs at enzyme level.
(b) State how reversible and irreversible members relate to specific therapeutic uses.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

A patient on long-term drug therapy develops hyperglycaemia consistent with diabetes mellitus.
(a) Identify the drug classes and mechanism involved.
(b) State the hormones, enzymes and organ systems affected.
(c) List differential causes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Drug- or chemical-induced diabetes is an 'other specific type': glucocorticoids, nicotinic acid, thiazides, hydantoins, protease inhibitors, atypical antipsychotics.
(b)
• Insulin raises glycogen synthase and glucokinase, lowers glucose-6-phosphatase and gluconeogenesis, and drives lipogenesis in adipose tissue and liver.
• Glucocorticoids control carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; growth hormone antagonises insulin.
• Type 2 diabetes is marked by insulin resistance, impaired insulin secretion and increased hepatic glucose output.
(c)
• Endocrinopathies: acromegaly, Cushing's syndrome, glucagonoma, pheochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism.
• Infections (congenital rubella, cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus), exocrine pancreas disease, and raised serum persistent organic pollutants linked to diabetes.

(a)
• 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) are the primary agents for preventing acute chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
• They also treat postoperative nausea and vomiting and emesis from whole-body or abdominal radiation.
(b)
Cytotoxic drugs release 5-HT from enterochromaffin cells; these drugs selectively block 5-HT3 receptors on visceral vagal afferents and in the CTZ (the primary site).
(c)
• Best given as a single IV dose 30 minutes before chemotherapy: ondansetron 8 mg, granisetron 1 mg, dolasetron 100 mg, palonosetron 0.25 mg.
• Extensively metabolized by the liver, excreted in urine; only ondansetron needs dose adjustment in hepatic insufficiency; palonosetron has higher receptor affinity and a half-life of 40 hours.
(d)
• Adverse effects: headache, dizziness, constipation; small QT prolongation (most with dolasetron); serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or SNRIs.
• Dolasetron should not be given in prolonged QT or with QT-prolonging drugs; alone they have little efficacy against delayed emesis (over 24 hours), so combine with dexamethasone, an NK1 antagonist and a D2 antagonist.
questions.question:
A patient is due to receive cisplatin chemotherapy and needs prevention of acute nausea and vomiting.
(a) Name the drug class indicated and its uses.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetics and dosing.
(d) State its adverse effects and contraindications.

A patient with severe active inflammatory bowel disease takes loperamide to reduce the frequency of bowel movements and develops toxic megacolon.
(a) Identify the causative drug class and reaction.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State how it can be prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Opioid antimotility antidiarrhoeals (loperamide, diphenoxylate, difenoxin) precipitating toxic megacolon in inflammatory bowel disease.
(b)
• They act on mu-receptors of the enteric plexus, epithelial cells and muscle, reducing intestinal motility and secretion.
• Overdose causes CNS depression, paralytic ileus and toxic megacolon in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
• Reducing motility is dangerous in infective diarrhoea, increasing the chance of systemic invasion by the organism, and can produce local complications such as toxic megacolon.
(c)
• Loperamide and diphenoxylate suit mild disease and are contraindicated in severe disease because they may predispose to toxic megacolon.
• Oral rehydration therapy is the cornerstone of acute diarrhoea; drug therapy is for significant or persistent symptoms.
• Loperamide: 4 mg to start, 2 mg after each loose stool, up to 16 mg in 24 hours; not recommended under 2 years; diphenoxylate is combined with atropine to discourage abuse.

(a)
• Genetic deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) predisposes to non-immune haemolytic anaemia.
• It is an idiosyncratic (type B) reaction caused by a congenital enzyme abnormality.
(b)
• G6PD is a cytosolic enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway that supplies reducing energy (NADPH) to cells such as erythrocytes.
• NADPH maintains glutathione, which protects red blood cells against oxidative damage; the organ system affected is the red cell/blood.
(c)
Drugs and chemicals shown to precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deficiency: acetanilide, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, methylene blue, sulfacetamide, nalidixic acid, naphthalene, sulfanilamide, sulfapyridine, sulfamethoxazole.
(d)
• Avoid the precipitating drugs in G6PD-deficient subjects; pharmacogenetics proposes treating predicted toxic responders with an alternative drug or dose.
• The at-risk group is people with genetic G6PD deficiency.
questions.question:
A patient develops non-immune haemolytic anaemia after receiving primaquine.
(a) Identify the underlying mechanism and type of adverse reaction.
(b) State the enzyme, pathway and organ system affected.
(c) List other drug-related precipitants of the same reaction.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for changing therapy and any at-risk population.

Classification of toxicity tests (acute, subacute, subchronic, chronic).
(a) Classify the toxicity tests and describe the design of each.
(b) Explain the pharmacological basis of the limitations of acute toxicity testing and LD50.
(c) Distinguish between NOAEL and LOAEL (and graded versus quantal dose-response).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acute: single exposure, usually in rodents, to estimate LD50 within 14 days; one control and four to five treatment groups of three to five animals, usually by the human route (often oral).
• Dose approaches: fixed dose (5 to 2000 mg/kg), stepwise procedure and up-and-down procedure; assessments include weight, behaviour, morbidity and food consumption, then necropsy and histopathology of over 40 organs.
• Subacute: repeated dosing in feed at three to four doses, clinical chemistry and histopathology after 14 or 28 days, to set doses for subchronic studies.
• Subchronic: usually 90 days (13 weeks), to establish NOAEL and characterise target organs.
• Chronic: longer than 3 months, 6 months to 2 years in rodents, about 1 year in non-rodents; highest dose is the maximum tolerated dose; carcinogenicity assessment.
(b)
• The LD50 is not a biological constant: strain, age, weight, feed, caging, fasting, method of administration, vehicle volume and observation duration alter it.
• LD50 need only be given within an order of magnitude (e.g. 5 to 50 mg/kg) and does not reflect the full spectrum of toxic responses.
• Some chemicals have carcinogenic, teratogenic or neurobehavioural effects at doses with no acute injury.
• Toxicity tests do not show that a chemical is safe but identify and characterise its toxic effects; FDA, EPA and OECD set good laboratory practice standards.
(c)
• NOAEL is the no observed adverse effect level and LOAEL is the lowest observed adverse effect level; both depend on dose spacing and animal numbers and have regulatory implications.
• Graded response describes an individual's response to rising doses; quantal response describes the distribution of individual responses across a population (ED50, TD50, LD50).
• Newer predictive in vitro approaches include organs-on-a-chip and stem cells.

questions.question:
A long-term user of high-dose cimetidine for ulcer disease develops gynaecomastia, reduced sperm count and impotence.
(a) Identify the causative drug and reaction.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) State the dosing precautions for these drugs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cimetidine, an H2-receptor antagonist (with ranitidine, famotidine and nizatidine), causing endocrine adverse effects.
(b)
• Long-term high-dose use decreases testosterone binding to the androgen receptor and inhibits a CYP that hydroxylates estradiol.
• In men this causes gynaecomastia, reduced sperm count and impotence; in women, galactorrhoea.
• H2 antagonists reversibly compete with histamine at parietal cell H2 receptors, suppress 24-hour acid secretion by about 70%, and are otherwise well tolerated.
• Other effects: diarrhoea, headache, drowsiness, fatigue, muscular pain, constipation; confusion, delirium or hallucinations with IV use or in the elderly; thrombocytopenia.
(c)
Dose reduction is recommended with decreased creatinine clearance; these drugs cross the placenta and enter breast milk.

(a)
• The phenomenon is tachyphylaxis: a rapid decrease in response to repeated doses over a short period.
• With nitroglycerin it develops over hours of infusion.
(b)
• Features: repeat administration, same dose, diminished physiological effect, short time course, not dose-dependent (a larger dose may not restore the maximum effect) and rate-sensitive (frequent dosing).
• The mechanism for nitroglycerin is not agreed and is thought to be multiple.
• Mechanisms resemble those of tolerance, except that receptors cannot be withdrawn and resynthesised at that speed.
• Contrast tolerance: a requirement for higher doses that is dose-dependent and chronic.
• Other examples: ephedrine and metaraminol (noradrenaline depletion from vesicles), methylphenidate, beta-2 agonists, nicotine, prazosin.
questions.question:
A patient on a continuous nitroglycerin infusion shows a progressively diminishing response over hours at the same dose.
(a) Identify the phenomenon and the causative drug.
(b) State the features, predisposing factors and pathophysiology.

For beta-adrenergic blockers:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their pharmacological effects.
(c) State their therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between non-selective and beta-1 selective blockers and the role of intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Non-selective: nadolol, penbutolol, pindolol, propranolol, timolol, carteolol, carvedilol, bucindolol, labetalol.
• Beta-1 selective: acebutolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol, betaxolol, celiprolol, nebivolol; beta-2 selective: butoxamine.
(b)
Reduced heart rate, contractility and output; slowed atrial and AV nodal conduction; longer AV refractory period; bronchoconstriction; prolonged hypoglycaemia; lower free fatty acids and HDL, higher LDL and triglycerides; hypokalaemia.
(c)
Angina, hypertension, arrhythmias, heart failure, pheochromocytoma, glaucoma, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, hyperthyroidism, migraine prophylaxis, acute panic symptoms, substance withdrawal, variceal bleeding.
(d)
• Adverse effects: bradycardia, negative inotropy, bradyarrhythmias, reduced AV conduction, fatigue, sleep disturbance, sexual dysfunction in men, drug interactions.
• Bronchoconstriction is of concern in asthmatics and COPD; hypoglycaemia is of concern in diabetics and hypoglycaemics; cold extremities and heart failure also occur.
• Contraindicated in Prinzmetal angina.
(e)
• Selective beta-1 agents act mainly on the heart; esmolol has quick onset and short duration, used in urgent settings.
• Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity is strong for pindolol and weak for penbutolol, carteolol, labetalol and betaxolol.
• Membrane stabilization occurs with propranolol, acebutolol, carvedilol and betaxolol only.
• Third-generation non-selective agents (carteolol, carvedilol, bucindolol, labetalol) add vasodilation; carvedilol and labetalol also block alpha-1 receptors.
• Propranolol crosses the blood-brain barrier while nadolol does not.

(a)
• Grapefruit juice is a cytochrome P450 inhibitor; atorvastatin is among drugs whose metabolism it inhibits (with alprazolam, cisapride, cyclosporine, midazolam, triazolam).
• CYP3A4 metabolises a large share of prescribed drugs.
(b)
• The active components include furanocoumarins such as 6',7'-dihydroxybergamottin.
• Enzyme inhibition reduces metabolism and raises the concentration of the substrate drug, with increased intensity, duration and toxicity.
• Some inhibitors are isoform-selective (ketoconazole) whereas cimetidine inhibits all P450-mediated metabolism.
(c)
A general preventive step is to check for drug interactions.
questions.question:
A patient taking atorvastatin regularly drinks grapefruit juice.
(a) State the interaction and why toxicity is a risk.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the interaction.
(c) State a general step to prevent such interaction toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Iron crosses the luminal membrane of intestinal cells by active transport of ferrous iron (Fe2+) and as heme; cell iron is stored as ferritin or transported across the basolateral membrane by ferroportin and oxidized to Fe3+ by a ferroxidase.
• Ferric iron is carried by transferrin; excess is stored in GI epithelial cells, macrophages and hepatocytes, and in overload in skin, heart and other organs.
• Most body iron is in haemoglobin; iron also forms myoglobin and cytochromes.
• Iron-containing heme is also an essential component of myoglobin, cytochromes and other proteins.
(b)
• Oral ferrous sulfate, gluconate or fumarate are effective and cheap; ferrous iron is most efficiently absorbed.
• Parenteral iron (iron dextran, sodium ferric gluconate, iron sucrose) is for patients who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron or have extensive chronic anaemia.
• Iron dextran is given IM or IV (50 mg elemental iron/mL); a test dose is needed; high molecular weight forms carry greater anaphylaxis risk.
• Monitor ferritin and transferrin saturation in chronic parenteral therapy; ferumoxytol interferes with MRI so do MRI first.
(c)
• Acute toxicity in young children: vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea, shock, lethargy, dyspnoea, then possible acidosis, coma and death.
• Treat with whole bowel irrigation and IV deferoxamine; supportive therapy for bleeding, acidosis and shock; activated charcoal does not bind iron.
• Parenteral administration bypasses intestinal regulation and delivers more iron than can be stored.
• Chronic overload (hemochromatosis) deposits iron in heart, liver and pancreas, leading to organ failure; treat with weekly phlebotomy or chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox).
questions.question:
For iron:
(a) Describe its absorption, transport, storage and excretion pathways.
(b) State the dosing considerations and routes, with monitoring.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of acute and chronic toxicity and its management.

Pharmacodynamics of hormone action at cell-surface and nuclear receptors.
(a) Describe how peptide/amino acid hormones and steroid/thyroid hormones act at receptor level.
(b) State how members relate to specific disorders.
(c) Explain why drug effects may extend to other organ systems.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Amino-acid derivative and peptide hormones are water-soluble and bind cell-surface membrane receptors, working through second messengers (cAMP, cGMP, phospholipase C-Ca2+, tyrosine kinase).
• Steroids, thyroid hormones, vitamin D and retinoids are lipophilic, carried by transport proteins and bind intracellular nuclear receptors.
• The hormone-receptor complex binds DNA, switching genes on or off and altering mRNA and protein amounts.
• Release is under negative feedback from hypothalamus to anterior pituitary to target gland.
(b)
• Growth hormone: deficiency gives short stature; excess gives gigantism or acromegaly.
• Glucocorticoid excess gives Cushing's syndrome and deficiency Addison's disease; aldosterone excess gives Conn's disease.
• Insulin deficiency gives diabetes mellitus and excess insulinoma; vasopressin deficiency gives diabetes insipidus.
• Excess prolactin gives galactorrhoea; excess TSH gives goitre.
(c)
• Glucocorticoids control carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism and suppress inflammation and immune response.
• Drug-induced diabetes arises with glucocorticoids, nicotinic acid, thiazides, hydantoins, protease inhibitors and atypical antipsychotics.
• Growth hormone antagonises insulin; hormones also have effects on reproduction, growth, electrolytes and energy metabolism.
• Corticosteroids may cause cataracts.

questions.question:
A patient with acute promyelocytic leukaemia is to receive arsenic trioxide.
(a) Name the drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on mechanism and pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Arsenic trioxide is approved by the FDA as an anticancer agent for acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
• It is also thought to have therapeutic potential in myeloma.
(b)
• Its therapeutic action is attributed to induction of apoptosis in leukaemia cells; it is a tumour-specific agent causing cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis.
• Arsenic trioxide is methylated (non-enzymatically to monomethylarsonic acid, then enzymatically to dimethylarsinic acid) before urinary excretion.
• Some methylated trivalent metabolites may be more toxic than arsenite.
(c)
• Arsenic(III) binds thiol groups and can inactivate over 200 enzymes; arsenic impairs mitochondrial respiration and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation.
• Inorganic arsenic is a human carcinogen with long-term exposure.

(a)
Penicillin is given intravenously to treat bacterial meningitis.
(b)
• Penicillin cannot pass through the blood-brain barrier normally, but intense inflammation in bacterial meningitis disrupts the barrier's integrity.
• Penicillin is a weak acid and is metabolised by gastric acid; the intravenous route gives 100% bioavailability and bypasses first-pass metabolism.
• Penicillin comes from Penicillium chrysogenum.
(c)
Drug allergy is an immune-mediated reaction largely independent of dose, occurring in a small percentage of the population.
questions.question:
A patient with bacterial meningitis is given intravenous penicillin.
(a) Name the drug therapy.
(b) Give the rationale based on pharmacokinetics.
(c) State the major adverse effect.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase 1 (COX-1).
• Prostaglandin improves mucosal blood supply and encourages mucosal repair; NSAIDs inhibit PGE2 and PGI2 secretion.
• Pharmacologically, aspirin decreases pain and also decreases fever.
(b)
• Members named: aspirin, diclofenac, meloxicam, naproxen, ibuprofen, indomethacin.
• Diclofenac, meloxicam and naproxen are CYP2C9 substrates; ibuprofen undergoes aliphatic hydroxylation; indomethacin is secreted in bile.
• Aspirin is a weak acid, absorbed in the stomach, with excretion enhanced by alkaline urine.
(c)
• GI: NSAIDs increase gastric secretion and reduce mucosal protection, causing ulcer formation; GI irritation is a type A undesired effect; peptic ulcer is a drug-induced disease.
• Cardiovascular/renal: NSAIDs antagonise beta-blockers, diuretics and ACE inhibitors; analgesic nephropathy is a type C effect.
• Fetal: NSAIDs can cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus.
• Liver: acyl glucuronidation of NSAIDs may form reactive species causing hepatotoxicity.
• A defective CYP2C9 gene (which handles diclofenac, meloxicam, naproxen) gives bleeding tendency; H. pylori infection also contributes to ulcers.
questions.question:
Pharmacodynamics of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
(a) Describe their action at enzyme level.
(b) State how members relate to specific uses and handling.
(c) Explain why effects extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

A patient with recurrent asthma attacks is prescribed a pressurised metered-dose salbutamol inhaler.
(a) Identify the drug class indicated and the receptors on which it acts.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action.
(c) Describe the pharmacokinetic features of the inhalation route that suit this therapy.
(d) State the adverse effects or limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Class: beta-agonist bronchodilators (e.g. albuterol/salbutamol) used for asthma attacks; they act on adrenergic receptors of the sympathetic nervous system.
(b)
• They attach to adrenergic receptors and mimic the action of norepinephrine.
• The beta-adrenoceptor is a G-protein coupled receptor (seven membrane-spanning helices) using cAMP as second messenger; effect is seen within seconds.
(c)
• Gaseous/aerosol drugs are absorbed through the pulmonary epithelium and reach the circulation rapidly (large surface area, thin membranes, high blood flow).
• Pressurised metered-dose aerosols hold the drug in a liquefied inert propellant; absorption is instantaneous, hepatic first-pass loss is avoided, and the drug is applied locally at the site of action in pulmonary disease.
(d)
• Rapid tolerance (tachyphylaxis) to the bronchodilator effect of beta-2 agonists develops after 1 dose and takes a week to resolve; the mechanism is uncoupling of the receptor from its intracellular effector.
• Continuous agonist exposure causes receptor down-regulation, giving a reduced response to beta-agonists in asthmatics.
• Other limitations of the route: irritation/inflammation with poorly soluble drugs, difficulty regulating the dose, transport to the site not guaranteed, and some patients find inhalers hard to use.
• Antagonism: propranolol antagonises salbutamol; beta-blockers such as atenolol block the action of norepinephrine at adrenergic receptors.

questions.question:
A patient with asthma is started on a non-selective beta-blocker and develops wheeze and breathlessness.
(a) Identify the causative drug class and reaction.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) State the drugs used for asthma in general.
(d) Name the beta-1 selective blockers that exist.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A non-selective beta-blocker (for example propranolol, nadolol, timolol) causing bronchoconstriction.
(b)
• Bronchoconstriction is of concern in asthmatics and COPD, because beta-2 receptors mediate bronchial smooth muscle relaxation through Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP.
• Blocking beta-2 receptors removes this relaxation; the effects depend largely on the degree of sympathoadrenal tone.
• Other effects of beta-blockade: bradycardia, reduced contractility and cardiac output, slowed AV conduction, fatigue, sleep disturbance, prolonged hypoglycaemia, sexual dysfunction in men, adverse lipid changes.
(c)
Selective beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol) are the agents used for asthma in general.
(d)
Beta-1 selective blockers exist (acebutolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol, betaxolol, celiprolol, nebivolol).

(a)
• Rapidly absorbed orally with 100% bioavailability and little individual variation.
• Highly bound to plasma albumin, which limits diffusion into CSF, urine and breast milk; it readily crosses the placenta.
• Mean half-life about 40 hours, highly variable between individuals.
• Conjugated to glucuronic acid; inactive metabolites are excreted in urine and faeces.
(b)
• It has a narrow therapeutic index; the International Normalized Ratio (INR) is the standard, and frequent monitoring may be required.
• Peak effects are delayed 72-96 hours; vitamin K reverses the effect but takes about 24 hours.
• Interactions: CYP2C9 induction (barbiturates, carbamazepine, rifampin) and binding to cholestyramine reduce effect; CYP2C9 inhibitors (amiodarone, azoles, metronidazole, etc.) raise bleeding; antibiotics raise INR via gut flora.
• Displacement from albumin by sulfonamides gives transient elevated activity.
(c)
• Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X, so the principal toxicity is bleeding (oral or IV vitamin K, plasma, factor concentrates).
• Rare toxicities: skin lesions and necrosis, purple toe syndrome; it is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy.
• Therapeutic failure: reduced absorption, enzyme induction, large vitamin K intake, raised clotting factors in pregnancy; hypoproteinemia lowers volume of distribution and half-life.
• Enhanced effect: hepatic impairment, heart failure and hyperthyroidism.
questions.question:
For warfarin:
(a) Describe its pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion).
(b) State its dosing considerations, monitoring and interactions.
