(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of its toxicity and of therapeutic failure.

A patient is brought in after taking a larger-than-therapeutic dose of aspirin.
(a) State the risk factors that determine toxicity and the property of aspirin that governs its elimination.
(b) Explain the mechanism by which urinary pH alters its excretion.
(c) Outline management of the overdose.
(d) Justify the preferred option over the opposite urinary manipulation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Toxicity depends on route, dose, and duration/frequency of exposure; larger-than-therapeutic doses may prolong absorption, alter protein binding and distribution, and change metabolic fate.
• Aspirin is a weak acid; its unionised (protonated) form is lipid-soluble and relatively readily absorbed in the acidic stomach.
(b)
• Only unionised, lipid-soluble drug moves freely back across the tubular membrane into blood; ionised, water-soluble drug stays in the filtrate and becomes concentrated as water is reabsorbed.
• In alkaline medium a weak acid ionises (A-), so its reabsorption falls and excretion rises (the 'ion trap').
(c)
• Make the urine more alkaline with sodium bicarbonate: aspirin becomes ionised, reabsorption decreases and excretion increases.
• Urinary pH is purposely altered in overdose or poisoning to raise the rate of drug excretion.
(d)
• Alkalinising the urine promotes excretion of acidic drugs, whereas acidifying it is used for basic drugs (e.g. diazepam with ammonium chloride).
• In acidic urine a weak acid is more lipophilic and less ionised, so it is reabsorbed largely and renal excretion is reduced; hence alkalinisation is preferred.

(a)
• Type 1 DM results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells with absolute loss of insulin secretion; insulin is a hormone from pancreatic beta cells.
• Insulin is also a drug source from animals, and bacteria engineered by recombinant DNA make human insulin.
(b)
• It raises glycogen synthase and lowers glycogen phosphorylase; raises glucokinase and lowers glucose-6-phosphatase; raises glycolysis and lowers gluconeogenesis.
• It drives amino-acid uptake into muscle and promotes lipogenesis and triglyceride storage.
• Insulin acts on enzyme-linked receptors with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity (a relatively slow response).
(c)
• As a polypeptide it is metabolised by digestive enzymes and undergoes pre-systemic loss, so it is effective by one route only (not orally).
• Subcutaneous absorption is slow and constant, limited by blood flow, and slowed by a vasoconstrictor; nicotine-induced skin vasoconstriction delays absorption.
(d)
Hypoglycaemic shock after insulin is an exaggerated desired (type A) effect.
questions.question:
A patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus requires insulin.
(a) State why insulin is indicated.
(b) Explain its mechanism of action and receptor type.
(c) Describe its pharmacokinetic considerations, including route.
(d) State the adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Absorption routes: oral GIT (small intestine is the major site), inhalation (particles smaller than 1 micrometre reach alveoli) and dermal (stratum corneum is the rate-limiting barrier).
• Absorption depends on molecular weight, lipid solubility (log P), ionisation (pKa and pH), concentration, physical form, blood flow and surface area.
• Storage: plasma proteins, liver and kidney (metallothionein binds cadmium), fat (DDT, PCBs), bone (lead replaces calcium; fluoride, strontium).
• Redistribution: lead goes first to liver and in a month to bone; barriers are the blood-brain barrier (lipid-soluble only, immature at birth) and the placenta (molecular weight under 1000).
• Excretion: urinary, faecal (biliary, intestinal), respiratory and milk, sweat or saliva; urine pH is altered in acute intoxication.
(b)
• Plasma protein binding interactions lead to toxicity; binding prolongs half-life and affects the toxic threshold dose.
• Monitoring exposure: blood cadmium reflects recent exposure and urinary cadmium/creatinine reflects body burden.
• Albumin or blood cells in urine indicate glomerular damage.
(c)
• No absorption means no toxicity; when absorption exceeds elimination the toxicant accumulates and reaches a critical target concentration.
• Distribution to non-target tissue decreases toxicity, and equal absorption can give different toxicity through biotransformation.
• Enterohepatic circulation prolongs half-life and can enhance toxicity; storage releases toxicant as it is biotransformed or excreted.
• Toxic response depends on potency, site specificity and the organism's ability to dispose of the toxicant.
questions.question:
Toxicokinetics: disposition of toxicants (absorption, distribution, biotransformation and excretion).
(a) Describe the absorption routes, storage depots, redistribution, barriers and excretion of toxicants.
(b) State the considerations affecting interactions and monitoring.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity.

A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease on haemodialysis and erythropoietin therapy has a hypochromic, microcytic anaemia with low mean cell volume and low mean cell haemoglobin concentration.
(a) Identify the drug class or mechanism involved.
(b) State the receptors, enzymes or organ systems affected.
(c) State the differential causes and conditions in which the drug is wrong.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for the choice of therapy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Iron deficiency anaemia, treated with iron preparations; its only indication.
(b)
• Iron is the component of heme in haemoglobin; without enough iron small erythrocytes with insufficient haemoglobin form.
• Erythropoietin is produced by the kidney; its reduced synthesis underlies the anaemia of renal failure; ESAs act on erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow.
(c)
• Causes: blood loss (most common in adults), increased requirements (infants, pregnancy, lactation), malabsorption (gastrectomy, small bowel disease) and haemodialysis with erythropoietin therapy.
• Iron should not be given in haemolytic anaemia because iron stores are elevated.
(d)
• Oral ferrous salts correct the anaemia as well as parenteral iron when GI absorption is normal; parenteral iron is preferred in haemodialysis patients on erythropoietin.
• Iron dextran needs a test dose (hypersensitivity; more anaphylaxis with high molecular weight forms); sodium ferric gluconate and iron sucrose are IV only and less likely to cause hypersensitivity.
• Monitor serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to avoid overload; ESA haemoglobin should not exceed 12 g/dL (hypertension, thrombosis).

questions.question:
Classification of drug dependence and related terms.
(a) Classify psychological and physical dependence, abuse, addiction, habituation and withdrawal with examples.
(b) Explain the pharmacological basis of withdrawal reactions and rebound.
(c) Distinguish between drug addiction and drug habituation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Drug dependence is a state in which use for personal satisfaction takes higher priority than basic needs despite awareness of health risks; it may be psychological or physical.
• Psychological dependence: belief that well-being needs the drug; it begins with liking and may progress to craving and compulsive use (opioids, cocaine, benzodiazepines).
• Physical dependence: altered physiological state requiring continued presence of the drug; stopping gives a withdrawal syndrome (alcohol, opioids, antidepressants, stimulants).
• Drug abuse is self-medication deviating from approved medical and social patterns; for regulators it is any use of an illicit drug.
• Addiction: compulsive drug seeking and relapse after promising to stop (cocaine, cannabis, amphetamines).
• Habituation: less intense involvement with mild discomfort on withdrawal, no physical dependence (tea, coffee, tobacco, social drinking).
(b)
• Withdrawal reactions also occur with non-dependence drugs: seizure frequency rises on sudden stopping of antiepileptics and hypertension may worsen with some BP drugs.
• Gradual withdrawal minimises these reactions; type E end-of-treatment effects include opioid and anxiolytic withdrawal and hypnotic rebound.
• Up-regulation of receptors after continuous antagonist exposure explains rebound after abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal.
(c)
• Addiction is intense, compulsive and prone to relapse; habituation is mild with no physical dependence.
• Nicotine is highly addictive: it stimulates nicotinic receptors, releasing dopamine and activating the reward system.

questions.question:
For antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) drugs:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanism of action.
(c) State their pharmacological effects.
(d) State their therapeutic uses.
(e) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(f) Distinguish between atropine and scopolamine.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Natural alkaloids: atropine and hyoscine (scopolamine) from belladonna; semisynthetic: atropine methonitrate, homatropine.
• Synthetic: ipratropium, tiotropium, tolterodine, oxybutynin, flavoxate, propantheline, glycopyrrolate, dicyclomine, pirenzepine, cyclopentolate, tropicamide, benztropine, trihexyphenidyl.
(b)
Competitive reversible antagonists at muscarinic receptors: affinity but no efficacy, slow dissociation; blockade is lessened by more ACh or agonist.
(c)
• Effects: mydriasis and cycloplegia; decreased gastric and intestinal secretions and motility; tachycardia from vagal blockade; bronchodilation; decreased secretions, salivation and sweating.
• Also urinary retention (relaxed detrusor, constricted sphincter) and CNS stimulation at higher doses.
(d)
• Parkinson's disease and drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions; motion sickness (scopolamine); symptomatic bradycardia; asthma, COPD and bronchitis.
• Peptic ulcer, irritable bowel and GI hypersecretory states; overactive bladder and enuresis; ophthalmic refraction and retinal examination.
(e)
• Adverse effects arise from blocking muscarinic receptors everywhere: dry mouth, dry skin and fever, blurred vision, raised intraocular pressure, tachycardia, constipation, urinary retention.
• Central effects include irritability, disorientation, hallucinations and delirium; overdose gives hyperthermia, ileus and seizures; they are contraindicated in glaucoma and prostatic hypertrophy.
(f)
• Atropine is the prototype with potent mydriatic, antisecretory and cardiovascular effects, and is an antidote in organophosphate poisoning.
• Scopolamine (hyoscine) has more CNS effects: it depresses the CNS, causing amnesia, drowsiness, euphoria and sleep, and is good for motion sickness; it is given parenterally, orally or transdermally.
• Peripheral effects are similar for both.

(a)
• HIV is a lentivirus (retrovirus): single-stranded RNA transcribed to double-stranded DNA by reverse transcriptase, which integrates into the host genome and can lie dormant in resting memory CD4+ T cells.
• NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase through two different mechanisms, preventing proviral DNA formation.
• Protease inhibitors interrupt protein processing and virus assembly, blocking virion maturation; integrase inhibitors act on integration; fusion inhibitors stop fusion with CD4 cells.
(b)
• NRTI members: zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), emtricitabine (FTC), didanosine (ddI), tenofovir (TDF), with combinations such as Combivir and Truvada; integrase inhibitor: dolutegravir.
• HIV-1 responds better to NNRTIs, whereas HIV-2 does not respond to them; zidovudine was the first antiretroviral (1986).
• Treatment is a 'test and treat' approach guided by viral load and drug sensitivity testing.
(c)
• Lactic acidosis, mostly with NRTIs, can be fatal; lipodystrophy affects 33-75% on HAART with raised lipids and hyperglycaemia.
• Indinavir causes renal calculi in 10% of patients (adequate hydration is the mainstay); pentamidine, amphotericin B, adefovir, cidofovir and foscarnet are linked to renal damage.
• NNRTIs, abacavir and amprenavir are known for severe skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
• Zidovudine is associated with elongated eyelashes and bluish nails; interferon with nucleoside analogue therapy can cause reversible cardiomyopathy.
• Ketoconazole toxicity may cause adrenal gland disease; abacavir hypersensitivity is strongly associated with HLA-B*5701.
• Immune reconstitution after therapy may cause hepatic injury.
questions.question:
Pharmacodynamics of antiretroviral drug classes.
(a) Describe the action of each class at enzyme or receptor level in the viral life cycle.
(b) State how members relate to specific uses.
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• PPIs (omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole) are prodrugs requiring activation in acid; they are given as enteric-coated capsules or tablets, powder or IV solution (esomeprazole, pantoprazole).
• They are rapidly absorbed, highly protein bound and extensively metabolized by hepatic CYP2C19 and CYP3A4.
• H2 antagonists (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine, nizatidine) are rapidly absorbed with peak serum levels in 1-3 hours, little protein binding, excreted by filtration and tubular secretion.
(b)
• PPIs are given about 30 minutes before meals; 2-5 days of once-daily dosing reach about 70% inhibition; suppression lasts 24-48 hours.
• H2 antagonists need a reduced dose in decreased creatinine clearance; tolerance may occur; they suppress 24-hour acid by about 70% and nocturnal secretion.
• PPI interactions: warfarin, diazepam, cyclosporin; omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and induces CYP1A2; reduced acidity lowers absorption of ketoconazole, ampicillin esters, iron salts and calcium.
• In hepatic disease reduce esomeprazole and lansoprazole doses in severe cases.
(c)
• PPIs bind the H+/K+-ATPase irreversibly, so acid returns only after new pumps form; adverse effects: nausea, abdominal pain, constipation, flatulence, diarrhoea, myopathy, arthralgias, headache, rash; chronic use linked to hip fractures.
• H2 antagonists compete reversibly with histamine, so are less potent than PPIs.
• Cimetidine at high doses blocks androgen binding and estradiol hydroxylation: gynaecomastia, reduced sperm count, impotence, galactorrhoea.
• CNS effects (confusion, hallucinations) occur with IV use or in the elderly; they cross the placenta and breast milk.
• Thrombocytopenia and other blood dyscrasias can occur.
questions.question:
For proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2-receptor antagonists:
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics.
(b) State their dosing considerations and interactions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of their toxicity or therapeutic limitations.

For dabigatran and the direct oral factor Xa inhibitors:
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics.
(b) State their dosing considerations, interactions and monitoring.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of their toxicity or therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Dabigatran etexilate is a prodrug given orally and hydrolysed by plasma esterases to the active thrombin inhibitor dabigatran; it is a P-glycoprotein substrate and eliminated renally.
• Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban and betrixaban are adequately absorbed orally.
• Rivaroxaban is metabolized by CYP3A4/5 and CYP2J2 to inactive metabolites, about one-third excreted unchanged in urine.
• Apixaban is mainly metabolized by CYP3A4 with about 27% renal excretion; edoxaban and betrixaban are minimally metabolized (urine and faeces respectively).
(b)
• Dabigatran levels need not be monitored, an advantage over warfarin; use caution in renal impairment and over age 75.
• P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, dronedarone, quinidine, ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise dabigatran; rifampicin lowers it.
• For Xa inhibitors reduce doses (or avoid) with P-gp inhibitors such as clarithromycin, verapamil and amiodarone; avoid strong P-gp/CYP3A4 inducers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin, St. John's wort) with apixaban and rivaroxaban.
• Renal dosage adjustments are recommended for the Xa inhibitors.
(c)
• Direct inhibition of thrombin or factor Xa reduces fibrin and platelet aggregation, so bleeding is the major adverse effect; declining kidney function prolongs effect and raises bleeding risk.
• Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; Xa inhibitors currently have no antidote.
• Dabigatran can cause GI effects (dyspepsia, esophagitis); abrupt discontinuation raises thrombotic risk.
• Dabigatran is contraindicated in mechanical prosthetic heart valves.

(a)
• Absorption: immature GI function in children and declining function in the elderly delay or reduce absorption.
• Distribution: the blood-brain barrier is not fully developed at birth; disease states such as hypoalbuminaemia, heart failure and cirrhosis also alter distribution.
• Metabolism: in newborns phase I and phase II pathways may not be active at birth because of maturational changes.
• In the elderly hepatic blood flow falls by 40% or more, liver size by about 17-36%, with diminished enzyme activity.
• Excretion: infants and the aged have decreased hepatic and renal function, lowering efficiency of excretion.
(b)
• Children may form metabolites not seen in adults, e.g. caffeine from theophylline in neonates; valproic acid, paracetamol, chloramphenicol, cimetidine and salicylamide also change.
• Elderly patients have more adverse effects, especially with multiple drug therapy.
• Dose adjustment is required for narrow therapeutic index drugs when excretion falls.
(c)
• Newborns may be more sensitive to xenobiotics that cross an immature blood-brain barrier.
• Reduced hepatic and renal clearance prolongs half-life, so drugs accumulate and toxic effects appear.
• Delayed or reduced absorption in children and the elderly is the age-related limitation of oral therapy.
questions.question:
Pharmacokinetics of drugs at the extremes of age (neonates and the elderly).
(a) Describe age effects on absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
(b) State dosing considerations and interactions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity and therapeutic failure.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels; binding of two ACh molecules opens a cation-selective pore equally permeable to Na+ and K+, with small Ca2+ permeability.
• Net inward current depolarizes the cell briefly (under 10 ms) because AChE rapidly degrades ACh; subunits include alpha, beta, gamma and delta.
• Subtypes: NN at autonomic ganglia and adrenal medulla; NM at the neuromuscular junction; neuronal (CNS) receptors also exist.
(b)
• Neuromuscular blockers act at NM receptors: non-depolarizing (tubocurarine, pancuronium, vecuronium, atracurium) are competitive antagonists; depolarizing (succinylcholine, decamethonium) are agonists.
• Uses: surgical relaxation, tracheal intubation, controlled ventilation and attenuating convulsions.
• Ganglion blockers (hexamethonium, mecamylamine, trimetaphan) are now rarely used; nicotine replacement and varenicline treat tobacco dependence.
• Curare-like drugs block ACh receptors at the motor end plate and are used therapeutically during surgery to relax musculature.
(c)
• Ganglionic blockade reduces both sympathetic and parasympathetic transmission: vasodilation and hypotension, tachycardia, mydriasis, cycloplegia, GI hypomotility, urinary retention, xerostomia and anhidrosis.
• Nicotine first stimulates then depresses all ganglia, produces neuromuscular blockade by desensitization, and stimulates the CNS (large doses depress and may cause respiratory failure).
• Non-depolarizing blockers such as tubocurarine cause hypotension and histamine release; gallamine and pancuronium block muscarinic receptors causing tachycardia.
• Succinylcholine may cause bradycardia, raised intraocular pressure and malignant hyperthermia.
• Neuromuscular blockers do not cross the blood-brain barrier.
questions.question:
For nicotinic receptors:
(a) Describe the pharmacodynamics at receptor level (structure, ion selectivity and action).
(b) State how the subtypes relate to specific therapeutic uses (ganglionic and neuromuscular drugs).
(c) Explain why effects may extend to other organ systems and cause adverse effects or special precautions.

For loperamide and diphenoxylate:
(a) Describe their pharmacokinetics.
(b) State their dosing considerations and cautions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of their toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Loperamide is an orally active piperidine butyramide derivative with mu-receptor activity, 40-50 times more potent than morphine as an antidiarrhoeal, and penetrates the CNS poorly.
• Loperamide has a half-life of about 11 hours, peak blood level at 3-5 hours and extensive first-pass metabolism.
• Diphenoxylate and difenoxin are more powerful than morphine; extensively absorbed orally, peak levels in 1-2 hours, half-life about 12 hours; diphenoxylate is rapidly de-esterified to difenoxine.
(b)
• Loperamide: 4 mg to start, then 2 mg after each loose stool, up to 16 mg in 24 hours; not recommended under 2 years.
• Loperamide has antisecretory activity against cholera toxin and some E. coli, raises anal sphincter tone and lengthens small intestine and mouth-caecum transit times.
• It is effective for travellers' diarrhoea alone or with antimicrobials and as an adjunct in chronic diarrhoea.
• Diphenoxylate is marketed with a small dose of atropine to discourage abuse; increasing doses give CNS and anticholinergic effects.
(c)
• Mu-receptor action reduces motility and secretion, which is dangerous in infective diarrhoea (systemic invasion) and can induce toxic megacolon.
• Loperamide overdose: CNS depression, paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon in inflammatory bowel disease; use is contraindicated in severe IBD.
• Diphenoxylate at 40-60 mg/day has CNS effects with potential for abuse and addiction.
• Oral rehydration therapy is the cornerstone of acute diarrhoea; antimotility drugs give symptomatic treatment only.
• With larger doses of the diphenoxylate-atropine preparation, anticholinergic effects appear in addition to CNS effects.

questions.question:
A worker is found to have an elevated urine cadmium to creatinine ratio.
(a) Identify the laboratory clue and what it indicates.
(b) State the target organs and molecular mechanisms.
(c) List differential toxicant causes and exposure origins.
(d) Give the pharmacological reasoning for management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Urine cadmium (adjusted by the cadmium/creatinine ratio) indicates accumulation or kidney burden; a value above 2 microgram/g creatinine is a marker of chronic exposure.
• Blood cadmium reflects recent exposure (e.g. smoking); levels are higher in smokers than in former smokers and non-smokers.
(b)
• Target organs: lung (emphysema, lung cancer), kidney, bone (reduced density, osteoporosis), GI tract (acute irritation), blood vessels.
• Cadmium generates reactive oxygen species, damages DNA, blocks calcium channels and induces metallothionein, a cysteine-rich binding protein.
(c)
• Sources: food (liver, mushrooms, shellfish, cocoa powder, dried seaweed), cigarette smoking, mining, smelting, batteries and pigments.
• Other priority metals with systemic toxicity: arsenic, chromium, lead and mercury.
(d)
Management is by reducing exposure sources (smoking, workplace).

(a)
• Digoxin has a low therapeutic index (as do cocaine and vancomycin).
• Its Vd is up to 10 times total body water (greater than 42 L): it accumulates in tissue.
(b)
• It is a substrate of P-glycoprotein (MDR1), together with quinidine and verapamil.
• Enterohepatic circulation can retain up to 20% of total drug and prolong action (digoxin, morphine, chloramphenicol).
• Renal disease lowers clearance so drugs normally eliminated by the kidney are retained, producing toxic effects.
• Phenytoin enhances metabolism of digitoxin; hallucinations are a nervous-system effect of digitalis.
• Parenteral digoxin is used as a loading dose before oral maintenance.
(c)
Justification: the therapeutic goal is concentration below the toxic level and not below the efficacy level.
questions.question:
A patient taking digoxin is at risk of toxicity.
(a) State the risk factors for toxicity.
(b) Explain the pharmacokinetic basis of the toxicity.
(c) State the therapeutic goal for digoxin.

For antiplatelet drugs:
(a) Classify them with examples.
(b) State their mechanism of action.
(c) State their therapeutic uses.
(d) Explain the pharmacological basis of their adverse effects and limitations.
(e) Distinguish between abciximab and the synthetic GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors (tirofiban, eptifibatide).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Aspirin (COX inhibitor); P2Y12 antagonists (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor); GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, tirofiban, eptifibatide).
• Miscellaneous: cilostazol and dipyridamole; protease-activated receptor-1 antagonists (vorapaxar, atopaxar).
(b)
• Aspirin irreversibly blocks COX-1 so thromboxane A2 is not made; P2Y12 antagonists block ADP receptors reducing aggregation.
• GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors block fibrinogen binding to activated platelets, preventing interplatelet bridges; cilostazol and dipyridamole inhibit phosphodiesterase, block adenosine uptake and inhibit TXA2 synthesis.
(c)
• They prevent platelet-rich arterial thrombi: aspirin and others reduce MI and stroke; abciximab in coronary angioplasty with heparin and aspirin; tirofiban and eptifibatide in acute coronary syndrome.
• Dipyridamole reduces stroke and death after transient ischaemic attacks by about 15%.
(d)
• Aspirin: GI bleeding, Reye's syndrome in children, tinnitus, worsened asthma (due to COX inhibition).
• Clopidogrel's CYP dependence limits it; ticagrelor causes dyspnoea; dipyridamole causes dizziness, headache, GI upset but unlike aspirin does not raise bleeding risk; cilostazol and dipyridamole also vasodilate.
(e)
• Abciximab: humanized mouse monoclonal antibody, IV, binds platelets within 1 minute, loading dose for over 80% receptor block, half-life 10-15 minutes but long biological activity.
• Tirofiban and eptifibatide: synthetic IV agents that bind reversibly and dissociate in 10-15 seconds; half-lives 2 and 2.5 hours; tirofiban has greater receptor affinity.
• Both compete with fibrinogen at the receptor; occupancy tracks plasma concentration.
• All are adjuncts to aspirin and heparin.

(a)
Mercury (methylmercury); sewage with mercury from a chemicals works entered Minamata Bay in Japan, with the first poisoning incidents in 1952 and nearly 1000 deaths.
(b)
• Algae and bacteria methylate mercury; it passes through the food chain into fish, shellfish and humans.
• Methylmercury is readily absorbed in the GI tract, crosses the placenta and blood-brain barrier, and has a very low excretion rate, accumulating in kidneys, nervous tissue and liver.
• Hg2+ and MeHg bind cysteine residues, deplete antioxidants, raise reactive oxygen species in mitochondria and alter calcium homeostasis.
• Effects: nervous system disruption, brain damage, DNA and chromosome damage, allergic reactions, sperm damage, birth defects and miscarriage.
(c)
• Prevention: strict environmental laws followed in Japan, and bans on mercury additives in paints and pesticides.
• In rat studies selenium pretreatment and vitamin E reduced HgCl2-induced lipid peroxidation.
questions.question:
Residents who eat fish from a bay polluted by industrial effluent develop disturbed nervous system function and brain damage.
(a) Identify the causative agent.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State how it can be prevented and any protective agents shown in animal studies.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Heavy metals are metallic elements of high density that are toxic at low concentrations; they are natural crust components and cannot be degraded.
• Essential nutrients: Co, Cu, Cr, Fe, Mg, Mn, Mo, Ni, Se, Zn; non-essential: Al, Sb, As, Ba, Be, Bi, Cd, Pb, Li, Hg, Pt, Ag, Tl, Sn, Ti, V, U and others.
• As, Cd, Cr, Pb and Hg are priority metals: systemic toxicants causing multi-organ damage at low exposure and known or probable human carcinogens.
• Origins: mining, smelting, industry, agriculture, domestic effluents, corrosion, volcanoes; exposure through food, water, air, paint, dental amalgams and fish.
(b)
• Arsenic: As(III) binds thiol groups and inactivates over 200 enzymes; As(V) replaces phosphate; it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation and inhibits pyruvate and fatty acid oxidation.
• Cadmium: damages cells via reactive oxygen species, single-strand DNA breaks, blocks calcium channels; blood vessels are main targets; lung is the established carcinogenic site.
• Lead: inhibits or mimics calcium, replaces it in bone, binds sulfhydryl and amide groups, and impairs haemoglobin synthesis; the nervous system is most vulnerable.
• Mercury: Hg2+ and MeHg bind cysteine residues, deplete antioxidants, raise reactive oxygen species in mitochondria and alter calcium homeostasis; targets are the GI tract, nervous system and kidney.
(c)
• Chromium(III) is an essential nutrient (shortage may cause heart conditions and diabetes) but excess causes skin rashes.
• Chromium(VI) is dangerous in steel and textile workers and smokers, causing skin allergy, nose irritation, ulcers, kidney and liver damage, altered genetic material and lung cancer.
• Arsenite (As III) is 2-10 times more toxic than arsenate (As V); inorganic arsenic is more toxic than organic forms.
questions.question:
Classification of heavy metals and their toxicity.
(a) Classify heavy metals (essential and non-essential, priority metals) and describe origins and routes of exposure.
(b) Explain the pharmacological basis of the toxicity of arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury.
(c) Distinguish between chromium(III) and chromium(VI) (and arsenite and arsenate).

Pharmacokinetics of drug metabolism and cytochrome P450 enzymes.
(a) Describe the sites, enzymes, reaction types and cytochrome P450 cycle.
(b) State dosing considerations, interactions (induction and inhibition) and monitoring.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity and therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The liver is the principal site, with GIT, lungs, skin and kidney also active; metabolism makes drugs more polar, usually inactive; prodrugs (enalapril, cyclophosphamide, levodopa) become active.
• Phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) introduces functional groups; phase II (glucuronidation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione, glycine, sulphate, water conjugation) forms polar conjugates.
• CYP450 is a haem-containing superfamily in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, absorbing light at 450 nm; CYP1, 2 and 3 families handle drugs, CYP3A4 handling about 50% of drugs.
• Oxidation needs P450, NADPH-P450 reductase, NADPH and molecular oxygen: drug binds Fe3+ P450, two electrons from NADPH reduce oxygen to activated oxygen, which oxidises the drug.
(b)
• Inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, St John's wort, chronic alcohol) speed metabolism of the inducer and co-administered drugs.
• Inhibitors (cimetidine, ketoconazole, erythromycin, valproate, isoniazid, grapefruit juice, omeprazole, metronidazole) raise levels of substrate drugs.
• Examples: warfarin plus barbiturate gives decreased anticoagulation; warfarin plus metronidazole gives haemorrhage.
• Other factors: protein binding, disease (liver disease prolongs diazepam half-life), age, nutrition, sex and genetics.
• Monitoring: drug concentrations during therapy; genotype tests for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19.
(c)
• Inducers cause reduced pharmacological action or therapeutic failure; where metabolites are reactive, induction worsens toxicity (paracetamol).
• Some conjugations form reactive species: acyl glucuronidation of NSAIDs and N-acetylation of isoniazid cause hepatotoxicity; sulfation activates minoxidil.
• Inhibition causes drug accumulation with increased intensity, duration and toxicity.

(a)
• The kidney is the main site of excretion; water-soluble drugs and polar metabolites are excreted effectively; metabolites are generally more polar than the parent drug.
• Filtration: unbound low-molecular-weight drugs are filtered; blood cells, protein-bound drugs and macromolecules (heparin) are not.
• Reabsorption is passive: only unionised lipid-soluble drugs return to blood; about 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed and ionised drugs become concentrated.
• Active secretion: carrier-mediated in proximal tubule, via OATs (acids) and OCTs (bases), effective even for protein-bound drugs.
• Clearance = rate of elimination / concentration; organ clearances add up (renal + liver + other).
(b)
• Urinary pH is altered in overdose: sodium bicarbonate for aspirin, ammonium chloride for diazepam.
• Competition for OAT and OCT carriers is a site of drug-drug interactions.
• Renal blood flow, protein binding, age and disease (liver or kidney failure) change excretion; narrow therapeutic index drugs need dose adjustment.
(c)
• When clearance falls in renal failure, drugs normally eliminated by the kidney are retained for long periods with toxic effects.
• Gentamicin accumulation harms the kidney and ear at high concentration over long periods.
• The kidney is vulnerable because of high blood flow and concentrating of filtered toxicants.
questions.question:
Pharmacokinetics of renal drug excretion.
(a) Describe filtration, tubular reabsorption, active secretion and clearance.
(b) State dosing considerations and interactions.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of toxicity.

Classification of drugs by affinity and efficacy at receptors.
(a) Classify agonists, partial agonists, inverse agonists and antagonists, stating the properties of each.
(b) Describe dose-response curves, potency, efficacy and therapeutic index.
(c) Explain the pharmacological basis of the differences between competitive and non-competitive antagonism and other non-receptor antagonism.
(d) Distinguish between potency and efficacy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Agonist: affinity plus intrinsic activity (full agonist has maximal efficacy; partial agonist has less than maximal efficacy and competes with a full agonist).
• Inverse agonist: affinity plus a reverse effect, e.g. beta-carbolines binding the benzodiazepine receptor produce anxiety, hypertonia and convulsions.
• Antagonist: affinity but no efficacy; it binds the receptor without changing it (competitive or non-competitive).
(b)
• Dose-response is graphed with dose on the x-axis and response on the y-axis; a log dose scale turns the hyperbola into a sigmoid and straightens the line; ED50 is the dose giving 50% response.
• The position of the curve on the dose axis indexes potency; the upper limit (ceiling) indexes efficacy; therapeutic index = TD50 (or LD50) divided by ED50, higher meaning safer (ranges from 1.0 for some cancer drugs to over 1000 for penicillin).
(c)
• Competitive antagonist: competes with agonist for the receptor, is surmountable by raising agonist concentration, shifts the curve to the right (dextral shift) and reduces apparent agonist affinity.
• Non-competitive antagonist: binds and stays bound (irreversible); gives a slight dextral shift at low concentration, but as more receptors are bound the agonist cannot elicit a maximal effect.
• Non-pharmacological forms of antagonism: physiological and chemical; examples of antagonism: salbutamol vs propranolol, NSAIDs vs beta-blockers, diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
• Receptor occupancy theory: response is proportional to receptors occupied, one molecule per receptor, and drug concentration far exceeds receptor number.
(d)
• Potency is the amount of drug needed to produce an effect of given intensity (enalapril vs captopril; alprazolam vs diazepam); a highly potent drug works at low concentration.
• Efficacy is the maximum response achievable regardless of dose; drugs X and Z may have equal efficacy while X is more potent.
• Drug Y can be more potent than Z yet have lower maximal efficacy; low therapeutic index drugs include digoxin, cocaine and vancomycin.

(a)
Glucocorticoids induce remission in moderate and severe active disease; budesonide is used for ileum and proximal colon involvement; they are not used to maintain remission.
(b)
• They inhibit phospholipase A2, gene transcription of NO synthase and COX-2, and production of cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1) and chemokines (IL-8).
• Budesonide is a potent prednisolone analogue with high glucocorticoid receptor affinity, given as controlled-release tablets releasing drug in the ileum and colon; oral bioavailability about 10% with first-pass metabolism.
• Oral prednisone or prednisolone are absorbed more and have more adverse effects than rectal hydrocortisone.
(c)
For azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine: bone marrow depression, GI toxicity, hepatic dysfunction; complete blood count and liver function tests in all patients.
(d)
• Immunomodulators (azathioprine/6-MP, methotrexate) induce remission in active severe or steroid-resistant disease.
• Infliximab (IV, 5-10 mg/kg, chimeric antibody) or adalimumab (subcutaneous, fully humanized) for patients not responding to immunomodulators or glucocorticoids.
• Infliximab risks: infusion reactions, latent tuberculosis, sepsis, hepatitis B, antibodies causing loss of response.
questions.question:
A patient has moderate to severe active Crohn's disease involving the ileum and proximal colon.
(a) State the first-line drug therapy for induction.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Activation of coagulation also activates the fibrinolytic system: endogenous plasminogen activators cleave plasminogen on fibrin strands to release plasmin locally.
• Plasmin is a trypsin-like protease that digests fibrin, fibrinogen, factors II, V and VIII and other proteins.
• Fibrinolytic drugs increase fibrinolysis; antifibrinolytic drugs inhibit it.
• Fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) drugs stimulate dissolution of a blood clot (thrombus); anticoagulants only slow clotting.
(b)
• Fibrinolytics reopen occluded arteries in acute myocardial infarction or stroke, and less often treat life-threatening venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
• Streptokinase is a plasminogen-activating protein from streptococci, infused IV; it reduces mortality in MI, additive with aspirin.
• Alteplase and duteplase are recombinant tissue plasminogen activators, clot selective (more active on fibrin-bound plasminogen), non-antigenic, short half-life so given as IV infusion; reteplase has a longer half-life allowing bolus.
• Tranexamic acid inhibits plasminogen activation; used for bleeding after prostatectomy or dental extraction, menorrhagia and bleeding after thrombolytics.
(c)
• Plasmin also digests fibrinogen and clotting factors, so bleeding (GI haemorrhage, haemorrhagic stroke) is the main hazard; treat serious bleeding with tranexamic acid, fresh plasma or coagulation factors.
• Streptokinase is antigenic: allergic reactions and fever; antibodies appear after 4 days or more, so do not repeat; it causes a burst of plasmin generating kinins, giving hypotension.
• Contraindications: active internal bleeding, haemorrhagic cerebrovascular disease, bleeding diatheses, pregnancy, uncontrolled hypertension, invasive procedures, recent trauma including vigorous CPR.
• Fibrinolytic drugs do not act on the coagulation phase; anticoagulants do not lyse clots.

(i)
Exfoliative cytology (bronchial washing/brushing) is the appropriate technique.
(ii)
The principle is that desquamated cells from the bronchial lining are collected in the washing fluid, or brushed directly from a lesion, and prepared as a smear for microscopic examination for diagnosis of lung disease/cancer.
(iii)
Materials required include the collection fluid/brush, glass slides for smearing, and a wet fixative such as 95% isopropyl alcohol or a spray fixative.

questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Formaldehyde is gaseous and soluble in water up to 37-40% w/v; a formaldehyde solution in water is called formalin.
• Formalin is cheap, penetrates tissue rapidly, does not over-harden tissue, preserves proteins by forming cross-linkages, denatures proteins, and preserves glycogen partially; it demonstrates some enzymes but neither preserves nor destroys fat.
• Pure (undiluted) formalin over-hardens tissue and is unsatisfactory; a 10% dilution in water (tap or distilled) is satisfactory for routine use.
• Formalin oxidises to formic acid on prolonged storage; unless neutralised with phosphates/calcium carbonate it becomes acidic, and it also becomes cloudy in cold storage due to paraformaldehyde precipitate.
A(ii)
• Formalin pigment is a brown, granular, doubly-refractile deposit seen both within and outside cells of tissue fixed with a simple formalin solution such as formal-saline; it is also called acid formaldehyde haematin, being formed by the action of formaldehyde at an acid pH on haemoglobin-derived material, and it is more common in bloody tissues such as spleen.
• Formalin pigment can form quickly (overnight or within days) if the formalin is distinctly acidic, or slowly over extended storage even in correctly buffered formalin.
B(i)
• Formalin is used routinely as a 10% solution (10% formal-saline/neutral buffered formalin), with fixation time at room temperature of about 12 hours (4-6 hours for small biopsies) or 2 hours at 65 degrees C.
• Formalin pigment is avoided by using 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF), since buffering to pH 7 stops the acidity that forms the pigment; NBF should be changed at least every six months to prevent the pigment forming even on extended storage.
C(i)
• The pigment arises because formaldehyde, in the presence of an acid pH generated by oxidation of formalin to formic acid, reacts with haemoglobin-derived material to form the brown acid-formaldehyde-haematin deposit.
• Where NBF is unavailable and plain 10% formalin/formal saline is used, the solution should be stored over marble chips or crushed oyster shells to neutralise acid as it is produced, preventing pigment formation.
• Once present, the pigment is removed by immersing sections in saturated alcoholic picric acid for about 20 minutes and washing in water until the yellow colouration is removed; heavy deposits may be left overnight, and treatment with lithium carbonate is only needed if picric-acid discolouration interferes with subsequent staining.
• Bleaching agents such as potassium permanganate/oxalic acid, hydrogen peroxide, and periodic and chromic acids also remove formalin pigment to varying extents.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the physical and chemical properties of formaldehyde/formalin as used in histopathology.
A(ii) Describe how formalin pigment forms and its appearance.
B(i) State the standard concentration/site at which formalin is used as a routine fixative.
C(i) Explain the basis of the formalin-pigment artefact that arises from its use.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Epithelia are traditionally classified according to three morphological characteristics: the number of cell layers (simple epithelium - a single layer; stratified epithelium - several layers), the shape of the component cells (e.g. squamous, cuboidal, columnar), and the presence of surface specialisations such as cilia or keratin.
• Simple epithelia (a single layer of cells) are almost always found at interfaces involved in selective diffusion, absorption or secretion, and provide little protection against mechanical abrasion; examples given include simple squamous epithelium (e.g. lining of blood vessels/endothelium, lining body cavities/mesothelium) and simple columnar epithelium.
• Other recognised forms include pseudostratified columnar (ciliated) epithelium and transitional epithelium.
• Epithelium primarily involved in secretion forms glandular epithelium.
• Exocrine glands maintain a duct connection to the epithelial surface and discharge secretions through it, whereas in endocrine glands the duct degenerates during development, leaving isolated islands of secretory epithelial cells whose products (hormones) pass directly into the bloodstream.
• All epithelia are supported by a basement membrane of variable thickness, which is never penetrated by blood vessels, so epithelial cells depend on diffusion of oxygen/metabolites from underlying supporting tissue.
B(i)
• Epithelial (surface-lining) tumours are classified as benign epithelial tumours, such as papillomas and adenomas.
• Malignant epithelial tumours include squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, scirrhous carcinoma and medullary carcinoma.
• Semimalignant epithelial tumours include basalioma and ameloblastoma, indicating that the same broad epithelial classification (squamous versus glandular) underlies the naming of both benign and malignant epithelial neoplasms.
C(i)
• Neoplastic transformation of epithelium is recognised cytologically by the criteria for malignancy, including nuclear hyperchromasia, anisokaryosis, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, multinucleation, increased or abnormal mitotic figures.
• Large or variably shaped nucleoli, together with cytoplasmic features such as vacuolisation, keratinisation and cannibalism.
• These nuclear/cytoplasmic changes are the measurable morphological abnormalities by which a laboratory distinguishes a malignant epithelial lesion (e.g. squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma) from benign or reactive/regenerative epithelial changes, which can mimic many of the same criteria.
questions.question:
A(i) State the general classification of epithelial tissue.
B(i) State how epithelial classification relates to the classification of epithelial tumours.
C(i) Explain how neoplastic disturbance of epithelium leads to a measurable cytological abnormality.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Formalin pigment is caused by the action of formaldehyde at an acid pH on haemoglobin-derived material, forming a brown, granular, doubly-refractile deposit within and outside cells, particularly in bloody tissue.
• Removal procedure for formalin pigment: bring sections to water.
• Immerse in saturated alcoholic picric acid in a coplin jar for about 20 minutes; wash in water until all yellow colouration is removed from the section, then continue with the required staining method.
• Most formalin pigment is removed fairly rapidly by this method; heavy deposits may require the sections to be left overnight, and treatment with lithium carbonate is only required if picric-acid discolouration itself interferes with staining.
• Bleaching agents such as potassium permanganate/oxalic acid, hydrogen peroxide, and periodic and chromic acids have also been shown to remove formalin pigment, to varying extents, from tissue fixed in formaldehyde-acetic-acid-alcohol.
• Mercuric-chloride (mercury) pigment removal: solutions used are Lugol's iodine (solution I) and 5% sodium thiosulphate (solution II).
• Procedure: bring the section to water (dewax in xylene, hydrate through descending grades of alcohol, rinse in water); immerse in Lugol's iodine for about 10 minutes; wash in water.
• Bleach in the sodium thiosulphate (hypo) solution for 2 minutes; wash thoroughly in water; then continue with the required staining procedure.
B(i)
• Removing fixation pigment is essential before staining and diagnostic reporting because the retained pigment (brown formalin pigment or black mercury pigment) can obscure cellular and nuclear detail, mimic other pigments/deposits, or produce confusing background colouration that could lead to misinterpretation of the slide.
C(i)
• Formalin pigment is removed with saturated alcoholic picric acid, which bleaches the brown acid-formaldehyde-haematin deposit and is washed out with water until the yellow colour disappears.
• Mercury pigment is instead removed with Lugol's iodine followed by sodium thiosulphate (hypo), a different chemical sequence that converts/dissolves the black mercuric precipitate rather than bleaching an organic pigment.
• The two procedures therefore differ in both the chemical basis of pigment formation (acid-formaldehyde-haematin versus mercuric chloride precipitate) and in the specific reagents required to remove each.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the removal of fixation pigment as a technique, under the headings: cause, procedure and reagents used.
B(i) Explain the diagnostic significance of removing fixation pigment before reporting a slide.
C(i) Distinguish the removal of formalin pigment from the removal of mercuric-chloride (mercury) pigment.

questions.answerText:

This is an exfoliative cytology specimen (nipple discharge), examined for diagnosis of breast carcinoma.
(ii)
Because the secretion is scant, the smear is restricted to a small area of the slide to prevent it drying out before fixation, and the slide is immediately immersed in 95% isopropyl alcohol or sprayed with fixative.

A(i) Describe the karyopyknotic index and eosinophilic index as techniques for assessing hormonal cytology smears.
B(i) State the diagnostic significance of these indices in gonadal hormonal assessment.
C(i) Distinguish the karyopyknotic index from the eosinophilic index.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Methods of assessment of a hormonal cytology smear include the karyopyknotic index (KI), eosinophilic index (EI), maturation index (MI), folded cell index (FCI) and crowded cell index (CCI).
• The karyopyknotic index expresses the percentage of superficial squamous cells with pyknotic nuclei relative to the percentage of all mature squamous cells, counted over 200-400 consecutive cells in three to four different fields.
• The eosinophilic index expresses the percentage of mature squamous cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm relative to the percentage of all mature squamous cells, regardless of the state of the nuclei.
• The maturation index expresses the percentage of parabasal cells to intermediate cells to superficial cells, with counts performed on single cells.
• The folded cell index and crowded cell index assess, respectively, the relationship of mature cells with folded cytoplasm, or lying in clusters of four or more cells, to all mature squamous cells.
B(i)
• These indices are used to assess ovarian function and gonadal hormonal activity, for example after hysterectomy, during the menstrual cycle, in premature menses, in assessing abnormal hormone production (pregnancy, abortion, retained placenta, endocrine disorders, hormone-producing ovarian tumours) and in guiding hormonal therapy.
• Reports on hormonal status are given with reference to age, menstrual history and possible clinical significance, comparing the current smear pattern with baseline/reference smear patterns.
C(i)
• The karyopyknotic index specifically measures the proportion of superficial cells with pyknotic (condensed) nuclei.
• Its peak coincides with the time of ovulation, when it is estimated at 50-80% of total cells.
• The eosinophilic index instead measures the proportion of mature squamous cells showing eosinophilic cytoplasm, irrespective of nuclear state.
• Its peak also coincides with the peak of the karyopyknotic index and may reach 50-70% at ovulation.
• Thus KI is a nuclear-based index while EI is a cytoplasmic-staining-based index, although both reflect the same oestrogenic peak around ovulation and are interpreted together.

(i)
This is bone dust artefact.
(ii)
It is produced mechanically during sectioning of bone on the microtome, and tends to be more prominent with thicker sections.
(iii)
The laboratory should recognise this as a processing artefact rather than a true pathological calcification, and take care during microtomy (e.g. using a sharp knife and appropriate section thickness) to minimise its production, since there is no reliable method to prevent it entirely.
questions.question:
Fine, grit-like material staining strongly with haematoxylin is seen scattered within and around bony trabeculae in a section, unrelated to the patient's underlying disease.
(i) Identify this finding.
(ii) State the basic principle/cause behind it.
(iii) State the correct laboratory action regarding this finding.

A(i) Describe the structure/composition of granulation tissue formed during wound repair.
B(i) State the standard site/process in wound healing where granulation tissue forms.
C(i) Explain the basis of the abnormal states (hypertrophic scar/keloid) that can arise from disturbed granulation tissue formation.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Repair is the replacement of lost tissue by granulation tissue, which consists of fibroblasts and proliferating capillary loops, and is also formed from the surrounding connective tissue.
• Fibroblasts initially synthesise collagen type III, which is later converted to collagen type I as the granulation tissue matures.
• As maturation of the granulation tissue proceeds, nerve fibres and lymphocytes are formed within it.
• Myofibroblasts are specialised cells at the edge of the wound, intermediate between fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, that differentiate, invade and help repair/remodel the injured tissue, and are the cause of wound contraction.
• Wound contraction is a decrease in the original size of the injury, starting 2-3 hours into the first days and reaching its maximum by 14 days, when the wound may have contracted to about 50% of its original size.
• Contraction helps the wound heal faster and reduces the amount of granulation tissue needed (more granulation tissue means longer healing).
B(i)
• Granulation tissue forms in the incision/wound space during the process of repair, following the earlier stage of wound contraction.
• By day 5 of primary healing the incisional space is typically filled with granulation tissue, with collagen fibre formation continuing into the second week as the granulation tissue eventually disappears and a scar forms by the end of the month.
C(i)
• Deficient scar formation can lead to wound dehiscence (rupture), while excessive scar formation produces a hypertrophic scar or keloid, in which the scar grows beyond its original boundary and does not regress.
• These represent disturbances of the normal, self-limiting accumulation and later disappearance of granulation tissue/collagen: too little collagen/granulation tissue weakens the wound (dehiscence), whereas excessive, unregulated collagen accumulation and failure of the granulation tissue to regress produces keloid/hypertrophic scarring.
• An exaggerated form of the normal wound-contraction process can likewise produce contracture, another complication of disturbed healing.
• These complications, alongside malignant transformation, are recognised complications of wound healing arising from abnormal regulation of the repair process.

A(i)
• A typical 18-hour automatic tissue-processing schedule passes tissue through: 10% formol saline (post-fixation), a graded alcohol series (70%, 80%, 90%, 95% twice, then two changes of absolute alcohol), two changes of xylene, and two wax baths.
• A routine manual processing method similarly passes fixed tissue through 70%, 90% and 95% alcohol, two changes of absolute alcohol, and chloroform or cedar-wood oil.
• Two changes of xylene/toluene may be used as an alternative to chloroform/cedar-wood oil, and the schedule finishes with three changes of paraffin wax.
• Where chloroform or cedar-wood oil is unavailable, tissue may instead be left in the second absolute-alcohol bath overnight and then treated with two changes of xylene.
B(i)
• The processing time given in a schedule varies with the type of tissue and the type of tissue processor used, and can be reduced or increased depending on when the laboratorian is ready for embedding.
• Tissue should not be more than about 4 mm thick for the routine schedules described, since thicker tissue needs longer at each stage for adequate reagent penetration.
• Agitation, heat and vacuum can each be used during automated processing to speed fluid exchange at each of these stages.
• Heat is typically limited (e.g. to about 45 degrees C) to avoid the shrinkage, hardening and antigen loss that excessive heat would cause.
C(i)
• Tissue should not be left in xylene overnight, because prolonged exposure of some tissues to xylene makes them brittle.
• If dehydration is incomplete before clearing, xylene will appear milky when the tissue/section is immersed in it, signalling that the alcohol series was not properly completed.
• Wrong timing/sequencing of any stage (for example, insufficient time in absolute alcohol, or omission of a wax change) is a processing mishap that can produce tissue specimens that cannot be sectioned and yield no diagnostic information.
• Because in diagnostic work the whole specimen may have been processed, there is no spare tissue to repeat the process, making correct schedule timing a critical laboratory-quality control.
questions.question:
A(i) State the classification of dehydrating, clearing and infiltrating reagents used together in a routine automatic tissue-processing schedule.
B(i) State how the duration at each stage relates to the thickness/type of tissue being processed.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance (wrong timing/sequence) leads to a measurable processing failure.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Physical/mechanical method: the tissue is bent, palpated or a needle is passed through it; if the needle passes freely or the tissue bends easily, calcium is assumed absent, but this method is crude, damages the tissue and is considered unreliable.
• A related physical test is the bubble test, in which acid reacting with calcium carbonate produces carbon-dioxide bubbles on the bone surface that become smaller as less calcium remains; this is subjective and used only as a rough guide.
• Chemical method: 5 ml of used decalcifying fluid is placed in a test tube, a piece of red litmus paper is added, and concentrated ammonia is added drop-wise until the litmus turns blue.
• If the solution remains clear (no turbidity) at this stage, 0.5 ml of saturated aqueous ammonium oxalate is added and the tube left to stand for about 30 minutes.
• If the solution remains clear, end-point is reached, but if it turns cloudy (calcium oxalate/hydroxide precipitate), decalcification is incomplete and the fluid is renewed.
• Radiographic method: the specimen is placed on photographic (x-ray) film and exposed; the film is developed, and clear/transparent areas indicate absence of calcium, while opaque/dark areas indicate residual calcium salts.
B(i)
• Accurate end-point determination is essential because tissue must be left in decalcifying fluid for the minimum time possible.
• Excessive exposure causes disruption and loss of tissue constituents and impairs staining reactions (over-decalcification), while premature removal leaves residual calcium that tears sections and damages the microtome knife (incomplete decalcification).
C(i)
• The chemical method depends on detecting dissolved calcium in the decalcifying fluid itself (via ammonia/ammonium oxalate precipitation), so it can only test the fluid, not the tissue directly, and it cannot be used following EDTA decalcification.
• The radiographic method is the most sensitive and reliable test, directly visualising residual calcium in the tissue itself as opaque areas on the film, but it is more costly, requires specialised equipment/expertise, and cannot be used on tissue fixed in radio-opaque (mercuric-chloride-containing) fixatives.
• Because it tests the fluid rather than the tissue, the chemical method may occasionally under- or over-estimate completeness compared with radiography, which examines the actual specimen; radiography is therefore preferred where mercuric-chloride fixation has not been used.
• In practice, small biopsies of cancellous bone are typically checked chemically after 24 hours and other specimens daily, whereas radiography is reserved for definitive confirmation, particularly where chemical testing is unsuitable (e.g. following ion-exchange-resin or EDTA decalcification).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the methods used to determine the end-point of decalcification under the headings: physical/mechanical method, chemical method and radiographic method.
B(i) State the diagnostic significance of accurately determining the end-point of decalcification.
C(i) Distinguish the chemical method from the radiographic (x-ray) method of end-point determination.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The best routine fixative for the brain is formol saline, which allows special fixatives/techniques to be used subsequently if desired; the brain should, if possible, be fixed by injection.
• Sections of central nervous system tissue may be prepared from paraffin- or celloidin-embedded tissue, or from frozen tissue, depending on the technique to be employed.
• Vacuum-bath embedding is not recommended for central nervous system tissue, since it tends to render sections brittle and can cause them to float off slides during staining or silver-impregnation techniques.
• Instead the tissue should be impregnated with paraffin wax for 12-18 hours, with at least four changes of wax.
• Sections are cut routinely at a thickness of 7 micrometres.
• Sections for myelin techniques should be at least 10-15 micrometres thick, and sections in which complete neurones (dendrites and axons) are to be demonstrated should be even thicker (15-20 micrometres).
• As routine staining methods for nervous tissue, haematoxylin and van Gieson, Mallory's and PTA (phosphotungstic acid) haematoxylin are employed, as with other tissues.
• Other special methods (for elastic tissue, reticulin, mucin and fat) are also used for differential diagnosis.
B(i)
• Because neuro-histology techniques are highly specialised and many are lengthy, requiring solutions with involved preparation, correct fixation and processing are essential to allow the special silver-impregnation and myelin-staining techniques to succeed and to avoid brittle, floating or poorly-oriented sections that would compromise diagnostic interpretation of nervous tissue.
C(i)
• Paraffin embedding of CNS tissue must avoid vacuum-bath impregnation and requires prolonged wax impregnation (12-18 hours with at least four wax changes) because vacuum embedding renders CNS sections brittle and prone to floating off during staining or silver-impregnation procedures.
• Celloidin (or frozen) embedding is an alternative routinely used for nervous tissue, chosen particularly when thicker sections (needed for myelin techniques or for demonstrating complete neurones) or reduced shrinkage/hardening compared with paraffin is required.
• The choice between paraffin and celloidin/frozen methods for CNS tissue therefore depends on the technique to be employed subsequently (routine staining versus special silver-impregnation/myelin methods requiring thicker, less brittle sections).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the fixation and processing of central nervous system tissue as a technique under the headings: fixation, processing (paraffin embedding) and section cutting.
B(i) State the diagnostic significance of correctly processing nervous tissue.
C(i) Distinguish paraffin embedding from celloidin embedding for central nervous system tissue.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The Kaiserling technique for museum specimens comprises three main solutions/stages: Kaiserling I (fixation), Kaiserling II (restoration), and Kaiserling III (preservation).
• Basic museum handling more broadly follows six steps: reception, preparation, fixation, restoration, preservation and presentation.
• Kaiserling I solution consists of formalin, potassium acetate, potassium nitrate and distilled water; the specimen is stored in it, with 3-4 times its volume of fixative, for about one month depending on size.
• Kaiserling II restoration involves washing the specimen in running water, transferring it to 95% alcohol for 10 minutes to 1 hour depending on size, and observing it for colour change for around 1-1.5 hours.
• A rejuvenator solution (pyridine, sodium hydrosulphite, distilled water) is used because formalin decreases the natural colour of the specimen and the rejuvenator restores it.
• Kaiserling III solution (potassium acetate, glycerine and distilled water, with thymol crystals to prevent moulds and 1% pyridine as a stabiliser) is the final permanent-fixative solution in which the specimen remains for display; the specimen initially floats but later sinks.
B(i)
• Kaiserling I fixes and preserves cell/tissue constituents in a life-like state and arrests autolysis and bacterial decomposition, forming the necessary first step before colour restoration.
• Kaiserling II specifically restores the natural colour lost during formalin fixation, preparing the specimen for long-term display.
• Kaiserling III is used specifically for long-term preservation/display because it is glycerine-based and acts as a permanent fixative, unlike the initial formalin (KI) and alcohol (KII) stages.
C(i)
• The Kaiserling III solution easily turns yellowish and needs to be replaced to restore the colour of the specimen, so failure to replace it in time leads to a measurably discoloured, less presentable specimen.
• Perspex jars cannot be used to store specimens fixed in alcohol or methyl salicylate because they react with the plastic, so using the wrong jar material for the fixative used would damage the container/specimen.
• If the specimen is allowed to rest on the bottom or an artificial flat surface during Kaiserling I fixation, an unnatural flattened surface will be produced on hardening, a measurable morphological defect in the preserved specimen.
questions.question:
A(i) State the classification/stages of the Kaiserling museum technique for specimen preservation.
B(i) State how each Kaiserling solution/stage relates to a specific step of specimen preparation.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance in this process leads to a measurable defect in the preserved specimen.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Within the cytoplasm of nerve cells are found neurofibrils, which are fine fibres arranged throughout the cytoplasm, extending into the cell processes.
• Nissl substance (Nissl granules) is granular in fixed tissue and stains intensely with basic aniline dyes; it is usually evenly distributed throughout the cytoplasm except immediately around the origin of the axon, and may spread into the dendrites.
• Mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus may also be well demonstrated in nerve cells.
• Certain cells, such as those of the substantia nigra, contain melanin granules, and all ageing nerve cells may contain yellow lipofuscin granules.
• Nerve fibres consist of naked axons (found in the grey matter of brain and spinal cord), axons with a neurilemmal sheath (surrounded by flattened Schwann cells, usually in the sympathetic nervous system).
• Myelinated nerve fibres (axons surrounded by a lipid myelin sheath, itself surrounded by a neurilemmal sheath).
• Nerve fibres also exist as sensory (afferent) fibres, whose dendrites convey impulses to the nerve cell, and motor (efferent) fibres, whose myelinated processes leave the peripheral nerve.
B(i)
• Nissl substance is demonstrated by staining with basic aniline dyes, since the material stains intensely with them in fixed tissue; the Luxol fast blue-cresyl violet technique also selectively stains Nissl substance.
C(i)
• Damage to a nerve fibre usually results in loss of Nissl substance from the parent nerve cell body.
• This loss reflects disruption of the normal cytoplasmic organisation and protein-synthetic apparatus of the neurone that follows axonal injury.
• The Nissl-staining pattern is therefore used, alongside the routine methods (haematoxylin and van Gieson, Mallory's, P.T.A. haematoxylin) applied to nervous tissue, to assess the state of the neurone following injury.

A(i) Describe decalcification as a technique under the headings: definition/principle, stages/steps, and criteria of a good decalcifying agent.
B(i) Explain the diagnostic significance of decalcification.
C(i) Distinguish the ion-exchange resin method from the electrolytic method of decalcification.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Decalcification is the process by which calcium ions/salts (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluorite) are completely removed from a bony or calcified tissue so that fine sections can be cut.
• The technique is divided into the stages: selection of tissue, fixation, decalcification, neutralisation of acid, and tissue processing/staining.
• Selection of tissue: thin slices not exceeding 4-5 mm thickness are cut with a fine-toothed saw and re-trimmed to remove saw-damaged areas.
• Fixation: the tissue must be thoroughly fixed before decalcification (buffered formalin is satisfactory) since tissue damage during acid decalcification is about four times greater when tissue is unfixed.
• Decalcification: the tissue is immersed in a chosen decalcifying fluid at 20-100 times the tissue volume until calcium is removed.
• Neutralisation of acid: acid is removed/neutralised, e.g. by immersion in 5-10% lithium or sodium sulphate solution, or by washing in running water overnight.
• Criteria of a good decalcifying agent: it should remove calcium ions/salts completely, not damage cells or tissue fibres, not impair subsequent staining or histochemistry, and act with reasonable speed.
B(i)
• Decalcification is essential diagnostically because the deposition of calcium salts makes it very difficult to cut fine sections by the usual methods, and failure to remove calcium results in torn, ragged sections and damage to the microtome knife edge, preventing accurate microscopic diagnosis.
C(i)
• The ion-exchange resin method incorporates an ammonium-form polystyrene resin into the decalcifying solution; the resin removes calcium from the fluid, speeding decalcification and improving staining, but the chemical method cannot be used to test its end-point (x-ray is used instead).
• The electrolytic method uses hydrochloric and formic acid as an electrolytic medium with a continuous 6-volt direct current passed between a platinum-wire anode (holding the specimen) and a brass/carbon cathode.
• Positively-charged calcium ions migrate to the cathode, and heat (up to 45 degrees C) generated by the current speeds decalcification more than electrolysis itself.
• The ion-exchange method thus relies on chemical binding of calcium by resin, whereas the electrolytic method relies on an electric field to draw calcium ions out of the tissue, and the two therefore differ in their applicable end-point tests and in the equipment required.

A(i)
• Post-chromation, also called post-chroming or post-chromatisation, is the practice of treating tissue or sections already fixed in a primary fixative (such as potassium dichromate or 10% formalin saline) with a further chromium-containing solution.
• Its purpose is to improve the preservation of materials such as lipoproteins and lipids that would otherwise be removed by strong reagents during subsequent processing.
• To preserve materials such as mitochondria and myelin so they can be demonstrated in paraffin sections.
• Procedure: fixed tissue is placed in a 2.5-3% solution of potassium dichromate in distilled water for a few days to weeks; the tissue is then removed and washed with running tap water overnight to remove all remaining dichromate.
• Post-chroming must be carried out in the dark, because potassium dichromate is photosensitive and absence of light is desirable.
• The length of the washing step is determined by the length of the post-chroming step; the longer the post-chroming, the longer the required washing.
B(i)
• Post-chromation preserves lipoprotein/lipid and mitochondrial/myelin detail that would otherwise be lost during routine processing, which is important where these structures (e.g. myelin, using Altmann's method) need to be demonstrated diagnostically or for research.
• Even though its effect is not absolute, a simple potassium dichromate solution may take days to weeks to act effectively.
C(i)
• Post-chromation is essentially a secondary fixation/preservation step using potassium dichromate to protect lipid/mitochondrial/myelin structures from being removed by later processing reagents.
• Post-chromation is not simply a fixation step, however; it also acts as a mordant, because the chromium is a good and effective mordant for certain dyes and may mordant the tissue itself, for example in Altmann's method for demonstrating myelin.
• Post-mordanting, by contrast, is the application of a mordant (a polyvalent metal ion, e.g. ferric chloride) to tissue sections before staining in order to form coordination complexes/salt bridges that allow proper union between dye molecules and the tissue, as in Heidenhain's iron haematoxylin.
• Thus post-chromation is primarily aimed at preserving specific tissue constituents against loss during processing (with a secondary mordanting effect), whereas post-mordanting is applied specifically to enable or intensify a particular staining reaction.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe post-chromation (post-chroming) as a technique under the headings: purpose, principle and procedure.
B(i) State the diagnostic significance of post-chromation.
C(i) Distinguish post-chromation from post-mordanting.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A ribbon of sections curved instead of straight is caused by the edges of the block not being parallel to each other and to the knife, or by a dull point on part of the knife edge causing one border of the section to crumble.
• Ribbons curling upward as sections are cut are caused by too great a tilt of the knife.
• Sections that cut well individually but fail to ribbon are caused either by wax that is too hard for the cutting temperature, or by too slow a rate of sectioning.
• Sections that crumble are caused by paraffin wax that is too soft or by a blunt knife edge.
• Sections that are longitudinally scratched are caused by a serrated or debris-coated knife edge, or by foci of calcification within the tissue.
• Alternate thick and thin sections cut are caused by a faulty feed mechanism requiring oiling, an improperly clamped knife or loose block holder, or a block not securely attached to its wooden chuck.
• Thick and thin zones (chatter) on the same section are caused by knife vibration due to hardness of the tissue, excessive tilt, or vibration from the table (especially with sledge-type microtomes).
• Uneven section thickness with a harsh metallic sound on knife contact is caused by too great a tilt of the knife; width of section much less than that of the block is caused by too broad a cutting facet on the knife edge, bad processing, or an unsuitable embedding medium.
B(i)
• Recognising these characteristic faults and their causes allows the laboratory scientist to correct the specific underlying problem (knife tilt, wax hardness, processing quality, block preparation) promptly, preventing repeated loss of valuable, often irreplaceable diagnostic tissue.
C(i)
• Where ribbons curl upward because the knife tilt is too great, the remedy is to reduce the tilt of the knife.
• Where sections are individually well cut but fail to ribbon because the wax is too hard for the cutting temperature, the remedy is to coat the block edge with softer, lower-melting-point wax, warm the room or place a lit Bunsen burner nearby, or cut the sections more rapidly; where the cause is instead too slow a rate of sectioning, the specific remedy is simply to cut more rapidly.
• Thus the two faults, though both concerning the microtome and knife, require different corrective actions: adjusting the knife's tilt angle in one case, versus adjusting the wax temperature/hardness or cutting speed in the other.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe common faults encountered in section cutting on the microtome, and their causes.
B(i) State the diagnostic/quality-control significance of recognising these faults.
C(i) Distinguish the remedy for "ribbons curling upward" from the remedy for "sections that fail to ribbon although individually well cut".

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Papanicolaou staining is the most important staining method in cytology; it stains the nucleus, chromatin and nucleolus very well, enhancing differentiation between malignant and non-malignant cells.
• It also stains the cytoplasm and its contents, such as keratin, vacuoles and granules.
• It differentiates between acidophilic and basophilic materials, staining extracellular substances such as fibrin, crystals and pigments.
• Smears to be stained by the Papanicolaou technique must be fixed while they are still wet, since delayed fixation causes air-drying artefact that impairs the staining and interpretation.
B(i)
• Because it clearly demonstrates nuclear chromatin detail and differentiates malignant from non-malignant cells, the Papanicolaou technique is the standard method for cervical/vaginal cytology screening and for detecting malignant, precancerous, inflammatory and hormonally-related cellular changes.
C(i)
• Papanicolaou staining requires wet fixation of the smear immediately after preparation, whereas Romanowsky stains (Leishman, Giemsa, Wright) require the smear to be rapidly air-dried immediately after spreading.
• Papanicolaou staining gives superior nuclear/chromatin detail suited to distinguishing malignant from benign squamous and other epithelial cells.
• Romanowsky stains are better suited to smears containing leucocytes, such as cerebrospinal fluid, aspirates and marrow cells.
• Two Romanowsky stains may be used in sequence (for example, a Giemsa-stained smear counterstained with May-Grunwald) to give a panoptic staining effect, a combination approach not used with Papanicolaou staining.
• Haematoxylin and eosin is, by contrast, a general-purpose stain that may be used for sputum and other specimens where Papanicolaou stain is unavailable, with Schaudinn's fluid as the cytological fixative of choice before H&E.
• Shorr stain is yet another alternative, used specifically for endocrine (cytohormonal) studies.
• It gives good cytoplasmic differentiation but less cytoplasmic transparency and poorer nuclear definition than the Papanicolaou stain, and is not very satisfactory for detection of malignant cells.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the Papanicolaou staining technique under the headings: significance and requirement for fixation.
B(i) State the diagnostic significance of the Papanicolaou technique.
C(i) Distinguish the Papanicolaou technique from the Romanowsky staining technique.
