A(i) State the classification of secondary fixatives used for secondary fixation.
B(i) State how secondary fixation relates to the preservation of specific tissue constituents.
C(i) Explain how inadequate secondary fixation leads to a measurable loss of a specific tissue constituent.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Secondary fixation is the process of re-fixing tissue in a second (different) fixative for about 4 hours, following initial fixation in formol saline.
• The fixatives usually selected for secondary fixation are Zenker's formal, formal sublimate, and Heidenhain's susa.
• Post-chromation (treatment with potassium dichromate solution) is a related, though distinct, secondary treatment used to improve preservation of lipoproteins, lipids, mitochondria and myelin.
B(i)
• Secondary fixation gives tissue a firmer texture, preserves certain tissue constituents better, and improves subsequent staining, compared with formol-saline fixation alone.
• Post-chromation specifically improves preservation of materials such as lipoproteins and lipids that would otherwise be removed by strong reagents during later processing, and helps preserve mitochondria and myelin so that they can be demonstrated in paraffin sections.
• Because secondary fixation is applied after the tissue has already undergone primary fixation, it is generally carried out on small, thin pieces of tissue so that the second fixative can adequately penetrate within the shorter (about 4 hour) time available.
C(i)
• If a tissue requiring demonstration of myelin or mitochondria receives only primary formol-saline fixation without the appropriate secondary fixation/post-chromation, these lipid-rich structures are vulnerable to removal by the strong reagents (alcohols, clearing agents) used later in processing.
• The measurable result is poor or absent demonstration of myelin/mitochondria in the final paraffin section, since a simple potassium-dichromate post-chromation solution itself may take days to weeks to act effectively, and any inadequate exposure time would leave these constituents under-preserved.
• Zenker's formal, formal sublimate and Heidenhain's susa are mercuric-chloride-containing fixatives, so tissue subjected to secondary fixation with them will develop the black mercury-pigment precipitate that must subsequently be removed with Lugol's iodine followed by sodium thiosulphate before the section can be stained.
• Failure to remove this mercury pigment after secondary fixation produces a black precipitate artefact obscuring cellular detail.
• The requirement to wash out dichromate/mercury reagents thoroughly in running water overnight, as with post-chromation, further shows that secondary fixation demands careful additional handling beyond routine primary fixation.
• Adequate secondary fixation/post-chromation therefore directly determines whether the specific tissue constituents of interest remain demonstrable, illustrating why the choice and duration of secondary fixative is significant to diagnostic or research outcome.

questions.question:
A(i) State the classification of fixing agents based on their mechanism of action.
B(i) State how each class relates to the specific tissue component it best preserves or demonstrates.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance (e.g. failure to remove a fixative-derived pigment) leads to a measurable artefact.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Fixatives are classified, according to mechanism of action, into five major groups: aldehydes, mercurials, alcohols, oxidising agents, and picrates.
• Aldehydes (e.g. formaldehyde) preserve proteins by cross-linking and denaturation and are considered to come closest to the ideal, all-purpose fixative.
• Mercurials (e.g. mercuric chloride) precipitate proteins and penetrate tissue rapidly, but leave a black mercury-pigment precipitate in the tissue.
• Alcohols act as protein precipitants/dehydrating fixatives and are also used as histochemical fixatives (e.g. absolute ethyl alcohol) because they do not interfere with the chemical nature of tissue components.
• Oxidising agents (e.g. osmium tetroxide, potassium dichromate) are strong oxidisers; osmium tetroxide is the only substance that permanently fixes fat, rendering it insoluble in alcohol and xylene.
• Picrates (e.g. picric acid) combine with proteins to form water-soluble picrates that must not be exposed to water before treatment with alcohol, which renders them insoluble.
B(i)
• Aldehyde fixatives are suited to general microanatomical preservation of routine diagnostic tissue.
• Mercurial fixatives are chosen where rapid, deep penetration and strong protein precipitation are required.
• Oxidising agents such as osmium tetroxide are chosen specifically where fat needs to be permanently fixed and demonstrated, since aldehydes and alcohols do not achieve this.
• Alcohol-based histochemical fixatives are chosen where the chemical/enzymatic reactivity of tissue constituents must be preserved for subsequent histochemical demonstration.
C(i)
• Mercurial fixatives leave a black mercury-pigment precipitate in the tissue which, if not removed (using Lugol's iodine followed by sodium thiosulphate) before staining, obscures cellular detail and produces a measurable staining/interpretation artefact.
• Similarly, tissue fixed in an aldehyde fixative that has become acidic can develop the brown formalin pigment, which likewise obscures detail unless removed with alcoholic picric acid, showing that each class of fixative carries its own characteristic, correctable pigment artefact if not properly managed.

(i)
This is formalin pigment (acid formaldehyde haematin).
(ii)
It is formed by the action of formaldehyde, at an acid pH (from oxidation of formalin to formic acid), on haemoglobin-derived material in blood-containing tissue such as spleen.
(iii)
The next step is to remove the pigment by immersing the section in saturated alcoholic picric acid for about 20 minutes and washing in water until the yellow colouration disappears (heavy deposits may need overnight treatment); for future specimens, using 10% neutral buffered formalin, changed regularly, prevents the pigment forming.
questions.question:
Sections of spleen fixed in a simple, unbuffered formalin solution show a brown, granular, doubly-refractile deposit both within and outside the cells, obscuring cellular detail.
(i) Identify the artefact seen.
(ii) State the basic principle behind why it appears.
(iii) State the correct handling/next laboratory step to deal with it.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Any specimen received in a museum is recorded in a reception book and given a number followed by the year (e.g. 32/2013).
• This number stays with the specimen for life, is written on an indelible tie-on label attached to the specimen, and the reception book records the clinical, gross and microscopic findings.
• An ideal specimen is received fresh and unfixed, but is more commonly received already formalin-fixed from the pathology laboratory; part of an organ can be reserved for museum use (e.g. one half of a bisected kidney) without disturbing the rest.
• The objective of fixation is to preserve cells and tissue constituents in as life-like a state as possible so they can undergo further preparative procedures without change; fixation arrests autolysis and bacterial decomposition and stabilises the cellular/tissue constituents.
• Museum fixatives worldwide are based on formalin fixation, derived from the Kaiserling technique.
• Kaiserling I solution (formalin, potassium acetate, potassium nitrate, distilled water) is used for initial fixation, with the specimen stored for about one month depending on size, not resting on the container bottom (to avoid an artificial flat surface forming on hardening).
B(i)
• A well-prepared, correctly labelled and fixed museum specimen serves permanent teaching and reference functions: exhibition of common specimens for undergraduate and postgraduate teaching, illustration of rare specimens.
• A permanent source of histologic material and gross/microscopic photography.
C(i)
• Kaiserling I solution (formalin-based) is used for the initial fixation stage, preserving cells/tissue in a life-like state and arresting decomposition, but it also decreases the specimen's natural colour.
• Kaiserling III solution (potassium acetate and glycerine in distilled water, with thymol crystals and pyridine stabiliser) is used at the final preservation stage, after colour has been restored by Kaiserling II/rejuvenator solution, and acts as the permanent display fixative.
• It easily turns yellowish and must be replaced periodically to maintain specimen colour.
• Thus Kaiserling I is the initial preservative fixative while Kaiserling III is the final, long-term display solution, with a distinct restoration (Kaiserling II) step required in between to reverse the colour loss caused by the initial formalin fixation.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe museum specimen fixation as a technique under the headings: reception, preparation and fixation.
B(i) State the diagnostic/teaching significance of a well-prepared museum specimen.
C(i) Distinguish Kaiserling I solution from Kaiserling III solution.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Microtomy is the process of cutting tissue sections from processed or frozen tissue for microscopy, using a machine called a microtome.
• Every microtome has four basic components: a knife held in a firm support; a device for holding the tissue block firmly.
• A mechanism for moving the tissue across the knife (or the knife across the tissue); and a mechanism for advancing the tissue a small, accurately measured distance to control section thickness.
• Types of microtome include the Cambridge rocker (rocking) microtome, the base sledge (sliding) microtome, the rotary microtome, the freezing microtome, and the cryostat.
• The Cambridge rocker microtome has the block attached to a pivoted arm that moves across the knife edge in an arc, automatically advancing the tissue at each stroke; it suits serial sections but not large or hard blocks.
• The base sledge microtome has a carriage that moves on rails carrying the tissue block under a fixed knife, and is versatile for soft, unusually hard, or large blocks, with simple attachments possible for frozen sections.
• The rotary microtome has the block attached to a carriage that travels up and down as a handle is turned, with the knife fixed edge-upward; it is best suited to paraffin blocks and serial/teaching sections but less suited to hard blocks.
• The freezing microtome keeps the block stationary with a cooling mechanism (thermoelectric or carbon-dioxide expansion) and is designed exclusively for frozen sections; the cryostat is a microtome enclosed in a refrigerated cabinet (-5 to -30 degrees C) used for cutting unfixed, frozen tissue for histochemistry.
B(i)
• Section quality depends on correctly set knife tilt: tilt angles vary between 10-40 degrees depending on knife shape and cutting-facet angle, and less tilt is used for soft tissue and more for hard tissue.
• There must be sufficient clearance (clearance angle) between the knife and the block surface to avoid compressing the tissue against the back of the knife; if tilt is too great, ribbons curl upward, sections may show uneven thickness, or thick/thin zones (chatter) appear.
C(i)
• The Cambridge rocking microtome moves the block across the knife edge in an arc on a pivoted arm, shows little wear over years apart from the ratchet pawl, and is suited to serial sectioning of soft/small blocks but not large or hard ones.
• The rotary microtome instead moves the block vertically on a carriage past a fixed, edge-upward knife by turning a handle, is best suited to paraffin blocks and cutting large numbers of serial/teaching sections, but is less satisfactory for hard blocks or for cutting only one or two sections from a large block.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe microtomy as a technique under the headings: definition, basic components of a microtome and types of microtome.
B(i) State the significance of correct microtome knife tilt for section quality.
C(i) Distinguish the (Cambridge) rocking microtome from the rotary microtome.

A(i) State the principle of fixation.
A(ii) State the aims and effects of fixation.
A(iii) State the properties a good fixative must possess and the amount of fixative required.
A(iv) List the common reagents employed as fixatives.
B(i) Explain the clinical/diagnostic significance of fixation.
C(i) Distinguish formaldehyde (formalin) fixation from mercuric-chloride-containing fixation.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Fixation is a complex series of chemical events which changes the chemical constituents of the cell (cell hardening); the fixative causes cross-linking of proteins, resulting in denaturation/coagulation, converting the semi-fluid cell state to a semi-solid state while preserving cell morphology and structural detail.
A(ii)
• Aims/effects: preserve tissue in as life-like a manner as possible; prevent postmortem autolysis and putrefaction; preserve chemical and micro-anatomic constituents so further histochemistry is possible.
• Hardening allows easy manipulation of soft tissue (e.g. brain, intestine); solidification converts the semi-fluid cell consistency to an irreversible semi-solid consistency.
• Optical differentiation is enhanced (unstained components become more visible) and staining, e.g. with haematoxylin, is intensified by fixatives such as formaldehyde.
A(iii)
• A good fixative should coagulate/precipitate tissue components, penetrate the tissue rapidly (penetration depends on molecular weight), be soluble in a suitable solvent (preferably water), be used at an isotonic or hypotonic concentration, and have a neutral reaction.
• The fixative should be at least 15-20 times the bulk of the tissue (over 50 times for museum specimens); large specimens should be sliced to about 1.5 cm thickness to allow easy penetration.
A(iv)
• Common fixative reagents include formaldehyde, ethyl alcohol, acetone, mercuric chloride, picric acid, potassium dichromate, osmium tetroxide, acetic acid and glutaraldehyde.
B(i)
• Fixation must be carried out immediately after removal of tissue (or soon after death) because unfixed tissue undergoes autolysis (enzymatic degradation) and putrefaction (bacterial degradation), which destroy the structural and chemical detail on which histopathological diagnosis depends.
• Fixation arrests these changes and preserves the tissue for subsequent processing, staining and histochemistry.
C(i)
• Formaldehyde is soluble in water up to 37-40% w/v (used as 10% formalin); it is cheap, penetrates tissue rapidly, does not over-harden tissue, preserves proteins by forming cross-linkages and partially preserves glycogen, but if it becomes acidic it forms a brown, granular "formalin pigment" in blood-containing tissue.
• Mercuric chloride precipitates proteins and penetrates tissue rapidly.
• Fixatives containing it leave a black precipitate (mercury pigment) in the tissue which must be removed (with Lugol's iodine followed by sodium thiosulphate) before staining, unlike formalin pigment which is removed with saturated alcoholic picric acid.

questions.question:
A(i) State the general classification of neuroglial cells found in the central nervous system.
B(i) State how each type of neuroglial cell relates to its location/function in the nervous system.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance in identifying these cells could lead to a measurable laboratory error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Neuroglial cells are classified as astrocytes (protoplasmic and fibrous), oligodendroglia, and microglia.
• Protoplasmic astrocytes have granular cytoplasm with long, branching, protoplasmic processes, some attached to blood vessels by 'sucker feet'; they contain no fibres.
• Fibrous astrocytes contain thick fibres that branch outside the cell and are also attached to capillaries by vascular feet, with longer, finer processes than protoplasmic astrocytes.
• Oligodendroglia are small, intensely-staining cells with no fibres or vascular feet, but fine, rarely-branching processes.
• Microglia are small, oval-shaped cells with a deeply-staining nucleus, from each end of which a thick process arises, branching freely into numerous small terminal processes.
B(i)
• Protoplasmic astrocytes are found most abundantly in the grey matter, whereas fibrous astrocytes are most abundant in the white matter.
• Oligodendroglia are abundant in the white matter, arranged in rows along myelinated fibres, and in the grey matter are found close to nerve cells or blood vessels.
• The meninges (dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater), composed of fibrous/elastic connective tissue, surround and protect the brain and spinal cord, with the sub-arachnoid space (between arachnoid and pia mater) containing the cerebrospinal fluid.
C(i)
• Because the different glial cell types are distinguished mainly by subtle differences in process branching, fibre content and location (grey versus white matter), mis-identification on a poorly stained or poorly oriented section could lead to an incorrect assessment of the tissue examined.
• Correct identification depends on appropriate special staining and section thickness (nervous tissue sections for demonstrating complete neurones require greater thickness, 15-20 micrometres, than the routine 7 micrometres).
• An error at this stage (wrong cell type reported) would constitute a measurable laboratory/reporting error affecting the microscopic description of the specimen.

A(i)
• There are three types of muscle tissue: skeletal muscle, visceral (smooth) muscle, and cardiac muscle.
• Skeletal muscle is responsible for movement of the skeleton and structures such as the globe of the eye and the tongue; it is often called voluntary muscle since it is under conscious control, and the arrangement of its contractile proteins produces prominent cross-striations, hence it is also called striated muscle.
• Visceral muscle forms the muscular component of structures such as blood vessels, the gastrointestinal tract, the uterus and the urinary bladder; being under autonomic/hormonal control it is called involuntary muscle, and since it does not show cross-striations it is also called smooth muscle.
• Cardiac muscle has structural and functional characteristics intermediate between skeletal and visceral muscle, providing continuous rhythmic contraction of the heart; although striated in appearance, it is distinguishable from skeletal muscle and should not be called "striated muscle".
• All three muscle types have specialised terminology for their organelles: plasma membrane/plasmalemma is called the sarcolemma, cytoplasm the sarcoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum the sarcoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria the sarcosomes.
• Cells of all three types are surrounded by a thin basement membrane binding them to adjacent cells and supporting tissue.
B(i)
• Skeletal muscle fibres are grouped into fasciculi bound by endomysium.
• Each fascicle is surrounded by perimysium.
• The whole muscle is invested in a dense collagenous epimysium, with the size of the fasciculi reflecting the precision of movement required (small fasciculi for finely controlled eye muscles, large fasciculi with little perimysium for gross-movement muscles such as the buttocks).
• Skeletal muscle contraction is controlled by large motor nerves whose branches supply groups of muscle fibres called motor units; excitation of a motor nerve causes simultaneous contraction of all fibres of its motor unit.
C(i)
• The vitality of skeletal muscle fibres depends on maintenance of their nerve supply.
• If the nerve supply is damaged, this results in atrophy of the corresponding muscle fibres, a measurable structural/functional abnormality (reduction in fibre size/function) directly attributable to disturbance of the normal nerve-muscle relationship.
questions.question:
A(i) State the general classification of muscle tissue.
B(i) State how each class of muscle relates to a specific structural/functional characteristic.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance (loss of nerve supply) leads to a measurable abnormality in skeletal muscle.

A specimen block containing bone, on being cut on the microtome, produces a ribbon of sections that is curved instead of straight, with one border of each section crumbling.
(i) Identify the fault occurring during section cutting.
(ii) State the basic principle/cause behind this fault.
(iii) State the correct remedy/next laboratory step.
questions.answerText:
(i)
This is the fault of a ribbon of sections cut curved instead of straight.
(ii)
It is caused by the edges of the block not being parallel to each other and to the knife, or by a dull point on part of the knife edge causing one border of the section to crumble.
(iii)
The remedy is to cut/trim the edges of the block until they are parallel to each other, and to move the knife until a uniformly sharp edge is presented to the block.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the structure/chemical nature of EDTA as a chelating decalcifying agent.
B(i) State the standard site/use of EDTA in the laboratory.
C(i) Explain the basis of the precipitate artefact that can arise from improper use of EDTA-decalcified tissue.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, disodium salt), also called sequestrene or versene, is a chelating agent soluble in distilled water to about 20-25%.
• It combines with calcium ions to form soluble, non-ionised compounds without destroying tissue structure, and deposits of iron and other metals may also be removed by EDTA.
• It is effective at neutral pH and gives excellent staining results with no observable deleterious effect on tissue no matter how long it is used.
• It is slow in action, and using a volume of 20-30 times that of the tissue, the solution is typically renewed every 5-7 days during decalcification.
• A neutral EDTA solution, with pH adjusted to 7.0 by addition of sodium hydroxide, is a common modification.
B(i)
• EDTA is the decalcifying agent of choice where speed is of secondary importance to quality of tissue preservation and staining reaction, for example for bone marrow biopsies or tissue on which antigen preservation for immunohistochemistry, or heat-sensitive enzyme demonstration, is required.
• Increased temperature can be used to speed EDTA decalcification without the maceration risk seen with acids, though this may not be acceptable for heat-sensitive antigens/enzymes.
C(i)
• The chemical (ammonium-oxalate) test for end-point cannot be used following EDTA decalcification, since it depends on detecting ionised calcium released by acid decalcifiers.
• X-ray (radiographic) examination is used instead for EDTA-decalcified tissue.
• Tissue decalcified in EDTA solutions should not be placed directly into 70% alcohol, because this causes residual EDTA to precipitate in the alcohol and within the tissue.
• Although this precipitate does not appear to affect subsequent tissue staining (since the EDTA is washed out during later processing), it may be noticeable during microtomy or storage as a crystalline crust forming on the surface of the block, a measurable, avoidable processing artefact.
• A water rinse after decalcification, or overnight storage in formol saline/phosphate-buffered saline, prevents this precipitate artefact from forming.

(i)
This pattern (a shift of the maturation index to the left, dominated by parabasal cells) is consistent with an atrophic, post-menopausal hormonal pattern.
(ii)
The assessment is made by hormonal cytology assessment of the smear, using indices such as the maturation index (percentage of parabasal to intermediate to superficial cells, counted on single cells over 200-400 consecutive cells) alongside the karyopyknotic and eosinophilic indices.
(iii)
The finding is reported with reference to the woman's age and menstrual history, comparing the pattern seen with baseline/reference smear patterns, and noting its possible clinical significance.
(iv)
The follow-up step is to correlate the reported hormonal cytology pattern with the clinical picture, and to note it may also be part of screening for cervical carcinoma performed on the same cervical smear.
questions.question:
A cervicovaginal (Pap) smear taken from a 55-year-old woman shows, on microscopy, mainly parabasal-type squamous cells with almost no superficial cells.
(i) Identify the pattern this finding is consistent with.
(ii) State the technique used to arrive at this assessment.
(iii) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(iv) State the follow-up practical step.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Cytological specimens are broadly obtained by exfoliative cytology (cells desquamated from an epithelial surface), aspiration cytology (e.g. fine-needle aspiration cytology, FNAC), and examination of body fluids.
• Exfoliative cytology specimens include normal desquamation products (e.g. bronchial secretion, urine, vaginal/cervical/endometrial secretions) and artificial mechanical desquamation samples (e.g. cervical scraping, buccal mucosal scraping, skin scraping).
• Cytology specimens for clinical examination include peritoneal, pericardial and pleural fluids, cerebrospinal fluid, nipple discharge, bronchial brushings/washings, sputum, gastric washings, urine sediment, prostatic secretions/fluid, and cervicovaginal (Pap) smears.
• Fluid samples require centrifugation before smearing, whereas semisolid samples can be smeared directly onto the glass slide.
B(i)
• Peritoneal, pericardial and pleural fluid (serous fluid/effusion) is examined for diagnosis of carcinoma; nipple discharge is examined for diagnosis of breast carcinoma.
• Bronchial brushings/washings and sputum are examined for diagnosis of lung disease/cancer; gastric washings are examined for diagnosis of stomach, gastrointestinal tract and oesophageal carcinoma.
• Urine sediment is examined for urinary tract carcinoma; prostatic secretions/fluid for prostate carcinoma; cervical (Pap) smear for cervical carcinoma.
• Vaginal smear for endocrine studies/cytohormonal evaluation; endocervical smear for screening for cervical carcinoma; and buccal smear for sex-chromatin determination.
C(i)
• Smears must generally be fixed immediately while still wet (e.g. dropped into fixative or sprayed with fixative) to prevent air-drying, which would distort cell and nuclear morphology.
• For example, in nipple-discharge collection, if the secretion is scant the smear must be restricted to a small area to prevent drying, and the slide is immediately immersed in 95% isopropyl alcohol or sprayed with fixative.
• If fixation is delayed or omitted, air-drying artefact results, causing cell swelling/flattening and loss of the fine nuclear chromatin detail needed to assess features such as hyperchromasia.
• Would compromise diagnostic accuracy and represent a measurable, avoidable laboratory error.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the classification of cytological specimens according to how they are obtained.
B(i) State how the type of specimen relates to the disease it is used to diagnose.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance (delayed or wrong fixation) leads to a measurable laboratory abnormality in the cytology specimen.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Nitric acid (HNO3) is a highly corrosive mineral acid; the pure compound is colourless, but samples may acquire a yellow tinge from decomposition into nitrogen oxides and water, and most commercially available nitric acid has a concentration of about 68%.
• It is a strong oxidising agent and a monoprotic-type mineral acid used at concentrations up to about 10% for decalcification, where it reacts with proteins (xanthoproteic reaction) and with keratin, staining skin yellow.
• Formol-nitric acid and aqueous nitric acid (stabilised with urea) are common fluids containing nitric acid used for decalcification, and Perenyi's fluid (nitric acid, absolute alcohol and chromic acid) is a slower but gentler nitric-acid-based decalcifying fluid.
• Nitric acid is a corrosive substance and a powerful oxidising agent.
• Its major hazard is chemical burns from acid hydrolysis of proteins and fats in skin/flesh, and standard first aid for skin contact is irrigation with large quantities of water for at least ten to fifteen minutes.
B(i)
• In the histopathology laboratory, nitric acid (as a 5-10% aqueous solution) is used mainly as a rapid decalcifying agent for small pieces of bone and for urgent biopsies where speed of decalcification is more important than tissue preservation.
• It is also incorporated into formol-nitric acid, a fluid recommended for the rapid decalcification of small bone slices or blocks already fixed in formalin.
C(i)
• Strong acids such as nitric acid are most rapid in action, but if used for an excessive time they cause loss of nuclear staining and can macerate tissue.
• Even brief exposure to nitric acid can render bone marrow unsatisfactory for staining with Giemsa, Maximow's azure-eosin, or Lillie's azure-eosin formula.
• Nitric acid also causes a yellow discolouration of the tissue (from nitrous acid formation) that interferes with subsequent staining reactions, an effect that can be reduced (though not eliminated) by adding 0.1% urea to the acid.
• The rate of decalcification with nitric acid actually accelerates as the yellow colour develops, so tissue can quickly become over-exposed if the end-point is not tested frequently.
• This gives the characteristic over-decalcification artefact of loss of nuclear staining and tissue maceration.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the physical and chemical properties of nitric acid as used in histopathology.
B(i) State the standard site/method of use of nitric acid in the laboratory.
C(i) Explain the basis of the tissue-damage artefact that results from prolonged use of nitric acid.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The three main dehydrating agents commonly used are alcohol (ethanol), acetone, and dioxane.
• The alcohol method passes tissue through a graded series of increasing alcohol concentrations, from about 70% up to three changes of absolute (100%) alcohol, to avoid the turbulence and tissue distortion that would occur if fresh tissue were placed directly into absolute alcohol.
• The acetone method is rapid (dehydration in 30 minutes to 2 hours) and cheap, but causes more hardening and shrinkage than alcohol and requires a greater volume, making it unsuitable for routine work though useful for urgent small biopsies.
• The dioxane method uses dioxane, which is miscible with water, alcohol, xylene, balsam and paraffin wax, producing little shrinkage.
• However, it is not recommended for routine use because it has a dangerous, cumulative toxic vapour with little warning odour.
B(i)
• The alcohol (ethyl alcohol) method is the standard, non-poisonous choice for routine dehydration of most tissue.
• The acetone method is chosen for very urgent biopsies where speed is essential and some shrinkage is acceptable, and only small pieces of tissue should be treated this way.
• The dioxane method is reserved for situations where its unique double miscibility (with both water and molten wax) is valued and its toxic vapour hazard can be managed.
• It can shorten the overall schedule by combining dehydration and clearing properties.
C(i)
• Tissue must be allowed sufficient time in absolute alcohol to achieve complete dehydration; if dehydration is not complete, the clearing agent and wax will not penetrate the tissue properly.
• Incomplete dehydration is detected because xylene becomes milky when an incompletely dehydrated tissue or section is immersed in it.
• The end result of incomplete dehydration is poor section cutting, since residual water blocks proper infiltration by the clearing agent and paraffin wax, producing a processing defect that compromises the quality of the final sections.
questions.question:
A(i) State the classification of dehydrating agents used in tissue processing.
B(i) State how each dehydrating agent relates to the specific tissue type or degree of urgency for which it is chosen.
C(i) Explain how incomplete dehydration leads to a measurable processing defect.

A(i) Describe the demonstration of myelin as a technique, naming the methods used and their principle.
B(i) State the diagnostic/research significance of demonstrating myelin.
C(i) Distinguish the Weigert-Pal technique from Holmes' silver technique for demonstrating myelin.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Normal myelin is demonstrated using the Weigert-Pal technique, which is performed on paraffin (or preferably frozen/celloidin) sections and is described as the routine method of demonstrating normal myelin.
• Holmes' silver technique is now a routine method for paraffin sections, often combined with Luxol fast blue to show the myelin sheaths, and normal and degenerate myelin can both be assessed using silver-impregnation approaches, of which several variants exist (the long standard method, the shorter Gros-Schultze method, and Glees and Marsland's modification for paraffin sections).
• The Luxol fast blue-cresyl violet technique is another method used, and it is noted as selectively staining Nissl substance in addition to myelin.
• As with all silver-impregnation methods, these techniques are reported to be reliable and to give good results with paraffin and most animal tissue.
• Sections prepared for myelin techniques must be cut at least 10-15 micrometres thick, distinctly thicker than the routine 7 micrometre sections used for general nervous-tissue staining, to adequately display the myelin sheath.
B(i)
• Demonstrating myelin is significant for assessing the structural integrity of nerve fibres in the central and peripheral nervous system, since myelinated fibres are found both in peripheral nerves (interrupted at nodes of Ranvier) and in the white matter of the brain and spinal cord, and loss/abnormality of myelin can be evaluated using these special stains where routine haematoxylin and eosin-type stains would not adequately show it.
• Because myelinated fibres consist of an axon surrounded by a lipid myelin sheath which is itself surrounded by a neurilemmal sheath, adequate demonstration of this lipid sheath is only possible with lipid/silver-selective methods such as Weigert-Pal or Holmes' silver rather than with routine stains.
C(i)
• The Weigert-Pal technique is the classical routine method for demonstrating normal myelin, historically the most popular technique in Great Britain for this purpose, performed on paraffin, frozen or celloidin sections.
• Holmes' silver technique is a routine paraffin-section method that demonstrates neurofibrils/silver-impregnable structures and is often combined with Luxol fast blue specifically to also show the myelin sheaths, whereas the Gros-Schultze method (a related silver technique) does not demonstrate neurofibrils as well as the standard technique.
• The two techniques therefore differ in their chemical basis (Weigert-Pal relies on a chromate/haematoxylin-type reaction with myelin lipid, whereas Holmes'/silver methods rely on metallic silver impregnation) and are often used in combination with different counterstains (Luxol fast blue for Holmes') to extend or confirm findings.
• Both methods can be applied to paraffin sections of central nervous system tissue provided the tissue was processed without vacuum-bath impregnation, which would otherwise render sections too brittle for these elaborate staining procedures.
• Selection between the two also depends on the embedding method already used for the block, since Weigert-Pal is traditionally applied to paraffin, frozen or celloidin sections, whereas Holmes' method is now most often used specifically on paraffin sections.

questions.question:
A(i) State the classification of body cells according to their regenerative capacity.
B(i) State how each class of cell relates to the healing capacity of specific organs/tissues.
C(i) Explain how injury to a class of cell with poor regenerative capacity leads to a measurable clinical/laboratory consequence.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• All cells in the body are divided into three groups according to their regenerative capacity: labile cells, stable cells, and permanent cells.
• Labile cells continuously divide throughout life, for example those of the bone marrow, skin, vagina and oral cavity.
• Stable cells do not divide under normal conditions but divide when stimulated, for example parenchymal cells of the liver, kidney and pancreas, and mesenchymal cells such as fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells.
• Permanent cells are non-dividing cells that have left the cell cycle completely and cannot undergo mitosis, for example neurones of the central nervous system and cardiac muscle cells.
• Regeneration (replacement of damaged cells by undamaged cells) involves proliferation and migration of adjacent cells to fill the gap created by a wound; regeneration and repair both occur in injured tissue, and which process dominates is determined by the tissue's ability to regenerate.
B(i)
• Tissues composed of labile cells (e.g. skin, bone marrow) heal predominantly by regeneration, since these cells continuously divide and can readily replace lost tissue.
• Tissues composed of stable cells (e.g. liver, kidney) can regenerate when stimulated by injury, as reflected in the special note that healing in the liver is total regeneration, whereas healing in the kidney occurs only in the tubules and not in the glomeruli.
• Tissues composed of permanent cells (neurones, cardiac muscle) cannot regenerate and must instead heal by repair (replacement with granulation tissue/scar), as reflected in bone healing being similar to skin except for formation of an immature callus.
C(i)
• Because permanent cells cannot re-enter the cell cycle, injury to them (e.g. neurones of the CNS or cardiac muscle) cannot be repaired by regeneration of functional tissue; the damaged area is instead replaced by non-functional scar/repair tissue.
• This is a measurable clinical/laboratory consequence: the tissue permanently loses the specific function of the destroyed cells (for example, cardiac contractile tissue replaced by fibrous scar cannot contract), unlike labile or stable-cell tissues, which can be restored to a functionally similar state after injury.
• This distinction underlies why healing in special tissues such as the heart, kidney, liver, bone and skeletal muscle differs.

questions.question:
A(i) State the classification/timeline of methods used for decalcification.
B(i) State how each decalcification method relates to a specific specimen size or clinical urgency.
C(i) Explain how over-decalcification leads to a measurable laboratory abnormality.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Methods of decalcification include the manual acid-solution method, microwave decalcification, the ion-exchange resin method, the electrolytic method, and the ultrasonic method.
• In the acid-solution method, the gauze-wrapped specimen is suspended in the centre of a jar of decalcifying fluid (about 100 times the tissue volume).
• Calcium is released by ion exchange with the acid anion to form a soluble calcium salt (e.g. calcium chloride with hydrochloric acid) that stays in solution.
• Microwave decalcification places the specimen and decalcifying agent in a microwave oven with intermittent irradiation and regular solution changes, accelerating decalcification about 10-30 fold compared with ambient-temperature methods.
• The ion-exchange resin method uses a mixture of formic acid and a commercial ion-exchange resin; calcium is rapidly removed from the formic acid solution into the resin, eliminating the need for frequent solution changes and giving well-preserved cellular detail.
• The electrolytic method suspends the specimen (as the anode) in an acid electrolytic solution (formic and hydrochloric acids) between electrodes carrying a direct current, so that calcium ions migrate to the cathode.
• Cancellous bone 3-5 mm thick can decalcify in 45 minutes or less, but only a limited number of specimens can be processed at a time.
• The ultrasonic method uses ultrasonic energy to accelerate diffusion processes, rapidly destroying calcium/magnesium phosphate and calcium carbonate crystalline structures while cooling the specimen to avoid warming, saving up to 75% of decalcification time for bone marrow biopsies with excellent tissue/antigen preservation.
B(i)
• Microwave and electrolytic methods are chosen where speed is essential (e.g. rapid bone marrow decalcification, transplant biopsies), while the ion-exchange resin method and standard acid method suit routine, larger specimens where daily monitoring is feasible.
• The ultrasonic method is preferred where maximum cell/tissue and antigen preservation combined with speed is required, such as bone marrow biopsies for immunohistochemistry.
C(i)
• Because the harmful effects of acid increase with time, tissue left in decalcifying fluid beyond the true end-point undergoes over-decalcification.
• Over-decalcified sections typically stain strongly with eosin and show a marked loss of nuclear haematoxyphilia, with poorly preserved nuclear and cytoplasmic detail, a measurable and irreversible laboratory abnormality distinct from the correctable artefact of incomplete decalcification.

(i)
The smear is obtained from the lateral wall of the mid-third of the vaginal epithelium and prepared for hormonal cytology assessment.
(ii)
The principle is that oestrogen and progesterone modulate the maturation of the vaginal squamous epithelium, so the proportion of parabasal, intermediate and superficial cells (assessed via the maturation, karyopyknotic and eosinophilic indices) reflects the current hormonal state.
(iii)
Materials required include a spatula or pipette for sample collection, a glass slide, and the appropriate wet fixative.
(iv)
Sources of error include inflammation, cytolysis, or recent medication/surgery, any of which can distort the maturation pattern independent of the true hormonal state.
(v)
Precautions include ensuring the smear is taken from the correct site (lateral mid-third of the vagina), and reporting the result with reference to the patient's age and menstrual history, comparing against baseline reference patterns.
questions.question:
A cervical smear is being collected from a patient for hormonal (cytohormonal) cytological evaluation.
(i) State the technique appropriate for obtaining this specimen.
(ii) State the principle behind the assessment to be made.
(iii) List the materials required.
(iv) State the sources of error that could affect the result.
(v) State the precautions needed for a valid evaluation.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Materials obtained in the histopathology laboratory include incisional biopsies (a small piece from a lesion/tumour), excisional biopsies (the whole of the tumour/lesion) and post-mortem tissue samples (from autopsy).
• Types of histological preparation include whole mounts (preparations of an entire small animal/organism, e.g. fungus or parasite, not more than 0.2-0.5 mm thick), sections (frozen or paraffin-wax tissue cut in 3-5 mm pieces, sectioned at about 5 micrometres on a microtome).
• Smears (for cytological examination, made from blood, bone marrow or fluid such as pleural or ascitic fluid, immediately fixed in alcohol, or made by crushing soft tissue between two slides or by pressing a clean slide onto a moist tissue surface as an impression smear).
• The diagnostic techniques used in pathology more broadly include histopathology, cytopathology, haematopathology, immunohistochemistry, microbiological examination, biochemical examination, cytogenetics, molecular techniques and autopsy.
B(i)
• Histopathological examination studies tissue obtained by biopsy under the microscope for abnormal structure, once the tissue has been fixed immediately in adequate 10% formalin.
• Cytopathology, using smears/preparations, is applied for screening of asymptomatic cancer (e.g. cervical cancer), diagnosis of symptomatic cancer, and diagnosis of cysts, inflammatory conditions and infections.
• Haematological examination investigates abnormalities of blood cells and their bone-marrow precursors to diagnose anaemias and leukaemias; immunohistochemistry detects specific antigens in tissue to identify disease type; microbiological examination identifies causative micro-organisms.
• Biochemical examination investigates metabolic disturbances (e.g. in diabetes mellitus, where it provides the best means of diagnosis and disease control); cytogenetics/molecular techniques detect chromosomal or genetic abnormalities; and autopsy identifies the cause of death for forensic or clinical purposes.
C(i)
• Because each investigation depends on the specimen being of the correct type and handled/fixed appropriately (e.g. a biopsy fixed immediately in formalin for histopathology versus a smear fixed while still wet for exfoliative cytology), use of the wrong preparation type or improper handling for a given investigation limits or invalidates the diagnostic information obtainable.
• For example, in the diagnosis of tumours, fine-needle aspiration cytology and histopathology contribute most, whereas in diabetes mellitus biochemical investigation is of greatest diagnostic value.
• Substituting one technique/specimen type for the wrong disease context would fail to give the best diagnostic yield, and for most diseases diagnosis actually depends on a combination of these pathological investigations.
questions.question:
A(i) State the general classification of specimens and preparations obtained in a histopathology laboratory.
B(i) State how each type of preparation relates to a specific diagnostic technique/investigation.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance (wrong specimen type/handling) leads to a measurable diagnostic limitation.

During trimming of a paraffin block of bony tissue, the microtome knife meets resistance, and the resulting sections are torn, ragged and scratched.
(i) Identify the underlying cause.
(ii) State the basic principle behind this fault.
(iii) State the correct next laboratory step.
questions.answerText:
(i)
This indicates incomplete decalcification, with residual foci of calcification remaining in the tissue.
(ii)
Residual calcium salts in the tissue resist cutting by the knife, tearing the section and damaging the knife edge as it encounters the hard calcified focus.
(iii)
The block should be removed from the microtome and surface-decalcified by immersion in 10% formic acid or 5% nitric acid for about an hour, then washed briefly in water, dried and replaced on the microtome for cutting; the area should never simply be cut away with a knife, especially in diagnostic histopathology.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the chemical nature and structure of mordants used in histology.
B(i) State the standard method/site of application of a mordant in a staining procedure.
C(i) Explain the basis of the abnormal (failed) staining reaction that occurs when a mordant is omitted.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Mordants are polyvalent metal ions that form coordination complexes with certain dyes; they are hydroxides or salts of divalent or trivalent metals.
• They form a salt bridge between the tissue and the dye, allowing proper union between the dye molecule and the tissue in some staining procedures.
• The two commonest metals used as mordants in the histology laboratory are aluminium and ferric iron.
• The use of potassium aluminium alum as a mordant has been reported to have no significant effect on the staining qualities in some procedures, while other mordants have been reported to affect certain stains.
• Bouin's solution is used as a mordant to intensify colour reactions, and the H&E staining method is a good example of a stain that uses a mordant.
B(i)
• A mordant may be mixed with the solution of the dye before staining, for example in Ehrlich's and Mayer's haematoxylin.
• Alternatively it may be applied to the tissue before the dye is applied, for example in Heidenhain's iron haematoxylin, where the section is mordanted in ferric chloride before being stained with haematoxylin.
• A mordant may also be applied after the dye, as in Lugol's iodine acting as a mordant after crystal violet in the Gram stain for bacteria and fibrin.
C(i)
• Without mordants forming the salt-bridge linkage, proper direct union between dye molecules and tissue will not take place in staining procedures that depend on mordanting.
• The result would be weak, uneven or absent staining of the intended structure, since the dye cannot attach firmly to the tissue in the absence of the coordination complex the mordant provides.
• In histology, mordants are therefore indispensable for fixing dyes to tissues in mordant-dependent techniques, and their omission constitutes a preventable technical error leading to unreliable or uninterpretable staining.
• Washing out (thorough washing in running tap water) is separately required after use of oxidising mordants/agents such as potassium dichromate or osmium tetroxide, to prevent their reduction on contact with subsequent alcohol steps.

A(i)
• Tissue processing refers to treatment of tissue by passing it gradually through a series of reagents necessary to impregnate it with a solid support medium, so that the tissue becomes sufficiently firm yet elastic for sections of the desired thickness to be cut on a microtome.
• The principle is to remove all extractable water from the tissue and replace it with a solid support medium that provides sufficient rigidity for sectioning without distortion or damage.
• Since most fixatives are aqueous, water, some lipids and other tissue fluids must be completely removed before paraffin embedding.
• The four stages of tissue processing are complete (post-) fixation, dehydration, clearing and infiltration/embedding.
• Dehydration removes water and residual fixative using graded alcohols; clearing removes the dehydrating agent and renders the tissue receptive to the infiltrating medium; infiltration permeates the tissue with a support medium; embedding orientates the tissue in the support medium and allows it to solidify.
• Factors influencing the rate of processing include agitation (can reduce processing time by up to 30% if efficient), heat (increases penetration/fluid exchange but must be limited, e.g. to about 45 degrees C, to avoid shrinkage/hardening and IHC interference), viscosity of the reagents, use of vacuum, and completeness of prior fixation.
B(i)
• Use of an inappropriate processing schedule, or a fundamental error such as wrong sequencing/replenishment of reagents, can produce tissue specimens that cannot be sectioned and therefore yield no useful microscopic/diagnostic information.
• Where the whole specimen has been processed ("all in"), there is no spare tissue for repeat processing, which can be disastrous for a patient awaiting diagnosis.
C(i)
• Manual (hand) tissue processing involves passing tissue cassettes through a fixed manual sequence of reagent baths (e.g. graded alcohols, clearing agent, wax) timed and changed by the operator, and is appropriate when only small numbers of specimens are processed.
• Automated tissue processing uses a tissue processor, either the tissue-transfer ("dip and dunk") type, where specimens are mechanically transferred between separate reagent containers, or the fluid-transfer ("enclosed") type, where specimens remain in a single retort/chamber and fluids are pumped in and out, often with heat, vacuum/pressure cycling and agitation to enhance and speed processing.
• Automated processors save time, allow larger specimen numbers to be processed efficiently, incorporate alarm/diagnostic systems for malfunction, and produce more consistent quality, whereas manual processing, though more flexible and simple, is slower and more prone to human error/mistiming across many specimens.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe tissue processing under the headings: definition, principle and the four stages involved.
B(i) State the diagnostic significance of correct tissue processing.
C(i) Distinguish manual (hand) tissue processing from automated tissue processing.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Decalcifying agents are classified into three main types: those based on strong mineral acids, those based on weaker organic acids, and those composed of chelating agents.
• Strong mineral acids (e.g. nitric acid, hydrochloric acid) at concentrations up to about 10% are the most rapid in action.
• Weak organic acids (formic acid being the main one used, with acetic and picric acids as minor/incidental decalcifiers found in fixatives such as Bouin's and Carnoy's) act more gently and slowly than the strong mineral acids.
• Chelating agents, principally EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, also called sequestrene or versene), combine with calcium ions to form soluble, non-ionised compounds without destroying tissue structure.
B(i)
• Nitric acid, being rapid, is recommended for urgent biopsies and small pieces of bone where speed is essential.
• Formic acid, being gentler, is recommended for post-mortem/research tissue and routine surgical specimens, particularly where immunohistochemical staining will be needed.
• EDTA, though very slow, is the decalcifying agent of choice where quality of tissue preservation, staining reaction, and preservation of antigens/enzymes are more important than speed, for example in bone marrow biopsies requiring subsequent special staining.
• Trichloroacetic acid is recommended for small pieces of delicate tissue requiring decalcification, while Ebner's fluid is particularly useful for decalcifying teeth.
C(i)
• The stronger the acid concentration and the longer the exposure, the faster calcium is removed, but this is accompanied by concomitant damage to cell structures.
• Prolonged exposure to nitric or hydrochloric acid inhibits nuclear staining and can macerate tissue, and hydrochloric acid at higher temperatures causes serious swelling of tissue and eventual digestion of bone matrix.
• Over-decalcified sections typically stain strongly with eosin and show a marked loss of nuclear haematoxyphilia, with poorly preserved nuclear and cytoplasmic detail, which is an irreversible artefact that can compromise diagnosis.
• EDTA, by contrast, decalcifies at a neutral pH and causes little tissue damage even with prolonged exposure, though it acts slowly and residual EDTA can precipitate as a crystalline crust if the tissue is placed directly into alcohol without a water rinse.
questions.question:
A(i) State the general classification of decalcifying agents.
B(i) Explain how each class of decalcifying agent relates to the specimen type or clinical situation for which it is chosen.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance (excessive acid strength or duration of exposure) leads to a measurable laboratory abnormality.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Cavity fluids that can be examined cytologically include abdominal (peritoneal), pleural, pericardial, synovial and cerebrospinal fluid.
• These fluids are classified into three types: transudate, exudate, and modified transudate.
• A transudate passes through a membrane or is squeezed through tissue into an extracellular space and has a protein concentration of less than 2.5 g/dL.
• An exudate is slowly discharged from blood vessels from inflamed tissue and has a protein concentration greater than 3.0 g/dL.
• A modified transudate has an intermediate protein concentration of 2.5-7.5 g/dL.
B(i)
• Transudates typically contain macrophages, mesothelial cells (the thin, double-layered lining covering the lungs, chest wall and diaphragm) and lymphocytes, reflecting a passive fluid-accumulation process such as ascites without primary inflammation of the cavity lining.
• Exudates instead reflect active inflammatory or malignant processes and may show neutrophilic, eosinophilic, mixed-cellularity or lymphocytic effusions, giant multinucleated cells, or cells of lupus erythematosus (an autoimmune disease).
• Exudates can also show malignant effusions containing primary tumour cells (e.g. mesothelioma), lymphoproliferative disorders, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple myeloma, large-cell lymphoma, or metastatic tumours such as adenocarcinoma, liposarcoma and malignant melanoma.
C(i)
• Because a transudate results from a passive process (fluid squeezed through a membrane) it has a low protein concentration (below 2.5 g/dL), whereas an exudate, discharged from blood vessels of inflamed tissue, has a higher protein concentration (above 3.0 g/dL).
• This measurable protein-concentration difference is the laboratory basis for classifying the fluid.
• A modified transudate, with its intermediate protein concentration (2.5-7.5 g/dL), indicates a disturbance of the underlying membrane/vessel that is more than purely passive but not as actively inflammatory/exudative as a full exudate.
• This illustrates how the degree of disturbance of the underlying process is reflected directly and measurably in the protein concentration of the fluid.
questions.question:
A(i) State the general classification of cavity fluids that can be examined cytologically.
B(i) State how each type of cavity fluid relates to the underlying disease process.
C(i) Explain how a disturbance in the underlying process leads to a measurable laboratory (protein concentration) abnormality.

A(i) Describe primary wound healing as a process under the headings: definition and stages/timeline.
B(i) State the clinical significance of primary healing.
C(i) Distinguish primary healing from secondary healing.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Primary healing (healing by primary intention) refers to healing of a clean, uninfected surgical incision that has been closed (apposed) by a surgical suture.
• Following injury and suturing, the narrow incision space is immediately filled by a blood clot and debris; dehydration of the surface clot forms a scab covering the wound.
• By the first day, within 2-3 hours, neutrophils appear at the wound margins and inflammation sets in.
• Within 24-48 hours, spurs of epithelial cells move from the cut edges and deposit basement-membrane components, eventually producing a thin, continuous epithelial layer that closes the wound.
• By the third day, macrophages appear to replace neutrophils, and granulation tissue invades the incision space with formation of collagen fibre; the epithelial covering continues to thicken.
• By the fifth day, the incisional space is filled with granulation tissue and the epidermis approaches its normal thickness, with differentiation of surface cells yielding a mature epidermal architecture and surface keratinisation.
• During the second week, there is continued accumulation of collagen and proliferation of fibroblasts, with disappearance of the granulation tissue; by the end of the month, there is a scar made of cellular, cutaneous connective tissue.
B(i)
• Primary healing is clinically significant because it occurs in a clean, uninfected, well-apposed incision and proceeds through an orderly, faster sequence with minimal granulation tissue and minimal scarring, which is the desired outcome after surgical wound closure.
C(i)
• Primary healing occurs in a clean, uninfected surgical incision with no gap between apposed edges, follows the ordered sequence described above, and produces minimal granulation tissue and a fine scar.
• Secondary healing occurs in an open wound with a gap and ragged edges, is typically infected and complicated by necrosis.
• It follows the same general pattern as primary healing but with much more extensive formation of granulation tissue and fibroblast proliferation, and examples of processes healing this way include infarction, inflammatory ulceration and abscess formation.
• Because secondary healing involves a larger tissue defect and more granulation tissue, it takes longer and carries a greater risk of the complications of wound healing (deficient scarring/dehiscence, hypertrophic scar/keloid, contracture) than primary healing.

A(i)
• The cells of connective/supporting tissue are divided into three types according to basic function: cells responsible for synthesis and maintenance of the extracellular material, cells responsible for storage and metabolism of fat, and cells with defence/immune functions.
• The cells responsible for synthesis/maintenance of extracellular material are fibroblasts, derived from precursor mesenchymal cells; fibroblasts with additional contractile function are called myofibroblasts.
• The cells responsible for storage and metabolism of fat are adipocytes, which collectively form adipose tissue.
• The cells with defence/immune functions are mast cells, tissue macrophages, and all types of white blood cells.
• Connective tissue has two major constituents: cells and extracellular material.
• The extracellular material consists of ground substance (a matrix of organic material) in which fibres are embedded, plus structural glycoproteins that mediate interaction between cells and the other constituents.
• Ground substance is an amorphous, semi-fluid gel composed of glycosaminoglycans (long, unbranched polysaccharide chains, e.g. hyaluronic acid) and proteoglycans (protein-carbohydrate complexes), through which metabolites diffuse.
B(i)
• In wound healing, repair is the replacement of lost tissue by granulation tissue, which is formed from surrounding connective tissue and consists of fibroblasts and proliferating capillary loops.
• The fibroblast is the cell responsible for initially synthesising collagen type III at the wound site, which is later converted to collagen type I as the granulation tissue matures into scar tissue.
C(i)
• If fibroblast/collagen activity is deficient, the resulting weak scar can lead to wound dehiscence (rupture).
• If fibroblast/collagen activity is excessive or unregulated, the result is a hypertrophic scar or keloid, in which the scar grows beyond its normal boundary and fails to regress, or an exaggerated contracture.
• Both outcomes are measurable, clinically-recognisable complications of wound healing that arise directly from disturbance of the normal fibroblast-driven granulation-tissue and collagen-remodelling process described for connective tissue repair.

questions.answerText:
(i)
An urgent/rapid processing schedule is appropriate, using the acetone dehydration method rather than the standard graded-alcohol schedule.
(ii)
The principle is that acetone dehydrates tissue rapidly (in 30 minutes to 2 hours) because only small pieces of tissue are treated this way, allowing a faster turnaround than the routine alcohol schedule.
(iii)
Materials/equipment required include acetone, a clearing agent (e.g. xylene) and paraffin wax, together with the small specimen container/cassette.

Sources of error include using acetone on tissue that is too large, which produces more hardening and shrinkage than alcohol and requires a greater volume of reagent, giving a poorly processed block.
(v)
Precautions include restricting the acetone method to only small pieces of tissue, and accepting the trade-off of some shrinkage in return for speed, since acetone is not recommended for routine work.

A small, delicate specimen of tuberculous tissue containing scattered foci of calcification requires decalcification without disrupting its friable structure.
(i) State the technique appropriate for this specimen.
(ii) State the principle behind choosing this approach.
(iii) List the materials required.
(iv) State the sources of error to avoid.
(v) State the precautions needed.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Surface decalcification, applied after the tissue has been embedded in wax, is the appropriate technique for such a delicate specimen, rather than full immersion decalcification of the unembedded tissue.
(ii)
The principle is that progressive decalcification takes place only at the exposed surface of the embedded block, with little or no adverse effect on the surrounding delicate tissue, avoiding the disruption that immersing a fragile specimen directly in acid would cause.
(iii)
Materials required are 10% formic acid or 5% nitric acid for surface treatment, applied for about one hour, with washing facilities to rinse the block afterward.
(iv)
A source of error is discovering unsuspected calcification only after sectioning has begun (torn sections, resistance to the knife); such areas should never be removed with a knife.
(v)
Precautions include removing the block from the microtome as soon as resistance/tearing is noticed, applying surface decalcification, washing and drying the block before replacing it for cutting.

questions.question:
A paraffin block containing a small focus of unsuspected calcification produces sections in which the microtome knife meets resistance and the sections show longitudinal scratches.
(i) State the technique appropriate to correct this during microtomy.
(ii) State the principle behind the technique.
(iii) List the materials required.
(iv) State the source of error responsible for this fault.
(v) State the precaution to prevent recurrence.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Surface decalcification of the block (rather than removing the calcified area with a knife) is the appropriate corrective technique.
(ii)
The principle is that acid applied to the exposed block surface removes the residual calcium salts causing the resistance and scratching, without disrupting the rest of the embedded tissue.
(iii)
Materials required are 10% formic acid or 5% nitric acid, with facilities to wash and dry the block afterward before replacing it on the microtome.
(iv)
The source of error is an unsuspected focus of calcification not detected or removed before embedding, discovered only through resistance to the knife and scratched sections during cutting.
(v)
The precaution is to test tissue for residual calcification (chemically or radiographically) before embedding, so that decalcification can be completed beforehand rather than being discovered during section cutting.

questions.question:
A(i) State the classification of embedding media used in histopathology.
B(i) State how the choice of embedding medium relates to the type/density of tissue being processed.
C(i) Explain how use of an unsuitable embedding medium leads to a measurable sectioning defect.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Several embedding media are in use, the major ones being paraffin wax, paraplast, esterwax, water-soluble wax (carbowax/polyethylene glycol), cellulose nitrate (celloidin/LVN), celloidin-paraffin double embedding, aqueous media/gelatin, synthetic resin, and freeze-drying/freeze-substitution media.
• Paraffin wax is the most widely used medium, giving reasonable processing speed, good consistency for serial sectioning, a wide range of section thickness and durable blocks, but it causes considerable hardening/shrinkage and dense cortical bone/large brain pieces are difficult to cut in it.
• Paraplast (purified paraffin wax plus polymers) has greater elasticity than plain paraffin wax, allowing bone sections to be cut more easily.
• Esterwax (dimethylene glycol distearate, glyceryl monostearate and polyethylene glycol) has a low melting point (45-47 degrees C) and is soluble in alcohol and xylene, though expensive.
• Water-soluble (carbowax/polyethylene glycol) waxes cause relatively little shrinkage and do not require dehydration/clearing before use, and are useful for enzyme work and lipid demonstration, but the medium dissolves in water and tissues with much fat are not easily penetrated.
• Cellulose nitrate (celloidin/LVN) causes little shrinkage (no heat required), gives improved cutting of large, dense blocks (e.g. bone) and preserves cohesion between tissue layers of different consistency (e.g. the eye).
• Impregnation/hardening is very slow, ribboning/serial sectioning is not possible, and thin (less than about 10 micrometre) sections are difficult.
B(i)
• Dense/hard tissues such as bone and brain are better embedded in paraplast, celloidin/LVN, or celloidin-paraffin double embedding (useful for bone, brain, eye, skin and muscle) because these reduce hardening/shrinkage or improve cohesion, whereas soft routine tissue is well suited to standard paraffin wax.
• Tissue requiring preservation of enzymes or lipids for special study is better embedded in water-soluble (polyethylene glycol) wax, since it avoids the high-temperature/dehydration steps of paraffin wax that would destroy or dissolve these substances.
C(i)
• If dense bone or brain tissue is embedded in ordinary paraffin wax, the resultant sections may show holes, folds and coarse chatter because the wax does not adequately support the dense tissue.
• If tissue containing large amounts of fat is embedded in water-soluble wax, the fat is not easily penetrated by the medium, giving a poorly infiltrated, structurally unstable block.
• Choosing an embedding medium unsuited to the tissue's density/consistency therefore directly produces the measurable sectioning defects (holes, folds, chatter, crumbling) recognised as processing artefacts.

questions.question:
A section of decalcified bone tissue, after staining, shows strong eosin staining throughout with marked loss of nuclear haematoxyphilia and poorly preserved nuclear/cytoplasmic detail.
(i) Identify the artefact seen.
(ii) State the basic principle/cause behind it.
(iii) State the correct laboratory approach to avoid this in future specimens.
questions.answerText:
(i)
This is the artefact of over-decalcification.
(ii)
It is caused by leaving the tissue in decalcifying fluid (particularly a strong acid) for longer than the true end-point, so that the harmful effects of the acid on tissue proteins and nuclear material accumulate with time.
(iii)
In future specimens, the end-point of decalcification should be tested at intervals (chemically or, more reliably, radiographically) so the tissue is removed from the decalcifying fluid as soon as calcium removal is complete, rather than left for a fixed or excessive period.

(i)
The specimen requires decalcification (e.g. using a weak acid such as formic acid, or the ion-exchange resin method) before it can be processed and sectioned.
(ii)
The principle is that the acid reacts with the calcium salts in the bone, releasing calcium ions to form a soluble calcium salt that passes into solution, allowing the bone matrix to soften sufficiently for microtomy.
(iii)
Materials/reagents/equipment required include a container of the chosen decalcifying fluid (about 20-100 times the tissue volume), a fine-toothed saw for trimming the specimen to 4-5 mm thickness, and materials for end-point testing (litmus paper and ammonium oxalate for the chemical test, or x-ray film for the radiographic test).
(iv)
Sources of error include using too strong an acid or leaving the tissue in the fluid too long (causing over-decalcification, loss of nuclear staining and tissue maceration), or removing the tissue too early (incomplete decalcification, causing torn sections and knife damage).
(v)
Precautions/quality-control checks include ensuring the tissue is thoroughly fixed before decalcification, using an adequate volume of fluid, changing the fluid regularly, and testing the end-point (chemically or radiographically) at intervals rather than relying on a fixed time.

A dense piece of cortical bone is received in the laboratory and needs to be prepared for routine histological sectioning.
(i) State the technique appropriate for this specimen before it can be processed.
(ii) State the principle of the technique.
(iii) List the materials/reagents/equipment required.
(iv) State the common sources of error associated with the technique.
