questions.question: A patient following spinal surgery reports new numbness and weakness in the lower limbs during a physiotherapy session. The most appropriate action is to
options: increase mobility training intensity to test tolerance
stop treatment immediately and alert the medical team urgently
reassure the patient that this is an expected finding
document the finding for review at the next scheduled visit
continue exercises to assess if symptoms resolve on their own
questions.explanation: New neurological symptoms such as numbness or weakness following spinal surgery may indicate a serious complication such as nerve compression or haematoma, requiring the physiotherapist to stop treatment immediately and escalate urgently to the medical team. Continuing treatment or delaying escalation could risk permanent neurological injury. Recognising red flag symptoms and responding promptly is an essential safety skill in postoperative musculoskeletal rehabilitation.

questions.question: A patient recovering from a fracture-dislocation of the elbow is cautioned against early aggressive passive stretching primarily because this joint is prone to developing
questions.explanation: The elbow joint is particularly prone to developing heterotopic ossification, an abnormal formation of bone in soft tissue, which can be provoked or worsened by aggressive passive stretching after fracture-dislocation. Gentle, active, patient-controlled movement is therefore generally preferred over forceful passive techniques in early elbow rehabilitation. Awareness of this specific joint vulnerability should guide the physiotherapist's choice of technique.

The third stage of general anaesthesia is called surgical anaesthesia and is marked by rhythmic, deep breathing that indicates the patient is ready for the operation to proceed. The preceding delirium stage instead shows irregular breathing, excitement, and marked muscle activity. The fourth stage, medullary paralysis, is dangerous and irreversible.
questions.question: The stage of general anaesthesia characterised by rhythmic breathing with deep respirations and surgical readiness is termed

questions.explanation: Oral temperature can be inaccurate if a hot or cold drink was taken within the previous half hour, as this directly alters the local mucosal temperature. The reading no longer reflects true core temperature until the mouth returns to equilibrium. Rectal or axillary sites avoid this specific source of error.
questions.question: A patient's oral temperature reading is likely to be falsely low immediately after they have
Which cosmetic surgical procedure specifically involves reshaping or firming of the abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: Abdominoplasty, commonly called a tummy tuck, involves reshaping and firming of the abdomen, typically by removing excess skin and tightening underlying musculature. Blepharoplasty and rhinoplasty, by contrast, address the eyelids and nose respectively. Each of these procedures falls under the broader specialty of aesthetic or cosmetic plastic surgery.

questions.question: The increased anteroposterior chest diameter commonly seen in patients with emphysema is clinically described as
questions.explanation: Barrel chest describes the increased anteroposterior diameter of the thoracic cage that develops in emphysema as a compensatory response to reduced alveolar surface area. This chest wall change is accompanied by diaphragmatic flattening, which further impairs efficient breathing mechanics. It is a hallmark clinical sign used when assessing patients with long-standing obstructive airway disease.

Starting pelvic floor muscle training before prostatectomy allows the patient to learn correct muscle activation while pain-free, which is associated with improved continence outcomes after surgery. This pre-operative preparation builds a foundation that postoperative training can then reinforce and progress. Early education also helps set realistic patient expectations about the gradual nature of continence recovery.
questions.question: Pre-operative pelvic floor muscle training before prostatectomy is recommended mainly because it
options: replaces the need for postoperative physiotherapy

questions.question: A prostatectomy patient is concerned that pelvic floor exercises are not showing improvement after only one week. The most appropriate physiotherapy explanation is that
options: surgery has permanently and irreversibly failed
the patient must have performed the exercises incorrectly only
continence recovery is typically gradual over weeks to months
exercises should be immediately abandoned as ineffective
full continence recovery always occurs within one week
questions.explanation: Recovery of continence after prostatectomy is typically a gradual process occurring over weeks to months, so it is appropriate to reassure the patient that early results should not be expected. Consistent adherence to a well-structured pelvic floor programme, combined with realistic expectations, supports better long-term outcomes. If concerns persist beyond the expected recovery window, further specialist assessment can be considered.

questions.question: Postoperative pain management is a physiotherapy priority after joint replacement surgery mainly because uncontrolled pain
options: limits participation in essential early exercise and mobilisation
only affects the surgical wound cosmetically
has no effect on rehabilitation progress
reduces the need for any exercise programme
improves long-term joint range of motion
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled pain after joint replacement surgery limits the patient's ability to participate in essential early exercise and mobilisation, both of which are critical for regaining function and preventing complications such as stiffness. Physiotherapists work closely with the medical team to ensure analgesia is optimised before and during treatment sessions. Effective pain control therefore directly supports, rather than merely accompanies, successful rehabilitation.

options: sit the patient fully upright immediately
apply ice packs to the trunk
tilt the patient head-down and check intravenous fluid patency
questions.question: During the immediate postoperative period, the most appropriate first action if a patient's blood pressure drops significantly is to
questions.explanation: A head-down tilt helps maintain cerebral perfusion when blood pressure falls, while checking the intravenous line ensures fluids are being delivered as prescribed. Increasing fluid input alongside high-flow oxygen administration is also part of the initial management. Sitting the patient upright would further reduce venous return and worsen hypotension.

Hip precautions following surgical management of a hip fracture, particularly with certain fixation or replacement approaches, aim to prevent dislocation of the repaired joint by avoiding the combined position of excessive flexion, adduction, and internal rotation. These precautions are reinforced throughout functional training, including transfers and dressing techniques. The duration of these precautions is guided by the specific surgical procedure performed and surgeon instruction.
options: dislocation of the surgically repaired joint
reduced swelling around the surgical site
accelerated bone healing at the fracture site
questions.question: A patient recovering from a hip fracture managed surgically is taught to avoid combined hip flexion beyond ninety degrees with adduction and internal rotation primarily to prevent
In microsurgical reconstruction, a segment of tissue moved to a new site and reconnected to a blood supply by suturing small vessels is called a
questions.explanation: A free flap involves transferring skin, muscle, bone, or fat, or a combination of these, to a distant site and reconnecting it to a new blood supply by suturing arteries and veins as small as one to two millimetres. This technique allows coverage of defects where no local tissue is available. It requires specialised microsurgical training and equipment.

options: early ambulation and improved dietary intake
strict bed rest until symptoms resolve
questions.explanation: Early ambulation stimulates bowel motility and, together with an improved dietary intake, is the first-line approach to postoperative constipation. Stool softeners may be added if prescribed to further assist bowel elimination. Prolonged inactivity, in contrast, tends to worsen rather than relieve constipation.
questions.question: Persistent constipation following abdominal surgery is best managed initially through
When counting a patient's pulse manually, the standard clinical technique is to palpate for at least 30 seconds and then
questions.explanation: Palpating the radial pulse for 30 seconds and multiplying by two is the accepted standard method for estimating beats per minute in a stable patient. This shortens assessment time while still giving a reliable rate. A full 60-second count is preferred if the rhythm is irregular.

questions.question: Regional anaesthesia is generally preferred over general anaesthesia in patients with significant cardiac, pulmonary, or renal disease mainly because it
options: avoids loss of consciousness and preserves protective reflexes
eliminates the need for patient monitoring
is easier to administer in emergencies
questions.explanation: Regional anaesthesia numbs a large body area without the patient losing consciousness, and it avoids the systemic cardiovascular and respiratory depression associated with general anaesthesia. This makes it a safer option for patients whose cardiac, pulmonary, or renal function is already compromised. It also provides good analgesia and muscle relaxation for the surgical field.

options: exclusive use of a stretcher for movement
questions.explanation: Teaching safe transfer techniques from bed to wheelchair early in rehabilitation promotes functional independence and reduces reliance on staff assistance for basic mobility. This skill is foundational before progressing to more advanced mobility training with or without a prosthesis. Building independence early also supports the patient's psychological adjustment to limb loss.
questions.question: A patient following amputation is taught transfer techniques from bed to wheelchair primarily to promote

questions.explanation: Huffing is a forced expiratory technique that moves secretions toward the larger airways while producing less airway irritation than a hard, explosive cough. Studies cited in physiotherapy teaching show it increases the efficiency of secretion clearance without triggering bronchospasm. It is therefore incorporated as a core technique alongside breathing exercises during postural drainage sessions.
questions.question: Huffing during postural drainage has been shown, compared with coughing alone, to
options: have no effect on secretion movement
increase secretion clearance without inducing bronchospasm

questions.question: A patient following shoulder arthroplasty is initially restricted from active abduction beyond a certain range mainly to protect the
options: repaired rotator cuff and surrounding soft tissue
questions.explanation: Early restriction of active abduction after shoulder arthroplasty protects the repaired rotator cuff and surrounding soft tissue while initial healing occurs, reducing the risk of re-tear or excessive strain on the surgical repair. Passive and active-assisted range of motion exercises are typically permitted earlier than unrestricted active movement. Progression follows a structured, surgeon-guided protocol based on tissue healing timelines.

questions.question: Postural drainage should generally be avoided immediately before or after a meal, with a recommended gap of approximately
questions.explanation: Postural drainage should never be carried out immediately before or after eating, and an interval of about one hour is recommended around meal times. This reduces the risk of reflux, discomfort, or aspiration during positioning. A warm drink beforehand can also help loosen secretions and assist the treatment session.

questions.question: A patient recovering from a fracture treated with a functional cast brace, compared with a rigid plaster cast, generally benefits from
options: guaranteed absence of any muscle wasting
elimination of the need for any physiotherapy input
complete immobilisation of all adjacent joints
a significantly longer period of total immobility
earlier joint movement at adjacent proximal and distal joints
questions.explanation: A functional cast brace is designed to allow earlier movement of the joints proximal and distal to the fracture site while still providing adequate fracture stability, in contrast to a rigid plaster cast that fully immobilises adjacent joints. This earlier movement helps reduce the degree of joint stiffness and muscle wasting that would otherwise accumulate. Physiotherapy exercise programmes can therefore often begin sooner with this type of immobilisation device.

Axillary web syndrome, sometimes called cording, presents as a tight, palpable cord extending from the axilla down the inner arm, restricting shoulder movement, particularly extension and abduction. It is thought to result from thrombosed or sclerosed lymphatic vessels following axillary surgery. Gentle stretching and manual therapy techniques are commonly used to help improve range of motion in this condition.
questions.question: A mastectomy patient reports a tight, cord-like structure running down the inner arm that restricts shoulder extension, most consistent with

questions.explanation: Hysterectomy involves surgical disruption of tissues surrounding the pelvic floor, which can affect the function of these support structures. Gentle pelvic floor awareness exercises, introduced as comfort allows, help maintain continence and pelvic support during recovery. This consideration is specific to gynaecological surgery and distinguishes it from other types of general abdominal surgery.
options: disrupts the surrounding pelvic support structures
has no effect on pelvic structures
questions.question: Pelvic floor awareness exercises are particularly relevant after hysterectomy mainly because the surgery

questions.explanation: Return to driving after hysterectomy is generally guided by the patient's ability to perform an emergency stop comfortably and without hesitation due to pain, since this reflects sufficient core control and confidence for safe vehicle control. This functional test is more meaningful than a fixed time frame alone. The physiotherapist can support this decision through progressive strengthening and functional advice during recovery.
questions.question: A hysterectomy patient asks when she can safely resume driving. The most appropriate physiotherapy-informed guidance is that this should generally wait until she can
options: perform an emergency stop comfortably without pain
stop taking all prescribed analgesia entirely
tolerate sitting upright for five minutes
climb one flight of stairs slowly
complete a single short walk indoors

questions.question: Among postoperative respiratory complications, the earliest to typically develop within the first 24 to 48 hours after surgery is
questions.explanation: Postoperative atelectasis, or collapse of lung segments, commonly develops early due to shallow breathing, retained secretions, and reduced lung volumes under anaesthesia. If untreated, it predisposes the patient to secondary infection such as bronchopneumonia later in the postoperative course. Early mobilisation and chest physiotherapy help prevent this complication.

options: instruct the patient to avoid using the arm at all
encourage gentle, gradual arm use within a comfortable range
ignore the posture as clinically insignificant
proceed directly to maximal resistance exercise
strap the arm firmly against the trunk
questions.explanation: A protective posture with the arm held close to the body is common after mastectomy and is addressed by encouraging gentle, gradual use of the arm within a comfortable range to prevent stiffness and promote normal movement patterns. Ignoring this posture risks the development of a fixed, guarded shoulder position over time. Education and reassurance support the patient's confidence in moving the arm safely.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a mastectomy patient consistently holding the affected arm close to the body in a protective posture. The most appropriate intervention is to
A patient following closed reduction of a shoulder dislocation is taught early physiotherapy exercises within the immobilisation period focusing on
questions.explanation: While the shoulder itself remains immobilised in a sling following reduction of a dislocation, gentle hand, wrist, and elbow movement is encouraged to maintain distal circulation and joint function. Shoulder range of motion exercises are introduced progressively once the immobilisation period, guided by the surgical or medical team, has been completed. This staged approach protects the healing joint capsule while preventing unnecessary stiffness in adjacent joints.
options: aggressive passive stretching into external rotation
resisted shoulder strengthening at maximal effort
complete immobilisation of the entire upper limb
gentle hand, wrist, and elbow movement to maintain distal function
full unrestricted shoulder range of motion immediately

questions.explanation: Diaphragmatic breathing exercises are the first-line intervention for a patient showing decreased chest expansion and accessory muscle use after upper abdominal surgery, as this incision site significantly restricts normal diaphragmatic movement. This gentle technique minimises the work of breathing while promoting basal lung expansion. Progression to thoracic expansion exercises and mobilisation follows as the patient's comfort and tolerance improve.
questions.question: A patient is noted to have decreased chest expansion and use of accessory muscles two days after upper abdominal surgery. The most appropriate initial physiotherapy intervention is

questions.explanation: An effective pelvic floor training programme includes both quick, strong contractions to address sudden increases in pressure, such as coughing, and sustained, held contractions to build endurance for ongoing support. Combining these two types of contraction addresses different functional demands placed on the pelvic floor throughout daily activities. Progression in both duration and repetition number is planned as the patient's control improves.
options: quick, strong contractions and sustained, held contractions
questions.question: A physiotherapist teaching pelvic floor exercises to a prostatectomy patient explains that exercises should include both
An increase in baroreceptor activity in the carotid sinus and aortic arch causes the vasomotor centre to
questions.explanation: Baroreceptors respond to a rise in arterial pressure by increasing their firing rate, which inhibits the vasomotor centre in the medulla. This reduces sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone to the arterioles, producing vasodilatation. The resulting fall in peripheral resistance helps return blood pressure toward normal.

questions.question: Chemical peels containing carbolic acid, trichloroacetic acid, or glycolic acid are primarily used to minimise the appearance of
questions.explanation: Chemical peels use agents such as phenol, trichloroacetic acid, glycolic acid, or salicylic acid to reduce the appearance of superficial scars, wrinkles, and sun-related photodamage, depending on the concentration used. They are not intended for deep structural correction such as bony asymmetry or muscle contracture. Deep furrows are also noted as an exception that chemical peels cannot fully address.

Pelvic floor muscle training is the primary physiotherapy intervention for managing urinary incontinence following radical prostatectomy, as the surgery can disrupt the muscles and nerves supporting continence. Ideally, this training begins before surgery and continues progressively afterward for best results. Consistent practice over weeks to months is usually required to achieve significant improvement in continence.
questions.question: A key physiotherapy intervention taught to patients following radical prostatectomy to address postoperative urinary incontinence is
A patient recovering from mastectomy with axillary node clearance develops swelling of the ipsilateral arm several weeks later. The most likely physiotherapy diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Lymphoedema is a recognised complication following axillary node clearance during mastectomy, resulting from disruption of normal lymphatic drainage pathways in the arm. Physiotherapy management includes techniques such as manual lymphatic drainage, compression garments, and specific exercises to encourage lymphatic flow. Early recognition and referral for specialist lymphoedema management improve long-term outcomes.

options: report the finding to the medical team and continue monitoring closely
ignore the finding as clinically insignificant
increase percussion intensity to disperse the air
apply firm pressure directly over the swollen area
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema, caused by air leaking into the tissue around a chest drain site, should be reported to the medical team for assessment, as it can occasionally indicate a significant air leak requiring further intervention. The physiotherapist continues to monitor the patient closely while awaiting medical review. Applying direct pressure or disconnecting the drain independently would be inappropriate and outside the physiotherapist's scope of practice.
questions.question: A patient following thoracic surgery is found to have subcutaneous emphysema around the chest drain site. The most appropriate physiotherapy response is to

questions.explanation: Keeping the chest drain bottle below the level of the chest at all times during mobilisation prevents retrograde flow of fluid or air back into the pleural space, which could compromise the drain's function. This safety check should be performed before initiating any movement or walking with a patient who has a chest drain in place. The drain should never be clamped or disconnected by the physiotherapist without explicit medical instruction.
questions.question: A patient with an intercostal chest drain following thoracic surgery is being mobilised for the first time. The physiotherapist should ensure the drainage bottle is
options: disconnected temporarily for ease of movement
raised above shoulder height during walking
placed on the same side as the unaffected lung only
kept below the level of the chest at all times

questions.explanation: The timing of prosthetic fitting depends primarily on adequate wound healing and appropriate shaping of the residual limb through bandaging and exercise, rather than a fixed universal time frame. Individual healing rates vary considerably, meaning the rehabilitation team assesses readiness on a case-by-case basis. Ongoing strengthening and desensitisation during this preparatory phase help optimise the limb for successful prosthetic use.
questions.question: A patient recovering from amputation asks when prosthetic fitting can typically begin. The most accurate physiotherapy-informed answer is that it depends primarily on
options: a fixed universal time frame for every patient
adequate wound healing and stump shaping

questions.explanation: Diaphragmatic breathing is taught with the patient in half lying or sitting, head and back fully supported, and the abdominal wall relaxed to allow free diaphragmatic movement. The therapist's hands rest lightly on the costal margins to palpate the movement produced. This positioning minimises the work of breathing and helps control episodes of breathlessness.
questions.question: In the technique of diaphragmatic breathing, the therapist positions the patient in
options: half lying or sitting, with the head and back fully supported
side lying with the affected side up
supine lying with legs elevated only

questions.explanation: A raised temperature with increasing abdominal tenderness after gynaecological surgery may indicate an evolving infective or other surgical complication requiring prompt medical reporting before physiotherapy proceeds further. Escalating unexpected clinical findings reflects the physiotherapist's role within the wider multidisciplinary surgical team. Treatment can be resumed and adapted once the underlying cause has been assessed and appropriately managed.
questions.question: A patient recovering from gynaecological surgery is found to have a raised temperature and increasing lower abdominal tenderness on postoperative day four. The most appropriate physiotherapy action is to
options: discharge the patient from physiotherapy immediately
report the finding promptly to the medical team before proceeding
apply direct pressure to the tender area during treatment
proceed with full-intensity mobilisation regardless of findings
increase the exercise programme to distract from discomfort

questions.question: Shoulder girdle exercises are routinely included in the physiotherapy programme after thoracotomy mainly because the surgical approach
questions.explanation: A posterolateral thoracotomy approach often involves division of muscles associated with the shoulder girdle, such as latissimus dorsi, making shoulder girdle exercises an important part of the postoperative physiotherapy programme to prevent stiffness and restore normal shoulder function. These exercises are introduced alongside breathing exercises from the early postoperative period. Ongoing range of motion work continues as the patient's tolerance and wound healing progress.
options: often involves division of shoulder girdle musculature
always damages the cervical spinal cord
has no impact on upper limb function
directly affects only the lower limb muscles
recommend immediate surgical revision of the repair
stop pelvic floor exercises as they are no longer needed
ignore the leakage as it will resolve without any action
avoid all future work-related activity permanently
continue training and use a pre-contraction before lifting
questions.explanation: Continuing pelvic floor training alongside teaching a pre-contraction, or 'the knack', technique before anticipated increases in intra-abdominal pressure such as lifting helps reduce residual stress incontinence. This functional strategy applies the strength gained through training directly to real-world activities. Gradual return to heavier work duties can be planned as control continues to improve.
questions.question: A prostatectomy patient is progressing well but reports mild leakage only with heavy lifting at work. The most appropriate physiotherapy advice is to
To reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis after surgery, physiotherapy intervention should routinely include
questions.explanation: Active calf pump exercises and early ambulation encourage venous return from the lower limbs, reducing venous stasis, which is a major contributor to deep vein thrombosis. Compression stockings and anticoagulants are used alongside these physical measures. Tourniquets should be minimised, as they can worsen venous stasis rather than prevent it.
options: passive stretching of the hip only
active calf pump exercises and early ambulation
prolonged bed rest with limb elevation only

questions.explanation: Blood pressure readings can vary by as much as 20 mmHg depending on arm position, so the arm should be supported horizontally at heart level for accuracy. An arm positioned too high or too low relative to the heart introduces hydrostatic error into the measurement. Consistent positioning allows readings to be compared reliably over time.
questions.question: For consistent and accurate blood pressure readings, the patient's arm should be positioned

questions.explanation: When uncertain of the most appropriate technique, diaphragmatic breathing combined with thoracic expansion exercise is recommended, as these remain effective and carry a low risk profile. Knowledge of the patient's history is emphasised before applying more specific or vigorous techniques such as postural drainage. Life-saving devices such as monitors and intravenous lines must also be safeguarded during any chest physiotherapy session.
options: diaphragmatic breathing with thoracic expansion exercise
prolonged postural drainage in all positions
questions.question: A first-line treatment approach recommended when a chest physiotherapist is uncertain which specific technique to apply is

questions.explanation: An extension lag with preserved passive range commonly reflects quadriceps inhibition, a recognised postoperative phenomenon related to pain, swelling, and altered neuromuscular activation rather than a mechanical problem with the prosthesis. Targeted quadriceps strengthening exercises, including static contractions and straight leg raises, are used to address this specific deficit. Persistent or worsening lag should prompt further review to exclude other contributing factors.
options: a mechanical block within the prosthesis
complete rupture of the patellar tendon
questions.question: A patient recovering from total knee replacement demonstrates a significant lag in active knee extension despite adequate passive range. This finding most likely reflects

questions.explanation: A stooped, forward-flexed posture during early ambulation after laparotomy commonly reflects protective guarding to reduce tension on the painful abdominal wound. Gentle postural correction and encouragement to stand as tall as comfortably possible help prevent this pattern from becoming habitual. Addressing pain control alongside postural cues supports a more normal walking pattern over time.
questions.question: During early postoperative mobilisation after laparotomy, the physiotherapist notices the patient adopting a stooped, forward-flexed posture while walking. The most likely reason is
options: underlying spinal deformity present before surgery
protective guarding of the abdominal wound
normal expected gait pattern requiring no correction

questions.question: A laparotomy patient exhibits shallow breathing and reluctance to move due to significant wound pain. The most appropriate first physiotherapy action is to
questions.explanation: Ensuring adequate analgesia before physiotherapy treatment allows the laparotomy patient to participate more effectively in breathing exercises and mobilisation. Proceeding with treatment despite poorly controlled pain is likely to be ineffective and increases patient distress. This principle of pain optimisation before intervention applies broadly across all major abdominal surgery.
options: ignore the pain and encourage forced deep breathing
discharge the patient from the physiotherapy list
proceed with full treatment regardless of pain level
liaise with nursing staff regarding analgesia before treatment

questions.question: The palpable landmark corresponding to the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra, where the trachea bifurcates, is the
questions.explanation: The sternal angle, also called the manubriosternal junction or angle of Louis, is an easily palpated landmark corresponding to the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. The bifurcation of the trachea into the right and left main bronchi occurs at this same level. The second costal cartilage also attaches at this junction, making it a useful reference point for counting ribs.

questions.question: Following hysterectomy, gradual progression of a patient's exercise programme from bed exercises to functional mobility is guided primarily by
questions.explanation: Progression of postoperative exercise should be individualised, guided by the patient's pain tolerance, vital sign stability, and overall clinical progress rather than a rigid, one-size-fits-all timeline. This patient-centred approach ensures safety while still promoting timely functional recovery. Regular reassessment allows the physiotherapist to adjust the programme as healing advances.
options: the patient's pain tolerance and clinical stability
the physiotherapist's personal treatment schedule only
the time of day the surgery was performed
a fixed protocol applied identically to all patients
the specific surgeon who performed the operation

questions.question: A key postoperative goal of physiotherapy following hysterectomy, in addition to preventing chest complications, is to
questions.explanation: Preventing venous thromboembolism through active leg exercises and early ambulation is a key postoperative physiotherapy goal after hysterectomy, given the pelvic location of surgery and associated risk of venous stasis. This goal works alongside chest physiotherapy to address the two most common categories of postoperative complication. Both goals depend on the patient's willingness and ability to move despite surgical discomfort.
options: reduce oral fluid intake to limit bladder strain
promote prolonged immobility for wound protection
prevent venous thromboembolism through leg exercises

questions.question: A patient recovering from cardiac surgery with sternal precautions in place should be specifically advised against
options: using a single arm to assist standing
lifting objects heavier than a few kilograms with both arms
questions.explanation: Sternal precautions after cardiac surgery typically restrict lifting objects heavier than a few kilograms, particularly with both arms simultaneously, to protect the healing sternal bone from excessive stress. Gentle exercises such as ankle pumps, breathing exercises, and supervised walking are encouraged and are compatible with these precautions. Adherence to these lifting restrictions is emphasised throughout the structured cardiac rehabilitation programme.

questions.question: A patient who has undergone major surgery is found to be disoriented and confused on the second postoperative day. This presentation is most consistent with
questions.explanation: Disorientation and confusion following major surgery are recognised features of postoperative delirium, a listed complication that can arise from factors such as anaesthesia, infection, or metabolic disturbance. The physiotherapist should report this finding to the medical team and adapt treatment communication accordingly. Safety during mobilisation becomes an especially important consideration in a confused patient.

questions.question: Which factor causes the systolic blood pressure to rise proportionally to the intensity of the activity performed?
questions.explanation: Physical exercise increases cardiac output, which produces a linear rise in blood pressure that is proportional to workload intensity. The systolic pressure typically shows a greater increment than the diastolic pressure during exertion. This response normally reverses once the activity ceases and the body returns to rest.

questions.question: Bronchiectasis is characterised pathologically by
options: collapse of an entire lung lobe
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis involves permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi resulting from destruction and alteration of the bronchial wall, often following inadequately treated pneumonia. The dilated airways become chronically colonised, leading to persistent purulent sputum production. Postural drainage and airway clearance techniques form the mainstay of physiotherapy management.

Promethazine has antiemetic, anticholinergic, and sedative properties, making it useful for combating the nausea and vomiting that anaesthetic agents commonly produce. It is given as part of premedication alongside sedatives to improve patient comfort before induction. Its anticholinergic action also modestly reduces respiratory secretions.
questions.question: Premedication with an antihistamine such as promethazine before surgery is primarily given to

options: a fixed calendar date regardless of healing
the physiotherapist's independent decision without surgical input
the patient's personal impatience to walk sooner
radiographic and clinical confirmation from the surgical team
the type of footwear available to the patient
questions.question: A patient following ankle fracture fixation is progressed from non-weight-bearing to partial weight-bearing status. The physiotherapist should ensure this progression is based primarily on
questions.explanation: Progression of weight-bearing status after fracture fixation should be based on radiographic and clinical confirmation of adequate healing from the surgical team, rather than the patient's preference or a rigid predetermined timeline. Premature weight-bearing before sufficient healing risks fixation failure or malunion. Physiotherapists work within these medically prescribed weight-bearing categories while progressing functional rehabilitation.

questions.question: Total loss of contact between the articulating surfaces of a joint defines a
questions.explanation: A dislocation is defined as complete loss of contact between the two articulating bone ends, distinguishing it from a subluxation, which involves only partial loss of contact. Dislocations are treated as emergencies because delayed reduction can compromise the articular cartilage through disruption of synovial nutrition. Prompt reduction also relieves the persistent pain caused by capsular stretch.

questions.question: An average healthy adult has a resting respiratory rate within the range of
questions.explanation: A normal resting adult respiratory rate falls between 12 and 18 breaths per minute, reflecting adequate ventilation for gas exchange without excessive effort. Newborns breathe much faster, at 30 to 60 breaths per minute, due to higher metabolic demand. Deviation from the adult range may indicate respiratory or metabolic disturbance.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing chest expansion in a laparotomy patient and records reduced movement on the right lower zone. The most appropriate targeted intervention is
options: thoracic expansion exercise targeting the right lower zone
generalised limb strengthening exercises for the body
postural drainage of the apical segments only
questions.explanation: When chest assessment identifies reduced movement in a specific lung zone, such as the right lower zone, thoracic expansion exercise with the therapist applying firm pressure over that area at end-expiration is used to target and encourage expansion of that region. This localised technique is more effective than generalised exercise alone for addressing a specific area of reduced lung movement. The patient can later be taught to apply this self-pressure independently.

questions.question: A key physiotherapy goal in the early postoperative period following mastectomy, in addition to arm mobility, is to
options: achieve full overhead range within 24 hours
replace the need for scar tissue management
prevent stiffness of the shoulder joint
promote complete immobilisation for wound protection
questions.explanation: Preventing shoulder stiffness is a key early physiotherapy goal after mastectomy, achieved through gentle, progressive exercise that respects the healing surgical site. Full overhead range is not expected in the first 24 hours and is instead built up gradually as tissue healing allows. This staged approach balances the competing needs of wound protection and functional recovery.

questions.question: A recognised contraindication to postural drainage in a postoperative surgical patient is
questions.explanation: Recent haemoptysis is a contraindication to postural drainage, along with conditions such as severe hypertension, cerebral oedema, and acute asthma, because positioning and vibration could worsen bleeding or cardiovascular instability. When postural drainage is contraindicated, diaphragmatic breathing and thoracic expansion exercises remain safe alternative techniques. Careful patient history review is essential before selecting any chest physiotherapy technique.

questions.question: A patient following thoracic surgery reports increasing breathlessness and is found to have decreased breath sounds on the operated side several hours after drain removal. This finding is most consistent with
questions.explanation: Decreased breath sounds with increasing breathlessness following chest drain removal raises concern for a recurrent or new pneumothorax, requiring urgent medical assessment and likely repeat chest imaging. The physiotherapist should recognise this presentation promptly and escalate rather than proceed with routine treatment. Early identification helps ensure timely re-intervention if a significant pneumothorax is confirmed.

questions.question: A patient following total hip replacement via a posterior surgical approach should be specifically advised to avoid
options: standing with equal weight through both limbs
active ankle pump exercises in bed
gentle hip flexion within a supported range
combined hip extension, abduction, and external rotation
combined hip flexion, adduction, and internal rotation
questions.explanation: A posterior approach to total hip replacement disrupts the posterior capsule and short external rotators, so patients are advised to avoid the combined movement of hip flexion, adduction, and internal rotation, as this position risks posterior dislocation. Precautions typically continue for a defined period as advised by the surgical team. Physiotherapists reinforce these precautions during all early functional training, including transfers and dressing techniques.

When pain is limiting participation and standard opioid analgesia is contraindicated due to allergy, the physiotherapist should liaise with the medical team to explore alternative analgesic strategies rather than proceeding with treatment the patient cannot tolerate. This collaborative approach ensures the patient receives safe, effective pain relief tailored to their specific needs. Physiotherapists do not prescribe or administer analgesic medication themselves.
questions.question: A laparotomy patient with a known allergy to opioid analgesics reports significant pain limiting participation in physiotherapy. The most appropriate physiotherapy response is to
options: instruct the patient to tolerate the pain silently
liaise with the medical team regarding alternative analgesic options

questions.question: A mastectomy patient with reduced shoulder flexion six weeks after surgery is most appropriately managed with
options: complete rest of the shoulder joint
progressive active and active-assisted range of motion exercises
questions.explanation: Persistent reduced shoulder flexion at six weeks after mastectomy is managed with progressive active and active-assisted range of motion exercises, building on the gentle movements introduced earlier in recovery. This graded exercise progression addresses stiffness that may have developed from post-surgical guarding or scar tissue restriction. Continued monitoring ensures the exercise programme is adjusted according to the patient's response.

options: breathing exercises replace the need for arm exercises
the surgery always requires a chest drain in the pleura
the mastectomy incision directly involves the lungs
abdominal muscles are always divided during mastectomy
general anaesthesia itself increases the risk of chest complications
questions.explanation: Even though the mastectomy incision is not abdominal, any patient undergoing general anaesthesia carries a risk of postoperative chest complications such as atelectasis, making breathing exercises a routine part of postoperative physiotherapy. This principle applies broadly across surgical specialties rather than being specific to abdominal procedures. Breathing and arm exercises are therefore both included, addressing different aspects of postoperative recovery.
questions.question: Deep breathing and coughing exercises remain important after mastectomy, even though the incision is not abdominal, mainly because

options: support the incision firmly with hands or a pillow while coughing
hold the breath instead of coughing
cough as forcefully as possible without support
questions.explanation: Supporting a midline laparotomy incision firmly with the hands or a pillow while coughing reduces pain and the sensation of the wound pulling apart, encouraging a more effective and confident cough. This technique is a cornerstone of postoperative chest care after any major abdominal incision. Avoiding coughing altogether would risk retained secretions and subsequent chest infection.
questions.question: A patient following exploratory laparotomy through a midline incision is being taught coughing technique. The most important instruction to give is to

questions.explanation: Phantom limb pain describes the perception of pain in the portion of the limb that has been surgically removed, and is a recognised and common experience following amputation. Physiotherapy management strategies include desensitisation techniques, mirror therapy, and graded motor imagery alongside medical pain management. Educating the patient that this phenomenon is a recognised and treatable part of amputation recovery helps reduce associated anxiety.
questions.question: A patient following below-knee amputation reports vivid sensation of pain in the missing foot. This phenomenon is termed

questions.explanation: An anterior hip dislocation classically produces a deformity of flexion, abduction, and external rotation of the affected limb. A posterior hip dislocation, by contrast, produces the opposite pattern of flexion, adduction, and internal rotation. Recognising these characteristic deformities aids rapid clinical diagnosis before imaging confirmation.
questions.question: The typical deformity produced by an anterior dislocation of the hip joint is
A patient following joint replacement surgery who reports increasing joint pain, warmth, and swelling on postoperative day five should be assessed for possible
questions.explanation: Increasing pain, warmth, and swelling several days after joint replacement surgery raises concern for periprosthetic infection, a serious complication requiring prompt medical assessment and investigation. The physiotherapist should recognise this presentation as distinct from the gradually improving, expected postoperative course and escalate the finding without delay. Early identification and treatment of infection are critical to preserving the function of the prosthetic joint.

questions.question: Balance training for a patient following unilateral lower limb amputation typically begins with
options: sitting balance progressing to supported standing
questions.explanation: Balance training after lower limb amputation follows a graded progression, beginning with sitting balance and advancing to supported standing on the remaining limb before more advanced activities are introduced. This staged approach builds the postural control required for eventual prosthetic use. Progression to unsupported and dynamic balance tasks occurs only once foundational stability has been established.

options: forceful passive stretching beyond pain tolerance
complete avoidance of any joint movement
gentle active and active-assisted range of motion within pain tolerance
questions.explanation: Joint stiffness following prolonged immobilisation is addressed initially with gentle active and active-assisted range of motion exercises performed within the patient's pain tolerance, gradually restoring movement without risking further tissue injury. Forceful stretching beyond tolerance can provoke inflammation and setback recovery. Strengthening exercises are introduced progressively as range of motion and comfort improve.
questions.question: A patient with joint stiffness following prolonged fracture immobilisation is commenced on a graded mobilisation programme. The most appropriate initial focus is

questions.explanation: Third-degree, or full-thickness, burns destroy both the epidermis and dermis, producing a dry, leathery, white or charred appearance without pain because the nerve endings have been destroyed. These burns rarely heal without surgical intervention, as the hair follicles needed for skin regeneration are also destroyed. Skin grafting is usually required for wound closure.
questions.question: A burn that appears white or charred, is dry and leathery, and shows no pain due to destroyed nerve endings is classified as

options: only after complete wound healing at several months
exclusively in the physiotherapy department under sedation
only once the patient has been discharged home
never, as the shoulder should remain fully immobilised
early in the postoperative period, within pain-free range
questions.explanation: Arm and shoulder exercises on the operated side are introduced early in the postoperative period, working within a pain-free range, to prevent stiffness resulting from the surgical approach and prolonged positioning during and after surgery. Waiting until complete wound healing at several months would allow significant, potentially harder-to-reverse stiffness to develop. Gradual progression of range and resistance continues throughout the recovery period as tolerated.
questions.question: A patient following thoracic surgery is taught arm and shoulder exercises on the operated side beginning

options: diaphragm on the unaffected side only
remaining lung tissue on the operated side
questions.question: Following lobectomy, thoracic expansion exercises are specifically targeted to encourage re-expansion of the
questions.explanation: After lobectomy, thoracic expansion exercises are specifically directed at encouraging re-expansion of the remaining lung tissue on the operated side, helping it fill the space left by the removed lobe. This targeted approach supports optimal use of the remaining functional lung tissue and reduces the risk of residual atelectasis. Regular reassessment of chest movement helps guide the ongoing focus of treatment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a mastectomy patient's posture six weeks postoperatively notes a rounded shoulder and forward head position on the affected side. This is most likely related to
options: compensatory postural guarding during early healing
a sign of active wound infection
questions.explanation: A rounded shoulder and forward head posture on the affected side commonly develops as compensatory guarding during the early postoperative period when the patient protects the healing chest wall and axilla. Postural correction exercises, combined with continued shoulder mobility work, help address this pattern before it becomes fixed. Early identification and intervention prevent longer-term musculoskeletal complications.

questions.question: The traditional sequence of management for a displaced fracture, in order, is
questions.explanation: The recognised order of managing a displaced fracture is resuscitation first, followed by reduction of the fragments, retention with an appropriate device, and finally rehabilitation. Resuscitation takes top priority if the patient is in shock. Rehabilitation, achieved through physiotherapy, completes the recovery process once the fracture has been adequately stabilised.

Gynaecological surgery, even when performed through an abdominal incision, can indirectly affect the surrounding pelvic support structures due to the proximity of the surgical field to the pelvic floor. Gentle pelvic floor awareness exercises are therefore included as a precaution to support ongoing pelvic health during recovery. This explanation helps patients understand the rationale behind exercises that may otherwise seem unrelated to their visible incision.
questions.question: A patient following gynaecological surgery asks why pelvic floor exercises are being introduced even though her main incision is abdominal. The most appropriate explanation is that the surgery
options: always directly damages the pelvic floor muscles severely
replaces the need for any abdominal exercise entirely
can indirectly affect the surrounding pelvic support structures
only affects pelvic floor function in caesarean section
has no relevance to pelvic floor function whatsoever

questions.question: The nerve supply to the anterior abdominal wall arises from the ventral rami of
questions.explanation: The abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin are innervated by the ventral rami of spinal nerves T7 through L1. These nerves run between the muscle layers before supplying the rectus abdominis and the skin of the abdomen. Damage to these nerves during surgical incisions can cause localised sensory loss or muscle weakness.

questions.question: A simple bedside clinical test used to screen for deep vein thrombosis in a postoperative patient is
questions.explanation: Homan's test involves passive dorsiflexion of the ankle to elicit calf pain, which may suggest deep vein thrombosis, and is part of the routine circulatory assessment of surgical patients. Although not fully reliable alone, it forms part of a broader clinical picture including swelling and warmth. Definitive diagnosis still requires imaging such as duplex ultrasonography.

options: apply firm massage to reduce the swelling
increase walking distance to disperse the swelling
record the finding calmly without any further action
continue vigorous leg exercises as originally planned
stop lower limb exercise and alert the medical team promptly
questions.explanation: New-onset unilateral leg swelling and warmth after gynaecological surgery raises concern for deep vein thrombosis, requiring the physiotherapist to stop exercise on the affected limb and alert the medical team promptly for further assessment. Continuing exercise or massaging the area could increase the risk of embolisation if a thrombus is present. Prompt recognition and escalation are essential to patient safety in this scenario.
questions.question: A patient following gynaecological surgery reports new-onset leg swelling and warmth on postoperative day three. The most appropriate physiotherapy response is to

questions.explanation: Return to upper body resistance training after mastectomy is guided by gradual progression once wound healing and shoulder mobility are adequate, rather than an immediate return to maximal effort or permanent avoidance. A structured, supervised progression helps rebuild strength safely while monitoring for signs of lymphoedema or shoulder complications. This individualised approach supports a return to valued physical activities over time.
questions.question: A mastectomy patient asks about resuming upper body resistance training at the gym. The most appropriate physiotherapy guidance is to
options: resume gym training only after one full year
avoid all future upper body exercise permanently
progress gradually under guidance once healing and mobility allow
begin maximal resistance training immediately after discharge
use only the unaffected arm for the rest of her life

questions.question: A patient develops sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain several days after abdominal surgery, most consistent with
questions.explanation: Sudden dyspnoea with pleuritic chest pain in the postoperative period is a classic presentation of pulmonary embolism, usually arising from a dislodged deep vein thrombus. This is a medical emergency requiring prompt investigation and treatment. Prevention through early mobilisation and anticoagulation is therefore a key physiotherapy goal after surgery.

The second stage of anaesthesia induction is delirium, during which consciousness is lost and excitement or involuntary muscle activity may occur. Breathing becomes irregular and rapid, and vomiting can happen at this point, raising aspiration risk. Modern rapid induction techniques aim to pass through this stage as quickly as possible.

options: shape the stump and control oedema in preparation for a prosthesis
permanently restrict all residual limb movement
prevent the wound from healing too quickly
eliminate the need for desensitisation techniques
replace the need for any exercise programme
questions.explanation: Residual limb bandaging, applied in a figure-of-eight technique, helps shape the stump into a conical form and controls postoperative oedema, both of which are important in preparing the limb for successful prosthetic fitting. This is combined with an active exercise programme rather than used as a substitute for movement. Correct bandaging technique requires specific training to avoid a tourniquet effect that could compromise circulation.

A patient two days after abdominal surgery reports feeling faint and dizzy when first standing at the bedside. The most appropriate physiotherapy response is to
options: increase walking distance without any delay
push the patient to continue walking regardless
sit the patient down and check vital signs
questions.explanation: Postural hypotension is common in early postoperative mobilisation due to reduced venous tone and fluid shifts, so the immediate priority is patient safety through sitting down and checking vital signs. Mobilisation should then be resumed gradually once the patient is stable. Discontinuing all future attempts would be excessive and could increase the risk of other complications from prolonged bed rest.

questions.question: A local anaesthetic technique that involves injecting the drug directly into the subcutaneous or deeper tissue at the surgical site is called
questions.explanation: Infiltration anaesthesia involves injecting local anaesthetic solution directly into the tissue to be operated on, either superficially into skin or into deeper structures. It provides anaesthesia without disturbing normal body activities, making it suitable for minor procedures such as drainage or excision. Larger operations require larger doses, raising the risk of systemic toxicity.

questions.question: When teaching arm exercises before abdominal surgery, the physiotherapist progresses from short lever to long lever exercises mainly to
questions.explanation: Progressing from short lever, elbow-bent arm exercises to long lever, elbow-extended movements gradually increases resistance and demand on the shoulder girdle musculature. This graded approach maintains upper limb strength and mobility, which supports functional activities such as transferring and using walking aids after surgery. It complements, rather than replaces, dedicated leg and breathing exercises used for other postoperative goals.
options: improve gas exchange in the lower lobes
reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis directly
gradually increase the demand on shoulder girdle muscles
prevent pressure sores on the sacrum
a walking stick and eventually independent gait
questions.question: A structured progression of gait re-education after lower limb joint replacement typically moves from a frame, to crutches, and finally to
questions.explanation: Gait re-education after lower limb joint replacement typically progresses from a walking frame, to crutches, and then to a single walking stick before independent, unaided gait is achieved, reflecting improving strength, balance, and confidence. This staged approach allows the physiotherapist to monitor safety at each level before advancing further. The pace of progression is individualised according to the patient's specific recovery and any surgical precautions in place.

questions.question: A patient is being progressed from a Zimmer frame to axillary crutches during early postoperative rehabilitation. This progression primarily reflects
options: a fixed hospital protocol regardless of progress
questions.explanation: Progression of walking aids from a Zimmer frame to crutches, and eventually to a stick, reflects the patient's improving limb strength and balance as recovery advances. This staged approach builds toward the goal of independent mobility. The pace of progression should always be guided by the individual patient's clinical status rather than a fixed timeline alone.

questions.question: The muscle layer of the anterior abdominal wall whose fibres run horizontally and give the greatest strength against raised intra-abdominal pressure is the
questions.explanation: The transversus abdominis is the innermost of the three flat abdominal muscles, and its horizontally disposed fibres run at an angle to the other layers. This layered, criss-crossing arrangement gives maximum strength to the abdominal wall. It helps resist the abdominal contents bursting through when intra-abdominal pressure rises.

options: permanent nerve damage at the site
systemic toxicity from rapid mucosal absorption
questions.question: Surface anaesthesia produced by direct application of a local anaesthetic to mucous membranes carries a notable risk of
questions.explanation: Because mucous membranes are highly vascular, local anaesthetics applied topically to structures such as the mouth, nose, or tracheobronchial tree are absorbed rapidly into the circulation. This absorption can raise plasma drug levels enough to cause systemic toxic effects. The anaesthetic effect itself remains superficial and does not extend to deeper submucosal structures.

questions.question: A chest physiotherapy technique specifically recommended during an episode of dyspnoea in chronic bronchitis is
questions.explanation: Positioning such as forward-leaning sitting or standing helps promote relaxation and eases the work of breathing during episodes of dyspnoea. This position allows accessory muscles to work more efficiently and can reduce the sensation of breathlessness. Breathing exercises are commonly combined with this positioning during acute episodes.

Patients recovering from major oncological gynaecological surgery often have reduced reserve due to the combined effects of surgery, underlying illness, and fatigue, so individualised, achievable functional goals with gradual progression are more appropriate than a standard fixed target. This patient-centred approach respects the person's current capacity while still working toward meaningful functional gains. Close communication with the wider multidisciplinary team supports coordinated care in this more complex patient group.
questions.question: A patient following major gynaecological surgery for ovarian malignancy is noted to have significantly reduced mobility due to fatigue and pain. The most appropriate physiotherapy approach is to
options: set individualised, achievable functional goals with gradual progression
insist on a standard mobility target regardless of tolerance
recommend permanent bed rest for symptom control
discharge the patient from physiotherapy care immediately
withhold all physiotherapy until fatigue resolves completely

questions.explanation: In the initial postoperative period after mastectomy, shoulder exercises are kept gentle, typically pendular and assisted movements within a pain-free range, to protect the healing wound and any drains in place. Full range of motion exercises are progressively introduced as swelling and pain subside and drains are removed. This graded approach reduces the risk of wound complications while still preventing shoulder stiffness.
questions.question: On the first postoperative day after mastectomy, shoulder exercises on the affected side are generally limited to
options: complete immobilisation of the entire arm
forceful passive stretching beyond pain tolerance
gentle pendular and assisted movements within pain-free range
resisted strengthening exercises at maximum effort

questions.question: An indentation on the surface of the left lung that accommodates the position of the heart is called the
questions.explanation: The cardiac notch is an indentation on the anterior border of the left lung that accommodates the projection of the heart into the left thoracic cavity. This feature explains why the left lung has only two lobes compared with the three lobes of the right lung. Its presence is an important consideration when interpreting chest imaging or planning thoracic procedures.

Thoracic expansion exercises improve movement of the chest wall and, principally, assist in the removal of retained secretions from specific lung regions. Firm pressure applied by the therapist at the end of expiration encourages the patient to expand that particular area on the next inspiration. Once learned, the patient can apply this self-pressure independently.

When a hysterectomy patient is taught to move from lying to sitting on the edge of the bed, the recommended technique to reduce strain on the wound is to
questions.explanation: Log rolling onto the side before pushing up to sitting minimises direct strain on the abdominal and pelvic incision by avoiding a sudden trunk flexion movement. This technique is taught early in the postoperative period and becomes a foundation for safe functional mobility. Reinforcing this movement pattern helps prevent unnecessary pain and protects the healing surgical site.
options: remain supine and avoid all repositioning
log roll onto the side before pushing up to sitting
swing both legs up rapidly while lying flat
perform a sudden trunk flexion movement
sit straight up using abdominal muscles alone
be located in the right upper quadrant
extend across the full thoracic cavity
be a low transverse or midline lower abdominal incision
questions.question: A patient is scheduled for an abdominal hysterectomy. The most appropriate incision-specific physiotherapy consideration before surgery is that the incision will
questions.explanation: An abdominal hysterectomy is typically performed through a low transverse or midline lower abdominal incision, which influences the positioning and support techniques taught to the patient for coughing and moving. Understanding the incision site helps the physiotherapist anticipate which movements are likely to provoke pain. This knowledge guides individualised wound-support and mobility advice.

After pneumonectomy, prolonged positioning directly on the unaffected side is avoided because it can compromise ventilation of the only remaining lung, whereas brief periods on the operated side may be tolerated and even encouraged in some protocols to protect the functioning lung. Positioning decisions after pneumonectomy require careful individual assessment and often specific surgical guidance. This differs notably from positioning principles following lobectomy, where the remaining lung tissue on the operated side is actively targeted for expansion.
options: prolonged lying directly on the unaffected side
lying on the operated side for short periods
questions.question: A patient following pneumonectomy is positioned in physiotherapy sessions to avoid

questions.explanation: Sternal precautions after median sternotomy typically advise against pushing up from a chair using both arms, as this movement places excessive strain across the healing sternum and could compromise bony union. Patients are instead taught alternative techniques, such as using the legs to rise or pushing from a single arm rest. These precautions are usually maintained for a defined period as guided by the cardiac surgical team.
questions.question: A patient following cardiac surgery through a median sternotomy is taught to avoid pushing up from a chair using both arms mainly to protect the

questions.explanation: Isometric quadriceps exercises performed within a cast help minimise muscle atrophy that would otherwise occur during a prolonged period of immobilisation, since the joint itself cannot move. This maintains a better baseline of strength for rehabilitation once the cast is removed and more functional exercises can begin. Isometric exercises do not directly influence the rate of bony healing, which depends on fracture biology rather than muscle activity.
questions.question: A patient in a long leg cast following tibial fracture is taught isometric quadriceps exercises primarily to
options: replace the need for any future rehabilitation
increase the range of knee flexion within the cast
minimise muscle atrophy during the period of immobilisation
reduce swelling in the immobilised limb directly

questions.question: A tissue graft harvested from a donor of a different species is specifically termed a
questions.explanation: A xenograft is tissue transferred from a donor of a different species, such as porcine skin used temporarily to cover a human burn wound. This differs from an allograft, which comes from a genetically non-identical donor of the same species. Xenografts are generally used as temporary biological dressings rather than permanent tissue replacement.

options: flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the limb
extension, abduction, and external rotation of the limb
extension, adduction, and internal rotation of the limb
flexion, abduction, and external rotation of the limb
neutral positioning of the limb throughout
questions.question: Following reduction of a posterior hip dislocation, the characteristic pre-reduction deformity that resolves after successful treatment includes
questions.explanation: A posterior hip dislocation classically presents with the limb held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation, a deformity that should resolve once successful closed or open reduction has been achieved. Recognising this pattern assists the physiotherapist in understanding the mechanism of injury when planning subsequent rehabilitation. Careful monitoring after reduction ensures the joint remains stable as mobilisation begins.

questions.question: A patient two days after laparotomy has a nasogastric tube in place for bowel decompression. Before starting treatment, the physiotherapist should
questions.explanation: Checking that a nasogastric tube is secure and correctly positioned before beginning treatment prevents accidental dislodgement during exercise or mobilisation. This falls under the general safety principle of protecting attached medical devices during any physiotherapy session. Any concerns about tube position should be reported to the nursing or medical team rather than adjusted independently.
options: ignore the tube during exercise sessions
reposition the tube without medical consultation
check the security and position of the nasogastric tube
remove the tube to allow full mobilisation
clamp the tube for the duration of treatment

questions.explanation: A greenstick fracture, common in children, involves an incomplete break with bending of the bone rather than full separation, and combined with the more active bone biology of children, this generally leads to faster healing compared with a complete fracture in an adult. This difference influences the expected rehabilitation timeline and the intensity of physiotherapy input required. Most greenstick fractures are managed conservatively with immobilisation rather than surgical fixation.
options: identical healing time regardless of age or fracture type
permanent growth plate closure in every single case
slower healing due to more extensive bone disruption
faster healing due to the incomplete break and younger bone
a mandatory surgical fixation required in every instance

Following hysterectomy, patients are typically advised to avoid heavy lifting for a period of approximately
questions.explanation: Patients recovering from hysterectomy are generally advised to avoid heavy lifting for around six weeks to allow adequate healing of the internal pelvic and abdominal tissues. This guidance forms part of the physiotherapist's discharge education alongside advice on gradual return to normal activity. Breathing and leg exercises continue to be encouraged throughout this recovery period.

options: keeping a pillow permanently under the residual limb
elevating the limb in flexion at all times
avoiding prolonged sitting and encouraging prone lying periods
maintaining constant hip flexion in a wheelchair
questions.question: Immediately after lower limb amputation, correct positioning of the residual limb to prevent hip flexion contracture involves
questions.explanation: Prolonged sitting and habitual placement of a pillow under the residual limb encourage hip flexion contracture, so patients are instead encouraged to spend periods in prone lying and to avoid sustained hip flexion positions. This positioning strategy is a key early physiotherapy intervention after lower limb amputation. Preventing contracture at this stage is essential for successful future prosthetic fitting and gait training.

questions.question: A laparotomy patient's family asks why the physiotherapist encourages walking so soon after major surgery. The most accurate explanation is that early mobilisation primarily helps
options: replace the need for breathing exercises
reduce the risk of chest and circulatory complications
questions.explanation: Early mobilisation after laparotomy is encouraged primarily because it reduces the risk of chest complications such as atelectasis and circulatory complications such as deep vein thrombosis. It works alongside, rather than replacing, dedicated breathing and leg exercises in the overall postoperative physiotherapy programme. Explaining this rationale to family members can help build support for the patient's active participation in recovery.

questions.question: Centrilobular emphysema, the most common type, is primarily caused by
questions.explanation: Centrilobular emphysema is the most common form and is caused by smoking, characteristically affecting the proximal and central part of the acinus in the upper lung zones. It occurs more frequently in men than women. Panacinar emphysema, by contrast, results from alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency and typically affects the lower lung lobes.

questions.question: A complication of spinal (regional) anaesthesia caused by seepage of cerebrospinal fluid is
questions.explanation: Post-dural puncture headache results from leakage of cerebrospinal fluid through the puncture site made during spinal anaesthesia. It is typically managed with analgesics and adequate hydration, and usually resolves without further intervention. Cauda equina syndrome, though far less common, results from direct nerve root damage rather than fluid loss.

Finger clubbing, characterised by increased curvature of the nails and enlargement of the finger pulps, is classically linked to chronic septic pulmonary conditions such as bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis. Bronchial tumours are another recognised cause. Its presence should prompt further respiratory investigation, as it is not a feature of most simple, self-limiting chest infections.
questions.question: Finger clubbing observed in chronic respiratory disease is most typically associated with

questions.explanation: The ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity, FEV1 divided by FVC, provides an objective measure of airway obstruction severity. In normal airways this ratio typically falls between 70 and 80 percent. A reduced ratio indicates significant airflow limitation, characteristic of obstructive rather than purely restrictive lung disease.
