Adult athletes over forty years of age
questions.explanation: In children under ten years old, the elbow is the most frequently dislocated joint, whereas in adults it ranks second behind the shoulder. This age-related difference likely reflects differences in ligamentous laxity and activity patterns between children and adults. Recognizing this pattern helps guide clinical suspicion when evaluating a paediatric elbow injury.

questions.question: What key chest X-ray sign helps distinguish pleural effusion from pulmonary fibrosis when only one lung field is affected?
options: The overall size of the cardiac silhouette
The presence of rib fractures on the film
The direction of tracheal deviation relative to the affected side
The visibility of the gastric air bubble
The width of the superior mediastinum
questions.explanation: When only one lung field is involved, pleural effusion characteristically pushes the trachea away from the affected side due to the volume of fluid, whereas pulmonary fibrosis or atelectasis pulls the trachea toward the affected side because of volume loss. Pneumonia, by contrast, typically leaves the trachea centralized. This distinction is a useful bedside interpretive rule.

Increasing the frequency of therapeutic ultrasound decreases its depth of penetration while concentrating the energy within more superficial tissues, making 3 MHz appropriate for structures located one to two centimetres deep, such as many tendons. A 1 MHz frequency is instead selected for deeper tissue up to about five centimetres. Matching frequency to target tissue depth is essential for effective and safe treatment.
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects a 3 MHz ultrasound frequency for a patient with a superficial tendon injury. What is the primary rationale for this frequency choice?
options: Higher frequency always penetrates more deeply into tissue
Higher frequency concentrates energy in more superficial tissue
Higher frequency eliminates the need for gel coupling
Higher frequency is used only for bone healing
Higher frequency reduces total treatment time to zero

questions.question: Why is chest X-ray periodically repeated in the long-term follow-up of patients with cardiac pacemakers, from a physiotherapy-relevant perspective?
options: To measure the patient's total lung capacity directly
To replace the need for any cardiac function testing
To assess unrelated abdominal organ pathology fully
To confirm stable lead position and detect complications
To determine the patient's bone mineral density
questions.explanation: Periodic chest X-ray monitoring helps confirm that pacemaker leads remain correctly positioned and detects complications such as fracture or migration that could influence the safety of prescribed physical activity. Awareness of this monitoring supports the physiotherapist in understanding any activity-related precautions relevant to the individual patient. This imaging complements, rather than replaces, functional cardiac assessment.

While clinical examination often diagnoses an acute Achilles rupture, MRI provides detailed visualization of the tendon gap and surrounding tissue that is particularly valuable for surgical planning in complex or chronic presentations. This is the most commonly ruptured tendon in the body. MRI helps the surgical team determine the extent of retraction and tissue quality.
options: Measuring total body bone mineral density
Surgical planning in complex or chronic cases
questions.question: Achilles tendon rupture is best evaluated with MRI primarily for which clinical purpose?

questions.explanation: A hyperechoic, well-organised appearance on ultrasound generally reflects relatively normal, organised collagen structure within the tendon, in contrast to hypoechoic, disorganised areas that suggest tendinopathy or partial tearing. This appearance does not indicate severe fibre disorganisation, complete rupture, active infection, or extensive calcification, each of which would have a different and more clearly abnormal ultrasound appearance. Recognising organised tissue on imaging can reassure the therapist that loading progression is likely to be well tolerated.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is using musculoskeletal ultrasound to assess a swollen Achilles tendon and notes the tendon appears hyperechoic and well organised on the scan. What does this appearance most likely suggest about tissue health?
options: Complete rupture of the tendon substance
Severe disorganisation of the tendon fibres
Active infection within the tendon sheath
Isolated upper limb resistance training only
Breathing retraining and airway clearance techniques
Complete avoidance of all respiratory exercises
Static stretching of the lower limb exclusively
questions.question: A patient with a chest X-ray showing hyperinflated lungs and a flattened diaphragm is referred for physiotherapy. Which intervention is most relevant given this imaging finding?
questions.explanation: Hyperinflation and diaphragmatic flattening on chest X-ray are characteristic of obstructive lung disease such as emphysema, and this imaging picture supports the inclusion of breathing retraining and airway clearance techniques within the physiotherapy plan. Recognizing the radiographic pattern helps the physiotherapist anticipate the patient's likely functional respiratory limitations. This integration of imaging and clinical reasoning supports a more targeted treatment approach.

questions.question: Interstitial pulmonary fibrosis in its late stages is classically described on chest imaging using which descriptive term?
questions.explanation: Advanced pulmonary fibrosis produces small cystic airspaces with thickened walls that create a characteristic honeycomb appearance on imaging, reflecting irreversible lung scarring. Earlier in the disease, ground glass opacification with volume loss predominates before honeycombing develops. This condition carries a poor prognosis, with transplantation being the main definitive treatment option.

options: A labral tear allowing contrast penetration
A ligamentous avulsion unrelated to the labrum
questions.explanation: Contrast extending into the substance of the labrum on MR arthrography is the classic sign of a labral tear, since intact labral tissue would not allow contrast to dissect into or beneath it in this way. This finding does not represent a normal intact labrum, an isolated cartilage defect, an unrelated ligamentous avulsion, or a simple synovial fluid collection, each of which would appear differently on the arthrogram. This pre-operative finding helps explain the indication for the arthroscopic procedure the patient subsequently underwent.
questions.question: A patient recovering from hip arthroscopy has a pre-operative MR arthrography report describing contrast extending into the substance of the labrum. What did this finding most likely indicate before surgery?

questions.explanation: STIR suppresses the normally bright fat signal, which dramatically increases the conspicuity of oedema within inflamed or infected vertebral bone marrow. This sensitivity makes it a key sequence for detecting early discitis or osteomyelitis. T1-weighted imaging alone is comparatively less sensitive to this early oedematous change.
options: Flow within the epidural venous plexus
questions.question: A STIR sequence is particularly favoured over T1-weighted imaging when evaluating suspected spinal infection because it best highlights what feature?

questions.explanation: In older individuals, proximal humeral fractures typically result from a relatively low-energy fall, often related to reduced bone density from osteoporosis, whereas in younger patients the same fracture usually requires substantially higher-energy trauma. This difference reflects the underlying bone quality between the two populations. Recognizing this pattern helps guide clinical suspicion in elderly fall patients.
questions.question: A proximal humeral fracture in an elderly patient most commonly results from which mechanism of injury?

A patient with chronic kidney disease is scheduled for a CT scan using iodinated contrast as part of pre-operative planning before a joint replacement. What pre-existing factor most increases this patient's risk during the scan?
options: Their age alone, regardless of kidney function
Pre-existing renal impairment increasing nephropathy risk
Their need for assistive walking devices
Their joint pain severity before surgery
questions.explanation: Pre-existing renal impairment is the key factor that increases the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy with iodinated contrast administration, since the kidneys are less able to clear the contrast agent efficiently. Age alone, joint pain severity, the planned physiotherapy programme, and the need for walking aids are not the mechanism responsible for this specific risk. Recognising renal function as the relevant factor helps explain why pre-scan kidney function tests are often required before contrast studies in at-risk patients.

questions.question: A patient with suspected carotid disease has duplex ultrasound findings reported alongside a request for cautious exercise progression. What does combining Doppler flow data with B-mode imaging in this test allow clinicians to assess?
options: Only respiratory function during the scan
Only the appearance of surrounding skin and muscle
Only bone density adjacent to the carotid artery
Both vessel structure and blood flow characteristics
Only the patient's resting heart rate pattern
questions.explanation: Duplex ultrasound combines B-mode structural imaging with Doppler flow assessment, allowing clinicians to evaluate both vessel wall structure, such as plaque, and the characteristics of blood flow through the carotid artery in a single non-invasive test. It does not primarily assess surrounding skin and muscle, bone density, resting heart rate pattern, or respiratory function, none of which are the focus of this vascular study. This combined structural and functional information helps guide safe exercise intensity in patients with known or suspected carotid disease.

Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor that contributes to the progression of chronic respiratory conditions, and physiotherapists play a role in patient education and behavioural change support as part of a comprehensive management approach. This complements, rather than replaces, other interventions such as exercise and airway clearance techniques. Addressing this modifiable factor supports better long-term respiratory outcomes.
options: It eliminates the need for any further respiratory treatment
It has no proven relationship to lung disease severity
It addresses a modifiable behavioural factor contributing to disease progression
It replaces the need for airway clearance techniques
It is unrelated to any physiotherapy scope of practice
questions.question: Why is smoking cessation education considered an important component of physiotherapy management for patients with chronic respiratory disease?

options: Central bony fusion across the joint
questions.question: Which radiographic finding is characteristic of chronic tophaceous gout at the joint margins?
questions.explanation: Chronic gout classically produces sharply marginated, punched-out erosions at the joint margins, often accompanied by an overhanging edge of bone, reflecting deposition of monosodium urate crystals over time. This differs from the diffuse osteopenia seen in rheumatoid arthritis. Recognizing this pattern helps distinguish gouty arthropathy from other inflammatory joint conditions on imaging.

options: A legal requirement unrelated to patient safety
An unnecessary formality with no clinical value
Appropriate informed consent for contrast administration
A step that can be skipped if time is limited
A process required only for surgical procedures
questions.explanation: Explaining the risks, benefits, and alternatives of contrast administration so the patient can make an informed decision represents appropriate informed consent, which protects patient autonomy and supports shared decision-making before any contrast-enhanced study proceeds. This is not an unnecessary formality without clinical value, it is not unrelated to patient safety despite also having legal significance, it is not a process limited only to surgical procedures, and it should not be skipped simply because time is limited. Respecting this principle is fundamental to ethical imaging practice.
questions.question: A patient is about to receive intravenous contrast for an imaging study relevant to her rehabilitation plan, and the radiographer explains the risks and benefits before the patient agrees to proceed. What principle does this process represent?

options: The Timed Up and Go test
questions.explanation: The Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire specifically evaluates upper limb function and is well suited to monitoring recovery after a wrist or forearm fracture. Balance and walking tests such as the Berg Balance Scale or Timed Up and Go are instead designed for lower limb and mobility assessment. Selecting an outcome measure matched to the affected region ensures clinically meaningful tracking of progress.
questions.question: Which outcome measure would be most appropriate for tracking upper limb functional recovery after a distal radius fracture?

options: It is faster to acquire in emergency settings
It provides better assessment of cortical bone detail
It requires no patient cooperation during scanning
It is universally available in every clinical setting
It gives superior visualization of the cord and soft tissue
questions.question: Why is MRI generally preferred over CT when evaluating suspected spinal cord compression from a soft tissue mass?
questions.explanation: MRI's excellent soft tissue contrast allows precise visualization of the spinal cord, discs, ligaments, and surrounding soft tissue masses that might be compressing neural structures. CT remains superior for assessing bony detail but is comparatively limited for soft tissue characterization. This is why MRI is considered the gold standard for evaluating cord compression.

questions.question: A patient with chronic liver disease relevant to her exercise tolerance has had liver stiffness assessed using elastography rather than biopsy. What tissue property does this technique measure, and why might it be preferred here?
questions.explanation: Elastography measures tissue stiffness, which correlates with the degree of fibrosis in conditions such as chronic liver disease, offering a non-invasive alternative to biopsy that is more comfortable and lower risk for monitoring disease progression. It does not measure blood flow velocity, bone mineral density, electrical conductivity, or oxygen saturation, each of which would require a different imaging or monitoring technique. Awareness of the patient's liver disease severity, informed by this test, can help guide safe exercise intensity prescription.
options: Tissue stiffness, offering a non-invasive alternative
Bone mineral density of the lower ribs
Electrical conductivity of the liver parenchyma
Blood flow velocity within the hepatic artery

questions.question: Why is deep vein thrombosis considered a significant early postoperative risk following lower limb joint replacement, and how does physiotherapy help mitigate it?
questions.explanation: Reduced mobility after lower limb surgery increases the risk of venous stasis and subsequent deep vein thrombosis, and physiotherapy interventions such as ankle pumps, early mobilization, and circulation exercises help maintain venous return and reduce this risk. This complements pharmacological prophylaxis often prescribed by the surgical team. Early and consistent movement is therefore a key rehabilitation priority in this population.
options: Surgery eliminates all clotting risk automatically
Physiotherapy has no role in preventing this complication
Only medication can address this risk, not exercise
This complication only affects upper limb surgery patients
Reduced mobility increases clot risk, addressed through circulation exercises
Side-lying on the unaffected side only
Supine, to allow fluid to layer posteriorly
questions.explanation: Erect or lateral decubitus positioning allows pleural fluid to layer along gravity-dependent surfaces, making even small effusions more visible on radiograph compared with a supine view, where fluid can be missed as it spreads diffusely across the posterior chest. Supine positioning, prone positioning, the Trendelenburg position, and restricting to side-lying on the unaffected side only do not optimise detection in the same way. This positioning principle is relevant when therapists are involved in patient preparation or interpreting the clinical reasoning behind a requested view.
questions.question: A patient with suspected pleural effusion is being prepared for radiographic assessment. Which patient position is recommended to optimise detection of even small amounts of pleural fluid?

options: Loading should be modified to reduce excessive stress on the affected compartment
The finding should be entirely disregarded during treatment
Maximal high-impact loading should be immediately prescribed
The patient should avoid all future physiotherapy involvement
The finding indicates the joint requires no further monitoring
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviewing a knee MRI report notes a bone marrow lesion with early cartilage loss. How should this information influence exercise prescription?
questions.explanation: Early bone marrow lesions and cartilage loss on MRI suggest increased mechanical stress within a specific joint compartment, and this information should guide the physiotherapist to modify loading strategies to protect the affected area while still promoting functional strengthening. This exemplifies how imaging findings are integrated into individualized exercise prescription. Ongoing reassessment helps track whether the chosen approach is effective.

A widely taught hip precaution following total hip replacement is to avoid flexing the operated hip beyond approximately ninety degrees, since excessive flexion increases the risk of prosthetic dislocation, particularly in the early postoperative period. This precaution is typically combined with avoiding excessive internal rotation and adduction. Patient education on these movement restrictions is a key component of early rehabilitation.
questions.question: Following total hip arthroplasty, physiotherapists commonly advise patients to avoid flexing the hip beyond what approximate angle to reduce dislocation risk?

options: Immediate notification to the referring physician
The finding should be discussed only at year-end review
The finding can be left for the next routine scan
Only the patient's family should be informed directly
No notification is required if therapy continues
questions.explanation: Unexpected, clinically significant findings identified incidentally on imaging require immediate notification to the referring physician, since timely communication can directly affect patient safety and the overall management plan, including the physiotherapy programme itself. Continuing therapy without any notification, deferring discussion to a year-end review, informing only family members directly, or waiting for the next routine scan would all risk unacceptable delays in addressing a potentially serious finding. Clear escalation pathways for incidental findings are an essential part of safe, coordinated patient care.
questions.question: A radiologist identifies an unexpected, clinically significant finding on a scan ordered for an unrelated reason during a patient's physiotherapy assessment pathway. What should happen regarding communication of this finding?

questions.explanation: A striped or banded appearance of alternating dense and lucent bone in the spine, sometimes called a rugger jersey pattern, is classically associated with renal osteodystrophy resulting from chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism. This is not simple age-related osteopenia, an isolated compression fracture, a benign vertebral haemangioma, or a normal variant in healthy individuals, each of which would have different radiographic features. Recognising this association helps the therapist appreciate the systemic, rather than purely mechanical, basis for some causes of back pain.
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease and bone pain has a radiograph described as showing alternating bands of dense and lucent bone in the spine, often called a striped appearance. Which metabolic bone condition is this most associated with?
options: Renal osteodystrophy with this striped pattern
Normal variant seen in healthy spines
Permanently sterilizing the surgical instruments used
Measuring the patient's core body temperature
Replacing the need for any postoperative X-ray
Providing real-time guidance for precise implant placement
questions.question: Intraoperative fluoroscopy during joint replacement surgery serves which primary function?
questions.explanation: Intraoperative fluoroscopy allows the surgical team to visualize implant positioning and bone alignment in real time during the procedure, helping ensure accurate component placement before the surgery is completed. This differs from standard postoperative radiography, which is performed afterward to confirm the final result. Both intraoperative and postoperative imaging play complementary roles in the overall surgical process.

Morning stiffness is a hallmark symptom of rheumatoid arthritis, and gentle range-of-motion exercises performed early in the day can help reduce stiffness and improve joint mobility before more demanding activity. This should be tailored to the individual patient's tolerance and current disease activity. Addressing this specific symptom pattern reflects an individualized approach to rheumatoid arthritis management.
options: Complete avoidance of movement until midday
Aggressive resisted strengthening immediately on waking
Gentle range-of-motion exercises performed in the morning
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with rheumatoid arthritis experiencing morning joint stiffness. Which intervention is most appropriate to address this specific symptom?

questions.explanation: Lead fractures near their attachment to the pulse generator are often triggered by repetitive physical exertion involving the upper limb on the side of the device, such as weightlifting, or by direct trauma to that region. For this reason, patients with implanted devices are commonly advised to avoid such repetitive strenuous activity. Physiotherapists should be aware of this precaution when designing exercise programmes for these patients.
options: Repetitive upper limb exertion such as weightlifting
Gentle passive range of motion exercises
Routine seated rest without limb movement
Light stretching of the lower limbs
questions.question: Which activity is most often associated with triggering fracture of a pacemaker lead near its attachment to the generator?

options: It helps prevent flare-ups and reduces cumulative joint damage
It eliminates the underlying disease process completely
It replaces the need for any medical management
It has no proven benefit in either condition
It is only relevant during acute hospital admission
questions.explanation: Patient education about joint protection, posture, and activity modification is emphasized because it helps reduce the frequency and severity of flare-ups and limits cumulative joint damage over the long term in both rheumatoid arthritis and gout. This educational component works alongside, rather than replacing, pharmacological management prescribed by the medical team. Empowering patients with this knowledge supports better long-term self-management.
questions.question: Why is patient education regarding joint protection strategies emphasized in the physiotherapy management of both rheumatoid arthritis and gout?

questions.explanation: Because the right middle lobe lies directly adjacent to the right heart border, consolidation in this lobe obscures that border through the silhouette sign, while sparing the right hemidiaphragm. Recognizing which border is lost helps localize the pneumonia to a specific lobe without needing a lateral film. This principle applies throughout the chest depending on anatomical proximity.

There is a posterolateral humeral head impaction
A rotator cuff tendon has fully ruptured
The clavicle has fractured at its midpoint
questions.question: A patient presents with anterior shoulder pain after a fall, and the physician mentions a possible Hill-Sachs lesion seen on imaging. What does this finding tell the physiotherapist about the underlying injury?
questions.explanation: A Hill-Sachs lesion is a posterolateral humeral head impaction fracture that occurs when the humeral head impacts the glenoid rim during an anterior shoulder dislocation, and its presence increases the risk of recurrent instability. It does not describe a rotator cuff rupture, a clavicular fracture, a scaphoid injury, or acromioclavicular dislocation, each of which is a distinct injury with different rehabilitation implications. Recognising this lesion helps the therapist anticipate instability risk during range of motion progression.

Spinal tuberculosis typically produces vertebral body destruction and collapse accompanied by a paraspinal soft tissue abscess, which may extend to compress the adjacent spinal cord. These combined findings help distinguish tuberculous spondylitis from simple degenerative disease. Early recognition allows prompt anti-tuberculous therapy before significant neurological compromise develops.
options: Isolated disc bulge without any bony change
Symmetrical marrow signal with normal alignment
Vertebral body collapse with a paraspinal abscess
A solitary calcified nodule in the canal
questions.question: Potts spine, or spinal tuberculosis, characteristically demonstrates which combination of MRI findings?

questions.explanation: Bone marrow oedema at the femoral neck may indicate an early stress fracture, and recognizing this on imaging should prompt the physiotherapist to exercise caution with weight-bearing and impact-loading activities to avoid progression to a complete fracture. This illustrates how imaging findings directly inform safe exercise prescription. Close communication with the referring physician supports appropriate activity modification.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes on an MRI report that a patient has significant bone marrow oedema at the femoral neck. What clinical precaution should this most directly prompt?
options: Immediate initiation of high-impact running training
Complete disregard of the imaging finding entirely
Encouragement of unrestricted heavy resistance training
Caution regarding weight-bearing and impact loading of the limb
No modification to the planned exercise programme

questions.question: A posterior hip dislocation most commonly results from which type of injury mechanism?
options: A minor twisting injury during walking
A low-impact fall from standing height
questions.explanation: Hip dislocations, most of which are posterior, typically require a substantial force such as that generated in a motor vehicle collision or a fall from a significant height, and are frequently associated with other injuries, including fractures. This reflects the inherent stability provided by the hip's deep bony socket and surrounding musculature. Because of the risk of avascular necrosis, this injury is considered a medical emergency requiring prompt reduction.

options: Immediate aggressive stretching of the wrist
Heavy resistance training of the forearm
Ignoring the swelling until it resolves alone
Elevation combined with gentle active movement
questions.question: A patient with a wrist dislocation is noted to have significant swelling on assessment. Which early physiotherapy intervention specifically addresses this finding?
questions.explanation: Elevation of the affected limb, combined with gentle active movement where appropriate, helps promote venous and lymphatic drainage to reduce swelling following a joint dislocation. This is typically combined with other modalities such as cryotherapy during the acute phase. Addressing swelling early supports subsequent range-of-motion recovery.

questions.question: A patient recovering from a recent ischaemic stroke is found to have a hyperdense MCA sign on the original CT scan. What does this specific imaging finding indicate about the underlying event?
questions.explanation: The hyperdense middle cerebral artery sign represents acute thrombus within the vessel itself, appearing brighter than expected on non-contrast CT, and it suggests a proximal occlusion associated with larger infarct volumes. It does not indicate chronic atrophy, a benign vascular variant, complete resolution of the stroke, or a subdural haematoma, each of which would appear differently and carry different implications. Understanding this sign helps the therapist appreciate the severity of the underlying vascular event when planning early rehabilitation goals.
options: A subdural haematoma overlying the cortex
A benign incidental vascular variant only
Complete resolution of the ischaemic event
A chronic, long-standing area of brain atrophy
Acute thrombus within the middle cerebral artery

questions.question: A patient with chronic Achilles tendinopathy has an ultrasound report describing increased vascularity within a thickened tendon. How should this finding influence the loading programme?
options: Only complete rest will resolve the finding
Surgery is the only appropriate next step
All loading should be stopped permanently
The finding indicates a complete tendon rupture
This supports a graded, progressive loading plan
questions.explanation: Increased vascularity in a thickened tendon on ultrasound is consistent with active tendinopathy and supports a graded, progressive loading programme, which is the evidence-based mainstay of treatment for this condition. Stopping all loading permanently, relying solely on complete rest, jumping to surgery, or assuming this finding represents a complete rupture all misinterpret what is a relatively common and manageable ultrasound appearance. Musculoskeletal ultrasound is well suited to monitoring tendon structure as loading is progressed over time.

options: A strong family genetic predisposition alone
Idiopathic onset without any known cause
questions.question: Which factor is most strongly associated with post-traumatic secondary osteoarthritis in young adults according to current understanding?
questions.explanation: Secondary osteoarthritis arising after significant trauma to a joint is recognized as a major cause of degenerative disease specifically in younger adults, distinguishing it from the idiopathic primary form more typical of older populations. Post-traumatic change accounts for a meaningful proportion of all osteoarthritis cases. Early identification helps guide long-term joint protection strategies.

Airway clearance techniques such as postural drainage, percussion, and vibration are specifically directed at mobilizing retained secretions in patients with chronic respiratory conditions such as COPD. These techniques complement, rather than replace, broader pulmonary rehabilitation strategies such as aerobic exercise. Selecting the appropriate technique depends on the location and nature of the retained secretions.

Passive range-of-motion exercises to the ankle

questions.explanation: The classic mechanism producing an anterior shoulder dislocation combines forced abduction, external rotation, and extension of the arm, which levers the humeral head anteriorly out of the glenoid fossa. This accounts for the vast majority of all shoulder dislocations. Understanding this mechanism helps anticipate the injury pattern in patients presenting after a fall onto an outstretched arm.
questions.question: Anterior shoulder dislocation, the most common type, typically results from which combination of forces?
options: Forced abduction, external rotation, and extension
Forced adduction and internal rotation only
Direct axial compression along the humeral shaft
Pure flexion of the shoulder without rotation

questions.explanation: External fixation devices such as the Ilizarov frame are specifically indicated for fractures that are comminuted, open, or otherwise unstable, since pins placed outside the fracture site allow bone alignment while avoiding further soft tissue disruption at the injury zone. This differs from a simple, stable, closed fracture that may be managed with casting alone. External fixation is particularly useful when the overlying soft tissue is significantly compromised.
options: A comminuted, open fracture of the tibia
A stable fracture healing without complication
A minor greenstick fracture in a child
questions.question: An Ilizarov external fixator would most appropriately be applied to which type of fracture?

This detail is irrelevant to imaging safety
The MRI should proceed without any further checks

Pacemakers are always compatible with any MRI scanner
questions.explanation: Certain implanted cardiac devices remain an absolute contraindication to MRI because the strong magnetic field can disrupt device function or cause dangerous heating, so this history must be flagged and verified with the imaging team before any scan proceeds. Not all pacemakers are universally MRI-compatible, the scan should not proceed without specific clearance, the concern relates specifically to MRI rather than CT, and this detail is highly relevant rather than irrelevant to safe imaging. Some newer MRI-conditional devices exist, but compatibility must always be confirmed rather than assumed.
questions.question: A patient scheduled for an MRI to investigate persistent knee pain reports having a cardiac pacemaker fitted two years ago. What should the physiotherapist understand about this situation?
A hydrocephalus patient's CT scan would most characteristically demonstrate which finding?
questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus results from excess accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid due to overproduction, obstruction, or impaired absorption, which enlarges the ventricular system on imaging. This distension can be seen affecting the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles depending on the site of obstruction. Left untreated, the rising intracranial pressure can damage surrounding brain tissue.
options: Diffuse thinning of the cerebral cortex
Bilateral collapse of the lateral ventricles
Fusion of the two cerebral hemispheres
Symmetrical dilation of the cerebral ventricles

questions.question: A patient reports mild claustrophobia before an MRI scan. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
questions.explanation: Mild claustrophobia can often be managed by explaining the procedure, using visualization or breathing techniques, and reassuring the patient during the scan. In more severe cases, sedation may be considered. Simply substituting CT is not appropriate when MRI is clinically indicated for the suspected pathology.
options: Cancel the scan and proceed directly to a CT instead
Increase the magnetic field strength to shorten scan time
Familiarize the patient with the process and consider relaxation techniques
Administer intravenous gadolinium before entering the bore
Remove the radiofrequency coil to widen the bore space

questions.question: A patient who fell on an outstretched hand has wrist pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. The physician orders imaging specifically because of the bone's vulnerable blood supply. Which bone is being assessed, and why does this matter for rehabilitation timelines?
options: The scaphoid, risking nonunion or avascular necrosis
The capitate, due to central wrist loading
The triquetrum, due to ligamentous attachment
The lunate, due to its risk of dislocation
The hamate, due to its hook fracture pattern
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is classically injured by a fall on an outstretched hand, and its unique blood supply makes proximal pole fractures particularly prone to nonunion or avascular necrosis, which can prolong or complicate rehabilitation timelines. The lunate, triquetrum, hamate, and capitate are not the structure typically implicated by this mechanism and clinical snuffbox tenderness. Awareness of this vulnerability helps the therapist appreciate why scaphoid fractures are monitored closely before progressing wrist loading.

Fetal radiation risk is generally considered highest during the early weeks of organogenesis, when developing organ systems are most vulnerable to radiation-related malformation, which is why imaging decisions in early pregnancy are made cautiously. Risk is highest immediately after delivery

In the early weeks of organogenesis

This differs from resistance or plyometric training, which are introduced later as healing progresses. This principle applies broadly across upper limb dislocation rehabilitation.
questions.question: Which exercise type is specifically recommended during the early phase of rehabilitation following an elbow dislocation to build strength without stressing the healing joint?

questions.explanation: Lucency and migration around an orthopaedic implant suggest possible loosening, which requires modified, protective weight-bearing and surgical consultation before therapy continues as planned. Progressing gait training unchanged, beginning high-impact work, increasing gait speed, or ignoring the finding because pain is controlled all risk accelerating implant failure. Serial radiographs are used specifically to catch this kind of change before it progresses further.
questions.question: A post-operative hip replacement patient's radiograph shows a lucent zone developing around the femoral component with slight migration compared with the prior film. What should this finding prompt in the rehabilitation plan?
options: Ignore the finding if pain is well controlled
Modify weight-bearing and seek surgical review
Increase gait speed to improve bone loading
Progress weight-bearing and gait training as planned

questions.explanation: A fine reticular pattern throughout both lungs on chest radiograph is suggestive of interstitial fibrotic change, which can reduce lung compliance and gas exchange efficiency and is therefore relevant to expected exercise tolerance and the pacing of rehabilitation activity. This pattern does not represent a normal variant, an isolated rib fracture, a solitary nodule, or acute bacterial pneumonia with consolidation, each of which would have a different radiographic appearance. Recognising this pattern helps the therapist anticipate possible breathlessness during exertional tasks.
questions.question: A patient with suspected interstitial lung disease has a chest radiograph described as showing a fine reticular pattern throughout both lungs. What does this pattern most likely represent, and how might it affect exercise tolerance?

An isolated rib fracture unrelated to the lungs
Fibrotic change that can reduce exercise capacity
A large solitary pulmonary nodule only

questions.question: Which general radiographic feature is NOT typically associated with osteoarthritis of a joint?
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis classically produces joint space narrowing rather than widening, as cartilage progressively breaks down and the bones move closer together. Sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts are all recognized radiographic hallmarks of the degenerative process. Joint space widening would instead suggest an alternative process such as effusion or instability.

options: Continue the exercise programme without any modification
Increase exercise intensity to test the device further
Ignore the symptoms if the patient appears comfortable
Independently adjust the pacemaker settings during treatment
Stop the activity and refer for prompt medical evaluation
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices signs of possible lead displacement in a pacemaker patient, such as new onset symptoms during exercise. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: New or worsening symptoms suggestive of pacemaker malfunction during physiotherapy treatment warrant stopping the activity and referring the patient for prompt medical evaluation, since lead displacement or fracture can have serious cardiac consequences. Physiotherapists are not qualified to adjust pacemaker settings and should never attempt to do so. Recognizing warning signs and escalating care appropriately is an essential safety responsibility.

Retrospective studies that examine existing records are particularly susceptible to selection bias and recall-related limitations in data quality, since the available records may not represent the full population of interest and important details may be incompletely documented. It is not accurate to say no bias is possible in retrospective designs, bias is not confined only to prospective studies, using imaging does not automatically eliminate bias, and this design does not guarantee a randomised sample. Recognising this limitation helps the therapist weigh the strength of evidence behind imaging-related research findings.
options: This study design guarantees a randomised sample
No bias is possible in any retrospective study
Bias is eliminated automatically by using imaging
Selection or recall bias inherent to retrospective design
Bias only ever affects prospective study designs
questions.question: A physiotherapy researcher reviewing imaging studies notices that several were conducted by examining medical records after the fact rather than following patients forward in time. What type of bias is most relevant to consider when interpreting this kind of study design?

options: High-impact loading carries increased fracture risk
This T-score reflects only soft tissue changes
High-impact activity is always required for this score
DEXA results are irrelevant to exercise prescription
The T-score indicates completely normal bone density
questions.question: A patient with osteoporosis diagnosed by DEXA with a T-score of -2.8 wants to start a high-impact aerobic class. What should the physiotherapist consider before approving this?
questions.explanation: A T-score of -2.8 confirms osteoporosis, meaning bone density and structural strength are reduced, so high-impact loading carries an increased risk of fracture and should be approached cautiously with a more graduated programme. The score does not indicate normal density, is not irrelevant to exercise planning, does not reflect soft tissue rather than bone, and does not mean high-impact activity is mandatory at this stage. Lower-impact weight-bearing and resistance exercise are generally safer starting points for this bone density level.

questions.question: What term describes the numeric value assigned to each tissue based on its degree of X-ray attenuation on CT?
questions.explanation: Each voxel in a CT image is assigned a Hounsfield unit that reflects how much the tissue attenuated the X-ray beam relative to water. Dense structures such as bone have high positive values, while air has strongly negative values. This numeric scale allows objective tissue characterization on CT.

options: Rehabilitation should be delayed indefinitely without reason
The finding means rehabilitation is now unnecessary
Maximal exertion should begin on the very first day
The CT finding has no role in rehabilitation planning
Exercise intensity should be guided by clinical findings
questions.explanation: Imaging findings consistent with recent myocardial infarction should be integrated with clinical assessment to guide the graded, individualised progression of exercise intensity typical of structured cardiac rehabilitation programmes. The CT finding is not irrelevant to planning, maximal exertion on day one would be unsafe, indefinite delay without clinical reason is overly cautious, and the finding certainly does not mean rehabilitation becomes unnecessary. Coordinated communication between cardiology and rehabilitation teams ensures safe, evidence-based progression following this kind of event.
questions.question: A patient recovering from a recent myocardial infarction undergoes cardiac CT, which shows a finding consistent with the recent infarction. How should this information shape the early phase of cardiac rehabilitation?

questions.explanation: Adjusting the window level and width to highlight high-density structures allows fine bony detail, including subtle fracture lines, to be seen clearly. The brain or soft tissue window instead emphasizes grey-white matter contrast and haemorrhage. Selecting the correct window is essential for detecting the pathology in question.
questions.question: Which CT window setting is specifically optimized to reveal subtle skull fractures and bony detail?

A patient with known bone metastases from breast cancer is referred for a general strengthening programme. Imaging shows lytic lesions in the femur. What is the primary safety concern this finding raises for the exercise prescription?
questions.explanation: Lytic bone lesions from metastatic disease weaken the structural integrity of the affected bone, increasing the risk of pathological fracture, particularly with resistance or high-impact loading at the involved site. This is not equivalent to the fracture risk of healthy bone, it does not indicate the bone has healed, lytic lesions affect bone rather than only soft tissue, and the finding is directly, not incidentally, relevant to fracture risk. Exercise prescription in this context should be guided by oncology input regarding safe loading limits at the affected site.
options: No increased risk compared with healthy bone
The lesion guarantees the bone has fully healed
This finding is unrelated to fracture risk
Increased risk of pathological fracture at the site
Lytic lesions only affect soft tissue strength

questions.question: Why is direct eye exposure specifically avoided during infrared radiation treatment of the face or neck region?
questions.explanation: Direct exposure of the eyes to infrared radiation can cause serious damage, including progressive opacity of the lens known as cataract, which can result in blurred vision. For this reason, the eyes must be specifically protected whenever infrared treatment is applied near the face or neck. This precaution is a standard safety measure in infrared therapy protocols.
options: It has no possible effect on ocular tissue at all
It can cause serious eye damage, including cataract formation
It permanently improves visual acuity in most patients
It is required to achieve the intended treatment effect
It only affects hearing rather than vision

questions.explanation: Proton density sequences provide the best contrast between meniscal tissue and tears without excessive fluid signal interference, making them the primary sequence radiologists rely on for meniscal evaluation, which helps the therapist understand why this detail is highlighted in the report. T1-weighted images are less specific for this purpose, FLAIR is used mainly in brain imaging, gradient echo is suited to detecting blood products, and STIR is most useful for marrow oedema rather than meniscal detail. Recognising which sequence was used supports accurate interpretation of the reported findings.
questions.question: A patient is referred for an MRI to investigate suspected meniscal tear of the knee. Which sequence is the radiologist most likely to rely on for optimal visualisation of this structure, and why does this matter to the therapist reviewing the report?
options: STIR sequence, primarily used for marrow oedema
T1-weighted sequence, since fluid contrast matters most
FLAIR sequence, used mainly for brain imaging
Gradient echo sequence, used for detecting bleeding
Proton density sequence, optimised for meniscal contrast

questions.question: Which specific precaution is emphasized in the physiotherapy management of a patient following total hip replacement to reduce dislocation risk?
questions.explanation: A standard hip precaution taught to patients after total hip arthroplasty is avoiding excessive hip flexion, generally beyond ninety degrees, along with avoiding excessive adduction and internal rotation, since these movements increase the risk of prosthetic dislocation. This precaution is typically most emphasized during the early postoperative period. Patient education on these movement restrictions is a core component of early rehabilitation.
options: Avoiding all lower limb movement indefinitely
Avoiding hip flexion beyond approximately ninety degrees

questions.explanation: Morbidly obese patients may exceed standard MRI table weight limits or the diameter of the scanner gantry, which can necessitate alternative arrangements such as open MRI or specialised bariatric equipment rather than proceeding with a standard protocol. This does not mean imaging is entirely impossible, it does not guarantee a need for general anaesthesia, it does not relate to radiation exposure since MRI does not use ionising radiation, and standard protocols may well need adjustment rather than remaining unchanged. Planning ahead for these physical constraints avoids delays or failed studies.
options: An absolute inability to perform any imaging study
Table weight limits and gantry diameter constraints
Complete elimination of all radiation exposure
No difference in protocol compared with other patients
A guaranteed need for general anaesthesia
questions.question: A morbidly obese patient is referred for MRI of the lumbar spine, and the radiology department raises a practical concern before scheduling. What is the most relevant consideration specific to this patient's body habitus?

questions.explanation: X-ray production requires electrons to be accelerated across a high voltage potential and strike the anode disc. Most of the kinetic energy converts to heat while a small fraction produces X-ray photons. The anode must rotate and be cooled because nearly all the applied energy becomes heat rather than radiation.
questions.question: An X-ray tube generates its beam when electrons are accelerated from a heated cathode filament and strike which component?

options: Complete tearing of the rotator cuff tendon
Free-floating loose bodies within the joint
Isolated fracture of the greater tuberosity
Fibrosis and contracture of the joint capsule
Calcified deposits within the biceps tendon
questions.explanation: Frozen shoulder, or adhesive capsulitis, results from progressive fibrosis and thickening of the joint capsule, which restricts both active and passive range of motion in all planes. This is distinct from a rotator cuff tear, which involves tendon disruption rather than capsular contracture. The axillary recess is often noted to be diminished on imaging.
questions.question: Frozen shoulder on MRI is best characterized by which finding involving the joint capsule?
Lateral epicondylitis, commonly called tennis elbow, most frequently involves inflammation of which structure?
questions.explanation: Tennis elbow is an overuse tendinopathy that most commonly involves the extensor carpi radialis brevis at its origin on the lateral epicondyle, though other extensor tendons may also be affected. MRI in these cases typically shows a thickened tendon with increased T2 signal. This condition is distinct from golfer's elbow, which affects the medial flexor tendon origin.
options: The extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon origin
The ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel

questions.explanation: Stiffness following a period of immobilization is a common and expected finding, and active-assisted range-of-motion exercises are an appropriate, graded way to restore joint mobility once adequate healing has occurred. This should be balanced against the stage of bone healing to avoid excessive early stress. Gradual progression helps prevent long-term contracture.
options: Permanent immobilization to prevent further injury
Ignoring the stiffness until symptoms fully resolve
Active-assisted range-of-motion exercises to restore mobility
questions.question: A patient three weeks post-fracture reports persistent joint stiffness in a previously immobilized limb. What is the most appropriate physiotherapy focus at this stage?

questions.explanation: The Visual Analogue Scale provides a simple, widely used method for patients to rate pain intensity along a continuous line, typically from zero to ten, making it appropriate for tracking pain following musculoskeletal injuries such as fractures. This differs from disease-specific composite scores or balance measures designed for other clinical purposes. Its simplicity makes it practical for frequent reassessment during rehabilitation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants to quantify pain intensity in a patient recovering from a fracture using a simple numerical scale. Which tool is most appropriate?

A patient with chronic low back pain has a lumbar MRI showing a small disc bulge with no nerve root compression and a normal neurological examination. How should the therapist interpret this for exercise progression?
questions.explanation: A minimal disc bulge without nerve root compression, supported by a normal neurological examination, indicates a stable presentation that allows safe progression to advanced lumbar exercises. Permanently avoiding loaded exercise, requiring surgical referral, prescribing bed rest, or assuming manipulation is absolutely contraindicated all overstate the risk implied by this relatively benign finding. Larger herniations accompanied by radiculopathy would warrant a more cautious, modified approach instead.
options: Advanced exercises can be progressed safely
All loaded exercise must be avoided permanently
Only bed rest is appropriate at this stage
Surgical referral is required before any exercise
Isolated ligamentous laxity without bony change
Complete absence of any degenerative finding
Uniform widening of every disc space
Joint space narrowing with osteophytosis and sclerosis
questions.explanation: Spondylosis is defined radiologically by the same degenerative triad seen elsewhere in the skeleton: joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis, along with cyst formation in more advanced cases. It most commonly affects the cervical and lumbar spine. Many affected individuals remain asymptomatic despite these imaging findings.
questions.question: Spinal osteoarthritis, or spondylosis, is radiologically defined by which combination of features?
Which outcome measure would be most appropriate for assessing functional exercise capacity in a patient with chronic lung disease?
questions.explanation: The six-minute walk test measures the distance a patient can walk in a fixed time, providing a practical, reproducible assessment of functional exercise capacity that is widely used in respiratory rehabilitation. It complements pulmonary function tests and dyspnoea scales when tracking a patient's progress. This measure is far more relevant to respiratory patients than joint-specific tools designed for musculoskeletal conditions.
options: The Shoulder Pain and Disability Index

questions.explanation: Unlike pleural effusion, which pushes the trachea away from the affected side, or fibrosis and atelectasis, which pull it toward the affected side, pneumonia typically leaves the trachea centralized since it does not substantially alter lung volume. Recognizing this distinction helps the physiotherapist anticipate the type of respiratory impairment present. This supports selection of appropriate breathing and mobility interventions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is informed that a patient's chest X-ray shows the trachea centralized despite a lobar consolidation. What condition does this finding most likely support?
options: A tension pneumothorax requiring emergency decompression
A massive pleural effusion causing significant shift
Extensive atelectasis with major volume loss
Pneumonia rather than a large pleural effusion or significant atelectasis
A normal chest X-ray with no pathology present

questions.question: A soft tissue mass visible adjacent to a joint on X-ray in a patient with chronic gout most likely represents what structure?
questions.explanation: A tophus is an aggregated deposit of monosodium urate crystals that can appear as a soft tissue mass adjacent to an affected joint on plain radiography, particularly in chronic, longstanding gout. These deposits continually recruit and remodel through monocyte and macrophage activity. Their presence on imaging supports a diagnosis of chronic tophaceous disease.
options: A benign lipoma unrelated to the joint
A simple ganglion cyst of the tendon
A tophus composed of urate crystal deposits
A calcified haematoma from old trauma

questions.question: Which imaging finding is most useful for confirming correct alignment following closed reduction of a dislocated joint?
options: A follow-up blood test measuring inflammatory markers
Post-reduction X-ray demonstrating restored joint congruity
A pulmonary function test assessing lung capacity
A nerve conduction study of the affected limb
questions.explanation: After manual reduction of a dislocated joint, a follow-up X-ray is essential to confirm that the articulating surfaces have been restored to their normal anatomical relationship and to exclude any associated fracture. This imaging step is a standard part of post-reduction care. Clinical stability testing should also be performed carefully once alignment is confirmed.

questions.question: A patient with knee osteoarthritis undergoing physiotherapy is best supported by MRI findings in which specific way?
questions.explanation: Understanding precisely which structures, such as cartilage, menisci, or ligaments, are affected allows the physiotherapist to tailor an exercise and manual therapy programme appropriate to the specific pathology present. This individualized approach supports better outcomes than a generic protocol. Imaging findings are integrated with, not a substitute for, clinical assessment.
options: By clarifying which structures are damaged to guide exercise selection
By eliminating the need for any exercise therapy
By determining the patient's blood pressure trend
By replacing manual therapy with passive rest alone
By confirming the patient's dietary preferences

questions.explanation: Primary or idiopathic osteoarthritis develops without an identifiable predisposing insult and has a strong genetic component, most often affecting middle-aged women. Secondary osteoarthritis, by contrast, follows an identifiable cause such as trauma, prior surgery, or inflammatory joint disease. Distinguishing between the two helps guide further clinical evaluation.
questions.question: Primary osteoarthritis, as opposed to secondary osteoarthritis, is best distinguished by which characteristic?
options: Presence of a prior significant joint injury
Association with a preceding inflammatory arthritis
Absence of a clear predisposing joint injury or disease
Occurrence only following crystal deposition disease

questions.question: A patient with peripheral vascular disease is referred for carotid imaging before starting a cardiac rehabilitation exercise programme. The report describes 75% stenosis. What is the clinical significance of this finding for exercise planning?
questions.explanation: Carotid stenosis of 70% or greater is considered clinically significant and meaningfully raises stroke risk, which is directly relevant when planning the intensity and monitoring of a cardiac or general exercise rehabilitation programme. This is not below any threshold of concern, it does have bearing on exercise planning, it is not relevant only during sleep, and it certainly does not eliminate the need for ongoing monitoring. Communication with the referring team about exercise intensity is appropriate given this level of stenosis.
options: This stenosis is below any threshold of concern
This finding has no bearing on exercise intensity
This level of stenosis is clinically significant
This finding rules out any need for monitoring
This stenosis only matters during sleep

questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews an MRI report showing a full-thickness supraspinatus tear before beginning treatment. How does this information most directly influence clinical decision-making?
questions.explanation: Understanding the specific extent and location of a rotator cuff tear from MRI findings allows the physiotherapist to select exercises and loading strategies appropriate to the tissue's current integrity, avoiding movements that could aggravate the injury. This integration of imaging with clinical assessment supports safer, more targeted rehabilitation. Imaging findings are considered alongside, not instead of, hands-on clinical evaluation.
options: It guides selection of appropriate exercises and loading parameters
It has no bearing on the physiotherapy treatment plan
It automatically dictates immediate surgical referral only
It replaces the need for any clinical examination
It determines the patient's unrelated dietary needs

questions.question: Advanced rheumatoid arthritis of the hand frequently demonstrates erosive subluxation most marked at which joints, together with ulnar deviation?
questions.explanation: In advanced rheumatoid disease, erosive subluxation is most pronounced at the metacarpophalangeal joints, frequently accompanied by characteristic ulnar deviation of the fingers. Prominent degenerative change may also be seen at the ulnar-carpal articulation in these advanced cases. This combination of findings reflects long-standing, poorly controlled joint destruction.

A Colles' fracture is the eponymous term for a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, typically resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand. Smith's fracture is essentially the reverse pattern, with volar rather than dorsal displacement. Distinguishing the direction of displacement is essential for appropriate reduction and management.
questions.question: A patient presents after falling onto an outstretched hand with dorsal angulation of the distal radius fragment. Which fracture is most likely?

options: Diffuse whitish infiltrates throughout both lungs
A rounded cavity with an air-fluid level
Blunting of the costophrenic angle bilaterally
A visible lucent rim without lung markings peripherally
Widening of the mediastinal silhouette centrally
questions.question: A pneumothorax on chest X-ray is best identified by which characteristic finding?
questions.explanation: A pneumothorax appears as an area of increased lucency at the lung periphery where normal vascular lung markings are absent, representing air trapped between the lung and chest wall. This should be distinguished from pleural effusion, which produces a white, fluid-density area typically at the lung base. Prompt recognition is essential given the risk of tension physiology.

Beyond conventional X-ray, both MRI and ultrasound are used to identify gouty erosions and tophi, often detecting early changes that are not yet visible on plain radiographs. These additional modalities support diagnosis when plain films are inconclusive or when early disease is suspected. Using multiple imaging tools improves overall diagnostic accuracy in gouty arthropathy.
questions.question: Which imaging modality, in addition to X-ray, is used to detect gouty erosions and tophi with comparable or greater sensitivity?

questions.explanation: Fluid accumulating within the pleural space layers dependently and produces a white, fluid-density opacity that classically blunts the normally sharp costophrenic angle. This should be distinguished from pneumothorax, which produces a dark, lucent area rather than a white opacity. A lateral decubitus view can further confirm free-flowing pleural fluid.
options: A dark, lucent rim without vascular markings
Hyperinflated lung fields with a flattened diaphragm
A localized air-fluid level within the lung
A white, fluid-density area obscuring the costophrenic angle
questions.question: Pleural effusion on chest X-ray is best characterized by which radiographic appearance at the lung base?

options: To measure the patient's total lung volume directly
To diagnose the underlying cause of the asthma
To replace the need for spirometry testing entirely
To evaluate how well the patient's symptoms are currently controlled
To assess unrelated musculoskeletal joint function
questions.explanation: The Asthma Control Test is a patient-reported questionnaire specifically designed to evaluate the current level of symptom control in individuals with asthma, complementing objective measures such as spirometry. It does not diagnose the underlying condition but helps monitor ongoing disease management. This outcome measure supports collaborative decision-making between the patient and the healthcare team.
questions.question: A patient with asthma undergoing physiotherapy assessment is asked to complete the Asthma Control Test. What is the primary purpose of this outcome measure?

options: Symptoms exclusively related to upper limb weakness
Symptoms of neurogenic claudication with walking
Symptoms that occur only during complete rest
Symptoms entirely unrelated to any positional change
Symptoms confined strictly to the cervical region
questions.explanation: Spinal stenosis classically produces neurogenic claudication, characterized by leg pain, numbness, or weakness that worsens with walking or standing and improves with flexion or sitting, and physiotherapists should monitor for this pattern when designing an exercise programme. Recognizing this presentation helps guide positioning strategies and appropriate exercise selection. Severe stenosis can also affect bladder or bowel function, which would warrant urgent medical referral.
questions.question: A patient with a spinal MRI report describing spinal stenosis is being assessed for an exercise programme. Which symptom pattern should the physiotherapist specifically monitor for?

questions.explanation: In the posterior-anterior projection, the heart lies closer to the film, minimizing magnification and allowing accurate assessment of the cardiothoracic ratio. The anterior-posterior view, used when a patient cannot stand, causes the heart to appear falsely enlarged because it is positioned further from the film. This is why cardiothoracic ratio cannot be reliably assessed on an AP film.
questions.question: Which chest X-ray view is generally considered the standard and preferred projection for assessing cardiac silhouette size?

options: It is limited to a scaphoid waist fracture
It describes a clavicular shaft fracture pattern
It is an isolated distal radius fracture only
It involves an ulnar fracture with radial dislocation
It involves a simple metacarpal neck fracture
questions.explanation: A Monteggia fracture-dislocation combines a proximal ulnar shaft fracture with dislocation of the radial head, and missing the radial head component has historically led to poor outcomes, so the therapist should anticipate combined forearm rotation and elbow function limitations. It is not an isolated distal radius fracture, a metacarpal neck fracture, a scaphoid fracture, or a clavicular fracture, each of which would carry different functional implications. Understanding the combined nature of this injury supports realistic goal-setting for forearm rotation recovery.
questions.question: A patient recovering from a Monteggia fracture-dislocation of the forearm needs a rehabilitation plan. Which detail about this injury should the therapist understand to anticipate functional limitations?

A patient with Paget's disease affecting the skull has imaging described as showing a patchy mixture of dense and lucent areas often called a cotton wool appearance. What functional consideration is most relevant when planning manual therapy near this region?
questions.explanation: The cotton wool appearance in skull Paget's disease reflects disorganised bone turnover that leaves the affected bone structurally weaker and more prone to deformity or fracture than normal bone, which should be factored into the force and technique used near this region. This is not a finding confined to soft tissue, the skull is clearly affected rather than spared, increasing manual therapy intensity would be inappropriate given the structural change, and the appearance reflects abnormal rather than absent bone activity. Awareness of this altered bone quality supports safer treatment planning.
options: The skull is completely unaffected by this disease
Manual therapy intensity should always increase
This appearance indicates active bone is absent
This finding only affects soft tissue, not bone
The bone is structurally weaker than normal
The ulnar nerve at the elbow
The radial nerve in the forearm
The median nerve at the wrist
questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when the median nerve becomes compressed as it passes through the carpal tunnel, and MRI often shows increased T2-weighted signal within the nerve at this level. This corresponds to the clinical symptoms of pain, numbness, and tingling in the hand. Identifying the nerve involved helps distinguish this condition from other peripheral neuropathies.
questions.question: Carpal tunnel syndrome on MRI is characteristically demonstrated by increased signal within which structure?

questions.explanation: A boxer's fracture classically involves the neck of the fifth metacarpal, most often resulting from striking an object with a closed fist. It should be distinguished from a Bennett's fracture, which instead involves the base of the first metacarpal at the thumb. The incidence of metacarpal fracture generally increases moving from the radial toward the ulnar side of the hand.
questions.question: A boxer's fracture most commonly involves the neck of which metacarpal bone?

questions.explanation: A strong burning sensation during infrared treatment indicates excessive heating and warrants immediately increasing the distance between the lamp and skin or discontinuing the session to prevent burn injury. Patients are specifically instructed to alert the therapist if heating exceeds a comfortable level. Prompt response to reported discomfort is a fundamental safety principle in physical agent application.
questions.question: A patient reports a strong burning sensation during infrared therapy. What is the most appropriate immediate physiotherapy action?
options: Move the lamp closer to intensify the sensation
Ignore the report and continue treatment unchanged
Increase treatment duration well beyond the plan
Increase the treatment distance or discontinue the session
Switch to an even higher wattage lamp immediately

questions.question: A patient with reduced kidney function is referred for an MRI with gadolinium contrast. What complication is this patient specifically at increased risk of, and why does this matter for the rehabilitation team?
questions.explanation: Patients with significant renal impairment are at increased risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis because gadolinium chelates can dissociate when clearance is delayed, releasing free gadolinium ions that deposit in tissue and cause progressive fibrosis, which can directly affect mobility and skin integrity relevant to rehabilitation. Bronchospasm, hearing loss, cardiac arrhythmia, and vision loss are not the recognised mechanism or complication associated with gadolinium in renal impairment. Awareness of this risk supports closer monitoring of skin and joint changes in affected patients.
options: Sudden hearing loss from gadolinium toxicity
Permanent loss of vision from optic toxicity
Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis from impaired clearance
Immediate cardiac arrhythmia from the contrast

questions.question: Which forearm fracture pattern most typically results from a twisting or rotational mechanism of indirect trauma?
questions.explanation: Indirect trauma, such as a twisting force applied to a limb while the distal segment is fixed, characteristically produces a spiral fracture pattern that follows the long axis of the bone obliquely. Direct blows, in contrast, more typically produce transverse or comminuted fracture patterns. Recognizing the fracture pattern can provide clues about the mechanism of injury.

questions.question: A patient is due to receive gadolinium contrast for a lumbar spine MRI and mentions she is currently breastfeeding. What advice reflects current safety guidance regarding gadolinium and breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: Current guidance recommends only a brief, defined delay in breastfeeding after gadolinium-based contrast administration, since the small amount excreted into breast milk is considered low risk rather than requiring permanent cessation. Stopping breastfeeding permanently, assuming no precaution is needed at all, treating gadolinium as fully contraindicated in lactation, or recommending a delay of several months all overstate or understate the actual recommended precaution. Patients can be reassured that a short interruption, rather than complete cessation, is generally sufficient.
options: Gadolinium is contraindicated in all lactating patients
A brief, defined delay in breastfeeding is recommended
Breastfeeding should stop only after several months
No precaution is needed regarding breastfeeding at all
Breastfeeding must stop permanently after gadolinium
Isolated grip strength training of the hand
Passive stretching of the lower limb only
Static balance training on a firm surface
Complete bed rest without any intervention
Deep breathing exercises to improve lung expansion
questions.explanation: Deep breathing exercises are specifically directed at improving lung expansion and ventilation in patients with reduced chest movement due to conditions such as pneumonia. This directly targets the underlying respiratory impairment rather than an unrelated body region. Airway clearance techniques may also be combined depending on the presence of retained secretions.
questions.question: A patient with pneumonia demonstrates reduced chest expansion on assessment. Which physiotherapy intervention most directly addresses this specific finding?

questions.explanation: The Health Assessment Questionnaire-Disability Index specifically evaluates a patient's functional ability to perform daily activities such as dressing, walking, and eating, making it particularly relevant for tracking disability in rheumatoid arthritis. This differs from pain scales or respiratory measures, which assess different clinical domains. Selecting the correct outcome measure ensures the assessment matches the clinical question being asked.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants to assess a patient's overall ability to perform daily activities such as dressing and walking following a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. Which outcome measure is most appropriate?
A patient recovering from a hip dislocation is being progressed through gait training. Which assistive device is typically introduced first to limit weight-bearing appropriately?
questions.explanation: Gait re-education following hip dislocation typically begins with mobility aids such as a walking frame or crutches to safely limit weight-bearing during the initial recovery period, with progression as tolerated and as advised by the treating team. This staged approach protects the healing joint while restoring functional mobility. Complete rehabilitation following hip dislocation can take several months.
options: No assistive device at any stage

questions.question: Spondylolisthesis, as visualized on spinal imaging, is best defined as what type of structural abnormality?
questions.explanation: Spondylolisthesis refers to the anterior slippage or displacement of one vertebral body relative to the vertebra below it, which can result in nerve compression and mechanical back pain depending on the degree of slip. This is distinct from scoliosis, which involves lateral curvature rather than forward displacement. Imaging helps grade the severity of the slippage to guide management.
options: Lateral curvature of the spine in the coronal plane
Forward slippage of one vertebral body relative to another
Complete fusion of two adjacent vertebral bodies
Isolated narrowing of a single disc space
Calcification confined to the anterior ligament

questions.explanation: A Galeazzi fracture involves a fracture of the radial shaft, typically in its distal third, combined with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint. This is essentially the counterpart to the Monteggia fracture, but affecting the distal rather than the proximal forearm relationship. Recognizing the associated joint dislocation is critical to avoid missing this injury.
questions.question: Which upper limb fracture is classically associated with a distal radial shaft fracture together with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint?

options: Free electrons circulating in blood plasma
Hydrogen protons in the body's water molecules
Photons emitted from a rotating anode
Gamma rays released from a radioisotope
questions.explanation: MRI exploits the abundance of hydrogen protons in water and fat throughout the body, which align with an applied magnetic field. Radiofrequency pulses temporarily disturb this alignment, and the signal released as protons realign is captured to construct the image. This process uses no ionizing radiation, unlike X-ray or CT imaging.
questions.question: The basic physical principle underlying magnetic resonance imaging depends on aligning which atomic particle within a strong magnetic field?
A radiographer notices that a chest film taken with excessively long exposure time appears overly dark. What has most likely occurred?
questions.explanation: Exposure duration governs how many photons accumulate on the film or digital detector. A prolonged exposure delivers excess photons, producing greater radiographic density and an overly dark image. Shorter exposures conversely risk an underexposed, overly light film.
options: Too few photons reached the detector, reducing contrast
The anode angle was set incorrectly for the study
The patient moved during the coronal acquisition
The collimator field size was reduced excessively
Too many photons reached the detector, increasing film blackening
Deposits within the tendon or subacromial bursa
Complete retraction of the supraspinatus muscle
Diffuse oedema throughout the deltoid muscle
Widening of the glenohumeral joint space
Erosion of the coracoid process tip
questions.explanation: Calcific tendinitis is characterized by single or multiple calcium deposits within the rotator cuff tendon or the adjacent subacromial bursa, which can be identified with high accuracy on MRI, particularly in chronic cases. These deposits may coexist with a full-thickness tendon tear in advanced disease. This condition produces significant shoulder pain and disability.
questions.question: Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff is best identified on MRI by the presence of what feature?
The definitive diagnostic test for confirming gout is based on which laboratory finding?
options: Elevated serum uric acid concentration alone
A positive rheumatoid factor blood test
An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate alone
Identification of urate crystals in synovial fluid
A positive tuberculin skin test result
