questions.explanation: While an elevated blood uric acid level supports the diagnosis, the definitive confirmatory test for gout is direct identification of monosodium urate crystals within synovial fluid obtained from an affected joint, examined using compensated polarized light microscopy. Uric acid levels alone can be misleading, as levels may be normal during an acute flare. In practice, however, this joint aspiration test is performed in only a minority of diagnosed patients.

Doppler compression ultrasound is the preferred non-invasive test for suspected deep vein thrombosis, showing non-compressible veins and abnormal flow with high sensitivity for proximal leg clots. Catheter angiography is invasive and not first-line for this purpose, bone scintigraphy and MR arthrography are unrelated to vascular assessment, and plain radiographs do not visualise venous thrombus at all. Until DVT is excluded or treated, aggressive lower limb exercise should generally be deferred given embolism risk.
questions.question: A patient with suspected deep vein thrombosis in the calf is referred for imaging before continuing an aggressive lower limb exercise programme. Which non-invasive test should the therapist expect to be used first?
options: Catheter angiography of the lower limb
Plain radiograph of the tibia and fibula

questions.question: A staging system for rheumatoid arthritis describes the presence of bony or fibrous ankylosis together with earlier features as which stage?
options: The earliest stage with no changes
An intermediate stage with mild osteoporosis only
A stage limited to soft tissue swelling
A stage seen only before symptom onset
questions.explanation: The most advanced radiographic stage of rheumatoid arthritis is characterized by bony or fibrous ankylosis in addition to the cartilage and bone destruction, joint deformity, and periarticular osteoporosis seen in earlier stages. This progression reflects the cumulative, destructive nature of uncontrolled disease over time. Recognizing the stage helps guide the intensity of both medical and physiotherapy management.

In the early stage of fracture management, physiotherapy focuses on gentle movement of adjacent uninvolved joints to prevent stiffness while protecting the healing fracture site itself. Aggressive strengthening or loading at this stage risks disrupting the healing process. Pain and swelling control through ice or electrical stimulation are also appropriate early measures.
questions.question: A physiotherapist receives a patient two days after a stable, immobilized forearm fracture. Which intervention is most appropriate at this early stage?
options: Aggressive resisted strengthening of the fractured limb
Deep friction massage directly over the fracture
Gentle range-of-motion exercises to nearby uninvolved joints
High-intensity plyometric exercises for the limb

questions.question: Which of the following best describes atelectasis as seen on chest imaging?
options: Increased lung volume with contralateral mediastinal shift
A fluid-filled cavity with a visible air-fluid level
Diffuse bilateral hyperinflation of both lung fields
A solitary calcified nodule within the lung apex
Volume loss from collapse of lung tissue with ipsilateral shift
questions.explanation: Atelectasis represents partial or complete collapse of lung tissue, resulting in volume loss that characteristically pulls the mediastinum and adjacent structures toward the affected side. This ipsilateral shift is a key feature distinguishing it from processes that increase volume, such as a large effusion. Elevation of the hemidiaphragm on the affected side is another common associated finding.

Joint space narrowing accompanied by osteophyte formation on X-ray is a classic radiographic pattern of osteoarthritis, and recognizing this supports a physiotherapy approach centred on patient education, exercise therapy, and manual techniques tailored to degenerative joint disease. This differs markedly from the imaging pattern expected with acute fracture or infection. Correlating the imaging pattern with the clinical presentation supports appropriate, evidence-based management.
options: These findings indicate an acute traumatic fracture requiring immobilization
These findings are entirely unrelated to the patient's hip symptoms
These findings mean physiotherapy is contraindicated entirely
These findings confirm an infectious process requiring antibiotics
These findings are consistent with osteoarthritis and support a tailored exercise approach
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviewing a hip X-ray report notes joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation. What is the most appropriate clinical interpretation to guide treatment?

questions.explanation: A Monteggia fracture is a complex forearm injury involving a fracture of the ulna together with dislocation of the proximal radial head, often resulting from a fall or direct blow to the forearm. This combination requires careful assessment of both the fracture and the joint dislocation for proper management. It is distinct from a Galeazzi fracture, which affects the distal rather than the proximal radioulnar relationship.
questions.question: A fracture of the ulna combined with dislocation of the radial head is best described using which eponym?

courses.title: Pain Management Nursing II
courses.objectives:
Concepts, Physiology and Effects of Pain: Q1–5
Classification of Pain: Acute, Chronic, Nociceptive, Neuropathic and Cancer Pain: Q6–12
Pain Assessment, including in Special Populations: Q13–23
Pharmacological Management of Pain: Q24–31
Non-Pharmacological, Multimodal and Psychological Pain Management: Q32–40

questions.question:
A 54-year-old male construction worker with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and chronic low back pain presents with severe low back pain that has worsened over the past week and is rated 8 out of 10 on the Numeric Pain Rating Scale. The pain began about 5 years ago, is persistent with acute exacerbations lasting several days, radiates from the lower back to the left leg, and is sharp and stabbing with intermittent dull aches. It is aggravated by prolonged standing, heavy lifting and bending, and relieved by rest, lying flat and over-the-counter analgesics that are no longer effective. He has numbness and tingling, decreased sensation in the left leg, limited lumbar flexion and extension with muscle spasm, and a positive straight leg raise test. Lumbar X-ray shows degenerative disc disease and MRI is pending.
(a) Identify the type(s) of pain this patient has by duration, by location and by etiology, stating the features that support each.
(b) Explain the underlying mechanism (pathophysiology) of the pain, from the peripheral pathway to central processing and modulation.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the parameters to be collected.
(d) Outline the pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions appropriate for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• By duration: chronic pain with acute exacerbations - onset about 5 years ago, persistent, recently intensified; chronic pain persists beyond expected healing time and may flare intermittently.
• By location: radiating pain - starts in the lower back and extends to the left leg, following the path of specific nerves.
• By etiology: sharp, stabbing pain with numbness and tingling matches neuropathic pain (burning, shooting or electric shock-like, tingling, numbness) arising from nerve damage or dysfunction; the medical diagnosis is acute exacerbation of chronic low back pain with radiculopathy.

(b)
• Noxious stimuli activate nociceptors, opening sodium channels and generating action potentials carried by A-delta fibers (fast, sharp pain) and C fibers (slow, dull or burning pain) to the dorsal root ganglion.
• Signals synapse with second-order neurons in the dorsal horn (glutamate and substance P released), ascend by the spinothalamic pathway to the thalamus and somatosensory cortex; limbic system and frontal cortex process emotional and cognitive aspects; descending pathways (endorphins, serotonin, norepinephrine) modulate transmission.
• Neuropathic pain results from abnormal processing of sensory input after damage to the peripheral or central nervous system; the nursing diagnosis links this patient's pain to inflammation of a spinal nerve.

(c)
• Priority: assess and document the pain characteristics, because the client's self-report is the most reliable information about the chronic pain experience.
• Parameters: onset, duration, location and radiation, quality, intensity (0-10 scale), frequency, pattern, associated symptoms (numbness, tingling), precipitating and alleviating factors, and impact on daily activities; include neurological and musculoskeletal examination (sensation, straight leg raising, tenderness, range of motion).

(d)
• Pharmacological: NSAIDs as initial treatment; acetaminophen for mild pain; muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine) for spasm; opioids reserved for severe pain not responding to other treatment.
• For the neuropathic component: antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine), anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin), topical lidocaine patches or capsaicin cream.
• Non-pharmacological: distraction, imagery, relaxation, massage, heat and cold application; immobilize or brace the affected part; plan care activities around periods of greatest comfort.
• Rationale and target: these methods can prompt release of endogenous opioids; expected outcome is pain below 2 on a 0-10 scale after 24 hours of intervention.

(a)
• Nonverbal communication: crying, grimacing, body movements and sleep changes are not specific to pain and overlap with hunger, discomfort or need for attention; individual variation in temperament, pain threshold and developmental stage.
• Vital signs (heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation) are nonspecific and are affected by fever, anxiety, activity, illness and medication.
• Preterm infants have immature nervous systems (atypical or less pronounced responses) and frequent procedures; caregiver subjectivity and parental anxiety cause inconsistent evaluation.
• Inconsistent use and limitations of tools such as FLACC and NIPS, cultural differences in pain expression, and inconsistent training of providers.

(b)
• Increased stress responses, altered sleep patterns, impaired immune function and delayed recovery from illness or procedures; poorer surgical outcomes, longer hospital stay and higher risk of complications.
• Uncontrolled or frequent early pain may lead to heightened pain sensitivity or maladaptive pain responses later in life.

(c)
• Options: consistent use of validated tools (CRIES, NIPS, PIPP, FLACC) with assessments at regular intervals and before and after painful procedures; comprehensive ongoing staff training; multidisciplinary team.
• Involve parents (they know the infant's normal behavior); combine pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions (skin-to-skin contact, swaddling, non-nutritive sucking, sucrose, environmental adjustments); support research.
• Priority: consistent use of a standardized tool suited to neonates (CRIES for NICU and postoperative pain), because it improves reliability, quantifies pain to guide analgesia and allows monitoring of response over time.
• Failure to assess and manage pain in infants can be considered neglect or suboptimal care.
questions.question:
A neonate in the neonatal intensive care unit has had surgery and undergoes frequent invasive procedures. The infant cannot verbalize pain, shows crying, grimacing and changes in sleep, and the unit uses pain assessment tools inconsistently.
(a) Identify the risk factors for inadequate pain control in this infant.
(b) Describe the complications of unrelieved or poorly managed pain in infants.
(c) State the nursing management options and justify the priority choice.

A post-operative patient is cared for on a busy ward with heavy nurse workload, insufficient staffing ratios and limited access to equipment such as TENS machines. Some nurses have negative attitudes toward non-pharmacological measures, training is inconsistent, documentation is incomplete, and the patient is skeptical of non-drug methods.
(a) Identify the risk factors (barriers) for inadequate pain control in this situation.
(b) Describe the complications of unrelieved or poorly managed post-operative pain.
(c) State the nursing management options and justify the priority choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Negative nurse attitudes and perceptions toward non-pharmacological interventions; nurse-related barriers - fatigue, heavy workload, multiple responsibilities and insufficient staffing.
• Resource constraints (equipment, space, time) and limited access to specialized equipment such as TENS machines; lack of consistent training leading to incorrect or inconsistent use.
• Complexity of selecting measures (preferences, culture, type of pain), patient instability or lack of cooperation, patient skepticism and cultural beliefs, time-consuming and inconsistent documentation, and gaps in evidence.

(b)
• Intense pain triggers the stress response (increased heart rate and blood pressure, suppressed immune response); cardiovascular insufficiency is three times more frequent and infection five times greater with poor control.
• Pain cycle: pain increases muscle tension and reduces blood flow, causing more pain; uncontrolled pain delays healing, prolongs hospital stay, hinders early mobilization and may lead to chronic pain.

(c)
• Options: give opioids at regular intervals rather than waiting for severe pain; use PCA; multimodal analgesia combining NSAIDs and acetaminophen with regional techniques to reduce opioid use; add non-pharmacologic methods (relaxation, massage, heat or cold).
• Address barriers: promote awareness and education, continuous professional development, interprofessional collaboration, consistent documentation, and respect for patient preferences and culture.
• Priority: prompt, regular assessment and timely multimodal analgesia, because effective pain management accelerates recovery by enabling early mobilization and reducing infection and cardiovascular complications.
• Regular monitoring of pain and side effects guides adjustment of the plan.

questions.question:
A patient with chronic low back pain and radiculopathy presents with limited range of motion, difficulty walking and changing positions, fatigue and inability to complete daily tasks.
(a) State the priority nursing diagnoses with their defining features.
(b) Explain the contributing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology underlying the functional limitation.
(d) Outline the nursing management with rationales and evaluation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Impaired physical mobility related to pain and discomfort, evidenced by limited range of motion and difficulty walking and changing positions.
• Activity intolerance related to pain and decreased physical endurance secondary to chronic low back pain and radiculopathy, evidenced by fatigue and inability to complete daily tasks.

(b)
Pain and discomfort, decreased physical endurance, and chronic low back pain with radiculopathy; pain and stiffness prevent full participation in care and activities.

(c)
• Unrelieved pain affects the musculoskeletal system (muscle spasm, impaired muscle function, fatigue, immobility); pain increases muscle tension and reduces blood flow, leading to more pain (pain cycle).
• The chronic pain is attributed to inflammation of a spinal nerve (sharp pain radiating down the leg, numbness); unrelieved pain also reduces quality of life (sleeplessness, anxiety).

(d)
• Assess pain and range of motion and strength before movement - shows what the patient is able to do; use a pain scale to establish baseline and monitor effectiveness.
• Medicate for pain before exercises or planned activities - ensures control to allow participation; teach non-pharmacological relief (heat/cold, relaxation, positioning).
• Encourage the patient to do as much as possible - decreases dependence and increases self-esteem; schedule activities around rest periods - prevents exhaustion; develop a gradual activity plan with regular rest.
• Provide passive range of motion several times a day - prevents contractures and muscle weakness; provide mobility aids (cane, walker) - enhances safety during movement.
• Evaluation: patient participates in activities of daily living and prescribed therapies within 1 week and shows improved activity tolerance after 1 week.

questions.question:
Describe the psychological approach to pain:
(a) the biopsychosocial model and cognitive behavioral therapy
(b) mindfulness-based stress reduction and acceptance and commitment therapy
(c) the HADS, Pain Catastrophizing Scale and Perceived Stress Scale.
State how these relate to pain conditions and treatment targets:
(d) psychosomatic and chronic pain
(e) treatment adherence.
Explain why pain may persist or become chronic and the resulting functional or psychosocial effect:
(f) the cycle with mood
(g) catastrophizing
(h) effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The biopsychosocial model targets cognitive responses to pain and maladaptive behaviors, plus social and environmental factors that modify reactions to pain.
• CBT develops coping skills - behavioral activation, structured relaxation, scheduling pleasurable events, assertive communication and behavior pacing to avoid prolonging or exacerbating flares - and uses cognitive restructuring for maladaptive thoughts and catastrophizing.

(b)
MBSR disconnects the sensory elements of pain from emotional and evaluative elements through awareness and meditation, so beliefs about pain are perceived as unattached events; ACT does not change thoughts but alters responses to them, with acceptance and behavior in line with goals and values.

(c)
• HADS (Zigmond and Snaith, 1983): 14 items, 7 anxiety and 7 depression, each scored 0-3, subscale totals 0-21; 0-7 normal, 8-10 borderline, 11-21 abnormal.
• PCS (Sullivan, Bishop and Pivik, 1995): 13 items covering magnification, rumination and helplessness. PSS (Cohen, Kamarck and Mermelstein, 1983): 10 items rated 0-4 over the past month, covering perceived helplessness and perceived overload.

(d)
• Psychosomatic pain is real physical pain caused or exacerbated by mental and emotional factors (stress, anxiety, depression, trauma, somatic symptom disorder), treated with CBT, mindfulness, yoga, antidepressants or anti-anxiety drugs, lifestyle changes and support groups.
• In older adults, depression can be screened with the Geriatric Depression Scale short form or CES-D, and anxiety with the Profile of Mood States or Pain Discomfort Scale.

(e)
Psychological support improves adherence to pain plans; understanding the psychological basis of pain motivates patients to follow treatments, exercises and lifestyle changes.

(f)
Anxiety, depression and stress amplify pain while positive emotions and relaxation reduce it; chronic pain is often accompanied by depression and anxiety, and psychological care can break the cycle of pain and depression.

(g)
Catastrophizing - exaggerating the threat of pain, ruminating and feeling helpless - amplifies perception; women are more likely to catastrophize.

(h)
• Effects include poor sleep, depression, anxiety, social isolation and mood swings; failure to treat a coexisting mood disorder leads to ineffective pain management.
• Family, friends and support groups reduce stress and improve tolerance; psychological support improves well-being and quality of life.

(a)
Pain scales such as the Numeric Rating Scale or Visual Analog Scale to measure pain intensity and the effectiveness of treatment.

(b)
Pain intensity, response to treatment, and side effects (gastrointestinal symptoms, sedation, signs of dependency).

(c)
• NSAIDs are first-line for mild to moderate pain and inflammation (e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen); acetaminophen when NSAIDs are not suitable; topical NSAIDs or capsaicin for localized joint pain; intra-articular corticosteroids for flares.
• Ibuprofen adult dose 400 mg orally every 6-8 hours, maximum 1.2 g, given with food; diclofenac 50 mg orally every 8 hours, maximum 150 mg daily, given with food; both work by inhibiting prostaglandin production.

(d)
• Adverse effects: stomach upset, peptic ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, gastritis, renal toxicity, and increased cardiovascular events with long-term use; COX-1 inhibition reduces protective prostaglandins in the gastric mucosa.
• Management: proton pump inhibitors or H2 receptor antagonists, misoprostol, or selective COX-2 inhibitors; if GI symptoms occur with diclofenac, discontinue it and give an H2 receptor antagonist (e.g. ranitidine).

(e)
• Education: take with food, report GI symptoms, do not exceed maximum doses; diclofenac carries serious risks after more than 7-10 days of use.
• Special populations: avoid ibuprofen and diclofenac in asthmatic patients; lower the ibuprofen maximum in liver impairment; diclofenac is not for renal failure.
• Older adults: NSAIDs cause GI, renal and cardiovascular side effects, so acetaminophen is often preferred for chronic pain; in pregnancy NSAIDs are avoided, especially in the third trimester.
questions.question:
An adult with osteoarthritis and mild to moderate joint pain and inflammation is prescribed an oral NSAID (ibuprofen or diclofenac).
(a) Name the pain assessment tool and method to be used.
(b) State the parameters to be assessed.
(c) State the analgesic options and the doses, with administration instructions.
(d) State the monitoring required and the adverse effects to watch for, with their management.
(e) State the patient education points and the special-population considerations.

A pregnant or lactating woman has mild to moderate pain that requires treatment.
(a) Name the pain assessment tool and method to be used.
(b) State the parameters to be assessed.
(c) State the analgesics chosen and those avoided, with reasons, and the non-pharmacological options.
(d) State the monitoring required and the adverse effects to watch for.
(e) State the special-population considerations and the patient and family education required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pain scales such as the Numeric Rating Scale or Visual Analog Scale to measure pain intensity and the effectiveness of treatment.

(b)
Pain intensity, treatment effectiveness, and side effects (gastrointestinal symptoms, sedation, signs of dependency), with patient feedback incorporated.

(c)
• Acetaminophen is generally considered safe in pregnancy and lactation and is first-line for mild to moderate pain.
• NSAIDs are avoided, especially in the third trimester, because of the risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and other complications.
• Opioids are controversial (risk of neonatal abstinence syndrome and developmental effects); when necessary use short-term at the lowest effective dose. Physical therapy, relaxation techniques and acupuncture are strongly encouraged to minimize medication use.

(d)
Careful monitoring is needed when opioids are used; opioid adverse effects include respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea and risk of dependence; hepatotoxicity can occur if acetaminophen exceeds the maximum daily dose (4 g in adults).

(e)
• Many medications are contraindicated or need caution because of teratogenic effects or excretion in breast milk; a thorough risk-benefit analysis weighs risks to the fetus or infant against maternal pain relief.
• Use an individualized plan developed by a multidisciplinary team (obstetricians, pediatricians, pain specialists) to optimize maternal and fetal outcomes.

(a)
Acute pain related to osteoarthritis exacerbated by urinary tract infection, evidenced by the reported pain score and joint pain that is aching and sharp on movement.

(b)
• Osteoarthritis of knees and hips with flares during infection; movement and prolonged standing aggravate the pain.
• Aging: degeneration of joint cartilage, fragile bones (osteoporosis), sarcopenia and higher incidence of painful inflammatory conditions such as arthritis.
• Dementia limits communication and confusion may mask pain; related diagnoses are acute confusion, risk for injury and impaired verbal communication.

(c)
Degenerative and inflammatory joint changes activate nociceptors (mechanical nociceptors respond to pressure, chemical nociceptors to chemicals released by damaged or inflamed tissue); signals travel by A-delta and C fibers to the spinal cord and brain.

(d)
• Assess pain regularly with a standardized scale suitable for dementia patients - ensures appropriate pain management.
• Give prescribed analgesics and monitor effectiveness - reduces discomfort and improves quality of life; NSAIDs prescribed with regular review of renal function because of elderly status.
• Apply heat or cold packs to painful joints - additional pain relief; encourage gentle physical activity - maintains joint function and reduces stiffness; physical therapy referral and assessment of a better-fitted cane.
• Supportive measures: calm quiet environment, frequent reorientation, simple clear communication, caregiver education, counseling referral for coping.
• Evaluation: patient verbalizes a pain score of 0/10 within 48 hours, shows less restlessness and engages more in physical activity; scheduled follow-up of pain levels, medication efficacy and function with adjustment of the plan.
questions.question:
An 82-year-old woman with moderate-stage Alzheimer's disease and osteoarthritis is admitted with a urinary tract infection and increased confusion. She complains of aching joint pain, sometimes sharp during movement, mainly in the knees and hips. The pain is chronic, worsens with urinary tract infections, movement and long periods of standing, and is relieved by rest, heat or cold packs and pain medication. She takes donepezil, acetaminophen and antibiotics, and her daughter is her caregiver.
(a) State the priority nursing diagnosis with its defining features.
(b) Explain the contributing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology relevant to her pain.
(d) Outline the nursing management with rationales and evaluation.

Describe transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS):
(a) the device and its components
(b) mechanism
(c) indications
(d) administration
State the safe-practice considerations:
(e) equipment and training
(f) nursing responsibilities.
Explain the rationale for monitoring and evaluating its use:
(g) monitoring
(h) evidence of effectiveness.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• TENS is an electrical device used to treat pain: a battery-powered unit with 2-4 leads connected to sticky pads positioned over the skin to cover or surround the painful area.
• It delivers a low-voltage electrical impulse to the padded surface electrodes in a series of alternating current impulses.

(b)
• The larger impulses are postulated to activate large myelinated fibers, and large fiber stimulation is thought to block small pain-transmitting fibers; analgesia results from stimulating large afferent fibers.
• Some experts believe it activates release of natural endorphins at the pituitary level using alternating low-frequency pulses.

(c)
Chronic back pain, arthritis and neuropathic pain; mild to moderate acute pain.

(d)
In a post-knee-replacement case, TENS was used for 30 minutes, 3 times daily, together with cryotherapy, guided imagery, progressive muscle relaxation and early mobilization.

(e)
Limited access to specialized equipment such as TENS machines and lack of consistent training hinder effective use; inadequate education can lead to incorrect or inconsistent application.

(f)
Nurses ensure interventions are safe, appropriate and aligned with patient preferences and cultural beliefs, monitor patients continuously, document each session, and collaborate with physical therapists and others.

(g)
Track the patient's response, assess changes in pain levels or symptoms and adjust the plan to optimize pain management.

(h)
The patient using TENS with other non-drug measures reduced breakthrough medication by 50%, reached pain 2/10 by day 5, and had improved knee range of motion and faster return to daily activities.

(a)
• Chronic (non-malignant) pain: constant or intermittent pain persisting beyond the expected healing time, often difficult to treat because the cause may be unclear.
• Likely source: musculoskeletal pain (lower back); chronic back pain is often due to degenerative disc disease, spinal stenosis or previous injuries, and postural strain from prolonged sitting can strain muscles and joints.

(b)
• Postural strain and sedentary office work, overuse and repetitive stress; ineffective reliance on over-the-counter medications.
• Chronic pain is often linked with stress, poor sleep and emotional impact (anxiety, depression), which can amplify pain perception.

(c)
• Acute injuries (sprains, strains); chronic conditions (arthritis, osteoporosis, fibromyalgia); overuse and postural strain; a neuropathic component (burning, shooting, tingling) or stress-related (psychosomatic) back pain.
• Assessment: medical history and physical examination (pain areas, range of motion, visible deformities), imaging (X-ray, MRI, CT), blood tests for inflammatory or autoimmune conditions, and pain assessment tools.

(d)
• Physical therapy improves mobility and strength; mindfulness and yoga reduce stress and improve mental and emotional well-being; ergonomic adjustments prevent recurrence of musculoskeletal pain.
• Non-pharmacological approaches have fewer side effects, avoid dependency, address root causes, empower the patient through active participation and offer long-term relief.
• Evaluation after 3 months: 60% reduction in pain intensity, improved flexibility and core strength, reduced reliance on pain medication, better sleep and reduced stress, and return to full-time work with minimal discomfort.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman, an office worker, has had chronic low back pain for 3 years and has relied heavily on over-the-counter pain medications without improvement. She decides on a non-pharmacological approach: physical therapy twice weekly for 8 weeks (core strengthening and posture correction), 15 minutes of mindfulness meditation daily, ergonomic workplace modifications (adjustable standing desk and ergonomic chair) and yoga twice weekly.
(a) Identify the type of pain and its likely source.
(b) Explain the factors that may be affecting her pain experience.
(c) State the differential considerations and how they are assessed.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning for the plan of care and how outcomes are evaluated.

A young adult student under significant stress describes pain in vague terms, minimizes symptoms to fit in with peers, and feels misunderstood and dismissed when reporting persistent pain.
(a) Identify the risk factors for inadequate pain control in this patient.
(b) Describe the complications of unrelieved or poorly managed pain in young adults.
(c) State the nursing management options and justify the priority choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Subjective nature of pain: varying thresholds and tolerances shaped by personal experience; communication barriers - vague descriptions, minimizing symptoms, limited medical vocabulary, cultural factors, reluctance to appear vulnerable.
• Psychosocial factors: anxiety, depression and stress amplify perception; life changes such as starting a career or education raise stress; social media and peer influence lead to downplaying or exaggerating; stigma, especially with chronic pain, causes underreporting.
• Gender norms (men may underreport to conform to stoicism), cultural norms and provider implicit bias also affect reporting and assessment.

(b)
• Unmanaged acute pain can transition to chronic pain; decreased physical activity, impaired academic or work performance, and social isolation.
• Chronic pain is often associated with anxiety and depression; inadequately managed pain contributes to the risk of substance misuse; underlying health issues may be missed.

(c)
• Options: combine self-report tools (NRS, VAS, VRS, VDS) with multidimensional tools (Brief Pain Inventory, painDETECT) and observational tools; assess anxiety, depression and stress with validated scales (HADS, Pain Catastrophizing Scale, Perceived Stress Scale).
• Address psychological factors (cognitive-behavioral therapy, support groups), consider cultural and social context, use wearables and mobile apps for continuous monitoring, and continue education and training.
• Priority: accurate, comprehensive multidimensional assessment - it identifies type, intensity, causes and impact on daily activities, enables an individualized plan and helps prevent the transition from acute to chronic pain.
• Good communication between patient and provider ensures pain is acknowledged and adequately addressed.

(a)
Onset: when the pain began and any triggering incident (acute pain often sudden, chronic gradual); duration: how long and whether constant or intermittent; frequency: how often; pattern: whether worsening, improving or unchanged.

(b)
• Location (precise site, radiation), quality (sharp, dull, throbbing, burning), intensity (NRS 0-10 or VAS), associated symptoms (nausea, dizziness, numbness, tingling), and precipitating and alleviating factors.
• Impact on daily activities: tasks no longer possible, interference with work, exercise and sleep.

(c)
• Inspection: posture, movements and facial expressions (limping, guarding, grimacing) and skin changes (redness, swelling, bruises, rashes).
• Palpation: tenderness and temperature differences (warmth suggests inflammation, coolness reduced blood flow or nerve damage); range of motion and pain during active and passive movement.

(d)
• Onset differentiates acute from chronic pain; location narrows possible causes; quality gives clues to etiology; intensity is essential for evaluating severity and effectiveness of interventions.
• Functional impact indicates severity and quality of life and supports individualized plans; history reveals patterns, potential causes and appropriate interventions.

(e)
• Children need age-appropriate scales (NIPS or FLACC for 0-2 years, Wong-Baker FACES for 2-5, NRS or VAS for 5-12 and adolescents) and behavioral indicators; elderly with cognitive impairment need PAINAD, scheduled assessments and caregiver input.
• Non-verbal or cognitively impaired patients need observational tools (Behavioral Pain Scale, Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool) and family reports of baseline behavior and symptom changes (appetite, sleep, agitation).

(f)
Subjective methods rely on self-report: NRS (0-10) and VAS (10 cm line); the client's self-report is the most reliable information about the pain experience.

(g)
• Objective methods: physiological indicators (heart rate and blood pressure rise with sympathetic activation), functional assessment (Timed Up and Go test; Katz ADL Scale, Barthel Index), and observed behaviors.
• These are valuable in non-verbal or sedated patients, but in infants vital signs are nonspecific and are also influenced by fever, anxiety or activity.
questions.question:
Describe the components of a pain assessment:
(a) onset, duration, frequency and pattern
(b) location, quality, intensity, associated symptoms, precipitating and alleviating factors and impact on function
(c) physical examination.
Explain the clinical basis:
(d) why each component matters
(e) why some patients (special populations) are more vulnerable to inadequate assessment.
Distinguish between subjective and objective methods of assessment:
(f) subjective methods
(g) objective methods.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Special populations include paediatric patients, the elderly, pregnant women, those with comorbidities (diabetes, cardiovascular disease), chronic illnesses and cognitive impairments; age, developmental stage, health condition, culture and pain characteristics guide the plan.

(b)
• Elderly: chronic pain from osteoarthritis, neuropathy and osteoporosis; use a multidisciplinary approach with non-opioid analgesics, physical therapy, CBT and acupuncture, with lower starting doses, slower titration and monitoring.
• Acetaminophen is preferred for chronic pain; NSAIDs cause GI, renal and cardiovascular effects; opioids carry fall risk, cognitive impairment and dependency and are used with caution.

(c)
• Children have difficulty communicating pain; use age-appropriate scales and involve parents; non-pharmacological measures (distraction, play therapy, relaxation) are often first-line.
• Acetaminophen and ibuprofen are commonly used with weight-based dosing; opioids are used cautiously for severe pain with monitoring for respiratory depression; multimodal analgesia combines drugs with complementary therapies.

(d)
Aging changes drug metabolism and excretion, making older adults more susceptible to side effects and drug interactions; comorbidities and altered pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics raise the risk of adverse reactions.

(e)
• Children have different pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, and barriers include inaccurate beliefs about pain mechanisms, fears about drugs, poor knowledge of assessment and personal values and beliefs.
• In pregnancy and lactation many medications are contraindicated or need caution because of teratogenic effects or excretion in breast milk.

(f)
Elderly: comorbidities, adverse drug reactions, low dose slow titration; children: communication difficulty, weight-based (not age-based) dosing, parental involvement in assessment.

(g)
• Pregnant or lactating: acetaminophen first-line; NSAIDs avoided, especially in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus); opioids controversial (neonatal abstinence syndrome) - short-term lowest effective dose with a risk-benefit analysis and a multidisciplinary plan.
• Cognitive impairment: difficulty expressing pain causes undertreatment, agitation or withdrawal may be the only indicators, tools for non-verbal individuals are used regularly, non-drug measures are preferred, and drugs start low and titrate slowly.
• Chronic illness (cancer, fibromyalgia, sickle cell disease): complex mechanisms need individualized multimodal plans combining medications, physical therapy, psychological support and lifestyle changes.
questions.question:
Describe pain management in special populations:
(a) the populations and the guiding principle
(b) the elderly
(c) children.
Explain the clinical basis:
(d) why older adults are more susceptible to adverse effects
(e) why children and pregnant or lactating women are vulnerable.
Distinguish between:
(f) pain management in the elderly and in children
(g) the approach in pregnant or lactating women, cognitively impaired individuals and chronic illness.

Describe multimodal pain management:
(a) definition and pharmacological components
(b) non-pharmacological components
(c) key features of the approach.
Explain the clinical basis:
(d) why it is used
(e) which patients benefit.
Distinguish between:
(f) scheduled dosing and breakthrough dosing
(g) the drugs, dose and routes for managing breakthrough pain.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A multimodal approach combines different classes of medications for more effective relief, using synergistic effects to enhance efficacy and potentially reduce the dose of each drug.
• Components: acetaminophen and NSAIDs first-line for mild to moderate pain; opioids for severe pain (monitored for dependency and side effects); adjuvants (antidepressants, anticonvulsants) for neuropathic pain; topical lidocaine or capsaicin.

(b)
Physical therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, complementary therapies (acupuncture, massage, relaxation) and lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise, sleep hygiene).

(c)
• Personalized plan based on type, intensity and cause of pain; multidisciplinary team (oncologists, pain specialists, physical therapists, psychologists); patient and family involvement; regular monitoring and adjustment.
• Routes include oral, intravenous, subcutaneous, transdermal and epidural depending on the patient's condition and type of pain; side effects (constipation, nausea, sedation) are managed.

(d)
It enhances pain relief, reduces reliance on medications and addresses the multifaceted nature of pain; in postoperative care it targets various pain pathways, reducing opioid consumption and side effects (ERAS protocols).

(e)
• Patients with chronic illnesses such as cancer, fibromyalgia and sickle cell disease have complex pain mechanisms needing comprehensive, individualized plans; also useful in children, elderly and postoperative patients.
• Combining NSAIDs and acetaminophen with regional anesthesia techniques reduces opioid consumption and improves pain control.

(f)
• Scheduled dosing is a regular schedule that maintains baseline control, with additional medication for breakthrough pain as needed.
• Breakthrough pain is a sudden, transient exacerbation despite well-controlled baseline pain, predictable or unpredictable, usually needing rapid-onset, short-acting medication.

(g)
• Short-acting immediate-release opioids (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl) at 10-20% of the total daily dose of the regular opioid; routes oral, sublingual, buccal, intranasal or parenteral; rapid-onset fentanyl preparations.
• Adjuncts: NSAIDs or acetaminophen alongside opioids, and anticonvulsants, antidepressants or corticosteroids depending on the type of breakthrough pain.

questions.question:
A school-aged child (5-12 years) needs pain management.
(a) Name the pain assessment tool and method to be used.
(b) State the parameters to be assessed.
(c) State the intervention and analgesic choices, with dosing principles.
(d) State the monitoring required and the adverse effects to watch for.
(e) State the special-population considerations and the family involvement required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Numeric Rating Scale or Visual Analog Scale, because children aged 5-12 years can rate pain from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable); Wong-Baker FACES is used at 2-5 years; age-appropriate scales are essential.

(b)
Pain intensity score; behavioral indicators - facial expressions (grimacing, furrowed brows), body movements (restlessness, rigidity, protective movements), crying and vocalizations, and behavior changes (withdrawal, irritability, changes in eating or sleeping).

(c)
• Non-pharmacological approaches such as distraction, play therapy and relaxation techniques are often first-line.
• When medication is needed, acetaminophen and ibuprofen are commonly used because of their safety profile; dosing is based on weight rather than age; opioids are used cautiously and reserved for severe pain; multimodal analgesia combines medications with complementary therapies.

(d)
Proper dosing is critical to avoid toxicity; opioids need close monitoring for adverse effects such as respiratory depression.

(e)
• Children have different pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics from adults and may have difficulty communicating pain; involve parents and caregivers in the assessment to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the child's pain.
• Barriers to address: inaccuracies about the pathophysiology of pain, fears about pharmacologic agents, deficits in knowledge of pain assessment, and personal values and beliefs that prevent adequate identification and relief of pain.
• Unrelieved pain can have developmental effects (altered temperaments, higher somatization, greater vulnerability to stress disorders and anxiety states).

(a)
• Psychosomatic pain: real (not imagined) physical pain caused or exacerbated by mental and emotional factors through the interaction of mind and body.
• Likely sources: stress, anxiety and depression, trauma, or somatic symptom disorder; typical presentation includes tension headaches or migraines, back pain, generalized muscle pain, abdominal pain and fatigue.

(b)
• Psychosocial factors: anxiety, depression and stress amplify pain perception; life changes such as starting a career or education heighten stress.
• Social media and peer influence may lead to downplaying or exaggerating symptoms; stigma about reporting pain may cause underreporting; vague descriptions and reluctance to appear vulnerable limit communication.
• Gender, cultural background and previous pain experiences also shape perception and expression of pain.

(c)
• Underlying physical conditions must be ruled out through medical history and physical examination; psychological assessment evaluates mental health and emotional well-being; symptom tracking monitors how pain correlates with stressors or emotional states.
• Tools: HADS (14 items, anxiety and depression; 0-7 normal, 8-10 borderline, 11-21 abnormal), Pain Catastrophizing Scale (13 items: magnification, rumination, helplessness) and Perceived Stress Scale (10 items).

(d)
• Cognitive behavioral therapy helps manage thoughts and behaviors contributing to pain; mindfulness, meditation and yoga reduce stress; antidepressants or anti-anxiety medications may relieve pain linked to mental health conditions.
• Lifestyle changes (exercise, healthy diet, adequate sleep), healthy coping, mind-body practices (yoga, tai chi) and support groups; psychological support improves adherence to the plan.
• Evaluation: pain assessment is an ongoing process requiring regular re-evaluation of pain intensity and treatment effectiveness, with adjustment of the plan based on patient feedback.
questions.question:
A young adult facing significant life changes such as starting a career or education reports recurring tension headaches, back pain, generalized muscle aches, abdominal pain and chronic fatigue without a clear physical cause. The pain worsens during periods of stress and anxiety.
(a) Identify the type of pain and its likely source.
(b) Explain the factors that may be affecting this patient's pain experience and reporting.
(c) State the differential considerations and how they are assessed.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning for the plan of care and how outcomes are evaluated.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Anxiety related to anticipation of the outcome of the disease process, evidenced by expressed fear of dying.

(b)
• Anticipation of the disease outcome; after fear of dying, pain is the second most common fear of newly diagnosed cancer patients, and pain is common - over half of 1,308 patients reported moderate to severe pain 50% of the time.
• Cancer pain may be directly associated with the cancer (bony infiltration, nerve compression), a result of treatment (surgery, radiation) or unrelated (trauma); most is a direct result of tumor involvement.

(c)
• Cancer pain is nociceptive (somatic or visceral; sharp, throbbing, aching), neuropathic (burning, shooting, tingling) or inflammatory (inflammatory mediators released by the tumor or treatment; swelling, redness, warmth).
• Anxiety, depression and stress amplify pain perception; unmanaged cancer pain in turn increases anxiety, depression and helplessness.

(d)
• Goals: patient expresses feelings about death and its effects and seeks help in coping during the shift; expresses acceptance of the prognosis by the end of the shift.
• Interventions: encourage the patient to verbalize thoughts and feelings; educate about the stages of grief; encourage family members to be involved in care; refer for grief counseling.
• Pain care: encourage non-pharmacologic relief, administer pain medications as needed, educate on the pain management plan, and offer resources for coping with the psychological impacts of pain.
• Palliative care adds support for physical, emotional, social and spiritual needs of patient and family.
• Evaluation: patient was able to express feelings about death, sought help in coping, and expressed acceptance of the prognosis.
questions.question:
A patient newly diagnosed with cancer and experiencing pain expresses fear of dying and anxiety about the outcome of the disease process.
(a) State the priority nursing diagnosis with its defining features.
(b) Explain the contributing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology of cancer pain and how it interacts with anxiety.
(d) Outline the nursing management with goals and evaluation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• FLACC assesses Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability, each scored 0-2, total 0-10; the higher the score, the greater the pain; widely validated, easy and reliable.
• Face: 0 no expression or smile, 1 occasional grimace or frown, 2 frequent to constant frown, clenched jaw, quivering chin. Legs: 0 normal or relaxed, 1 uneasy, restless, tense, 2 kicking or legs drawn up.
• Activity: 0 lying quietly, 1 squirming or tense, 2 arched, rigid or jerking. Cry: 0 none, 1 moans or whimpers, 2 crying steadily, screams or sobs. Consolability: 0 content, 1 reassured by touch or talking, 2 difficult to console.

(b)
• Used for infants and young children who cannot verbalise pain levels.
• Settings: postoperative units (adjust analgesics), emergency departments (prioritize treatment), ICUs (continuous monitoring), outpatient clinics (minor procedures, immunisations) and home care (caregivers communicating with providers).

(c)
The scale is scored from observed behavior, and scores are recorded regularly with time, type of procedure and behaviors observed.

(d)
Limitations: tools may not capture all aspects of the infant's pain, are used inconsistently across settings, and infant behaviors are not specific to pain.

(e)
Nursing responsibilities include regular scoring, adjusting analgesics, documenting and communicating with the team.

(f)
Use NIPS or CRIES for neonates, FLACC for infants and young children, PAINAD for dementia, and Behavioral Pain Scale or CPOT for non-verbal or ICU patients.

(g)
Implement validated tools consistently, train providers on behavioral and physiological indicators, interpret in context (baseline state, procedure) and involve parents.

(h)
Assess at regular intervals and before and after painful procedures to gauge effectiveness of pain relief; scores guide pain management decisions.

(i)
Continue observing after a procedure for residual pain, document consolability and return to baseline, and adjust doses according to response and adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Local anesthetics block nerve conduction, giving localized pain relief without affecting consciousness; used for surgical procedures, chronic pain and minor interventions.
• Mechanism: they block sodium channels on nerve cell membranes, preventing initiation and propagation of action potentials so pain signals do not reach the brain.

(b)
• Lidocaine: minor surgery, dental procedures, acute and chronic pain such as postherpetic neuralgia; topical creams, injections and transdermal patches.
• Bupivacaine: longer duration than lidocaine; epidural, spinal and peripheral nerve blocks; orthopedic surgery, labor analgesia, postoperative pain.

(c)
• Ropivacaine: long-acting, blocks sensory more than motor nerves; epidural and regional anesthesia, obstetric and postoperative pain; less cardiotoxic than bupivacaine.
• Mepivacaine: intermediate duration, dental, minor surgery, nerve blocks, favored in outpatients; procaine: ester-type, short action, rapidly metabolized by plasma esterases, for infiltration and nerve block and occasionally spinal anesthesia.

(d)
Local irritation, numbness and erythema (lidocaine); local site pain and swelling (bupivacaine, procaine, ropivacaine).

(e)
• Allergic reactions are more common with ester-type anesthetics (procaine) than amides.
• Systemic toxicity is rare but occurs if large amounts are absorbed into the bloodstream; bupivacaine carries the concern of inadvertent intravascular injection, and ropivacaine is a safer option for prolonged anesthesia.

(f)
• Lidocaine toxicity: dizziness, seizures, arrhythmias, hypotension; bupivacaine: severe cardiotoxicity (bradycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest) and seizures; ropivacaine: dizziness, seizures, hypotension, bradycardia.
• Mepivacaine toxicity at high plasma levels: tinnitus, confusion, hypotension, arrhythmias; large procaine doses cause CNS and cardiovascular symptoms.

(g)
General principles are regular side-effect monitoring and treatment review.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nonverbal cues (guarding, grimacing, restricted movement) are noted and information is gathered from the primary caregiver; one main purpose of history and examination is to identify the cause of pain, and older adults typically present with multiple pain etiologies.
• Search for conditions known to be painful and common in this population: arthritis, old fracture site pain, peripheral neuropathy, infections (pneumonia, urinary tract infection, skin and soft tissue infections) and painful procedures; palpate for tenderness, inflammation, deformity and trigger points.

(b)
• Age-related changes (cartilage degeneration, slower nerve conduction, reduced blood flow) and mood - depression and anxiety may alter perception or enhance pain intensity.
• Meaning of pain (loss, threat or challenge), coping resources, cultural, ethnic, spiritual, social and family factors, and sensory impairments (hearing, vision).

(c)
• Non-specific symptoms (fatigue, confusion, decreased appetite) and atypical presentation can mask pain; coexisting conditions overlap.
• Determine whether the mental status is typical for the patient (orientation to person, place and time; ask family about prior mental status; Mini-Mental State Examination or Orientation-Memory-Concentration Test).

(d)
• Use observational tools: PAINAD (5 items scored 0-2, maximum 10), Abbey Pain Scale (movement-based, observe during care such as pressure area care or showering), CNPI (score each item at movement and at rest; any behavior warrants further investigation) and PACSLAC.
• PACSLAC timing: at intake; at least every 8 hours for behavioral symptoms suggestive of pain; with any change in pain status; 1 hour after a pain intervention; quarterly in long-term care.
• Evaluation: regular scheduled reassessment, because cognitive impairment leads to underreporting; caregiver reports of behavior change and documentation guide adjustment of the plan.

(b) Explain the factors that may affect this patient's pain experience.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pain assessment in infants is evaluating and interpreting signs and behaviours that indicate presence and intensity of pain in infants who cannot verbally communicate.
• It improves comfort, prevents long-term consequences (increased stress response, altered sleep, impaired immunity, delayed recovery), improves parental satisfaction and communication, is an ethical imperative and optimizes surgical outcomes; early uncontrolled pain may produce heightened pain sensitivity later.

(b)
Respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, informed proxy consent from parents or guardians, and transparency and accountability.

(c)
Crying (high-pitched, continuous), facial expressions (furrowed brows, tightly closed eyes, quivering chin), body movements (stiffening, arching, agitation); physiological: heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure.

(d)
• Behaviors are not specific to pain (hunger, discomfort, attention) and vary with temperament, pain threshold and developmental stage; vital signs are also affected by fever, anxiety, activity or medication.
• Caregiver subjectivity and parental anxiety can lead to over- or underestimation; tools are used inconsistently and have limitations; cultural differences and inconsistent staff training also contribute.

(e)
Preterm infants have immature nervous systems producing less pronounced or atypical pain signals, are susceptible to frequent procedures, and need specialized approaches.

(f)
• NIPS (neonates): facial expression, cry, breathing, arms, legs, state of arousal, each scored 0-2 (total 0-7), primarily behavioral. CRIES (NICU, postoperative neonates and infants): Crying, Requires oxygen above 95% saturation, Increased vital signs, Expression, Sleeplessness, each 0-2, maximum 10.
• PIPP (premature infants): gestational age, behavioral state, facial actions and physiological responses (heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation), combining behavioral and physiological indicators. FLACC (infants and young children): Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability, each 0-2, total 0-10.

(g)
• Observational methods: direct observation before, during and after a procedure with documented time, procedure and behaviors, plus standardized tools (NFCS, NIPS, FLACC) and interpretation against baseline.
• Parental reports: parents know typical behavior and notice subtle changes, give history of previous pain and responses to relief, provide emotional support and enable timely intervention.
• Parents should be educated on indicators, asked structured questions (crying, reaction to touch, sleep), updated regularly, and approached with cultural sensitivity, while balancing their input against objective assessment because of anxiety.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Non-pharmacological therapies are categorized into physical (sensory) and psychological interventions; complementary therapies (acupuncture, massage, aromatherapy, mindfulness) and environmental adjustments also contribute.

(b)
• Physical interventions are patient-specific and inhibit nociceptive input and pain perception; massage increases blood and lymphatic circulation, has an analgesic effect, decreases inflammation and edema, releases spasm and increases endorphin release.
• Hot and cold therapy relieves muscle, joint, back and arthritis pain; positioning maintains alignment, reduces stress, prevents bed ulcers and alleviates pain; acupuncture uses needles to stimulate nerves and promote circulation and pain modulation.
• TENS: battery unit with 2-4 leads and sticky pads delivering low-voltage impulses, thought to activate large fibers that block small pain fibers; helps chronic back pain, arthritis, neuropathic pain and mild to moderate acute pain. Progressive muscle relaxation (tightening and relaxing muscle groups) is safe, used for back pain, phantom limb pain, headache and stress.

(c)
CBT builds coping skills (behavioral activation, relaxation, pacing) and cognitive restructuring of catastrophizing; mindfulness-based stress reduction disconnects sensory from emotional elements of pain; acceptance and commitment therapy changes responses to thoughts.

(d)
• Benefits: fewer adverse reactions and no dependency, addressing root causes, improved well-being, patient empowerment, long-term relief and prevention of recurrence, multidisciplinary and personalized care.
• Useful for patients with drug allergies or sensitivities; a patient sensitive to opioids after knee replacement used cryotherapy, TENS, guided imagery, progressive muscle relaxation and early mobilization, reducing breakthrough medication by 50% and reaching 2/10 pain by day 5.

(e)
• Barriers: negative nurse attitudes, constant monitoring needs, workload and staffing, resource and equipment limits (TENS machines), inconsistent training, patient instability, patient preferences and cultural beliefs, documentation burden and evidence gaps.
• Nurses assess, educate, implement, monitor, collaborate and advocate for patient-centered care to overcome these barriers.

(f)
Physical interventions act through sensory input to inhibit nociceptive transmission; psychological interventions target cognitive responses, maladaptive behaviors and the emotional and evaluative aspects of pain.

(g)
• Non-pharmacological methods do not involve ingesting chemical substances, so they are less likely to cause adverse reactions or interactions and avoid dependency.
• They require active patient participation and continuous monitoring, complement pharmacological treatment, and are combined with it in multimodal care.

(c) psychological interventions.

(e) barriers that make some patients vulnerable to inadequate use.
Distinguish between:

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute pain related to the surgical incision and tissue manipulation; related diagnoses are risk of limited movement due to pain and surgery, and risk of infection at the surgical site.

(b)
• Incision site and surgical procedure (location and extent of surgery affect pain levels); type and administration of anesthetic agent.
• Patient factors: age, emotional state, previous pain experiences, cultural background; internal factors: motivation, emotional states (anxiety and depression heighten sensitivity), cognitive perceptions; external factors: culture, supportive environment, previous experiences.

(c)
• Post-operative pain results from tissue damage, inflammation and nerve irritation - a natural response to surgical trauma.
• Intense pain triggers the stress response: increased heart rate and blood pressure and suppressed immune response, making the body more susceptible to infection.
• Poor control: cardiovascular insufficiency occurs three times more often and infection five times more often; pain cycle (muscle tension and reduced blood flow cause more pain); delayed healing, longer hospital stay and risk of chronic pain.

(d)
• Goals: pain level 3 or below on a 0-10 scale within 48 hours; increased movement and participation in physical therapy; no signs of infection.
• Assess vital signs and pain every 2 hours with a numeric scale; check surgical site for infection, swelling and bruising; watch for nausea, vomiting, constipation and breathing problems.
• Medication: opioid (e.g. morphine) by PCA pump per protocol and scheduled NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) to reduce inflammation and pain; monitor and manage side effects.
• Non-pharmacologic: ice packs, relaxation (deep breathing), guided imagery, reposition every 2 hours; gentle range-of-motion exercises with physical therapists on day 1, CPM machine, walking as tolerated.
• Aseptic dressing changes, teach signs of infection and when to report, ensure hydration and good intake.
• Evaluation: pain 3 or below within 48 hours, improved mobility and therapy participation, surgical site free of infection signs.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with hypertension has undergone total knee replacement for severe osteoarthritis. He reports pain at the incision site rated 6 out of 10 on the pain scale.

(c) Explain the pathophysiology of post-operative pain and the consequences of poor control.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Aging brings functional and anatomical changes (cognitive impairment, neurochemical alterations, brain volume reduction) that affect pain perception.
• Pain thresholds appear to increase (decreased sensitivity), yet chronic pain prevalence rises, showing that aging affects different aspects of the pain experience rather than the nociceptive system generally.

(b)
• Slower nerve conduction, loss of nerve fibers, diminished reflexes and altered sensation; brain atrophy and reduced neurotransmitter levels affect processing.
• Some older adults have reduced perception from decreased nerve function and receptor density; others have heightened sensitivity, especially with chronic conditions such as diabetes that affect nerve health.

(c)
Musculoskeletal: cartilage degeneration, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, arthritis; cardiovascular: reduced blood flow slows healing; endocrine: falling estrogen and testosterone influence pain sensitivity.

(d)
• Chronic pain from osteoarthritis, neuropathy and osteoporosis is common; pain is experienced regularly by 49-83% of those over 60 in care homes and 40% in the community; a Nigerian study found low back pain prevalence of 46.8%.
• Use lower starting doses, slower titration and careful monitoring; acetaminophen is often preferred, NSAIDs cause GI, renal and cardiovascular effects, and opioids carry fall risk, cognitive impairment and dependency.

(e)
Physical therapy improves mobility and reduces pain, CBT addresses psychological aspects, and acupuncture and other complementary therapies reduce reliance on opioids within a multidisciplinary approach.

(f)
Older adults underreport pain because of normalization of pain with aging or fear of medication dependency, and fear of being seen as complaining, leading to undertreatment.

(g)
Atypical presentation and non-specific symptoms (fatigue, confusion, decreased appetite) can mask pain; multiple chronic conditions overlap and provider bias attributes pain to aging.

(h)
• Functional: greater motor impairment, falls, decreased mobility, decreased appetite, impaired neurological function and worse health status.
• Psychosocial: depression, anxiety and social isolation; pain and depressed mood are strongly associated, and failure to treat a mood disorder makes pain management ineffective.
questions.question:
Describe how aging affects pain perception:
(a) overall effect on thresholds and prevalence
(b) nervous system changes and variation between individuals
(c) other body systems.
State how these changes relate to common pain conditions and treatment:
(d) conditions and drug choices
(e) non-pharmacological options.
Explain why pain may persist, be underrecognized or become chronic and its functional and psychosocial effect:
(f) underreporting and undertreatment
(g) atypical presentation

Describe the pain pathway:
(a) peripheral nociceptors, fibers and generation of the signal
(b) spinal cord synapse and ascending pathways
(c) brain processing and descending modulation.
State how parts of the pathway relate to pain conditions and treatment targets:
(d) neurotransmitters and drug or non-drug targets
(e) nociceptive and neuropathic pain.
Explain why pain may be referred, persist or become chronic, and the resulting functional or psychosocial effect:
(f) referred pain
(g) persistence and chronicity
(h) functional and psychosocial effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nociceptors are specialized receptors in skin, muscles, joints and internal organs that detect mechanical damage, extreme temperatures and chemicals (acids, histamine); types are mechanical, thermal and chemical.
• Tissue damage opens sodium channels; sodium influx depolarizes the nociceptor and generates action potentials, carried by A-delta fibers (fast, sharp pain) and C fibers (slow, dull or burning pain) to the dorsal root ganglion near the spinal cord.

(b)
• Signals synapse with second-order neurons in the dorsal horn, releasing glutamate (primary excitatory neurotransmitter) and substance P (amplifies pain signals and contributes to neurogenic inflammation).
• They ascend by the spinothalamic pathway to the thalamus and somatosensory cortex (intensity and location) and by the spinoreticular pathway to the brainstem reticular formation (arousal, attention, emotional responses).

(c)
• The thalamus relays information; the somatosensory cortex interprets location, intensity and quality; the limbic system and frontal cortex process emotional and cognitive aspects.
• Descending inhibitory pathways release endogenous opioids (endorphins), serotonin and norepinephrine to inhibit transmission; descending facilitatory pathways can enhance pain perception under certain conditions.

(d)
• Targets: opioids bind mu, delta and kappa receptors; gabapentin and pregabalin bind the alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunit, reducing glutamate and substance P; TCAs and SNRIs raise serotonin and norepinephrine; local anesthetics block sodium channels; NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins.
• TENS is thought to stimulate large afferent fibers that block small pain-transmitting fibers and may release endorphins; massage also increases endogenous endorphin release.

(e)
Nociceptive pain is normal transmission of noxious stimuli (cut, sprained joint, postoperative pain); neuropathic pain is abnormal processing after damage to the peripheral or central nervous system (diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia).

(f)
Referred pain is felt in a different area from its source (heart attack pain in the left arm or jaw) because nerves supplying different areas share pathways.

(g)
Pain becomes chronic when it persists beyond expected healing time; neuropathic pain is pathologic processing, descending facilitation can enhance pain, and poorly managed acute pain may lead to chronic syndromes.

(h)
Chronic pain leads to poor sleep, depression, anxiety, social isolation, decreased physical activity and impaired academic or work performance.

(a)
• Pain is a complex experience influenced beyond physical sensation; six dimensions cannot be easily separated, and some are more relevant than others in certain situations.
• Physiologic: organic etiology, location, onset, duration and type (in cancer pain tumor, treatment or other; visceral, somatic, neuropathic). Sensory: intensity, quality and pattern - somatic often sharp and stabbing, visceral dull and aching, neuropathic burning or paroxysmal.

(b)
• Affective: how pain makes the sufferer feel - mood, outlook and emotional states such as depression, anxiety and fear.
• Cognitive: meaning of pain, thought processes, conscious thoughts, opinions and experiences; behavioral: pain-related behaviors.

(c)
Sociocultural: ethnocultural, demographic, spiritual and social factors affecting perception and response in the patient, supporters (family, friends) and caregivers (nurses, physicians); attitudes and beliefs decide whether pain is acknowledged as needing action.

(d)
• Cancer pain shows condition-specific patterns (tumor pain often constant); in dementia, behavioral changes (agitation, withdrawal) may be the only indicator of pain.
• Targets: physiologic - analgesics; affective and cognitive - CBT, mindfulness and psychological therapies that change thoughts and behaviors; sociocultural - culturally respectful care, family support and support groups.

(e)
McGill Pain Questionnaire (sensory, affective and evaluative dimensions); Brief Pain Inventory (intensity and interference with mood, walking, work, sleep); pain charts to mark location.

(f)
Whether pain exacerbates depression, anxiety and fear or is exacerbated by them (or both) is unclear, but their interrelationship is established; mood states may alter perception or enhance intensity.

(g)
Chronic pain is often accompanied by depression and anxiety; failure to treat a concomitant mood disorder results in ineffective pain management, while psychological care can break the cycle of pain and depression.

(h)
• Pain leads to decreased physical activity, impaired academic or work performance and social isolation, and may signify loss of function or independence in older adults.
• Multidimensional assessment gives a holistic understanding, enables tailored treatment and improves outcomes and patient satisfaction.
questions.question:
Describe the multidimensional model of pain:
(a) the physiologic and sensory dimensions
(b) the affective, cognitive and behavioral dimensions
(c) the sociocultural dimension.
State how the dimensions relate to common pain conditions, assessment tools and treatment targets:
(d) conditions and treatment targets
(e) assessment tools.
Explain why pain may persist or become chronic and the resulting functional and psychosocial effect:
(f) interaction with emotions
