Describe the self-report pain assessment tools (VAS, NRS and verbal descriptor scale):
(a) description and administration
(b) indications
(c) merits
(d) limitations.
(e) State the safe-practice considerations in choosing a tool, particularly for older adults and cognitive impairment.
(f) Explain the rationale for regular monitoring and reassessment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• VAS: a 10 cm line with endpoints 'no pain' and 'worst pain imaginable'; the patient marks a point and the distance is measured in millimeters; first used in 1921 by Hayes and Patterson; paper-and-pencil or digital.
• NRS: a 0-10 whole-number scale (0 no pain, 10 worst pain imaginable) in which the patient chooses a number; a segmented 11-point version of the VAS. VDS/VRS: descriptive phrases (none, mild, moderate, severe, excruciating) from which the patient selects.

(b)
• VAS is a unidimensional measure of intensity used in research and in rheumatic disease, chronic pain and cancer; NRS is used across settings and populations including older adults with adequate cognition.
• VDS is the scale of choice for older adults including mild to moderate cognitive impairment and suits patients who struggle with numbers; the pain thermometer (vertical thermometer-like scale) suits older adults with mild to moderate cognitive impairment.

(c)
VAS: easy, no training beyond a ruler, minimal translation difficulty, most valuable for change within individuals. NRS: simple, quick, quantifiable and trackable. VDS: easy, no numeric understanding, quick.

(d)
• VAS: highly subjective, less valuable for comparing individuals, treats ordinal values as interval data, cannot be administered verbally or by phone, and needs cognitive ability.
• NRS: needs cognitive function, subjective interpretation, affected by hearing, speech or language barriers and the abstract nature of numbers; it may not capture pain characteristics or emotional aspects.
• VDS: subjective, limited sensitivity and range, cultural and language barriers; pain thermometer: limited sensitivity, possible misinterpretation, limited use in severe cognitive impairment.

(e)
• Match the tool to the patient's cognitive ability, language proficiency and cultural background; use multiple self-report tools for a fuller profile; use standardized protocols and train staff to use and interpret tools.
• In severe cognitive impairment use observational tools (PAINAD, Abbey Pain Scale, CNPI, PACSLAC), screen cognition (Mini-Mental State Examination, Mini-Cog) and obtain caregiver input.

(f)
• Scales give a numeric or descriptive value that can be recorded and tracked over time, allowing monitoring of trends and intervention effectiveness.
• Reassess regularly (for example, one hour after an intervention with PACSLAC), document findings, and adjust treatment according to response and adverse effects.

questions.question:
Describe non-opioid analgesics:
(a) examples and mechanism of action
(b) indications
(c) adult doses and administration of paracetamol, ibuprofen and diclofenac
(d) contraindications and cautions
(e) adverse effects.
(f) State the safe-practice considerations for these drugs.
Explain the rationale for monitoring and for managing NSAID-induced gastrointestinal complications:
(g) mechanism
(h) management strategies
(i) monitoring responsibilities.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin work mainly by inhibiting production of prostaglandins involved in pain and inflammation signaling; they form step 1 of the WHO ladder (mild pain), with or without adjuvants.

(b)
Used for mild to moderate pain, fever and inflammation (headaches, menstrual cramps, sprains, arthritis); paracetamol can be combined with an NSAID.

(c)
• Paracetamol: 500 mg-1 g by mouth every 6 hours, maximum 4 g per day.
• Ibuprofen: 400 mg by mouth every 6-8 hours, maximum 1.2 g, given with food. Diclofenac: 50 mg by mouth every 8 hours, maximum daily dose 150 mg, given with food.

(d)
Ibuprofen and diclofenac are avoided in asthmatic patients; the ibuprofen maximum should be lowered in liver impairment; diclofenac is not for use in renal failure and is used with caution with NSAIDs.

(e)
Gastrointestinal upset and ulcers, liver damage with high-dose acetaminophen, increased cardiovascular risk with long-term NSAIDs; diclofenac can cause GI bleeding or renal toxicity, particularly after more than 7-10 days.

(f)
• Hepatotoxicity can occur if more than the maximum paracetamol dose is given per day, so the daily maximum must not be exceeded.
• Give NSAIDs with food; acetaminophen is often preferred for chronic pain in older adults because of its safety profile; NSAIDs are avoided in pregnancy, especially the third trimester; children are dosed by weight.

(g)
• NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 and COX-2; inhibiting COX-1 reduces protective prostaglandins in the gastric mucosa, decreasing mucosal protection so the stomach lining is more susceptible to acid damage.
• Resulting problems: peptic ulcers (pain, nausea, bleeding), GI bleeding that may be severe and life-threatening, and gastritis (discomfort, nausea, vomiting).

(h)
Management: proton pump inhibitors or H2 receptor antagonists to reduce acid; misoprostol to protect the mucosa; selective COX-2 inhibitors with lower GI risk; if GI symptoms occur with diclofenac, discontinue it and give an H2 antagonist such as ranitidine.

(i)
Monitor regularly for adverse effects (GI symptoms, sedation, signs of dependency), measure effectiveness with pain scales, and adjust doses or change medication according to response and patient feedback.

questions.question:
A young adult sustains a sprain after a fall. The pain has a sudden onset after the accident, with stiffness, swelling and inflammation and reduced range of motion in the affected part.
(a) Identify the type of pain by duration, location and etiology, stating the supporting features.
(b) Explain the underlying mechanism (pathophysiology) of the pain.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the parameters to be collected.
(d) Outline the pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• By duration: acute pain - sudden onset from injury, well defined with predictable duration, resolving as the cause heals; if healing is expected in 3 weeks and pain continues, it should be considered chronic.
• By location: deep pain (muscles, tendons, bones), usually aching or throbbing; by etiology: nociceptive pain, from activation of nociceptors by injury, inflammation or mechanical pressure (for example a sprained joint); musculoskeletal acute injury (fractures, sprains, strains from accidents or falls).

(b)
• Mechanical damage activates nociceptors; sodium channels open and action potentials travel on A-delta fibers (sharp pain) and C fibers (dull or burning pain) to the dorsal root ganglion and dorsal horn, releasing glutamate and substance P.
• Signals ascend by the spinothalamic pathway to the thalamus and somatosensory cortex (location, intensity, quality); limbic system and frontal cortex process emotional and cognitive aspects; descending inhibitory pathways (endorphins, serotonin, norepinephrine) modulate transmission.

(c)
• History: onset and any specific incident, location and radiation, quality, intensity (NRS or VAS), aggravating and relieving factors, impact on daily activities.
• Inspect for swelling, bruising, redness and posture, guarding or limping; palpate for tenderness and temperature differences; test range of motion and pain during movement; imaging (X-ray, MRI, CT) for structural problems.

(d)
• Pharmacological: NSAIDs, muscle relaxants and analgesics to reduce pain and inflammation.
• Non-pharmacological: physical therapy with strengthening and flexibility exercises, hot and cold therapy, positioning, massage; alternative therapies such as acupuncture; lifestyle measures (ergonomic adjustments, regular exercise).

questions.question:
Describe pain under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) acute pain
(c) chronic or persistent pain, including its subcategories and breakthrough pain.
Explain the clinical basis for concern about unrelieved pain:
(d) the body systems affected
(e) why some patients are more vulnerable.
Distinguish between acute and chronic pain:
(f) onset and course
(g) management implications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage or described in terms of such damage.
• It is highly personal and subjective - whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever he says it does - and can affect psychosocial, emotional and physical functioning.

(b)
Acute pain usually involves tissue damage from surgery, trauma, burn or venipuncture; it has a sudden onset, is well defined, short in duration and resolves with normal healing (described as lasting seconds to 6 months).

(c)
• Chronic or persistent pain persists beyond the expected healing time, may be constant or intermittent (flares), and is described as lasting 6 months or longer (other descriptions give 3 months or over 12 weeks).
• It is subcategorized as cancer or noncancer origin; noncancer examples are diabetic peripheral neuropathy, back or neck pain after injury and osteoarthritis pain.
• Breakthrough pain: patients with cancer may have continuous chronic pain plus periodic, more intense acute exacerbations, and may also have acute pain from repetitive painful procedures.

(d)
• Unrelieved pain can affect every system: endocrine (increased ACTH, cortisol, ADH, epinephrine, norepinephrine), metabolic (hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, muscle protein catabolism), cardiovascular (increased heart rate, hypertension, hypercoagulation, DVT).
• Also respiratory (atelectasis, hypoxemia, sputum retention, infection), gastrointestinal (decreased motility), musculoskeletal (spasm, fatigue, immobility), immune depression, cognitive confusion, and poor quality of life (sleeplessness, anxiety, fear, hopelessness).

(e)
• Children: increased behavioral and physiologic responses, altered temperaments, higher somatization, possible altered development of the pain system and greater vulnerability to stress disorders, addictive behavior and anxiety states.
• Older adults with cognitive impairment or communication barriers underreport pain (fear of being seen as complaining, belief that pain is normal aging), leading to undertreatment; unrelieved pain may lead to chronic syndromes (postmastectomy, post thoracotomy, phantom pain, postherpetic neuralgia).

(f)
Acute pain has a sudden onset linked to an identifiable event and resolves; chronic pain develops gradually, persists, may have a poorly defined onset, and its cause may be unclear.

(g)
If healing is expected in 3 weeks and pain continues, it should be considered chronic and treated with chronic pain interventions; some conditions (e.g. cancer) produce both acute and chronic pain.

(a)
• Neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy), a chronic pain condition arising from damage or dysfunction of the nervous system.
• Findings: burning or shooting pain, tingling and numbness in hands and feet, allodynia (pain from stimuli that do not usually cause pain, such as light touch); hyperalgesia and muscle weakness may also occur.

(b)
• Neuropathic pain is pathologic, resulting from abnormal processing of sensory input after damage to the peripheral or central nervous system; diabetic neuropathy is nerve damage caused by long-term high blood sugar.
• Treatment targets in the pathway: gabapentin and pregabalin bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels, reducing release of glutamate and substance P; TCAs and SNRIs raise serotonin and norepinephrine, enhancing descending pain inhibition.

(c)
• Priority: medical history and physical examination to identify causes and assess pain characteristics, plus neurological examination of nerve function and reflexes; painDETECT (9 self-administered items, scored 0-5; higher scores mean greater likelihood of neuropathic pain).
• Investigations: electromyography and nerve conduction studies, MRI or CT for structural problems, blood tests for underlying conditions such as diabetes or vitamin deficiencies.

(d)
• Pharmacological: anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin), antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine), topical lidocaine patches or capsaicin cream; opioids (e.g. oxycodone) used cautiously if other medications fail.
• Watch for side effects: gabapentinoids - dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, weight gain, risk of dependency and misuse; TCAs - dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, sedation, orthostatic hypotension.
• Non-pharmacological: physical therapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy, nerve blocks and injections, acupuncture, biofeedback and meditation.
• Prevention: blood sugar control, healthy lifestyle (exercise, balanced diet, avoiding alcohol and smoking), protective measures, regular medical checkups for early detection.
questions.question:
A patient with long-standing diabetes and prolonged high blood sugar complains of burning, shooting, electric shock-like pain with tingling and numbness in the hands and feet, and pain from a light touch.
(a) Identify the type of pain and the specific sensory findings shown.
(b) Explain the underlying mechanism (pathophysiology).
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the diagnostic investigations.
(d) Outline the pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions and the preventive measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Cancer pain may be acute (short-term, from diagnostic or therapeutic procedures), chronic (long-lasting, beyond expected healing, associated with progression) or breakthrough (sudden intense flare despite ongoing management).

(b)
• Nociceptive pain from tissue damage is somatic (bones, joints, muscles, connective tissue) or visceral, described as sharp, throbbing or aching; neuropathic pain from nerve damage is burning, shooting or tingling.
• Inflammatory pain results from inflammatory mediators released by the tumor or cancer treatments, with swelling, redness and warmth.

(c)
Pain may be directly associated with cancer (bony infiltration, nerve compression), result from treatment (surgery, radiation) or be unrelated (trauma); most is a direct result of tumor involvement.

(d)
• WHO ladder (1986): step 1 non-opioids (acetaminophen, NSAIDs); step 2 weak opioids (codeine, tramadol); step 3 strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl); with or without adjuvants.
• Adjuvants: amitriptyline and gabapentin for neuropathic pain, corticosteroids (dexamethasone), bisphosphonates (pamidronate) and neurolytic blocks; EAPC 2012 gives no preference among oral morphine, oxycodone or hydromorphone and lists transdermal fentanyl and buprenorphine as alternatives.

(e)
Breakthrough pain is treated with short-acting immediate-release opioids (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl) at 10-20% of the total daily dose, by oral, sublingual, buccal, intranasal or parenteral routes, with rapid-onset fentanyl and adjuvant NSAIDs, acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, antidepressants or corticosteroids.

(f)
Breakthrough pain is a sudden, transient exacerbation despite well-controlled baseline pain, predictable or unpredictable; chronic cancer pain persists with disease progression.

(g)
• After fear of dying, pain is the second most common fear of newly diagnosed patients; over half of 1,308 patients reported moderate to severe pain 50% of the time.
• Pain impairs quality of life and daily activities, and unmanaged pain can lead to treatment interruptions or discontinuation.

(h)
• Unrelieved pain brings anxiety, depression and helplessness; effective management supports emotional well-being and improves adherence to treatment.
• Palliative care addresses physical, emotional, social and spiritual aspects with an interdisciplinary team and supports families; early integration improves symptom control and quality of life.
questions.question:
Describe cancer pain:
(a) types by duration
(b) pathophysiology by mechanism
(c) causes.
State how these relate to treatment targets:
(d) the WHO ladder and adjuvants
(e) breakthrough pain management.
Explain why cancer pain persists and its functional and psychosocial effect:
(f) breakthrough and chronic pain
(g) impact
(h) psychosocial and palliative response.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Breakthrough pain: a sudden, transient exacerbation of pain that occurs despite well-controlled baseline pain; it can be predictable or unpredictable.
• Source: cancer pain may be directly associated with the cancer (bony infiltration, nerve compression), result from treatment (surgery, radiation) or be unrelated to cancer (trauma); most is a direct result of tumor involvement.

(b)
• Patient factors such as age, emotional state, previous pain experiences and cultural background; anxiety and depression heighten pain sensitivity and cognitive perceptions shape the experience.
• Psychological state influences perception: anxiety, depression and stress amplify pain while positive emotions and relaxation reduce it; family and social support can reduce stress and improve tolerance.

(c)
• Acute pain (short-term, often from diagnostic or therapeutic procedures); chronic pain (long-lasting, beyond expected healing, with cancer progression); breakthrough pain (flare despite control).
• By mechanism: nociceptive (somatic or visceral; sharp, throbbing, aching), neuropathic (burning, shooting, tingling) and inflammatory (swelling, redness, warmth from inflammatory mediators released by the tumor or treatments).

(d)
• Continue scheduled dosing with additional medication for breakthrough pain; use short-acting immediate-release opioids (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl); dose typically 10-20% of the total daily dose of the regular opioid.
• Routes: oral, sublingual, buccal, intranasal or parenteral; rapid-onset fentanyl preparations; NSAIDs or acetaminophen alongside opioids; anticonvulsants, antidepressants or corticosteroids depending on pain type; consider switching opioid if relief is inadequate with severe adverse effects.
• Evaluation: continuous assessment of pain and side effects with adjustment of the plan; involve patient and family in decisions; combine non-pharmacological and complementary therapies.
questions.question:
A patient with cancer whose chronic baseline pain is well controlled on regular analgesics suddenly experiences an intense, transient flare of pain despite ongoing pain management.
(a) Identify the type of pain and its possible source.
(b) Explain the factors that may affect this patient's pain experience.
(c) State the differential considerations among the types of cancer pain.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning for the plan of care and how outcomes are evaluated.

Describe adjuvant analgesics (co-analgesics):
(a) definition and classes
(b) mechanism of action of TCAs, SNRIs and gabapentin or pregabalin
(c) indications
(d) adverse effects.
(e) State the safe-practice considerations.
Explain the rationale for monitoring and for managing adverse effects:
(f) monitoring and adjustment
(g) special populations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Adjuvant analgesics are not primarily designed for pain relief but enhance the effect of primary analgesics or address specific pain types; classes include antidepressants, anticonvulsants, muscle relaxants and corticosteroids.

(b)
• TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) inhibit reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine and also block sodium channels; SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine) raise the same neurotransmitters, enhancing descending pain inhibition.
• Gabapentin and pregabalin bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing calcium influx and release of glutamate and substance P; baclofen is a GABA_B agonist; cyclobenzaprine acts on the brainstem; corticosteroids reduce inflammatory mediators.

(c)
• TCAs: diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, fibromyalgia, tension headache, migraine prophylaxis; SNRIs: neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain; gabapentinoids: diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, spinal cord injury pain, fibromyalgia.
• Baclofen: spasticity pain (multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy); cyclobenzaprine: short-term muscle spasm in low back and neck pain; corticosteroids (prednisone, dexamethasone): inflammatory pain, cancer pain, nerve compression.

(d)
• TCAs: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, weight gain, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmias. SNRIs: nausea, dry mouth, dizziness, insomnia, sweating, hypertension at higher doses.
• Gabapentinoids: dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, weight gain, blurred vision, poor concentration and memory, risk of dependency and misuse; baclofen: drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, fatigue; cyclobenzaprine: drowsiness, dry mouth, anticholinergic effects.

(e)
• Do not stop SNRIs abruptly (withdrawal symptoms); abrupt discontinuation of baclofen can cause hallucinations and seizures; use cyclobenzaprine cautiously with a history of arrhythmias or heart disease.
• Long-term corticosteroids cause weight gain, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension and infection risk; short-term use may cause insomnia, mood swings and GI upset.

(f)
• Regular assessment of pain relief and side effects identifies adverse effects early; adjust dose, switch medication if effects are intolerable or ineffective, and add non-pharmacological methods.
• Pain scales (NRS, VAS) measure effectiveness; incorporate patient feedback and involve an interdisciplinary team (pain specialists, psychologists, physical therapists).

(g)
In older adults use lower starting doses, slower titration and careful monitoring because of altered pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics and the risk of adverse drug reactions.

questions.question:
Describe pain classified by etiology:
(a) nociceptive pain
(b) neuropathic pain
(c) inflammatory, psychogenic and cancer pain.
Explain the clinical basis:
(d) why descriptors differ with type and location
(e) why some patients are more vulnerable to neuropathic pain and how it is identified.
Distinguish between nociceptive and neuropathic pain:
(f) pathology
(g) treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nociceptive (physiologic) pain is the normal functioning of physiologic systems that leads to the perception of noxious stimuli (tissue injury) as painful - described as normal pain transmission.
• It occurs when nociceptors are activated by actual or potential tissue damage from injury, inflammation or mechanical pressure (a cut, sprained joint, postoperative pain) and may be somatic or visceral.

(b)
• Neuropathic (pathophysiologic) pain is pathologic, resulting from abnormal processing of sensory input after damage to the peripheral or central nervous system or both.
• It is described as shooting, burning, electric shock-like or tingling, with allodynia, hyperalgesia, numbness and muscle weakness if motor nerves are affected.

(c)
• Inflammatory pain results from immune activation and tissue inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, infections), with redness, swelling and heat.
• Psychogenic pain is primarily influenced by stress, anxiety or depression and may lack a clear physical cause (somatic symptom disorder, conversion disorder); cancer pain arises from tumor growth, invasion or treatment and may be nociceptive, neuropathic or both.

(d)
• Somatic pain is often sharp and stabbing, visceral pain dull and aching or cramp-like, neuropathic pain burning or paroxysmal; superficial pain is sharp, burning or tingling while deep pain is aching or throbbing.
• Visceral examples are appendicitis, kidney stones and menstrual cramps; superficial examples are a cut, sunburn or abrasion; deep examples are deep tissue injuries or fractures.

(e)
• Neuropathic pain follows injuries (spinal cord injury, nerve damage), infections (shingles), diabetes, autoimmune disease (multiple sclerosis, lupus), genetic disorders (Charcot-Marie-Tooth), chemotherapy, or may be idiopathic.
• Identification: neurological examination, EMG and nerve conduction studies, MRI or CT, blood tests; painDETECT (9 items, each scored 0-5) differentiates nociceptive from neuropathic components, higher scores meaning higher likelihood of neuropathic pain.

(f)
Nociceptive pain reflects normal transmission of noxious stimuli from tissue injury; neuropathic pain reflects pathologic processing from nervous system damage or dysfunction.

(g)
Neuropathic pain is treated with anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin), antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine) and topical lidocaine or capsaicin, with opioids used cautiously if these fail; nociceptive postoperative pain is managed with opioids, NSAIDs and acetaminophen.

questions.question:
A patient with cancer has severe, persistent pain caused directly by tumor involvement (for example bony infiltration or nerve compression) and is to be started on oral morphine.
(a) Name the pain assessment tool(s) and method you would use.
(b) State the pain parameters you would assess.
(c) State the analgesic step and drug chosen, with starting dose, formulations and use of adjuvants.
(d) State the monitoring required and the adverse effects to watch for, with their management.
(e) Outline the patient and family education required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Numeric Rating Scale (0 no pain to 10 worst pain imaginable), Visual Analog Scale (10 cm line), McGill Pain Questionnaire (quality and intensity through descriptive terms) and Brief Pain Inventory (severity and impact on daily function); comprehensive assessment guides the plan.

(b)
Location, intensity, duration (frequency and duration of episodes) and quality (sharp, dull, burning, throbbing).

(c)
• Step 3 of the WHO ladder (severe and persistent pain): strong opioid with or without non-opioid analgesics and with or without adjuvants; morphine is the gold standard.
• Adult starting dose 2.5-20 mg by mouth every 4 hours depending on age and previous opiate use; available as immediate-release or sustained-release.
• Adjuvants: antidepressants (amitriptyline) and anticonvulsants (gabapentin) for neuropathic pain; corticosteroids (dexamethasone), bisphosphonates (pamidronate) and neurolytic blocks for cancer pain.

(d)
• Monitor effectiveness and side effects of the drug, respiratory status, bowel functioning, and mental and cognitive functioning.
• Adverse effects: respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea, and risk of addiction and dependence.
• Management: laxatives or stool softeners, antiemetics, titration to the minimum effective dose, naloxone to reverse respiratory depression in emergencies, regular monitoring for dependence.

(e)
• Teach names of the pharmacologic agents, dosage schedules, side effects, and interventions for nausea and vomiting (antiemetics) and constipation.
• Explain the rationale for interventions, allow time for patient and family questions, and teach proper use and storage of opioids.
• Patient and family must know how to contact medical personnel in an emergency; education improves adherence and helps recognize and manage side effects.

questions.question:
An older adult living in a care home has dementia and hearing loss and several chronic conditions. The patient underreports pain for fear of being seen as complaining, believes pain is a normal part of aging and fears medication side effects and addiction. The patient presents with fatigue, confusion and decreased appetite, and staff tend to attribute the complaints to aging.
(a) Identify the risk factors for inadequate pain control in this patient.
(b) Describe the complications of unrelieved or poorly managed pain in older adults.
(c) State the nursing management options and justify the priority choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cognitive impairment (dementia) makes it difficult to describe pain intensity, location and nature; communication barriers include hearing loss, speech difficulties and language barriers.
• Underreporting: fear of being perceived as complaining, concern about medication side effects, belief that pain is a normal part of aging; reluctance to use medication because of fears of addiction, side effects or interactions.
• Atypical presentation and non-specific symptoms (fatigue, confusion, decreased appetite) can mask pain; multiple chronic conditions overlap; provider bias and misconceptions attribute pain to aging instead of treating it as a significant symptom.

(b)
• Chronic pain leads to depression, social isolation, decreased mobility and increased risk of falls; older adults in pain have greater motor impairment, decreased appetite and impaired neurological function.
• Pain is associated with worse health status, poorer quality of life, poor sleep and reduced daily functioning; effective management can reduce readmissions and need for intensive treatment.

(c)
• Options: obtain a complete history (including medication history) and identify sensory and cognitive impairments upfront (Mini-Mental State Examination or Mini-Cog); note nonverbal cues such as guarding, grimacing and restricted movement.
• Use observational tools: PAINAD (breathing, negative vocalization, facial expression, body language, consolability; 0-2 each, maximum 10) or Abbey Pain Scale; involve the caregiver for baseline behavior; pain chart or pointing to the painful body part.
• Start analgesics at lower doses with slow titration and careful monitoring; combine with non-pharmacological approaches (physical therapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy, complementary therapies).
• Priority: regular, scheduled pain assessment with a tool suited to the patient's cognition, because cognitive impairment leads to underreporting and the other options depend on pain being recognized.
• Address mood (depression screening with the Geriatric Depression Scale short form or CES-D), educate on medication concerns, and respect cultural beliefs about pain.

questions.question:
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with joint pain accompanied by redness, swelling and heat in the affected area.
(a) Identify the type of pain (by etiology) and the features that support it.
(b) Explain the underlying mechanism (pathophysiology).
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the parameters to be collected.
(d) Outline the pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Inflammatory pain: results from activation of the body's immune response leading to tissue inflammation; commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and infections.
• Supporting features: redness, swelling and heat in the affected area.

(b)
• Chemical nociceptors respond to chemicals released by damaged or inflamed tissue; activation opens sodium channels, producing action potentials carried by A-delta and C fibers to the dorsal horn, where glutamate and substance P are released.
• Substance P amplifies pain signals and contributes to neurogenic inflammation; signals ascend to the thalamus and somatosensory cortex; prostaglandins are involved in pain and inflammation signaling.

(c)
• Inspect the skin over the painful area for redness, swelling, bruises or rashes; palpate for tenderness and compare temperature with surrounding tissue (warmth suggests inflammation).
• Test range of motion and observe pain during active and passive movement; rate intensity with NRS or VAS; assess functional impact on daily activities; blood tests can detect inflammatory or autoimmune conditions.

(d)
• Pharmacological: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation; DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, biologics such as TNF inhibitors infliximab and etanercept) for long-term management; corticosteroids (prednisone) short-term for flares.
• Corticosteroid cautions: long-term use causes weight gain, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension and increased risk of infection.
• Non-pharmacological: hot and cold therapy, massage, positioning, TENS (helps patients with arthritis), progressive muscle relaxation, physical therapy and complementary therapies.

questions.question:
Describe the physiological effects of unrelieved pain:
(a) endocrine and metabolic
(b) cardiovascular and respiratory
(c) other systems.
State how these effects relate to postoperative conditions and treatment targets:
(d) complications
(e) interventions.
Explain why pain may persist or become chronic and the resulting functional and psychosocial effect:
(f) future pain syndromes
(g) the pain cycle
(h) quality of life and function.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Endocrine: increased ACTH, cortisol, ADH, epinephrine, norepinephrine, growth hormone, catecholamines, renin and angiotensin II.
• Metabolic: gluconeogenesis, hepatic glycogenolysis, hyperglycemia, glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, muscle protein catabolism and increased lipolysis.

(b)
• Cardiovascular: increased heart rate, cardiac workload, peripheral, systemic and coronary vascular resistance, hypertension, myocardial oxygen consumption, hypercoagulation and deep vein thrombosis.
• Respiratory: reduced flows and volumes, atelectasis, shunting, hypoxemia, decreased cough, sputum retention and infection.

(c)
Genitourinary: reduced urine output, retention, fluid overload, hypokalemia; GI: decreased motility; musculoskeletal: spasm, impaired function, fatigue, immobility; cognitive: confusion; immune: depressed response.

(d)
• Intense postoperative pain triggers the stress response (increased heart rate and blood pressure, suppressed immunity), making the body more susceptible to infection; with poor control cardiovascular insufficiency is three times more frequent and infection five times greater.
• Uncontrolled pain delays healing and prolongs hospital stay; effective control enables early mobilization and reduces infection and cardiovascular events.

(e)
Targets: opioids at regular intervals, PCA (reduces delay and maintains therapeutic level), epidural infusions, intrapleural anesthesia (allows coughing and deep breathing, reducing pulmonary complications), multimodal analgesia and ERAS protocols to reduce opioid use.

(f)
Poorly managed pain may lead to debilitating chronic pain syndromes (postmastectomy pain, post thoracotomy pain, phantom pain, postherpetic neuralgia), whereas properly managed acute pain can prevent chronic pain.

(g)
Pain cycle: pain increases muscle tension and reduces blood flow, leading to more pain, which perpetuates and worsens the experience if not managed; in children, possible altered development of the pain system.

(h)
• Quality of life: sleeplessness, anxiety, fear, hopelessness and increased thoughts of suicide.
• Function: decreased physical activity, impaired academic or work performance, social isolation.

(a)
Opioids are weak or strong by potency: weak (codeine, tramadol, hydrocodone; step 2 of the WHO ladder, with low-dose morphine used by some palliative experts) and strong (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, hydromorphone; step 3).

(b)
They bind mu, delta and kappa receptors in the brain, spinal cord and other tissues, reducing pain perception and modulating the pain response.

(c)
Used for moderate to severe pain from cancer, chronic pain conditions and acute injuries, and during and after surgery.

(d)
• Tramadol 50-100 mg by mouth every 4-6 hours, maximum 400 mg; codeine 30-60 mg every 4 hours, maximum 240 mg daily (if inadequate, move to a strong opioid; can combine with any step 1 analgesic).
• Morphine is the gold standard; adult starting dose 2.5-20 mg by mouth every 4 hours depending on age and previous opiate use, as immediate-release or sustained-release.

(e)
Tramadol: caution in epilepsy, especially with drugs that lower seizure threshold, and serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic medications; codeine: genetic variability in metabolism may make it ineffective or cause excessive side effects.

(f)
Respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea, and risk of addiction and dependence.

(g)
• Older adults: increased fall risk, cognitive impairment and dependency, so start low and titrate slowly; children: dosing by weight, close monitoring; pregnancy and lactation: neonatal abstinence syndrome risk, so short-term lowest effective dose.
• Give a laxative with codeine unless the patient has diarrhea; give postoperative opioids at regular intervals; use prescription monitoring programs, patient contracts, regular reviews and education on proper use and storage.

(h)
Opioids depress the brain's respiratory centers, reducing breathing rate and in severe cases causing arrest; titrate to the minimum effective dose, monitor respiratory status and sedation, use combination therapy to reduce dose, and give naloxone in emergencies.

(i)
Prescribe laxatives or stool softeners and antiemetics; monitor bowel functioning because these effects are common and affect comfort and adherence.

(j)
Risk factors: personal history of substance abuse, mental health disorders, family history, high doses and long duration; use risk screening and regular monitoring (risk is low in short-term postoperative use).
questions.question:
Describe opioid analgesics:
(a) classification and examples
(b) mechanism of action
(c) indications

options: Dried specimens are more recognizable than fresh
Herbarium specimens contain more medicinal properties

The definition encompasses physical and mental illness treatment while respecting cultural diversity.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Amylase is an enzyme belonging to the class of hydrolases that catalyse the breakdown of starch and glycogen, and is the smallest enzyme known, weighing between 50,000 and 55,000 daltons.
• It attacks the alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds in starch (amylose and amylopectin) and glycogen, producing glucose, maltose and dextrin fragments.
• Sources of amylase include the acinar cells of the pancreas (serum amylase), with lesser concentrations in skeletal muscle, the small intestine and the fallopian tube; salivary amylase is produced by the salivary glands.
• Because it is a small enzyme, it can be found in urine, having been filtered through the glomerulus.
(ii)
• Serum amylase is useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, in which it rises 2-12 hours after the onset of the insult, usually peaking after 24 hours and returning to normal within 3-5 days, with values ranging from 250-1000 IU.
• Elevated amylase can also occur in non-pancreatic conditions such as mumps, parotitis, perforated peptic ulcer, acute appendicitis, and ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
• Urine amylase, amylase clearance studies, and amylase isoenzymes offer a more specific way of achieving a diagnosis when serum amylase elevation is nonspecific.
(iii)
• Hyperamylasaemia (macroamylasaemia) results when the amylase molecule combines with immunoglobulins to form a complex too large to filter through the glomerulus.
• In this condition, serum amylase is high but urinary amylase is low.
• If only serum amylase were measured, a patient with macroamylasaemia could be mistaken for having pancreatitis or another cause of true hyperamylasaemia.
• Measuring urine amylase alongside serum amylase, or performing amylase clearance studies, helps distinguish macroamylasaemia (high serum, low urine amylase) from true pancreatic disease.
• This combined approach, together with amylase isoenzyme testing, offers a more specific way of reaching the correct diagnosis than serum amylase alone.
questions.question: (i) Describe the basic structure, sources and biochemical role of amylase. (ii) State the standard clinical setting in which serum and urine amylase are measured. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind measuring both serum and urine amylase, rather than serum amylase alone, when macroamylasaemia is suspected.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Lipoproteins are classified into five groups by density: chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL.
• The more protein a lipoprotein contains, the higher its density; the more lipid, the lower its density.
• Chylomicrons are the largest and least dense lipoproteins, while HDL particles are the most dense.
• They can also be classified according to their electrophoretic mobility, as chylomicrons, pre-beta-lipoprotein (VLDL), beta-lipoprotein (LDL) and alpha-lipoprotein (HDL).
(ii)
• If a lipaemic sample is left overnight at 4 degrees Celsius, the larger, less dense chylomicrons rise to form a creamy layer on the surface.
• The smaller, denser VLDL and IDL particles do not rise in this way, and the sample may instead appear diffusely turbid.
• LDL and HDL particles are small and do not scatter light, so they do not contribute to this turbidity.
• This appearance test is used to infer which class of lipoprotein is elevated in a turbid or lipaemic sample.
(iii)
• Fasting plasma from normal individuals contains only VLDL, LDL and HDL particles.
• After a meal, chylomicrons carrying dietary (exogenous) triglyceride and cholesterol are present in the circulation.
• A nonfasting sample would therefore contain chylomicrons in addition to the endogenous lipoprotein classes, giving turbidity and lipid values that reflect recent dietary intake rather than the individual's baseline lipid status.
• This makes the lipid profile result inaccurate for classifying dyslipidaemia or assessing cardiovascular risk, which is why a fasting specimen is required.

(ii) State how this classification is applied in interpreting the appearance of a stored plasma or serum sample. (iii) Explain why a nonfasting sample gives an inaccurate or invalid lipid profile result.

(i) Describe column chromatography under the headings of definition and phases involved. (ii) Explain why chromatography is a useful group of techniques in practical chemical pathology. (iii) Distinguish column chromatography from thin-layer chromatography (TLC) as different formats of the stationary phase.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Chromatography is a group of techniques for the separation of the compounds in a mixture, with the term derived from Greek words meaning colour and written.
• It is defined as a physical method of separation in which the components to be separated are distributed between two phases, one of which is stationary while the other, the mobile phase, moves in a definite direction.
• The stationary phase may be a solid, or a liquid supported on a solid or a gel; the mobile phase may be a liquid, a solvent, a mixture of solvents, or a gas.
• In column chromatography, the stationary phase is packed into a column.
(ii)
• Chromatography allows the components of a mixture to be separated on the basis of their differing distribution between the stationary and mobile phases.
• This separation ability is useful whenever a sample contains a mixture of compounds that need to be resolved before or as part of quantification, such as the historical separation of coloured leaf-extract constituents on a column of calcium carbonate.
• Different types of chromatography (liquid, gas, liquid-solid, liquid-liquid) provide flexibility to separate different kinds of mixtures depending on the nature of the compounds involved.
(iii)
• In column chromatography, the stationary phase is packed into a column, through which the mobile phase (liquid, solvent mixture, or gas) flows.
• In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), the stationary phase is instead spread as a layer on a glass or aluminium plate, rather than packed into a column.
• Both column chromatography and TLC are examples of adsorption chromatography, differing mainly in the physical format of the stationary phase.
• A high-performance version of the layer format is described as HPTLC, corresponding to the general TLC approach but with improved performance.
• The general principle, a stationary phase versus a moving mobile phase, is the same for both, but the choice between a packed column and a spread layer depends on the practical needs of the separation being performed.

(i)
• Alcohols are organic compounds with one or more hydroxyl (-OH) groups attached to a carbon of an alkyl group, and can be considered organic derivatives of water in which a hydrogen atom is replaced by an alkyl group.
• Ethanol is the most widely used and often abused alcohol; other toxicologically important alcohols include methanol, isopropanol, acetone and ethylene glycol.
• Alcohol is absorbed throughout the gastrointestinal tract, more slowly in the stomach than in the small or large intestine, and passes to the liver via the hepatic portal vein for first-pass metabolism before entering the general circulation.
• It is metabolised mainly by a group of six enzymes collectively called alcohol dehydrogenase, and further metabolised to acetaldehyde, a toxic and carcinogenic substance.
(ii)
• Blood alcohol content (BAC) is a measurement of alcohol intoxication used for legal or medical purposes, expressed as grams of alcohol per 100 mL of blood.
• Alcohol can also be analysed in urine, oral fluid, breath, and hair samples, in addition to blood.
• Serum, plasma and whole blood are all suitable blood-related specimens for the determination of ethanol.
(iii)
• The venipuncture site should be cleansed with an alcohol-free disinfectant, such as aqueous benzalkonium chloride.
• This precaution avoids introducing exogenous alcohol from the skin disinfectant into the sample, which would falsely raise the measured ethanol result.
• The specimen should be kept capped to avoid evaporative loss of the volatile alcohol.
• Blood may be stored, properly sealed, for 14 days at room temperature or at 4 degrees Celsius, with or without a preservative.
• For longer storage, or for non-sterile postmortem specimens, sodium fluoride should be used as a preservative.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Normal urine should naturally appear clear, without particles, and coloured straw yellow or yellow-amber.
• The presence of turbidity or cloudiness indicates a problem, such as excess crystals (crystalluria), excess pus (pyuria), or protein (proteinuria).
• Colour variations can be diagnostically informative: for example, a distinct yellow may indicate excess riboflavin intake, red may indicate red blood cells or haemoglobin, dark brown to black may indicate alkaptonuria, and a greenish hue may indicate jaundice/bile metabolism problems.
• Urine odour varies from odourless (dilute urine) to a stronger odour (concentrated, dehydrated urine), with an abnormal odour possible in diabetic ketoacidosis due to ketone bodies.
(ii)
• Urinalysis is one of the major screening tests done in the clinical laboratory to assist in the diagnosis of urinary tract infections, kidney diseases, liver diseases, diabetes mellitus, and other metabolic conditions.
• The basic approach in urinalysis is to check the appearance, check the chemical contents, and possibly assess the concentration of the contents.
• Specific tests performed include pH, specific gravity, protein, glucose, bilirubin, urobilinogen, blood, nitrite, and leukocyte esterase.
(iii)
• A fresh sample is described as being equivalent to a valid sample for urinalysis.
• Several chemical constituents of urine are unstable over time; for example, conjugated bilirubin hydrolyses to unconjugated bilirubin in an aged sample at room temperature, causing a false-negative bilirubin result.
• Exposure to ultraviolet light converts bilirubin to biliverdin, which is another cause of a false-negative bilirubin result if the sample is not analysed promptly.
• Bacteria can also multiply in urine left standing, which could alter pH and other parameters, and give an unreliable result.
• Because of these instabilities, only a freshly voided sample gives results that truly reflect the patient's urine composition at the time of collection.

(i) Describe the basic biochemical roles of sodium in the body. (ii) State the standard laboratory/clinical setting in which serum sodium is measured. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind investigating water intake and fluid loss history when a patient is found to have an elevated serum sodium.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Sodium is a major cation in extracellular fluid, playing a role in maintaining fluid balance by regulating osmotic pressure and the movement of water between cells and the extracellular space.
• Sodium is a key determinant of blood pressure, influencing blood volume and vascular resistance.
• Sodium is crucial for the generation and transmission of nerve impulses, participating in the depolarisation phase of action potentials.
• Sodium is involved in muscle contraction (influx into muscle cells in excitation-contraction coupling), acid-base balance (interacting with bicarbonate), and nutrient absorption via the sodium/potassium ATPase pump.
• The kidneys regulate sodium balance through reabsorption of sodium in the renal tubules.
(ii)
• Serum sodium is measured as part of assessing fluid balance, blood pressure regulation, and overall renal function.
• Hypernatraemia is defined as a serum sodium level above 145 mEq/L.
(iii)
• Causes of hypernatraemia include inadequate water intake, especially with increased fluid loss (for example, from hot weather or exercise).
• Excessive water loss, from dehydration due to vomiting, diarrhoea, excessive sweating, or high fever leading to increased evaporative water loss, is another cause.
• Diabetes insipidus, an impaired production of or response to antidiuretic hormone, is a further cause of hypernatraemia.
• Excessive sodium intake is a rarer cause, occurring with certain medical treatments or conditions of abnormally high sodium intake.
• Because these causes have different underlying mechanisms and management, a history of water intake, fluid losses and possible ADH dysfunction is needed to correctly identify the cause of an elevated sodium result.

• This avoids interference from haemoglobin in the whole blood sample.
• Serum, plasma or whole blood are all suitable specimens, but higher alcohol concentrations are obtained with serum compared with whole blood, which should be borne in mind when interpreting the result.
questions.question: A serum sample from a patient involved in a road traffic incident is to be analysed for ethanol using an enzymatic method. (i) State the test/method appropriate here. (ii) State the principle of this method. (iii) State the materials/reagents required. (iv) State a source of error that could falsely elevate the result. (v) State the precaution needed when using whole blood rather than serum for this method.

(i) Describe the pentagastrin stimulation test under the headings of preparation and procedure. (ii) Explain why a gastric acid stimulation test is used in the assessment of gastric function. (iii) Distinguish the pentagastrin stimulation test from the augmented histamine test.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Preparation: the patient is informed about the test and its purpose, fasted for at least 12 hours prior, and informed consent is obtained; baseline gastric acid secretion and baseline blood tests, including serum gastrin, are measured.
• Procedure: pentagastrin is administered intravenously at a standard dose (usually 0.5 mcg/kg) over 2-3 minutes.
• The patient is monitored for adverse reactions during and after administration, and gastric acid secretion is monitored over a period (usually 15-60 minutes) following administration.
• Gastric aspirates are collected, or pH monitoring is used, to assess changes in gastric acid production, and blood tests including serum gastrin are repeated as necessary.
(ii)
• Gastric acid secretion tests measure the amount of acid produced by the stomach, helping to diagnose conditions such as gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
• Baseline and post-stimulation gastric acid measurements can distinguish conditions of too little acid (achlorhydria) from conditions of too much acid (as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
• Serum gastrin measurement alongside acid secretion helps interpret the cause of an abnormal acid secretory pattern.
(iii)
• The pentagastrin stimulation test uses intravenous pentagastrin at a standard dose (usually 0.5 mcg/kg) to directly stimulate parietal cells.
• The augmented histamine test is similar to the basic histamine stimulation test, which uses intravenous histamine (usually 0.01 mg/kg) to stimulate gastric acid secretion.
• The augmented histamine test involves additional steps to assess the response of gastric acid secretion to further stimuli, such as caffeine or insulin, given before or after histamine administration.
• Both tests follow a similar overall structure: patient fasting, baseline gastric acid and serum gastrin measurement, administration of the stimulating agent, and monitoring of gastric acid secretion and repeat gastrin over 15-60 minutes.
• The pentagastrin test uses a single synthetic peptide stimulant, whereas the augmented histamine test layers an additional agent (caffeine or insulin) onto histamine stimulation to further probe the acid secretory response.

(i)
• The fasting value (75 mg/dl) is within the normal range (60-100 mg/dl), and there is a rise in blood glucose after the load with a peak value observed at 1 hour.
• This pattern is consistent with a normal glucose tolerance curve.
(ii)
This should be reported as a normal glucose tolerance test result, with all urine glucose values negative.
(iii)
• There is normally a rapid insulin response to ingestion of a large oral glucose load, peaking in 30 to 60 minutes and returning to normal in about 3 hours.
• Patients with an appropriate insulin response tolerate the glucose dose easily, with only a minimal and transient rise in plasma glucose within 1 to 2 hours, and glucose does not spill into the urine.
(iv)
No further glucose tolerance testing is indicated on the basis of this normal result.
questions.question: A patient's oral glucose tolerance test shows fasting blood glucose of 75 mg/dl, rising to a peak of 150 mg/dl at 60 minutes, and returning to 70 mg/dl by 150 minutes, with urine glucose negative at every time point. (i) Interpret this result. (ii) State how this result should be reported. (iii) State what this result indicates about the patient's insulin response. (iv) State the action that follows from this result.

(i) Describe the intravenous glucose tolerance test under the headings of procedure and calculation of the glucose disappearance rate. (ii) Explain why the intravenous glucose tolerance test is used in preference to the oral test in certain patients. (iii) Distinguish the intravenous glucose tolerance test from the mini (WHO-recommended) glucose tolerance test.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Procedure: 25g of glucose dissolved in 100mL is given intravenously within 5 minutes, with completion of infusion taken as time zero, and blood samples taken at 10-minute intervals for the next hour.
• In another described method, 0.5 g/kg body weight (maximum 35g) as a 25 g/dL solution is given over 3 minutes, with blood collected every 10 minutes after the mid-injection time for 1 hour.
• Blood glucose concentrations decrease in an exponential manner, and the rate of glucose disappearance (K) is calculated from K = 70/t half, where t half is the number of minutes required for the blood glucose value to fall to half of its 10-minute value.
• Glucose values are plotted on a log scale against time, the best-fitting straight line is drawn, and t half is read from the graph.
(ii)
• The intravenous test is used when poor absorption of orally administered glucose might give a flat oral tolerance curve.
• It is used in patients unable to tolerate a large oral carbohydrate load, or with altered gastric physiology, such as after gastric resection.
• It also allows measurement of the first-phase insulin response, which can identify individuals at greatest risk of progression to type 1 diabetes mellitus.
(iii)
• The intravenous glucose tolerance test involves injecting glucose directly into a vein and sampling blood at 10-minute intervals over about an hour to calculate the rate of glucose disappearance (K value).
• The mini or modern glucose tolerance test, as recommended by WHO, instead uses only two samples: fasting (zero hour) and 2 hours after an oral glucose load, with urine samples also collected at the same times.
• In the intravenous test, in healthy individuals K usually exceeds 1.5%, while values less than 1.0% are considered diagnostic of diabetes.
• In the mini test, diagnosis is made from the variation observed between the fasting and 2-hour results, rather than from a calculated disappearance rate.
• The intravenous test bypasses gastrointestinal absorption entirely, whereas the mini test still relies on oral ingestion and gastrointestinal absorption of the glucose load, like the standard oral test but with fewer sampling points.

questions.question: A forensic sample of capillary blood from a fingertip prick is analysed by diffusion in specially blown glassware, oxidation with potassium dichromate and sulfuric acid, addition of potassium iodide, and back-titration with sodium thiosulfate using a starch indicator. (i) Identify the test being performed. (ii) State the principle underlying this method. (iii) Describe the procedural steps of this method. (iv) Interpret how the final result is expressed and used.
questions.answerText:
(i)
This is Widmark's micro-method of blood-ethanol analysis.
(ii)
• Ethanol can be separated from blood by diffusion and then oxidised, with the extent of oxidation reflecting the amount of ethanol present.
• The liberated iodine from the oxidation reaction is measured by titration, which is proportional to the amount of ethanol originally present.
(iii)
• Blood is drawn by pricking a fingertip or earlobe.
• Ethanol is separated from the blood by diffusion in specially blown glassware.
• The ethanol is then oxidised with a mixture of potassium dichromate and sulfuric acid, followed by addition of potassium iodide to the reaction mixture after oxidation.
• The liberated iodine is back-titrated with standard sodium thiosulfate, using a starch indicator to detect the endpoint.
(iv)
• Results are reported in mass per mass units, specifically milligrams of ethanol per gram of whole blood.
• This value is used to assess blood alcohol content for legal or medical purposes.

questions.question: (i) Describe the method used for serum bilirubin analysis under the headings of principle and procedure. (ii) Explain why this reaction is useful in practical chemical pathology. (iii) Distinguish the estimation of conjugated (direct) bilirubin from that of total bilirubin using this method.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Serum bilirubin is usually measured by the Jendrassik-Grof modification of the Van den Bergh reaction.
• Principle: bilirubin pigments in serum are divided into two forms, conjugated bilirubin, which reacts directly with the diazo reagent alone, and unconjugated bilirubin, which reacts indirectly.
• For total bilirubin, the diazo reagent is combined with a solubiliser/accelerator so that both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin react.
• The colour produced is measured spectrophotometrically and is proportional to the bilirubin concentration.
(ii)
• It allows the two components of serum bilirubin to be distinguished, which is essential for classifying hyperbilirubinaemia as conjugated or unconjugated.
• This distinction helps to differentiate prehepatic causes of jaundice (unconjugated) from intrahepatic and posthepatic causes (conjugated).
• It is a simple colorimetric method suited to routine testing in the clinical laboratory.
(iii)
• Conjugated (direct) bilirubin reacts with the diazo reagent alone, without any solubiliser or accelerator, because it is water-soluble.
• Total bilirubin is measured by reacting the sample with the diazo reagent plus a solubiliser/accelerator, so that both the conjugated and the normally protein-bound unconjugated bilirubin react.
• Unconjugated bilirubin is calculated indirectly as the difference between total bilirubin and the directly measured conjugated bilirubin.
• Unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble and is not excreted in urine, so its presence in serum can only be inferred by this difference, not measured directly with the diazo reagent alone.
• If direct bilirubin makes up more than about 15% of total bilirubin, this points to a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia rather than an unconjugated one.

questions.question: (i) Describe the basic structure and cellular composition of the liver relevant to its function. (ii) State the standard setting in which understanding this structure helps interpret a pattern of liver injury. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind the centrilobular zone of the liver being most susceptible to drug-induced damage.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The liver contains mainly two populations of cells: hepatocytes, constituting 60% of liver cells, and the remaining endothelial cells and Kupffer cells (reticuloendothelial cells) lining the hepatic sinusoids, along with vascular and supporting tissue cells.
• Hepatocytes radiate, like spokes of a wheel, from the central vein, forming anastomosing, fenestrated plates of liver cells separated by large vascular spaces called hepatic sinusoids.
• Blood flowing in the sinusoids is prevented from directly contacting hepatocytes by an endothelial lining composed of fenestrated sinusoidal lining cells.
• Resident macrophages, called Kupffer cells, are associated with the sinusoidal lining cells and are capable of phagocytosing bacteria and other foreign matter in the blood.
• The functional unit of the liver, the lobule, is hexagonal, with a portal triad at each corner, and blood passes from the portal tract along the sinusoids toward the central vein.
(ii)
Understanding this zonal blood flow helps interpret which part of the liver acinus is most affected in a given disease process.
(iii)
• The acinus can be divided into three functional zones based on oxygen content: periportal (highest oxygen, least susceptible to ischaemic damage), mediolobular (intermediate), and centrilobular (lowest oxygen, most susceptible to ischaemic and drug-induced damage).
• The centrilobular zone is also described as most involved in drug metabolism.
• Oxygen concentration in the blood reduces the farther cells are from the portal tract towards the central vein, since well-oxygenated blood enters via the portal tract and percolates toward the centre of the lobule.
• Cells around the central vein region therefore receive the least oxygenated blood and are most susceptible to anoxia (lack of oxygen).
• The centrilobular zone is also described as most involved in drug metabolism, meaning it is exposed to higher concentrations of drug metabolites and reactive intermediates.
• The combination of lowest oxygen supply and highest drug-metabolising activity makes the centrilobular zone the region most susceptible to both ischaemic and drug-induced liver damage.

questions.question: (i) Describe the basic structure, classification and biochemical role of plasma lipoproteins. (ii) State the standard clinical setting in which lipoprotein/lipid measurements are used. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind requiring a fasting specimen for a lipid profile.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Lipoproteins are spherical, soluble protein complexes that transport lipids such as cholesterol and triglyceride in body fluids, with hydrophobic lipids in the core and amphiphilic lipids and proteins on the surface.
• They are classified into five main groups by density: chylomicrons, very low density lipoproteins (VLDL), intermediate density lipoproteins (IDL), low density lipoproteins (LDL) and high density lipoproteins (HDL).
• Chylomicrons, VLDL and IDL are triglyceride-rich, and because of their large size scatter light, giving plasma a turbid (lipaemic) appearance at high concentrations, while LDL and HDL are smaller and contain mainly cholesterol.
• Chylomicrons transport exogenous (dietary) lipid from the intestine to cells, VLDL transports endogenous lipid from the liver to cells, LDL carries cholesterol to cells, and HDL transports cholesterol from cells back to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport).
• Lipoproteins carry apolipoproteins on their surface, which activate metabolic enzymes, maintain structural integrity, and facilitate cellular uptake of the lipoprotein.
(ii)
• Lipoprotein and cholesterol measurements are used to assess cardiovascular risk, since increased LDL cholesterol is associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease and increased HDL cholesterol with decreased cardiac risk.
• They are also used to classify primary and secondary dyslipidaemias.
(iii)
• Fasting plasma from normal individuals contains only VLDL, LDL and HDL particles.
• After a meal, chylomicrons are present, and if a lipaemic sample is left overnight at 4 degrees Celsius, the larger and less dense chylomicrons form a creamy layer on the surface.
• The smaller, denser VLDL and IDL particles do not rise in this way and may make the sample appear diffusely turbid, whereas LDL and HDL particles are too small to scatter light and do not contribute to turbidity.
• A nonfasting sample containing chylomicrons would therefore give a falsely turbid or inaccurate lipid measurement that does not reflect the individual's usual (fasting) lipid state.
• A fasting specimen avoids the contribution of dietary (exogenous) chylomicrons and ensures that only the endogenous lipoprotein classes (VLDL, LDL, HDL) relevant to standard lipid profile interpretation are present.

(i)
• Hormones are classified as polypeptide or protein hormones (such as insulin, parathyroid hormone, and ACTH), steroid hormones (such as cortisol and oestrogen), and amino acid-related hormones (such as catecholamines).
• A hormone is a chemical substance produced by an organ, cells of an organ, or scattered cells, having a specific regulatory effect on an organ or organs, and is produced at one site but acts at distant sites through the endocrine system.
• Hormones act in growth and development, exert homeostatic control of metabolic pathways, and regulate the production, use and storage of energy.
(ii)
• Samples used for hormone measurement include plasma, serum, urine and saliva.
• Because the metabolic environment plays a crucial role in hormone production, it is often essential to obtain a simultaneous sample for measurement of both the hormone and the molecule(s) it regulates, for example insulin with glucose, or parathyroid hormone with calcium.
• When evaluating possible hormone deficiency or excess, it is often necessary to perform a stimulation or suppression test.
(iii)
• Preanalytical factors known to affect hormone results include stress, drugs (for example insulin), food (for example banana), and exercise.
• Some hormones are directly affected by food (for example, insulin) or by circadian variability (for example, cortisol).
• Because of this, the timing of sample collection relative to meals, activity and time of day needs to be standardised or accounted for when interpreting a hormone result.
• Uncontrolled stress, exercise or drug intake before sampling could otherwise produce a hormone level that does not reflect the patient's usual or basal state.
• This is also why a simultaneously collected sample for the regulated molecule (such as glucose alongside insulin) is required, so that the hormone result can be interpreted in its proper metabolic context.
• Standardised stimulation or suppression protocols are used specifically to control for these variable influences when hormone deficiency or excess is being evaluated.
questions.question: (i) Describe the basic classification of hormones measured in the clinical laboratory. (ii) State the standard specimen requirements for hormone measurement. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind controlling preanalytical factors such as stress, drugs, food and exercise before a hormone sample is taken.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Vitamin A occurs naturally as vitamin A1 and vitamin A2 (retinol and 3-dehydroretinol), derived directly from dietary sources (primarily as retinyl esters) or from metabolism of dietary carotenoids (provitamin A), primarily beta-carotene.
• Food sources include low-fat dairy products and deep yellow or orange vegetables (carotenoid sources), and animal products (retinyl ester sources).
• Vitamin A (retinol) is the precursor of retinal, the light-sensitive group in rhodopsin and other visual pigments, and is essential for vision, cellular differentiation, growth, reproduction and immune function.
• Vitamin A is stored in the liver and transported in the circulation complexed to retinol-binding protein and transthyretin.
(ii)
• Vitamin A status is assessed when deficiency is suspected, presenting with night blindness, dry eyes and skin, or degenerative retinal changes, and can be measured using the Carr-Price method, the Neeld-Pearson method, or HPLC.
• It is also relevant in assessing immune function, since vitamin A is described as an anti-inflammatory vitamin with regulatory roles in cellular and humoral immune responses.
(iii)
• Overdose of vitamin A can result in dry skin and headache.
• Overdose can also cause liver damage.
• Overdose can result in birth defects in pregnant women.
• Vitamin A derivatives such as isotretinoin (Accutane) can cause birth defects and have been associated with suicide.
• Because vitamin A is stored in the liver and can accumulate, excess intake is of particular concern, especially maternal accumulation, which is also linked to preterm birth, underscoring that vitamin A status affects pregnancy outcomes.
• This is why caution around vitamin A supplementation, and vitamin A-derived medications, is specifically emphasised in women who are or may become pregnant.
questions.question: (i) Describe the basic structure, sources and biochemical role of vitamin A. (ii) State the standard clinical setting in which vitamin A status is assessed. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution against vitamin A overdose, particularly in pregnancy.

questions.answerText:
(i)
A serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L is above the threshold of 5.0 mEq/L used to define hyperkalaemia.
(ii)
This should be reported as hyperkalaemia.
(iii)
• Recognised causes of hyperkalaemia include impaired renal function, certain medications (potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs), cellular shift of potassium from tissue damage, metabolic acidosis, hypoaldosteronism, excessive potassium intake, and Addison's disease.
• The muscle weakness and palpitations reported are consistent with the described features of hyperkalaemia, namely weakness/paralysis and irregular heartbeats from disrupted cardiac electrical activity.
(iv)
Given the risk of arrhythmia and cardiac arrest associated with hyperkalaemia, prompt further evaluation of the underlying cause and monitoring is warranted, along with confirming the result is not due to a haemolysed sample.
questions.question: A patient's serum potassium is reported as 5.8 mEq/L, with associated muscle weakness and palpitations. (i) Interpret this result. (ii) State how this result is reported. (iii) State what this result indicates about possible underlying causes. (iv) State the action that follows from this result.

A patient with a family history of diabetes is scheduled for a standard oral glucose tolerance test. (i) State the test appropriate for this patient. (ii) State the principle of the test. (iii) State the materials required to perform it. (iv) State factors that could interfere with (invalidate) the result. (v) State the precautions/patient preparation needed to obtain a valid result.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The standard oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is appropriate.
(ii)
The test measures the ability of the body to utilise glucose in the blood circulation, by measuring plasma glucose before and after a specific oral glucose load.
(iii)
• An oral glucose solution: 75g for non-pregnant patients (or 100g for pregnant patients), dissolved in 300mL of lemon juice/water.
• A method for measuring blood glucose and testing urine for glucose at each interval.
(iv)
• Smoking, stress, and exercise during the test can affect glucose levels.
• Fasting or reduced caloric intake before the test can cause glucose intolerance.
• Drugs (including tobacco) that could interfere with the test results should be discontinued before testing.
(v)
• The patient should have adequate food intake with adequate carbohydrate (150g) for at least 3 days before the test, and should fast for 12 hours before the test.
• The patient's weight should be obtained to determine the appropriate glucose loading dose, especially in children.
• During the test, only water is allowed; no other liquids, food, tobacco, or smoking are permitted, and the patient must ingest the entire glucose load.

questions.question: A blood sample is collected for insulin measurement, together with a simultaneous sample for glucose. (i) State the test appropriate for measuring the hormone. (ii) State the principle of this test. (iii) State the materials/reagents required. (iv) State the preanalytical factors that could interfere with the result. (v) State the precaution taken by collecting a simultaneous glucose sample.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Immunoassay is the appropriate test for measuring insulin.
(ii)
Immunoassays measure analyte concentration through antigen-antibody reactions, using an antibody specific to insulin, with a label used to generate a measurable signal.
(iii)
A specific antibody to insulin and a detection label (for example, an enzyme such as horseradish peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase).
(iv)
• Preanalytical factors known to affect hormone results include stress, drugs, food (for example banana), and exercise.
• Insulin is directly affected by food intake.
(v)
• Because the metabolic environment plays a crucial role in hormone production, a simultaneous sample for the regulated molecule (glucose, in the case of insulin) is collected.
• This allows the insulin result to be interpreted in its proper metabolic context, rather than in isolation.

questions.question: (i) Describe examples of classical vitamin deficiency diseases and the vitamins associated with them. (ii) State how a combination of dietary history, physical examination and laboratory measurement is applied in diagnosing a vitamin deficiency. (iii) Explain why relying on clinical symptoms alone can give an invalid diagnosis of vitamin deficiency in early or mild, chronic deficiency states.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Scurvy is associated with vitamin C deficiency, historically linked to sailors and the protective effect of lime consumption.
• Rickets is associated with vitamin D deficiency, notable in the early industrial age.
• Beriberi is associated with thiamine deficiency, notable in alcoholics, and pellagra is associated with niacin deficiency.
• Megaloblastic anaemia is associated with folic acid deficiency, and pernicious anaemia (with neuropathy) is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency.
• The term vitamin has a historical basis in deficiency states that were relieved by specific food intake.
(ii)
• Variabilities in the clinical expression of vitamin abnormalities result from differences in the specific cause, degree, and duration of vitamin inadequacy, the simultaneous presence of other nutritional insufficiencies, and increased metabolic demands from conditions such as pregnancy, infection and cancer.
• A combination of dietary history, physical examination, and laboratory measurements is often required to diagnose a vitamin deficiency.
(iii)
• The clinical symptoms of vitamin deficiencies are usually nonspecific in the early stages and in mild, chronic deficiency states.
• Because early symptoms are nonspecific, they can resemble those of other conditions or of no condition at all, making a diagnosis based on symptoms alone unreliable.
• Abnormal increases in metabolism that require a higher supply of a vitamin may be termed vitamin insufficiency or vitamin dependency, depending on the level of supply demanded, adding further variability to how a given intake level presents clinically.
• Simultaneous nutritional insufficiencies and increased metabolic demand (as in pregnancy, infection, or cancer) can also alter or mask the clinical picture of a specific vitamin deficiency.
• For these reasons, dietary history and laboratory measurement must be combined with physical examination, rather than relying on clinical symptoms alone, to reach a valid diagnosis of vitamin deficiency.

questions.question: A patient's investigations show urine sodium less than 20 mmol/L and a urine/serum osmolality ratio greater than 1.2, with disproportionately raised serum urea relative to creatinine. (i) Interpret this pattern. (ii) State how this is reported using the renal failure index. (iii) State what this pattern indicates about the cause of renal impairment. (iv) State the action that follows from this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Low urine sodium (less than 20 mmol/L) with a urine/serum osmolality ratio greater than 1.2, and a disproportionate rise in urea relative to creatinine, is the pattern described for pre-renal impairment.
• In pre-renal acute failure, the kidney excretes a small volume of concentrated urine with a low sodium concentration.
(ii)
This is reported as a renal failure index (RFI) of less than 1, calculated as (urinary sodium x plasma creatinine)/urine creatinine.
(iii)
• This pattern indicates pre-renal impairment, due to reduced renal perfusion, as seen with shock, hypotension, or heart failure.
• It is distinguished from intrinsic renal causes, which instead show urine sodium greater than 40 mmol/L and a urine/serum osmolality ratio less than 1.2.
(iv)
The underlying cause of reduced renal perfusion (for example, hypotension, hypovolaemia or heart failure) should be identified and corrected.

(i)
• Creatinine is derived from muscle creatine, with about 1-2% of muscle creatine converted to creatinine daily, so the amount produced relates to muscle mass.
• It is freely filtered at the glomerulus, with only a small amount (about 10%) also secreted by the renal tubules.
• It is produced at a fairly constant rate, is not reabsorbed or metabolised by the renal tubules, and its concentration is inversely related to the glomerular filtration rate.
• The reference interval given for serum creatinine is 53-115, and it is an endogenous substance that is routinely and easily assayed.
(ii)
• Creatinine is measured as part of renal function testing, to estimate glomerular filtration rate and to detect the presence and extent of renal damage.
• It is used together with the Cockcroft and Gault formula, which also requires the patient's age, sex and weight, to predict creatinine clearance.
(iii)
• Plasma creatinine can increase following a protein load, described as the goulash effect, with an 80% rise in creatinine reported after 300g of cooked beef.
• There is less variability in early morning creatinine measurements compared with other times of day.
• Strenuous exercise may increase creatinine by about 14%.
• Because creatinine reflects muscle mass, factors such as age, sex, race, body builders, amputees and recent ingestion of cooked meat can all influence estimated GFR calculations from creatinine.
• Muscle mass, and therefore creatinine, is more difficult to predict in oedematous patients, in late pregnancy, and in patients with muscle wasting or liver disease.
• Formulae for predicting clearance from plasma creatinine apply only in a steady state and are not reliable in acute renal failure, so a stable period of renal function of about 4 days is required.
