• The appearance of the sample (clear, diffusely turbid, or with a creamy surface layer) is then examined visually.
(iv)
• A creamy surface layer on an otherwise clear lower layer indicates the presence of chylomicrons, which should not normally be present in a fasting sample.
• Given that this is stated to be a fasting sample, the presence of chylomicrons suggests a disorder of chylomicron clearance, such as familial hyperchylomicronaemia (Type I) or a combined hyperlipidaemia (Type V).
• If the sample had instead been diffusely turbid without a creamy layer, this would suggest elevated VLDL/IDL rather than chylomicrons.
• Correlation with a formal lipid profile and clinical assessment is needed to classify the specific dyslipidaemia.

questions.question: (i) Describe the different patterns (curves) that may be seen on a glucose tolerance test. (ii) State how each curve pattern is applied in identifying the underlying condition. (iii) Explain why failing to also test urine glucose alongside blood glucose can give an incomplete picture of a patient's glucose tolerance curve.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Curve patterns described include the normal curve, the diabetic curve (moderate or severe), the renal glycosuria pattern, the lag curve, and the flat curve.
• In a normal curve, fasting blood glucose is within the normal range, glucose rises after the load with a peak around 1 hour, and returns to normal in about 3 hours, with urine glucose remaining negative throughout.
• In a diabetic curve, fasting and post-load blood glucose values are elevated compared with normal, and urine glucose becomes positive as blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold, with the severe diabetic curve showing higher absolute values than the moderate diabetic curve.
• In the lag curve, fasting blood glucose is normal but there is a sharp rise within 30 minutes to 1 hour that exceeds the renal threshold, followed by a rapid decline back to normal, with transient urine glucose positivity, due to increased gut glucose absorption or delayed insulin action.
• The renal glycosuria pattern shows blood glucose within normal limits (a normal glucose tolerance curve) but with urine glucose positive at some sampling points, due to a lowered renal threshold from a renal tubular defect in glucose reabsorption.
• The flat curve shows fasting blood glucose 80mg/dl or below, with all samples showing low blood glucose and negative urine glucose, seen in hypoactivity of other endocrine organs such as hypopituitarism and Addison's disease, and in malabsorption.
(ii)
• The lag curve is associated with hyperthyroidism, pregnancy, post-gastroenterostomy states, and early diabetes mellitus.
• Renal glycosuria can be caused by early diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, renal disease, heavy metal poisoning, and can be seen in children of diabetic parents.
(iii)
• In renal glycosuria, blood glucose values remain within normal limits and the glucose tolerance curve itself is normal, yet urine glucose is positive at some points.
• If only blood glucose were measured, without urine glucose, this pattern (normal blood glucose curve with positive urine glucose) would be missed entirely.
• Testing urine glucose alongside blood glucose at each time point is therefore necessary to detect a lowered renal threshold for glucose, which is a distinct finding from the shape of the blood glucose curve itself.
• This combined blood-and-urine approach is also how the standard oral glucose tolerance test protocol is structured, since urine is collected and analysed for glucose at each sampling interval alongside the blood sample.

questions.question: (i) Describe the one-step uricase enzymatic method for estimating uric acid under the headings of principle and reaction. (ii) Explain why the one-step uricase method is used as the reference method for uric acid estimation. (iii) Distinguish the uricase method from the phosphotungstic acid (PTA) reduction chemical method.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Principle: uric acid is oxidised by the enzyme uricase in the presence of oxygen.
• Reaction: uric acid plus oxygen, catalysed by uricase, forms allantoin and hydrogen peroxide.
(ii)
• This one-step uricase reaction is described as the reference method for uric acid determination.
• It is designated the reference method, implying it is the most accurate and widely accepted standard against which other methods are compared.
• It is an enzymatic method, using the specific action of uricase on uric acid, which gives it greater specificity than a purely chemical reduction reaction.
• Coupled enzymatic reactions can also be built from this basic reaction (for example, further reacting the hydrogen peroxide produced) to allow spectrophotometric measurement of the reaction product.
(iii)
• The uricase method oxidises uric acid enzymatically with oxygen to form allantoin and hydrogen peroxide, which is the reference method.
• The phosphotungstic acid (PTA) reduction technique is a chemical method in which PTA reacts with uric acid under alkaline conditions to form allantoin and tungsten blue, measured at 680 nm.
• The PTA method is also known by named variants such as the Caraway method and the Brown method.
• Coupled enzymatic variants of the uricase method exist, for example reacting the hydrogen peroxide produced with ethanol and catalase to generate acetaldehyde, measured via an aldehyde dehydrogenase/NADH reaction at 340 nm, or reacting the hydrogen peroxide with methanol to form formaldehyde, measured as a coloured compound at 410 nm.
• The chemical (PTA) method relies on a colour-forming chemical reduction reaction, while the enzymatic (uricase) methods rely on a specific enzyme-catalysed oxidation of uric acid.
• Because it is enzyme-based and specific to uric acid, the uricase method is preferred as the reference method over the less specific chemical PTA reduction technique.

(i)
This is the pentagastrin stimulation test of gastric function.
(ii)
• Pentagastrin stimulates parietal cells to secrete gastric acid, so the response to a standard dose reflects the stomach's acid secretory capacity.
• Comparing baseline (unstimulated) and post-pentagastrin (stimulated) gastric acid secretion and serum gastrin distinguishes different patterns of gastric acid abnormality.
(iii)
• The patient fasts for at least 12 hours, informed consent is obtained, and baseline gastric acid secretion and serum gastrin are measured.
• Pentagastrin is administered intravenously at a standard dose (usually 0.5 mcg/kg) over 2-3 minutes, with monitoring for adverse reactions.
• Gastric acid secretion is monitored over 15-60 minutes following administration, using gastric aspirates or pH monitoring, with serum gastrin repeated as necessary.
(iv)
• This test helps diagnose conditions such as gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
• It can help distinguish achlorhydria (lack of stomach acid) from excessive acid secretion, as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
• The combination of gastric acid response and serum gastrin level helps interpret the underlying cause of an abnormal acid secretory pattern.
questions.question: A fasted patient has baseline gastric acid secretion and serum gastrin measured, is then given intravenous pentagastrin at 0.5 mcg/kg, and gastric aspirate/pH is monitored over the next 15-60 minutes, with serum gastrin repeated. (i) Identify the test being performed. (ii) State the principle underlying this test. (iii) Describe the procedure followed in this scenario. (iv) Interpret what this test result would be used to diagnose.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Absorption spectroscopy is a spectroscopic technique that measures the frequency or wavelength of light absorbed as a result of interaction between light and a sample.
• Principle: materials possess an absorption spectrum, a range of radiation absorbed at different frequencies depending on their atomic and molecular composition.
• Apparatus/materials: a spectrophotometer, with the solvent and the sample solution held in separate cuvettes.
• Procedure: the solvent blank is read first to determine light loss from the solvent alone, then the sample cuvette is read at frequencies usually ranging from 200-800 nm, and absorbance is plotted against known concentrations to read off an unknown concentration.
(ii)
• The absorbance of a sample depends on the number of excited electrons, which in turn depends on the concentration of molecules in the sample, allowing quantification of a substance.
• It allows the presence of a particular substance to be determined and then quantified.
• It permits determination of the atomic and molecular structure and composition of substances.
• It has been applied to remote sensing, allowing the concentration of hazardous substances to be determined without direct contact between the instrument and the sample.
(iii)
• Absorption spectroscopy measures the absorbance of molecules already in solution across a wavelength range, using cuvettes and a spectrophotometer.
• Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) instead vaporises the liquid sample into a gas using a fuel-rich flame, and measures absorption of a specific wavelength of light by free electrons in that gaseous atomic state.
• AAS uses a lamp set to the necessary wavelength as a light source and a detector to record absorbance of the atoms in the gas, with a graph of absorbance against concentration plotted from standards.
• AAS is applied to quantitative and qualitative determination of metallic elements in biological systems, water, soil and pharmaceutical products, whereas absorption spectroscopy is used more generally for determining the presence and concentration of a substance in solution.
questions.question: (i) Describe the technique of absorption spectroscopy under the headings of principle, apparatus/materials, and procedure. (ii) Explain why this technique is preferred for measuring analyte concentration in a chemical pathology laboratory. (iii) Distinguish absorption spectroscopy from atomic absorption spectroscopy as methods for analysing a sample.

(i) Describe the classification of the causes of acute renal failure. (ii) State how urine and blood indices are applied to differentiate pre-renal from intrinsic renal acute failure. (iii) Explain why using only serum urea and creatinine, without urine sodium or osmolality indices, can give an incomplete or invalid classification of acute renal failure.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Acute renal failure is classified into pre-renal causes (decreased renal perfusion, due to shock, hypotension or heart failure), renal causes (nephrotoxic drugs, kidney diseases such as glomerulonephritis or acute tubular necrosis, and systemic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis), and post-renal causes (obstruction to the urinary pathway, such as stones, tumours or prostatic enlargement).
• Acute renal failure is a rapid, reversible loss of renal function, in contrast to chronic renal failure, which is irreversible with slow loss of renal function.
• Chronic renal failure shows increased urea, creatinine, potassium, phosphate and magnesium, with decreased creatinine clearance, sodium, calcium, calcitriol, proteins and pH, along with fixed specific gravity and polyuria.
(ii)
• In pre-renal acute failure, the kidney excretes a small volume of concentrated urine with a low sodium concentration: urine sodium less than 20 mmol/L, urine/serum osmolality ratio greater than 1.2, urine urea to serum urea ratio greater than 20, renal failure index less than 1, and fractional sodium excretion less than 1.
• In renal (intrinsic) causes, the pattern differs: urine sodium greater than 40 mmol/L, urine osmolality less than 400, urine/serum osmolality ratio less than 1.2, fractional sodium excretion greater than 2, renal failure index greater than 2, and urine urea to serum urea ratio less than 10.
• In post-renal causes, the laboratory pattern is described as similar to pre-renal causes.
• The renal failure index is calculated as (urinary sodium x plasma creatinine)/urine creatinine, with a value below 1 indicating pre-renal impairment and above 2 indicating tubular impairment.
(iii)
• Urea and creatinine both rise in all three categories (pre-renal, renal, post-renal) of acute renal failure, so their absolute levels alone do not distinguish between the categories.
• It is the urine sodium concentration, urine/serum osmolality ratio, fractional sodium excretion, and renal failure index that differentiate a pre-renal pattern from an intrinsic renal pattern.
• Without these urine-based indices, reliance on serum urea and creatinine alone cannot tell whether reduced renal perfusion (pre-renal) or actual tubular/glomerular damage (renal) is responsible for the abnormal results.
• Because pre-renal and post-renal patterns can appear laboratory-similar, urine indices combined with clinical assessment of a possible obstruction are both needed to tell them apart.
• Relying on urea and creatinine alone, without these urine indices, therefore risks an incomplete or invalid classification of the type of acute renal failure present.

(i)
• Principle: proteins complex with copper ions in an alkaline environment, and coordination of peptide bonds with the copper ions forms a violet-coloured complex that is quantified spectrophotometrically.
• Reagent preparation: Biuret reagent is prepared by mixing copper sulfate with sodium potassium tartrate and sodium hydroxide, creating an alkaline solution containing copper ions.
• Procedure: the protein sample is mixed with the Biuret reagent, and the complexation reaction is facilitated in the alkaline environment.
• Colour development: the copper-protein complex changes colour from blue to violet, with the intensity of colour directly proportional to the protein concentration in the sample.
(ii)
• The Biuret method shows a linear response over a wide range of protein concentrations, allowing accurate quantification.
• It is more sensitive than the older Kjeldahl method, making it suitable for samples with lower protein concentrations.
• It is a classical colorimetric assay that can be read spectrophotometrically, making it convenient for routine laboratory use.
• It reacts with the peptide bonds common to all proteins, making it a general method for estimating total protein rather than one specific protein.
(iii)
• The Biuret method depends on complexation of copper ions with peptide bonds in an alkaline medium, producing a violet colour, whereas the Lowry method is based on reduction of Folin-Ciocalteu reagent by amino acid residues in proteins under alkaline conditions, producing a blue colour.
• Biuret reagent is prepared from copper sulfate, sodium potassium tartrate and sodium hydroxide, while the Lowry reagent additionally includes Folin-Ciocalteu phenol reagent.
• The Lowry method is more sensitive than the Biuret method, allowing detection of lower protein concentrations, though the Biuret method is not specific to protein and can react with other peptide-bond-containing substances leading to overestimation.
• The Lowry method's reagent preparation is more time-consuming, and both methods can suffer interference, from reducing or chelating agents in the Biuret method, and from detergents and reducing agents in the Lowry method.
questions.question: (i) Describe the Biuret method for total protein determination under the headings of principle, reagent preparation, and procedure. (ii) Explain why the Biuret method is commonly used for estimating total protein in practical chemical pathology. (iii) Distinguish the Biuret method from the Lowry method of protein estimation.

(i) Describe the basic biochemical roles of potassium in the body. (ii) State the standard clinical setting in which serum potassium is measured. (iii) Explain the reasoning behind treating tissue damage or trauma as a cause of a raised potassium result.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Potassium is crucial for the repolarisation phase of nerve impulses, restoring the resting membrane potential after sodium causes depolarisation.
• Potassium is essential for muscle function, including contraction and relaxation, and influences the excitability of muscle cells.
• Potassium is critical for the normal electrical activity of the heart, helping establish and maintain the resting membrane potential of cardiac cells and regulate heart rate.
• Potassium, as primarily an intracellular cation, helps regulate osmotic pressure inside cells and contributes to acid-base balance through cellular exchange of hydrogen ions.
• Potassium influences enzyme activity and participates in protein and nucleic acid synthesis, and the kidneys help excrete excess potassium and reabsorb it when levels are low.
(ii)
• Serum potassium is measured to assess cardiac electrical activity, muscle function, acid-base status and renal handling of electrolytes.
• Hyperkalaemia is defined as a serum potassium level above 5.0 mEq/L.
(iii)
• Potassium is primarily an intracellular cation, so cells contain much higher potassium concentrations than plasma.
• Tissue damage or trauma can cause the release of potassium from cells into the bloodstream, listed as a cause of hyperkalaemia through a cellular shift of potassium.
• Because of this large intracellular-to-extracellular potassium gradient, even localised tissue damage can release enough potassium to significantly raise the measured serum level.
• Metabolic acidosis, such as diabetic ketoacidosis or severe kidney disease, similarly causes a shift of potassium out of cells and into the blood.
• Recognising cellular shift as a cause is important so that a raised potassium result is correctly attributed to tissue damage or acidosis, rather than being assumed to reflect a primary renal or hormonal cause such as impaired excretion or reduced aldosterone.

questions.question: (i) Describe the classification of laboratory methods for estimating amylase. (ii) State how each method measures the amylase reaction. (iii) Explain why a chromogenic method might be selected in preference to an amyloclastic method for estimating amylase in practice.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Laboratory methods of estimating amylase are classified as amyloclastic, saccharogenic, and chromogenic methods.
• The amyloclastic method measures the disappearance of the starch substrate.
• The saccharogenic method measures the appearance of the reaction product, while the chromogenic method measures the increasing colour of the product coupled with a chromogenic dye.
(ii)
• Amyloclastic methods track the loss of starch as amylase hydrolyses it, so the substrate concentration decreases as the reaction proceeds.
• Saccharogenic methods track the appearance of the breakdown products (such as glucose, maltose and dextrin) as amylase acts on starch.
• Chromogenic methods couple the product of the amylase reaction to a dye whose colour intensity increases as more product is formed, allowing spectrophotometric measurement.
• A chromogenic method produces a coloured product that can be measured spectrophotometrically, which is well suited to automated, routine laboratory analysis.
(iii)
• Because the colour intensity increases with the amount of product formed, it can give a more direct and readily quantifiable signal than tracking the disappearance of a substrate.
• The amyloclastic method depends on measuring a decreasing substrate concentration, which can be less sensitive at the endpoint compared with measuring an increasing coloured product.
• The choice of method in a given laboratory therefore depends on which produces a signal (colour) that is convenient to measure with the equipment available.
• All three approaches (amyloclastic, saccharogenic, chromogenic) are ways of assessing amylase's action on starch, but they differ in whether they monitor loss of substrate, appearance of product, or a colour reaction coupled to the product.
• Selecting a chromogenic method reflects a general preference in routine laboratories for assays with an easily and reliably measured colorimetric endpoint.

(i)
• Vitamins are classified into two classes: water-soluble vitamins and fat-soluble vitamins.
• The fat-soluble vitamins are vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin E and vitamin K.
• Vitamins are organic nutrients required in small quantities for growth, maintenance and reproduction; they generally cannot be synthesised by the body and must be supplied in the diet.
(ii)
• Vitamin A is stored in the liver and can be stored to prevent deficiency for as long as 10 months.
• Vitamin D can be stored to prevent deficiency for 3 to 4 months.
• Vitamin B12 (a water-soluble vitamin) can be stored to last for at least 1 year and maybe several years, but fat-soluble vitamins in general are described as being stored in the body's fat and liver reserves rather than being readily excreted.
(iii)
• Because fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate in fatty tissue and the liver, prolonged high intake builds up body stores over time.
• Vitamin A overdose can result in dry skin, headache, liver damage, and birth defects in pregnant women, and vitamin A derivatives can cause birth defects and have been linked to suicide.
• Because vitamin A (a fat-soluble vitamin) is stored in the liver rather than being readily excreted, repeated or excessive intake accumulates and increases the risk of reaching toxic levels.
• This storage and accumulation property is characteristic of the fat-soluble vitamins as a group (vitamin A, D, E and K), which are stored in the body's fat and liver reserves.
• In contrast, the clinical picture described for vitamins overall emphasises deficiency, and the classical vitamin-deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, beriberi, pellagra, megaloblastic anaemia, pernicious anaemia) rather than routine toxicity.
• It is therefore the storage characteristic of the fat-soluble vitamin class that explains why toxicity is a particular concern for this group, distinguishing them from the general vitamin deficiency-oriented picture described for vitamins as a whole.
questions.question: (i) Describe the classification of vitamins into fat-soluble and water-soluble groups. (ii) State how this classification affects the way each group is stored and supplied in the body. (iii) Explain why fat-soluble vitamins carry a greater risk of toxicity from overdose than is generally described for the vitamins overall.

A patient's fasting, 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150 minute blood glucose values after an oral glucose load are 230, 300, 345, 365, 350 and 330 mg/dl, with urine glucose strongly positive throughout. (i) Identify the specimens and test being performed. (ii) State the biochemical principle underlying this test. (iii) Describe the standard procedure for carrying out this test. (iv) Interpret this pattern of results.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The specimens are venous blood and urine, collected as part of a glucose tolerance test.
• Blood glucose is estimated in all samples and urine is analysed for the presence of glucose.
(ii)
• Glucose tolerance means the ability of the body to utilise glucose in the blood circulation, measured as plasma glucose before and after a specific oral glucose load.
• It is used to assist in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and to evaluate patients with hypoglycaemia.
(iii)
• The patient is prepared with adequate carbohydrate intake for at least 3 days and a 12-hour fast, then fasting (zero-hour) blood and urine samples are collected.
• An oral glucose solution (75g for non-pregnant patients or 100g for pregnant patients) dissolved in 300mL of lemon juice/water is given.
• Venous blood and urine samples are then collected at 30-minute intervals for up to 150 minutes, with only water permitted during the test.
• Glucose is estimated in every blood sample, and urine is analysed for glucose at each interval.
(iv)
• This pattern, with markedly elevated fasting and post-load blood glucose values and strongly positive urine glucose throughout, corresponds to a severe diabetic curve.
• Blood glucose remains well above the renal threshold at every sampling point, so glucose spills into the urine throughout the test.
• This result is consistent with diabetes mellitus, distinct from the moderate diabetic curve, which shows somewhat lower blood glucose values.

questions.question: (i) Describe the fecal elastase-1 test under the headings of principle and specimen used. (ii) Explain why fecal elastase-1 is preferred as a practical screening test of pancreatic exocrine function. (iii) Distinguish fecal elastase-1 from fecal chymotrypsin as tests of pancreatic function.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Fecal elastase-1 measures the amount of elastase, an enzyme secreted by the exocrine pancreas, present in a stool specimen.
• A stool sample is collected and analysed for the presence and concentration of elastase.
• A low fecal elastase (less than 200 micrograms per gram) after 4 weeks of age indicates pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
(ii)
• It is a noninvasive test, not requiring gastrointestinal intubation, making it simpler and cheaper to perform than the secretin-CCK test.
• Fecal elastase remains the test of choice among the noninvasive tests described.
• It is used to separate patients with normal from impaired pancreatic function without the discomfort of intubation.
(iii)
• Fecal chymotrypsin is based on the reduction in secretion of pancreatic enzymes, measured by directly assaying chymotrypsin activity in feces.
• Chymotrypsin is completely digested during its passage through the gut in adults, but its residual activity in feces is stable for several days.
• Output of chymotrypsin in stool correlates poorly with chymotrypsin secretion in duodenal contents measured after secretin-CCK stimulation.
• In patients without pancreatic disease, the incidence of falsely low fecal chymotrypsin results is between 10-15%.
• Fecal elastase-1, by contrast, is described as remaining the test of choice among the noninvasive pancreatic function tests, implying better reliability than fecal chymotrypsin.
• Both are noninvasive, stool-based tests, but they measure different pancreatic enzymes (elastase versus chymotrypsin) with different degrees of correlation to true pancreatic secretory function.

questions.question: A midstream urine sample from a patient with dysuria and frequency gives a positive nitrite test and a positive leukocyte esterase test on dipstick. (i) Identify the test being performed and what each positive result detects. (ii) State the principle behind the nitrite and leukocyte esterase reactions. (iii) Describe how the dipstick test is carried out. (iv) Interpret this combination of results.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• This is dipstick urinalysis; a positive nitrite result detects bacteria capable of converting urinary nitrate to nitrite, and a positive leukocyte esterase result detects the presence of white blood cells, whole or lysed.
• Both are chemical screening tests performed on a fresh urine sample.
(ii)
• Nitrates in the urine are converted to nitrites in the presence of Gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli; a positive nitrite test is a surrogate marker of bacteriuria.
• Leukocyte esterase gives a positive result from the presence of white blood cells (whole or lysed), so pyuria can be detected even if the white cells are damaged.
(iii)
• A reagent strip is dipped into a freshly voided urine sample.
• The colour changes on the nitrite and leukocyte esterase pads are read and compared with the reference chart.
(iv)
• A positive nitrite test suggests infection, with a positive predictive value of about 95%, while a negative nitrite test does not completely rule out infection (negative predictive value about 25%).
• A positive leukocyte esterase test indicates pyuria, and a negative leukocyte esterase test rules out infection in most cases.
• Together, a positive nitrite and positive leukocyte esterase result is consistent with a urinary tract infection, likely due to a Gram-negative organism such as E. coli.
• Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity should be pursued, since it should only be omitted when there is no additional evidence of urinary tract infection, and here the dipstick findings constitute that evidence.

questions.question: A jaundiced patient's urine dipstick shows a positive bilirubin result and a normal urobilinogen result. (i) Identify the tests being performed on this urine sample. (ii) State the principle behind bilirubin appearing in urine. (iii) Describe how urine bilirubin and urobilinogen are tested. (iv) Interpret this combination of findings.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The tests performed are the urine bilirubin test and the urine urobilinogen test, both part of a standard urinalysis dipstick panel.
• Both are chemical screening tests on a urine sample.
(ii)
• Bilirubin is not present in the urine of normal healthy individuals; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not water-soluble, so it is not filtered by the kidney or excreted in urine.
• Bilirubin appears in urine only when conjugated bilirubin is elevated in the plasma, since conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and can be filtered and excreted.
(iii)
• Urine bilirubin can be tested by dipstick, with false positives seen in patients on phenothiazines and false negatives with ascorbic acid, aged samples, rifampicin, or exposure to UV light.
• Urine urobilinogen is tested using Ehrlich's reagent, which gives a magenta colour, and urobilinogen is reported as normal or raised, since it is a normal component of urine.
(iv)
• A positive urine bilirubin result indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and may be an early indicator of liver disease, sometimes occurring before clinical jaundice is apparent.
• A normal (not raised) urobilinogen, in this context, does not support the increased urobilinogen pattern seen in some hepatic or haemolytic conditions.
• The combination of positive bilirubin with normal urobilinogen is more in keeping with a cholestatic or obstructive process impairing excretion of conjugated bilirubin into the gut, rather than a purely haemolytic process, which would be expected to raise urobilinogen.
• Further liver function tests (bilirubin fractionation, ALP, GGT, transaminases) would help confirm the pattern.

(i)
• Fasting blood glucose is normal, but there is a sharp rise within 30 minutes to 1 hour that exceeds the renal threshold, followed by a rapid decline back to normal levels.
• Some urine samples contain glucose where blood glucose is above the renal threshold, but this resolves as blood glucose falls.
(ii)
This pattern is reported/named as a lag curve.
(iii)
• A lag curve is due to an increased rate of glucose absorption from the gut and a delay in insulin action (insulin function lagging behind).
• Recognised causes include hyperthyroidism, pregnancy, a post-gastroenterostomy state, and early diabetes mellitus.
(iv)
The result should be correlated with the clinical picture (for example, thyroid status, pregnancy, surgical history) to identify the underlying cause.
questions.question: A patient's blood glucose is 90 mg/dl fasting, rises sharply to 230 mg/dl at 30 minutes, then declines rapidly to 90 mg/dl by 180 minutes, with urine glucose transiently positive at 30 and 60 minutes only. (i) Interpret this pattern. (ii) State how this pattern is reported/named. (iii) State what conditions this pattern indicates. (iv) State the action that follows from this finding.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Causes of hypernatraemia include inadequate water intake, excessive water loss (dehydration from vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating, or fever), diabetes insipidus, and excessive sodium intake.
• Causes of hyperkalaemia include impaired renal function, certain medications (potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs), cellular shift of potassium from tissue damage or trauma, metabolic acidosis, hypoaldosteronism, excessive potassium intake, and Addison's disease (adrenal insufficiency).
• Features of hypernatraemia range from thirst, dry mucous membranes, restlessness and confusion, to muscle twitching, seizures, elevated heart rate, orthostatic hypotension and decreased urine output.
• Features of hyperkalaemia range from weakness/paralysis and tingling or numbness, to irregular heartbeats, respiratory distress, abdominal cramping, mental confusion, oliguria/anuria and, in extreme cases, cardiac arrest.
(ii)
• Identifying whether hypernatraemia results from inadequate intake, excessive loss, diabetes insipidus, or excess intake directs the appropriate correction.
• Identifying whether hyperkalaemia results from impaired renal excretion, medication effect, cellular shift, acidosis, or reduced aldosterone directs management, such as addressing the causative drug, correcting acidosis, or treating adrenal insufficiency.
• Because both hypernatraemia and hyperkalaemia can have serious systemic effects, recognising the underlying cause helps direct prompt, cause-specific treatment.
• Individual responses and presentation can vary, and underlying health conditions or comorbidities can influence how these electrolyte imbalances present.
(iii)
• Potassium is primarily an intracellular cation, present in blood cells at much higher concentration than in plasma.
• Tissue damage or trauma is a recognised cause of hyperkalaemia because it causes potassium to shift out of damaged cells into the bloodstream.
• Haemolysis of a blood sample similarly ruptures red blood cells and releases their intracellular potassium into the serum/plasma being tested.
• This artefactually raises the measured potassium concentration without reflecting the patient's true in-vivo potassium status, so a haemolysed sample can give an invalid, falsely elevated potassium result that should be confirmed with a fresh, non-haemolysed sample.
questions.question: (i) Describe the classification of causes of hypernatraemia and hyperkalaemia. (ii) State how identifying the cause guides clinical assessment of each condition. (iii) Explain why a haemolysed blood sample can give an invalid (falsely high) serum potassium result.

A urine sample is submitted for routine chemical screening using a multi-parameter reagent strip. (i) State the test appropriate for this specimen. (ii) State the principle behind the protein and glucose reactions on the strip. (iii) State the materials required. (iv) State sources of error/interference affecting these reactions. (v) State the precaution needed to obtain a reliable result.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Urine dipstick (reagent strip) urinalysis is appropriate for this specimen.
(ii)
• The protein test detects protein by a colour change with an indicator dye, bromophenol blue, most sensitive to albumin, and detects globulins and Bence-Jones protein poorly.
• The glucose test employs the glucose oxidase reaction, so other sugars such as galactose and fructose are easily missed.
(iii)
A multi-parameter urine reagent strip.
(iv)
• False-positive protein results can occur with concentrated urine, alkaline urine (pH greater than 7.5), trace residue of bleach, acetazolamide, cephalosporins, or sodium bicarbonate.
• False-negative protein results can occur with dilute urine or acidic urine (pH less than 5.0).
• False-positive glucose results can occur with hydrogen peroxide or bleach contamination, and false-negative glucose results can occur with ascorbic acid or some fruit juices.
(v)
• A freshly voided sample should be used, since a fresh sample is equivalent to a valid sample.
• Awareness of these interferences (concentrating/diluting factors, contaminants, ascorbic acid) is needed when interpreting a dipstick result, and confirmatory methods (such as Benedict's reaction or Clinitest for reducing substances in newborns) may be used when other sugars are suspected.

(i)
• Immunoassays measure the concentration of an analyte through antigen-antibody reactions, utilising at least one antibody reagent specific to the analyte.
• The reagent antibodies serve to selectively capture the analyte and/or generate a detection signal, relying on the ability of an antibody to recognise and bind a specific antigen in a complex mixture.
• Labels used to produce a measurable signal include enzymes (such as horseradish peroxidase, alkaline phosphatase or glucose oxidase), radioactive isotopes (as in radioimmunoassay), DNA reporters, fluorogenic reporters, and electrochemiluminescent tags.
• Depending on the specific method protocol, immunoassays can be performed within a timeframe of a few hours up to two days.
(ii)
• Immunoassays rely on the specific binding of an antibody to its target antigen, giving them good specificity for the hormone being measured.
• Enzyme labels allow detection through an observable colour change in the presence of certain reagents, which is convenient for routine laboratory use.
• The variety of available labels (enzyme, radioactive, DNA-based, fluorogenic, electrochemiluminescent) allows immunoassays to be adapted to different sensitivity and workflow needs.
(iii)
• Immunoassays depend on an antibody binding a specific antigen (the hormone), with a labelled component producing a detectable signal.
• Receptor-based assays instead depend on the in vitro interaction of a hormone with its own biological receptor, where unlabelled hormone displaces a radioactively labelled hormone from receptor sites, or a response such as cAMP production is measured.
• Receptor-based assays have an advantage over immunoassays in that they reflect the biological function of the hormone (its capacity to bind its receptor), whereas immunoassays only reflect antibody recognition of the hormone molecule.
• However, receptor-based assays are not as sensitive as immunoassays, and enzymes in the biological specimen may degrade the receptor preparation or destroy the labelled tracer.
• The added complexity and lability of receptor preparations contribute to the more limited use of receptor-based assays in routine clinical laboratories compared with immunoassays.

(ii) Explain why immunoassays are widely used for hormone measurement in the clinical laboratory. (iii) Distinguish immunoassay technique from receptor-based assay technique for measuring hormones.

Most people achieve the desired response to theophylline, with minimum adverse effects when the serum theophylline concentration is maintained between 10-20 mcg/mL. Fewer patients are managed effectively at <10 mcg/mL, but some may respond quite appropriately at lower levels. The frequency of adverse effects increases as the level increases above the upper limit of the therapeutic range, but a few patients are managed effectively, without adversity, above the range.

questions.question: The therapeutic range for theophylline is often stated as 10-20 mcg/mL. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: A therapeutic range is a probabilistic concept, not an absolute cutoff: it represents the concentration range within which the majority of patients achieve an effective response with minimal toxicity. As option B correctly states, most patients respond well and safely within 10-20 mcg/mL, but a minority of patients will respond adequately at concentrations below 10 mcg/mL, and some patients will tolerate concentrations above 20 mcg/mL without toxicity, even though the probability of adverse effects rises as levels climb above the upper limit. This is why the therapeutic range guides, rather than dictates, individualized dosing decisions - it is not tied to a fixed percentage of responders (ruling out options A and C), it has nothing to do with dosing frequency (ruling out option D), and levels outside the range are not automatically ineffective or unsafe for every patient (ruling out option E), since patient-specific therapeutic ranges can differ from the population range.

questions.explanation: A measured potassium in the 'normal' range can be misleading in acidosis. As a general rule, for every 0.1-unit drop in pH below 7.4, the serum potassium rises by about 0.6 mEq/L because acidosis shifts intracellular potassium into the extracellular space. Here the pH is 7.1, a drop of 0.3 units from 7.4, corresponding to a shift of 0.3/0.1 x 0.6 = 1.8 mEq/L. Correcting the measured value: 4.8 - 1.8 = 3.0 mEq/L, which reveals that her true potassium status is actually low. This means her total body potassium is depleted (from osmotic diuresis/glycosuria and acidosis-driven losses) despite the deceptively 'normal' measured value, so supplementation is needed as the acidosis is corrected and potassium shifts back intracellularly — making statement A the false (and therefore correct) exception.

questions.explanation: A positive nitrogen balance of 3-6 g of nitrogen per day is the target goal indicating that protein intake is exceeding losses and that anabolism/tissue repletion is occurring. Prealbumin is actually a preferred marker for short-term nutritional progress because of its short half-life; transferrin tends to be falsely elevated (not depressed) in iron deficiency; and rapid weight gain of 1.5-2 lb/day reflects fluid retention rather than true lean body mass gain, since genuine lean tissue accrual occurs much more slowly.
options: Prealbumin is not the optimal marker to follow for short-term nutritional progress.
Transferrin is falsely depressed in patients with iron deficiency.
Albumin is falsely elevated in renal failure.
A positive nitrogen balance of 3-6 g of nitrogen daily is optimal.
A weight gain of 1.5-2 lb/day indicates optimal lean body weight gain.

Which of the following drugs is considered to be the agent of choice for anaphylactic reactions?
questions.explanation: Of the adrenergic agonists listed, only epinephrine, because of its broad, nonselective alpha- and beta-agonist activity, is the agent of choice for anaphylactic reactions. Its alpha-mediated vasoconstriction reverses the hypotension of anaphylaxis, and its beta2-mediated bronchodilation reverses the bronchospasm, together improving circulatory and respiratory function and counteracting the vascular effects of histamine release.

Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents can cause muscarinic responses such as bradycardia and increased glandular secretions?
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular blocking agents act primarily at nicotinic receptors of the skeletal neuromuscular junction. Succinylcholine, however, is also capable of stimulating autonomic muscarinic receptors, producing responses such as bradycardia, increased glandular secretions, and even cardiac arrest, which is not typical of the other agents listed.

Vancomycin, methicillin, and cefazolin all have excellent activity against staphylococci, but none is effective when given orally for systemic/soft-tissue infection: vancomycin is poorly absorbed orally (oral vancomycin is used only for gastrointestinal infections such as C. difficile colitis), and methicillin and cefazolin are not available or reliable as oral formulations for systemic therapy. Most hospital- and community-acquired staphylococci are also resistant to penicillin (penicillin V), so it is not appropriate empiric therapy either. Of the choices listed, dicloxacillin, an orally bioavailable penicillinase-resistant penicillin, is the appropriate oral therapy for staphylococcal cellulitis.

All of the following statements regarding use of nonprescription H2RAs in gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) are correct except which one?
questions.explanation: Nonprescription-strength H2-receptor antagonists are dosed too low to heal severely damaged esophageal mucosa; healing significant esophageal damage requires prescription-strength H2RA doses or proton pump inhibitors, which more completely suppress acid secretion. The other statements are correct: common adverse effects include headache, diarrhea, dizziness, and nausea; cimetidine inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and can raise serum levels of warfarin, theophylline, and phenytoin; and onset of symptom relief with OTC H2RAs is around 1-2 hours.
options: The most common adverse effects of nonprescription H2RAs are headache, diarrhea, dizziness, and nausea.
Cimetidine may increase serum concentrations of warfarin, theophylline, and phenytoin.

questions.question: As the pharmacist providing services for the neonatal intensive care unit, you evaluate medication orders and make recommendations to the medical team. Which of the following would be the most appropriate recommendation for AH's care?
questions.explanation: Because pediatric dosing relies on weight-based calculations and often requires converting between units or diluting small doses, pediatric orders are at particularly high risk for decimal-point and calculation errors, which can have serious consequences given neonates' narrow margins of safety; carefully double-checking all calculations is therefore the most appropriate and universally applicable recommendation. Switching to oral antibiotics would not be advisable in a neonate with presumed sepsis because oral absorption is unreliable in this population; there is no need to specifically dilute gentamicin further simply to ease measurement, since standard pediatric IV preparation techniques already accommodate small volumes accurately; the therapeutic range for gentamicin is the same in pediatric patients as in adults, so no separate pediatric-specific range is used; and switching to Bactrim would not be appropriate empiric single-agent therapy for neonatal sepsis, nor is it indicated by anything in this scenario.
options: Change to oral antibiotics for better absorption.
Double-check the calculations to avoid decimal errors.
Dilute the gentamicin with a larger volume of IV fluids to make it easier to measure.
Use a pediatric-specific therapeutic range for monitoring gentamicin.
Change to sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim (Bactrim) for single-agent antibacterial coverage.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs should NOT be prepared in a horizontal laminar flow hood?
questions.explanation: CisPlatin is an antineoplastic agent and, consequently, should be prepared only in a vertical laminar flow hood because of the potential hazard of these toxic agents to the operator.

questions.question: Which of the following formulas represents the zwitterion form of an amino acid?
questions.explanation: The structures shown represent an amino acid (general formula R-CH(NH2)-COOH) in different ionization states. A zwitterion is a single molecular species that carries both a positive and a negative charge simultaneously (an 'internal salt'), with no net overall charge. In option D, the amino group has picked up a proton to become -NH3+ (positively charged) while the carboxyl group has donated its proton to become -COO- (negatively charged); the two charges cancel to give a net charge of zero, which is the defining feature of a zwitterion. Amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions at physiological pH, such as within a cell or in the bloodstream. Options A and B show only one ionized group (a net negative or net positive charge, not a zwitterion), option C shows the fully un-ionized (neutral, non-zwitterionic) form, and option E depicts a dipeptide rather than a single amino acid.
options: H2N-CH(R)-COO- (amino group neutral/unprotonated, carboxyl group ionized/deprotonated - net negative charge)
H3N+-CH(R)-COOH (amino group protonated, carboxyl group neutral/protonated - net positive charge)
H2N-CH(R)-COOH (both amino and carboxyl groups neutral/un-ionized)
H3N+-CH(R)-COO- (amino group protonated and carboxyl group deprotonated - net charge of zero)
H2N-CH(R)-CONH-CH(R)-COOH (a dipeptide formed by an amide/peptide bond between two amino acids)

I. liver
II. spleen

questions.explanation: After intravenous administration, 99mTc sulfur colloid particles localize within the reticuloendothelial system: approximately 80-90% of the dose is phagocytized by the Kupffer cells of the liver, 5-10% by the spleen, and the remaining fraction by bone marrow macrophages, allowing all three organs (liver, spleen, and bone marrow) to be visualized on a sulfur colloid scan.
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct
if I, II, and III are correct

questions.question: RJ is a 28-year-old pregnant woman in the 9th week of pregnancy, diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum. Her pregravid weight was 57 kg and her height is 5 ft. 5 in. (165 cm). She has lost 7 kg (12.3%) during her pregnancy and was placed on a central glucose PN program. Which one of the following represents the best estimate of her daily caloric requirements?
questions.explanation: The basal energy expenditure (BEE) is calculated from the Harris-Benedict equation using the patient's pregravid weight: for women, BEE = 655 + (9.6 × weight in kg) + (1.8 × height in cm) - (4.7 × age in years). Substituting: BEE = 655 + (9.6 × 57) + (1.8 × 165) - (4.7 × 28) = 655 + 547.2 + 297 - 131.6 ≈ 1368 kcal. An additional 300 kcal/day is then added to the BEE to meet the increased caloric requirement of pregnancy, giving a total of approximately 1668 kcal/day, which rounds to the closest listed answer of 1675 kcal.

Antimetabolites are structural analogs of naturally occurring substrates used in biochemical reactions. They exert their cytotoxic effect by acting as false substitutes for the natural substrates during DNA (and nucleic acid) synthesis, thereby inhibiting DNA production — this is distinct from the intercalation mechanism of the antitumor antibiotics and from the microtubule-directed mechanisms of the mitotic inhibitors.
options: inhibiting DNA synthesis by sliding between DNA base pairs
inhibiting RNA synthesis by sliding between RNA base pairs
acting as false metabolites in the microtubules
acting as false substitutions in the production of nucleic acids

A 65-year-old man presents with stage I hypertension. He has diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease and is intolerant to lisinopril. Which of the following agents would be an appropriate selection for initial treatment in this patient based on the guidelines from the 'Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure' (JNC-7)?
questions.explanation: Candesartan, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), inhibits the binding of angiotensin II to its receptor, blocking both its vasoconstrictor effects and angiotensin II-mediated aldosterone release. Because this patient has diabetes and chronic kidney disease (compelling indications favoring renin-angiotensin system blockade) but cannot tolerate the ACE inhibitor lisinopril, an ARB is an appropriate substitute. A beta-blocker (propranolol) or thiazide diuretic (chlorothiazide) would not specifically address his compelling indications as well, and nitroprusside/clonidine are not used for routine initial hypertension therapy (nitroprusside is reserved for hypertensive emergencies).

questions.question: Which of the following antigout medications acts by decreasing serum levels but increasing urine levels of uric acid, thus increasing the risk of kidney stone development?
questions.explanation: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that promotes renal excretion of uric acid, lowering plasma urate concentration while simultaneously raising the concentration of uric acid in the urine. If urinary uric acid exceeds its solubility limit, it can crystallize and precipitate, causing stone formation (urinary lithiasis). For this reason, patients on probenecid should be counseled to maintain generous fluid intake.

questions.explanation: Onset time is the interval from drug administration until the absorbed drug reaches the minimum effective concentration (MEC) -- the plasma concentration that is proportional (though not necessarily equal) to the minimum concentration at the receptor site needed to produce a pharmacologic response.

begin to be eliminated from the body.

questions.question: For the same carbenicillin infusion patient, assuming no loading intravenous dose was given, how long after initiation of the infusion would the plasma drug concentration reach 95% of the theoretic steady-state concentration?
questions.explanation: The time to reach a given fraction of steady state during a constant infusion depends only on the drug's half-life, independent of dose or infusion rate. The time to reach 95% of Css is 4.32 times the half-life (while 99% of Css requires 6.6 half-lives). With t1/2 = 1 hr, the time to reach 95% of Css = 4.32 x 1 hr = 4.3 hr.

questions.question: S.M., a 38-year-old woman, received a living-related kidney transplant 2 months ago. At clinic today she complains of tiredness, shortness of breath, and pedal edema. Serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL and BUN 43 mg/dL (versus 1.2 mg/dL and 24 mg/dL 4 weeks ago), and tacrolimus level 3 ng/mL (therapeutic range 5-15 ng/mL). She was diagnosed with acute graft rejection, admitted, and treated with thymoglobulin. The physician asks whether daclizumab (Zenapax) would be useful in treating this patient's acute rejection. Which of the following is an appropriate response?
questions.explanation: Daclizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody (about 90% human IgG, with roughly 10% mouse-derived binding region) directed against the interleukin-2 (IL-2) receptor on T cells; by binding this receptor, it blocks the IL-2-driven T-cell proliferation and growth that is central to graft rejection. It is indicated only for the prevention (prophylaxis) of acute rejection, not for treating established rejection, and unlike OKT3 or antithymocyte globulin it does not cause serious infusion-related side effects, so premedication with agents such as acetaminophen, diphenhydramine, and corticosteroids is not required.
options: It is a humanized IgG product against IL-2 receptor and it is useful only in preventing acute rejection.
It is a useful agent to treat rejection, but chest x-ray and monitoring of patient's fluid status are required before this therapy.
It is useful, but patient's weight gain should be less than 3% from the dry weight before therapy
It is a chimeral IgG with specificity against IL-2 receptor and it is useful only for prevention of rejection.
It is a humanized horse serum against T-cells and it is a new agent useful for prevention and treatment of rejection.

questions.question: For the same carbenicillin infusion patient, what is the recommended loading dose?
questions.explanation: A loading dose is designed to immediately establish the target plasma concentration: DL = Css x VD. Using Css = 150 mg/L and VD = 9 L: DL = 150 mg/L x 9 L = 1350 mg).

questions.question: For the same cephalosporin antibiotic patient, how much drug remains in the patient's body (DB) 8 hr after the dose?
questions.explanation: The amount of drug remaining in the body at any time equals the plasma concentration at that time multiplied by the apparent volume of distribution: DB = Cp x VD. Using Cp(8 hr) = 1.11 mg/L and VD = 21 L: DB = 1.11 mg/L x 21 L = 23.3 mg).

questions.question: Hypotension, acute renal failure, cholestatic jaundice, and agranulocytosis is a group of adverse effects most closely related to which of the following drug classes?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors can cause first-dose hypotension and, particularly in patients with compromised renal perfusion (such as bilateral renal artery stenosis), acute renal failure. They have also been reported to cause blood dyscrasias, including agranulocytosis, as well as cholestatic jaundice, distinguishing their adverse effect profile from the other cardiovascular drug classes listed.

questions.question: Hematological studies are most likely to show a low reticulocyte count in a patient who has which of the following abnormalities?
questions.explanation: The reticulocyte count measures circulating immature RBCs and therefore reflects bone marrow production. A low reticulocyte count is expected in aplastic anemia, a disorder in which a lack of hematopoietic stem cells (often from chemotherapy) leaves the marrow unable to produce new red cells. In contrast, hemolytic anemia and acute blood loss stimulate the marrow to increase RBC output, and successful treatment of an iron, B12, or folate deficiency triggers a brisk reticulocytosis as the marrow ramps up production of new, previously deficiency-limited red cells — so options B, C, D, and E would all show an increased, not decreased, reticulocyte count.
options: aplastic anemia secondary to cancer chemotherapy
acute hemolytic anemia secondary to quinidine treatment
severe bleeding secondary to an automobile accident
iron-deficiency anemia 1 week after treatment with ferrous sulfate
megaloblastic anemia owing to folate deficiency 1 week after treatment with folic acid

questions.explanation: Glucose, urea, and sucrose are nonelectrolytes, and sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte. Electrolytes are substances that form ions when dissolved in water, allowing them to conduct an electric current through the solution; cations are positively charged ions and anions are negatively charged ions. Strong electrolytes are completely ionized in water at all concentrations, while weak electrolytes (such as ephedrine) are only partially ionized at most concentrations. Because nonelectrolytes do not form ions in solution, they are nonconductors.

questions.question: If this patient's renal clearance for carbenicillin is 86 mL/min, what is the hepatic clearance for carbenicillin?
questions.explanation: Total body clearance is the sum of all individual organ clearances, so hepatic clearance = total body clearance - renal clearance: ClH = ClT - ClR. questions.explanation: Specialized pregnancy-exposure databases and reference resources, such as REPROTOX or Teris, along with published references like Briggs' Drugs in Pregnancy and Lactation, provide the most reliable, systematically compiled evidence for assessing drug safety in pregnancy. The FDA letter classification system is a poor tool for risk assessment, particularly for category C drugs, since this category lumps together a very wide range of actual risk levels; case reports of pregnancy exposures tend to be biased toward capturing adverse outcomes (since normal outcomes are less likely to be reported), and general physician knowledge, while valuable clinically, is not a systematic evidence source compared to dedicated reproductive-risk databases.

Evaluation parameters include both efficacy parameters (what should be monitored to confirm the therapeutic goal is being met) and toxicity parameters (what should be monitored to ensure adverse effects or toxicity are not occurring). Note that 'efficacy issues' (choice B) is a related but distinct concept — it is one of the PRIME problem categories (the 'E' in PRIME), not the CORE plan's evaluation component.

Phase I metabolites are often only modestly more polar than their parent drugs, whereas phase II metabolites (with the exception of acetylated and methylated products) are always much more polar than their parents. Because phase I metabolites retain more lipid solubility, they are more likely to cross cell membranes than the highly polar phase II metabolites. It is unusual for a drug to yield only a single metabolite - most drugs produce a mixture. Because phase II metabolites are highly polar and rapidly excreted, they rarely undergo further metabolism, whereas phase I metabolites commonly go on to undergo phase II conjugation. Although the liver is the major site of metabolism, many extrahepatic tissues also contain drug-metabolizing enzymes. Finally, while many metabolites are less active than their parent drugs, some have equal or greater pharmacologic activity (and sometimes greater toxicity), and prodrugs by definition always form at least one active metabolite.

questions.explanation: Polypharmacy - taking multiple medications, often with complicated regimens - is a well-recognized risk factor for medication noncompliance in the elderly, since complex regimens are harder to remember and follow correctly. Lower socioeconomic status, living alone, complicated drug regimens, poor (not good) relationships with healthcare providers, and having multiple disease states are the recognized risk factors; hypertension itself (a disease state, not inherently a compliance barrier), living with a spouse (a form of social support rather than isolation), and a good physician relationship would not be expected to increase noncompliance risk.

questions.question: Ingestion of which of the following vitamins should be avoided by a patient taking an oral anticoagulant?
questions.explanation: Oral anticoagulants such as warfarin act by inhibiting hepatic synthesis of prothrombin (and other vitamin K-dependent clotting factors), the precursor of thrombin that converts fibrinogen to fibrin during clot formation. One of the key substrates for prothrombin biosynthesis is vitamin K, with which warfarin competitively interferes. Because this competition is reversible, dietary vitamin K intake can antagonize (reduce the effectiveness of) oral anticoagulant therapy, so patients should avoid large or inconsistent intake of vitamin K-rich foods.

Hematological testing of a patient with AIDS is most likely to show which of the following abnormalities?
questions.explanation: HIV/AIDS selectively attacks and depletes the CD4 (T-helper, TH4) subset of T lymphocytes. Because T lymphocytes make up a large share of circulating lymphocytes, this destruction lowers the total lymphocyte count, producing lymphopenia — a finding that also signals an underlying immunodeficiency in general. Basophilia is more typical of chronic myelogenous leukemia; eosinophilia accompanies allergic/parasitic disease; reticulocytosis reflects a bone marrow response to hemolysis or blood loss; and agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia) is a distinct, usually drug-induced process, not the classic hematologic hallmark of AIDS.

Once such an emergency oral prescription is dispensed, the quantity must be strictly limited to what is needed to cover the emergency period only (choice B), and the authorizing practitioner is legally required to follow up with a written prescription delivered to the pharmacist within 7 days of the oral authorization, which must be marked 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' (choice A). questions.question: A pharmacist prepares 1 gal of KCl solution by mixing 565 g of KCl (valence = 1) in an appropriate vehicle. How many milliequivalents of K+ are in 15 mL of this solution? (atomic weights: K = 39; Cl = 35.5)
questions.explanation: NOTE ON SOURCE TEXT: the source PDF's question lists the atomic weight of potassium as 'K = 30,' but this does not reproduce the book's own answer; the chapter's own worked milliequivalent example (Ch. 2, VII.A) explicitly uses K = 39 (39 + 35.5 = 74.5 = mol wt of KCl), and only K = 39 reproduces the stated correct answer, so K = 39 is used here as the corrected value. Molecular weight of KCl = 39 + 35.5 = 74.5 g/mol; since valence = 1, the milliequivalent weight is also 74.5 mg/mEq. Total KCl = 565 g = 565,000 mg, giving 565,000 mg / 74.5 mg/mEq = 7583.9 mEq of K+ in the full 1-gallon (3785 mL) preparation. Concentration = 7583.9 mEq / 3785 mL = 2.004 mEq/mL. In 15 mL: 2.004 mEq/mL x 15 mL = 30.06 mEq, which rounds to 30 mEq.

She was diagnosed with acute graft rejection, admitted, and treated with thymoglobulin. Which of the following regarding thymoglobulin is (are) true? I. It is a horse serum against human B cells. II. It is an IL-2 receptor antagonist against human T-cells. III. It is a rabbit immunoglobulin against human T-cells.
questions.explanation: Thymoglobulin is a rabbit-derived antibody directed against human thymocytes (T cells), used either to prevent rejection or to treat ongoing rejection, typically dosed at 1.5 mg/kg daily for 7-10 days. This distinguishes it from Atgam, which is the horse-derived antibody against human thymocytes, and from daclizumab (Zenapax) or basiliximab (Simulect), which are monoclonal antibodies against the IL-2 receptor — so thymoglobulin is neither a horse serum against B cells nor an IL-2 receptor antagonist, making only statement III correct.

This effect is thought to result in part from nicotine decreasing biliary and pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, which reduces the duodenum's ability to neutralize acid (II), as well as from smoking accelerating gastric emptying of acid into the duodenum, which predisposes to duodenal ulcer and slows healing (III). questions.explanation: Desensitizing agents should not be abrasive or used on a chronic basis unless directed by a dentist. The products approved by the ADA include the ingredients 5% potassium nitrate, 10% strontium chloride, and dibasic sodium citrate 2% in Pluronic gel.

questions.question: Which of the following have been shown to be effective in the acute management of digitalis toxicity? I. cholestyramine resin (Questran) II. Fab fragment antibody (Digibind) III. potassium administration
questions.explanation: Cholestyramine resin binds digoxin within the GI tract, reducing further absorption if administered before all the drug has been absorbed. Potassium administration helps protect the myocardium from digitalis' toxic effects while excess drug levels are cleared. Fab fragment antibody (Digibind), though costly, directly binds and inactivates circulating digoxin (roughly 40 mg of Digibind binds 0.6 mg of digitalis) and is effective for managing very high, life-threatening digoxin levels. All three approaches have a role in acute management.
options: if I and II are correct

questions.question: A vancomycin solution containing 1000 mg of vancomycin hydrochloride diluted to 250 mL with D5W is to be infused at a constant rate with an infusion pump in 2 hr. What is the rate of drug administration?
questions.explanation: This is a constant-rate IV infusion problem. The total dose (1000 mg) is infused over 2 hours = 120 minutes. Rate of administration = 1000 mg / 120 min = 8.33 mg/min.

questions.question: Has anticholinergic activity with few side effects
questions.explanation: Anticholinergic agents such as atropine and ipratropium bromide produce bronchodilation by competitively inhibiting cholinergic (muscarinic) receptors in the airway. Atropine, however, has disadvantages including dry mouth, tachycardia, and urinary retention because of its systemic anticholinergic absorption. Ipratropium bromide is three to five times more potent than atropine as a bronchodilator and, because it is poorly systemically absorbed when given by inhalation, does not produce these same systemic anticholinergic side effects, giving it anticholinergic activity with comparatively few side effects.

questions.question: Which of the following nonprescription products is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for treatment of impacted cerumen? I. olive oil II. carbamide peroxide III. isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glycerin
questions.explanation: Carbamide peroxide is the only FDA-approved agent for cerumen removal. Olive oil and mineral oil are used to remove cerumen, but are not FDA approved. Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glycerin is FDA approved for water-clogged ears, but not cerumen removal.

questions.explanation: Unfractionated heparin therapy is monitored using the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) or a heparin assay, correlating the aPTT ratio to a target heparin level (0.2-0.4 units/mL by protamine titration assay, or 0.3-0.7 units/mL by plasma-amidolytic assay), since aPTT reagent sensitivity varies between laboratories. The international normalized ratio (INR) is used to monitor oral vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) therapy, not heparin, so only II and III apply.

A 30-year-old female is 10 weeks pregnant with her second child. During her first pregnancy, she became depressed and was started on Prozac 20 mg every day. She is already beginning to notice early symptoms of depression during her second pregnancy. She would like to try St. John's wort for her depression. Which of the following statements is correct regarding St. John's wort?
questions.explanation: St. John's wort has a significant interaction with serotonin reuptake inhibitors (such as this patient's Prozac/fluoxetine), with the combination raising the risk of serotonin syndrome, so combining the two should be avoided. St. John's wort should specifically be avoided in pregnancy because it is an emmenagogue and abortifacient (a defined risk, not merely 'unknown'), it is Commission E-approved for mild-to-moderate depression (so it is helpful for mild depression), and its notable food interaction involves tyramine-containing foods such as cheese, beer, wine, herring, and yeast (similar to MAOI food interactions) rather than dairy products like milk and eggs.
options: The safety of St. John's wort in pregnancy is unknown.
St. John's wort is not helpful in treating mild depression.
St. John's wort may interact with serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
St. John's wort may interact with dairy products like milk and eggs.
St. John's wort may interact with proton pump inhibitors.

Management at this stage focuses on treating those underlying risk factors, and ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) are recommended for their beneficial effect on cardiac remodeling as first-line therapy for select stage A patients. All three statements accurately describe this stage.

questions.question: A pharmacist is presented a prescription for 250 mcg of levothyroxine. Which of the following dosages would be equivalent to that amount?
questions.explanation: This is a straightforward metric unit conversion, and getting it right (or wrong) is exactly the type of error the chapter emphasizes as a common and dangerous source of medication mistakes. The conversion factor is 1 mg = 1,000 mcg (equivalently, 1 mcg = 0.001 mg). So: 250 mcg ÷ 1,000 = 0.25 mg. Checking the distractors: 2.5 mg (choice A) is off by a factor of 10 (would correspond to 2,500 mcg); 0.25 gm (choice B) is off by a factor of 1,000,000 (0.25 g = 250,000 mcg, since 1 g = 1,000 mg = 1,000,000 mcg); and 25 gm (choice D) is even further off. This type of unit-conversion slip is precisely why the chapter stresses caution with abbreviations like 'mcg' vs. 'mg' — a levothyroxine dose off by a factor of 10 or more could cause serious iatrogenic hyper- or hypothyroidism.

questions.question: Which comminution technique is described by: 'Reducing and subdividing a substance by adding an easily removed solvent'?
questions.explanation: Pulverization by intervention is often used for substances that tend to agglomerate or resist grinding. A small amount of an easily removed (often volatile) solvent is added; after pulverization, the solvent is allowed to evaporate or is otherwise removed.

Lutein is an antioxidant pigment that functions to filter and protect the visual apparatus and its vascular supply. Lutein, is therefore, thought to be beneficial for improvement in vision in patients with dry age-related macular degeneration and prevention of cataracts. Vitamin D is not an antioxidant vitamin.

A patient with renal failure is inadvertently given 3 doses of potassium chloride 40 mEq IV in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over a 3-hr period. This error is immediately discovered and a STAT serum potassium level is 8.0 mEq/L. The patient is bradycardic with a markedly prolonged QRS complex. The patient should receive which of the following?
options: Insulin 10 U and 50% dextrose 50 mL IV push
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g by mouth every 3 hr for 4 doses
questions.explanation: This patient has severe, symptomatic hyperkalemia (serum K⁺ of 8.0 mEq/L with life-threatening cardiac manifestations — bradycardia and a markedly widened QRS complex). Although all of calcium, sodium bicarbonate, and insulin/dextrose are legitimate treatments for hyperkalemia, when a patient is unstable with these dangerous ECG changes, the very first priority is to stabilize the cardiac cell membrane immediately, which is exactly what IV calcium (calcium chloride 10%, 10-20 mL IV push) does. Sodium bicarbonate and insulin/dextrose (choices B and C) work by shifting potassium intracellularly and are important next steps, but they act more slowly and do not directly protect the myocardium the way calcium does; sodium polystyrene sulfonate (choice D) works even more slowly, by removing potassium from the body via the GI tract, and is not appropriate as the first intervention in an unstable, symptomatic patient.

questions.question: TW is a 52-year-old female with a history of schizophrenia and diabetes mellitus type 2. She has been treated for many years with haloperidol with good response; however, she has recently developed lip smacking and tongue chewing. Which of the following medications has been used to treat the adverse effect described in question 6 (tardive dyskinesia)?
questions.explanation: Vitamin E, along with benzodiazepines, baclofen, and reserpine, has been used in attempts to treat tardive dyskinesia, although none of these agents has been definitively proven effective. Propranolol is used for antipsychotic-induced akathisia, and diphenhydramine and amantadine are used for acute dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism (drug-induced parkinsonism), respectively — not tardive dyskinesia.

questions.question: Match the chemotherapy agent to the adverse effect with which it is most closely associated (each effect is used only once). Paclitaxel
questions.explanation: Paclitaxel is most closely associated with hypersensitivity reactions, which are largely attributed to its Cremophor EL diluent rather than to the drug itself; patients are typically premedicated with corticosteroids and antihistamines before infusion to reduce this risk.

questions.question: When spironolactone (Aldactone) is used in a patient with heart failure (HF), it works through what primary mechanism?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone was the first aldosterone-receptor antagonist available for clinical use. In the RALES trial, spironolactone (12.5-25 mg daily) added to ACE inhibitor therapy in patients with class IV HF symptoms reduced the risk of death and hospitalization. Although it is only a weak diuretic, its clinical benefit in HF is attributed primarily to its direct antagonism of aldosterone's harmful effects, not to any inotropic, chronotropic, or angiotensin-blocking action.

Cost-minimization analysis (CMA) assumes that the health outcomes (consequences) of the alternatives being compared are clinically equivalent. Because the consequences are assumed equal, the analysis focuses purely on comparing costs, and the least expensive alternative is selected.

Removing one of these hydroxyl groups increases the lipophilicity of the molecule, favoring its uptake into the brain and into adrenergic nerve terminals, where it can displace stored norepinephrine from vesicles and promote transmitter release—that is, it shifts the compound toward indirect sympathomimetic activity rather than enhancing direct receptor potency.

Diphenhydramine, which possesses substantial anticholinergic activity, is effective against nausea and vomiting arising from vestibulocochlear stimulation, vertigo, and motion sickness. Brompheniramine, omeprazole, and ranitidine do not directly reduce nausea or vomiting through this mechanism, making diphenhydramine the best choice.

Using the same set of metabolic pathway options (ether glucuronidation, ester glucuronidation, nitroreduction, oxidative deamination, ester hydrolysis), amphetamine, which contains a primary amine, is metabolized primarily by which pathway?
questions.explanation: The principal functional group in amphetamine is its primary amine, and oxidative deamination is a very common metabolic pathway for primary amines. Amphetamine can occasionally undergo phase II acetylation (a less common pathway for primary amines) and can also undergo aromatic hydroxylation, but oxidative deamination is its most likely major pathway.

questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate causes acid rebound, and when taken with milk or another alkaline substance over prolonged periods it can precipitate milk-alkali syndrome, along with other adverse effects such as hypercalcemia, alkalosis, azotemia, and nephrocalcinosis.

Capping (a tablet-processing defect) is most likely the result of:
questions.explanation: Capping is separation of the top or bottom crown of a tablet from its main body, implying that the compressed powder mass is not sufficiently cohesive. questions.question: The appropriate dose of pseudoephedrine for a 3-year-old child is
questions.explanation: For children 2-5 years of age, the recommended pseudoephedrine dose is 15 mg every 4-6 hours, up to a maximum of 60 mg in 24 hours.
