A 3-year-old falls in the 2-5 year age band, making 15 mg q4-6h correct.

questions.question: Two biotransformation reactions are shown: reaction I is an acetylation reaction (masking an amine with an acetyl group), and reaction II is a glycine conjugation reaction (masking a carboxylic acid with the amino acid glycine); reaction III represents oxidative deamination, a change to an existing amine functional group. Which of the following reactions can be classified as phase II metabolism?
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct
if I, II, and III are correct
questions.explanation: Phase II metabolic reactions involve masking an existing functional group by attaching a natural endogenous constituent, such as an acetyl group (reaction I, acetylation) or the amino acid glycine (reaction II, glycine conjugation) - both of statements I and II are phase II reactions. Reaction III, oxidative deamination, instead represents a change to an existing functional group rather than the addition of an endogenous conjugate, making it a phase I, not phase II, reaction.

questions.question: Sulfasalazine is a prodrug that is activated in the intestine by bacterial enzymes. The enzyme most likely responsible is
questions.explanation: Sulfasalazine has both anti-inflammatory and antibacterial activity once it is converted in the body to aminosalicylic acid and sulfapyridine. This conversion occurs through reductive cleavage of the azo linkage in the sulfasalazine molecule, catalyzed by bacterial azoreductase in the intestine. Because the intact drug is not absorbed from the stomach or upper intestine and reaches the colon before being metabolized, this represents a form of site-specific (colon-targeted) drug delivery, which is why sulfasalazine is effective for ulcerative colitis.

questions.question: Sulfonylurea agents (as monotherapy or in combination) are a primary mode of therapy in the treatment of
options: diabetes patients experiencing severe hepatic or renal dysfunction.
questions.explanation: Sulfonylureas require functioning pancreatic β-cells to work, so they are appropriate only for type 2 (non-insulin-dependent) DM and are not effective or indicated in type 1 DM. They should also be avoided in patients with severe hepatic or renal dysfunction, in pregnancy, and in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — DKA must always be treated with insulin, fluids, and electrolyte replacement rather than oral agents.

options: relation between the physical and the chemical properties of a drug and its systemic absorption
measurement of the rate and amount of therapeutically active drug that reaches the systemic circulation
movement of the drug into body tissues over time
dissolution of the drug in the gastrointestinal tract
amount of drug destroyed by the liver before systemic absorption from the gastrointestinal tract occurs
questions.question: Which statement best describes bioavailability?
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is the measurement of the rate and extent (amount) of therapeutically active drug that reaches the systemic circulation. The relationship between a drug's physical/chemical properties and its systemic absorption is instead called biopharmaceutics; movement of drug into body tissues over time is an aspect of pharmacokinetics; GI dissolution is a physicochemical process that affects (but does not define) bioavailability; and destruction of drug by the liver before systemic absorption is the first-pass effect, which decreases bioavailability rather than defining it.

questions.question: If treating a patient with HF, which of the following dosages of dopamine would be used to elicit its positive inotropic effects?
questions.explanation: Dopamine's effects are dose-dependent: at low doses of about 2-5 ug/kg/min it acts on dopaminergic receptors to increase renal blood flow; at intermediate doses of about 5-10 ug/kg/min it stimulates beta-adrenergic receptors to increase cardiac output (its positive inotropic effect); and at higher doses of about 10-20 ug/kg/min alpha-adrenergic stimulation predominates, increasing peripheral vascular resistance. Because these ranges overlap and vary between patients, close titration to individual response is required.

continue the present meperidine dosage because she will eventually get relief.
decrease the meperidine dose to avoid side effects.
questions.explanation: Both oxycodone (as previously dosed) and meperidine have short durations of effect, and repeated, frequent meperidine dosing risks normeperidine accumulation and myoclonic seizures. For a chronic cancer pain patient, converting to an around-the-clock, controlled-release oral morphine or oxycodone regimen is the appropriate next step; with proper titration, an every 8- to 12-hour regimen should provide good, sustained pain relief without the toxic metabolite buildup seen with meperidine.

Cardiac arrhythmias are not a recognized adverse effect of aspirin.

Poor communication practices is a latent defect in this pharmacy system and significantly contributed to the error

questions.question: A hospital pharmacy begins stocking new intravenous mini-bags of a neuromuscular-blocking agent. The packaging is similar to a commonly used intravenous antibiotic. The addition of the new mini-bags was not widely communicated to all personnel. One weekend, several doses of this new product were accidentally dispensed in place of the intended doses of antibiotic. Several patients suffered respiratory arrest and one of the patients eventually died. What would a root cause analysis of this error find?
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis (RCA) is a structured process for identifying all direct and indirect factors that contributed to an error — it is explicitly not intended to assign individual blame. In this scenario, the failure to widely communicate the addition of a look-alike, high-risk neuromuscular-blocking agent to stock is a textbook example of a latent defect: a systemic weakness (poor communication of a change plus confusing/similar packaging) that does not cause harm immediately but sets the stage for a serious error under the right circumstances — here, unfamiliar staff pulling the wrong look-alike product during a weekend shift. Choices A and C incorrectly try to pin the error entirely on one individual (the pharmacist or the technicians), which contradicts the entire premise of RCA; firing an individual doesn't fix the underlying system failure and only invites a repeat error. Choice D is factually wrong — this is a wrong-drug error (the wrong medication was substituted for the intended antibiotic), not an extra-dose error (which involves receiving more doses of the correctly intended drug than ordered).

questions.question: A beta-blocker with an ultrashort duration of action
questions.explanation: Esmolol was the first beta-blocker with an ultrashort duration of action, given only as a continuous IV infusion. Because of this short duration and the need for IV administration, it is not used routinely for chronic hypertension but is useful for perioperative hypertension or tachycardia.

loop diuretics to rapidly eliminate potassium
magnesium sulfate or magnesium chloride intravenously
questions.question: Life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias due to hyperkalemia should be treated with
questions.explanation: Intravenous calcium chloride or calcium gluconate acts within minutes to stabilize the cardiac cell membrane against the arrhythmogenic effects of hyperkalemia, making it the treatment of choice for a life-threatening arrhythmia. Digoxin is not indicated (and hyperkalemia can potentiate digoxin toxicity). Loop diuretics and sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS) lower total body potassium, but too slowly to abort an acute arrhythmia; they, along with dialysis, are used afterward to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: If 3.17 kg of a drug is used to make 50,000 tablets, how many milligrams will 30 tablets contain?
questions.explanation: This is solved by proportion. First find the mass per tablet: 3.17 kg = 3,170,000 mg; 3,170,000 mg / 50,000 tablets = 63.4 mg/tablet. For 30 tablets: 63.4 mg/tablet x 30 tablets = 1902 mg, which rounds to approximately 1900 mg.

questions.question: A mass of adipose tissue that develops at the injection site is usually the result of the patient's neglect to rotate the insulin injection site. This is known as
questions.explanation: Lipohypertrophy refers to masses of adipose tissue that build up at repeatedly used injection sites, typically from failure to rotate the injection location; these masses generally resolve gradually once injections in that area are avoided. Lipoatrophy is a different, less common phenomenon involving loss (not accumulation) of subcutaneous fat at injection sites.

questions.question:
Ingredients that may be used as suspending agents include:
I. methylcellulose.
II. acacia.
III. talc.
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct
if I, II, and III are correct
questions.explanation: I and II are correct; III is not. Acacia (a natural product) and methylcellulose (a synthetic polymer) are both common suspending agents; by increasing the viscosity of the liquid vehicle, they help particles remain suspended longer. Talc is not a suspending agent.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with jaundice has spillage of bilirubin into his urine. All of the following statements could apply to this patient except which one?
questions.explanation: Only conjugated (direct) bilirubin is water-soluble and can be filtered by the glomerulus into the urine, so bilirubinuria requires an increase in direct bilirubin. In hemolytic anemia, the bilirubin elevation is predominantly unconjugated (indirect); direct bilirubin is normal or only slightly increased, so no bilirubin spills into the urine, and urine color remains normal. Viral hepatitis (liver cell necrosis) and cholestatic hepatitis (biliary obstruction) both raise direct bilirubin and are associated with dark urine containing bilirubin, and total bilirubin is increased in all three conditions.

questions.question: For two drug products, generic (test) and brand (reference), to be considered bioequivalent I. there should be no statistical difference between the extent of bioavailability of the drug from the test product compared to the reference product. II. the 90% confidence intervals about the ratio of the means of the Cmax and AUC values for the test product to reference product must be within 80%-125% of the reference product. III. there should be no statistical differences between the mean Cmax and AUC values for the test product compared to the reference product.
questions.explanation: Although Tmax is an indication of rate of drug absorption, it is a discrete measurement and usually too variable to use for statistical comparisons in bioequivalence studies. Statistical comparisons use AUC and Cmax values from test and reference drug products as the basis of bioequivalence.

questions.question: The parameters used to describe bioavailability are
questions.explanation: AUC relates to the extent of drug absorption. Cmax and Tmax relate to the rate of drug absorption. The elimination t1/2 of the drug is usually independent of the route of drug administration and is not used as a measure of bioavailability. For the FDA, only the Cmax and AUC parameters must meet 90% confidence intervals of 80-125% of the reference (brand) product (Table 7.1).

questions.question: A new cardiac glycoside has an elimination half-life of 24 hr, an apparent volume of distribution of 3 L/kg, an effective concentration of 1.5 ng/mL, toxic effects above 4 ng/mL, is 25% plasma-protein bound, and is 75% bioavailable orally. What is the oral maintenance dose, given once a day, for a 68-year-old man who weighs 65 kg, has CHF, and normal renal function?
questions.explanation: The oral maintenance dose that sustains an average target plasma concentration is calculated as D0 = (Css,avg x k x VD x tau) / F, where F is bioavailability, k is the elimination rate constant, VD is the apparent volume of distribution, and tau is the dosing interval. Here: k = 0.693/24 hr, VD = 3 L/kg x 65 kg = 195 L, Css,avg = 1.5 ng/mL = 1.5 ug/L, tau = 24 hr, F = 0.75. Substituting: D0 = (1.5 ug/L x [0.693/24 /hr] x 195 L x 24 hr) / 0.75 = 270 ug = 0.270 mg).

questions.explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics are fast (sodium) channel blockers that slow impulse conduction by depressing sodium influx during phase 0 of the action potential, prolonging depolarization (and, on the ECG, the P wave or QRS complex). Class II agents (beta-blockers) act mainly on AV nodal conduction via sympathetic blockade; Class III agents prolong the refractory period/action potential without affecting conduction velocity; Class IV agents (calcium-channel blockers) act on the slow calcium channels active during phase 2. There is no recognized 'class V' of antiarrhythmics.

An overdose victim presents to the emergency department with an elevated heart rate, decreased blood pressure, dilated pupils, and lethargy. Upon arrival to the intensive care unit (ICU), she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that is treated with IV diazepam and fosphenytoin. Which of the following is the most likely intoxicant?
questions.explanation: This clinical picture — tachycardia, hypotension, mydriasis (dilated pupils), lethargy progressing to seizures — is the classic anticholinergic/cardiotoxic and CNS toxidrome of tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose, and amitriptyline is a prototypical TCA. TCA toxicity produces anticholinergic effects (mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperpyrexia), cardiopulmonary toxicity (tachyarrhythmias, conduction blocks, hypotension), and CNS effects ranging from agitation and confusion to seizures and coma; the cardiac and CNS manifestations of TCA toxicity classically respond to sodium bicarbonate therapy. Ethanol (choice A) and acetaminophen (choice C) toxicity do not typically present with this seizure/anticholinergic picture. Oxycodone (choice D), an opioid, would be expected to cause the opposite presentation — miosis (constricted pupils), respiratory depression, and decreased heart rate/blood pressure from CNS/respiratory depression, not seizures with dilated pupils. Methanol (choice B) toxicity classically presents with visual disturbances and severe metabolic acidosis rather than this anticholinergic/seizure picture.

naloxone reduces the Emax for morphine.
naloxone reduces the ED50 for morphine.
naloxone increases the Emax for morphine.
naloxone increases the ED50 for morphine.
questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive antagonist of opiate receptor. If one compares the log dose-response curve of both morphine and naloxone to that of morphine alone, the morphine-naloxone curve is shifted to the right. As a result, the ED50 for morphine is increased. This means that a larger than previous dose of morphine is required for achieving the same analgesic effect.

questions.explanation: Tenecteplase is a fibrinolytic (tissue plasminogen activator) that converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve clot. Current guidelines reserve fibrinolytic therapy for STEMI, where a fully occlusive thrombus is present; fibrinolytics are not part of the recommended management of unstable angina or NSTEMI. Sublingual nitroglycerin, beta-blockers, aspirin, and morphine, in contrast, are all standard components of initial NSTEMI/ACS management.

questions.question: A patient suffering from acute infectious diarrhea caused by Shigella can be managed in all of the following ways except which one?
options: No treatment necessary because signs and symptoms usually resolve in 48 hr.
Use glucose solutions (e.g., soda, apple juice) to settle the stomach and decrease the number of stools.
Avoid food for at least 6 hr, then slowly increase fluid intake.
Use antibiotics (e.g., Bactrim, doxycycline) for 7 days.
Use antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide, diphenoxylate) to settle the stomach and decrease the number of stools.
questions.explanation: Highly osmotic glucose-containing beverages such as soda or apple juice actually draw more water into the intestinal tract osmotically and can worsen diarrhea rather than settle the stomach or reduce stool frequency, making this the incorrect (and thus correct answer to the except) management strategy. Appropriately, many episodes of infectious diarrhea resolve within about 48 hours without specific treatment, food can be withheld briefly (about 6 hours) before slowly reintroducing fluids, and antibiotics such as Bactrim or doxycycline are appropriate for confirmed bacterial pathogens like Shigella.

questions.question: A 29-year-old white man is seen in the emergency room. His white blood cell (WBC) count is 14,200 with 80% polys. All of the following conditions could normally produce these laboratory findings except which one?
options: a localized bacterial infection on the tip of the index finger
acute bacterial pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae
a gunshot wound to the abdomen with a loss of 2 pints of blood
questions.explanation: The patient has leukocytosis with neutrophilia. A purely localized infection, confined to a small area such as a fingertip, typically does not raise the total circulating WBC or neutrophil count enough to produce this degree of leukocytosis. Systemic bacterial infection (pneumonia), tissue necrosis (myocardial infarction), acute hemorrhage/physical stress (gunshot wound), and acute inflammatory conditions (gout) are all recognized causes of neutrophilic leukocytosis.

questions.question: Using the same patient profile (moderate hypertension, glaucoma, and mild osteoarthritis, on metoprolol, pilocarpine gel, epinephrine drops, isoflurophate, and timolol), which two agents could have an additive effect to produce excessive bradycardia?

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines can serve as preanesthetic medications and as induction agents for general anesthesia (statement I). questions.question: RC is a 33-year-old male with a history of HIV for 10 years who now presents with Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI). Which of the following drugs has demonstrated in vitro activity against MAI?
questions.explanation: Clarithromycin, a macrolide related to erythromycin, has demonstrated in vitro activity against Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI) and is more active than erythromycin against this organism as well as against staphylococci and streptococci; it is also active against Toxoplasma gondii and Cryptosporidium spp. Vancomycin-class and penicillinase-resistant penicillins such as cloxacillin are used to treat staphylococci and streptococci but have no demonstrated activity against MAI.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with ovarian cancer presents with pain. Her pain was reasonably well controlled with two capsules of oxycodone every 4 hr until 2 weeks ago, when she was hospitalized for pain control. She was placed on meperidine (75 mg) every 3 hr but still complained of pain, so her meperidine dosage was increased to 100 mg every 2 hr. questions.explanation: CNS excitation, including myoclonus and other seizure-like activity, can develop with frequent, high-dose meperidine because of accumulation of its metabolite, normeperidine. Given this patient's escalating, frequent meperidine dosing (100 mg every 2 hr), myoclonic seizures are the expected complication rather than adequate analgesia.

You are counseling the grandmother of a 3-year-old boy who has a prescription for amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin) to treat uncomplicated otitis media. Which of the following issues would be least likely to affect medication adherence (compliance)?
questions.explanation: Autonomy - the child's own ability to independently manage or administer medication - is not a meaningful adherence factor for a 3-year-old, since a child this young is entirely dependent on a caregiver (in this case, the grandmother) to administer every dose; autonomy becomes a much more relevant issue later, during adolescence, when patients begin taking more responsibility for their own medication-taking behavior. In contrast, the grandmother's understanding of how and why to give the medication (education), the cost of the prescription, how often doses must be given during the day (dosing interval), and whether the child will tolerate or resist the medication's taste are all practical, well-established barriers to adherence in young pediatric patients.

A 48-year-old black man has a history of mild to severe hypertension, poorly controlled with enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide due to inconsistent compliance. He has no history of diabetes mellitus or heart disease. He completed a 14-day course of clarithromycin for an upper respiratory infection in the past month and now returns for follow-up. He complains of dizziness, loss of energy, increased urinary frequency, and lower-extremity edema. Exam: overweight man, standing BP 175/100 mmHg, moderate ankle edema, slight third heart sound. Labs: BUN 45 mg/dl, serum creatinine 3.7 mg/dl, serum calcium 5.3 mg/dl, serum potassium 6.3 mg/dl, hematocrit 25%. Serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin saturation, and ferritin are normal. Urinalysis shows mild proteinuria and a specific gravity of 1.010. 1. The history, physical examination, laboratory values, and current signs and symptoms suggest that the patient has which of the following conditions?
options: Acute renal failure brought on by a nephrotoxic drug (clarithromycin, enalapril)
Acute renal failure resulting from renal obstruction by a kidney stone
Acute renal failure precipitated by severe dehydration
Chronic renal failure resulting from hypertension
Chronic renal failure resulting from diabetes
questions.explanation: The fixed, low urine specific gravity (1.010) with no crystals or casts, combined with the gradual onset of fatigue, edema, and hypertension, points to chronic rather than acute renal failure. Neither clarithromycin nor enalapril is nephrotoxic, and the patient's blood pressure and fluid status give no indication of a prerenal (dehydration) cause. Long-standing, poorly controlled hypertension is a leading cause of chronic renal failure (CKD), and the clinical picture here — elevated BUN and creatinine, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, and a normocytic anemia from decreased erythropoietin production — is classic for CKD secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis rather than a new acute insult.

I. avoidance of first-pass effects.
II. suitability when the oral route is not feasible.
III. predictable drug release and absorption.
questions.explanation: I and II are correct; III is not. questions.question: Ethyl alcohol (EtOH) is administered to patients who have ingested either ethylene glycol or methanol because EtOH
questions.explanation: Both ethylene glycol and methanol are themselves relatively nontoxic, but they are metabolized by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase into highly toxic metabolites (for ethylene glycol: glycolaldehyde → glycolic acid → the especially toxic oxalic acid; for methanol: formaldehyde and formic acid, which are analogous toxic products). Ethanol works as an antidote because it has a much higher affinity for alcohol dehydrogenase than either ethylene glycol or methanol, so it competitively saturates the enzyme and blocks (rather than increases) the formation of these toxic metabolites — the opposite of choice B. It does not act primarily as a sedative in this context (choice A) or increase renal clearance of the parent compounds (choice D), and it is very much a recognized antidote (ruling out choice E), although fomepizole (Antizol), a more selective alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor with fewer adverse metabolic/CNS effects, has become the preferred agent, with ethanol reserved for situations where fomepizole is unavailable.

questions.question:
How many grams of boric acid should be used in compounding the following prescription?
Phenacaine HCl 1.0% (NaCl eq = 0.17); Chlorobutanol 0.5% (NaCl eq = 0.18); Boric acid, qs (NaCl eq = 0.52); Purified H2O, ad 30 mL; Make isotonic solution; Sig: 1 drop in each eye.
questions.explanation: This is a sodium chloride equivalent isotonicity problem. Step 1: Find the NaCl equivalent contributed by each active ingredient. Phenacaine HCl: 1.0% x 30 mL = 0.3 g x 0.17 = 0.051 g NaCl equivalent. Chlorobutanol: 0.5% x 30 mL = 0.15 g x 0.18 = 0.027 g NaCl equivalent. Combined, the actives represent 0.051 + 0.027 = 0.078 g of NaCl. Step 2: Find the total NaCl needed for 30 mL to be isotonic: 0.9% x 30 mL = 0.27 g. Step 3: Subtract to find the NaCl still needed: 0.27 g - 0.078 g = 0.192 g. Step 4: Convert this remaining NaCl requirement to boric acid using its NaCl equivalent: 0.192 g / 0.52 = 0.369 g, which rounds to 0.37 g.

questions.question: An unconscious patient is brought to the emergency department with a history of an unknown drug overdose. Which of the following actions should the physician perform?
questions.explanation: Management of an unconscious patient with an unknown overdose follows a comprehensive, layered approach: first and always, support the vital functions (airway, breathing, circulation) and stabilize the patient (choice B); then give empiric antidotal therapy targeting the most common reversible causes of depressed mental status — dextrose (to treat occult hypoglycemia), thiamine (to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome when glucose is given), and naloxone (in case an opioid is involved) (choice A); and simultaneously obtain baseline laboratory studies such as a CBC, electrolytes, and a toxicology screen to help identify the causative agent and guide further, more specific treatment (choice C). questions.explanation: Pain or difficulty when swallowing (odynophagia/dysphagia) is a warning symptom suggesting significant esophageal mucosal damage, stricture, motility disorder, or malignancy, and requires referral for medical diagnosis and prescription-level treatment rather than self-treatment with nonprescription agents. questions.explanation: Patients responding to antidepressant therapy should continue treatment through the continuation phase, which is generally 6-9 months, to consolidate the acute response and reduce the risk of relapse. questions.question: All of the following statements concerning antacid therapy used in the treatment of duodenal or gastric ulcers are correct except which one?
questions.explanation: Antacids have been shown to both heal peptic ulcers and effectively control ulcer pain, so the claim that they are 'ineffective in controlling ulcer pain' is the false statement. The other statements are correct: antacids neutralize acid and reduce pepsin activity; when used alone they should be dosed 1 hr and 3 hr after meals (the meal prolongs the acid-buffering effect) and at bedtime; if an antacid mixture causes diarrhea, alternating with constipating aluminum hydroxide can help; and calcium carbonate is generally avoided because of acid rebound and constipation.

questions.question: A 48-year-old black man has a history of mild to severe hypertension, poorly controlled with enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide due to inconsistent compliance. options: A major cause of chronic renal failure
A major cause of acute renal failure
A major cause of both chronic and acute renal failure
Only seen in patients whose renal failure has caused excessive fluid retention
A minor cause of acute renal failure
questions.explanation: Systemic, long-standing hypertension is the second most common cause of chronic renal failure (CKD) after diabetes. Only malignant (severely accelerated) hypertension causes acute renal failure, and even then it is an uncommon cause. Elevated blood pressure is a common consequence of both CKD and ARF once substantial renal damage has occurred, but ordinary hypertension is specifically a major cause of chronic, not acute, renal failure.

questions.question: Which of the following mood stabilizers would be most appropriate in a patient with liver disease?
questions.explanation: Lithium is not known to cause hepatic dysfunction and is not metabolized by the liver — it is eliminated almost entirely by the kidneys unchanged — making it the most appropriate mood stabilizer of these choices for a patient with liver disease. Both valproic acid and carbamazepine, by contrast, undergo hepatic metabolism and can impair liver function, so they would be less desirable in this patient.

Certain types of ethers such as glycosides also undergo hydrolysis, but they usually require strongly alkaline conditions or a catalyst such as an enzyme. Ketones, amines, or carboxylic acids do not undergo hydrolysis.

questions.explanation: Doxorubicin is an antitumor antibiotic that inhibits DNA synthesis by intercalating between DNA base pairs. questions.question: In antiviral immunity, what directly recognizes and kills viral-infected cells? I. Cytotoxic T cells (CTLs) II. Antiviral antibodies III. Interferons
questions.explanation: Antiviral antibodies are probably most important in extracellular immunity to viruses, binding virus particles for opsonization and preventing additional infection of cells. Interferons are secreted from viral-infected and other cells (e.g., macrophages, T cells) and, after binding to receptors, induce the appearance of antiviral proteins in other cells. CTLs recognize viral- infected cells and cause direct cytotoxicity.

questions.question: Which of the following medications would most likely exacerbate a preexisting seizure disorder?
questions.explanation: Although all antidepressants can lower the seizure threshold to some degree, bupropion is specifically contraindicated in patients with a seizure disorder because of its comparatively higher seizure risk. Paroxetine was associated with only about a 0.1% incidence of seizures in clinical trials, seizures with venlafaxine occur infrequently (roughly 1 in 100 to 1 in 1000 patients), and trazodone is not thought to alter the seizure threshold at normal therapeutic doses (seizures have been reported mainly in overdose).

questions.question: The passage of drug molecules from a region of high drug concentration to a region of low drug concentration is known as
questions.explanation: Transport of a drug across a cell membrane by passive (simple) diffusion follows Fick's law of diffusion, moving with the concentration gradient -- from high to low concentration. This is the opposite of active transport, in which drugs move against a concentration gradient.

Myocardial oxygen demand is governed by the heart's contractile state, the ejection time, left ventricular volume/wall tension, and systolic pressure (afterload) — as contractility falls, ventricular volume and wall tension rise, each independently increasing the oxygen the heart muscle requires per cardiac cycle. Right atrial pressure, a right-heart filling pressure, is not one of the classic determinants of left ventricular myocardial oxygen demand and is therefore the exception.

Metoprolol, a beta-adrenergic blocker, produces the opposite effect: it decreases heart rate, blood pressure, and contractility, thereby reducing (not increasing) myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.explanation: Graves disease (diffuse toxic goiter) is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism; it occurs most often in women in their 3rd-4th decades and results from an autoimmune reaction between IgG antibodies and the thyroid gland that stimulates excess hormone production. Endemic (iodine-deficiency) goiter, surgical thyroid excision, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and goitrin-induced iodine deficiency are all recognized causes of hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A beta-blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity
questions.explanation: Pindolol was the first beta-blocker shown to possess high intrinsic sympathomimetic activity — the ability to partially stimulate the receptors it also blocks, which helps maintain a satisfactory heart rate and may reduce the risk of bronchoconstriction compared with agents lacking this property.

questions.question: A 16-year-old woman is reported to have overdosed on 40 sustained-release theophylline tablets. She is transported to the emergency department, where gastric lavage was performed and she was given one dose of activated charcoal. An initial theophylline level is 42 µg/mL, but a follow-up level in the intensive care unit (ICU) is 95 µg/mL. What is the most appropriate course of therapy?
questions.explanation: This patient's theophylline level rose sharply (from 42 to 95 µg/mL, far above the 5-20 µg/mL therapeutic range) despite an initial single dose of activated charcoal, because large ingestions of sustained-release products can act as a drug reservoir in the GI tract, continuing to release drug for absorption over time and overwhelming a single decontamination attempt. The appropriate escalation is repeat (multiple-dose) activated charcoal to enhance ongoing elimination, combined with charcoal hemoperfusion, which is specifically noted to be more effective at removing theophylline from the blood than hemodialysis and is used for unstable patients (e.g., those approaching or in status epilepticus). Syrup of ipecac (choice B) is not recommended for theophylline overdose management. Forced alkaline diuresis (choice C) is used for weak-acid drugs like salicylates or phenobarbital, not theophylline. Sodium-polystyrene sulfonate (choice D) is a potassium-binding resin used for hyperkalemia, not for enhancing theophylline elimination.
options: Charcoal hemoperfusion and multiple-dose activated charcoal
Forced diuresis and multiple-dose activated charcoal

questions.question: A patient who overdoses on acetaminophen is admitted to the hospital for antidotal therapy with N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC). The patient has the following medication orders: NAC 140 mg/kg loading dose followed by 70 mg/kg for a total of 17 doses, ranitidine 50 mg IV every 8 hr, prochlorperazine 10 mg IM every 6 hr as needed for nausea, thiamine 100 mg IV every day for 3 doses, and Darvocet N-100 1-2 tablets every 4 hr as needed for headache. What is the best course of action?
options: Call the physician to increase the dosage of ranitidine to 50 mg IV every 6 hr
Call the physician to have the Darvocet N-100 discontinued
Call the physician to initiate hemodialysis therapy
Have the patient prophylactically intubated to protect the airway
Administer ethanol 10% at a loading dose of 7.5 mL/kg over 1 hr, followed by a continuous infusion of 1.4 mL/kg/hr for 48 hr
questions.explanation: The critical safety issue in this order set is that Darvocet N-100 is a combination product that contains acetaminophen (in addition to propoxyphene). Giving any additional acetaminophen-containing product to a patient who is already being treated for acetaminophen toxicity would add further hepatotoxic burden exactly when the goal of NAC therapy is to prevent (or limit) liver injury — so the pharmacist's most important intervention is to catch this and have the physician discontinue the Darvocet N-100. The NAC dosing itself (140 mg/kg loading, then 70 mg/kg for a total of 17 doses) is the standard oral regimen and does not need adjustment (making choice A, an unrelated and unnecessary ranitidine dose change, a distractor). Hemodialysis (choice C) is not standard therapy for acetaminophen overdose. Prophylactic intubation (choice D) is not indicated based on the information given. And the ethanol infusion regimen described (choice E) is the antidote used for ethylene glycol or methanol poisoning, not acetaminophen — including it here is meant to test whether the reader recognizes it as an irrelevant, distractor treatment for the wrong toxin.

Volatile anesthetics act colligatively as solutes in the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane. Drug receptors are endogenously expressed, but their level can be modulated by exogenously added drugs. Down-regulation of receptor level can lead to desensitization, not sensitization, of the target cell to the receptor agonist.

questions.question: DG is a 23-year-old female committed to the inpatient psychiatric ward by her parents. They also state that she angers more easily than she used to as a child, and this morning they found her with a knife trying to slit her wrists. questions.question: In choosing a study perspective, the current pharmacoeconomic (PE) guidelines have suggested which one of the following perspectives to be included?
questions.explanation: Current pharmacoeconomic guidelines recommend that the societal perspective be included in an analysis. Identifying the perspective from which a decision is made is critical because it directly affects the conclusion — for example, a decision to fund a high-cost, moderately effective therapy for hospitalized septic patients might look quite different from a hospital formulary committee's in-house budgetary viewpoint than it would from the broader societal viewpoint of saving lives at whatever expense.

questions.question: Which of the following resources would be appropriate for identifying a drug manufactured in a foreign country?
options: AHFS (American Hospital Formulary Service Drug Information)

questions.question: The termination of heparin activity by protamine sulfate is the result of

questions.explanation: Heparin is a highly acidic mucopolysaccharide, while protamine is a highly basic protein. When protamine is administered after heparin, it chemically combines with heparin, presumably through an acid-base interaction, and inactivates its anticoagulant effect, making protamine an effective heparin antidote. Caution is required because excess protamine can itself produce an anticoagulant effect.

questions.question: Which statement regarding phase-specific chemotherapeutic agents is correct? They
questions.explanation: Phase-specific chemotherapy agents exert their maximal cytotoxic effect during one particular phase of the cell cycle (for example, antimetabolites act in S phase and mitotic inhibitors act in M phase), and they have essentially no activity against cells in G0, the resting phase. Examples include the mitotic inhibitors, asparaginase, the antimetabolites, and etoposide. Alkylating agents and antitumor antibiotics, by contrast, are phase-nonspecific — they act throughout the cell cycle, including in resting cells.

questions.question: Correct statements about dobutamine include which of the following? I. questions.explanation: Dobutamine, dosed at 5-20 ug/kg/min, is a positive inotropic agent used in HF (statement I is correct). Unlike dopamine, however, dobutamine lacks significant effects on renal blood flow and tends to produce peripheral vasodilation rather than an increase in peripheral vascular resistance, making statement II incorrect. Dobutamine is also a sympathomimetic amine (a synthetic catecholamine), not a 'nonsympathomimetic' agent, making statement III incorrect as well. Only statement I is correct.

questions.explanation: The term enantiomer and the D and L indicate that the β-methacholine has a chiral center and exhibits optical isomerism. questions.explanation: These two compounds are neither true isomers nor the same compound, since one contains three oxygens while the other substitutes one oxygen for a sulfur. questions.explanation: Digitoxin has only one alcohol (hydroxyl) group on its steroidal nucleus, whereas digoxin has two, and this small structural difference significantly reduces digitoxin's polarity (statement II). Because of its greater lipophilicity, digitoxin undergoes more extensive renal tubular reabsorption (statement III), enterohepatic recycling, hepatic microsomal metabolism, and plasma protein binding (statement I), all of which combine to give digitoxin a longer duration of action and greater potential for cumulative effects compared with digoxin.

questions.question: A major error in a hospital pharmacy resulted in a total parenteral nutrition solution being mistaken for a cardioplegic solution for coronary bypass surgery. Which of the following is true regarding the root cause analysis that was done at the hospital after the error?
questions.explanation: A root cause analysis systematically investigates all the direct and indirect contributing factors behind an error — asking questions such as what happened and why, what staffing or workload pressures were present, whether look-alike products were stored near each other, whether labeling or communication was inadequate, and whether training was sufficient. It is not a blame-finding exercise (ruling out choice A) and it is not merely a formal acknowledgment that an error occurred (ruling out choice B, which understates its purpose); rather, its entire value lies in comprehensively identifying and analyzing every systemic factor that contributed, so that similar tragic mix-ups (like confusing a TPN solution with a cardioplegic solution) can be prevented going forward. Given the severity of this error, an RCA is exactly the appropriate response, not an inappropriate one (ruling out choice D).
options: The primary objective is to find out which pharmacist made the mistake that allowed this to take place
The result of the analysis would be the admission that an error had taken place
All factors that could have contributed to this error would be identified and analyzed
A root cause analysis would be inappropriate in this case
All individuals who might have directly witnessed this incident would be interviewed and documented

This is a worked renal-dose-adjustment calculation using the Sarubbi-Hull approach, following the same method demonstrated in the chapter's gentamicin example (Section IV.D):

Step 1 - Estimate the patient's creatinine clearance (Clcr) using the Cockcroft-Gault equation for a male patient:
Clcr = [(140 - age) x weight(kg)] / (72 x Crs)
Clcr = [(140 - 70) x 80] / (72 x 3) = (70 x 80) / 216 = 5600 / 216 = approximately 26 mL/min

Step 2 - Estimate the patient's prolonged half-life (t1/2)ri caused by reduced renal function, using the fraction of drug eliminated unchanged (F = 0.98 for aminoglycosides) and the ratio of the patient's Clcr to the normal population Clcr (120 mL/min):
(t1/2)ri = (t1/2)n / [F x (Clcr,ri / Clcr,n) + (1 - F)]
(t1/2)ri = 2.5 / [0.98 x (26/120) + 0.02] = 2.5 / [0.98 x 0.216 + 0.02] = 2.5 / [0.212 + 0.02] = 2.5 / 0.232 = approximately 10.9 hours

Step 3 - Calculate the loading dose (DL) needed to reach the target Cmax,ss of 7.5 mcg/mL, using the patient's population V, S, and f:
DL = (Cmax,ss)(V) / (S)(f) = (7.5 mcg/mL)(0.25 L/kg) / (1)(1) = 1.9 mg/kg

Step 4 - Determine the fraction of drug lost during a 24-hour dosing interval (tau), using the patient's adjusted (t1/2)ri of 10.9 hours:
fraction lost = 1 - 10^[-0.3(tau/t1/2)] = 1 - 10^[-0.3(24/10.9)] = 1 - 10^(-0.661) = 1 - 0.22 = 0.78

Step 5 - Calculate the maintenance dose per tau, which replaces the fraction of drug lost during each interval to maintain the same peak and trough at steady state:
D per tau(ri) = (DL)(fraction lost) = (1.9 mg/kg)(0.78) = 1.5 mg/kg

Therefore, a loading dose of approximately 1.9 mg/kg (within the 1.8-2.0 mg/kg range) followed by a maintenance dose of 1.5 mg/kg every 24 hours is expected to achieve the desired Cmax,ss (~7.5 mcg/mL) and Cmin,ss (<2 mcg/mL) in this renally impaired patient, confirming option B. As with any dosing estimate built on population parameters and estimated Clcr and t1/2, if the patient's actual measured Cmax,ss and Cmin,ss differ from these predictions, the discrepancy is most likely explained by the patient's true Clcr, t1/2, or V differing from the estimated values used in the calculation, and the regimen should be adjusted based on a measured serum concentration.
options: A loading dose of 1.8-2.0 mg/kg followed by 1.0 mg/kg qd
A loading dose of 1.8-2.0 mg/kg followed by 1.5 mg/kg qd

Which of the following statements are true for sodium pertechnetate technetium-99m (99mTc) USP?
I. It is used to radiolabel all other 99mTc radiopharmaceuticals.
II. The molybdenum-99 (99Mo) breakthrough limit is < 0.15 microCi 99Mo/mCi 99mTc (< 0.15 kBq/MBq).

questions.explanation: Sodium pertechnetate 99mTc USP, eluted from the 99Mo/99mTc generator, is the starting material used to radiolabel essentially all other 99mTc-based radiopharmaceutical kits (statement I). Regulatory limits require that molybdenum-99 breakthrough (contamination of the eluate with the longer-lived parent) not exceed 0.15 microCi 99Mo per mCi 99mTc, an important quality-control check performed on each eluate (statement II). However, 99mTc decays by isomeric transition with a physical half-life of approximately 6 hours, not 16 hours, so statement III is incorrect.

What do the following abbreviations MS, MSO₄, and MgSO₄ have in common?
questions.explanation: MS and MSO₄ are abbreviations that have historically been used for morphine sulfate, while MgSO₄ is an abbreviation for magnesium sulfate — two very different drugs that have been dangerously confused with one another when abbreviated this way, contributing to serious patient harm. Because of this look-alike/mix-up risk, all three abbreviations appear on JCAHO's 'Do Not Use' list, and the chapter specifically recommends that morphine sulfate and magnesium sulfate be spelled out in full rather than abbreviated. Choices A and B are each only partially correct (they each describe only one of the two drugs represented across the three abbreviations), so choice C — capturing the shared prohibition against using any of them — is the best overall answer.

questions.explanation: The margin of safety of the two drugs can be helpful in guiding selection of a drug. Margin of safety is the ratio of TD0.1 to ED99.9. Thus the margin of safety for drug A is 20 mg ÷ 0.4 mg, or 50, whereas the margin of safety for drug B is 15 mg ÷ 0.2 mg, or 75. Because drug B has a greater margin of safety than drug A, drug B is relatively safe at the dosage given to produce the desired effect.

Both drugs have the same margin of safety, so more information is needed.

Digoxin is a hapten, a molecule that is too small to stimulate responses (be an immunogen) in its free form, but can be recognized by antibodies. To obtain sheep antidigoxin antibodies, the sheep is immunized with digoxin that has been coupled to a larger molecule, in this case, a protein. The antibodies obtained from the sheep are cleaved with proteolytic enzymes to yield the Fab fragment. This fragment is specific to and can bind digoxin, blocking its biologic activity. Animal antibodies have a shorter serum half- life when injected into humans, and all Fab fragments, even human, have a short half-life compared to complete antibody molecules. Only complete human IgG has a half-life of approximately 1 month.

What is the most important focus of pharmaceutical care?
questions.explanation: Pharmaceutical care is defined as a collaborative, patient-centered process. Unlike traditional pharmacy practice, which is oriented around the prescription/order or drug product, and clinical pharmacy, which is process-oriented, pharmaceutical care is oriented around patient outcomes. A pharmacist can build a caring, empathetic relationship only with a real patient — not with a chart or a drug profile — which is why the patient, not the prescription or the record, is the central focus of pharmaceutical care.

questions.question: An 80-year-old man takes warfarin for his mechanical heart valve. He would also like to take the following herbs: Asian ginseng, feverfew, garlic, and dong quai. Which of the these herbs may decrease the effectiveness of warfarin?
questions.explanation: Asian ginseng is unique among the listed herbs in that it may decrease the INR, thereby reducing warfarin's anticoagulant effectiveness and potentially raising clotting risk in this patient with a mechanical heart valve. Feverfew, garlic, and dong quai, in contrast, all tend to increase the INR and enhance warfarin's effect, raising bleeding risk instead. Metronidazole is not an herb (it is a prescription antimicrobial) and is listed only as a distractor, though it too is known to increase the INR when combined with warfarin.

questions.question: The definition of a surfactant (an ingredient in toothpaste) can best be described by which of the following statements?
options: It prevents drying of the preparation.
It removes debris by its detergent action and causes foaming, which is usually desired by the patient.
It physically removes plaque and debris.
It determines the texture, dispersiveness, and appearance of the product.
It adds flavor to the preparation, which makes it more appealing to the patient.
questions.explanation: Sodium lauryl sulfate is used frequently as a surfactant in most dentifrices. Its detergent action aids in the removal of debris, and the foaming is usually desired by the patient. There is no evidence that surfactants possess anticaries activity or decrease periodontal disease. The FDA considers surfactants an inactive ingredient in dentifrices.

questions.question: A patient in the intensive care unit on a ventilator was placed on a glucose system parenteral nutrition (PN) formulation providing 2040 kcal/day and 98 g protein/day. A measured energy expenditure (MEE) of 2038 kcal and a respiratory quotient (RQ) of 1.1 were subsequently obtained. Which of the following is correct based on this information?
options: The patient is receiving adequate glucose calories, and an adjustment in the program is not necessary.
The daily protein intake has to be decreased to reduce the patient's RQ.
The PN formulation should be switched to a lipid system formulation to reduce the carbon dioxide load.
The patient is retaining oxygen from the glucose calories in the PN formulation.
Lipid emulsion should be added to the current PN formulation to enhance lipogenesis.
questions.explanation: An RQ above 1.0 indicates that excess carbohydrate calories are being converted to fat (lipogenesis), a process that generates more carbon dioxide than oxidation does — a concerning finding in a ventilated patient because the added CO2 load increases ventilatory demand. Even though the caloric intake (2040 kcal) closely matches the measured energy expenditure (2038 kcal), the elevated RQ signals overfeeding with glucose specifically. Switching to a lipid system formulation, where lipid supplies 40%-50% of nonprotein calories, reduces the CO2 load because lipolysis produces less carbon dioxide than glycolysis, easing ventilatory demand.

Using the same set of metabolic pathway options (ether glucuronidation, ester glucuronidation, nitroreduction, oxidative deamination, ester hydrolysis), acetaminophen, which contains a phenol group, is metabolized primarily by which pathway?
questions.explanation: The principal functional group in acetaminophen is a phenol. Like the carboxylic acid group in benzoic acid, a phenol commonly undergoes glucuronide conjugation, but because it is an alcohol/phenol rather than a carboxylic acid, conjugation produces an ether glucuronide rather than an ester glucuronide. Phenols such as acetaminophen also commonly undergo sulfate conjugation and, less frequently, O-methylation.

Precipitation may occur when mixing aqueous solutions of meperidine hydrochloride with which of the following solutions? I. Sodium bicarbonate injection II. Atropine sulfate injection III. Sodium chloride injection
questions.explanation: When meperidine hydrochloride solution is mixed with the alkaline solution of sodium bicarbonate, a neutralization reaction occurs with the possible precipitation of the water-insoluble free base meperidine. A neutralization reaction occurs when acidic solutions are mixed with basic solutions, or conversely. No reaction, in terms of acid-base, occurs when solutions are mixed with other acidic or neutral solutions or when basic solutions are mixed with other basic or neutral solutions. There should be no reaction, then, when the meperidine hydrochloride solution, which is acidic, is mixed with the acidic solution of atropine sulfate or the neutral solution of sodium chloride.
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct

questions.question: IT is a 58-year-old male admitted to the intensive care unit with acute respiratory failure and thrombocytopenia. He is at high risk for an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Which of the following agents is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the prevention of this type of bleed?
questions.explanation: Although sucralfate and H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine have been used successfully off-label for stress-ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients, omeprazole (as an oral powder suspension) is specifically the agent that carries FDA approval for prevention of upper GI bleeding due to stress ulcers in critically ill patients. Esomeprazole and lansoprazole, despite being proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole, do not carry this specific approved indication.

questions.question: For the same cephalosporin antibiotic patient, how long after the dose is exactly 75% of the drug eliminated from the patient's body?
questions.explanation: For any first-order elimination process, 50% of the drug present is eliminated during each successive half-life. After one half-life, 50% has been eliminated (50% remains); after a second half-life, half of that remaining 50% is further eliminated, so a cumulative 75% has been eliminated (25% remains). Since this drug's half-life is 2 hr, 75% elimination occurs after two half-lives, or 2 hr x 2 = 4 hr).

questions.question: Allopurinol is recommended instead of probenecid in the treatment of hyperuricemia in which of the following situations? questions.explanation: Allopurinol is preferred over probenecid when large tophi are present, when creatinine clearance is markedly reduced (probenecid becomes ineffective with impaired renal function, generally below about 50-60 mL/min, whereas the allopurinol dose is simply reduced), and when there is a need to prevent large urate loads — such as in leukemia, where tumor-cell turnover risks renal urate precipitation. All three situations (I, II, and III) therefore favor allopurinol.

questions.question: Which statement about pneumococcus and meningococcus vaccines is true? I. They are composed of purified polysaccharides. II. They are recommended for children < 2 years of age. III. The vaccines protect against all serotypes of disease causing pneumococcus or meningococcus.
questions.explanation: The pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines are multivalent and contain purified polysaccharide from a number of different serotypes. However, these vaccines do not contain polysaccharide from all the relevant infectious agents. Purified polysaccharides do not stimulate immune responses in children younger than 2 years of age. For polysaccharide vaccines to be effective in young children, the polysaccharide must be conjugated to a protein as in the Hib vaccine.

questions.explanation: 'Warfarin 1.0 mg' contains a trailing zero — a decimal point followed by a zero after a whole number. This is a recognized dangerous notation because if the decimal point is missed or overlooked when the prescription is read or transcribed, '1.0' can easily be misread as '10,' resulting in a tenfold overdose exactly as described in this scenario. This is why best practice (and JCAHO's 'Do Not Use' list) calls for writing doses like this simply as 'warfarin 1 mg,' without the unnecessary trailing zero. Choice B describes the opposite problem (a missing leading zero before a decimal, such as writing '.5 mg' instead of '0.5 mg'), which is not what happened here. Choice C is irrelevant since there is no second, similarly named drug involved. Choice D is incorrect because a tenfold dispensing overdose that caused patient harm squarely meets the NCCMERP definition of a preventable medication error.

questions.question: The structure shown is a diethylaminoethyl p-aminobenzoate ester: it contains a hydrophilic amino group in the alcohol portion of the molecule connected via an ester linkage to a lipophilic aromatic acid group. questions.explanation: This structure is that of procaine, a diethylaminoethyl p-aminobenzoate ester and the prototype of the ester-type local anesthetics. Its combination of a hydrophilic amine linked through an ester bond to a lipophilic aromatic acid is the classic structural pattern of ester-type local anesthetics.

questions.question: The characteristics of an active transport process include all of the following except for which one?
questions.explanation: Statement B is the false exception: Fick's law of diffusion describes passive diffusion of drug molecules from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration -- a process that is not saturable and does not require energy. Active transport, by contrast, is a carrier-mediated, energy-requiring process that can move drug molecules against a concentration gradient and can become saturated at high drug concentrations.

questions.explanation: The positive predictive value (PPV) of a diagnostic test is defined as the proportion of patients with a positive test result who actually turn out to have the positive outcome the test is meant to predict - that is, it answers the question 'given that this test was positive, how likely is it that the patient truly has the condition (e.g., toxicity or therapeutic response)?' For example, if a serum drug concentration above a defined cutoff is being used to predict drug-induced toxicity and the PPV is 0.8, then 80% of patients whose SDC is above that cutoff will actually experience toxicity; if instead the test is being used to predict an effective therapeutic response, 80% of patients above the cutoff will actually respond effectively. Option A describes the reverse relationship (sensitivity-like framing, i.e., the fraction of true positive-outcome patients who test positive), while options B, C, and E do not correctly define PPV in terms of test-result-to-outcome accuracy.

questions.question: All of the following statements concerning zero-order degradation are true except
questions.explanation: Statement D is the false exception: in zero-order degradation, drug concentration decreases over time (it does not stay unchanged) -- what stays constant is the rate (velocity) at which the concentration changes, expressed as dC/dt being a constant negative value. a plot of concentration versus time yields a straight line on rectilinear paper.
its half-life is a changing parameter.

questions.question: A 60-year-old hypertensive woman is currently being treated with nitroglycerin, carvedilol, furosemide, nifedipine (Procardia), ramipril, aspirin, and digoxin. She is admitted with a diagnosis of stage C heart failure. Q3: Which agent is most likely to be discontinued in this patient?
questions.explanation: Calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine have negative inotropic effects and are one of the drug classes (along with certain antiarrhythmics and NSAIDs) generally identified as best avoided in most heart failure patients because they can worsen HF symptoms. Carvedilol (a beta-blocker with proven mortality benefit in HF), furosemide (diuretic for volume control), ramipril (an ACE inhibitor), aspirin, and digoxin are all appropriate components of chronic HF management and would be continued.

questions.question: According to the principles of drug excretion into the breast milk, which combination of the following properties would result in the highest drug concentration in breast milk? I. low molecular weight, moderately lipophilic  II. low plasma protein bound, weakly basic  III. highly plasma protein bound, weakly acidic
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct
if I, II, and III are correct
questions.explanation: A drug that is low in molecular weight and moderately lipophilic passes easily across the membranes separating maternal plasma from breast milk, so statement I describes properties that favor high milk concentrations. Likewise, a drug that has low plasma protein binding has a larger free (unbound) fraction available to diffuse into milk, and a weakly basic drug tends to become ionized ('ion trapped') once it reaches the more acidic environment of breast milk, becoming trapped there and further raising milk concentrations, so statement II is also correct. Statement III describes the opposite, unfavorable combination: high plasma protein binding limits the free fraction available to cross into milk, and a weakly acidic drug does not become ion-trapped in breast milk the way a weakly basic drug does, so this combination would not produce a high milk concentration. Therefore, I and II together (not III) describe the properties that maximize drug transfer into breast milk.

Alavert contains loratadine, a second-generation antihistamine that preferentially binds peripheral H1-receptors, producing minimal CNS penetration and therefore minimal sedation, anticholinergic effects, and impairment of intellectual/motor function. Benadryl, Dimetapp, and Drixoral all contain first-generation antihistamines, which cross the blood-brain barrier and cause significant sedation and cognitive impairment - an important drawback for a student who needs to remain alert during final exams, even though first-generation agents are typically less expensive.

Losartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker with a distinct uricosuric effect — it increases urinary uric acid excretion and can lower serum urate — making it a preferred antihypertensive choice in a patient with gout. Hydrochlorothiazide, by contrast, reduces urinary uric acid excretion and should be used cautiously (if at all) in gout patients, while clonidine, lisinopril, and irbesartan have little to no effect on serum uric acid.

The pharmacist receives a prescription for hydromorphone (Dilaudid) injection to be compounded to a solution of 15 mg per mL. Dilaudid is commercially available in an ampule but the concentration is 10 mg per mL. The physician would like a more concentrated solution prepared so that 50 mls can be instilled into the titanium resevoir of a Medtronic infusion pump. The hydromorphone solution will be continuously infused, intrathecally, over approximately 30 days, for a patient with chronic back pain, uncontrolled with oral narcotics. The pharmacist checks his inventory and finds a bottle of Hydromorphone powder, USP. He proceeds to weigh out enough powder for a 60 mL preparation. The weighing step is checked by a colleague pharmacist. According to USP Chapter 797 this sterile preparation would be considered a
questions.explanation: The hydromorphone preparation is a high risk level CSP because it is made from non-sterile powder. Derived calculation: the prescribed strength is 15 mg/mL, and the pharmacist weighs powder for a 60 mL batch (extra volume to allow for losses during compounding and filtration, since only 50 mL is needed for the pump reservoir). Required hydromorphone mass = 15 mg/mL x 60 mL = 900 mg of hydromorphone powder. Because the preparation starts from a non-sterile bulk powder (not from a sterile, commercially manufactured product), USP <797> classifies it as a high-risk level compounded sterile preparation (CSP), which carries the strictest requirements for testing, environment, and beyond-use dating of the three CSP risk levels.

questions.question: Following principles of teratogenicity, drug exposure during the following times could cause fetal abnormalities? I. first 2 weeks of gestation  II. weeks 3-8 of gestation  III. the fetal period
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct
if I, II, and III are correct
questions.explanation: During the first 2 weeks after fertilization, the developing embryo follows an 'all-or-none' principle: it is essentially impervious to teratogens, so exposure during this earliest window either has no lasting effect or results in loss of the embryo, but does not typically cause the structural birth defects associated with teratogenicity, making statement I incorrect. Weeks 3-8 of gestation constitute the classic period of organogenesis, when the embryo is most vulnerable to structural teratogenic effects, making statement II correct. Exposure during the fetal period (after organogenesis) can still cause harm; teratogenic effects during this later period are not always structural, but can instead be functional or behavioral in nature, making statement III correct as well. Therefore, II and III (not I) are the periods during which drug exposure can cause fetal abnormalities.

questions.question: S.M., a 38-year-old woman, received a living-related kidney transplant 2 months ago. At clinic today she complains of tiredness, shortness of breath, and pedal edema. Serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL and BUN 43 mg/dL (versus 1.2 mg/dL and 24 mg/dL 4 weeks ago), and tacrolimus level 3 ng/mL (therapeutic range 5-15 ng/mL). She was diagnosed with acute graft rejection, admitted, and treated with thymoglobulin. Six months later her renal function is good (creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, BUN 28 mg/dL), but today her BP is 160/105. Which of the following medication(s) contribute(s) to her hypertension? I. Tacrolimus II. Prednisone III. Mycophenolate mofetil
questions.explanation: Tacrolimus promotes vasoconstriction and renal dysfunction, both of which contribute to hypertension, and prednisone increases fluid and sodium retention, which also raises blood pressure. Mycophenolate mofetil is an antimetabolite that inhibits DNA synthesis and cell proliferation; its main side effects are leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, and it is not associated with hypertension, so only tacrolimus and prednisone (I and II) contribute here.

questions.question: Patients with angina pectoris receiving propranolol plus diltiazem must be monitored for which adverse drug effect?
questions.explanation: Propranolol (a beta-blocker) and diltiazem (a calcium-channel blocker) both produce negative chronotropic effects (slowed heart rate) and negative inotropic effects (reduced contractility). Used together, their effects are additive, so patients must be watched for both bradycardia and reduced cardiac output/decompensation — corresponding to options A and B together.

questions.question: The structure shown is a benzothiadiazine (sulfonamide-containing) nucleus, the hallmark of the thiazide diuretics. This structure is characteristic of which of the following agents?
questions.explanation: The benzothiadiazine nucleus is the defining structural feature of hydrochlorothiazide, a sulfonamide diuretic and the prototype thiazide. Other sulfonamide-containing diuretic subclasses, such as the carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) and loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), do not contain this benzothiadiazine nucleus and are chemically distinct.

questions.question: The standard recommended dose of glyburide is
questions.explanation: The standard recommended dosing range for glyburide is 1.25-20 mg/day; doses above 20 mg/day are not recommended by the manufacturer. Patients are typically started on a low dose, such as 1.25 mg/day, and titrated upward to an effective, clinically indicated dose.

questions.question: After the acute illness (DKA) has resolved in this 20-year-old with newly diagnosed type 1 DM, what therapy would be appropriate?
options: Start a second-generation sulfonylurea, plus dietary modification and physical activity regimen
Daily administration of a regimen of neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH; isophane insulin suspension) and regular insulin, plus dietary modification and physical activity regimen
Daily administration of a fixed regimen of glargine (Lantus; long-acting basal analog insulin) and lispro insulin, plus dietary modification and physical activity regimen
questions.explanation: Type 1 DM always requires ongoing insulin therapy — there is no functioning endogenous insulin secretion to rely on, so diet alone, observation alone, or a sulfonylurea (which depends on functioning β-cells) are never appropriate. A typical maintenance regimen for type 1 DM is a total daily insulin dose of about 0.5 Units/kg/day divided into multiple injections — commonly combining an intermediate-acting insulin such as NPH with a shorter-acting regular insulin — together with consistent dietary carbohydrate management and regular physical activity. Option E describes a real, plausible modern alternative (a basal-bolus regimen using glargine and lispro analogs) and is not inherently wrong pharmacologically, but the text's model answer for this scenario is the NPH-plus-regular-insulin regimen in option C, so E functions as a distractor rather than the expected answer.

Rizatriptan and related triptans act as 5-HT1 agonists, producing three distinct beneficial effects in migraine: direct vasoconstriction that returns dilated cerebral blood vessels to their normal diameter; inhibition, via neuronal receptors, of the release of vasodilating and pain-transmitting substances such as neurokinin A and substance P; and a direct antinociceptive action that prevents pain-transmitting neurons from firing. All three mechanisms contribute to the drug's antimigraine effect.

questions.question: Which of the following preparations is used to attain remission of thyrotoxicosis?
questions.explanation: Propylthiouracil (PTU) induces remission of thyrotoxicosis through two mechanisms: it interferes with iodination of tyrosyl residues (reducing T4 production), and it inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Propranolol is useful as an adjunct for symptomatic control of hyperthyroid symptoms but does not itself reduce thyroid hormone production, while liotrix, levothyroxine, and desiccated thyroid are all thyroid hormone replacement products used for hypothyroidism, not treatments for thyrotoxicosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a component of acute coronary syndrome (ACS)? I. unstable angina II. non-ST-segment elevated myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) III. ST-segment elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI)
questions.explanation: Acute coronary syndrome is the umbrella term for the acute ischemic presentations of coronary artery disease and encompasses unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI — each of which reflects a different degree of coronary occlusion and carries its own treatment pathway (UA/NSTEMI share similar management; STEMI's differs). Stable angina, by contrast, is not part of ACS; it represents the chronic, exertional starting point of ischemic heart disease rather than an acute event.

questions.explanation: Furosemide, a loop diuretic, remains effective even at markedly reduced creatinine clearance and is the initial diuretic of choice when creatinine clearance falls below 25 mL/min. Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide have little effect at this level of renal impairment. Bumetanide, torsemide, and ethacrynic acid are reserved for patients who are allergic to furosemide or in whom repeated furosemide dosing is ineffective.

Uncoupling this linkage is the reverse of this reaction, a hydrolysis reaction. A hydrolase is an enzyme that catalyzes hydrolysis reactions. More specific terms for an enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of proteins are amidase or peptidase. A ligase catalyzes the coupling of two molecules. questions.explanation: Under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA) of 1994, dietary supplements are not classified as drugs or foods, and manufacturers are permitted to make claims regarding the product's effect on the structure or function of the body (though not disease claims). Supplements are not required to be proven safe and effective before marketing (unlike drugs), do not need to be standardized to qualify as dietary supplements, and the FDA-mandated disclaimer statement ('This product has not been evaluated by the FDA...') is a required element of labeling, not an optional one.

questions.explanation: Pramoxine has a chemically distinct structure from the other local anesthetics listed, giving it minimal cross-sensitivity with lidocaine and the other 'caine' anesthetics. It is therefore the preferred topical anesthetic for a patient with an established lidocaine allergy, whereas tetracaine, dibucaine, and benzocaine share structural similarities with lidocaine that carry a higher risk of cross-reactive allergic reactions.

The p-phenyl-N-alkylpiperidine moiety is characteristic of the structurally specific opioid analgesics. Meperidine, chemically ethyl 1-methyl-4-phenylpiperidine-4-carboxylate, is built on exactly this N-methyl-p-phenylpiperidine scaffold. Phenobarbital is a barbiturate sedative-hypnotic, chlorpromazine is a phenothiazine antipsychotic, diazepam is a benzodiazepine anxiolytic, and imipramine is a dibenzazepine tricyclic antidepressant, none of which share this piperidine-based opioid structure.

Which of the following drugs is a class IV antiarrhythmic that is primarily indicated for the treatment of supraventricular tachyarrhythmias?
questions.explanation: Verapamil, a calcium-channel blocker, is the class IV agent among the choices and is used for its direct effects on impulse conduction to treat and prevent supraventricular arrhythmias. Ibutilide is class III (used for atrial fibrillation/flutter conversion), quinidine is class IA, mexiletine is class IB, and propranolol (a beta-blocker) is class II — all are also effective for various supraventricular arrhythmias, but only verapamil is the class IV agent specified in the question.

questions.question: All of the following chemotherapy agents work through affecting microtubule function except
questions.explanation: Docetaxel is a taxane that works by promoting microtubule assembly and stabilization, which blocks cell division; vinblastine, vincristine, and vinorelbine are vinca alkaloids that work by the opposite mechanism, preventing microtubule formation. Mitoxantrone, by contrast, is an antitumor antibiotic that works through DNA intercalation, not through any effect on microtubules.

questions.question: Which of the following topics would not be included in the assessment portion of the FARM note?
questions.explanation: The Assessment (A) portion of a FARM note is the pharmacist's evaluation of the findings — it includes statements about what additional information is needed to fully assess the problem, the severity/priority/urgency of the problem, and the short- and long-term goals of the proposed intervention. Actual recommendations made to the patient or caregiver (choice A) belong instead in the Resolution (R) portion of the note, which documents the actual or proposed actions taken by the pharmacist (e.g., counseling the patient, informing the prescriber, or recommending a therapy change) along with the rationale for that intervention.

questions.explanation: A hypermetabolic stress state such as major trauma, combined with several days of protein deprivation, can rapidly precipitate a moderate to severe kwashiorkor-type malnutrition, characterized by hypoalbuminemia, edema, and impaired cellular immune function — unlike marasmus, which develops from chronic calorie deprivation over a much longer period. This places the patient at elevated (not low) risk for hospital-acquired infection and makes him an appropriate candidate for aggressive nutritional support.

questions.explanation: II and III are correct; I is not. questions.question: Which of the following metabolites would be the least likely excretion product of orally administered aspirin?
questions.explanation: Aspirin's functional groups allow it to undergo several metabolic reactions: aromatic hydroxylation, conjugation of the carboxyl group with glycine, conjugation of the carboxyl group with glucuronic acid (forming an ester glucuronide), hydrolysis of the acetate ester, and conjugation of the resulting phenol with glucuronic acid (forming an ether glucuronide). Because aspirin's acetate ester is readily hydrolyzed in the acidic stomach before absorption, and any absorbed intact drug is further hydrolyzed by esterases in the circulation and liver, essentially none of the acetylated (unchanged) drug survives intact to reach the glomerular filtrate. Excretion of unchanged aspirin is therefore highly unlikely.

As a worked illustration (using representative values, since none are given in the question stem): if a patient's TT4 is 10 µg/dL and their RT3U is 33% against a population mean RT3U of 30%, then FTI = 10 × (33/30) ≈ 11.0, which falls within the normal euthyroid FTI range of about 5.5-12. Cost-of-illness methodology, by contrast, only assesses the resources (measured in dollars) required to treat a designated illness — there are no comparator groups or consequences evaluated, so it does not address both cost and consequences.

questions.question: Which drug is a non-ergot dopamine agonist and has a side-effect profile different from the rest of the dopaminergic agents?
questions.explanation: Ropinirole is a non-ergot dopamine agonist indicated for both early and advanced stages of Parkinson disease. Non-ergot agonists selectively bind and activate the D2 dopamine receptor (with little or no D1 affinity and greater affinity for D3 than D2) and, unlike the older ergot-derived dopamine agonists, have a low incidence of pleuropulmonary and retroperitoneal fibrosis, coronary vasoconstriction, erythromelalgia, and Raynaud phenomenon. This gives ropinirole a side-effect profile that is distinctly different from the ergot-derived dopaminergic agents.

questions.question: A patient diagnosed with depression was unsuccessfully treated with fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was discontinued, and 14 days later, the patient started therapy with phenelzine. Then, 3 days after phenelzine was started, the patient presented with hyperreflexia, fever, elevated blood pressure, confusion, and diarrhea. What is the most likely cause of this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: Serotonin syndrome can occur when an MAOI (such as phenelzine) is started too soon after discontinuing another serotonergic agent, since the combination causes an excess of serotonergic activity. A washout period of about 2 weeks is generally recommended between stopping most SSRIs and starting an MAOI; however, fluoxetine specifically requires about a 5-week washout period because of its long-acting active metabolite, norfluoxetine. Because phenelzine was started only 14 days after stopping fluoxetine — before adequate clearance of norfluoxetine — this patient developed serotonin syndrome, characterized by hyperreflexia, fever, elevated blood pressure, confusion, and diarrhea.

questions.question: Which of the following agents would not be an alternative to phenobarbital in the treatment of partial seizures?
