questions.question: Drugs that act systemically must I. undergo biotransformation into an active form after reaching their active site. II. be in a form capable of passage through various membrane barriers. III. be in or be converted to a form that is readily excreted from the body.
questions.explanation: Generally, drugs must be lipophilic to pass through lipoprotein membranes and hydrophilic to be excreted by the kidney. Drugs do not have to be converted into an active form at their active site, although most drugs must be in their active form when they reach their active site. Many drugs are active in the form in which they are administered. Some drugs, usually referred to as prodrugs, are biotransformed into their active form after administration. Theoretically, drugs that reach their active site and then are metabolically activated should be more specific in their action and have fewer side effects. Currently, research efforts are under way to develop site-specific delivery systems and processes.

questions.question:
Situations that can potentially lead to drug interactions include
I. multiple-drug therapy
II. multiple prescribers
III. patient compliance
questions.explanation: A patient's medication profile might not capture the complete drug history if the patient is on multiple medications (increasing the chance two of them interact), sees multiple prescribers (who may not be aware of each other's prescriptions), or has variable compliance (taking OTC medications or supplements, or missing doses, without informing the pharmacist or physician). All three situations can contribute to unrecognized or unmanaged drug interactions.

questions.question: Define therapeutic drug monitoring. What is meant by the term TDM?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is defined as the practice, applied to a limited group of drugs, of using serum drug concentrations (SDCs) in conjunction with clinical observation to individualize and optimize a patient's drug therapy. TDM is reserved for drugs that meet two key criteria: (1) there is a direct, meaningful relationship between the serum concentration and the pharmacological response, and (2) the range of concentrations that are both effective and safe is narrow, so that small deviations above or below this therapeutic range risk toxicity or therapeutic failure. Because SDC alone does not fully capture a patient's clinical status, it is always interpreted alongside other clinical observations rather than in isolation, which is exactly what option A describes. The other options describe unrelated or narrower uses (determining population half-life values, verifying assay accuracy, general drug observation, or classifying drugs as effective/ineffective) that do not capture the actual definition of TDM.

questions.question: A patient presents with pressured speech, inability to sleep for 72 hr, bizarre dress, inappropriate makeup, and grandiose delusions that interfere with social functioning. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This clinical presentation — pressured speech, severe insomnia, bizarre dress and grooming choices, and grandiose delusions that impair social functioning — is consistent with mania. Hypomania is a less severe mood elevation that, by definition, does not impair functioning, which rules it out here since this patient's symptoms clearly interfere with social functioning. Euthymia refers to a normal mood state, and depression typically presents with neurovegetative symptoms (low mood, low energy), which is the opposite of this presentation.

questions.question: Contraindications to the administration of syrup of ipecac include which of the following?
questions.explanation: The classic contraindications to inducing emesis with syrup of ipecac are remembered as the '3 C's': Caustic ingestion, patient is Convulsing (seizing), and patient is unConscious (CNS-depressed). Each poses a serious aspiration or re-injury risk: an unconscious patient cannot protect their own airway during vomiting; a seizing patient is also at high aspiration risk and emesis could worsen the clinical picture; and inducing vomiting after a caustic (strong acid/alkali) ingestion would re-expose the esophagus to the corrosive substance, causing additional tissue damage. Because all three specific scenarios listed (unconscious, seizing, caustic ingestion) are recognized contraindications, 'All of the above' is correct.

A metabolic reaction converts a primary amine group on a molecule into a carbonyl (ketone) group, with loss of the amino group and introduction of oxygen, without any change in the carbon skeleton or removal of an alkyl group from nitrogen. Terms that may be used to describe this metabolic reaction include
I. N-dealkylation
II. oxidative deamination
III. phase I metabolism
questions.explanation: Converting an amine functional group into a carbonyl group represents a change to an existing functional group, which by definition is a phase I metabolic reaction (statement III). Because this conversion involves introduction of oxygen (oxidation) with loss of the amino group, it is specifically classified as oxidative deamination (statement II). N-Dealkylation, in contrast, refers to removal of an alkyl group attached to a nitrogen atom, which is not what occurs in this reaction, so statement I does not apply.

questions.question: Preventable adverse drug reactions (ADRs)
questions.explanation: None of the listed statements is true. Preventable ADRs are not necessarily mild — they can cause serious medical problems requiring intensive medical care and, as noted in the chapter, are estimated to account for a large share of ADR-related morbidity, mortality, and cost. They are also not always easily recognized: although some preventable ADRs may appear obvious in retrospect upon review of a patient's medication history, this is frequently not the case, since recognizing an ADR requires assessing multiple causality factors (timing, dechallenge/rechallenge, prior reports, drug interactions, etc.) that are not always straightforward.

questions.question: A 48-year-old black man has a history of mild to severe hypertension, poorly controlled with enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide due to inconsistent compliance. He has no history of diabetes mellitus or heart disease. He completed a 14-day course of clarithromycin for an upper respiratory infection in the past month and now returns for follow-up. He complains of dizziness, loss of energy, increased urinary frequency, and lower-extremity edema. Exam: overweight man, standing BP 175/100 mmHg, moderate ankle edema, slight third heart sound. Labs: BUN 45 mg/dl, serum creatinine 3.7 mg/dl, serum calcium 5.3 mg/dl, serum potassium 6.3 mg/dl, hematocrit 25%. Serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin saturation, and ferritin are normal. Urinalysis shows mild proteinuria and a specific gravity of 1.010. 5. When should peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis be considered to treat this patient's renal failure?
questions.explanation: Both peritoneal dialysis and hemodialysis carry significant associated complications and morbidity, so they are not started prematurely. Dialysis is indicated once conservative measures (dietary/fluid restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives, phosphate binders, and so on) can no longer maintain adequate fluid, electrolyte, and waste-product balance. Patients can be maintained on dialysis indefinitely, so eligibility for transplantation is not a prerequisite.

Only when renal function has decreased to a point where fluid and electrolyte status cannot be maintained using conservative measures
On an intermittent basis as the situation demands
Only if the patient is a kidney transplant candidate

questions.explanation: This patient has ingested 20 tablets × 500 mg = 10,000 mg (10 g) of acetaminophen, which meets the threshold (>10 g in adults) at which treatment is generally indicated. However, the treatment (NAC) decision and duration are formally guided by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, which specifically requires a level drawn at 4 hours post-ingestion (the earliest reliable time point) to accurately assess the risk of hepatotoxicity — a level obtained only 2 hours after ingestion, before absorption is complete, cannot be reliably plotted on the nomogram and may underestimate the peak level. Given the large ingested dose, the safest and most appropriate course is to begin a loading dose of NAC empirically while awaiting a properly timed 4-hour level to confirm whether the full antidotal course is needed; if that 4-hour level falls in the toxic range, the complete NAC regimen should be continued. Repeated charcoal alone (choice A) is insufficient given the large, potentially toxic ingestion; ipecac (choice B) is inappropriate this many hours after ingestion and in general is not favored; and discharging the patient (choice D) would be dangerous given the significant ingested dose and alcohol co-ingestion, which further increases hepatotoxicity risk.

options: Aspirin is indicated for mild to moderate analgesia, inflammatory diseases, antipyresis, and prophylaxis for patients with ischemic heart disease.

questions.explanation: Aspirin is the only OTC analgesic with FDA-approved labeling covering all four uses: analgesia, anti-inflammatory action, antipyresis, and prophylaxis in patients with ischemic heart disease. questions.question: Which of the following agents have been shown to interact with oral thyroxine (T4) replacement therapy? (I) atenolol (II) calcium carbonate (III) ciprofloxacin (IV) levothyroxine (V) raloxifene
questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate (II) reduces T4 bioavailability by adsorbing levothyroxine at acidic pH, lowering free and total T4 and raising TSH unless doses are separated; ciprofloxacin (III) and raloxifene (V) have similarly been shown to interact with levothyroxine when co-administered, requiring separation of about 6 hours for ciprofloxacin and about 12 hours for raloxifene. This matches option E's wording ('if II, III, and V are correct'); atenolol (I) is not a recognized levothyroxine interaction, and levothyroxine (IV) obviously does not 'interact' with itself. Note: the original textbook's printed answer key lists this as '(I, III, V)', which appears to be a typographical error, since it is internally inconsistent with option E's own text ('II, III, and V') and with the accompanying explanation, which discusses calcium carbonate, ciprofloxacin, and raloxifene — not atenolol. This CSV follows the internally consistent reading (II, III, and V).
options: if I and IV are correct

questions.explanation: The quality control (QC) unit is the group within the manufacturer responsible for establishing product specifications and for testing the finished dosage form to verify that those specifications have actually been met — including acceptance or rejection of raw materials, packaging components, drug products, water systems, and environmental conditions used during manufacture. Conditions that tend to increase the action of an orally administered drug that undergoes phase II metabolism include
I. enterohepatic circulation
II. enzyme saturation
III. first-pass effect
options: if I and II are correct
if II and III are correct
if I, II, and III are correct
questions.explanation: Enterohepatic circulation occurs when glucuronide conjugates secreted into the intestine via bile are hydrolyzed by intestinal bacterial beta-glucuronidase, regenerating free (non-polar) drug that can be reabsorbed and prolong drug action (statement I). If the phase II conjugating enzyme system becomes saturated, active drug cannot be inactivated through that pathway, and if no alternative pathway exists, plasma levels of active drug rise, increasing activity or toxicity (statement II). The first-pass effect, by contrast, results in hepatic metabolism of a drug before it ever reaches its site of action, which decreases, rather than increases, its overall activity - so statement III is incorrect.

questions.question: The dispensing pharmacist usually blends potent powders with a large amount of diluent by
questions.explanation: Geometric dilution is used to mix potent substances with a large amount of diluent. The potent drug is first mixed with an equal amount of diluent by trituration; then a further volume of diluent equal to the mixture already in the mortar is added and triturated again. This doubling procedure is repeated until all diluent has been incorporated, ensuring uniform distribution of the potent ingredient.

questions.explanation: Levodopa can cause gastrointestinal side effects such as nausea and vomiting, particularly at the start of treatment, along with bowel irregularity and gastrointestinal bleeding. A patient who has received citalopram 40 mg/day for 2 weeks for the treatment of major depression complains that the medication is not working and would like to be switched to another agent. What is the appropriate recommendation?
questions.explanation: An antidepressant must be given at an adequate, maximally tolerated dose for 4-6 weeks before it can be considered a true therapeutic failure. Since this patient has only been on citalopram for 2 weeks, the best recommendation is to continue the current regimen for at least 2 more weeks to allow an adequate trial. MAOIs are reserved for refractory depression and are not indicated at this early stage, and lithium augmentation is not appropriate until the patient has failed two or three different antidepressant trials.

questions.question: Alice is 27 years old and in the first trimester of her pregnancy. She needs a recommendation for sneezing, rhinorrhea, and nasal itching, which started 2 days ago. She feels miserable with her symptoms, which worsen when she cleans the house. Her current medications include calcium carbonate and docusate sodium. Which of the following would be the best recommendation for Alice's symptoms?
questions.explanation: Alice's symptoms (sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal itching worsened by house-cleaning/dust exposure) are classic allergic rhinitis, not nasal congestion, so pseudoephedrine and Breathe Right Nasal Strips (which relieve congestion) are not appropriate. Chlorpheniramine, a first-generation antihistamine, and intranasal cromolyn are both considered acceptable during pregnancy for allergic rhinitis symptoms, but cromolyn requires 1-2 weeks of regular use before symptom improvement is seen, whereas chlorpheniramine relieves symptoms within hours. Because Alice feels miserable now and needs prompt relief, chlorpheniramine is the better choice.

questions.explanation: The Controlled Substances Act sets out specific required findings for each schedule. Choice A ('high potential for abuse') and choice C ('no currently accepted medical use') describe schedule I criteria, not schedule III. Choice E ('lack of accepted safety under medical supervision') is also a schedule I criterion. Choice B, describing dependence 'relative to schedule IV,' is actually the schedule IV finding language (relative to schedule III), not the schedule III finding, so it does not fit here either.

Abuse of the drug or other substance may lead to limited physical dependence or psychological dependence relative to the drugs or other substances in schedule IV
The drug or other substance has no currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States
Abuse of the drug or other substance may lead to moderate or low physical dependence or high psychological dependence
There is a lack of accepted safety for use of the drug or other substance under medical supervision

questions.explanation: Relative bioavailability compares two formulations given at the same dose (here, both the generic and reference tablets were given as a 200 mg dose), so it is calculated directly from the ratio of their AUC0-∞ values, with no dose-correction needed: Relative bioavailability = (AUC generic tablet / AUC reference tablet) x 100% = (2822 / 2715) x 100% = 103.94%, which rounds to 103.9%. Because relative bioavailability compares one dosage form to another (rather than to an intravenous dose, which is 100% bioavailable by definition), it can exceed 100%, whereas absolute bioavailability -- which is always referenced to the IV dose -- cannot exceed 100%. This is why the generic tablet can show a relative bioavailability of 103.9% relative to the reference tablet even though neither tablet could exceed 100% absolute bioavailability relative to the IV bolus injection.

Drugs with linear clearance have shorter t1/2 values than drugs with nonlinear clearance.

questions.explanation: Linear (first-order) pharmacokinetics assumes that clearance (Cl) and half-life (t1/2) remain constant regardless of dose, so that a proportional change in dose produces the same proportional change in steady-state serum concentration (Css) - for example, doubling the dose doubles Css. Nonlinear (zero-order, or capacity-limited/saturable) clearance behaves differently: as the dose or the amount of drug in the body increases, the elimination pathway (often enzymatic or transporter-mediated) becomes saturated, causing Cl to decrease and t1/2 to lengthen as dose increases. This means proportional increases in dose produce disproportionately large increases in Css - a small dose increase can trigger a much larger-than-expected rise in serum concentration and toxicity risk. This distinction matters greatly for TDM: with linear drugs, clinicians can reliably predict how a dose adjustment will change Css using simple proportional (linear) equations, whereas with nonlinear drugs, the relationship between dose and Css is not predictable by simple proportion, requiring more caution, more frequent monitoring, and different (Michaelis-Menten-type) equations when adjusting doses of drugs such as phenytoin. Options C, D, and E reverse or misstate these relationships, and option B does not address the actual defining pharmacokinetic difference between the two clearance types.

Contrary to option C, pentamidine does have a clinically significant effect on serum glucose — blood glucose must be carefully monitored during therapy because the drug can cause either hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia (including delayed, sometimes irreversible, hypoglycemia from islet cell injury).

questions.question: Assume that for a digoxin, the therapeutic range is cited as Cavg,ss = 0.8-2 ng/mL. If the patient is assumed to have an estimated digoxin t1/2 of 48 hours, how long would you wait to take a serum digoxin concentration measurement, and when during tau would you schedule it?
questions.explanation: Because steady state is clinically assumed to be reached after 3-4 half-lives (representing about 88%-94% of true steady state), and the patient's estimated digoxin t1/2 is 48 hours, the wait time is 3-4 x 48 hours = 144-192 hours, or approximately 6-8 days; 7 days is the closest and most reasonable choice among the options. Once steady state has been reached, the timing of the blood draw within the dosing interval (tau) must match the reference point used to establish the therapeutic range. Since the therapeutic range here is defined as Cavg,ss (the average concentration during tau, i.e., near the midpoint of the dosing interval), the level should be drawn near the midpoint of tau rather than shortly after a dose (which would approximate Cmax,ss) or right before the next dose (which would approximate Cmin,ss). For a once-daily digoxin regimen, the midpoint of the 24-hour interval falls around 10-14 hours after the dose, matching option C. The other options either wait too short a time to approximate steady state (1, 3 days) or too long (14, 28 days), and/or schedule the level at a point in tau (3-4 hr, 6-8 hr, 1-2 hr, 18-22 hr) that would better approximate a Cmax,ss or Cmin,ss measurement rather than the Cavg,ss the therapeutic range is referenced to.
options: 28 days, then 3-4 hours after the dose is administered
14 days, then 6-8 hours after the dose is administered
7 days, then 10-14 hours after the dose is administered
3 days, then 1-2 hours after the dose is administered
1 day, then 18-22 hours after the dose is administered

Patients with ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease present in similar ways, but there are several clinical differences that can help differentiate them. Which of the following clinical features is more common in Crohn's disease than in ulcerative colitis?
questions.explanation: Fistula formation is a hallmark feature of Crohn's disease, reflecting its characteristic transmural (full-thickness bowel wall) inflammation, and is extremely rare in ulcerative colitis, which involves only the mucosal and submucosal layers. Abnormal bowel movements, gradual disease onset, and joint pain can occur in both conditions and are less useful for distinguishing between them. Option E (rectal bleeding) is actually more characteristic of ulcerative colitis than Crohn's disease, the opposite of what the question asks for.

questions.question: Which one of these statements is not true for the differences between economic studies and randomized clinical trials (RCTs)?
questions.explanation: Clinical and economic end points are generally not the same thing — in the typical sequence of drug development, efficacy (the RCT clinical end point, measured under controlled conditions) is established before effectiveness (the real-world economic end point) is assessed. RCTs, by design, also tend to show inflated benefit estimates and carry additional protocol-driven costs compared with real-world use, and economic studies typically enroll larger, more heterogeneous populations with different generalizability than RCTs — so the statement that clinical and economic end points are identical is the false one.

They state that she has recently been under a large amount of stress from college, and they have noticed over the past year that she has become more withdrawn from her friends and social activities. They also state that she angers more easily than she used to as a child, and this morning they found her with a knife trying to slit her wrists. She does not admit to any visual hallucinations but describes multiple voices (male and female) talking to her continuously telling her that she should harm herself or that people are out to get her. questions.explanation: DG has a history of good response to risperidone but is now relapsing because of nonadherence rather than treatment failure. A long-acting (depot) formulation is indicated specifically to help address medication compliance problems. Because she has not yet failed multiple antipsychotic trials, she is not a candidate for clozapine monotherapy or adjunctive clozapine, which are reserved for treatment-refractory disease. questions.explanation: Not every potential drug interaction is clinically significant; many can be managed or avoided through proper patient instruction and compliance rather than requiring a drug change. Before contacting the prescriber, the pharmacist should evaluate and document whether a given drug combination is likely to produce a clinically meaningful effect in that specific patient, since the clinical significance of any interaction must be assessed on a case-by-case basis rather than assumed. Pharmacodynamic and pharmaceutical interactions can be just as clinically significant as pharmacokinetic interactions, so restricting concern to pharmacokinetic interactions alone is incorrect.

A constant ratio of drug metabolites is formed as the administered dose increases.
The elimination half-life (t1/2) increases as the administered dose increases.
The area under the plasma drug concentration versus time curve (AUC) increases in direct proportion to an increase in the administered dose.
Both low and high doses follow first-order elimination kinetics.
The steady-state drug concentration increases in direct proportion to the dosing rate.
questions.explanation: Nonlinear pharmacokinetics means first-order elimination does not hold at all drug concentrations. For drugs like phenytoin, as plasma concentration rises, the elimination pathway becomes saturated and the apparent half-life increases with dose. Consequently, AUC is NOT proportional to dose, metabolite formation is not a constant ratio, not all doses follow first-order kinetics, and steady-state concentration does not rise in direct proportion to dosing rate -- all of which are hallmarks of nonlinear (capacity-limited) kinetics.

He has no history of diabetes mellitus or heart disease. He completed a 14-day course of clarithromycin for an upper respiratory infection in the past month and now returns for follow-up. questions.explanation: Fluid restriction, loop or thiazide-type diuretics (furosemide, metolazone), antihypertensive therapy, and digoxin (if heart failure is present) are all first-line conservative measures for fluid retention and edema in chronic renal failure. questions.question: Osteoporosis is associated with the use of which of the following drugs used in rheumatoid arthritis (RA)?
questions.explanation: Chronic glucocorticoid therapy (e.g., prednisone), commonly used for symptom control in RA, promotes bone resorption and is a well-recognized cause of osteoporosis; patients on long-term steroid therapy should therefore be started on calcium supplementation and a bisphosphonate. Methotrexate, leflunomide, penicillamine, and hydroxychloroquine are not primarily associated with osteoporosis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning drug recall classification is true?
questions.explanation: The FDA assigns one of three classifications to a drug recall based on the severity of the health hazard involved. A Class I recall is the most serious category: a situation where there is a reasonable probability that use of or exposure to the violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death — exactly matching choice C. By contrast, a Class II recall (mischaracterized in choice D) is a situation where the product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, or where the probability of serious harm is remote (this is actually the description wrongly assigned to Class I in choice B). A Class III recall (mischaracterized in choice E) is a situation where use of or exposure to the product is not likely to cause any adverse health consequences at all (which is actually the description wrongly assigned to Class I in choice A). Each incorrect option essentially takes the correct definition of one class and mislabels it as belonging to a different class.
options: A Class I recall is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product is not likely to cause adverse health consequences

A Class I recall is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or in which the probability of serious health consequences is remote
A Class I recall is a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of, or exposure to, a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death
A Class II recall is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product is not likely to cause adverse health consequences
A Class III recall is a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of, or exposure to, a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death

questions.question: S.M., a 38-year-old woman, received a living-related kidney transplant 2 months ago. At clinic today she complains of tiredness, shortness of breath, and pedal edema. questions.question: The selective cyclooxygenase (COX) 2 inhibitors have been associated with which of the following adverse drug reactions?
questions.explanation: The primary safety concerns with selective COX 2 inhibitors are gastrointestinal bleeding and, more significantly, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events. The thrombotic risk reflects loss of the normal contribution of vascular COX 2 to the daily balance of platelet and vascular function. Severe ischemic colitis has instead been linked to alosetron; torsade de pointes to older, second-generation antihistamines and cisapride (no longer marketed); acute liver failure to acetaminophen overdose; and Churg-Strauss syndrome to zafirlukast combined with corticosteroid withdrawal - none of which are associated with the COX 2 selective inhibitors.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs, based on its mechanism of action, is effective in treating diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)?
questions.explanation: Alosetron blocks the 5-HT3 receptor, inhibiting serotonin-mediated increases in intestinal motility, thereby slowing peristalsis and gut transit, which is beneficial in diarrhea-predominant IBS. Tegaserod, by contrast, is a serotonergic agonist that stimulates GI motility and would worsen diarrhea-predominant IBS. Naratriptan is a 5-HT1 agonist used for migraine and has little effect on GI motility.

questions.explanation: This item is one of three linked questions (Q14-16) that refer to a single drug molecule depicted in the chapter. The compound contains three aromatic phenyl rings, an aliphatic alkyl chain connecting the central phenyl ring to a basic alicyclic (piperidine-type) nitrogen, one or more hydroxyl groups, and a carboxylic acid group. Lipophilic functional groups increase a drug's ability to cross cell membranes: the three aromatic phenyl rings and the aliphatic alkyl chain are all lipophilic (hydrophobic) and contribute to the drug's passage through cell membranes, so functional groups I and II (the phenyl rings and the central alkyl chain) are responsible for membrane permeability, while the hydroxyls are hydrophilic and do not contribute to lipophilicity. Since I and II (the phenyl rings and the alkyl chain) are correct and III (the hydroxyls) is not, the answer is C.

questions.explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) is a cause of hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism — it is an autoimmune condition with elevated antithyroglobulin antibody titers (a titer <1:32 is seen in over 85% of patients) that is more common in women, in whites, and with advancing age, and it may present as either glandular fibrosis or idiopathic thyroid atrophy. Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, T3 toxicosis, and Plummer disease are all recognized causes of hyperthyroidism.

he is showing evidence of some liver damage owing to the heavy alcohol intake
he has experienced a heart attack
he received an intramuscular (IM) injection a few hours before the blood sample was drawn
he pulled a muscle that day when lifting a heavy concrete slab
questions.explanation: CK is found primarily in cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, and brain tissue — it is not present in the liver — so alcoholic liver damage would not raise the CK level. Blunt trauma/bruising, myocardial infarction, an IM injection, and a strained skeletal muscle all release CK from cardiac or skeletal muscle and would plausibly explain an elevated CK.

Freely filtered, this drug limits tubular reabsorption of water and is useful in reducing cerebral edema and intracranial pressure. Which of the following drugs does this describe?
questions.explanation: Mannitol is a highly polar, water-soluble osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered at the glomerulus but poorly reabsorbed from the renal tubule. By increasing the osmolarity of the glomerular filtrate, it limits tubular reabsorption of water and promotes diuresis. This osmotic effect is also useful for drawing water out of the brain and eye, which is why mannitol is used to reduce cerebral edema, decrease intracranial pressure, and lower intraocular pressure.

questions.question: For questions 9-10: JB, a 42-year-old white male, complains of a scratchy throat, nasal congestion, and a cough that started 2 days ago. When he coughs, he brings up yellow-white phlegm. He has hypertension and dyslipidemia. Which of the following would be the best recommendation for JB's cough?
questions.explanation: JB's cough is productive, as shown by the yellow-white phlegm he brings up, so an expectorant is appropriate rather than an antitussive. Guaifenesin is the only available OTC expectorant; it works by irritating the gastric mucosa, which reflexively increases respiratory tract secretions, thins bronchial mucus, and loosens sputum so it can be cleared more effectively. Codeine, dextromethorphan, and diphenhydramine are all antitussives, which would suppress the productive cough rather than help clear secretions.

questions.question: A satisfactory suppository base must meet all of the following criteria except
options: it should have a narrow melting range.
it should be nonirritating and nonsensitizing.
it should dissolve or disintegrate rapidly in the body cavity.
questions.explanation: Statement D is the false exception: a good suppository base should remain firm at room temperature and preferably should NOT melt below 30 degrees C, to avoid premature softening during storage and insertion -- rather, it should melt just below body temperature. The other listed criteria (narrow melting range, nonirritating/nonsensitizing, rapid dissolution/disintegration in the body cavity, and inertness) are all genuine requirements of a good suppository base.

questions.question: First-dose syncope, postural hypotension, and palpitations
questions.explanation: Prazosin is a peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic blocker that causes vasodilation of both arteries and veins. Its hallmark adverse effect is 'first-dose syncope' — a marked drop in blood pressure with the first dose (or a dose increase) owing to profound venous and arterial dilation — along with postural hypotension and reflex-mediated palpitations; the incidence of reflex tachycardia is nonetheless lower with alpha-1 blockers than with direct vasodilators like hydralazine.

questions.question: All of the following descriptions match the therapeutic agent for poison ivy except
options: calamine: phenolphthalein gives it the pink color.
Ivy Block: useful in preventing poison ivy dermatitis.
benzocaine: data regarding incidence of hypersensitivity are conflicting.
hydrocortisone: useful for its antipruritic and anti-inflammatory effects.
witch hazel: acts as a mild astringent.
questions.explanation: Ferric oxide provides the pink color of calamine. All of the other descriptions match their associated agents.

questions.question: A 67-year-old white female presented with a 3-month history of progressive difficulty swallowing and a 10-kg weight loss. She is 160 cm tall and weighs 50 kg. She has just undergone a distal esophagectomy and proximal gastrectomy for distal esophageal cancer, with a feeding jejunostomy tube inserted at surgery. The dieticians who are adept at using the Harris-Benedict equation have gone home for the day, and the surgeon calls you for your best guess at what the hourly goal rate for this patient should be using an isotonic enteral formula that provides 0.85 nonprotein calories (NPCs)/mL. Your answer should be
questions.explanation: Using the simple nomogram method (appropriate here since a full Harris-Benedict calculation isn't available) at roughly 30 kcal/kg/day for a mildly to moderately stressed postoperative patient: 30 kcal/kg × 50 kg = 1500 kcal (NPC) per day. Dividing by the formula's caloric density gives the daily volume: 1500 kcal ÷ 0.85 kcal/mL ≈ 1765 mL/day. Dividing by 24 hours yields the hourly rate: 1765 mL ÷ 24 hr ≈ 73.5 mL/hr, which rounds to the closest listed answer of 75 mL/hr.

questions.question: The pharmacist's role in the selection of therapeutic alternatives requires which of the following clinical skills?
questions.explanation: Effective selection of therapeutic alternatives requires the pharmacist to use drug information resources effectively, review and critique the drug literature, and construct comparative analyses to support therapeutic decisions. 'Motivate and inspire patients' (choice B) falls instead under patient education and counseling skills; performing DUEs (choice C) falls under drug-treatment protocol monitoring; and knowledge of community resources (choice D) falls under patient-specific care-plan skills related to referrals — none of these is the specific skill set tied to choosing among therapeutic alternatives.

questions.question: The inhibition of pituitary thyrotropin secretion is controlled by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Rising circulating free T4 (and free T3) levels signal the pituitary via negative feedback to suppress TSH secretion; it is specifically the unbound (free), biologically active hormone fraction — not the protein-bound total hormone (TT4) or the calculated FTI — that is available to act at pituitary receptors and control this feedback loop.

Because they extend from the drug's known pharmacologic effect, they can be provoked or worsened by concomitant disease states, drug-drug interactions, or drug-food interactions — matching choice C. Idiosyncratic reactions and reactions that are primarily a function of individual patient susceptibility (choices A and B) are instead the hallmark of Type B reactions, which are unpredictable, not usually dose-dependent, and tend to concentrate in specific organ systems (liver, blood, skin, kidney, nervous system).

questions.question: A patient with stage I hypertension who has bronchospastic airway disease and who is noncompliant would be best treated with which of the following beta-blocking agents?
questions.explanation: Acebutolol combines relative cardioselective (beta-1) blocking activity — an advantage in patients with bronchospastic airway disease/COPD, since it is less likely than nonselective agents to block bronchial beta-2 receptors — with a long duration of action allowing once-daily dosing, which helps a noncompliant patient. Penbutolol has a long duration of action and intrinsic sympathomimetic activity but lacks relative cardioselectivity; timolol and propranolol are long-acting but nonselective (they block both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors); and esmolol, given only as a continuous IV infusion with an ultrashort duration of action, is unsuited to chronic ambulatory therapy.

questions.question: Which of the following benzodiazepines is expected to cause the least amount of adverse effects in the elderly?
questions.explanation: Oxazepam is considered the safest benzodiazepine choice in elderly patients because it has a relatively short elimination half-life, lacks active metabolites, and is eliminated via glucuronidation (conjugation) rather than oxidative phase I hepatic metabolism, a pathway that is less affected by aging and hepatic changes in the elderly. Chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, and flurazepam should all be avoided in elderly patients because they have long half-lives and active metabolites that can accumulate and cause prolonged sedation, confusion, and fall risk.

Classic signs of muscarinic blockade with atropine include mydriasis (causing photophobia), dry mouth and constipation from reduced GI secretory activity and motility, and tachycardia from loss of normal vagal (cholinergic) restraint on the heart. Diarrhea, by contrast, is a sign of excess cholinergic (muscarinic) activity, not of antimuscarinic blockade, and would not be expected with atropine.

questions.explanation: One of the most common causes of type III hypersensitivity is the response to drugs. This type of reaction is often seen after long-term, high-dose therapy. The treatment of choice is to discontinue treatment and substitute an unrelated drug.

The principle of superposition in designing multiple-dose regimens assumes that
options: each dose affects the next subsequent dose, causing nonlinear elimination.
each dose of drug is eliminated by zero-order elimination.
steady-state plasma drug concentrations are reached at approximately 10 half-lives.
early doses of drug do not affect subsequent doses.
the fraction of drug absorbed is equal to the fraction of drug eliminated.
questions.explanation: The superposition principle underlying multiple-dose regimen design assumes that earlier doses do not affect the pharmacokinetics of subsequent doses (i.e., linear, dose-independent kinetics). If the elimination rate constant or total body clearance changes during multiple dosing -- for example, due to enzyme induction, enzyme inhibition, or saturation of an elimination pathway -- the superposition principle no longer holds and the drug instead displays nonlinear pharmacokinetics.

questions.explanation: Acetaminophen toxicity is characterized primarily by profound hepatotoxicity, caused by a reactive metabolic intermediate that accumulates once the normal glucuronide/sulfate conjugation pathways become saturated and depleted. Unlike ergot toxicity, it does not cause vasoconstriction; unlike aspirin toxicity, it does not typically cause severe GI cramping/diarrhea or profound CNS stimulation and seizures (only mild GI upset may occur early). Liver damage and potential hepatic failure is the hallmark of acetaminophen overdose.

questions.explanation: Complex, or conjugated, enzymes contain a nonprotein group called a cofactor, which is required for biologic activity. In many cases, the cofactor is quite firmly bound to the protein. In others, the binding occurs only during the reaction that the enzyme catalyzes. Cofactors that are firmly bound to the protein are known as prosthetic groups, whereas those that are actively bound to the protein only during catalysis are referred to as coenzymes. A holoenzyme is a complete, catalytically active enzyme system. A transferase is an enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of groups from one substance to another, such as catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT). A heteropolysaccharide is a polysaccharide that contains two or more different monomeric units, such as heparin.

questions.explanation: Procardia XL uses an osmotic system, in which a semipermeable membrane coating surrounds an osmotically active core. Water diffuses in through the membrane (which does not allow drug to diffuse out), dissolving the drug, and a laser-drilled hole allows the resulting drug solution to exit at a rate matching the rate of water influx -- maintaining a constant osmotic pressure gradient and zero-order drug release as long as excess osmotically active solute remains in the core.

Individual pharmacists, pharmacy interns, pharmacy technicians, and other employees or agents of a properly registered pharmacy are specifically exempt from having to register themselves, provided they are acting within the usual course of their employment at that registered pharmacy — the pharmacy's registration covers their activity. This is why 'pharmacists who dispense controlled substances' (as individuals) is the entity that does NOT need its own separate DEA registration, distinguishing them from the pharmacy itself, which does need to register.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man complains of dysuria and urinary urgency and is diagnosed to have uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis. He is given procaine penicillin G intramuscularly. In addition, probenecid is given to prolong the duration of action of penicillin. This type of combined drug effect is known as
questions.explanation: Probenecid alone is inactive against gonococci. However, it can compete with penicillin for urinary excretion. Thus probenecid can reduce the elimination rate of penicillin, whose duration of action becomes prolonged. Therefore, probenecid potentiates the activity of penicillin when the two are given together.

questions.question: Current criteria used in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus (DM) include all of the following symptoms except
questions.explanation: The classic diagnostic picture of DM includes fasting hyperglycemia (fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, or a random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms), polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss (the latter especially in type 1 DM). Tinnitus (ringing in the ears) is not a recognized diagnostic feature of diabetes and is unrelated to glucose metabolism.

NSAIDs are the primary nonprescription pharmacological treatment for dysmenorrhea pain because prostaglandins drive the uterine cramping of dysmenorrhea, and NSAIDs directly inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, giving them a logical and evidence-supported mechanistic advantage. OTC options such as ibuprofen (200 mg every 4-6 hr, maximum 1200 mg/day) and naproxen (200 mg every 8-12 hr, maximum 600 mg/day) are recommended, begun at the onset of pain since there is no proven benefit to starting therapy before symptoms appear. questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding pharmacogenetic polymorphisms is not true?
options: An extensive metabolizer (EM) taking metoprolol for hypertension begins to take OTC Tagamet regularly for heartburn. He is at increased risk for bradycardia and cardiac arrhythmias.
An extensive metabolizer (EM) taking methadone begins taking Tegretol for neuropathic pain. He is at risk for treatment failure and pain crisis.
A poor metabolizer (PM) taking atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia is placed on ketoconazole for a fungal infection. He is at increased risk for myalgia and rhabdomyolysis.
A poor metabolizer (PM) taking metoprolol for tachycardia begins taking Benadryl for sleep. He is not at risk for significant bradycardia and cardiac block.
An ultra-rapid metabolizer (UM) taking codeine for pain relief is at increased risk for opioid toxicity because of accelerated conversion of codeine to morphine.
questions.explanation: A poor metabolizer (PM) already has reduced (inhibited) metabolism of atorvastatin at baseline. Adding another inhibitor such as ketoconazole will not meaningfully increase atorvastatin levels further, since the metabolic pathway is already maximally impaired, so significant additional risk of dose-related toxicity (myalgia/rhabdomyolysis) is unlikely - making this statement false, as the question requires. The other statements are true: an EM taking metoprolol plus cimetidine (Tagamet, a CYP inhibitor) will show an exaggerated rise in metoprolol levels because the EM's normally efficient metabolism is now blocked, raising bradycardia/arrhythmia risk; an EM taking methadone plus carbamazepine (Tegretol, an enzyme inducer) will have increased methadone metabolism, lowering methadone levels and risking treatment failure and pain crisis; a PM taking metoprolol plus diphenhydramine (Benadryl, a CYP2D6 inhibitor) will show further inhibition of an already-impaired metabolic pathway and increased risk of bradycardia and cardiac block; and an ultra-rapid metabolizer taking codeine will convert an unusually large proportion of the prodrug codeine into its active metabolite morphine via CYP2D6, genuinely increasing the risk of opioid toxicity.

questions.question: The structure of prochlorperazine is shown in the source text. Which of the following medications, because of its chemical relationship to prochlorperazine, would most likely cause similar side effects?

Alprazolam, buspirone, and pentobarbital are not phenothiazines at all and are structurally unrelated to prochlorperazine.

How many grams of talc should be added to 1 lb of a powder containing 20 g of zinc undecylenate per 100 g to reduce the concentration of zinc undecylenate to 3%?
questions.explanation: This is a dilution problem where the active ingredient's mass stays constant while diluent is added. One pound equals 454 g of the original 20% w/w powder, which contains 454 g x (20/100) = 90.8 g of zinc undecylenate. To dilute this same 90.8 g down to a 3% concentration, the total final mass must be 90.8 g / 0.03 = 3026.7 g. The amount of talc to add is the difference between the final mass and the original mass: 3026.7 g - 454 g = 2572.7 g.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man who weighs 70 kg and has normal renal function needs an IV infusion of carbenicillin. The desired steady-state plasma concentration is 15 mg/dL, infused over 10 hr. Carbenicillin has an elimination half-life of 1 hr and an apparent volume of distribution of 9 L in this patient. Assuming no loading dose was given, what rate of intravenous infusion is recommended?
questions.explanation: At steady state during a constant IV infusion, the infusion rate R equals Css x k x VD, where k is the first-order elimination rate constant. Converting Css to consistent units: 15 mg/dL = 150 mg/L. k = 0.693/t1/2 = 0.693/1 hr = 0.693/hr. Therefore R = 150 mg/L x 0.693/hr x 9 L = 936 mg/hr).

Other enteric-coating materials include povidone (polyvinylpyrrolidone), polyvinyl acetate phthalate, and hydroxypropyl methylcellulose phthalate (note: this is a different, phthalate-containing form from plain hydroxypropyl methylcellulose). Hyperkalemia is not a cause of ARF — it is a consequence of decreased renal function and altered acid-base balance seen in both acute and chronic renal failure.

The pH value is calculated mathematically as the
questions.explanation: pH is a measure of the acidity, or hydrogen ion concentration, of an aqueous solution. It is defined as the logarithm of the reciprocal of the hydrogen ion (H+) concentration expressed in moles per liter; since the logarithm of a reciprocal equals the negative logarithm of the number, pH equals the negative logarithm of the H+ concentration. A pH of 7.0 indicates neutrality, and acidity increases as pH decreases (e.g., arterial blood is 7.35-7.45, gastric juice is about 1.4). Alkalinity, by contrast, is the negative logarithm of [OH-] and is inversely related to acidity.
options: log of the hydroxyl ion (OH-) concentration.

He also carries numerous additional VTE risk factors — age over 40, recent major surgery, a history of malignancy (lymphoma, even in remission), heart failure with a severely reduced ejection fraction of 15%, prior myocardial infarction, and obesity — making deep venous thrombosis of the lower extremity by far the most likely diagnosis, rather than a musculoskeletal or infectious cause of leg pain.

questions.explanation: Inulin is filtered by the glomerulus but is neither reabsorbed nor actively secreted by the renal tubules, so it is eliminated by glomerular filtration alone. This makes inulin clearance the gold-standard measurement of GFR, useful both clinically and in new-drug development.

Torsades de pointes is a ventricular tachyarrhythmia associated with marked QT-interval prolongation, and it has been reported with several antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, disopyramide, dofetilide, flecainide, ibutilide, procainamide, quinidine, sotalol) as well as certain non-antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g., erythromycin, certain fluoroquinolones, pentamidine). Of the choices listed, only amiodarone is classified as a class III antiarrhythmic; lidocaine is class IB, quinidine is class IA, flecainide is class IC, and diltiazem is a class IV calcium-channel blocker (and is not typically implicated in torsades).

John is a 48 year old male interstate truck driver with a chief complaint of a dry, hacking cough. He states the cough started yesterday, but he has not had any fever, chills, sore throat, or congestion. His only medical condition is hypertension, which is controlled with hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ). What would be the best recommendation for John's cough?
questions.explanation: A dry, hacking, nonproductive cough calls for an antitussive rather than an expectorant, ruling out guaifenesin. Among the antitussive options, codeine and diphenhydramine both cause sedation, which is unsuitable for a truck driver who must remain alert while driving; codeine is also subject to restricted sale in some states and carries allergic-reaction potential. Dextromethorphan controls cough with minimal sedation and few adverse effects at recommended doses, making it the best recommendation, along with counseling that common-cold symptoms typically resolve on their own over time.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a harmful food-drug interaction?
options: Raw green salads for patients on warfarin DVT prophylaxis
Grapefruit juice and cyclosporin to prevent graft vs. host rejection of a transplanted kidney
Omeprazole beads in applesauce for a patient with problems swallowing capsules secondary to GERD
Milk with doxycycline to treat H. pylori
Aged cheese with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) for depression
questions.explanation: Omeprazole capsules contain enteric-coated beads designed to protect the acid-labile drug from destruction in the stomach. When the capsule cannot be swallowed, opening it and sprinkling the still-intact enteric-coated beads into an acidic food such as applesauce preserves the enteric coating through the acidic stomach environment, allowing the drug to reach the more basic duodenum intact for absorption - this improves, rather than harms, drug delivery. In contrast, vitamin K-rich green salads can antagonize warfarin, grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and can raise cyclosporine levels to toxic ranges, calcium in milk chelates doxycycline and reduces its absorption, and aged cheese contains high levels of tyramine that, when its metabolism is blocked by an MAOI, can precipitate a life-threatening hypertensive crisis - all genuinely harmful interactions.

Which of the following drugs is a volatile substance that is administered by inhalation?
questions.explanation: General anesthetics fall into two broad classes: volatile gases or liquids given by inhalation, and nonvolatile agents given intravenously or orally. Halothane, a halogenated hydrocarbon, belongs to the inhaled class and, unlike older volatile agents such as ether or cyclopropane, is nonflammable. Thiopental, alprazolam, buspirone, and phenytoin are all nonvolatile drugs administered orally or parenterally; thiopental is an intravenous basal anesthetic, alprazolam and buspirone are anxiolytics, and phenytoin is an anticonvulsant.

questions.question: Thallous chloride 201Tl USP localizes in tissue by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Thallous chloride 201Tl USP is a monovalent cation whose biological distribution closely parallels that of the potassium ion (K+). Myocardial (and other tissue) uptake of thallium occurs via active transport through the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, the same membrane transport system responsible for cellular potassium uptake.

questions.question: All of the following statements about sodium (Na) are true except which one?
options: The normal range for sodium is 135-147 mEq/L.
Sodium is the major cation of the extracellular fluid, and the laboratory test is used mainly to detect disturbances in water balance.
Hyponatremia usually results from the total body depletion of sodium or through a dilutional effect.
Control of the sodium concentration is mainly through regulation of arterial pH.
Control of the sodium concentration is mainly through actions of aldosterone and ADH.
questions.explanation: Sodium concentration is controlled mainly through the hormones aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which govern renal handling of sodium and water — not through regulation of arterial pH (pH is instead governed largely by the bicarbonate/CO2 buffer system and potassium handling). The other statements are accurate: normal sodium is 135-147 mEq/L, sodium is the major extracellular cation and its measurement mainly reflects water balance/osmolality, and hyponatremia arises either from true total-body sodium depletion (e.g., GI or renal losses) or from a dilutional effect (e.g., CHF, cirrhosis, SIADH, excess water intake).

The two structures shown are simply two different conformations of the same molecule generated by rotation around the side-chain single bond linking the ring nitrogen to the tertiary nitrogen, so the answer is E, conformational isomers.

Content uniformity is required for coated tablets, tablets in which the active ingredient makes up less than 50% of the tablet, suspensions in single-unit containers or soft capsules, and many solids containing added substances; weight variation applies instead to liquid-filled soft capsules and to dosage forms containing at least 50 mg of a single drug that makes up at least 50% of the bulk, among other cases.

questions.question: The recommended maintenance dose of aminophylline for children is 1.0 mg/kg/hr by injection. If 10 mL of a 25-mg/mL solution of aminophylline is added to a 100-mL bottle for dextrose, what should be the rate of delivery in mL/hr for a 40-lb child?
questions.explanation: This combines a dose calculation with a concentration/infusion-rate calculation. Convert weight: 40 lb / 2.2 lb/kg = 18.18 kg. Required dose rate: 1.0 mg/kg/hr x 18.18 kg = 18.18 mg/hr. Next, determine the concentration of the final infusion bag: 10 mL x 25 mg/mL = 250 mg of aminophylline added to the 100-mL bottle, giving a total volume of 110 mL and a concentration of 250 mg / 110 mL = 2.27 mg/mL. Finally, the infusion rate needed to deliver 18.18 mg/hr at this concentration is 18.18 mg/hr / 2.27 mg/mL = 8.0 mL/hr.

Finally, it should localize rapidly in the target organ or tissue of interest while clearing quickly from nontarget tissue, maximizing image contrast and minimizing the radiation-absorbed dose to the rest of the body (statement III). questions.question: As part of a comprehensive management strategy to treat peptic ulcer disease, patients should be encouraged to do all of the following except
questions.explanation: Restricting patients to bland foods is no longer recommended, since evidence shows bland or milk-based diets do not accelerate ulcer healing; patients can generally eat a normal diet but should avoid specific foods that aggravate their own symptoms. Decreasing caffeine, stopping smoking, avoiding alcohol, and not relying on milk as a treatment (milk can transiently buffer acid but triggers rebound acid secretion) are all appropriate components of comprehensive ulcer management.

questions.question: All of the following statements about calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (PO4) are true except which one?
options: An alcoholic with a serum albumin of 2 g/dL and a serum total calcium of 8.0 mg/dL has a corrected total calcium of 9.6 mg/dL.
Calcium and PO4 levels should be interpreted together because many of the same factors influence both minerals.
Metastatic cancer often induces a decrease in serum calcium levels
A patient with renal failure may present with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.
Hypoparathyroidism often induces a decrease in serum calcium levels
questions.explanation: Metastatic cancer and other malignant/granulomatous diseases are classic causes of hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia, so statement C is false. The calcium correction in statement A is accurate: the rule of thumb is to add 0.8 mg/dL to the measured total calcium for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below its normal value of about 4 g/dL. Here albumin is decreased by 2 g/dL (4 - 2), so the correction is 2 x 0.8 = 1.6 mg/dL, giving a corrected calcium of 8.0 + 1.6 = 9.6 mg/dL — a normal value once low albumin (and therefore low protein-bound calcium) is accounted for. Statements B and D are also correct: calcium and phosphate are influenced by many shared factors (PTH, vitamin D, renal function) and are interpreted together, and renal failure classically causes hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia because failing kidneys cannot excrete phosphate and cannot activate vitamin D.

All three of these agents accumulate in the thyroid gland and can be used for thyroid imaging, but they differ in their handling by the gland: sodium iodide 123I is actively trapped and organified into thyroid hormone, giving it ideal imaging characteristics with a favorable radiation dose profile. Sodium pertechnetate 99mTc USP is also trapped by the thyroid but is not organified into hormone, which somewhat limits the functional information the image provides. Sodium iodide 131I is trapped and organified like 123I but delivers a much higher radiation dose and is used more selectively (e.g., for thyroid ablation or whole-body imaging in thyroid cancer) rather than routine imaging. All three, however, are capable of producing a thyroid image.

questions.explanation: Digoxin has a large volume of distribution (7-10 L/kg) and requires 6-8 hours to fully equilibrate between the serum and myocardial tissue after a dose. A level drawn only 1 hour post-dose therefore reflects the drug still largely confined to the vascular/serum compartment and will read falsely elevated compared to the true tissue-equilibrated level — it does not, by itself, indicate a dangerous overdose requiring immediate treatment. The correct clinical response is to wait and repeat the level at the appropriate 6-8 hour equilibration window while reassessing the patient clinically for actual signs/symptoms of toxicity. Digoxin immune Fab antibodies (choice A) should be reserved for symptomatic patients with confirmed toxicity, not triggered off a premature, falsely elevated level. Activated charcoal (choice B) can bind digoxin in the gut but is not the priority action here since this was an IV dose, bypassing the GI tract entirely. Hemodialysis (choice C) is explicitly stated to be of no value in managing digoxin overdose, since digoxin's large volume of distribution and extensive tissue binding make it poorly dialyzable.

Manufacturers may make a change in the formulation after market approval. If the change in the formulation is considered a minor change, the manufacturer needs to report the change to the FDA only in the:
questions.explanation: All post-approval formulation changes must be reported to the FDA in some form — there is no such thing as an unreported change. A minor change is one with only minimal potential to adversely affect the identity, strength, quality, purity, or potency of the product (and thus its safety or effectiveness). Because such changes are unlikely to have any detectable effect on formulation quality and performance, they can be instituted without prior FDA approval and need only be disclosed in the manufacturer's annual report. Larger changes require a CBE-30 supplement (moderate risk) or a full pre-approval supplement (major risk, requiring FDA approval before the change can be implemented).

questions.question: A physician receives a call from the parent of a 2-year-old child who has ingested an unknown quantity of morphine controlled-release tablets and is now unconscious. The physician's initial recommendation is to
questions.explanation: Any patient with unstable vital signs resulting from a poisoning exposure — and an unconscious 2-year-old following an unknown-quantity opioid ingestion certainly qualifies — must be immediately connected with emergency medical services and transported to a hospital emergency department for advanced life support and further management; this is the mandatory first step before any decontamination or antidote strategy is even considered. Home administration of activated charcoal or ipecac (choices B and C) is inappropriate and dangerous here: ipecac-induced emesis is specifically contraindicated in a patient with a depressed level of consciousness because of the risk of aspiration, and giving anything by mouth to an unconscious child similarly risks aspiration. Hemodialysis (choice D) and acid diuresis (choice E) are not indicated interventions for opioid (morphine) overdose at all — the antidote for opioid toxicity is naloxone, administered in the emergency department after the airway and vital signs are secured.

Administer 1 g/kg of activated charcoal with sorbitol

Suggest that the child receive emergency hemodialysis

questions.question: Which of the following agents has been shown to interact with oral thyroxine (T4) replacement therapy?
questions.explanation: Euthyroid patients on oral T4 replacement have become hypothyroid when a bile acid sequestrant such as cholestyramine was given concomitantly, because close dosing intervals reduce T4 bioavailability through binding in the gut. Option E uses the same regimen structure but an inadequate infusion rate (2 Units/hr, roughly 0.03 Units/kg/hr for this patient) and inappropriately sends a patient in active DKA to outpatient follow-up rather than admitting him.

questions.explanation: Nitroprusside is a potent, direct-acting arterial and venous dilator used for rapid blood pressure control in hypertensive emergencies. questions.explanation: FARM is the abbreviated documentation format pharmacists use to record their interventions in a patient's chart when the full Pharmacist's Workup of Drug Therapy (PWDT) is too lengthy for routine notation. The acronym stands for Findings (the patient-specific subjective/objective information that prompted the pharmacist's attention), Assessment (the pharmacist's clinical judgment about the findings, including severity, priority, and short/long-term goals), Resolution/Recommendation (the actual or proposed action, such as counseling the patient, informing the prescriber, or recommending a therapy change), and Monitoring and follow-up (the parameters, frequency, and duration used to track whether the intervention worked). Some institutions use an analogous SOAP note (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) instead, but the content and purpose are the same.

Under the NIH classification, if any one of the assessed parameters indicates a more severe category, the patient is classified according to that more severe level — so because his PEFR indicates moderate persistent disease, he is classified overall as having moderate persistent asthma.
questions.question: A 45-year-old male with a history of asthma has a peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) of 65%, nocturnal wheezing once a month, and daytime wheezing usually less than twice a week. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines for the treatment of asthma, he has which type?
What is the average replacement dose of levothyroxine for an otherwise healthy adult?
questions.explanation: The average adult levothyroxine maintenance dose is 75-150 µg/day, corresponding to about 1.5-1.7 µg/kg/day of body weight — for example, a healthy 70 kg adult would require roughly 1.6 × 70 ≈ 105-115 µg/day, squarely within this range. Elderly or chronically ill patients typically need a lower dose (about 50-100 µg/day, i.e., 25-50 µg/day less than an otherwise healthy adult of the same size), and doses are usually titrated in 25-50 µg/day increments every 4 weeks based on TSH response.

questions.question: P.A. is a 60-year-old man recently diagnosed with stage IIB lung cancer. After evaluation, he underwent surgical resection of the primary tumor and then received chemotherapy with carboplatin and docetaxel. If P.A. has recurrence of his lung cancer after therapy with carboplatin and docetaxel, which targeted agent may be considered for second-line therapy?
questions.explanation: Erlotinib is a targeted agent directed against the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase and is used as second-line therapy in non-small cell lung cancer. Busulfan and cyclophosphamide are non-cell-cycle-specific alkylating agents, and bleomycin and doxorubicin are phase-nonspecific antitumor antibiotics that intercalate with DNA — none of these are targeted molecular agents.

questions.question: Match the chemotherapy agent to the adverse effect with which it is most closely associated (each effect is used only once). Bleomycin
questions.explanation: Bleomycin's dose-limiting toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis associated with cumulative dosing; in this matching set it is paired with gastrointestinal hemorrhage as its most closely associated listed adverse effect, distinguishing it from doxorubicin (cardiotoxicity), paclitaxel (hypersensitivity), irinotecan (diarrhea), and vincristine (constipation).
