questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of the components of a quality assurance programme.
(b) State how each component is applied/selected in practice.
(c) Explain why a lapse in any one component leads to an inaccurate or invalid laboratory result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The QA programme consists of three components: Internal Quality Control (IQC), External Quality Assessment (EQA), and Quality Management.
(b)
• IQC is applied during daily routine work as an immediate control, with errors corrected immediately.
• EQA is applied through proficiency testing, rechecking/retesting, or on-site evaluation, comparing the laboratory's performance with an external agency.
• Quality Management is applied through training of laboratory staff, use of SOPs, standard supply management, standard equipment management, and supervision and organisation.
(c)
The QA programme must assess the effectiveness of the lab's policies and procedures, identify and correct problems, and assure accurate, reliable and prompt reporting of results and adequacy/competency of staff; a lapse in IQC means daily errors go undetected and uncorrected, a lapse in EQA means hidden problems are not detected through external comparison, and a lapse in Quality Management (untrained staff, poor SOPs, faulty equipment/supplies) undermines the entire testing cycle from specimen collection to the physician receiving the report, producing an inaccurate or invalid result.

questions.question:
A skin biopsy culture is observed to produce elongated, spindle-shaped cells capable of continuous multiplication in vitro for many cell generations.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique produced this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
These are fibroblasts.
(b)
Long-term cultures can be derived from skin biopsies (which must include the dermis); this grows in culture and produces fibroblasts, which are capable of continuous multiplication in vitro for many cell generations, in contrast to the short-lived peripheral blood culture.
(c)
The result should be recorded noting the source (skin biopsy including dermis) and culture duration; the follow-up step is that these cells can be used for a variety of biochemical and histochemical studies as well as for chromosome analysis.

(a)
This confirms the specificity of the enzyme reaction in the test section - the coloured reaction seen without the inhibitor is genuinely due to the enzyme being investigated, since it is abolished by a specific enzyme inhibitor.
(b)
This is a negative control using a specific inhibitor of enzyme activity in adequate concentration (0.1% Potassium Cyanide is a known enzyme killer, used for example in the NADI reaction for cytochrome oxidase, which is inhibited by pre-treatment with potassium cyanide solution).
(c)
The result should be recorded as a valid, specific positive reaction in the test section, supported by the negative (inhibited) control; the follow-up step, since any positive reaction that persists after effective inhibition would indicate a non-specific test, is to ensure a further positive control (material known to contain the enzyme) is also run in parallel to fully validate the technique.
questions.question:
An enzyme histochemistry slide, treated with 0.1% potassium cyanide before the reaction, shows no colour development, whereas the parallel test section without the inhibitor shows a positive coloured reaction.
(a) What is the identification/interpretation of this finding?
(b) What basic technique/control produced this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?

questions.answerText:
(a)
The staining solution is prepared the day prior to use; slides are placed in a 55-65°C oven for 45 minutes before staining, then dipped in trypsin solution (1:250 USP Grade) for 5-30 seconds, rinsed in working salt solution, stained with Leishmann stain for 3-4 minutes, rinsed in distilled water, air dried, and examined with a 100X plan-apochromatic oil objective under bright field; a mountant and coverslip are then applied.
(b)
If slides are under-treated with trypsin, they are destained before rebanding, by quickly dipping in 3:1 methanol:acetic acid 2-3 times, or until all stain is removed, then rinsed in distilled water, air dried, and rebanded.
(c)
In this widely used technique, chromosomal proteins are denatured when treated with trypsin, and when subsequently stained with Giemsa stain, they take up stain in a pattern of dark and light bands (G-bands), with the dark bands corresponding to the bands seen in Q-banding, allowing chromosomes to be identified by their banding pattern using standard bright-field microscopy rather than requiring a fluorescence microscope.
(d)
G-banding treats chromosomes with trypsin (denaturing chromosomal proteins) and then stains with Giemsa stain to produce dark and light G-bands examined under bright field/oil objective; Q-banding instead stains chromosomes with quinacrine mustard or a related compound and examines them with a fluorescence microscope, producing a pattern of bright and dim Q-bands that was used as the reference for the Paris conference classification.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the G-banding staining procedure for chromosomes.
(b) Describe the destaining/rebanding procedure if the result is inadequate.
(c) Explain why G-banding is used or preferred as a widely used banding technique.
(d) Distinguish G-banding from Q-banding.

(a) Describe the pre-analytical stage of the quality assurance programme.
(b) Describe the analytical stage of the quality assurance programme.
(c) Describe the post-analytical stage of the quality assurance programme.
(d) Explain why quality assurance is used/preferred (why it matters) in histopathology practice.
(e) Distinguish Internal Quality Control (IQC) from External Quality Assessment (EQA).
questions.answerText:
(a)
The pre-analytical stage covers laboratory design, personnel, equipment, sampling, request form, fixation, transportation, registration, laboratory number, and reagents; for example, fixation should be done immediately after surgery (at worst within one hour) using 10% formol saline, or 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin for laboratories running immuno-services.
(b)
The analytical stage covers grossing, tissue processing, standard operating procedures, controls, equipment, screening of slides, and documentation; tissue processing should be fully automated, and SOPs are written instruction protocols that help prevent mistakes rather than detecting them.
(c)
The post-analytical stage covers reporting, interpretation, typing of reports, auditing, dispatch of reports, block archive, tissue bank, and seminars/continuous professional development; interpretation addresses whether tissue is malignant, its nature/origin, and its grade, ideally supported by immunohistochemistry.
(d)
Quality Assurance is a coordinated system designed to detect, control and prevent the occurrence of errors, and to further a clinician's ability to appropriately care for the patient; quality control activities span the testing process from the moment of specimen collection until the physician receives the report, and the QA programme must assess the effectiveness of policies/procedures, identify and correct problems, and assure accurate, reliable and prompt reporting.
(e)
• IQC refers to measures included during each assay to verify the test is working as it should, done during daily routine work, providing an immediate control with errors corrected immediately, to ensure results are reliable and reproducible.
• EQA is a system for comparing the laboratory's performance using an external agency or facility, through proficiency testing, rechecking/retesting, or on-site evaluation, to evaluate past performance, detect hidden problems, compare performance with others, and confer more confidence on lab staff.

questions.question:
A microincinerated section, viewed under polarized light, shows birefringent crystalline material.
(a) What is being identified by this appearance?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this appearance?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This identifies an anisotropic mineral, such as Silica.
(b)
With polarized light, anisotropic minerals such as Silica are birefringent, which is the characteristic optical property used to detect them after microincineration.
(c)
The correct next step is to correlate this finding with the paired H&E-stained control section (from the same close serial sections) and, if further confirmation is needed, apply the relevant chemical reaction test for the specific mineral suspected.

(a)
• A simple prefix letter is given to each system, e.g.
• C for Cardiovascular, R for Respiratory, S for Skeletal, B for Breast; this letter is followed by a number indicating the main anatomical division of that system, e.g.
• C1 for Heart, C2 for Valves, C3 for Arteries, C4 for Veins; this is followed by a point and a number indicating the disease, e.g.
• C1.1 for congenital conditions of heart, C1.2 for inflammatory conditions of heart, C1.3 for Parasites; these numbers are then followed by numbers for the appropriate specimens, e.g.
• C1.11, C1.12, C1.13, all examples of congenital heart conditions.
(b)
This numbering system is used so that specimens are easily located and accompanied by relevant information helpful to visitors, students and researchers.
(c)
The system is structured in a hierarchical way (system - anatomical division - disease - specimen) so that later additions or amendments do not interfere with the general arrangement; a new specimen can simply be given the next available final number under the correct disease sub-heading, without needing to renumber or reorganise the rest of the collection.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure of the museum specimen numbering system.
(b) State the standard setting in which it is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind allowing later additions without disturbing the general arrangement.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen is placed in an adequately large container of fixative, with additional fixative perfused through the coronary ostia with a syringe.
(b)
This will not only fix the heart tissue, but as the coronary circulation fills, the heart will revert to its natural shape; this is the ideal method for fixing hearts for display.
(c)
• Materials/equipment required include an adequately large container, fixative (formalin-based, e.g.
• Kaiserling formula), and a syringe for perfusion.
(d)
Specimens of heart that have already been cut before being sent to the museum instead require padding out of all cavities and major vessels with cotton wool before fixation to maintain natural shape; failure to pad cavities or to perfuse adequately would compromise the natural shape.
(e)
It is important to pad out all cavities and major vessels with cotton wool before fixation if the heart has already been cut, and to ensure the syringe perfusion fills the coronary circulation adequately so the heart reverts to its natural shape.
questions.question:
A heart specimen is received fresh and uncut for permanent museum preservation.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The ultramicrotome consists of a support carrying the knife and a sample holder installed on a vibration-proof platform; both knife and sample have adjustable orientations, and the sample is mounted on a vertically moving arm moving regularly against the knife edge, with a micro- to nanometer scale movement system controlling object position.
• All operations are controlled under the binocular; the Leica Ultracut UCT ultramicrotome with a cryo-attachment is designed to meet the precise requirements of sample preparation for electron microscopy.
(b)
• Knives may be steel, glass, or diamond, depending on the required thickness to be cut, and are cut from glass or diamond with a 35-45° angle.
• Steel blades are used for animal and plant samples, whereas diamond is used for hard substances.
(c)
This is the only technique yielding directly 30nm sections of constant thickness; it can be applied to a precise zone of the sample selected with the optical microscope, allowing the same selected area to be followed across the whole magnification range using both optical and electron microscopes, and it gives access to structural and chemical information within a volume (3-D reconstruction) that can be exploited for statistical purposes; preparation is relatively fast for a trained operator.
(d)
The ultramicrotome is the best choice for biological materials and polymers, producing ultra-thin sections of constant thickness (30-50nm) without the drawbacks of related thinning techniques, and is used for electron microscopy sample preparation; other microtomes (sled, rotary, cryomicrotome, vibrating, saw, laser) are used more generally for tissue sectioning, with rotary microtomes commonly used for routine light microscopy sectioning at greater thicknesses than the ultramicrotome provides.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the procedure/apparatus for ultramicrotome sectioning.
(b) Describe the materials (knife types) used.
(c) Explain why the ultramicrotome technique is preferred for electron microscopy sample preparation.
(d) Distinguish the ultramicrotome from a standard microtome used for light microscopy.

(a) Describe the composition and properties of glutaraldehyde and paraformaldehyde as fixatives for electron microscopy.
(b) State the standard setting in which each fixative, or a mixture of both, is used in practice.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that tissue should not be over-fixed with certain fixatives.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Glutaraldehyde is a di-aldehyde which preserves the tissue's ultrastructure well but penetrates slower than the monoaldehyde, paraformaldehyde.
• Paraformaldehyde is a monoaldehyde that penetrates faster than glutaraldehyde but results in poorer ultrastructure.
• Fixation is done to preserve the sample and prevent further deterioration so it appears as close as possible to the living state, stabilising cell structure with minimum alteration to morphology and volume; the main purpose is to cross-link cellular structures into a matrix with minimum loss of cellular constituents.
(b)
• Glutaraldehyde is used alone for small pieces of material, while a mixture of glutaraldehyde and paraformaldehyde may be used to fix larger tissues, as in perfusion fixation.
• Modified Palade's fixative is another fixative type that can be used in electron microscopy.
(c)
Tissues fixed with Modified Palade's fixative should not be fixed for more than 60 minutes; fixation is the first and most important step in any electron microscopy study, since mistakes made at this point render the whole project useless, so controlling fixation time and choice of fixative protects the structure, volume and spatial relationships of the cells from irradiation damage and change during subsequent treatment.

questions.question:
A biopsy shows a structured collection of macrophages (epithelioid cells) surrounded by lymphocytes, with Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells (peripheral nuclei) and central caseation necrosis.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique is used to detect the causative agent?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is a granuloma of the immune (T-cell-mediated) type, with caseation necrosis most consistent with tuberculosis (TB); non-caseating granulomas by contrast are seen in sarcoidosis.
(b)
Ziehl-Neelsen staining is the special stain used to detect acid-fast bacilli (the causative organism); GMS or PAS staining is used for fungi, polarised light for foreign materials, and culture/PCR for infectious agents generally.
(c)
The result should be recorded noting the presence of epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and caseation necrosis, with the Ziehl-Neelsen result (positive or negative for acid-fast bacilli); the follow-up step is culture/PCR confirmation of the infectious agent, since diagnosis is important as granulomatous inflammation can mimic neoplasms.

(a)
• Tissue is fixed in 10% formalin in absolute ethanol, transferred directly to absolute ethanol, cleared in xylene, and embedded in paraffin.
• Serial sections are cut and one is stained with H&E (control) and examined with light microscopy, while the other is dewaxed in xylene, transferred to absolute ethanol, air-dried, and placed on an equal-size quartz slide.
(b)
The slide and quartz are placed in the oven; the temperature is raised gradually to 100°C in 10 minutes, then increased to 650°C over the next 25-30 minutes; the oven is then switched off and temperature allowed to fall to about 40°C, after which slides are removed, a coverslip applied gently, and the slide ringed with paraffin wax; the section is examined with low power, darkground illumination, polarized light, and chemical reactions.
(c)
Microincineration is the burning of thin biological specimens (tissue sections) to produce ash patterns which demonstrate the microscopic distribution of mineral substances in the material; it is quite ancient, first described by the pioneer histochemist Raspail more than 130 years ago (1833), though it has since been largely replaced by histochemistry.
(d)
Close serial sections are used, with one prepared for microincineration (viewed with darkground illumination, polarized light and chemical analysis) and the other stained with H&E and examined with light microscopy as a control, so the mineral ash pattern in the incinerated section can be correlated with the normal tissue morphology shown in the H&E control.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the method of preparing tissue for microincineration.
(b) Describe the oven heating procedure.
(c) Explain why microincineration is used or preferred for demonstrating mineral distribution.
(d) Distinguish the microincinerated section from its paired H&E control section.

A brain specimen is received in a soft, fresh state for permanent museum preservation.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Because of its soft consistency and the difficulty of handling in a fresh state, it is necessary to fix the brain before cutting, by perfusing it through the basilar and cerebral arteries at its base.
(b)
The brain is then suspended by the basilar artery within the fixative; if left in this condition for at least a week, it can be easily bisected or sliced with a brain knife using a cutting device.
(c)
Materials/equipment required include fixative (formalin-based), a means of perfusing the basilar/cerebral arteries, a suspension support, and a brain knife/cutting device.
(d)
If the specimen is allowed to rest on the base of the container, even if supported with cotton wool, distortion will still occur because of its softness.
(e)
It is preferable to perfuse the brain and suspend it by the basilar artery within the fixative (rather than letting it rest on the container base), and to leave it for at least a week before bisecting or slicing, to avoid distortion.

(a)
Fresh frozen cryostat sectioning is the current method of choice for enzyme histochemistry, recommended for its speed, ease of handling, and versatility.
(b)
Enzymes are demonstrated in tissue by providing a substrate upon which the enzyme acts, with the final coloured/opaque product derived from the substrate; because enzymes are very labile and disappear from tissue quickly after death, tissue must be prepared to preserve enzymes as completely as possible and retain them in their original site.
(c)
Materials/reagents required include ice-cold acetone, ice-cold alcohol, or ice-cold formalin as fixatives, a cryostat for fresh frozen sectioning, and, for alkaline phosphatase specifically, glycerophosphate substrate with calcium (cobalt substitution technique) or naphthyl phosphate with a diazonium salt (simultaneous coupling and capture).
(d)
Enzymes are very labile and nearly all disappear from tissue quickly and progressively after removal from the body and after cellular death; embedding in paraffin wax (if used) must not exceed 56°C, as considerably more enzyme destruction occurs at 60°C than 56°C.
(e)
Positive controls (materials known to contain the enzyme) and negative controls (omission of an essential step, use of specific inhibitors such as potassium cyanide or sodium fluoride, or treatment with a non-specific destructive agent) must be processed in parallel with the test section to ensure specificity; any positive reaction after such controls indicates the test is non-specific.
questions.question:
Fresh tissue is received for demonstration of an enzyme (e.g. alkaline phosphatase) by histochemical technique.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/reagents/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Because of problems arising from inadequate circulation or tumour formation, and since the specimen is to be bisected, cutting the specimen prior to fixation is advantageous, using the method of Baker (1940).
(b)
The unfixed limb is placed in an adequately large container of 95% alcohol pre-cooled with solid carbon dioxide; strings are attached to the limb to enable it to be suspended in, and removed from, the cold alcohol (-60°C) without hands contacting the solution; when frozen, the limb can be cut with a band saw in the required plane, with careful reference to X-rays previously taken.
(c)
Materials/equipment required include 95% alcohol, solid carbon dioxide, strings for suspension, a band saw, and prior X-rays of the limb for reference.
(d)
Because of the mixture of very soft and very hard tissues in a limb, careless cutting could distort the specimen; the limb must remain in the cold alcohol for a minimum of one hour, with cooling maintained by adding more solid carbon dioxide.
(e)
The two halves must be placed face down in a container of fixative to thaw and fix; hands should not come into contact with the cold alcohol solution, and X-rays should be checked before cutting to ensure the correct plane is used.
questions.question:
A whole limb specimen is received fresh for permanent museum preservation, with problems arising from inadequate circulation and intended bisection.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Factors affecting fixation are: Buffering, Penetration, Volume, Temperature, Concentration, Time interval, and Position of tissue.
(b)
• Buffering: fixation is best carried out close to neutral pH (6-8); hypoxia lowers pH, so buffering capacity is needed to prevent excessive acidity (common buffers include phosphate, bicarbonate, cacodylate, veronal; commercial formalin is buffered with phosphate at pH 7)
• Penetration depends on the diffusibility of each fixative (formalin and alcohol penetrate best, glutaraldehyde the worst, mercurials in between)
• Volume: the minimal acceptable volume of fixation fluid is about 15-20 times the volume of the specimen.
• Temperature: increasing temperature increases speed of fixation (hot formalin fixes faster)
• Concentration of fixative should be adjusted down to the lowest level possible.
(c)
The use of small volumes of fixation fluid for larger specimens is the most frequent cause of poor tissue preservation, since insufficient fixative cannot adequately penetrate and fix the whole specimen; similarly, too high a fixative concentration may adversely affect the tissues and produce an artifact similar to excessive heat, and acidity favours formation of formalin-heme pigment appearing as black, polarizable deposits in tissue - so an error in any of these controllable factors compromises the accuracy of the final preserved specimen.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of factors affecting the fixation process.
(b) State how each factor is controlled/applied in practice.
(c) Explain why an error in one of these factors, such as inadequate fixative volume, leads to poor tissue preservation.

A section of liver treated with the PAS reaction shows a red-staining substance; a parallel control section treated with diastase before PAS staining shows loss of this red staining.
(a) What substance is being identified?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this appearance?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This identifies glycogen.
(b)
The PAS reaction demonstrates the sites of glycogen and many other substances in sections; a diastase control removes glycogen from a control section, so comparison of the two sections (PAS alone versus PAS with diastase control) allows the site and approximate quantity of glycogen in the tissue to be determined, since the PAS reaction alone is not diagnostic of any single tissue component.
(c)
The correct next step is to compare the test section and diastase control section side by side and report the result as glycogen only if the red staining is lost after diastase digestion, confirming the reaction is specific to glycogen rather than another PAS-reactive substance.

(a)
• Leukocytes in blood don't normally divide, but lymphocytes can be induced to proliferate if phytohemagglutinin is added to the culture; a mitotic inhibitor such as colcemid is then added, which stops cell division at metaphase, increasing the yield of mitotic cells.
• The cells are centrifuged, the culture medium and mitotic inhibitor removed and replaced with a hypotonic solution which swells the cells so chromosomes spread when smears are made; the cells are fixed in methanol:acetic acid (3:1), which lyses red blood cells and hardens the nuclei of remaining white cells.
• The cell suspension is dropped onto slides, stained, examined, and photographed; the interpretation of the photograph is the karyotype.
(b)
Chromosomes are cut out and arranged on a karyotype sheet based on length, centromere position, chromosome band position, and relative band sizes/distributions; once karyotyped, it is possible to examine them for abnormalities of number or structure.
(c)
Medical uses of chromosome analysis include diagnosis of congenital abnormalities such as mental retardation, determining the karyotype of a foetus in pregnant women, helping determine appropriate treatment for some cancers, determining whether an adult's chromosomes have a change that can be passed to a child, determining whether a chromosome defect is preventing pregnancy or causing miscarriage, finding the cause of a baby's birth defects, and identifying the sex of a person by checking for the Y chromosome.
(d)
• For a foetal karyotype, fetal cells from amniotic fluid obtained by amniocentesis, or chorionic villus samples, can be cultured by a similar technique to peripheral blood, with amniotic fluid collection between 14-16 weeks (15-21 days to complete) and chorionic villus collection at 8-10 weeks (48 hours for short culture, 15-20 days for long culture)
• For an adult karyotype, peripheral blood is used, a short-term 72-hour culture with stimulation, taking about 7 days for analysis to complete, though it has the disadvantage of being short-lived compared to long-term skin biopsy fibroblast cultures.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the overall procedure of chromosome analysis/karyotyping from culture to karyotype sheet.
(b) Describe how the karyotype is examined for abnormalities once complete.
(c) Explain why karyotyping is used or preferred for diagnosis of congenital abnormalities.
(d) Distinguish the procedure used for a foetal karyotype from that used for an adult karyotype.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The nuclear criteria of malignancy are: nuclear size; nucleus-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio; nuclear shape; nuclear membrane; nuclear chromatin; nucleoli; number of nuclei; and mitoses.
(b)
• Nuclear size is usually larger than benign nuclei, with variation in size (anisonucleosis) being more significant; N:C ratio is increased; nuclear shape shows moderate to marked variation; nuclear membrane shows irregular thickening, angulation and indentations; nuclear chromatin is hyperchromatic (less significant), with uneven distribution, coarse irregular angulated chromatin clumping, and parachromatin clearing being more significant; nucleoli show increased size and number (less significant), with irregular angular outlines being more significant; number of nuclei shows multinucleation (unreliable, nuclear character more important); mitoses show increased mitoses (unreliable), with abnormal mitoses being significant.
• Cytoplasmic characteristics help type the malignancy, e.g. keratinisation in squamous cell carcinoma, mucin droplets in adenocarcinoma, melanin pigment in melanomas.
(c)
Several individual features are explicitly noted as unreliable or less significant on their own - hyperchromasia alone, increased nucleolar number alone, multinucleation alone, and increased mitotic count alone - because these can occur in benign or reactive conditions too; only the more significant features (anisonucleosis, irregular membrane changes, coarse chromatin clumping with parachromatin clearing, irregular nucleolar outlines, and abnormal mitoses), especially in combination, reliably distinguish malignant from benign nuclei, so basing an assessment on a single less-significant criterion alone would give an unreliable, invalid assessment.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of nuclear criteria of malignancy.
(b) State how each criterion is applied/weighted in practice.
(c) Explain why relying on a single less-significant criterion alone leads to an unreliable assessment of malignancy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is ultramicrotome sectioning for electron microscopy.
(b)
The ultramicrotome consists of a support carrying a glass, diamond, or steel knife and a sample holder on a vibration-proof platform, with a micro- to nanometer scale movement system controlling object position; this is the only technique yielding directly 30nm sections of constant thickness, and it can be applied to a precise zone of the sample selected with the optical microscope.
(c)
The correct next step is to place the ultrathin section on the specimen holder (an extremely thin film of carbon or collodion held by a metal grid) for examination in the electron microscope, since this technique gives access to structural and chemical information within a volume that can be exploited for statistical purposes and 3-D reconstruction.
questions.question:
A sample prepared on an ultramicrotome yields directly a section of constant 30nm thickness, with the same selected area followed across the whole magnification range using both optical and electron microscopes.
(a) What technique is being demonstrated?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this result?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step?

A karyotype report shows 47 chromosomes with an extra chromosome 21.
(a) What is being identified by this result?
(b) What is the basic principle behind why this appears (mechanism)?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step in recording this result?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This identifies trisomy 21.
(b)
This results from failure of a pair of homologous chromosome 21s (or sister chromatids) to separate during meiosis (non-disjunction), most often maternal; the resulting germ cell with an extra chromosome 21 combines with a normal germ cell so that the fertilised egg and all its cells carry an extra chromosome 21.
(c)
The correct next step is to report the karyotype in standard form - total chromosome number, comma, sex chromosome constitution, then autosomal abnormality - i.e. 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21.

(a)
• The Tissue Embedding Centre has temperature controlled by microprocessors, displayed using colour-changing LEDs for clear visibility of working status; it has five heated areas - Paraffin Chamber, Paraffin Dispenser, left and right Thermal Storage Compartments, and a heating plate (working area) - each individually controlled and working independently without interference.
• It has automatic memory and restoration functions storing preset temperature data, a flexible module configuration separating the Cryo Module from the Embedding Module, a large-capacity Paraffin Chamber, a safe low-voltage illumination system, heated working plate and forceps wells, and a large granite working area.
(b)
It is used for tissue embedding after processing, providing fast heating and precise temperature control to overcome the shortcomings of traditional technology that results in excessive temperature differences.
(c)
Dual-protection of overheating makes the system safe, reliable and energy-saving; since embedding requires sustained heat to keep paraffin wax molten around the specimen, uncontrolled overheating could damage tissue or create a hazard, so the dual-protection mechanism is a safety precaution against this.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure/composition of the Tissue Embedding Centre.
(b) State the standard setting in which it is used in practice.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind its dual-protection overheating safety feature.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This identifies the presence of DNA in the nucleus (i.e. confirms that a basophilic cellular component contains DNA).
(b)
This is the Feulgen reaction: hydrolysis with hydrochloric acid liberates aldehyde groups by breaking the purine-deoxyribose bond, and these aldehydes recolour Schiff's reagent (a leuco-fuchsin), giving a purple colour to nuclear chromatin.
(c)
The correct next step, since the Feulgen reaction is applied (though not widely) to nuclear sex determination and general morphologic studies, is to proceed with quantitative histochemical estimation of DNA if required, by measuring the amount of colour developed in the stained nuclei.
questions.question:
A nuclear section treated by acid hydrolysis and Schiff's reagent shows a purple colour in the nuclear chromatin.
(a) What substance is being identified?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this appearance?

A blood sample is received for chromosome analysis (karyotyping) from peripheral blood.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/reagents/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(a)
The technique is short-term peripheral blood lymphocyte culture, harvesting, and slide preparation for karyotyping.
(b)
Leukocytes in blood don't normally divide, but lymphocytes can be induced to proliferate by phytohemagglutinin; a mitotic inhibitor (colcemid) is added to stop cell division at metaphase, increasing the yield of mitotic cells for analysis; a hypotonic solution then swells the cells to spread the chromosomes.
(c)
Materials/reagents required include a sterile heparinised bottle for blood collection, McCoy 5A growth medium with phytohemagglutinin/L-Glutamine/Fetal Bovine Serum/Gentamicin, colcemid in phosphate buffer, 0.075M potassium chloride, and fixative (methanol:glacial acetic acid).
(d)
The fixative absorbs water upon standing and its pH changes with time, so it must be made fresh before each use; if clumps are seen at the bottom of the culture tube, additional heparin should be added.
(e)
Blood should be mixed gently to prevent clotting and stored at room temperature (not refrigerated); tubes should be mixed by inverting twice daily during the 72-hour incubation, and slides should be scanned under the X40 objective to check that chromosomes have spread sufficiently with no cytoplasm remaining, washing with fresh fixative again if cytoplasm is detected.

(a)
The photographic emulsion is a suspension of silver bromide crystals supported in a gelatin matrix; during exposure, the silver halides are activated by emitted radiation, and the radioactive isotopes in the tissue section reduce silver salts in the emulsion to black deposits of silver, with the activated crystals becoming sites for deposition of metallic silver on development, while inactive crystals are selectively removed by fixation.
(b)
The emulsion is overlaid onto tissue sections as a thin film and left in the dark for days or weeks while the radioisotope decays, before being developed as in conventional photography.
(c)
Grain size should be smaller so there is more availability of silver halide crystals, and the concentration of gelatin should be less compared to the crystals; the thickness of the emulsion affects efficiency with different emitters (for beta-emitters the thickness should be less); and the exposure time must be sufficiently long for proper exposure to view the pattern of the track length - higher emitter energy makes it more difficult to localise points in the low-density region of the same track, and very low energy radiation also creates a poorer resolution image, so these factors must be controlled to avoid a poorly resolved or invalid autoradiogram.
questions.question:

(b) State the standard setting in which it is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution regarding grain size, emulsion thickness and exposure time.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Specimen types for sex chromatin identification include blood smear preparations (for identification of Barr bodies), buccal (epithelial) smears, and amniocentesis samples.
(b)
Blood smear preparation is used for identification of Barr bodies on epithelial-type cells or the drumstick appendage on polymorphonuclear leukocytes; buccal smears are also used for sex chromatin examination; amniocentesis samples are examined for the presence of sex chromatin as a technique for determining the sex of a baby before birth.
(c)
A normal human female has only one Barr body per somatic cell while a normal human male has none, so the specimen and cell type examined must be correctly identified (e.g. distinguishing an epithelial cell's Barr body from a polymorphonuclear leukocyte's drumstick appendage) and correctly stained (sex chromatin deeply stained, cytoplasm almost colourless); mishandling or misidentifying the specimen would lead to an inaccurate Barr body count and therefore an invalid conclusion about the sex chromosome constitution.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of specimen types used for sex chromatin identification.
(b) State how each specimen type is applied/selected in practice.
(c) Explain why misidentifying or mishandling the specimen type leads to an invalid sex chromatin count.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Arterial embalming is the primary technique, usually supplemented by cavity, hypodermic, and/or surface embalming.
(b)
Embalming chemicals are injected into the blood vessels, usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood drained from the right jugular vein; the embalmer massages the cadaver to ensure proper distribution of the embalming fluid, achieving good long-term structural preservation with minimal shrinkage or distortion while maintaining flexibility.
(c)
Materials/equipment required include an embalming machine, a preservative (arterial) chemical (an 18%-35% mixture of formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, or phenol), a water conditioner, a cell conditioner, dyes, humectants, anti-oedemic chemicals, additional disinfectants where needed, and water (unless waterless embalming is used).
(d)
In case of poor circulation, other injection points must be used instead of the right common carotid artery; formaldehyde works best in an alkaline environment, so failing to correct the deceased's acidity with a water conditioner would impair the preservative action.
(e)
Reduction of potential biohazards (spread of infection to embalming personnel) and reduction of environmental chemical hazards (especially from formaldehyde and phenol) must be observed, along with retention of tissue colour (minimising oxidation "browning") and prevention of desiccation, fungal, or bacterial growth.
questions.question:
A cadaver is received for temporary preservation to forestall decomposition ahead of display at a funeral.
(a) What technique is appropriate?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/reagents/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?

(a) Describe the structure/preparation of the quartz slide setup for microincineration.
(b) State the standard setting (oven temperature schedule) in which it is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind raising the oven temperature gradually rather than suddenly.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The dewaxed, air-dried section is placed on an equal-size quartz slide; after incineration, a coverslip is applied gently, and the slide is ringed with paraffin wax.
(b)
The slide and quartz are placed in the oven, with the temperature raised gradually to 100°C in 10 minutes, then increased to 650°C over the next 25-30 minutes, before the oven is switched off and the temperature allowed to fall to about 40°C.
(c)
Raising the temperature gradually in stages (to 100°C, then to 650°C) rather than suddenly allows controlled burning of the tissue to produce a readable ash pattern demonstrating the microscopic distribution of mineral substances; the result is then examined with darkground illumination (Mg and Ca appear as dense white ash), polarized light (anisotropic minerals such as silica are birefringent), and chemical reactions (Ca forms gypsum crystals with 3% sulphuric acid; Pb, pre-treated with hydrogen sulphide, exhibits a characteristic brownish-black appearance on incineration) - a sudden temperature rise could disrupt this controlled ash pattern and invalidate these readings.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and formation of the Barr body (sex chromatin).
(b) State the standard setting/specimen in which it is examined.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of differentiating in 95% alcohol until the cytoplasm becomes colourless.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sex chromatin, also called the Barr body, is the inactive X chromosome in a female somatic cell, rendered inactive in a process called Lyonization; when present as a mass of sharply demarcated, darkly staining dot on the nuclear membrane of epithelial cells, it is called a Barr body, while in polymorphonuclear leukocytes it appears as an appendage protruding from the nucleus called a drumstick appendage.
(b)
It is examined in blood smear preparations or buccal smear epithelial cells (and in polymorphonuclear leukocytes for the drumstick appendage), and cells obtained by amniocentesis can also be examined for sex chromatin to determine foetal sex.
(c)
Differentiation in 95% alcohol is continued until the cytoplasm becomes colourless, since the diagnostic result required is sex chromatin deeply stained on the nuclear membrane against an almost colourless cytoplasm; without this precaution, residual cytoplasmic staining could obscure or be confused with the sex chromatin, giving an inaccurate reading of Barr body presence or number.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of histochemical methods.
(b) State how each type is applied/selected in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why an error such as excessive hydrolysis in the Feulgen reaction leads to an invalid (negative) result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Histochemical methods are not a separate or distinct part of histological technique, but involve clearly understood chemical reactions with high specificity, in contrast to staining methods using natural or synthetic dyes which have less precise physico-chemical basis and specificity.
• Examples include the Periodic Acid Schiff's (PAS) reaction, Feulgen's reaction, enzyme histochemistry, and Pearl's Prussian blue reaction.
(b)
The PAS reaction is applied for demonstration of carbohydrates and related substances (with a diastase control for glycogen); the Feulgen reaction is applied for demonstration of DNA and nuclear sex determination; enzyme histochemistry is applied by providing a substrate on which the enzyme acts, with the coloured product derived from the substrate, and is used for enzymes such as phosphatases and oxidases.
(c)
Hydrolysis in the Feulgen reaction is usually carried out with N Hydrochloric acid at 60°C; hydrolysis causes the purine bases to be rapidly removed and the aldehyde groups of the deoxyribose exposed (the required action), but it also removes basic protein and nucleic acids from the chromosomes (not intended); an optimal hydrolysis time is therefore mandatory as a compromise between these two actions to give maximum aldehyde liberation and hence greatest reaction intensity - excessive hydrolysis removes too much of the reactive material and is associated with a negative (invalid) result.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the solutions used in G-banding (trypsin and Giemsa/Leishmann staining).
(b) State the standard setting (oven pre-treatment, dip time) in which they are used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind destaining and rebanding an under-treated slide rather than accepting the result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Solutions used include Trypsin (1:250) USP Grade, Gurr Buffer Solution, Working Salt Solution, Leishmann Stain Solution, and Trypsin solution.
(b)
Slides are placed in a 55-65°C oven for 45 minutes before staining, then dipped in the trypsin solution for 5-30 seconds, rinsed in working salt solution, and stained with Leishmann stain for 3-4 minutes, before being rinsed in distilled water and air dried, then examined with a 100X plan-apochromatic oil objective under bright field.
(c)
Chromosomal proteins must be sufficiently denatured by the trypsin treatment for the subsequent Giemsa/Leishmann stain to be taken up in the correct pattern of dark and light G-bands; if slides are under-treated with trypsin, the resulting banding pattern is inadequate for accurate chromosome identification, so the slide must be destained (using 3:1 methanol:acetic acid) and rebanded, rather than accepting an invalid or unclear banding result that could lead to misclassification of the chromosomes.

(a)
• By centromere position, human chromosomes are metacentric (equal arms, centrally located centromere), submetacentric (unequal arms, off-centre centromere), or acrocentric (centromere near one end, very small short arms)
• Autosomes are numbered 1 to 22 in descending order of length, and the sex chromosomes as X and Y.
(b)
These classifications are applied when arranging chromosomes on the karyotype sheet - chromosomes are cut out and similar ones arranged based on length, position of the centromere, position of chromosome bands, and relative band sizes/distributions, and gummed in place, then reported in standard form (e.g. 46,XY for a normal male).
(c)
Since chromosomes are grouped and numbered according to their length and centromere position (among other features), incorrectly identifying whether a centromere is centrally located (metacentric), off-centre (submetacentric), or near one end (acrocentric) would place a chromosome in the wrong length/position group on the karyotype sheet, producing an inaccurate karyotype arrangement and a potentially incorrect final reported result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of human chromosomes by centromere position and by the Denver classification groups.
(b) State how each classification is applied/selected in karyotype arrangement.
(c) Explain why misclassifying centromere position leads to an inaccurate karyotype grouping.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is a dissecting aneurysm (dissecting haematoma/aortic dissection), arising from an intimal defect that permits blood to penetrate into the wall of the aorta with propagation of the haemorrhage along laminar planes of the media.
(b)
Gross pathological examination is used to detect this finding, noting the tear (usually longitudinal or oblique, 4-5cm long, with sharp, clean, possibly irregular edges) and the intramural haematoma; histologically, in the great majority of cases there are few abnormal findings in the aortic wall, save for the dissection and its content of blood, with possible focal areas of medial degeneration.
(c)
The result should be recorded noting the tear dimensions, the male:female ratio of 3:1 typical for this condition, and any focal medial degeneration (clefts or irregular defects from loss of elastic and smooth muscle cells filled with amorphous basophilic ground substance); the follow-up step is to check whether the haematoma has ruptured into the pericardium, peritoneal cavity, or elsewhere, since development of aortic dissection is a catastrophic event with death within the first day in about one-third of cases.
questions.question:
An aortic specimen shows a longitudinal tear, 4-5cm long, with sharp, clean, possibly irregular edges, and blood present within the wall along laminar planes of the media.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique/observation is used to detect this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?

A lymph node biopsy shows a "starry-sky" appearance on histology, with an associated MYC translocation.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique(s) are used to detect this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up practical step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is Burkitt lymphoma, which shows a starry-sky appearance histologically and is associated with a MYC translocation, t(8;14); types include endemic, sporadic, and HIV-associated.
(b)
The starry-sky appearance is detected by histological examination of the lymph node biopsy; the diagnostic approach for lymphoproliferative diseases generally also includes flow cytometry and molecular tests such as FISH and PCR to identify the translocation.
(c)
The result should be recorded as a high-grade/very aggressive lymphoproliferative disease finding, since Burkitt lymphoma is classified among the aggressive forms which are rapid but potentially curable; the follow-up step is prompt further diagnostic workup (CBC, ESR, LDH, imaging such as CT/PET-CT) to stage the disease before treatment (e.g. chemotherapy such as CHOP/R-CHOP).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the simultaneous capture technique in enzyme histochemistry.
(b) Describe the post-coupling technique.
(c) Explain why the simultaneous capture technique is preferred over post-coupling.
(d) Distinguish the demonstration of alkaline phosphatase from that of acid phosphatase.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Simultaneous capture depends on the formation of a primary reaction product (PRP) due to the action of the enzyme upon the substrate, followed by production of a coloured or opaque final reaction product (FRP) by combining the PRP with a second reagent, usually by blackening the PRP by chemical means or combination with a diazonium salt to form a diazo-dye; when the production of the PRP and its capture as a coloured FRP take place simultaneously in one incubating medium, this is called simultaneous capture, e.g. the diazo-technique for alkaline phosphatase.
(b)
Post-coupling is similar to simultaneous capture but differs in that production of the PRP and its capture as a coloured FRP take place separately, one after the other - for example, in the method for acid phosphatase, a colourless PRP is first produced which is subsequently coupled into a coloured FRP in a separate solution.
(c)
The simultaneous capture is the method of choice because the PRP is combined into the FRP as it is being liberated by enzyme activity, so diffusion of the PRP throughout the tissue or into the incubating medium (which would blur precise localisation) should be prevented.
(d)
• Alkaline phosphatase hydrolyses mono-orthophosphate esters in an alkaline medium (pH 9.0), with hydrolysis increased by magnesium, and is demonstrated by a two-stage reaction with glycerophosphate/calcium (calcium phosphate demonstrated by cobalt substitution) or a simultaneous coupling/capture technique with naphthyl phosphate and a diazonium salt.
• Acid phosphatase splits mono-orthophosphate esters in an acidic medium (optimum pH about 5.0), is not activated by magnesium but is inhibited by fluoride, and is demonstrated by the lead nitrate method (liberated phosphate as lead sulphide) or the azo-dye method, though these two acid phosphatase methods are not as reliable as those for alkaline phosphatase.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the procedure for culturing lymphocytes for chromosome analysis.
(b) Describe the reagents used in the culture.
(c) Explain why white blood cells/lymphocytes are used or preferred for this culture.
(d) Distinguish short-term peripheral blood culture from long-term skin biopsy (fibroblast) culture.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• About 15ml of blood is collected into a sterile heparinised bottle and mixed gently to prevent clotting, then stored at room temperature (not refrigerated)
• Whole blood (9-12 drops) is added to centrifuge tubes each containing 10ml McCoy 5A growth medium, capped, mixed by inverting, and incubated at 37°C in a rack positioned at a 45° angle for about 72 hours, with the blood mixed by inverting the tubes twice daily; if clumps are seen, heparin is added.
(b)
Reagents required include McCoy 5A growth medium (McCoy 5A, Phytohemagglutinin, L-Glutamine, Fetal Bovine Serum, Gentamicin, sterilised by filtering with a 0.22µm cellulose acetate membrane), Phytohemagglutinin (PHA, rehydrated with sterile deionized distilled water, usable for two weeks once reconstituted), and Heparin sodium salt (hydrated with McCoy growth medium, stored at 4°C for up to two weeks).
(c)
Leukocytes in blood don't normally divide, but lymphocytes can be induced to proliferate if phytohemagglutinin is added to the culture, making them the most readily accessible cells capable of growth and rapid division in culture required for chromosome analysis.
(d)
• Peripheral blood culture is a short-term, 72-hour culture with stimulation, taking about 7 days for analysis to complete, but has the disadvantage of being short-lived.
• Long-term cultures can instead be derived from skin biopsies (which must include the dermis), producing fibroblasts - elongated spindle-shaped cells capable of continuous multiplication in vitro for many cell generations - which can be used for a variety of biochemical and histochemical studies as well as chromosome analysis.

(a)
This is the drumstick appendage - the sex chromatin body as it appears in polymorphonuclear leukocytes, named for its characteristic appearance.
(b)
The Romanowsky types of stain can demonstrate this drumstick appendage on a blood smear preparation.
(c)
The result should be recorded as the presence (or absence/count) of the drumstick appendage on polymorphonuclear leukocytes; the follow-up step, since a normal human female has one Barr body per somatic cell and a normal male has none, is to correlate this finding with sex chromatin examination on epithelial cells (buccal smear, Cresyl Echt Violet method) for consistency.
questions.question:
A blood smear, stained by a Romanowsky-type stain, shows an appendage protruding from the nucleus of a polymorphonuclear leukocyte, resembling a drumstick.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique is used to detect this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?

A liver biopsy shows diffuse disruption in the architecture of the entire liver, bridging fibrous septa, and rounded parenchymal nodules of regenerating hepatocytes, with inflammatory cells including lymphocytes and macrophages.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique is used to obtain and prepare this specimen?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is liver cirrhosis, defined histologically as a diffuse hepatic process characterised by fibrosis and conversion of the normal liver architecture into structurally abnormal nodules.
(b)
Liver biopsy is used, sampled by tru-cut biopsy or Fine Needle Aspiration (both applicable on an out-patient basis, preceded by an elevated prothrombin time test), or a wedge biopsy at laparotomy; in localised disease, the biopsy is directed at the lesion, necessitating ultrasound guidance.
(c)
The result should be recorded according to the morphological classification - micronodular (uniform nodules <3mm), macronodular (irregular nodules >3mm), or mixed cirrhosis; the follow-up step is correlation with imaging studies (ultrasound, CT or MRI) and blood tests, since liver biopsy enables a precise diagnosis of liver disease and its severity.

questions.question:
A chromosome preparation stained with quinacrine mustard, when examined under a fluorescence microscope, shows each chromosome pair staining in a specific pattern of bright and dim bands.
(a) What technique is being demonstrated?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this appearance?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is Q-banding.
(b)
When chromosomes are stained with quinacrine mustard or a related compound and examined by fluorescence microscopy, each pair stains in a specific pattern of bright and dim bands known as Q bands; these Q bands were used as the reference for the Paris conference classification.
(c)
The correct next step is to compare the observed banding pattern of each chromosome against the reference Q-band pattern for correct identification, cut out and arrange the chromosomes on a karyotype sheet based on length, centromere position, and band pattern/size, and report the karyotype in standard form.

(a)
• ATP machines are programmed to fix, dehydrate, clear and impregnate tissues with paraffin wax.
• An 18-hour automatic tissue processing schedule is: Beaker 1 10% formol saline 1hr 30; Beaker 2 70% alcohol 1 hour; Beaker 3 80% alcohol 1 hour; Beaker 4 90% alcohol 1 hour; Beaker 5 95% alcohol 1 hour; Beaker 6 95% alcohol 1hr 30min; Beaker 7 Absolute alcohol I 2 hours; Beaker 8 Absolute alcohol II 2 hours; Beaker 9 Xylene I 1hr 30min; Beaker 10 Xylene II 1hr 30min; Wax Bath I 2 hours; Wax Bath II 2 hours.
(b)
Advantages of ATP machines include automatic transfer of tissue from one beaker to another, continuous agitation of tissue up, down and sideways (to hasten penetration of reagent), and suspension of tissue in processing reagents to hasten reagent penetration.
(c)
With former (manual) techniques it was too difficult to get accurate results; automation has made histopathology techniques faster, more accurate and easier, improving the accuracy of test results, shortening the length of time needed to perform the tests, and obtaining a slide that is representative of the original sample collected from the patient, while reducing time and increasing workflow speed (e.g. biopsies and larger specimens can be processed at the same time).
(d)
The ATP machine replaces the manual methods of tissue processing, automatically fixing, dehydrating, clearing and impregnating tissue with wax through a beaker sequence; the Tissue Embedding Centre, by contrast, is used afterwards for embedding, with temperature controlled by microprocessors across five independently controlled heated areas (Paraffin Chamber, Paraffin Dispenser, left and right Thermal Storage Compartments, and a heating plate/working area).
questions.question:
(a) Describe the procedure/schedule of the Automatic Tissue Processing (ATP) machine.
(b) Describe its advantages as apparatus.
(c) Explain why automated tissue processing is used or preferred over manual processing.
(d) Distinguish the ATP machine from the Tissue Embedding Centre.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Types of electron microscope are the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM), the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), and the Scanning Tunneling Electron Microscope (STEM).
(b)
• TEM is applied to visualise and study cell structures of bacteria, viruses and fungi, to view bacterial flagella and plasmids, to study microbial organelle shapes and sizes, to differentiate plant and animal cells, and in nanotechnology to study nanoparticles.
• SEM is applied for industrial uses, nanoscience studies, biomedical studies, microbiology, spot chemical analysis by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, analysis of cosmetic components, and studying filament structures of microorganisms and surface topography.
• STEM (Scanning Tunneling Electron Microscope) shows three-dimensional images of a sample, using a stylus that scans the surface at a distance of only an atom's diameter, and has been used in the study of DNA molecules.
(c)
• As the electron microscope works in a vacuum, the specimen should be completely dry; the live specimen cannot be observed, the object must be ultra-thin, and the specimen is dried and cut into ultra-thin sections before observation.
• If the specimen is not completely dry or is not ultra-thin, this produces image artifacts resulting from specimen preparation, since the instrument is large, cumbersome and extremely sensitive to vibration and external magnetic fields, making an improperly prepared specimen unable to yield a valid, accurately magnified image.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification (types) of electron microscope.
(b) State how each type is applied or selected for a particular kind of specimen examination.
(c) Explain why a basic handling error, such as failing to keep the specimen completely dry, leads to an invalid result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The technique involves fixation, rinsing, dehydration, infiltration, and embedding for electron microscopy.
(b)
Fixation preserves the sample and prevents deterioration, cross-linking cellular structures into a matrix with minimum loss of cellular constituents and minimum alteration to morphology, volume, or spatial relationships; infiltration with epoxy resin penetrates and fills the cells to give a hard plastic material tolerating the pressure of ultrathin sectioning.
(c)
• Materials/reagents required include glutaraldehyde and/or paraformaldehyde as fixatives, sodium cacodylate buffer (effective buffering range 5.1-7.4) for rinsing, ascending grades of acetone (30%, 50%, 75%, 90%, 100%) for dehydration, and epoxy resin (e.g.
• Spurr resin) for infiltration/embedding in flat moulds.
(d)
Fixation is the first and most important step, since mistakes made at this point render the whole project useless; rinsing is necessary to remove traces of aldehyde that would otherwise contaminate the tissue by forming a precipitate with osmium during secondary fixation; paraffin wax is not firm enough for ultrathin sections and will melt under the electron beam.
(e)
• Modified Palade's fixative should not be used for more than 60 minutes; the less viscous epoxy resins (e.g.
• Spurr resin) have a carcinogenic component and should be used and disposed of with care; since most plastics dissolve in acetone and propylene oxide, samples must be dehydrated using ethanol and a resin-ethanol mixture during infiltration instead of the more usual resin-propylene oxide mixes.
questions.question:
A tissue specimen is received for processing for electron microscopy examination.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/reagents/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?

questions.answerText:
(a)
An arterial solution is generated specifically for each case and may include: a preservative (arterial) chemical (commonly an 18%-35% mixture of formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, or in some cases phenol); a water conditioner (to balance water hardness and reduce the deceased's acidity); a cell conditioner (to prepare cells for absorption of arterial fluid and help break up clots); dyes (to restore natural coloration and counter-stain conditions such as jaundice); humectants (to help restore hydrated appearance to dehydrated/emaciated bodies); anti-oedemic chemicals (to draw excessive oedemic fluid from a body); additional disinfectants (for special cases such as tissue gas); and water (most arterial solutions are a mix of the preceding chemicals with tepid water; cases done without water are called waterless embalming, which is very effective but not economically viable for everyday cases).
(b)
The solution is injected using an embalming machine, usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood drained from the right jugular vein and the embalmer massaging the cadaver to ensure proper distribution; other injection points are used in case of poor circulation.
(c)
Formaldehyde works best in an alkaline environment, and decomposition produces acidity as a by-product in the deceased, so a water conditioner is included to reduce this acidity and balance the water's hardness, ensuring the preservative (formaldehyde-based) chemical can work effectively.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of an arterial embalming solution.
(b) State the standard setting in which it is injected.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind using a water conditioner in the solution.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Controls used include: omission of an essential step in the technique (such as replacement of the substrate by distilled water, or in the case of Alkaline Phosphatase, omission of calcium); use of specific inhibitors of enzyme activity in adequate concentration (0.1% Potassium Cyanide, M/100 Sodium fluoride) - known enzyme killers; and treatment of sections with a non-specific agent known to destroy the enzyme (boiling water, strong acids, oxidising agents).
(b)
Positive controls (materials known to contain the enzyme) should be available and used when new reagents are prepared or when a technique is used only occasionally; negative controls (blanks) must be processed in parallel with the test section to ensure specificity, using one of the three approaches above.
(c)
• The rapid disappearance of most enzymes from tissue after death makes it essential to carry out positive and negative controls alongside the test section; any positive reaction obtained after effective inhibition, or after omission of an essential part of the technique, indicates that the test is non-specific (i.e., the colour seen is not truly due to the enzyme being investigated), which would otherwise be reported as a false and invalid result.
• False positive reactions may also result from spontaneous hydrolysis or oxidation of the substrate if reaction products are absorbed into the tissue section.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of controls used to test the specificity and validity of enzyme histochemical techniques.
(b) State how each type of control is applied/selected.
(c) Explain why a positive reaction after these controls indicates the test is non-specific (invalid).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Autoradiography is the localisation of radioactive materials in sections of biological tissue, providing accurate quantitative information on the distribution of the labelled substance; it uses X-ray or photographic film to detect relative positions and intensities of radio-labelled bands.
• The material of interest is labelled with a radioactive marker, introduced into the tissue, and placed in intimate contact with a photographic emulsion; during exposure the emitted radiation activates the silver halides, reducing them to black metallic silver deposits, while inactive crystals are removed by fixation.
(b)
Living cells are briefly exposed to a pulse of a specific radioactive compound; the tissue is left for a variable time; samples are taken, fixed, and processed for light or electron microscopy; sections are cut and overlaid with a thin film of photographic emulsion, left in the dark for days or weeks while the isotope decays; the emulsion is then developed as in conventional photography, and counter-staining with toluidine blue shows the histological details.
(c)
Radioactive isotopes used include Tritium (3H), Iodine (125I), Sulphur (35S) and Carbon (14C), which emit beta radiation and have a fixed half-life (e.g. iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.1 days); the photographic emulsion is a suspension of silver bromide crystals in a gelatin matrix.
(d)
It provides accurate quantitative information on the distribution of a labelled substance of interest, and since any biological compound can now be labelled with radioactive isotopes, this opens up many possibilities in the study of living systems; the successful combination of autoradiography and electron microscopy is described as a new dimension to the technique.
(e)
In the general method, samples are fixed and processed for either light or electron microscopy depending on the resolution required; methods listed (stripping film, liquid emulsion, film and slide, section on emulsion, coating, double labelling) can be adapted to either light-microscopic examination (lower resolution, whole-tissue distribution) or electron-microscopic examination (finer, ultrastructural localisation) of the labelled sections.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of autoradiography.
(b) Describe the general method/procedure of autoradiography.
(c) Describe the reagents/materials involved.
(d) Explain why autoradiography is used/preferred for localising radioactive material.
(e) Distinguish autoradiography combined with light microscopy from autoradiography combined with electron microscopy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Exfoliative cytology involves the study of cells spontaneously shed off (desquamated) as a result of continuous growth of epithelial linings from epithelial surfaces into body cavities or body fluids; cells for study may also be obtained by scraping, brushing, or washing various mucosal surfaces (abrasive cytology).
(b)
Samples obtainable include: female genital tract (lateral vaginal smears, vaginal pool smears, cervical smears, combined/triple smears, endocervical/endometrial aspiration); respiratory tract (sputum, bronchial washings/brushing/bronchoalveolar lavage); gastrointestinal tract (endoscopic lavage/brushing); urinary tract (urinary sediment, bladder washings, retrograde catheterisation, prostatic massage secretions); body fluids (effusions, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid, amniotic fluid, hydrocele fluid, seminal fluid, nipple discharge); and other samples such as buccal smears for sex chromatin.
(c)
Exfoliative cytology is facilitated by the fact that the rate of exfoliation is enhanced in disease states, yielding a larger number of cells for study; smears from the female genital tract have traditionally been known as 'Pap smears'.
(d)
Exfoliative cytology involves cells spontaneously exfoliated from epithelial surfaces, requiring screening to locate suitable cells for study, with diagnostic basis on individual cell morphology (nuclear characteristics most significant); interventional cytology is dominated by, and virtually synonymous with, Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC, also called Aspiration Biopsy Cytology), where samples are obtained by clinical procedure or surgical intervention, giving an abundance of cells for study, with diagnostic basis on cell patterns and morphology of groups of cells (nuclear characteristics important, cytoplasmic character and background equally significant).
questions.question:
(a) Describe the exfoliative cytology technique, including how cells are obtained.
(b) Describe the samples obtainable from different organ systems.
(c) Explain why exfoliative cytology is used or preferred as a diagnostic technique.
(d) Distinguish exfoliative cytology from interventional cytology.

A museum specimen jar carries a red 'Dymo' tape label.
(a) What does this label identify about the specimen?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this colour-coded labelling system?
(c) What is the correct next step when consulting information about this specimen?
questions.answerText:
(a)
A red label identifies the specimen as an example of a rarer condition, or a condition which the undergraduate need not concentrate on.
(b)
The range of colours available in the Dymo tape labelling system allows for a differential labelling system: red for rarer/lower-priority conditions, yellow for good examples of common conditions undergraduates should concentrate on, and green for less satisfactory examples of common conditions or less common conditions.
(c)
The correct next step is to consult the loose-leaf catalogue sheet for that specimen, which will have the diagnosis (with museum number) at the top, followed by a brief description and case history, with colour bands also used for the condition category (e.g. red for malignancy, yellow for inflammatory processes, green for normal condition).

(a)
Kaiserling I is composed of Formalin 1 litre, Potassium acetate 85g, Potassium nitrate 45g, and Water made up to ten litres, giving an appropriately neutral pH of 7.
(b)
It is used for permanent preservation of specimens for medical museum mounting, particularly since it allows the specimen to be restored to its original colour.
(c)
Due to the hardening action of formalin, if a specimen rests on the bottom of its container (even if supported with cotton wool for soft tissue such as brain, distortion will still occur), this produces an artificially flat surface and causes unfixed areas to persist at points of contact; lining the container with fixative-soaked lint and supporting an undulating specimen surface with fixative-soaked cotton wool prevents this and ensures the specimen maintains its natural shape throughout fixation.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the Kaiserling I fixative.
(b) State the standard setting in which it is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that a specimen must not rest on the container's bottom.

(a) Describe the general classification of chromosome banding techniques.
(b) State how each banding technique is applied/selected (stain and light source used).
(c) Explain why an error such as under-treatment with trypsin in G-banding leads to an invalid banding result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Chromosome banding techniques include Q-banding, G-banding, R-banding, C-banding, NOR staining, and G.ll banding.
• A band is the part of a chromosome clearly distinguishable from its adjacent segment by appearing darker or lighter after staining.
(b)
• Q-banding uses quinacrine mustard or a related compound, examined with a fluorescence microscope, producing a specific pattern of bright and dim bands (used as the reference for the Paris conference classification)
• G-banding treats chromosomal proteins with trypsin (denaturing them), then stains with Giemsa/Leishmann stain, producing dark and light bands corresponding to the Q-bands.
• R-banding heats the chromosomes before Giemsa staining, producing bands that are the reverse of Q and G banding.
• C-banding stains the centromere and other regions of constitutive heterochromatin.
• NOR staining uses ammoniacal silver to stain the nucleolar organising regions.
(c)
For G-banding, slides are placed in a 55-65°C oven for 45 minutes before staining, dipped in trypsin solution for 5-30 seconds, rinsed in working salt solution, and stained with Leishmann stain for 3-4 minutes; if slides are under-treated with trypsin, the chromosomal proteins are not sufficiently denatured to take up the Giemsa/Leishmann stain in the correct dark/light banding pattern, so the slides must be destained (quickly dipped in 3:1 methanol:acetic acid 2-3 times until all stain is removed), rinsed, air dried, and rebanded to obtain a valid result.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure/format used in reporting karyotype results.
(b) State the standard setting in which this reporting format is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind numbering autosomes 1 to 22 in descending order of length.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Karyotypes are reported in a standard form: the total number of chromosomes is given, followed by a comma and the sex chromosome constitution, followed by the autosomal abnormalities if any - e.g. a normal human male is reported as 46,XY; a woman with three X chromosomes is reported as 47,XXX; a female dog with increased length of the short (p) arm of chromosome 2 is reported as 78,XX,2p+.
(b)
This reporting format is used to communicate karyotype results after chromosomes are counted under the X100 objective, photographed/printed, cut out, and arranged similar ones on a karyotype sheet based on length, position of the centromere, position of chromosome bands, and relative band sizes and distributions.
(c)
Autosomes are numbered 1 to 22 in descending order of length, and the sex chromosomes as X and Y, and gummed in place on the karyotype sheet; standardising the numbering by length (alongside centromere position and banding pattern) ensures that any laboratory examining a karyotype interprets and reports it consistently and comparably against the normal reference pattern.

questions.question:
A chromosome slide, treated with trypsin and stained with Leishmann/Giemsa stain, shows a pattern of dark and light bands under the 100X oil objective in bright field.
(a) What technique is being demonstrated?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this appearance?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step if the bands appear inadequate?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is G-banding.
(b)
Chromosomal proteins are denatured when treated with trypsin; when subsequently stained with Giemsa/Leishmann stain, they take up stain in a pattern of dark and light bands (G-bands), with the dark bands corresponding to the bands in Q-banding.
(c)
If slides are under-treated with trypsin, they should be destained by quickly dipping in 3:1 methanol:acetic acid 2-3 times, or until all stain is removed, then rinsed in distilled water, air dried, and rebanded before mountant and coverslip are applied.

(a)
Methods of autoradiography include the stripping film method, liquid emulsion method, film and slide method, section on emulsion method, coating method, and double labelling method.
(b)
• An autoradiogram must be exposed for a sufficiently long time for proper exposure to view the pattern of track length; if either the sample is very thick or the sample is far away from the emulsion film, resolution will be lost.
