• Since the distance and thickness of the sample, along with grain size, emulsion thickness, exposure time and energy of emitter, all determine efficiency and resolution, an error in any of these factors leads to a poorly resolved or invalid autoradiographic result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of methods of autoradiography.
(b) Explain why an error such as incorrect exposure time or sample thickness/distance leads to an invalid result.

A cytology smear shows cells with an increased nucleus-cytoplasmic ratio, irregular nuclear membrane thickening and angulation, and coarse irregular chromatin clumping with parachromatin clearing.
(a) What is the identification/interpretation of this finding?
(b) What basic technique produced this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
These nuclear features indicate malignancy; the described features (increased N:C ratio, irregular nuclear membrane changes, and coarse chromatin clumping with parachromatin clearing) are among the more significant nuclear criteria of malignancy.
(b)
This finding is produced by exfoliative or interventional cytology, with cytopathologic diagnosis resting upon alterations in morphology observed in single cells or small groups of cells.
(c)
The result should be recorded describing the specific nuclear features observed (since these carry more diagnostic weight than less significant features such as hyperchromasia or multinucleation alone); the follow-up step is that cytodiagnosis, in its traditional role, is a valuable adjunct to histopathology for establishing the tissue diagnosis, so further histopathological correlation/confirmation would be pursued.

(a)
This is Kaposi sarcoma; early lesions are difficult to distinguish from granulation tissue.
(b)
Skin biopsy is used, with tissue examined histopathologically for the characteristic spindle cell proliferation, vascular channels, and hyaline globules; CD34 immunostaining confirms positivity of the spindle cells and hyaline globules.
(c)
The result should be recorded noting the spindle cell morphology, vascular channels, inflammatory infiltrate, and CD34 positivity; the follow-up step, since Kaposi sarcoma commonly spreads to the lungs and gastrointestinal tract, is chest X-ray and, if indicated by symptoms (coughing blood, breathing problems, blood in stool, abdominal pain, or anaemia), bronchoscopy or endoscopy/colonoscopy.
questions.question:
A skin biopsy shows proliferation of spindle cells arranged in fascicles with interspersed vascular channels filled with red blood cells, inflammatory infiltrate, extravasated red blood cells, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and PAS-positive diastase-resistant hyaline globules; the spindle cells and hyaline globules are positive for CD34.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique is used to detect/confirm it?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Automated machines in the histopathology laboratory include the Automatic Tissue Processing Machine, the Tissue Embedding Centre, the Microtome, the Automated Tissue Slide Stainer, the Automated Glass Coverslipper, and the Automated Cryostat.
(b)
• The Automatic Tissue Processing Machine is applied to fix, dehydrate, clear and impregnate tissue with wax; the Tissue Embedding Centre is applied for embedding tissue in wax after processing; the microtome (manual, semi-automated, or fully automated) is applied for sectioning; the Automated Tissue Slide Stainer is applied for simultaneous routine staining of slide racks (e.g.
• H&E and Papanicolaou staining) with a monitored process; the Automated Glass Coverslipper is applied to produce slides with superb optical quality for long-term storage; the Automated Cryostat is applied for fully automatic frozen sectioning with motor-controlled specimen movement.
(c)
• Automation improves the accuracy of test results, shortens the time needed to perform tests, and obtains a slide representative of the original sample; automation also provides pathologists with higher quality sections due to standardisation of specimen thickness.
• Without automation (or with improper manual substitution), test results and specimen sections lack this standardisation, so inconsistent specimen thickness and slower, less accurate workflow lead to a less reliable, less representative result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of automated machines used in the histopathology laboratory.
(b) State how each type is applied/selected in the workflow.
(c) Explain why a lack of automation (or its improper use) leads to an inaccurate or inconsistent result.

(a) Describe the Kaiserling fixation technique for museum specimens, including the fixative formula.
(b) Describe the container/duration requirements.
(c) Explain why this technique is used or preferred for permanent museum specimens.
(d) Distinguish the fixation method for hollow viscera from that for solid organs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The fixatives in use today in most medical museums are derived from Kaiserling's (1896) technique: initial fixation in a formalin-based fixative containing salts to give a neutral pH. The formula is: Formalin 1 litre, Potassium acetate 85g, Potassium nitrate 45g, Water made up to ten litres; this solution is pH 7 and is known as Kaiserling I (K I).
(b)
• The specimen should be placed in an adequately oversized container with three to four times its volume of fixative; one fixation solution usually suffices, but larger specimens may need it changed once or twice.
• The period the specimen remains in the solution depends on its size, from three days for a small specimen up to fourteen days for large specimens (e.g. whole lung, liver, limbs); all containers should be lined with fixative-soaked lint (non-furry side up), with an undulating surface supported by fixative-soaked cotton wool.
(c)
In order to preserve a specimen as a permanent museum mount and restore it to its original colour, the only acceptable fixative is formalin; due to formalin's hardening action, the way the specimen is ultimately presented depends on it maintaining its natural shape during fixation.
(d)
• Cut hollow organs are padded out with cotton wool, but if uncut they can be pressure-inflated (e.g. through the urethra into the bladder, through the ureter into the pelvicalyceal system, through the trachea into the lung, or by direct injection for cysts) using a Higginson syringe or hypodermic syringe, avoiding over-inflation.
• Solid organs such as liver and spleen may be perfused through the main artery, but if impossible, are immediately sliced in the required plane with a long flat-bladed knife (at least 30cm) in one even cutting stroke, and placed cut-face downwards on the lint-covered container base.

(a)
Schiff's reagent is a leuco-fuchsin which is colourless; when aldehyde groups (liberated by hydrolysis in the Feulgen reaction, or by periodic acid oxidation in the PAS reaction) react with it, it recolours to give a red (PAS) or purple (Feulgen) colour at the site of the reactive groupings.
(b)
Schiff's reagent is the reagent of choice for the demonstration of aldehydes that have been freed by hydrolysis in both the Feulgen reaction (for DNA) and the PAS reaction (for carbohydrates).
(c)
Schiff's reagent should be stored in a brown bottle and preserved in a refrigerator; storing it away from light and heat in this way protects the reagent's chemical stability so that it remains colourless until it is deliberately reacted with liberated aldehydes, preventing an inaccurate (e.g. prematurely recoloured or degraded) result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and colour-change property of Schiff's reagent.
(b) State the standard setting in which Schiff's reagent is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution for its storage.

(a) Describe the preparation of tissue for enzyme histochemical technique.
(b) State the standard setting/reason this preparation method is chosen.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution on embedding temperature.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tissues must be prepared to preserve enzymes as completely as possible and retain them in their original sites; fixation should not allow enzymes to deteriorate or diffuse, and the final colour reaction should be sharply precise for exact localisation.
• Fixatives used include ice-cold acetone, ice-cold alcohol, and ice-cold formalin.
• Freeze substitution is a compromise method in which water frozen within the cell is replaced by an organic solvent at subzero temperatures, involving initial quenching, simultaneous fixation and removal of ice by immersion in a solvent such as absolute alcohol or acetone at low temperature (-60 to -70°C) for several days, then gradual raising of temperature and completion of embedding.
(b)
The use of fresh frozen cryostat sections of fresh tissue has brought enzyme histochemistry within reach of most histological labs, and is the current method of choice, recommended for its speed, ease of handling and versatility, since enzymes are very labile (unstable) and nearly all disappear from tissues quickly and progressively after removal from the body and after cellular death.
(c)
Embedding in paraffin wax must be carried out rapidly in the vacuum oven, which should not exceed 56°C, as considerably more enzyme destruction takes place at 60°C than at 56°C; this temperature limit is the precaution that preserves enzyme activity so that the histochemical reaction still reflects the original site and amount of enzyme in the living tissue.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the Cresyl Echt Violet method for demonstrating sex chromatin (Barr body).
(b) Describe the expected result of the staining.
(c) Explain why this method is used/preferred for demonstrating sex chromatin.
(d) Distinguish this method from the Romanowsky-type stain used to demonstrate the drumstick appendage.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Smears are fixed in equal volumes of alcohol-ether for 2 hours, hydrated through 70% and 50% alcohol for 5 minutes each, rinsed in distilled water, then put in 1% aqueous cresyl echt violet (or Gurr's cresyl fast violet acetate) for 5 minutes; they are differentiated in 95% alcohol until the cytoplasm becomes colourless (2 to 5 minutes), then dehydrated very rapidly in alcohol, cleared in xylene, and mounted.
(b)
The result shows sex chromatin deeply stained on the nuclear membrane, with the cytoplasm almost colourless.
(c)
A normal human female has only one Barr body (sex chromatin) per somatic cell, while a normal human male has none; examination of cells for the presence of sex chromatin is a technique used for determining the sex of a baby before birth, and this method allows the sex chromatin to be sharply demarcated as a darkly staining dot on the nuclear membrane of epithelial cells.
(d)
The Cresyl Echt Violet method is used on blood smear or buccal smear epithelial cells to demonstrate the Barr body as a sharply demarcated dark dot on the nuclear membrane; in polymorphonuclear leukocytes, however, the sex chromatin body appears instead as a drumstick appendage protruding from the nucleus, and this can be demonstrated using the Romanowsky types of stain.

(a)
• Colcemid (in phosphate buffer) interferes with the action of the spindle by binding specifically to tubulin of the spindle microtubules and prevents the centromeres from dividing, stopping mitosis at metaphase so that cells in metaphase accumulate in the culture. 0.075M Potassium Chloride (KCl) is a hypotonic solution added to swell the cells and separate the chromatids while leaving the centromeres intact.
• The fixative is Methanol (4°C) 75ml with Glacial acetic acid 25ml.
(b)
Colcemid (0.25ml of 10µg/ml) is added to the culture and incubated at 37°C for 10-20 minutes; after centrifuging and aspirating the supernatant, the hypotonic KCl solution is added slowly (1-3ml at a time up to 10ml total) and incubated for 18 minutes at 37°C; the fixative is then added drop by drop (1:3 methanol:acetic acid), which quickly fixes the cells in a swollen shape and lyses the red blood cells.
(c)
The fixative absorbs water upon standing and its pH changes with time; therefore it should be made fresh before each use, so that the fixation quality (fixing cells in the swollen shape needed to spread the chromosomes, and lysing red blood cells) remains consistent and the resulting metaphase spread is valid for analysis.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the reagents used in harvesting cultured lymphocytes and their function.
(b) State the standard setting/timing in which each reagent is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that fixative must be made fresh before use.

(a) Describe the principle of the Periodic Acid Schiff's (PAS) reaction.
(b) Describe how a diastase control is used with the PAS reaction.
(c) Explain why the PAS reaction is used or preferred for demonstrating carbohydrates.
(d) Distinguish the PAS reaction from the Feulgen reaction.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The PAS reaction is the most important staining technique for carbohydrates and is a development of the Feulgen reaction.
• Periodic acid replaces the hydrochloric acid used in the Feulgen reaction, breaking the carbon bonds (C-C) of structures present as adjacent 1:2 glycol groups (CHOH-CHOH), turning them into aldehydes (CHO) - a configuration present in carbohydrates.
• The liberated aldehydes then react with Schiff's reagent (a colourless leuco-fuchsin), and the site of PAS-reactive groupings is shown by a red colour.
• Periodic acid is the most satisfactory oxidising reagent because it does not continue to oxidise the aldehydes to carboxyl (COOH) groups once produced.
(b)
The PAS reaction is used in conjunction with a diastase control in the identification of glycogen: the PAS reaction demonstrates the sites of glycogen and many other substances in sections, and by removal of glycogen from a control section with diastase, the site and approximate quantity of glycogen in the tissue can be determined by comparing the two sections.
(c)
It is histochemically specific, being a true histochemical technique dependent on satisfactory fixation or freshly prepared cryostat sections, and can demonstrate amyloid, basement membrane, cartilage, cellulose, cerebrosides, epithelial mucus, fungi, glycogen, hyaline membrane of neonatal lung, lipochrome pigments, mucoid cells of the anterior pituitary, pancreatic zymogen granules, starch, and thyroid colloid; since many components give a true reaction, it is used with enzyme or chemical controls, blocking techniques, or additional staining methods to improve identification value.
(d)
The PAS reaction uses periodic acid to break C-C bonds of glycol groups in carbohydrates and is not diagnostic of any single tissue component (requiring additional controls), giving a red result; the Feulgen reaction uses hydrochloric acid hydrolysis to liberate aldehydes specifically from the purine-deoxyribose bond of DNA, giving a purple colour to nuclear chromatin, and is the most reliable and specific histochemical method for DNA.

questions.question:
A hollow organ specimen (e.g. bladder, lung, or pelvicalyceal system) is received uncut for permanent museum preservation.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(a)
If uncut, hollow organs can be pressure-inflated, e.g. through the urethra into the bladder, through the ureter into the pelvicalyceal system, through the trachea into the lung, and by direct injection in the case of cysts.
(b)
The fixative is injected into such organs with a Higginson syringe or a conventional hypodermic syringe, with the injection pressure required usually obvious, allowing the organ to be fixed in its natural, inflated shape.
(c)
Materials/equipment required include a Higginson syringe or hypodermic syringe, and fixative (formalin-based).
(d)
It is important to avoid over-inflation, and there is a particular problem when dealing with an elastic organ such as the lung, especially if affected by a disease such as emphysema.
(e)
When dealing with a number of such specimens, or an elastic/diseased organ, apparatus using a re-cycling pump calculated to produce a fixed pressure is recommended, rather than free-hand syringe injection, to avoid over-inflation.

(a)
Metaphase cells required to prepare a standard karyotype can be obtained from bone marrow, blood, amniotic fluid, cord blood, tumour, or tissues (including skin, umbilical cord, liver, and many other organs).
(b)
Amniotic fluid specimens for amniocentesis can be collected between 14 and 16 weeks of gestation and take 15-21 days to complete; chorionic villus specimens can be collected during the first trimester between 8 and 10 weeks and can be completed for short culture in 48 hours or long culture in 15-20 days; peripheral blood is a 72-hour culture with stimulation, taking about 7 days for analysis to complete; tumour specimen timing depends on the type of tumour.
(c)
Peripheral blood cultures have the disadvantage of being short-lived, whereas long-term cultures can be derived from skin biopsies (which must include the dermis) producing fibroblasts capable of continuous multiplication in vitro for many cell generations; choosing a specimen source unsuited to the required culture duration, or one that does not include the necessary tissue component (e.g. a skin sample without dermis), would fail to yield sufficient dividing cells, producing an invalid or delayed karyotype result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of specimen sources used to prepare karyotypes.
(b) State how each source is applied/selected, including timing.
(c) Explain why using a degraded or inappropriate specimen source leads to an invalid or delayed karyotype result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This identifies the presence of Magnesium and/or Calcium in the tissue, since with darkground illumination, Mg and Ca appear as dense white ash.
(b)
Microincineration is the burning of thin biological specimens to produce ash patterns which demonstrate the microscopic distribution of mineral substances in the material; the tissue is heated in an oven (gradually raised to 100°C, then to 650°C), and the mineral content remains as a characteristic ash pattern readable under darkground illumination.
(c)
The correct next step is to confirm the specific mineral by chemical reaction - Calcium forms gypsum crystals when treated with 3% Sulphuric acid - and to compare the ash pattern with the paired H&E-stained control section (from the same close serial sections) to correlate the mineral distribution with tissue morphology.
questions.question:
A microincinerated tissue section, viewed under darkground illumination, shows areas of dense white ash.
(a) What is this appearance identifying?
(b) What is the basic principle behind why it appears this way?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step?

(a) Describe the sample types obtainable for exfoliative cytology from different body sites.
(b) State the standard setting in which the buccal smear specifically is applied.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind screening smears to locate suitable cells before interpretation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sample types include, from the female genital tract, lateral vaginal smears, vaginal pool smears, cervical smears, combined/triple smears, and endocervical/endometrial aspiration; from the respiratory tract, sputum and bronchial washings/brushing/bronchoalveolar lavage; from the gastrointestinal tract, endoscopic lavage/brushing; from the urinary tract, urinary sediment, bladder washings, retrograde catheterisation, and prostatic massage secretions; from body fluids, effusions, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid, amniotic fluid, hydrocele fluid, seminal fluid, and nipple discharge; and other samples, buccal smears for sex chromatin.
(b)
The buccal smear is applied for cytogenetic studies, specifically for demonstrating sex-chromatin, e.g. the Barr body.
(c)
In exfoliative cytology, smears require screening to locate suitable cells for study, since the samples are prepared and forwarded by the clinician to the pathologist and the cytopathologist interprets them in isolation (unlike interventional cytology, where the cytopathologist often performs the clinical procedure and interacts with the patient); screening ensures that only smears with adequate, representative cellular material are used for diagnostic interpretation, avoiding an invalid reading from an inadequate sample.

(a)
Detection methods are darkground illumination, polarized light, and chemical reactions.
(b)
• With darkground illumination, Magnesium and Calcium appear as dense white ash.
• With polarized light, anisotropic minerals such as Silica are birefringent.
• With chemical reactions, Calcium forms gypsum crystals when treated with 3% Sulphuric acid, while Lead can be identified in sections following pre-treatment with hydrogen sulphide (which converts Pb to lead sulphide); on subsequent incineration, lead sulphide exhibits a characteristic brownish-black appearance.
(c)
Each mineral is identified by a specific detection method matched to its physical/chemical property (density producing white ash under darkground, crystal anisotropy producing birefringence under polarized light, or a specific chemical reaction producing a characteristic crystal or colour); applying the wrong method - for example, looking only under darkground illumination for a mineral that is only identifiable by a chemical reaction, such as lead - would fail to reveal or correctly identify that mineral, giving a missed or invalid result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of methods used to detect minerals after microincineration.
(b) State how each method is applied/selected.
(c) Explain why using the wrong detection method leads to a missed or invalid mineral identification.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Presentation methods include fluorescent lighting, photographs showing patient appearance, illustration of aetiological and environmental factors, statistical significance of each disorder, illustration of X-ray and laboratory findings, and colour codes for aetiology, epidemiology, pathology, clinical treatment, prognosis and prevention.
(b)
Fluorescent lighting is used because it gives better results than other lighting; photographs and illustrated factors are used to present a visitor or student with the full picture of human disease; colour codes are used to differentiate the various aspects (aetiology, epidemiology, pathology, clinical treatment, prognosis, prevention) of each condition on the catalogue sheet.
(c)
A poorly lit museum is useless, since in any museum the best-lit exhibits are the ones most frequently examined and visited; without good lighting and a full presentation of the relevant information (photographs, factors, statistics, findings), visitors and students cannot properly study or learn from the specimen, so it fails to serve its teaching and research purpose.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of museum lighting and presentation methods.
(b) State how each is applied/selected.
(c) Explain why poor lighting or presentation leads to an ineffective (unused) museum specimen.

Living cells are to be examined for the distribution of a radioactively labelled substance of interest.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/reagents/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Autoradiography is the appropriate technique.
(b)
The material of interest is labelled with a radioactive marker and introduced into the tissue; the labelled tissue is placed in intimate contact with a photographic emulsion, and during exposure, the emitted radiation activates the silver halides, reducing them to black metallic silver deposits, providing accurate quantitative information on the distribution of the labelled substance.
(c)
• Materials/reagents required include a radioactive isotope (e.g.
• Tritium, Iodine-125, Sulphur-35, or Carbon-14), photographic emulsion (silver bromide crystals in a gelatin matrix), and toluidine blue for counter-staining to show histological detail.
(d)
Factors affecting the result include grain size and amount of silver halide crystals, thickness of the emulsion, exposure time, energy of the emitter, and distance/thickness of the sample - if the sample is too thick or too far from the emulsion film, resolution will be lost.
(e)
The emulsion should have smaller grain size for more availability of silver halide crystals, with less gelatin concentration relative to crystals; emulsion thickness should be reduced for beta-emitters; and the autoradiogram must be exposed for a sufficiently long time for proper exposure to view the pattern of track length.

(a)
Ultramicrotome knives may be steel, glass or diamond, depending on the required thickness to be cut; they are cut from glass or diamond with a 35-45° angle.
(b)
Steel blades are used for animal and plant samples, whereas diamond is used for hard substances (such as bone).
(c)
• The technique may introduce compressions in the material, tearing off of the hardest zones, and tears along zones differing in hardness, and metal samples may suffer strain hardening; it cannot be applied to very heterogeneous, very hard, very soft, or very fragile samples.
• Selecting the correct knife material and angle for the specimen's hardness is therefore necessary to avoid these compressions, tears, or strain hardening artefacts, so that the constant, undistorted 30-50nm thickness the technique is meant to provide is actually achieved.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and composition of the different ultramicrotome knife types.
(b) State the standard setting in which each knife type is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind selecting the knife angle and material appropriate to the sample.

questions.answerText:
(a)
SOPs are written instruction protocols that include all aspects of laboratory work practice, following a standard format that includes name of author, title, principle, purpose, procedure, warning, hazards, precautions, date, supervisor, date to be reviewed, and references.
(b)
SOPs are an important part of the quality assurance programme, run following widely acceptable international standards, and are used across all methods and processes in the histopathology laboratory.
(c)
• SOPs help prevent mistakes rather than detecting them; they are written in simple language readily understood by employees, contain sufficient procedural detail to enable trained staff to perform the task without supervision, and are written by qualified and experienced laboratory officers.
• Because SOPs must be followed exactly by all staff, and are reviewed and updated regularly, exact adherence is the precaution that ensures the mistake-prevention purpose of the SOP is actually achieved rather than undermined by inconsistent practice.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure/composition of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP).
(b) State the standard setting in which SOPs are used in practice.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that SOPs must be followed exactly by all staff.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Types of microtome include the sled microtome, rotary microtome, cryomicrotome, ultramicrotome, vibrating microtome, saw microtome, and laser microtome.
• Rotary microtomes may further be manual (completely manipulated by the operator), semi-automated (one motor advancing either the fine or coarse hand wheel), or fully automated (two motors driving both the fine and coarse advance hand wheel).
(b)
Standard rotary microtomes are used for routine light microscopy sectioning of paraffin-embedded tissue; the ultramicrotome is used specifically for electron microscopy sample preparation, being the only technique yielding directly 30nm sections of constant thickness; the cryomicrotome/cryostat is used for rapid frozen sectioning.
(c)
The ultramicrotome technique cannot be applied to very heterogeneous, very hard, very soft, or very fragile samples, and metal samples may suffer strain hardening if this technique is wrongly used on them; using an unsuitable microtome for a given tissue type may introduce compressions, tearing off of the hardest zones, and tears along zones differing in hardness, which compromises the goal of obtaining a slide that is representative of the original sample, thereby producing an inaccurate or invalid section.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification (types) of microtome.
(b) State how each type is applied or selected in the histopathology laboratory.
(c) Explain why using the wrong microtome for a given sample leads to an inaccurate or invalid section.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hazards of embalming include Tuberculosis (TB) transmitted from a cadaver to an embalmer, and infectious HIV, which has been reported in the pleural fluid, pericardial fluid, and blood of such patients after storage at 2°C for up to 16.5 days post mortem, and has also been recovered from bone fragments, brain, bone marrow, spleen, and lymph nodes of a patient with AIDS at autopsy six days after death.
(b)
These hazards are relevant because the embalmer handles bodily fluids and tissues directly during arterial, cavity, hypodermic, and surface embalming, and reduction of potential biohazards (spread of infection to dissection personnel and students) and reduction of environmental chemical hazards are both listed among the properties required for successful embalming.
(c)
Since TB can be transmitted from a cadaver to an embalmer, and HIV can remain infectious in body fluids and tissues for many days after death (up to 16.5 days in pleural/pericardial fluid/blood, and recoverable from bone, brain, marrow, spleen and lymph nodes six days after death in an AIDS patient), failing to take adequate precautions while handling these fluids and tissues during embalming creates a real risk of occupational transmission of infection to the embalmer.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of hazards associated with embalming.
(b) State how each hazard is relevant to embalmer safety/handling.
(c) Explain why inadequate precaution against these hazards leads to occupational transmission of infection.

A chromosome slide requires banding to allow identification of individual chromosomes and their structural features.
(a) What technique is appropriate for this specimen?
(b) What is the principle of this technique?
(c) What materials/reagents/equipment are required?
(d) What sources of error or interfering factors are relevant?
(e) What precautions or quality-control checks should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(a)
G-banding is a widely used technique appropriate for this purpose.
(b)
Chromosomal proteins are denatured when treated with trypsin; when subsequently stained with Giemsa stain, they take up stain in a pattern of dark and light bands (G-bands), with the dark bands corresponding to the bands in Q-banding, allowing identification of each chromosome pair by its banding pattern.
(c)
Materials/reagents/equipment required include Trypsin (1:250) USP Grade, Gurr Buffer Solution, Working Salt Solution, Leishmann Stain Solution, an oven (for pre-treatment at 55-65°C), and a 100X plan-apochromatic oil objective for bright-field examination.
(d)
Slides should be placed in the oven for 45 minutes before staining and dipped in trypsin solution for only 5-30 seconds; if slides are under-treated with trypsin, the banding pattern will be inadequate.
(e)
If under-treated, slides must be destained (quickly dipped in 3:1 methanol:acetic acid 2-3 times, or until all stain is removed), rinsed in distilled water, air dried, and rebanded before a mountant and coverslip are applied, to ensure a valid, readable banding pattern.

(a)
• The electron microscope uses a beam of accelerated electrons as a source of illumination, giving high resolution and the ability to magnify objects in nanometers; it has much higher magnification and greater resolving power than a light microscope, allowing it to see much smaller objects in finer detail.
• All electron microscopes use electromagnetic and/or electrostatic lenses to control the path of electrons, in the form of a tall, vertically mounted vacuum column.
(b)
Parts include the electron gun (a heated tungsten filament generating electrons), electromagnetic lenses (a condenser lens focusing the beam on the specimen, a second condenser lens forming a thin tight beam, the objective lens forming the intermediate magnified image, and projector/ocular lenses producing the final magnified image), the specimen holder (an extremely thin film of carbon or collodion held by a metal grid), and the image viewing and recording system (a fluorescent screen with a camera below it).
(c)
The electron gun generates electrons; condenser lenses focus the beam onto the specimen and into a thin tight beam; an accelerating voltage (100kV-1000kV) moves electrons down the column; ultra-thin sections (20-100nm) are examined; the beam passes through the specimen and electrons scatter depending on thickness/refractive index (denser regions scatter more electrons and appear darker, transparent regions are brighter); the beam then passes to the objective lens forming the intermediate image, and the ocular lenses produce the final magnified image on the fluorescent screen.
(d)
It is used to investigate the ultrastructure of biological and inorganic specimens, offering very high magnification, incredibly high resolution, minimal material distortion by preparation, and the ability to investigate a greater depth of field, making it valuable for studying microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses and thereby making disease treatment more effective.
(e)
• TEM uses a beam of electrons focused on a specimen to produce a highly magnified, detailed image (magnification over 2 million times), used to visualise cell structures of bacteria, viruses and fungi, view flagella/plasmids, and study organelle shapes and sizes.
• SEM scans the surfaces of microorganisms using a beam of electrons moving at low energy, producing images from secondary electrons (detecting morphology/topography) and backscattered electrons (showing compositional contrast), and is used for spot chemical analysis and studying surface topography.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of the electron microscope.
(b) Describe its main parts (apparatus).
(c) Describe the working procedure by which an image is formed.
(d) Explain why this technique is used or preferred in histopathology practice.
(e) Distinguish the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) from the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM).

(a) Describe the four parts of the modern embalming process.
(b) Describe specialist embalming for autopsy cases.
(c) Explain why embalming is used or preferred to preserve a body.
(d) Distinguish arterial embalming from cavity embalming.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The modern embalming process usually involves four parts: Arterial embalming (injection of embalming chemicals into the blood vessels, usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood drained from the right jugular vein, using an embalming machine, and the embalmer massaging the cadaver for proper distribution; other injection points are used if circulation is poor); Cavity embalming (suction of internal fluids and injection of embalming chemicals into body cavities using an aspirator and trocar); Hypodermic embalming (injection of embalming chemicals under the skin as needed); and Surface embalming (supplementing the other methods, especially for visible, injured body parts).
(b)
Embalming autopsy cases differs from standard embalming as the post-mortem irrevocably disrupts the circulatory system with removal of organs for examination; in these cases a six-point injection is made via the two femoral arteries, axillary vessels, and common carotids, with the viscera treated separately with cavity fluid in a viscera bag.
(c)
Embalming is the art of temporarily preserving the human body to prevent post-mortem degeneration, to forestall decomposition and make it suitable for display at a funeral, and for anatomical research and study; properties required for successful embalming include good long-term structural preservation with minimal shrinkage/distortion, prevention of over-hardening while maintaining flexibility, prevention of desiccation, and prevention of fungal or bacterial growth.
(d)
Arterial embalming involves injecting embalming chemicals into the blood vessels (usually via the right common carotid artery, with blood drained from the right jugular vein) to distribute the embalming fluid throughout the vascular system; cavity embalming instead involves suctioning the internal fluids of the cadaver and injecting embalming chemicals directly into the body cavities using an aspirator and trocar, treating the viscera rather than the vascular system.

(a)
This is the fungating carcinoma of the stomach, also known as the "leather bottle stomach" or linitis plastica, which has a very poor prognosis; most gastric carcinomas are adenocarcinoma with mucin secretion.
(b)
Barium meal is used especially for early lesions, demonstrating the morphology of the lesion; endoscopy and biopsy provide confirmatory diagnosis.
(c)
The result should be recorded noting the site (pyloric antrum is the most common site), the gross pattern (fungating/linitis plastica), and histological type (adenocarcinoma, mucin-secreting); the follow-up step is a full blood count, since spread is usually through the lymphatic system, with the portal vein enhancing spread to the liver.
questions.question:
A gastric specimen from the pyloric antrum shows a large tumour that infiltrates the wall deeply and diffusely, converting it into a rigid structure with a nodular growth into the gastric lumen.
(a) What is the identification of this finding?
(b) What basic technique is used to detect/confirm this finding?
(c) How should the result be recorded/reported, and what is the follow-up step?

A buccal smear stained by the Cresyl Echt Violet method shows a sharply demarcated, darkly staining dot on the nuclear membrane of epithelial cells, with the cytoplasm almost colourless.
(a) What is being identified in this smear?
(b) What is the basic principle behind this appearance?
(c) What is the correct next laboratory step?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This identifies sex chromatin, the Barr body - the inactive X chromosome in a female somatic cell, rendered inactive by a process called Lyonization.
(b)
A normal human female has only one Barr body per somatic cell, while a normal human male has none; the Cresyl Echt Violet method stains the sex chromatin deeply on the nuclear membrane while the cytoplasm remains almost colourless, giving the sharply demarcated dark dot appearance.
(c)
The correct next step is to count the number of Barr bodies present, since this number relates to the number of X chromosomes present, and this count can be used (e.g. via amniocentesis samples) as a technique for determining the sex of a baby before birth or investigating a sex chromosome abnormality.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and composition of a human chromosome.
(b) State the standard setting (cell cycle stage) in which chromosome structure is examined.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind correctly identifying centromere position for classification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chromosomes are complex structures located in the cell nucleus, composed of DNA, histone and non-histone proteins, RNA, and polysaccharides - the "packages" that contain the DNA. Under the microscope, chromosomes appear as thin, thread-like structures with a short arm (p) and a long arm (q) separated by a primary constriction called the centromere, which is the location of spindle attachment and essential for normal chromosome movement and segregation during cell division.
(b)
Chromosome structure is examined under the microscope at metaphase, when chromosomes condense into visible rod-shaped structures, following culture, harvesting with a mitotic inhibitor, hypotonic treatment, fixation, and slide preparation.
(c)
Human metaphase chromosomes come in three basic shapes categorised by centromere location: metacentric (short and long arms of almost equal length, centromere centrally located), submetacentric (arms of unequal length, centromere not centrally located), and acrocentric (centromere very close to one end, very small short arms); correctly identifying this centromere position, together with chromosome length and banding pattern, is essential because it is one of the features used to arrange and classify each chromosome into its correct group on the karyotype sheet - an error here would misclassify the chromosome.

(a)
A conventional 'Dymo' tape label is used; the range of colours available allows a differential labelling system - specimens with a red label are examples of rarer conditions or conditions undergraduates need not concentrate on, yellow labelled specimens are good examples of common conditions undergraduates should concentrate on, and green labelled specimens are less satisfactory examples of common conditions or less common conditions.
(b)
• A simple loose-leaf catalogue holds all necessary information relating to each specimen, and it is helpful to have a separate catalogue for each anatomical system; each catalogue sheet has the diagnosis (with museum number) at the top, followed by a brief description of the specimen and a brief case history, and different colour bands can be used for each condition (e.g. red for malignancy, yellow for inflammatory processes, green for normal condition)
• A plan of the museum room should be visible to the visitor on entering, with each section clearly labelled.
(c)
Older glass jars with hand-painted labels are easily chipped off and can become confusing or illegible, and Perspex jars with machine-engraved labels are expensive to produce and not easily replaced; the Dymo tape label is a compromise which, while not as attractive as the first, is cheap and easily renewed.
(d)
Specimens can be classified either by anatomical system (e.g. all liver conditions together, all heart conditions together) or by disease system (e.g. all tuberculous specimens, all parasites together); most medical teaching is carried out by anatomical systems, which usually proves the most practical arrangement, but if a disease process needs to be studied, a simple numbering system enables such specimens to be easily selected from the general collection.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the labelling method used for museum specimens.
(b) Describe the cataloguing method used.
(c) Explain why the 'Dymo' tape label is used or preferred over other labelling options.
(d) Distinguish anatomical-system arrangement of specimens from disease-based arrangement.

(a) Describe the procedure for slide preparation of cells at metaphase.
(b) Describe how the slides are scanned/checked for quality after preparation.
(c) Explain why this dropping technique is used or preferred to spread the chromosomes.
(d) Distinguish air-drying slides at a slant from air-drying them horizontally.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Slides are washed with absolute alcohol for several minutes and wiped clean; the old fixative above the cell pellet is aspirated and the pellet resuspended in 1.5ml of fresh fixative. 100µl of the cell suspension is dropped from 3-4 inches above the slide surface, one drop at a time, moving the pipette so that no two drops fall exactly on the same area, though all 100µl should fall within the scratched area on the slide.
(b)
• Slides are quickly scanned using the X40 objective, green filter and L20 phase annulus to check that the chromosomes have spread sufficiently and that no cytoplasm (halo or dark area) is observed around the chromosomes; if cytoplasm is detected, it is dispersed by washing the cells several times with fresh fixative before preparing more slides.
• Slides are then washed in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) for 5 minutes, then in ascending grades of ethanol (70, 90, 100%), which hardens the chromosomes and makes them more resistant to conventional banding procedures such as G or Giemsa banding.
(c)
Dropping the fixative slowly, one drop at a time from a set height, allows the fixative to quickly evaporate from under and around the cell so the cell flattens completely, forcing the chromosomes to spread for analysis.
(d)
The slides are air-dried either at a slant if the chromosomes are well spread, or horizontally if the chromosomes are not well spread, in order to control how the drying process finishes the chromosome spreading before microscopic evaluation and banding.

questions.explanation: When a port wine stain mimics the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, further malformations in the eyes (glaucoma), meninges, or brain (epilepsy) may be suspected. This is known as Sturge-Weber syndrome. Parents and the child may need substantial psychological support.
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the complication of Sturge-Weber syndrome associated with a port wine stain?
options: Port wine stain with Sturge-Weber causes bilateral renal agenesis
Port wine stain associated with aortic coarctation and Turner syndrome
Port wine stain causing progressive skin thickening and necrosis
Port wine stain associated with VSD and pulmonary hypertension
Port wine stain mimicking distribution of ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve associated with glaucoma and epilepsy

questions.question: Postnatal exercises in the puerperium should be performed:
questions.explanation: Postnatal exercises should be performed daily in the puerperium to promote uterine involution, strengthen the pelvic floor, improve circulation, and aid general recovery. These exercises are an essential component of postnatal care for all women regardless of mode of delivery or perineal status. Waiting until 6 weeks or until lochia ceases delays beneficial recovery. Simple exercises can begin from the first postpartum day with gradual progression.
options: Only after the 6-week postnatal check confirms full pelvic floor recovery
Only for women who had perineal lacerations requiring suturing after delivery
Three times weekly, starting from the 10th postpartum day
Every other day, commencing only after lochia has completely ceased
Onset of true labour after a prolonged latent phase
Normal transition to the second stage
Uterine rupture at the scar site
questions.explanation: Sudden severe abdominal pain, an abnormal fetal heart rate pattern, and cessation of previously effective contractions in a woman with a uterine scar are classic warning signs of uterine rupture, a life-threatening obstetric emergency requiring immediate surgical intervention. This presentation differs markedly from normal labour progress or benign causes of abdominal discomfort. Continuous monitoring of women with previous caesarean section is essential during labour.
questions.question: A woman with a previous caesarean scar develops sudden severe abdominal pain, fetal heart rate abnormality, and cessation of previously strong contractions during labour. This presentation is MOST suggestive of:

options: Flexion of fingers when an object is placed in the palm
Extension of arm and leg on the side the head is turned toward
Stepping movements when feet are placed on a firm surface
Symmetrical abduction and extension then flexion of arms on sudden head extension
Turning of the head toward stimulation of the cheek
questions.explanation: The Moro reflex involves symmetrical abduction and extension followed by flexion and adduction of the arms with accompanying cry, triggered by sudden head extension. It is present from 37 weeks' gestation and disappears around 4 months. Unilateral absence implies fractured clavicle, hemiplegia, or brachial plexus palsy.
questions.question: The Moro (startle) reflex in a newborn is described as which of the following?

questions.explanation: Pain relief during the second stage is guided by the woman's preferences (as documented in her birth plan), maternal and fetal condition, and available options. The midwife continues to support the woman's comfort and hygiene, including sponging the face and neck. Bladder care and positioning are also important.
options: Epidural anaesthesia is mandatory for all women in the second stage
Regional analgesia must be discontinued at the onset of second stage
The woman's pain relief preferences from the birth plan guide management
Pharmacological pain relief is contraindicated during active pushing
IV opioids are routinely administered at the onset of the second stage
questions.question: Pain relief during the second stage is primarily managed in which way?

options: Increases placental separation risk due to fundal displacement
Stimulates increased prostaglandin production leading to coagulopathy
Causes maternal hypertension through autonomic stimulation
Promotes membrane rupture leading to chorioamnionitis
Prevents uterine contractions by mechanically interfering with uterine retraction
questions.question: A full bladder is a predisposing factor for PPH because it causes which specific mechanism?
questions.explanation: A full bladder is a predisposing factor for PPH because it mechanically interferes with uterine contraction and retraction. The overdistended bladder displaces the uterus and prevents it from contracting effectively. Women must be encouraged to void before delivery and early catheterisation is important if retention is suspected.

questions.question: A midwife counsels a mother that the measles vaccine is typically given at what age in the routine immunisation schedule?
questions.explanation: The measles vaccine is typically given at nine months of age in many national immunisation schedules, timed to occur after the decline of maternally transferred antibodies, which would otherwise interfere with the infant's own immune response to the vaccine. Giving it earlier, such as at birth or six weeks, would result in reduced vaccine effectiveness due to these residual maternal antibodies. A second dose may be given later, such as at 15 to 18 months, depending on the specific national schedule.

The presentation of high fever greater than 40°C for 4 to 7 days, followed by a maculopapular rash starting on the face, combined with Koplik's spots on the buccal mucosa, is characteristic of measles. Koplik's spots are pathognomonic (uniquely diagnostic) of measles. Roseola rash appears as fever breaks (not during), rubella has a fine rash with lymphadenopathy, and chickenpox produces vesicular not maculopapular lesions.
options: Rubella (German measles), with a fine petechial rash and posterior lymphadenopathy
Measles, presenting with characteristic prodromal signs and buccal Koplik's spots
Roseola infantum (HHV-6), with rash appearing as fever breaks
Scarlet fever, with the sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue
Chickenpox (varicella), with vesicular rash beginning on the trunk
questions.question: A child presenting with high fever greater than 40°C for 4 to 7 days, followed by a maculopapular rash starting on the face, with Koplik's spots on the buccal mucosa, is MOST LIKELY diagnosed with:

questions.explanation: Correct use of the Pinard stethoscope involves placing the wide end firmly against the maternal abdomen, typically over the fetal back where heart sounds are clearest, while the midwife's ear rests against the narrow end without using hands to hold it in place, allowing accurate auscultation without applying additional pressure. It is used throughout labour, not only the second stage. Correct technique and positioning are essential for obtaining an accurate fetal heart rate.
options: Hold the device away from the abdomen while listening
Use it exclusively during the second stage of labour
Place the wide end firmly against the maternal abdomen over the fetal back without using her hands to hold it against her ear
Apply it only over the fetal limbs for accuracy
Press it firmly against the maternal ear only
questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman confirms fetal wellbeing using a Pinard fetal stethoscope. Correct use of this instrument requires the midwife to:

questions.explanation: By eighteen months, most toddlers can walk independently and typically use a vocabulary of several single words, representing normal gross motor and early language development at this age. Running confidently, complex sentence formation, tricycle riding, and writing are skills that develop later in the second, third, and fourth years of life. Recognising the expected range of milestones helps identify children who may benefit from further developmental assessment.
options: Walk independently and say several single words
Speak in complete sentences of five words or more
Write simple letters of the alphabet
questions.question: A midwife assessing an eighteen-month-old toddler expects the child to typically be able to:

options: Spontaneous onset of labour at term
Normal third stage lasting under 15 minutes
Induction or augmentation of labour with oxytocin
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised predisposing factor for postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)?
questions.explanation: Induction or augmentation of labour with oxytocin is a recognised predisposing factor for PPH as it may lead to uterine exhaustion and atony after delivery. Other factors include grand multiparity, uterine overdistension, retained placenta, and mismanagement of the third stage.

options: Caesarean section delivery regardless of indication
Male baby gender requiring additional care adjustments
Primiparity with prolonged labour requiring episiotomy
Personal and family history of depression
questions.question: Which of the following correctly identifies a risk factor for postpartum blues consistently shown in the literature?
questions.explanation: The factors most consistently shown to be predictive of postpartum blues are personal and family history of depression. There is a bidirectional relationship: a history of postpartum depression is a risk factor for postpartum blues, and postpartum blues confers a higher risk of subsequent postpartum depression.

questions.question: Which of the following infant formula types is MOST suitable for a healthy term infant experiencing digestive difficulties such as colic?
questions.explanation: Whey-dominant formula, with a 60:40 whey-to-casein ratio approximating human milk, is recommended for infants experiencing digestive issues such as colic or lactose intolerance. Whey protein is faster-digesting and easier to absorb. Casein-dominant formula is intended for hungrier babies but is not recommended for young babies.
options: Whey-dominant formula with a 60:40 whey-to-casein ratio
Casein-dominant formula designed for hungrier babies
Soya-based formula for all colic due to anti-inflammatory properties
Goat's milk formula for all term infants with digestive difficulties
Amino acid-based formula as first choice for all colic
Diethylcarbamazine and metronidazole, for broad anti-protozoal coverage
Ferrous sulphate and folic acid, for haematinic supplementation
Mebendazole and pyrantel, for anti-helminthic treatment
questions.explanation: Amoxycillin and cotrimoxazole are listed as antibacterial drugs on the essential drug list. These are commonly used at the primary healthcare level for the treatment of bacterial infections. Pyrimethamine/Sulfadoxine is an antimalarial, ferrous sulphate and folic acid are haematinics, mebendazole and pyrantel are anti-helminthics, and metronidazole is an amoebicide. Each drug category serves a specific treatment purpose in primary health care delivery.
questions.question: In the essential drug list, which combination drug is listed specifically as an antibacterial agent at the primary healthcare level?

A midwife assesses a child with a grey-white pseudomembrane covering the tonsils and pharynx, along with fever and a 'bull neck' appearance from cervical lymphadenopathy. This is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Diphtheria is characterised by the formation of a tough, grey-white pseudomembrane over the tonsils, pharynx, or larynx, which can cause airway obstruction, along with significant cervical lymphadenopathy producing the classic 'bull neck' appearance. This is a medical emergency due to both airway compromise and the systemic effects of diphtheria toxin, requiring urgent antitoxin and antibiotic treatment. This presentation is distinct from other causes of sore throat, which typically do not produce a true adherent pseudomembrane.

options: Size of the fetal head using external cephalometry
Sagittal suture direction, fontanelle position, and moulding
Biparietal diameter by internal palpation technique
Degree of asynclitism by assessing parietal bones only
Fetal head station measured in centimetres above the ischial spines
questions.explanation: During vaginal examination, the midwife notes the slope of the sagittal suture (normally in right or left oblique in early labour), the position of the fontanelles to determine fetal head position, and the degree of moulding. This information guides management and identifies malposition or malpresentation.
questions.question: During vaginal examination in labour, what information should be obtained regarding the fetal head?

questions.explanation: Weight-for-age is particularly useful for monitoring growth in small infants who normally gain weight fast. Normal weight gain suggests the infant is healthy and growing normally. Failure to gain weight normally or losing weight is often the earliest sign of illness or malnutrition. For older children, height becomes a more useful indicator of long-term nutritional status, and head circumference is most useful under 36 months for brain growth assessment.
options: Assessing brain growth in children over 36 months of age
Detecting wasting and stunting in children between 2 and 5 years
Older children where height is more reflective of long-term nutritional status
Small infants who normally gain weight fast, detecting early illness or malnutrition
Monitoring head circumference changes in the neonatal intensive care setting
questions.question: In assessing a child's growth, weight-for-age is particularly useful for:

questions.explanation: Heart rate normalises by 10 days postpartum. Cardiac output does not normalise until 24 weeks after birth. Blood pressure normalises by 6–8 weeks. Peripheral vascular resistance remains elevated above normal at 6 weeks postpartum. Stroke volume normalises by 4–12 weeks.
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the cardiovascular return to normal in the puerperium?
options: Cardiac output returns to normal by 6 weeks postpartum
Blood pressure returns to normal immediately after delivery
Peripheral vascular resistance normalises within the first 48 hours
Heart rate normalises by day 10; cardiac output not until 24 weeks
Stroke volume normalises by day 3 postpartum

questions.explanation: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion are greatly inhibited by placental progesterone and oestrogen during pregnancy. This inhibition prevents further follicular development and ovulation during the gestational period. While HCG does stimulate the corpus luteum in early pregnancy, it is the placental sex steroids (progesterone and oestrogen) that specifically suppress FSH and LH through negative feedback on the anterior pituitary.
questions.question: Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) secretion during pregnancy is greatly inhibited by:
options: Rising levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) from the placenta
Increased prolactin from the anterior pituitary gland
Elevated ACTH and cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Posterior pituitary oxytocin acting on a negative feedback loop

questions.explanation: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is always considered pathological and requires urgent investigation to identify the underlying cause, such as haemolytic disease of the newborn, as it carries a higher risk of rapidly rising bilirubin levels and kernicterus if untreated. This contrasts with physiological jaundice, which appears later and follows a more predictable, self-limiting course. Prompt recognition and referral are critical to prevent serious neurological complications.
options: A normal variant related to delayed cord clamping
Expected in all breastfed infants without concern
A finding to be reassessed only after one week
Normal physiological jaundice needing no action
questions.question: A midwife identifies jaundice in a newborn within the FIRST 24 hours of life. This finding should be considered:

questions.explanation: Prevention of PPH includes AMTSL and preventing specific causes, including precipitate labour, retained products, over-distension of the uterine muscle, and prolonged labour leading to uterine inertia. Precipitate labour is listed alongside placenta praevia, placental abruption, and episiotomy or perineal tear.
options: Elective caesarean section before labour onset
Administration of prophylactic antibiotics in all cases
Prevention and management of precipitate labour as a cause of PPH
Insertion of balloon catheter after precipitate delivery
Manual exploration of the uterus after every precipitate labour
questions.question: Prevention of PPH includes which of the following specific interventions for precipitate labour?

questions.explanation: Fatigue is most characteristically experienced in the first trimester, and the recommended relief measure is frequent rest until this period is over. The woman is reassured that fatigue typically disappears at the end of the first trimester. In the third trimester, while fatigue returns, there is usually a surge of nesting energy. The specific association with 'first trimester fatigue' is a distinct clinical feature taught in midwifery.
options: Throughout all three trimesters equally due to increased metabolic demands
Predominantly in the second trimester when weight gain is maximum
In the first trimester, usually disappearing at the end of the first trimester
In the third trimester when the woman experiences increased nesting energy
Mainly after 30 weeks due to impaired sleep from urinary frequency
questions.question: Fatigue as a minor disorder of pregnancy is MOST characteristically experienced during which period?
A midwife is performing active management of the third stage of labour. The three components of this approach are administration of an oxytocic, controlled cord traction, and:
questions.explanation: Active management of the third stage of labour comprises three components: administration of a uterotonic drug soon after birth, controlled cord traction to deliver the placenta, and uterine massage after delivery of the placenta to maintain contraction. This approach significantly reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage compared with expectant management. Routine early cord clamping within 10 seconds is not part of current recommended practice, as slightly delayed clamping is now preferred.
options: Routine episiotomy repair before placental delivery
Manual removal of the placenta routinely
Fundal pressure before the placenta separates
Early clamping of the cord within 10 seconds
Neonatal tetanus in the infant born to a tetanus-infected mother
Puerperal tetanus from septic procedures during delivery
Incidental tetanus from any type of wound sustained during pregnancy
Postabortal tetanus from septic abortion procedures
Postpartum tetanus from unhygienic delivery practices within 42 days
questions.question: Maternal tetanus is defined as tetanus occurring during pregnancy or within 6 weeks of end of pregnancy. Which of the following is NOT a form of maternal tetanus?
questions.explanation: Maternal tetanus includes postpartum (puerperal) tetanus from septic delivery, postabortal tetanus from septic abortion, and tetanus incidental to pregnancy from any wound during pregnancy. Neonatal tetanus is a separate category defined as tetanus occurring within the first 28 days of the neonate's life. While neonatal tetanus shares common risk factors with maternal tetanus (unclean delivery practices), it is classified separately under neonatal tetanus, not as a form of maternal tetanus.

options: Adverse drug reactions in patients receiving essential medicines
Drug resistance development from inadequate or incomplete treatment courses
Expired drug administration through first-in-first-out stock rotation tracking
Theft, wastage, and stockouts through documented accountability of every transaction
Counterfeit drug infiltration into the supply chain at the facility level
questions.question: Good drug inventory management using stock cards serves to prevent which PRIMARY problem in essential drug management?
questions.explanation: Good drug inventory management using stock cards prevents theft, wastage (including expired drugs), and stockouts through documented accountability of every drug transaction. The card records quantity received or issued, stock balanced, date, and signature, creating an audit trail for all drug movements. This protects drug quality, ensures drug availability (preventing stockouts), and safeguards against theft. While first-in-first-out rotation also helps prevent expiry, the primary purpose of stock cards is comprehensive accountability.

questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman on day ten postpartum notes lochia that is now pale yellow to white in colour. This is termed:
questions.explanation: Lochia alba is the final stage of lochial discharge, pale yellow to white in colour, occurring from around day ten to as late as six weeks postpartum as the discharge decreases in blood content and increases in leucocytes and mucus. This progression from rubra to serosa to alba reflects normal healing of the uterine lining. A return to red bleeding after this stage would be abnormal and require assessment.

questions.question: How is the baby delivered by lateral flexion toward the mother's abdomen during the mechanism of labour?
options: Lateral flexion occurs before shoulders reach the pelvic outlet
After anterior shoulder escapes under symphysis pubis, posterior shoulder sweeps perineum and baby born by lateral flexion
The head is laterally flexed by the midwife before restitution is complete
Lateral flexion occurs during crowning after the posterior shoulder appears
Lateral flexion is a maternal movement without specific anatomical basis
questions.explanation: The anterior shoulder escapes under the symphysis pubis and the posterior shoulder sweeps the perineum, then the baby is born by lateral flexion of the trunk toward the mother's abdomen. The midwife grasps the baby around the chest to aid birth of the trunk, completing the mechanism of labour.

options: Five fused vertebrae with the anterior surface being concave (Hollow of the Sacrum)
Four fused vertebrae with the posterior surface being concave
Six fused vertebrae with the lateral surfaces forming the alar wings
Five fused vertebrae with the posterior surface being concave
Three fused vertebrae with a prominent promontory on the anterior surface
questions.question: The Sacrum is described as a wedge-shaped bone consisting of how many fused vertebrae, with which surface being concave?
questions.explanation: The sacrum consists of five fused vertebrae forming a wedge-shaped bone. Its anterior surface is concave, referred to as the Hollow of the Sacrum. The upper border of the first sacral vertebra juts forward as the sacral promontory (the most important landmark in the female pelvis). The posterior surface is roughened to receive attachment of muscles. The lateral sacrum extends into a wing or ala. The coccyx (not sacrum) consists of four fused vertebrae.

questions.question: Essential drugs are defined as those that satisfy the health care needs of the majority of the population. Which criterion is NOT part of the WHO essential drug selection process?
questions.explanation: Essential drugs are selected based on disease prevalence and public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness. Brand name recognition or pharmaceutical company reputation is not a criterion — indeed, generic drugs are generally preferred. The concept aims to ensure the most effective, safe, and affordable medicines are available at all health system levels, particularly primary healthcare.
options: The brand name recognition and pharmaceutical company reputation
Disease prevalence and public health relevance
Comparative cost-effectiveness relative to available alternatives
Evidence of efficacy and safety in clinical settings
Availability at all operational health levels in adequate amounts
Reassure the woman and discharge her home
Administer oral iron only and observe
Delay examination of the placenta until the next day
Examine the placenta and membranes for completeness and arrange urgent obstetric review
Apply fundal pressure repeatedly until bleeding stops
questions.question: A midwife suspects retained placental fragments after finding continued bleeding and a uterus that fails to remain well contracted following apparently complete placental delivery. The MOST appropriate immediate step is to:
questions.explanation: When retained fragments are suspected, the midwife should carefully examine the delivered placenta and membranes for completeness and arrange urgent obstetric review, as retained tissue prevents effective uterine contraction and predisposes to ongoing haemorrhage and infection. Evacuation of retained products may be required. Delaying assessment risks worsening haemorrhage and sepsis.

Marked moulding and caput formation together with arrested descent despite good contractions suggest that the fetal head diameters are too large relative to the maternal pelvis, known as cephalopelvic disproportion. This requires urgent obstetric assessment as continued labour risks obstructed labour and uterine rupture. Mild moulding without arrest of progress can be a normal adaptive finding.
questions.question: A midwife assessing a labouring woman finds arrest of descent despite strong contractions, with marked moulding and caput formation. This clinical picture is MOST suggestive of:
options: Normal physiological moulding in active labour

questions.explanation: A well-applied fetal head fills the pelvic brim and forms a seal that reduces the space through which the umbilical cord could prolapse if the membranes rupture. This is why membrane rupture with a poorly applied or high presenting part carries higher risk of cord prolapse. It does not by itself indicate dilatation, second stage, or fetal wellbeing.
questions.question: A woman in labour has ruptured membranes with clear liquor draining, and the midwife notes the fetal head is well applied to the cervix. This finding is significant because it:
options: Reduces the risk of cord prolapse
Indicates the second stage has begun

questions.explanation: External rotation follows restitution and occurs as the shoulders rotate internally within the pelvis to lie in the anteroposterior diameter, causing the already-born head to turn further to maintain alignment. This allows the anterior shoulder to escape beneath the symphysis pubis. It is a normal and expected part of the mechanism of labour in vertex delivery.
questions.question: A midwife observes that after restitution, the fetal head continues to turn further as the shoulders rotate to lie in the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet. This subsequent movement is known as:
options: Internal rotation of the shoulders only

questions.question: During the third trimester, a pregnant woman experiences a SURGE OF ENERGY described as:
options: A nesting energy surge as the woman prepares for the infant
Peak physical strength from elevated progesterone supporting musculoskeletal function
Increased libido and sexual activity in preparation for postpartum recovery
Final trimester adrenaline release triggered by fetal cortisol in anticipation of labour
Reduced fatigue from the placenta taking over all hormonal functions from the corpus luteum
questions.explanation: In the third trimester, there is usually a surge of energy as the woman prepares a nest for the infant — a phenomenon commonly called 'nesting instinct.' This surge is distinct from the general pattern of increased fatigue and decreased interest in sexual activity that characterizes the third trimester. Pride about the pregnancy coexists with anxiety about labour and birth. Physical discomforts increase and the woman is eager for the pregnancy to end.

Low birth weight is defined as a birth weight below 2,500 grams, regardless of gestational age, so a term infant weighing 2,300 grams falls into this category and requires closer monitoring for complications such as hypothermia and hypoglycaemia. Very low birth weight refers to infants below 1,500 grams, and extremely low birth weight to those below 1,000 grams, neither of which applies here. Understanding these classifications helps guide appropriate levels of neonatal care.
questions.question: A midwife weighs a newborn at birth and records 2,300 grams at term gestation. This baby is classified as:
A midwife counsels a woman about depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injectable contraception. She explains that repeat injections are typically required every:
questions.explanation: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is administered by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection every three months to maintain effective contraceptive protection through sustained suppression of ovulation. Missing this schedule significantly increases the risk of unintended pregnancy, so women should be counselled on the importance of returning on time for repeat doses. This differs from other injectable or implant methods, which have different dosing intervals.

questions.question: A midwife performing bag-and-mask ventilation on a newborn observes no chest rise despite good technique. The MOST likely corrective step is to:
questions.explanation: When chest rise is not observed during bag-and-mask ventilation, the midwife should first reposition the airway and check for an adequate mask seal, as poor technique is the most common cause of ventilation failure. Chest compressions and medications are only indicated if effective ventilation has been established and the heart rate remains low. Abandoning resuscitation without correcting technique would be inappropriate.
options: Reposition the head and check the mask seal before reattempting ventilation
Increase ventilation rate above 60 breaths per minute without checking technique

questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman receiving epidural analgesia in labour must prioritise which additional monitoring?
questions.explanation: Epidural analgesia can cause maternal hypotension due to sympathetic blockade, so frequent blood pressure monitoring is essential to detect and treat this promptly, as it can also reduce placental perfusion and affect the fetus. Bladder care is also important since the woman may have reduced sensation. Blood glucose and urinary protein are not the primary concerns related specifically to epidural use.
options: Frequent maternal blood pressure monitoring for hypotension
Hourly temperature only, no blood pressure needed
100 to 120 grams, including cervix and lower segment
30 to 40 grams, lighter than commonly described in older texts
75 to 80 grams, heavier than the myometrium alone
200 to 250 grams in nulliparous women and less in multiparae
questions.question: The non-pregnant uterus is described as pear-shaped with specific dimensions. Its weight is:
questions.explanation: The non-pregnant uterus is a pear-shaped hollow thick-walled muscular organ approximately 7.5 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2.5 cm thick, weighing 57 to 60 grams. At term, the myometrium grows from 50 to 60 grams to approximately 1,000 grams. The figures of 30 to 40 grams, 100 to 120 grams, or 200 grams do not correspond to documented standard anatomical measurements for the non-pregnant uterus.

questions.question: A midwife counsels a woman about reduced fetal movements reported at 32 weeks gestation. The MOST appropriate immediate action is to:
questions.explanation: Reduced fetal movements reported by a pregnant woman should always be promptly assessed, including fetal heart auscultation and further evaluation such as cardiotocography if indicated, as this can be an early warning sign of fetal compromise or placental insufficiency. Reassurance without assessment or advising a delay of a week would risk missing a potentially serious underlying problem. This symptom should be taken seriously regardless of gestational age within the viable range.
options: Advise her to wait one week before any assessment
Attribute this solely to normal fetal sleep cycles without assessment
Discharge her with no further instructions
Arrange prompt assessment including fetal heart auscultation and further evaluation as needed
Reassure her this is normal and requires no follow-up
Counter-traction applied above the symphysis pubis while cord traction is applied
Applying gentle traction while the uterus is contracting strongly
Cupping the placenta in both hands as it appears at the introitus
Applying fundal pressure from above to prevent uterine descent
Using a clamp on the cord to maintain constant steady traction
questions.question: Which characteristic of CCT technique is specifically designed to prevent uterine inversion?
questions.explanation: Counter-traction applied with the non-dominant hand above the symphysis pubis, pushing the uterus upward and backward, while cord traction is applied downward and backward with the dominant hand, specifically prevents uterine inversion. The counter-traction stabilises the uterus so it is not drawn down with the placenta.

Weight should be measured and recorded every month for the first year of life, every 2 months for the second year, and then every 6 months thereafter to the age of 5 years. This decreasing frequency reflects the slowing rate of growth after infancy. However, it is often measured routinely at every visit to a clinic, hospital, or general practitioner. The structured schedule represents the minimum recommended monitoring frequency, not a ceiling on how often weight can be measured.
questions.question: Weight monitoring frequency for children between 2 and 5 years of age (after the second year of life) is:
options: Monthly, maintaining the same frequency as the first year
Every 2 months, as in the second year of life
Annually, as growth rate is stable and changes are gradual
Only when the child is brought for immunization visits or illness

questions.explanation: Subsequent care begins after the first 24 hours and includes ambulation (6 to 12 hours after delivery), which promotes well-being, good circulation, and drainage of lochia, and allows the woman to participate in her baby's care.
