Absorbable haemostatic materials (oxidised cellulose/Surgicel, gelatin foam/Gelfoam) promote clot formation at the bleeding site and are biodegraded/absorbed over days to weeks, eliminating the trauma of pack removal. They are particularly suitable for anterior bleeds and post-operative haemostasis. Their self-degrading nature prevents secondary bleeding from mucosal stripping during removal of non-absorbable packs.
options: They promote clot formation and do not require removal after bleeding stops
They are non-absorbable and provide permanent tamponade
They contain antibiotics that sterilise the nasal cavity as the sole finding
They are only indicated for posterior bleeds
They replace damaged mucosal cells directly
questions.question: Haemostatic absorbable packing materials such as oxidised cellulose (Surgicel) and gelatin foam are specifically used in epistaxis because:

questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) classically presents in adolescents with exudative tonsillitis, palatal petechiae, anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and a positive heterophile (Monospot) test. The posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and systemic features (hepatosplenomegaly, fatigue) distinguish it from streptococcal tonsillitis. Ampicillin/amoxicillin should be avoided as it causes a drug rash in EBV infection.
questions.question: Acute tonsillitis with palatal petechiae, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and heterophile-positive test in an adolescent most likely represents infection with:
A patient with a maxillary sinus mass has an embryological origin traced to the primitive nasal capsule. Which structure specifically gives rise to the maxillary sinus during development?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus develops embryologically as an outpouching of mucosa from the middle meatus into the developing maxillary bone, beginning in fetal life and continuing to expand postnatally through the described biphasic growth pattern. Understanding this origin helps explain why the natural maxillary ostium is consistently located high on the medial wall, in the region of the middle meatus. This developmental relationship also underlies the pattern of recirculation seen with accessory ostia.
options: An outpouching of the middle meatus mucosa

questions.question: In paediatric patients, microsuction of cerumen is generally tolerated from which age?
questions.explanation: Most children only tolerate microsuction from age 4 years or older. For younger children, a Jobson Horne probe or ring curette may be a viable alternative. Careful explanation, allowing the child to touch equipment, and slow introduction of the suction device can help children as young as 3 tolerate the procedure.

questions.question: In a patient suspected to have food allergy, which investigation is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Elimination tests, where suspected foods are removed from the diet and symptoms monitored, are particularly useful in diagnosing food allergies. This approach identifies the offending food without the risks of challenge tests and is practical for multi-food sensitivity assessment.

CN XII (hypoglossal nerve) exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone, a separate foramen from the jugular foramen (CN IX-XI). Inferior clival extension of NPC or erosion of the occipital condyle region can directly compress CN XII here, causing ipsilateral tongue weakness and deviation toward the paralysed side. This finding indicates advanced disease with skull base invasion and necessitates comprehensive cranial nerve assessment.
questions.question: Involvement of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) in NPC indicates spread through which skull base foramen?

questions.explanation: The uncinate process and the ethmoid infundibulum form the key gateway of the ostiomeatal complex. During FESS, the uncinate process is resected first to open the infundibulum and allow access to the maxillary, anterior ethmoid, and frontal drainage pathways. Careful preservation of adjacent structures prevents scarring and recurrent obstruction.
questions.question: During functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), the structure that must be preserved to prevent disruption of frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid drainage is the:

options: Penetration into adjacent paranasal sinuses causing sinusitis
Trismus and temporomandibular joint involvement at all times
questions.question: Sharp nasal foreign bodies (e.g., pins, needles) may cause which specific and serious complication beyond simple mucosal damage?
questions.explanation: Sharp nasal foreign bodies (pins, needles, sharpened pencils) can penetrate the thin nasal mucosa and walls of the paranasal sinuses — particularly the thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid or the medial wall of the maxillary sinus — causing secondary sinusitis. They can also penetrate the orbit or skull base in severe cases. This is why sharp nasal foreign bodies always require careful extraction technique and post-removal imaging.

options: As first-line treatment for all glomus tumours found
Beyond surgical margins, recurrence, or unfit for surgery
questions.explanation: Radiotherapy is recommended for glomus tumours extending beyond surgically manageable boundaries, for postoperative recurrences, and for patients who are not surgical candidates. Surgical removal ranges from simple transcanal tympanotomy to extensive base-of-skull resection depending on tumour extent. Glomus tumours are the most common ear neoplasms.
questions.question: Radiotherapy for glomus tumours of the ear is specifically recommended in which situations?

questions.explanation: Capillary haemangioma of the nasal cavity (usually arising from the nasal septum or lateral nasal wall) presents predominantly with recurrent epistaxis from the highly vascular tumour. The mass is typically bright red, soft, compressible, and bleeds easily on contact. Other symptoms include nasal obstruction. Treatment is endoscopic surgical excision with cauterisation of the vascular pedicle.
questions.question: Capillary haemangioma of the nasal cavity most commonly presents with which symptom?
options: Recurrent epistaxis from the vascular mass
Anosmia as the first well-defined symptom
Has been misdiagnosed and is not truly allergic
Has an active bacterial sinus infection
questions.explanation: Reactivity to multiple, unrelated allergens on skin testing reflects an underlying atopic tendency in which the immune system is broadly predisposed to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reactions. This pattern is common in patients with a personal or family history of other atopic conditions such as asthma and eczema. It does not indicate misdiagnosis, but instead a broader allergic constitution requiring comprehensive environmental control.
questions.question: A patient undergoes skin testing for suspected allergic rhinitis and reacts positively to multiple unrelated allergens simultaneously. This pattern MOST likely indicates that the patient:

questions.explanation: Widening of the prevertebral soft tissue shadow on lateral neck X-ray in a febrile, drooling infant with stridor is characteristic of a retropharyngeal abscess, which arises from suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes. This is a surgical emergency requiring airway assessment, imaging confirmation, and often incision and drainage alongside intravenous antibiotics. Delay in diagnosis risks airway obstruction or mediastinal spread of infection.
questions.question: An infant under six months develops rapidly worsening stridor, drooling, and high fever. Lateral neck X-ray shows marked widening of the prevertebral soft tissue shadow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Extensive loss of septal cartilage, as seen with progressive cocaine-induced perforation, removes the structural support for the nasal dorsum, leading to collapse and the characteristic saddle nose deformity. This is a late structural complication distinct from the acute bleeding or crusting symptoms typically seen earlier in the disease course. Reconstructive surgery is complex in this setting given the ongoing tissue fragility and need for cessation of the causative drug use.
options: Saddle nose deformity from cartilage loss
questions.question: A patient with a large nasal septal perforation from chronic cocaine use is being evaluated. What additional structural complication can result if the perforation progresses further?
Distant metastases in NPC most commonly occur to which sites?
questions.explanation: The most common distant metastatic sites for NPC are bone (most frequent, often osteolytic), lung, and liver. Brain metastases are uncommon. Unlike many head and neck cancers where locoregional disease is the primary cause of treatment failure, NPC has a relatively higher propensity for distant haematogenous spread. This influences surveillance protocols, including chest/abdominal imaging and bone scans, particularly in patients with advanced nodal disease at presentation.

Warming the mirror prevents condensation from the warm oral cavity, while nasal breathing helps the soft palate remain relaxed and away from the posterior pharyngeal wall, opening the space needed to view the nasopharynx. Failure to do either step commonly results in a fogged mirror or an obstructed view. This combination is essential for a successful indirect examination.
questions.question: For indirect nasopharyngoscopy, a small angled mirror is introduced behind the soft palate. The mirror must be warmed and the patient instructed to breathe through the nose PRIMARILY to:
options: Prevent fogging and relax the soft palate
Reduce gag reflex in the ear canal

questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space contains retropharyngeal lymph nodes lateral to the midline raphe, which divides the space into two lateral compartments. This is why retropharyngeal abscesses typically appear as unilateral or asymmetric rather than strictly midline bulges. The midline raphe serves as a partial barrier to contralateral spread. Knowledge of this anatomy guides surgical drainage lateral approach avoids injury to the midline raphe and vascular structures.
questions.question: During external surgical drainage of a deep neck abscess, the surgeon identifies a midline raphe connecting the superior constrictor to the deep cervical fascia. The space lateral to this raphe in the retropharyngeal area contains:
The preventive measure recommended for patients who have had otitis externa from swimming is:
questions.explanation: For recurrent otitis externa from swimming, 70% ethyl alcohol or 2% acetic acid non-aqueous solutions applied after swimming or bathing are recommended as preventive measures. These drops restore the acidic pH of the canal and prevent pathogen growth. Cotton bud trauma should also be avoided as it disrupts the protective epithelial barrier.
options: Ethyl alcohol or acetic acid drops after swimming
Avoiding all forms of water contact permanently afterward

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis is noted to have nasal polyps at age 8. What percentage of cystic fibrosis patients develop nasal polyps?
questions.explanation: Nasal polyps occur in 6–48% of patients with cystic fibrosis, a much higher prevalence than in the general paediatric population (0.1%). Any child under 16 presenting with nasal polyps should be investigated for cystic fibrosis with a sweat test and CFTR mutation analysis, as it can be the presenting feature of the disease.

questions.question: A patient presents with sudden hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and otalgia after a slap to the ear. Baseline audiogram and management of the ear should prioritise:
options: Just an immediate CT scan and surgery
Keep ear dry; watch for fistula signs
questions.explanation: Following traumatic TM perforation, initial management includes a baseline audiogram, keeping the ear dry, and monitoring. Vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus may indicate a labyrinthine or round window fistula requiring exploration and repair to preserve hearing. Most traumatic perforations heal spontaneously without surgical intervention.

questions.question: Acoustic trauma from a single intense noise exposure (e.g., gunshot at close range) causes immediate hearing loss. This pattern of hearing loss is:
options: Reversible within 24 hours in all cases
Conductive, from tympanic membrane rupture always
Sensorineural, typically maximal at 4 kHz, potentially permanent
Sensorineural only at low frequencies below 1 kHz
Bilateral in more than 90% of cases
questions.explanation: Acute acoustic trauma from a single intense noise exposure causes immediate sensorineural hearing loss, typically with a notch at or around 4 kHz (the resonance frequency of the outer ear canal making that region most vulnerable). The injury ranges from temporary threshold shift (TTS reversible within hours to days with cochlear rest) to permanent threshold shift (PTS) from irreversible cochlear hair cell damage, depending on the intensity and duration of the acoustic insult. Tympanic membrane perforation can also occur with very high-intensity blasts, adding a conductive component, but sensorineural loss from hair cell damage is the primary mechanism.

questions.question: A patient with nasal polyps and asthma takes ibuprofen for a headache and develops acute bronchospasm and worsening congestion. What is the underlying mechanism of this reaction?
questions.explanation: In aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, inhibition of the cyclooxygenase pathway by NSAIDs shunts arachidonic acid metabolism toward the lipoxygenase pathway, causing excessive leukotriene production that triggers bronchospasm and nasal symptoms. This is a pharmacological, non-IgE-mediated mechanism, distinguishing it from classic drug allergy. Management includes strict NSAID avoidance and consideration of leukotriene-targeted therapy.
options: Excess leukotriene production from NSAID use

questions.question: When assessing a patient with suspected conductive hearing loss, which instrument provides the MOST direct assessment of tympanic membrane mobility?
questions.explanation: Pneumatic otoscopy directly visualises tympanic membrane mobility by applying positive and negative pressure via a sealed speculum. It is the gold standard for diagnosing acute and chronic otitis media. Tympanometry provides an objective measurement of middle ear compliance but does not allow direct visualisation.

questions.question: A patient with ear cancer presents with new facial weakness. Involvement of which structure does this presenting feature indicate?
questions.explanation: Facial weakness in a patient with ear cancer indicates tumour involvement or compression of the facial nerve as it courses through the temporal bone, reflecting locally advanced or aggressive disease. This finding carries prognostic significance and influences treatment planning, often necessitating more extensive surgical and adjuvant therapy. Its presence should prompt urgent further staging investigation.
options: The external auditory canal skin only

questions.question: A negative Rinne with reduced tympanic membrane mobility in a patient with known middle ear carcinoma most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Conductive hearing loss with reduced TM mobility in a middle ear carcinoma patient is due to mass effect of the tumour on the ossicular chain and middle ear space, impeding normal sound conduction. Sensorineural hearing loss suggests cochlear or auditory nerve involvement by more advanced disease. Audiological assessment helps stage functional impairment.
options: Just a sensorineural loss from cochlear invasion
Conductive loss from middle ear mass effect

questions.explanation: Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by multiple mucocutaneous telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations. Recurrent epistaxis is the most common presenting symptom (>90% of patients). Telangiectasias are visible on the nasal mucosa, lips, tongue, fingertips, and face. Coagulation studies are characteristically normal.
questions.question: Which condition is characterized by recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasias on the nasal mucosa and lips, and autosomal dominant inheritance?
A patient sustains a temporal bone fracture and develops cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea. What does this specific finding imply about the injury?
options: A benign, self-limiting bruise with no deeper injury
A fracture with dural tear allowing CSF leakage
A simple, isolated tympanic membrane perforation only
Isolated external ear canal laceration only
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea following temporal bone fracture indicates a dural tear allowing communication between the subarachnoid space and the middle ear or external canal, carrying risk of ascending meningitis if not properly managed. This finding signifies a more significant injury than a simple tympanic membrane perforation or external laceration. Prompt recognition and appropriate management, including close monitoring for infection, are essential given the intracranial communication.

questions.question: In managing AOM in the developing world context, which factor specifically justifies empirical antibiotic therapy despite viral predominance arguments?
options: The overall high cost of laboratory services
Mixed infection and humid environment promote superinfection
questions.explanation: In the developing world, most AOM cases involve mixed bacterial-viral infections, and humid environments plus native cultural practices encourage secondary bacterial infections. This justifies empirical antibiotic therapy. Studies from Africa show a different bacteriological spectrum with S. aureus and S. pyogenes predominating.

questions.question: A zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture is typically displaced inferiorly and medially. Which clinical sign specifically indicates inferior displacement of the zygomatic arch?
options: Ecchymosis in the buccal sulcus only
Trismus from impingement on the coronoid process of the mandible
Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia from foramen injury
Step deformity at the frontozygomatic suture only
questions.explanation: Inferior and medial displacement of the zygomatic arch in a ZMC fracture causes it to impinge on the underlying coronoid process of the mandible during mouth opening, producing trismus (limited mouth opening) from mechanical obstruction rather than muscle spasm. This is one of the specific indications for surgical reduction of ZMC fractures persistent trismus from coronoid impingement does not resolve spontaneously and requires elevation/fixation of the zygomatic arch. Other features of ZMC fractures include infraorbital nerve paraesthesia, malar flattening, and periorbital swelling.

options: Erosion into the horizontal semicircular canal
questions.explanation: A positive fistula test occurs when cholesteatoma has eroded through the bony labyrinth, most commonly the horizontal semicircular canal, allowing pressure changes to directly stimulate the vestibular endorgan and produce vertigo with nystagmus. This finding indicates significant disease extent and mandates prompt surgical intervention to prevent labyrinthitis or further complications. Preoperative CT helps confirm the extent of bony erosion.
questions.question: A patient with a large cholesteatoma develops a positive fistula test, where vertigo and nystagmus occur with pneumatic otoscopy pressure. What does this indicate?

options: It replaces the need for tympanometry entirely in all cases
It assesses tympanic membrane mobility in addition to appearance
It eliminates the need for any further testing
questions.question: Pneumatic otoscopy is described as the gold standard in diagnosing otitis media. What specifically makes this technique superior to simple otoscopy?
questions.explanation: Pneumatic otoscopy combines visual assessment of the tympanic membrane with evaluation of its mobility in response to applied air pressure, providing functional information about middle ear status that static visual inspection alone cannot reliably provide. Reduced or absent mobility strongly suggests the presence of middle ear effusion. This combination of visual and functional assessment underlies its status as the clinical gold standard.

Suspected perilymph fistula is often initially managed conservatively with bed rest, head elevation, and avoidance of activities that raise intracranial or middle ear pressure such as straining or heavy lifting, since some small fistulas can seal spontaneously. Persistent or worsening symptoms despite these measures may then warrant surgical exploration and repair. Deliberately performing Valsalva manoeuvres would risk worsening rather than helping a suspected fistula.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected perilymph fistula following stapes surgery reports fluctuating hearing loss and vertigo worsened by straining. What conservative measure is typically tried before considering revision surgery?
options: Immediate revision surgery in every case regardless of severity
Vigorous physical exercise to improve circulation
Bed rest with head elevation and avoidance of straining
High-dose oral antibiotics as first-line treatment
Aggressive Valsalva manoeuvres to test the fistula

questions.question: What is the FIRST change observed on otoscopy during the stage of hyperaemia in acute suppurative otitis media?
questions.explanation: During the hyperaemia stage, otoscopy shows dilated vessels along the handle of the malleus and along the rim of the tympanic membrane. Bulging with loss of landmarks occurs later in the exudation stage. Antibiotic therapy during the hyperaemia stage can prevent progression to more advanced stages.
options: A bulging drum with visible pus
Dilated vessels along the malleus handle

questions.explanation: While bilateral nasal polyps are typical of the usual inflammatory eosinophilic process, unilateral polypoid disease should raise suspicion for alternative diagnoses such as antrochoanal polyp, inverted papilloma, or malignancy, warranting further imaging and histological confirmation before treatment. Assuming a unilateral mass is a simple inflammatory polyp without appropriate workup risks missing a significant underlying diagnosis. This cautious approach is a recurring principle across several sinonasal conditions.
questions.question: A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps is noted on examination to have unilateral, rather than the more typical bilateral, polypoid disease. Why does unilateral presentation warrant particular caution?
options: It is always a normal anatomical variant
It is always due to septal deviation
Higher suspicion for tumour or other pathology
It excludes the need for imaging

questions.question: The vasomotor imbalance theory of nasal polyp pathogenesis proposes that increased vascular permeability leads to marked oedema in the polyp pedicle. What histological feature of polyps supports this theory?
options: Dense vascular network and extensive innervation
Abundant smooth muscle cells in vessel walls
Cell-poor, poorly vascularized stroma lacking vasoconstrictor innervation
questions.explanation: The vasomotor imbalance theory is supported by the characteristic histological finding in nasal polyps of a cell-poor, oedematous, poorly vascularized stroma that lacks vasoconstrictor (adrenergic) innervation. This absence of vasomotor regulation allows prolonged effects of histamine and other mast cell products, resulting in the profound stromal oedema that characterizes polyp tissue.

The Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy require recurrent sore throat episodes that are well-documented, sufficiently frequent (7 in one year, 5/year for 2 years, or 3/year for 3 years), and severe enough to require antibiotic treatment. Documentation of antibiotic prescriptions substantiates that episodes were bacterial and clinically significant. Mere frequency without documented severity and antibiotic use may not meet the threshold for surgery.
questions.question: A 7-year-old child with recurrent tonsillitis has had 6 documented episodes in the past year. According to standard criteria, which additional feature would strengthen the recommendation for tonsillectomy?

questions.explanation: Cleft palate is a contraindication to adenoidectomy because removal of the adenoid pad disrupts the velopharygneal mechanism that compensates for palatal insufficiency, causing permanent hypernasal speech. Recent URTI is a contraindication due to haemorrhage risk from hyperaemic mucosa and anaesthetic risk. Bleeding diathesis must be corrected pre-operatively. Cleft palate is unique in that the contraindication is functional rather than haemorrhagic.
questions.question: Which adenoidectomy contraindication is unique because it relates to the risk of post-operative scarring causing tube dysfunction rather than surgical risk?

questions.explanation: The Paradise criteria specify three thresholds: 7 episodes in one year, 5 episodes per year for two consecutive years, or 3 episodes per year for three consecutive years. All episodes must be sufficiently documented and severe (temperature >38.3C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive Group A Strep test). Meeting any one threshold justifies tonsillectomy as the expected benefit exceeds surgical risk.
questions.question: In the Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy, the minimum number of documented sore throat episodes per year for three consecutive years that justifies surgery is:
Palatal involvement by maxillary sinus malignancy presents clinically as:
options: Unilateral deafness and tinnitus as the sole finding
Loose/shaking teeth, palatal bulge, trismus, or intraoral mass
questions.explanation: Downward extension of maxillary sinus malignancy through the floor of the sinus (alveolar surface of the maxilla) causes palatal involvement presenting as dental pain, loose or shaking teeth, palatal bulge (mass visible in the mouth), and trismus (restricted jaw opening from pterygoid muscle involvement). These are important clinical signs that distinguish advanced antral malignancy from sinusitis.

Prophylactic antibiotics are specifically indicated in auricular burns to prevent suppurative perichondritis, which can destroy the cartilage framework. Stenting of a burned meatus is also necessary to prevent stenosis. Management otherwise follows general burn principles but with extra attention to cartilage protection.
questions.question: In the management of burns to the auricle, prophylactic antibiotics are specifically indicated to prevent:

options: Involvement of the lateral pterygoid only
Extension to the parapharyngeal space only
Intracranial extension or involvement of cranial nerves
questions.question: In NPC staging, which of the following T4 criteria is present in a patient with cavernous sinus involvement?
questions.explanation: According to the AJCC/UICC TNM staging system for NPC, T4 disease is defined by direct extension to the intracranial compartment, cranial nerve involvement, orbit, infratemporal fossa, hypopharynx, or masticator space with pterygoid muscle invasion. Cavernous sinus involvement implies intracranial extension and cranial nerve involvement (CN III-VI), fitting the T4 classification. Stage T4 NPC carries a significantly worse prognosis and typically requires aggressive concurrent chemoradiotherapy.

Keratosis obturans is a reactive condition characterised by keratin accumulation without the prominent erythema seen in eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis, mycosis, or acute trauma. Identifying erythema helps differentiate active inflammatory from quiescent accumulative disorders. Keratosis obturans presents primarily with a keratin plug rather than inflammatory signs.
questions.question: Erythema in the EAC is LEAST consistent with which condition?
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vertigo. The Dix-Hallpike test is positive when it provokes:
questions.explanation: A positive Dix-Hallpike test for posterior canal BPPV provokes: (1) a latency period of 5-20 seconds before nystagmus onset, (2) brief rotary/upbeat geotropic nystagmus lasting 20-60 seconds (corresponding to canalith movement), (3) reversal of nystagmus on sitting up, and (4) fatigability on repeated testing. The latency, brief duration, direction-specific pattern, and fatigability are characteristic of canalith displacement distinguishing BPPV from central causes (which produce immediate, sustained, non-fatigable nystagmus). Treatment is the Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre.
options: Sustained nystagmus lasting more than 5 minutes
Immediate sustained horizontal nystagmus on head turning
Brief (20-60 second) rotary upbeat nystagmus after a latency of 5-20 seconds
Brief horizontal nystagmus maximal with eye closure

questions.question: A 6-year-old presents with mouth breathing, snoring, and hypernasality. Examination reveals a long face with prominent upper teeth, high-arched palate, and hypoplastic maxilla. Which term best describes this constellation of features?
questions.explanation: Adenoid facies (long face syndrome) results from chronic nasal obstruction due to adenoid hypertrophy, forcing the child to breathe through the mouth. Features include underdeveloped nostrils, short upper lip, prominent upper teeth, narrow upper alveolus, high-arched palate, and hypoplastic maxilla. The chronic mouth-open posture remodels facial skeletal development over years of childhood growth.

questions.question: A patient with tonsillitis develops trismus, muffled 'hot potato' voice, bulging of the superior tonsil pole with uvular deviation. The next most appropriate step is:
questions.explanation: The triad of trismus, muffled voice, and superior tonsil pole bulging with uvular deviation is diagnostic of peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). Needle aspiration or incision-and-drainage is both diagnostic and therapeutic as the first intervention, providing immediate relief of pus under pressure. IV antibiotics are adjunctive but insufficient alone for an established abscess requiring surgical drainage.

questions.question: A patient with unilateral neck swelling that is painful and progressive is MOST likely to have which type of neck lesion?
questions.explanation: Painful neck swelling indicates an inflammatory or infectious process, most commonly lymphadenopathy. Malignant neck masses are characteristically painless and progressive, making infection the most likely diagnosis here.

Simultaneous dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the outset is the hallmark of achalasia a motility disorder as opposed to mechanical obstruction (which initially causes solid dysphagia only, progressing to liquids). Absent peristalsis means neither liquids nor solids can be propelled effectively past the non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter. Oesophageal dilatation leads to nocturnal regurgitation (overflow) of retained material causing aspiration pneumonia. The simultaneous onset of solid and liquid dysphagia is the key diagnostic discriminator from malignancy.
questions.question: A patient presents with progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids simultaneously from the onset, with nocturnal regurgitation and recurrent aspiration pneumonia. The most likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: In the Weber test, the vibrating tuning fork is placed on the midline forehead or vertex of the skull. Bone conduction vibrations are transmitted equally to both cochleae, and any lateralization indicates either conductive or sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.question: The tuning fork used for hearing assessment is placed on which position for the Weber test?

options: It improves the odds of complete recovery
Steroids treat the presumed bacterial cause
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is thought to involve viral reactivation, commonly herpes simplex, with secondary inflammatory oedema compressing the facial nerve within its bony canal. Corticosteroids reduce this oedema while antivirals target possible viral aetiology, and starting therapy within 72 hours is associated with better recovery outcomes. Delayed initiation significantly reduces the benefit of treatment.
questions.question: A patient with Bell's palsy is started on prednisolone and acyclovir within 72 hours of onset. What is the primary rationale for this combination?

questions.explanation: Renal disease, particularly Alport syndrome and nephritis, is associated with sensorineural hearing loss due to shared basement membrane pathology in the cochlea and glomeruli. This systemic association is critical in ENT history.
questions.question: During ENT history taking, a patient with renal disease presents with progressive hearing loss. Which type of hearing loss is MOST associated with nephritis?

options: Acute dental abscess causing sudden onset trismus
New primary tumour of the mandible in all cases
Radiation-induced fibrosis of the masticatory muscles and temporomandibular joint
Simple muscle strain from chewing hard food
questions.question: A patient with a history of head and neck radiotherapy several years ago presents with progressive trismus. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: Late radiation fibrosis affecting the muscles of mastication and the temporomandibular joint is a recognised long-term complication of head and neck radiotherapy, causing progressive, often irreversible trismus that can significantly impair oral intake, hygiene, and quality of life. Jaw stretching exercises and physiotherapy, ideally started early or even prophylactically during treatment, can help limit severity. This differs from acute dental causes, which typically have a more sudden onset and localised findings.

questions.question: A patient requires posterior nasal packing for uncontrolled epistaxis. What is the maximum recommended duration the pack should remain in place to avoid serious infective complications?
questions.explanation: Posterior packs should generally not remain longer than 48 to 72 hours because prolonged placement increases the risk of toxic shock syndrome and sinusitis from stasis of secretions. Prophylactic antibiotics are often given while the pack is in place. If bleeding recurs after removal, alternative measures such as embolisation or surgical ligation should be considered rather than simply re-packing indefinitely.

questions.question: In ENT examination, 'ABC always first' refers to the principle of:
questions.explanation: The ABC principle (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) is fundamental in clinical medicine and must always be assessed before proceeding to detailed ENT examination. This ensures that life-threatening conditions are identified and managed first.

questions.question: A patient reports difficulty initiating a swallow with nasal regurgitation of liquids and coughing immediately at onset of swallowing. The phase of swallowing most likely affected is:
questions.explanation: Nasal regurgitation and immediate coughing at the onset of swallowing indicate pharyngeal phase dysphagia, where failure of velopharyngeal closure and laryngeal elevation allows material to enter the nasopharynx and larynx before the food bolus is safely propelled past the hypopharynx. The pharyngeal phase is the most complex and neurologically demanding phase of swallowing, coordinated by the brainstem swallowing centre. Oesophageal phase dysfunction typically causes dysphagia for solids minutes after initiating swallowing.

questions.question: Treatment of croup (LTB) with inhaled adrenaline (epinephrine) works through which mechanism?
options: Stimulating corticosteroid release from the adrenal glands
Stimulating surfactant production in the lungs
Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction reducing subglottic mucosal oedema
questions.explanation: Inhaled adrenaline (racemic or L-epinephrine) in croup acts through alpha-adrenergic receptor stimulation to cause vasoconstriction of the subglottic mucosal blood vessels, reducing oedema and mucosal swelling. This provides rapid (within 30 minutes) but transient (2–3 hours) relief. Because of rebound oedema, children treated with adrenaline must be observed for 3–4 hours. Systemic corticosteroids provide more durable anti-inflammatory benefit.

questions.question: A patient with a history of nasal trauma develops a septal haematoma. Why must this be drained urgently rather than observed?
options: It always resolves without any risk of complication
Untreated haematoma can cause septal cartilage necrosis and saddle nose deformity
It only causes temporary cosmetic swelling with no cartilage risk
It is exclusively a cosmetic concern requiring no urgent action
It poses no risk of secondary infection
questions.explanation: A septal haematoma separates the septal cartilage from its overlying perichondrium, which supplies its only blood source, so if left undrained the cartilage can undergo avascular necrosis, leading to saddle nose deformity, and the haematoma itself is also prone to secondary infection and abscess formation. Urgent incision and drainage, followed by nasal packing to prevent reaccumulation, is required to preserve septal integrity. This is considered an ENT emergency distinct from simple nasal fracture management.

Epstein-Barr virus has a well-established aetiological association with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, particularly the undifferentiated subtype seen across high-incidence populations including parts of Africa and Southeast Asia. Serological markers of EBV infection are used both in diagnosis and in monitoring treatment response. Human papillomavirus is instead more strongly linked to oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.question: A patient with nasopharyngeal carcinoma from a high-incidence region in West Africa is being counselled on aetiology. Which viral agent is most strongly implicated?

questions.explanation: The most common organism in perichondritis is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Treatment involves betadine or boric acid wet-to-dry dressings to open wounds. If perichondritis progresses to chondritis with abscess formation, incision, drainage, and debridement of non-viable cartilage is necessary.
questions.question: Perichondritis of the auricle following trauma requires treatment primarily targeting which organism?

options: Unidirectional horizontal nystagmus that fatigues with repeated testing
Rotary nystagmus with a clear fast and slow phase
Nystagmus only present with eyes closed (Frenzel lenses required)
Direction-changing (gaze-evoked) or purely vertical nystagmus that does not fatigue
Nystagmus beating toward the lesion side
questions.question: Central causes of vertigo are distinguished from peripheral causes by which pattern of nystagmus?
questions.explanation: Central vestibular lesions (brainstem/cerebellum) produce nystagmus patterns not consistent with peripheral disease: direction-changing nystagmus (gaze-evoked nystagmus that changes direction with gaze direction), purely vertical nystagmus (upbeat or downbeat never seen in peripheral lesions), non-fatigable nystagmus, or nystagmus without associated hearing loss or tinnitus. Peripheral vertigo (BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Mnire's) produces unidirectional horizontal or horizontal-torsional nystagmus that fatigues with repetition and is associated with auditory symptoms. These patterns guide urgent MRI ordering.

questions.question: A rugby player sustains a facial blow and develops flattening of the midface, mobility of the maxilla with the nasal bones, but a stable zygoma. This corresponds to which fracture pattern?
questions.explanation: LeFort II fractures produce a pyramidal separation involving the maxilla and nasal bones while the zygomatic arches remain attached to the skull base, distinguishing it from LeFort III craniofacial disjunction. LeFort I involves only the tooth-bearing maxillary segment. Correct classification guides the surgical approach to fixation.

questions.question: The Woodruff plexus is responsible for approximately what percentage of nosebleeds and is located at which anatomical site?
questions.explanation: The Woodruff plexus accounts for approximately 5–10% of epistaxis cases and is located over the posterior end of the middle turbinate (and inferior turbinate). It is composed primarily of venous anastomoses of branches of the internal maxillary artery (posterior nasal, sphenopalatine, and ascending pharyngeal arteries). Posterior epistaxis is generally more severe, more common in the elderly, and less amenable to simple first aid.
options: 5–10%, over the posterior end of the middle turbinate
20%, on the floor of the nasal well-defined cavity

questions.explanation: The higher incidence of sinonasal malignancies in Africa and Asia is partly attributed to higher prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma and sinonasal lymphomas) and Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, combined with occupational exposure to wood dust, leather industry chemicals, and other carcinogens more prevalent in these regions' industrial settings.
options: Higher prevalence of EBV and HPV infections combined with industrial dust exposure
Higher smoking rates in Africa and Asia
Genetic racial susceptibility to squamous cell carcinoma
Poor access to nasal steroid sprays in developing countries at all times
Higher prevalence of chronic sinusitis in tropical climates
questions.question: Sinonasal malignancy is commoner in Africa and Asia than in America or Europe. Which of the following BEST explains this geographic variation?

questions.explanation: CT scan offers better resolution than plain X-rays and is very important in suspected OME from nasopharyngeal tumours. In developing countries, cost limits CT use, making X-rays still relevant. MRI provides additional soft tissue detail for nasopharyngeal tumour extent and intracranial involvement.
questions.question: Which imaging modality provides the BEST resolution for evaluating suspected nasopharyngeal tumour causing OME in an adult?

A patient gives a history of recurrent episodes of facial pain and pressure that worsen on bending forward, associated with purulent nasal discharge for over twelve weeks. This history supports a diagnosis of:
questions.explanation: Symptoms persisting beyond twelve weeks with facial pressure worsened by bending and purulent discharge fulfil the duration criterion for chronic rhinosinusitis. Acute bacterial sinusitis is defined by a much shorter symptom course. The postural worsening reflects sinus pressure changes typical of chronic mucosal disease.

questions.question: A young man presents with recurrent epistaxis, and examination reveals multiple small telangiectasias on his lips and oral mucosa. His father had a similar history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Recurrent epistaxis with mucocutaneous telangiectasias and a clear autosomal dominant family history is characteristic of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease). Bleeding arises from structurally fragile, dilated vessels rather than a clotting factor deficiency. Screening for visceral arteriovenous malformations, particularly pulmonary and cerebral, is important once the diagnosis is suspected.

Sinonasal tumours are staged using the UICC (International Union Against Cancer) TNM classification, also endorsed by the AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer). T describes the primary tumour (size and local extension), N describes regional lymph node involvement, and M describes distant metastasis. Proper staging guides treatment planning, determines operability, and predicts prognosis.
questions.question: The TNM classification for sinonasal tumours uses which international system?

questions.explanation: Pure tone audiometry provides frequency-specific threshold information for each ear independently, covering typically 250–8000 Hz. It is reliable from age 3 years. Unlike tuning fork tests, which give gross lateralisation information, pure tone audiometry quantifies the degree and configuration of hearing loss at each frequency.
questions.question: Which audiological test provides frequency-specific information about cochlear function at each ear independently?

questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome involves mandibulofacial dysostosis with micrognathia, malar hypoplasia, and cleft palate abnormalities. The resulting small jaw and abnormal craniofacial anatomy can cause severe upper airway obstruction from birth, requiring tracheostomy for airway protection.
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome is listed as a congenital indication for tracheostomy. This syndrome involves which primary anatomical anomalies requiring airway intervention?
options: Laryngeal web and vocal cord absence
Mandibular hypoplasia and choanal atresia causing
Warming mirrors to prevent condensation fogging
Heating the speculum for patient comfort
Providing emergency light during power outage
questions.question: An oil lamp in an ENT kit is MOST important for which specific procedural step?
questions.explanation: The oil lamp is specifically used to warm the laryngeal or postnasal mirror before use, preventing fogging from the patient's warm breath during indirect laryngoscopy or nasopharyngoscopy. A fogged mirror makes visualization impossible.

questions.question: Tracheostomy patients are nursed in a humidified environment PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: The upper airway normally warms and humidifies inspired air, a function bypassed once air enters directly through a tracheostomy tube; artificial humidification prevents thickening of secretions and mucosal crusting that could otherwise obstruct the tube. It does not directly influence wound infection, tube displacement, or bleeding risk. This is a fundamental principle of tracheostomy aftercare.
options: Reduce the risk of wound infection
Compensate for loss of natural airway humidification

questions.question: A patient's allergic symptoms are noted to have begun shortly after starting a new job involving exposure to flour dust in a bakery. This history is classified as:
questions.explanation: Symptoms with a clear temporal onset linked to a specific workplace exposure, such as flour dust in bakers, are classified as occupational in origin, a recognised and important category in allergy history-taking. This differs from seasonal patterns tied to pollen or perennial patterns tied to constant indoor allergens. Identifying an occupational trigger has implications for workplace modification or, if severe, change of occupation.

questions.question: The MOST common injury resulting in significant disability from ear syringing is:
questions.explanation: Perforation of the tympanic membrane is by far the most common injury resulting in significant disability from ear syringing, accounting for the majority of medicolegal claims. Otitis externa and pain are more common but usually less severe complications. Sharp et al. suggested a rate of major complications in 1 per 1000 ears syringed.

Patients with tracheostomy tubes cannot produce normal voice because exhaled air bypasses the vocal cords through the stoma. A bell (for alerting), pen, and paper must be available at the bedside for non-verbal communication until the patient can use a speaking valve or be decannulated.
questions.question: A tracheostomy patient cannot communicate verbally. Which specific item should be placed at the bedside for communication?

questions.explanation: Silent aspiration identified on swallowing assessment after stroke requires immediate cessation of oral intake, with an alternative feeding route such as nasogastric tube used while a full speech and language therapy assessment determines the safest longer-term feeding plan. Thin liquids are often the most likely consistency to be aspirated, so this option would be inappropriate. Many post-stroke swallowing deficits improve over time, so reassessment is important before committing to permanent feeding solutions like gastrostomy.
options: Continue normal oral diet without any restriction
Immediate permanent gastrostomy without further assessment
Encourage thin liquids only to reduce aspiration risk
Nil by mouth with alternative feeding route until formal swallowing assessment
Discharge home with no dietary advice given
questions.question: A patient recovering from a stroke has a modified barium swallow suggesting silent aspiration. What is the most appropriate immediate management step?
A patient with recurrent sinusitis is found to have low serum IgG2 and IgG3 levels on immunological workup. How does this predispose to rhinosinusitis?
questions.explanation: IgG2 and IgG3 subclasses are particularly important for opsonising encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, so deficiency impairs bacterial clearance and predisposes to recurrent sinopulmonary infections including rhinosinusitis. This differs mechanistically from ciliary dyskinesia or allergic eosinophilic disease. Identification of subclass deficiency may prompt consideration of immunoglobulin replacement therapy in severe, recurrent cases.
options: Direct fungal invasion of the mucosa

questions.question: Epiglottitis in children is characteristically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B and presents with which classic triad?
questions.explanation: Epiglottitis (supraglottitis) caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B presents acutely with high fever, severe sore throat, drooling (dysphagia causing refusal to swallow saliva), muffled 'hot potato' voice, and a characteristic forward-leaning 'tripod' posture (sitting up and leaning forward to maximise airway opening). Management: secure the airway immediately (intubation/tracheostomy) before antibiotics.
options: Barking cough, stridor, and normal temperature
Drooling, high fever, muffled voice, and a 'tripod' posture
Gradual onset stridor, normal voice, and low-grade well-defined fever
Bilateral neck swelling, inspiratory stridor, and anosmia

questions.question: The most common bacterial organism isolated in retropharyngeal abscess pus culture is:
questions.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess pus grows mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms in 91% of cultures. This polymicrobial nature dictates that antibiotic therapy should cover both aerobic and anaerobic organisms, typically a beta-lactamase resistant penicillin with metronidazole.

Adenoid hypertrophy obstructs both Eustachian tube orifices symmetrically in the midline nasopharynx, predisposing either ear with approximately equal probability. However, unilateral presentations can occur due to asymmetric adenoid growth or differential Eustachian tube anatomy. The bilateral nature of the obstruction is why adenoidectomy rather than unilateral grommets alone addresses the underlying cause of recurrent bilateral otitis media with effusion.
questions.question: A child with adenoid hypertrophy is most likely to present with otitis media with effusion in which ear?
A diabetic patient in ketoacidosis develops black necrotic nasal mucosa, facial pain, and rapidly progressive orbital signs. Which organism must urgently be excluded?
questions.explanation: Black necrotic eschar with rapid orbital and intracranial extension in an immunocompromised or ketoacidotic patient is the hallmark of rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, an angioinvasive fungal infection. It is a surgical and medical emergency requiring urgent debridement and systemic antifungal therapy. Aspergillus more typically causes a chronic, indolent fungal sinus disease rather than this fulminant necrotising picture.

options: Exudative tonsils only, with no other systemic features as the sole finding
Vesicular ulcers on tonsils and soft palate
Unilateral purulent tonsil with fever and trismus
Grey pharyngeal membrane not bleeding on removal
Epitrochlear lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytes on blood film caused by EBV
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus infection) distinguishes from streptococcal tonsillitis by systemic features: epitrochlear lymphadenopathy (a characteristic site), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, a maculopapular rash (especially after amoxicillin), and atypical lymphocytes (activated T-cells) on blood film. Monospot test (heterophile antibody) or EBV-specific serology confirms the diagnosis.
questions.question: Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is an important differential of exudative tonsillopharyngitis. Its specific features distinguishing it from streptococcal tonsillitis include:

options: Voice, Resonance, Fluency and Articulation only
Phonation, Articulation, Fluency and Resonance only
Pitch, Loudness, Quality and Fluency only
questions.explanation: Speech disorders are classified into four groups: Voice (respiration, phonation, resonance), Articulation (articulatory process), Fluency (coordination), and Language (symbolization). This comprehensive classification guides assessment and management of all speech and communication disorders.
questions.question: Speech disorders are classified into four groups. Which of the following represents the correct complete classification?

questions.explanation: Ultrasound can confirm the presence of a discrete fluid collection versus solid cellulitis without exposing the patient, often a child, to ionising radiation, making it an attractive first-line screening tool. It does not provide the bony or deep anatomical detail that CT offers for complex or deep-space infections. For this reason, CT is still often required if ultrasound findings are inconclusive or if deep extension is suspected.
options: Replaces the need for any further imaging
Provides superior bony detail compared to CT
Cannot differentiate solid from cystic masses
Avoids ionising radiation while confirming fluid collections
questions.question: Ultrasound is increasingly used in the initial assessment of neck abscesses PRIMARILY because it:

questions.explanation: Bilateral spread of ophthalmoplegia and a fixed pupil distinguish cavernous sinus thrombosis from the unilateral orbital complications of sinusitis, because the two cavernous sinuses communicate directly. This represents the most severe intracranial extension in Chandler's classification and is a neurosurgical emergency. Orbital cellulitis and abscess remain confined to one orbit without early contralateral involvement.
questions.question: A patient with acute sinusitis develops sudden proptosis, a fixed dilated pupil, and complete ophthalmoplegia of one eye, with early spread to the other eye. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options: It absorbs all available oxygen from the nasal mucosa
It blocks all nasal drainage causing acute sinusitis within 24 well-defined hours
Magnetic properties attract other metals into the nasal cavity
Electrical current and leaking alkali cause rapid tissue liquefaction necrosis within hours
questions.question: A button battery lodged in the nasal cavity is a medical EMERGENCY because:
questions.explanation: Button batteries are a rhinological emergency requiring immediate removal. They generate electrical current (electrolysis) and can leak alkaline hydroxide solution, causing rapid liquefactive necrosis of the nasal septum within 1–2 hours of contact. This can result in septal perforation, saddle-nose deformity, and extension to surrounding structures. No other nasal foreign body causes such rapid, severe tissue destruction.

questions.question: Aphonia is defined as complete loss of voice. Which combination of vocal fold positions can cause aphonia?
questions.explanation: Aphonia results from either completely abducted (open) vocal folds that cannot adduct to produce voice, or from total laryngectomy which removes the larynx entirely. Both eliminate the ability to produce phonation, resulting in complete absence of voice.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the clinical significance of a painless growth on the pinna in an elderly patient?
questions.explanation: A painless growth on the pinna in an elderly patient is suspicious for malignancy (SCC, BCC, or melanoma) and requires biopsy for histological examination. Any pinna ulcer, swelling, or growth is among the classic clinical presentations of ear cancer. Pain or painlessness does not reliably distinguish benign from malignant pinna lesions.
options: A simple haematoma of the auricle

questions.question: A 10-year-old child with moderate-severe hearing loss is being assessed for rehabilitation options. What level of hearing rehabilitation would MOST likely be required?
questions.explanation: Moderate-severe hearing loss in a school-aged child typically requires hearing aid amplification combined with appropriate educational support to optimise language development and academic performance, reserving cochlear implantation for more severe or profound losses with limited hearing aid benefit. A multidisciplinary approach involving audiology and educational specialists is important for this age group. Regular reassessment ensures the rehabilitation plan remains appropriate as the child's needs evolve.
options: No intervention is required at this severity
Complete reliance on sign language exclusively
Isolated speech therapy without any amplification
Hearing aid amplification with educational support
Cochlear implantation only, with hearing aids never considered
Stimulating alpha-adrenergic receptors causing mucosal vasoconstriction
Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis to stop bleeding
Acting on muscarinic receptors to dry secretions
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine and other topical vasoconstrictors act as alpha-adrenergic agonists, causing constriction of the superficial blood vessels of the nasal mucosa. Applied before examination or packing, they reduce active bleeding, improve visualisation, and facilitate identification of the bleeding point. They also reduce mucosal oedema, improving nasal airway. Their action is purely vasoconstrictive with no direct effect on coagulation.
questions.question: Topical vasoconstrictor nasal sprays (e.g., phenylephrine) used acutely in epistaxis management act by:

questions.explanation: A carotid body tumour, a paraganglioma arising from chemoreceptor tissue at the carotid bifurcation, classically presents as a pulsatile, compressible neck mass with an audible bruit, and displaces rather than invades the carotid vessels, producing the characteristic splaying appearance on imaging. Fine needle aspiration is generally avoided due to bleeding risk and low diagnostic yield. Surgical excision requires careful vascular control given the tumour's proximity to major vessels.
questions.question: A patient presents with a painless, slowly enlarging neck mass found on examination to be pulsatile and compressible, with a bruit on auscultation, located at the carotid bifurcation. What is the likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Maxillary sinus carcinoma can destroy any wall of the antrum depending on tumour origin and spread direction. Wall destruction identified radiologically dictates surgical resection planning, with anterior wall involvement often being detected earliest clinically.
questions.question: In the radiological assessment of maxillary sinus carcinoma, bone destruction is most commonly identified in which wall?
A 55-year-old patient presents with sensation of a lump in the throat without visible lesion on examination. This symptom is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Globus pharyngeus refers to the persistent sensation of a lump in the throat in the absence of an organic lesion. It is a common functional ENT symptom that requires careful history-taking and examination to exclude serious pathology.

questions.question: Mucociliary transport in the nasal cavity normally directs mucus toward the:
questions.explanation: The mucociliary apparatus moves mucus toward the choanae and into the nasopharynx, where it is then swallowed. Crucially, even when an accessory ostium is present, sinus mucus recirculates through the natural ostium rather than taking the shorter route through the accessory ostium, illustrating the directional nature of mucociliary flow.

questions.question: A patient on warfarin presents with severe epistaxis and an INR of 6. Beyond standard nasal packing, what additional step is required?
questions.explanation: An excessively elevated INR in the setting of significant bleeding requires correction of anticoagulation, using vitamin K or specific reversal agents as appropriate to the clinical severity, alongside mechanical haemostatic measures. Simply packing the nose without addressing the underlying coagulopathy is likely to fail. Close liaison with haematology is important to balance bleeding risk against the patient's indication for anticoagulation.
options: Immediate surgical ligation regardless of severity

questions.explanation: Opening the Thudicum speculum blades in the vertical plane avoids exerting undue pressure on the sensitive nasal septum, minimising patient discomfort and the risk of septal trauma or epistaxis. Horizontal over-opening can bruise the septal mucosa. Correct technique preserves both patient comfort and examination accuracy.
questions.question: During anterior rhinoscopy with a Thudicum speculum, the blades are opened vertically rather than horizontally. This technique is MOST important because it:
options: Avoids pressure on the nasal septum

questions.question: A patient's ciliary function is being assessed after recurrent sinus infections. Which of the following would most specifically impair ciliary beating and mucus transport?
options: Recurrent viral damage to the epithelium
questions.explanation: Recurrent viral or bacterial infection can directly damage the ciliated respiratory epithelium, reducing ciliary density and beat frequency and thereby impairing mucociliary clearance, which in turn predisposes to further infection in a self-perpetuating cycle. This is a more direct cause of ciliary dysfunction than simple structural issues like turbinate hypertrophy or septal deviation, which primarily cause obstruction rather than epithelial damage. Saline irrigation, by contrast, generally supports rather than impairs ciliary function.

options: Around 4000 Hz, producing a notch on the audiogram
questions.question: A factory worker with years of occupational noise exposure undergoes audiometry. Which frequency is characteristically affected FIRST in noise-induced hearing loss?
questions.explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss characteristically produces an audiometric notch centred around 4000 Hz before spreading to affect other frequencies with continued exposure, reflecting the particular vulnerability of cochlear regions tuned to this frequency range. Recognising this characteristic notch pattern helps distinguish noise-induced hearing loss from other causes such as presbycusis. Hearing protection in occupational settings is key to preventing this pattern of loss.

options: Killing organisms through ciliary impact force
Sweeping mucus and particles back up to
Warming inspired air by ciliary movement
Trapping only large particles above 10 micrometres
questions.explanation: Tracheal cilia beat rhythmically in the mucociliary escalator system, sweeping mucus laden with trapped particles and organisms upward from the trachea toward the pharynx for swallowing or expectoration. Tracheostomy bypasses this protective mechanism, predisposing to tracheobronchial infections.
questions.question: The cilia of the tracheal mucosa function in airway defense by:
A patient with facial trauma reports that his hearing suddenly worsened after a loud blast. He also reports ear fullness but no discharge. The most likely mechanism is:
questions.explanation: Blast injury classically disrupts the delicate ossicular chain, particularly the incudostapedial joint, producing sudden conductive hearing loss. Infection and cerumen impaction develop gradually rather than instantly after trauma. The temporal relationship to the blast is the key diagnostic clue.

questions.question: Which surgical procedure specifically addresses ossicular discontinuity to restore conductive hearing?
questions.explanation: Ossiculoplasty involves reconstruction of the ossicular chain to restore the mechanical transmission of sound. Myringoplasty repairs tympanic membrane perforations. Stapedectomy or stapedotomy is performed specifically for otosclerosis affecting the stapes footplate, while mastoidectomy removes diseased mastoid air cells.

questions.question: A patient loses smell after a head injury with a fracture through the anterior skull base. Which structure was most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: Olfactory filaments pass through the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb, and shearing of these fibres during anterior skull base fracture is a classic cause of post-traumatic anosmia. The perpendicular plate and vomer form the septum and are unrelated to olfaction. This injury also carries a risk of concurrent cerebrospinal fluid leak.

Otitis media with effusion, or 'glue ear', describes persistent middle ear fluid without signs of acute infection, commonly following resolution of acute otitis media, and is a leading cause of conductive hearing loss in children. It often resolves spontaneously over weeks to months but may require ventilation tube insertion if persistent and affecting hearing or speech development. Regular audiological follow-up is important in affected children.
questions.question: A child recovering from acute otitis media is found on follow-up to have persistent fluid behind an intact eardrum without pain or fever, and reduced hearing. What is this condition called?

questions.explanation: Second branchial cleft anomalies are by far the most common branchial anomalies, typically presenting as a cystic swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, often becoming apparent in late childhood or early adulthood after an upper respiratory infection causes enlargement. Complete surgical excision, tracing the tract if present between the internal and external carotid arteries, is the definitive treatment. Recurrence is more likely with incomplete excision of an associated tract.
questions.question: A patient with a lateral neck cystic swelling anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle is diagnosed with a branchial cleft cyst. From which branchial arch remnant does this most commonly arise?
A 3-year-old presents with unilateral foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge lasting two weeks, with no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Unilateral, foul-smelling, purulent discharge in a young child without systemic fever is highly suggestive of a retained nasal foreign body causing secondary infection, since children commonly insert small objects into the nose. Bilateral symptoms would be more typical of adenoiditis or rhinosinusitis. Anterior rhinoscopy, and if needed examination under anaesthesia, is required to identify and remove the object.

Dysphagia lusoria is caused by an aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) that arises as the last branch of the aortic arch rather than from the brachiocephalic trunk. It passes posterior to the oesophagus from left to right, compressing it posteriorly and causing intermittent dysphagia, typically for solids. It is usually identified on barium swallow (posterior indentation of the oesophagus) or CT angiography. Most cases are asymptomatic; symptomatic cases may require surgical correction.
questions.question: Dysphagia lusoria refers to oesophageal compression caused by which vascular anomaly?

questions.explanation: A positive intranasal provocation test produces watery rhinorrhoea (watery nose) or lacrimation (eye watering), confirming sensitivity to the tested allergen. This direct challenge test helps identify specific allergens causing allergic rhinitis.
questions.question: An intranasal provocation test involves placing a drop of test solution in the nose. A positive result is indicated by:

options: Granulomatous inflammation causing crusting, mucosal friability, and septal destruction
Arteriovenous malformations in the nasal septum at all times
questions.explanation: Wegener's granulomatosis (GPA) involves destructive necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of the upper respiratory tract. In the nose, this causes crusting, mucosal ulceration, friability, and progressive destruction of the nasal septum and turbinates. The resulting friable, granulomatous mucosa bleeds easily and causes recurrent epistaxis. cANCA testing confirms the diagnosis.
questions.question: Wegener's granulomatosis (GPA) causes recurrent epistaxis through which pathological mechanism?

questions.explanation: Type B (flat) tympanogram indicates immobile tympanic membrane from middle ear fluid (or mass/fixation), combined with absent acoustic reflexes (from fluid preventing ossicular movement) and conductive hearing loss this audiometric triad is classic for otitis media with effusion (glue ear/serous OM). Otosclerosis produces type As (shallow compliance, not flat) with absent reflexes and conductive loss. Mnire's produces a low-frequency SNHL pattern with a normal tympanogram (type A). In an adult with new OME, NPC must be excluded by nasopharyngoscopy.
questions.question: An audiogram showing absent acoustic reflexes, type B tympanogram (flat), and conductive hearing loss in an adult with aural fullness and fluctuating hearing suggests:
options: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) as the most likely diagnosis
Mnire's disease in the endolymphatic hydrops phase
Presbycusis with central auditory processing disorder

questions.question: A patient presents with a preauricular pit that has become recurrently infected and discharging. What is the recommended definitive management?
options: Observation since pits always resolve spontaneously
Complete surgical excision of the sinus tract
questions.explanation: Preauricular sinus tracts that become recurrently infected should be managed with complete surgical excision of the entire tract, since incomplete removal or simple drainage without excision leads to high recurrence rates. Excision is best performed after the acute infection has settled to reduce operative complications. These congenital tracts arise from incomplete fusion of the auricular hillocks during embryological development.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent sinusitis and a history of intranasal cocaine use presents with a large septal perforation and saddle nose deformity. What is the mechanism of tissue damage in this context?
options: Direct allergic reaction to cocaine causing perforation
Bacterial infection introduced solely by nasal insufflation
Vasoconstriction-induced ischaemic necrosis of the nasal mucosa and cartilage
Mechanical trauma from repeated nose blowing alone
Autoimmune vasculitis unrelated to any drug exposure
questions.explanation: Cocaine causes profound vasoconstriction of the nasal mucosal blood supply, and chronic use leads to ischaemic necrosis of the septal cartilage and overlying mucoperichondrium, resulting in progressive septal perforation and, in severe cases, saddle nose deformity from loss of structural cartilage support. This cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion can closely mimic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, requiring careful history taking and sometimes biopsy to differentiate the two conditions. Cessation of cocaine use is essential before considering any reconstructive surgery.

questions.question: A patient with suspected mastoiditis complicating otitis media requires imaging to rule this out. Which imaging view or modality is MOST useful?
questions.explanation: CT scanning of the temporal bone provides detailed assessment of the mastoid air cells, bony septae, and any associated complications such as abscess formation or intracranial extension, making it the most useful imaging modality when mastoiditis is suspected. This allows for both diagnosis and surgical planning if intervention is required. Plain X-rays lack the resolution needed to reliably assess these fine bony and soft tissue details.
options: CT scan of the temporal bone

questions.explanation: Tympanoplasty combined with myringoplasty addresses middle ear mucosa clearance, ossicular reconstruction, and TM closure in COM. Myringoplasty alone closes isolated TM perforations. Total disease eradication must be confirmed before undertaking reconstructive surgery to prevent recurrence.
questions.question: Which surgical procedure is indicated specifically for the removal of exuberant granulation tissue and restoration of the tympanic membrane in COM?

questions.explanation: Xerostomia (dry mouth) is a common complication of head and neck radiotherapy caused by damage to the parotid and other major salivary glands within the radiation field. The parotid glands are particularly susceptible, and radiation-induced hyposecretion significantly impairs quality of life.
options: Parotid and other major salivary glands
Mucous glands of the pharyngeal wall
questions.question: Xerostomia as a complication of nasopharyngeal radiotherapy results from irradiation of which structure?

questions.explanation: The Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre works by moving the misplaced calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia/otoliths) that have migrated into the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle, where they are reabsorbed. A series of sequential head and body positions guides the loose otoliths along the arc of the posterior canal and out through the common crus into the utricular macula. The success rate of a single manoeuvre is approximately 80%, making it the definitive first-line treatment for posterior canal BPPV with no medication required.
options: Directing loose otoliths from the posterior semicircular canal into the utricle through sequential head positions
Breaking up otolith aggregates by rapid head shaking
Surgically plugging the posterior semicircular canal
Increasing endolymph flow to flush debris out
Abolishing the cupulolithiasis by sustained head-down positioning
questions.question: The Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre treats posterior canal BPPV by:
A patient with deep neck space infection requires surgical drainage under general anaesthesia. The anaesthetic consideration of greatest concern before intubation is:
options: Risk of postoperative pain requiring opioids
Prolonged surgery requiring neuromuscular blocking agents
Potential airway distortion from abscess mass effect
questions.explanation: The paramount anaesthetic concern is distortion of normal airway anatomy by the abscess, which may deviate the trachea, impair mouth opening (trismus), and make visualisation of the glottis during laryngoscopy impossible. Forceful laryngoscopy risks rupturing the abscess with aspiration of pus. Strategies include awake flexible fibreoptic intubation, awake tracheostomy, or careful inhalational induction maintaining spontaneous ventilation. Rapid sequence intubation may be catastrophic if laryngoscopy fails.

questions.question: A patient undergoing sinus surgery is found to have a large ethmoid air cell pneumatizing into the orbital floor and narrowing the maxillary ostium. Intraoperative recognition of this cell is important because it predisposes to which complication if injured?
questions.explanation: This describes a Haller cell, which sits just below the orbital floor near the maxillary ostium, so aggressive instrumentation risks breaching the lamina papyracea and entering the orbit. Onodi cells, not Haller cells, are the ones that lie close to the optic nerve. Recognising Haller cells preoperatively on CT helps the surgeon plan a safer dissection trajectory.

questions.question: The laryngeal mirror is used to perform indirect laryngoscopy. It differs from the postnasal mirror primarily in:
questions.explanation: The laryngeal mirror has a larger mirror head angled at approximately 90 degrees for viewing the larynx when introduced into the oropharynx, while the postnasal mirror is smaller and differently angled for nasopharyngeal visualization.

Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, the Holman-Miller or antral sign, reflects the expansile growth pattern of JNA pushing anteriorly through the pterygopalatine fossa. This finding, together with the demographic of an adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis, is highly suggestive of JNA. Biopsy is generally avoided due to the tumour's vascularity.
questions.question: A teenage boy presents with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and nasal obstruction. CT shows anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall. What does this finding, known as the Holman-Miller sign, indicate?
A patient with confirmed malignant otitis externa requires systemic antibiotic therapy. Which class of antibiotics is MOST appropriately included in this regimen?
questions.explanation: Since Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the predominant causative organism in malignant otitis externa, systemic antibiotics with reliable anti-pseudomonal activity, such as fluoroquinolones, are a key component of prolonged treatment for this life-threatening infection. Treatment duration is typically extended over weeks to months guided by clinical and imaging response. Multidisciplinary input, including endocrinology for glycaemic control, is often required.

options: OME has been present for over 1 year
Allergy is identified as a contributing factor
questions.explanation: Anti-allergic drugs are indicated in OME when allergy is identified as a contributing aetiological factor. Allergy causes Eustachian tube mucosal oedema and contributes to fluid accumulation. Control of allergy reduces recurrence. Antibiotics are used for concurrent bacterial infections, not routinely for allergic OME.
questions.question: Anti-histamine therapy in the management of OME is indicated specifically when:

questions.explanation: Neck flexion in patients with upper airway obstruction from deep neck infections reduces the airway lumen, worsening respiratory distress. These patients instinctively maintain neck extension to maximize the already compromised airway space, making forced flexion potentially dangerous.
questions.question: Children with deep neck abscess prefer to sit upright and refuse to flex their neck. Flexing the neck in these patients MOST likely causes:

questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT scan is the gold standard for evaluating deep neck space infections because it provides rapid, detailed anatomical imaging that distinguishes cellulitis (diffuse enhancement without central lucency) from abscess (rim-enhancing fluid collection). It also defines the extent of spread into adjacent spaces and guides surgical planning. Although MRI offers superior soft tissue resolution, it is slower and less practical in the acute setting.
questions.question: Which imaging modality provides the best differentiation between cellulitis and abscess in deep neck space infections?

questions.explanation: Adenoid tissue produces immunoglobulin A (IgA) locally at mucosal surfaces, forming a critical first-line immune defence at the nasopharyngeal portal of entry. IgG and IgM are produced systemically rather than locally. This secretory IgA function explains why adenoids represent an important immunological sentinel against respiratory pathogens, particularly in early childhood.
