questions.explanation: Cerumen has been shown to reduce the viability of H. influenzae, S. aureus, and variants of E. coli by up to 99%. The antimicrobial properties arise from fatty acids and the low pH (around 6.1) of cerumen. Two common fungi (candida) present in the EAC are also significantly inhibited by human cerumen.
questions.question: Cerumen has been shown to have bactericidal properties MOST effective against which organisms?

options: At night during sleep when ciliary function decreases at all times
After meals due to blood flow diversion
During dry weather and upper respiratory tract infections when mucosa dries
During exercise when intravascular pressure rises
In humid weather due to mucosal oedema
questions.explanation: In children, epistaxis is most common during the winter months and during upper respiratory tract infections, when the nasal mucosa of Little's area becomes dry, inflamed, and fragile due to low humidity, mouth breathing, and rhinorrhoea. Digital manipulation (nose-picking) then easily ruptures the superficial vessels of Kiesselbach's plexus. These are the most common predisposing factors in paediatric anterior epistaxis.
questions.question: Epistaxis in children under 10 years most commonly occurs at which time due to the nasal mucosa being most vulnerable?
Which investigation is MOST important in the initial workup of malignant otitis externa?
questions.explanation: CT of the temporal bones in malignant otitis externa shows mastoid clouding and bony destruction, establishing the diagnosis and extent. Technetium-99m scan shows an acute infective focus. MRI is used to monitor cerebral and vascular involvement in advanced cases.

options: Plain chest X-ray alone is sufficient for diagnosis
Barium swallow using standard barium contrast
Pulmonary function testing as the first investigation
Contrast swallow study or CT with water-soluble contrast
questions.explanation: Suspected oesophageal perforation requires prompt imaging with a water-soluble contrast swallow study or CT, since barium is avoided due to the risk of mediastinitis if it leaks into surrounding tissues through the perforation. Surgical emphysema and fever in this context indicate a surgical emergency requiring urgent multidisciplinary management, often involving thoracic or upper GI surgery alongside ENT. Delay in diagnosis significantly increases morbidity and mortality from mediastinal contamination.
questions.question: A patient with suspected oesophageal perforation after foreign body removal develops chest pain, surgical emphysema, and fever. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?

options: Eustachian tube dysfunction from nasopharyngeal extension of tumour
Allergic reaction to tumour products at all times
questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion (OME) in a patient with maxillary antral carcinoma results from the tumour extending posteriorly into the nasopharynx and obstructing the eustachian tube orifice on the affected side. Eustachian tube dysfunction causes negative middle ear pressure and serous effusion. This is a recognised presenting sign of advanced posterior maxillary/sinonasal tumours and of primary nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.question: A squamous cell carcinoma of the right maxillary antrum presented with loose teeth and right-sided OME. The OME is caused by:

questions.explanation: Prenatal rubella infection is a classic cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss through cochlear damage during fetal development. It is part of the TORCH group of congenital infections affecting hearing. Rubella vaccination programmes have dramatically reduced this cause of childhood deafness globally.
questions.question: The MOST common cause of sensorineural hearing loss in a child exposed to rubella in utero is:
A patient with cystic fibrosis undergoes nasal mucosal biopsy for a research study assessing mucus transport. Which finding would most directly explain her tendency toward chronic sinus disease?
questions.explanation: In cystic fibrosis, defective chloride channel function leads to dehydrated, viscous periciliary fluid that impairs normal mucociliary transport even though the cilia themselves are structurally normal and motile. This differs from primary ciliary dyskinesia, where the cilia are structurally abnormal or immotile. The resulting stasis of thick secretions predisposes to chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyposis.
options: Thick, dehydrated periciliary mucus impairing clearance

questions.question: Otitis media with effusion (OME, 'glue ear') following AOM is defined as:
questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion (OME) is defined as an asymptomatic middle ear effusion (fluid) with an intact but immobile tympanic membrane, often following AOM. It may also arise without an antecedent AOM history. Unlike AOM, there is no acute pain, fever, or perforation. OME causes conductive hearing loss and is the most common cause of hearing impairment in children. Most cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months.
options: Asymptomatic middle ear effusion, often following AOM, with immobile tympanic membrane
Acute purulent middle ear infection requiring antibiotics
Chronic perforation of the tympanic membrane with discharge at all times
Eustachian tube polyp causing persistent blockage
Vestibular dysfunction from chronic middle ear disease

questions.question: In a patient with a deep neck space infection, gentle lateral displacement of the larynx and trachea produces pain and a grating sensation rather than the normal free lateral excursion. This abnormal finding MOST suggests:
questions.explanation: Loss of the normal free lateral mobility of the larynx and trachea, with associated pain or crepitus on gentle displacement, suggests inflammatory infiltration of the perivisceral tissues surrounding the airway and oesophagus. This finding is not expected with more superficial or localised infections such as tonsillitis or simple pharyngitis. Its presence should heighten concern for deeper space involvement requiring further imaging.
options: Infection tracking around the visceral (perivisceral) space

questions.explanation: Unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus and an absent stapedial reflex should raise suspicion for vestibular schwannoma, and a cerebellopontine angle mass on MRI confirms this diagnosis. These tumours arise from Schwann cells of the vestibular portion of the eighth nerve and can compress adjacent structures as they enlarge. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the gold standard for detection.
questions.question: A patient with unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus is found to have absent stapedial reflex and a cerebellopontine angle mass on MRI. What is the likely diagnosis?
Temporal bone fracture associated with CSF otorrhea implies which injury?
questions.explanation: CSF otorrhea following temporal bone trauma implies a basilar skull fracture with breaching of the dural covering. It is classified as a danger sign alongside vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus. These signs may also indicate oval or round window fistula or labyrinthine concussion requiring urgent evaluation.

In allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS), surgery (FESS) removes obstructing polyps, evacuates eosinophilic mucin, and opens the sinuses, thereby allowing subsequent topical and systemic antifungal medications to reach the sinus mucosa and reduce the antigenic fungal load. Surgery alone has high recurrence, while antifungals alone cannot penetrate obstructed sinuses effectively — hence the combined approach is required.
options: Surgery alone is curative, but antimycotics prevent postoperative infection
Both treatments target bacterial superinfection rather than fungi
Antimycotics are given first to shrink polyps before surgery
Surgery corrects the underlying immune deficiency
questions.question: Allergic fungal sinusitis is treated surgically, followed by topical and systemic antimycotics. What is the rationale for the combined surgical and medical approach?

questions.explanation: MRI with gadolinium contrast is the gold standard for identifying small acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) in the internal auditory canal. CT may show flaring of the IAC only in large tumours. Characteristic audiometric findings include abnormal acoustic reflex, poor discrimination, and abnormal ABR.
questions.question: Which imaging modality is considered the gold standard for evaluating small acoustic tumours of the internal auditory canal?
A patient with recurrent epistaxis is noted to have hypertension poorly controlled on current medication. What is the relationship between hypertension and epistaxis in this context?
questions.explanation: While hypertension is not typically the primary initiating cause of epistaxis, elevated blood pressure can make bleeding more severe, more difficult to control, and more likely to recur once a vascular source is disrupted, so blood pressure control is an important adjunct to local haemostatic measures in these patients. Abruptly stopping antihypertensive medication is not appropriate and can create additional cardiovascular risk. Identifying and treating the local nasal source of bleeding remains essential regardless of blood pressure status.
options: It is always the sole cause of epistaxis
Blood pressure has no influence on bleeding
It may worsen bleeding severity rather than solely cause it

questions.explanation: A glomus tympanicum tumour, a paraganglioma arising from glomus bodies along the tympanic plexus, characteristically presents as a red-blue retrotympanic mass with pulsatile tinnitus synchronous with the heartbeat, distinguishing it from other causes of a middle ear mass. Positive Brown's sign, where the mass blanches with positive pressure on pneumatic otoscopy, supports the diagnosis. Imaging with CT and sometimes MRI or angiography helps define tumour extent before surgical planning.
questions.question: A patient with a unilateral pulsatile tinnitus and a red-blue mass visible behind the tympanic membrane is being evaluated. What vascular lesion should be suspected?

questions.explanation: Bulbar palsy involves cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal), which collectively control swallowing, laryngeal, and pharyngeal function. Lesions of these nerves impair the swallowing mechanism, causing aspiration requiring airway protection via tracheostomy.
questions.question: Bulbar palsy producing dysphagia and aspiration is listed under tracheobronchial toileting indications. The nerve groups involved in bulbar palsy are:
options: Cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII (lower cranial
Cranial nerves III, IV, VI (eye movement nerves)
Cranial nerves I, II, III (olfactory, optic, oculomotor)
Peripheral motor nerves of the arm

questions.question: In the management of Bell's palsy, combination therapy with corticosteroids and antivirals (e.g., prednisolone plus acyclovir) given within 72 hours achieves which outcome?
options: No benefit over steroids alone in any study
Significantly higher rate of complete facial recovery compared to steroids alone
Equivalent outcome to untreated Bell's palsy
Prevention of ipsilateral eye blindness as primary benefit
Reduction in time to complete recovery from 3 months to 1 week
questions.explanation: Multiple randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews demonstrate that combination therapy with corticosteroids plus antivirals (acyclovir or valacyclovir) initiated within 72 hours of Bell's palsy onset achieves significantly higher rates of complete facial recovery (House-Brackmann Grade I) compared to corticosteroids alone. The Scottish and Sullivan trials showed combined therapy outcomes of approximately 83% complete recovery versus 79% with steroids alone. While the difference is modest, it is statistically significant and supports the combined regimen, particularly in complete or severe palsy, given the minimal risk of antivirals.

options: Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas spp., and Gram-negative rods (E. coli)
Group B Streptococcus and Candida albicans at all times
questions.question: Acute Otitis Media (AOM) in neonates is most commonly caused by which organisms, differing from older children?
questions.explanation: In neonates, AOM is caused by organisms reflecting the birth canal and neonatal intensive care unit flora: Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas spp., Escherichia coli, and other Gram-negative rods. This differs sharply from older children and adults, where Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis predominate. Neonatal AOM requires parenteral antibiotics (cefuroxime plus amikacin) rather than oral amoxicillin.

options: The patient cannot eat or drink
The risk of aspiration if the patient vomits
The radiological difficulty in locating it
The risk of oesophageal perforation and mediastinitis
The need for general anaesthesia for removal
questions.question: In a patient with an impacted sharp foreign body in the oesophagus, the PRIMARY risk that makes it an emergency is:
questions.explanation: Impacted sharp foreign bodies in the oesophagus carry a high risk of perforating the oesophageal wall, potentially causing mediastinitis, which is a life-threatening complication with high mortality. Disc batteries carry the same risk due to their electrochemical tissue damage mechanism.

The glottic radiotherapy field is designed to encompass both true vocal cords and the anterior commissure, which are the sites at highest risk of malignant involvement in glottic carcinoma. The bilateral opposing field arrangement ensures homogeneous dose delivery to both cords.
questions.question: In glottic radiotherapy, the treatment field extends from the thyroid notch to the cricoid cartilage. This field includes which bilateral structures?
options: Both true vocal cords and anterior commissure

questions.question: After wearing the head mirror on the forehead, the FIRST action to confirm proper setup is to:
options: Reflect the light onto your own palm
Ask the patient to open their mouth
Focus the beam directly on the patient's ear
questions.explanation: After positioning the head mirror, the examiner reflects light onto their own palm to confirm the mirror is properly positioned, the light source is correctly placed, and the reflected beam is focused. This test run prevents a failed examination.

New dysphagia developing 2 years after completing chemoradiation for nasopharyngeal carcinoma must first exclude local NPC recurrence or a radiation-induced second primary tumour in the hypopharynx or oesophagus before attributing dysphagia to late radiation-induced benign fibrosis. This requires nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy of any suspicious lesions, and CT/MRI of the neck and chest. Only after malignancy is excluded should radiation fibrosis, trismus, or other benign late sequelae be presumed as the cause of the new dysphagia.
questions.question: A patient with nasopharyngeal cancer who completes chemoradiation develops dysphagia 2 years later. The specific complication to first exclude is:
options: Local recurrence or second primary in the hypopharynx
Radiation-induced oesophageal stenosis at the thoracic level
Dental abscess from osteoradionecrosis causing trismus

questions.explanation: Pierre Robin sequence involves micrognathia (small jaw), glossoptosis (posterior displacement of the tongue), and often cleft palate. The recessed mandible displaces the tongue base posteriorly, obstructing the airway. Severe cases may require tracheostomy when other positioning interventions fail.
questions.question: Pierre Robin sequence is listed as a congenital indication for tracheostomy. The PRIMARY airway problem in this condition is:

questions.explanation: Presbycusis produces a characteristic high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss audiogram, beginning at 4-8 kHz (corresponding to the basal turn of the cochlea, where the highest-frequency hair cells are located) and progressing over years to affect speech frequencies (1-4 kHz). This pattern reflects the progressive apical-to-basal pattern of cochlear degeneration from cumulative lifetime noise exposure, metabolic changes, and strial atrophy. When speech frequencies (2-4 kHz) are affected, the patient notices difficulty understanding speech, particularly in background noise the classic functional complaint of presbycusis.
options: Ultra-high frequencies above 12 kHz only, never speech range
Low frequencies (250-500 Hz) selectively in early stages
Mid frequencies (1-2 kHz) corresponding to speech
High frequencies (4-8 kHz) with progressive extension to speech frequencies
questions.question: Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss) most characteristically affects which frequencies first?

questions.explanation: Cochlear implantation is indicated for profound sensorineural deafness where hearing aids provide insufficient benefit. The device bypasses damaged hair cells and directly stimulates the auditory nerve. Careful patient selection including pre-lingual versus post-lingual deafness affects rehabilitation outcomes.
questions.question: Cochlear implantation is MOST appropriately indicated in which category of hearing loss?
Which approach combines external and endoscopic techniques for resection of JNA with significant infratemporal fossa extension but no intracranial involvement?
questions.explanation: For JNA with significant infratemporal fossa extension (Stage IIB-III) without intracranial involvement, the endoscopic-assisted mid-facial degloving approach combines the wide exposure of the mid-facial degloving (sublabial incision with elevation of facial soft tissues) with endoscopic visualisation of the skull base components. This approach provides adequate access to the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae while minimising facial scarring. Purely endoscopic resection may be insufficient for large infratemporal extension, and a combined approach optimises tumour removal.

questions.question: The reaction between allergen and reagenic antibody on tissue cells leads to release of histamine. Histamine causes changes in which specific tissue layer?
questions.explanation: Histamine and histamine-like substances released from the allergen-IgE reaction cause changes in the non-epithelial or ground substances of affected tissues. These ground substance changes manifest as the classic allergic symptoms of oedema, mucus secretion, and inflammation.

Nasal fractures are the most common facial fractures, accounting for approximately 50% of all facial bone fractures. They are caused by direct nasal trauma (sports, assault, road traffic accidents) and present with periorbital ecchymosis, nasal congestion, epistaxis, and external nasal deformity. Diagnosis is primarily clinical; radiographic evaluation with plain X-rays or CT confirms the fracture and guides surgical planning. Reduction is performed within 2-3 weeks, before consolidation of the fracture, either closed (manipulation under anaesthesia) or open.
questions.question: The most common facial fracture overall is:
A patient with a level VI neck node metastasis from papillary thyroid carcinoma is being planned for surgery. Which structures are most at risk during dissection of this nodal level?
questions.explanation: Level VI, the central compartment of the neck, contains the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands in close proximity to thyroid and paratracheal lymph nodes, making these structures particularly vulnerable during central compartment neck dissection for thyroid malignancy. Careful identification and preservation of these structures is essential to avoid voice change or hypoparathyroidism. Intraoperative nerve monitoring is increasingly used to reduce this risk.
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands
Spinal accessory nerve and jugular vein
Vagus nerve trunk in the carotid sheath

questions.question: Inhalation burns from steam or smoke causing upper airway obstruction are listed as traumatic indications for tracheostomy. The PRIMARY mechanism of obstruction is:
options: Aspiration of carbon particles causing bronchial obstruction
Progressive supraglottic and glottic oedema from thermal
Vocal cord scarring from direct burn
questions.explanation: Inhalation burns cause progressive supraglottic and glottic mucosal oedema from thermal injury and chemical irritants in smoke. This oedema evolves over hours, and early tracheostomy or intubation must be performed before the airway becomes critically obstructed and impossible to manage.

JNA classically derives its dominant blood supply from the internal maxillary artery, a branch of the external carotid system, which is a key diagnostic and pre-embolisation finding. Larger tumours may recruit additional supply from the ascending pharyngeal or internal carotid systems as they extend intracranially. This vascular pattern distinguishes JNA from other nasopharyngeal masses on imaging.
questions.question: On angiography, a suspected JNA characteristically shows blood supply predominantly from which artery?

questions.explanation: Exostosis of the external auditory canal is a pathology of the external ear, not the middle ear. Middle ear causes of conductive hearing loss include tympanosclerosis, haemotympanum, otitis media, cholesteatoma, ossicular discontinuity, and Eustachian tube dysfunction. Accurate localisation guides surgical planning.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a pathology of the middle ear that produces conductive hearing loss?

questions.explanation: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery provides the majority of blood supply to the palatine tonsils. Secondary contributions come from the ascending pharyngeal, descending palatine, and dorsal lingual arteries. Knowledge of this vascular anatomy is critical during tonsillectomy to anticipate the site of primary bleeding when the tonsillar pedicle is ligated.
questions.question: The blood supply to the palatine tonsils is predominantly from which artery?

questions.explanation: Undifferentiated (lymphoepithelioma) nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the most radiosensitive histological type, showing excellent response to radiotherapy. Well-differentiated squamous cell carcinomas tend to be relatively more radioresistant, making histological typing important in radiotherapy planning.
questions.question: Which histological type of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is classified as 'highly radiosensitive' and responds best to radiotherapy?

questions.explanation: Foreign bodies entering via penetrating wounds to the nose are most commonly projectile injuries — bullets, shrapnel, or blast fragments from explosions. These foreign bodies may be deeply embedded in the nasal cavity, sinuses, orbit, or skull base, requiring imaging (CT) before retrieval. Road traffic accidents may cause penetrating injuries but projectile injuries are the classic cause listed for this specific entry route.
questions.question: Nasal foreign bodies entering via penetrating wounds are MOST commonly associated with:
options: Road traffic accidents affecting facial bones

questions.question: A patient has middle ear effusion without the acute signs and symptoms typically associated with infection, such as fever or severe pain. What subtype of otitis media does this represent?
questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion is specifically characterised by the presence of middle ear fluid without the acute inflammatory signs and symptoms of infection, distinguishing it from acute suppurative otitis media. This condition is often insidious and may present primarily with hearing loss rather than pain. Management differs from acute infection, focusing on monitoring and addressing persistent effusion if it does not resolve spontaneously.
options: Chronic suppurative otitis media, active discharge
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the nasal mucosa
Sensory fibres of the trigeminal nerve
questions.explanation: The Vidian nerve carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibres responsible for glandular secretion and vasodilation in the nasal mucosa, and interrupting it reduces excessive rhinorrhoea and congestion. It is not primarily a sensory or olfactory pathway. Because of variable outcomes and risk of dry eye, this procedure has largely been superseded by medical therapy.
questions.question: Vidian neurectomy has historically been performed as a surgical treatment for severe allergic rhinitis. The rationale for this procedure relates to interruption of:

questions.explanation: On indirect laryngoscopy, the tongue base is the most anteriorly positioned structure in the view, with the vallecula, epiglottis, false cords, and vocal cords positioned progressively more posteriorly and inferiorly.
questions.question: On indirect laryngoscopy, the view shows the tongue base, vallecula, epiglottis, false cords, and vocal cords. Which structure is MOST anteriorly positioned in this view?

questions.explanation: The triad of painless cervical lymphadenopathy, epistaxis, and unilateral conductive hearing loss (from Eustachian tube obstruction causing middle ear effusion) in a middle-aged Chinese male is classic for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. In endemic populations, unilateral unexplained secretory otitis media in an adult must be investigated by nasopharyngoscopy to exclude NPC before attributing it to benign causes. The painless cervical mass may be the presenting feature in up to 50% of NPC patients.
questions.question: A 45-year-old Chinese male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, epistaxis, and unilateral conductive hearing loss. The most likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: A dose of approximately 1 mg/kg/day of oral corticosteroid is a typical adjunctive regimen sometimes used alongside antibiotics in acute otitis media to help reduce inflammation and associated symptoms in selected cases. This dosing reflects standard paediatric corticosteroid dosing principles used cautiously and for a limited duration. Steroid use is adjunctive rather than a substitute for appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
questions.question: A child with acute otitis media is prescribed a short course of oral steroid therapy alongside antibiotics. At what dose is this typically administered?

A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis is noted on nasal endoscopy to have a deviated nasal septum contributing to unilateral obstruction and recurrent sinusitis on that side. What is the most appropriate surgical option to address this specific contributing factor?
options: Total rhinectomy for the deviated septum
Radiotherapy directed at the nasal septum
Septoplasty to correct the deviation and improve airflow
questions.explanation: Septoplasty corrects a deviated nasal septum by realigning or removing the deviated cartilage and bone, improving nasal airflow and reducing the anatomical predisposition to recurrent unilateral sinusitis when the deviation is a significant contributing factor. It is often performed alongside functional endoscopic sinus surgery when both septal deviation and sinus disease coexist. Tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy address different anatomical sites and would not correct a structural septal problem.

questions.question: A patient with malignant otitis externa develops facial nerve palsy. What does this indicate about disease extent?
options: The infection is now fully resolved and self-limiting
This is an unrelated coincidental Bell's palsy
Skull base osteomyelitis has extended to involve the stylomastoid foramen region
The infection has remained confined to the ear canal
This confirms a fungal rather than bacterial cause
questions.explanation: Facial nerve palsy in malignant otitis externa signals progression of skull base osteomyelitis to involve the nerve near the stylomastoid foramen, indicating more extensive disease and a worse prognosis. Other cranial nerves, including the lower cranial nerves at the jugular foramen, can become involved as infection spreads further along the skull base. This progression mandates escalation of imaging and prolonged antimicrobial therapy.

questions.question: A 2-year-old with suspected bacterial tracheitis is being distinguished from viral croup. Which causative organism is most classically implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation: Bacterial tracheitis is most classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus as a secondary bacterial infection complicating an initial viral tracheal insult, producing thick purulent secretions and membranous debris that can cause severe airway obstruction. This differs from the primary viral aetiology of uncomplicated croup, caused by agents such as parainfluenza virus. Recognition of bacterial tracheitis prompts a shift toward intravenous antibiotics and often airway intervention rather than purely supportive care.

questions.question: Pott's disease affecting the cervical spine can cause prevertebral space abscess. The causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Pott's disease (spinal tuberculosis) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the classic cause of a cold prevertebral abscess. The indolent infection destroys vertebral bodies, and pus tracking anteriorly through the prevertebral fascia creates a large, often bilateral prevertebral collection. Unlike pyogenic abscesses, tuberculous prevertebral abscesses may be painless initially and present with progressive neurological deficit from cord compression. Anti-tuberculous therapy and surgical debridement are required.

options: Direct fungal invasion of blood vessels
Type I and Type III hypersensitivity reactions
questions.question: A patient with allergic fungal rhinosinusitis has thick, dark, tenacious mucin removed at surgery. Which immunological mechanism underlies this condition?
questions.explanation: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is driven by a combined Type I (IgE-mediated) and Type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity response to environmental fungal antigens colonising the sinuses, rather than true tissue invasion by the fungus. This distinguishes it from invasive fungal sinusitis, which involves angioinvasion and tissue destruction, particularly in immunocompromised hosts. Management combines surgical removal of the allergic mucin with anti-inflammatory and sometimes antifungal therapy.

Furunculosis (localised abscess in the EAC) is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the principal cause of diffuse and malignant otitis externa. S. aureus can also rarely cause malignant otitis externa as an alternative to Pseudomonas.
questions.question: Furunculosis of the external auditory canal is MOST commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: In chronic suppurative otitis media, the most frequent organisms include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Corynebacterium species, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Common anaerobes include Peptostreptococcus spp., Prevotella melaninogenica, and Bacteroides fragilis. This bacteriological profile differs significantly from AOM.
questions.question: In chronic suppurative otitis media, the MOST frequent bacterial organisms include:
The maxillary sinus reaches adult size after which period of biphasic growth?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus undergoes biphasic growth: the first phase occurs around age 3 and the second phase between ages 7 and 18. It is present at birth and is the largest of the four paired paranasal sinuses with an adult volume of approximately 15 ml and a pyramidal shape.
options: First growth at birth and second at age 3
First at age 2 and second at age 12
First at age 5 and second between ages 10 and 15
First at birth and second at puberty
First at age 3 and second between ages 7 and 18
Direct tumour invasion of the ossicles
Tumour obstruction of the Eustachian tube orifice
Cholesteatoma formation in the middle ear
questions.question: A patient with nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with unilateral conductive hearing loss and a middle ear effusion. What is the underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: NPC frequently arises in the fossa of Rosenmuller adjacent to the Eustachian tube opening, and tumour growth obstructs the tube leading to negative middle ear pressure and effusion. Unilateral serous otitis media in an adult should always prompt nasopharyngeal examination to exclude NPC. This presentation is often an early clue before nasal symptoms develop.

questions.question: The osteomeatal complex (OMC) is a functional unit whose obstruction most directly leads to disease in the:
options: Maxillary, anterior ethmoid, and frontal sinuses
Lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal well-defined duct
questions.explanation: The osteomeatal complex is a functional drainage pathway for the maxillary, anterior ethmoid, and frontal sinuses into the middle meatus. Obstruction at this key anatomical site — from mucosal edema, polyps, or anatomical variants — leads to impaired drainage of these sinuses, creating the conditions for chronic rhinosinusitis.

Sweat glands in the EAC produce secretions with a pH between 3 and 5, which is lethal for most human pathogens. This acidic environment maintains the sterility of the canal. Ceruminous and sebaceous glands contribute to the waterproof nature of the canal lining.
questions.question: The external auditory canal (EAC) maintains its antimicrobial environment primarily because of the secretions from which glands?

options: Isolated external ear canal disease only
A completely localised, early-stage tumour confined to skin
Invasion of the inner ear or vestibular structures
No relationship to underlying disease extent
questions.question: A patient with ear cancer presents with vertigo as part of their symptom complex. What does this specific symptom suggest regarding disease extent?
questions.explanation: Vertigo as a presenting symptom in ear cancer suggests invasion of the inner ear or vestibular apparatus by the tumour, indicating more advanced local disease extending beyond the external and middle ear compartments. This symptom therefore carries important implications for staging and prognosis. Its presence should prompt detailed imaging to assess the full extent of inner ear involvement.

questions.question: A patient with suspected endolymphatic hydrops undergoes electrocochleography (ECOG). What is this test MOST useful for diagnosing?
questions.explanation: Electrocochleography measures electrical potentials generated within the cochlea and can demonstrate an abnormally elevated summating potential to action potential ratio characteristic of endolymphatic hydrops in Meniere's disease. This provides objective supportive evidence in cases where the clinical diagnosis is uncertain. It is a specialised test used alongside clinical criteria rather than as a sole diagnostic tool.

questions.question: A laceration of the external auditory canal is particularly prone to which complication?
questions.explanation: Lacerations of the external auditory canal are prone to stenosis (narrowing) from scarring during healing. Management requires careful examination, cleaning under microscope, reapproximation of skin, and covering denuded areas with split-thickness skin grafts supported by antibiotic-impregnated gauze. Stenting of a burned or traumatised meatus prevents stenosis.

In patients with true penicillin allergy, a macrolide such as erythromycin provides effective alternative coverage against Group A Streptococcus for treating exudative tonsillopharyngitis. This avoids cross-reactivity risk associated with other beta-lactam antibiotics. Treatment aims to reduce symptom duration and prevent non-suppurative complications such as acute rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.
questions.question: A child presents with sore throat, exudative tonsillitis, and is allergic to penicillin. Which antibiotic is the most appropriate alternative for treating streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis?

options: Moderate croup — nebulised adrenaline and steroids indicated
Stage I (mild) — oral dexamethasone and discharge
questions.question: Croup management includes grading the severity of obstruction. A child with marked sternal recession, tachycardia, but no cyanosis represents which grade of severity?
questions.explanation: In the clinical grading of croup severity, marked sternal/intercostal recession with tachycardia but without cyanosis represents moderate-to-severe croup requiring hospital admission, nebulised adrenaline (for immediate relief of subglottic oedema), and systemic corticosteroids (dexamethasone or prednisolone for sustained inflammation reduction). Cyanosis or depressed consciousness indicates imminent complete obstruction requiring immediate airway intervention.

options: Antibody-mediated opsonisation and clearance of encapsulated bacteria
Mast cell degranulation in allergic responses
NK cell activation against tumour well-defined cells
questions.question: IgG subclass deficiency (especially IgG2 and IgG3) predisposes to rhinosinusitis by impairing which immune function?
questions.explanation: IgG subclass deficiencies (particularly IgG2, which opsonises capsulated organisms) impair antibody-mediated opsonisation and phagocytic clearance of encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae — the most common rhinosinusitis pathogens. This creates a selective immunodeficiency manifesting as recurrent sinopulmonary infections despite normal total IgG levels. SUBTOPIC 3: NASAL POLYPS AND POLYPOSIS

Learning-disabled children show impaired language acquisition function without deficits in sensory, motor, intellectual, or emotional domains. This distinguishes them from aphasia (cortical lesion), cerebral palsy (neuromotor), and intellectual disability, requiring specialized educational intervention.
options: Developmental language disorder with learning disability
questions.question: A child with developmental language disorder has impaired language acquisition WITHOUT impairment of specific sensory, motor, intellectual, or emotional functions. This is called:

A patient with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in a level II cervical lymph node has no obvious primary tumour found on examination. Where should endoscopic biopsy focus to identify an occult primary?
options: Tonsil, base of tongue, and nasopharynx
questions.explanation: When squamous cell carcinoma presents as a neck node with an unknown primary, the most common occult sites are the tonsil, base of tongue, and nasopharynx due to their lymphoid-rich mucosa and tendency for early nodal spread before the primary becomes clinically apparent. Panendoscopy with directed biopsies, including ipsilateral tonsillectomy, is standard in the work-up. PET-CT and HPV/EBV testing on the node further help localise the likely primary site.

The pterygopalatine fossa is a pyramidal fat-filled space between the maxillary sinus anteriorly and the pterygoid plates posteriorly, serving as a crossroads for neurovascular structures. JNA extension into this fossa represents lateral spread from the sphenopalatine foramen (the tumour's origin) and is present in most cases. It increases surgical complexity because the fossa contains the internal maxillary artery and its branches, the maxillary nerve, and communicates with multiple spaces. This is why pterygopalatine fossa involvement is a specific staging criterion.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa is an important surgical landmark in JNA because extension into this space:
options: Represents lateral spread and increases surgical complexity
Confirms the benign nature of the tumour
Makes the tumour amenable to radiation alone

questions.explanation: NPC characteristically spreads through the foramen lacerum into the cavernous sinus, affecting the trigeminal nerve, causing facial numbness, and the abducens nerve, causing diplopia from lateral rectus weakness, reflecting the tumour's propensity for skull base and perineural invasion. Recognition of these cranial neuropathies is important for staging, as they indicate more advanced, locally invasive disease. MRI is superior to CT for delineating this pattern of skull base and intracranial extension.
questions.question: A patient with NPC develops diplopia and facial numbness. Which cranial nerves are most likely affected by skull base extension of the tumour?
options: Cranial nerves V and VI via cavernous sinus spread
Cranial nerves I and II exclusively
Cranial nerves VII and VIII exclusively
Cranial nerves IX and X exclusively
Preseptal cellulitis only, an early mild stage
Simple orbital cellulitis without abscess formation
Subperiosteal abscess without any visual changes
Stage one disease requiring no urgent intervention
Orbital abscess or later stage with optic nerve compromise
questions.question: A patient with a suspected orbital complication of sinusitis is found to have proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and reduced visual acuity. According to Chandler's classification, what stage does this represent?
questions.explanation: Reduced visual acuity together with proptosis and ophthalmoplegia indicates advanced orbital complications of sinusitis, corresponding to orbital abscess or beyond in Chandler's classification, and represents a vision- and potentially life-threatening emergency requiring urgent surgical drainage and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Earlier stages such as preseptal cellulitis do not typically cause visual disturbance or significant ophthalmoplegia. Prompt recognition of progression through these stages is critical to prevent permanent visual loss or intracranial spread.

questions.question: A patient with liver failure is referred for ENT evaluation. Which symptom in this patient is DIRECTLY attributable to the systemic disease?
questions.explanation: Liver failure leads to coagulopathy due to impaired synthesis of clotting factors, resulting in bleeding tendencies including epistaxis. This systemic clue during review of systems is a vital ENT clerkship finding.

The minimum masking level (MML) is an audiometric tinnitus quantification tool defined as the lowest intensity level of a narrowband or broadband noise stimulus that completely suppresses (masks) the patient's tinnitus. It is expressed in dB sensation level (above hearing threshold) and is used clinically to predict response to masking therapy and to monitor treatment effects. The MML is typically only a few decibels above the audiometric threshold at the tinnitus frequency a characteristic feature that distinguishes tinnitus from external sounds and informs the paradox of how a quiet sound can be so distressing.
options: The tinnitus pitch match frequency in hertz
The threshold difference between the tinnitus ear and the normal ear
The lowest speech recognition score in the tinnitus ear
The decibel level of the tinnitus as reported subjectively
The lowest level of a narrowband noise that completely masks the tinnitus
questions.question: The minimum masking level (MML) is an audiometric measure used to quantify tinnitus. It is defined as:

questions.explanation: The ribbed end of the Jobson-Horne probe is designed to carry cotton wool for cleaning and mopping the external auditory meatus. The other looped end is used for removing foreign bodies or wax from the ear canal.
questions.question: A Jobson-Horne probe has two distinct ends. The ribbed end is used for:
options: Carrying cotton wool for ear cleaning
Removing foreign bodies from the ear

questions.question: Hormonal rhinitis is most commonly encountered in which clinical setting?
questions.explanation: Hormonal rhinitis is associated with conditions of hormonal imbalance. Rhinitis of pregnancy (gestational rhinitis) is very common, resulting from oestrogen-mediated vascular changes and mucosal hyperaemia. Hypothyroidism causes nasal mucosal oedema. Acromegaly (growth hormone excess) can also cause nasal changes. These are distinct from allergic rhinitis.

Moderate-severe hearing loss is defined as 56–70 dB and may cause difficulty with speech and decreased speech intelligibility. Patients at this level do not hear most conversational speech. This grade requires more powerful hearing aids or consideration of surgical rehabilitation compared to mild or moderate losses.
questions.question: Moderate-severe hearing loss is defined as a pure-tone average in which range?

questions.explanation: Ear cancer cause is unknown but is associated with chronic ear infection. Unlike skin cancers elsewhere, UV radiation is not the primary aetiological factor for middle ear cancer. External ear cancer (pinna and canal) may have some UV component for sun-exposed areas. Chronic inflammation is the strongest documented association.
questions.question: The aetiology of ear cancer is unknown but is MOST closely associated with:

questions.explanation: Palpating first from in front and then from behind ensures systematic coverage of all cervical lymph node groups including submandibular, anterior cervical, posterior cervical, and supraclavicular regions, preventing missed pathology.
questions.question: On neck examination, systematically palpating from the front and THEN from behind the patient is recommended PRIMARILY to:
options: Ensure all nodal groups are systematically
Allow simultaneous comparison of both sides
Partial impairment of voice quality with some phonation preserved
Total absence of any vocal sound
A disorder exclusively of language comprehension
questions.question: Dysphonia, in contrast to complete aphonia, is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Dysphonia refers to any degree of altered or impaired voice quality, pitch, or loudness while phonation is still at least partially present, distinguishing it from aphonia, where voice is completely absent. It is a broad descriptive term that can result from structural, neurological, or functional causes. This distinction is important because dysphonia represents a spectrum of severity rather than an all-or-nothing voice loss.

options: Correct a coexisting septal deviation obstructing airflow
questions.explanation: Submucous resection addresses a structurally deviated septum that is contributing to nasal obstruction alongside the allergic mucosal swelling, improving overall airflow. It has no direct effect on the underlying allergic immune process. It is therefore considered an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, medical management of the allergy itself.
questions.question: Submucous resection (SMR) of the nasal septum is sometimes performed in a patient with allergic rhinitis. Its role in this context is PRIMARILY to:

In radiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, optic nerve complications are prevented by using the shrinking field technique. The reported rate of optic nerve and hypothalamic complications is approximately:
questions.explanation: With the shrinking field technique and careful treatment planning to protect the optic nerves, hypothalamus, and pituitary, the reported complication rate for optic nerve and hypothalamic injury in nasopharyngeal carcinoma radiotherapy is approximately 5%. This emphasizes the importance of critical structure shielding.

options: Extension into the intracranial compartment extradurally
Involvement of the nasal cavity and nasopharynx only
questions.explanation: The Fisch staging system classifies JNA by extent of spread: Stage I (nasal cavity, nasopharynx), Stage II (pterygoid region, maxillary sinus, sphenoid sinus), Stage III (orbital region and infratemporal fossa), Stage IIIA (without intracranial extension), Stage IIIB (with extradural intracranial extension), Stage IV (intradural intracranial extension). Stages I-II are amenable to endoscopic resection; stage IIIB-IV may require open craniofacial approaches. Extradural intracranial extension (Stage IIIB) represents significant surgical risk but remains potentially curable.
questions.question: Using the Fisch classification of JNA, a tumour in stage III is defined as:

options: Haemophilus influenzae type B in neonates
Staphylococcus aureus in toxic-appearing young children
questions.question: Bacterial tracheitis is caused by which organism and characteristically presents in which age group?
questions.explanation: Bacterial tracheitis (bacterial croup or membranous laryngotracheobronchitis) is predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and characteristically affects young children under 2 years (older than typical viral croup). It presents with high fever, a toxic appearance, erythematous rash, and notably thick, purulent, adherent secretions forming pseudomembranes in the subglottis and trachea requiring intensive care airway management.

questions.question: A patient with acute frontal sinusitis develops a spiking fever, headache, and a boggy frontal scalp swelling. What complication does this describe?
questions.explanation: Pott's puffy tumour is a subperiosteal abscess of the frontal bone resulting from osteomyelitis secondary to frontal sinusitis, presenting as a tender, boggy forehead swelling with systemic signs of infection. This complication indicates direct bony spread of infection and carries risk of further intracranial extension if untreated. Combined ENT and neurosurgical management with imaging is required.

questions.question: Chest X-ray is indicated in a patient with deep neck infection PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: Chest X-ray is mandatory in deep neck infections to identify downward spread of infection to the mediastinum (mediastinitis) and aspiration pneumonia. These are life-threatening complications that significantly worsen prognosis and require aggressive management.
options: Diagnose pneumonia from aspiration of secretions
Assess for aspiration pneumonia and mediastinitis

questions.explanation: T3/T4 pyriform sinus cancers require total laryngopharyngectomy (removal of the larynx and pharynx) followed by post-operative radiotherapy for locoregional control. This combined modality approach addresses both the primary tumour and the high risk (69%) of regional lymph node metastases in this site.
questions.question: In head and neck cancer management, a patient with T3/T4 pyriform sinus cancer typically receives which treatment combination?

questions.explanation: Higher prevalence of chronic suppurative otitis media in developing regions is largely attributable to limited access to timely healthcare, delayed or inadequate treatment of acute otitis media, and higher burden of predisposing factors such as malnutrition and overcrowding. This contrasts with settings where prompt treatment of acute infections reduces progression to chronic disease. Addressing these systemic healthcare access issues is key to reducing disease burden.
questions.question: Chronic suppurative otitis media is noted to be more prevalent in developing countries. What is the PRIMARY reason for this observed pattern?
options: Widespread availability of advanced surgical care
Limited access to timely healthcare for acute infections
Lower rates of childhood respiratory infections
Complete absence of any bacterial pathogens

questions.explanation: Eustachian tube dysfunction is the most important factor in middle ear disease. Obstruction leads to negative middle ear pressure, impaired mucociliary drainage, and aspiration of pathogens from the nasopharynx. The nasopharyngeal mucosa at the pharyngeal end is part of the mucociliary system protecting the middle ear.
questions.question: The MOST important single factor in the pathophysiology of both acute and chronic middle ear disease is:

questions.explanation: Topical corticosteroids reduce polyp size primarily by suppressing the underlying eosinophilic and cytokine-driven inflammatory cascade, reducing mucosal oedema and inflammatory cell infiltration within the polyp tissue. This anti-inflammatory action differs fundamentally from the rapid vasoconstriction produced by decongestant sprays, and their benefit accrues gradually over weeks of regular use. Long-term maintenance therapy is often required to sustain reduction in polyp size and prevent regrowth.
options: Suppression of local eosinophilic inflammation and oedema
Direct antibacterial killing within the sinus
questions.question: A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis undergoes topical corticosteroid therapy as first-line medical treatment. What is the primary mechanism by which these agents reduce nasal polyp size?

questions.explanation: Occupational exposure to nickel, chromium, and other industrial dusts causes chronic mucosal irritation, inflammation, and increased fragility of the nasal mucosa, predisposing to recurrent epistaxis. These substances are both irritants (causing direct mucosal damage) and carcinogens (associated with sinonasal malignancy after long exposure). They are listed among local aetiological factors for epistaxis in otolaryngology texts.
options: These metals cause systemic haematological changes
They cause allergic sensitisation through IgE-mediated reactions
They inhibit platelet aggregation specifically in nasal capillaries at all times
They cause direct mucosal irritation, chronic inflammation, and increased vascularity
They produce carcinomatous change within 6 months
questions.question: Industrial dust exposure to nickel and chromium compounds is a recognized LOCAL cause of epistaxis primarily because:

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery (from the internal carotid system) that supplies the superior-anterior part of the nasal septum and lateral wall. The posterior ethmoidal artery also derives from the ophthalmic artery but supplies more posterior and superior structures including the olfactory area.
questions.question: Which artery, a branch of the internal carotid system, primarily supplies the superior and posterior nasal septum?
A child with recurrent acute otitis media is found to have a shorter, more horizontal Eustachian tube compared to adults. How does this anatomical difference contribute to increased infection risk?
questions.explanation: In young children, the Eustachian tube is shorter, wider, and more horizontally oriented compared with the adult tube, which becomes more oblique and longer with craniofacial growth, making it easier for nasopharyngeal secretions and pathogens to reflux into the middle ear and contributing to the higher incidence of acute otitis media in this age group. This anatomical difference resolves gradually as the child grows, correlating with declining infection rates. Adenoid hypertrophy can further compound Eustachian tube dysfunction in this population.
options: It improves middle ear ventilation compared to adults
It has no clinical significance for infection risk
It prevents pathogen entry more effectively than in adults
It allows easier reflux of nasopharyngeal secretions and pathogens into the middle ear
It is unrelated to middle ear pressure regulation

questions.question: An angled metal tongue depressor is preferred over a wooden spatula for examination of the oropharynx because it:
questions.explanation: The angled metal tongue depressor is reusable, sterilisable, and its angled design provides better access to the oropharynx and post-nasal space compared to straight wooden spatulas. It gives superior structural visualization during examination.
options: Is reusable and allows better access
Does not trigger the gag reflex
Provides tactile feedback on palatal movement

questions.explanation: Traditional posterior nasal packing uses a nasopharyngeal gauze pack secured by three strings (one protruding from each nostril anteriorly and one from the mouth for removal), often combined with an anterior nasal pack to tamponade the posterior nasal space. Modern alternatives include a Foley catheter (balloon inflated in the nasopharynx) with anterior gauze packing, or specially designed bilateral balloon epistaxis catheters (e.g., Epistat).
questions.question: Posterior nasal packing using the 'three-strings' technique involves the use of which instrument?
options: Foley catheter with balloon inflated in the nasopharynx
Gelfoam placed directly in the posterior choana
Surgicel rolls placed via an endoscope
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray first
Avoid the throat and secure the airway
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with high fever, drooling, muffled voice, and a preference for sitting upright leaning forward. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for acute epiglottitis, and any attempt to examine the throat or agitate the child can precipitate complete airway obstruction, so the child should be kept calm and taken directly to a controlled setting such as theatre for airway securing under anaesthesia. Investigations and blood tests should be deferred until the airway is safe. Haemophilus influenzae type B is the classic causative organism, though incidence has fallen with vaccination.

The postnasal (nasopharyngeal) mirror is a small angled mirror on a long handle used to view the nasopharynx indirectly by reflecting light from the throat into the postnasal space. It is distinct from the laryngeal mirror used for laryngoscopy.
questions.question: For indirect nasopharyngoscopy, which instrument is used to view the nasopharynx?

questions.explanation: Normal hearing sensitivity is the ability to detect sounds in the audio-frequency range of about 20 to 20,000 Hz. Frequencies outside this range are generally inaudible to humans. Clinical audiometry typically evaluates the speech range of 250–8,000 Hz.
questions.question: Normal hearing sensitivity covers the audio-frequency range of approximately:

questions.explanation: Caseous necrotic material combined with vertebral body destruction on imaging is characteristic of tuberculous spondylitis extending into the prevertebral space, a chronic process quite distinct from the acute purulent picture of ordinary pyogenic retropharyngeal abscess. Cystic congenital lesions such as branchial or thyroglossal cysts do not typically cause vertebral destruction. This combination of findings should prompt investigation and treatment for underlying spinal tuberculosis.
questions.question: A prevertebral abscess in a patient with known pulmonary tuberculosis is found to contain caseous material on drainage, with vertebral body destruction on imaging. This presentation is MOST consistent with:

options: Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy if suspicious lesion seen
Audiometry and watchful waiting for 3 months
questions.question: A patient presents with unilateral serous otitis media (glue ear) with no prior history of ear disease. The patient is 40 years old with southern Chinese ethnicity. The mandatory investigation is:
questions.explanation: Unilateral adult-onset secretory otitis media without prior ear disease, particularly in a patient from an NPC-endemic population or ethnicity, mandates urgent nasopharyngoscopy to exclude NPC obstructing the Eustachian tube. Any suspicious mucosal lesion in the nasopharynx must be biopsied. Proceeding to grommet insertion without exclusion of NPC risks missing a potentially curable early-stage tumour. The nasopharynx is the clinical blind spot where significant disease may be present without other symptoms.

Angiography is indicated for highly vascular sinonasal tumours (e.g., juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, haemangiomas) to map the arterial supply, identify feeding vessels, and plan pre-operative embolisation to reduce intraoperative blood loss. It is not used for staging (CT/MRI is used) or histological diagnosis (EUA and biopsy provides this). Modern CT angiography may partly replace conventional angiography in planning.
options: Identify vascular supply for pre-operative embolisation
questions.question: Angiography for sinonasal tumours is specifically indicated to:

options: Central necrosis with peripheral rim enhancement
Uniform T2 hyperintensity without flow voids
Salt-and-pepper appearance from flow voids interspersed with fibrous high signal
questions.question: On contrast-enhanced MRI, which signal pattern is considered characteristic of JNA?
questions.explanation: The 'salt-and-pepper' appearance on MRI is the characteristic finding of JNA: multiple signal voids ('pepper') from rapidly flowing blood in large tumour vessels interspersed with higher-signal fibrous stroma ('salt'). Post-contrast T1 images show intense homogeneous enhancement of the vascular component. This pattern distinguishes JNA from other nasopharyngeal masses (NPC shows more homogeneous intermediate signal, lymphoma is uniformly T2 bright) and, combined with the clinical context, makes the diagnosis with high confidence without biopsy.

questions.question: During ENT clerkship, a patient speaks with a high-pitched nasal tone. This MOST likely indicates pathology in which anatomical region?
questions.explanation: A nasal tone of voice indicates disease in the nasal cavity or nasopharynx, causing abnormal resonance. This is called rhinolalia and directly implicates nasopharyngeal pathology during the clinical clerkship assessment.

Failure to respond to appropriate antibiotic therapy with persistent bulging and severe symptoms is an indication for myringotomy, which relieves pressure, provides symptomatic relief, and allows collection of a sample for culture to guide further targeted antibiotic therapy. This is a less invasive surgical option compared to mastoidectomy, which is reserved for more extensive complications. Prompt intervention prevents progression to complications such as mastoiditis.
options: Myringotomy to relieve pressure and culture
Immediate mastoidectomy without medical therapy trial
questions.question: A patient with acute suppurative otitis media develops persistent high fever and severe pain despite 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy, with a bulging drum. What is the appropriate SURGICAL indication here?

questions.explanation: Gustatory rhinitis results from a parasympathetic reflex triggered by trigeminal nerve stimulation from capsaicin and other compounds in spicy food, leading to glandular hypersecretion and watery rhinorrhoea, distinct from a true IgE-mediated food allergy. This explains why it occurs consistently and immediately with spicy food exposure rather than showing the variable timing typical of allergic reactions. Anticholinergic nasal sprays can be used to reduce symptoms if bothersome.
questions.question: A patient develops gustatory rhinitis with profuse watery rhinorrhoea specifically triggered by eating hot spicy food. Through which pathway is this reflex mediated?
A culture swab taken from the ear canal in otitis externa should specifically include:
questions.explanation: A culture swab should be taken for microbiological culture including fungal culture and antibiotic/antimycotic sensitivity. This comprehensive approach ensures both bacterial and fungal aetiologies are identified. Culture results guide definitive topical and systemic therapy, especially in resistant or recurrent cases.

options: Repetitive tongue pumping movements causing bolus fragmentation
questions.question: A 65-year-old with Parkinson's disease develops dysphagia. The characteristic swallowing abnormality in Parkinson's disease is:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease characteristically causes a repetitive rolling or pumping motion of the tongue (festination) during the oral phase, fragmenting the bolus and producing multiple inefficient swallowing attempts before pharyngeal triggering. Reduced pharyngeal muscle velocity and delayed swallow trigger also contribute. The oral phase 'pumping' is pathognomonic of Parkinson's swallowing dysfunction and distinguishes it from other neurological dysphagia. Lee Silverman Voice Treatment and swallowing therapy can partially compensate for these deficits.

Children with Down syndrome have multiple anatomical and physiological risk factors for obstructive sleep apnoea, including midface hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, generalised hypotonia, and a higher prevalence of adenotonsillar hypertrophy, all of which narrow the upper airway. This markedly elevated risk means polysomnography is recommended even in the absence of overt symptoms in this population. Surgical outcomes from adenotonsillectomy can be less predictable than in the general paediatric population due to these anatomical factors.
questions.question: A patient with suspected obstructive sleep apnoea in a child with Down syndrome is being evaluated. Why is this population at particularly high risk for OSA?
options: Down syndrome patients never develop adenotonsillar hypertrophy
Increased airway size compared with typically developing children
Combination of midface hypoplasia, macroglossia, and hypotonia narrowing the airway
Down syndrome exclusively affects nasal septal anatomy only
Absence of any craniofacial anomalies in this population

questions.question: Transverse temporal bone fractures characteristically cause sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo because they:
questions.explanation: Transverse temporal bone fractures run perpendicular to the long axis of the petrous bone, crossing the internal auditory canal and/or bony labyrinth. This path directly transects or contuses the otic capsule (bony labyrinth), cochlea, and vestibular apparatus, causing sensorineural hearing loss (often complete and permanent) and severe vertigo with nystagmus. Facial nerve involvement is more common with transverse fractures (up to 50%) compared to longitudinal (20%), often at the labyrinthine segment. Transverse fractures are caused by frontal or occipital impacts.
options: Compress the cochlear nerve at the internal auditory meatus
Commonly involve the bony labyrinth and cochleovestibular apparatus
Tear the tympanic membrane at its annulus
Disrupt the ossicular chain at the incudostapedial joint

questions.question: Atelectasis is a post-bronchoscopy complication of foreign body removal. Its expected management includes:
options: Repeat X-ray and watchful waiting only
Antibiotics and expectant management with physiotherapy
questions.explanation: Atelectasis following foreign body bronchoscopy is typically managed expectantly with antibiotics (to prevent superinfection) and chest physiotherapy (to mobilize secretions and assist re-expansion). Most cases resolve with conservative management without requiring repeat bronchoscopy.

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles. Involvement by NPC through hypoglossal canal erosion causes ipsilateral tongue weakness, wasting (atrophy), and fasciculations, with deviation of the tongue toward the paralysed side on protrusion. Dysarthria results from impaired tongue mobility. Dysphagia for solids may follow if bilateral involvement occurs, though unilateral CN XII palsy rarely causes significant swallowing difficulty.
questions.question: Which symptom in NPC results from direct involvement of the hypoglossal nerve?
A child with chronic otitis media with effusion undergoes grommet insertion. What is the primary physiological benefit of this procedure?
options: Ventilation of the middle ear cavity
Prevention of future upper respiratory infections
questions.explanation: Grommet insertion creates a temporary artificial opening through the tympanic membrane that ventilates the middle ear and allows effusion to drain, restoring normal air pressure and improving conductive hearing loss while the tube remains patent. It does not permanently correct underlying Eustachian tube dysfunction, and effusion can recur after extrusion. Most grommets extrude spontaneously within 6 to 12 months.

questions.question: Which benign sinonasal tumour consists of compact bony tissue and is most commonly located in the frontal sinus, often as an incidental finding?
questions.explanation: An osteoma is a benign tumour consisting of mature compact or cancellous bone, most commonly found in the frontal sinus (followed by ethmoid, maxillary, and sphenoid sinuses). Small osteomas are typically asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on sinus X-rays or CT. Larger osteomas may obstruct sinus drainage causing mucocele or chronic sinusitis, or may erode into the orbit or intracranium, requiring surgical removal.

The lateral rhinotomy incision provides excellent direct exposure of the nasal cavity, ethmoid sinuses, and adjacent structures, allowing complete tumour resection under direct vision for lesions not amenable to purely endoscopic removal. It does leave a visible facial scar, which is an accepted trade-off for adequate oncological access in appropriately selected cases. Reconstruction and wound closure techniques help minimise the cosmetic impact of this incision.
options: Avoidance of any visible facial scar
Avoiding the need for general anaesthesia
Wide direct access to the nasal cavity
Preservation of smell in every case
questions.question: A patient requires a lateral rhinotomy approach for excision of an extensive nasal cavity tumour. What is the main advantage of this surgical approach?
A very large rhinolith in the nasal cavity is managed under GA by:
options: Fragmentation with forceps followed by piecemeal removal
En bloc removal intact via the anterior nares
Antral washout through the inferior meatus
questions.explanation: Large rhinoliths cannot be removed intact through the relatively narrow nasal vestibule. The standard technique is to break the rhinolith into smaller pieces using strong forceps (bone-cutting forceps) under general anaesthesia, then remove the fragments piecemeal. Very large rhinoliths that have extended into the maxillary antrum require a Caldwell-Luc approach for adequate access. Laser and acid dissolution are not standard techniques.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the common differential diagnoses of ear cancer?
questions.explanation: Glomus jugulare is a paraganglioma (vascular tumour), not a primary carcinoma, and while it affects the ear region, it is not in the same differential as carcinoma. Common carcinomas of the ear include squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, melanoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and adenocarcinoma. Any ear structure can develop into cancer.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs the paranasal sinus with its primary drainage location?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinus drains posterosuperiorly into the sphenoethmoidal recess, which lies between the superior turbinate and the nasal septum. The maxillary sinus and anterior ethmoid cells drain into the middle meatus; the posterior ethmoid cells drain into the superior meatus; and the frontal sinus drains into the middle meatus via the frontal recess.

The hallmark of glomus tumours is unilateral pulsatile tinnitus that is synchronous with the pulse rate. Progressive hearing loss and otalgia also occur. Cranial nerve involvement (VII–XII) indicates advanced disease. Physical examination reveals a bluish mass behind the tympanic membrane. Diagnosis is confirmed with arteriography or jugular venogram.
questions.question: The hallmark clinical feature of glomus tympanicum tumour is:

questions.explanation: At the C2 level, the normal prevertebral soft tissue space is narrow, and a measurement greater than approximately 7 millimetres is considered abnormally widened, raising suspicion for retropharyngeal abscess or haematoma. The C6 level has a different, larger normal threshold due to the adjacent oesophagus and larynx. This measurement is a key screening tool before proceeding to CT confirmation.
questions.question: On lateral neck X-ray in a child with suspected retropharyngeal abscess, widening of the prevertebral soft tissue space at the level of C2 is defined as a measurement exceeding:

options: Nasal capsule without a pouch as the sole finding
Lateral wall of the nasal cavity via an outgrowth
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus develops as an outgrowth (evagination) from the lateral wall of the developing nasal cavity, specifically from the region of the infundibulum. It is the first sinus to develop and is present at birth as a small cavity. The sphenoid sinus uniquely arises within the nasal capsule without a distinct pouch.
questions.question: Which embryological structure gives rise to the maxillary sinus?

options: Herpes simplex virus with cold sores on the lips as the sole finding
Adenovirus causing follicular conjunctivitis and pharyngitis
Coxsackievirus A causing vesicles or ulcers on the soft palate, tonsils, and uvula
Parainfluenza virus causing croup in adults
questions.explanation: Herpangina is caused by Coxsackievirus A (an enterovirus) and presents with vesicles and ulcers on the soft palate, anterior pillars of the fauces, tonsils, and uvula, along with high fever, sore throat, and dysphagia. It is clinically important as a differential of exudative tonsillitis. Treatment is symptomatic. It differs from HSV gingivostomatitis (which affects the anterior oral cavity and lips) in its posterior pharyngeal distribution.
questions.question: Herpangina (vesicular tonsillopharyngitis) is caused by which virus and is characterised by which distinctive finding?
Which investigation is mandatory before biopsy of a nasopharyngeal mass to rule out a highly vascular lesion?
options: CT or MRI of the nasopharynx with contrast
Biopsy can always be safely performed under local anaesthesia
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the nasopharynx must be performed before biopsy to exclude a highly vascular lesion such as juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma or paraganglioma. Biopsy of an angiofibroma without prior imaging can cause catastrophic haemorrhage. Once imaging characterises the lesion as epithelial carcinoma or lymphomatous mass rather than a vascular tumour, biopsy under appropriate conditions (with suction, cautery, and haemostatic packing available) is appropriate for histological diagnosis.

questions.question: Which surgical approach is appropriate for Stage I and Stage II JNA without intracranial extension?
questions.explanation: Advances in endoscopic skull base surgery have made endoscopic endonasal resection the standard approach for Stage I and II JNA, and even selected Stage III cases without orbital involvement. Endoscopic resection offers equivalent oncological outcomes to open approaches while avoiding facial incisions, reducing hospitalisation, and allowing earlier rehabilitation. Stage IIIB-IV tumours with intracranial extension typically require open craniofacial approaches (mid-facial degloving, Le Fort osteotomy, or combined transcranial-endoscopic).

questions.question: Tympanocentesis is indicated in all of the following clinical scenarios EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Tympanocentesis is not indicated for uncomplicated AOM in a healthy child. Specific indications include infants under 6 weeks, immunocompromised patients, failure of antimicrobial therapy, and complications. Tympanocentesis allows aspiration of middle ear contents for diagnostic microbiology to guide targeted therapy.

questions.question: An awake (urgent) tracheostomy is performed under local anaesthesia in which specific clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: Awake tracheostomy under local anaesthesia is preferred in patients with severe partial airway obstruction where induction of general anaesthesia and muscle relaxants would cause complete airway collapse before intubation can be secured. Maintaining consciousness preserves respiratory drive and airway muscle tone.

The steeple sign on anteroposterior neck X-ray shows tapering of the subglottic airway due to mucosal oedema in croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). This symmetrical narrowing contrasts with the 'thumb sign' of epiglottitis and helps distinguish these two acute paediatric airway emergencies.
questions.question: The 'steeple sign' on neck X-ray is associated with which ENT condition?

questions.explanation: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) is by far the most common precipitating event for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Viral infection causes mucosal oedema that obstructs the ostiomeatal complex, impairs mucociliary clearance, and creates a hypoxic environment within the sinuses, facilitating secondary bacterial superinfection.
options: Dental infection spreading from adjacent roots
questions.question: The most common inciting event for bacterial acute rhinosinusitis is:
Pressure equalization (PE) tubes are inserted into which part of the tympanic membrane for OME?
questions.explanation: Pressure equalisation tubes are inserted into the antero-inferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane via the myringotomy incision. This location avoids the ossicular chain and the risk of sensorineural damage. Tube insertion allows chronic ventilation of the middle ear and drainage of accumulated effusion.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis despite maximal medical therapy is being considered for functional endoscopic sinus surgery. What is the primary surgical goal of this procedure?
questions.explanation: Functional endoscopic sinus surgery aims to restore normal mucociliary clearance by widening natural sinus ostia and removing obstructive anatomical or inflammatory tissue, thereby allowing the sinuses to drain and ventilate through their physiological pathways rather than creating artificial openings or radically removing mucosa. This functional, mucosa-preserving philosophy distinguishes modern sinus surgery from older radical approaches. Postoperative medical therapy remains important to control the underlying inflammatory disease process even after successful surgery.
options: Completely strip all sinus mucosa for permanent cure
Restore normal mucociliary drainage by widening natural sinus ostia
Create entirely new artificial drainage pathways only
Remove the turbinates in every case regardless of findings
Perform total maxillectomy for chronic sinus disease
Pterygoid muscle invasion through the pterygoid fossa
questions.question: Which clinical feature of NPC is described as 'trismus' and indicates direct extension of the primary tumour?
questions.explanation: Trismus in NPC results from direct lateral extension of the tumour into the parapharyngeal space and masticator space, invading the pterygoid muscles. The medial and lateral pterygoid muscles control mandibular movement, and infiltration by tumour causes muscle spasm and fibrosis, reducing mouth opening. This finding indicates T4 disease with masticator space invasion. Radiation-induced trismus from fibrosis is also a late complication in survivors.

Despite common belief, there are no pathognomonic nasal findings for allergic rhinitis. The paroxysmal nature of allergy makes examination findings variable and often normal between attacks. Blue-hued turbinates can occur in many rhinitic conditions.
questions.question: In an allergic patient, the presence of enlarged blue-hued turbinates on examination is:

options: Simple Bell's palsy caused by herpes simplex virus
Ramsay Hunt syndrome caused by varicella-zoster virus reactivation
Malignant otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas
Acute otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae
questions.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus within the geniculate ganglion, producing the triad of facial paralysis, ear pain, and a vesicular rash affecting the pinna or external auditory canal, and generally carries a worse prognosis for facial nerve recovery than simple Bell's palsy. Treatment combines high-dose corticosteroids with antivirals, ideally started early. Associated sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo can occur due to eighth nerve involvement.
