questions.question: A patient develops sudden facial nerve palsy associated with a vesicular rash on the pinna and severe ear pain. What is the diagnosis and causative organism?
The MOST important anatomical reason cerumen does not normally accumulate deep in the external ear canal is:
questions.explanation: Epithelial migration is the primary mechanism — cells formed at the umbo of the tympanic membrane migrate outward along the canal walls, carrying cerumen and debris toward the canal entrance. This conveyor-belt process is equivalent in speed to fingernail growth. Jaw movement assists by dislodging debris attached to the walls.
options: Gravity simply pulling the wax outward
Epithelial migration from the TM outward

questions.explanation: Interleukin-5 is a key cytokine driving eosinophil differentiation, recruitment, and prolonged survival within polyp tissue, contributing to the chronic eosinophilic inflammation characteristic of many nasal polyps. This understanding has led to the development of biologic therapies targeting the IL-5 pathway for severe refractory disease. Its role is distinct from neutrophil-driven or purely IgE-mediated inflammatory pathways.
questions.question: A patient with nasal polyposis is noted to have very high tissue levels of interleukin-5. What is the primary pathophysiological role of this cytokine in polyp formation?
options: Increasing goblet cell mucus secretion only

questions.explanation: CT and MRI are complementary in sinonasal tumour assessment. CT excels at showing bony erosion, remodelling, calcification within tumours, and anatomical relationships to bony walls. MRI provides superior soft tissue characterisation, distinguishes tumour from adjacent secretions/inflammatory tissue, and best demonstrates intracranial and orbital invasion, perineural spread, and skull base involvement. Both are required for comprehensive staging.
options: Bone erosion and calcification; soft tissue extent
questions.question: The combination of MRI and CT for sinonasal tumour assessment provides complementary information: CT shows ___ while MRI shows ___.

questions.explanation: The risk for complications associated with otitis media increases if an acute episode persists longer than 2 weeks or if symptoms recur within a 2–3 week period. This threshold triggers the stage of coalescence where bony destruction begins. Close clinical monitoring during this window is essential to prevent complications.
questions.question: The risk for complications associated with otitis media increases significantly if an acute episode persists beyond:

options: CT scan of the paranasal sinuses
Plain X-ray of the paranasal sinuses at all times
Full blood count, coagulation screen, and urgent blood crossmatch
questions.explanation: In a haemodynamically compromised patient with profuse epistaxis, the immediate priorities are resuscitation (airway, breathing, circulation) with large-bore IV access and urgent blood tests: full blood count for anaemia and platelet count, coagulation screen (PT, APTT) for coagulopathy, and blood crossmatch for urgent transfusion. CT scanning and endoscopy are secondary to stabilisation. questions.question: The most important investigation to perform immediately in a patient presenting with profuse epistaxis and haemodynamic compromise is:
An allergic patient has a cat at home. The allergenic component of cat exposure is PRIMARILY:
questions.explanation: The major cat allergen (Fel d 1) is found in cat saliva, sebaceous glands, and dander (shed skin cells). It adheres to soft furnishings and becomes airborne, making cat allergy highly pervasive and persistent even after cat removal from the home.

questions.question: In radiotherapy planning, the 'target volume' is the concept of identifying the tumour plus an appropriate margin. This margin PRIMARILY accounts for:
questions.explanation: The target volume includes a margin around the gross tumour volume to account for microscopic tumour extension beyond visible margins and set-up uncertainty in daily positioning. This ensures adequate dose to all tumour cells while attempting to spare adjacent normal structures.
options: Tumour microscopic extension and set-up uncertainty
The type of radiation machine used
The histological grade of the tumour

questions.explanation: The acute epithelial reaction in otitis externa consists of vesication, parakeratosis, and spongiosis, along with dilated dermal vessels. Granulation tissue formation is a feature of chronic otitis media or necrotising otitis externa. These acute changes explain the clinical signs of a red, hot, oedematous, tender canal.
questions.question: In the acute phase of otitis externa, the epithelial reaction is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Children and young adults under 20 years
questions.explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents, with the head and neck region (including the paranasal sinuses and orbit) being the most frequent primary site. In the paranasal sinuses, it presents with rapid onset nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and local invasion in children and young adults under 20 years. Treatment involves multimodality therapy: surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.
questions.question: Rhabdomyosarcoma of the paranasal sinuses most commonly affects which age group?

options: Sudden pressure change, e.g. Valsalva or diving
A typical acute case of viral labyrinthitis
questions.question: Oval window rupture with perilymph leakage is MOST commonly associated with which precipitating event?
questions.explanation: Oval or round window rupture with perilymph fistula is most commonly associated with sudden pressure changes: Valsalva manoeuvre, sneezing, nose blowing, scuba diving, or flying. The resulting hearing loss is often sudden and fluctuating, frequently accompanied by vertigo. Initial management is bed rest, with surgery for non-resolving cases. questions.question: Which of the following is the most common organism implicated in acute rhinosinusitis in older children and adults?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial pathogen in acute rhinosinusitis in older children and adults, responsible for approximately 30–40% of cases. Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis are the next most common pathogens. In immunocompromised patients and those with cystic fibrosis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa becomes important.

options: Congenital septal defect present from birth
questions.question: A patient with septal perforation reports whistling during breathing and crusting. What is the most common cause of septal perforation in adults?
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic causes, particularly previous septal surgery, along with nasal trauma or chronic nose picking, are the most common causes of septal perforation in adults, disrupting the mucoperichondrial blood supply to the cartilage. Other causes include cocaine use, granulomatous disease, and occupational chromium exposure. Small perforations may be managed with silicone septal buttons, while larger symptomatic ones may require surgical repair.

questions.question: A patient with chronic tonsillitis is also noted to have halitosis that persists despite good oral hygiene. What tonsillar feature most directly explains this symptom?
options: Simple tonsillar erythema without crypt involvement
Deep crypts harbouring debris and anaerobic bacteria
Enlarged adenoid tissue unrelated to the tonsils
questions.explanation: Deep tonsillar crypts can trap food debris, desquamated cells, and anaerobic bacteria, producing volatile sulphur compounds responsible for halitosis independent of general oral hygiene measures. This is distinct from tongue-coating-related halitosis and often persists until the tonsillar debris or tonsilloliths are addressed. Tonsillectomy or crypt debridement can be considered when this significantly affects quality of life.

questions.question: A child is brought in after inserting a button battery into the nostril several hours earlier. Why is this considered a nasal emergency requiring immediate removal?
questions.explanation: Button batteries generate a local electrical current and leak alkaline contents that cause rapid liquefactive necrosis of adjacent mucosa, leading to septal perforation and significant tissue destruction within hours if not promptly removed. This differs from inert foreign bodies, which can often be safely left for a period before elective removal. Immediate removal, ideally within hours, is essential to limit permanent damage.

questions.question: Squamous cell carcinoma of the middle ear can resemble chronic otitis media. The distinguishing clinical feature most often prompting biopsy is:
questions.explanation: Blood-stained (sanguineous) discharge combined with a non-healing otic polyp unresponsive to standard COM treatment should prompt biopsy to exclude malignancy. Squamous cell carcinoma of the middle ear may be indistinguishable from COM on clinical grounds. Histological examination of polyps and granulation tissue in atypical COM is therefore essential.

questions.question: A 55-year-old presents with progressive diplopia and a maxillary sinus mass on CT. Which anatomical spread best explains his diplopia?
questions.explanation: Diplopia in the context of a maxillary sinus tumour indicates superior extension through the orbital floor into the orbit, causing restriction or displacement of the extraocular muscles. This finding upstages the tumour and significantly affects surgical planning, often requiring orbital exenteration or preservation strategies. Infratemporal or palatal extension would instead produce trismus or palatal swelling rather than diplopia.

The cricopharyngeus muscle (at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction) is the narrowest point of the oesophagus and the commonest site of foreign body impaction. Other common sites include the level of the aortic arch and the gastro-oesophageal junction where physiological narrowing occurs.
questions.question: The commonest site of oesophageal foreign body impaction is:
What is the correct initial first aid position for a patient with anterior epistaxis?
options: Head tilted back to prevent blood entering the throat
Standing with arms raised above the head
Head forward with neck flexed and nose pinched for 10–20 minutes
Head to the bleeding side to direct blood away from airway
questions.explanation: The correct first aid for anterior epistaxis is to sit the patient upright with the head inclined forward (not back), flex the neck slightly, and firmly pinch the soft cartilaginous part of the nose for 10–20 minutes without releasing. The forward position prevents blood from flowing into the nasopharynx and stomach (which can cause nausea and vomiting), allows blood to be collected, and quantifies blood loss.

questions.question: A furniture factory worker develops chronic nasal obstruction, and biopsy of a nasal mass reveals adenocarcinoma. Which specific occupational exposure is most strongly implicated?
questions.explanation: Long-term exposure to hardwood dust in furniture and cabinet making is strongly associated with intestinal-type adenocarcinoma arising in the ethmoid sinus region. This association justifies occupational screening and protective measures in affected industries. Nickel and chromium exposures are more classically linked to squamous cell carcinoma rather than adenocarcinoma.

questions.question: Coins account for what percentage of ingested foreign bodies in children?
questions.explanation: Coins account for 75% of ingested foreign bodies in children, making them the commonest type. Their round, flat shape allows them to sit in the oesophagus at the cricopharyngeus, aortic arch level, or gastro-oesophageal junction, and they are radiopaque and visible on plain X-ray.

options: A completely normal finding requiring no further action
questions.question: A patient with chronic ear discharge is noted to have blood-stained otorrhoea. What diagnosis should this prompt consideration of?
questions.explanation: Blood-stained ear discharge in the context of a chronic ear history is a red-flag symptom that should prompt consideration of an underlying malignancy, since chronic infection alone less commonly produces frank blood-staining without another explanation such as granulation tissue or tumour. Prompt further evaluation, including examination and biopsy of any suspicious tissue, is warranted rather than assuming ongoing simple infection. Early recognition improves the chance of successful treatment if malignancy is confirmed.

questions.question: Examination Under Anaesthesia (EUA) for nasal foreign body is indicated when:
questions.explanation: EUA (Examination Under Anaesthesia) for a suspected nasal foreign body is indicated when clinical history (unilateral foetid discharge, nasal obstruction) strongly suggests a foreign body but rhinoscopy fails to identify it. General anaesthesia provides patient cooperation, adequate light and instrumentation, and airway protection needed for thorough examination, especially in children and for posteriorly positioned objects.
options: The foreign body is visible anteriorly in all patients at all times
A foreign body is clinically suspected but cannot be found on rhinoscopy
Only for rhinoliths extending into the antrum
Only for animate foreign bodies requiring chloroform
Only when a child refuses examination
Modify hormonal influences on mucosal reactivity
questions.question: Ophthalmic and systemic oestrogen-containing preparations are classified, in some older allergy texts, under a specific category of anti-allergic drug therapy. This classification is based on their action to:
questions.explanation: Hormonal agents such as oestrogens and steroids were historically grouped separately from antihistamines and mast cell stabilisers because their proposed benefit in allergy related to modifying hormonal and mucosal reactivity rather than a direct anti-histaminic or membrane-stabilising action. This distinguishes their mechanism from cromoglycate, which acts directly on mast cell membranes. Modern practice relies far more on corticosteroids for their anti-inflammatory rather than purely hormonal effect.

options: Less than 3 months in the year
More than 4 days per week and more than 4 consecutive weeks
More than 2 days per week all year round
Less than 4 days per week or less than 4 consecutive weeks
questions.question: Allergic rhinitis is classified as intermittent when symptoms are present for:
questions.explanation: According to the ARIA (Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma) classification, allergic rhinitis is categorized as intermittent when symptoms occur for fewer than 4 days per week or fewer than 4 consecutive weeks. Persistent allergic rhinitis is defined by symptoms occurring for 4 or more days per week AND for 4 or more consecutive weeks.

A hard, painless, fixed node in the supraclavicular fossa (Virchow's node on the left) strongly suggests metastatic malignancy, often from abdominal, thoracic, or head and neck primary tumours. This is an important clinical examination finding.
questions.question: During systematic neck palpation, the supraclavicular fossa is examined. Finding a hard painless node here MOST likely represents:

questions.explanation: The first stage is hyperaemia, characterised by oedema of the mucoperiosteum due to vascular engorgement. Subsequent stages are exudation, suppuration, and resolution. The stage of complication (coalescent mastoiditis) may follow if infection persists beyond 2 weeks without adequate treatment.
questions.question: The FIRST stage in the pathological progression of acute suppurative otitis media is:

questions.explanation: A clear temporal association with a precipitating event such as barotrauma, head injury, or forceful straining helps distinguish a perilymph fistula from Meniere's disease, which typically follows a more spontaneous, episodic course without such a clear precipitant. Both conditions can share overlapping symptoms of hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo, making the history particularly important in differentiation. Certain provocative manoeuvres reproducing symptoms can further support a fistula diagnosis.
options: A clear history of a precipitating pressure-related or traumatic event
A completely normal audiogram in both conditions
The presence of any hearing loss
questions.question: A patient presents with sudden hearing loss and vertigo, and an oval window fistula is suspected but Meniere's disease remains a differential. What feature BEST differentiates a fistula from Meniere's disease?

questions.explanation: The postnasal mirror is introduced into the oropharynx and angled behind the soft palate to reflect an image of the nasopharynx. The soft palate must be elevated using a tongue depressor, and the mirror must be warmed to prevent fogging.
questions.question: For examining the nasopharynx (post-nasal space), the mirror is introduced into the:

questions.explanation: Tertiary syphilis of the nose causes gummatous osteomyelitis with sequestration of nasal bone — the dead bone behaves as a foreign body causing unilateral discharge, crusting, and nasal obstruction clinically mimicking a nasal foreign body. The Treponema pallidum infection destroys the nasal septum and causes saddle nose deformity. VDRL and TPHA tests confirm syphilis.
questions.question: Nasal syphilis as a differential of nasal foreign body presents with which specific clinical feature?
options: Unilateral nasal obstruction with anosmia only
Pale nasal polyps with foul smell
Septal destruction with bone sequestrum and crusting

questions.explanation: Bilateral posterior nasal packing carries serious risks including hypoxaemia (due to nasal airway obstruction and nasopulmonary reflex), aspiration of blood (with packs dislodging), toxic shock syndrome from Staphylococcal colonisation of the pack, and mucosal pressure necrosis. Inpatient monitoring with pulse oximetry, oxygen supplementation, and consideration of prophylactic antibiotics are required for all posterior packs.
questions.question: The complication most feared from bilateral nasal packing for posterior epistaxis is:
options: Permanent anosmia from pack pressure at all times
Hypoxia, aspiration of blood, and toxic shock syndrome

questions.question: Maxillary sinus carcinoma constitutes what percentage of paranasal sinus malignancies?
questions.explanation: Maxillary sinus carcinoma constitutes approximately 80% of all paranasal sinus malignancies, making it by far the most common. This high prevalence makes the maxillary sinus the most clinically significant sinus in terms of malignant disease and the primary focus of sinus cancer management.

options: Symptoms under four days weekly or four weeks
Symptoms in a single lifetime episode
Daily symptoms for over four weeks
questions.explanation: The ARIA classification defines intermittent allergic rhinitis as symptoms occurring less than four days per week or for less than four consecutive weeks, in contrast to persistent disease which exceeds both these thresholds. This classification, alongside severity grading, helps guide stepwise pharmacological management. It has largely replaced the older seasonal versus perennial classification, which did not always accurately reflect symptom burden.
questions.question: A patient with intermittent allergic rhinitis is being distinguished from persistent disease according to symptom duration. Which pattern defines the intermittent subtype?

options: Raccoon eyes indicating anterior skull base fracture
CSF from the nose indicating cribriform plate fracture
Postauricular ecchymosis indicating temporal bone fracture
questions.question: A patient presents with Battle's sign after head trauma. This finding is:
questions.explanation: Battle's sign is postauricular (mastoid region) ecchymosis occurring 12-24 hours after temporal bone fracture, resulting from extravasation of blood from the fracture site tracking along the posterior auricular tissue planes. It is a classic clinical indicator of temporal bone fracture and may take 24-36 hours to become apparent. Raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis) indicate anterior skull base/cribriform plate fracture. CSF rhinorrhoea also suggests anterior skull base fracture, while haemotympanum and Battle's sign together strongly suggest temporal bone fracture.

Tympanic membrane perforations resulting from acute barotrauma, sudden pressure change, or minor instrumentation trauma heal spontaneously in the majority of cases, given the membrane's generally good capacity for epithelial regeneration when the perforation is not chronically infected. This informs a generally conservative initial management approach with observation before considering surgical repair. Persistent perforations beyond an expected healing period may then warrant tympanoplasty.
questions.question: A patient's tympanic membrane perforation from acute barotrauma is being monitored. In what proportion of such cases does the perforation typically heal spontaneously?
options: Only a small minority of cases
None of the cases ever heal spontaneously
Exactly half of all cases without exception

questions.question: The primary function of the tuning fork in ENT examination is to:
questions.explanation: The tuning fork is fundamental for performing Rinne and Weber tests, which compare air conduction (via the external canal) and bone conduction (via the skull bones) to classify hearing loss as conductive, sensorineural, or mixed.

questions.question: At the level of C6 on lateral neck X-ray, widening of prevertebral soft tissue is defined as exceeding:
questions.explanation: At C6, the normal prevertebral soft tissue width should not exceed 14 mm. A measurement greater than 14 mm at this level indicates abnormal retropharyngeal swelling, such as from a retropharyngeal abscess, haematoma, or tumour, and requires further investigation.

Contact granulomas of the larynx are typically caused by repetitive mechanical trauma from habits such as forceful throat clearing or vocal misuse, often compounded by laryngopharyngeal reflux, so first-line management focuses on voice therapy to modify these behaviours alongside reflux treatment rather than surgery, which carries a high recurrence risk if the underlying cause persists. Surgical removal is reserved for lesions causing airway compromise or failing conservative measures. Recurrence after excision without addressing the underlying habit is common.
options: Immediate surgical excision as the only effective option
High-dose oral antibiotics for presumed bacterial cause
Voice therapy addressing the throat-clearing habit and reflux control
questions.question: A patient with a chronic laryngeal granuloma is found on history to have a habit of frequent, forceful throat clearing. What is the most effective initial management strategy?
Which genetic type of cerumen is predominantly found in Asians and Native Americans?
questions.explanation: Asian and Native American people are more likely to have dry-type cerumen (grey and flaky), which is determined by an autosomal recessive gene. White and African populations are more likely to have wet-type cerumen (honey-brown to dark-brown and moist), which is autosomal dominant. The difference is traced to a single nucleotide polymorphism in the ATP-binding cassette gene.

Globus pharyngeus characteristically occurs between meals and paradoxically improves or disappears during the act of swallowing, unlike true dysphagia which occurs during swallowing and worsens with eating. This paradoxical improvement during eating is a key distinguishing feature. Globus is most commonly associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), anxiety, or no identifiable cause. It does not cause weight loss and does not represent true dysphagia. However, persistent globus requires investigation to exclude hypopharyngeal or oesophageal pathology.
options: It is always associated with true dysphagia
It occurs between meals and paradoxically improves during eating
It represents early oesophageal carcinoma in most cases
It requires immediate endoscopy in all patients
It only affects patients with documented reflux disease
questions.question: Globus pharyngeus is defined as persistent or intermittent non-painful sensation of a lump in the throat. Which statement about globus pharyngeus is most accurate?

On otoscopic examination, the pars tensa of the tympanic membrane is noted to be intact while an area above the lateral process of the malleus appears retracted. This retraction pocket is located in the:
questions.explanation: A retraction pocket occurring above the lateral process of the malleus involves the attic, or pars flaccida, a thinner and less supported area of the tympanic membrane prone to retraction and cholesteatoma formation. The pars tensa quadrants and umbo are structurally different regions less prone to this specific type of retraction. Early identification of an attic retraction pocket is important because of its association with progressive cholesteatoma.

questions.question: Tympanic membrane perforations from acute barotrauma, sudden pressure change, or instrumentation heal spontaneously in what proportion of cases?
questions.explanation: Approximately 80% of tympanic membrane perforations from trauma heal spontaneously. The remaining 20% may require tympanoplasty for closure. Initial management includes a baseline audiogram, keeping the ear dry, and antibiotics only if infection develops. Fistulae of the labyrinthine windows may require exploration and repair.

options: Entire midface from the skull base at the orbital level
Nasal bones from the frontal bone
Maxillary sinus walls only without alveolar involvement
Maxillary alveolus and hard palate from the upper midface (pterygoid plates detached)
Orbital rims from the zygomatic arches
questions.explanation: Le Fort I (horizontal maxillary fracture) runs horizontally through the lower maxilla, separating the maxillary alveolus and hard palate (as a single mobile segment) from the upper midface. The fracture passes through the piriform aperture, across the anterior maxillary walls, through the posterior maxillary walls, and through the pterygoid plates bilaterally (all Le Fort fractures involve the pterygoid plates). The mobile segment includes the teeth-bearing alveolus and hard palate, creating 'floating palate' mobility of the dentition independent of the upper face. Treatment requires ORIF with titanium plates.
questions.question: Maxillary fractures are described by the Le Fort classification. The Le Fort I fracture specifically separates which structures?

questions.explanation: The osteomeatal complex is the key common drainage pathway through which the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses empty into the nasal cavity, so even minor anatomical narrowing or mucosal swelling here can obstruct multiple sinuses and predispose to recurrent rhinosinusitis. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery targets widening this area to restore normal mucociliary drainage. This explains why disease in one sinus often coexists with disease in others sharing this pathway.
options: It drains only the sphenoid sinus
It has no role in sinus physiology
It drains the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses
It is the site of olfactory epithelium
It only regulates nasal airflow resistance
questions.question: A patient with recurrent acute rhinosinusitis is found on CT to have a narrowed osteomeatal complex. Why is this area clinically significant?
A 5-year-old with grade 4 tonsillar hypertrophy has witnessed apnoeic episodes, snoring, and daytime somnolence but only 2 episodes of tonsillitis this year. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnoea from tonsillar hypertrophy is an independent indication for adenotonsillectomy regardless of infection frequency. Untreated paediatric OSA risks cor pulmonale, failure to thrive, and neurocognitive impairment. The Paradise criteria for recurrent infection do not apply when obstruction is the primary problem.

questions.question: Foreign body ingestion in a mentally retarded patient is MOST common because:
options: They are given inappropriate food sizes
They experience more frequent seizures causing aspiration
They have impaired cognitive assessment of edibility
questions.explanation: Mentally retarded individuals share the risk factors of toddlers, having impaired cognitive ability to assess whether objects are edible and diminished understanding of danger, combined with oral exploration tendencies. These cognitive and behavioural characteristics explain the elevated foreign body ingestion risk.

Unilateral foetid (foul-smelling) mucopurulent nasal discharge is the most pathognomonic symptom of a retained nasal foreign body. The asymmetric presentation — strictly unilateral obstruction and discharge — combined with the foul smell from secondary bacterial infection distinguishes a foreign body from sinusitis, polyps, and rhinitis, which are typically bilateral or have different discharge characteristics.
questions.question: The MOST pathognomonic symptom of a nasal foreign body is:

questions.explanation: Acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) usually arise from the vestibular nerve, not the cochlear nerve, despite commonly presenting with hearing loss. Progression of vestibular nerve involvement is typically so slow that dizziness is not noticed by the patient. Characteristic findings include abnormal acoustic reflex, poor discrimination, and abnormal ABR.
questions.question: The MOST common type of acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) arises from which nerve?
The prevertebral space is resistant to infection spread primarily because:
options: Dense fibrous attachments between fascia and deep muscles
It is filled with dense adipose tissue
It communicates only upward toward the skull base
questions.explanation: The prevertebral space shows resistance to infection spread due to dense fibrous attachments between the prevertebral fascia and the deep paraspinal muscles. Unlike the danger space with its loose areolar tissue, these firm attachments limit the dissection and spread of infection.

questions.question: A previously well child develops sudden-onset unilateral wheeze and stridor after playing with small toys, without preceding fever or coryza. What should be strongly suspected?
questions.explanation: Sudden onset of unilateral respiratory symptoms in a previously well child, particularly following play with small objects and without a preceding viral prodrome, is highly suggestive of foreign body aspiration into the airway. This requires urgent bronchoscopy for both diagnosis and removal, as delayed recognition risks complications such as post-obstructive pneumonia. The absence of the gradual coryzal prodrome typical of croup helps distinguish this presentation clinically.

Unilateral, progressive obstruction combined with recurrent unilateral epistaxis over several months is a red-flag pattern for a nasal or sinus neoplasm until excluded. Allergic and vasomotor rhinitis typically cause bilateral, fluctuating symptoms. The persistent unilaterality is the key discriminating history feature.
questions.question: A patient reports epistaxis that always occurs from the same nostril and is accompanied by unilateral nasal obstruction that has progressively worsened over four months. This history should MOST urgently prompt evaluation for:
In plain radiography of the paranasal sinuses, bony walls are seen as white lines on X-ray. The presence of fluid level in a sinus on plain X-ray MOST indicates:
questions.explanation: A fluid level in a paranasal sinus on plain X-ray indicates accumulation of secretions or pus, consistent with acute sinusitis with fluid collection. This radiological finding confirms clinical suspicion and guides the need for further imaging or drainage.

questions.question: A neonate has episodes of stridor and cyanosis at rest that do not improve with typical croup measures, present since birth without a preceding viral illness. What distinguishes this from croup and points toward congenital subglottic stenosis?
questions.explanation: Congenital subglottic stenosis presents from birth or early infancy without the preceding coryzal illness typical of croup, and symptoms tend to be persistent rather than episodic in relation to viral infections. Endoscopic airway assessment is required to confirm the diagnosis and assess the degree of narrowing. Management may range from observation for mild cases to surgical airway reconstruction for severe stenosis.
options: Absence of a preceding viral illness
Presence of a barking cough sound
Onset between six months and years

questions.explanation: Partial inferior turbinectomy reduces the volume of hypertrophied inferior turbinates that cause persistent nasal obstruction in allergic and vasomotor rhinitis. It is reserved for patients who fail medical treatment, improving airflow without eliminating mucosal function.
questions.question: Partial turbinectomy is performed in allergic rhinitis PRIMARILY to relieve:
A patient with confirmed allergic rhinitis is noted on examination to have pale, oedematous, blue-hued nasal turbinates. This finding is MOST useful for:
options: Supporting the clinical diagnosis of allergy
questions.explanation: Pale, oedematous, blue-tinged turbinate mucosa is a classical examination finding in allergic rhinitis, reflecting chronic venous engorgement from repeated allergen exposure. Bacterial infection typically produces erythematous, purulent-appearing mucosa instead. This colour change is a supportive, though not solely diagnostic, clinical sign that should be interpreted alongside the history.

Desensitisation (allergen immunotherapy) involves subcutaneous or sublingual administration of gradually increasing doses of the specific allergen. This induces immune tolerance, shifts the immune response, and reduces symptoms upon natural allergen exposure.
questions.question: Desensitisation therapy for allergic rhinitis works by:
A child presents with acute otitis media, and the tympanic membrane shows a 'lighthouse sign' with a visible pulsating light reflex. What does this sign indicate?
questions.explanation: The lighthouse sign describes a pulsating reflection of light from a bulging, inflamed tympanic membrane under pressure, indicating that spontaneous perforation may be imminent as pus accumulates under tension in the middle ear. Recognising this sign can prompt consideration of myringotomy to relieve pressure in a controlled manner rather than awaiting spontaneous rupture. It reflects an advanced stage in the progression of acute suppurative otitis media.
options: Impending spontaneous perforation from bulging under pressure
Chronic otitis media with effusion only

questions.question: A bus driver presents with recurrent otitis media and sinusitis. The MOST likely occupational cause for this pattern is:
questions.explanation: Drivers are specifically exposed to barotrauma from rapid pressure changes during travel, which can rupture the tympanic membrane and cause sinusitis. This occupational association is a critical clerkship observation for ENT patients.

Repetitive obstructive apnoeic events during sleep prevent normal sleep cycling through slow-wave and REM stages, resulting in non-restorative sleep architecture. The consequent sleep deprivation manifests as daytime hypersomnolence, inattention, behavioural problems, and even enuresis (due to altered arousal thresholds and altered secretion of antidiuretic hormone). Adenotonsillectomy normalises sleep architecture and resolves these neurobehavioural sequelae.
questions.question: Daytime hypersomnolence, poor school performance, and enuresis in a child with adenotonsillar hypertrophy are best explained by which mechanism?
options: Fragmented sleep architecture from apnoeic events

questions.question: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) is a benign tumour listed as a tracheostomy indication. Tracheostomy in this condition is performed as a last resort because it carries a specific risk of:
questions.explanation: Tracheostomy in RRP is avoided when possible because it risks implantation and spread of papillomata to the tracheostomy site. These HPV-driven lesions can seed into the trachea and stoma, making control more difficult. Tracheostomy is used only when the airway is critically compromised.

Sitting upright and leaning slightly forward while applying pressure prevents blood from trickling down the throat, which can cause aspiration, nausea, or vomiting of swallowed blood. Tilting the head backward is a common but incorrect practice that increases the risk of airway compromise. This position also allows the patient to spit out any blood rather than swallowing it.
questions.question: A patient with anterior epistaxis is correctly positioned for first aid. Which position should be adopted while pressure is applied?

questions.explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is known for its propensity for perineural invasion with skip metastases along nerve sheaths, making complete surgical resection challenging. Late local recurrences are common even after apparently complete excision. The facial nerve is particularly at risk during surgery due to this perineural spread pattern.
questions.question: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the ear has which characteristic behaviour that makes it particularly sinister?

questions.explanation: The distraction test is a behavioural test appropriate for infants aged 6–18 months. The cooperation test is used for 18–30 months. Performance testing is for children over 30 months, while pure tone audiometry is reliable from age 3 years. Selecting the correct test avoids misdiagnosis due to developmental mismatch. SUBTOPIC 2: OTITIS EXTERNA
questions.question: The distraction test for hearing in infants is appropriate for which age group?
A tracheostomy is defined as a surgical opening maintained by a tube on which aspect of the trachea?
questions.explanation: Tracheostomy is specifically defined as a surgical creation of an opening maintained by a tube on the anterior aspect of the cervical tracheal wall. The anterior position avoids the posterior membranous wall and allows safe access to the tracheal lumen with minimal vascular risk.
options: Anterior aspect of cervical tracheal wall
Anterolateral wall at the mid-cervical level
Lateral wall at thyroid cartilage level

questions.question: A tuning fork test demonstrates bone conduction greater than air conduction in a patient's right ear. This finding is consistent with:
questions.explanation: A Rinne-negative result (BC > AC) on the right side indicates conductive hearing loss in the right ear. In normal hearing and sensorineural loss, air conduction exceeds bone conduction (Rinne positive). Weber test lateralises to the side of conductive loss, helping to differentiate unilateral from bilateral pathology.

questions.question: COM is MORE prevalent in the developing world primarily because of:
questions.explanation: COM is commoner in developing countries where prevalence can be as high as 2–5%, driven by poverty, overcrowding, poor hygiene, limited access to medical care, and dearth of specialists. Seasonal variations have been noted, with inactive COM becoming active during rainy seasons in West Africa. Malnutrition also predisposes.

questions.question: Otitis media with effusion (OME) is also known by all of the following names EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Purulent otitis media implies active bacterial suppuration, which is incompatible with OME. OME is characterised by middle ear effusion without signs and symptoms of acute infection. Its other names — glue ear, secretory OM, mucoid OM, and serous OM — all reflect the nature of the non-purulent fluid present.

options: The radiation field would be too large
The neck lymph nodes are not at risk
questions.question: A patient with early-stage nasal vestibule carcinoma does NOT receive prophylactic neck radiotherapy PRIMARILY because:
questions.explanation: Prophylactic neck radiotherapy is avoided in early-stage cancers of the nasal septum, nasal vestibule, larynx, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses because the neck lymph node drainage and metastatic risk are low. Treating the neck unnecessarily exposes the patient to radiation-related morbidity.

questions.question: Syphilitic otitis media primarily causes which type of hearing loss?
questions.explanation: Syphilitic OM is caused by a spirochete that affects both the cochlear and semicircular canals, causing severe sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo. Diagnosis is made through dark-field microscopic examination of ear discharge. Treatment includes penicillin G, aminoglycosides, or azithromycin.

questions.question: Contact dermatitis of the external ear most commonly results from which allergen?
questions.explanation: The most common cause of contact dermatitis of the external ear is nickel allergy from earrings. Other agents include shampoos, hair sprays, perfumes, earplugs, and cosmetics. Treatment involves removal of the allergen and application of topical corticosteroids. Symptoms include burning, itching, pain, and variable erythema to hyperpigmentation.

questions.question: On indirect laryngoscopy, the mirror image shows structures in reverse superior-inferior orientation compared with direct laryngoscopy. The epiglottis and tongue base therefore appear:
questions.explanation: Because a mirror reverses the vertical orientation of the image, anterior structures such as the tongue base and epiglottis appear at the top of the mirror view, while posterior structures like the arytenoids appear lower. Understanding this reversal is essential for correct interpretation during indirect laryngoscopy. Failure to account for this can lead to misidentification of pathology location.

Increased eosinophils in nasal secretions are a well-established marker supporting a diagnosis of allergic rhinitis, reflecting the underlying type 1 hypersensitivity inflammatory process. Neutrophil predominance instead suggests bacterial superinfection. This simple cytological test complements the clinical history and skin testing in confirming an allergic aetiology.
questions.question: Nasal secretion analysis in a patient with suspected allergic rhinitis is sent for cytology. Which cell type, when found in increased numbers, MOST supports the allergic diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Myringotomy involves a controlled surgical incision of the tympanic membrane to relieve pressure and allow drainage of purulent middle ear fluid, providing rapid symptomatic relief in cases of severe or unresponsive acute suppurative otitis media. It also allows collection of fluid for microbiological culture to guide further treatment. This procedure is used alongside, not as a replacement for, appropriate antibiotic therapy.
options: To improve cosmetic appearance of the ear
To relieve pressure and drain purulent middle ear fluid
To permanently seal the tympanic membrane
To replace the need for any antibiotic therapy
To directly treat an underlying cholesteatoma
questions.question: A patient undergoes myringotomy for acute suppurative otitis media. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this procedure?

questions.explanation: Passavant's ridge is the most inferior aspect of the adenoid pad, which may overlap the superior constrictor muscle. It plays a role in velopharyngeal closure during speech. During adenoidectomy, curettage must be cautious in this area to avoid damaging the superior constrictor, which would further compromise velopharyngeal function and cause hypernasal speech post-operatively.
questions.question: Passavant's ridge is located at which anatomical position relative to the adenoid?
options: Lateral surface near the Eustachian tube
Superior pole adjacent to the skull base
Most inferior aspect, overlapping the superior constrictor
Posterior surface near the prevertebral fascia
To allow the patient to communicate during procedure
To prevent distal migration of the foreign body
Spontaneous ventilation gives better bronchoscopic visualization
questions.explanation: Spontaneous ventilation is maintained during foreign body bronchoscopy to avoid positive pressure ventilation, which can drive the foreign body distally to a more inaccessible location or convert a partial obstruction to complete ball-valve obstruction. Natural respiratory effort keeps the airway in its most open state.
questions.question: A patient with foreign body aspiration undergoes bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia with spontaneous ventilation. The reason for maintaining spontaneous ventilation (rather than controlled ventilation) is:
An elderly man presents with a unilateral, red, fleshy, friable nasal mass with a granular surface that bleeds on light touch. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: A unilateral mass that is friable, granular, and bleeds easily is atypical for a simple inflammatory nasal polyp and raises strong suspicion for malignancy, most commonly squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma in an older patient. Histological confirmation via biopsy is mandatory before any conservative or medical management is pursued. Treating this empirically as a benign polyp risks delaying cancer diagnosis and treatment.
options: Reassure and review in six months

questions.question: Infection spreading from the mastoid to form a collection in the sternocleidomastoid region is known as:
questions.explanation: Bezold's abscess forms when pus from coalescent mastoiditis tracks through the mastoid tip into the sternocleidomastoid muscle region. Luc's abscess occurs in the temporalis region. Citelli's abscess forms in the subperiosteal (digastric triangle) region. These extratemporal complications require surgical drainage.

questions.question: A patient with a tracheostomy stoma is asked to occlude the tube and count aloud during examination. This manoeuvre is PRIMARILY used to assess:
questions.explanation: Occluding the tracheostomy tube diverts airflow through the upper airway and larynx, allowing the examiner to judge whether the airway above the stoma is patent enough to support phonation and breathing. This is a functional test of the upper airway rather than a direct test of vocal cord movement alone. It helps determine readiness for decannulation.

A pinna ulcer in an elderly patient with chronic sun exposure should raise suspicion for squamous cell carcinoma or basal cell carcinoma, as the pinna is a sun-exposed area. BCC classically shows smooth raised edges with a central crater; SCC presents as raised ulcerated lesion. Biopsy is mandatory for any suspicious pinna lesion.
questions.question: A pinna ulcer in an elderly patient with a history of chronic sun exposure should raise suspicion for:

options: Membranous and bony labyrinthine developmental abnormalities
questions.question: A child is found to have Scheibe and Mondini-Michelle inner ear abnormalities on imaging. Under which category of congenital sensorineural hearing loss do these fall?
questions.explanation: Scheibe and Mondini-Michelle abnormalities represent examples of congenital membranous and bony labyrinthine developmental defects respectively, resulting in structural inner ear malformation and associated sensorineural hearing loss present from birth or early life. Recognising these as congenital structural anomalies, rather than acquired pathology, is important for genetic counselling and prognosis. Imaging characterisation of the specific abnormality can also guide cochlear implant candidacy assessment if needed.

Adenoids (nasopharyngeal tonsils) are covered by pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium with few crypts, consistent with their nasopharyngeal location. Palatine tonsils are covered by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium with deep crypts. After repeated infections, the ciliated epithelium of the adenoid thins, impairing mucociliary clearance and causing mucus stasis that perpetuates infection.
questions.question: Adenoids differ histologically from palatine tonsils in that adenoids are covered by:
Otomycosis of the EAC caused by Aspergillus niger characteristically shows which clinical finding?
questions.explanation: Aspergillus niger produces a characteristic grayish membrane with hyphae visible under microscopy. Candida albicans produces debris resembling wet blotting paper. Otomycosis causes severe itching, and secondary bacterial infection may produce intense pain requiring treatment with otomycotic drugs.

options: Response to adrenaline nebulisation at all times
A preceding upper respiratory tract infection
questions.question: Congenital subglottic stenosis in an infant under 6 months is clinically distinguished from viral croup by the absence of:
questions.explanation: Congenital subglottic stenosis presents in infants under 6 months with stridor (often biphasic) without a preceding viral URTI — the hallmark that distinguishes it from viral croup (which always follows a cold). There may also be a history of previous neonatal intubation (suggestive of acquired subglottic stenosis). Endoscopy confirms the diagnosis. Tracheostomy may be required for severe cases pending airway expansion procedures.

options: Systemic hypertension causing posterior epistaxis at all times
Direct mucosal vasoconstriction causing ischaemia and septal perforation
questions.question: Cocaine snorting as a local cause of epistaxis acts through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Cocaine is a potent local vasoconstrictor (via alpha-adrenergic stimulation and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition) that when insufflated causes severe ischaemia of the nasal septal mucosa. Repeated use causes progressive mucosal and cartilaginous destruction, leading to septal perforation, saddle-nose deformity, and recurrent epistaxis. It is both a local and (via systemic effects) a potential systemic cause of nosebleeds.

options: It may seed or disseminate tumour cells
It requires general anaesthesia unavailable urgently
It is only used for allergic disease
It cannot reach the maxillary sinus
questions.explanation: Antral washout involves instrumentation and irrigation of the maxillary sinus, which in the presence of an unrecognised malignancy risks tumour seeding along the needle tract or spreading malignant cells within the sinus. Investigation of a suspected tumour should instead proceed via imaging and biopsy under controlled conditions. This principle underlies the general caution against blind instrumentation of a mass lesion.
questions.question: A patient with epistaxis secondary to a suspected sinonasal tumour is being considered for antral washout. Why is this procedure contraindicated in this context?

questions.explanation: When medical therapy fails to resolve chronic rhinosinusitis, functional endoscopic sinus surgery is indicated to restore normal ventilation and drainage by addressing the osteomeatal complex. It aims to correct anatomical obstruction while preserving as much normal mucosa as possible. Antral washout alone provides only temporary symptomatic relief and does not address the underlying obstructive pathology.
questions.question: A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis fails maximal medical therapy including topical steroids and saline irrigation. Endoscopy shows persistent mucopus in the middle meatus. What is the next appropriate step?

questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma requires complete excision with a margin of normal tissue, typically via superficial parotidectomy with careful facial nerve dissection and preservation, because simple enucleation risks tumour rupture, seeding, and high recurrence rates. The facial nerve is preserved unless there is evidence of malignant invasion. Recurrent pleomorphic adenoma is notoriously more difficult to treat than the primary tumour due to multifocal seeding.
questions.question: A patient presents with a painless, slow-growing mass at the angle of the jaw that has been present for several years. Fine needle aspiration suggests pleomorphic adenoma. What is the appropriate surgical approach?
options: Simple enucleation of the tumour alone
Total parotidectomy sacrificing the facial nerve routinely
Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation
Radical neck dissection as first-line treatment

questions.question: Stenver's view (postero-anterior oblique) of the temporal bone is BEST for demonstrating:
questions.explanation: Stenver's view demonstrates the whole length of the petrous bone, the mastoid bone tip, and the superior and horizontal semicircular canals. It provides excellent detail of petrous bone pathology and is valuable in assessing labyrinthine disorders.

Because infants have a shorter Eustachian tube, reflux of liquid from the nasopharynx into the middle ear is more likely. The supine position, which is common in infants, further enhances flow of liquid into the middle ear. This anatomical factor explains the higher prevalence of otitis media in infants.
questions.question: A shorter Eustachian tube in infants compared to adults increases the risk for:
During classical tracheostomy, the skin incision is made at which specific anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: The standard horizontal skin incision for classical tracheostomy is made midway between the sternal notch and the cricoid cartilage. This positions the incision optimally over the 2nd-4th tracheal rings after dissection, avoiding both the cricoid and the thoracic inlet structures.
options: At the level of thyroid notch
At the level of the cricoid cartilage
Two finger-breadths above the sternal notch
Midway between the sternal notch and cricoid

questions.question: A patient with a deviated nasal septum causing obstruction of the middle meatus develops recurrent maxillary sinusitis on the narrowed side. Which anatomical relationship best explains this?
questions.explanation: A severely deviated septum can encroach on the middle meatus and narrow the osteomeatal complex on the convex side, impairing drainage and ventilation of the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses and predisposing to recurrent sinusitis. This mechanical obstruction is a recognised anatomical risk factor considered when medical treatment for recurrent sinusitis fails. Septoplasty may be considered as part of management when this anatomical contribution is significant.
options: Septal deviation directly infecting the sinus
Septal deviation narrowing the osteomeatal complex
Septal deviation obstructing the sphenoid ostium only

questions.question: An infant with Pierre Robin sequence has a small jaw causing posterior displacement of the tongue and airway obstruction. At which anatomical level does this obstruction primarily occur?
questions.explanation: In micrognathia, the small mandible allows the tongue to fall backward into the oropharynx, causing glossoptosis and obstruction at the oropharyngeal level, particularly when the infant is supine. Prone positioning often improves symptoms by allowing the tongue to fall forward away from the airway. Severe cases may require a nasopharyngeal airway or surgical intervention such as mandibular distraction or tongue-lip adhesion.

questions.question: In the classification of rhinosinusitis by duration, 'recurrent acute rhinosinusitis' is defined as:
options: Four or more episodes per year with complete resolution between attacks
Two or more episodes per year with persistent symptoms between attacks
Symptoms persisting for more than 12 weeks continuously
Symptoms lasting 4–12 weeks with partial resolution
questions.explanation: Recurrent acute rhinosinusitis is defined as four or more distinct episodes of acute rhinosinusitis per year, with complete resolution of symptoms between episodes. This distinguishes it from chronic rhinosinusitis (where symptoms persist without complete resolution) and is an important indication for surgical evaluation of the ostiomeatal complex.

questions.question: Ampicillin-sulbactam is empirically appropriate for deep neck space infections primarily because it covers which problematic resistance mechanism?
questions.explanation: Up to 17-47% of isolates from deep neck space infections produce beta-lactamases, which inactivate plain penicillins and aminopenicillins. Sulbactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects ampicillin from enzymatic inactivation, restoring its efficacy against these resistant aerobic and anaerobic organisms. Metronidazole is added for enhanced anaerobic coverage. This combination addresses the polymicrobial nature and anticipated resistance patterns of contemporary deep neck infections.

Loss of cervical lordosis (straightening of the normal cervical curve) on lateral neck X-ray is caused by paraspinal muscle spasm secondary to retropharyngeal infection or abscess. This indirect sign, combined with prevertebral swelling, supports the diagnosis.
questions.question: Loss of cervical lordosis on lateral soft tissue neck X-ray in a child is MOST associated with:

questions.explanation: Glycerine carbolic ear drops or warm olive oil are used to reduce pain before tympanic membrane perforation in acute otitis media. After perforation and discharge, ear drops are used differently. Adequate analgesia at this stage prevents unnecessary patient distress and is an essential supportive measure.
questions.question: Glycerine carbolic ear drops in the management of AOM are primarily indicated for:
Bimanual palpation during oral cavity examination is MOST useful for assessing:
questions.explanation: Bimanual palpation, with one finger inside the mouth and one hand externally under the jaw, provides optimal assessment of floor of mouth masses and submandibular salivary gland lesions, especially for detecting deep structures.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a proposed aetiology for idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis causes gradual progressive conductive or mixed hearing loss, not sudden SNHL. Proposed aetiologies for idiopathic sudden SNHL include viral, autoimmune, vascular, and allergic causes. The diagnosis is one of exclusion after extensive workup. Treatment includes bed rest and possibly steroid and inhalation therapies.

MRI with gadolinium contrast is the gold standard imaging modality for detecting small acoustic tumours (vestibular schwannomas) of the internal auditory canal, offering superior soft tissue resolution compared to CT. Early detection of small tumours by MRI allows for more conservative management options such as observation or radiosurgery. CT is less sensitive for small lesions and is generally reserved for assessing bony anatomy.
questions.question: A patient with suspected small acoustic tumour of the internal auditory canal requires imaging. Which modality is the GOLD STANDARD for this purpose?

questions.explanation: When air conduction exceeds bone conduction (positive Rinne) bilaterally and Weber does not lateralize to either ear, this is the expected pattern of normal hearing. Both tests together help confirm the absence of significant hearing loss.
questions.question: Tuning fork tests are performed during ENT examination. A positive Rinne test (AC > BC) with a negative Weber lateralization to either side MOST likely indicates:

options: Apply a local anaesthetic drop and then continue
Postpone removal; prescribe bicarbonate drops for 1–2 weeks
questions.explanation: If the procedure becomes painful, cerumen removal should be postponed for 1 or more weeks and the patient instructed to instil softening drops such as sodium bicarbonate 5% twice daily. Softened cerumen is significantly easier and less painful to remove. Pain likely indicates trauma to the canal skin or inadvertent contact with the malleus.
questions.question: If cerumen removal becomes painful during the procedure, the RECOMMENDED course of action is to:
Fibrous dysplasia of the maxillary sinus most characteristically causes which clinical finding?
questions.explanation: Fibrous dysplasia is a benign condition in which normal bone is replaced by fibrous tissue, leading to expansion of the affected sinus wall. In the maxillary sinus, expansion of the roof displaces the orbital floor upward, causing proptosis of the eye on the affected side. This characteristic presentation distinguishes it from sinusitis and mucocele.
options: Displacement of orbital floor causing proptosis
Air-fluid level on plain well-defined X-ray
Eustachian tube obstruction occurring entirely alone
Mass effect on cochlea or nerve
questions.question: Tinnitus as a presenting feature of ear cancer is MOST likely caused by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Tinnitus in ear cancer is caused by mass effect of the tumour on the cochlea, auditory nerve, or middle ear structures. In glomus tumours, pulsatile tinnitus is pathognomonic due to the vascular nature of the tumour. Any middle ear mass can cause tinnitus and hearing loss through disruption of normal sound transmission.

options: Absence of metastatic potential despite local invasion
questions.question: JNA is classified as a locally aggressive benign tumour. The feature that distinguishes it from a malignant tumour is:
questions.explanation: JNA is classified as benign because despite its locally aggressive behaviour (bone erosion, extension into multiple anatomical spaces, skull base invasion), it does not metastasise to regional lymph nodes or distant sites. This distinguishes it fundamentally from malignant vascular tumours (angiosarcoma, Kaposi's sarcoma) which share the property of local invasion but additionally disseminate. The absence of metastatic potential means complete surgical resection, even when requiring multiple approaches, is curative without need for systemic therapy.

The primary cause of conductive hearing loss in NPC is Eustachian tube obstruction by tumour in the fossa of Rosenmueller, which impairs middle ear ventilation and creates a serous otitis media with effusion (glue ear). This is why unilateral otitis media with effusion in an adult without prior ear disease is an ENT red flag requiring nasopharyngoscopy. Sensorineural hearing loss may additionally occur from cranial nerve involvement in advanced disease.
options: Eustachian tube obstruction causing middle ear effusion
CN VIII compression at the internal auditory meatus
Middle ear cholesteatoma from chronic negative pressure
questions.question: The conductive hearing loss in NPC is caused by which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Sinonasal malignant melanoma typically presents at a more advanced stage due to the hidden location and non-specific early symptoms, resulting in a generally worse prognosis compared with cutaneous melanoma, which is more often detected early through visual inspection. It also shows less clear correlation between depth of invasion and outcome compared with skin lesions. Multidisciplinary management combining surgery and adjuvant therapy is standard, though outcomes remain guarded.
questions.question: A patient with a sinonasal malignant melanoma is being counselled on prognosis. How does the biological behaviour of this tumour typically compare with cutaneous melanoma?
options: It presents late with a worse prognosis
Wide excision alone always cures it
It behaves identically to skin melanoma
It never metastasises unlike skin melanoma
It has a better prognosis overall

questions.question: The self-cleaning mechanism of the external auditory canal is primarily driven by:
questions.explanation: Cells formed at the centre of the tympanic membrane migrate outward from the umbo at a rate equivalent to fingernail growth, carrying cerumen and debris toward the canal entrance. Jaw movement assists this process by dislodging debris from the canal walls. This physiological conveyor belt process eliminates the need for ear cleaning in most people.

questions.question: A child undergoing adenoidectomy inadvertently suffers dislocation of the temporomandibular joint during mouth-gag insertion. This complication is more likely in patients with:
questions.explanation: Temporomandibular joint dislocation is a recognised complication of adenoidectomy related to the forceful and sustained opening of the mouth with the Boyle-Davis gag or similar instruments. Patients with pre-existing joint hypermobility or ligamentous laxity (such as those with connective tissue disorders or Down syndrome) are at increased risk. Careful positioning and avoiding excessive mouth-gag tension mitigate this risk.

Percutaneous tracheostomy uses a needle puncture followed by sequential dilation of the tract, often under bronchoscopic guidance, to place the tube without formal open surgical dissection of the strap muscles and trachea. It still requires a skin incision, though smaller than the open technique. This less invasive approach is popular in critical care settings for ventilated patients.
questions.question: A 'percutaneous' tracheostomy, as opposed to a formal open surgical tracheostomy, is characterised by which key technical feature?
options: Use of only a permanent metal tube
Performance only under local anaesthesia awake
Guided dilation of a needle tract, not formal dissection

questions.explanation: Technetium scan shows the acute infective focus in malignant otitis externa and reverts to normal with clinical resolution. Gallium scan shows osteoblastic activity and may remain abnormal for many months after clinical resolution, making it useful for monitoring true disease eradication. CT shows bony destruction. SUBTOPIC 5: HEARING LOSS
questions.question: Imaging study typically used to monitor osteoblastic activity and response to treatment in malignant otitis externa is:

questions.explanation: Rhinolalia clausa refers to hyponasality, where the nasal cavity is blocked anteriorly or posteriorly, preventing adequate nasal resonance. It causes the typical 'blocked nose' voice quality where nasal consonants (m, n, ng) sound muffled or absent.
questions.question: Rhinolalia clausa is the correct term for which resonance disorder?

options: The level of the hard palate
questions.explanation: The parapharyngeal space extends from the skull base superiorly to the hyoid bone inferiorly, with the pterygomandibular raphe anteriorly, prevertebral fascia posteriorly, buccopharyngeal fascia medially, and superficial layer of deep cervical fascia laterally. Its communication with multiple other deep neck spaces (peritonsillar, submandibular, retropharyngeal, parotid, masticator spaces) makes parapharyngeal abscess particularly dangerous for spread.
questions.question: The parapharyngeal space is also known as the pharyngomaxillary space. Its superior boundary is:

questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinus ostium is located on the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, opening into the sphenoethmoidal recess between the superior turbinate and the nasal septum. Its small size (0.5–4 mm), variable position, and proximity to the sella turcica, carotid artery, and optic nerve make sphenoid sinus surgery technically demanding.
questions.question: The sphenoid sinus ostium is characteristically located on the:
options: Anterior wall, in the sphenoethmoidal recess
Lateral wall, superior to middle turbinate
Inferior wall, draining into the inferior meatus
Floor, draining into the maxillary sinus

questions.question: Which paranasal sinus drains into the middle meatus via the infundibulum?
options: Frontal sinus as the sole route
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoid cells and the maxillary sinus drain via the ethmoid infundibulum into the middle meatus. The frontal sinus drains through the frontal recess into the middle meatus as well. The posterior ethmoid cells drain into the superior meatus, and the sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

questions.question: A patient with otitis media with effusion in adulthood is being evaluated. What underlying cause should be specifically EXCLUDED in this age group?
options: Normal ageing change without further workup
Simple allergic rhinitis without further workup
questions.explanation: Unilateral otitis media with effusion in an adult should prompt evaluation of the nasopharynx to exclude an obstructing tumour, since this presentation can be an early sign of nasopharyngeal carcinoma affecting eustachian tube function. This is a critical distinction from the typically benign, self-limiting effusion seen in children following viral infections. Nasendoscopy or imaging is warranted in adults with unexplained unilateral effusion.

Otalgia that is worse on lying down is characteristic of acute otitis media, likely due to increased middle ear pressure in the recumbent position. In OME, otalgia is intermittent and typically worse at night. Chronic suppurative OM usually features otorrhea as the predominant symptom rather than severe otalgia.
questions.question: Otalgia in otitis media that is worse on lying down is MOST characteristic of which subtype?
Tinnitus is defined as perception of sound produced involuntarily within the body. The type with the most serious clinical implications because it may indicate vascular pathology is:
questions.explanation: Objective tinnitus is audible to the examiner as well as the patient and includes pulsatile tinnitus from vascular causes (arteriovenous malformations, glomus tumours, benign intracranial hypertension, arterial bruits) and non-pulsatile types from myoclonus (palatal myoclonus, stapedial muscle spasm). Pulsatile objective tinnitus is particularly significant because it may indicate a vascular neoplasm (glomus jugulare/tympanicum), AVM, or venous abnormality that requires urgent imaging. Subjective tinnitus originates within the auditory system and does not carry the same vascular risk implications.
options: Tinnitus in the context of presbycusis

questions.question: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) in West Africa is most strongly associated with which viral aetiology?
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly and consistently associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection worldwide, including in West Africa. Elevated EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA IgA) and early antigen (EA) antibody titres serve as serum biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring. EBV DNA in plasma is also used. Geographic variations in NPC incidence relate to the interaction between EBV, genetic susceptibility, and dietary/environmental factors.

options: Simple, non-bloody mucoid discharge responding well to treatment
Persistent bleeding and lack of response to standard therapy
Isolated, occasional tinnitus with no discharge
questions.explanation: Persistent, blood-stained discharge that fails to respond to standard antimicrobial therapy for presumed chronic otitis media should raise clinical suspicion for underlying malignancy rather than assuming ongoing benign infection. This atypical treatment-resistant pattern is a key clinical red flag prompting biopsy and further staging investigation. Maintaining vigilance for this pattern helps avoid delayed cancer diagnosis in patients with a background of chronic ear disease.
questions.question: A patient with long-standing presumed chronic otitis media develops a new, persistent, foul-smelling blood-stained discharge unresponsive to standard treatment. Which clinical feature should raise suspicion of underlying middle ear carcinoma rather than benign disease?
A nasal polyp that is red, fleshy, friable with a granular surface, especially in an older patient, should immediately raise suspicion for:
questions.explanation: The classic teaching is that any polyp that is red, fleshy, friable, bleeds easily, or has a granular surface — especially in an older patient — must raise strong suspicion for underlying malignancy. All nasal polyps should ideally be subjected to histological examination. A simple nasal polyp may also masquerade as a malignancy underneath, reinforcing the importance of histology.

options: Antibiotic therapy must never be delayed at all
Most cases improve spontaneously; some need only observation
questions.explanation: Most cases of otitis media improve spontaneously, and cases requiring treatment may be managed with antibiotics and analgesics or with observation alone. Watchful waiting is a valid approach in mild uncomplicated AOM in children over 2 years. Immediate antibiotic treatment is recommended for severe cases, young infants, or bilateral disease.
questions.question: Which of the following statements is MOST accurate regarding the management of AOM in children?

A patient with a nasal cavity mass undergoes biopsy showing an inverted growth pattern arising from Schneiderian mucosa. Why is careful complete excision of this lesion important even though it is histologically benign?
options: It is only used in allergic disease
It may seed tumour cells locally
It cannot access the maxillary sinus
questions.explanation: Inverted papilloma, despite being histologically benign, has a marked tendency toward local recurrence if incompletely excised and carries a recognised risk of harbouring or later developing squamous cell carcinoma. Complete surgical excision, often via an endoscopic or open approach with wide margins, is therefore essential. Long-term endoscopic follow-up is required to detect recurrence early.

Perichondritis of the auricle, particularly following piercing of the cartilaginous portion, is commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and empirical antibiotic therapy should provide reliable anti-pseudomonal cover. Delayed or inadequate treatment risks progression to chondritis with cartilage destruction and permanent auricular deformity. Prompt recognition and targeted treatment help preserve the structural integrity of the ear.
questions.question: A patient develops perichondritis of the auricle following ear piercing trauma. Which organism should treatment PRIMARILY target?

questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery lies approximately 2 centimetres posterolateral to the deep surface of the palatine tonsil. In roughly 1% of patients, it may be anomalously positioned just deep to the superior constrictor muscle, presenting a catastrophic haemorrhage risk during tonsillectomy. Pre-operative identification of vascular anomalies and maintaining the correct surgical plane within the tonsil capsule avoids this serious complication.
questions.question: The internal carotid artery lies in what relationship to the deep surface of the palatine tonsil?

options: Vocal cord nodules from voice overuse
questions.question: A patient develops stridor and voice change after prolonged intubation for ICU ventilation. Laryngoscopy reveals bilateral posterior glottic scarring. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prolonged endotracheal intubation can cause pressure injury to the posterior larynx at the site of the endotracheal tube and arytenoid cartilages, leading to granulation tissue and subsequent scarring that narrows the airway, known as posterior glottic or subglottic stenosis. This differs from vocal cord palsy, which shows immobile but non-scarred cords on examination. Dilation, laser therapy, or open reconstruction may be needed depending on severity.

questions.question: Tympanostomy tubes (ventilation tubes/grommets) in OME are MOST recommended when effusion has persisted for more than:
questions.explanation: Tympanostomy tubes are recommended for OME that persists for more than 3 months, particularly with a hearing handicap. Adenoidectomy may provide additional benefit alongside tube insertion. Three to four episodes of OM per year in an ear with chronic or recurrent OME is another indication.

Reactive or eczematous otitis externa results from an underlying dermatological condition such as eczema, psoriasis, or seborrhoeic dermatitis affecting the ear canal skin, producing intense itching and scaling without an infective organism as the primary driver. Management focuses on treating the underlying skin condition alongside gentle aural hygiene, rather than antimicrobial therapy alone. Distinguishing reactive from infective otitis externa avoids unnecessary or ineffective antibiotic use.
questions.question: A patient presents with intense itching and scaling of the external ear canal with no infective organism identified, related to an underlying skin condition. What is the MOST likely cause?

questions.explanation: The most useful initial investigations in severe recurrent epistaxis include: full blood count (FBC) to assess anaemia and platelet count, clotting profile (PT, APTT, fibrinogen) to identify coagulopathy, and blood grouping and cross-matching for potential transfusion. Lipid profile is mentioned for atherosclerosis risk. Paranasal sinus X-rays or CT scan are additional if sinonasal pathology is suspected.
questions.question: Which of the following investigations is MOST useful in the initial assessment of a patient with severe recurrent epistaxis?
options: Plain sinus X-ray in Waters' view
Clotting profile, FBC, and blood grouping

questions.question: Which of the following bones does NOT contribute to the lateral wall of the nasal cavity?
questions.explanation: The vomer forms the inferior part of the nasal septum (medial wall), not the lateral wall. The lateral wall is formed by the lacrimal, ethmoid, palatine, maxilla, and inferior turbinate bones. The septum and lateral wall are entirely separate structures anatomically.

Amoxicillin-induced maculopapular rash in the setting of tonsillitis is the hallmark of infectious mononucleosis (EBV infection). The reaction occurs in up to 90% of EBV patients given aminopenicillins, compared to only 3-5% in those without EBV. It is not a true penicillin allergy but an immune-mediated drug-viral interaction. Correct diagnosis avoids labelling the patient as penicillin-allergic and guides appropriate antiviral supportive care.
questions.question: In a child with acute tonsillitis, treatment with amoxicillin results in a widespread maculopapular rash covering the trunk and limbs. The most likely underlying diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) is an immune-mediated condition causing eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal mucosa. Endoscopic findings include: concentric mucosal rings giving a 'trachealized' or 'feline' appearance, longitudinal linear furrows, white eosinophilic exudates, and mucosal fragility ('crpe paper' mucosa). EoE typically presents in young males with intermittent solid food dysphagia and food bolus impaction. Diagnosis requires biopsy showing =15 eosinophils per high-power field, and treatment involves proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical steroids, or elemental diet.
questions.question: Eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) presenting with dysphagia is characterised on endoscopy by:
options: Concentric rings (trachealization), linear furrows, and white exudates
Diffuse mucosal erythema without structural changes
Single large ulcer in the mid-oesophagus
Smooth regular stricture at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Diverticula along the posterior oesophageal wall
Superior canal BPPV diagnosed by straight head hanging
Multiple canal BPPV resolved by the Semont manoeuvre
Horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV diagnosed by the roll test
Central BPPV from posterior fossa tumour
Cupulolithiasis variant requiring only prolonged positioning
