The combination of restriction of upgaze with diplopia on upgaze especially in a young patient after direct orbital trauma requires urgent CT to assess entrapment and timely surgical decompression to avoid permanent diplopia.
questions.question: An orbital blow-out fracture causes the globe to be displaced and the inferior rectus/orbital fat to herniate. The clinical sign that most specifically suggests inferior rectus muscle entrapment is:

A patient with neurological disease develops dysarthria affecting respiration, phonation, articulation, resonance, and both voluntary and involuntary movement. Which type of movement is UNIQUELY mentioned as part of dysarthria?
questions.explanation: Dysarthria uniquely involves both voluntary and involuntary movements due to the neuromotor nature of the lesion. This distinguishes it from purely voluntary articulation disorders and explains why involuntary movements (tremors, spasms) in dysarthric patients interfere with speech even during non-speech activities.

questions.question: Downbeat nystagmus (fast phase beating downward) in a patient with chronic dizziness and ataxia most specifically indicates a lesion at:
questions.explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (fast phase directed downward, worst in lateral gaze) is a specific sign of pathology at the craniovertebral junction (foramen magnum region) or the flocculus/paraflocculus of the cerebellum most commonly Chiari malformation, cerebellar degeneration, or drug toxicity (lithium, anticonvulsants). It is a central sign that never occurs in peripheral vestibular lesions. Its presence mandates MRI of the posterior fossa and craniovertebral junction. Upbeat nystagmus indicates lower brainstem/medulla lesions (Wernicke's, medullary lesions).

questions.question: A patient with suspected laryngeal trauma after a direct blow to the neck presents with hoarseness, surgical emphysema, and a palpable loss of the normal laryngeal contour. What is the priority in immediate management?
questions.explanation: Blunt laryngeal trauma with surgical emphysema and loss of normal laryngeal landmarks indicates significant structural injury with a high risk of airway compromise that can progress rapidly, so securing the airway, sometimes via awake tracheostomy rather than orotracheal intubation which can worsen injury, takes priority over other investigations. CT imaging and further definitive management follow once the airway is secured. Delayed recognition of laryngeal trauma severity can result in life-threatening airway obstruction.
options: Immediate discharge with outpatient ENT follow-up only
Urgent airway assessment and secure airway management before further evaluation
Delayed imaging after several days of observation
Voice rest alone without airway assessment

questions.question: Treatment of ear cancer generally involves which combination approach?
questions.explanation: Ear cancer treatment generally involves surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy in a multimodal approach. The specific combination depends on tumour type, location, stage, and patient factors. Early external ear cancers (e.g., small BCC or SCC) may be managed with surgery or Mohs chemosurgery alone, while advanced tumours require multimodal treatment.

Posterior (poststyloid) compartment parapharyngeal abscess typically lacks trismus or tonsillar displacement but presents with toxicity and fever of unknown origin. Involvement of the neurovascular structures (carotid sheath contents) in this space can cause cranial neuropathies and Horner's syndrome.
questions.question: A patient with parapharyngeal abscess has no trismus but appears toxic with fever of unknown origin. This pattern MOST suggests involvement of:
options: Prestyloid compartment with medial pterygoid irritation

questions.explanation: Laryngeal mucosa lacks the protective mechanisms of the oesophagus and is far more sensitive to even brief acid exposure, so patients can develop significant laryngeal symptoms like hoarseness and throat clearing with minimal or no classic heartburn. This explains why LPR is often called silent reflux. Empirical proton pump inhibitor trials combined with laryngoscopy findings support the diagnosis.
options: Laryngopharyngeal reflux never involves gastric acid
Laryngeal mucosa is far more acid-sensitive than oesophageal mucosa
The larynx is fully protected from acid normally
Heartburn is required for any reflux diagnosis
Only nocturnal reflux causes laryngeal symptoms
questions.question: A patient with laryngopharyngeal reflux presents with hoarseness and chronic throat clearing but denies heartburn. Why might this patient lack typical reflux symptoms?

questions.explanation: Longitudinal temporal bone fractures account for up to 80% of all temporal bone fractures. They run parallel to the long axis of the petrous bone, typically from the squamoparietal suture through the tegmen tympani and along the external auditory canal. They are characteristically caused by temporoparietal head impacts. Longitudinal fractures more commonly cause conductive hearing loss, haemotympanum, EAC lacerations, and ossicular chain disruption, but less commonly cause facial nerve injury or sensorineural hearing loss compared to transverse fractures.
questions.question: Temporal bone fractures are classified by their orientation relative to the long axis of the petrous bone. Which type is most common, accounting for up to 80% of cases?
The MOST common route by which foreign bodies enter the nasal cavity in children is:
questions.explanation: Children most commonly insert foreign bodies into their own nasal cavities (anterior nares) during play and periods of unsupervised activity. Common objects include beads, peas, buttons, paper, and rubber erasers. This is the most prevalent route, distinguishing paediatric foreign bodies from adult ones where occupational or traumatic routes are more common. Animate foreign bodies may enter through the mouth during regurgitation.
options: Through penetrating wounds to the nose
Through the posterior nares during regurgitation at all times
Via the anterior nares by self-insertion during play

questions.question: During clinical assessment of speech disorders, indirect laryngoscopy is performed to look for all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Indirect laryngoscopy assesses the larynx including vocal cord polyps, nodules, degree of approximation, and other laryngeal lesions. Nasal cavity anatomy is assessed by anterior rhinoscopy or nasendoscopy, not by laryngoscopy, which looks only at the laryngopharynx.

options: Using a masking noise in the opposite ear
questions.question: A 'free field test' during audiological examination assesses hearing by:
questions.explanation: The simple free field test assesses hearing by noting the patient's response to normal and loud conversational voice at specific distances. While not precise, it provides a quick bedside estimate of functional hearing ability before formal audiometry.

questions.question: Which congenital condition predisposes to rhinosinusitis by causing a defect in mucociliary transport without absent cilia?
questions.explanation: Young syndrome consists of a triad of chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and azoospermia in males. The mechanism involves abnormal viscosity of secretions impairing mucociliary clearance, though the cilia themselves are structurally and functionally normal (distinguishing it from primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome). Sputum and sinus mucus are abnormally viscous.

questions.question: Erysipelas of the external ear is caused by:
questions.explanation: Erysipelas, a superficial skin infection with intense erythema and clear demarcation, is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Impetigo of the ear can also be caused by S. pyogenes or S. aureus. Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes diffuse and malignant otitis externa, not erysipelas.

options: Immobilising with topical lignocaine before removal
Irrigating the ear with cold water
questions.explanation: Insects in the EAC should first be immobilised with topical lignocaine (lidocaine) or ether before removal with gentle irrigation or alligator forceps under direct vision. A live insect moving in the canal causes intense pain and distress. Attempting forceps extraction of a live, moving insect risks incomplete removal and trauma.
questions.question: An insect in the external auditory canal should be managed FIRST by:

options: Identical prognosis regardless of onset timing
questions.question: A patient with facial nerve palsy following temporal bone trauma has complete paralysis with delayed onset 48 hours after injury. What does this timing suggest about prognosis?
questions.explanation: Delayed-onset facial palsy after trauma suggests oedema and compression rather than nerve transection, and generally carries a more favourable prognosis for spontaneous recovery than immediate complete paralysis, which more often indicates direct nerve injury. Electrodiagnostic testing helps guide the decision for surgical exploration in cases that fail to improve. Immediate paralysis is more likely to require decompression.

The head mirror is designed with a focal length of approximately twelve inches (one foot), allowing the examiner to work at a comfortable distance while maintaining a focused beam of reflected light on the structure being examined.
questions.question: When wearing the head mirror, the focal length for optimal examination is maintained at approximately:
Through which landmark do olfactory axon filaments pass to reach the olfactory bulb?
questions.explanation: Olfactory epithelium lies in the roof of the nasal cavity and its axons pass as filaments through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach neurons in the olfactory bulb, which lies on the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. This route explains how fractures of the cribriform plate can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.question: The primary risk of unmanaged facial palsy in the short term that requires urgent attention is:
questions.explanation: In complete facial palsy, lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the upper eyelid due to orbicularis oculi paralysis) exposes the cornea to desiccation, trauma, and infection. Corneal exposure keratopathy can progress rapidly to corneal ulceration, scarring, and permanent visual loss. Eye care is therefore the most urgent priority: frequent lubricant eye drops during the day, ointment and eye taping at night, moisture chamber spectacles, and ophthalmological review. Surgical eye procedures (tarsorrhaphy, gold weight implant) are required for severe or prolonged lagophthalmos.
options: Permanent facial disfigurement from muscle atrophy
Parotid gland inflammation from reduced secretion
Corneal exposure keratopathy from inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos)

questions.question: A patient with nasal polyps and topical steroid use develops epistaxis and is later found to have a septal perforation. Which practice most likely contributed to this complication?
questions.explanation: Repeated direct spraying of topical nasal steroid onto the septal mucosa, rather than angling laterally toward the turbinates, causes local mucosal thinning that can progress to perforation. Patients should be taught to aim the spray away from the septum toward the lateral nasal wall. This complication is preventable with correct technique and is not an inherent property of properly used steroid sprays.
options: Spraying steroid directly onto the septum repeatedly
Using the spray once daily as directed
Storing the spray at room temperature
Using saline irrigation before the spray
Tilting the head forward during administration

questions.explanation: Hardwood dust exposure (mahogany, teak, and other hardwoods used in the furniture and cabinet-making industries) is most specifically associated with intestinal-type adenocarcinoma of the ethmoid sinus. Nickel and chromium dusts are associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the nasal cavity and antrum. Wood dust carcinogenesis is thought to be related to specific organic chemical components of hardwood species.
questions.question: Exposure to which occupational substance is most specifically associated with intestinal-type adenocarcinoma of the ethmoid sinus?

questions.explanation: Inverted papilloma carries a recognised risk of malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma in a proportion of cases and has a high tendency for local recurrence if incompletely excised, making complete surgical removal with clear margins the standard of care. Endoscopic resection has become the preferred approach in appropriately selected cases, replacing more invasive open techniques. Long-term surveillance is required due to recurrence risk even after complete excision.
options: The tumour is always metastatic at presentation
Radiotherapy alone reliably cures the condition
The tumour has a recognised risk of malignant transformation and local recurrence
The tumour resolves spontaneously without treatment
Biopsy alone is curative in most cases
questions.question: A patient with an inverted papilloma of the nasal cavity is being counselled about management. Why is complete surgical excision with tumour-free margins critical?

options: Head rotation to close the weaker piriform sinus
Effortful swallowing to increase pharyngeal pressure
Prolonged laryngeal elevation, increasing UOS opening duration
questions.explanation: The Mendelsohn manoeuvre involves the patient voluntarily sustaining laryngeal elevation at its peak position during swallowing (holding the 'Adam's apple' up). This prolongs the duration of hyoid and laryngeal elevation, which mechanically holds the cricopharyngeus open for a longer duration, increasing upper oesophageal sphincter opening time and improving bolus passage from the pharynx into the oesophagus. It is particularly useful for patients with reduced laryngeal elevation and incomplete UOS opening as the underlying dysphagia mechanism.
questions.question: The Mendelsohn manoeuvre is a compensatory swallowing technique used in dysphagia rehabilitation. The effect it achieves is:
A child aged 3 presents with recurrent hoarseness and biphasic stridor. Direct laryngoscopy reveals multiple wart-like lesions on the vocal cords. What is the underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis in young children is caused by human papillomavirus, typically acquired perinatally from an infected maternal genital tract, and produces wart-like laryngeal lesions causing hoarseness and stridor. It characteristically requires multiple repeated surgical debulking procedures because of its tendency to recur. Airway obstruction can become significant if lesions are not regularly managed.

questions.question: A 35-year-old mushroom farmer presents with recurrent sneezing and wheezing. The MOST likely etiology of his symptoms is:
questions.explanation: Mushroom farmers are exposed to fungal spores, which are potent allergens causing allergic rhinitis and asthma. This occupational fungal allergy is a key history-taking point in ENT and respiratory ENT assessments.

questions.question: Vertigo as a presenting symptom in ear cancer suggests invasion of which structure?
questions.explanation: Vertigo in ear cancer suggests invasion of the labyrinth (inner ear), specifically the membranous labyrinth or its bony housing. This indicates advanced local disease extension beyond the middle ear. Combined with hearing loss, facial palsy, and blood-stained discharge, labyrinthine invasion signals a poor prognosis.

Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is by far the most common cause of obstructive sleep apnoea in otherwise healthy children, and adenotonsillectomy is typically curative in this group. Other causes such as micrognathia or laryngomalacia are less common and often relate to specific craniofacial or laryngeal abnormalities rather than simple lymphoid hypertrophy. Polysomnography can help confirm severity and guide the urgency of surgical referral.
questions.question: A child with obstructive sleep apnoea is assessed for the most common underlying cause in the paediatric population. What is this most common cause?
Which anatomical structure forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa and is relevant to JNA origin?
options: Posterior wall of the maxillary sinus
Anterior surface of the pterygoid process
Lateral wall of the sphenoid sinus
Perpendicular plate of the palatine bone with the sphenopalatine foramen
questions.explanation: The medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa is formed by the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, which contains the sphenopalatine foramen the opening through which the sphenopalatine artery and nasopalatine nerve pass into the nasal cavity. This foramen is at the posterosuperior wall of the nasal cavity and is the consistent site of origin of JNA. Understanding this anatomy is essential both for explaining JNA's origin and for planning endoscopic surgery, where ligating the sphenopalatine artery at this foramen is a key early step.

questions.question: Oral prednisone in AOM is administered in combination with which other primary treatment?
questions.explanation: Oral prednisone/prednisolone at 1mg/kg/day is administered in combination with antibiotics in AOM management. The combination reduces mucosal inflammation while antibiotics address the bacterial infection. Steroids are not used as monotherapy in AOM because bacterial infection must be concurrently treated.

questions.question: In a properly conducted head mirror examination, the focal point of reflected light should be adjusted by:
questions.explanation: After initial setup, the examiner reflects the head mirror light onto their palm to confirm effectiveness, then readjusts the mirror angle to focus the reflected light beam onto the specific structure being examined. This active readjustment is essential for optimal visualization.

The 'bird-beak' or 'rat-tail' appearance on barium swallow a smooth, tapered narrowing of the lower oesophagus at the gastro-oesophageal junction is the classic radiological sign of achalasia. It represents the non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter viewed in profile, with the dilated oesophageal body above and the narrowed sphincter below. In carcinoma of the cardia, the narrowing is irregular and asymmetric. Peptic stricture produces a smoother but shorter and more irregular narrowing higher in the oesophagus above a hiatus hernia.
questions.question: Dysphagia associated with a smooth, tapered narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction on barium swallow (the 'bird-beak' appearance) is diagnostic of:

questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging, such as CT or MRI, is the appropriate first-line investigation for a suspected vascular middle ear mass presenting with pulsatile tinnitus, allowing characterisation of the lesion's extent and vascularity to guide further management. Simple bedside hearing tests do not provide the anatomical detail required to evaluate a suspected mass lesion. Appropriate imaging is essential before any biopsy or surgical planning given the vascular nature of such lesions.
questions.question: A patient presents with pulsatile tinnitus and a bluish mass visible behind the tympanic membrane. What is the FIRST-LINE investigation to evaluate this presentation?
options: Contrast-enhanced imaging such as CT or MRI

questions.explanation: Bulbar palsy impairs the cranial nerve-mediated swallowing mechanism, causing repeated aspiration of saliva and food into the airway. Tracheostomy allows direct suction of the tracheobronchial tree (toileting) and may be cuffed to prevent further aspiration, protecting the lower airways.
questions.question: Bulbar palsy causing aspiration is listed as an indication for tracheobronchial toileting via tracheostomy. This is because:
options: Bulbar palsy causes direct laryngeal paralysis
Tracheostomy allows vocal rehabilitation in bulbar palsy
Impaired swallowing causes repeated aspiration requiring suction
Bulbar palsy causes complete respiratory arrest

questions.question: Squamous cell carcinoma of the external ear MOST commonly presents as:
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma most commonly presents as a raised, ulcerated lesion on the helix of the auricle. Treatment is wide surgical excision or Mohs surgery. Pre- or postoperative radiation is used for advanced lesions. Invasion of the external auditory canal or temporal bone requires temporal bone resection.
options: A discrete nodule with raised edges
Raised ulcerated lesion on the helix

questions.question: Palatal perforation or incompetence (e.g., cleft palate) predisposes to nasal foreign bodies entering via which route?
questions.explanation: Patients with palatal perforation or incompetence (e.g., cleft palate, palatal fistulas) are at risk of food and objects entering the nasal cavity from the oral cavity via the posterior nares during swallowing or regurgitation, as the soft palate cannot adequately seal the nasopharynx from the oropharynx. This is the mechanism for the posterior nares route of entry for nasal foreign bodies.

questions.question: A patient with primary ciliary dyskinesia presents with a combination of chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and infertility. Which additional classic finding, when present, defines Kartagener syndrome specifically?
questions.explanation: Kartagener syndrome is a specific subtype of primary ciliary dyskinesia defined by the additional presence of situs inversus, alongside chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and reduced fertility due to impaired ciliary and flagellar motility. Not all patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia have situs inversus, since normal organ situs depends on functioning embryonic nodal cilia in only about half of affected individuals. Recognition of this triad prompts genetic and ciliary function testing for confirmation.

Caloric vertigo during ear syringing results from thermal stimulation of the vestibular labyrinth when irrigation fluid temperature differs from body temperature, inducing convection currents within the semicircular canals that trigger nystagmus and a sensation of vertigo. Using body-temperature water for irrigation minimises this uncomfortable but generally self-limiting effect. Warning patients of this possible sensation beforehand helps reduce anxiety if it occurs.
questions.question: A patient undergoing ear syringing develops sudden vertigo and nystagmus during the procedure. What is the underlying mechanism of this caloric response?
options: Direct mechanical damage to the cochlea
Thermal stimulation of the vestibular labyrinth by irrigation fluid temperature
Psychogenic response unrelated to the procedure
An allergic reaction to the irrigation solution

questions.question: Which hormonal characteristic of JNA supports its exclusive occurrence in pre/adolescent males?
options: Androgen receptors demonstrated on tumour cells
questions.explanation: Androgen receptors have been demonstrated immunohistochemically on JNA tumour cells, supporting the hypothesis that androgens drive the growth of these tumours during the surge of puberty. This explains the exclusive occurrence in males and the tendency toward spontaneous regression in adulthood as androgen levels stabilise. Anti-androgen therapy (flutamide) has been explored as adjuvant treatment to reduce tumour size pre-operatively, though surgical resection remains the primary treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a well-known complication of diabetes mellitus and other immunocompromised states. It is a life-threatening infection requiring aggressive management.
questions.question: A patient with diabetes mellitus presents with severe earache and purulent otorrhea that does not respond to standard antibiotics. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
In plain radiographs, malignancy of the paranasal sinuses is MOST suggested by which finding?
questions.explanation: Bone destruction (erosion) of sinus walls on plain X-ray is the hallmark feature of malignancy in the paranasal sinuses. Opacification and fluid levels can occur in benign conditions, but bone destruction strongly suggests invasive carcinoma or aggressive tumour.

The Seigle's speculum creates a sealed system allowing alternating positive and negative pressure to be applied, testing the mobility of the tympanic membrane in response to pressure changes. Reduced mobility suggests middle ear effusion or ossicular fixation. Colour and cerumen are assessed by direct visual inspection, not pneumatic testing.
questions.question: A Seigle's pneumatic speculum is used during otoscopic examination. Its PRIMARY purpose is to assess:
Oestrogen and steroids are classified under which category of drug therapy for allergy?
questions.explanation: Oestrogen and steroids are classified as endocrine-based drug therapies in ENT allergy treatment. Steroids reduce allergic mucosal inflammation while oestrogen changes can affect nasal mucosal vasoreactivity, explaining allergy exacerbation with hormonal changes.

Conductive hearing loss in longitudinal temporal bone fractures results primarily from haemotympanum (blood filling the middle ear space, causing a maximum 30 dB conductive loss) and ossicular chain disruption. The most common ossicular injury is incudostapedial joint separation. Haemotympanum typically resolves spontaneously over 4-6 weeks with recovery of hearing; persistent conductive loss suggests ossicular discontinuity requiring surgical exploration and ossiculoplasty. Up to 80% of conductive hearing loss from temporal bone fractures resolves spontaneously.
questions.question: The conductive hearing loss seen in longitudinal temporal bone fractures is most commonly caused by:
options: Cochlear hair cell damage from concussive force
Serous otitis media from Eustachian tube injury

questions.question: Glomus tumours of the ear are often described as 'malignant by location' despite frequently benign histology. What does this specifically mean?
options: They stay confined to the canal only
Their growth can cause serious local destruction
They spread only through the bloodstream
They never cause local tissue damage
They are always malignant with metastatic potential
questions.explanation: Glomus tumours are frequently histologically benign but described as 'malignant by location' because their anatomical position and locally invasive growth pattern can cause significant destruction of surrounding vital structures such as cranial nerves and bone, leading to serious functional complications despite lacking true malignant metastatic potential in most cases. This distinction is important for counselling patients about prognosis and the rationale for treatment even in histologically benign tumours. Management therefore focuses on controlling local growth and preserving function.

options: Oropharyngeal SCC shows strong HPV-16 association; NPC shows EBV association
Both are equally associated with HPV
NPC shows HPV association; oropharyngeal cancer shows EBV
NPC is HPV-positive only in non-endemic regions
questions.question: Oropharyngeal cancer differs from NPC in which clinically important way regarding HPV association?
questions.explanation: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsillar and base of tongue) has a well-established association with Human Papillomavirus type 16 (HPV-16), which drives distinct molecular carcinogenesis through E6/E7 oncoproteins inactivating p53 and pRb. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has better prognosis than HPV-negative. In contrast, NPC is driven by EBV and not HPV. These distinct viral associations reflect different epithelial types, anatomical sites, and patient demographics (younger, non-smoker, HPV-positive OPSCC vs middle-aged endemic-region NPC).

Little's area on the anterior nasal septum contains Kiesselbach's plexus, an anastomotic network of vessels from the anterior and posterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, and greater palatine arteries, making it the most common site of anterior epistaxis. Direct pressure over the nasal alae for 10 to 15 minutes usually controls bleeding from this location. Posterior bleeds from Woodruff's plexus are less common but more severe.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent epistaxis from Little's area is being treated. Which vascular plexus is the source of bleeding in this location?

questions.explanation: Sequestration of bone in situ refers to devascularized bone fragments that form in the nasal cavity following nasal trauma (fractures with devascularised bone) or tertiary syphilis, which causes osteonecrosis and gummatous destruction of nasal bones and cartilage. The sequestrated bone behaves as a foreign body, causing infection, discharge, and nasal obstruction similar to exogenous foreign bodies.
questions.question: Sequestration of bone in situ is listed as an aetiological route for nasal foreign bodies. This most commonly occurs following:
options: Nasal polyp surgery leaving bone fragments
Nasal bone trauma or tertiary syphilis

questions.explanation: Atlantooccipital dislocation in retropharyngeal abscess results from inflammatory ligamentous laxity and direct involvement of the atlantooccipital ligaments by adjacent infection. This potentially catastrophic complication causes cervical instability and may lead to spinal cord injury.
questions.question: Atlantooccipital dislocation is listed as a complication of retropharyngeal abscess. This occurs because:
options: Abscess causes direct vertebral erosion at C1-C2
The abscess tracks along the prevertebral space
Ligamentous laxity and inflammation destabilize the atlantooccipital
Surgical drainage disrupts the atlantoaxial ligament
Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity only
Combined Type I and Type III hypersensitivity
Autoimmune IgG antibodies against sinus epithelium
questions.question: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) is associated with which immunological mechanism?
questions.explanation: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis involves both Type I (IgE-mediated, causing immediate reaction) and Type III (immune complex deposition) hypersensitivity reactions to fungal antigens (usually Aspergillus and dematiaceous fungi). Diagnosis requires a positive RAST/skin test to fungus, nasal polyps, eosinophilic mucin, CT evidence of hyperdense material, and fungal identification.

questions.question: Retropharyngeal abscess in children under 6 months presents with stridor, drooling, and pyrexia. Lateral soft tissue X-ray of the neck typically shows:
questions.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess — a collection of pus in the retropharyngeal space (between the posterior pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral fascia) — is confirmed on lateral soft tissue neck X-ray by widening of the prevertebral soft tissue space (>7 mm at C2 or >14 mm at C6 in children). The 'thumbprint sign' on AP neck X-ray indicates epiglottitis; the 'steeple sign' (subglottic narrowing) indicates croup.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms is the most common cause of bacterial tonsillitis requiring antibiotics?
questions.explanation: Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is the predominant bacterial cause of tonsillitis requiring antibiotic therapy, accounting for approximately 15-30% of cases in children. Its identification is clinically important because penicillin treatment prevents rheumatic fever and suppurative complications. Viral causes are more common overall, but bacterial tonsillitis with exudate warrants antibiotic treatment.

questions.question: Chondrosarcoma is the malignant counterpart of chondroma. In the nose, the most common benign cartilaginous tumour (chondroma) arises from which structure?
options: Maxillary sinus floor at all times
questions.explanation: Chondroma is a benign tumour of hyaline cartilage arising most commonly from the nasal septum (quadrilateral cartilage) or turbinate cartilage in the nasal cavity. Its malignant counterpart, chondrosarcoma, is more common than chondroma in the sinonasal region and characteristically appears on CT as a heterogeneous mass with ring-and-arc calcification pattern in a destructive lesion.

Research available on endoscopic sinus surgery suggests that radical endoscopic procedures involving complete fronto-sphenoidectomies lead to greater perceived benefits by patients in terms of symptom relief. This is attributed to more complete removal of the disease burden and better restoration of sinus drainage compared to limited procedures, though at the cost of greater surgical complexity.
questions.question: Which surgical approach for nasal polyps combines complete fronto-sphenoidectomy and is reported to provide the greatest perceived benefit to patients?
options: Radical endoscopic sinus surgery with fronto-sphenoidectomy
External ethmoidectomy via Lynch well-defined incision
Osseous metastasis to the cervical spine
questions.explanation: Bone metastases to the spine, particularly the cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae, are the most common form of distant NPC recurrence and can present with pain, neurological deficits, and instability 18 months after treatment completion. PET-CT showing increased FDG uptake in a vertebral body in a patient with prior NPC is highly suspicious for osseous metastasis rather than post-radiation change (which shows decreased uptake). Biopsy or MRI correlation should confirm the diagnosis before systemic therapy.
questions.question: A patient with NPC post-treatment develops neck stiffness and unsteady gait 18 months later. PET-CT shows increased uptake in the upper cervical spine. The most likely explanation is:

options: Without the patient present to prevent intimidation
Always with the patient present to respect autonomy
After the patient has independently chosen treatment
Only after surgery has been performed
Simultaneously with the patient in all circumstances
questions.question: In the multidisciplinary cancer clinic setting, treatment discussions involving specialists should occur:
questions.explanation: Multidisciplinary treatment discussions are conducted without the patient present to allow frank specialist deliberation without intimidating the patient. Once the team reaches consensus on the optimal treatment plan, the decision is communicated to the patient with appropriate explanation and consent.

options: Early mucosal disease with no spread
Erosion through the sinus floor into palate
questions.explanation: Loose teeth and palatal swelling reflect inferior tumour extension through the floor of the maxillary sinus into the hard palate and alveolar ridge, indicating locally advanced rather than early disease. This clinical sign often prompts patients to first present to a dentist rather than an ENT surgeon, contributing to delayed diagnosis. Imaging is required to fully define the extent of bony erosion before surgical planning.
questions.question: A patient with maxillary sinus carcinoma develops loosening of the upper molar teeth and a palatal swelling. What does this indicate about tumour extent?
Palatal myoclonus as a cause of objective non-pulsatile tinnitus is characterised by:
options: Intermittent tinnitus only during REM sleep
Pulsatile tinnitus synchronous with the heartbeat
High-pitched ringing matching the audiometric pure-tone threshold
Rhythmic clicking tinnitus from involuntary palatal muscle contractions at 60-240/min
Tinnitus audiometry showing a pure-tone match below 500 Hz
questions.explanation: Palatal myoclonus produces objective, non-pulsatile, rhythmic clicking tinnitus from involuntary contractions of the levator veli palatini and tensor veli palatini muscles at a rate of 60-240 contractions per minute (often perceived as a regular clicking or crackling sound). The myoclonus opens and closes the Eustachian tube orifice, creating the clicking noise. The clicks can be heard by the examiner with a stethoscope placed near the patient's ear and observed as rhythmic palatal movements on inspection. It can result from brainstem stroke, MS, or occur idiopathically.

The lamina papyracea is the very thin lateral wall of the ethmoid labyrinth that separates it from the orbital contents. Its thinness explains why ethmoid sinusitis is a common cause of orbital complications such as periorbital cellulitis and orbital abscess, and why it is prone to inadvertent penetration during sinus surgery.
questions.question: The ethmoid sinus is separated from the orbit by which bony structure that is surgically significant?

questions.explanation: Initial management of deep neck infection with respiratory distress includes supplemental oxygen, IV fluid resuscitation, intravenous antibiotics, and preparation for emergency surgery. A systematic approach addressing airway, fluid, and antimicrobial therapy simultaneously is essential.
questions.question: Initial management of a paediatric patient with suspected retropharyngeal abscess and respiratory distress should include:

questions.explanation: Penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae in rhinosinusitis is generally overcome by using high-dose amoxicillin to achieve adequate tissue concentrations, or by switching to a respiratory fluoroquinolone with reliable pneumococcal activity in resistant or treatment-failure cases. Standard low-dose penicillin regimens are unlikely to be effective against resistant strains. Culture-directed therapy improves outcomes compared with continued empirical treatment in non-responders.
questions.question: A patient with sinusitis is treated empirically, and culture later confirms penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which antibiotic is most appropriate for this organism?

A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis undergoes functional endoscopic sinus surgery. Intraoperatively, CSF leak is suspected after violation of the skull base. Which structure was most likely breached?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate and fovea ethmoidalis form the thin, variably positioned roof of the ethmoid sinuses adjacent to the anterior skull base, making them the most common sites of iatrogenic CSF leak during endoscopic sinus surgery. The Keros classification describes variations in cribriform plate depth that influence this risk. Immediate recognition and repair, often with a mucosal or fascial graft, prevents ascending meningitis.

Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) are delayed non-suppurative complications of Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis. They are immune-mediated (due to molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and host tissues) rather than direct infection complications. Suppurative complications include peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, and sinusitis.
options: Direct toxic complication of streptococcal exotoxin
questions.question: Complications of exudative streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis can be classified as suppurative and non-suppurative. Acute rheumatic fever is which class of complication?

questions.explanation: When anterior packing fails to control epistaxis, posterior bleeding is suspected and a balloon catheter or traditional postnasal pack is inserted to tamponade the posterior nasal cavity, often requiring hospital admission for monitoring given the risk of hypoxia and cardiac complications from the pack. This step precedes more invasive options such as endoscopic artery ligation or embolisation, which are reserved for cases where packing fails. Careful monitoring for pressure necrosis and airway compromise is required with posterior packs.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent epistaxis from the posterior nasal cavity fails anterior packing. What is the next appropriate step before considering surgical ligation?
options: Posterior nasal packing with a balloon catheter
Discharge home with oral iron supplementation

questions.question: Upregulation of which gene is implicated in the host predisposition to otitis media via mucin production?
questions.explanation: Upregulation of the MUC5B gene leads to increased mucin production, contributing to middle ear effusion in otitis media. Cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutation) also predisposes to OME through mucus abnormalities. Genetic predisposition to otitis media involves multiple interacting pathways.

Immediate complete facial paralysis after temporal bone trauma is more suggestive of direct nerve transection or severe injury than the oedema-related mechanism seen in delayed-onset palsy, and often warrants surgical exploration and possible nerve repair or grafting. In contrast, delayed-onset palsy following trauma usually reflects oedema and has a better prognosis with conservative management. Electrodiagnostic testing helps clarify the extent of nerve injury and guide decision-making.
questions.question: A patient with a transverse temporal bone fracture develops immediate complete facial paralysis and profound sensorineural hearing loss. What does the immediate onset suggest?
options: Simple nerve oedema with excellent spontaneous recovery expected
A benign self-limiting Bell's palsy coincidentally
Delayed onset injury from post-traumatic swelling
No urgency for further assessment or imaging
Direct nerve transection requiring surgical exploration

questions.question: A cervical bruit heard on auscultation of the neck MOST likely indicates pathology in which structure?
questions.explanation: A cervical bruit results from turbulent blood flow, most commonly due to carotid artery stenosis or a carotid body tumour. Auscultation of the neck is a critical step in systematic ENT examination to detect vascular pathology.

questions.question: A patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with nasal crusting, septal perforation, and saddle nose deformity, alongside renal impairment. Which serological marker supports this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is strongly associated with c-ANCA, targeting proteinase 3, and this serological marker, combined with the characteristic triad of upper respiratory tract, lower respiratory tract, and renal involvement, supports the diagnosis alongside tissue biopsy showing necrotising granulomatous vasculitis. Recognising this systemic vasculitis is essential in patients presenting with destructive nasal disease and additional systemic features such as renal impairment, since management requires immunosuppressive therapy rather than surgery alone. Early diagnosis significantly improves long-term renal and overall prognosis.

questions.question: In COM, the bacteriological method of choice to avoid contamination during otorrhea sampling is:
questions.explanation: The micropipette technique of deeply seated otorrhea within the middle ear cavity via the perforation is the method of choice in active COM to avoid contamination from EAC commensals. Standard EAC swabs may be contaminated by surface organisms. Culture results guide targeted antibiotic selection.

MRI of the petromastoid is superior to CT in evaluating soft tissue extent, intracranial involvement, and vascular involvement by ear tumours including glomus tumours and carcinomas. CT provides better bony detail. Together, CT and MRI are complementary investigations providing a complete picture of tumour extent for surgical planning.
questions.question: MRI of the petromastoid region in ear cancer is specifically superior to CT in evaluating:
options: Soft tissue extent and vascular involvement
Full mastoid air cell pneumatisation pattern

questions.explanation: Otitis externa is defined as inflammation of the skin of the external auditory meatus (EAM). Middle ear inflammation is termed otitis media. The external auditory meatus includes the cartilaginous and bony portions of the external ear canal up to the tympanic membrane.
questions.question: Otitis externa is most precisely defined as inflammation of the skin of the:

questions.explanation: In peritonsillar abscess, the inflammatory oedema and pus push the soft palate and uvula away from the affected side, producing contralateral deviation of the uvula. This is the opposite of the deviation seen in palatal motor paralysis (where the uvula deviates toward the intact side). Identifying the side of uvular deviation helps the clinician locate the abscess for needle aspiration, directing the needle toward the contralateral (deviated away) side where the abscess is expanding.
questions.question: In a patient with peritonsillar abscess, the uvula characteristically deviates to which side?

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid and runs in close proximity to the thyroid gland, making it vulnerable during thyroidectomy. Injury causes vocal cord paralysis in the paramedian position, producing breathiness and an ineffective cough due to poor glottic closure. Careful nerve identification during surgery reduces this risk.
options: Vagus nerve trunk proximal to the larynx
questions.question: A patient with a unilateral vocal cord palsy following thyroidectomy is noted to have a breathy voice and weak cough. Which nerve was most likely injured?

questions.explanation: Hearing aids amplify sound to improve the patient's perception of speech and environmental sounds. They do not restore normal cochlear function or repair damaged hair cells. Careful fitting is critical in SNHL because cochlear distortion and central processing deficits may limit the benefit obtained from amplification.
questions.question: The primary objective of hearing aid fitting in sensorineural hearing loss is to:
A patient with parapharyngeal abscess is found on CT to have a small (<3 cm), unilocular, non-extending abscess. The most appropriate management is:
questions.explanation: Small, unilocular, non-extending deep neck abscesses are amenable to minimally invasive CT-guided needle aspiration, which allows early specimen collection for culture, avoids a neck scar, and reduces cost and hospital stay compared to open drainage. Up to 80% of carefully selected patients can be successfully treated with needle aspiration. Larger, multilocular, or rapidly extending abscesses require formal external surgical drainage.

questions.question: CT scan of the petromastoid region in ear cancer assessment provides which information NOT available on plain X-ray?
questions.explanation: CT scan of the petromastoid provides superior resolution compared to plain X-rays, demonstrating bony destruction, extent of disease spread, and involvement of adjacent structures. MRI provides additional soft tissue detail. High-resolution CT scanning also evaluates the extent of glomus tumour disease and guides surgical approach.
options: The presence of a mass only
Shows bony destruction with superior resolution
Glue-like fluid in the middle ear
Retracted TM stuck to middle ear
questions.question: Adhesive otitis media is best described as:
questions.explanation: Adhesive otitis media occurs when a thin retracted tympanic membrane becomes sucked into the middle ear cavity and adheres to middle ear structures. It is a distinct classification from OME, AOM, and chronic suppurative OM. It can lead to conductive hearing loss and predispose to cholesteatoma formation.

questions.question: Subglottis is defined as the region extending from the free margin of the true vocal cords to what distance inferiorly?
questions.explanation: The subglottis extends from 5 cm below the free margin of the true vocal cords to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage. This anatomical definition is important in staging laryngeal cancer and planning radiotherapy fields for subglottic or transglottic tumours.

Patients with asthma have approximately twice the risk of polyp recurrence following surgical treatment compared to non-asthmatic patients. This is attributed to the shared underlying eosinophilic inflammatory process affecting both the upper and lower airways. Samter's triad (polyps + asthma + aspirin hypersensitivity) is associated with the most refractory polyposis and highest recurrence rates.
questions.question: Recurrence after surgical treatment of nasal polyps is highest in patients with which comorbidity?
Laryngomalacia is characterized by which clinical features and natural history?
options: Onset at birth with stridor, hoarse voice, and worsening until age 5
Progressive stridor from birth due to subglottic stenosis
Acute onset stridor after viral URTI in an older child
Bilateral vocal cord paralysis causing biphasic stridor from birth
questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia (congenital flaccidity of the laryngeal structures) is the most common cause of stridor in neonates and infants. Characteristic features: inspiratory stridor present from birth, completely normal voice (unlike vocal cord pathology), stridor worsens when supine and improves in the prone position, paroxysmal episodes during feeding or crying. Natural history: usually resolves spontaneously by age 2 as cartilage matures.

questions.question: Which investigation provides the best information on intracranial extension and soft tissue boundaries of JNA?
questions.explanation: MRI with gadolinium contrast provides the best characterisation of soft tissue extent, intracranial extension, dural involvement, and orbital invasion in JNA. JNA demonstrates intense homogeneous enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted sequences. The 'salt-and-pepper' appearance on MRI (mixed signal from vascular flow voids and fibrous elements) is characteristic. CT complements MRI by better demonstrating bone erosion and foraminal widening. Both modalities together provide comprehensive pre-operative staging information.
options: High-resolution CT of the skull base
Cortex and association paths of dominant
Peripheral cranial nerves VII and XII
questions.explanation: Aphasia results from lesions in the cerebral cortex and association pathways of the dominant hemisphere (usually left hemisphere in right-handed individuals). These cortical areas (Broca's and Wernicke's areas) are responsible for language production and comprehension.
questions.question: Aphasia is caused by lesions in which neurological structures?

options: A raised ulcerated lesion on the helix
Nodule with raised edges, central crater
questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma presents classically as a discrete nodule with smooth, raised edges, a central crater (ulcer), and superficial telangiectasias. It is locally invasive and may invade the EAC, middle ear, TMJ, or parotid if poorly controlled. Treatment of choice is wide surgical excision or Mohs chemosurgery.
questions.question: Basal cell carcinoma of the external ear characteristically presents as:

options: Urgent ear syringing regardless of insect state
Instil oil to immobilise or kill the insect
Refer for surgery without first aid
Apply a topical steroid cream directly
questions.question: A patient presents with an insect trapped in the external auditory canal, causing significant discomfort. What is the FIRST step in managing this situation?
questions.explanation: The first step in managing a live insect in the ear canal is to instil oil or a similar liquid to immobilise or kill the insect, which reduces further movement-related discomfort and trauma before attempting extraction. Attempting immediate forceful extraction of a live, moving insect risks pushing it deeper or causing canal injury. Once immobilised, careful removal under direct visualisation can then be performed safely.

Subjective sensorineural tinnitus shows increasing prevalence with age, reflecting cumulative cochlear hair cell damage, noise exposure, and presbycusis. It affects both sexes approximately equally unlike BIH, which predominantly affects women. Severity of tinnitus symptoms also increases with age. The increased prevalence with ageing is consistent with its association with age-related cochlear degeneration, but tinnitus can occur at any age following noise exposure, ototoxicity, or otological disease. Approximately 10-15% of adults have chronic tinnitus.
options: Predominantly affects young women in reproductive years
Exclusively affects those with complete deafness
Rare after age 60 due to cochlear atrophy
Occurs only with conductive hearing loss
Prevalence and severity increase with age, equal sex distribution
questions.question: Subjective tinnitus originating within the auditory system is more prevalent in which epidemiological pattern?

questions.explanation: Nasal polyps in a child are unusual and, combined with recurrent chest infections and malabsorption, strongly suggest cystic fibrosis due to thick secretions affecting the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. A sweat chloride test is the key confirmatory investigation. Around a significant minority of children with cystic fibrosis go on to develop nasal polyposis during childhood.
questions.question: A child presents with bilateral nasal polyps, recurrent chest infections, and failure to thrive with steatorrhoea. Which underlying condition must be excluded?

A 55-year-old with bilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo is found to have positive VHIT (reduced VOR gain bilaterally) and absent OAEs. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Bilateral Mnire's disease with bilateral cochlear and vestibular involvement
Acoustic neuroma of both internal auditory canals (bilateral vestibular schwannoma in NF2)
Bilateral BPPV causing bilateral VOR suppression
questions.explanation: Bilateral progressive SNHL developing over weeks to months with episodic vertigo, tinnitus, absent OAEs (indicating bilateral OHC loss), and reduced bilateral VOR gain in a middle-aged adult describes autoimmune inner ear disease (AIED). AIED is a rare autoimmune condition causing rapidly progressive bilateral SNHL, potentially responding to systemic corticosteroids. Bilateral Mnire's does occur but is less common. NF2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas) would show mass lesions on MRI. AIED is the most clinically important diagnosis because it is the most treatable (steroid-responsive) bilateral cochleo-vestibular disorder.

options: Direct bronchodilation of the lower airways only
questions.explanation: Nebulised adrenaline causes vasoconstriction of the oedematous laryngeal and subglottic mucosa, providing rapid though short-lived improvement in airway calibre and work of breathing in significant croup. Its effect typically lasts around two hours, so children treated with adrenaline require a period of observation for potential rebound symptoms. It does not have direct antiviral or long-acting anti-inflammatory properties, which is why corticosteroids are used concurrently for more sustained benefit.
questions.question: A child with croup is treated with nebulised adrenaline for significant respiratory distress. Through which mechanism does this treatment provide rapid, though temporary, benefit?
Paranasal sinus malignancies constitute what percentage of all head and neck cancers?
questions.explanation: Paranasal sinus malignancies constitute approximately 3% of all head and neck cancers. Their rarity, combined with overlapping symptoms with common upper respiratory tract infections, contributes to late diagnosis and poorer outcomes compared to other head and neck sites.

questions.question: Nasal smear cytology showing more than 25% eosinophils (or more than 6 eosinophils per high-power field) is most consistent with which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nasal cytology (smear) showing abundant eosinophils (>25% of cells or >6/hpf) indicates allergic or non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophilia syndrome (NARES). Eosinophilic predominance distinguishes these from bacterial and viral rhinitis (which show neutrophils) and from atrophic rhinitis (which shows epithelial atrophy without eosinophilia).

questions.question: A nasal polyp discovered in a child should always be aspirated and the fluid examined for CSF before surgical removal because:
options: Polyps in children are always malignant
Children require IV sedation for all nasal procedures
May be a glioma or encephalocele, risking CSF leak
Aspiration confirms the diagnosis of antrochoanal polyp
CSF aspiration determines if the polyp is vascular
questions.explanation: A nasal mass in a child that appears to be a simple polyp may actually be a glioma, encephalocele, or meningoencephalocele — all lesions that communicate with the intracranial space. Careless removal without recognizing this would result in CSF rhinorrhoea and meningitis. Aspiration of fluid and examination for beta-2 transferrin or glucose can confirm CSF before surgery.

Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa predominantly affects elderly patients with poorly controlled diabetes or other immunocompromised states. It is usually caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is characterised by otalgia and otorrhea persisting more than one month, unresponsive to medical therapy.
questions.question: Malignant otitis externa is a life-threatening condition typically affecting which patient population?
A neonate presents with inspiratory stridor that worsens with crying and feeding, and improves in the prone position. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of neonatal stridor, arising from floppy supraglottic structures that collapse inward during inspiration, and characteristically worsens with agitation or feeding while improving with prone positioning that reduces posterior collapse. Most cases are mild and resolve spontaneously by 18 to 24 months as the cartilage matures. Severe cases with feeding difficulty or failure to thrive may require supraglottoplasty.

questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the infratemporal fossa through which opening?
questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure (between the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus and the anterior surface of the pterygoid plates) is the lateral opening through which the pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the infratemporal fossa. JNA expanding laterally from the pterygopalatine fossa passes through this fissure to reach the infratemporal fossa, producing the characteristic anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary antral wall (Holman-Miller sign) as it expands anteriorly against the posterior antrum.

options: Permanent silence with no rehabilitation possible
Botulinum toxin injection into the pharynx
questions.explanation: Tracheoesophageal puncture with placement of a voice prosthesis is the most widely used and generally most effective method of voice restoration after total laryngectomy, allowing pulmonary air to be shunted into the oesophagus to produce vibratory sound, referred to as tracheoesophageal speech. Alternative options include an electrolarynx or oesophageal speech, but these generally produce less natural-sounding voice. Prosthesis maintenance and replacement are ongoing aspects of long-term care.
questions.question: A patient with laryngeal cancer treated with total laryngectomy asks about voice restoration options. What is the most commonly used method for voice rehabilitation after this surgery?

questions.explanation: Malignant otitis externa is a life-threatening, invasive infection typically occurring in elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patients, characterised by severe pain, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal floor, and potential cranial nerve involvement as infection spreads to the skull base. Urgent imaging and prolonged targeted antibiotic therapy are required to prevent life-threatening progression. Recognition of the specific at-risk population is key to prompt diagnosis.
questions.question: An elderly diabetic patient presents with severe, unrelenting otalgia, granulation tissue in the ear canal floor, and cranial nerve palsies. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
A patient with a known juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma presents with brisk epistaxis. Why is nasal packing alone considered inadequate definitive management?
questions.explanation: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is an extremely vascular benign tumour, so simple packing may temporarily control bleeding but does not address the underlying lesion, which requires preoperative embolisation followed by surgical excision. Attempting biopsy or aggressive instrumentation without this preparation risks catastrophic haemorrhage. Imaging to define vascular supply is essential before any definitive intervention.
options: It spreads readily to the brain
It is an extremely vascular tumour
It is usually a malignant tumour

questions.explanation: Rhinoplasty (septal reconstruction or submucous resection) is indicated for recurrent epistaxis caused by anatomical nasal abnormalities such as nasal spurs or sharp deviations that create areas of turbulent airflow and chronic trauma to the nasal mucosa, exposing blood vessels to repeated injury. Straightening the septum removes the traumatic stimulus and relieves the recurrent epistaxis.
questions.question: Rhinoplasty may be indicated as a treatment for recurrent epistaxis in which specific clinical scenario?
options: Epistaxis from nasal spur or septal deviation

questions.explanation: Barotrauma most commonly occurs during airplane or diving descent when ambient pressure increases but the middle ear cannot equilibrate because the Eustachian tube fails to open. The resulting negative pressure relative to the environment causes TM and mucosal retraction, pain, and potential transudate or haemorrhage. Decongestants and Valsalva manoeuvres help prevent it.
questions.question: Barotrauma to the middle ear most commonly occurs during:
T1 glottic carcinoma is treated with radiotherapy alone to preserve which function?
questions.explanation: T1 and T2 glottic carcinomas confined to the vocal cords are treated with radiotherapy alone because it provides equivalent tumour control to surgery while preserving the voice. This organ-preservation approach is superior to laryngectomy in quality-of-life terms for early-stage disease.

External auditory canal diameters vary considerably between patients of different ages and anatomies. Multiple aural speculum sizes ensure an adequate seal and optimal visualization regardless of canal diameter, which is critical for accurate examination.
questions.question: Different sizes of aural specula are available in an ENT kit. The primary reason for having multiple sizes is:
options: To match different ear canal diameters
To provide varying degrees of magnification
To allow deeper insertion as needed

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized systemic cause of epistaxis?
questions.explanation: Nasal foreign body is a LOCAL cause of epistaxis (causing mucosal irritation, inflammation, and secondary infection), not a systemic cause. Systemic causes include hypertension, coagulopathies (haemophilia, thrombocytopenia, liver disease), anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel), granulomatous diseases, haematological malignancies, and SLE.

The danger space, located between the alar and prevertebral layers of deep cervical fascia, extends from the skull base to the diaphragm with minimal anatomical barriers, providing a direct route for infection to spread rapidly from the neck into the posterior mediastinum, resulting in descending necrotising mediastinitis. This is one of the most feared complications of deep neck space infection due to its high associated mortality. Early recognition and aggressive combined ENT and thoracic surgical drainage are essential for survival.
options: Direct haematogenous spread from the tonsil exclusively
Lymphatic spread through the thoracic duct only
Danger space (space 4) extending along the prevertebral fascia
Spread via the oesophageal submucosa exclusively
questions.question: A patient with a deep neck space infection is found to have mediastinitis as a complication. Through which route does infection most commonly reach the mediastinum from the neck?

questions.explanation: Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, and non-healing ulcer in a patient with alcohol and tobacco history are classic red flag symptoms of hypopharyngeal or oropharyngeal malignancy. These together mandate urgent oncological evaluation.
questions.question: A patient presents with progressive dysphagia, weight loss, and a non-healing throat ulcer. Which finding in this patient's history MOST urgently suggests malignancy?

questions.explanation: In adults, the external auditory canal has a natural curve that is straightened by pulling the pinna upward, outward, and backward. This manoeuvre provides the best visualization of the tympanic membrane during otoscopy.
questions.question: During otoscopic examination, the examiner must pull the pinna in which direction to best straighten the external auditory canal in an adult?
The diagnostic triad for bronchial foreign body (unilateral wheeze, cough, and ipsilateral diminished breath sounds) is present in what proportion of cases?
questions.explanation: The classic diagnostic triad of unilateral wheeze, cough, and ipsilateral diminished breath sounds occurs in less than 50% of bronchial foreign body cases. This means the diagnosis must be considered even without the complete triad, especially with a positive history of choking.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy has progressive unilateral nasal obstruction and discharge. CT shows a solitary polypoidal mass extending from the maxillary sinus through the ostium into the postnasal space. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A single polyp arising in the maxillary sinus and extending through its ostium into the choana and postnasal space describes the trilobed antrochoanal (Killian's) polyp, which typically occurs in children and young adults. It is unilateral, unlike the usually bilateral ethmoidal polyps of adults. Complete surgical removal including the antral component is required to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: A patient with a frontal sinus mass found incidentally on imaging has a well-circumscribed, dense, bony lesion with no symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An osteoma is a benign, slow-growing lesion of compact bony tissue most commonly found incidentally in the frontal sinus on imaging performed for unrelated reasons. Most remain asymptomatic and require only periodic observation unless they obstruct sinus drainage or cause cosmetic deformity. Malignant bony lesions such as osteosarcoma typically show more aggressive, poorly defined margins and associated symptoms.

questions.question: A patient with tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma is found to be HPV-positive on testing. How does this affect prognosis compared with HPV-negative disease?
questions.explanation: HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, including tonsillar cancer, is associated with a significantly better prognosis and improved response to chemoradiotherapy compared with HPV-negative disease, which is more strongly linked to tobacco and alcohol use. This distinction has led to ongoing research into treatment de-escalation strategies for HPV-positive patients to reduce long-term toxicity while maintaining survival outcomes. HPV status is now a standard part of staging for oropharyngeal cancers.
options: HPV-positive tumours generally have a better prognosis and treatment response
HPV-positive tumours always carry a worse prognosis
HPV status has no bearing on prognosis at all
HPV-positive tumours never respond to radiotherapy
HPV-positive status indicates certain distant metastasis

questions.question: Aural polyp in COM represents which pathological entity?
questions.explanation: An aural polyp is a coalition of exuberant granulation tissue formed following chronic irritation of the middle ear mucosa. It can occlude the entire perforation and prolapse into the external auditory canal. Its presence indicates active chronic disease and is not a benign finding.

Within the tonsillar lymphoid follicle, mature B lymphocytes reside in the mantle zone that encircles the germinal centre. The germinal centre is where antigen-stimulated B cells proliferate, undergo somatic hypermutation, and differentiate into plasma cells secreting high-affinity antigen-specific immunoglobulins. The mantle zone serves as a reservoir of naive and memory B cells surrounding this reactive germinal centre.
questions.question: The lymphoid follicle in tonsillar tissue has germinal centres where B lymphocytes produce immunoglobulin. These germinal centres are surrounded by the:
Gustatory rhinitis (food-induced rhinitis) is triggered by hot spicy foods and is mediated through:
questions.explanation: Gustatory rhinitis is a non-allergic form triggered by hot, spicy foods containing capsaicin. Capsaicin stimulates sensory C-fibre nociceptors in the nasal mucosa, inducing release of tachykinins and other neuropeptides (neurogenic inflammation) that cause rhinorrhoea. This mechanism is distinct from IgE-mediated allergic rhinitis.
options: COX-1 inhibition by natural food compounds at all times
Capsaicin stimulation of sensory nerve fibres releasing tachykinins

questions.explanation: In longitudinal temporal bone fractures, the facial nerve is most vulnerable at the perigeniculate region (geniculate ganglion and the adjacent proximal tympanic segment), where the nerve makes its first genu bend. This area is anatomically exposed where the fracture line typically passes through the tegmen tympani and roof of the middle ear. In transverse fractures, the labyrinthine segment (shortest, narrowest, and least mobile segment) is most commonly injured as the fracture crosses the otic capsule.
questions.question: The overall incidence of facial nerve injury in temporal bone fractures is approximately 7%, with 25% of these being permanent. The most common site of facial nerve injury in longitudinal temporal bone fractures is:

questions.explanation: Sensory loss refers to SNHL arising from degenerative, toxic, immune-mediated, infectious, or traumatic damage to the cochlea itself. Neural transmission impairment involves traumatic nerve damage, neoplastic nerve impingement, or central defects. The distinction guides both the diagnostic workup and treatment approach.
questions.question: Sensorineural hearing loss due to pathology in the cochlea's sensory end-organ is classified under which pathophysiologic mechanism?

questions.explanation: A persistent tongue ulcer in a patient with major risk factors for oral squamous cell carcinoma, namely tobacco and alcohol use, must be biopsied promptly to exclude malignancy rather than treated empirically or observed. Delay in biopsy risks disease progression and worse oncological outcomes. Any oral ulcer failing to heal within two to three weeks warrants tissue diagnosis regardless of risk factor status.
questions.question: A patient with a chronic non-healing ulcer of the tongue and a history of heavy tobacco and alcohol use is being evaluated. What is the most important next step?
options: Reassurance and review in three months
Systemic antihistamines causing drying of mucosa
questions.explanation: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound rhinitis) develops from prolonged use (typically beyond 10 days to 2 weeks) of intranasal vasoconstrictors (alpha-adrenergic agonists such as oxymetazoline and phenylephrine). Rebound vasodilatation and intravascular oedema develop when the drug wears off, creating a dependency cycle.
questions.question: Rhinitis medicamentosa is defined as rebound nasal obstruction resulting from:

questions.explanation: Percussion tenderness over a tooth suggests inflammation extending to the periapical or periodontal tissues, commonly from an underlying dental abscess. Salivary and tonsillar pathology are assessed by other examination techniques such as bimanual palpation or direct visual inspection. This simple test helps localise a source of orofacial pain to a specific tooth.
questions.question: On examination of the oral cavity, gentle percussion of individual teeth is performed. This manoeuvre is used PRIMARILY to detect:

questions.explanation: Unlike the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, which are present at birth, the sphenoidal sinus arises within the nasal capsule without a pouch and begins significant pneumatization at approximately age 3. This has clinical relevance because sphenoidal sinusitis is distinctly uncommon in young children.
questions.question: The sphenoidal sinus begins to pneumatize at approximately which age?

questions.explanation: A high tracheostomy, performed above the second tracheal ring, is generally avoided in elective cases because of the increased risk of subglottic stenosis from proximity to the cricoid cartilage. A low tracheostomy, between the third and fourth rings, is the preferred elective site. Knowing the classification helps anticipate complication risk based on the level of the stoma.
questions.question: A tracheostomy tube is inserted between the second and third tracheal rings, above the level used for a standard low tracheostomy. This is classified as:
For a radiolucent foreign body in the oesophagus that cannot be seen on plain X-ray, which specialized radiological investigation is performed?
questions.explanation: Barium swallow using wisps of cotton wool impregnated with barium helps detect radiolucent foreign bodies in the oesophagus by demonstrating the filling defect or hold-up of swallowed material. This technique is used when plain films fail to identify the foreign body.

Tympanometry is an objective test that measures the compliance (mobility) of the tympanic membrane and middle ear system in response to varying air pressure, providing information about middle ear status such as the presence of effusion or ossicular abnormality. It does not directly assess cochlear or neural function, distinguishing it from audiometric threshold testing. This makes it a valuable complementary test alongside pure-tone audiometry in the overall hearing assessment.
options: Middle ear pressure and tympanic membrane compliance
questions.question: A patient undergoes tympanometry as part of a hearing evaluation. What does this test PRIMARILY measure?

questions.explanation: A safe central perforation without cholesteatoma or significant ossicular disease is appropriately managed electively with myringoplasty, which repairs the tympanic membrane defect and reduces recurrent infection risk while improving or maintaining hearing. This differs from unsafe perforations with cholesteatoma, which require mastoid exploration. Surgery is typically deferred until the ear has been dry for a period to optimise graft success.
questions.question: A patient with a longstanding central tympanic membrane perforation has occasional discharge but preserved hearing. What is the most appropriate elective management?
options: Observation with no intervention ever offered

questions.question: A neonate develops acute otitis media with systemic sepsis. Which combination of antibiotics is most appropriate to cover the likely causative organisms in this age group?
options: Broad-spectrum cover for likely neonatal organisms
questions.explanation: Neonatal acute otitis media with sepsis differs from disease in older children because the causative organisms more often include Group B Streptococcus and Gram-negative bacilli acquired perinatally, requiring broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic cover rather than the typical oral regimens used in older children. Blood and, where appropriate, middle ear fluid cultures should guide targeted therapy once available. Prompt treatment is essential given the higher risk of systemic complications in neonates.

The great majority of temporal bone fractures are managed conservatively head elevation, avoidance of nose blowing (to prevent pneumocephalus), observation for CSF leak (most close spontaneously within 10-14 days), and hearing assessment after resolution of haemotympanum. Immediate surgery is rarely indicated except for: immediate-onset complete facial palsy with >90% ENoG degeneration, expanding intracranial haematoma from vascular injury, or persistent CSF leak beyond 10-14 days. The principle reflects the excellent natural history of most temporal bone injuries without operative intervention.
questions.question: An important principle in managing suspected temporal bone fracture is that the vast majority are managed:
options: With emergency surgical decompression within 24 hours
With immediate dural repair via craniotomy

questions.explanation: Acute respiratory infections (ARI) are defined as infections of the respiratory tract lasting less than 21 days (3 weeks). ARI is subdivided into acute upper respiratory tract infections (AURI — including common cold, acute otitis media, acute tonsillopharyngitis, rhinosinusitis) and acute lower respiratory tract infections (ALRI — including bronchiolitis, pneumonia). This temporal definition distinguishes acute from subacute (3–12 weeks) and chronic conditions.
questions.question: Acute upper respiratory infections (AURI) are defined as infections of the respiratory tract of less than what duration?

options: Stimulates regulatory T cells to reduce inflammation
Harbours bacteria resistant to antibiotic penetration
questions.explanation: Bacterial biofilms are structured communities of organisms embedded in self-produced extracellular matrix on adenoid and tonsillar surfaces. The matrix physically impedes antibiotic penetration and concentrations adequate to eradicate biofilm-dwelling bacteria require up to 1000 times higher than planktonic minimum inhibitory concentrations. This explains why recurrent and chronic tonsillitis/adenoiditis often fails to resolve with standard antibiotic courses and ultimately requires surgical removal.
questions.question: A biofilm produced in adenoid and tonsillar tissue is significant clinically because it:

questions.explanation: In children, adenoidal and tonsillar hypertrophy is by far the most common cause of OSA, causing mechanical obstruction of the nasopharynx and oropharynx during sleep. Complications include snoring, hypoxaemia, growth failure, cardiovascular sequelae, and in severe cases, sudden death during sleep. Adenotonsillectomy is the first-line surgical treatment for paediatric OSA secondary to adenotonsillar hypertrophy.
options: Obesity and fatty deposits in the pharynx
Allergic rhinitis causing chronic nasal obstruction
questions.question: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) in children is most commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: Persistent maxillary disease despite an adequate antrostomy usually reflects unresolved osteomeatal complex obstruction, since this common channel drains the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. Disease anywhere along this narrow unit perpetuates sinus disease even after individual sinus surgery. The frontal recess and sphenoid ostium are separate drainage pathways not directly responsible for maxillary recurrence.
questions.question: During FESS, a surgeon widely opens the maxillary antrostomy but the patient continues to have recurrent maxillary sinusitis. Which structure was most likely left obstructed?

questions.explanation: Although the clinical picture is consistent with ethmoidal nasal polyps, CT of the paranasal sinuses is the single most important investigation before surgical treatment. It maps the extent of polyps in the sinuses, identifies anatomical variants at the ostiomeatal complex that predispose to recurrence, and delineates proximity of the polyps to the orbit and skull base for surgical safety.
