questions.question: A 40-year-old man with bilateral nasal obstruction has pale, insensitive, grape-like nasal masses on anterior rhinoscopy that do not bleed on palpation. The SINGLE most important investigation to determine treatment is:
options: CT scan of the paranasal sinuses
MRI of the paranasal well-defined sinuses

questions.explanation: NPC genetic susceptibility is associated with HLA-A2 and HLA-B Sin2 genotypes, which are common in southern Chinese populations but rare in Black and White populations. These HLA alleles influence how the immune system presents EBV antigens and recognises EBV-transformed cells. The rarity of these alleles in non-endemic populations is consistent with the low NPC incidence outside Southeast Asia and North Africa, supporting the gene-environment interaction model.
questions.question: The genetic susceptibility to NPC is associated with which HLA genotypes that are rare in black and white populations?

questions.explanation: At around 22 months, behavioural tests such as the distraction test or visual reinforcement audiometry are developmentally appropriate, using the child's natural responses to sound stimuli including head-turning behaviour. Formal pure-tone audiometry with headphones typically requires the cooperation of an older child. Selecting age-appropriate testing ensures reliable results and avoids under- or over-diagnosis of hearing impairment.
questions.question: A child aged 22 months requires hearing assessment. Which test is MOST developmentally appropriate for this age?
options: Distraction test or visual reinforcement audiometry

questions.question: Hearing results from the transduction of sound energy. Which type of energy is ultimately converted into neural impulses?
questions.explanation: Hearing results from the transduction of sound (mechanical energy) into neural impulses interpreted by the central nervous system. The ossicular chain transmits mechanical vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the cochlea. Hair cells in the cochlea convert mechanical movement into electrochemical signals.

questions.question: T-stage in maxillary sinus carcinoma specifically describes:
options: Only the histological grade (well, moderate, poorly differentiated) as the sole finding
The surgical approach selected for treatment
The number of lymph nodes involved
The primary tumour size and extent of local invasion into adjacent structures
questions.explanation: The T (tumour) in TNM staging describes the primary tumour characteristics: for maxillary sinus carcinoma, T-stage reflects both the size of the tumour and the extent of its invasion into adjacent structures (nasal cavity, ethmoid sinus, pterygoid plates, orbit, skull base, cranial cavity). T1–T2 are confined or minimally invasive; T3–T4 involve adjacent structures. N describes nodes; M describes metastases.

Haemophilus influenzae type b was historically the predominant cause of paediatric acute epiglottitis, and widespread Hib vaccination has substantially reduced the incidence of this life-threatening condition in children, though cases still occur from other organisms and in unvaccinated individuals. Adult epiglottitis has a broader range of causative organisms. Recognition of the classic presentation remains essential regardless of the causative organism, given the rapid potential for airway compromise.
questions.question: A patient with acute epiglottitis is stabilised with a secured airway. Which organism, now less common due to vaccination, was historically the leading cause of this condition in children?

options: The gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex in response to rapid passive head rotations
Nystagmus pattern in response to caloric irrigation
Static vestibulospinal reflex through the Romberg test
Otolith function using off-vertical axis rotation
Central vestibular processing via brainstem evoked potentials
questions.explanation: The video Head Impulse Test (vHIT) quantifies the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) gain the ratio of compensatory eye velocity to head velocity during rapid passive head rotations. A normal VOR gain approaches 1.0 (eye moves equally and opposite to head to stabilise gaze). In vestibular hypofunction (from vestibular neuritis, vestibular schwannoma, or labyrinthitis), reduced gain on the affected side produces a catch-up corrective saccade visible on video recording. vHIT assesses all six semicircular canals individually and is more sensitive than caloric testing for detecting canal-specific hypofunction.
questions.question: Vestibular function testing using the video Head Impulse Test (vHIT) measures:

options: Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with absent peristalsis
Spastic contraction of the cricopharyngeal muscle
Mucosal inflammation from reflux causing stricture
Motor neurone loss causing tongue weakness
questions.explanation: Achalasia is caused by degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells (containing VIP and nitric oxide synthase) in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, resulting in failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation on swallowing and absent or disordered oesophageal peristalsis. Food accumulates in the oesophagus producing dysphagia for both solids and liquids (simultaneously unlike malignancy, where solids are affected first). Regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain, and weight loss are additional features. Treatment options include pneumatic dilatation, Heller myotomy, or POEM.
questions.question: Achalasia causes dysphagia through which primary mechanism?

options: Nasal trauma including digital manipulation (nose picking)
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia as the sole finding
questions.explanation: The most common local cause of epistaxis in children is nasal trauma, predominantly from digital manipulation (nose-picking), sport, or play. This irritates the richly vascular mucosa of Kiesselbach's plexus on the anteroinferior septum. Epistaxis in children under 10 is predominantly anterior, self-limiting, and benign, unlike epistaxis in the elderly where hypertension and systemic disorders are more important.
questions.question: A child aged 7 presents with recurrent anterior nosebleeds. Rhinoscopy shows a red vascular lesion on the anterior nasal septum. The MOST common local cause of paediatric epistaxis is:

questions.explanation: The Heimlich manoeuvre (abdominal thrusts) is used for older children and adults with complete airway foreign body obstruction. For infants under 1 year, back blows are used instead, as the Heimlich manoeuvre risks abdominal organ injury in infants due to their anatomical proportions.
questions.question: The Heimlich manoeuvre is performed in which specific group for airway foreign body obstruction?

questions.explanation: Severe itching is characteristically associated with eczema, neurodermatitis, or mycotic (fungal) infection of the EAC. In contrast, otalgia is the predominant symptom of furunculosis, diffuse otitis externa, and herpetic infections. Clinical history is a valuable pointer toward the specific aetiology.
questions.question: Severe itching in the EAC is MOST suggestive of which aetiology?

questions.explanation: The cooperation test is used for children aged 18–30 months. The distraction test is appropriate for children aged 6–18 months. Pure tone audiometry is reliable from age 3 years and above. Performance testing is used for children over 30 months. These age-specific tests account for developmental milestones.
questions.question: Which of the following hearing tests is MOST appropriate for a child aged 22 months?
A child presents with sensorineural hearing loss, a white forelock, and heterochromia iridis. What hereditary condition is this MOST characteristic of?
questions.explanation: Waardenburg syndrome is a hereditary cause of sensorineural hearing loss characteristically associated with pigmentary abnormalities such as a white forelock, heterochromia iridis, and wide-set eyes, reflecting the underlying neural crest cell developmental defect. Recognising this constellation of features helps direct genetic counselling and further systemic evaluation. Hearing loss severity can vary considerably even within affected families.

options: They metastasise early to lymph nodes
Slow growth erodes nearby vital structures
They arise from malignant schwann cells
questions.explanation: Glomus tumours (nonchromaffin paragangliomas) are the most common neoplasms of the ear and are described as malignant by location because their slow, relentless growth erodes surrounding vital structures including cranial nerves and blood vessels. The hallmark presentation is unilateral pulsatile tinnitus synchronous with the pulse.
questions.question: Glomus tumours of the ear are described as malignant by location because:

options: Acute OM not responding to amoxicillin
questions.question: Anti-tuberculous therapy is specifically indicated for which variant of otitis media?
questions.explanation: Anti-tuberculous therapy is the treatment for confirmed tuberculous OM where Mycobacterium tuberculosis has been isolated from ear discharge. Standard TB treatment regimens are applied. The global re-emergence of tuberculosis means this diagnosis should be considered in cases of painless multiperforated TM discharge.

questions.question: A Bjork flap, used in some paediatric and adult tracheostomies, is specifically designed to:
questions.explanation: A Bjork flap involves suturing an inferiorly based tracheal flap to the skin, creating a more stable, epithelialising tract that facilitates safer tube changes and reduces the risk of losing the airway if accidental decannulation occurs. It does not close the stoma or eliminate the need for future tube changes. This technique is particularly valued in situations where reinsertion would otherwise be difficult.
options: Eliminate the need for tube changes
Create a stable, epithelialised tract to reduce accidental decannulation risk

questions.question: Hearing outcome following tympanostomy tube insertion for OME is BEST compared to conservative management in that:
questions.explanation: Evidence has shown a better outcome and fewer complications in OME managed with tympanostomy tubes compared to conservative management, particularly for persistent or viscous effusion. Recent studies also demonstrate that adenoidectomy provides additional benefit alongside tube insertion. Hearing improvement is the primary goal.
options: Tubes show better outcomes with fewer complications
Tubes cause more complications than conservative care
Tubes are only beneficial in adults

questions.question: A 45-year-old teacher presents with chronic hoarseness of voice for 3 months. During clerkship, which aspect of occupational history is MOST diagnostically significant?
questions.explanation: Teachers use their voices extensively, predisposing them to chronic laryngitis and vocal nodules. Occupational voice overuse is the most diagnostically relevant factor in this context, often leading to vocal abuse and hoarseness.

options: The infection erodes through the skull base directly
The danger space and prevertebral space are contiguous
Blood-borne spread to the epidural space occurs
questions.explanation: Epidural abscess complicates deep neck infection because the prevertebral space and danger space lie immediately adjacent to the spinal epidural space. Direct extension of infection through contiguous fascial planes from the neck into the epidural space can cause this severe neurological complication.
questions.question: Epidural abscess as a complication of deep neck infection can occur because:

questions.explanation: Radiotherapy for JNA is reserved for specific situations: unresectable disease (extensive intracranial involvement), recurrence after multiple surgical attempts, or when surgery carries prohibitive risk. While JNA is responsive to radiation, concerns about radiation-induced malignant transformation (secondary sarcomas), growth retardation in young patients, and radiation-related long-term morbidity limit its routine use. Surgery is the primary curative modality; radiotherapy is a second-line option for cases not amenable to surgical cure.
questions.question: Which statement about radiation therapy in JNA management is most accurate?
options: Radiotherapy is used prophylactically to prevent recurrence
Radiotherapy is the first-line treatment for all stages
JNA is radioresistant and radiotherapy is never used
Radiotherapy is reserved for unresectable residual or recurrent disease only
Radiotherapy cures JNA as effectively as surgery in stage I

questions.explanation: Granulation tissue in the medial canal or middle ear space during chronic suppurative otitis media indicates ongoing active inflammatory mucosal disease, often associated with persistent discharge and potential for further complications such as an aural polyp. Its presence should prompt further evaluation and consideration of surgical management if medical treatment fails to control the disease. It differs from a healed, quiescent perforation without active inflammation.
options: A simple foreign body reaction only
questions.question: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media is found to have granulation tissue in the middle ear on otoscopy. What does this finding MOST likely represent?
After resolution of acute otitis externa, treatment should continue for at LEAST how long to prevent recurrence, particularly in otomycosis?
questions.explanation: Treatment should continue for at least one week after clinical resolution because of the tendency to recurrence, particularly in otomycosis. Prolonged treatment ensures complete eradication of the organism. Premature discontinuation is a common cause of recurrent episodes, especially with fungal infections.

questions.question: Referred otalgia (ear pain) in an adult presenting with an oesophageal foreign body occurs through which mechanism?
options: Direct extension of oesophageal inflammation to the ear
Referred pain via the vagus nerve (CN X)
Haematogenous spread to the middle ear
Pressure on the carotid artery causing ear pain
questions.explanation: Referred otalgia from oesophageal pathology occurs via the vagus nerve (CN X), which supplies the oesophagus and also provides auricular sensation. Painful oesophageal stimulation is referred to the ear via this shared nerve pathway, a clinically important diagnostic sign in adults.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent parotitis in childhood is diagnosed with juvenile recurrent parotitis. What is the typical natural history of this condition?
options: It tends to resolve spontaneously around puberty
It always progresses to require parotidectomy
It is caused by an underlying malignancy in most cases
It represents an untreatable chronic autoimmune disease
questions.explanation: Juvenile recurrent parotitis is characterised by repeated episodes of non-suppurative parotid gland swelling and pain in childhood, with sialectasis on imaging, and the condition typically improves and resolves spontaneously around puberty in most children. Management during episodes is largely supportive with hydration, massage, and sialogogues. Sialendoscopy can be both diagnostic and therapeutic in recurrent or severe cases.

Diplopia (double vision) in the context of sinonasal malignancy indicates orbital involvement, specifically displacement or infiltration of the extraocular muscles or orbital apex, disrupting the coordinated movement of the eyes. Proptosis (forward protrusion of the eyeball) and epiphora (excessive tearing from nasolacrimal duct obstruction) are other orbital symptoms. Orbital involvement significantly affects staging and prognosis.
options: Orbital involvement causing displacement or infiltration of extraocular muscles
Skull base erosion at the clivus at all times
questions.question: Diplopia as a presenting symptom of sinonasal malignancy indicates spread to which anatomical region?
A patient with a suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is scheduled for imaging before any biopsy. Why is biopsy typically avoided in the outpatient clinic setting?
questions.explanation: JNA is an extremely vascular tumour, and unplanned biopsy in an unprepared setting risks life-threatening haemorrhage, so diagnosis is instead based on characteristic clinical presentation in an adolescent male combined with imaging findings such as the Holman-Miller sign and angiographic vascular pattern. If tissue confirmation is required, it is performed with full surgical and anaesthetic preparedness for potential bleeding. This cautious approach distinguishes JNA work-up from that of most other nasopharyngeal masses.
options: Biopsy is technically impossible to perform in the nasopharynx
The tumour is always benign so tissue diagnosis is unnecessary
Local anaesthesia cannot achieve adequate analgesia there
The highly vascular tumour carries a significant risk of severe haemorrhage
Outpatient biopsy risks tumour seeding into the bloodstream
Eliminates the need for suction during the case
Improves visualisation of the vocal cords only
Allows faster completion of the procedure
Reduces the risk of pushing the foreign body further distally
questions.explanation: Positive pressure ventilation risks forcing an impacted foreign body further down the tracheobronchial tree or converting a partial obstruction into a complete one, whereas spontaneous ventilation maintains more predictable airway dynamics during instrumentation. It is not primarily chosen for muscle relaxation or speed, which are unrelated benefits. This anaesthetic technique reflects a specific safety consideration unique to foreign body bronchoscopy.
questions.question: A patient with foreign body aspiration undergoes bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia with spontaneous ventilation maintained. Spontaneous ventilation is preferred over controlled positive pressure ventilation because it:
Radical radiotherapy dose for ENT malignancies ranges between:
questions.explanation: Radical (curative intent) radiotherapy for ENT malignancies is delivered at doses of 50-80 Gy, sufficient to eradicate the tumour. Palliative radiotherapy uses lower doses of 8-25 Gy to achieve symptom relief without intending cure. The higher radical doses require careful fractionation to protect normal tissues.

options: Bilateral foetid green discharge with polyps
A unilateral purulent discharge with fever above 39°C
A grey-white unilateral serosanguineous discharge with a membranous crust
A painless unilateral nasal mass with no well-defined discharge
questions.explanation: Nasal diphtheria produces a characteristic grey-white, serosanguineous (blood-tinged serous) unilateral or bilateral nasal discharge with adherent pseudomembranous crust. The pseudomembrane, caused by the diphtheria toxin, bleeds when removed. Unlike a nasal foreign body, diphtheria lacks an identifiable object on rhinoscopy, and throat examination may show the classic pharyngeal membrane. Culture confirms Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
questions.question: Nasal diphtheria, listed as a differential of nasal foreign body, is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae and characteristically produces:

questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion (OME) is defined as middle ear effusion of any duration that lacks associated signs and symptoms of infection. It often follows an episode of acute otitis media. This distinguishes it from acute suppurative OM where systemic and local signs of infection are present.
questions.question: Which otitis media subtype specifically lacks the associated signs and symptoms of infection despite middle ear effusion?

questions.explanation: A post-cricoid mass causing dysphagia with cervical lymphadenopathy requires tissue diagnosis through rigid hypopharyngoscopy under general anaesthesia. This allows direct visualisation, precise biopsy of the hypopharyngeal lesion under controlled conditions with airway protection, assessment of tumour extent, and simultaneous staging of the lesion. FNAC of the cervical node is complementary but insufficient alone because it may not yield adequate material for histological typing needed for treatment planning. Direct laryngoscopy and biopsy are the gold standard.
questions.question: A patient presents with dysphagia and examination reveals a post-cricoid hard mucosal mass with cervical lymphadenopathy. The most appropriate biopsy approach is:
options: Fine needle aspiration of the neck node only

questions.question: The trachea is lined with mucus glands that humidify inspired air. Tracheostomy bypasses these glands, and this is compensated MOST effectively by:
questions.explanation: The nose and upper airway normally humidify and warm inspired air; tracheostomy bypasses this system. Compensation requires nursing in a humidified room and regular instillation of normal saline or sodium bicarbonate to maintain mucosal moisture and prevent crusting.

questions.question: A patient develops high-grade fever, severe throat pain, trismus, and inability to swallow on day 5 of treated tonsillitis. The uvula is midline but there is asymmetric parapharyngeal swelling. Which complication has likely developed?
questions.explanation: Parapharyngeal abscess presents with fever, trismus, dysphagia, and a medial bulge of the lateral pharyngeal wall without the typical superior tonsil pole swelling and uvular deviation of a peritonsillar abscess. It may arise from spread of peritonsillar or dental infection. Because the parapharyngeal space communicates with the carotid sheath and mediastinum, complications of carotid artery erosion and mediastinitis are serious risks requiring urgent surgical drainage.

Ear barotrauma occurs when the Eustachian tube fails to equalise rapidly changing ambient pressure during aircraft descent, causing negative middle ear pressure that can lead to mucosal oedema, effusion, and even haemorrhage in more severe cases. Symptoms are usually self-limiting and managed with decongestants and Valsalva manoeuvres, though a minority may develop persistent effusion requiring further treatment. Prevention includes chewing, swallowing, or using nasal decongestants before descent.
options: Direct rupture of the round window membrane always
Acute bacterial infection triggered by altitude change
Sudden onset otosclerosis from pressure change
Failure of Eustachian tube pressure equalisation during descent
Permanent ossicular chain dislocation in most cases
questions.question: A patient with barotrauma from air travel develops sudden ear pain and mild conductive hearing loss during descent. What is the underlying mechanism?

questions.explanation: Progressive dysphagia beginning with solids and advancing to liquids over weeks to months, accompanied by significant weight loss (>10% body weight), is the classic presentation of mechanical obstruction from oesophageal or hypopharyngeal malignancy. This alarming progression pattern must be urgently investigated with endoscopy and CT. Globus presents without true dysphagia; Zenker's diverticulum causes regurgitation of undigested food; reflux dysphagia is usually intermittent. Malignancy must be excluded before attributing symptoms to benign causes.
questions.question: A 55-year-old presents with progressive dysphagia for solids only, which has gradually extended to liquids over 6 months. He has lost 8 kg. The most concerning underlying diagnosis is:
Which of the following is NOT a host factor predisposing to otitis media?
questions.explanation: Passive smoke exposure is an environmental factor, not a host factor predisposing to otitis media. Host factors include immune system deficiency, familial genetic predisposition, MUC5B gene upregulation, anatomic palate abnormalities (cleft palate, Down syndrome), ciliary dysfunction, and vitamin A deficiency. Environmental factors include passive smoke, daycare attendance, and infant feeding methods.

options: Direct bacterial spread to the heart
questions.explanation: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxia in untreated obstructive sleep apnoea triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction, and if sustained, leads to pulmonary hypertension and eventual right ventricular strain, known as cor pulmonale. This underscores the importance of timely adenotonsillectomy in children with significant OSA to prevent long-term cardiovascular consequences. Screening for OSA severity, sometimes with polysomnography, helps guide the urgency of surgical referral.
questions.question: A child with adenotonsillar hypertrophy and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea develops signs of right heart strain over time. Which mechanism explains this cardiovascular complication?

questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa contains the mandibular nerve (CN V3) and its branches (inferior alveolar, lingual, auriculotemporal nerves), the internal maxillary artery and its branches (including the sphenopalatine artery the primary JNA feeder), the pterygoid venous plexus, the chorda tympani, and the otic ganglion. During JNA resection in the infratemporal fossa, the mandibular nerve and the internal maxillary artery require careful identification to avoid postoperative trismus, facial numbness, and catastrophic haemorrhage.
questions.question: The infratemporal fossa is accessed during JNA surgery. Which important structure passes through the infratemporal fossa and is at risk during tumour resection?
options: Facial nerve and superficial temporal artery
Glossopharyngeal nerve and ascending pharyngeal artery
Mandibular nerve (CN V3) and internal maxillary artery

questions.explanation: 8% aluminium acetate acts as an astringent in resistant cases of otitis externa. Beclomethasone ear drops address the itchy reactive component. Aluminium acetate or acetic acid ear spray is also recommended for chronic otitis externa after the acute infection has been eradicated.
questions.question: 8% aluminium acetate ear drops are recommended in otitis externa primarily for their:
Follow-up of treated otitis externa should particularly monitor for which complication in otomycosis?
questions.explanation: Otomycosis has a strong tendency to recur, which is why treatment must continue for at least one week after resolution. Regular follow-up ensures complete eradication of fungal infection. Beclomethasone ear drops help itchy reactive conditions, and 8% aluminium acetate is recommended to maintain an antimicrobial canal environment. SUBTOPIC 3: OTITIS MEDIA

questions.question: A patient complains of difficulty swallowing solids more than liquids, with gradual worsening over several months and associated weight loss. This pattern of dysphagia MOST suggests:
questions.explanation: Progressive difficulty with solids before liquids is the classic pattern of a mechanical, structural obstruction such as a stricture or tumour narrowing the lumen. Motor disorders typically cause difficulty with both liquids and solids from the outset. The associated weight loss further supports an organic, progressive cause requiring urgent endoscopic evaluation.

questions.question: Healed (dry) COM with a permanent central perforation and no active disease requires which primary management?
questions.explanation: Healed COM — a dry ear with a permanent central perforation and no active inflammation — requires no further active intervention other than regular review of the patient. Surgical closure of the TM is considered depending on the degree of hearing loss and patient's functional requirements. Inserting active ear canal water protection is advisable.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal is treated with wide surgical excision, which may extend to temporal bone resection depending on tumour extent, combined with adjuvant radiotherapy where indicated based on staging and margin status. This aggressive combined approach reflects the tumour's potential for local invasion into critical adjacent structures. Early diagnosis before extensive local spread significantly improves the chances of successful treatment.
questions.question: A patient is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal. What is the treatment of choice for this tumour?

questions.explanation: Topical vasoconstrictor nasal decongestants reduce oedema in the Eustachian tube, nasal, and middle ear mucosa, thereby encouraging better aeration of the middle ear. Current evidence-based research, however, questions the usefulness of vasoconstrictors in OME. Appropriate antibiotics treat underlying infections.
questions.question: In medical management of OME in adults, topical vasoconstrictors (nasal decongestants) are used primarily to:

questions.explanation: This presentation describes malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, a severe infection almost always caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, occurring predominantly in elderly diabetics or immunocompromised patients, with granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction being a classic sign. Untreated, it can progress to skull base osteomyelitis and cranial nerve palsies. Prolonged systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics and glycaemic control are central to management.
questions.question: An elderly diabetic patient presents with severe ear pain, purulent discharge, and granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the ear canal. What organism is most commonly responsible for this presentation?

questions.explanation: Nasal obstruction in NPC results from tumour bulk extending anteriorly from the nasopharynx into the posterior nasal cavities (choana), physically obstructing airflow. This is the basis for epistaxis as well surface ulceration or submucosal vascular engorgement causes intermittent bleeding, typically presenting as postnasal drip of blood rather than frank anterior epistaxis. Tinnitus occurs from Eustachian tube dysfunction with serous otitis media.
options: Cribriform plate invasion causing mucus accumulation
Tumour extension into the posterior nasal cavity
questions.question: A patient with NPC presents with nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and tinnitus. Nasal obstruction in NPC is caused by:

questions.explanation: Weaning a patient off chronic topical decongestant use is best supported by intranasal corticosteroids, which reduce mucosal inflammation and congestion during the withdrawal period without perpetuating receptor downregulation. Substituting one decongestant for another, including oral agents, does not address the underlying rebound mechanism. Patient education about the cause of rhinitis medicamentosa improves adherence to the weaning process.
questions.question: A patient presents with rebound nasal congestion after prolonged decongestant spray use. Correct management includes gradual withdrawal supported by which class of medication to ease symptoms?

options: It directly shows active bacteria present right away
Shows osteoblastic activity persisting after clinical cure
questions.explanation: Gallium scan shows osteoblastic activity and remains abnormal for many months after clinical resolution of malignant otitis externa, whereas the Technetium scan reverts to normal with clinical resolution. This makes gallium scanning useful for monitoring true disease eradication in long-term follow-up, independent of symptoms. MRI monitors cerebral and vascular involvement.
questions.question: Gallium scan in malignant otitis externa has utility over Technetium scan specifically because:

questions.explanation: The internal carotid arteries are in direct contact with the lateral walls of the sphenoid sinus, separated only by a thin shell of bone that can be dehiscent in up to 25% of individuals. JNA extending within the sphenoid sinus is in close proximity to the ICA, and tumour removal from this location risks catastrophic haemorrhage from ICA injury. This is why meticulous pre-operative imaging with attention to ICA position in relation to the tumour, and selective ICA angiography, are essential before endoscopic sphenoid sinus surgery for JNA.
questions.question: A 16-year-old male with JNA extending into the sphenoid sinus has pre-operative embolisation and proceeds to endoscopic surgery. The sphenoid sinus component is at higher risk of which intraoperative complication specifically?
Hematoma of the auricle following blunt trauma accumulates between which structures?
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma to the auricle causes accumulation of blood between the perichondrium and cartilage. If not drained promptly, organisation and calcification of the clot with cartilage necrosis leads to the deformity known as 'cauliflower ear'. Treatment is repeated aspiration under sterile conditions with mastoid pressure dressings.

questions.question: EBV serology is used in NPC screening. The antibody with highest sensitivity for early NPC is:
questions.explanation: Elevated IgA antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus viral capsid antigen (IgA-VCA) are the most sensitive serological marker for NPC screening in endemic populations. IgA-VCA is elevated in approximately 90% of NPC patients, often before clinical presentation. Population screening with IgA-VCA and IgA-EA has been used in southern China, enabling detection at earlier, more curable stages. Persistently elevated titres in an endemic population warrant nasopharyngoscopy even in the absence of symptoms.

questions.question: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss combined with unilateral tinnitus in an adult necessitates exclusion of which specific diagnosis by MRI?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss, particularly with unilateral tinnitus and/or unilateral vestibular dysfunction, is the hallmark presentation of vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). These benign tumours arise from Schwann cells of the vestibular portion of CN VIII and grow slowly in the internal auditory canal, producing gradual unilateral SNHL and tinnitus. MRI with gadolinium (high-resolution T2 and T1+Gd) is the gold standard investigation, detecting tumours as small as 2-3 mm. All patients with unexplained asymmetric SNHL or unilateral tinnitus must undergo MRI to exclude this diagnosis.
options: Malignant external otitis with skull base invasion
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) of the internal auditory canal

questions.question: Which of the following BEST distinguishes a nasal foreign body from unilateral chronic sinusitis clinically?
questions.explanation: The most definitive clinical distinction between a nasal foreign body and unilateral sinusitis is the direct visualisation of a foreign object on anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy. When present, this is pathognomonic. In sinusitis, no foreign body is seen and CT typically shows mucosal thickening in the sinus. Both may respond partially to antibiotics, making antibiotic response unreliable as a distinguishing feature. SUBTOPIC 6: SINONASAL TUMOURS
options: Direct visualisation of the foreign object

questions.explanation: An Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell extends posterolaterally to lie adjacent to, or even surround, the optic nerve and internal carotid artery, so unrecognised entry into it during sphenoid surgery risks direct optic nerve injury. Preoperative CT identification of this cell allows the surgeon to orient dissection safely. The vidian nerve lies more inferiorly within the sphenoid floor rather than laterally.
questions.question: During endoscopic sphenoidotomy, the surgeon deliberately keeps dissection medial and low within the sphenoid face because a laterally placed air cell in this region may abut which critical structure?

options: Imaging facilities are unavailable in most centres
Symptoms mimic common upper respiratory tract infections,
These tumours are asymptomatic until very advanced
questions.question: Paranasal sinus malignancies are usually diagnosed late. The PRIMARY reason for this delayed diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Paranasal sinus malignancies present with symptoms (nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pain) that overlap with common upper respiratory tract infections and sinusitis. This symptomatic overlap leads to repeated treatment for presumed benign conditions, delaying imaging and biopsy that would reveal malignancy.

Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome (Plummer-Vinson in North America) consists of: dysphagia from a post-cricoid mucosal web, iron deficiency anaemia (hypochromic microcytic), and mucosal changes (angular cheilitis, glossitis, koilonychia). It affects predominantly middle-aged women and carries a predisposition to post-cricoid carcinoma. The web is best demonstrated on barium swallow as an anterior web in the post-cricoid hypopharynx. Treatment of the iron deficiency often causes regression of the web; persistent webs require endoscopic dilatation.
questions.question: Paterson-Brown Kelly (or Plummer-Vinson) syndrome is characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and which other feature?
Cholesteatoma is MOST commonly associated with which type of tympanic membrane pathology?
questions.explanation: Cholesteatoma most commonly forms from marginal perforations at the pars flaccida or retraction pockets that allow squamous epithelium to migrate inward. Evidence has shown cholesteatoma can form with either central or marginal perforations, nullifying strict classification by perforation location. It causes progressive bone erosion and hearing loss. SUBTOPIC 4: MANAGEMENT OF OTITIS MEDIA

A retained bronchial foreign body can present subtly with chronic cough and recurrent localised chest infection even without a clearly witnessed choking episode, since parents or caregivers may not always observe the aspiration event, and a ball-valve effect can cause air trapping and hyperinflation distal to the obstruction. Persistent, unexplained, localised respiratory symptoms in a child should prompt consideration of bronchoscopy to exclude this possibility. Delayed diagnosis increases the risk of complications such as bronchiectasis in the affected segment.
options: Retained foreign body causing a ball-valve obstruction
Simple viral bronchiolitis with no foreign body
Congenital lobar emphysema unrelated to any foreign object
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in a child
Primary tuberculosis without any foreign body
questions.question: A child presents with a several-week history of unexplained cough and recurrent chest infection localised to one lung segment. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation on the affected side. What diagnosis should be strongly considered despite no witnessed choking episode?

questions.explanation: Impetigo is an infection of the superficial layers of the epidermis, usually by S. aureus or occasionally S. pyogenes. It is distinct from perichondritis, which involves deeper peri-cartilaginous structures. Identifying the correct layer of involvement directs both antibiotic choice and route of administration.
questions.question: Impetigo of the external ear involves infection of which skin layer?

questions.explanation: Meningitis is the most common intracranial complication of rhinosinusitis. The frontal sinus is the most frequently implicated sinus in intracranial spread, which occurs via small diploic veins that communicate with venous plexi of the dura, periorbita, and cranial periosteum. All intracranial complications require neurosurgical consultation, high-dose antibiotics, and drainage procedures.
questions.question: The most common intracranial complication of rhinosinusitis is:

options: Sharp foreign body impaction in adults
Nasal foreign bodies in young children
questions.explanation: In airway foreign body aspiration in children, a positive history of choking must always be taken seriously even without current symptoms, because asymptomatic intervals are common. A negative history, however, can be misleading as children may not describe the episode and complications can still develop.
questions.question: In foreign body management, the adage 'a positive history must never be ignored, while a negative history may be misleading' MOST accurately applies to:
A patient with recurrent severe epistaxis undergoes endoscopic surgical ligation. Which artery is most commonly targeted by this approach?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation has become the preferred surgical approach for refractory posterior epistaxis because it directly and precisely addresses the dominant blood supply to the posterior nasal cavity with minimal morbidity. External carotid ligation is a less targeted, more invasive alternative used historically or when endoscopic access fails. Anterior ethmoidal artery ligation is reserved for bleeding localised to the superior nasal cavity.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent otitis externa is prescribed 8% aluminium acetate ear drops. What is the PRIMARY property of this preparation that benefits the condition?
questions.explanation: Aluminium acetate solution acts as an astringent, reducing oedema and drying the inflamed, moist canal skin, which helps create an environment less favourable to bacterial and fungal growth. This differs from antimicrobial agents that directly target the causative organism. It is often used as an adjunct alongside more specific antimicrobial treatment in otitis externa management.
options: Astringent, drying action on the inflamed canal skin

questions.question: Emotional disturbance in a child can cause developmental language disorder PRIMARILY by:
questions.explanation: Emotional disturbance disrupts the social interaction, motivation, and attention processes fundamental to language learning. Language acquisition requires social engagement and communicative intent; severe emotional disturbance can impair these prerequisites without causing organic neurological damage.
options: Producing structural changes in the articulators
Interfering with the motivation and social

questions.explanation: Amoxicillin/clavulanate provides additional beta-lactamase coverage and is used when there is recent antibiotic exposure, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis suggesting H. influenzae, or penicillin allergy (in which case second/third-generation cephalosporins may be used). Clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamase-producing resistant organisms.
questions.question: Amoxicillin/clavulanate (co-amoxiclav) is used instead of amoxicillin alone in AOM when there is:
A patient develops forehead fluctuance and scalp oedema after frontal sinusitis. Imaging shows osteomyelitis of the frontal bone anterior wall. This condition is eponymously called:
questions.explanation: Pott's puffy tumour is a subperiosteal abscess overlying the frontal sinus with underlying osteomyelitis of the frontal bone outer table, first described by Percivall Pott. It presents as a fluctuant, doughy forehead swelling and can spread intracranially. Gradenigo syndrome involves petrous apex osteomyelitis, and Bezold abscess is a complication of mastoiditis.

questions.question: A patient with rhinosinusitis develops the most common orbital complication seen in children specifically. What is this complication?
questions.explanation: Subperiosteal abscess is the most common orbital complication of sinusitis in children, typically arising from ethmoid sinusitis with pus collecting between the periosteum and lamina papyracea. It often responds to intravenous antibiotics in young children, though drainage may be required if there is progression or visual compromise. Cavernous sinus thrombosis, while more severe, is comparatively rarer than subperiosteal abscess in the paediatric population.

Primary sinonasal mucosal melanoma is a rare, aggressive malignancy arising from melanocytes in the nasal and sinus mucosa. It carries a significantly worse prognosis than cutaneous melanoma due to its anatomical location limiting surgical margins, late presentation (often advanced stage at diagnosis), and inherent biological aggressiveness. Unlike cutaneous melanoma, it is not related to UV exposure. Five-year survival is approximately 20–30%.
options: Always presents with skin pigmentation changes
Is exclusively seen in dark-skinned patients
Has a worse prognosis from mucosal melanocytes
questions.question: Malignant melanoma of the sinonasal tract differs from cutaneous melanoma in that it:

questions.explanation: Otoacoustic emissions testing measures sound generated by healthy outer hair cells of the cochlea in response to an auditory stimulus, providing an objective, rapid assessment of peripheral cochlear function suitable for newborn screening. It does not directly assess neural or central auditory pathways, which require complementary tests such as ABR if OAEs are absent or if retrocochlear pathology is suspected. This makes OAE testing a useful first-line screening tool rather than a comprehensive diagnostic test.
questions.question: A newborn undergoes an otoacoustic emissions (OAE) screening test. What aspect of hearing function does this test specifically measure?

questions.explanation: A long-standing nasal foreign body causing granulation tissue, mucosal inflammation, unilateral purulent discharge, and nasal obstruction can clinically mimic both unilateral sinusitis (same discharge and obstruction) and sinonasal malignancy (granulation tissue and possible bony erosion). Careful rhinoscopy, imaging, and examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with biopsy are important to differentiate these conditions.
questions.question: A nasal foreign body causing granulation tissue in the nasal cavity closely mimics which clinical condition?
options: Both unilateral sinusitis and sinonasal malignancy
Bilateral nasal polyposis at all times

questions.question: A wood carpenter presents with a painless progressive unilateral nasal mass. Which occupational exposure BEST explains the likelihood of malignancy in this patient?
questions.explanation: Wood dust exposure is a well-established risk factor for adenocarcinoma of the maxillary sinus. The occupational history of wood dust directly correlates with cancer of the maxilla, making it the most critical finding here.

questions.question: Which segment of the facial nerve within the Fallopian canal has the least diameter relative to the bony canal, making it most susceptible to pressure-related injury?
questions.explanation: The labyrinthine segment (between the fundus of the internal auditory canal and the geniculate ganglion) is the shortest (2-4 mm) and narrowest segment of the Fallopian canal, with the smallest ratio of nerve diameter to bony canal diameter. This means that even modest oedema produces proportionally greater pressure increase in this segment compared to the wider mastoid segment. This anatomical vulnerability explains why the labyrinthine segment and the meatal foramen are the most common sites of facial nerve compression in Bell's palsy and herpes zoster, and the most common injury site in transverse temporal bone fractures.

questions.question: A patient with nasal polyps undergoes surgery using a powered micro-debrider rather than traditional forceps avulsion. What is the main advantage of this instrument?
questions.explanation: The micro-debrider allows controlled, precise removal of polyp tissue while better preserving surrounding healthy mucosa compared with blunt forceps avulsion, which can strip normal tissue and increase bleeding and scarring. This precision improves postoperative healing and visualisation during endoscopic sinus surgery. It does not, however, eliminate the underlying inflammatory tendency that drives polyp recurrence.
options: More precise tissue removal with reduced mucosal trauma
Ability to operate without endoscopic visualisation
No need for postoperative steroid therapy

questions.question: A patient with confirmed ear cancer is being planned for definitive treatment. What combination approach does treatment of ear cancer generally involve?
options: Observation alone without any active treatment
Surgery combined with radiotherapy, depending on stage and histology
Radiotherapy alone in all cases without exception
Topical treatment alone with no systemic or surgical therapy
questions.explanation: Treatment of ear cancer generally involves a combined multimodal approach of surgical resection and radiotherapy, individualised according to tumour stage, histological type, and extent of local invasion, reflecting the complex anatomy and aggressive potential of malignancies in this region. This differs from treatment of benign or purely infective ear conditions, which do not require oncological therapy. A multidisciplinary team approach optimises outcomes for this relatively rare but potentially aggressive group of tumours.

questions.question: A patient using over-the-counter oxymetazoline nasal spray for three weeks now reports worsening congestion that improves only briefly after each spray. What is the underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: Prolonged topical decongestant use downregulates alpha-adrenergic receptors, so rebound vasodilation and congestion occur once the drug effect wears off, driving a cycle of dependence known as rhinitis medicamentosa. The correct management is to withdraw the spray, often with a short course of nasal steroids to ease withdrawal symptoms. This is distinct from an infectious or allergic process.

questions.question: Burkitt lymphoma involving the sinonasal region is characteristically described as:
questions.explanation: African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma characteristically presents as a rapidly expanding, grotesque jaw or facial mass primarily affecting children in sub-Saharan Africa, strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and malaria co-infection. In the sinonasal region, it produces rapid facial swelling. Without treatment it can double in size within days. Chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide) produces dramatic responses.
options: A vascular tumour with profuse epistaxis
A firm unilateral submandibular mass in the elderly
A painless unilateral neck mass with night sweats at all times
A rapidly expanding, grotesque facial swelling most commonly affecting African children

questions.question: Surgical ligation for recalcitrant epistaxis most commonly targets which artery as the primary endoscopic approach?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation at the sphenopalatine foramen has become the preferred surgical approach for recalcitrant posterior epistaxis. It is minimally invasive and has high success rates. It can be combined with ethmoidal artery ligation if anterior ethmoidal artery bleeding is present. External carotid artery ligation in the neck is reserved for rare cases of life-threatening haemorrhage.
options: External carotid artery in the neck
Maxillary artery in the pterygopalatine fossa
Facial artery in the submandibular region
Sphenopalatine artery endoscopically at the sphenopalatine foramen
Anterior ethmoidal artery via an external ethmoidectomy

questions.question: Oval window fistula can be differentiated from Meniere's disease primarily by:
questions.explanation: Oval window fistula is associated with a clear history of sudden pressure change (Valsalva, sneeze, dive) and confirmed by surgical exploration finding perilymph leakage. Meniere's disease features endolymphatic hydrops without such precipitating events. Definitive diagnosis of perilymph fistula can only be made by surgical exploration.
options: Just a simple pure tone audiometry pattern
History of pressure change and surgical findings

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a reactive (non-infective) form of otitis externa?
questions.explanation: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is classified as a reactive (non-infective) condition causing otitis externa. The reactive category also includes eczema, neurodermatitis, keratitis obturans, and psoriasis. Distinguishing reactive from infective causes determines whether topical steroids or antimicrobials (or both) are indicated.

questions.question: The Scheibe and Mondini-Michelle abnormalities are examples of which category of congenital SNHL?
questions.explanation: Scheibe and Mondini-Michelle abnormalities represent developmental inner ear malformations causing congenital SNHL. They fall under the category of hereditary hearing loss with abnormal inner ear morphology. CT and MRI imaging of the temporal bones can identify these structural inner ear anomalies preoperatively before cochlear implantation.

questions.question: A patient with a history of prolonged nasogastric tube feeding develops new-onset stridor and hoarseness. What complication should be suspected?
options: Posterior glottic or subglottic pressure injury from the tube
Allergic reaction to the feeding formula
questions.explanation: Prolonged nasogastric tube presence can cause pressure-related mucosal injury and subsequent scarring at the posterior larynx or subglottis, similar to the mechanism seen with prolonged endotracheal intubation, leading to new stridor and voice change that should prompt laryngoscopic evaluation. Recognising the tube as a potential contributing factor is important for both diagnosis and future prevention. Early removal or repositioning of the tube when symptoms develop can help prevent progression to fixed stenosis.

options: Toward the floor of the canal
Toward the canal roof and posteriorly
questions.explanation: The nozzle of the syringe should be aimed slightly upward and backward (toward the roof and posteriorly) so that water flows as a cascade along the canal roof and exits along the floor with wax and debris. Direct irrigation onto the tympanic membrane risks perforation. Water should be at or near body temperature to prevent caloric vertigo.
questions.question: When irrigating the ear canal for cerumen removal, the water jet should be directed:

options: Controlling the bleeding first, then addressing hypertension as the bleeding itself elevates BP
Performing bilateral anterior nasal packing without blood pressure control as the sole finding
questions.explanation: In epistaxis associated with elevated blood pressure, the priority is to control active bleeding first, as pain and anxiety from the epistaxis themselves elevate blood pressure. Antihypertensive therapy is important but secondary. Uncontrolled hypertension is both a risk factor for epistaxis and an aggravating factor preventing vessel constriction, and long-term BP control reduces recurrence risk.
questions.question: In the management of epistaxis due to hypertension, the MOST important initial step is:

questions.explanation: Wedge filters are used in maxillary sinus radiotherapy to achieve dose homogeneity across the irregular tissue thickness of the head and face. Without wedges, the dose distribution would be non-uniform, with higher doses in thinner tissue and lower doses in thicker tissue along each beam path.
options: Better dose homogeneity across the tumour volume
Treatment of ipsilateral neck nodes simultaneously
Reduction of exit dose to the contralateral eye
questions.question: Maxillary sinus cancer radiotherapy uses anterior and lateral wedged fields at 45 degrees. Wedging the fields PRIMARILY achieves:

options: Canal oedema from negative middle ear pressure
Irritation of canal skin by persistent otorrhea
questions.explanation: Secondary otitis externa from chronic or acute otitis media occurs because the persistent purulent otorrhea irritates and inflames the external auditory canal skin. This distinguishes it from primary otitis externa where the canal itself is the initial site. Treatment must address both the middle ear source and the secondary canal inflammation.
questions.question: Secondary otitis externa as a complication of chronic suppurative otitis media results from which mechanism?

options: Total laryngectomy as the only curative option
Observation with repeat biopsy in six months
Radical neck dissection without primary site treatment
Radiotherapy or endoscopic laser excision with similar cure rates
questions.question: A patient with a T1 glottic squamous cell carcinoma confined to one vocal cord with normal mobility is being counselled on treatment. What is an appropriate first-line option?
questions.explanation: Early-stage T1 glottic carcinoma confined to the vocal cord with preserved mobility has excellent outcomes with either radiotherapy or transoral laser microsurgery, both offering comparable cure rates while preserving voice function and avoiding total laryngectomy. Choice between modalities depends on patient factors, voice quality goals, and institutional expertise. Total laryngectomy is reserved for advanced or recurrent disease.

The voice test and watch-tick test are simple, low-technology screening tests of hearing that assess a patient's ability to detect speech or a ticking sound at graded distances, historically useful where formal audiometric equipment was unavailable. While useful for rapid screening, they lack the precision of formal audiometry for quantifying hearing thresholds. They remain a practical bedside tool in resource-limited settings.
questions.question: Which hearing tests, historically used in general practice before audiometry became widely available, rely on the examiner's voice and clock sound at graded distances?

options: Chronic rhinosinusitis with active mucosal disease
Normal variant requiring no further action
questions.question: A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps undergoes endoscopy showing polypoid mucosal change specifically within the middle meatus. What does this endoscopic finding most specifically suggest?
questions.explanation: Polypoid change specifically within the middle meatus, the common drainage pathway for the anterior sinuses, is a specific endoscopic marker supporting a diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis with ongoing mucosal inflammation, distinguishing it from simple allergic rhinitis without sinus involvement. This finding often correlates with radiological evidence of osteomeatal complex disease. It also helps guide the surgeon toward the likely areas requiring attention during functional endoscopic sinus surgery.

questions.question: Which medical treatment has been investigated as neo-adjuvant therapy to reduce JNA size and vascularity before surgery?
questions.explanation: Flutamide, a non-steroidal anti-androgen, has been studied as pre-operative neo-adjuvant therapy for JNA based on the demonstrated androgen receptor expression on tumour cells. Some studies report tumour volume reduction of 30-44% after 3 months of flutamide therapy, potentially reducing intraoperative blood loss and facilitating complete resection. It is not universally adopted as standard of care, and pre-operative embolisation remains the mainstay of pre-surgical haemostatic preparation.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent severe posterior epistaxis fails nasal packing. Which artery is most often ligated or embolised to control this bleeding?
questions.explanation: Posterior epistaxis refractory to packing most commonly originates from the sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, and endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation is the definitive treatment. This approach has largely replaced older techniques such as internal maxillary artery ligation via the antrum. Success rates for endoscopic ligation exceed 90 percent.

The classic triad of episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus without prior infection points to Meniere's disease. This endolymphatic hydrops disorder is distinguished by its fluctuating, recurrent nature.
questions.question: A patient presents with episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating hearing loss. In the history, he reports no prior ear surgery or infection. These symptoms MOST suggest:

questions.explanation: Stapedectomy is performed for otosclerosis (fixation of the stapes footplate), not for chronic otitis media. COM surgery includes myringoplasty (TM repair), tympanoplasty (middle ear and TM), ossicular reconstruction, and mastoidectomy. The choice depends on the extent of disease and degree of functional hearing loss.
questions.question: All of the following are surgical options in the management of COM EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Topical preparations combining an antibiotic with a steroid mixture are standard first-line treatment for diffuse bacterial otitis externa. The steroid component reduces inflammation and oedema. The antibiotic addresses the bacterial pathogen, most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
questions.question: The FIRST-LINE topical treatment for bacterial diffuse otitis externa is a preparation combining antibiotic with:
A patient with a parapharyngeal space abscess develops ipsilateral tongue deviation on protrusion. Which nerve within this space has been compromised?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve traverses the parapharyngeal space and, when compressed or infiltrated, causes ipsilateral tongue deviation toward the affected side on protrusion due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus. Recognising cranial nerve involvement helps localise the extent of a deep neck infection. Prompt imaging and drainage prevent further neurological compromise.

questions.question: A patient presents with recurrent nosebleeds and is found to be on long-term anticoagulant therapy for atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate initial approach to epistaxis management in this context?
options: Immediately and permanently discontinue all anticoagulation
Ignore the epistaxis since anticoagulation cannot be adjusted
Increase the anticoagulant dose to prevent clot formation
Refer only for cardiology review without local treatment
Local measures first while carefully reviewing anticoagulation rather than stopping it reflexively
questions.explanation: In anticoagulated patients with epistaxis, local haemostatic measures such as pressure and nasal packing should be attempted first, and any decision to withhold or reverse anticoagulation must carefully balance bleeding risk against thromboembolic risk, ideally in consultation with the prescribing team rather than stopping therapy reflexively. Over-correction can precipitate serious thrombotic events such as stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Most epistaxis in anticoagulated patients can be controlled without complete cessation of therapy.

When a rhinolith extends into the maxillary antrum beyond reach of anterior instrumentation, a Caldwell-Luc approach through the canine fossa provides direct surgical access to remove the calcified mass completely. Incomplete removal risks recurrent infection and persistent symptoms. Preoperative imaging helps define the exact extent of the rhinolith before planning the surgical approach.
questions.question: A rhinolith has extended posteriorly into the maxillary antrum and cannot be removed via a simple anterior approach. What surgical access is required?
On examination of the external ear, palpation of the mastoid process reveals exquisite tenderness. This finding is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Tenderness over the mastoid process indicates inflammation of the mastoid air cells, most commonly as a complication of acute otitis media. This physical sign is pathognomonic of mastoiditis and requires urgent management.

An obturator prosthesis is fitted to fill the surgical palatal defect after maxillectomy, restoring the separation between the oral and nasal cavities to enable near-normal speech and swallowing. This is often the initial and sometimes definitive rehabilitation option, though free flap reconstruction may be used in select cases. Regular follow-up is needed to adjust the obturator as healing progresses.
questions.question: A patient with a maxillary sinus tumour undergoes total maxillectomy leaving a large palatal defect affecting speech and swallowing. What is the standard rehabilitation approach?
Which first-line antibiotic is recommended for treating acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in children with mild to moderate severity?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin at standard or high dose is the recommended first-line antibiotic for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in children with mild to moderate severity. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for non-responders, patients with more severe initial disease, and those at high risk for resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae. Ciprofloxacin (a quinolone) is used as a second-line adult agent.

options: Radiation-induced fibrosis of pharyngeal constrictor muscles
Surgical resection of the soft palate
questions.question: Which nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal cancer treatment complication is the most common long-term cause of dysphagia in survivors?
questions.explanation: Radiation-induced pharyngeal constrictor muscle fibrosis is the most common and challenging long-term dysphagia mechanism in head and neck cancer survivors. Doses above 50-55 Gy to the pharyngeal constrictors cause progressive fibrosis and reduced contractile force, resulting in incomplete pharyngeal stripping, residue, aspiration, and severe dietary restriction years after treatment. IMRT-based dose reduction to uninvolved pharyngeal constrictors and early swallowing exercises ('preventive rehabilitation') during radiation reduce this complication.

Exostoses are benign bony growths of the external auditory canal strongly associated with repeated cold-water exposure, thought to result from a periosteal reaction to cold stimulus. They differ from solitary osteomas, which are typically single, pedunculated, and unrelated to cold-water exposure. Symptomatic exostoses causing recurrent canal obstruction or infection may require surgical removal.
questions.question: A cold-water swimmer presents with a bony projection growing into the external auditory canal causing recurrent water and debris trapping. What is this condition called?
The Caldwell view in sinus radiology is PRIMARILY used to visualize which sinus?
questions.explanation: The Caldwell (postero-anterior) view is the preferred projection for visualising the frontal sinuses and ethmoid sinuses. It complements the Water's view (maxillary sinuses), and together both views provide comprehensive assessment of all paranasal sinuses on plain films.

options: Hennebert's sign (pressure-induced nystagmus with intact TM)
Otolith crisis of Tumarkin (sudden drop attack)
questions.question: Superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD) causes a specific symptom triggered by pressure or loud sounds. This symptom is called:
questions.explanation: Tullio's phenomenon vertigo and/or nystagmus triggered by loud sounds is the pathognomonic symptom of superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD). The thin bone dehiscence overlying the superior canal creates a 'third mobile window' into the membranous labyrinth, allowing sound or pressure energy that should move the stapes footplate to instead deflect the superior canal ampulla, triggering inappropriate vestibular responses. SSCD also causes autophony, pulsatile tinnitus, and bone conduction hyperacusis. High-resolution CT of the temporal bones is the diagnostic investigation.

options: No further action needed since the tonsil has been removed
Simple observation with review only if symptoms recur
Urgent referral for full oncological staging and haemato-oncology input
Repeat tonsillectomy on the contralateral side as treatment
Antibiotic course to treat presumed residual infection
questions.question: A patient with recurrent tonsillitis has a tonsillectomy performed and histology unexpectedly reveals non-Hodgkin lymphoma. What should guide subsequent management?
questions.explanation: Unexpected diagnosis of lymphoma on tonsillectomy histology requires urgent referral for full staging investigations, including imaging and bone marrow assessment, and management by a haemato-oncology team, since treatment is systemic rather than further local surgery. This scenario highlights why unusual, asymmetric, or rapidly enlarging tonsillar tissue should always raise suspicion for malignancy. Tonsillar lymphoma often presents as painless unilateral enlargement rather than the typical infective symptoms of tonsillitis.

questions.question: A mucocele of the frontoethmoidal sinus region is best described as:
options: An infected mucosal cyst with rapid expansion as the sole finding
A chronic cystic lesion lined by pseudostratified epithelium expanding over years
An acute abscess requiring immediate drainage
A retention cyst without bony erosion
questions.explanation: A mucocele is a chronic, slowly expanding cystic lesion lined by pseudostratified or columnar epithelium that develops when sinus ostia are obstructed. These lesions expand over many years (often requiring more than 10 years to become symptomatic) and cause bony erosion of adjacent structures such as the orbit, skull base, or cranial cavity.

options: Lubricate the tube for easier suction
Reduce bleeding from the tracheal mucosa
Prevent crusting or soften formed crusts
Maintain tube patency by dilating the trachea
questions.explanation: Instilling sodium bicarbonate or normal saline through the tracheostomy tube helps prevent the formation of thick crusts or softens existing crusts within the tube lumen. This regular care prevents tube obstruction, one of the most serious immediate complications of tracheostomy.
questions.question: Sodium bicarbonate or normal saline is instilled into a tracheostomy tube PRIMARILY to:

options: Multiple pale bilateral masses in the middle meatus
Purulent discharge from the posterior ethmoid
A globular smooth mass filling the choana or nasopharynx
Granulations on the posterior nasal surface
A pedunculated mass arising from the soft well-defined palate
questions.question: The posterior rhinoscopy finding most typical of an antrochoanal polyp is:
questions.explanation: On posterior rhinoscopy (or nasopharyngoscopy), an antrochoanal polyp characteristically appears as a globular, smooth, grey mass filling the posterior choana or nasopharynx. It does not bleed on probing and is insensitive to probing. It may not be visible on anterior rhinoscopy if it has grown entirely posteriorly — a reason why posterior rhinoscopy is essential in evaluating suspected antrochoanal polyp.

The nose and paranasal sinuses drain primarily to the submandibular and upper deep cervical lymph node groups, which is relevant when assessing regional spread of sinonasal infection or malignancy. This drainage pattern differs from the retropharyngeal first-echelon drainage more specific to posterior nasal and nasopharyngeal structures. Awareness of this pattern guides clinical examination and staging in patients with sinonasal disease.
questions.question: A patient with chronic sinusitis is noted to have enlarged cervical lymph nodes on examination. To which nodal group does the nose and paranasal sinuses primarily drain lymphatically?
Waldeyer's ring comprises several lymphoid tissue components. Which of the following is NOT a recognized constituent of Waldeyer's ring?
questions.explanation: Waldeyer's ring consists of: nasopharyngeal tonsils (adenoids), palatine tonsils, tubal tonsils (near Eustachian tube orifice), lingual tonsils, and posterior pharyngeal wall lymphoid follicles. Thymic remnants are mediastinal structures unrelated to Waldeyer's ring. This lymphoid ring provides immune surveillance at the aerodigestive junction.

questions.question: An elderly diabetic patient presents with severe otalgia out of proportion to examination findings, along with headache and facial nerve weakness. Which history feature MOST strongly suggests malignant (necrotising) otitis externa?
questions.explanation: Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus is the principal predisposing factor for malignant otitis externa, an aggressive Pseudomonas infection extending into skull base bone. Pain disproportionate to clinical signs plus cranial nerve involvement should raise immediate suspicion in this population. Swimming and cotton bud use cause simple otitis externa, not the necrotising form.

questions.question: At birth, which paranasal sinuses are already present?
questions.explanation: At birth, the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are already present. The frontal sinus develops from the frontal bone during the first year of life and becomes radiologically visible around age 5. The sphenoid sinus arises within the nasal capsule and begins significant pneumatization at approximately age 3.

options: The infant eustachian tube is longer, narrower, and more angled
The infant cartilaginous eustachian tube lacks a tensor veli palatini muscle
The infant eustachian tube is lined by respiratory epithelium only
The infant eustachian tube is shorter, wider, and more horizontal
The infant eustachian tube opens directly into the nasopharynx without a tubal torus
questions.explanation: In infants, the eustachian tube is shorter, wider, and more horizontal than in older children and adults. This anatomical configuration allows easier reflux of nasopharyngeal bacteria and secretions into the middle ear, particularly during feeding and upper respiratory infections, explaining the high frequency of AOM in infants. As the child grows, the tube elongates, narrows, and acquires a more vertical angle.
questions.question: Acute otitis media (AOM) in infants is more common than in older children primarily because of which anatomical difference in the eustachian tube?
Melanoma of the ear pinna is best managed with:
options: Wide excision with sentinel node biopsy
Incisional biopsy followed by radiotherapy treatment
questions.explanation: Melanoma of the pinna requires wide surgical excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy to assess regional spread. Any structure in the ear can develop into melanoma, which is more aggressive than basal or squamous cell carcinoma. Adjuvant therapy (immunotherapy or targeted therapy) depends on staging and molecular testing.

questions.question: A patient with Meniere's disease presents with the classic triad. Which combination of symptoms confirms this diagnosis?
options: Sudden hearing loss with facial weakness
Progressive hearing loss with headache only
Fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo
questions.explanation: Meniere's disease is defined by the triad of fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo attacks typically lasting 20 minutes to several hours, along with a sensation of aural fullness. This distinguishes it from BPPV, which lacks auditory symptoms, and from vestibular neuritis, which causes a single prolonged episode. Endolymphatic hydrops is the presumed underlying pathology.

For infants below one year with complete airway obstruction from foreign body or abscess, back blows (five firm back blows between the shoulder blades) are the recommended first intervention. Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) are used for children over one year old.
questions.question: In paediatric retropharyngeal abscess, children aged below 1 year who present with complete airway obstruction should have which specific intervention first?

questions.explanation: Aspergillus niger otomycosis characteristically produces black or dark grey fungal debris within the ear canal, often described as resembling wet newspaper or having visible fungal filaments, distinguishing it from bacterial or other fungal aetiologies. Recognising this appearance supports antifungal rather than antibacterial topical treatment. Adequate aural toilet to remove debris is an essential part of effective treatment.
options: Pulsatile bluish mass behind the drum
Black or dark grey fungal debris resembling wet newspaper
Pure white, dry, flaky debris only
questions.question: A patient with otomycosis caused by Aspergillus niger is examined. What characteristic clinical finding is typically seen?

questions.explanation: When perichondritis progresses to chondritis with abscess formation, incision and drainage combined with debridement of non-viable cartilage is necessary. Betadine or boric acid wet-to-dry dressings are used for open wound management. Cultures should be obtained for antibiotic guidance, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa being the most common organism.
questions.question: In perichondritis progressing to chondritis with abscess, which surgical intervention is required?
options: Systemic antibiotics given alone, with nothing else
Incision, drainage, debridement of dead cartilage

questions.question: A 50-year-old asthmatic develops severe bronchospasm and nasal congestion minutes after taking ibuprofen for headache. He also has known nasal polyps. Which triad does this represent?
questions.explanation: The combination of nasal polyps, asthma, and hypersensitivity reaction to aspirin or NSAIDs defines Samter's triad, driven by dysregulated arachidonic acid metabolism favouring leukotriene overproduction. Affected patients must avoid NSAIDs and may benefit from leukotriene receptor antagonists. Aspirin desensitisation protocols are sometimes used in refractory cases under specialist supervision.

questions.question: During anterior rhinoscopy using a Thudicum speculum, the examiner should hold the speculum correctly. The MOST important reason for proper speculum technique is to:
questions.explanation: The nasal mucosa is highly vascular and fragile, making proper Thudicum speculum technique essential to prevent trauma, bleeding, and patient discomfort. Inadequate technique can also obscure findings with blood or trigger vasovagal reactions.

In adults, the external auditory canal has a natural S-shaped curve that obscures the view of the tympanic membrane on direct insertion. Pulling the pinna upward, backward, and outward straightens this curve, allowing a clear line of sight. In infants the pinna is instead pulled downward and backward because the canal curves differently.
questions.question: During otoscopic examination of an adult, the examiner pulls the pinna upward, backward, and outward before insertion of the speculum. The PRIMARY purpose of this manoeuvre is to:
The act of swallowing involves three distinct phases. In a healthy adult, the entire swallowing sequence from oral placement to oesophageal clearance takes approximately:
questions.explanation: The complete swallowing sequence oral preparation, oral phase, pharyngeal phase, and oesophageal phase takes approximately 8-10 seconds in a healthy adult. The pharyngeal phase alone is extremely rapid (less than 1 second) and involuntary once triggered. The oesophageal phase takes the longest (6-8 seconds) as the bolus is propelled by peristalsis from the upper oesophageal sphincter to the lower oesophageal sphincter. Prolonged total swallowing time suggests dysmotility.

options: Waters' view showing erosion of the orbital floor
Caldwell (PA) view showing opacification of the maxillary sinus
Submentovertex view showing skull base erosion
Lateral sinus view showing anterior bowing of the posterior antral wall
AP view showing nasal septum deviation
questions.question: The Holman-Miller sign on sinus X-ray is considered pathognomonic of JNA. This sign is seen on which view?
questions.explanation: The Holman-Miller sign is best seen on the lateral sinus view as anterior bowing (displacement) of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum. This pathognomonic finding results from JNA expanding through the pterygomaxillary fissure from the pterygopalatine fossa into the retromaxillary space, pushing the posterior antral wall forward. While modern CT has largely replaced plain sinus films, the Holman-Miller sign remains a classic teaching point and may still be the initial clue suggesting JNA in a resource-limited setting.

options: It requires no electricity and frees
It is lighter and more comfortable
