Patient preference is an important consideration listed under 'the patient factors' influencing the choice between radical and palliative treatment. Other patient factors include age, general condition, morbidity/mortality risk, function, cosmetics, and reliability for follow-up.
questions.question: In head and neck cancer management, the patient's 'preference' is listed as a factor influencing treatment choice under which category?
Silver nitrate cauterisation should NEVER be performed bilaterally on the nasal septum simultaneously because:
options: Bilateral simultaneous cauterisation risks septal perforation by ischaemic necrosis
Silver nitrate dissolves bilateral cartilage within 24 well-defined hours
It would scar both olfactory mucosae
questions.explanation: Silver nitrate cauterisation should always be performed on only one side of the nasal septum at a time, with a minimum waiting period of 4–6 weeks before treating the opposite side. Simultaneous bilateral cauterisation creates two opposing zones of chemical burn-induced ischaemia in the thin avascular septum, risking central ischaemic necrosis and septal perforation — a serious complication causing chronic crusting and breathing difficulty. SUBTOPIC 5: FOREIGN BODIES IN THE NOSE

options: Isolated cricopharyngeal dysfunction without pharyngeal weakness
Delayed swallow trigger with reduced pharyngeal contraction strength
Loss of taste causing reduced appetite rather than dysphagia
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis develops progressive dysphagia. The most characteristic swallowing dysfunction in MS involves:
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis affects the brainstem and corticobulbar pathways that coordinate pharyngeal swallowing. The characteristic dysfunction involves delayed triggering of the pharyngeal swallow reflex and reduced pharyngeal contraction strength, causing incomplete bolus clearance, pyriform sinus residue, and aspiration risk. The combination of delayed trigger (increased aspiration risk for thin liquids) and reduced pharyngeal contractile strength (causing residue and overflow aspiration) often necessitates dietary texture modification and compensatory swallowing manoeuvres.

questions.question: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the nasopharynx differs from NPC in which feature?
options: Rapid nodal spread before skull base invasion
Strong EBV association similar to NPC
Perineural spread tendency without EBV association
questions.explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the nasopharynx is a salivary gland-type tumour with characteristic perineural invasion along cranial nerve sheaths, often causing pain and progressive cranial nerve deficits. Unlike NPC, ACC has no EBV association, is not radiosensitive (surgery is the primary modality), tends to have indolent locoregional growth with late distant metastases, and does not have the same endemic geographic distribution. These differences significantly affect management strategy.

options: A local anaesthetic combined with an antiviral
An analgesic combined with a decongestant
An antifungal combined with an antihistamine
An antiseptic combined with a mucolytic
An antibiotic combined with a corticosteroid
questions.explanation: First-line topical treatment for bacterial diffuse otitis externa typically combines an antibiotic to target the causative organism with a corticosteroid to reduce the accompanying inflammation and oedema of the canal. This combination addresses both the infective and inflammatory components of the condition simultaneously. Selection of a non-ototoxic preparation is important if there is any possibility of a tympanic membrane perforation.
questions.question: A patient with diffuse bacterial otitis externa is prescribed a first-line topical preparation. What combination does this preparation typically contain?
Balloon catheter extraction of oesophageal foreign bodies is effective in what percentage of cases?
questions.explanation: Balloon catheter extraction is effective in approximately 90% of appropriately selected oesophageal foreign body cases. Failures require endoscopic retrieval. The technique involves passing a balloon catheter beyond the foreign body, inflating it, and withdrawing to remove the impacted object.

options: Common bacterial pathogens including Staphylococcus and Escherichia species
questions.question: Cerumen has recognised antimicrobial properties. Against which type of organisms has this bactericidal effect been MOST demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Cerumen has demonstrated bactericidal properties against a range of common bacterial pathogens, including certain Staphylococcus and Escherichia species, contributing to the ear canal's natural defence against infection. This antimicrobial function, combined with its acidic pH and waterproofing properties, helps explain why excessive or inappropriate cerumen removal can predispose to otitis externa. Recognising this protective role supports conservative management of asymptomatic cerumen.

questions.question: Prophylactic neck radiotherapy is avoided in early laryngeal cancers PRIMARILY because these tumours have low rates of:
questions.explanation: Early laryngeal (glottic) carcinomas, particularly T1 lesions, have a very low incidence of cervical lymph node metastases (approximately 2%). This low nodal risk means that prophylactic neck irradiation would expose the patient to radiation toxicity without meaningful oncological benefit.

questions.question: Occupational rhinitis in woodworkers is most specifically associated with which type of wood dust and tumour risk?
options: Softwood (pine) dust causing squamous cell carcinoma at all times
Hardwood dust (mahogany, teak) causing adenocarcinoma of the ethmoid sinus
questions.explanation: Exposure to hardwood dust (particularly mahogany and Western Red Cedar in furniture and cabinet-making industries) is strongly associated with occupational rhinitis and a markedly elevated risk of intestinal-type adenocarcinoma of the ethmoid sinus. This occupational cancer risk is a well-recognized association requiring long-term surveillance of affected workers.

questions.question: Which benign sinonasal tumour is described as consisting of inverted (endophytic), everted (exophytic), or transitional papilloma types and arises from Schneiderian mucosa?
questions.explanation: Papillomas (Schneiderian papillomas) arise from the Schneiderian mucosa (ectodermal-derived sinonasal epithelium) and are classified into three types: inverted (most common, endophytic growth pattern with malignant potential), fungiform or everted (exophytic, rare), and cylindrical/transitional papilloma. Inverted papilloma is the most clinically significant due to local recurrence and malignant transformation risk.

questions.question: The anterior approach for external surgical drainage of deep neck abscesses involves retraction of which structures?
options: Lateral retraction of larynx and medial retraction of carotid sheath
Lateral retraction of carotid sheath and medial retraction of larynx,
Inferior retraction of clavicle and superior retraction of mandible
Lateral retraction of sternocleidomastoid and medial retraction of carotid
Medial retraction of sternocleidomastoid and lateral retraction of larynx
questions.explanation: The anterior approach to deep neck abscess drainage involves lateral retraction of the carotid sheath and medial retraction of the larynx, trachea, and thyroid. This allows access to the retropharyngeal, danger, and prevertebral spaces via the anterior neck.

options: JNA shows central necrosis while NPC is solid throughout
NPC always shows bone erosion while JNA does not
JNA has bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy while NPC has none
EBV in situ hybridisation is positive in JNA and negative in NPC
Young male, lateral origin, intense enhancement with flow voids vs older patient, midline mucosa, heterogeneous mass in NPC
questions.explanation: JNA and NPC are distinguished radiologically by: JNA young adolescent male, lateral nasopharyngeal wall origin (sphenopalatine foramen), intense homogeneous enhancement, salt-and-pepper flow voids on MRI, characteristic pterygopalatine fossa involvement and antral bowing. NPC middle-aged patient from endemic region, nasopharyngeal mucosa origin (often fossa of Rosenmueller), heterogeneous enhancement, cervical lymphadenopathy, and positive EBV in situ hybridisation on biopsy. The combination of patient demographics and imaging characteristics reliably distinguishes the two entities.
questions.question: JNA can be distinguished from nasopharyngeal carcinoma on MRI by which set of features?

options: Directly reduces eosinophil counts in mucosa
Desensitizes C-fibre nociceptors, reducing neurogenic inflammation
Kills fungal organisms in the sinuses
Shrinks polyp vascularity like a decongestant
Blocks IgE receptors on mast cells
questions.question: Topical capsaicin has been used in nasal polyposis as a therapeutic agent because it:
questions.explanation: Topical capsaicin (derived from chilli peppers) has been shown to be effective in treating non-allergic rhinitis and some forms of nasal polyposis. Its mechanism involves desensitization of TRPV1 receptors on C-fibre nociceptors in the nasal mucosa, depleting substance P and reducing neurogenic inflammation. It has been shown to reduce polyp size and symptoms in some studies.

options: Severe throbbing acute pain as the dominant feature
Multiple painless tympanic membrane perforations with profuse discharge
Rapid onset over hours with high fever
A single small central perforation with minimal discharge
questions.question: A patient with tuberculous otitis media is being evaluated. What clinical feature is characteristically associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Tuberculous otitis media characteristically presents with multiple, painless tympanic membrane perforations and profuse, often pale watery discharge, a pattern that helps distinguish it from typical acute pyogenic otitis media. The relative painlessness despite significant findings is a notable diagnostic clue. Suspicion should be raised in patients from high-tuberculosis-burden settings with an atypical, indolent presentation.

questions.question: A patient presents with a three-day history of severe throat pain, muffled 'hot potato' voice, and difficulty opening the mouth. This combination of history features is MOST suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Trismus, a muffled voice, and severe unilateral throat pain together form the classic triad of peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). Simple pharyngitis rarely causes trismus. Recognising this triad in the history prompts urgent examination for a fluctuant peritonsillar swelling requiring drainage.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile cilia syndrome) when combined with situs inversus (dextrocardia and abdominal organ transposition) constitutes Kartagener syndrome. The defective cilia result in chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and infertility. Samter's triad describes polyps plus asthma plus aspirin hypersensitivity, while Young syndrome is sinusitis plus azoospermia.
options: Nasal polyps, asthma, and aspirin sensitivity (Samter's triad)
Sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome)
questions.question: A patient with known primary ciliary dyskinesia is MOST likely to present with which combination of findings?
A tonsillectomy patient returns to the operating theatre on day 7 post-operatively with brisk oropharyngeal haemorrhage. This complication is classified as:
questions.explanation: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage is classified by timing: primary haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours of surgery (during the operation or immediately after), reactionary haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours related to rising blood pressure as anaesthetic wears off, and secondary haemorrhage occurs 5-10 days post-operatively due to sloughing of the fibrinous eschar covering the tonsillar bed. Day 7 bleeding is therefore secondary haemorrhage, typically caused by wound infection.

options: Peak size is reached at puberty
Adenoids begin shrinking after age 5-7 years
questions.question: Which statement about adenoid growth in children is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Adenoid tissue begins to enlarge after birth, with symptomatic enlargement possible between 18-24 months. Growth typically peaks at age 5-7 years, after which progressive involution occurs. By adolescence, adenoid tissue is substantially reduced in most individuals. Surgical intervention is therefore often timed carefully around this natural history of spontaneous regression.

A deviated septum toward the right narrows the right nasal passage, predisposing to impaired ventilation and mucociliary drainage of the right maxillary sinus. The left inferior turbinate compensatorily hypertrophies to fill the wider left nasal cavity. This combination on CT is classic for unilateral sinusitis with paradoxical compensatory turbinate changes.
questions.question: A coronal CT scan showing opacification of the right maxillary sinus with a hypertrophied left inferior turbinate and a rightward septal deviation is MOST consistent with:
Broadening of the nasal bridge with increased intercanthal distance in longstanding nasal polyposis suggests which complication?
questions.explanation: Longstanding, large, neglected nasal polyps can exert gradual pressure on the nasal bones and craniofacial skeleton, causing widening of the nasal bridge and increased intercanthal distance (widening between the inner corners of the eyes). This is a recognized but less common complication in severe, untreated polyposis, reflecting the potential for nasal polyps to physically remodel bone over time.

options: A preceding viral respiratory tract infection
questions.explanation: The majority of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis cases follow a preceding viral upper respiratory tract infection, which causes mucosal oedema and ciliary dysfunction that predisposes to secondary bacterial superinfection of the sinuses. Other causes such as dental infection, trauma, or barotrauma are recognised but far less common overall. Recognising this typical sequence helps clinicians judge when antibiotics are appropriate rather than treating every cold as bacterial from the outset.
questions.question: A patient's sinusitis symptoms are triggered by a preceding common cold that led to secondary bacterial superinfection. What is the most common inciting event for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in the general population?

questions.explanation: The Epistat is a specially designed double-balloon catheter system that provides simultaneous anterior and posterior nasal packing. The posterior balloon is inflated first in the nasopharynx to occlude the choanae and block posterior bleeding, then the anterior balloon is inflated to tamponade the anterior nasal cavity. It is more comfortable and reliable than traditional three-string posterior pack and gauze combination.
options: A gauze pack soaked in thrombin
An arterial clip for sphenopalatine artery ligation as the sole finding
A specially designed bilateral balloon catheter for anterior and posterior packing
questions.question: The Epistat is classified as what type of device used in posterior epistaxis management?
A 40-year-old man has bilateral, pale, insensitive, grape-like nasal masses that do not bleed on palpation. Before planning definitive treatment, which single investigation is most important?
questions.explanation: CT of the paranasal sinuses defines the full extent of polyp disease, identifies any bony erosion suggestive of malignancy, and guides safe surgical planning, particularly around the skull base and orbit. It is far more sensitive than plain X-ray for delineating fine anatomical detail. Nasal smear cytology and allergy testing may support an allergic aetiology but do not inform anatomical extent or surgical safety.

questions.question: Which feature of facial nerve palsy indicates a central rather than peripheral lesion?
options: Complete unilateral facial weakness including the forehead
Ipsilateral hyperacusis from stapedius muscle paralysis
Sparing of the forehead (frontalis) on the affected side
questions.explanation: Central (upper motor neurone) facial nerve palsy spares the forehead because the frontalis muscle receives bilateral cortical representation corticobulbar fibres from both hemispheres converge on the facial motor nucleus for the upper face. Therefore, a unilateral cortical or internal capsule lesion causes contralateral lower face weakness with relative sparing of frontalis (forehead raises bilaterally). Peripheral facial nerve palsy causes complete ipsilateral weakness including the forehead (unilateral forehead weakness). This clinical distinction is fundamental to neurological localisation.

options: Moderate dysfunction with obvious asymmetry at rest
Mild dysfunction with complete eye closure
Complete paralysis with no facial movement
questions.question: In the House-Brackmann grading system for facial nerve function, Grade VI represents:
questions.explanation: The House-Brackmann scale grades facial nerve function from I (normal) to VI (total paralysis). Grade VI represents complete paralysis with no discernible facial movement in any distribution, absence of tone, and complete lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye). Grade I is normal symmetric function. Grades II-V represent progressive degrees of dysfunction. The scale is the international standard for documenting facial nerve outcomes and guides surgical decision-making in temporal bone fractures and parotid surgeries.

questions.question: In ear cancer staging using imaging, which modality best evaluates perineural spread along the facial nerve?
questions.explanation: MRI with gadolinium contrast is best for evaluating perineural spread along the facial nerve, as it shows enhancement of the nerve if involved by tumour. This is particularly important for adenoid cystic carcinoma, which has a propensity for perineural invasion. CT shows bony erosion but is inferior to MRI for soft tissue and neural involvement.

questions.question: The most common malignant tumour type in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses is:
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, accounting for approximately 80% of sino-nasal malignancies. The maxillary antrum is the most common site (60% of all sinonasal tumours), followed by the nasal cavity (30%) and ethmoid sinus (10%). Squamous cell carcinoma is strongly associated with tobacco smoking and exposure to chemical carcinogens.

questions.question: An emergency 'slash' tracheostomy (emergent type) is defined as being performed when:
questions.explanation: An emergent ('slash') tracheostomy is performed when the patient is in actual respiratory arrest, requiring the fastest possible airway access without time for standard preparation. The urgency dictates a rapid vertical midline incision through all layers to achieve airway access above all other considerations.
options: The patient is awake under local anaesthesia
The patient is in actual respiratory arrest
The patient has an elective surgical indication

questions.explanation: Cocaine causes intense local vasoconstriction, and repeated use leads to chronic mucosal and cartilaginous ischaemia, ultimately resulting in septal perforation and recurrent bleeding from the compromised, poorly vascularised tissue. This is distinct from a simple chemical burn or allergic process. Cessation of use is essential, alongside management of any resulting nasal deformity or ongoing epistaxis.
questions.question: A young cocaine user presents with recurrent epistaxis and is later found to have a septal perforation. What is the mechanism by which cocaine caused this damage?

questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea is a thin, often dehiscent bony plate separating the ethmoid sinuses from the orbit, making it the most common route through which ethmoid sinus infection spreads to cause orbital cellulitis. Chandler's classification stages the severity of this spread from preseptal cellulitis to orbital abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Urgent imaging and drainage prevent vision-threatening progression.
questions.question: A patient develops orbital cellulitis as a complication of acute ethmoiditis. Which anatomical structure allows this spread of infection?

questions.explanation: Postoperative vertigo after stapedectomy can result from a perilymph fistula or a prosthesis that is too long, both of which cause excessive inner ear stimulation or fluid leakage, requiring prompt otological assessment and possible surgical revision. While mild transient dizziness can occur with normal healing, persistent or severe vertigo is not expected and warrants investigation. Careful intraoperative measurement of prosthesis length helps reduce this risk.
questions.question: A patient with otosclerosis undergoes stapedectomy. Postoperatively, they report severe vertigo. What is a recognised complication explaining this symptom?
options: Simple wound infection at the incision site
Expected transient tinnitus with no vertigo link
Unrelated benign paroxysmal positional vertigo coincidentally
Normal healing response requiring no evaluation
Perilymph fistula or excessive prosthesis length

questions.explanation: Animate foreign bodies such as maggots or leeches are first killed or immobilised using an agent such as chloroform water instilled into the nose, which prevents the organism from burrowing deeper or causing further tissue trauma during extraction. Attempting extraction of a live, mobile organism without immobilisation risks incomplete removal and ongoing tissue damage. Once immobilised, the organism can be removed under direct vision.
questions.question: A live foreign body such as a maggot is identified in the nasal cavity. Which agent is classically used to immobilise it prior to removal?

options: 30 dB or greater across at least 3 consecutive frequencies within 72 hours
10 dB across any single frequency within 24 hours
Any measurable hearing loss occurring without warning
Total deafness (>90 dB) within one week
questions.explanation: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL) is defined by audiometric criteria as a loss of 30 dB or greater across at least 3 consecutive frequencies occurring within a 72-hour period. This standardised definition excludes minor fluctuations and distinguishes true SSHL (requiring urgent intervention) from gradual loss. The aetiology is identified in only about 10% of cases (viral labyrinthitis, perilymph fistula, Mnire's, vascular). Systemic corticosteroids given within the first 2 weeks significantly improve recovery rates and are the standard of care.
questions.question: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL) is defined as hearing loss of at least how many dB occurring over what time period?

A patient with recurrent epistaxis from the Woodruff plexus is noted to have this bleeding arise from a predominantly venous rather than arterial source. How does this influence the typical clinical presentation compared to anterior arterial bleeding?
questions.explanation: Because the Woodruff plexus is largely venous, bleeding from this site tends to present as persistent oozing rather than the pulsatile, easily visualised bleeding typical of anterior arterial sources, making it harder to localise on simple anterior rhinoscopy. This often necessitates posterior packing or endoscopic examination to identify and control the source. Recognising this distinction is important when initial anterior measures fail to control bleeding.
options: It is easily seen on anterior rhinoscopy
It never requires any medical intervention
It is always painless and self-limiting
It always causes massive sudden haemorrhage

questions.explanation: Symptoms that consistently correlate with the workplace and remit away from it strongly suggest an occupational trigger, whether an inhaled allergen or irritant specific to that environment. Identifying and removing the causative exposure is central to management, alongside standard rhinitis therapy. Vasomotor rhinitis, in contrast, is triggered by non-specific stimuli without such a clear temporal work pattern.
questions.question: A 45-year-old office worker notices nasal congestion and rhinorrhoea that are worse at work than at home, improving completely over weekends and holidays. What is the most likely underlying cause?

questions.explanation: A child with a short history of strictly unilateral foetid mucopurulent nasal discharge without significant fever, combined with nasal obstruction on one side, is the classic presentation of a retained nasal foreign body until proven otherwise. The asymmetric, unilateral, foul-smelling nature is the distinguishing feature. Sinusitis typically produces bilateral symptoms; choanal atresia presents from birth; antrochoanal polyp lacks the foul odour.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with 2-week history of unilateral purulent foul-smelling discharge, nasal obstruction, and mild facial discomfort. No fever. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

options: Material has definitely entered the trachea and bronchi
Material enters the laryngeal vestibule but does not pass below the vocal cords
The patient has entirely normal swallowing function
The oesophageal phase of swallowing is severely impaired
No further dietary modification is required at all
questions.explanation: Laryngeal penetration refers to material entering the laryngeal vestibule above the level of the vocal cords without passing below them into the trachea, which is distinct from aspiration where material passes below the cords, and represents an intermediate finding on the penetration-aspiration scale used in videofluoroscopic swallow studies. This distinction guides the degree of dietary modification and swallowing therapy required. Silent aspiration, occurring without a cough reflex, is a particularly concerning finding requiring careful assessment.
questions.question: A patient with dysphagia is found on videofluoroscopy to have laryngeal penetration without aspiration during the pharyngeal swallow. What does this finding specifically indicate?

questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the most common causative organism in otogenic meningitis arising as a complication of acute or chronic otitis media, spreading via haematogenous routes or direct bony erosion into the intracranial space. Prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics covering this organism, combined with urgent ENT assessment for source control, are essential. Pseudomonas is more typically associated with chronic suppurative disease and malignant otitis externa rather than meningitis.
questions.question: A patient with otitis media develops sudden onset severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. Lumbar puncture confirms meningitis. What is the most common causative organism in otogenic meningitis?
The airway management strategy of choice for a patient with retropharyngeal abscess requiring surgical drainage is:
questions.explanation: In retropharyngeal abscess, the airway may overlie the trachea and tissue planes are distorted by oedema and pus, making emergency intubation dangerous. Direct laryngoscopy risks rupture of the abscess with aspiration of purulent material. The ideal approach is a planned awake tracheostomy under local anaesthesia, providing a secure airway before manipulation of the infected tissues. Flexible fibreoptic intubation is an alternative when tracheostomy facilities are unavailable.
options: Awake planned tracheostomy under local anaesthesia

questions.explanation: Micrognathia (hypoplastic mandible) causes the tongue to be relatively too large for the oral cavity, resulting in posterior tongue displacement (glossoptosis) that obstructs the hypopharynx. This is the mechanism in Pierre Robin sequence (micrognathia + glossoptosis + cleft palate). Prone positioning relieves obstruction by allowing the tongue to fall anteriorly. Severe cases require airway intervention (nasopharyngeal airway, surgical jaw distraction, or tracheostomy).
questions.question: In micrognathia (small jaw), upper airway obstruction in the oropharynx results from:
options: Oversized adenoid tissue obstructing the nasopharynx
Posterior displacement of the tongue obstructing the hypopharynx
Macroglossia pushing the tongue upward against the palate
Stage of exudation without systemic toxicity
questions.question: Which of the following is a SURGICAL indication in acute suppurative otitis media?
questions.explanation: Coalescent mastoiditis and subperiosteal abscess are surgical complications of acute suppurative otitis media requiring surgery under adequate antibiotic cover. Myringotomy may be performed for refractory cases not responding to medical management. The stage of hyperaemia responds well to oral amoxicillin alone.

questions.question: The MOST common type of carcinoma affecting the external ear canal and middle ear is:
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the external ear canal and middle ear. It is also the most common middle ear malignancy. Symptoms include aural discharge, bleeding, pain, decreased hearing, and otic polyps. It can resemble chronic otitis media, emphasising the need for biopsy in atypical chronic ear disease.

questions.question: Maxillofacial trauma patients frequently require airway management. The involvement of an ENT surgeon in maxillofacial trauma is most critical because of:
options: Frequency of airway compromise requiring immediate intervention
Need for dental occlusion assessment only
Management of associated tympanic membrane perforations
questions.explanation: ENT surgeons are frequently involved in maxillofacial trauma management primarily because of the high frequency of airway problems in this population. Fractures of the mandible, maxilla, or combined midface injuries can cause posterior displacement of the tongue and palate, haematoma formation, oedema, and bleeding all causing upper airway obstruction. Surgical airway management (tracheostomy, cricothyroidotomy) may be required urgently. The high-speed nature of maxillofacial trauma from motor vehicle accidents and industrial injuries has increased its incidence and complexity.

Sinus X-rays in allergic patients are performed to exclude associated upper respiratory tract infection (sinusitis) that may coexist with or complicate allergic disease. Distinguishing pure allergy from allergic rhinosinusitis with infection changes the management approach.
questions.question: In investigating allergy, an X-ray of the sinuses is ordered. Its PRIMARY purpose in allergic workup is:

options: It becomes infected and forms an abscess
It is discovered incidentally in the neck
It grows large enough to cause extrinsic
It causes pain or cosmetic concern
questions.explanation: Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) can grow to involve the floor of the mouth, tongue, and neck, causing extrinsic compression of the trachea. When compression causes significant airway obstruction, tracheostomy provides emergency airway bypass until definitive treatment of the malformation.
questions.question: Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) is listed as a benign indication for tracheostomy. It requires tracheostomy when:

options: Loose areolar tissue allows rapid spread of
It is bounded by the prevertebral fascia
It communicates only with the parapharyngeal space
questions.explanation: The danger space, located between the alar and prevertebral layers of deep fascia, contains loose areolar tissue that offers little resistance to infection spread. It extends from the skull base to the diaphragm, allowing rapid mediastinal extension of neck infections.
questions.question: The danger space in deep neck anatomy is clinically significant because:
Subperiosteal abscess complicating AOM requires treatment with:
questions.explanation: Subperiosteal abscess is a surgical complication of AOM formed by erosion of the outer mastoid cortex. These patients require surgery under adequate antibiotic cover. Coalescent mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess must be distinguished from simple mastoiditis, which may respond to IV antibiotics without surgery.

questions.question: Waardenburg syndrome, a hereditary cause of SNHL, is characteristically associated with which clinical finding?
questions.explanation: Waardenburg syndrome is a hereditary sensorineural hearing loss syndrome characterised by a white forelock, hypertelorism, and heterochromia iridis. It is an autosomal dominant condition with variable penetrance. Identifying associated anomalies in hearing loss workup guides genetic counselling and multidisciplinary management.

questions.question: Post-operative radiotherapy for maxillary sinus carcinoma gives better outcomes than pre-operative radiotherapy because:
questions.explanation: Post-operative radiotherapy benefits from complete surgical specimen assessment of tumour margins, nodal status, and pathological staging, allowing precise radiation field planning. Pre-operative radiotherapy must treat a larger, unstaged volume and may complicate subsequent surgery through tissue fibrosis.
options: The radiation dose can be higher post-operatively
It allows proper histological staging before planning radiotherapy
Post-operative radiotherapy avoids wound healing problems
Pre-operative radiotherapy causes increased bleeding during surgery
Surgical specimen allows assessment of margins and pathological
Nasal polyp tissue from normal inflamed mucosa
questions.explanation: Nasal polyps characteristically show a thickened, hyalinised basement membrane with oedematous stroma, a histological pattern that helps differentiate polypoid tissue from ordinary inflamed sinus mucosa, which lacks this degree of basement membrane change. This finding is a supportive histological feature rather than a marker of malignancy. It reflects chronic tissue remodelling from persistent inflammation rather than an acute infective process.
questions.question: A patient with nasal polyps undergoes histological examination showing oedematous stroma with scattered eosinophils but an intact basement membrane. What does this basement membrane finding help distinguish?

options: Directly in front of the patient
On the same side as the examiner
Six inches behind the patient's ear
questions.explanation: The light source should be placed approximately six inches behind the patient's ear, on the side opposite to the examiner's dominant hand. This positioning allows optimal reflection of light by the head mirror into the structures being examined.
questions.question: When setting up for ENT examination, the light source should be positioned in which location relative to the patient?
A patient has hereditary hearing loss that does not manifest until later in life, despite a genetic cause present from birth. How is this type of hearing loss classified?
questions.explanation: Some hereditary hearing loss conditions have a genetic basis present from birth but do not clinically manifest until later childhood or adulthood, and this pattern is classified as delayed-onset hereditary hearing loss. Recognising this category is important for genetic counselling, as apparently normal hearing at birth does not exclude an inherited predisposition to later hearing loss. Family history remains an important clue even when initial newborn screening is normal.
options: Congenital hearing loss present at birth

questions.question: Acute coalescent mastoiditis differs from simple catarrhal mastoiditis in that coalescence involves:
questions.explanation: Coalescent mastoiditis involves dissolution of calcium from bone (decalcification) and coalescence of mastoid air cells due to local acidosis and venous stasis. Simple catarrhal mastoiditis involves mucosal oedema of the air cells without bony destruction. Coalescent mastoiditis requires surgical intervention.

questions.question: Chemical cauterisation of the nasal septum for Kiesselbach's plexus bleeding uses which agent?
questions.explanation: Silver nitrate sticks (AgNO3) are the standard agents for chemical cauterisation of the nasal septum. When applied to the bleeding point, silver nitrate creates a chemical burn that obliterates the superficial blood vessels of Little's area. Only one side of the septum should be cauterised at a time to avoid septal perforation. Silver nitrate is an alternative to electrical (bipolar or monopolar) cauterisation.

The Thudicum nasal speculum is specifically designed for anterior rhinoscopy, providing dilated access to the anterior nasal cavity for inspection of the inferior turbinate, nasal septum, and middle meatus. It does not reach the posterior nasal space.
questions.question: The Thudicum speculum is used for examining which anatomical structure?

questions.explanation: The foramen lacerum (irregular jagged foramen at the skull base between the petrous apex and sphenoid body) is considered the major pathway of intracranial extension for NPC, along with direct bone erosion. The internal carotid artery traverses the fibrocartilaginous plug of the foramen lacerum, and NPC extending superiorly through this corridor can reach the cavernous sinus, middle cranial fossa, and clivus. Its recognition on MRI guides radiation treatment planning for skull base coverage.
questions.question: Which anatomical space is described as the 'gateway to the skull base' in NPC, allowing superior tumour extension?

questions.explanation: Mucociliary clearance in the maxillary sinus is genetically programmed to move secretions toward the natural ostium in a fixed pattern, so even if an accessory ostium is created or present, mucus can recirculate through it back into the sinus rather than draining out, perpetuating disease. This is why surgical creation of a large, well-positioned opening incorporating the natural ostium is preferred over simply making an additional opening elsewhere. Understanding this principle underlies modern functional endoscopic sinus surgery technique.
options: Cilia beat away from the ostium
The natural ostium is the sole route
Mucus always flows toward the natural ostium
questions.question: A patient with chronic maxillary sinusitis undergoes surgery, and the surgeon carefully identifies and preserves the natural maxillary ostium rather than creating an accessory opening. Why is preservation of mucociliary flow through the natural ostium important?

options: Neck and back pain worse on swallowing
questions.question: The prevertebral space houses the prevertebral muscles and extends along the entire vertebral column. The most distinctive clinical feature of prevertebral space infection compared with retropharyngeal abscess is:
questions.explanation: Prevertebral space infection (often from Pott's disease/tuberculous spondylitis, osteomyelitis, or extension from adjacent spaces) classically presents with back, shoulder, and neck pain that is distinctively worsened by swallowing (deglutition). This distinguishes it from retropharyngeal abscess, whose symptoms are primarily those of pharyngeal obstruction. Prevertebral infection can also cause dysphagia and dyspnoea from posterior displacement of the pharynx.

options: Endoscope with irrigation through the middle meatus
Balloon catheter through the natural ostium
questions.question: Antral lavage (washout) allows removal of sinus secretions by introducing which instrument through the inferior meatus?
questions.explanation: Traditional antral washout is performed by passing a Lichtwitz trocar and cannula through the inferior meatus into the maxillary sinus, then irrigating with normal saline to wash out secretions. The natural ostium also facilitates drainage. Modern practice has largely replaced this procedure with endoscopic middle meatal antrostomy (FESS), especially for chronic cases.

Initial management of perilymph fistula is bed rest to allow spontaneous healing of the round window membrane or oval window fistula. Surgical exploration and repair of the leak is indicated only if there is no improvement or if deterioration occurs. The condition is usually associated with sudden pressure change events.
questions.question: Perilymph fistula presenting with sudden hearing loss and vertigo is INITIALLY managed with:
Adenoidectomy in the management of paediatric OM is considered because the adenoid:
questions.explanation: Adenoidectomy provides benefit in recurrent otitis media because the adenoid tissue harbours pathogenic bacteria, and adenoid enlargement can obstruct the pharyngeal orifice of the Eustachian tube. In adults, adenoid hypertrophy can cause OME through Eustachian tube obstruction. Surgery for cleft palate and Down syndrome also reduces OM recurrence.
options: Harbours bacteria, obstructs the ET orifice
Only ever simply produces excess cerumen

questions.question: A 6-year-old child is brought in with episodic nocturnal awakening, daytime drowsiness, and morning headaches. These symptoms are MOST consistent with which ENT condition?
questions.explanation: Waking frequently at night, daytime somnolence, and morning headaches are classic symptoms of sleep apnoea secondary to pharyngeal or nasal obstruction. This triad distinguishes sleep apnoea from other ENT conditions listed.

questions.question: The 5-year survival rate for early-stage (stage I-II) NPC treated with radiotherapy is approximately:
questions.explanation: Early-stage NPC (stages I-II, T1-2N0-1M0) treated with definitive radiotherapy achieves 5-year overall survival rates exceeding 80%, reflecting the tumour's exceptional radiosensitivity. This contrasts sharply with stage IV disease where survival falls to 30-40% despite chemoradiotherapy. The dramatic stage-dependent survival difference underscores the importance of EBV serological screening programs in endemic regions to detect disease at early, curable stages.

Pyriform sinus pooling of secretions or food on FEES indicates that material reaching the hypopharynx is not passing through the pharyngo-oesophageal segment (PES) the cricopharyngeal muscle and surrounding upper oesophageal sphincter. Failure of cricopharyngeal relaxation (achalasia of the UOS) causes backed-up secretions in the pyriform sinuses, which eventually overflow into the larynx causing aspiration. This finding may indicate a cricopharyngeal bar or pharyngeal muscle weakness with relative obstruction at the PES.
questions.question: A patient with dysphagia is found to have pooling of secretions in the pyriform sinuses on flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES). This finding most specifically indicates dysfunction at which level?

questions.explanation: Vestibular neuritis is presumed to result from HSV-1 reactivation causing inflammation of the superior vestibular nerve. The HINTS (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) bedside examination distinguishes it from a posterior fossa stroke: a positive head impulse test (corrective saccade indicating peripheral lesion), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus beating toward the healthy side, and absence of vertical skew deviation all point to peripheral vestibular neuritis. A normal HIT (no corrective saccade) plus direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation indicates a central/stroke cause requiring urgent MRI.
options: Ischaemic infarction of the AICA; normal HIT
Viral (HSV-1) neuritis; positive HINTS exam (Head Impulse Test abnormal, no skew deviation, unidirectional nystagmus)
questions.question: Vestibular neuritis causes prolonged vertigo lasting days. The presumed aetiology and the clinical finding that distinguishes it from a stroke is:

questions.explanation: In aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad), COX enzyme inhibition by aspirin or NSAIDs (including ibuprofen) shunts arachidonic acid metabolism away from prostaglandins toward the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, causing massive overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes. This triggers bronchoconstriction, nasal polyp swelling, and rhinorrhoea. The reaction is non-immunological (pharmacological), not IgE-mediated allergy.
options: COX inhibition causing arachidonic acid shunting to leukotriene pathway
Direct mucosal irritation by the drug at all times
questions.question: The Samter's triad patient with nasal polyps and asthma develops worsening symptoms after taking ibuprofen for joint pain. This reaction is MOST consistent with which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss requires evaluation to exclude a retrocochlear cause such as a vestibular schwannoma, given the asymmetry that would not be expected with typical bilateral causes like presbycusis or noise exposure. MRI imaging is often indicated as part of this workup. Missing this evaluation risks delayed diagnosis of a potentially treatable but progressively enlarging tumour.
questions.question: A patient presenting with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss requires further evaluation. What additional finding should ALWAYS be specifically assessed in this presentation?
options: Asymmetry warranting evaluation to exclude a retrocochlear lesion
Within the substance of the tonsil itself
Between the tonsillar capsule and superior constrictor
questions.explanation: These findings describe a peritonsillar abscess, which forms in the potential space between the tonsillar capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle. Trismus results from pterygoid muscle irritation, and uvular deviation reflects mass effect pushing the soft palate contralaterally. Needle aspiration or incision and drainage at this specific site relieves the collection.
questions.question: A patient develops trismus, muffled voice, and uvular deviation away from a swollen tonsil. Where is pus most likely collecting?
Inert nasal foreign bodies (e.g., plastic, rubber) may produce which pathological changes in the nasal cavity if left unremoved?
options: No pathological changes; they remain inert indefinitely at all times
Granulation tissue formation, ulceration of mucosa, and possible cartilage necrosis
Calcification and hardening of adjacent turbinates
questions.explanation: Even inert nasal foreign bodies, if left in situ, eventually produce pathological changes: chronic mucosal inflammation (from mechanical irritation), bacterial colonisation, granulation tissue formation, mucosal ulceration, and in advanced cases, necrosis of adjacent cartilage or bone. Sharp objects additionally risk penetrating into adjacent sinuses. Only truly inert materials in an ideal location remain without complications for an extended period.

questions.question: A child swallows a coin that becomes lodged causing drooling and refusal to eat. Chest X-ray shows the coin in the oesophagus in the coronal (en-face) orientation. What does this orientation suggest about location?
questions.explanation: On plain radiographs, a coin lodged in the oesophagus typically appears en-face (coronal orientation) because the oesophagus is flattened anteroposteriorly, whereas a coin in the trachea usually appears in profile (sagittal orientation) due to the trachea's cartilaginous rings creating a different flattening plane. This radiographic clue helps localise the foreign body before endoscopic removal. Oesophageal coins require prompt removal to prevent pressure necrosis and fistula formation.
options: It is definitely already in the stomach
It has passed into the right bronchus
The orientation gives no location information
It is likely lodged in the oesophagus, not the trachea

questions.question: Lemierre's syndrome following peritonsillar abscess is characterised by internal jugular vein thrombosis complicated by:
questions.explanation: Lemierre's syndrome (postanginal sepsis) involves Fusobacterium necrophorum thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein following tonsillar/pharyngeal infection. The thrombotic IVJ vegetation produces septic emboli that shower primarily the lungs, causing multiple cavitating pulmonary abscesses. Less commonly, emboli seed joints, bones, or liver. Aggressive prolonged antibiotic therapy targeting anaerobes (metronidazole) is required; anticoagulation remains controversial.

Granulation tissue in the medial canal or middle ear space is characteristic of chronic otitis media. The external auditory canal in CSOM may be oedematous though not usually tender. The discharge varies from fetid and purulent to serous, and the middle ear mucosa may be oedematous, polypoid, pale, or erythematous.
questions.question: Granulation tissue seen in the medial canal or middle ear space during otoscopy is most consistent with:
A patient with acute otitis media progresses to coalescent mastoiditis. What specifically defines this progression from simple catarrhal mastoiditis?
questions.explanation: Coalescent mastoiditis is defined by breakdown and destruction of the bony septae separating individual mastoid air cells, resulting in a confluent infected cavity, distinguishing it from the earlier, reversible mucosal inflammation of catarrhal mastoiditis. This progression indicates a more advanced, destructive infective process requiring surgical intervention in many cases. Prompt recognition prevents further extension to intracranial or extracranial complications.
options: Breakdown of bony septae between air cells
Simple mucosal congestion of air cells

questions.question: Post-tonsillectomy, a child develops bright red bleeding from the throat on day 7. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage classically occurs between days 5 and 10 as the eschar covering the tonsillar bed separates. It is usually related to infection loosening the healing clot rather than a surgical vascular injury. Management includes admission, antibiotics, and examination under anaesthesia if bleeding persists.
options: Injury to the internal carotid artery
Foreign body retained in the fossa
Separation of eschar from the tonsil bed

questions.explanation: Beta-lactam resistance through beta-lactamase production is found in 17-47% of bacterial isolates from deep neck space infections. This high prevalence directly justifies the use of beta-lactamase-inhibitor combinations (ampicillin-sulbactam) rather than plain penicillin as empirical therapy. Culture and sensitivity results should guide de-escalation, but empirical coverage must assume the possibility of resistant organisms given this documented prevalence.
questions.question: In deep neck space infection management, cultures from aspirated pus frequently demonstrate beta-lactam resistance at what prevalence?

questions.explanation: Fatigability that worsens with use and improves with rest is a hallmark of neuromuscular junction disorders such as myasthenia gravis affecting laryngeal muscles. Structural lesions like nodules or polyps cause a constant, use-independent hoarseness. This diurnal pattern should prompt neurological evaluation rather than laryngoscopy alone.
questions.question: A patient reports that his voice becomes progressively weaker throughout the day but recovers fully after a night's rest. This pattern of fatigability is MOST characteristic of:

options: Instil oil or lidocaine into the canal to immobilise the insect
Attempt immediate forceps extraction without preparation
Irrigate forcefully with water at first presentation
Give oral antibiotics before any local treatment
Refer for general anaesthesia in all cases
questions.explanation: Instilling mineral oil, alcohol, or topical lidocaine into the ear canal kills or immobilises a live insect first, preventing further painful movement and reducing the risk of tympanic membrane injury during subsequent removal with forceps or irrigation. Attempting extraction of a struggling live insect without this step can cause significant patient distress and canal trauma. Most insects can then be removed safely with microscopic visualisation.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected foreign body in the ear presents with a live insect causing severe discomfort. What is the first step in management before attempting removal?
Which of the following is NOT among the differential diagnoses of acute otitis media?
questions.explanation: Labyrinthitis, though a complication of otitis media, is not a differential diagnosis of AOM presenting primarily as otalgia. Differential diagnoses of AOM include acute sinusitis, paediatric allergic rhinitis, URTI, foreign body, cholesteatoma, impacted earwax, nasal polyps, and otitis externa. Each must be excluded before confirming AOM.

options: They have no activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae
They are contraindicated in all adults
To limit resistance development and reserve broader-spectrum cover
They are ineffective against all sinus pathogens
questions.explanation: Respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin and moxifloxacin have excellent broad-spectrum activity including resistant pneumococcus, but are reserved as second-line agents to limit the emergence of fluoroquinolone resistance and to preserve their effectiveness for more severe or resistant infections. First-line therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate is preferred for uncomplicated cases given its narrower spectrum and established efficacy. This stepwise approach reflects broader antimicrobial stewardship principles.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent acute rhinosinusitis is being counselled on antibiotic choice. Why are respiratory fluoroquinolones generally reserved as second-line rather than first-line agents in adults?

questions.explanation: Primary atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) is characterized by progressive atrophy of nasal mucosa and underlying bone, with Klebsiella ozaena being the most commonly implicated organism. The wide nasal cavity becomes filled with copious foul-smelling crusts (ozaenae), causing paradoxical nasal obstruction, hyposmia, and a constant bad smell perceived by others but not by the patient (cacosmia).
questions.question: Atrophic rhinitis (primary form) is caused by progressive atrophy of the nasal mucosa and bone. The organism most commonly implicated is:

questions.explanation: T1 nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated with radiotherapy achieves approximately 70% five-year disease-free survival. Outcomes decline with advancing T-stage: T2 achieves 60%, T3 achieves 40%, and T4 achieves 30% five-year disease-free survival, reflecting the importance of early diagnosis.
questions.question: In the five-year disease-free survival of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, T1 disease achieves approximately what percentage survival?

questions.explanation: Merocel is a compressed, polyvinyl acetate expandable sponge that is inserted dry and then expands on contact with blood or saline, providing tamponade of the bleeding vessel. It is primarily used for anterior nasal bleeds. Absorbable materials like oxidised cellulose (Surgicel) and gelatin foam increase clot formation and are suitable for anterior bleeds. Traditional petrolatum gauze is used for more extensive packing.
options: Compressed expandable polyvinyl acetate sponge for anterior bleeds
Oxidised cellulose (Surgicel) for posterior cavity bleeds
Foley catheter balloon for posterior nasal well-defined packing
questions.question: Merocel is a type of nasal packing material described as:

questions.explanation: Bezold's abscess occurs when mastoid infection erodes through the thin mastoid tip and tracks along the sternocleidomastoid muscle into the neck, presenting as a tender swelling along the muscle border with systemic sepsis features. This complication requires urgent mastoid surgery with abscess drainage. Failure to recognise it can lead to further spread into deep neck spaces.
questions.question: A patient with chronic otitis media develops a spiking fever, severe headache, and a tender swelling behind the mastoid tip along the sternocleidomastoid. What complication is suggested?
options: Simple furunculosis of the ear canal

questions.question: Pott's abscess represents a prevertebral abscess resulting from:
questions.explanation: Pott's abscess is a prevertebral abscess arising from extension of tuberculous infection of a vertebral body (Pott's disease). It was historically the most common cause of prevertebral abscess before antituberculous therapy became widely available.

Sentinel bleeding (herald bleed) from the ear, nose, or mouth in a patient with deep neck abscess is a warning sign of impending carotid artery erosion and rupture. This potentially catastrophic complication requires immediate vascular surgical evaluation.
questions.question: Carotid artery rupture in a patient with deep neck abscess may be heralded by:

questions.explanation: The classic triad of JNA is progressive unilateral nasal obstruction, profuse recurrent epistaxis (often severe and life-threatening), and a smooth nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male. The epistaxis is typically more severe than expected from benign nasopharyngeal pathology and may be the presenting emergency. Diagnosis of JNA in an adolescent male with this triad should prompt imaging before any biopsy attempt, as inadvertent biopsy can precipitate massive uncontrollable haemorrhage.
questions.question: The classic presenting triad of JNA is:
options: Sore throat, neck mass, and conductive hearing loss
Nasal obstruction, profuse epistaxis, and nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male

questions.explanation: Brief, positionally-triggered vertigo without cochlear symptoms is the classic history of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo caused by displaced otoconia. Meniere's disease and labyrinthitis typically include hearing loss or tinnitus. The short duration and clear positional trigger distinguish it from longer-lasting vestibular disorders.
questions.question: A patient presents with vertigo that occurs only when turning over in bed, lasting less than one minute, without hearing loss or tinnitus. This history is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space extends from the base of the skull down to the level of the first and second thoracic vertebrae (T1-T2), where the fascial layers forming its walls join together. Below this, infection can enter the mediastinum, causing the dreaded complication of mediastinitis.
questions.question: The retropharyngeal space extends from the base of skull inferiorly to the level of which vertebra where fascial layers join?

questions.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst characteristically moves upward on tongue protrusion and swallowing because of its embryological connection to the foramen caecum via the tract of thyroid descent, a feature not seen in branchial cysts or lymphadenopathy. Before excision via the Sistrunk procedure, ultrasound should confirm the presence of normal thyroid tissue elsewhere in the neck. The Sistrunk procedure removes the cyst, tract, and central portion of the hyoid bone to reduce recurrence.
questions.question: A patient presents with a midline neck swelling that moves upward with tongue protrusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Immediate CT scan before any attempt
Nasal douching to flush it out
Reassurance and review in one month
Examination and removal under general anaesthesia
questions.explanation: When a child is too uncooperative for safe bedside removal, or the object is impacted or poorly visualised, examination under general anaesthesia provides controlled conditions to prevent the foreign body being pushed further back or aspirated. Blind attempts at removal in an uncooperative child risk airway compromise. Imaging is generally reserved for radio-opaque objects or suspected complications rather than as a routine first step.
questions.question: A child with a suspected nasal foreign body is uncooperative, and the object cannot be visualised or removed safely at the bedside. What is the most appropriate next step?

questions.explanation: Localised circumscribed otitis externa typically represents furunculosis — a localised abscess in a hair follicle. Diffuse localised infection involves a wider spread of the canal skin. Generalised infection can be either primarily otological or primarily dermatological (as in eczema extending from head skin).
questions.question: In localised otitis externa, infection can be described as circumscribed or diffuse. Which form typically presents as furunculosis?
Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis — EGPA) is associated with nasal polyps during which phase of the disease?
questions.explanation: Churg-Strauss syndrome (EGPA) progresses through three phases: the prodromal allergic phase (asthma, allergic rhinitis, and nasal polyposis), the eosinophilic infiltration phase (tissue eosinophilia and organ damage), and the vasculitic phase (necrotizing vasculitis). Nasal polyps are characteristically associated with the prodromal allergic stage, occurring in approximately 50% of EGPA patients overall.

questions.question: A patient with nasopharyngeal carcinoma is noted to have elevated Epstein-Barr virus serology. How is this used clinically?
options: As the sole method required for definitive diagnosis without biopsy
As proof the tumour is of squamous rather than lymphoepithelial origin
As a supportive diagnostic and monitoring marker for disease activity
As an indicator that radiotherapy is contraindicated
As confirmation that surgery is the only effective treatment
questions.explanation: Elevated EBV DNA titres and serology are strongly associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, particularly the undifferentiated non-keratinising type, and are used as supportive diagnostic evidence alongside tissue biopsy, as well as for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence. EBV serology alone cannot replace histological confirmation via biopsy of the primary tumour or an involved lymph node. This viral association is a distinctive epidemiological and biological feature of NPC compared with other head and neck cancers.

Stapedectomy is a procedure specifically indicated for otosclerosis causing fixation of the stapes footplate, not for chronic suppurative otitis media, distinguishing it from the other listed procedures, which directly address chronic middle ear and mastoid disease. Selecting the correct procedure depends on the specific underlying pathology being treated. Confusing these distinct surgical indications could lead to inappropriate or ineffective treatment.
questions.question: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media has failed medical management. Which of the following is NOT typically considered a surgical option for this condition?

options: Assessing the severity of hearing loss
questions.question: The histological examination of tissue biopsy is MOST useful in ear cancer to:
questions.explanation: Tissue biopsy for histological examination confirms the diagnosis of ear cancer and determines the tumour type (e.g., squamous cell, basal cell, melanoma). This is essential because treatment varies by histological type. Mastoid X-ray, CT, and MRI delineate the extent of bony and soft tissue involvement for surgical planning.

options: A single episode of otitis media with mild symptoms
Any episode of common cold with ear discomfort
Three or more episodes within six months despite adequate antibiotics
One episode of otitis media that resolved fully
questions.explanation: Recurrent acute otitis media, generally defined as three or more episodes in six months or four or more in a year despite appropriate antibiotic treatment, is an accepted indication for grommet insertion to reduce the frequency of infections and associated complications. This threshold helps distinguish children who genuinely benefit from surgery from those with self-limiting isolated episodes. Persistent effusion between episodes further supports the case for surgical intervention.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent acute otitis media despite antibiotic therapy is being considered for grommet insertion. What is an accepted indication for surgical intervention over continued medical therapy?
Which space communicates directly with the peritonsillar space and serves as the common pathway for spread of peritonsillar abscess to the deep neck?
questions.explanation: The peritonsillar space (medial to the palatine tonsil capsule and lateral to the superior constrictor) communicates directly with the parapharyngeal space. This anatomical adjacency means that untreated or inadequately drained peritonsillar abscess can spread through the superior constrictor into the parapharyngeal space, and from there into the retropharyngeal, danger, and mediastinal spaces. This cascade of spread is the basis for the term 'angina Ludovici' in severe cases.

options: Obstructs maxillary sinus ventilation near the ostium
Extends laterally toward the optic nerve
Forms the roof of the middle turbinate
Lies entirely within the frontal bone
questions.question: A Haller cell is best described as an ethmoid air cell that:
questions.explanation: Haller cells are ethmoid cells located near the maxillary sinus ostium that may obstruct ventilation and drainage of the maxillary sinus, often without producing symptoms. They differ from Onodi cells, which extend toward the sphenoid sinus and optic nerve, and from a concha bullosa, which pneumatizes the middle turbinate.

questions.question: In the modified barium swallow study (videofluoroscopy), which consistency is tested LAST when assessing a dysphagic patient, after safer consistencies have proven adequate?
questions.explanation: Modified barium swallow studies begin with the safest, most viscous consistencies (thick puree) and progressively introduce more challenging consistencies. Thin liquids are tested last because they are the most difficult to control they spread rapidly, are most prone to penetrate the larynx before the protective swallowing reflex completes, and are the consistency most commonly aspirated in neurological dysphagia. If thin liquids demonstrate safe swallowing, the patient may not require thickening agents, which improve compliance and quality of life.

options: The patient can still breathe normally through the nose and mouth
Standard mouth-to-mouth resuscitation remains appropriate if needed
The patient breathes exclusively through the neck stoma with no nose-to-lung airway connection
The stoma is a temporary opening that will eventually close
Swimming is safe without any special precautions
questions.question: A patient with a total laryngectomy is being educated about their permanent tracheostome. What critical safety information must be emphasised?
questions.explanation: After total laryngectomy, the trachea is permanently diverted to open directly onto the neck as a stoma, completely separating the airway from the nose and mouth, so all breathing occurs exclusively through this opening. This has critical implications for emergency care, since resuscitation must be directed at the stoma rather than the mouth, and for safety, since water entering the stoma directly enters the lungs. Medical alert identification is strongly recommended for these patients.

questions.question: A 60-year-old with longstanding sinusitis develops sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, and reduced consciousness. Which intracranial complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: Meningitis is the most common intracranial complication of rhinosinusitis and typically presents with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered consciousness due to direct or haematogenous spread of infection. Urgent lumbar puncture, once safe, and intravenous antibiotics are required alongside sinus source control. Other complications such as brain abscess more typically present with focal neurological deficits rather than meningism alone.

questions.question: A patient undergoing bronchoscopy for foreign body removal has multiple foreign bodies detected. Surgically, this means the bronchoscopist must:
options: Remove all foreign bodies in one pass of the bronchoscope
Discontinue the procedure and plan open thoracotomy
Prioritize the most distal foreign body first
Repeat bronchoscopy to systematically inspect the entire tracheobronchial tree
Accept incomplete removal if the patient is stable
questions.explanation: When multiple foreign bodies are detected (occurring in 5-19% of cases), repeat bronchoscopy is required after each removal to systematically inspect the entire bronchial tree. Missing a foreign body risks ongoing complications including pneumonia, atelectasis, and lung abscess.

Otitis externa haemorrhagica is classified under viral otitis externa with a presumptive viral aetiology. It is characterised by haemorrhagic bullae on the tympanic membrane and deep canal skin. The condition typically causes sudden severe otalgia and may present with bloody otorrhea.
questions.question: Otitis externa haemorrhagica is believed to have which aetiology?

questions.explanation: Blood-stained discharge combined with facial nerve weakness and enlarged cervical lymph nodes is highly suspicious for middle ear carcinoma rather than benign otitis media. Malignant otitis media can resemble COM and must be biopsied. Histological examination is essential to distinguish malignancy from inflammatory middle ear disease.
options: Blood-stained discharge, facial weakness, neck nodes
Conductive hearing loss with normal otoscopy
questions.question: Which of the following clinical features should raise suspicion of middle ear carcinoma rather than benign otitis media?
Fracture of the cervical vertebrae with spinal cord injury is listed as a respiratory insufficiency indication for tracheostomy. The DIRECT cause of respiratory failure in this scenario is:
options: Direct tracheal injury from the fracture
Paralysis of respiratory muscles from high
questions.explanation: High cervical spinal cord injuries (C3-C5 or above) disrupt the phrenic nerve and intercostal nerve pathways, causing paralysis of the diaphragm and respiratory muscles. This neurogenic respiratory failure requires mechanical ventilation via tracheostomy for long-term respiratory support.

questions.question: In foreign body ingestion, a dehydrated child with late presentation MOST likely has which additional clinical feature?
questions.explanation: Late-presenting foreign body ingestion cases show dehydration (from inability to swallow), fever (from developing infection or perforation), and potential respiratory compromise (from transmitted sounds or aspiration). These features indicate complications requiring urgent management.

Amoxicillin remains the first-line drug of choice for acute suppurative otitis media due to its efficacy against the most common causative organisms, favourable safety profile, and low cost, making it practical in most clinical settings. Alternative agents are reserved for penicillin allergy or treatment failure. Appropriate dosing and duration are important to ensure eradication and minimise recurrence.
questions.question: A child with acute suppurative otitis media requires antibiotic therapy. What is the drug of choice for first-line treatment?

questions.explanation: Hereditary delayed-onset hearing loss may present in adult life despite genetic origin, presenting as dominant or recessive with numerous syndromes. This differs from congenital prelingual deafness. Identifying the genetic basis allows counselling regarding progression, family planning, and eligibility for cochlear implantation.
questions.question: Hereditary hearing loss that is delayed in onset and may present in adult life is classified as:

questions.explanation: LeFort III (craniofacial dysjunction) is the most severe midface fracture, separating the entire midfacial skeleton from the skull base. LeFort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla, and LeFort II is a pyramidal fracture involving the nasal bones and orbital rims. LeFort III involves the zygomatic arches, orbital walls, and nasal bones.
questions.question: The LeFort III fracture is characterized by:
options: Complete craniofacial dysjunction separating midface from skull base
Pyramidal fracture including the nasal bones
Transverse fracture of the maxilla above the teeth
Isolated fracture of the zygomatic arch
Fracture limited to the orbital floor

questions.explanation: In the AJCC 8th edition staging for NPC, retropharyngeal lymph node involvement (with or without unilateral cervical involvement and regardless of laterality) is classified as N1. Bilateral cervical node involvement ipsilateral to the primary and contralateral cervical nodes below the clavicle represent N2 and N3 respectively. Because the nasopharynx is a midline structure with bilateral drainage, bilateral retropharyngeal involvement is common and should not be misclassified as advanced nodal disease.
questions.question: A patient with NPC has bilateral involvement of retropharyngeal lymph nodes. The N-stage according to AJCC 8th edition is:
options: M1 (bilateral lymph nodes indicate distant metastasis)

questions.explanation: MRI provides the best soft tissue detail and is ideal for radiotherapy planning, but its high cost, limited availability, and contraindications in certain patients (metallic implants) make it dispensable in low-resource settings where CT and plain films must suffice.
questions.question: A patient with head and neck cancer undergoes radiotherapy planning. Which imaging modality is described as most dispensable in low-resource settings despite its advantages?

questions.explanation: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign vascular tumour that occurs almost exclusively in prepubertal and adolescent males, typically between the ages of 10-20 years. Despite being histologically benign, it is locally aggressive with a tendency to expand along natural foramina and fissures into the skull base, orbit, and intracranial compartments. The male exclusivity and age restriction suggest a hormonal (androgen-dependent) growth mechanism, with some tumours expressing androgen and oestrogen receptors.
questions.question: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is characterised by which combination of epidemiological features?
options: Malignant, prepubertal males with rapid metastasis
Benign, any age and both sexes equally

questions.explanation: Brain stem evoked response audiometry (ABR) is an objective test that does not require patient cooperation, making it ideal for infants and uncooperative patients. It measures brainstem electrical activity in response to clicks. ABR is also useful in diagnosing acoustic neuromas by showing prolonged or absent wave V latencies.
questions.question: Brain stem evoked response audiometry (BERA/ABR) is MOST useful in assessing hearing in which patient group?

questions.explanation: Samter's triad (also called the ASA triad or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease — AERD) comprises nasal polyposis, bronchial asthma, and aspirin/NSAID hypersensitivity. It accounts for approximately 10% of nasal polyp cases. The pathophysiology involves COX inhibition shunting arachidonic acid metabolism toward excess leukotriene production.
questions.question: Samter's triad consists of which three conditions?
options: Situs inversus, sinusitis, and well-defined bronchiectasis
Asthma, aspirin hypersensitivity, and nasal polyposis

questions.explanation: Most aspirated foreign bodies cause partial rather than complete airway obstruction, allowing adequate ventilation and time for proper preparation before endoscopy. Rushing to perform bronchoscopy without adequate preparation, anaesthesia, and instruments increases the risk of complications.
questions.question: In foreign body aspiration, endoscopy is described as 'usually not a dire emergency.' The PRIMARY reason for this is:
options: Conservative management resolves most cases spontaneously
Antibiotic therapy can substitute for endoscopy in most cases
Most patients can breathe adequately around a partial obstruction
Waiting allows the foreign body to move to a more accessible location
Most children expel the foreign body spontaneously

questions.question: A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis reports anosmia, nasal obstruction, and a constant bad smell. Rhinoscopy shows wide nasal cavities with green-yellow crusts. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) is characterized by progressive atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones, creating paradoxically wide nasal cavities filled with foul-smelling crusts. Patients have hyposmia or anosmia and experience the foul odour from crusts (cacosmia), unlike others who can also smell it. Primary atrophic rhinitis involves Klebsiella ozaena.

questions.question: A patient with uncontrolled epistaxis fails endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation. What is the next most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: When surgical ligation fails to control bleeding, angiographic embolisation of the culprit vessel, most often a branch of the internal maxillary artery, provides an effective minimally invasive alternative to further surgery. It is particularly useful when the bleeding source is difficult to access surgically or the patient is a poor surgical candidate. Careful patient selection and awareness of the small risk of stroke or tissue ischaemia are important.

questions.question: Sodium cromoglycate is used prophylactically in allergic rhinitis. Its mechanism of action is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Sodium cromoglycate stabilises mast cell membranes, preventing degranulation and the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators upon allergen exposure. It does not act as an antihistamine or a vasoconstrictor and has no direct effect on IgE production. Because of this mechanism, it is most effective when used prophylactically before allergen exposure rather than during an acute attack.

questions.question: A patient with a suspected skull base osteomyelitis secondary to malignant otitis externa is being investigated. What is the most sensitive imaging modality to assess bone marrow involvement and monitor treatment response?
options: MRI with technetium or gallium scanning as an adjunct
questions.explanation: MRI is highly sensitive for detecting bone marrow oedema and soft tissue extension in skull base osteomyelitis, while nuclear medicine studies such as technetium bone scan and gallium scan are useful for both initial diagnosis and monitoring resolution of active infection over the prolonged treatment course. Plain radiographs lack the sensitivity to detect early or subtle skull base changes. Treatment duration is often guided by clinical response together with serial imaging rather than a fixed antibiotic course alone.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides the primary afferent sensory input from the posterior tongue, soft palate, and posterior pharyngeal wall that triggers the involuntary pharyngeal swallow reflex when the bolus contacts these regions. This afferent signal reaches the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem, activating the central pattern generator for swallowing. CN X provides additional sensory input from the laryngopharynx and is critical for laryngeal closure during swallowing, but CN IX is the primary trigger.
questions.question: The pharyngeal phase of swallowing is primarily coordinated by the brainstem. Which nerve is most critical for the sensory trigger that initiates the involuntary pharyngeal swallow reflex?
