It requires two examiners and careful technique to avoid visual cueing. Beyond this age range, more sophisticated behavioural or play audiometry techniques become more appropriate.
options: Newborns in the first week of life

questions.question: Chronic suppurative otitis media is defined as chronic inflammation persisting for at least:
questions.explanation: Chronic suppurative OM is defined as chronic inflammation of the middle ear that persists at least 6 weeks and is associated with otorrhea through a perforated tympanic membrane, tympanostomy tube, or surgical myringostomy. The 6-week threshold distinguishes it from acute otitis media. Early and adequate treatment of AOM prevents progression to CSOM.

questions.question: Acute otitis media is, by convention, defined as infection lasting less than:
questions.explanation: Acute otitis media is defined as suppurative infection of the middle ear cleft lasting less than 3 weeks by convention. Chronic suppurative otitis media is defined as chronic inflammation persisting at least 6 weeks with otorrhea through a perforated tympanic membrane. Duration is a fundamental distinguishing criterion in classification.

The timing of facial palsy onset after temporal bone fracture has critical prognostic significance. Immediate onset (at the time of injury) suggests direct neural transection or severe axonotmesis, with poor spontaneous recovery and a strong indication for surgical decompression or repair. Delayed onset (developing 24-72 hours later) implies neuropraxia or secondary oedema compressing the nerve within its bony canal these cases have excellent spontaneous recovery rates (>95%) with conservative management (steroids) and rarely require surgery. This distinction guides treatment decisions.
options: Only immediate palsy requires surgical exploration
Delayed palsy implies transection; immediate palsy has better recovery
Both carry identical prognosis regardless of onset timing
Immediate palsy implies neural transection; delayed palsy has better prognosis from neuropraxia/oedema
questions.question: A patient with temporal bone fracture and immediate complete facial palsy is compared to one with delayed (24-48 hours post-trauma) onset of palsy. The prognosis distinction is:

A teenager with exudative tonsillitis, marked cervical lymphadenopathy, and prolonged fatigue lasting several weeks is suspected to have a viral rather than bacterial cause. Which feature would most support infectious mononucleosis over streptococcal tonsillitis?
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis characteristically produces generalised lymphadenopathy, often including posterior cervical nodes, along with splenomegaly and prolonged fatigue, distinguishing it from the more localised anterior cervical adenopathy of streptococcal tonsillitis. Administration of amoxicillin in unrecognised mononucleosis can precipitate a florid maculopapular rash. Monospot or specific serology testing helps confirm the diagnosis when clinical suspicion is high.

options: Improving nasal mucociliary clearance measured by the saccharine test
Shrinking polyp size through osmotic effect
Raising pH to alkaline levels that dissolve well-defined polyps
questions.explanation: Saline nasal douching improves nasal mucociliary clearance, as demonstrated by improvement in saccharine test times in nasal polyp patients. It also mechanically rinses polyp surfaces, removes secretions and allergens, and enhances penetration of subsequently applied topical medications. It is recommended as an adjunct to all medical and surgical therapy for nasal polyposis.
questions.question: Simple nasal saline douching benefits nasal polyp patients primarily by:

questions.explanation: Symptoms concentrated in the early morning and triggered by dusty environments point toward house dust mite, which accumulates in bedding and is disturbed during sleep and waking activity. Pollen allergy instead follows a seasonal rather than daily pattern. Identifying this temporal clue helps direct targeted environmental control measures.
questions.question: A patient reports profuse sneezing specifically on waking each morning and after exposure to household dust. This temporal pattern MOST strongly suggests sensitivity to:
A patient with a parotid gland mass is noted to have facial nerve weakness on the same side. What does this finding suggest about the tumour?
options: Benign pleomorphic adenoma as the most likely diagnosis
Warthin's tumour, which is typically benign
questions.explanation: Facial nerve weakness in association with a parotid mass is a strong indicator of malignancy, as benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma typically displace rather than invade the nerve, whereas malignant tumours infiltrate perineural planes causing weakness. This finding should prompt urgent imaging and biopsy, as it significantly changes the surgical and prognostic approach. Preservation of the facial nerve becomes more difficult when tumour has already invaded it.

Fourth branchial cleft anomalies classically present with recurrent left-sided cervical abscesses, particularly thyroid abscesses or thyroid region abscesses, because the fourth cleft sinus tract descends through the left thyroid lobe and terminates in the piriform sinus. This characteristic left-sided thyroid predilection distinguishes fourth cleft anomalies from second cleft cysts (lateral neck), first cleft anomalies (parotid/EAC region), and thyroglossal duct cysts (midline).
questions.question: Which clinical scenario would prompt consideration of a fourth branchial cleft anomaly as a source of recurrent deep neck infection in a child?

options: Excessive regulation of airflow and resistance
questions.explanation: The turbinates normally regulate nasal airflow and resistance by adjusting their vascular engorgement, but chronic hypertrophy, often from allergic or vasomotor rhinitis, exaggerates this function to the point of causing persistent obstruction. This differs from a structural or neoplastic cause of obstruction, which would typically show an asymmetric mass rather than symmetric turbinate enlargement. Management may range from medical therapy to turbinate reduction surgery in refractory cases.
questions.question: A patient with chronic nasal obstruction is found to have hypertrophied inferior turbinates on examination, with normal mucosa elsewhere. Which turbinate function, when exaggerated, explains this obstructive picture?
A patient reports nasal obstruction, rhinorrhoea, and facial pressure that are worse in the office building than at home on weekends. The MOST likely aetiology is:
options: Seasonal allergic rhinitis to tree pollen
Perennial allergic rhinitis to house dust mites
Rhinitis medicamentosa from workplace nasal sprays
Occupational rhinitis triggered by workplace agents
Vasomotor rhinitis with no occupational link
questions.explanation: Symptoms that improve away from the workplace and worsen on return strongly suggest occupational rhinitis. Workplace triggers include animal dander, wood dust, latex, grain dust, chemicals, and solvents. The temporal relationship — improved on weekends and holidays, worse on working days — is the hallmark diagnostic clue distinguishing occupational from other forms of rhinitis.

questions.question: A child develops acute otitis media as a complication of a preceding viral URI. Which anatomical feature of the infant eustachian tube predisposes to this complication compared with older children?
questions.explanation: In infants, the eustachian tube is shorter, wider, and more horizontally oriented than in older children and adults, allowing easier reflux of nasopharyngeal secretions and pathogens into the middle ear, which explains the higher incidence of acute otitis media in this age group. As children grow, the tube elongates and becomes more angled, reducing this predisposition. This anatomical difference underlies much of the age-related variation in otitis media incidence.
options: Longer and more vertical tube shape

questions.question: Which of the following represents an early clinical symptom of carcinoma of the maxillary sinus, before bony walls are eroded?
questions.explanation: Early maxillary sinus carcinoma (Stage I-II, confined within the sinus walls) is often clinically silent or produces only subtle symptoms such as persistent unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, or mild facial fullness — symptoms easily mistaken for sinusitis. More dramatic symptoms (proptosis, trismus, palatal bulge, diplopia) appear later when the tumour erodes through bony walls into adjacent spaces, by which time the disease is usually advanced.
options: Subtle facial asymmetry or unilateral nasal obstruction

questions.explanation: JNA has a recurrence rate of approximately 20-25% after surgical resection, even when the tumour appears completely removed. Recurrence most commonly arises from residual tumour cells in the pterygoid base, infratemporal fossa, or other bony crevices that are difficult to completely excise. Regular post-operative surveillance with MRI at 3-6 month intervals is essential for early detection of recurrence, which can be treated by repeat resection or, in selected cases, radiotherapy.
questions.question: A 15-year-old male with JNA who undergoes complete surgical resection has a recurrence rate of approximately:

questions.explanation: The secretions of the sebaceous glands keep the stratum corneum watertight and supple, preventing desiccation and cracking. Sweat gland secretions are responsible for the acidic pH (3–5). The combined glandular secretions form the basis of cerumen.
questions.question: The sebaceous glands of the external auditory canal serve which primary protective function?
NPC presenting with double vision, facial numbness, and cervical lymphadenopathy indicates involvement of which structure?
questions.explanation: NPC can extend superiorly through the skull base foramina or directly invade the cavernous sinus, involving the cranial nerves that traverse it: CN III (oculomotor - diplopia), CN IV (trochlear - diplopia), CN V (trigeminal - facial numbness), and CN VI (abducens - lateral gaze palsy). This syndrome of multiple cranial nerve palsies indicates advanced disease with intracranial extension and significantly worsens the prognosis, requiring combined chemoradiotherapy.
options: Foramen magnum with CN XII involvement
Parotid gland with CN VII compression
Jugular foramen with CN IX-XI involvement
Cavernous sinus and cranial nerves III, IV, V, VI
Orbital apex with CN II compression

questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the audiometric pattern in pure sensorineural hearing loss on Rinne and Weber tests?
questions.explanation: In pure sensorineural hearing loss, the Rinne test is positive (AC>BC) in the affected ear. Weber lateralises to the better-hearing ear (away from the affected side). This pattern contrasts with conductive hearing loss where Rinne is negative and Weber lateralises toward the affected ear.
options: Positive Rinne bilaterally, Weber to better ear
Negative Rinne, Weber to the affected side
Negative Rinne, Weber cannot be determined

questions.explanation: Following chemoradiation for base of tongue SCC, severe dysphagia results from the combination of fibrosis of the tongue base (reducing the posterior propulsive force that squeezes the bolus into the pharynx) and pharyngeal constrictor fibrosis (reducing the peristaltic stripping wave that clears the pharynx). These two mechanisms together eliminate effective bolus transit, leaving residue that then aspirates. This pattern of 'frozen pharynx' from fibrosis at multiple levels is more severe than single-structure dysfunction and often necessitates long-term gastrostomy dependence.
questions.question: A patient with a T3 base of tongue SCC undergoes primary chemoradiation. Post-treatment, they report inability to swallow even soft foods. Nasogastric feeding is required. The most likely underlying mechanism is:
options: Fistula formation between oropharynx and carotid sheath
Laryngeal stenosis from direct radiation injury
Tongue base fibrosis with reduced posterior propulsion combined with pharyngeal constrictor fibrosis
Oesophageal stricture at the lower third from radiation scatter
Trismus from pterygoid fibrosis preventing mouth opening

questions.question: Otosclerosis causing conductive hearing loss is specifically treated surgically with:
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis causes fixation of the stapes footplate in the oval window, resulting in conductive hearing loss. Stapedectomy (removal and replacement) or stapedotomy (creating a small hole in the footplate) with a prosthesis restores ossicular mobility. Fluoride treatment may slow sensorineural progression associated with cochlear otosclerosis.

questions.question: A patient with keratosis obturans presents with bilateral ear pain and conductive hearing loss, and examination reveals a widened ear canal packed with keratin debris. How does this differ from cholesteatoma of the ear canal?
options: Keratosis obturans typically causes canal widening without bone erosion, unlike canal cholesteatoma
Keratosis obturans always causes bone destruction identical to cholesteatoma
Keratosis obturans occurs only in elderly patients exclusively
Cholesteatoma of the canal never causes localised bone erosion
Keratosis obturans is a malignant condition requiring wide excision
questions.explanation: Keratosis obturans results from abnormal epithelial migration causing keratin accumulation and canal widening, typically bilateral and associated with conditions like bronchiectasis or sinusitis, without the localised bone erosion characteristic of external auditory canal cholesteatoma, which tends to be unilateral and erosive. This distinction guides management, with keratosis obturans treated by regular debris removal and cholesteatoma requiring more definitive surgical clearance. Both conditions require regular follow-up to prevent complications.

questions.question: A patient with achalasia-like dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset undergoes barium swallow showing a 'bird's beak' narrowing at the lower oesophagus. How does this presentation differ from a mechanical stricture?
options: Achalasia only ever affects solid food swallowing
Achalasia affects both solids and liquids equally from onset, unlike mechanical strictures
Mechanical strictures always affect liquids before solids
Achalasia has no radiological findings on barium swallow
Mechanical strictures never cause weight loss
questions.explanation: A key distinguishing feature of achalasia, a motility disorder from failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation, is dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset, whereas mechanical strictures typically cause progressive dysphagia beginning with solids before progressing to liquids as the lumen narrows further. This history is an important clinical clue guiding further investigation with manometry. Barium swallow findings and endoscopy help confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy.

One recognized function of the paranasal sinuses is to absorb mechanical shock, acting as crumple zones that protect the brain and orbital contents during frontal impacts. Other functions include humidifying and warming inspired air, lightening the skull weight, providing resonance, and contributing to facial growth and olfaction.
questions.question: The function of paranasal sinuses that helps protect the brain during frontal impact is:
A patient undergoing parotidectomy develops Frey's syndrome postoperatively, with facial sweating and flushing during eating. What is the underlying mechanism of this complication?
options: Direct facial nerve injury causing abnormal sweating
Simple wound infection at the surgical site
Aberrant regeneration of parasympathetic fibres innervating sweat glands instead of the parotid
Allergic reaction to surgical dressing materials
questions.explanation: Frey's syndrome occurs when severed parasympathetic secretomotor fibres originally destined for the parotid gland aberrantly regenerate and innervate the sweat glands of the overlying skin, so that stimuli that would normally trigger salivation instead produce localised facial sweating and flushing during eating, known as gustatory sweating. This is a well-recognised long-term complication of parotid surgery rather than a wound complication or unrelated skin condition. Botulinum toxin injection into the affected skin is an effective treatment for bothersome symptoms.

While excessive cerumen removal can predispose to otitis externa by stripping the canal's protective acidic and waterproof lining, complete absence of cerumen production as a distinct predisposing factor is not a recognised typical cause compared to the other listed factors. Water exposure, mechanical trauma from cotton buds, occlusive devices, and anatomical narrowing are all well-established predisposing factors. Identifying and addressing modifiable risk factors helps reduce recurrence.
options: Use of cotton buds in the ear canal
Narrow or tortuous ear canal anatomy
questions.question: A patient's history is reviewed for predisposing factors to otitis externa. Which of the following is NOT typically considered a predisposing factor?

questions.explanation: Cytoplasmic ANCA (cANCA) directed against proteinase 3 is the serological hallmark of Wegener's granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis — GPA). This systemic vasculitis causes destructive granulomatous rhinosinusitis, renal disease, and pulmonary haemorrhage. ACE levels and rheumatoid factor are useful in sarcoidosis, while sweat testing confirms cystic fibrosis.
questions.question: The antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA) test is most useful in confirming which cause of rhinosinusitis?
Adenoidectomy is considered in the management of recurrent paediatric otitis media because the adenoid contributes to disease through which mechanism?
options: Obstructing the tube orifice and harbouring bacteria
questions.explanation: Enlarged or chronically infected adenoid tissue can mechanically obstruct the eustachian tube orifice in the nasopharynx and serve as a reservoir for pathogenic bacteria, both contributing to recurrent middle ear disease. Adenoidectomy addresses this contributing factor, particularly in children with recurrent otitis media or persistent effusion. This procedure is often considered alongside, rather than instead of, tympanostomy tube insertion in appropriate cases.

Coronal CT scan of the paranasal sinuses is the gold standard pre-operative investigation for FESS. It delineates the ostiomeatal complex anatomy, identifies mucosal thickening, polyps, and bony anatomical variants (e.g., concha bullosa, Haller cells, septal deviation), and shows critical relationships to the orbit and skull base. MRI is superior for soft tissue characterisation and suspected malignancy.
questions.question: The most specific radiological investigation for planning functional endoscopic sinus surgery is:
options: Coronal CT scan of the paranasal sinuses
MRI of the paranasal sinuses at all times

questions.explanation: A midline neck swelling that moves upward on swallowing is attached to the larynx or thyroid gland and moves with these structures. Thyroid masses characteristically exhibit this movement due to fascial attachment to the trachea.
questions.question: A patient presents after being asked to swallow during neck examination. Midline neck swelling that moves upward on swallowing MOST likely represents:

A patient reports nasal obstruction, thick green-yellow crusting, and a persistent foul smell that family members notice but the patient does not. Rhinoscopy shows widened nasal cavities. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of foul-smelling crusting, widened nasal cavities from mucosal and bony atrophy, and the patient's own anosmia preventing self-perception of the odour is classic for atrophic rhinitis (ozaena). Treatment focuses on regular nasal douching and crust removal rather than antibiotics alone. This condition is more prevalent in regions with lower socioeconomic status and nutritional deficiency.

questions.question: Foreign body sinusitis most commonly affects which sinus due to proximity of dental roots to its floor?
questions.explanation: The floor of the maxillary sinus is formed by the alveolar surface of the maxilla, and the roots of the upper premolar and first molar teeth project into or are very close to the sinus floor. This anatomical relationship makes the maxillary sinus vulnerable to foreign bodies from dental origins (displaced root fragments, dental materials, packing after tooth extraction), causing odontogenic maxillary sinusitis.

questions.question: Saline nasal irrigation works in rhinosinusitis by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Saline nasal irrigation benefits rhinosinusitis through multiple mechanisms: it increases mucociliary clearance rates, has a brief vasoconstrictive effect, mechanically rinses crusts and secretions, and when combined with sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) creates an alkaline medium that reduces mucus viscosity. Isotonic saline is generally better tolerated than hypertonic solutions.
options: Acting as a local anaesthetic as the sole finding
Increasing mucociliary flow, mechanically rinsing secretions, and thinning mucus

questions.question: A young adult with progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss has a normal tympanic membrane and a family history of similar hearing loss. Audiometry shows a Carhart notch. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss due to abnormal bone remodelling fixing the stapes footplate, typically presenting bilaterally with a normal-appearing tympanic membrane and a positive family history. The Carhart notch, a dip in bone conduction around 2 kHz, is a characteristic audiometric artefact of stapes fixation. Stapedectomy or hearing aids are the main treatment options.

questions.question: The osteoplastic flap procedure (with or without obliteration) addresses which specific sinus?
options: Frontal sinus via bicoronal or eyebrow incision
All sinuses via combined craniofacial well-defined approach
questions.explanation: The osteoplastic flap is a surgical procedure specifically designed for the frontal sinus. Through a bicoronal or eyebrow incision, the anterior wall of the frontal sinus is elevated as a vascularized flap to allow access for removal of diseased mucosa. Obliteration with fat is performed when complete mucosal eradication is required to prevent mucocele formation.

options: Antibiotics have no role in deep neck infections
Surgery should precede antibiotics in all cases
Surgery is always preferable to antibiotics alone
Antibiotics should be stopped once surgery is performed
Antibiotics should be used in conjunction with, not
questions.explanation: Levitt's principle emphasizes that antibiotics alone are insufficient for established deep neck abscesses and must be combined with appropriate surgical drainage. Antibiotic monotherapy without drainage allows ongoing infection and risks serious complications like mediastinitis and airway obstruction.
questions.question: In deep neck infection management, Levitt's dictum states: 'Antibiotics are not a substitute for surgery.' This principle implies:
A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyposis is found to have aspirin sensitivity and asthma. What is this triad called?
questions.explanation: Samter's triad, also known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, consists of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, asthma, and hypersensitivity reactions to aspirin and other NSAIDs. Recognising this association is important because these patients often have severe, recurrent polyposis and can experience bronchospasm if given NSAIDs. Aspirin desensitisation is a recognised treatment strategy in refractory cases.

questions.question: An infant develops harsh inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine and improves when prone, beginning in the first weeks of life, with no acute infective symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Positional stridor beginning shortly after birth, worsening supine and improving prone, without fever or acute illness, is characteristic of laryngomalacia caused by collapse of immature supraglottic structures during inspiration. Most cases are self-limiting and resolve as the larynx matures over the first one to two years of life. Severe cases with feeding difficulty or failure to thrive may require surgical supraglottoplasty.

options: Mucopurulent discharge from the middle meatus or oedema at sinus ostia
Clear watery discharge from the cribriform area as the sole finding
Pale mucosa with eosinophils on smear
questions.question: Endoscopically, which finding most specifically suggests chronic rhinosinusitis?
questions.explanation: The most specific endoscopic signs for chronic rhinosinusitis per the Rhinosinusitis Task Force are: polyps in the middle meatus, mucopurulent discharge emanating from the middle meatus, and oedema or mucosal obstruction of the sinus ostia at the middle meatus. These findings directly indicate inflammation at the ostiomeatal complex and active sinus disease.

questions.question: A post-laryngectomy patient complains that a swallowing rehabilitation procedure has restored voice but is now experiencing dysphagia. The most likely cause is hypertonia of which structure?
questions.explanation: After total laryngectomy with tracheo-oesophageal puncture for voice restoration, dysphagia can result from cricopharyngeal spasm (hypertonia of the pharyngo-oesophageal segment). The cricopharyngeus, which normally coordinates with laryngeal elevation for UOS relaxation, loses its normal reflex regulation after laryngectomy. Botulinum toxin injection into the cricopharyngeus or cricopharyngeal myotomy relieves the spasm and restores normal bolus passage. This is distinct from prosthesis malfunction, which affects voice but not swallowing.

options: Failure to respond to standard treatment with atypical, persistent findings
Complete and rapid resolution with standard antibiotic therapy
A single episode of mild, self-limiting discomfort
Symptoms present for less than forty-eight hours only
Normal otoscopic findings throughout the entire course
questions.question: A patient's chronic ear disease resembling otitis media is eventually diagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma of the middle ear. What clinical feature most often prompts the biopsy that leads to this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical feature most often prompting biopsy and eventual diagnosis of underlying malignancy is failure of presumed chronic otitis media to respond as expected to standard treatment, combined with atypical or persistent findings such as bleeding, pain out of proportion to examination findings, or unusual granulation tissue. This treatment-resistant pattern should trigger a heightened index of suspicion rather than repeated courses of standard therapy. Early biopsy in such atypical cases is key to timely cancer diagnosis.

questions.question: According to case management principles, what should guide the choice of frequency for monitoring an outcome measure?
options: The convenience of the physiotherapist's personal schedule
A logical relationship to the expected rate of change in the condition
A fixed universal frequency applied to every patient
The number of staff available on a given day
The patient's preference regardless of clinical need
questions.explanation: The frequency of measuring and monitoring an outcome should have a logical relationship to the expected rate of change in the patient's condition. When the rate of change increases, monitoring frequency may also need to increase accordingly. This principle ensures that clinical decisions are based on timely, relevant data.

The progressive increase in six-minute walk distance across three consecutive assessments indicates a genuine improvement in functional exercise capacity in response to the pulmonary rehabilitation programme. This positive trend supports continuing the current treatment approach, potentially with further progression of exercise intensity. Using serial objective measurements in this way exemplifies evidence-based monitoring of rehabilitation outcomes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews a patient's serial six-minute walk test distances: 250 metres at baseline, 310 metres after four weeks, and 340 metres after eight weeks of pulmonary rehabilitation. How should this trend be interpreted?
options: A worsening of the patient's underlying respiratory condition
Measurement error requiring the results to be discarded
No meaningful change in the patient's functional status
A progressive improvement in functional exercise capacity in response to treatment
Evidence that the programme should be discontinued immediately

questions.explanation: The upright position is favoured during mobilization because it takes advantage of gravitational effects on central and peripheral hemodynamics and fluid shifts. This physiologic positioning enhances the overall benefit of the mobilization or exercise stimulus. Combining this posture with graded exercise supports optimal oxygen transport in acutely ill patients.
questions.question: Why is the upright position generally preferred when prescribing mobilization for patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction?
options: It eliminates the need for supplemental oxygen therapy
It optimises central and peripheral hemodynamics and fluid shifts
It prevents any further disease progression permanently
It reduces the requirement for medication entirely
It replaces the need for airway clearance techniques

questions.explanation: The un-sticking phase of autogenic drainage specifically requires a big breath out followed by a small breath in, targeting the small peripheral airways where secretions often first accumulate. Teaching this specific breath pattern accurately is essential for the technique's effectiveness, distinguishing it from the subsequent collecting and evacuating phases. This equipment-free technique is well suited to a motivated, independent patient like the one described.
options: Using rapid, shallow panting throughout the entire technique
Using only maximal breath holds without any exhalation
Using forceful huffing exclusively without controlled breathing
Using equally sized breaths throughout every phase
Using a big breath out followed by a small breath in
questions.question: A physiotherapist is teaching autogenic drainage to a motivated adult patient with chronic bronchiectasis who wants a technique requiring no equipment. Which core teaching point should be emphasised regarding breath size during the initial un-sticking phase?

questions.explanation: Manual hyperinflation is specifically contraindicated in the presence of an undrained pneumothorax, since the increased tidal volumes and pressures involved risk worsening the pneumothorax or precipitating a tension pneumothorax. Other routine interventions such as auscultation, suctioning, and passive range of motion remain appropriate and should continue as part of standard care. Recognising this specific contraindication is essential for patient safety in the ICU setting.
questions.question: A ventilated ICU patient requires airway clearance, but the physiotherapist notes an undrained pneumothorax on the chart. Which intervention should specifically be avoided in this situation?
options: Standard suctioning of the endotracheal tube
Passive range of motion of the limbs

questions.explanation: In emphysema, hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis are relatively uncommon because the breathing imbalance is often compensated for by an increased respiratory rate. This contrasts with chronic bronchitis, where hypoxemia and eventual hypercapnia are more frequent due to significant ventilation-perfusion mismatch. This distinction helps explain some of the differing clinical presentations between the two COPD phenotypes.
options: Hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis are more common in emphysema than in chronic bronchitis
Hypercapnia never occurs in either chronic bronchitis or emphysema
Respiratory acidosis is exclusively associated with emphysema and never bronchitis
Hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis are uncommon in emphysema because increased respiratory rate compensates
Hypercapnia occurs equally and independently of respiratory rate in both conditions
questions.question: Which statement accurately reflects the relationship between hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis in emphysema compared to chronic bronchitis?

questions.explanation: Active vomiting is listed as an absolute contraindication to non-invasive ventilation because of the significant risk of aspiration through the mask interface. Other absolute contraindications include facial trauma or burns, fixed upper airway obstruction, and respiratory or cardiac arrest. Relative contraindications include recent facial surgery and haemodynamic instability.
options: Stable chronic COPD without acute exacerbation
questions.question: Which of the following is listed as an absolute contraindication to non-invasive ventilation?

questions.explanation: Pyothorax, also called empyema, refers to a pleural effusion consisting of pus, typically resulting from an underlying infective process. Hydrothorax contains serous fluid, haemothorax contains blood, and chylothorax contains lymphatic chyle. Identifying the type of fluid helps direct appropriate medical and physiotherapy management.
questions.question: Which term describes a pleural effusion containing pus?

questions.explanation: Positive end-expiratory pressure maintains a constant positive pressure in the airway throughout expiration, which is functionally similar to continuous positive airway pressure. Both help splint airways open, preventing atelectasis, and increase functional residual capacity and oxygenation. A key difference is that PEEP is typically applied during mandatory or assisted ventilator breaths, while CPAP is used in spontaneously breathing patients.
options: Both are used exclusively during inspiration only
Both eliminate the need for supplemental oxygen
Both maintain a constant positive airway pressure at the end of expiration
Both are delivered only through invasive endotracheal tubes
Both directly measure arterial blood gas values
questions.question: What is the functional similarity between positive end-expiratory pressure and continuous positive airway pressure?

A physiotherapist notes a ventilated patient's peak inspiratory pressure has risen sharply from 25 to 45 cmH2O. Which clinical possibility should be considered before continuing airway clearance techniques?
questions.explanation: A sharp rise in peak inspiratory pressure above the 40 cmH2O threshold associated with increased barotrauma risk should prompt consideration of causes such as sputum plugging, bronchospasm, or reduced compliance. This finding may actually support the case for airway clearance intervention, but must be interpreted alongside other clinical data before proceeding. Recognising this change promptly supports safe and effective ventilator management.
options: A normal expected variation requiring no further assessment
Sputum plugging or bronchospasm causing reduced compliance
Definite evidence of improved lung compliance
Confirmation that extubation criteria have been met
Confirmation that the endotracheal tube has been removed
Continue non-invasive ventilation without any modification
Discontinue non-invasive ventilation immediately due to aspiration risk
Increase the mask pressure to compensate
Ignore the vomiting since it is unrelated to ventilation
Switch immediately to a tighter-fitting mask
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that a patient on non-invasive ventilation for a COPD exacerbation has developed active vomiting. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: Active vomiting is an absolute contraindication to non-invasive ventilation because of the significant risk of aspiration through the mask interface. The physiotherapist should discontinue non-invasive ventilation immediately and alert the medical team for reassessment and airway protection. Recognising and acting promptly on absolute contraindications is critical to patient safety.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the pathogenesis of chronic bronchitis at the tissue level?
options: Inhalation of noxious particles directly destroys alveolar walls without inflammation
Chronic bronchitis arises exclusively from viral infection without irritant exposure
Inhalation of noxious particles triggers inflammation, goblet cell hypertrophy, and excess mucus production
Chronic bronchitis results primarily from surfactant deficiency
Chronic bronchitis develops solely due to pleural fluid accumulation
questions.explanation: In chronic bronchitis, inhaled noxious particles and gases activate inflammatory cells that release chemical mediators, causing vasodilation, congestion, mucosal oedema, and goblet cell hypertrophy. This hypertrophy drives excessive mucus production that obstructs the airways. Over time, recurrent infections further impair ciliary function and worsen airway degeneration.

questions.question: Which factor is a well-documented genetic risk factor for the development of COPD?
questions.explanation: Severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is the best documented genetic risk factor for COPD, predisposing affected individuals to early and often more severe emphysema. This deficiency impairs the body's ability to counteract enzymatic destruction of lung tissue. Cigarette smoking remains the most common encountered risk factor overall, but genetic susceptibility can significantly influence disease severity.

questions.question: The BODE index used in COPD outcome assessment includes which of the following components?
questions.explanation: The BODE index is a multidimensional scoring system combining body mass index, degree of airflow obstruction, dyspnoea severity, and exercise capacity. It provides a more comprehensive prognostic picture than FEV1 alone in COPD patients. This composite score is commonly used to monitor disease progression and guide pulmonary rehabilitation planning.
options: Blood pressure, oxygen saturation, dyspnoea, and endurance
Body temperature, oxygen delivery, dyspnoea, and effort
Bicarbonate level, obstruction severity, dyspnoea, and energy
Body mass index, airflow obstruction, dyspnoea, and exercise capacity
Blood gas values, oedema, dyspnoea, and expiratory flow

questions.explanation: A change in sputum from mucoid to thick green purulent material suggests a possible acute infective exacerbation, warranting closer monitoring and likely medical review for consideration of antibiotic therapy. This change should not be dismissed as normal variation, given its clinical significance in chronic bronchiectasis management. Physiotherapy input, particularly airway clearance, often becomes even more important during such exacerbations to manage the increased secretion burden.
options: A possible acute infective exacerbation requiring closer monitoring and possibly medical review
A normal, expected daily variation requiring no action
Definite evidence that airway clearance is no longer needed
Confirmation that the underlying bronchiectasis has resolved
An isolated finding unrelated to respiratory status
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to review a patient with chronic bronchiectasis whose sputum has recently changed from mucoid to thick green purulent material. What is the most likely clinical significance of this change?

questions.explanation: Kussmaul respiration describes deep, rapid breathing that occurs as a compensatory response to metabolic acidosis, helping to reduce PaCO2 and raise blood pH. This pattern differs from Cheyne-Stokes respiration, which is more commonly linked to cardiac or neurological conditions. Recognising Kussmaul breathing can prompt further evaluation of underlying metabolic derangement.
questions.question: Kussmaul respiration is most classically associated with which underlying condition?
options: Central nervous system depression from sedatives

questions.explanation: According to recommended short-term goals for asthma management, educating the patient about their condition and triggers should occur during the very first treatment session. This early education empowers the patient to recognise and avoid precipitating factors. More physically demanding interventions such as resistance training or vigorous conditioning are introduced later as tolerated.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a newly diagnosed asthma patient during the first treatment session, according to recommended short-term goals. What should be prioritised first?
options: Teaching advanced respiratory muscle resistance training
Performing chest percussion regardless of symptoms
Initiating postural drainage in Trendelenburg position
Educating the patient about their condition and known triggers

questions.explanation: Atelectasis refers specifically to the collapse of previously expanded lung tissue, commonly occurring after upper abdominal or thoracic surgery due to altered pulmonary mechanics. Pneumonia, by contrast, refers to infective consolidation, while pulmonary embolism refers to vascular obstruction. Distinguishing between these complications helps guide targeted physiotherapy intervention.
questions.question: Which post-surgical pulmonary complication specifically refers to the collapse of previously expanded lung tissue?

questions.explanation: In an obese patient following abdominal surgery, elevating the head of the bed helps reduce diaphragmatic splinting caused by abdominal contents pressing upward, thereby supporting more effective ventilation and reducing atelectasis risk. Flat supine positioning for extended periods could worsen this splinting effect and increase respiratory compromise. This positioning consideration is particularly important given the combined risk factors of obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea, and recent abdominal surgery.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning positioning for an obese patient with obstructive sleep apnoea who has just undergone abdominal surgery. Which positioning consideration is most relevant to reducing postoperative respiratory complications in this patient?
options: Placing the patient in full flat supine positioning for extended periods
Elevating the head of the bed to reduce diaphragmatic splinting from abdominal contents
Avoiding any elevation of the head of the bed under all circumstances
Restricting the patient to prone positioning exclusively
Ignoring body habitus entirely when selecting positioning

questions.explanation: Paradoxical inward abdominal movement during inspiration suggests diaphragmatic dysfunction, since a normally functioning diaphragm should descend and displace the abdominal contents outward during inspiration. This finding is an important objective sign that may correlate with neuromuscular disease, phrenic nerve injury, or severe fatigue. Recognising this abnormal pattern helps guide further assessment and appropriate breathing retraining strategies.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices marked paradoxical abdominal movement, with the abdomen drawing inward during inspiration, in a patient with suspected diaphragmatic weakness. What does this finding most likely indicate?
options: Diaphragmatic dysfunction impairing effective descent during inspiration
A finding unrelated to respiratory muscle function
Confirmation that mechanical ventilation is no longer required
It forms carbonic acid, releasing hydrogen ions that stimulate deeper, faster breathing
It directly stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in the aorta only
It reduces cerebrospinal fluid pH without altering breathing rate
It binds directly to central chemoreceptors as a gas without conversion
It lowers hydrogen ion concentration in cerebrospinal fluid
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide diffuses into cerebrospinal fluid where it hydrates to form carbonic acid. This acid dissociates to release hydrogen ions, lowering cerebrospinal fluid pH. Central chemoreceptors sense this drop and increase the depth and rate of breathing to eliminate excess carbon dioxide.
questions.question: What effect does a rise in blood carbon dioxide have on cerebrospinal fluid chemistry and breathing?

questions.explanation: Unlike the gravity-dependent Flutter valve, the Acapella device uses a counterweighted plug and magnet mechanism to achieve valve closure regardless of position. This allows patients to use the device while sitting, standing, or reclining. It also offers adjustable flow and frequency settings across different model variants.
options: It relies solely on gravity to move an internal steel ball
It cannot be used with a nebulizer adapter
It provides no adjustable resistance settings
It is designed exclusively for use in the supine position
It uses a counterweighted magnet mechanism that is not gravity dependent
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the Acapella device from the traditional Flutter valve?
Which structure houses the vocal cords and therefore contributes to voice production?
questions.explanation: The larynx houses the vocal cords and therefore serves the important function of voice production, alongside providing an open airway and routing air and food appropriately. The pharynx and trachea, while part of the respiratory passageway, do not themselves house the vocal cords. Understanding this anatomy is relevant when assessing patients with voice changes secondary to respiratory or laryngeal pathology.

Hyper-resonance on percussion typically indicates the presence of trapped air within the pleural space, as seen in pneumothorax, because air conducts percussion sound differently from normal lung tissue. This contrasts with the dull note heard over consolidation or atelectasis and the stony dull note heard over pleural effusion. Recognising these differences assists in rapid bedside differentiation of chest pathology.
questions.question: What does hyper-resonance on chest percussion typically indicate?

questions.explanation: In assist-control ventilation, the ventilator assists every breath the patient initiates while also guaranteeing a minimum preset respiratory rate. If the patient's spontaneous rate drops below this preset value, the ventilator delivers mandatory breaths to maintain the minimum rate. This ensures adequate minute ventilation even if the patient's respiratory drive weakens.
options: The ventilator stops delivering any breaths until the patient resumes effort
The ventilator takes over and delivers mandatory breaths at the preset rate
The ventilator switches automatically to CPAP mode
The ventilator increases tidal volume without changing rate
The ventilator triggers an alarm but delivers no additional breaths

This reversibility distinguishes it from COPD, where the GOLD definition specifically excludes reversible airflow limitation. Airway inflammation is common to both, but the reversibility of obstruction is the key differentiator.
questions.question: In asthma, what is the underlying pathophysiological hallmark distinguishing it from COPD?

It describes both lateral curvature and rotation of the spine

It describes generalised hyperinflation of the chest wall

Pectus carinatum, in contrast, describes an outward protrusion of the sternum. Recognising these distinct deformities is part of the objective chest shape assessment.
questions.question: Which statement about chest shape abnormalities is correct regarding pectus excavatum?

questions.explanation: Combining manual techniques during supervised sessions with a home-based positive expiratory pressure device supports both effective in-session secretion clearance and a sustainable, independent self-management strategy for ongoing home use. This dual approach reflects a realistic, long-term management plan for a chronic condition such as bronchiectasis, rather than relying solely on clinic-based intervention. Empowering patients with home-based tools supports better long-term adherence and self-efficacy.
options: Ensuring the patient never needs to attend any further physiotherapy sessions
Providing effective in-session secretion clearance alongside a sustainable self-management tool for ongoing home use
Replacing the need for any medical follow-up permanently
Avoiding the need for any outcome measurement of treatment effectiveness
Ensuring the patient avoids all future exacerbations permanently
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify why a patient's chest physiotherapy plan specifically includes both manual techniques and a home-based positive expiratory pressure device. What is the most likely clinical rationale for this combined approach?

The patient has copious uncleared airway secretions
The patient shows worsening cardiovascular instability
The patient can maintain adequate gas exchange without pressure support
The original indication for intubation remains unresolved
questions.explanation: Successful extubation requires that the original indication for intubation has resolved and that the patient can maintain adequate gas exchange without pressure support. Additional criteria include absence of auto-PEEP, adequate cardiovascular reserve, minimal secretions, and the ability to protect the airway. Failure to meet these criteria increases the risk of extubation failure.

A physiotherapist is asked to assist in preparing a long-term ventilated patient for a tracheostomy tube change. Which timing consideration, based on standard practice, is most relevant to when tracheostomy is typically considered?
questions.explanation: Tracheostomy is generally considered when a patient is expected to require ventilation for longer than approximately ten days, as this route reduces risks associated with prolonged endotracheal intubation such as laryngeal or tracheal trauma. Recognising this timeframe helps the physiotherapist anticipate airway management changes and adjust treatment planning accordingly. It also has implications for positioning and secretion clearance strategies once the tracheostomy is established.
options: It is only ever considered after twelve months of ventilation
It is never used for patients requiring prolonged ventilation
It is considered immediately for every ventilated patient regardless of duration
It is used only for patients who are fully extubated already
It is generally considered once ventilation is expected to exceed approximately ten days

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to justify continuing chest physiotherapy for a patient whose sputum volume remains unchanged after one week of treatment despite full technique compliance. What would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue the identical treatment plan indefinitely without any change
Discontinue all physiotherapy input immediately without further assessment
Reassess the treatment approach and consider alternative techniques or further medical review
Assume the patient is not truly compliant without further discussion
Increase treatment frequency without reconsidering technique selection
questions.explanation: When sputum volume remains unchanged despite a full week of compliant treatment, it is appropriate to reassess the overall approach, potentially trialling alternative airway clearance techniques or seeking further medical review to investigate other contributing factors. Simply continuing an ineffective plan unchanged, or abandoning treatment entirely without reassessment, would not reflect sound clinical reasoning. This scenario illustrates the importance of using outcome data to guide treatment modification.

questions.question: In the context of respiratory assessment, what does 'focal fremitus' refer to during chest palpation?
options: Audible wheezing heard without a stethoscope
Visible chest wall retraction during inspiration
Palpable vibrations transmitted through the chest wall during speech
A palpable pleural friction rub during expiration only
questions.explanation: Focal fremitus refers to palpable vibrations felt on the chest wall as the patient speaks, typically assessed by placing the hands symmetrically on the chest. Increased fremitus may suggest consolidation, while decreased fremitus may suggest pleural effusion or pneumothorax. This palpation technique complements percussion and auscultation during a comprehensive objective respiratory assessment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist auscultates a ventilated patient and hears coarse crackles bilaterally with visible secretions in the endotracheal tube. Blood pressure and heart rate are stable. What is the most appropriate immediate physiotherapy action?
questions.explanation: Coarse crackles with visible secretions and stable haemodynamics support proceeding with airway clearance techniques such as suctioning, positioning, and manual techniques as appropriate. There is no indication here for withholding treatment or escalating to invasive procedures such as chest tube insertion. This scenario reflects a typical, appropriate case for standard secretion clearance intervention.
options: Immediately request emergency chest tube insertion
Proceed with airway clearance techniques such as suctioning and positioning
Administer intravenous fluids without medical consultation

questions.question: A physiotherapist working in a low-resource setting does not have access to a formal incentive spirometer for a post-surgical patient with mild atelectasis. Which alternative intervention would most appropriately address the same underlying goal of lung re-expansion?
options: Complete avoidance of any respiratory intervention until equipment becomes available
Structured deep breathing and thoracic expansion exercises with verbal coaching
Reliance solely on bed rest without any breathing exercise
Immediate referral for surgical intervention regardless of severity
Discharge without any further respiratory follow-up
questions.explanation: In the absence of a formal incentive spirometer, structured deep breathing and thoracic expansion exercises delivered with verbal coaching can achieve a similar goal of promoting lung re-expansion and preventing further atelectasis. This adaptation reflects practical, resource-appropriate clinical reasoning while maintaining the core therapeutic objective. Physiotherapists should be prepared to modify techniques based on available resources without compromising fundamental treatment goals.

An FEV1/FVC ratio below 70 percent confirms airflow obstruction, and an FEV1 of 45 percent predicted falls within the range defining Stage 3, severe COPD, according to GOLD staging. This classification helps guide the intensity of pharmacological and rehabilitative management appropriate to disease severity. Correctly applying staging criteria supports accurate documentation and communication within the multidisciplinary team.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to interpret a patient's spirometry showing FEV1/FVC of 0.55 with FEV1 at 45 percent predicted. According to GOLD staging, which severity classification does this most closely correspond to?
A physiotherapist is mobilising a post-operative patient and monitors a drop in oxygen saturation from 96 percent to 89 percent during the activity. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
options: Stop the activity, reassess the patient, and consider supplemental oxygen as needed
Continue the activity at the same intensity without any changes
Increase the intensity of the activity to improve oxygen saturation
Ignore the reading since pulse oximetry is often inaccurate
Discharge the patient immediately from physiotherapy care
questions.explanation: A significant drop in oxygen saturation during activity warrants stopping the activity, reassessing the patient's clinical status, and considering supplemental oxygen or other supportive measures as needed. Continuing or intensifying the activity despite desaturation would risk further clinical deterioration. This response reflects safe, responsive clinical decision-making during exercise-based physiotherapy.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify the most likely reason a patient's chest physiotherapy plan includes a specific note to avoid positioning the patient flat immediately after a large meal, in addition to standard postural drainage timing advice. What is the most likely combined rationale?
questions.explanation: Avoiding flat positioning immediately after a large meal helps reduce the combined risk of gastro-oesophageal reflux and the discomfort or vomiting risk already associated with postural drainage timing near meals. This layered consideration reflects careful, patient-centred planning that accounts for multiple overlapping risk factors rather than a single isolated concern. Thoughtful timing and positioning decisions such as this improve both safety and patient comfort during treatment.
options: Ensuring the patient remains hungry throughout the treatment session
Eliminating any need to consider meal timing in future sessions
Avoiding any consideration of digestive comfort during physiotherapy
Reducing the combined risk of gastro-oesophageal reflux and treatment-related discomfort or vomiting
Ensuring the treatment session lasts as long as possible regardless of comfort

questions.explanation: Increased sputum production combined with coarse crackles on auscultation directly indicates active secretion retention, providing clear justification for prioritising airway clearance techniques during the session. questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify which finding, among several documented in a patient's chart, would most specifically justify prioritising airway clearance techniques over other available interventions during today's session. Which finding is most directly relevant?

Withholding breathing exercises entirely until pain fully resolves
Recommending strict bed rest without any respiratory input

Splinting the incision during breathing exercises alongside analgesia review
questions.explanation: Splinting the surgical incision, for example with a pillow, during breathing exercises helps reduce pain-related guarding while supporting more effective lung expansion. Vigorous percussion directly over a fresh incision would be inappropriate and potentially harmful.
questions.question: A patient recovering from major abdominal surgery demonstrates a shallow breathing pattern and reluctance to take deep breaths due to pain. Which combination of physiotherapy interventions best addresses both the pain and the breathing limitation?

options: Scheduling airway clearance only at midday regardless of symptom pattern
Scheduling airway clearance sessions to coincide with periods of increased secretion mobility, such as mornings
Avoiding airway clearance entirely due to purulent sputum
Scheduling airway clearance only once weekly regardless of symptoms
Delaying all treatment until sputum becomes non-purulent
questions.explanation: Because this patient reports increased secretion mobility in the morning and with position change, scheduling airway clearance to coincide with these periods maximises treatment effectiveness. Purulent sputum itself is not a contraindication to airway clearance; rather, it reinforces the need for regular, well-timed treatment. Adjusting timing to match the patient's individual secretion pattern reflects patient-centred clinical reasoning.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning airway clearance for a bronchiectasis patient who reports morning hypersecretion of purulent sputum with change in position. Which timing consideration is most clinically relevant?

questions.explanation: Energy conservation techniques, such as sitting to perform tasks where possible and pacing activities with planned rest breaks, help reduce the overall oxygen demand and breathlessness experienced during household chores in COPD patients. Encouraging the patient to push through discomfort without modification would likely worsen symptoms and reduce activity tolerance over time. Teaching practical, activity-specific strategies supports improved quality of life and functional independence.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is teaching energy conservation techniques to a COPD patient who reports severe breathlessness during household chores. Which specific strategy best exemplifies this approach?
options: Completing all chores as quickly as possible without any rest breaks
Sitting to perform tasks where possible and pacing activities with rest breaks
Avoiding all household activity permanently regardless of task
Performing all tasks standing to maximise physical exertion
Ignoring breathlessness symptoms and pushing through discomfort

questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning positioning for a mechanically ventilated patient with unilateral right lower lobe collapse. Which position would most directly support the goal of improving ventilation to the affected area?
questions.explanation: Positioning the unaffected, healthier lung dependent, in this case left side-lying with the collapsed right lower lobe uppermost, can improve ventilation-perfusion matching and promote re-expansion of the affected segment. This principle draws on the physiological relationship between gravity, ventilation, and perfusion. Careful positioning is a low-risk, evidence-based intervention that complements other airway clearance and re-expansion techniques.
options: Right side-lying, placing the affected lung lowermost
Left side-lying, placing the affected lung uppermost
Prone positioning regardless of the affected side
Sitting fully upright at all times
Definite confirmation that the lung has fully re-expanded
A normal and expected finding requiring no further action

Confirmation that the patient is ready for immediate discharge
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that a chest drain's underwater seal is not swinging with respiration in a patient two days post-thoracotomy. What is the most likely clinical concern this finding raises?
questions.explanation: Absence of the expected swinging in the underwater seal chamber may indicate tube blockage, kinking, or complete lung re-expansion, all of which require further clinical assessment to distinguish. The physiotherapist should report this finding to the nursing or medical team rather than assuming lung re-expansion without confirmation. Recognising abnormal chest drain behaviour is an important safety observation during post-surgical respiratory care.

questions.explanation: A near-normal pH despite a markedly elevated PaCO2, together with an elevated bicarbonate level, indicates renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis, consistent with long-standing severe COPD. Recognising this chronic compensated pattern, rather than mistaking it for acute deterioration, helps guide appropriately measured physiotherapy and oxygen therapy decisions. Sudden changes from this baseline, rather than the baseline itself, would be the more concerning clinical signal.
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews arterial blood gas results showing pH 7.36, PaCO2 68 mmHg, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L in a patient with known severe COPD. How should this pattern most likely be interpreted?

questions.question: A patient recovering from a stroke is referred for respiratory physiotherapy due to reduced cough effectiveness and risk of aspiration. Which specific consideration should guide the choice of airway clearance and positioning techniques in this patient?

questions.question: During a spontaneous breathing trial using a T-piece, the physiotherapist observes increasing respiratory rate and accessory muscle use in a patient with a tracheostomy and prolonged ventilator days. What should this observation prompt?
questions.explanation: Increasing respiratory rate and accessory muscle use during a spontaneous breathing trial are signs of fatigue, particularly significant in a patient with a tracheostomy and prolonged ventilator days who requires cautious weaning. This observation should prompt close monitoring and consideration of returning the patient to fuller ventilatory support rather than persisting with the trial. Careful, staged weaning trials help avoid weaning failure and unnecessary patient distress.

questions.question: A patient with a large pleural effusion is referred for airway clearance techniques to address unrelated mild secretion retention. What is the most appropriate initial clinical consideration?
options: Large pleural effusion has no bearing on airway clearance safety
Large pleural effusion is a listed contraindication requiring caution before proceeding
Airway clearance should be intensified specifically due to the effusion
The effusion should be ignored entirely during treatment planning
Postural drainage in steep Trendelenburg is strongly recommended in this case
questions.explanation: Large pleural effusions are specifically listed among the contraindications for airway clearance techniques, meaning the physiotherapist must exercise caution and likely modify or avoid certain manual techniques until the effusion is appropriately managed. questions.explanation: A Borg scale score indicating very severe exertion suggests the current exercise intensity exceeds an appropriate and safe therapeutic level for the patient, warranting a reduction in intensity. The Borg scale is specifically designed to guide real-time adjustment of exercise intensity based on the patient's own perceived effort. questions.explanation: Metabolic equivalents, or METs, derived from exercise testing protocols, help determine the appropriate intensity for mobilization and exercise prescriptions. questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with suspected pulmonary embolism who has been referred for chest physiotherapy due to reduced mobility. What is the most appropriate immediate approach before initiating standard respiratory techniques?

questions.question: What is the normal daily volume of airway secretions produced and cleared in a healthy individual?
questions.explanation: In health, between 10 and 100 millilitres of airway secretions are continuously produced and cleared by the mucociliary escalator, aided by transient increases in expiratory airflow. Alveolar gas composition differs from atmospheric air because oxygen continuously diffuses out into the blood while carbon dioxide diffuses in. Humidification by the conducting airways adds water vapour, and incomplete mixing with each tidal breath further alters the composition. These combined processes explain the higher CO2 and lower O2 levels found in alveolar air.

Direct equalisation of alveolar and atmospheric pressures without exchange

questions.question: Which mechanism explains why alveolar CO2 and O2 levels differ from atmospheric composition?

questions.explanation: Transport of respiratory gases refers to the movement of oxygen from the lungs to the tissue cells and carbon dioxide from the tissue cells back to the lungs, accomplished by the cardiovascular system using blood as the transport medium. This differs from external respiration, which occurs between the lungs and blood, and internal respiration, which occurs between blood and tissue cells. Together these processes complete the overall respiratory cycle.
questions.question: Which process describes the transport of oxygen from the lungs to the tissue cells of the body via the cardiovascular system?

options: Dismiss the patient's concern entirely and proceed exactly as before
Immediately discontinue all future airway clearance techniques permanently
Ignore the emotional component and focus only on technique mechanics
Insist the patient perform the technique at maximal intensity regardless of distress
Acknowledge the patient's concern, review and adjust technique intensity, and provide reassurance before proceeding gradually
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the patient's fear, reviewing and adjusting technique intensity, and providing clear reassurance before gradually reintroducing the huffing technique reflects a patient-centred approach that addresses both the physical and psychological aspects of the concern. Dismissing the patient's fear or insisting on maximal intensity could worsen anxiety and reduce future cooperation with necessary treatment. Balancing therapeutic necessity with sensitive, responsive communication supports better long-term treatment adherence.

questions.explanation: Repeating a chest radiograph after a course of physiotherapy for atelectasis allows objective evaluation of whether the affected lung segment has re-expanded in response to treatment, directly informing decisions about continuing, modifying, or stepping down intervention. This use of imaging as an outcome measure complements clinical findings such as auscultation and percussion. Using repeat objective investigations appropriately supports evidence-based monitoring of treatment response.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify the most likely reason a chest radiograph is repeated for a patient one week into physiotherapy treatment for atelectasis. What is the most likely clinical purpose of this repeat imaging?

questions.explanation: Trendelenburg positioning is specifically contraindicated following recent oesophageal surgery due to the increased risk of complications such as anastomotic strain or reflux. The physiotherapist should select alternative, less steep positioning options to achieve secretion drainage goals safely. This illustrates the importance of considering recent surgical history when selecting postural drainage positions.
questions.question: A patient recovering from oesophageal surgery requires positioning for secretion drainage. Which specific postural consideration applies given this recent surgical history?

Oesophageal surgery has no bearing on positioning choices
Only prone positioning is contraindicated after oesophageal surgery
Trendelenburg positioning is contraindicated following recent oesophageal surgery

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a ventilated patient with an inflated endotracheal tube cuff and needs to auscultate for a cuff leak before extubation. What finding would most likely suggest an adequately sealed cuff?
questions.explanation: An adequately sealed endotracheal tube cuff should prevent an audible air leak around the tube during positive pressure breaths, ensuring effective delivery of the set tidal volume. A loud, continuous leak would suggest cuff underinflation or tube malposition requiring correction before proceeding further. Assessing cuff integrity is an important safety check the physiotherapist should be aware of, particularly around suctioning and hyperinflation procedures.

options: Chronic cough increasing intra-abdominal pressure repeatedly over time
A completely unrelated urological condition with no respiratory link
Reduced fluid intake secondary to breathlessness alone
Increased renal blood flow caused by hypoxaemia
Decreased abdominal muscle tone caused by inactivity alone
questions.question: A patient reports chronic cough and has recently developed stress urinary incontinence. Which underlying respiratory-related mechanism most plausibly explains this new symptom?
questions.explanation: Chronic cough is recognised as a cause of stress urinary incontinence because the repeated, forceful increases in intra-abdominal pressure during coughing can weaken pelvic floor support over time. Recognising this connection is important when taking a subjective history in respiratory patients, as it may also indicate the severity and chronicity of the underlying cough. Addressing the cough itself, alongside pelvic floor considerations, may be relevant to overall management.

options: The lower lobes have thinner bronchial walls prone to collapse
The upper lobes have a higher density of mucus-secreting glands
The lower lobes lack any ciliated epithelium
The upper lobes are anatomically inaccessible for drainage
The upper lobes drain more effectively by gravity in the upright position
questions.question: Why are the lower lobes generally identified as requiring postural drainage more frequently than the upper lobes?
questions.explanation: Because the upper lobes benefit from gravitational drainage during normal upright posture, they generally require less frequent postural drainage. The lower lobes, by contrast, tend to accumulate secretions more readily and therefore require drainage most frequently. This anatomical relationship guides prioritisation of postural drainage positions in clinical practice.

questions.question: According to the physiological hierarchy for treating impaired oxygen transport, which intervention is generally considered before initiating mobilization and exercise?
questions.explanation: The physiological hierarchy for treating impaired oxygen transport progresses from body positioning through breathing control maneuvers and coughing maneuvers, culminating in mobilization and exercise. This structured approach ensures that foundational interventions are addressed before progressing to more demanding activity. Following this hierarchy helps optimise oxygen transport safely in compromised patients.

In progressive neuromuscular conditions such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, respiratory muscle weakness often impairs the ability to generate an effective spontaneous cough, making manually or mechanically assisted cough techniques particularly valuable for secretion clearance. Relying solely on an unassisted cough would likely be inadequate as the disease progresses. Adapting airway clearance strategy to the specific pattern of muscle weakness reflects individualised neuromuscular respiratory care.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is working with a patient who has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and progressive respiratory muscle weakness. Which airway clearance approach would be most appropriate given the likely limitation in generating an effective spontaneous cough?
options: Reliance solely on the patient's unassisted voluntary cough
Vigorous unassisted postural drainage without any cough assistance
Withholding any airway clearance intervention entirely
Manually or mechanically assisted cough techniques
High-intensity resistance training of respiratory muscles regardless of fatigue

questions.explanation: The St George's Respiratory Questionnaire is specifically designed to evaluate health-related quality of life in patients with chronic respiratory conditions such as COPD and bronchiectasis. It covers symptoms, activity limitations, and psychosocial impact of the disease. This distinguishes it from generic tools such as the Short Form 36, which is not respiratory-specific.
questions.question: Which questionnaire is specifically designed to assess health-related quality of life in patients with chronic respiratory disease?

questions.explanation: The active cycle of breathing technique can be performed independently by the patient without reliance on a caregiver, making it particularly suitable for a mobile patient who values independence. Postural drainage, particularly when combined with manual percussion, may still require caregiver assistance in certain positions. Considering patient preference and independence is an important part of individualised treatment selection.
options: It requires the patient to remain in Trendelenburg position at all times
It cannot be combined with any other airway clearance method
It can be performed independently without reliance on a caregiver
It requires expensive mechanical equipment unavailable at home
It is only suitable for ventilated patients
questions.question: A physiotherapist is deciding whether to use postural drainage or an active cycle of breathing technique for a mobile bronchiectasis patient who prefers independence. Which factor most strongly supports selecting the active cycle of breathing technique?

questions.explanation: Chronic hyperinflation of the lungs, commonly seen in advanced COPD, often produces a barrel-shaped chest due to persistent air trapping and increased anteroposterior chest diameter. This differs from pectus excavatum or kyphoscoliosis, which are structural spinal or sternal deformities rather than a direct consequence of hyperinflation. Recognising this chest shape assists in identifying underlying chronic obstructive disease.
options: Flat diaphragmatic excursion only on the left side

questions.explanation: Transudative pleural effusions arise from systemic imbalances in oncotic and hydrostatic pressure, commonly seen in conditions such as congestive heart failure and cirrhosis. Exudative effusions, in contrast, result from inflammatory processes or impaired lymphatic drainage, as seen in malignancy or tuberculosis. Correctly classifying the effusion type helps guide the underlying diagnostic workup.
questions.question: Which classification of pleural effusion results from an imbalance in oncotic and hydrostatic pressures, such as in congestive heart failure?

questions.explanation: Vibration uses the therapist's hands and arms to create small-amplitude, high-frequency oscillations over the chest wall. Shaking, by contrast, utilises the whole arm and body to generate larger-amplitude, lower-frequency oscillations. Both techniques aim to reinforce expiratory airflow and enhance the shearing action on retained secretions.
questions.question: What primarily distinguishes shaking from vibration as manual airway clearance techniques?
options: Shaking uses smaller amplitude and higher frequency oscillations than vibration
Shaking uses larger amplitude and lower frequency oscillations than vibration
Shaking is performed only during inspiration while vibration occurs during expiration
Shaking requires mechanical devices while vibration is always manual
Shaking is contraindicated in all respiratory conditions while vibration is not
