questions.answerText:
(a)
The fetal head comprises the scalp (skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose tissue and periosteum), the skull and its contents; about 95% of babies present by the head.

(b)
Vault bones are two frontal, two parietal and the occipital bone (plus part of the temporal); the sutures are sagittal, coronal, lambdoidal and frontal and they allow moulding.

(c)
The anterior fontanelle is diamond-shaped (about 2.5 cm), closes at about 18 months; the posterior fontanelle is triangular.

(d)
The vertex lies between the two fontanelles and the parietal eminences; the sinciput is the frontal area, the face lies between the root of the nose and the chin, and the occipital area extends from the posterior fontanelle to the foramen magnum.

(e)
Longitudinal diameters: suboccipito-bregmatic 9.5 cm, suboccipito-frontal 10 cm, occipito-frontal 11.5 cm, submento-vertical 11.5 cm, mento-vertical 13.5 cm, submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm; transverse: biparietal 9.5 cm and bitemporal 8.2 cm.

(f)
Attitude is the degree of flexion or extension of the head on the neck; with a well-flexed vertex the suboccipito-bregmatic (9.5 cm) presents; with a brow presentation the mento-vertical 13.5 cm and with face the submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm.

(g)
Moulding is slight overriding of the vault bones that shortens one diameter and lengthens another; abnormal if excessive (prolonged labour, prematurity), sudden (breech, caesarean section) or in the wrong direction (persistent occipito-posterior).

(h)
Caput succedaneum is oedema of the scalp over the presenting part, pits on pressure and normally resolves within 24 hours without treatment; a large caput can protrude through a not-fully-dilated cervix and mislead the midwife.

(i)
In brow presentation vaginal delivery is extremely unlikely because of the mento-vertical diameter; in persistent occipito-posterior the occipito-frontal diameter distends the vaginal orifice.

(j)
Excessive or sudden moulding can be harmful.

(k)
Complications of unfavourable presenting diameters spreading to the mother (bruising or laceration of the pelvic floor and perineum) are described for the android pelvis.

(a) Objectives and precautions
(b) Face, head and neck

(d) Genitalia, limbs and spine
(e) Measurements

(i) Cord and abdominal checks
Explain the rationale and the consequences of incorrect practice.
(j) Why the room must be warm
(k) Why the examination is done in the mother's presence
(l) Why findings must be documented and reported
questions.answerText:
(a)
Objectives: to ascertain normality externally, detect abnormality and assess adaptation to extra-uterine life; ensure a warm, draught-free room, diligent handwashing and gentle handling.

(b)
Observe the skin colour, activity and symmetry; check the mouth (tongue-tie, gums, palate high-arched and intact, uvula central, cleft by feeling the palate, precocious teeth), eyes (spacing up to 3 cm), ears (pinna level with canthus, patency), head (shape, fontanelles, caput or cephalhaematoma) and neck.

(c)
Chest: synchronous respiratory and abdominal movement, nipple spacing; abdomen rounded (scaphoid may mean malnourishment or diaphragmatic hernia); cord with 3 vessels (2 arteries and 1 vein), bleeding or protrusions; ectopic bladder from imperfect closure of the abdominal wall.

(d)
Genitalia and anus: sex, ambiguous genitalia, hypospadias, epispadias, anal patency; limbs and digits: count digits, talipes, polydactyly, joint movement; spine: prone, inspect and palpate for defects, dimples or hairy patches.

(e)
Use a non-stretchy tape: head circumference 34-38 cm in a term baby (moulding may reduce it), length about 52 cm and weight 2.5-3.5 kg.

(f)
Moro, rooting, sucking and swallowing, gag, cough and sneeze, blinking and corneal, grasp, walking and stepping, traction response and ventral suspension, elicited when the baby is quiet and alert to show neurological normality.

(g)
Warm, draught-free environment, handwashing and gentle handling, with the baby naked, good light and an orderly head-to-toe sequence.

(h)
Ortolani (both hips together, a clunk if dislocated) and Barlow (one hip at a time, pelvis stabilised, hip rotated through 70-90 degrees, a clunk if dislocated).

(i)
Check the cord for bleeding and number of vessels; absence of an artery indicates renal or cardiac anomalies and must be brought to the paediatrician's attention.

(j)
The newborn loses heat easily, and the environment must be warm and draught free to avoid cooling.

(k)
The examination is done in the presence of the mother or caregiver so findings are explained and parents are prepared for the screening.

(l)
Findings are documented and abnormalities reported to the paediatrician so that medical intervention can be sought early.

questions.question:
A newborn baby has persistent vomiting within 24 to 36 hours of birth, and another baby has bilious vomiting with abdominal distension.
(a) Identify the likely diagnoses.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology and causes.
(c) State the immediate midwifery management and emergency actions.
(d) State the definitive management and referral.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Intestinal obstruction from atresia (oesophageal or duodenal atresia, where persistent vomiting within 24-36 hours of birth is the first feature if not diagnosed prenatally) or from malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting and abdominal distension).

(b)
• Oesophageal atresia results from incomplete canalisation of the oesophagus in early intrauterine development; duodenal atresia can occur at any level of bowel but the duodenum is the commonest site.
• Atresia is commonly associated with chromosomal disorders, particularly trisomy 21.
• Malrotation is a developmental abnormality with incomplete rotation of the small bowel, predisposing to intermittent twisting (volvulus) and obstruction; the baby may be asymptomatic in the neonatal period.
• Many are diagnosed before birth by fetal ultrasound screening at 18-20 weeks' gestation.

(c)
General newborn care includes checking the abdominal shape (normally rounded; scaphoid or protrusions are noted) and anal patency, keeping the baby warm, documenting and reporting.

(d)
• Atresia is treated by surgical repair.
• Malrotation with episodes of obstruction needs surgical correction.
• Referral: report to the paediatrician.

questions.question:
Describe the cardiovascular system and blood physiology of the newborn:
(a) Blood volume and cord clamping
(b) Haemoglobin and white cells
(c) Heart rate and circulation changes
(d) Vitamin K and clotting
(e) Peripheral pulses and murmurs
State how its parts relate to common complications.
(f) Coarctation of the aorta
(g) Tachycardia and bradycardia
(h) Haemorrhagic disease
(i) Iron deficiency anaemia
Explain how a complication may spread or affect another system and cause a functional deficit.
(j) Cardiac compensation and respiration
(k) Heart failure and shock
(l) Cardiac defect and growth
questions.answerText:
(a)
Delaying cord clamping for at least the first minute lets oxygenated blood pass from the placenta, so blood volume at birth may exceed 80-90 ml/kg.

(b)
Haemoglobin may exceed 18-22 g, with fetal haemoglobin converting to adult haemoglobin from 36 weeks and completing in 1-2 years; fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen; white cell count is initially high (18 x 10^9/l) and falls quickly.

(c)
Heart rate is 100-160 beats per minute (120-160 average); the foramen ovale, a temporary opening between the atria, closes within days to weeks of birth.

(d)
Vitamin K is poorly transferred across the placenta and low in breast milk; clotting factors II, VII, IX and X depend on it and on bowel colonisation by E. coli.

(e)
The brachial pulse is easiest to feel and is counted over 10 seconds; benign murmurs are short, soft, systolic and at the left sternal border, and many babies have murmurs in the first 24 hours without a defect.

(f)
Strong arm pulses with weak leg pulses suggest coarctation of the aorta; a stronger right than left brachial pulse suggests constriction before the left subclavian artery.

(g)
Sinus tachycardia above 160 per minute first prompts a check for pyrexia; sinus bradycardia below 80 may follow hypothermia, hypoxia, raised intracranial pressure or hypothyroidism.

(h)
Exclusively breastfed babies are at higher risk of classic haemorrhagic disease, so vitamin K prophylaxis is given; early-onset disease (within 24 hours) is caused by maternal anticoagulant medicines.

(i)
Delayed cord clamping helps ward off neonatal iron-deficiency anaemia.

(j)
Respiratory distress may be a sign of cardiac compensation, shown by tachypnoea above 60, nasal flaring, recession, head bobbing and grunt.

(k)
A weak thready pulse occurs in congestive heart failure and circulatory shock, and capillary refill over 2 seconds is abnormal.

(l)
Smallness for gestational age could indicate growth disruption when major organs were forming, and poor feeding and failure to thrive are signs of a congenital heart defect.

(a)
The gastrointestinal tract is structurally complete but functionally immature; the mouth mucosa is pink and moist, teeth are buried in the gums, ptyalin secretion is low, and sucking and swallowing are coordinated.

(b)
The stomach holds 15-30 ml and enlarges rapidly; gastric emptying takes 2-3 hours; acidity equals the adult level within hours then falls, and by the 10th day the baby is virtually achlorhydric.

(c)
Bowel sounds are heard within an hour; sterile meconium present from 16 weeks is passed within 24 hours and fully excreted by 48-72 hours; E. coli then colonises the bowel and stools become brownish-yellow, then yellow.

(d)
Breast-milk stools are loose, bright yellow, acid and inoffensive (8-10 a day); formula-fed stools are paler, semi-formed, less acidic and more offensive, with a real risk of constipation.

(e)
Glycogen stores deplete rapidly so early feeding maintains blood glucose (2.6-4.4 mmol/L); weight loss is normal at first, birth weight is regained in 7-10 days and gain is 150-200 g per week.

(f)
The weak cardiac sphincter predisposes to regurgitation of milk (posseting).

(g)
Achlorhydria from about day 10 increases the risk of infection from the mouth, and the intestine is susceptible to infection across the mucosa for the first six months.

(h)
Melaena is a tar-like stool of digested blood from high in the gut, from blood swallowed at birth, bleeding maternal nipples or gut damage; low bleeding gives frank blood.

(i)
Milk plaques on the tongue must be distinguished from Candida albicans, which needs treatment.

(j)
Neonates are very susceptible to infection entering through respiratory and gastrointestinal mucosa; localisation is poor, so minor infections can generalise easily.

(k)
Because glycogen stores are rapidly depleted, inadequate early feeding risks low blood glucose, which affects the baby's metabolism and energy supply.

(l)
Poor attachment and lactose overload can cause gas, distension and loose green stools and, in severe cases, dehydrating diarrhoea.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Maternal: hypertension, pre-eclampsia including HELLP, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, malnutrition, anaemia, smoking, alcohol and substance misuse, heart or respiratory disease, thyroid disorders, epilepsy.
• Uterine and placental: abruption, placenta praevia, reduced uterine and placental blood flow, chorioamnionitis, abnormal cord insertion, oligohydramnios; fetal: multiple gestation, ToRCH and syphilis infection, congenital and chromosomal abnormalities; familial smallness.
• Symmetric IUGR (up to 30%) is from intrinsic fetal factors; asymmetric IUGR (up to 80%) is from reduced placental perfusion with a normal head size.

(b)
Baby: decreased oxygen levels, low Apgar scores, meconium aspiration, hypoglycaemia, difficulty keeping warm, polycythaemia, low resistance to infection, trouble with the stress of vaginal delivery, and in severe cases stillbirth or long-term growth problems.

(c)
• Options: temperature-controlled beds or incubators, tube feeds if the suck is weak, blood tests for hypoglycaemia, oxygen monitoring, and oxygen and mechanical help if also preterm.
• Choice of treatment depends on gestational age, overall health, extent of the condition, tolerance of therapies and the parents' preference.
• Justified choice: temperature control with hypoglycaemia checks and feeding support, because SGA babies may be weak, tolerate large feeds poorly and cool easily, and asymmetric SGA babies have depleted fat stores.
questions.question:
A baby is small for gestational age, thin and pale with loose dry skin and a thin, dull umbilical cord.
(a) State the risk factors for the condition.
(b) State the complications for the baby and the mother.
(c) Describe the management options and justify the one you would choose.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Postpartum (baby or maternity) blues: very common and self-limited, beginning shortly after childbirth and affecting up to 85% of new mothers, with symptoms starting within a few days and lasting up to two weeks.
• Symptoms: tearfulness, mood swings, irritability, anxiety, fatigue, difficulty sleeping, eating, concentrating and making choices, loss of appetite and questioning ability to care for the baby.

(b)
• Pathophysiology: after delivery of the placenta there is an abrupt fall in oestrogen and progesterone; symptoms relate to the woman's sensitivity to hormone change (genetic predisposition and psychosocial stressors) rather than absolute levels.
• Factors most consistently predictive are personal and family history of depression; a history of postpartum depression is also a risk factor.
• Contributing circumstances: fatigue, 24-hour newborn care, sleep deprivation, lack of support, relationship strain, changed routines, financial stress, unrealistic expectations and pressure to bounce back; age, marital status, delivery complications and low birth weight are not consistently linked.

(c)
• Treatment is supportive: adequate sleep, emotional support, education and reassurance; the midwife explores the cause in relation to the woman's history, uses a kindly approach, assurance, assistance and advice, and some relaxants may be given.
• Escalate if symptoms affect daily functioning or last over two weeks (evaluate for postpartum depression or anxiety); postpartum psychosis (mania, hallucinations, delusions; 1-2 per 1000 women) is a psychiatric emergency needing hospital admission.
• No specific screening exists for blues, but routine screening for depression and emotional wellbeing is recommended in pregnancy and postpartum.
questions.question:
A mother a few days after childbirth cries easily, has mood swings, is irritable and doubts her ability to care for her baby.
(a) Identify the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the management and midwifery care.

Describe the care of the healthy low birth weight baby:
(a) Definitions of low, very low and extremely low birth weight
(b) Classification by gestation and weight (AGA, SGA, LGA)
(c) Feeding and breastfeeding
(d) Thermoregulation
(e) Prevention of infection
(f) Sleeping position, handling, noise and light
State the safe practice, precautions and monitoring required.
(g) Weight gain monitoring
(h) Room temperature and clothing
(i) Monitoring during feeding
Explain the rationale and the consequences of incorrect practice.
(j) Why heat loss is high
(k) Why feeding needs support
(l) Why the supine position is used
questions.answerText:
(a)
Low birth weight is defined by weight alone; very low birth weight is below 1500 g and extremely low birth weight is below 1000 g, regardless of gestational age.

(b)
AGA is between the 10th and 90th centile, SGA below the 10th centile and LGA above the 90th, plotted on centile charts using gestational age and birth weight.

(c)
Breastfeeding is especially important because breast milk has all the nutrients and antibodies; preterm babies have weak musculature so positioning and attachment are crucial; a nasogastric tube may delay sucking and swallowing, and cup feeding aids the transition.

(d)
Newborns cannot shiver and use brown fat; use a pre-warmed hat, clothing and swaddling; keep the incubator room at 26 degrees C and the cot room at 24 degrees C for babies of 2.0-2.5 kg.

(e)
Wash hands frequently, ask others to do so and avoid crowds and sick people.

(f)
Place supine and nest in soft bedding; limit noise and keep dim lighting; give a calm, nurturing environment with holding and comfort.

(g)
Closely monitor weight gain; some babies need more frequent feeds or higher-calorie milk or supplements, and regular check-ups monitor growth and development.

(h)
Dress warmly and adjust the room temperature; the head loses heat through a large surface area and wide sutures.

(i)
Parents and midwives give physical support and monitor the baby's breathing during feeding to avoid bradycardia and apnoea.

(j)
The baby has less body fat and a large surface area, and exposure to cold causes multisystem changes including decreased digestion and increased oxygen consumption.

(k)
Weak muscle tone and flexor control make feeding difficult, so proper positioning and attachment are vital.

(l)
The supine position promotes self-regulatory behaviour and prevents asphyxia; healthy LBW babies should always be placed supine.

questions.question:
Describe neural tube defects:
(a) Definition and types
(b) Causes and timing of development
(c) Spina bifida
(d) Anencephaly
(e) Hydrocephalus
(f) Management and prevention
Explain the clinical basis for their associated problems.
(g) Why hydrocephalus accompanies spina bifida
(h) Why folic acid is important
(i) Effect of a large encephalocele on labour
Distinguish between a meningocele and a meningomyelocele.
(j) Contents
(k) Effects
(l) Management
questions.answerText:
(a)
Neural tube defects are the commonest malformations of the central nervous system, arising from abnormal formation and closure of the neural tube; the two commonest are spina bifida and anencephaly, and they can affect spinal bones, the cord or nerve roots.

(b)
The cause is unclear but may relate to genetics, maternal nutrition including folic acid deficiency and other factors; the tube forms about one month after conception, often before the woman knows she is pregnant; spina bifida affects about 1 in 1000 newborns.

(c)
Spina bifida is failure of fusion of the vertebral column: meningocele, meningomyelocele (lumbosacral most common) and encephalocele at the skull base.

(d)
Anencephaly is absence of the forebrain and skull vault, incompatible with sustained life; the midwife wraps the baby carefully before showing the parents, since seeing and holding the baby helps grieving.

(e)
Hydrocephalus is a blockage in circulation or absorption of CSF; the ventricles enlarge and compress the brain; signs of raised pressure are a large tense fontanelle, splayed sutures, an inappropriate rise in head circumference, sun-setting eyes and irritability; a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is used, replaced as the baby grows, with risks of blockage and infection.

(f)
Prenatal screening is very effective at identifying these malformations; folic acid supplements before conception and early in pregnancy reduce incidence; surgery may address the defects.

(g)
Hydrocephalus commonly accompanies severe spina bifida because of a structural defect near the foramen magnum (Arnold-Chiari malformation) and may develop after closure of a meningomyelocele; aqueduct stenosis is the commonest cause without a meningomyelocele.

(h)
The neural tube forms very early, so folic acid taken before conception and in early pregnancy has reduced these anomalies.

(i)
A large encephalocele whose sac contains brain tissue may impede normal progress of labour.

(j)
A meningocele is protrusion of meninges (a flat or sac-like membrane with or without CSF) containing no neural tissue; a meningomyelocele involves the spinal cord and may rupture, exposing neural tissue.

(k)
A meningomyelocele usually causes neurological damage with paralysis distal to the defect and impaired bladder and bowel function.

(l)
Open lesions are covered with a non-adherent dressing and enclosed lesions handled with care to limit meningitis; myelomeningocele surgery closes the skin well but does not change existing cord damage.

(a)
This is the left occipito-anterior (LOA) position: the lie is longitudinal, the attitude complete flexion, the denominator is the occiput, and the sagittal suture lies in the right oblique diameter.

(b)
The engaging diameter is the suboccipito-frontal of 10.4 cm at the pelvic brim; with increased flexion and descent it reduces to the suboccipito-bregmatic of 9.5 cm.

(c)
• The expected mechanism is: flexion and descent, the occiput leads, internal rotation 1/8 of a circle forward along the left side, crowning, then extension to deliver the head.
• Then restitution, internal rotation of the shoulders with external rotation of the head, the anterior shoulder escapes under the symphysis, the posterior shoulder sweeps the perineum and the baby is born by lateral flexion.

(d)
• In a normal LOA position labour progresses normally; the midwife monitors descent and the engaging diameter on vaginal examination (sagittal suture slope, fontanelles and moulding).
• Bandl's ring visible above the symphysis signals mechanically obstructed labour.
questions.question:
A woman in labour has a longitudinal lie with the fetal head completely flexed, the occiput as the denominator, and the sagittal suture in the right oblique diameter of the pelvis, with the occiput on the left anterior side.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the structure and diameter involved.
(c) State the differential and the expected mechanism.
(d) State the midwifery reasoning and decision to escalate.

A woman gave birth one hour ago and the placenta has still not been delivered.
(a) Identify the problem.
(b) Name the procedure to be done and describe the preparation, steps and key points.
(c) State the risks or complications to the mother.
(d) Describe the aftercare, health education and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Retained placenta: the placenta has not been delivered up to one hour after birth; a normal third stage lasts 5-15 minutes and up to 1 hour is within normal limits; retained placenta is a predisposing factor for PPH.

(b)
• Procedure: manual removal of the placenta.
• Pre-requisites: an IV line in place, analgesia or anaesthetic given, full aseptic precautions, explanation and consent, and privacy.
• Hold the cord taut with the non-dominant hand; insert the coned dominant hand into the vagina following the cord; once the placenta is located release the cord and support the fundus abdominally to prevent uterine inversion or rupture.
• Extend the fingers and ease them gently between the placenta and the uterine wall with the palm facing the placenta; detach the placenta sideways with a slicing movement.
• When completely separated, rub up a contraction with the non-dominant hand and withdraw the dominant hand with the placenta in its grasp; examine the placenta for completeness and give a uterotonic once it is complete.

(c)
Risks: uterine inversion or rupture if the fundus is not supported, and PPH if placental tissue is retained or the uterus does not contract; infection risk at the raw placental site.

(d)
• Aftercare: discard used equipment, make the woman comfortable, document and report findings; observe for PPH, shock and uterine contraction.
• Prevention: active management of the third stage (uterotonic, cord clamping, controlled cord traction) and avoiding mismanagement of the third stage.

questions.question:
Describe the physiology of the urinary system in the puerperium:
(a) Conditions affecting the system
(b) Diuresis
(c) Renal changes
(d) Stress incontinence
State how these physiological features relate to urinary complications.
(e) Physiological reason for retention
(f) Neurological reasons for retention
(g) Mechanical reasons and overflow incontinence
(h) Warning signs of infection
Explain how urinary complications affect other systems and cause functional problems.
(i) Effect on the uterus
(j) Effect of delayed management
(k) Management of incontinence
(l) Effect on assessment of involution
questions.answerText:
(a)
Three conditions affect the urinary system in the puerperium: urinary retention, incontinence and diuresis.

(b)
Diuresis is normal from about day 2 for 3-4 days as fluid and salt balance return to non-pregnant values; plasma volume falls and haematocrit may rise unless blood loss was excessive.

(c)
The dilation of the renal calyces that occurred in pregnancy reverses by the end of the puerperium.

(d)
Stress incontinence (leaking on laughing, straining, coughing) is assumed to result from stretching of the base of the bladder in pregnancy and delivery and resolves naturally in most women.

(e)
Retention is common and the bladder can easily become over-distended on days 1-2; physiologically there is persistent reduced bladder smooth muscle tone from pregnancy with increased postvoid residual volume.

(f)
Neurologically, epidural analgesia temporarily impairs bladder function and micturition reflexes may be inhibited with suturing of the peritoneum.

(g)
Mechanically, urethral oedema or urethral compression from postdelivery vulval oedema contributes; the overfilled bladder can cause overflow incontinence, so women are encouraged to pass urine within a few hours of delivery.

(h)
Pain or burning on micturition can be a sign of bladder infection.

(i)
Emptying the bladder prevents its mechanical interference with uterine contractions.

(j)
Inappropriate or delayed diagnosis and management of retention can lead to bladder dysfunction, urinary tract infection and catheter-related complications.

(k)
Pelvic floor exercises help incontinence; specialist help should be provided if the problem persists.

(l)
A full bladder or rectum can displace the uterus and give a false fundal height reading, so the bladder and rectum should be emptied before measurement.

questions.question:
Describe the physiology of the second stage of labour:
(a) Definition and transitional period
(b) Uterine action and the Ferguson reflex
(c) Soft tissue displacement
(d) Presumptive and confirmatory signs of the second stage
(e) Phases and duration
State how its parts relate to common complications.
(f) Premature pushing
(g) Misleading signs
(h) Crowning and perineal injury
(i) Blood loss to distinguish
Explain how a complication may affect another system and cause a functional deficit.
(j) Effect on the bladder and urethra
(k) Effect on the rectum
(l) Effect on the pelvic floor
questions.answerText:
(a)
The second stage is from full dilatation to birth; a transitional period before pushing begins is marked by restlessness, discomfort, desire for pain relief and demands for the birth to be over quickly.

(b)
Contractions become stronger and longer but less frequent; membranes often rupture, letting the head press on the cervix; fetal axis pressure increases flexion; pressure on pelvic floor nerve receptors (Ferguson reflex) causes the urge to push, then the abdominal muscles and diaphragm are used.

(c)
The bladder is pushed up into the abdomen, stretching and thinning the urethra; the rectum flattens into the sacral curve; the levator ani muscles dilate, thin and move laterally and the perineal body flattens, stretches and thins.

(d)
Presumptive: expulsive contractions, rupture of forewaters, anal dilatation and gaping, presenting part visible, vulval congestion, show; confirmed by vaginal examination revealing no cervix.

(e)
Duration is as little as 5 minutes in multigravidae and up to 2 hours in primigravidae; the latent phase has gradual stretching of soft tissues with little urge and the active phase has a compulsive urge to push.

(f)
The urge to push may occur before full dilatation (for example in occipito-posterior position or a full rectum), and enthusiastic premature pushing may cause vulval congestion.

(g)
Excessive moulding may form a large caput that protrudes through the cervix before full dilatation, and a breech may be visible at 7-8 cm dilatation, more in women of high parity.

(h)
Expulsive crowning can cause perineal laceration, so fingers are placed on the advancing head and one shoulder is delivered at a time; episiotomy is given if necessary.

(i)
Show (blood-stained mucus) must be distinguished from fresh blood loss caused by partial placental separation or ruptured vasa praevia.

(j)
The bladder moves up out of risk of injury during fetal descent, but the urethra is stretched, so bladder care and encouraging urination are needed.

(k)
The rectum is flattened and residual faecal matter is expelled.

(l)
The levator ani and perineal body are stretched and thinned, so they are at risk of injury.

questions.question:
During routine newborn hip screening, with the baby warm and on a firm flat surface and a parent present, the examiner feels a clunk at one hip during the Barlow manoeuvre. The baby was a breech presentation and there was oligohydramnios.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the structure affected.
(c) State the differential and associated conditions.
(d) Describe the midwifery reasoning and the decision to escalate or refer.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A clunk indicates a dislocated or dislocatable hip: the Barlow manoeuvre screens for a dislocatable hip (displaced out of the joint) and the Ortolani manoeuvre for a dislocated hip (felt clunking into place).
• On the affected side the knee may be lower because the femoral head has dropped into soft tissue; equal knee height may mean normal hips or bilateral dislocation.

(b)
The hip joint (femoral head and acetabulum) is affected: developmental dysplasia of the hip may be dislocated, dislocatable or subluxated; the left hip is more often affected, and it is commoner in girls and in primigravidae.

(c)
• Associated findings: oligohydramnios, postural foot deformities (talipes), plagiocephaly, scoliosis, prominent sacral dimple, IUGR and dysmorphic features.
• Predisposing factors: squashed hips in utero (breech, external cephalic version, oligohydramnios), genetic predisposition (identical twins), family history, ligament hyperlaxity, and swaddling with legs together (10 per 1000 versus 0.25 per 1000).

(d)
• Screening aims at early identification and minimising long-term complications through timely hip ultrasound, further expert assessment and early intervention; the ideal time is 7 days and the examination should be done by experienced staff.
• Examine one hip at a time with Barlow (stabilising the pelvis) and Ortolani; both hips may be examined together by an experienced examiner; leg length is measured after the hip examination so as not to upset the baby.
• Decision: report the findings to the paediatrician, arrange selective ultrasound and document.

questions.question:
Describe effective positioning and attachment for breastfeeding:
(a) Positioning of the mother
(b) Positioning of the baby
(c) The proper way to breastfeed
(d) Signs of a proper latch
(e) Common breastfeeding positions
State the safe practice, precautions and monitoring required.
(f) Mother's back and support
(g) Baby's airway
(h) Role of the midwife
(i) Care of the breasts
Explain the rationale and the consequences of poor attachment.
(j) Rationale for good attachment
(k) Consequences for the baby
(l) Consequences for the mother
questions.answerText:
(a)
A comfortable position is a prerequisite; after caesarean section or a painful perineum, lying on her side may be the only tolerable position, with help placing the baby; sitting, her back should be upright at a right angle to her lap, with back and feet supported.

(b)
The baby's body is turned towards the breast at the same angle as the breast comes down; with the nose opposite the nipple and the neck slightly extended, the mouth is correctly placed.

(c)
Touch the nipple to stimulate the baby's mouth to open, let the baby open wide, and bring the baby to the breast.

(d)
Signs of a latch: wide-open mouth, chin touching the breast, flanged lips, round full breast, audible sucking and swallowing and a long round nipple after the feed.

(e)
Side-lying; football (clutch) hold for engorgement or sore nipples, which helps empty the bottom ducts; cross-cradle for new learners and small babies; cradle hold, the commonest position.

(f)
Support the back with pillows and tuck a pillow under the ribs when feeding from the lower breast in side-lying.

(g)
Make sure the baby's nose is not obstructed.

(h)
The midwife helps with positioning, may need to assist in placing the baby, and teaches how to breastfeed and maintain lactation, including when separated from the baby.

(i)
Wear a supportive but not tight bra, change damp pads, wash nipples with clear water only (soap removes natural lubricant), rest, eat well and drink fluids.

(j)
The baby needs to be well attached so the tongue strips milk from the breast rather than relying only on the let-down reflex.

(k)
A poorly attached baby may not get fat-rich hindmilk, feeds very frequently, and may develop colic-like symptoms.

(l)
Poor attachment may produce sore, cracked nipples, engorgement and infection; milk may not be emptied properly.

(a)
• Ophthalmia neonatorum (gonococcal conjunctivitis), which can present from 1 to 3 days with a profuse purulent discharge and swelling of the conjunctiva and lids.
• Chlamydial conjunctivitis presents later, at 5-14 days; a sticky eye demands microbiological investigation to exclude gonococcal and/or chlamydial infection.

(b)
• The mother and her sexual contact(s) need referral to the genitourinary clinic.
• If untreated, gonococcal infection can rapidly lead to corneal ulceration and blindness.
• Chlamydial conjunctivitis is associated with neonatal pneumonia if the initial systemic antibiotic treatment is inadequate.

(c)
• The examiner should treat assessment of an infected eye as no casual task and consider the gravity of ophthalmia neonatorum; check the colour of the sclera and for any discharge.
• Take a swab for microscopy and culture, then perform saline irrigation.
• Document findings for each eye and inform the parents.

(d)
• Treatment: topical and systemic antibiotics, usually penicillin.
• Refer the mother and sexual contact(s) to the genitourinary clinic.
questions.question:
A newborn at 2 days of age has a sticky eye with a profuse purulent discharge and swollen conjunctiva and lids.
(a) Identify the diagnosis and the likely causative organisms.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology, causes and complications.
(c) State the immediate midwifery management and emergency actions.
(d) State the definitive medical management and referral, including the mother's care.

Describe the physiology of thermoregulation in the newborn:
(a) Normal range and why temperature is unstable
(b) Routes of heat loss
(c) Non-shivering thermogenesis and brown fat
(d) The neonatal energy triangle
State how these features relate to complications.
(e) Early signs of cooling
(f) Hyperthermia
(g) Babies most vulnerable
(h) Multisystem effects of cold
Explain how cold stress affects other systems and how it is prevented.
(i) Metabolic effect
(j) Respiratory effect
(k) Prevention measures
(l) Assessment of temperature
questions.answerText:
(a)
The acceptable range is 36.5-37.5 degrees C; in the first week core temperature is unstable as the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata adapt from a hot intrauterine environment to cooler air, and the baby has a large surface area to body mass ratio and little subcutaneous fat.

(b)
Heat is lost by evaporation (wet skin and towels), conduction (contact with cold items, scales, clothes), convection (draughts) and radiation (heat drawn to colder objects, windows, walls).

(c)
Cooling babies cannot shiver; they use brown adipose tissue (2-7% of weight, deposited from 28 weeks, largest mass around the kidneys and adrenals, activated only after birth) and raise metabolic rate, increasing glucose and oxygen consumption.

(d)
Aerobic glycolysis needs oxygen and glucose; anaerobic glycolysis needs more than 20 times the glucose for the same energy, so the baby becomes hypoxic and glycogen stores are used, leading to hypoglycaemia if prolonged (the neonatal energy triangle).

(e)
A transient respiratory grunt may be the first sign of cooling, followed by nasal flaring, tachypnoea and sternal or subcostal recession.

(f)
Pyrexia above 37.7 degrees C may indicate infection; hyperthermia can follow an inappropriate heat source or over-dressing and raises metabolic rate, drawing on glucose and oxygen, so respiratory distress may follow unless the baby cools slowly.

(g)
Low birth weight babies and asymmetric SGA babies with depleted fat stores are more vulnerable to hypoglycaemia and cooling; the head loses heat through its large surface area and wide sutures.

(h)
Exposure to cold causes multisystem changes including decreased digestion and increased tissue oxygen consumption.

(i)
Cooling raises glucose demand, depletes glycogen and may cause hypoglycaemia.

(j)
Oxygen shortage leads to respiratory distress; respiratory difficulty can also arise from neurological, metabolic, circulatory or thermoregulation dysfunction.

(k)
Prevention: warm, draught-free room kept at 18-21 degrees C, skin-to-skin contact, a hat, adequate clothing without tight swaddling, adequate nutrition, reassessment after 30 minutes, and a supine cot position with feet to the foot of the cot to reduce overheating and sudden infant death.

(l)
Feel the head and chest, then measure temperature by the axilla, tympanic membrane or groin.

questions.question:
A newborn is assessed at 1 minute: the body is pink with blue hands and feet, the heart rate is below 100 beats per minute, the baby grimaces to stimulation, there is some flexion of the limbs, and respirations are slow and irregular.
(a) Interpret the findings and calculate the score.
(b) State the systems being assessed.
(c) State the differential considerations.
(d) State the midwifery reasoning and decision to escalate.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Colour 1 (pink body, blue extremities), pulse 1 (below 100), grimace 1, activity 1 (some flexion), respiration 1 (slow irregular): total 5.
• A score of 4-6 is moderately abnormal, below normal, and the baby likely needs medical intervention; 7-10 is normal and 0-3 critically low.

(b)
The Apgar components assess skin colour/perfusion, heart rate, reflex irritability, muscle tone and respiratory effort; heart rate is the most critical part in deciding on resuscitation.

(c)
• Low scores may arise from maternal sedation or anaesthesia, congenital abnormalities, trauma or prematurity; most infants score 1 for colour because peripheral cyanosis is common.
• Colour may be misleading in non-white infants; a low score alone is not evidence of asphyxia.

(d)
• Escalate: a score below 8 after drying and stimulation is managed with oxygen by bag and mask; call for the clinician and assess heart rate.
• Reassess and record at 5 minutes; if below 7, repeat every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes; scores below 5 at 5 minutes should have umbilical artery blood gas sampling.
• The 5-minute score and the change from 1 to 5 minutes indicate response to resuscitation.
• Document and communicate with the family.

(a)
• In non-lactating women the first menstruation occurs 45-64 days postpartum and the first ovulation at 45-94 days, though the earliest reported ovulations were at 25-27 days, so women who do not breastfeed risk conceiving rapidly without contraception.
• Between 20% and 80% of first menses are anovulatory.
• In breastfeeding women suckling suppresses GnRH release and so luteinising hormone, delaying ovulation in proportion to the intensity of breastfeeding; supplementary feeds and reduced frequency bring ovulation back sooner.

(b)
Family planning improves maternal health and child survival, reduces the number of abortions especially unsafe ones, helps prevent STIs including HIV/AIDS and empowers women.

(c)
• Options: short-acting (natural, barrier, hormonal), long-acting (implants, IUCDs) and permanent surgical methods.
• The Lactational Amenorrhoea Method is effective for the first 6 months, is low cost and available to all, but only while breastfeeding intensity is maintained.
• Women should receive counselling and be referred to the family planning clinic for a method suited to them.
• Justified choice: for a non-breastfeeding woman LAM does not apply, so a suitable alternative method chosen after counselling.
questions.question:
A woman who is not breastfeeding wants to know about contraception after childbirth.
(a) State the risk factors for early conception and the effect of breastfeeding on the return of fertility.
(b) State the complications of unplanned or closely spaced pregnancy.
(c) Discuss the contraceptive options and justify one.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The pelvis has two innominate bones (ilium, ischium, pubis), the sacrum and the coccyx; joints are the symphysis pubis, two sacro-iliac joints and the sacro-coccygeal joint, which loosen in pregnancy and the coccyx deflects backwards at birth.

(b)
The true pelvis comprises the brim, the cavity (round plane between the second and third sacral vertebrae, ischial spines and symphysis) and the outlet.

(c)
Brim: true conjugate at least 11.5 cm, obstetric conjugate 10.2 cm, diagonal conjugate 12 cm, oblique 12 cm, greatest transverse 13.5 cm; outlet: anteroposterior (increased by backward movement of the coccyx) and transverse between the ischial spines or tuberosities (reduced if the spines are prominent).

(d)
Gynaecoid (round brim, best for childbearing), android (heart-shaped), anthropoid (oval, narrow transversely) and platypelloid (kidney-shaped, narrow anteroposteriorly).

(e)
The deep layer is the levator ani (pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, ischiococcygeus) and the superficial layer is the superficial perineal muscles.

(f)
The perineal body is wedge-shaped tissue between the anal canal and vagina, formed by levator ani and superficial perineal muscle fibres, important in delivery and at risk of laceration.

(g)
In an android pelvis the head engages transversely or posteriorly and deep transverse arrest often occurs because of prominent ischial spines; the acute pubic arch bruises or lacerates the pelvic floor and perineum.

(h)
Contracted pelvis (justo-minor, Robert's, rickets, osteomalacia, kyphosis) causes cephalopelvic disproportion; severe contraction needs caesarean section while a trial of labour may be tried in minor degrees.

(i)
The perineal body is likely to be injured in delivery and tears are graded first, second and third degree.

(j)
Extra strain on the pelvic floor during labour weakens the ligamentous supports of the uterus formed by pelvic fascia round the cervix.

(k)
This can result in prolapse of the uterus, and the vaginal walls weaken slightly with each pregnancy, contributing to genital prolapse with age.

(l)
A pelvic floor weakened or deformed by contraction also distorts rotation: the pelvic floor normally directs the head forward in internal rotation.
questions.question:
Describe the anatomy of the bony pelvis and pelvic floor:
(a) The pelvic bones and joints
(b) The true pelvis: brim, cavity and outlet
(c) The main diameters of the brim and outlet
(d) Pelvic types
(e) Layers and muscles of the pelvic floor
(f) The perineal body
State how its parts relate to common complications of labour.
(g) Android pelvis
(h) Contracted pelvis
(i) Perineal injury
Explain how a complication may spread or affect another system and cause a functional deficit.
(j) Effect of labour on pelvic support
(k) Effect of pelvic floor weakening
(l) Effect of the pelvis on the head

questions.answerText:
(a)
Indications: to determine presentation and engagement, whether the forewaters have ruptured, to exclude cord prolapse after rupture (especially with an ill-fitting presenting part or heart rate changes), assess progress, confirm full dilatation and fetal axis, and confirm the presentation of the second twin.

(b)
Preparation: preceded by an abdominal examination, empty bladder, privacy, explanation and consent, aseptic technique, positioning and swabbing the vagina.

(c)
Observe varicosities, oedema, warts or sores, previous tear or episiotomy scar, scar from female genital mutilation, discharge or bleeding, smell of discharge and colour of amniotic fluid.

(d)
Palpate: length of the cervical canal, proximity of the presenting part, effacement, dilatation, consistency, membranes, moulding of the head, slope of the sagittal suture (oblique or transverse early, later anteroposterior) and position of the fontanelles.

(e)
Assess the pelvis: ischial spines should be blunt and the sub-pubic angle should accommodate 2 examining fingers; prominent spines and a reduced angle are unfavourable features associated with the android pelvis.

(f)
Maintain aseptic technique, seek consent, provide privacy and position the woman.

(g)
The sensitive part of the examining finger should face upwards.

(h)
Report and document findings, discuss them with the woman, discard waste and make her comfortable.

(i)
To confirm the second stage the examination finds no cervix; it ensures the woman is not pushing before full dilatation and gives a baseline for timing the second stage.

(j)
An abdominal examination first and an empty bladder are prerequisites.

(k)
Confirming full dilatation prevents premature pushing, which may cause vulval congestion, and gives a start time for the second stage.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• HIV may be transmitted in breast milk, so the risk is the transmission to the baby through breastfeeding.
• Lactoferrin in milk has antiviral action against HIV, CMV and HSV by interfering with virus absorption or penetration.

(b)
Breastfeeding: the risk of transmitting HIV; formula feeding: in some countries a significant cause of infant mortality.

(c)
• Option 1: formula feeding, where it is relatively safe (developed countries), with the mother advised not to breastfeed.
• Option 2: exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, which may be the safer option where formula feeding is a significant cause of infant mortality.
• Other WHO and UNICEF advice: breastfeed within the first hour, no other food or drink, breastfeeding on demand, and avoid bottles, teats and pacifiers.
• Justified choice: depends on the setting; exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months is the safer option where formula feeding causes infant deaths, and formula feeding where it is safe.

A baby is born before the completion of the 37th week of pregnancy and is smaller than expected.
(a) State the risk factors (spontaneous and elective) for preterm labour.
(b) State the characteristics of the preterm baby and the complications for the mother and the baby.
(c) Describe the management options for feeding and warmth and justify the one you would choose.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Spontaneous: 40% unknown; multiple gestation (higher multiples, greater chance); hyperpyrexia from viral or bacterial infection, often urinary tract infection; premature rupture of membranes from chorioamnionitis, polyhydramnios.
• Also spontaneous: short maternal stature, age <18 or >35 years, parity, uterine malformation (bicornuate uterus, fibroids), poor obstetric history including previous preterm labour.
• Elective: pregnancy-induced hypertension, pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, maternal renal or heart disease, placenta praevia, abruptio placenta, rhesus incompatibility, congenital abnormality of the baby, IUGR.

(b)
• Preterm means born before the end of the 37th week irrespective of birth weight (extremely preterm <28 weeks, very preterm 28-31, moderately preterm 32-33, late preterm 34 to <36 weeks).
• Characteristics: low-set umbilicus, thin red transparent skin with little subcutaneous fat (laid down from 28 weeks), abundant vernix and lanugo, flat pinna, bulging eyes, poorly developed nipple areola, absent plantar creases before 36 weeks, labia majora not covering minora in girls.
• Baby complications: serious health problems, lifelong cerebral palsy, later learning disabilities, weak feeding with risk of bradycardia and apnoea, heat loss, hypoglycaemia and higher risk of infection.

(c)
• Feeding options: breastfeeding with correct positioning and attachment; nasogastric tube (may delay sucking and swallowing reflexes); cup feeding (stimulates oral experience and aids transition to breastfeeding); more frequent feeds or higher-calorie milk supplements.
• Warmth options: incubator with bedding in a room at 26 degrees C; cot in a room at 24 degrees C for most preterm babies of 2.0-2.5 kg; pre-warmed hat; clothing and swaddling.
• Justified choice: breast milk (with cup feeding as a bridge), because it contains all nutrients and antibodies and lowers infection risk; tube feeding is reserved for a baby without a strong suck.
• Supine position, calm environment, dimmed light, reduced noise and regular weight and check-ups support care.

(a)
Uterine involution is being assessed; the uterus loses 50% of its weight in the first week and the fundal height falls gradually towards the pre-pregnant state.

(b)
• Skill: measuring fundal height by abdominal palpation, ideally by the same person, with the same instrument at a fixed time each day.
• The woman must have emptied her bladder and rectum first because a full bladder or rectum can displace the uterus and give a false reading.
• She lies on her back; the midwife palpates the abdomen, locates the fundus and the upper border of the symphysis pubis and uses a flat graduated ruler or spatula to estimate the distance between them.
• Percuss the lower abdomen to determine whether the bladder is properly emptied.

(c)
• Delayed involution may signal retained products of conception, endometritis, or a high uterus from pelvic haematoma or abscess.
• Uterine tenderness is checked for on puerperal rounds; persistent red lochia may mean retained tissue; green, malodorous lochia suggests infection.

(d)
• Education: aid involution by early ambulation, postnatal exercises, breastfeeding, prevention of infection and good health.
• Some authorities think daily fundal measurement is outdated but it offers an opportunity for training.
• Give the mother advice on danger signs and where to seek help.

(a) Interpret the finding.
(b) State the structure affected.
(c) State the differential considerations.
(d) State the midwifery reasoning and decision to escalate or refer.
questions.answerText:
(a)
About 20% of babies pass urine in the birthing room, 90% by 24 hours and 99% by 48 hours; a delay at 24 hours is therefore within the range of 10% of babies but needs attention.

(b)
The renal system, and the lower urinary tract and bladder, are the structures involved; neonatal kidneys are immature with a low glomerular filtration rate that matures in the first month.

(c)
• The commonest cause of initial delay or decreased urine production is inadequate perfusion of the kidney; other causes are physiological stress, intrinsic renal abnormalities or obstruction of the urinary tract.
• Oligohydramnios on antenatal scans may indicate fetal problems passing urine; many syndromes involve kidney function (low-set ears, abnormal genitalia, anal atresia, lower spine anomalies).

(d)
• The midwife asks the mother about wet nappies, checks the records and antenatal scan findings, and assesses for dehydration, infection and a palpable bladder.
• Normal urine is dilute, straw coloured and odourless; because tubular reabsorption is limited there is a narrow margin between under- and over-hydration.
• Refer for further investigation as necessary.

(a)
The third stage lasts 5-15 minutes (up to 1 hour is normal); emptying the uterus lets retraction accelerate, the placental attachment area shrinks, and the non-elastic placenta detaches, usually centrally with a retroplacental clot.

(b)
Schultze: separation begins centrally, a retroplacental clot forms, its weight strips the lateral borders and peels off the membranes, and the placenta descends fetal surface first in a membranous bag with complete shearing and less blood loss.

(c)
Matthews Duncan: detachment starts unevenly at a lateral border, blood escapes without a clot, the placenta slips down sideways maternal surface first; it takes longer with ragged incomplete membranes and higher blood loss.

(d)
Haemostasis depends on retraction of oblique uterine muscle fibres at the upper segment, vigorous uterine contraction, and activation of the coagulation and fibrinolytic systems.

(e)
Fundal height: start of third stage 2.5 cm below the umbilicus (15 cm above the symphysis); placenta in lower segment 1.5 cm above the umbilicus (19 cm); end of third stage 4 cm below the umbilicus (14 cm).

(f)
Signs: small fresh blood loss or gush, the cord lengthens, the fundus becomes rounder, smaller, harder and more mobile, the vulva may bulge and the woman may feel pressure or a contraction.

(g)
PPH arises from incomplete placental separation, retained products, precipitate or prolonged labour (uterine inertia), overdistension (multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios), placenta praevia, abruption, tears, oxytocin induction, full bladder and general anaesthesia.

(h)
The Duncan method is linked to ragged incomplete expulsion of membranes and higher blood loss, whereas Schultze is linked to less blood loss.

(i)
Tension applied to the cord without a contraction may cause uterine inversion.

(j)
PPH occurs in 10-11% of women having live births; the time from onset of massive bleeding to death is about 2 hours.

(k)
Stage 2 (1000-1500 ml): reduced urine output, raised pulse and respiratory rate, postural hypotension, narrow pulse pressure; stage 3 (1500-2000 ml): hypotension, tachycardia, cold clammy extremities, tachypnoea; stage 4 (>2000 ml): profound shock.

(l)
The signs show failing circulation, reduced urine output and respiratory compensation as blood loss rises.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Musculoskeletal defects are the second commonest birth defects after central nervous system anomalies and can be due to fetal viral infection, toxin ingestion or neurological disorders.

(b)
Syndactyly (webbing) commonly affects the hands, alone or in Apert's syndrome (premature fusion of skull sutures, cleft palate and syndactyly of hands and feet); surgery depends on the degree of fusion.

(c)
Polydactyly (extra digits) may be fully formed or tissue on a pedicle; better results come from surgical excision than tying off, and excision is mandatory in complex cases.

(d)
Limb reduction deficiencies are classified by site (upper or lower limb) and type (transverse or longitudinal).

(e)
Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant with a small baby, large head and short limbs; osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) is due to disordered collagen production causing fractures, with eight types.

(f)
Developmental dysplasia of the hip may be dislocated, dislocatable or subluxated; talipes equinovarus (club foot) is a downward-bent ankle with the forefoot turned inwards.

(g)
Hip dysplasia is commoner with breech at term, oligohydramnios, foot deformity or a first-degree relative affected; it is commoner in primigravidae and girls, and the left hip is more often affected.

(h)
About 80% of achondroplasia cases are new mutations of fibroblast growth factor receptor genes, so families may not anticipate it without antenatal diagnosis.

(i)
Osteogenesis imperfecta can cause multiple fractures in utero or at birth, with severity varying between types.

(j)
Syndactyly is fusion or webbing of digits; polydactyly is extra digits (so count and separate the digits and open the fist to find hidden extra digits).

(k)
In a transverse defect the limb is normal to a level beyond which no skeletal elements exist; in a longitudinal defect there is reduction or absence of an element within the long axis.

(l)
Syndactyly division depends on the degree of fusion, whereas polydactyly is managed by surgical excision rather than tying off.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Physiological: persistent reduction of bladder smooth muscle tone that begins in pregnancy, with increased postvoid residual volume; retention is commonest on days 1-2.
• Neurological: epidural analgesia temporarily impairs bladder function and micturition reflexes may be inhibited with suturing of the peritoneum.
• Mechanical: urethral oedema or urethral compression from postdelivery vulval oedema.

(b)
Maternal complications: overflow incontinence from an overfilled bladder, mechanical interference with uterine contractions, and bladder dysfunction, urinary tract infection and catheter-related complications when diagnosis or management is inappropriate or delayed.

(c)
• Options: encourage the woman to try to pass urine within a few hours of delivery; percuss the lower abdomen at puerperal rounds to check the bladder is emptied; reassure and watch for pain or burning on micturition; obtain specialist help if the problem persists.
• Justified choice: early encouragement to pass urine with abdominal assessment, because emptying the bladder prevents overflow incontinence and interference with uterine contractions and avoids the infection and dysfunction that follow delayed management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The Apgar score is a simple, non-invasive, standardised method, devised by Dr Virginia Apgar in 1952, for quickly assessing the clinical status of the newborn and the need for prompt intervention to establish breathing.

(b)
It is done at 1 and 5 minutes (the 1-minute score shows tolerance of birth, the 5-minute score shows how the baby is doing outside the womb) and repeated at 10 minutes or every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes when the score is below 7.

(c)
Appearance (pale/blue 0, pink body with blue extremities 1, all pink 2); pulse (absent 0, below 100 = 1, above 100 = 2); grimace (none 0, grimace 1, cry/cough/sneeze 2); activity (floppy 0, some flexion 1, active motion 2); respiration (absent 0, slow/irregular 1, vigorous cry 2).

(d)
7-10 is normal and reassuring, 4-6 is moderately abnormal (below normal, likely needs intervention), 0-3 is critically low; heart rate is the most critical element in deciding on resuscitation.

(e)
A doctor, midwife or nurse performs it; the nurse documents the 1- and 5-minute scores, assists with resuscitation, informs the clinician of changes, and educates the family.

(f)
Maternal sedation or anaesthesia, congenital abnormalities, gestational age, trauma and interobserver variability affect the score.

(g)
A healthy preterm baby with no hypoxia may score low because tone, reflexes and respiratory effort depend on maturity; low scores are inversely related to birth weight.

(h)
A low score alone is not evidence of asphyxia; other findings such as fetal heart rate patterns, cord arterial blood gases and cerebral function must be considered.

(i)
Components are subjective and one baby could be scored 7 by one person and 6 by another (55-82% consistency), so the same person should ideally score both times.

(j)
The Silverman and Andersen index evaluates chest movement, intercostal retraction, xiphoid retraction, nares dilatation and expiratory grunt; the Apgar score assesses colour, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration.

(k)
Each Silverman and Andersen criterion scores 0 to 2, so totals run from 0 to 10, as in the Apgar score.

(l)
On the Silverman and Andersen index 0 means no respiratory distress, 4-6 moderate and 7-10 severe distress, which is the opposite of the Apgar score where a high score is good.

questions.answerText:
(a)
It is a policy of giving a prophylactic uterotonic regardless of assessed risk status, with the aim of reducing the risk of PPH; it has three parts: uterotonic, cord clamping and controlled cord traction (CCT).

(b)
The uterotonic (syntometrine, syntocinon, ergometrine or prostaglandins) is given IV, IM or rarely orally, at crowning, at delivery of the anterior shoulder or before placental expulsion; oxytocin 10 IU or ergometrine 0.5 mg, larger 40 IU IV infusion doses for women at risk.

(c)
The cord is clamped in the first minute after birth regardless of pulsation in one account, and normally 30 seconds to 3 minutes after birth in another.

(d)
Place the non-dominant hand above the symphysis, palm towards the umbilicus, pushing upwards (counter-traction); the other hand firmly grasps the cord and applies traction downward and backward along the birth canal, without force or jerks; if unsuccessful, pause, check for contraction and repeat.

(e)
Cup the visible placenta and ease the membranes out with artery forceps; inspect perineum and vagina, repair, estimate blood loss, note time of placental delivery, examine placenta and membranes, then care for mother and baby and keep records.

(f)
Ensure the uterotonic has been given and had time to act, the uterus is well contracted, counter-traction is applied, signs of separation and descent are present and a strong contraction is palpable.

(g)
Release traction before counter-traction; use a gentle upward and downward movement; if the uterus relaxes, release tension until a good contraction returns.

(h)
Signs: fundus rounder, smaller, more mobile and at umbilical level, cord lengthens, small fresh blood loss.

(i)
Do not hurry, to avoid tearing the friable membranes; cup the placenta to ease tension.

(j)
CCT enhances the normal physiological delivery of the placenta, reduces blood loss, shortens the third stage and minimises the time the mother is at risk of haemorrhage.

(k)
Tension on the cord without a contraction may cause uterine inversion.

(l)
Hurrying the process may tear the membranes; a gentle movement increases the chance of delivering the placenta intact.

During a vaginal examination in labour, performed after an abdominal examination with the woman's bladder empty, the midwife notes an effaced and dilated cervix, moulding of the fetal head, an oblique sagittal suture, prominent ischial spines and a reduced sub-pubic angle.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the structure affected.
(c) State the differential considerations.
(d) Describe the midwifery reasoning and the decision to escalate or refer.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The examination assesses effacement, dilatation and consistency of the cervix, state of membranes, moulding and the slope of the sagittal suture (oblique or transverse in early labour, later anteroposterior) and fontanelles to judge position and progress of labour.
• Normally the ischial spines are blunt and the sub-pubic angle accommodates 2 examining fingers; prominent spines and a reduced angle are unfavourable.

(b)
The bony pelvis (cavity and outlet) is the structure affected: these features are associated with the android pelvis.

(c)
• Android pelvis: heart-shaped brim, straight sacrum, converging side walls, narrow sciatic notch and sub-pubic angle, prominent spines, reduced transverse diameter.
• Compared with the gynaecoid pelvis (round brim, best for childbearing), anthropoid (oval brim), platypelloid (kidney-shaped brim) and other contracted pelves.

(d)
• In an android pelvis the head often engages transversely or posteriorly, deep transverse arrest may occur, and the acute pubic arch forces the head back causing bruising or laceration of the pelvic floor and perineum.
• Adequacy of the pelvis is reassessed; contracted pelvis is confirmed by external, internal (vaginal) or x-ray pelvimetry, but external pelvimetry is inaccurate and not relied on.
• Caesarean section is needed in severe contraction; in minor degrees a trial of labour may be carried out; report and document findings and discuss them with the woman.

Distinguish between cyanotic and acyanotic congenital heart disease.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Congenital heart defects form the second largest group of malformations; about 90% have no single cause, 8% are chromosomal or genetic and 2% teratogenic.

(b)
Cyanosis, rapid breathing, poor feeding, failure to thrive, murmur, abnormal pulse, sweating and respiratory distress with grunting.

(c)
Transposition of the great arteries, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, univentricular heart and tetralogy of Fallot.

(d)
Left-to-right shunts: atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus (surgical closure if ibuprofen or indomethacin fails).

(e)
Obstructive lesions: coarctation of the aorta, pulmonary valve stenosis, aortic stenosis and hypoplastic left heart; coarctation and aortic stenosis are usually amenable to surgery.

(f)
Detection by detailed prenatal ultrasound and careful neonatal examination; the definitive investigation is echocardiography.

(g)
Cyanosis occurs when there is more than 5 g/dl of circulating deoxygenated haemoglobin, from mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood or inadequate pulmonary blood flow.

(h)
In transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left, creating two parallel circuits incompatible with life; balloon septostomy enlarges the foramen ovale and prostaglandin keeps the ductus open.

(i)
Tetralogy of Fallot combines ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, a misplaced aorta and ventricular hypertrophy; with transposition it is the commonest cyanotic condition.

(j)
Cyanotic disease has central cyanosis from mixing of blood or poor lung flow; acyanotic disease has no central cyanosis.

(k)
In a left-to-right shunt fully oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs, an inefficient arrangement for gas exchange.

(l)
Cyanotic: balloon septostomy and prostaglandin; acyanotic: surgical closure of the ductus or repair of coarctation and aortic stenosis.

questions.question: A patient develops sudden, maximally severe hemiplegia with no preceding warning symptoms, and echocardiography later reveals a cardiac thrombus. Which stroke mechanism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Embolic strokes classically present abruptly at their worst severity because a clot, often originating from the heart, suddenly occludes a cerebral vessel, matching the cardiac thrombus finding. Thrombotic and lacunar strokes typically evolve more gradually rather than presenting instantly at maximal deficit. Subarachnoid haemorrhage and vasospasm are unrelated to embolic cardiac sources.

questions.question: A client with diabetes develops sudden facial drooping on one side with no other neurological deficits. Which type of diabetic neuropathy MOST likely explains this?
options: Autonomic neuropathy of the vagus nerve
Focal mononeuropathy of the facial nerve
questions.explanation: Focal or mononeuropathy in diabetes affects a single nerve, and involvement of the facial nerve produces a presentation resembling Bell's palsy with isolated facial weakness. Symmetrical peripheral neuropathy would affect both limbs distally rather than the face alone, while autonomic and thigh-related neuropathies present with entirely different symptom patterns. Recognising the single-nerve pattern supports this specific diagnosis.

options: Bile duct epithelium; forms biliary obstructions
questions.explanation: Angiosarcoma begins from blood vessels in the liver and grows rapidly, making it an aggressive hepatic malignancy with a poor prognosis. It is rare compared to HCC and cholangiocarcinoma. The rapid growth and vascular origin of angiosarcoma distinguish its clinical behaviour from other primary liver tumours, and it often presents at an advanced, unresectable stage.
questions.question: Angiosarcoma of the liver originates from which specific cell type and is notable for which growth characteristic?
During otoscopic examination of the tympanic membrane, which finding specifically indicates the presence of acute otitis media?
questions.explanation: In acute otitis media, otoscopic examination reveals a red, bulging, and immobile tympanic membrane with loss of the normal cone of light reflex. These findings reflect the pressure of middle ear effusion or pus pushing against the tympanic membrane. Otoscopy is the primary diagnostic tool for evaluating middle ear pathology, and recognising these findings is fundamental to nursing assessment of ear disorders.
options: A grey, translucent, mobile tympanic membrane
A retracted, dull, immobile tympanic membrane
A thin, scarred tympanic membrane without perforation
A red, bulging, immobile tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex
A pearly white tympanic membrane with prominent landmarks

questions.question: A client with Cushing's Disease is being distinguished from other causes of Cushing Syndrome. Which feature is specific to this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cushing's Disease specifically refers to hypercortisolism caused by a pituitary adenoma that secretes excess adrenocorticotropic hormone, stimulating the adrenal glands. This pituitary origin distinguishes it from adrenal, ectopic, iatrogenic or alcohol-related causes of Cushing Syndrome. The term is reserved specifically for the pituitary-driven subtype.
options: A lung tumour secreting ACTH ectopically
An adrenal tumour secreting cortisol directly
A pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH

questions.question: Liver cancer in patients with chronic HBV infection develops even without cirrhosis through which unique molecular mechanism?
questions.explanation: HBV can cause hepatocellular carcinoma even without cirrhosis because the virus integrates its DNA into the host hepatocyte genome, causing genomic instability and chromosomal rearrangements that promote malignant transformation. This DNA integration mechanism is unique to HBV; HCV uses RNA and does not integrate into the host genome, requiring cirrhosis as an intermediary for HCC development.
options: HBV stimulating iron overload in hepatocytes
HBV directly suppressing tumour suppressor genes through RNA
HBV integrating DNA into host genome causing chromosomal instability

questions.explanation: Otitis externa, commonly called swimmer's ear, is inflammation or infection of the external auditory canal, often related to moisture trapped in the ear that promotes bacterial or fungal growth. The middle ear ossicles, cochlea, eustachian tube, and mastoid bone are structures associated with other conditions rather than otitis externa.
questions.question: Otitis externa, sometimes called 'swimmer's ear,' is best described as inflammation or infection of which structure?
A nurse removes excess bedding and applies cool sponging to reduce fever in an unconscious patient. What is the primary goal of these measures?
questions.explanation: Removing bedding and providing cool sponging are external cooling strategies aimed directly at reducing an elevated body temperature in an unconscious patient. These measures are not intended to increase intracranial pressure, and in fact controlling fever helps limit metabolic demand that could otherwise raise ICP. They do not directly promote diuresis, prevent pressure injuries, or improve nutrition.

A thrombotic stroke occurs due to injury of a blood vessel with local clot formation and accounts for the majority of ischemic strokes, with 30% to 50% of cases preceded by a transient ischemic attack. Embolic strokes originate from clots formed elsewhere that travel to the brain, while lacunar strokes specifically involve small penetrating arteries, and subarachnoid and intraventricular hemorrhages are hemorrhagic processes.
questions.question: A stroke caused by injury to a blood vessel with formation of a local clot, frequently preceded by a transient ischemic attack in many patients, is classified as which type?
A comminuted fracture is specifically characterised by which pattern of bone fragmentation?
options: A single break at a right angle to the long axis of bone
The fracture spirals along the length of the bone
The fracture involves only one cortex of the bone
The bone is broken into multiple fragments at the fracture site
The fracture fragments are impacted into each other
questions.explanation: A comminuted fracture involves the bone being broken into more than two fragments at the fracture site. Comminution typically results from high-energy trauma such as road traffic accidents or gunshot wounds. Comminuted fractures are more challenging to reduce and stabilise than simple two-part fractures and often require operative fixation with plates, screws, or intramedullary nails to restore alignment and allow early mobilisation.

questions.question: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by progressive degeneration of motor neurons leading to weakness and wasting of muscles, generally without affecting which other domains?
questions.explanation: ALS is characterized by weakness and wasting of muscles without sensory or cognitive changes, as it specifically affects motor neurons in the brain stem and spinal cord. While respiratory muscles are eventually involved, the disease is distinguished by sparing of sensory and cognitive domains, unlike cardiac muscle, bone density, blood pressure regulation, and skin integrity, which are not the defining unaffected systems described.

Documented complications of encephalitis include cognitive disabilities, personality changes, ongoing seizures, motor deficits, and blindness. Improved vision, enhanced memory, increased appetite alone, and hair regrowth are not listed complications and would represent improvements rather than the deficits associated with encephalitis.
questions.question: Complications of encephalitis listed in the documentation include cognitive disabilities, personality changes, ongoing seizures, motor deficits, and which additional finding?

questions.explanation: Hyperuricaemia in gout results from either impaired renal excretion of uric acid (the most common cause, accounting for 90% of cases) or increased uric acid production from excessive purine metabolism. Dietary purines from red meat, organ meats, and shellfish contribute to uric acid load. Identifying whether the patient is an underexcretor or overproducer of uric acid guides the choice of urate-lowering therapy — probenecid for underexcretors and allopurinol for overproducers.
questions.question: The primary biochemical cause of hyperuricaemia that leads to gout involves which purine metabolism disorder?
options: Decreased xanthine oxidase activity reducing uric acid production
Impaired renal uric acid excretion or increased uric acid production
Excess dietary calcium absorption increasing crystal formation
Increased urea production from protein catabolism
Decreased hepatic glycogen storage causing urate accumulation

questions.explanation: Meniere's disease is characterized by a triad of episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss that often affects lower frequencies first, believed to result from abnormal fluid accumulation (endolymphatic hydrops) within the inner ear. Complete permanent vision loss, severe joint pain, chronic cough, and skin rash are not part of this classic triad.
questions.question: Meniere's disease is characterized by a triad of symptoms including episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and which additional finding?
options: Complete and permanent loss of vision
Fluctuating hearing loss affecting low frequencies first
It highlights blood flow and leakage within retinal vessels
It dilates the pupil for better visualisation
It treats existing retinal haemorrhage directly
It numbs the retina to prevent discomfort
It measures intraocular pressure during the scan
questions.explanation: Fluorescein dye is injected into a vein and travels to the retinal vessels, where it highlights blood flow patterns and any abnormal leakage under specialised photography. It does not numb the retina, dilate the pupil, treat haemorrhage, or measure pressure, which are separate procedures. This imaging helps identify areas requiring laser treatment.
questions.question: During fluorescein angiography, a client asks why dye is injected before retinal photographs are taken. Which nursing explanation is MOST accurate?

questions.explanation: Deep brain stimulation involves surgical implantation of an electrode into either the globus pallidus or subthalamic nucleus, where stimulation may increase dopamine release or block anticholinergic activity, improving tremor and rigidity. The cerebellum, medulla, corpus callosum, occipital cortex, and spinal cord are not the target structures for this procedure.
questions.question: Deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease involves surgical implantation of an electrode into which target areas?
The characteristic joint distribution of rheumatoid arthritis in the hands specifically involves which joints while typically sparing which other joints?
options: Involves PIPs and MCPs; spares DIPs
Involves DIPs; spares PIPs and MCPs
Involves DIPs and MCPs; spares PIPs
Involves only wrists; spares hand joints
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically involves the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of the hands while typically sparing the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. This distribution distinguishes RA from osteoarthritis, which involves the DIP and PIP joints (Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes). Symmetrical involvement of the same joints on both hands is a hallmark feature that helps confirm the RA diagnosis.

questions.question: A patient with chronic otitis media who develops new-onset facial nerve palsy should be immediately assessed for which serious complication?
options: Acute labyrinthitis from inner ear involvement
Cholesteatoma with erosion into the facial nerve canal
questions.explanation: Facial nerve palsy in a patient with chronic otitis media is a serious complication suggesting cholesteatoma (an abnormal collection of keratinising squamous epithelium) eroding into the facial nerve canal within the temporal bone. Cholesteatoma is an aggressive lesion that erodes bone and can cause facial palsy, labyrinthitis, meningitis, or brain abscess. Immediate surgical assessment and temporal bone CT imaging are required when this complication is suspected.

questions.question: A stroke patient experiences loss of the same visual field in each eye, causing them to ignore one side of a dinner tray. This finding is termed:
questions.explanation: Homonymous hemianopsia is a loss of the same visual field in both eyes, which can cause a patient to ignore one side of objects such as a dinner tray or neglect one side of the body. Diplopia is double vision, nystagmus is rhythmic involuntary eye movement, ptosis is eyelid drooping, and anisocoria refers to unequal pupil size, none of which describe this homonymous field loss.

Cerebral autoregulation protects the brain from changes in mean systemic arterial blood pressure within a range of approximately 50 to 150 mmHg by adjusting cerebral vessel diameter to keep blood flow constant. Pressures outside this range, whether too low or too high, overwhelm autoregulatory capacity, so the other ranges do not describe the protected zone.
questions.question: Cerebral autoregulation maintains constant cerebral blood flow despite changes in mean systemic arterial pressure within approximately which range?
Of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves, how many are classified as purely sensory in function?
questions.explanation: Three cranial nerves are entirely sensory: the olfactory (I), optic (II), and acoustic/vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves. Five cranial nerves are purely motor (III, IV, VI, XI, XII), and four are mixed sensory and motor (V, VII, IX, X), so neither five, six, nor all twelve is correct.
