Washing the face twice daily with cleansing soap is also recommended for mild acne management.
questions.question: For mild acne management, nutritional advice given to patients includes the elimination of which types of foods when associated with acne flare-ups?
options: Red meat and spicy foods only
Chocolate, cola, fried foods, or milk products

questions.question: Which laboratory result specifically reflects acute metabolic decompensation when reviewing a patient admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: Ketones in the urine (ketonuria) are a key indicator of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), reflecting the metabolic shift to fat catabolism when insulin is severely deficient. Urinalysis for ketones also screens for poor glycaemic control or missed insulin doses during annual review. Ketonuria warrants urgent clinical reassessment and may require hospital admission for management of acute diabetic decompensation.
options: Presence of ketones in the urine

questions.explanation: As soon as consciousness is regained, a bladder-training program is initiated for the previously unconscious patient, alongside frequent skin monitoring for irritation and breakdown. Bladder training cannot occur before unconsciousness develops, is not delayed until after discharge, is not assumed to require permanent catheterization, and is a standard nursing intervention rather than something initiated only upon patient request.
questions.question: Bladder training programs for a previously unconscious patient are initiated at which point in the recovery process?
options: Only after discharge from the hospital
Only if the patient requests it
As soon as consciousness is regained

questions.explanation: The dorsal (posterior) columns carry proprioception, vibration and fine touch, so their damage selectively impairs joint position sense while pain fibres remain intact. The spinothalamic tracts instead carry pain and temperature, which this patient still perceives. The corticospinal and spinocerebellar tracts govern motor output and coordination, not conscious proprioception.
questions.question: During assessment, a patient can feel pinprick sensation but cannot identify joint position with eyes closed. Which pathway is most likely impaired?

questions.explanation: Fat embolism syndrome most commonly follows fractures of the long bones (particularly the femur and tibia) and pelvic fractures, where fat globules released from bone marrow enter the venous circulation and lodge in the pulmonary vasculature and microvasculature of other organs. Clinical features include the classic triad of respiratory distress, neurological dysfunction, and petechial rash. FES typically develops 24 to 72 hours post-fracture and requires supportive intensive care management.
options: Long bones such as the femur and tibia, and pelvic fractures
questions.question: Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a serious complication that most commonly follows fractures of which bones?

questions.explanation: The middle ear, also known as the tympanic cavity, is an air-filled chamber located within the temporal bone of the skull. It lies between the external ear and the inner ear and plays a vital role in sound conduction. The temporal bone's structure protects the delicate middle ear ossicles and houses both the middle ear and inner ear, making it central to auditory and vestibular function.
questions.question: The middle ear, also known by which anatomical name, is located within which bone of the skull?

questions.explanation: The International League Against Epilepsy generally defines epilepsy as at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart, or one seizure with a high risk of recurrence. Stating exactly one is always sufficient overstates the general rule. Requiring five or ten seizures, or only continuous seizure activity, considerably overstates the diagnostic threshold used in practice.
questions.question: A patient asks how many unprovoked seizures are needed before a diagnosis of epilepsy is confirmed under current classification. What should the nurse answer?

questions.explanation: Because corticospinal fibres decussate as they descend to the spinal cord, damage to the right cerebral hemisphere produces weakness on the opposite, left side of the body. Right-sided weakness would instead be expected with a left hemisphere lesion. Bilateral or absent involvement does not fit a typical unilateral hemispheric stroke.
questions.question: A stroke affects the right cerebral hemisphere. Which side of the body would the nurse expect to show weakness, given that nerve fibres cross over?
A client who had a vitrectomy with gas bubble insertion is being discharged. Which specific instruction is MOST important for the nurse to include?
questions.explanation: Gas bubbles inserted during vitrectomy expand at altitude, so clients must avoid air travel until the bubble has fully resorbed to prevent a dangerous rise in intraocular pressure. Reading, sleep position restrictions, caffeine intake and permanent avoidance of corrective lenses are not the critical safety concerns here. This instruction directly prevents a serious ocular complication during air travel.
options: Avoid lying flat while sleeping only
Avoid air travel until the gas bubble fully resolves
Avoid caffeine intake for six weeks

questions.explanation: Excessive dilute urine output with rising serum sodium after intracranial surgery suggests diabetes insipidus, caused by insufficient antidiuretic hormone secretion or action. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH would instead cause fluid retention and low serum sodium, the opposite pattern. Acute kidney injury and adrenal insufficiency, as well as hyperaldosteronism, do not typically present with this specific combination of dilute polyuria and hypernatraemia.
questions.question: A patient recovering from intracranial surgery develops excessive dilute urine output along with rising serum sodium. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

questions.explanation: Malunion is defined as fracture healing that occurs with the fragments in an unsatisfactory anatomical position, resulting in deformity, limb shortening, or rotational malalignment. It occurs when inadequate reduction was achieved or when displacement recurred after immobilisation. Malunion can cause functional impairment, abnormal gait, and secondary osteoarthritis of adjacent joints. Corrective osteotomy may be required in symptomatic cases.
questions.question: Malunion as a complication of fracture healing is defined as which specific outcome?
options: Failure of fracture fragments to unite at all
Fracture healing with fragments in an unsatisfactory position causing deformity
Delayed fracture union beyond the expected time frame
Infection of the fracture site causing osteomyelitis
Avascular necrosis of a fracture fragment

questions.explanation: Clear fluid drainage at a craniotomy site raises concern for cerebrospinal fluid leakage, which increases the risk of ascending infection such as meningitis and requires prompt reporting. This finding is not a normal or expected part of wound healing. It does not reflect hydration status, cerebral perfusion, or resolution of oedema.
questions.question: A nurse observes leakage of clear fluid at a craniotomy site. Why is this finding significant?
options: Indicates possible CSF leak and infection risk

questions.explanation: Mastoiditis occurs when infection from the middle ear spreads to the mastoid air cells within the temporal bone, typically as a complication of inadequately treated acute otitis media. Clinical features include post-auricular swelling, tenderness, erythema, and protrusion of the ear (pinna) anteriorly. Mastoiditis requires prompt intravenous antibiotic therapy and may necessitate surgical drainage (mastoidectomy) to prevent intracranial complications.
questions.question: Mastoiditis as a complication of otitis media occurs when infection spreads to which adjacent anatomical structure?
options: The mastoid air cells within the temporal bone
The parotid gland adjacent to the ear

questions.question: Peripheral neuropathy in diabetes most commonly affects which body regions in a characteristic distribution?
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuropathy affects the outer peripheral parts of the body, most commonly the feet, legs, hands, and arms in a 'glove and stocking' distribution. In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, chronic hyperglycaemia damages peripheral nerve fibres, initially causing tingling or numbness and progressing to pain or complete loss of sensation. Early detection through monofilament testing is critical for preventing diabetic foot complications.

options: Oxidation of sulfhydryl groups in synovial proteins
questions.explanation: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are directed against proteins that have undergone citrullination — the post-translational modification of arginine residues to citrulline by the enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD). Citrullinated proteins accumulate in the inflamed rheumatoid synovium and trigger the autoimmune response. Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for RA (approximately 95% specificity) and are associated with more severe, erosive joint disease.
questions.question: Anti-CCP antibodies in rheumatoid arthritis are directed against proteins that have undergone which specific post-translational modification?

questions.explanation: Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid at a surgical site increases the danger of meningitis, since it creates a pathway for organisms to enter the subarachnoid space, making vigilant monitoring for CSF leakage an important nursing responsibility after intracranial surgery. Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, cataract formation, and gastrointestinal bleeding are not the complications specifically associated with CSF leakage.
questions.question: Watching for leakage of cerebrospinal fluid at a craniotomy site is important because CSF leakage increases the danger of which complication?
Avulsion fractures occur through which specific mechanism involving soft tissue attachment sites on bone?
options: Direct impact causing cortical bone shattering at the site
Repetitive microtrauma causing fatigue failure of cortical bone
Pathological bone weakening allowing fracture without trauma
Compressive loading exceeding trabecular bone strength
Sudden muscle contraction pulling a bone fragment from its attachment
questions.explanation: Avulsion fractures occur when a sudden, forceful muscle contraction or ligament strain pulls a fragment of bone away from its insertion or origin site. Common examples include avulsion of the tibial tubercle (patellar tendon), the base of the fifth metatarsal (peroneus brevis tendon), and the anterior superior iliac spine (sartorius). They are particularly common in adolescent athletes whose growth plate apophyses are more vulnerable than in adults where soft tissue tears occur instead.

questions.question: Which endocrine gland is referred to as the 'master gland' due to its influence over multiple other endocrine glands?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland is found at the base of the brain behind the sinuses and is called the 'master gland' because it influences many other glands, especially the thyroid. It controls bone growth, a woman's menstrual cycles, and breast milk release. Dysfunction of the pituitary can have widespread effects across multiple organ systems.

options: Meticulous wound care, nutritional optimisation, and infection prevention
Applying tight wound dressings to compress the surgical site
Early removal of surgical sutures within 48 hours
Immobilising the patient completely in bed post-surgery
Applying antibiotic ointment without covering the wound
questions.explanation: Wound dehiscence (breakdown of the surgical wound) is prevented by meticulous wound care including keeping the wound clean and dry, monitoring for signs of infection, optimising nutritional status (adequate protein, vitamin C, and zinc for wound healing), and controlling blood glucose in diabetic patients. Sutures or staples should be maintained until the wound is fully healed. Smoking cessation is also important as nicotine impairs wound healing through vasoconstriction and reduced collagen synthesis.
questions.question: Wound dehiscence as a complication of surgical fracture fixation is best prevented by which nursing intervention?

options: Oxidation of melanin and lipids at the open follicle
Blood infiltrating the follicle from inflammation
Excess iron deposited in the keratin plug
questions.explanation: Open comedones appear black because the follicular opening is exposed to air, causing oxidation of the melanin and lipid contents of the plug, giving it a characteristic dark colour. This is not due to dirt or bacterial pigment. In contrast, closed comedones (whiteheads) remain white because the follicle opening is sealed, preventing oxidation. Clarifying this distinction is important when educating patients about acne pathophysiology.
questions.question: Open comedones (blackheads) are black in colour due to which specific factor?

questions.explanation: When properly prescribed and taken, anticonvulsant medications control seizures in roughly 70 to 80 percent of patients, reflecting generally favourable but not universal treatment success. Lower percentages such as 10, 30 or 50 percent understate typical medication effectiveness. Stating nearly 100 percent always would overstate the certainty of complete seizure control for every patient.
questions.question: A patient asks what proportion of people with epilepsy achieve seizure control with properly prescribed and taken anticonvulsant medication. What is the best response?

questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a classic example of focal mononeuropathy affecting the median nerve at the wrist. It causes tingling, numbness, and pain in the hand and fingers. In diabetics, nerve susceptibility is increased by chronic hyperglycaemia, making carpal tunnel syndrome more prevalent and potentially more severe than in the general population.
questions.question: Focal or mononeuropathy in diabetes affects only a single nerve. Which common example of this type affects the median nerve at the wrist?

questions.explanation: Nonmodifiable stroke risk factors include characteristics that cannot be changed, such as increasing age, sex, and family or genetic history. Hypertension, smoking, obesity, inactivity, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, alcohol use and diet are all modifiable factors that can be addressed through lifestyle and medical intervention. Distinguishing the two categories helps guide prevention counselling.
questions.question: A nurse reviews a patient's history for nonmodifiable stroke risk factors. Which combination best fits this category?

questions.explanation: Beta-blocker eye drops such as timolol lower intraocular pressure primarily by decreasing the production of aqueous humor by the ciliary body, in contrast to miotic agents, which primarily increase outflow. These drops do not primarily increase outflow, dilate the pupil, increase corneal thickness, or stimulate tear production.
options: Decreasing the production of aqueous humor
questions.question: A patient with glaucoma is taught that beta-blocker eye drops such as timolol lower intraocular pressure primarily by which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Autonomic neuropathy results from damage to nerves controlling involuntary functions such as blood pressure regulation, bladder emptying and bowel motility, explaining this combination of symptoms. Peripheral sensory neuropathy would instead present with numbness or pain, while focal and mononeuritis patterns affect single or scattered nerves rather than systemic autonomic control. Diabetic amyotrophy primarily causes proximal leg weakness, not autonomic symptoms.
questions.question: A client with diabetes reports postural dizziness, bladder dysfunction, and erratic bowel habits. Which type of nerve damage explains this combination?

questions.explanation: Children's fractures can involve the physis (growth plate) — the cartilaginous zone of endochondral bone growth at the ends of long bones. These physeal injuries are classified by the Salter-Harris system (Types I to V) based on the fracture line's relationship to the growth plate, epiphysis, and metaphysis. Physeal injuries carry the risk of premature growth plate closure and limb length discrepancy or angular deformity if the germinal cells of the physis are damaged.
options: Cortical fracture through dense adult periosteum
Comminuted fracture from brittle bone disease
Stress fracture from repetitive loading in sports
Avulsion fracture from ligament insertion sites
questions.question: Which type of fracture in children differs from adult fractures by involving damage to which growth structure unique to the immature skeleton?

questions.explanation: The purpose of a Thomas splint in managing femoral shaft fractures is to achieve longitudinal traction and stabilisation of the fracture, reducing pain and preventing further soft tissue injury before definitive treatment. A cervical collar stabilises the neck, while a figure-of-eight bandage and sling and swathe are used for clavicle and shoulder injuries. A volar splint is used for wrist and hand injuries, none of which suit femoral shaft stabilisation.
questions.question: A client with a femoral shaft fracture is placed in a specific splint designed to provide longitudinal traction and support before surgical fixation. Which device does the nurse expect?
A client with chronic hepatitis B infection develops liver cancer even though liver biopsy shows no cirrhosis. Which mechanism BEST explains this finding?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus can integrate directly into hepatocyte DNA, causing genetic mutations that lead to cancer development independent of cirrhosis, unlike hepatitis C which typically requires cirrhotic change first. This direct oncogenic mechanism explains liver cancer occurring without cirrhosis in hepatitis B carriers. Alcohol metabolism, iron overload and autoimmune destruction are separate, unrelated mechanisms.
options: Alcohol metabolism directly causes the mutation
Direct viral integration into hepatocyte DNA
Iron overload from the virus alone
Cirrhosis is always present but undetected

questions.question: A client's previous history of corticosteroid use is most critically relevant to suspecting which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: A history of long-term corticosteroid use is directly relevant to exogenous Cushing Syndrome, the most common cause overall. Glucocorticoids like prednisone mimic cortisol and cause all features of hypercortisolism. Identifying this medication history during endocrine assessment enables the nurse to correlate symptoms like moon face, weight gain, and hypertension with iatrogenic hypercortisolism.

questions.question: A child with untreated otitis media develops fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status. What complication should the nurse suspect?
questions.explanation: Infection can spread contiguously from the middle ear to the meninges, so otitis media complicated by fever, neck stiffness and altered mentation raises strong suspicion for secondary meningitis. A simple febrile seizure would not typically present with neck stiffness and altered mentation together. Gastroenteritis, cardiac arrhythmia and appendicitis do not explain this specific combination of findings.

Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common type of primary liver cancer and originates specifically from hepatocytes, the main functional liver cells. Cholangiocarcinoma instead arises from bile duct lining cells, while angiosarcoma arises from blood vessel cells. Metastatic liver cancer originates from a distant primary site rather than the liver itself.
questions.question: A client's liver biopsy reveals a tumour originating from hepatocytes rather than bile duct cells. Which type of primary liver cancer does this represent?

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) are antihypertensive medications used in diabetic patients that specifically help ameliorate cardiovascular risk and protect kidney function by reducing intraglomerular pressure. They are particularly beneficial in patients with diabetic nephropathy. Their use is reviewed alongside other cardiovascular medications such as diuretics, beta-blockers, and aspirin during the annual diabetes review.
questions.question: Which antihypertensive medication class specifically listed in the diabetes medication review also protects kidney function in diabetic patients?

questions.explanation: Following liver resection, reduced hepatic glycogen storage and glucose synthesis capacity increases the risk of hypoglycaemia, making constant dextrose infusion necessary in the immediate postoperative period. This is not intended to replace blood volume, prevent infection, reduce embolism risk, or specifically maintain sodium levels. Close glucose monitoring remains essential during this recovery phase.
options: It prevents hypoglycaemia from reduced hepatic glucose reserves
It maintains normal serum sodium levels
It reduces the risk of pulmonary embolism
It replaces lost blood volume directly
questions.question: A client recovering from liver cancer surgery requires a constant infusion of dextrose solution in the first two days postoperatively. Which nursing rationale BEST explains this order?

options: Corneal injury from incomplete eyelid closure
questions.question: A patient with Bell's palsy is taught to use an eye patch or tape the eyelid shut at night primarily to prevent which complication?
questions.explanation: Because Bell's palsy causes flaccidity of the affected side of the face and inability to close the eyelid, good eye care including patching or taping the eye shut at night is essential to prevent corneal injury from dryness or exposure. It is not aimed at preventing hearing loss, facial cellulitis, increased intracranial pressure, or tinnitus.

questions.question: A patient presenting with sudden severe symptoms following an embolic stroke would most likely have which clinical course compared to a thrombotic stroke?
questions.explanation: Patients with embolic stroke typically experience a rapid occurrence of severe clinical symptoms because the embolus suddenly occludes a vessel without prior collateral development. Thrombotic strokes, by contrast, may evolve gradually and are often preceded by TIAs over time. Complete resolution within minutes describes a TIA rather than an embolic stroke, and absence of deficit would be atypical.
options: Slow progression with warning TIAs over months
Rapid occurrence of severe clinical symptoms
Symptoms that resolve completely within minutes
Prevent pressure ulcers on the scalp
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with increased intracranial pressure avoids excessive neck flexion and rotation. What is the primary rationale for this precaution?
questions.explanation: Excessive neck flexion or rotation can compress the jugular veins and obstruct venous outflow from the brain, further raising intracranial pressure, so this position is avoided. While airway concerns exist separately, the primary reason in this context relates to venous drainage. Skin breakdown, scalp pressure ulcers and comfort are not the main clinical rationale behind this specific precaution.

Meniere's disease presents with a classic triad of episodic vertigo (lasting 20 minutes to several hours), tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, often accompanied by a sensation of aural fullness. It is caused by endolymphatic hydrops — an increase in endolymph volume within the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear. Management includes dietary sodium restriction, diuretics, vestibular suppressants, and in refractory cases, endolymphatic sac decompression or gentamicin ablation.
options: Conductive hearing loss, fever, and ear discharge
Chronic otorrhoea, otalgia, and aural fullness
Progressive deafness, headache, and facial numbness
Episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss
questions.question: Meniere's disease is a condition of the inner ear characterised by a classic triad of which three symptoms?

questions.explanation: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease is believed to happen because of problems with how the body uses a protein called alpha-synuclein; when this protein misfolds, it accumulates in clumps known as Lewy bodies, causing toxic effects and cell damage. Beta-amyloid and tau are associated with Alzheimer's disease, huntingtin relates to Huntington's disease, and acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme rather than a misfolded protein causing Lewy bodies.
questions.question: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease is believed to result from problems with protein folding involving which specific protein, which accumulates in toxic clumps called Lewy bodies?

options: Fluid accumulation under the retina from infection
Elevated intraocular pressure compressing the retina
Direct vitreous haemorrhage into the retinal layers
Scar tissue from abnormal vessels pulling the retina away
questions.question: Retinal detachment as a complication of diabetic retinopathy occurs through which pathological mechanism?
questions.explanation: Retinal detachment in diabetic retinopathy occurs when abnormal blood vessels stimulate the growth of scar tissue, which then pulls the retina away from the back of the eye. This tractional mechanism causes visual symptoms including floaters, flashes of light, and potentially severe vision loss. It differs from rhegmatogenous detachment, which is caused by retinal tears rather than traction.

questions.question: A tympanostomy tube (ear tube) is surgically placed in the tympanic membrane primarily to manage which condition in children with recurrent infections?
questions.explanation: Tympanostomy tubes are surgically placed through the tympanic membrane to allow drainage and ventilation of the middle ear, primarily to manage recurrent or chronic otitis media with effusion in children prone to repeated ear infections. Glaucoma, cataracts, retinal detachment, and macular degeneration are eye conditions unrelated to this ear-specific procedure.

Nuchal rigidity refers specifically to stiffness and resistance of the neck on flexion caused by meningeal inflammation. Cogwheel rigidity is a Parkinsonian finding in the limbs, not the neck. Decorticate posturing and opisthotonos describe abnormal whole-body positioning, and trismus refers to jaw muscle spasm seen in tetanus.
questions.question: A patient with meningitis resists passive neck flexion, and the nurse notes stiffness on attempted movement. Which term describes this finding?
A client reports knee pain that worsens throughout the day with activity and improves with rest. Which condition does this pattern MOST strongly suggest?
questions.explanation: The characteristic symptom pattern of osteoarthritis involves pain that worsens with activity throughout the day and improves with rest, distinguishing it from inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis where stiffness is typically worse in the morning. Reactive arthritis, gout and septic arthritis present with more acute, inflammatory patterns rather than this activity-related mechanical pain. This distinction supports differentiating degenerative from inflammatory joint disease.

questions.question: The testes function as part of the endocrine system by producing which substances essential to male physiology?
questions.explanation: The testes are the male reproductive glands that produce both sperm and sex hormones, primarily testosterone. As endocrine organs, they respond to luteinizing hormone (LH) from the pituitary to regulate testosterone secretion. Testosterone is essential for male secondary sexual characteristics, libido, muscle mass, and bone density maintenance.

questions.question: The parathyroid glands, described as four tiny glands in the neck, primarily contribute to which physiological process?
questions.explanation: The parathyroid glands are four tiny glands in the neck that play a role in bone development through the regulation of calcium and phosphorus metabolism. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) acts on bone, kidneys, and the intestines to maintain serum calcium levels. Dysfunction leads to disorders such as hyperparathyroidism or hypoparathyroidism affecting skeletal integrity.

questions.question: Gout is classified as a crystal-induced arthropathy caused by deposition of which specific crystal within joints and soft tissues?
questions.explanation: Gout is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals within joints, bursae, and soft tissues, resulting from elevated serum uric acid levels (hyperuricaemia). When uric acid levels exceed the saturation threshold, crystals precipitate and trigger an intense acute inflammatory response. Understanding the crystal aetiology of gout is fundamental to selecting appropriate treatment targeting both acute inflammation and long-term urate-lowering therapy.

Dragging a patient across the bed surface creates shear and friction forces that can damage the skin and underlying tissue, so proper lifting techniques are used to prevent this injury. This action is not primarily linked to cardiac arrhythmia, aspiration pneumonia, or electrolyte imbalance. While excessive exertion could theoretically affect ICP, the main concern with dragging technique is skin integrity.
questions.question: A nurse avoids dragging an unconscious patient up in bed and instead uses a proper lifting technique. What is the primary risk being avoided?

options: Only sensory function, with motor function preserved
Reflex activity, motor function, and sensation, often with hypotension and bradycardia
Permanent and irreversible loss of all function
questions.question: Spinal shock following acute spinal cord injury is characterized by temporary loss of which functions below the level of injury?
questions.explanation: Spinal shock is a temporary loss of reflex activity, motor function, and sensation below the level of spinal cord injury, often accompanied by hypotension and bradycardia due to loss of sympathetic tone, and typically resolves within days to weeks. It does not spare motor function while affecting sensation alone, is not limited only to bowel and bladder function, is not permanent by definition, and does not present with increased reflexes immediately during the acute phase.

questions.question: A client with liver cancer develops prolonged bleeding after a minor procedure and abnormal clotting studies. Which liver function deficit BEST explains this finding?
questions.explanation: The liver synthesises most clotting factors, and impaired hepatic function from cancer or associated cirrhosis reduces this synthesis, leading to prolonged bleeding and abnormal clotting studies postoperatively. Reduced bile salt production, ammonia detoxification, albumin synthesis and glucose storage cause different clinical problems such as malabsorption, encephalopathy, oedema or hypoglycaemia rather than coagulopathy. This distinction directs the nurse toward monitoring clotting parameters specifically.

questions.question: Which nursing priority is most critical in the immediate management of a patient admitted with a suspected hip fracture?
questions.explanation: In the immediate management of a patient with a suspected hip fracture, nursing priorities include thorough pain assessment and providing adequate analgesia (including nerve blocks such as fascia iliaca block), pressure area care to prevent sacral and heel pressure ulcers in the immobile patient, fluid management to correct dehydration, nutritional assessment, and prevention of complications including DVT, chest infection, and urinary retention. Optimising the patient's condition for surgery is the overarching nursing goal.
options: Preparing the patient for immediate weight-bearing mobilisation
Ordering plain X-rays before any nursing intervention
Applying traction to the fractured limb
Pain assessment and management, pressure area care, and fluid management
Commencing antibiotics immediately for fracture prophylaxis

questions.question: A patient taking phenytoin also uses oral contraceptives for birth control. What should the nurse advise regarding contraceptive effectiveness?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives through hepatic enzyme induction, so patients should be advised to use an additional barrier method to prevent unintended pregnancy. Assuming no additional precautions are needed risks contraceptive failure. Doubling the contraceptive dose or switching phenytoin's route are not recommended or evidence-based solutions to this interaction, and stopping a needed anticonvulsant is not advised without medical guidance.

questions.question: A patient with trigeminal neuralgia reports that pain is triggered by chewing, brushing teeth, or a cold blast of air on the face, but is relieved during which activity?
questions.explanation: Sleep provides a period of relief from the pain of trigeminal neuralgia, while triggers include chewing, brushing teeth, and exposure to hot or cold air on the face. Eating spicy foods, talking loudly, bright light exposure, and vigorous exercise are not described as relieving factors for this condition.

questions.question: Cushing Syndrome is defined as a clinical condition arising from chronic hypercortisolism. Which cause accounts for approximately 70% of endogenous cases?
questions.explanation: Cushing's Disease, caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, accounts for approximately 70% of endogenous Cushing Syndrome cases. The adenoma stimulates the adrenal glands to produce excess cortisol, leading to hypercortisolism. It predominantly affects women between 20 and 40 years of age and requires pituitary-directed treatment.

courses.title: Medical Surgical Nursing II

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Atherosclerosis affects the intima of large and medium arteries through accumulation of lipids, calcium, blood components, carbohydrates and fibrous tissue (atheromas or plaques); arteriosclerosis is hardening of the arteries.
• Lesions are fatty streaks (yellow, smooth, usually symptom-free) and fibrous plaque (white to yellow, may completely obstruct the lumen); sites at bifurcations are more vulnerable.

(b)
• Non-modifiable risk factors: age and gender; modifiable: nicotine, diet, hypertension, diabetes, stress, sedentary lifestyle.
• Manifestations: chest or limb pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, palpitations, fatigue, weakness and myalgia.

(c)
• Direct results: stenosis, thrombosis obstruction, aneurysm, ulceration and rupture; indirect results: malnutrition and fibrosis of the organs supplied (ischaemic necrosis replaced by fibrous tissue).
• Peripheral arterial disease (narrowing or blockage of arteries to the extremities, more common in legs) begins with intermittent claudication.

(d)
• Distant effects: pain in the chest if coronary arteries are involved or in the legs if peripheral arteries are involved; PAD features include burning foot pain at night, cool skin, colour changes, infections and non-healing foot sores.
• Diagnosis of PAD: ankle-brachial index, ultrasound, CT angiography, duplex and angiography.
• Management: risk factor modification, controlled exercise, medication (statins, aspirin, nitrates, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, ranolazine; cilostazol and pentoxifylline for PAD), and angioplasty, stents or grafts.
• Nursing diagnoses: ineffective peripheral tissue perfusion, chronic pain, risk for impaired skin integrity and deficient knowledge on self-care.
• Health education: regular exercise, diet and lifestyle changes.
questions.question:
Discuss atherosclerosis and peripheral arterial disease.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and morphological types of the lesions.
(b) State the risk factors and manifestations.
(c) State how the lesions relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how the disease may affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management and health education.

Discuss metabolic syndrome.
(a) Define the condition and state its causes and risk factors.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology.
(c) State the clinical manifestations, diagnosis and management.
(d) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Distinguish between metabolic syndrome and obesity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A cluster of risk factors specific for cardiovascular disease, also called syndrome X, the insulin resistance syndrome and the deadly quartet; it results mainly from obesity and insulin resistance.
• Risk factors: age, obesity, insulin resistance, genetics and history, gender and race, sedentary lifestyle, diet, drug use and other diseases.

(b)
The WHO emphasises the central role of insulin resistance (diabetes, impaired fasting glucose or fasting glucose above 110 mg/dL) plus two of: BP above 140/90, triglycerides above 150 mg/dL, low HDL, obesity or raised waist-hip ratio, raised urinary albumin.

(c)
• Features: atherogenic dyslipidaemia, raised BP and raised plasma glucose; diagnosed with at least 3 of 5: fasting glucose 100 mg/dL or more, BP 130/85 or more, triglycerides 150 or more, low HDL (below 40 men, below 50 women), waist 102 cm men or 88 cm women.
• Management: lifestyle change and weight loss first (no smoking, activity, less atherogenic diet); drugs for BP (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, beta-blockers), lipids (statins, niacin), sugar (thiazolidinediones), weight-loss drugs and surgery.
• Nursing: recognise eating habits to change, report BP above 160 mmHg and give antihypertensives, dietitian advice, examine activity and hyperglycaemia symptoms, monitor weight and avoid crash diets.

(d)
• Susceptibility factors are those above (age, obesity, insulin resistance, genetics, sedentary lifestyle).
• Complications: type 2 diabetes, heart and blood vessel disease (heart attack, stroke).

(e)
• Obesity is abnormal or excessive fat accumulation presenting a health risk (BMI of 30 or more) and is the main contributor to metabolic syndrome.
• Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of conditions (increased BP, high blood sugar, central obesity, abnormal cholesterol or triglycerides) that together raise the risk of heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes.
• Prevention: exercise, weight loss, quitting smoking and regular check-ups.

questions.question:
A man who fell from a height has pain, tenderness, swelling and bruising, deformity, shortening of the limb, loss of function, abnormal mobility and crepitus. X-ray confirms a break in the continuity of the bone, and open reduction with internal fixation is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and the diagnostic procedure used.
(b) Describe the treatment principles used in fracture management.
(c) State the complications to monitor for.
(d) Outline patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Fracture: a break in the continuity of a bone (closed/simple or open/compound); caused by direct or indirect violence, muscular violence or pathological causes; diagnosed by history, physical appraisal and bone X-ray (also CT or MRI).

(b)
• Treatment principles: reduction, immobilisation and restoration of full function; reduction may be closed (manipulation or traction) or open (operation); internal fixation uses plates, nails and screws of vitallium or titanium.
• Traction (ropes, pulleys, weights) regains length and alignment, immobilises the fracture, lessens muscle spasm and reduces pain; POP/cast holds the bone in reduction.

(c)
Complications: surgical shock, fat embolism, injuries to blood vessels, hypovolaemic shock from severe bleeding, malunion, non-union, delayed union and hypostatic pneumonia.

(d)
Rehabilitation: exercise by the patient, physiotherapy and full restoration of the part to normal function; bone healing passes through haematoma (within 24 hours), callus (6-10 days) and remodelling stages, and depends on age and type of bone.

(a)
Pulmonary oedema: abnormal accumulation of fluid in the extravascular compartment of the lung (respiratory system); cardiogenic causes include hypertension, left ventricular failure and cardiomyopathy.

(b)
Fluid moves into the interstitium and alveolar walls, damages the alveolar epithelium and impairs effective respiration (gas exchange, oxygenation); right ventricular failure may show hepatomegaly, jugular vein distension and peripheral oedema.

(c)
Differentials: pleurisy, empyema, acute pulmonary failure and ARDS; non-cardiogenic and neurogenic causes of pulmonary oedema.

(d)
• Assessment: history, physical examination, vital signs every 15-30 minutes, pulse oximetry, ABG, chest X-ray; pulmonary artery catheterisation if causes are uncertain or oedema is refractory.
• Diagnosis/planning: priorities are correcting hypoxaemia, reducing preload and afterload and supporting perfusion.
• Implementation: oxygen or mechanical ventilation, upright position, furosemide, vasodilators, captopril, inotropes; help the patient relax; record time and dose of morphine; watch for electrolyte depletion; explain procedures.
• Evaluation/education: urge compliance with medication and emphasise early reporting of signs of fluid overload.
questions.question:
A patient has dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety and thin frothy sputum, with rhonchi and crackles on auscultation. Pulse oximetry is below 85%, arterial PaO2 is 30-50 mmHg and the chest X-ray shows an area of 'white out'. The patient also has a history of left ventricular failure.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Name the differential conditions.
(d) Using the nursing process, explain the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy): a disorder of malabsorption caused by an autoimmune response to gluten (gliadin in wheat, rye and barley); digestive system, small intestine.

(b)
• Gliadin presented to helper T cells triggers an immunologically mediated inflammatory response; villi are lost and crypts lengthen, destroying the absorptive surface and causing maldigestion and malabsorption.
• Functions affected beyond the gut: fatigue, anaemia, osteopenia, hypothyroidism, migraine, seizures, paraesthesia, depression and dermatitis herpetiformis.

(c)
If the patient fails to respond to corticosteroids, comorbid conditions such as lymphomas of the small intestine must be ruled out; complications include increased malignancy (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, adenocarcinomas).

(d)
• Assessment: family history, risk factors, symptoms, serology and biopsy; the patient must keep eating gluten during testing or serology may be falsely negative.
• Planning/implementation: a lifelong gluten-free diet is the primary management (full recovery of villi takes a year); teach reading labels on food and non-food items (drugs, toothpaste, lipstick); corticosteroids if refractory; folate, cobalamin or iron for anaemia; osteoporosis treatment for osteopenia.
• Evaluation: persistent or recurrent symptoms occur in up to 20%.
questions.question:
An adult presents with diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, abdominal pain and distension, flatulence and weight loss, together with fatigue, anaemia, osteopenia and an itchy vesicular rash on the elbows and knees. A serologic test (IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase) is positive and endoscopic biopsy shows absence of intestinal villi.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Name the related or differential conditions to exclude.
(d) Using the nursing process, explain the nursing assessment, planning and evaluation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• It allows direct visualisation of the oesophageal, gastric and duodenal mucosa through a lighted flexible fibreoptic scope (gastroscope).
• Indications: diagnose oesophageal, gastric or duodenal abnormalities or inflammatory, neoplastic or infectious processes; evaluate oesophageal and gastric motility; collect secretions and tissue specimens.
• Preparation: no food or drink for 6 to 12 hours before; spray or gargle with local anaesthetic; intravenous muscle relaxant just before the scope is introduced.

(b)
• Position the patient on the left side to facilitate saliva drainage and scope access.
• After the procedure: no food or drink until the gag reflex returns (1 to 2 hours); Simms position until awake, then semi-Fowler's until discharge.

(c)
Perforation is the complication to assess for: pain, bleeding and fever.

(d)
Withhold oral intake until the gag reflex returns and keep the patient positioned as above; assess for signs of perforation after the procedure.

(e)
• Left-side positioning drains saliva and gives easy scope access; fasting beforehand is part of the preparation.
• Delaying food and fluids until the gag reflex returns prevents aspiration of food or fluids into the lungs.
• Post-procedure positioning (Simms then semi-Fowler's) is the care given until the patient is awake and ready for discharge.
• Neglecting these steps risks aspiration and unrecognised perforation.
questions.question:
Discuss upper gastrointestinal fibroscopy (oesophagogastroduodenoscopy).
(a) State the indications and preparation.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities.
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

questions.answerText:
(a)
FBC (anaemia, neutrophilia), ESR, blood culture, chest X-ray, CT scan and bronchoscopy.

(b)
Percutaneous catheter drainage or surgical resection: lobectomy or pneumonectomy.

(c)
• Pre-operative: teach what to expect (anaesthesia, thoracotomy, chest tube, oxygen, possible ventilator, ICU stay of 1 to 3 days); teach turning, incentive spirometry, diaphragmatic pursed-lip breathing, cough technique and splinting the incision.
• Pre-operative: clear the airway (humidification, postural drainage, chest percussion after bronchodilator, antibiotics), estimate sputum volume, relieve anxiety, and begin pain control.
• Post-operative: maintain a clear airway and closed chest drainage, oxygen therapy, haemodynamic monitoring, vital signs every 15 minutes then hourly then every 2-4 hours, semi-Fowler's position, regulated fluids, coughing with the incision supported, abdominal breathing, morphine for pain, passive arm exercises, fluids and a protein and vitamin C diet.

(d)
Monitor the incision for bleeding and for subcutaneous emphysema (air leak into soft tissue); report blood on the dressing at once and record time and amount. Deep breathing, coughing and airway clearance reduce atelectasis and infection.

(e)
Patient must continue antibiotics for the prescribed period (4-6 weeks, oral therapy continuing a further 4-8 weeks), attend routine check-ups, cough effectively, use chest physiotherapy and postural drainage, and have rest, good nutrition and adequate fluids.
questions.question:
A patient with a lung abscess (necrosis of pulmonary tissue with a cavity containing necrotic debris or fluid, with swinging fever and purulent foul-smelling sputum) does not respond to medical therapy and is scheduled for lobectomy.
(a) Name the investigations used to confirm the condition.
(b) State the surgical procedures considered.
(c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(d) State one complication to monitor for after surgery and how it is prevented or detected.
(e) Outline patient education and discharge planning.

A 40-year-old woman has fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever and weight loss, followed by pain, stiffness and symmetrical swelling of the fingers, wrists, elbows, knees and ankles with morning stiffness lasting more than an hour and subcutaneous nodules. The rheumatoid factor is positive and the ESR is elevated.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Rheumatoid arthritis: a chronic systemic degenerative and inflammatory disease of connective tissue manifested primarily in and around peripheral joints.

(b)
Cause unknown; autoimmune reaction and genetic/familial factors; women are three times more likely to be affected, with onset usually between 35 and 50 years.

(c)
• Congestion and oedema of the synovial membrane and joint capsule lead to synovitis; thickened granulation tissue destroys cartilage and joint capsule, and fibrous granulation tissue deforms, ossifies, occludes and immobilises the joint.
• The disease eventually spreads systemically to organs such as the heart, lungs, kidneys and eyes.

(d)
• Moist compresses to increase blood supply and reduce pain; paraffin gloves to reduce pain and oedema; exercise to maintain range of motion and strength; balance between rest and activity.
• Psychological and emotional support, walking aid, physical care, balanced diet, health education and administering prescribed drugs.
• Medical context: aspirin or NSAIDs, gold compounds and penicillamine, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants; surgery includes synovectomy, osteotomy and arthroplasty.

(a)
• Amputation: surgical removal of a limb or part of the body; indications include arteriosclerosis, trauma, chronic osteomyelitis, sarcoma, severe infection, correcting deformity and life-saving measures.
• Types: guillotine/open (serious trauma or moist gangrene; wound closed later), closed/flap (immediate closure, healing within 2 weeks, good limb fitting), traumatic amputation and disarticulation (at a joint).

(b)
• Pre-operative: inform and educate the patient and significant others, observe vital signs, obtain consent, physical and psychological care, pre-operative exercise, IV infusion or blood transfusion as prescribed, pre-operative medication and nil per oral.
• Post-operative: observe vital signs, check for haemorrhage, elevate the stump on a pillow for 12-24 hours to reduce oedema, stump care (dry dressing, lanolin, gentle massage), exercise, psychological care, nutrition, antibiotics, analgesics and vitamin C, and bedside rails for safety.

(c)
Complications: haemorrhage, wound infection, wound separation, contracture, stump lesions, phantom pain and delayed grieving; phantom limb pain is managed with nerve injection of 5% ethanol, opioid analgesia or re-amputation if it persists.

(d)
Health education on home care of the stump and use of crutches and prosthesis; emotional, physical (physiotherapy, prosthesis) and social rehabilitation; emotional reactions are influenced by lack of information, stigma, loss of mobility and isolation.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic osteomyelitis and moist gangrene of the lower limb is scheduled for amputation.
(a) Name the procedure, its indications and the types of amputation.
(b) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(c) State the complications to monitor for and how they are managed or prevented.
(d) Outline patient education and discharge planning.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Empyema is an accumulation of thick purulent fluid in the pleural space, often with fibrin; causes: bacterial pneumonia or lung abscess, penetrating chest trauma, haematogenous infection and iatrogenic causes (after thoracic surgery or thoracentesis).
• Organisms and risk factors release inflammatory mediators, raising capillary permeability, attracting white cells and letting protein escape, producing protein-rich pleural fluid; worsening inflammation produces purulent exudate and fibroblastic activity.
• The two pleural membranes adhere and form a 'peel'.

(b)
• Exudative stage (days 1-3): outpouring of fluid with low cellular content; simple para-pneumonic effusion with normal pH and glucose.
• Fibrinopurulent stage (days 4-14): polymorphonuclear leukocytes and fibrin accumulate and the effusion becomes purulent and viscous.
• Organisation stage (after 14 days): fibroblasts grow into the exudate and form an inelastic peel, most common in S. aureus infection.

(c)
In the organisation stage a thickened peel restricts lung movement, termed trapped lung; surgical complications are persistent air leak, bleeding from pulmonary vessels, intercostal nerve damage, single-lung ventilation problems and re-expansion pulmonary oedema.

(d)
• Spread through the blood (haematogenous infection) is a recognised cause; manifestations include fever, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, cyanosis, abdominal pain, vomiting and splinting of the affected side.
• Functional deficit: impaired gas exchange from a compressed lung (trapped lung restricts movement).
• Management: control infection, drain pleural fluid, IV antibiotics 10-14 days, oxygen, thoracentesis, oral antibiotics for 1-3 weeks after discharge if complicated.
• Nursing diagnoses: impaired gas exchange, acute pain and risk for activity intolerance.
questions.question:
Discuss empyema.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) Describe the stages of the disorder.
(c) State how the stages relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how the disorder may spread or affect distant systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Severe mitral regurgitation (cardiovascular system) causing cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; blood regurgitates from the left ventricle back into the left atrium in systole.

(b)
The left atrium stretches, hypertrophies and dilates; the lungs become congested (pulmonary oedema), adding strain on the right ventricle; cardiac output falls.

(c)
Other structural and inflammatory disorders to consider: mitral valve prolapse, mitral stenosis, aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, endocarditis and pericarditis.

(d)
• Assessment cues: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, fatigue, pitting oedema, SpO2 82%, crepitations. Nursing diagnoses: activity intolerance, decreased cardiac output, ineffective breathing pattern.
• Planning and implementation: monitor respirations, pulse, oxygen saturation and BP with activity; paced activity with rest; supplemental oxygen as prescribed; restful environment, semi-recumbent rest to lower cardiac workload and dyspnoea; diuretics as prescribed.
• Evaluation: stable BP, heart rate and SpO2 (95-100%) through the shift, tolerating sitting to walking, respiratory rate 18 per minute, and no symptoms of heart failure.
questions.question:
A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, hypertension and mitral valve prolapse has acute shortness of breath, orthopnoea and fatigue. Heart rate is 107, respiratory rate 25 and oxygen saturation 82% on room air. A 3/6 pansystolic murmur, raised jugular venous pressure, pitting oedema and coarse bibasal inspiratory crepitations are found. Chest X-ray shows pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions, and transoesophageal echocardiogram shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet with ruptured chordae tendineae.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Name the differential conditions.
(d) Using the nursing process, explain the nursing assessment, planning and evaluation.

A patient presents with anorexia, low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, dyspnoea, chest tightness and mucopurulent sputum with haemoptysis. The patient lives in substandard conditions and has had close contact with someone with active disease.
(a) Identify the condition and the causative organism.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pulmonary tuberculosis, an infection of the lung parenchyma most often caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by inhaling droplets from an infected person's cough or sneeze.

(b)
• Droplet nuclei carry bacilli to the alveoli where they multiply; neutrophils and macrophages engulf them, forming granulomas that become a fibrous mass with a Ghon tubercle; necrotic cheesy material calcifies into a scar and bacteria become dormant.
• With inadequate immune response the dormant bacteria reactivate, the Ghon tubercle ulcerates into the bronchi, and the lung becomes inflamed; bacilli can also spread by the bloodstream.

(c)
• History, physical examination, tuberculin skin test, chest X-ray, acid-fast bacillus smear, sputum culture, bronchoscopy, chest CT and interferon-gamma release (QFT-Gold) test.
• Nursing problems: ineffective airway clearance, ineffective breathing pattern, imbalanced nutrition, ineffective coping and knowledge deficit about self-care.

(d)
• Anti-TB drugs for 6 to 12 months: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and streptomycin or ethambutol daily for 8 weeks, then isoniazid and rifampin for a further 4 months.
• A person is considered non-infectious after 2 to 3 weeks of continuous therapy; pyridoxine is given with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy; directly observed therapy is the best way to ensure adherence.

(a)
• CT gives cross-sectional images of abdominal organs from multiple x-ray images digitised by computer; indicated for diseases of the liver, spleen, kidney, pancreas and pelvic organs and for inflammatory conditions of the colon (appendicitis, diverticulitis, regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis).
• MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to supplement ultrasonography and CT; useful for abdominal soft tissues, blood vessels, abscesses, fistulas, neoplasms and sources of bleeding; oral contrast can enhance the image.
• MRI is contraindicated with permanent pacemakers, artificial heart valves, defibrillators, implanted insulin pumps or TENS devices, internal metal devices (e.g. aneurysm clips) and intraocular metallic fragments.

(b)
• CT: no food or drink for 6 to 8 hours; an IV or oral contrast agent may be prescribed, so ask about contrast dye allergies.
• MRI: no food or drink for 6 to 8 hours; remove jewellery and metals; the procedure takes 30 to 90 minutes.

(c)
• CT disadvantages: not useful for cachectic patients (detail depends on fat), painless but radiation doses are considerable.
• MRI disadvantages: heartbeat, respiration and peristalsis artefacts may blur the image (newer fast-imaging techniques help); close-fitting scanners may cause claustrophobia and the machine makes a knocking sound.

(d)
• Schedule barium studies after CT scanning so they do not interfere with imaging.
• Warn patients about claustrophobia and noise; open MRIs are less close-fitting and remove claustrophobia.

(e)
• Magnetic fields can cause implanted devices to malfunction, which is why those patients are excluded.
• Asking about contrast allergy protects against reaction to contrast.
• Neglecting barium scheduling or metal removal compromises imaging or safety.
questions.question:
Discuss abdominal computed tomography (CT) scanning and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
(a) State the indications, contraindications and preparation.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities.
(c) State the complications or disadvantages.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the problems that follow when they are neglected.

A patient who recently had abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia develops cough, sputum production, low-grade fever, dyspnoea, tachycardia, tachypnoea, pleural pain and central cyanosis, and is anxious and breathless when supine. Breath sounds are decreased with crackles over the affected area, SpO2 is below 90%, and the chest X-ray shows a sharply defined opacity with volume loss.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Atelectasis: collapse or closure of the alveoli/lung with reduced or absent gas exchange, usually unilateral; obstructive atelectasis is the most common type.

(b)
• Age younger than 5 or older than 60 years; lung disease (asthma in children, COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis); conditions that interfere with coughing, yawning and sighing; premature birth; respiratory muscle weakness; general anaesthesia; abdominal or chest surgery.
• Causes: obstructive (foreign body, blood clot, airway tumour) or non-obstructive (pleural effusion, pneumothorax, tumour, chest injury, pneumonia).

(c)
• Reduced alveolar ventilation or blockage stops air passing to and from the alveoli; trapped alveolar air is absorbed into the bloodstream and outside air cannot replace it, causing lung injury.
• Injury damages type II alveolar cells, so surfactant is lacking or inactivated; this creates alveolar tension, decreases compliance and recoil and results in atelectasis.

(d)
• Treat the cause: suctioning of secretions, bronchoscopy for foreign body, mucous plug or tumour, pleural effusion management, incentive spirometry, nebulised bronchodilators (albuterol, metaproterenol) and chest physiotherapy (postural drainage, percussion).
• Post-operatively avoid narcotics as much as possible, ambulate if haemodynamically stable, and use physiotherapy; chronic cases may need lobectomy or segmental resection.
• Nursing diagnoses: ineffective breathing pattern, impaired gas exchange, activity intolerance, acute pain, anxiety, knowledge deficit and risk for fluid volume deficit.

questions.question:
Discuss bone neoplasms.
(a) Define bone neoplasms and describe the types.
(b) State the clinical manifestations and diagnostic procedures.
(c) State the common complications of bone neoplasms.
(d) Explain how the disorder may spread or affect distant body systems and describe the related medical, surgical and nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A bone neoplasm is a new growth on the bone which may be benign or malignant.
• Primary bone neoplasms are common in children and young adults under 40 years.
• Secondary bone neoplasms are malignant bone growths from metastasis of tumours elsewhere in the body and have higher incidence than primary types.

(b)
• Persistent progressively increasing bone pain, reduced activity of the part, local tenderness, swelling and warmth, weight loss and anaemia.
• Diagnosis: bone scan and bone X-ray.

(c)
Pathological fracture is a recognised cause of fracture in neoplastic disease (benign osteochondroma, malignant sarcoma and myeloma).

(d)
• Secondary neoplasms show spread from other body parts to bone; weight loss and anaemia show systemic effects.
• Surgical: excision and curettage, radical excision, limb amputation.
• Medical: hormonal treatment, cytotoxic drugs (methotrexate, fluorouracil, mercaptopurine; cyclophosphamide, mustine) and radiation therapy.
• Nursing management: general nursing care.

questions.question:
A patient with a laryngeal tumour causing upper airway obstruction is scheduled for a tracheostomy.
(a) Name the procedure and state its indications.
(b) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(c) State the complications to monitor for and how they are recognised or prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tracheostomy: a surgical incision into the trachea to establish an airway (the stoma is the resulting opening). Indications: upper airway obstruction (e.g. laryngeal tumour), prolonged mechanical ventilation, access to retained secretions, and prevention of recurrent aspiration.

(b)
• Pre-operative: explain the procedure to patient and family, obtain informed consent, assess understanding, reassure that someone will be in constant attendance, arrange communication by writing, and allow questions.
• Preparation to receive the patient: sterile suction, oxygen, ventilator if indicated, a tray of sterile tracheostomy tubes of various sizes, an ambu bag connector, and mouth-care equipment.
• Post-operative: head of bed at about 45 degrees if stable; monitor BP, respiratory rate and sounds, pulse and colour; suction as needed (saline may be instilled); humidify inspired gas to prevent encrustation; fluid intake of at least 3000 ml unless contraindicated; keep wound clean, change tapes with two nurses.
• Mouth care every 2 hours; call bell, pad and pencil for communication; family encouraged to talk to the patient; no oral food or fluids initially (given IV or by nasogastric tube).

(c)
• Early: tube dislodgement, accidental decannulation, bleeding, pneumothorax, air embolism, aspiration, subcutaneous or mediastinal emphysema (inspect the neck), laryngeal nerve damage, posterior tracheal wall penetration.
• Long-term: airway obstruction from secretions or cuff protrusion, infection, innominate artery rupture, dysphagia, tracheoesophageal fistula, tracheal dilation, ischaemia and necrosis.

(a)
• Chest drainage is used after thoracic surgery and in spontaneous or traumatic pneumothorax.
• Pre-operative: teach what to expect (anaesthesia, thoracotomy, chest tube and drainage, oxygen, possible ventilator, ICU for 1 to 3 days), turning, incentive spirometry, diaphragmatic pursed-lip breathing, coughing and splinting the incision.
• Pre-operative: clear the airway (humidification, postural drainage, chest percussion after bronchodilator, antibiotics), listen to fears, and begin pain control with non-opioid NSAIDs.

(b)
• Maintain a clear airway and closed drainage, give oxygen, monitor haemodynamics, and keep the patient flat or head slightly raised (20 degrees) until BP is controlled, then semi-Fowler's.
• Vital signs every 15 minutes until recovered from anaesthesia, hourly until stable, then every 2-4 hours; assist coughing with the incision supported; promote abdominal breathing; give morphine every 3-4 hours for 48-72 hours.
• Passive arm exercises from the evening of surgery; fluids then a diet adequate in protein and vitamin C; monitor chest tubes and drainage.

(c)
Subcutaneous emphysema (air leak from the pleural space into soft tissue) and bleeding from the incision; atelectasis or infection; fluid overload with pulmonary oedema.

(d)
Regulate prescribed fluids; report blood on the dressing to the surgeon at once and record time and amount; the provider decides the method and pace of ventilator weaning.

(e)
• Clearing secretions before surgery reduces post-operative atelectasis and infection.
• Abdominal breathing improves ventilation without increasing pain and helps effective coughing; arm exercises prevent restriction of function.
• Fluids liquefy secretions so they are easier to expectorate; protein and vitamin C help wound healing; chest drainage re-expands the lung and removes air, fluid and blood (the chest cavity normally has negative pressure and an open chest causes lung collapse).
• Neglect leads to atelectasis, infection, pulmonary oedema, unrecognised bleeding or subcutaneous emphysema, and lung collapse.
questions.question:
Discuss the care of a patient undergoing thoracic surgery.
(a) State the indications and preparation (pre-operative management).
(b) State the post-operative nursing responsibilities.
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

A patient has vague periumbilical pain with anorexia that progresses to sharp, well-localised right lower quadrant pain with nausea and a low-grade fever. There is local tenderness at McBurney point, rebound tenderness and pain felt in the right lower quadrant when the left lower quadrant is palpated. The white cell count and neutrophils are raised and a CT scan shows appendix enlargement of at least 6 mm. Surgery is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and the diagnostic test that supports it.
(b) Describe the pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(c) State the complication to monitor for and how it is prevented.
(d) State the goals of nursing care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Appendicitis: inflammation of the inner lining of the vermiform appendix, spreading to its other parts, from obstruction of the lumen; supported by FBC (raised WBC and neutrophils), raised C-reactive protein and CT scan (appendix enlarged by at least 6 mm).

(b)
• Pre-operative: IV infusion to replace fluid loss and promote renal function, antibiotics to prevent infection, analgesics for pain; no enema (risk of perforation) and no laxatives or cathartics with fever, nausea and abdominal pain.
• Intra-operative: appendectomy as soon as possible under general anaesthesia by laparotomy (low abdominal incision) or laparoscopy.
• Post-operative: high Fowler position (reduces tension on incision, promotes thoracic expansion, lessens atelectasis); incentive spirometer at least every 2 hours while awake; parenteral opioid (morphine) then oral agent; IV then oral fluids; food when bowel sounds are present; listen for bowel sounds and ask about flatus; monitor urine output.

(c)
Perforation, gangrene, peritonitis, abscess or portal pylephlebitis; perforation generally occurs within 6 to 24 hours of pain onset, so surgery is done as soon as possible; complicated cases get 3-5 days of post-operative antibiotics.

(d)
Goals include pain relief, preventing fluid volume deficit, reducing anxiety, preventing or treating surgical site infection and atelectasis, maintaining skin integrity and optimal nutrition.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman presents to emergency services in cardiogenic shock with progressively worsening breathlessness over the past year. Her pulse is 110 beats per minute, regular and of low volume, blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg, and a third heart sound is heard with no murmurs. She then has a systolic cardiac arrest and is resuscitated and mechanically ventilated.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Dilated cardiomyopathy: an acquired or hereditary disease of the heart muscle that makes it hard for the heart to deliver blood to the body and can lead to heart failure.

(b)
Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the myocardium with structural or functional abnormalities (often ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation) that impair the pump function of the heart; the cause is often unknown, or follows long-term high blood pressure, heart attack damage, long-term rapid heart rate, valve problems, infection, metabolic disorders, alcohol and some chemotherapy.

(c)
• Assessment: chief complaint (fever, syncope, aches, fatigue, palpitations, dyspnoea), aetiological factors (alcohol, pregnancy, recent infection, endocrine history), family history, vital signs; inspect skin for pallor and cyanosis.
• Interventions: establish rapport, monitor and record vital signs as baseline, semi-Fowler's position to increase oxygen saturation, measure tidal volume and vital capacity; inotropic support (dopamine, noradrenaline) and mechanical ventilation were used.

(d)
• Diagnostic tests: chest X-ray, echocardiogram, ECG, treadmill stress test, cardiac catheterisation, cardiac CT and MRI, blood tests.
• Drugs: anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin), diuretics (furosemide, metolazone), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins, antiarrhythmics (flecainide, sotalol).
• Surgically implanted devices: implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, ventricular assist device, pacemaker. Complications to guard against: heart failure, blood clots, valve problems, cardiac arrest and sudden death.

questions.question:
Discuss osteomalacia.
(a) Define the condition and state its causes.
(b) Explain the clinical basis (pathogenesis).
(c) State the clinical manifestations, diagnosis and management.
(d) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Distinguish between osteomalacia and osteoporosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• An adult disorder comparable to rickets in children (adult rickets) with softening and weakness of bone due to low plasma calcium.
• Causes: dietary insufficiency of calcium, steatorrhoea or prolonged diarrhoea, inadequate calcium during pregnancy, and acidosis in renal failure causing excess calcium excretion.

(b)
Low plasma calcium leads to softening and weakening of bone.

(c)
• Softening and weakening of bone, tenderness and pain, long bone deformity, tetany (painful muscular spasms), loss of weight and muscle strength, low plasma calcium.
• Diagnosis: CBC shows decreased plasma calcium.
• Medical: calcium, vitamin C and vitamin D supplements and IV calcium gluconate 10%.

(d)
Susceptible: people with low dietary calcium, chronic diarrhoea or steatorrhoea, pregnancy with inadequate calcium, and renal failure with acidosis.

(e)
• Osteoporosis is a generalised progressive reduction of bone mass in which resorption exceeds formation, causing fractures with little force; common in postmenopausal or elderly women.
• Osteoporosis causes include hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, COPD, renal and liver disease, malabsorption and prolonged corticosteroid or heparin use.
• Osteoporosis signs: vertebral fractures, pain, muscle spasm, loss of lumbar curve, kyphosis; managed with oestrogen plus progesterone, calcitonin, calcium gluconate and vitamin D.
• Osteomalacia is softening due to low plasma calcium with tetany and deformity; osteoporosis is loss of bone mass.
• Both are helped by calcium and vitamin D.

questions.question:
Discuss specialised nutrition support (enteral and parenteral nutrition).
(a) State the indications and contraindications.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and mode of administration.
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nutrition support is delivery of formulated nutrients by feeding tube or intravenous infusion, for patients unable to eat enough (severe swallowing difficulty, GI obstruction, critical illness, ventilation, burns, anorexia, eating disorders, congenital anomalies).
• Enteral contraindications: functional GI problems, hyperglycaemia, electrolyte abnormalities and severe fluid overload.
• Parenteral is for patients without a functioning GI tract (fistulas, obstruction, short-bowel syndrome, severe pancreatitis, malabsorption, severe burns); it should not be used when the GI tract works; glucose of 300 mg/dL or more, electrolyte abnormalities and fluid overload must be corrected first.

(b)
• Enteral routes: nasogastric, orogastric, nasoduodenal/nasojejunal; position the head properly, confirm tube placement, flush tubes after each feed or medication, stop the infusion if resistance occurs.
• Parenteral: central or peripheral vein, given continuously (24 hours) or cyclically (10-16 hours) by a team with catheter insertion and care, monitoring and discontinuation when GI function returns.

(c)
Parenteral complications: catheter-related infection, hyperglycaemia, bone disease and electrolyte imbalance; for enteral feeding, monitor for distension, nausea and bloating.

(d)
• Monitor feeding tolerance, auscultate the abdomen, watch for gastric distension, nausea and bloating.
• Prevent and treat catheter infection per CDC guidance; check glucose at least every 6 hours until stable; adjust free water and monitor for refeeding syndrome.

(e)
• Correct head positioning and correct tube placement are the key enteral safety actions.
• Glucose monitoring addresses hyperglycaemia; calcium, vitamin D and regular exercise address bone disease.
• Catheter infection prevention addresses catheter-related infection, a recognised complication.
• Neglect leads to infection, hyperglycaemia, bone disease, electrolyte imbalance and refeeding syndrome.

questions.question:
A patient complains of dyspepsia with belching, bloating and heartburn, early satiety, unexplained weight loss and recurrent vomiting, and has passed black tarry stools (melena) or vomited blood. Upper endoscopy shows an excavation in the mucosa of the duodenum.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Peptic ulcer disease: an excavation that forms in the mucosa of the stomach, pylorus, duodenum or oesophagus (gastric, duodenal or oesophageal ulcer), usually from H. pylori infection.

(b)
• Erosion of a circumscribed area of mucosa, which may extend to the muscle layers or through to the peritoneum, from disturbed balance between acid/pepsin secretion and the mucosal barrier; damaged mucosa cannot secrete enough mucus to protect against hydrochloric acid.
• H. pylori colonises the mucus layer, causes chronic active inflammation, produces cytotoxins and urease, and raises gastrin and acid secretion; NSAIDs also disrupt the mucosal barrier.

(c)
• Assess pain with a pain scale; watch for haematemesis, tachycardia, hypotension; examine all stools for frank or occult blood and notify the provider; monitor intake and output and electrolytes; periodic FBC to judge blood loss.
• Reduce anxiety with a calm approach; give anti-ulcer drugs and teach the patient to avoid foods that cause pain; encourage stopping smoking (it reduces pancreatic bicarbonate and delays healing).

(d)
• Medical: triple therapy for 14 days (PPI such as omeprazole plus clarithromycin 500 mg bid plus amoxicillin 1 g bid; metronidazole replaces amoxicillin only in penicillin allergy); quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline) when standard therapy fails.
• Surgery for life-threatening haemorrhage, perforation, obstruction, or failure to heal after 12-16 weeks: vagotomy with or without pyloroplasty, antrectomy with Billroth I or II anastomosis; laparoscopy reduces postoperative bleeding, pain, infection and recovery time.
• Diet: avoid extremes of temperature, alcohol, coffee (including decaffeinated) and caffeinated drinks; eat three regular meals a day.

questions.question:
A patient who regularly takes aspirin or ibuprofen and drinks alcohol complains of epigastric pain, indigestion, anorexia, nausea and vomiting and has passed black tarry stools.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors (causes).
(b) State the complications that may develop.
(c) Outline the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority nursing intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Gastritis (here erosive acute gastritis): inflammation of the gastric mucosa when the protective mucosal barrier breaks down and allows autodigestion by hydrochloric acid and pepsin.
• Causes: NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen), alcohol, H. pylori (most frequent), other infections, acute stress (shock), radiation, allergy and food poisoning, bile reflux, ischaemia and direct trauma.

(b)
• Superficial ulceration may lead to haemorrhage (haemorrhagic gastritis: haematemesis, tachycardia, hypotension; melena or haematochezia); chronic gastritis leads to atrophy and loss of intrinsic factor, causing vitamin B12 malabsorption and pernicious anaemia.
• Emergency surgery may be needed for gangrenous or perforated tissue; gastric outlet (pyloric) obstruction may need gastric resection or gastrojejunostomy.

(c)
