• Medical: refrain from alcohol and food until symptoms subside, then a non-irritating diet; IV fluids if symptoms persist; NG intubation, antacids, H2 blockers (famotidine, ranitidine), PPIs (omeprazole, lansoprazole); H. pylori regimen of PPI, antibiotics and sometimes bismuth.
• Nursing: reduce anxiety; keep NPO for possibly a few days then ice chips and clear liquids, introducing solids as soon as possible; discourage caffeine, alcohol and smoking and refer for counselling; monitor intake and output (at least 1.5 L/day, urine 0.5 mL/kg/h) and electrolytes every 24 hours.
• Priority: detect bleeding early (haematemesis, tachycardia, hypotension, examine all stools) because haemorrhage is the dangerous complication; teach diet, medication completion and stress management.

questions.question:
Discuss osteoarthritis.
(a) Define osteoarthritis.
(b) State the causes.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) State the clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible to osteoarthritis.
(f) Distinguish between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A chronic non-inflammatory degenerative disease of the joints found in weight-bearing joints of the lower extremities (hips and knees), the lumbar vertebrae and the hands.

(b)
Causes: unknown/idiopathic, strain on the joint (obesity, abnormal posture), wear and tear of ageing, septicaemia, fracture and malignancy.

(c)
With ageing, cartilage loses water content and elasticity, softens, frays and thins; friction and new bone formation (bony spurs) make the joint stiff; eroded bone ends contact, causing severe pain, restricted movement, muscle spasm and contracture.

(d)
Stiffness and pain, reduced range of motion, contracture, crepitation, joint enlargement and instability, hard irregular joints, inability to carry out daily activities, and Heberden's nodes.

(e)
• Primary osteoarthritis relates to ageing and genetic factors; secondary follows joint trauma, disease and obesity.
• It affects both sexes, but onset occurs earlier in men and incidence rises in women after menopause.

(f)
• Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic systemic degenerative and inflammatory connective tissue disease, with autoimmune cause, three times commoner in women with onset at 35-50 years.
• Rheumatoid arthritis has bilateral symmetrical joint involvement, morning stiffness over an hour, subcutaneous nodules, raised ESR and positive rheumatoid factor, and spreads to heart, lungs, kidneys and eyes.
• Osteoarthritis synovial fluid analysis is normal; diagnosis uses history, examination, arthroscopy and arthrography.
• Osteoarthritis treatment: rest, heat, exercise, NSAIDs (ibuprofen), corticosteroid; surgery is arthroplasty or arthrodesis.
• Osteoarthritis of the spine compressing the cord can cause bladder and bowel incontinence, weakness of the extremities and impotence.
• Rheumatoid arthritis management: aspirin/NSAIDs, gold, penicillamine, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants; surgery includes synovectomy, osteotomy and arthroplasty.

(a)
• Bronchiectasis: chronic dilatation of medium-sized airways with destruction of the bronchial elastic and muscular structure; it may be congenital or acquired (types: saccular and cylindrical).
• Causes: pulmonary collapse from obstruction of small bronchi, bronchial distension by pus beyond an obstruction, congenital abnormality (e.g. cystic fibrosis), and bronchial wall damage from infection (e.g. whooping cough, measles).

(b)
Complications: haemoptysis, bronchopneumonia, septicaemia, emphysema and pericarditis.

(c)
• Medical: amoxicillin (adult 500 mg-1 g every 8 hours for 5-7 days) or cotrimoxazole (adult 960 mg every 12 hours for 5-7 days), appropriate antibiotics once culture results are available, and bronchodilators such as salmeterol.
• Nursing: adequate rest, diet and mild exercise; avoid superimposed infection such as colds; good hydration to liquefy secretions; good general and oral hygiene; oxygen when necessary.
• Priority: postural drainage to mobilise secretions to the large airways where they can be coughed up, because obstructed bronchi stay filled with exudate and only forceful coughing and postural drainage empty them.
• Prevention: avoid smoking and air pollution, treat bacterial infection promptly and effectively, and give respiratory care during childhood measles.
questions.question:
A patient who had whooping cough in the past now has a cough that is worse in the morning, foul-smelling purulent sputum, occasional fever, general malaise, haemoptysis, loss of appetite and weight loss. Chest radiography shows cystic spaces with air-fluid levels.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors (causes).
(b) State the complications that may develop.
(c) Outline the nursing, medical and preventive management options and justify the priority intervention.

Discuss pleurisy (pleuritis).
(a) Define the condition and state its causes.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology.
(c) State the clinical manifestations.
(d) Explain why certain people are more susceptible or vulnerable.
(e) Distinguish between pleurisy and empyema.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pleurisy is inflammation of both layers of the pleura (parietal and visceral) that cover the lungs and chest wall, with sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing.
• Causes: tuberculosis, pulmonary infarction or embolism, pneumonia, pulmonary abscess, upper respiratory infection, chest wall trauma and pulmonary neoplasm.

(b)
• Infection or trauma causes inflammation of the pleura, which irritates the sensory fibres of the parietal pleura.
• The inflamed membranes rub together, especially on inspiration, causing severe knife-like pain; extra fluid in the pleural space is called a pleural effusion.

(c)
Chest pain, shortness of breath, local tenderness, fever, malaise, raised white cell count, cough and chills.

(d)
Those with the following conditions (TB, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or infarction, abscess, upper respiratory infection, neoplasm) or chest trauma are vulnerable.

(e)
• Pleurisy is inflammation of the pleural layers with pain on breathing; empyema is thick purulent fluid in the pleural space, often with fibrin.
• Empyema follows bacterial pneumonia, lung abscess, penetrating trauma, haematogenous infection or thoracic surgery/thoracentesis, and passes through exudative, fibrinopurulent and organisation stages.
• Empyema presents like bacterial pneumonia with acute febrile response, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, possible cyanosis and splinting.
• Pleurisy is treated with antibiotics for bacterial infection, aspirin or ibuprofen, cough medicine and bronchodilators.
• Empyema requires drainage of the pleural fluid, IV antibiotics and oxygen.
• Diagnosis of pleurisy: X-ray (pleural thickening), sputum, thoracentesis fluid smear and culture, pleural biopsy and CT.

(a)
• A pacemaker is an electronic device giving electrical stimuli to the heart muscle; used for slower-than-normal impulse formation or a conduction disturbance causing symptoms, and to control some tachydysrhythmias that do not respond to drugs.
• Components: electronic pulse generator and electrodes; types: temporary (endocardial, epicardial, transcutaneous) and permanent (single chamber, dual chamber, rate-responsive).
• How it works: battery, computerised generator and wires with sensors at the tips detect heart activity and send pulses when the rhythm is abnormal.

(b)
Nursing management covers pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative care and patient and family teaching.

(c)
Complications: infection, haematoma, haemothorax, ventricular ectopy and tachycardia, lead dislocation and cardiac tamponade.

(d)
• Pacemaker clinics monitor patients and test pulse generators for impending battery failure.
• Surveillance also assesses lead fracture, muscle inhibition and insulation disruption.

(e)
• Rationale: regular surveillance detects battery or lead failure before the device stops pacing.
• Neglect of surveillance risks undetected battery failure, lead fracture or insulation disruption.
• Related device: the implantable cardioverter-defibrillator detects and stops dangerous rhythms such as ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; risks include infection.
questions.question:
Discuss pacemaker therapy.
(a) State the indications and preparation.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities.
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A systemic inflammatory disorder of the spinal column and large peripheral joints; 3-4 times commoner in men, onset between 20 and 40 years; cause idiopathic, genetic or environmental.
• It begins mostly in the sacroiliac area; the intervertebral disc becomes inflamed, cartilage and bone deteriorate, and fibrous tissue infiltrates and ossifies the disc space.
• Inflammation then spreads up the lumbar, thoracic and cervical spine, leading to kyphosis.

(b)
• Early: recurrent low back or large joint pain, morning stiffness, stooped posture, limited range of motion, fatigue, fever, anorexia, weight loss, reduced chest expansion and red painful eyes.
• Late: kyphosis, vertebral fractures, impotence, incontinence, diminished bladder and rectal sensation, angina, pericarditis, pulmonary fibrosis and fixed flexion of the hips.

(c)
• Complications: skeletal deformities, spinal subluxation, spinal cord compression and death.
• Diagnosis: clinical evaluation and family history, X-ray, positive HLA-B27, slightly raised ESR and negative rheumatoid factor.

(d)
• Distant effects: heart (angina, pericarditis), lungs (pulmonary fibrosis, reduced chest expansion), eyes (red painful eyes) and bladder and bowel (incontinence, diminished sensation).
• Functional deficit: limited range of motion, stooped posture and fixed hip flexion.
• Medical: analgesics (paracetamol) and NSAIDs (ibuprofen); surgical: correction of kyphosis, hip flexion repair, cervical fusion, traction and spica cast.
• Nursing: physical care, regular stretching and exercise, good posture, prone position on a firm mattress without pillows, regular position changes.
questions.question:
Discuss ankylosing spondylitis.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State the classification or stages of the manifestations (early and late).
(c) State how the stages relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how the disorder may spread or affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related medical and nursing management.

Discuss emphysema.
(a) Define emphysema and state its causes.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology.
(c) State the clinical manifestations.
(d) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Distinguish between centrilobular and panlobular emphysema.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Emphysema is a condition in which the walls between the alveoli (air sacs) lose their ability to stretch and recoil.
• Causes: cigarette smoking (by far the commonest, responsible for 80-90% of COPD deaths) and deficiency of alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT), a lung-protector protein.

(b)
• Alveoli are destroyed, reducing the area for exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide; the damage is irreversible and leaves permanent holes in the lower lung tissue.
• The work of breathing rises: ribs are raised, the chest becomes barrel shaped and accessory muscles are used; loss of alveolar walls and capillaries raises pulmonary artery pressure and strains the right ventricle.

(c)
Shortness of breath, cough, limited exercise tolerance and great difficulty exhaling.

(d)
• Smokers are most susceptible; AAT deficiency symptoms usually begin between 32 and 41 years and smoking greatly increases severity in those individuals.
• Emphysema rarely occurs under 45 years (91% of diagnosed cases were 45 or older) and men have higher rates.

(e)
• Centrilobular emphysema involves the respiratory bronchiole, which is enlarged and destroyed, forming irregular confluent spaces among normal lung tissue.
• Panlobular emphysema is a more uniform, diffuse and extensive enlargement and destruction of the alveoli.
• Centrilobular is more common in the upper lungs, while panlobular involves the lower lungs.
• Right ventricular failure, a common cause of death in chronic bronchitis and emphysema, follows the rise in pulmonary artery pressure.
• Complications: pneumothorax, pneumonia, respiratory failure, respiratory acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.

(a)
• GERD is troublesome symptoms impairing quality of life, or injury or complications from retrograde flow of gastric contents into the oesophagus, oropharynx and/or respiratory tract.
• Causes/contributors: lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) dysfunction, delayed gastric emptying, hiatal hernia and obesity.

(b)
• The oesophagus functions as a pump, the LES as a valve and the stomach as a reservoir; abnormality in any part can cause GERD.
• Poor oesophageal motility and decreased acid clearance, a dysfunctional LES allowing reflux, and delayed gastric emptying raising reservoir volume and pressure until the valve fails.

(c)
• Manifestations: heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, coughing, chest pain and wheezing; patients may develop oesophagitis, stricture and Barrett's oesophagus.
• Diagnosis: upper GI endoscopy and manometry, 24-hour pH test, upper GI series and gastric emptying study.
• Management: antacids after each meal and at bedtime; H2 antagonists (ranitidine, cimetidine, famotidine) for nocturnal acid breakthrough; PPIs (omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole) are the most powerful.
• Nursing: low-fat diet, avoid caffeine, tobacco, beer, milk, peppermint and carbonated drinks, avoid eating 2 hours before bed, normal weight, loose clothing, head of bed raised at least 30 degrees. Complications: erosive oesophagitis, stricture, Barrett's oesophagus, adenocarcinoma.

(d)
• Western dietary habits make GERD common; prevalence increases in people over 40.
• Esophagitis occurs in men 2:1 to 3:1 over women and Barrett's oesophagus 10:1.

(e)
• Reflux is a normal physiological phenomenon experienced intermittently by most people, particularly after a meal; GERD occurs when the amount refluxed exceeds the normal limit, causing symptoms with or without oesophagitis.
• Many people control symptoms with over-the-counter medication, so actual numbers are probably higher.
questions.question:
Discuss gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
(a) Define GERD and state its causes.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology.
(c) State the clinical manifestations and management.
(d) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Distinguish between normal gastro-oesophageal reflux and GERD.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anal fistula: a tunnel that connects an infected gland inside the anus to an opening on the skin around the anus; leading causes are clogged anal glands and anal abscesses (also Crohn's disease, radiation, trauma, STDs, TB, diverticulitis, cancer).
• Tests: examination of the perianal area for the tract, anoscopy, ultrasound or MRI of the anal area, blood tests, X-rays and colonoscopy (under conscious sedation).

(b)
• Surgery is always necessary to cure an anal fistula; it is usually done as an outpatient procedure, and large or deep fistulas may need a short hospital stay.
• Post-operative: sitz bath in a warm bath, stool softeners or laxatives for a week, pain relief (e.g. diclofenac) and antibiotic to prevent infection (e.g. ciprofloxacin).

(c)
Incontinence is the risk if the anal sphincter muscles are damaged; the surgical goal is to remove the fistula while protecting the sphincter muscles.

(d)
• Keep the perineal area clean with warm water and dry with absorbent cotton wipes; take sitz baths 3-4 times daily; use ice and analgesic ointment for sphincter spasm in the first 24 hours.
• Drink at least 2 L of water daily, eat high-fibre foods, use bulk laxatives or stool softeners, set a regular bowel time and heed the urge to defecate; most patients go home the same day.
questions.question:
A patient has pain, redness and swelling around the anus, bleeding, painful bowel movements, fever and a foul-smelling liquid oozing from a hole near the anus. An opening is found on the skin and the diagnosis is confirmed by anoscopy and MRI. Surgery is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and name the diagnostic tests.
(b) Describe the surgical approach and the post-operative nursing care.
(c) State the complication to monitor for and how it is prevented.
(d) Outline patient education and discharge planning.

Discuss mechanical ventilation.
(a) State the indications and the preparation.
(b) Describe the classification, modes and nursing responsibilities (monitoring).
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Indications: respiratory failure or compromised airway, continuous decrease in PaO2, increase in PaCO2, drug overdose, shock, and multiple system failure and coma.

(b)
• Positive-pressure ventilators (volume cycled, pressure cycled, high-frequency oscillatory) push air into the alveoli, expiration is passive, and an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube is needed; negative-pressure ventilators are no longer used.
• Modes: controlled mechanical ventilation (for apnoeic patients), assist control, intermittent mandatory ventilation and synchronised IMV (reduces fighting the ventilator).
• Monitor control modes, tidal volume and rate, FiO2 (21-100%, PaO2 above 60 mmHg or SpO2 above 92%), peak inspiratory pressure (normal 15-20 cm H2O), sensitivity, I:E ratio (usually 1:2) and minute volume.

(c)
A complication to monitor for is infection related to ventilator dependency.

(d)
• Keep alarms on and functioning at all times; check for water in the tubing, disconnection or kinking; check humidifier water and temperature.
• Adjust the ventilator so the patient is comfortable and breathes synchronously with the machine.

(e)
• Correct volume settings give satisfactory arterial blood gas values with little or no cardiovascular compromise.
• Peak inspiratory pressure rises with increased airway resistance or decreased compliance, so monitoring it detects these problems.
• Good outcomes depend on understanding ventilation principles, a weaning plan and open team communication.
• Neglect leads to impaired gas exchange, ineffective airway clearance and infection.

(a)
• Diarrhoea is the passage of abnormally liquid or unformed stools with increased frequency (three or more bowel movements a day); four basic mechanisms may coexist: osmotic, secretory, inflammatory/infectious and deranged motility.
• Osmotic: poorly absorbed solutes (e.g. lactose in lactose intolerance, sorbitol, magnesium) hold water in the lumen; it stops on fasting.
• Secretory: secretion of water into the lumen exceeds absorption (e.g. cholera toxin raising cyclic AMP, opening chloride channels); it does not resolve with a 2-3 day fast.
• Inflammatory/infectious: epithelial disruption causes exudation and poor water absorption; deranged motility: accelerated transit reduces absorption.

(b)
Acute: sudden onset in a healthy person, self-limiting, 1 or 2 days; persistent: 2 to 4 weeks; chronic: more than 4 weeks, with fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weight loss and weakness.

(c)
• Complications: hypovolaemic shock with multiple organ failure, intestinal septicaemia, perforation, GI bleeding and paralytic ileus.
• Secretory diarrhoea (e.g. cholera) is often lethal unless hydration is aggressively maintained.

(d)
• Dehydration and fluid and electrolyte imbalance follow; nocturnal diarrhoea may reflect diabetic neuropathy; oil droplets suggest pancreatic insufficiency; greasy stools suggest malabsorption.
• Objectives: adequate hydration, eliminate the infectious agent, treat complications; oral rehydration (500 ml over 2-3 hours, 3-4 times daily) for mild to moderate dehydration; IV 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L 2-6 hourly for moderate to severe.
• Zinc 20 mg daily for 10-14 days shortens diarrhoea in children (10 mg under 6 months); anti-infectives (metronidazole), antiperistaltic drugs (loperamide), adsorbents (kaolin, pectin).
• Assessment: duration, onset, frequency, consistency, blood or mucus, recent food and travel, signs of dehydration, FBC, serum chemistries, urinalysis and stool examination.
questions.question:
Discuss diarrhoea.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology (mechanisms).
(b) State the classification of diarrhoea.
(c) State the common complications of diarrhoea.
(d) Explain how diarrhoea may affect other body systems and describe the related management and assessment.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Anaemia is a low haemoglobin concentration (below 8 g/dL severe; 8-9.5 moderate; 9.5-11 mild); normal red cell production needs iron, vitamin B12, folic acid, B6 and protein, with erythropoietin from the kidney stimulating the marrow.

(b)
• Physiological classification: hypoproliferative (decreased production, low reticulocyte count), haemolytic (premature red cell destruction) and haemorrhagic (acute or chronic blood loss).
• Hypoproliferative causes: marrow damage by drugs or chemicals, lack of iron, B12, folate or erythropoietin; iron deficiency gives small (microcytic) hypochromic cells; megaloblastic anaemia gives abnormally large cells.
• Haemolytic: inherited (sickle cell, thalassaemia, G-6-PD deficiency) or acquired (antibody-related, trauma, infection, DIC, toxins, hypersplenism).

(c)
• Megaloblastic anaemia can progress to pancytopenia; aplastic anaemia causes severe anaemia with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
• Haemolysis raises bilirubin and causes yellow sclera and an increased reticulocyte count; iron deficiency in an adult may signal gastrointestinal bleeding or colon cancer.
• The more rapidly anaemia develops, the more severe the symptoms; patients with heart, vascular or lung disease are more symptomatic.

(d)
• Severe anaemia: fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, headache, dyspepsia, angina, pallor, tachycardia, heart failure, murmur, cardiac enlargement, jaundice, koilonychia and spontaneous bruising.
• In renal disease anaemia results from reduced erythropoietin, shortened red cell life span, and iron and folate loss in haemodialysis; epoetin alfa with oral iron raises haematocrit to 33-38%.
• Functional deficit: reduced oxygen carrying capacity causing fatigue and breathlessness.
• Nursing management: evaluate haemodialysis patients for iron and folate deficiency and treat.
questions.question:
Discuss the anaemias.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State the classification of anaemia.
(c) State how the types of anaemia relate to common complications and manifestations.
(d) Explain how anaemia affects other body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management.

An adult with a family history of obesity, an unhealthy diet with regular overeating, a sedentary lifestyle, chronic stress and lack of sleep has excess body fat, shortness of breath, sweating, trouble sleeping, fatigue, back and joint pain, and a body mass index above 30.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) State the complications and effects on health.
(c) Outline the medical, lifestyle and surgical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Obesity: abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that presents a risk to health (BMI of 30 or more; class I 30 to <35, class II 35 to <40, class III 40+).
• Risk factors: family history, unhealthy diet and regular overeating, sedentary lifestyle, age, medication and medical problems, pregnancy, stress, lack of sleep and smoking; causes include genetics, hormonal imbalance (cortisol, ghrelin, leptin, glucagon), processed food and sugar, emotional eating.

(b)
Cardiovascular (chronic inflammation, heart disease), type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome, GERD and gallstones, sleep apnoea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (reduced chest wall compliance, increased work of breathing, reduced lung capacity), cartilage deterioration, cancers (thyroid, liver, kidney, colorectal, breast, endometrial, gallbladder), and psychosocial problems (stigma, low self-esteem, depression).

(c)
• Diagnosis: BMI, skinfold thickness, waist-to-hip ratio, ultrasound, CT or MRI, cholesterol and glucose tests, liver function, diabetes screening, thyroid tests and ECG.
• Lifestyle and behavioural change: healthy eating plan, structured exercise and increased daily activity (up to 300 minutes a week), counselling or support groups for triggers and emotional eating; medication or weight-loss surgery may be recommended.
• Priority: lifestyle and behavioural change is presented as the preferred method (for children, unless extremely overweight); obesity must be treated as a chronic disease like diabetes and hypertension.

(a)
Indications: inability to breathe effectively or maintain oxygenation because of airway obstruction or respiratory failure; cardiopulmonary arrest during advanced cardiac life support; general anaesthesia with mechanical ventilation.

(b)
• Assess respiratory status and tube placement regularly; auscultate lungs bilaterally; secure the tube with tape or a Velcro holder.
• Suction if the patient cannot cough effectively, explaining it carefully even to an unresponsive patient; monitor ABG and oxygen saturation and notify the physician of changes; wean slowly from the ventilator.

(c)
Intubation can damage the vocal cords and surrounding tissues, so it is usually short term; ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP); laryngeal oedema or respiratory distress after removal.

(d)
• Secure the tube; tell the alert patient not to pull on it; obtain an order for soft wrist restraints only if absolutely necessary for a confused patient.
• Wash hands well and give frequent mouth care; before removal suction the mouth and tube and deflate the cuff; afterwards keep the patient in high Fowler's position.

(e)
• Bilateral auscultation detects displacement of the tube into one bronchus; securing the tube prevents dislodging.
• Repositioning oral tubes to the opposite side of the mouth every 24 hours prevents tissue damage.
• Hand washing and mouth care reduce aspiration of oral microorganisms and so help prevent VAP.
• Close observation after removal detects laryngeal oedema or respiratory distress; high Fowler's position maximises chest expansion.
• Neglect leads to dislodgement, tissue damage, bronchial displacement and VAP.
questions.question:
Discuss endotracheal intubation.
(a) State the indications and the preparation.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities during care.
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

An older adult with a chronic illness and recent viral respiratory infection develops a rapidly rising fever, pleuritic chest pain, a rapid bounding pulse, tachypnoea, purulent sputum, fatigue and loss of appetite. Chest X-ray shows a lobar distribution.
(a) Identify the condition and its types or classification.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pneumonia: inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by microorganisms (bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, viruses) with abnormal alveolar filling with fluid (consolidation and exudation).
• Types/classification: lobar and bronchopneumonia; community-acquired, hospital-acquired, health care-associated, aspiration pneumonia and pneumonia in the immunocompromised host.

(b)
Age 65 or older, smoking, chronic illness, weakened immune system, recent viral respiratory infection, chronic chemical exposure, recent surgery or trauma, infancy, alcohol and drug abuse, and ICU hospitalisation.

(c)
• Normal flora (with compromised resistance) or aspirated oropharyngeal flora reach the sterile lower tract and stimulate alveolar inflammation; exudate interferes with diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
• White cells enter the air spaces; secretions and mucosal oedema partly occlude bronchi or alveoli, lowering alveolar oxygen tension; ventilation-perfusion mismatch sends poorly oxygenated blood to the left heart, causing arterial hypoxaemia.

(d)
• Maintain a patent airway and oxygenation, obtain sputum specimens (suction if unable), perform chest physiotherapy, and give a high-calorie, high-protein soft diet.
• Check tube position and feed slowly during nasogastric feeding to prevent aspiration; provide a quiet, calm environment with frequent rest; monitor ABG if hypoxic; auscultate breath sounds at least every 4 hours.
• Nursing diagnoses: impaired gas exchange, ineffective airway clearance, acute pain, ineffective breathing pattern and risk for deficient fluid volume.

questions.question:
Discuss anorexia nervosa.
(a) Define the condition and state its causes.
(b) State the clinical manifestations, diagnosis and treatment.
(c) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(d) Distinguish between anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• An eating disorder characterised by weight loss, difficulty maintaining appropriate body weight for height, age and stature, and in many a distorted body image; it affects people of all ages, genders and races.
• Exact cause unknown: personality traits, emotions, thinking patterns, environmental and biological factors, inadequacy, low self-esteem, loneliness, troubled relationships, peer pressure, heredity and hormonal imbalance.

(b)
• Dramatic weight loss, denies hunger, cooks for others without eating, stomach cramps, dizziness, fainting, sleep problems, dry skin, muscle weakness and impaired immunity.
• Diagnosis by DSM-5: restricted energy intake with low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and disturbed body image or denial of the seriousness of low weight.
• Treatment: psychotherapy, medications, nutrition counselling, group or family therapy and hospitalisation.

(c)
• Eating disorders often affect women aged 12 to 35, up to 5% of the population, and co-occur with other psychiatric disorders (OCD, mood and anxiety disorders).
• Assessment: physical (height, BP, teeth and gums), nutritional, interviews, mental health screening and tools such as the Eating Attitudes Test.

(d)
• Bulimia nervosa is recurrent binge eating followed by purging (or fasting, excessive exercise, extreme dieting).
• Bulimia signs: uncontrolled eating then purging, frequent bathroom use after meals, dental problems, sore throat, swollen glands, heartburn and irregular periods; weight is normal or slightly overweight.
• Bulimia risk factors: being female, depression and anxiety, substance use, trauma and stress; diagnosis uses the SCOFF questionnaire and tests; treated with cognitive therapy, SSRIs, nutritional counselling and a nutrient-dense sugar-free diet.
• Anorexia is characterised by restriction and low weight, whereas bulimia is binge-purge behaviour with usually normal weight.

questions.question:
Discuss constipation.
(a) Define constipation.
(b) State the causes.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) State the clinical manifestations and management.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible to constipation.
(f) Distinguish between acute and chronic constipation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A change in bowel habit or defecatory behaviour causing symptoms that resolve when constipation is relieved; a clinical condition of infrequent bowel opening and/or passage of hard stools (usually fewer than three bowel movements per week).
• It is a symptom and not a disease, but may indicate an underlying disease or GI motility disorder.

(b)
• Drugs (anticholinergics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, calcium channel antagonists, diuretics, opioids, aluminium/calcium antacids, iron); anal, rectal and colon disease; irritable bowel syndrome; hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia.
• Ignoring the urge to defecate, low fibre and fluid intake, lack of exercise and stress.

(c)
• Colonic dysmotility: failure of coordinated motor activity to move stool through the colon, with dietary, drug or systemic causes and enteric nerve abnormalities.
• Pelvic floor dysfunction: anorectal and pelvic floor disorders cause outlet dysfunction and inability to evacuate the rectum; both mechanisms may coexist.

(d)
• Hard stools, bloating, excessive flatulence, hard faecal matter with or without blood; treat by removing causes and evacuating faeces (bisacodyl 10 mg at night, suppositories, liquid paraffin 5-15 ml); complications: megacolon, anal fissure, haemorrhoids, rectal bleeding.
• Nursing: educate to avoid precipitants, high-fibre diet and adequate fluids; laxatives are generally avoided and needed only for a few days.

(e)
More likely in women (particularly pregnant women), patients who recently had surgery, older adults and those of lower socioeconomic status.

(f)
• Acute constipation in older people can occur with acute illness or dietary alterations.
• Chronic constipation usually has an insidious onset over many years, often dating to childhood.
• Investigations include barium enema, sigmoidoscopy, occult blood test, anorectal manometry, defecography, transit studies and thyroid hormone levels.

questions.question:
Discuss pulmonary tuberculosis.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and stages of the disease.
(b) State the types of tuberculosis.
(c) State how its stages or types relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how the disease may spread to or affect distant body systems and describe the related nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Droplet nuclei carry bacilli through the airway to the alveoli, where they are deposited and multiply; bacilli can be carried to other body parts by the bloodstream.
• Neutrophils and macrophages phagocytose them; masses of live and dead bacilli are walled off as granulomas, which become a fibrous mass with a Ghon tubercle.
• The necrotic cheesy mass calcifies into a collagenous scar and the bacteria become dormant; an inadequate immune response reactivates them.

(b)
Types: pulmonary TB, avian TB (M. avium), bovine TB (M. bovis) and miliary/disseminated TB.

(c)
• After reactivation the Ghon tubercle ulcerates and releases cheesy material into the bronchi; the lung becomes inflamed and develops pneumonia and tubercle formation.
• Unless arrested, the process spreads downward to the hilum and then to the adjacent lobe; it may present as non-resolving bronchopneumonia.

(d)
• TB may spread to any part of the body, including the meninges, kidney, bones and lymph nodes.
• Nursing diagnoses: ineffective airway clearance, ineffective breathing pattern, imbalanced nutrition, ineffective coping and knowledge deficit about self-care after discharge.
• Treatment is with anti-TB drugs for 6 to 12 months; directly observed therapy (DOT) is the best way to ensure adherence.
• Pyridoxine is given with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy; a person is non-infectious after 2 to 3 weeks of continuous therapy.
• Risk factors to address: close contact with active TB, immunocompromise, drug abuse, alcoholism, diabetes, renal failure and substandard living conditions.

(a)
Achalasia ('does not relax'): a motility disorder of the oesophagus with absent peristalsis in the distal oesophagus and failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax, causing obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction.

(b)
Cause unknown, with some evidence it is autoimmune (linked to the MHC region of chromosome 6); commonest at 25-40 years, only 5% in children, also in elderly with malignancy; incidence increases in spinal cord injury and altered motility is sometimes seen in anorexia nervosa.

(c)
• Lower oesophageal pressure and relaxation are regulated by excitatory (acetylcholine, substance P) and inhibitory (nitric oxide, VIP) neurotransmitters.
• Patients lack non-adrenergic non-cholinergic inhibitory ganglion cells, causing an imbalance that results in a hypertensive, non-relaxed oesophageal sphincter.

(d)
• Nursing: instruct the patient to eat slowly and drink fluids with meals.
• Medical: temporary oral calcium channel blockers and nitrates; botulinum toxin injected endoscopically into oesophageal quadrants to inhibit smooth muscle contraction.
• Procedures: pneumatic dilation (high success, low perforation risk, moderate sedation), or laparoscopic Heller myotomy with anterior or posterior (Toupet) partial fundoplication.
questions.question:
A young adult presents with dysphagia (most marked), regurgitation, chest pain, heartburn and weight loss. X-ray shows oesophageal dilation above a narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction, and manometry shows absent peristalsis.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing and medical management.

After a bout of forceful vomiting, a patient develops excruciating retrosternal pain and dysphagia, then fever, leukocytosis and severe hypotension, with pneumothorax and subcutaneous emphysema.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oesophageal perforation (here Boerhaave syndrome, spontaneous perforation from forceful vomiting): a surgical emergency in which an opening in the oesophagus lets infection and inflammation spread to nearby vital organs.

(b)
• The oesophagus lacks a serosal layer (which gives stability through elastin and collagen fibres), so it is more vulnerable than the rest of the alimentary tract; perforation may occur by piercing, shearing, bursting from radial forces or thinning from necrosis.
• It is surrounded by loose connective tissue, so infection disseminates easily; mediastinal sepsis can occur with Boerhaave syndrome.

(c)
• Assessment: history, physical assessment, X-ray, barium swallow or esophagram, chest CT to locate the site and scope of injury.
• Immediate care: transport to the emergency unit with IV access, supplemental oxygen with a secure airway and pain medication; intensive-care level supportive monitoring and preparing the patient for surgery.

(d)
• Medical: morphine sulphate, antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, ondansetron) and antibiotics (imipenem-cilastatin, piperacillin-tazobactam).
• Surgical: repair; if repair is not possible, drainage, diversion, stent placement or esophagostomy. Post-operatively NPO about 7 days, enteral (jejunal) or parenteral feeding from day 2-3, repeat esophagram on day 7 before NG removal, antibiotics 7-10 days.

(a)
• Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes (bronchi), the air passage between the nose and the lungs.
• Chronic bronchitis is a long-term, irreversible respiratory illness with a daily mucus-producing cough for at least 3 months a year.

(b)
• Causes: viruses, bacteria and other particles that irritate the bronchial tubes.
• Risk factors: tobacco smoking, weak immune system, bacterial or viral infection, GERD, air pollution, influenza A and B virus and Mycoplasma pneumonia.

(c)
Infections, smoke and other pollutants irritate the airway, stimulating inflammatory reactions and hypersecretion of mucus; the bronchial lining thickens and mucus may plug the airway and impede alveolar function.

(d)
• Bronchial inflammation or swelling, coughing, clear, white, yellow, grey or green sputum, and wheezing.
• Fatigue, shortness of breath, fever and chills, running nose, chest pain or discomfort and sore throat.

(e)
• Those exposed to tobacco smoke, air pollution or infection, those with a weakened immune system and those with GERD are more exposed or less protected.
• Health education points to avoidable exposures: second-hand smoke, people with colds or flu, and cold, damp or heavily polluted places.

(f)
• Acute bronchitis is a shorter illness that commonly follows a cold or viral infection such as flu, and usually lasts a few days or weeks.
• Chronic bronchitis is long term and irreversible, with a daily mucus-producing cough for at least 3 months a year.
• Complications of chronic bronchitis include asthma, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis and sinusitis.
questions.question:
Discuss chronic bronchitis.
(a) Define bronchitis and chronic bronchitis.
(b) State the causes and risk factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) List the clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why some people are more susceptible to chronic bronchitis.
(f) Distinguish between acute bronchitis and chronic bronchitis.

An adult with a history of tobacco smoking has a persistent cough with mucoid sputum, wheezing, dyspnoea, chest tightness, cyanosis, frequent hypoxia and a barrel-shaped chest. Airflow obstruction is only partially reversible with bronchodilators.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) State the complications that may develop.
(c) Outline the medical, nursing and surgical management options and justify the priority nursing intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COAD/COPD): chronic airflow limitation in the small airways in which chronic bronchitis and emphysema combine; obstruction is only partially reversible with bronchodilators.
• Risk factors: tobacco smoking, air pollution/occupational exposure, infection, genetic abnormalities and ageing.

(b)
Complications: cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure) and respiratory failure; emphysema may also cause pneumothorax, pneumonia, respiratory acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.

(c)
• Medical: long-acting beta-2 agonist (salmeterol 50 micrograms twice daily in adults), theophylline, and antibiotics when necessary to control infection (e.g. erythromycin, co-amoxiclav).
• Nursing: take history and examine on admission, assist airway clearance, hydrate, give oxygen at the prescribed pressure and flow rate, give steam inhalation, teach diaphragmatic breathing, keep the room warm, monitor for complications and give health education and discharge advice.
• Surgical: lung volume reduction surgery (removes diseased parenchyma not contributing to ventilation; it does not cure but may reduce dyspnoea and improve function and quality of life).
• Surgical: single lung transplantation for end-stage emphysema, usually for patients younger than 60 years and relatively healthy, often with alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency; organs are in short supply.
• Priority: airway clearance and improved gas exchange, because of excess mucus, exudate in the bronchial tree, dyspnoea, cyanosis and frequent hypoxia.

(a)
Proctitis: inflammation of the rectal mucosa (within 15 cm of the dentate line), acute or chronic; gastrointestinal system (rectum/anorectum).

(b)
Mucosal cell loss, acute inflammation of the lamina propria, eosinophilic crypt abscess and arteriolar oedema; progression causes fibrosis and endarteritis, rectal ischaemia, friability, bleeding, ulcers, strictures and fistula formation.

(c)
• Causes/differentials: radiation or antibiotic side effects, sexually transmitted infections (gonorrhoea, chlamydia, lymphogranuloma venereum, herpes, syphilis), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, celiac disease, chemical or traumatic injury, C. difficile and idiopathic proctitis; proctitis is similar to proctosigmoiditis but usually does not evolve into ulcerative colitis.
• Complications: chronic ulcerative colitis, fistula formation, abscess, treatment failure and perforation.

(d)
• Assessment: history, examination, sigmoidoscopy, FBC (leukocytosis or anaemia), rectal swab cultures, vesicular fluid culture for HSV, VDRL and dark field for syphilis, stool for C. difficile toxin.
• Implementation: antibiotics (ceftriaxone, cefixime, doxycycline, penicillin G), acyclovir for viral, metronidazole for amoebic, ciprofloxacin for Shigella; sitz baths, antispasmodics, stool softeners and low-residue diet for relief; steroid enemas or suppositories for ulcerative proctitis.
questions.question:
A patient has mucopurulent rectal discharge, bleeding, rectal pain and diarrhoea. Sigmoidoscopy shows inflammation of the rectal lining, the full blood count shows leukocytosis, a rectal swab culture is positive for gonorrhoea or chlamydia, and stool is tested for C. difficile toxin.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Name the differential conditions.
(d) Using the nursing process, explain the nursing assessment and implementation.

A patient who is pregnant and has had long-standing low-fibre intake with straining on defecation reports bright red rectal bleeding, pain, protrusion of tissue through the anus, soiling with mucus discharge and pruritus, and a change in bowel habits.
(a) Identify the condition and its classification.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Haemorrhoids (piles): dilated portions of veins in the anal canal / swollen blood vessels in the lower rectum; classified as internal or external relative to the dentate line. Internal haemorrhoids are graded I to IV by degree of prolapse.

(b)
Low-fibre diet with small-calibre stools and straining (decreased venous return), straining and constipation, pregnancy, chronic diarrhoea, colon malignancy, obesity, higher socioeconomic status, raised anal resting pressure, spinal cord injury, loss of rectal muscle tone, rectal surgery, episiotomy, anal intercourse and inflammatory bowel disease.

(c)
• Anal cushions are present in healthy people and cause symptoms when enlarged, inflamed, thrombosed or prolapsed; abnormal swelling causes dilatation and engorgement of the arteriovenous plexuses, stretching the suspensory muscles and eventual prolapse.
• The engorged mucosa is easily traumatised and bleeds bright red; prolapse leads to soiling, mucus discharge (pruritus) and predisposes to incarceration and strangulation.

(d)
• Keep the perineal area clean with warm water and absorbent cotton wipes (avoid toilet tissue); teach sitz baths (3-4 times daily, after each bowel movement for 1-2 weeks after surgery), ice and analgesic ointment within 24 hours of rectal surgery, and prone position at intervals to reduce oedema.
• Encourage at least 2 L of water daily, high-fibre foods, bulk laxatives (psyllium) and stool softeners (docusate); advise a set time for bowel movements and heeding the urge promptly; encourage moderate exercise.
• Medical context: increased fibre and fluids first; banding, sclerotherapy or infrared coagulation for grades I-III; haemorrhoidectomy for very symptomatic grade III-IV.

questions.question:
A patient with a vitamin B12 deficiency has fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, pallor, tachycardia and jaundice. Blood tests show a haemoglobin of 4 to 5 g/dL, a WBC count of 2,000 to 3,000/mm3, platelets below 50,000/mm3, very large red cells with hypersegmented neutrophils, and bone marrow hyperplasia.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Name the differential conditions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Megaloblastic anaemia: anaemia from deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid (no DNA synthesis), producing abnormally large megaloblastic red cells; haematological system (bone marrow and blood).

(b)
• Many abnormal cells die or are trapped in the marrow, so pancytopenia (low red cells, WBCs and platelets) can develop; other myeloid cells (non-lymphoid WBCs, platelets) are abnormal, and cells vary widely in shape (poikilocytosis).
• Severe anaemia signs: fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, headache, dyspepsia, angina, pallor, tachycardia, heart failure, murmur, cardiac enlargement, jaundice, koilonychia and spontaneous bruising.

(c)
• Other anaemias: hypoproliferative (iron deficiency, renal disease, aplastic), haemolytic (sickle cell, thalassaemia, G-6-PD deficiency, autoimmune) and haemorrhagic.
• B12 absorption needs intrinsic factor, so gastrectomy reduces absorption; effects of decreased intake or absorption take 2 to 4 years to appear.

questions.question:
Discuss disorders of the salivary glands (parotitis, sialadenitis and sialolithiasis).
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and causes.
(b) State the classification of the disorders.
(c) State how the types relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how the disorders may affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Parotitis is inflammation of the parotid gland; Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest bacterial pathogen and mumps the commonest viral cause in children; predisposing factors include dehydration, malnutrition, immunosuppression, dental infection, tracheostomy and drugs that reduce salivary flow.
• Sialadenitis (inflammation of the glands) is caused by dehydration, radiation, stress, malnutrition, stones or poor oral hygiene, commonly with S. aureus (MRSA in hospitalised patients).

(b)
• Parotitis: acute or chronic (by onset), bacterial or viral (by cause); sialolithiasis is calcified structures in the gland or duct.
• Bacterial parotitis occurs mostly in neonates and the elderly or debilitated; bilateral infection is more associated with neonates.

(c)
• Parotitis signs: sudden warm erythematous swelling of the pre- and post-auricular area, pain, high fever, chills and systemic toxicity; complications: septicaemia, osteomyelitis and organ failure.
• Sialolithiasis affects the submandibular gland in 80-90% of cases; stones may be symptomless, with postprandial pain and swelling.

(d)
• In chronically obstructed glands, necrosis of acini and lobular fibrosis cause complete loss of secretion from the gland.
• Parotitis diagnosis: needle aspiration culture, ultrasound, CT and MRI; treatment: hydration, IV antistaphylococcal antibiotics, surgical drainage and parotidectomy for long-standing infection.
• Sialadenitis management: antibiotics, massage, hydration, warm compresses and sialagogues (e.g. hard candy, lemon juice); surgical drainage or gland and duct excision if recurrent or refractory.
• Chronic sialadenitis is typically due to decreased salivary flow.

questions.question:
Discuss sickle cell disease.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology.
(b) State the types of sickle cell crisis and classification of the condition.
(c) State how the types of crisis relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how the disease may affect distant body systems and describe the related medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sickle cell disease is a family of inherited haemoglobin disorders (HbSS sickle cell anaemia and sickle beta thalassaemia); HbAS is sickle cell trait, which cannot develop into sickle cell anaemia.
• In HbSS glutamine is replaced by valine at the 6th position; deoxygenated HbS links into chains that stiffen the cell into a sickle shape, causing premature destruction (haemolysis), microcirculation occlusion and tissue infarction.

(b)
• Painful crisis (commonest): tissue hypoxia and necrosis from inadequate blood flow; aplastic crisis: human parvovirus infection, haemoglobin falls and no reticulocytes; sequestration crisis: organs pool sickled cells, often the spleen.
• Incidence in Africa is approximately 25%; diagnosis is by low haematocrit, sickled cells on smear and confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis.

(c)
• In children the spleen is the usual organ for sequestration and by age 10 most have had splenic infarction and autosplenectomy; in adults the liver and, more seriously, the lungs are involved.
• Early death in childhood is from infection; average life expectancy is still about 42 years with severe complications.

(d)
• Pain can occur in the chest, abdomen, back, jaw, legs and arms, with lethargy, pallor, breathlessness, jaundice, fever, seizures and dehydration.
• Severe crisis is life-threatening and requires prompt assessment and management.
• Medical management modalities: bone marrow transplant (potential cure), hydroxyurea and long-term RBC transfusion.
• Antibiotics and parent teaching have greatly improved outcomes for children.
• Symptoms and complications diminish by 30 years in some patients, who live into the sixth decade or longer.

(a)
• Hiatal hernia: protrusion of the stomach upward into the mediastinal cavity through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm; types are sliding (more common, often small) and fixed/paraoesophageal.
• Risk factors: a larger than usual hiatal opening from birth, injury, ageing changes in the diaphragm, and belly pressure from pregnancy, obesity, coughing, heavy lifting or straining on the toilet.

(b)
Reflux symptoms (GERD heartburn); in a fixed hernia blood flow to the trapped part of the stomach could be blocked, causing serious damage and a medical emergency.

(c)
• Medical: antacids, proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers; diagnosis by barium swallow, endoscopy and oesophageal manometry.
• Surgical: fundoplication, wrapping the stomach fundus around the lower oesophagus, done laparoscopically with a 3-5 day hospital stay.
• Nursing: assess for signs of hiatal hernia, instruct on dietary restrictions and symptom-reducing measures, give general post-operative care, and assess for dysphagia at the first post-operative meal (notify the physician if it occurs).
• Priority: teaching to reduce symptoms and assessment for dysphagia after fundoplication are the key nursing actions.
questions.question:
A patient who is obese and often strains on the toilet complains of heartburn, chest pain, bloating, burping, trouble swallowing, bad taste in the mouth, regurgitation and shortness of breath. Barium swallow shows part of the stomach protruding upward through the diaphragm.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) State the complications that may develop.
(c) Outline the nursing, medical and surgical management options and justify the priority nursing intervention.

A postmenopausal woman who is underweight, smokes, drinks alcohol, has a low calcium diet and has used corticosteroids for a long time complains of back pain and is found to have a vertebral fracture after minimal force, with loss of the normal lumbar curve and progressive kyphosis.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) State the complications that may develop.
(c) Outline the medical and nursing management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Osteoporosis: a generalised progressive reduction of bone mass as bone resorption exceeds bone formation, causing skeletal weakness and fracture with little force; common in postmenopausal or elderly women; primary (unknown cause) or secondary (e.g. diabetes, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption).
• Risk factors: female gender, European race, underweight stature, inactivity, alcohol and smoking, inadequate calcium, vitamin C, vitamin D and protein, family history, menopause (falling oestrogen), hypogonadism, endocrine disorders and prolonged steroid or heparin use.

(b)
Fractures of any bone particularly the vertebrae, pain, tenderness, muscle spasm, loss of the normal lumbar curve, progressive kyphosis and decreased mobility.

(c)
• Medical: oestrogen plus progesterone for postmenopausal women, calcitonin to reduce resorption, calcium gluconate 1200-1500 mg for women, vitamin D supplement, testosterone replacement for men.
• Nursing: diet high in calcium, vitamins C and D and protein (dairy); discourage carbonated drinks (phosphorus linked to bone resorption); regular weight-bearing exercise (jogging, walking); discourage smoking and alcohol.
• Priority: prevention of further bone loss and fracture through diet, weight-bearing exercise and avoiding smoking and alcohol, since immobility and these habits increase resorption.

questions.question:
Discuss cardiac dysrhythmias.
(a) Describe the pathophysiology (normal conduction and how it is disturbed).
(b) State the classification of dysrhythmias.
(c) State how the types relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how dysrhythmias may affect other body systems and describe the related management and assessment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A dysrhythmia (arrhythmia) is an abnormal or irregular heartbeat; the SA node normally fires 60-100 times per minute, the impulse passes through the atria, AV node (brief delay), bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres.
• Sympathetic stimulation raises heart rate, AV conduction and contraction force; parasympathetic stimulation lowers them; increased sympathetic stimulation may increase dysrhythmias.

(b)
• Sinus node: sinus arrhythmia, sinus bradycardia (rate below 60) and sinus tachycardia.
• Atrial: atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, premature atrial complex; junctional: junctional bradycardia, escape, accelerated rhythm and tachycardia (AV node as pacemaker).
• Ventricular: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation and long QT (predisposes to torsade de pointes); conduction abnormalities are also classified.

(c)
• Ventricular dysrhythmias can cause cardiogenic shock and sudden cardiac arrest; complications are cardiac failure, heart failure and stroke.
• Ventricular fibrillation typically causes collapse and loss of consciousness, sometimes without warning.

(d)
• Symptomatic sinus bradycardia causes shortness of breath, altered mental status, angina and hypotension; sinus node dysfunction in people over 50 causes reduced exercise capacity, fatigue and confusion.
• Management: atropine 0.5 mg IV every 3-5 minutes up to 3 mg for symptomatic bradycardia; cardioversion (synchronised) for planned treatment; defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT; pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators.
• Assessment: ECG (12-lead, ten electrodes), Holter and ambulatory monitors, history and examination; ask about CHAPS symptoms (chest pain, hypotension, altered mental status, poor perfusion, shortness of breath).
• The nursing process for dysrhythmia is outlined as a heading.

(a)
Acute osteomyelitis: inflammation and infection of the bone and marrow, commonly occurring in children under sixteen; caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus; predisposing factors: inadequate nutrition, poor hygiene and injuries such as fracture.

(b)
• Organisms invade, causing vascular engorgement and exudation, release of white cells and pus formation; pus tracks down the medullary canal or under the periosteum, causing a sub-periosteal abscess and separation of the periosteum from bone.
• Vessel thrombosis causes bone ischaemia and bone death (sequestrum).

(c)
• Assessment: admission and bed rest, observation of vital signs, culture and sensitivity, bone X-ray, WBC count and ESR.
• Immediate nursing care: physical care, nutrition, psychological care, prescribed medications and limb rest by immobilisation, then health education, advice on discharge and follow-up.

(d)
• Medical: antibiotic of choice (e.g. penicillin 250,000 units in divided doses 4-hourly for 2 weeks), analgesics (paracetamol), vitamin C or calcium tablets for 2 weeks.
• Surgical: drainage of the sub-periosteal abscess, sequestrectomy (removal of dead bone), and POP or cast may be applied.
questions.question:
A child under sixteen has a sudden onset of fever, rigor, rapid pulse, furred tongue, localised pain, tenderness and heat over the upper end of the tibia, with scanty urine and inability to move the limb.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Traction applies force in a set direction (ropes, pulleys, weights) to overcome muscle pull and align fractured ends; types: skin, skeletal, cervical, pelvic, fixed and balanced suspension.
• Purposes of traction: regain length and alignment, reduce and immobilise the fracture, relieve muscle spasm, prevent deformity, give bed activity freedom, reduce pain and stretch adhesions.
• POP/cast is made of plaster bandages (gypsum, calcium sulphate dihydrate), fibre or resin; purposes: immobilise fragments, apply uniform compression, permit early weight bearing, correct chronic deformities and prevent deformities.

(b)
• Types: short arm, gauntlet/thumb spica, long arm, short leg, long leg, spica/body and cervical casts, each with defined limits (e.g. long leg cast from upper middle third of thigh to base of toes, foot at right angle).
• Cast removal uses an electric cast cutter, cast spreader, plaster knife and surgical scissors.
• After immobilisation, rehabilitation involves patient exercise, physiotherapy and restoration of full function.

(c)
Fracture complications: surgical shock, fat embolism, injury to blood vessels, hypovolaemic shock, malunion, non-union, delayed union and hypostatic pneumonia.

(d)
• Immobilisation maintains reduction until union occurs; external splintage by POP and internal by plates, nails and screws.
• Bone healing passes through haematoma, callus (6-10 days) and remodelling stages, and depends on age and type of bone.
• Neglecting alignment and immobilisation risks malunion, non-union and delayed union.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indication: pulmonary TB, treated primarily with anti-tuberculosis agents for 6 to 12 months.
• First line: streptomycin, isoniazid (5 mg/kg, max 300 mg/day), rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol.
• Second line: capreomycin, ethionamide, para-aminosalicylate, cycloserine; third line: rifabutin, rifapentine, amoxicillin-clavulanate, linezolid and high-dose INH.

(b)
• Guideline: INH, rifampin, pyrazinamide and streptomycin or ethambutol daily for 8 weeks; pyrazinamide stopped after 8 weeks, then INH and rifampin for a further 4 months.
• If cultures show sensitivity before 8 weeks, ethambutol or streptomycin can be discontinued.
• Directly observed therapy (DOT): the health worker watches the patient swallow each dose; best way to ensure adherence and used with all intermittent regimens.

(c)
INH-associated peripheral neuropathy.

(d)
• Pyridoxine (vitamin B) is given with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
• Use multiple-drug regimens rather than a single drug.

(e)
• DOT ensures every dose is taken, since treatment is prolonged and adherence is critical.
• A person is considered non-infectious after 2 to 3 weeks of continuous therapy, which guides infection control.
• Neglect leads to non-adherence, treatment failure and neuropathy without pyridoxine.

questions.question:
A patient presents with episodic dyspnoea, cough, wheezing, tachypnoea, tachycardia and prolonged expiration. Rhonchi are heard on both inspiration and expiration, and airway narrowing is reversible after an inhaled beta-adrenergic agonist.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the attack.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management of the acute episode and the chronic management according to severity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bronchial asthma: a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways with hyper-responsiveness of the tracheobronchial tree, causing widespread airway narrowing and paroxysmal dyspnoea, cough and wheezing.

(b)
• The attack starts with an antigen-antibody reaction that releases histamine and the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis.
• The inflammation causes vascular congestion, oedema, thick tenacious mucus, bronchial muscle spasm, thickened airway walls and increased bronchial hyper-responsiveness.

(c)
• Assess the degree and progression of respiratory distress, note any increase in restlessness, and monitor vital signs (especially during the attack and when drugs are given) and blood gases; treat acidosis if present.
• Position for maximum lung expansion; give parenteral fluids in the acute phase, avoid ice-cold fluids (may stimulate bronchospasm), monitor intake and output; assess anxiety, give psychological support and evaluate the need for sedation.

(d)
• Acute episode: nebulised salbutamol (2.5 mg, repeated up to 4 times daily, may increase to 5 mg), slow IV aminophylline (250-500 mg over 20 minutes with close monitoring), IV steroids, adequate hydration and oxygen.
• Intermittent symptoms: inhaled salbutamol as needed. Mild persistent: salbutamol plus inhaled corticosteroid (beclomethasone).
• Moderate persistent: salbutamol plus beclomethasone plus a long-acting beta-agonist (salmeterol 50 micrograms twice daily in adults).
• Severe persistent: inhaled salbutamol plus oral corticosteroid (prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for a few days, then reduced gradually).
• Health education: avoid exertion, irritants and offending allergens, use only physician-prescribed drugs, and keep follow-up appointments.

(a)
• OSA is cessation of breathing (apnoea) during sleep, usually caused by repetitive upper airway obstruction.
• Risk factors: obesity, male gender, increasing age, family history, alcohol or sedative use and smoking.

(b)
• The pharynx is a collapsible tube compressed by surrounding soft tissue; loss of neuromuscular compensation and reduced pharyngeal muscle activity narrow or collapse the airway during sleep.
• Repetitive apnoeic events cause hypoxia and hypercapnia that trigger a sympathetic response.

(c)
• Signs: loud chronic snoring, nocturnal gasping and choking, excessive daytime sleepiness, fatigue, morning headaches; examination: upper-body obesity, thick neck (17-18 in males, 16 in females) and hypertension.
• Medical: modafinil for daytime sleepiness, protriptyline for respiratory drive and airway tone, acetazolamide for chronic alveolar hypoventilation.
• Surgical: tonsillectomy for large tonsils, uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, nasal septoplasty; nursing: weight loss, avoid alcohol, positional therapy (not on the back), supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula.

(d)
• Estimated prevalence is about 26% of adults aged 30-70, and rates have risen with obesity; between 4-9% of women and 9-24% of men in the US.
• OSA interferes with rest, affecting memory, learning and decision making; automobile and work accidents may occur.

(e)
• Nasal obstruction is blockage of the nasal cavity affecting airflow in and out of the nose, from turbinate hypertrophy, deviated septum, foreign bodies, large adenoids, choanal atresia, polyps or pyriform aperture stenosis.
• Nasal obstruction forces mouth breathing with dry oral mucosa and cracked lips, and is treated by removing the obstruction, antihistamines, nasal steroids and antibiotics; surgery is usually outpatient.
• OSA is a sleep-related collapse of the pharyngeal airway with apnoea and hypoxia, whereas nasal obstruction is a structural blockage of the nasal passage.

A 54-year-old man with hyperlipidaemia and hypertension, who had a flu-like illness a month earlier, presents with mid-sternal chest pain aggravated by cough, mild shortness of breath, fatigue and pedal oedema. The jugular venous pulse is raised, there are mild bibasal crackles, serology for infection is negative and the C-reactive protein is 244 mg/L.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pericarditis: inflammation of the pericardium, the fibrous two-layered fluid-filled sac surrounding the heart.

(b)
It can arise after a heart attack or heart surgery, or from an inflammatory autoimmune condition such as arthritis; irritants such as bacteria, chemicals or viruses can cause inflammation of the heart; risk factors include age, sex, family history and genetics, environment, lifestyle and medical conditions.

(c)
• Inflammation is accompanied by increased fluid in the pericardial sac (pericardial effusion), which can compress the cardiac chambers, limiting diastolic filling and causing cardiac tamponade.
• Complications: constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion, heart failure and sudden cardiac death.

(d)
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain related to pericardial inflammation, decreased activity tolerance (imbalance between oxygen supply and demand), decreased cardiac output, anxiety and imbalanced nutrition.
• Pain: assess vital signs and do a comprehensive pain assessment (location, characteristics, frequency, quality, intensity, cause), give prescribed analgesics and re-rate pain 30 to 60 minutes later.
• Activity: set activity goals with the patient, evaluate the need for help at home, encourage participation; also bed rest, anxiety management, patient and family education; medical: antibiotics, NSAIDs, pericardiocentesis or pericardial window.

(a)
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS): sudden, progressive respiratory failure with acute hypoxaemia, increased alveolar-capillary permeability, severe dyspnoea and refractory hypoxaemia (respiratory system).

(b)
• Insult activates inflammatory cells and mediators (serotonin, histamine, bradykinin) which damage the alveolar-capillary membrane; protein-rich oedema fluid fills air spaces, and surfactant function is lost, compromising gas exchange.
• Phases: exudative (0-6 days, hypoxaemia most severe), proliferative (7-10 days, 'stiff lung'), fibrotic (beyond 10-14 days, oxygenation improves).

(c)
Differentials: pulmonary oedema, acute pulmonary (respiratory) failure, pneumonia and pleural conditions; non-cardiogenic and neurogenic causes of pulmonary oedema are also considered.

(d)
• Assessment: history, examination, pulse oximetry, ABG (PaO2 below 60 mmHg on room air), FBC, chest X-ray and CT.
• Diagnosis: impaired gas exchange, ineffective airway clearance, imbalanced nutrition, self-care deficit and knowledge deficit.
• Medical measures include diuretics, nitrates, morphine, dopamine and bronchodilators.

questions.question: Total Quality Management (TQM) differs from QMS primarily in that TQM:
questions.explanation: TQM is a holistic approach involving all aspects of the organization from products and services to processes and culture.
