A drug development team studies the biosynthetic route that produces oestradiol from cholesterol in the ovary, in order to find which step an oestrogen-dependent breast cancer drug should block.
(a) Identify the end hormone and the three natural forms.
(b) Outline the biosynthetic route, naming the key intermediates, the enzymes and the steps.
(c) Identify the step or site at risk of blockade by a drug and the drug class.
(d) State the synthetic or conjugated variants and how secretion is regulated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oestradiol (E2), with estrone (E1) and estriol (E3) as the other natural forms (E2 > E1 > E3)
(b)
• Cholesterol to pregnenolone by P450scc (CYP11A1); pregnenolone to progesterone by 3β-HSD; progesterone to 17α-hydroxyprogesterone by CYP17A1
• 17α-Hydroxyprogesterone to androstenedione by 17,20-lyase (CYP17A1); androstenedione to testosterone by 17β-HSD; testosterone to estradiol by aromatase (CYP19A1)
• In the placenta and other tissues androstenedione is converted to estrone by aromatase; estrone to estradiol by 17β-HSD
(c)
The aromatase step is blocked by aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane); letrozole is non-steroidal and reversible
(d)
• Variants: synthetic ethinyl estradiol and diethylstilbestrol; conjugated, for example Premarin
• Regulation: hypothalamus releases GnRH, the pituitary secretes FSH and LH, the ovaries produce oestrogens; high oestrogen inhibits GnRH, FSH and LH, and a pre-ovulation oestradiol surge triggers an LH and FSH peak

(a)
Vitamin B6: pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine, interchangeable with similar activity
(b)
Synthesis is from ethyl-N-formyl-dl-alanine
(c)
• Oxidation (via the pyridoxal aldehyde) gives 4-pyridoxic acid, the carboxylic acid metabolite
• Unstable to metal ions (decomposition), light in dilute solution and H2O2 and other oxidising agents
(d)
• Active form: pyridoxal-5-phosphate, formed in the liver; coenzyme in decarboxylation, transaminases and racemisation
• Uses: formation of haemoglobin and blood cells, acne, megaloblastic anaemia not due to Fe deficiency; deficiency causes convulsive seizures
• Stable as a solid to air and light; acidic solution stable at pH below 5
• Assay: spectrophotometry, colorimetry, microbiological method and animal bioassay; sources: liver, fish meal, rice, yeast, cereals

Describe the chemical-stabilisation approach used for vitamins:
(a) The liabilities that need to be countered
(b) The stabilisation measures used
Relate the approach to common examples:
(c) Fat-soluble vitamins
(d) Water-soluble vitamins
Explain why the strategy improves stability or handling and what trade-off or limitation remains:
(e) Improvement
(f) Limitations
questions.answerText:
(a)
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D and E are unstable to O2 and UV; trace metals decompose A and D; surface-active compounds isomerise and decompose D
(b)
Stabilisation uses antioxidants (α-tocopherol, hydroquinone), protective coatings, optimum pH and esterification
(c)
• Vitamin A: esters are more stable and optimum pH is 6; vitamin E: esters (acetates and benzoates) are more stable
• Vitamin K is stable to heat but unstable to sunlight and alkali; vitamin D assay and stability follow UV inactivation
(d)
• Pantothenic acid is a hygroscopic viscous unstable oil, so calcium salts are used to reduce hygroscopicity; maximum stability at pH 6–7
• Thiamine: stored in glass and protected from light; unstable above pH 5; riboflavine: protect from light at pH 7
• Ascorbic acid is stored airtight and cold, and is stable to air in the dry state
• Nicotinamide is used as a solubiliser for riboflavin and folic acid
(e)
Ester forms and salts counter oxidation, hygroscopicity and photolysis; antioxidants protect the oxidisable groups
(f)
• Limitation: each vitamin has a different pH optimum (A pH 6; B12 pH 4.5–5.0; B5 pH 6–7; B1 below pH 5), so no single pH suits a mixture
• Cross-reactions persist: ascorbic acid cleaves folic acid, riboflavin cleaves folic acid at pH 4–6.5, and ascorbic acid, nicotinamide and thiamine destabilise cyanocobalamin
• Light, trace Cu/Fe and heat remain risks even after chemical modification

(a)
Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist of the ergot-derivative class (also pergolide and cabergoline); the non-ergot derivative is quinagolide
(b)
• A synthetic ergot alkaloid; dose starts at 1.25 mg and is raised every 3–17 days to 5 mg 12-hourly or 2.5 mg 8-hourly; only 7% reaches the systemic circulation; elimination half-life 2–8 h
• Given at bedtime to minimise side effects
(c)
• Interacts with D2 receptors on lactotrophes (dopamine is the major prolactin regulator) to inhibit spontaneous and TRH-induced prolactin release
• Dopamine agonists also reduce GH release in acromegaly, though not effectively
(d)
• Uses: hyperprolactinaemia (first-line), shrinking prolactin-secreting tumours, restoring ovulation; acromegaly at 20–30 mg/day; Parkinson's disease at higher doses
• Normalises serum prolactin in 70–80% of patients with prolactinomas and shrinks tumours in over 50%
• Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, light-headedness, orthostatic hypotension, fatigue; less often nasal congestion, digital vasospasm, hallucination, nightmares, insomnia
questions.question:
A woman with a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma, amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea is given a synthetic ergot alkaloid that interacts with the D2 receptor and is taken at bedtime.
(a) Identify the drug and its chemical class, naming other members of the class.
(b) State the structural class feature and the pharmacokinetic features that matter.
(c) Describe the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State the therapeutic uses and the key adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Thiamine: thiazole and pyrimidine rings joined by a methylene bridge; oxidised by air, H2O2, KMnO4 and alkaline potassium ferricyanide, and attacked by reducing agents
• Riboflavine: benzo[g]pteridine-2,4-dione ring system with a tetrahydroxypentyl chain, sensitive to O2 and light; folic acid: pteridine, PABA and glutamic acid units; ascorbic acid: enediol system, strong reducing agent
(b)
• Ascorbic acid oxidises in solution in air and alkaline conditions, catalysed by trace Cu and Fe and by riboflavin; its reducing action cleaves folic acid
• Riboflavin causes oxidative cleavage of folic acid at pH 4–6.5; thiamine reacts with aldehydes to give inactive Schiff bases
(c)
• Thiamine is unstable at pH above 5; riboflavine is stable in acidic pH but unstable in alkaline pH, forming lumiflavine, lumichrome and others with O2 and light
• Folic acid is unstable at pH below 5, in UV and sunlight, with heat and reducing agents, but its aqueous solution is stable to O2, air and autoclaving
(d)
• Thiamine is stored in glass protected from light; riboflavine is protected from light at pH 7; ascorbic acid is stored airtight and cold, and is stable to air in the dry state
• Nicotinamide is used as a solubiliser for riboflavin and folic acid
questions.question:
A formulator proposes a single aqueous solution containing thiamine, riboflavine, nicotinamide, folic acid and ascorbic acid at pH 5 to 6.5, in clear glass exposed to light, with traces of copper from the vehicle.

(b) Explain the degradation or incompatibility pathways between the components.

Describe the oestrogens under the following headings:
(a) Classification and members
(b) General structure and biosynthesis
(c) Mechanism of action
Explain the chemical or biological basis of activity and limitation:
(d) The receptor types and tissue distribution
(e) The basis of the pharmacological actions and adverse effects
Distinguish between related compounds:
(f) Natural, synthetic and conjugated oestrogens
(g) Pure antagonists, SERMs and aromatase inhibitors
questions.answerText:
(a)
Natural: estradiol (E2) > estrone (E1) > estriol (E3); synthetic: ethinyl estradiol and diethylstilbestrol (DES); conjugated: for example Premarin
(b)
• Steroid hormones; cholesterol to pregnenolone (P450scc, CYP11A1), to progesterone (3β-HSD), to 17α-hydroxyprogesterone (CYP17A1), to androstenedione (17,20-lyase), to testosterone (17β-HSD)
• Aromatase (CYP19A1) converts testosterone to estradiol and androstenedione to estrone; 17β-HSD converts estrone to estradiol
(c)
Oestrogens bind nuclear oestrogen receptors that control gene expression through direct binding to gene promoter sequences (genomic) or without direct DNA binding (non-genomic)
(d)
ERα is mainly in the uterus, breast and ovaries; ERβ is in the ovary, prostate, brain and bone, with roles in bone health and neuroprotection
(e)
• Bone: increased expression of osteonectin, collagen, osteocalcin and alkaline phosphatase, reduced osteoclast maturation and activity, and generation of vitamin D3
• Actions: development and maintenance of female secondary sex characteristics, bone mass, endometrial growth, positive Ca balance, decreased LDL and increased HDL, raised SHBG, TBG and CBG, oedema (salt and water retention)
• Adverse effects: thromboembolic disorders, endometrial carcinoma with irregular bleeding, accelerated breast cancer growth, gall stones, hepatomas, feminisation in males; stilbestrol raised cervical carcinoma incidence in female offspring
(f)
Preferred route is oral but parenteral for large doses; estradiol 2.5–10 mg/ml i.m. and ethinyl estradiol tablets are examples
(g)
• Clomiphene and fulvestrant are pure antagonists; tamoxifen, raloxifene and toremifene are tissue-selective SERMs; letrozole, anastrozole and exemestane inhibit aromatase
• Drug interactions: enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenytoin), enzyme inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin), warfarin
• Contraindications: thromboembolic history, hormone-sensitive cancers, severe liver disease, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, pregnancy, hypertension, cardiovascular disease

(a)
• Natural: testosterone, androstenedione, androsterone and 5-dehydroepiandrosterone, secreted by the testes, adrenal cortex and ovaries
• Synthetic predominantly androgenic: methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone, esters of testosterone; predominantly anabolic: nandrolone, oxandrolone, stanozolol, methandienone, ethylestrenol
(b)
Non-aromatic steroid with oxygen functions at C3 and C17, no side chain at C17 and Me at C18 and C19; the C17 oxygen corresponds to that of oestradiol and oestrone
(c)
• Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone bind the intracellular androgen receptor (nuclear receptor NR3A); the receptor dissociates from the heat shock protein complex, dimerises, translocates to the nucleus and binds androgen response elements
• Testosterone is converted by 5α-reductase to dihydrotestosterone (dominant androgen in skin, prostate, seminal vesicles, epididymis) and by aromatase (CYP19) to estradiol
(d)
• Unsaturated compounds have maximum activity; rings A and B must be trans; 17β-OH is required (β orientation, receptor binding); oxidation of OH to carbonyl decreases androgenic activity
• 17α-Methyl gives oral stability (methyltestosterone); 11β-OH with 9α-F (fluoxymesterone) gives 20x anabolic and 9x androgenic activity
(e)
Most synthetic androgens and anabolic agents are 17-alkyl-substituted steroids; these cause dose-related hepatic dysfunction and reversible cholestatic jaundice, and high doses cause peliosis hepatis, hepatic failure, adenomas and carcinomas
(f)
Testosterone (17β-hydroxyandrost-4-en-3-one) is orally inactive and rapidly inactivated; esters (propionate, cyclopentylpropionate, enanthate) are given i.m. in oil base; implants and transdermal forms exist
(g)
Methyltestosterone and fluoxymesterone are 17-alkylated and active by mouth, but carry the hepatic risk of 17-alkyl steroids
(h)
• Anabolic effects (muscle trophic effects, reduced nitrogen excretion) can be separated from androgenic effects in animals, but separation is less marked in humans and all are potent androgens
• Adverse effects in women include hirsutism, acne, amenorrhoea, clitoral enlargement and deepening of the voice; androgens lower HDL
questions.question:
Describe androgens and anabolic steroids under the following headings:
(a) Classification
(b) General structure
(c) Mechanism of action
Explain the chemical basis of activity and toxicity:
(d) Structural requirements for activity and oral stability
(e) The basis of hepatic toxicity
Distinguish between related drugs and classes:
(f) Testosterone and its esters
(g) Methyltestosterone and fluoxymesterone
(h) Androgenic and anabolic activity

Describe the prodrug and ester-derivative approach to drug design:
(a) Steroid and corticosteroid examples
(b) Thyroid, analgesic and antimalarial examples
Relate the parts of the approach to common examples:
(c) Esters of testosterone
(d) Medroxyprogesterone derivatives and vitamin esters
Explain why the strategy improves a property and what trade-off or limitation results:
(e) The property improved
(f) The limitation arising from variable enzyme activation
(g) A clinical illustration
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cortisone and prednisone are inactive prodrugs until converted to cortisol by the liver enzyme 11β-HSD1
(b)
• Carbimazole is rapidly converted to its active metabolite methimazole
• Codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6 O-demethylation; proguanil is converted to its active metabolite cycloguanil by CYP2C19; clopidogrel is also a prodrug
(c)
• Testosterone is orally inactive and rapidly inactivated, so it is used as esters (propionate, cyclopentylpropionate, enanthate) given i.m. in an oil base; the esters are hydrolysed to free testosterone at the injection site
• Esters have more prolonged absorption and greater activity (propionate, enanthate, undecanoate, cypionate); propionate is potent but short-acting
(d)
• Medroxyprogesterone acetate and caproate: increased lipid solubility, decreased first-pass metabolism and enhanced oral activity; acetylation of 17β-OH increases duration of action
• Vitamin esters are more stable (vitamin A esters; vitamin E acetates and benzoates)
• Medroxyprogesterone acetate (Depo Provera) and caproate (Primolut Depot) are depot injectable forms
(e)
Progesterone and testosterone are rapidly metabolised and ineffective orally, so ester and 17α-modified forms improve absorption, oral activity and duration
(f)
Prodrug activation depends on the enzyme: in CYP2D6 poor metabolisers there is decreased prodrug activation (codeine) and decreased response; in ultra-rapid metabolisers response and toxicity risk rise (respiratory depression)
(g)
• A 62-year-old on codeine 25 mg three times daily developed coma, with plasma morphine 80 μg/L (normal 1–4) and ultra-rapid CYP2D6 genotype
• CYP2C19 poor metabolisers potentially have reduced effect of prodrugs such as proguanil and clopidogrel; oral testosterone undecanoate is not recommended because of liver tumours

questions.question:
Describe the chemistry and pharmacology of octreotide:
(a) Its origin and relationship to the natural hormone
(b) Potency and pharmacokinetic properties
State the structural or pharmacological basis of its action:
(c) The receptor and the hormones inhibited
(d) The clinical indications
Explain the basis of toxicity and loss of activity:
(e) The limitation of the natural hormone
(f) Adverse effects and the antagonist pegvisomant
questions.answerText:
(a)
Octreotide is a somatostatin analogue (lanreotide is another); somatostatin occurs in the hypothalamus, other parts of the CNS, pancreas and GIT
(b)
• Octreotide is 45x more potent than somatostatin in inhibiting GH and 2x as potent in reducing insulin secretion
• Half-life 80 min, presented as a long-acting suspension; given SC, or IM monthly in long-acting formulations
(c)
Agonist at somatostatin receptors; reduces production of GH and also glucagon, insulin and gastrin (to a lesser extent)
(d)
Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, gastrinoma, glucagonoma, insulinoma and other hormone-secreting tumours; acute control of bleeding from the oesophagus
(e)
Natural somatostatin is rapidly cleared (half-life 1–3 min), so has limited therapeutic benefit; the kidney plays an important role in its metabolism and excretion
(f)
• Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, flatulence, steatorrhoea with bulky stools; biliary sludge and gallstones after 6 months (20–30%); sinus bradycardia and conduction disturbances
• Pegvisomant, a GH receptor antagonist (PEG derivative of mutant GH B2036), is used if hypersecretion persists; it does not inhibit GH secretion, which may raise GH level and adenoma growth
• Other GH antagonists: dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine, which reduce GH production but not effectively
• Lanreotide shares the GH-lowering mechanism and indications, with subcutaneous and intramuscular administration
• Somatostatin is primarily an inhibitory pancreas factor and inhibits release of GH, TSH, glucagon, insulin and gastrin

questions.question:
A hypogonadal man is prescribed a steroid hormone that is stored in clear glass in sunlight and in an alkaline vehicle, and he asks for a tablet. The hormone is orally inactive, rapidly inactivated in the body, and several derivatives of it are available.
(a) Identify the hormone and its structural liability.
(b) Explain the degradation and incompatibility pathways.
(c) Differentiate the related derivatives (esters and 17-alkyl compounds).
(d) Reason from the chemistry to the choice of formulation, route and monitoring.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Testosterone (17β-hydroxyandrost-4-en-3-one); liabilities: the Δ4-3-ketone and the 17β-OH
(b)
Light sensitive; unstable to alkali because of keto–enol tautomerism; in vivo oxidation of 17-OH to C=O and liver reduction to androsterone and etiocholanolone
(c)
• Esters (propionate, cyclopentylpropionate/cypionate, enanthate, undecanoate) release testosterone at the injection site; enanthate and cypionate are long-acting, propionate is potent but short-acting
• 17α-Alkyl derivatives (methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone) are active by mouth but carry hepatic dysfunction risk
(d)
• Choice: long-acting i.m. esters in oil; transdermal patches or gels (two applications daily); implanted pellets; oral undecanoate not recommended because of liver tumours
• Replacement in hypopituitarism: enanthate or cypionate 50 mg i.m. every 4, then 3, then 2 weeks, then 100 mg every 2 weeks, finally 200 mg every 2 weeks
• Monitoring: haemoglobin, haematocrit, liver function, cholesterol, PSA, prostate exam, blood pressure; reduce dose if polycythaemia or hypertension develops
• Contraindications: prostate cancer, breast cancer, severe liver disease, apnoea, heart disease

questions.question:
Describe vitamin D under the following headings:
(a) Classification and members
(b) General structure and pharmacophore
(c) Activation and mechanism of action
Explain the chemical basis of activity and limitation:
(d) The structural features and the effect of modification
(e) Stability and toxicity
Distinguish between related compounds and states:
(f) Deficiency and its treatment, and the assay
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A mixture of chemically related compounds: ergocalciferol (D2), cholecalciferol (D3) and 22,23-dihydroergocalciferol (D4)
• Sources: fish liver oil, milk and eggs
(b)
Cholecalciferol: 9,10-seco(5Z,7E)-5,7,10(19)-cholestatriene-3β-ol; important features: the unsaturated section, C3-OH and the double bonds at C5 and C7
(c)
• Activity is in bone formation; it promotes reabsorption of Ca and P from the GIT and resorption of Ca from bones
• PTH stimulates conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to the active calcitriol, which acts through high-affinity vitamin D receptors to stimulate Ca and phosphate absorption and inhibit PTH production
(d)
Epimerisation of C3-OH or reduction to a ketone decreases activity in D2 and D3
(e)
• Unstable to O2; trace metals and surface-active compounds cause isomerisation and decomposition; UV inactivates
• Antioxidants (α-tocopherol, hydroquinone) and protective coatings stabilise it
• Excess causes hypercalcaemia (excess Ca deposit)
(f)
• Deficiency: rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; hypoparathyroidism is treated with vitamin D supplement
• Assay: UV (λmax 265 nm), colorimetry and HPLC

questions.question:
Describe the sulfonylurea class of oral hypoglycaemic agents under the following headings:
(a) Classification by generation with named members
(b) General structure and physicochemical properties
(c) Mechanism of action
Explain the chemical basis of activity and limitation:
(d) The roles of the aryl moiety, urea moiety and alkyl group
(e) Why second-generation agents are more potent and better tolerated
Distinguish between tolbutamide and chlorpropamide in terms of substituents, potency, duration, metabolism and metabolites.
(f) Tolbutamide
(g) Chlorpropamide
(h) Features and adverse effects common to both
questions.answerText:
(a)
First generation: carbutamide, chlorpropamide, tolbutamide, tolazamide (acetohexamide is also included); second generation: glibenclamide (glyburide), glipizide, glimepiride, gliclazide
(b)
• Sulphonamide derivatives; carbutamide was the first clinically useful member (reported 1942)
• Acidic, easily absorbed from the GIT and plasma protein bound; assayed by titration with NaOH and phenolphthalein, based on acidity
(c)
• They stimulate insulin release from functioning pancreatic β cells by blocking ATP-sensitive K channels
• This causes depolarisation, opening of voltage-dependent Ca channels and a rise in intracellular Ca that stimulates insulin release
(d)
The aryl moiety is important (NH2 at R1 is not required); modification of the urea moiety causes loss of activity; the alkyl group gives maximum activity at 3–4 carbons
(e)
• Second generation: main modification at the aryl and alkyl groups; bulky groups increase lipid solubility and so potency
• They have longer duration (12–24 h for glibenclamide and glimepiride), less frequent dosing, fewer adverse effects and fewer drug interactions
(f)
Tolbutamide: R1 = CH3, active; short-acting, t½ 4–5 h, duration 6–8 h; the p-methyl group is oxidised to COOH and excreted in urine as inactive metabolite; safe in old patients and renal impairment
(g)
Chlorpropamide: R1 = Cl, R2 = CH2CH2CH3, giving increased potency and longer action; long-acting, t½ 24–40 h, duration 20–60 h, inactive metabolites excreted in urine
(h)
• Both are well absorbed and metabolised; adverse effects are hyperinsulinaemia and hypoglycaemia (less with tolbutamide), weight gain and GIT upset
• Contraindications of the class: hepatic impairment, renal insufficiency, pregnancy and lactation, type I diabetes

questions.question:
Describe the non-sulfonylurea oral hypoglycaemic classes under the following headings:
(a) Classification with named members
(b) General structure and physicochemical properties
(c) Mechanism of action
Explain the chemical or pharmacological basis of activity or limitation:
(d) The secretagogue and sensitiser concepts
(e) The basis of the adverse effects
Distinguish between related classes:
(f) Metformin and pioglitazone
(g) Repaglinide and the sulfonylureas
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Meglitinides: repaglinide, nateglinide; biguanides: phenformin, metformin; thiazolidinediones: rosiglitazone, pioglitazone
• α-Glucosidase inhibitors: acarbose, miglitol; incretin agonists: exenatide, liraglutide; DPP-4 inhibitors: sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin
(b)
• Biguanides are guanylguanidine derivatives, colourless solids, soluble in water giving a basic solution; metformin is 1,1-dimethylbiguanide, available as the HCl salt
• Thiazolidinediones (rosiglitazone, pioglitazone) are insulin sensitisers that act on intracellular metabolic pathways to enhance insulin action
(c)
• Meglitinides: block ATP-sensitive K channels, causing Ca influx and insulin exocytosis; rapid onset (peak 1 h), short duration (4 h), taken before each meal
• α-Glucosidase inhibitors reversibly inhibit intestinal brush-border α-glucosidases and decrease postprandial hyperglycaemia; DPP-4 inhibitors block the enzyme that metabolises incretin hormones, increasing insulin and decreasing glucagon secretion
(d)
Insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas, meglitinides) increase insulin secreted by the pancreas; insulin sensitisers (biguanides, thiazolidinediones) increase sensitivity of target organs to insulin
(e)
• Secretagogues: hypoglycaemia and weight gain; biguanides: GIT upset, metallic taste, lactic acidosis; thiazolidinediones: hepatotoxicity, oedema; α-glucosidase inhibitors: flatulence, diarrhoea
• Acarbose is poorly absorbed, metabolised by intestinal bacteria and excreted in stool and urine; sitagliptin is given once daily, with dose reduced in renal impairment
(f)
• Metformin needs no functioning β cells, is not metabolised and is excreted unchanged in urine; pioglitazone activates PPAR-γ, is 99% albumin bound and metabolised in the liver
• Metformin lowers hepatic glucose output; pioglitazone raises glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue
(g)
Repaglinide is a sulfonylurea-free, rapidly acting secretagogue useful in patients allergic to sulfur or sulfonylureas, with short duration compared with long-acting sulfonylureas

(a)
• GnRH analogues are synthetic peptides: agonists first stimulate pituitary release of FSH and LH, then downregulate GnRH receptors and decrease FSH and LH production
• Antagonists directly block the receptors, preventing release of FSH and LH from the pituitary
(b)
Pulsatile administration mimics GnRH and raises FSH and LH; continuous administration downregulates receptors and lowers FSH and LH
(c)
Agonists: leuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin, gonadorelin, buserelin, nafarelin; given IV, SC, IM or intranasally (nafarelin 1–2 times daily); injectable forms monthly or quarterly
(d)
• Antagonists: ganirelix, cetrorelix, abarelix, degarelix; SC injection with bioavailability above 90%
• Degarelix is approved for advanced prostate cancer; ganirelix and cetrorelix prevent premature LH surge in controlled ovarian stimulation
(e)
• Agonists have a longer half-life than GnRH; indications: stimulation (female and male infertility, diagnosis of LH responsiveness) and suppression (endometriosis, uterine fibroids, prostate cancer, central precocious puberty, controlled ovarian stimulation)
• GnRH analogues may help protect ovarian function in women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer
(f)
• Adverse effects: hot flashes, vaginal dryness, reduced libido, headache, fatigue, mood swings, decreased bone mineral density; hypogonadism with continuous treatment
• Contraindications: pregnancy, hypersensitivity, prostate cancer (aggravation by agonists), hormone-sensitive tumours, severe liver or kidney disease
• Interactions: estrogen or testosterone alters efficacy; anticoagulants may raise haemorrhage risk
• Monitoring: FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone levels, bone mineral density, blood pressure, lipids and the menstrual cycle

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5): pantoic acid coupled to β-alanine; prosthetic group of coenzyme A
• Prominent in acyl group transfer and critical in all enzymatic acylation
(b)
Synthesis from isobutyraldehyde via a pantolactone intermediate
(c)
• The free acid is a hygroscopic viscous oil which is unstable; it is stable to air and light, with maximum stability at pH 6–7
• Stereoisomer: the R form is active
(d)
• Variants: the alcohol derivative pantothenol has similar vitamin activity; calcium salts reduce the hygroscopic property
• Assay: colorimetry (pure compound) and microbiological method using Lactobacillus plantarum
• Sources: animal – liver, dairy products (milk, cheese), eggs, yeast; plants – leafy vegetables, cereal brans
questions.question:
A hygroscopic, viscous, unstable oil is the coupling product of pantoic acid with β-alanine and forms the prosthetic group of coenzyme A.
(a) Identify the vitamin and state its biochemical role.
(b) Outline its synthetic route, naming the starting material and key intermediate.
(c) Identify the structural features or sites at risk: stereochemistry, hygroscopicity, stability and pH.
(d) State the derivative, salt or variant forms, the assay and the natural sources.

An orally active thiazolidinedione insulin sensitiser is given once daily. It is highly bound to plasma albumin (99%), has a slow onset of activity and a half-life of 3 to 4 h, is metabolised in the liver and is excreted in urine (64%) and bile.
(a) Identify the compound and its drug class, naming related agents.
(b) State how it is assayed.
(c) State its mechanism of action, metabolic fate and pharmacokinetics, including active or inactive metabolites.
(d) State the clinical consequences: uses, adverse effects and contraindications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pioglitazone (Actos), a thiazolidinedione (glitazone) insulin sensitiser; related: rosiglitazone and troglitazone
(b)
Assay is by bioassay
(c)
• Activates the nuclear receptor PPAR-γ, decreasing insulin resistance and increasing sensitivity of target tissues to insulin; increases glucose uptake and utilisation in muscle and adipose tissue
• Acts on intracellular metabolic pathways to enhance insulin action; given orally once daily; metabolised in the liver; excreted 64% in urine and in bile
(d)
• Uses: type II diabetes with insulin resistance, alone or combined with sulfonylurea or biguanide; no risk of hypoglycaemia when used alone
• Adverse effects: hepatotoxicity (liver function tests during the first year of therapy), fluid retention (oedema), precipitation of congestive heart failure, mild weight gain
• Contraindications: congestive heart failure, pregnancy, lactating women, significant liver disease
